nodes.label: Definition 2.1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.1 Definition. A differentiable manifold of dimension \( n \) is a set \( M \) and a family of injective mappings \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha } : {U}_{\alpha } \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  M \) of open sets \( {U}_{\alpha } \) of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) into \( M \) such that:

(1) \( \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{\alpha }{\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {U}_{\alpha }\right)  = M \) .

(2) for any pair \( \alpha ,\beta \) , with \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {U}_{\alpha }\right)  \cap  {\mathbf{x}}_{\beta }\left( {U}_{\beta }\right)  = W \neq  \phi \) , the sets \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }^{-1}\left( W\right) \) and \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\beta }^{-1}\left( W\right) \) are open sets in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) and the mappings \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\beta }^{-1} \circ  {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha } \) are differentiable (Fig. 1).

(3) The family \( \left\{  \left( {{U}_{\alpha },{\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }}\right) \right\} \) is maximal relative to the conditions (1) and (2).

The pair \( \left( {{U}_{\alpha },{\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }}\right) \) (or the mapping \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha } \) ) with \( p \in  {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {U}_{\alpha }\right) \) is called a parametrization (or system of coordinates) of \( M \) at \( p \) ; \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {U}_{\alpha }\right) \) is then called a coordinate neighborhood at \( p \) . A family \( \left\{  \left( {{U}_{\alpha },{\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }}\right) \right\} \) satisfying (1) and (2) is called a differentiable structure on \( M \) .

The condition (3) is included for purely technical reasons. Indeed, given a differentiable structure on \( M \) , we can easily complete it to a maximal one, by taking the union of all the parametriza-tions that, together with any of the parametrizations of the given structure, satisfy condition (2). Therefore, with a certain abuse of language, we can say that a differentiable manifold is a set provided with a differentiable structure. In general, the extension to the maximal structure will be done without further comment.

nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 2.2 REMARK. A comparison between the definition 2.1 and the definition of a regular surface in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) shows that the essential point (except for the change of dimension from 2 to \( n \) ) was to distinguish the fundamental property of the change of parameters (which is a theorem for surfaces in \( {\mathrm{R}}^{3} \) ) and incorporate it as an axiom. This is precisely condition 2 of Definition 2.1. As we shall soon see, this is the condition that allows us to carry over all of the ideas of differential calculus in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) to differentiable manifolds.

nodes.label: Remark 2.3
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.3 REMARK. A differentiable structure on a set \( M \) induces a natural topology on \( M \) . It suffices to define \( A \subset  M \) to be an open set in \( M \) if and only if \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }^{-1}\left( {A \cap  {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {U}_{\alpha }\right) }\right) \) is an open set in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) for all \( \alpha \) . It is easy to verify that \( M \) and the empty set are open sets, that a union of open sets is again an open set and that the finite intersection of open sets remains an open set. Observe that the topology is defined in such a way that the sets \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {U}_{\alpha }\right) \) are open and that the mappings \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha } \) are continuous.

The Euclidean space \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) , with the differentiable structure given by the identity, is a trivial example of a differentiable manifold. Now we shall see a non-trivial example.

nodes.label: Example 2.4
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.4 EXAMPLE. The real projective space \( {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) . Let us denote by \( {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) the set of straight lines of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) which pass through the origin \( 0 = \left( {0,\ldots ,0}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) ; that is, \( {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) is the set of "directions " of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) .

Let us introduce a differentiable structure on \( {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) . For this, let \( \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n + 1}}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) and observe, to begin with, that \( {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) is the quotient space of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} - \{ 0\} \) by the equivalence relation:

\[
\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n + 1}}\right)  \sim  \left( {\lambda {x}_{1},\ldots ,\lambda {x}_{n + 1}}\right) ,\;\lambda  \in  \mathbf{R},\;\lambda  \neq  0.
\]

The points of \( {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) will be denoted by \( \left\lbrack  {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n + 1}}\right\rbrack \) . Observe that, if \( {x}_{i} \neq  0 \) ,

\[
\left\lbrack  {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n + 1}}\right\rbrack   = \left\lbrack  {\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{i}},\ldots ,\frac{{x}_{i - 1}}{{x}_{i}},1,\frac{{x}_{i + 1}}{{x}_{i}},\ldots ,\frac{{x}_{n + 1}}{{x}_{i}}}\right\rbrack  .
\]

Define subsets \( {V}_{1},\ldots ,{V}_{n + 1} \) , of \( {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) , by:

\[
{V}_{i} = \left\{  {\left\lbrack  {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n + 1}}\right\rbrack  ;{x}_{i} \neq  0}\right\}  ,\;i = 1,\ldots , n + 1.
\]

Geometrically, \( {V}_{i} \) is the set of straight lines \( {R}^{n + 1} \) which pass through the origin and do not belong to the hyperplane \( {x}_{i} = 0 \) . We are now going to show that we can take the \( {V}_{i} \) ’s as coordinate neighborhoods, where the coordinates on \( {V}_{i} \) are

\[
{y}_{1} = \frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{i}},\ldots ,{y}_{i - 1} = \frac{{x}_{i - 1}}{{x}_{i}},\;{y}_{i} = \frac{{x}_{i + 1}}{{x}_{i}},\ldots ,{y}_{n} = \frac{{x}_{n + 1}}{{x}_{i}}.
\]

For this, we will define mappings \( {\mathbf{x}}_{i} : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {V}_{i} \) by

\[
{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\left( {{y}_{1},\ldots ,{y}_{n}}\right)  = \left\lbrack  {{y}_{1},\ldots ,{y}_{i - 1},1,{y}_{i},\ldots ,{y}_{n}}\right\rbrack  ,\;\left( {{y}_{1},\ldots ,{y}_{n}}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n},
\]

and will show that the family \( \left\{  \left( {{\mathbf{R}}^{n},{\mathbf{x}}_{i}}\right) \right\} \) is a differentiable structure on \( {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) .

Indeed, any mapping \( {x}_{i} \) is clearly bijective while \( \bigcup {x}_{i}\left( {\mathbf{R}}^{n}\right) \; = {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) . It remains to show that \( {\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{-1}\left( {{V}_{i} \cap  {V}_{j}}\right) \) is an open set in

\( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) and that \( {\mathbf{x}}_{j}^{-1} \circ  {\mathbf{x}}_{i}, j = 1,\ldots , n + 1 \) , is differentiable there. Now, if \( i > j \) , the points in \( {\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{-1}\left( {{V}_{i} \cap  {V}_{j}}\right) \) are of the form:

\[
\left\{  {\left( {{y}_{1},\ldots ,{y}_{n}}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n};\;{y}_{j} \neq  0}\right\}  .
\]

Therefore \( {\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{-1}\left( {{V}_{i} \cap  {V}_{j}}\right) \) is an open set in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) , and supposing that \( i > j \) (the case \( i < j \) is similar),

\[
{\mathbf{x}}_{j}^{-1} \circ  {\mathbf{x}}_{i}\left( {{y}_{1},\ldots ,{y}_{n}}\right)  = {\mathbf{x}}_{j}^{-1}\left\lbrack  {{y}_{1},\ldots ,{y}_{i - 1},1,{y}_{i},\ldots ,{y}_{n}}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
= {\mathbf{x}}_{j}^{-1}\left\lbrack  {\frac{{y}_{1}}{{y}_{j}},\ldots ,\frac{{y}_{j - 1}}{{y}_{j}},1,\frac{{y}_{j + 1}}{{y}_{j}},\ldots ,\frac{{y}_{i - 1}}{{y}_{j}},\frac{1}{{y}_{j}},\frac{{y}_{i}}{{y}_{j}},\ldots ,\frac{{y}_{n}}{{y}_{j}}}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
= \left( {\frac{{y}_{1}}{{y}_{j}},\ldots ,\frac{{y}_{j - 1}}{{y}_{j}},\frac{{y}_{j + 1}}{{y}_{j}},\ldots ,\frac{{y}_{i - 1}}{{y}_{j}},\frac{1}{{y}_{j}},\frac{{y}_{i}}{{y}_{j}},\ldots ,\frac{{y}_{n}}{{y}_{j}}}\right) ,
\]

which is clearly differentiable.

In summary, the space of directions of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) (real projective space \( {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) ) \) can be covered by \( n + 1 \) coordinate neighborhoods \( {V}_{i} \) , where the \( {V}_{i} \) are made up of those directions of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) that are not in the hyperplane \( {x}_{i} = 0 \) ; in addition, in each \( {V}_{i} \) we have coordinates

\[
\left( {\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{i}},\ldots ,\frac{{x}_{i - 1}}{{x}_{i}},\frac{{x}_{i + 1}}{{x}_{i}},\ldots ,\frac{{x}_{n + 1}}{{x}_{i}}}\right) ,
\]

where \( \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n + 1}}\right) \) are the coordinates of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) . It is customary, in the classical terminology, to call the coordinates of \( {V}_{i} \) "inhomogeneous coordinates" corresponding to the "homogeneous coordinates" \( \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n + 1}}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) .

2.5 Definition. Let \( {M}_{1}^{n} \) and \( {M}_{2}^{m} \) be differentiable manifolds. A mapping \( \varphi  : {M}_{1} \rightarrow  {M}_{2} \) is differentiable at \( p \in  {M}_{1} \) if given a parametrization \( y : V \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \rightarrow  {M}_{2} \) at \( \varphi \left( p\right) \) there exists a parametrization \( \mathbf{x} : U \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {M}_{1} \) at \( p \) such that \( \varphi \left( {\mathbf{x}\left( U\right) }\right)  \subset  \mathbf{y}\left( V\right) \) and the mapping

(1)

\[
{\mathbf{y}}^{-1} \circ  \varphi  \circ  \mathbf{x} : U \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{m}
\]

is differentiable at \( {x}^{-1}\left( p\right) \) (Fig. 2). \( \varphi \) is differentiable on an open set of \( {M}_{1} \) if it is differentiable at all of the points of this open set.

It follows from condition (2) of Definition 2.1 that the given definition is independent of the choice of the parametrizations. The mapping (1) is called the expression of \( \varphi \) in the parametrizations \( \mathbf{x} \) and \( \mathbf{y} \) .

2.6 Definition. Let \( M \) be a differentiable manifold. A differentiable function \( \alpha  : \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)  \rightarrow  M \) is called a (differentiable) curve in \( M \) . Suppose that \( \alpha \left( 0\right)  = p \in  M \) , and let \( \mathcal{D} \) be the set of functions on \( M \) that are differentiable at \( p \) . The tangent vector to the curve \( \alpha \) at \( t = 0 \) is a function \( {\alpha }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  : \mathcal{D} \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) given by

\[
{\alpha }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) f = {\left. \frac{d\left( {f \circ  \alpha }\right) }{dt}\right| }_{t = 0},\;f \in  \mathcal{D}.
\]

A tangent vector at \( p \) is the tangent vector at \( t = 0 \) of some curve \( \alpha  : \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)  \rightarrow  M \) with \( \alpha \left( 0\right)  = p \) . The set of all tangent vectors to \( M \) at \( p \) will be indicated by \( {T}_{p}M \) .

If we choose a parametrization \( \mathrm{x} : U \rightarrow  {M}^{n} \) at \( p = \mathrm{x}\left( 0\right) \) , we can express the function \( f \) and the curve \( \alpha \) in this parametrization by

\[
f \circ  \mathbf{x}\left( q\right)  = f\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right) ,\;q = \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right)  \in  U,
\]

and

\[
{x}^{-1} \circ  \alpha \left( t\right)  = \left( {{x}_{1}\left( t\right) ,\ldots ,{x}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right)
\]

respectively. Therefore, restricting \( f \) to \( \alpha \) , we obtain

\[
{\alpha }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) f = {\left. \frac{d}{dt}\left( f \circ  \alpha \right) \right| }_{t = 0} = {\left. \frac{d}{dt}f\left( {x}_{1}\left( t\right) ,\ldots ,{x}_{n}\left( t\right) \right) \right| }_{t = 0}
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{x}_{i}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}_{i}}\right)  = \left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{x}_{i}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) {\left( \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}}\right) }_{0}}\right) f.
\]

8 Differentiable manifolds

In other words, the vector \( {\alpha }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) can be expressed in the parametrization \( \mathbf{x} \) by

(2)

\[
{\alpha }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{x}_{i}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) {\left( \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}}\right) }_{0}.
\]

Observe that \( {\left( \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}}\right) }_{0} \) is the tangent vector at \( p \) of the "coordinate curve" (Fig. 3):

\[
{x}_{i} \rightarrow  \mathbf{x}\left( {0,\ldots ,0,{x}_{i},0,\ldots ,0}\right) .
\]

![019eafa4-c1ab-71ca-a069-1af7cc3160f3_22_245_861_1356_575_0.jpg](images/019eafa4-c1ab-71ca-a069-1af7cc3160f3_22_245_861_1356_575_0.jpg)

Figure 3

The expression (2) shows that the tangent vector to the curve \( \alpha \) at \( p \) depends only the derivative of \( \alpha \) in a coordinate system. It follows also from (2) that the set \( {T}_{p}M \) , with the usual operations of functions, forms a vector space of dimension \( n \) , and that the choice of a parametrization \( x : U \rightarrow  M \) determines an associated basis \( \left\{  {{\left( \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{1}}\right) }_{0},\ldots ,{\left( \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{n}}\right) }_{0}}\right\} \) in \( {T}_{p}M \) (Fig. 3). It is immediate that the linear structure in \( {T}_{p}M \) defined above does not depend on the parametrization \( \mathbf{x} \) . The vector space \( {T}_{p}M \) is called the tangent space of \( M \) at \( p \) .

Let \( \mathrm{x} : U \rightarrow  {M}_{1} \) and \( \mathbf{y} : V \rightarrow  {M}_{2} \) be parametrizations at \( p \) and \( \varphi \left( p\right) \) , respectively. Expressing \( \varphi \) in these parametrizations, we can write

\[
{\mathbf{y}}^{-1} \circ  \varphi  \circ  \mathbf{x}\left( q\right)  = \left( {{y}_{1}\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right) ,\ldots ,{y}_{m}\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
q = \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right)  \in  U,\;\left( {{y}_{1},\ldots ,{y}_{m}}\right)  \in  V.
\]

On the other hand, expressing \( \alpha \) in the parametrization \( \mathbf{x} \) , we obtain

\[
{\mathbf{x}}^{-1} \circ  \alpha \left( t\right)  = \left( {{x}_{1}\left( t\right) ,\ldots ,{x}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) .
\]

Therefore,

\[
{\mathbf{y}}^{-1} \circ  \beta \left( t\right)  = \left( {{y}_{1}\left( {{x}_{1}\left( t\right) ,\ldots ,{x}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) ,\ldots ,{y}_{m}\left( {{x}_{1}\left( t\right) ,\ldots ,{x}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) }\right) .
\]

It follows that the expression for \( {\beta }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) with respect to the basis \( \left\{  {\left( \frac{\partial }{\partial {y}_{i}}\right) }_{0}\right\} \) of \( {T}_{\varphi \left( p\right) }{M}_{2} \) , associated to the parametrization \( y \) , is given by

(3)

\[
{\beta }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = \left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\frac{\partial {y}_{1}}{\partial {x}_{i}}{x}_{i}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,\ldots ,\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\frac{\partial {y}_{m}}{\partial {x}_{i}}{x}_{i}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) .
\]

The relation (3) shows immediately that \( {\beta }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) does not depend on the choice of \( \alpha \) . In addition,(3) can be written as

\[
{\beta }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = d{\varphi }_{p}\left( v\right)  = \left( \frac{\partial {y}_{i}}{\partial {x}_{j}}\right) \left( {{x}_{j}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) ,
\]

\[
i = 1,\ldots , m;\;j = 1,\ldots , n,
\]

where \( \left( \frac{\partial {y}_{i}}{\partial {x}_{j}}\right) \) denotes an \( m \times  n \) matrix and \( {x}_{j}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) denotes a column matrix with \( n \) elements. Therefore, \( d{\varphi }_{p} \) is a linear mapping of \( {T}_{p}{M}_{1} \) into \( {T}_{\varphi \left( p\right) }{M}_{2} \) whose matrix in the associated bases obtained from the parametrizations \( \mathbf{x} \) and \( \mathbf{y} \) is precisely the matrix \( \left( \frac{\partial {y}_{i}}{\partial {x}_{j}}\right) \) .

nodes.label: Definition 2.9
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.9 Definition. Let \( {M}_{1} \) and \( {M}_{2} \) be differentiable manifolds. A mapping \( \varphi  : {M}_{1} \rightarrow  {M}_{2} \) is a diffeomorphism if it is differentiable, bijective, and its inverse \( {\varphi }^{-1} \) is differentiable. \( \varphi \) is said to be a local diffeomorphism at \( p \in  M \) if there exist neighborhoods \( U \) of \( p \) and \( V \) of \( \varphi \left( p\right) \) such that \( \varphi  : U \rightarrow  V \) is a diffeomorphism.

The notion of diffeomorphism is the natural idea of equivalence between differentiable manifolds. It is an immediate consequence of the chain rule that if \( \varphi  : {M}_{1} \rightarrow  {M}_{2} \) is a diffeomorphism, then \( d{\varphi }_{p} : {T}_{p}{M}_{1} \rightarrow  {T}_{\varphi \left( p\right) }{M}_{2} \) is an isomorphism for all \( p \in  {M}_{1} \) ; in particular, the dimensions of \( {M}_{1} \) and \( {M}_{2} \) are equal. A local converse to this fact is the following theorem.

nodes.content:
2.10 Theorem. Let \( \varphi  : {M}_{1}^{n} \rightarrow  {M}_{2}^{n} \) be a differentiable mapping and let \( p \in  {M}_{1} \) be such that \( d{\varphi }_{p} : {T}_{p}{M}_{1} \rightarrow  {T}_{\varphi \left( p\right) }{M}_{2} \) is an isomorphism. Then \( \varphi \) is a local diffeomorphism at \( p \) .

The proof follows from an immediate application of the inverse function theorem in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) .

nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry

nodes.label: Definition 3.1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
3.1 Definition. Let \( {M}^{m} \) and \( {N}^{n} \) be differentiable manifolds. A differentiable mapping \( \varphi  : M \rightarrow  N \) is said to be an immersion if \( d{\varphi }_{p} : {T}_{p}M \rightarrow  {T}_{\varphi \left( p\right) }N \) is injective for all \( p \in  M \) . If, in addition, \( \varphi \) is a homeomorphism onto \( \varphi \left( M\right)  \subset  N \) , where \( \varphi \left( M\right) \) has the subspace topology induced from \( N \) , we say that \( \varphi \) is an embedding. If \( M \subset  N \) and the inclusion \( i : M \subset  N \) is an embedding, we say that \( M \) is a submanifold of \( N \) .

It can be seen that if \( \varphi  : {M}^{m} \rightarrow  {N}^{n} \) is an immersion, then \( m \leq  n \) ; the difference \( n - m \) is called the codimension of the immersion \( \varphi \) .

3.6 EXAMPLE. It is clear that a regular surface \( S \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) has a differentiable structure given by its parametrizations \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha } : {U}_{\alpha } \rightarrow  S \) . With such a structure, the mappings \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha } \) are differentiable and, indeed, are embeddings of \( {U}_{\alpha } \) into \( S \) ; that is an immediate consequence of conditions (a) and (b) of the definition of regular surface given in the introduction. We are going to show that the inclusion \( i : S \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) is an embedding, that is, \( S \) is a submanifold of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) .

![019eafa4-c1ab-71ca-a069-1af7cc3160f3_27_379_233_1207_558_0.jpg](images/019eafa4-c1ab-71ca-a069-1af7cc3160f3_27_379_233_1207_558_0.jpg)

In fact, \( i \) is differentiable, because for all \( p \in  S \) there exists a parametrization x: \( U \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{2} \rightarrow  S \) of \( S \) at \( p \) and a parametrization \( j : V \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \rightarrow  V \) of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) at \( i\left( p\right) \) ( \( V \) is a neighborhood of \( p \) in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) and \( j \) is the identity mapping), such that \( {j}^{-1} \circ  i \circ  x = x \) is differentiable. In addition, from condition (b), \( i \) is an immersion and, from condition (a), \( i \) is a homeomorphism onto its image, which proves the claim.

nodes.label: Proposition 3.7
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 3.7 Proposition. Let \( \varphi  : {M}_{1}^{n} \rightarrow  {M}_{2}^{m},\;n \leq  m \) , be an immersion of the differentiable manifold \( {M}_{1} \) into the differentiable manifold \( {M}_{2} \) . For every point \( p \in  {M}_{1} \) , there exists a neighborhood \( V \subset  {M}_{1} \) of \( p \) such that the restriction \( \varphi  \mid  V \rightarrow  {M}_{2} \) is an embedding.
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.7 Proposition. Let \( \varphi : {M}_{1}^{n} \rightarrow {M}_{2}^{m},\;n \leq m \) , be an immersion of the differentiable manifold \( {M}_{1} \) into the differentiable manifold \( {M}_{2} \) . For every point \( p \in {M}_{1} \) , there exists a neighborhood \( V \subset {M}_{1} \) of \( p \) such that the restriction \( \varphi \mid V \rightarrow {M}_{2} \) is an embedding.

nodes.proof:
This fact is a consequence of the inverse function theorem. Let \( {x}_{1} : {U}_{1} \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {M}_{1} \) and \( {x}_{2} : {U}_{2} \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \rightarrow  {M}_{2} \) be a system of coordinates at \( p \) and at \( \varphi \left( p\right) \) , respectively, and let us denote by \( \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right) \) the coordinates of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) and by \( \left( {{y}_{1},\ldots ,{y}_{m}}\right) \) the coordinates of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) . In these coordinates, the expression for \( \varphi \) , that is, the mapping \( \widetilde{\varphi } = {x}_{2}^{-1} \circ  \varphi  \circ  {x}_{1} \) , can be written

\[
\widetilde{\varphi } = \left( {{y}_{1}\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right) ,\ldots ,{y}_{m}\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right) }\right) .
\]

Let \( q = {\mathrm{x}}_{1}^{-1}\left( p\right) \) . Since \( \varphi \) is an immersion, we can suppose, renumbering the coordinates for both \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) and \( {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) , if necessary, that

\[
\frac{\partial \left( {{y}_{1},\ldots ,{y}_{n}}\right) }{\partial \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right) }\left( q\right)  \neq  0.
\]

To apply the inverse function theorem, we introduce the mapping \( \phi  = {U}_{1} \times  {R}^{m - n = k} \rightarrow  {R}^{m} \) given by

\[
\phi \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n},{t}_{1},\ldots ,{t}_{k}}\right)  =
\]

\[
= \left( {{y}_{1}\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right) ,\ldots ,{y}_{n}\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right) ,{y}_{n + 1}\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right)  + {t}_{1},\ldots }\right. \text{ , }
\]

\[
\left. {,\ldots ,{y}_{n + k}\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right)  + {t}_{k}}\right)
\]

where \( \left( {{t}_{1},\ldots ,{t}_{k}}\right)  \in  {\mathrm{R}}^{m - n = k} \) . It is easy to verify that \( \phi \) restricted to \( {U}_{1} \) coincides with \( \widetilde{\varphi } \) and that

\[
\det \left( {d{\phi }_{q}}\right)  = \frac{\partial \left( {{y}_{1},\ldots ,{y}_{n}}\right) }{\partial \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right) }\left( q\right)  \neq  0.
\]

It follows from the inverse function theorem, that there exist neighborhoods \( {W}_{1} \subset  {U}_{1} \times  {\mathbf{R}}^{k} \) of \( q \) and \( {W}_{2} \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) of \( \phi \left( q\right) \) such that the restriction \( \phi  \mid  {W}_{1} \) is a diffeomorphism onto \( {W}_{2} \) . Let \( \widetilde{V} = {W}_{1} \cap  {U}_{1} \) . Since \( \phi  \mid  \widetilde{V} = \widetilde{\varphi } \mid  \widetilde{V} \) and \( {\mathbf{x}}_{i} \) is a diffeomorphism, for \( i = 1,2 \) , we conclude that the restriction to \( V = {x}_{1}\left( \widetilde{V}\right) \) of the mapping \( \phi  = {\mathbf{x}}_{2} \circ  \widetilde{\varphi } \circ  {\mathbf{x}}_{1}^{-1} : V \rightarrow  \varphi \left( V\right)  \subset  {M}_{2} \) is a diffeomorphism, hence an embedding.

nodes.title: 0.4. Other examples of manifolds. Orientation
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry

nodes.label: Example 4.1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
4.1 EXAMPLE. (The tangent bundle). Let \( {M}^{n} \) be a differentiable manifold and let \( {TM} = \left\{  {\left( {p, v}\right) ;p \in  M, v \in  {T}_{p}M}\right\} \) . We are going to provide the set \( {TM} \) with a differentiable structure (of dimension 2n); with such a structure \( {TM} \) will be called the tangent bundle of \( M \) . This is the natural space to work with when treating questions that involve positions and velocities, as in the case of mechanics.

Let \( \left\{  \left( {{U}_{\alpha },{\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }}\right) \right\} \) be a maximal differentiable structure on \( M \) . Denote by \( \left( {{x}_{1}^{\alpha },\ldots ,{x}_{n}^{\alpha }}\right) \) the coordinates of \( {U}_{\alpha } \) and by \( \left\{  {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{1}^{\alpha }},\ldots }\right. \) , \( \left. \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{n}^{\alpha }}\right\} \) the associated bases to the tangent spaces of \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {U}_{\alpha }\right) \) . For every \( \alpha \) , define

\[
{\mathbf{y}}_{\alpha } : {U}_{\alpha } \times  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {TM},
\]

by

\[
{\mathbf{y}}_{\alpha }\left( {{x}_{1}^{\alpha },\ldots ,{x}_{n}^{\alpha },{u}_{1},\ldots ,{u}_{n}}\right)  =
\]

\[
= \left( {{\mathrm{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {{x}_{1}^{\alpha },\ldots ,{x}_{n}^{\alpha }}\right) ,\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{u}_{i}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}^{\alpha }}}\right) ,\;\left( {{u}_{1},\ldots ,{u}_{n}}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n}.
\]

Geometrically, this means that we are taking as coordinates of a point \( \left( {p, v}\right)  \in  {TM} \) the coordinates \( {x}_{1}^{\alpha },\ldots ,{x}_{n}^{\alpha } \) of \( p \) together with the coordinates of \( v \) in the basis \( \left\{  {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{1}^{\alpha }},\ldots ,\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{n}^{\alpha }}}\right\} \) .

We are going to show that \( \left\{  \left( {{U}_{\alpha } \times  {\mathbf{R}}^{n},{\mathbf{y}}_{\alpha }}\right) \right\} \) is a differentiable structure on \( {TM} \) . Since \( \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{\alpha }{\mathrm{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {U}_{\alpha }\right)  = M \) and \( {\left( d{\mathrm{x}}_{\alpha }\right) }_{q}\left( {\mathbf{R}}^{n}\right)  = \; {T}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }\left( q\right) }M,\;q \in  {U}_{\alpha } \) , we have that

\[
\mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{\alpha }{\mathbf{y}}_{\alpha }\left( {{U}_{\alpha } \times  {\mathbf{R}}^{n}}\right)  = {TM}
\]

which verifies condition (1) of Definition 2.1. Now let

\[
\left( {p, v}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{y}}_{\alpha }\left( {{U}_{\alpha } \times  {\mathbf{R}}^{n}}\right)  \cap  {\mathbf{y}}_{\beta }\left( {{U}_{\beta } \times  {\mathbf{R}}^{n}}\right) .
\]

Then

\[
\left( {p, v}\right)  = \left( {{\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {q}_{\alpha }\right) , d{\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {v}_{\alpha }\right) }\right)  = \left( {{\mathbf{x}}_{\beta }\left( {q}_{\beta }\right) , d{\mathbf{x}}_{\beta }\left( {v}_{\beta }\right) }\right) ,
\]

where \( {q}_{\alpha } \in  {U}_{\alpha },{q}_{\beta } \in  {U}_{\beta },{v}_{\alpha },{v}_{\beta } \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . Therefore,

\[
{\mathbf{y}}_{\beta }^{-1} \circ  {\mathbf{y}}_{\alpha }\left( {{q}_{\alpha },{v}_{\alpha }}\right)  = {\mathbf{y}}_{\beta }^{-1}\left( {{\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {q}_{\alpha }\right) , d{\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {v}_{\alpha }\right) }\right)  =
\]

\[
= \left( {\left( {{\mathrm{x}}_{\beta }^{-1} \circ  {\mathrm{x}}_{\alpha }}\right) \left( {q}_{\alpha }\right) , d\left( {{\mathrm{x}}_{\beta }^{-1} \circ  {\mathrm{x}}_{\alpha }}\right) \left( {v}_{\alpha }\right) }\right) .
\]

Since \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\beta }^{-1} \circ  {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha } \) is differentiable, \( d\left( {{\mathbf{x}}_{\beta }^{-1} \circ  {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }}\right) \) is as well. It follows that \( {\mathbf{y}}_{\beta }^{-1} \circ  {\mathbf{y}}_{\alpha } \) is differentiable, which verifies condition (2) of the definition 2.1 and completes the example.

nodes.label: Example 4.2
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
4.2 EXAMPLE. (Regular surfaces in \( {\mathrm{R}}^{n} \) ). The natural generalization of the notion of a regular surface in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) is the idea of a surface of dimension \( k \) in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n},\;k \leq  n \) . A subset \( {M}^{k} \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is a regular surface of dimension \( k \) if for every \( p \in  {M}^{k} \) there exists a neighborhood \( V \) of \( p \) in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) and a mapping \( \mathbf{x} : U \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{k} \rightarrow  M \cap  V \) of an open set \( U \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{k} \) onto \( M \cap  V \) such that:

(a) \( x \) is a differentiable homeomorphism.

(b) \( {\left( dx\right) }_{q} : {\mathbf{R}}^{k} \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is injective for all \( q \in  U \) .

Except for the dimensions involved, the definition is exactly the same as was given in the Introduction for a regular surface in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) .

In a similar way as was done for surfaces in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) (M. do Carmo [dC2], p. 71), it can be proved that if \( \mathrm{x} : U \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{k} \rightarrow  {M}^{k} \) and \( \mathrm{y} : V \subset \; {\mathbf{R}}^{k} \rightarrow  {M}^{k} \) are two parametrizations with \( \mathbf{x}\left( U\right)  \cap  \mathbf{y}\left( V\right)  = W \neq  \phi \) , then the mapping \( h = {\mathbf{x}}^{-1} \circ  \mathbf{y} : {\mathbf{y}}^{-1}\left( W\right)  \rightarrow  {\mathbf{x}}^{-1}\left( W\right) \) is a diffeomorphism. For completeness, we give a sketch of this proof in what follows.

First, we observe that \( h \) is a homeomorphism, being a composition of homeomorphisms. Let \( r \in  {\mathbf{y}}^{-1}\left( W\right) \) and put \( q = h\left( r\right) \) . Let \( \left( {{u}_{1},\ldots ,{u}_{k}}\right)  \in  U \) and \( \left( {{v}_{1},\ldots ,{v}_{n}}\right)  \in  {\mathrm{R}}^{n} \) , and write \( \mathbf{x} \) in these coordinates as

\[
\mathbf{x}\left( {{u}_{1},\ldots ,{u}_{k}}\right)  = \left( {{v}_{1}\left( {{u}_{1},\ldots ,{u}_{k}}\right) ,\ldots ,{v}_{n}\left( {{u}_{1},\ldots ,{u}_{k}}\right) }\right) .
\]

From condition (b), we can suppose that

\[
\frac{\partial \left( {{v}_{1},\ldots ,{v}_{k}}\right) }{\partial \left( {{u}_{1},\ldots ,{u}_{k}}\right) }\left( q\right)  \neq  0
\]

Extend \( \mathbf{x} \) to a mapping \( F : U \times  {\mathbf{R}}^{n - k} \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) given by

\[
F\left( {{u}_{1},\ldots ,{u}_{k},{t}_{k + 1},\ldots ,{t}_{n}}\right)
\]

\[
= \left( {{v}_{1}\left( {{u}_{1},\ldots ,{u}_{k}}\right) ,\ldots ,{v}_{k}\left( {{u}_{1},\ldots ,{u}_{k}}\right) ,}\right.
\]

\[
\left. {{v}_{k + 1}\left( {{u}_{1},\ldots ,{u}_{k}}\right)  + {t}_{k + 1},\ldots ,{v}_{n}\left( {{u}_{1},\ldots ,{u}_{k}}\right)  + {t}_{n}}\right) ,
\]

where \( \left( {{t}_{k + 1},\ldots ,\ldots {t}_{n}}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n - k} \) . It is clear that \( F \) is differentiable and the restriction of \( F \) to \( U \times  \{ \left( {0,\ldots ,0}\right) \} \) coincides with \( \mathbf{x} \) . By a simple calculation, we obtain that

\[
\det \left( {d{F}_{q}}\right)  = \frac{\partial \left( {{v}_{1},\ldots ,{v}_{k}}\right) }{\partial \left( {{u}_{1},\ldots ,{u}_{k}}\right) }\left( q\right)  \neq  0.
\]

We are then able to apply the inverse function theorem, which guarantees the existence of a neighborhood \( Q \) of \( \mathbf{x}\left( q\right) \) where \( {F}^{-1} \) exists and is differentiable. By the continuity of \( y \) , there exists a neighborhood \( R \subset  V \) of \( r \) such that \( \mathbf{y}\left( R\right)  \subset  Q \) . Note that the restriction of \( h \) to \( R, h\left| {R = {F}^{-1} \circ  \mathbf{y}}\right| R \) is a composition of differentiable mappings. Thus \( h \) is differentiable at \( r \) , hence in \( {\mathbf{y}}^{-1}\left( W\right) \) . A similar argument would show that \( {h}^{-1} \) is differentiable as well, proving the assertion.

From what we have just proved, it follows by an entirely similar argument as in Example 3.6 that \( {M}^{k} \) is a differentiable manifold of dimension \( k \) and that the inclusion \( i : {M}^{k} \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is an embedding, that is, \( {M}^{k} \) is a submanifold of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) .

nodes.content:
4.3 EXAMPLE. (Inverse image of a regular value). Before discussing the next example, we need some definitions.

Let \( F : U \subset  {\mathrm{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {\mathrm{R}}^{m} \) be a differentiable mapping of an open set \( U \) of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . A point \( p \in  U \) is defined to be a critical point of \( F \) if the differential \( d{F}_{p} : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) is not surjective. The image \( F\left( p\right) \) of a critical point is called a critical value of \( F \) . A point \( a \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) that is not a critical value is said to be a regular value of \( F \) . Note that any point \( a \notin  F\left( U\right) \) is trivially a regular value of \( F \) and that if there exists a regular value of \( F \) in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{m} \) , then \( n \geq  m \) .

Now let \( a \in  F\left( U\right) \) be a regular value of \( F \) . We are going to show that the inverse image \( {F}^{-1}\left( a\right)  \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is a regular surface of dimension \( n - m = k \) . From what was seen in Example 4.2, \( {F}^{-1}\left( a\right) \) is then a submanifold of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) .

To prove the assertion we use, again, the inverse function theorem. Let \( p \in  {F}^{-1}\left( a\right) \) . Denote by \( q = \left( {{y}_{1},\ldots ,{y}_{m},{x}_{1},\ldots {x}_{k}}\right) \) an arbitrary point of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n = m + k} \) and by \( F\left( q\right)  = \left( {{f}_{1}\left( q\right) ,\ldots ,{f}_{m}\left( q\right) }\right) \) its image by the mapping \( F \) . Since \( a \) is a regular value of \( F, d{F}_{p} \) is surjective. Therefore, we can suppose that

\[
\frac{\partial \left( {{f}_{1},\ldots ,{f}_{m}}\right) }{\partial \left( {{y}_{1},\ldots ,{y}_{m}}\right) }\left( p\right)  \neq  0.
\]

Define a mapping \( \varphi  : U \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{n = m + k} \) by

\[
\varphi \left( {{y}_{1},\ldots ,{y}_{m},{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{k}}\right)  = \left( {{f}_{1}\left( q\right) ,\ldots ,{f}_{m}\left( q\right) ,{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{k}}\right) .
\]

Then

\[
\det {\left( d\varphi \right) }_{p} = \frac{\partial \left( {{f}_{1},\ldots ,{f}_{m}}\right) }{\partial \left( {{y}_{1},\ldots ,{y}_{m}}\right) }\left( p\right)  \neq  0.
\]

By the inverse function theorem, \( \varphi \) is a diffeomorphism of a neighborhood \( Q \) of \( p \) onto a neighborhood \( W \) of \( \varphi \left( p\right) \) . Let \( {K}^{m + k} \subset  W \subset \; {R}^{m + k} \) be a cube of center \( \varphi \left( p\right) \) and put \( V = {\varphi }^{-1}\left( {K}^{m + k}\right)  \cap  Q \) . Then \( \varphi \) maps the neighborhood \( V \) diffeomorphically onto \( {K}^{m + k} = {K}^{m} \times  {K}^{k} \) . Define a mapping \( \mathbf{x} : {K}^{k} \rightarrow  V \) by

\[
\mathbf{x}\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{k}}\right)  = {\varphi }^{-1}\left( {{a}_{1},\ldots ,{a}_{m},{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{k}}\right) ,
\]

where \( \left( {{a}_{1},\ldots ,{a}_{m}}\right)  = a \) . It is easy to check that \( \varphi \) satisfies conditions (a) and (b) of the definition of regular surface given in Example 4.2. Since \( p \) is arbitrary, \( {F}^{-1}\left( a\right) \) is a regular surface in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) , as asserted.

Before going on to other examples of differentiable manifolds, we should introduce the important global notion of orientation.

4.4 Definition. Let \( M \) be a differentiable manifold. We say that \( M \) is orientable if \( M \) admits a differentiable structure \( \left\{  \left( {{U}_{\alpha },{\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }}\right) \right\} \) such that:

(i) for every pair \( \alpha ,\beta \) , with \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {U}_{\alpha }\right)  \cap  {\mathbf{x}}_{\beta }\left( {U}_{\beta }\right)  = W \neq  \phi \) , the differential of the change of coordinates \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\beta }^{-1} \circ  {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha } \) has positive determinant.

In the opposite case, we say that \( M \) is non-orientable. If \( M \) is ori-entable, a choice of a differentiable structure satisfying (i) is called an orientation of \( M \) . \( M \) is then said to be oriented. Two differentiable structures that satisfy (i) determine the same orientation if their union again satisfies (i).

It is not difficult to verify that if \( M \) is orientable and connected there exist exactly two distinct orientations on \( M \) .

Now let \( {M}_{1} \) and \( {M}_{2} \) be differentiable manifolds and let \( \varphi  : {M}_{1} \rightarrow  {M}_{2} \) be a diffeomorphism. It is easy to verify that \( {M}_{1} \) is orientable if and only if \( {M}_{2} \) is orientable. If, additionally, \( {M}_{1} \) and \( {M}_{2} \) are connected and are oriented, \( \varphi \) induces an orientation on \( {M}_{2} \) which may or may not coincide with the initial orientation of \( {M}_{2} \) . In the first case, we say that \( \varphi \) preserves the orientation and in the second case, that \( \varphi \) reverses the orientation.

Indeed, since the determinant of the differential of the coordinate change is \( \neq  0 \) , it does not change sign in \( {V}_{1} \cap  {V}_{2} \) ; if it is negative at a single point, it suffices to change the sign of one of the coordinates to make it positive at that point, hence on \( {V}_{1} \cap  {V}_{2} \) .

4.6 EXAMPLE. The simple criterion of the previous example can be used to show that the sphere

\[
{S}^{n} = \left\{  {\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n + 1}}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1};\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{{n + 1}}{x}_{i}^{2} = 1}\right\}   \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1}
\]

is orientable. Indeed, let \( N = \left( {0,\ldots ,0,1}\right) \) be the north pole and \( S = \left( {0,\ldots ,0, - 1}\right) \) the south pole of \( {S}^{n} \) . Define a mapping \( {\pi }_{1} : {S}^{n} - \{ N\}  \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) (stereographic projection from the north pole) that takes \( p = \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots {x}_{n + 1}}\right) \) in \( {S}^{n} - \{ N\} \) into the intersection of the hyperplane \( {x}_{n + 1} = 0 \) with the line that passes through \( p \) and \( N \) . It is easy to verify that (Fig. 9)

\[
{\pi }_{1}\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n + 1}}\right)  = \left( {\frac{{x}_{1}}{1 - {x}_{n + 1}},\ldots ,\frac{{x}_{n}}{1 - {x}_{n + 1}}}\right) .
\]

The mapping \( {\pi }_{1} \) is differentiable, injective and maps \( {S}^{n} - \{ N\} \) onto the hyperplane \( {x}_{n + 1} = 0 \) . The stereographic projection \( {\pi }_{2} : {S}^{n} - \{ S\}  \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) from the south pole onto the hyperplane \( {x}_{n + 1} = 0 \) has the same properties.

Therefore, the parametrizations \( \left( {{\mathbf{R}}^{n},{\pi }_{1}^{-1}}\right) ,\left( {{\mathbf{R}}^{n},{\pi }_{2}^{-1}}\right) \) cover \( {S}^{n} \) . In addition, the change of coordinates:

\[
{y}_{j} = \frac{{x}_{j}}{1 - {x}_{n + 1}} \leftrightarrow  {y}_{j}^{\prime } = \frac{{x}_{j}}{1 + {x}_{n + 1}},
\]

\[
\left( {{y}_{1},\ldots ,{y}_{n}}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n},\;j = 1,\ldots , n,
\]

is given by

\[
{y}_{j}^{\prime } = \frac{{y}_{j}}{\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{y}_{i}^{2}}
\]

(here we use the fact that \( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{{n + 1}}{x}_{k}^{2} = 1 \) ). Therefore, the family \( \left\{  {\left( {{\mathbf{R}}^{n},{\pi }_{1}^{-1}}\right) ,\left( {{\mathbf{R}}^{n},{\pi }_{2}^{-1}}\right) }\right\} \) is a differentiable structure on \( {S}^{n} \) . Observe that the intersection \( {\pi }_{1}^{-1}\left( {\mathbf{R}}^{n}\right)  \cap  {\pi }_{2}^{-1}\left( {\mathbf{R}}^{n}\right)  = {S}^{n} - \{ N \cup  S\} \) is connected, thus \( {S}^{n} \) is orientable and the family given determines an orientation of \( {S}^{n} \) .

![019eafa4-c1ab-71ca-a069-1af7cc3160f3_34_244_260_1318_772_0.jpg](images/019eafa4-c1ab-71ca-a069-1af7cc3160f3_34_244_260_1318_772_0.jpg)

Figure 9

Now let \( A : {S}^{n} \rightarrow  {S}^{n} \) be the antipodal map given by \( A\left( p\right)  = \; - p, p \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) . \( A \) is differentiable and \( {A}^{2} = \) ident. Therefore, \( A \) is a diffeomorphism of \( {S}^{n} \) . Observe that when \( n \) is even, \( A \) reverses the orientation of \( {S}^{n} \) and when \( n \) is odd, \( A \) preserves the orientation of \( {S}^{n} \) .

We are now in a position to exhibit some other examples of differentiable manifolds.

nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
4.7 EXAMPLE. (Another description of projective space). The set \( {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) of lines of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) that pass through the origin can be thought of as the quotient space of the unit sphere \( {S}^{n} = \left\{  {p \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1};\left| p\right|  = 1}\right\} \) by the equivalence relation that identifies \( p \in  {S}^{n} \) with its antipodal point, \( A\left( p\right)  =  - p \) . Indeed, each line that passes through the origin determines two antipodal points and the correspondence so obtained is evidently bijective.

Taking into account this fact, we are going to introduce another differentiable structure on \( {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) (Cf. Example 2.4). For this, we initially introduce on \( {S}^{n} \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) the structure of a regular surface, defining parametrizations

\[
{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{ + } : {U}_{i} \rightarrow  {S}^{n},\;{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{ - } : {U}_{i} \rightarrow  {S}^{n},\;i = 1,\ldots , n + 1,
\]

in the following way:

\[
{U}_{i} = \left\{  {\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n + 1}}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1};{x}_{i} = 0,}\right.
\]

\[
\left. {{x}_{1}^{2} + \ldots  + {x}_{i - 1}^{2} + {x}_{i + 1}^{2} + \ldots  + {x}_{n + 1}^{2} < 1}\right\}
\]

\[
{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{ + }\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{i - 1},{x}_{i + 1},\ldots ,{x}_{n + 1}}\right)
\]

\[
= \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{i - 1},{D}_{i},{x}_{i + 1},\ldots ,{x}_{n + 1}}\right) ,
\]

\[
{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{ - }\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{i - 1},{x}_{i + 1},\ldots ,{x}_{n + 1}}\right)
\]

\[
= \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{i - 1}, - {D}_{i},{x}_{i + 1},\ldots ,{x}_{n + 1}}\right) ,
\]

where \( {D}_{i} = \sqrt{1 - \left( {{x}_{1}^{2} + \ldots  + {x}_{i - 1}^{2} + {x}_{i + 1}^{2} + \ldots  + {x}_{n + 1}^{2}}\right) } \) . It is easy to verify that conditions (a) and (b) of the definition in Example 4.2 are satisfied. Therefore, the family

\[
\left\{  {\left( {{U}_{i},{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{ + }}\right) ,\left( {{U}_{i},{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{ - }}\right) }\right\}  ,\;i = 1,\ldots , n + 1
\]

is a differentiable structure on \( {S}^{n} \) . Geometrically, this is equivalent to covering the sphere \( {S}^{n} \) with coordinate neighborhoods that are hemi-spheres perpendicular to the axes \( {x}_{i} \) and taking as coordinates on, for example, \( {\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{ + }\left( {U}_{i}\right) \) , the coordinates of the orthogonal projection of \( {\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{ + }\left( {U}_{i}\right) \) on the hyperplane \( {x}_{i} = 0 \) (Fig. 10).

![019eafa4-c1ab-71ca-a069-1af7cc3160f3_35_495_1395_781_763_0.jpg](images/019eafa4-c1ab-71ca-a069-1af7cc3160f3_35_495_1395_781_763_0.jpg)

Figure 10

Let \( \pi  : {S}^{n} \rightarrow  {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) be the canonical projection, that is, \( \pi \left( p\right)  = \{ p, - p\} \) ; observe that \( \pi \left( {{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{ + }\left( {U}_{i}\right) }\right)  = \pi \left( {{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{ - }\left( {U}_{i}\right) }\right) \) . We are going to define a mapping \( {\mathbf{y}}_{i} : {U}_{i} \rightarrow  {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) by

\[
{\mathbf{y}}_{i} = \pi  \circ  {\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{ + }.
\]

Since \( \pi \) restricted to \( {\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{ + }\left( {U}_{i}\right) \) is one-to-one, we have that

\[
{\mathbf{y}}_{i}^{-1} \circ  {\mathbf{y}}_{j} = {\left( \pi  \circ  {\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{ + }\right) }^{-1} \circ  \left( {\pi  \circ  {\mathbf{x}}_{j}^{ + }}\right)  = {\left( {\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{ + }\right) }^{-1} \circ  {\mathbf{x}}_{j}^{ + },
\]

which yields the differentiability of \( {\mathbf{y}}_{i}^{-1} \circ  {\mathbf{y}}_{j} \) , for all \( i, j = 1,\ldots , n + 1 \) . Thus the family \( \left\{  \left( {{U}_{i},{y}_{i}}\right. \right. \) is a differentiable structure for \( {P}^{n}\left( \mathrm{R}\right) \) .

In fact, this differentiable structure and that of Example 2.4 give rise to the same maximal structure. Indeed, the coordinate neighborhoods are the same and the change of coordinates are given by:

\[
\left( {\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{i}},\ldots ,\frac{{x}_{i - 1}}{{x}_{i}},1,\frac{{x}_{i + 1}}{{x}_{i}},\ldots ,\frac{{x}_{n + 1}}{{x}_{i}}}\right)  \leftrightarrow
\]

\[
\leftrightarrow  \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{i - 1},{D}_{i},{x}_{i + 1},\ldots ,{x}_{n + 1}}\right)
\]

which, since \( {x}_{i} \neq  0 \) and \( {D}_{i} \neq  0 \) , is differentiable.

As we shall see in Exercise 9, \( {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) is orientable if and only if \( n \) is odd.

4.8 EXAMPLE. (Discontinuous action of a group). There is a way of constructing differentiable manifolds that generalizes the process above, which is given by the following considerations.

We say that a group \( G \) acts on a differentiable manifold \( M \) if there exists a mapping \( \varphi  : G \times  M \rightarrow  M \) such that:

(i) For each \( g \in  G \) , the mapping \( {\varphi }_{g} : M \rightarrow  M \) given by \( {\varphi }_{g}\left( p\right)  = \; \varphi \left( {g, p}\right) ,\;p \in  M \) , is a diffeomorphism, and \( {\varphi }_{e} = \) identity.

(ii) If \( {g}_{1},{g}_{2} \in  G,\;{\varphi }_{{g}_{1}{g}_{2}} = {\varphi }_{{g}_{1}} \circ  {\varphi }_{{g}_{2}} \) .

Frequently, when dealing with a single action, we set \( \varphi \left( {g, p}\right)  = {gp} \) ; in this notation, condition (ii) can be interpreted as a form of associativity: \( \left( {{g}_{1}{g}_{2}}\right) p = {g}_{1}\left( {{g}_{2}p}\right) \) .

We say that the the action is properly discontinuous if every \( p \in  M \) has a neighborhood \( U \subset  M \) such that \( U \cap  g\left( U\right)  = \phi \) for all \( g \neq  e \) .

When \( G \) acts on \( M \) , the action determines an equivalence relation \( \sim \) on \( M \) , in which \( {p}_{1} \sim  {p}_{2} \) if and only if \( {p}_{2} = g{p}_{1} \) , for some \( g \in  G \) . Denote the quotient space of \( M \) by this equivalence relation by \( M/G \) . The mapping \( \pi  : M \rightarrow  M/G \) , given by

\[
\pi \left( p\right)  = \text{ equiv. class of }p = {Gp}
\]

will be called the projection of \( M \) onto \( M/G \) .

Now let \( M \) be a differentiable manifold and let \( G \times  M \rightarrow  M \) be a properly discontinuous action of a group \( G \) on \( M \) . We are going to show that \( M/G \) has a differentiable structure with respect to which the projection \( \pi  : M \rightarrow  M/G \) is a local diffeomorphism.

For each \( p \in  M \) choose a parametrization \( \mathbf{x} : V \rightarrow  M \) at \( p \) so that \( \mathbf{x}\left( V\right)  \subset  U \) , where \( U \subset  M \) is a neighborhood of \( p \) such that \( U \cap  g\left( U\right)  = \phi , g \neq  e \) . Clearly \( \pi  \mid  U \) is injective, hence \( \mathbf{y} = \pi  \circ  \mathbf{x} : V \rightarrow \; M/G \) is injective. The family \( \{ \left( {V,\mathbf{y}}\right) \} \) clearly covers \( M/G \) ; for such a family to be a differentiable structure, it suffices to show that given two mappings \( {y}_{1} = \pi  \circ  {x}_{1} : {V}_{1} \rightarrow  M/G \) and \( {y}_{2} = \pi  \circ  {x}_{2} : {V}_{2} \rightarrow  M/G \) with \( {y}_{1}\left( {V}_{1}\right)  \cap  {y}_{2}\left( {V}_{2}\right)  \neq  \phi \) , then \( {y}_{1}^{-1} \circ  {y}_{2} \) is differentiable.

For this, let \( {\pi }_{i} \) be the restriction of \( \pi \) to \( {x}_{i}\left( {V}_{i}\right) ,\;i = 1,2 \) . Let \( q \in  {\mathbf{y}}_{1}\left( {V}_{1}\right)  \cap  {\mathbf{y}}_{2}\left( {V}_{2}\right) \) and let \( r = {\mathbf{x}}_{2}^{-1} \circ  {\pi }_{2}^{-1}\left( q\right) \) . Let \( W \subset  {V}_{2} \) be a neighborhood of \( r \) such that \( \left( {{\pi }_{2} \circ  {\mathbf{x}}_{2}}\right) \left( W\right)  \subset  {\mathbf{y}}_{1}\left( {V}_{1}\right)  \cap  {\mathbf{y}}_{2}\left( {V}_{2}\right) \) (Fig. 11). Then, the restriction to \( W \) is given by

\[
{\mathbf{y}}_{1}^{-1} \circ  {\mathbf{y}}_{2} \mid  W = {\mathbf{x}}_{1}^{-1} \circ  {\pi }_{1}^{-1} \circ  {\pi }_{2} \circ  {\mathbf{x}}_{2}.
\]

Therefore, it is enough to show that \( {\pi }_{1}^{-1} \circ  {\pi }_{2} \) is differentiable at \( {p}_{2} = {\pi }_{2}^{-1}\left( q\right) \) . Let \( {p}_{1} = {\pi }_{1}^{-1} \circ  {\pi }_{2}\left( {p}_{2}\right) \) . Then \( {p}_{1} \) and \( {p}_{2} \) are equivalent in \( M \) , hence there is a \( g \in  G \) such that \( g{p}_{2} = {p}_{1} \) . It follows easily that the restriction \( {\pi }_{1}^{-1} \circ  {\pi }_{2} \mid  {\mathbf{x}}_{2}\left( W\right) \) coincides with the diffeomorphism \( {\varphi }_{g} \mid  {\mathbf{x}}_{2}\left( W\right) \) , which proves that \( {\pi }_{1}^{-1} \circ  {\pi }_{2} \) is differentiable at \( {p}_{2} \) , as stated.

From the very way in which this differentiable structure is constructed, \( \pi  : M \rightarrow  M/G \) is a local diffeomorphism. A criterion for the orientability of \( M/G \) is given in Exercise 9. Observe that the situation in the previous example reduces to the present one, by taking \( M = {S}^{n} \) and \( G \) the group of diffeomorphisms of \( {S}^{n} \) formed by the antipodal mapping \( A \) and the identity \( I = {A}^{2} \) of \( {S}^{n} \) .

4.9 (a). Consider the group \( G \) of "integral" translations of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{k} \) where the action of \( G \) on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{k} \) is given by

\[
G\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{k}}\right)  = \left( {{x}_{1} + {n}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{k} + {n}_{k}}\right) ,\;{n}_{1},\ldots ,{n}_{k} \in  \mathbb{Z},
\]

\[
\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{k}}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{k}.
\]

nodes.label: Definition 5.1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.section_title: 0.5. Vector fields; brackets. Topology of manifolds
nodes.content:
5.1 Definition. A vector field \( X \) on a differentiable manifold \( M \) is a correspondence that associates to each point \( p \in  M \) a vector \( X\left( p\right)  \in  {T}_{p}M \) . In terms of mappings, \( X \) is a mapping of \( M \) into the tangent bundle \( {TM} \) (see Example 4.1). The field is differentiable if the mapping \( X : M \rightarrow  {TM} \) is differentiable.

Considering a parametrization \( \mathbf{x} : U \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  M \) we can write

(4)

\[
X\left( p\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{a}_{i}\left( p\right) \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}},
\]

where each \( {a}_{i} : U \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) is a function on \( U \) and \( \left\{  \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}}\right\} \) is the basis associated to \( \mathbf{x},\;i = 1,\ldots , n \) . It is clear that \( X \) is differentiable if and only if the functions \( {a}_{i} \) are differentiable for some (and, therefore, for any) parametrization.

Occasionally, it is convenient to use the idea suggested by (4) and think of a vector field as a mapping \( X : \mathcal{D} \rightarrow  \mathcal{F} \) from the set \( \mathcal{D} \) of differentiable functions on \( M \) to the set \( \mathcal{F} \) of functions on \( M \) , defined in the following way

(5)

\[
\left( {Xf}\right) \left( p\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{a}_{i}\left( p\right) \frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}_{i}}\left( p\right) ,
\]

where \( f \) denotes, by abuse of notation, the expression of \( f \) in the parametrization \( \mathbf{x} \) . Indeed, this idea of a vector as a directional derivative was precisely what was used to define the notion of tangent vector. It is easy to check that the function \( {Xf} \) obtained in (5) does not depend on the choice of parametrization \( \mathbf{x} \) . In this context, it is immediate that \( X \) is differentiable if and only if \( X : \mathcal{D} \rightarrow  \mathcal{D} \) , that is, \( {Xf} \in  \mathcal{D} \) for all \( f \in  \mathcal{D} \) .

Observe that if \( \varphi  : M \rightarrow  M \) is a diffeomorphism, \( v \in  {T}_{p}M \) and \( f \) is a differentiable function in a neighborhood of \( \varphi \left( p\right) \) , we have

\[
\left( {{d\varphi }\left( v\right) f}\right) \varphi \left( p\right)  = v\left( {f \circ  \varphi }\right) \left( p\right) .
\]

Indeed, let \( \alpha  : \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)  \rightarrow  M \) be a differentiable curve with \( {\alpha }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = v \) , \( \alpha \left( 0\right)  = p \) . Then

\[
\left( {{d\varphi }\left( v\right) f}\right) \varphi \left( p\right)  = {\left. \frac{d}{dt}\left( f \circ  \varphi  \circ  \alpha \right) \right| }_{t = 0} = v\left( {f \circ  \varphi }\right) \left( p\right) .
\]

The interpretation of \( X \) as an operator on \( \mathcal{D} \) permits us to consider the iterates of \( X \) . For example, if \( X \) and \( Y \) are differentiable fields on \( M \) and \( f : M \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) is a differentiable function, we can consider the functions \( X\left( {Yf}\right) \) and \( Y\left( {Xf}\right) \) . In general, such operations do not lead to vector fields, because they involve derivatives of order higher than one. Nevertheless, we can affirm the following.

nodes.content: 5.2 LEMMA. Let \( X \) and \( Y \) be differentiable vector fields on a differentiable manifold \( M \) . Then there exists a unique vector field \( Z \) such that, for all \( f \in  \mathcal{D},\;{Zf} = \left( {{XY} - {YX}}\right) f \) .

nodes.proof:
First, we prove that if \( Z \) exists, then it is unique. Assume, therefore, the existence of such a \( Z \) . Let \( p \in  M \) and let \( \mathbf{x} : U \rightarrow  M \) be a parametrization at \( p \) , and let

\[
X = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{a}_{i}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}},\;Y = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{b}_{j}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{j}}
\]

be the expressions for \( X \) and \( Y \) in these parametrizations. Then for all \( f \in  \mathcal{D} \) ,

\[
{XYf} = X\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{b}_{j}\frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}_{j}}}\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i, j}}{a}_{i}\frac{\partial {b}_{j}}{\partial {x}_{i}}\frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}_{j}} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i, j}}{a}_{i}{b}_{j}\frac{{\partial }^{2}f}{\partial {x}_{i}\partial {x}_{j}}
\]

\[
{YXf} = Y\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{a}_{i}\frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}_{i}}}\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i, j}}{b}_{j}\frac{\partial {a}_{i}}{\partial {x}_{j}}\frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}_{i}} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i, j}}{a}_{i}{b}_{j}\frac{{\partial }^{2}f}{\partial {x}_{i}\partial {x}_{j}}.
\]

sec. 5]Vector fields; brackets. Topology of manifolds 27

Therefore, \( Z \) is given, in the parametrization \( \mathbf{x} \) , by

\[
{Zf} = {XYf} - {YXf} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i, j}}({a}_{i}\frac{\partial {b}_{j}}{\partial {x}_{i}} - {b}_{i}\frac{\partial {a}_{j}}{\partial {x}_{i}})\frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}_{j}}
\]

which proves the uniqueness of \( Z \) .

To show existence, define \( {Z}_{\alpha } \) in each coordinate neighborhood \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {U}_{\alpha }\right) \) of a differentiable structure \( \left\{  \left( {{U}_{\alpha },{\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }}\right) \right\} \) on \( M \) by the previous expression. By uniqueness, \( {Z}_{\alpha } = {Z}_{\beta } \) on \( {x}_{\alpha }\left( {U}_{\alpha }\right)  \cap  {x}_{\beta }\left( {U}_{\beta }\right)  \neq  \phi \) , which allows us to define \( Z \) over the entire manifold \( M \) .

(b) \( \left\lbrack  {{aX} + {bY}, Z}\right\rbrack   = a\left\lbrack  {X, Z}\right\rbrack   + b\left\lbrack  {Y, Z}\right\rbrack \) (linearity),

\]

nodes.content:
Let \( M \) be a differentiable manifold. A family of open sets \( {V}_{\alpha } \subset  M \) with \( \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{\alpha }{V}_{\alpha } = M \) is said to be locally finite if every point \( p \in  M \) has a neighborhood \( W \) such that \( W \cap  {V}_{\alpha } \neq  \phi \) for only a finite number of indices. The support of a function \( f : M \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) is the closure of the set of points where \( f \) is different from zero.

We say that a family \( \left\{  {f}_{\alpha }\right\} \) of differentiable functions \( {f}_{\alpha } : M \rightarrow \) R is a differentiable partition of unity if:

(1) For all \( \alpha ,{f}_{\alpha } \geq  0 \) and the support of \( {f}_{\alpha } \) is contained in a coordinate neighborhood \( {V}_{\alpha } = {\mathrm{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {U}_{\alpha }\right) \) of a differentiable structure \( \left\{  \left( {{U}_{\beta },{\mathbf{x}}_{\beta }}\right) \right\} \) of \( M \) .

(2) The family \( \left\{  {V}_{\alpha }\right\} \) is locally finite.

(3) \( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }{f}_{\alpha }\left( p\right)  = 1 \) , for all \( p \in  M \) (this condition makes sense, because for each \( p,{f}_{\alpha }\left( p\right)  \neq  0 \) only for a finite number of indices).

It is customary to say that the partition of unity \( \left\{  {f}_{\alpha }\right\} \) is subordinate to the covering \( \left\{  {V}_{\alpha }\right\} \) .

nodes.label: Remark 5.7
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.section_title: 0.5. Vector fields; brackets. Topology of manifolds
nodes.content:
5.7 REMARK. Recall that given \( p \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) and an open ball \( {B}_{r}\left( p\right)  \subset \; {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) centered at \( p \) with radius \( r \) , there exists a neighborhood \( U \) of \( p \) with \( \bar{U} \subset  {B}_{r}\left( p\right) \) and a differentiable function \( f : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) such that \( 0 \leq  f\left( q\right)  \leq  1 \) for all \( q \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) and

\[
f\left( q\right)  = \left\{  \begin{array}{lll} 1, & \text{ if } & q \in  \bar{U}, \\  0, & \text{ if } & q \notin  {B}_{r}\left( p\right) . \end{array}\right.
\]

Indeed, if we take, for simplicity, \( r = 2 \) , we can choose \( U = {B}_{1}\left( p\right) \) and define \( f \) by \( f\left( q\right)  = \beta \left( {-\left| {p - q}\right| }\right) , q \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) , where \( \beta  : \mathbf{R} \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) is given by

\[
\beta \left( t\right)  = \frac{{\int }_{-\infty }^{t}\alpha \left( s\right) {ds}}{{\int }_{-2}^{-1}\alpha \left( s\right) {ds}},
\]

and \( \alpha  : \mathbf{R} \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) is the smooth function equaling \( \exp \left( {-\frac{1}{\left( {t + 2}\right) \left( {-1 - t}\right) }}\right) \) on \( \left\lbrack  {-2, - 1}\right\rbrack \) and zero off this interval. It is easy to check that \( f \) satisfies the required conditions.

Clearly, the same thing happens in a neighborhood contained in a coordinate neighborhood on a differentiable manifold \( M \) . In other words, if \( p \in  M \) and \( V \subset  M \) is a neighborhood of \( p \) contained in a coordinate neighborhood of \( p \) which is diffeomorphic to an open ball, then there exists a neighborhood \( U \) of \( p \) with \( \bar{U} \subset  V \) and a differentiable function \( f : M \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) with \( 0 \leq  f\left( q\right)  \leq  1 \) if \( q \in  M, f\left( q\right)  = 1 \) if \( q \in  \bar{U} \) , and \( f\left( q\right)  = 0 \) if \( q \notin  V \) . This fact allows us to show that certain globally defined objects on \( M \) are, in reality, local, that is, their behavior at \( p \) only depends on how \( M \) behaves in a neighborhood of \( p \) (cf. the definition of the bracket of two vector fields in this chapter and the definition of an affine connection in Chapter 2).

1. (Product manifold). Let \( M \) and \( N \) be differentiable manifolds and let \( \left\{  \left( {{U}_{\alpha },{\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }}\right) \right\}  ,\left\{  {{V}_{\beta },{\mathbf{y}}_{\beta }}\right\} \) differentiable structures on \( M \) and \( N \) , respectively. Consider the cartesian product \( M \times  N \) and the mappings \( {\mathbf{z}}_{\alpha \beta }\left( {p, q}\right)  = \left( {{\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }\left( p\right) ,{\mathbf{y}}_{\beta }\left( q\right) }\right) , p \in  {U}_{\alpha }, q \in  {V}_{\beta } \) .

(a) Prove that \( \left\{  \left( {{U}_{\alpha } \times  {V}_{\beta },{\mathbf{z}}_{\alpha \beta }}\right) \right\} \) is a differentiable structure on \( M \times  N \) in which the projections \( {\pi }_{1} : M \times  N \rightarrow  M \) and \( {\pi }_{2} : M \times  N \rightarrow  N \) are differentiable. With this differentiable structure \( M \times  N \) is called the product manifold of \( M \) with \( N \) .

(b) Show that the product manifold \( {S}^{1} \times  \ldots  \times  {S}^{1} \) of \( n \) circles \( {S}^{1} \) , where \( {S}^{1} \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{2} \) has the usual differentiable structure, is diffeomorphic to the \( n \) -torus \( {T}^{n} \) of example 4.9 (a).

3. Prove that:

(a) a regular surface \( S \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) is an orientable manifold if and only if there exists a differentiable mapping of \( N : S \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) with \( N\left( p\right)  \bot  {T}_{p}\left( S\right) \) and \( \left| {N\left( p\right) }\right|  = 1 \) , for all \( p \in  S \) .

(b) the Möbius band (Example 4.9 (b)) is non-orientable.

nodes.content:
4. Show that the projective plane \( {P}^{2}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) is non-orientable.

Hint: Prove that if the manifold \( M \) is orientable, then any open subset of \( M \) is an orientable submanifold. Observe that \( {P}^{2}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) contains an open subset diffeomorphic to a Möbius band, which is non-orientable.

5. (Embedding of \( {P}^{2}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{4} \) ). Let \( F : {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{4} \) be given by

\[
F\left( {x, y, z}\right)  = \left( {{x}^{2} - {y}^{2},{xy},{xz},{yz}}\right) ,\;\left( {x, y, z}\right)  = p \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{3}.
\]

Let \( {S}^{2} \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) be the unit sphere with the origin \( 0 \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) . Observe that the restriction \( \varphi  = F \mid  {S}^{2} \) is such that \( \varphi \left( p\right)  = \varphi \left( {-p}\right) \) , and consider the mapping \( \widetilde{\varphi } : {P}^{2}\left( \mathbf{R}\right)  \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{4} \) given by

\[
\widetilde{\varphi }\left( \left\lbrack  p\right\rbrack  \right)  = \varphi \left( p\right) ,\left\lbrack  p\right\rbrack   = \text{ equiv. class of }p = \{ p, - p\} .
\]

Prove that:

(a) \( \widetilde{\varphi } \) is an immersion.

(b) \( \widetilde{\varphi } \) is injective; together with (a) and the compactness of \( {P}^{2}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) , this implies that \( \widetilde{\varphi } \) is an embedding.

7. (Infinite Möbius band).

Let \( C = \left\{  {\left( {x, y, z}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{3};{x}^{2} + {y}^{2} = 1}\right\} \) be a right circular cylinder, and let \( A : C \rightarrow  C \) be the symmetry with respect to the origin \( 0 \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) , that is, \( A\left( {x, y, z}\right)  = \left( {-x, - y, - z}\right) \) . Let \( M \) be the quotient space of \( C \) with respect to the equivalence relation \( p \sim  A\left( p\right) \) , and let \( \pi  : C \rightarrow  M \) be the projection \( \pi \left( p\right)  = \{ p, A\left( p\right) \} . \)

(a) Show that it is possible to give \( M \) a differentiable structure such that \( \pi \) is a local diffeomorphism.

(b) Prove that \( M \) is non-orientable.

nodes.label: Exercise 12
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
12. (The orientable double covering). Let \( {M}^{n} \) be a non-orientable differentiable manifold. For each \( p \in  M \) , consider the set \( B \) of bases of \( {T}_{p}M \) and say that two bases are equivalent if they are related by a matrix with positive determinant. This is an equivalence relation and separates \( B \) into two disjoint sets. Let \( {\mathcal{O}}_{p} \) be the quotient space of \( B \) with respect to this equivalence relation. \( {O}_{p} \in  {\mathcal{O}}_{p} \) will be called an orientation of \( {T}_{p}M \) . Let \( \bar{M} \) be the set

\[
\bar{M} = \left\{  {\left( {p,{O}_{p}}\right) ;p \in  M,{O}_{p} \in  {\mathcal{O}}_{p}}\right\}  .
\]

Let \( \left\{  \left( {{U}_{\alpha },{\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }}\right) \right\} \) be a maximal differentiable structure on \( M \) , and define \( {\overline{\mathbf{x}}}_{\alpha } : {U}_{\alpha } \rightarrow  \bar{M} \) by

\[
{\overline{\mathbf{x}}}_{\alpha }\left( {{u}_{1}^{\alpha },\ldots ,{u}_{n}^{\alpha }}\right)  = \left( {{\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {{u}_{1}^{\alpha },\ldots ,{u}_{n}^{\alpha }}\right) ,\left\lbrack  {\frac{\partial }{\partial {u}_{1}^{\alpha }},\ldots ,\frac{\partial }{\partial {u}_{n}^{\alpha }}}\right\rbrack  }\right)
\]

where \( \left( {{u}_{1}^{\alpha },\ldots ,{u}_{n}^{\alpha }}\right)  \in  {U}_{\alpha } \) and \( \left\lbrack  {\frac{\partial }{\partial {u}_{1}^{\alpha }},\ldots ,\frac{\partial }{\partial {u}_{n}^{\alpha }}}\right\rbrack \) denotes the element of \( {\mathcal{O}}_{p} \) determined by the basis \( \left\{  {\frac{\partial }{\partial {u}_{1}^{\alpha }},\ldots ,\frac{\partial }{\partial {u}_{n}^{\alpha }}}\right\} \) . Prove that:

(a) \( \left\{  {{U}_{\alpha },{\overline{\mathbf{x}}}_{\alpha }}\right\}  \} \) is a differentiable structure on \( \bar{M} \) and that the manifold \( \bar{M} \) so obtained is orientable.

(b) The mapping \( \pi  : \bar{M} \rightarrow  M \) given by \( \pi \left( {p,{O}_{p}}\right)  = p \) is differentiable and surjective. In addition, each \( p \in  M \) has a neighborhood \( U \subset  M \) such that \( {\pi }^{-1}\left( U\right)  = {V}_{1} \cup  {V}_{2} \) , where \( {V}_{1} \) and \( {V}_{2} \) are disjoint open sets in \( \bar{M} \) and \( \pi \) restricted to each \( {V}_{i}, i = 1,2 \) , is a diffeomorphism onto \( U \) . For this reason, \( \bar{M} \) is called the orientable double cover of \( M \) .

(c) The sphere \( {S}^{2} \) is the orientable double cover of \( {P}^{2}\left( \mathbf{R}\right) \) and the torus \( {T}^{2} \) is the orientable double cover of the Klein bottle \( K \) .

nodes.title: 1.2. Riemannian Metrics
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry

nodes.label: Definition 2.1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.1 Definition. A Riemannian metric (or Riemannian structure) on a differentiable manifold \( M \) is a correspondence which associates to each point \( p \) of \( M \) an inner product \( \langle  \cdot  , \cdot  {\rangle }_{p} \) (that is, a symmetric, bilinear, positive-definite form) on the tangent space \( {T}_{p}M \) , which varies differentiably in the following sense: If \( x : U \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  M \) is a system of coordinates around \( p \) , with \( \mathbf{x}\left( {{x}_{1},{x}_{2},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right)  = q \in \; \mathbf{x}\left( U\right) \) and \( \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}}\left( q\right)  = d{\mathbf{x}}_{q}\left( {0,\ldots ,1,\ldots ,0}\right) \) , then \( {\left\langle  \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}}\left( q\right) ,\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{j}}\left( q\right) \right\rangle  }_{q} = \; {g}_{ij}\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right) \) is a differentiable function on \( U \) .

It is clear this definition does not depend on the choice of coordinate system.

Another way to express the differentiability of the Riemannian metric is to say that for any pair of vector fields \( X \) and \( Y \) , which are differentiable in a neighborhood \( V \) of \( M \) , the function \( \langle X, Y\rangle \) is differentiable on \( V \) . It is immediate that this definition is equivalent to the other.

It is usual to delete the index \( p \) in the function \( \langle \) , \( {\rangle }_{p} \) whenever there is no possibility of confusion. The function \( {g}_{ij}\left( { = {g}_{ji}}\right) \) is called the local representation of the Riemannian metric (or "the \( {g}_{ij} \) of the metric") in the coordinate system \( \mathbf{x} : U \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  M \) . A differentiable manifold with a given Riemannian metric will be called a Riemannian manifold.

After introducing any type of mathematical structure, we must introduce a notion of when two objects are the same.

nodes.label: Definition 2.2
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.2 Definition. Let \( M \) and \( N \) be Riemannian manifolds. A diffeomorphism \( f : M \rightarrow  N \) (that is, \( f \) is a differentiable bijection with a differentiable inverse) is called an isometry if:

(1)

\[
\langle u, v{\rangle }_{p} = {\left\langle  d{f}_{p}\left( u\right) , d{f}_{p}\left( v\right) \right\rangle  }_{f\left( p\right) }\text{ , for all }p \in  M, u, v \in  {T}_{p}M\text{ . }
\]

A diffeomorphism \( f : M \rightarrow N \) (that is, \( f \) is a differentiable bijection with a differentiable inverse) is called an isometry if: (1) \[ \langle u, v{\rangle }_{p} = {\left\langle d{f}_{p}\left( u\right) , d{f}_{p}\left( v\right) \right\rangle }_{f\left( p\right) }\text{ , for all }p \in M, u, v \in {T}_{p}M\text{ . } \]

nodes.label: Definition 2.3
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.3 Definition. Let \( M \) and \( N \) be Riemannian manifolds. A differentiable mapping \( f : M \rightarrow  N \) is a local isometry at \( p \in  M \) if there is a neighborhood \( U \subset  M \) of \( p \) such that \( f : U \rightarrow  f\left( U\right) \) is a diffeomorphism satisfying (1).

It is common to say that a Riemannian manifold \( M \) is locally isometric to a Riemannian manifold \( N \) if for every \( p \) in \( M \) there exists a neighborhood \( U \) of \( p \) in \( M \) and a local isometry \( f : U \rightarrow  f\left( U\right)  \subset  N \) .

What follows are some non-trivial examples of the notion of Riemannian manifold.

nodes.label: Example 2.4
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 2.4 EXAMPLE. The almost trivial example. \( M = {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) with \( \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}} \) identified with \( {e}_{i} = \left( {0,\ldots ,1,\ldots ,0}\right) \) . The metric is given by \( \left\langle  {{e}_{i},{e}_{j}}\right\rangle   = {\delta }_{ij} \) . \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is called Euclidean space of dimension \( n \) and the Riemannian geometry of this space is metric Euclidean geometry.

The metric is given by \( \left\langle {{e}_{i},{e}_{j}}\right\rangle = {\delta }_{ij} \) . \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is called Euclidean space of dimension \( n \) and the Riemannian geometry of this space is metric Euclidean geometry.

nodes.label: Example 2.5
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.5 EXAMPLE. Immersed manifolds. Let \( f : {M}^{n} \rightarrow  {N}^{n + k} \) be an immersion, that is, \( f \) is differentiable and \( d{f}_{p} : {T}_{p}M \rightarrow  {T}_{f\left( p\right) }N \) is injective for all \( p \) in \( M \) . If \( N \) has a Riemannian structure, \( f \) induces a Riemannian structure on \( M \) by defining \( \langle u, v{\rangle }_{p} = {\left\langle  d{f}_{p}\left( u\right) , d{f}_{p}\left( v\right) \right\rangle  }_{f\left( p\right) } \) , \( u, v \in  {T}_{p}M \) . Since \( d{f}_{p} \) is injective, \( \langle ,{\rangle }_{p} \) is positive definite. The other conditions of Definition 2.1 are easily verified. This metric on \( M \) is then called the metric induced by \( f \) , and \( f \) is an isometric immersion.

A particularly important case occurs when we have a differentiable function \( h : {M}^{n + k} \rightarrow  {N}^{k} \) and \( q \in  N \) is a regular value of \( h \) (that is, \( d{h}_{p} : {T}_{p}M \rightarrow  {T}_{h\left( p\right) }N \) is surjective for all \( p \in  {h}^{-1}\left( q\right) \) ). It is known then that \( {h}^{-1}\left( q\right)  \subset  M \) is a submanifold of \( M \) of dimension \( n \) ; hence, we can put a Riemannian metric on it induced by the inclusion.

For example, let \( h : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) be given by \( h\left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right)  = \; \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} - 1 \) . Then 0 is a regular value of \( h \) and \( {h}^{-1}\left( 0\right)  = \{ x \in \; \left. {{\mathbf{R}}^{n} : {x}_{1}^{2} + \ldots  + {x}_{n}^{2} = 1}\right\}   = {S}^{n - 1} \) is the unit sphere of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . The metric induced from \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) on \( {S}^{n - 1} \) is called the canonical metric of \( {S}^{n - 1} \) .

nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.6 EXAMPLE. Lie groups. A Lie group is a group \( G \) with a differentiable structure such that the mapping \( G \times  G \rightarrow  G \) given by \( \left( {x, y}\right)  \rightarrow  x{y}^{-1}, x, y \in  G \) , is differentiable. It follows then that translations from the left \( {L}_{x} \) and translations from the right \( {R}_{x} \) given by: \( {L}_{x} : G \rightarrow  G,{L}_{x}\left( y\right)  = {xy};{R}_{x} : G \rightarrow  G,{R}_{x}\left( y\right)  = {yx} \) are diffeomor-phisms.

We say that a Riemannian metric on \( G \) is left invariant if \( \langle u, v{\rangle }_{y} = \langle d{\left( {L}_{x}\right) }_{y}u, d{\left( {L}_{x}\right) }_{y}v{\rangle }_{{L}_{x}\left( y\right) } \) for all \( x, y \in  G, u, v \in  {T}_{y}G \) , that is, if \( {L}_{x} \) is an isometry. Analogously, we can define a right invariant Riemannian metric. A Riemannian metric on \( G \) which is both right and left invariant is said to be bi-invariant.

We say that a differentiable vector field \( X \) on a Lie group \( G \) is left invariant if \( d{L}_{x}X = X \) for all \( x \in  G \) . The left invariant vector fields are completely determined by their values at a single point of \( G \) . This allows us to introduce an additional structure on the tangent space to the neutral element \( e \in  G \) in the following manner. To each vector \( {X}_{e} \in  {T}_{e}G \) we associate the left invariant \( X \) defined by \( {X}_{a} = d{L}_{a}{X}_{e}, a \in  G \) . Let \( X, Y \) be left invariant vector fields on \( G \) . Since for each \( x \in  G \) and for any differentiable function \( f \) on \( G \) ,

\[
d{L}_{x}\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  f = \left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  \left( {f \circ  {L}_{x}}\right)  = X\left( {d{L}_{x}Y}\right) f - Y\left( {d{L}_{x}X}\right) f =
\]

\[
= \left( {{XY} - {YX}}\right) f = \left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  f
\]

we conclude that the bracket of any two left invariant vector fields is again a left invariant vector field. If \( {X}_{e},{Y}_{e} \in  {T}_{e}G \) , we put \( \left\lbrack  {{X}_{e},{Y}_{e}}\right\rbrack   = \; {\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }_{e} \) . With this operation, \( {T}_{e}G \) is called the Lie algebra of \( G \) , denoted by \( \mathcal{G} \) . From now on, the elements in the Lie algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) will be thought of either as vectors in \( {T}_{e}G \) or as left invariant vector fields on \( G \) .

To introduce a left invariant metric on \( G \) , take any arbitrary inner product \( \langle \) , \( {\rangle }_{e} \) on \( \mathcal{G} \) and define

(2)

\[
\langle u, v{\rangle }_{x} = \left\langle  {{\left( d{L}_{{x}^{-1}}\right) }_{x}\left( u\right) ,{\left( d{L}_{{x}^{-1}}\right) }_{x}\left( v\right) {\rangle }_{e},\;x \in  G, u, v \in  {T}_{x}G.}\right.
\]

Since \( {L}_{x} \) depends differentiably on \( x \) , this construction actually produces a Riemannian metric, which is clearly left invariant.

In an analogous manner we can construct a right invariant metric on \( G \) . If \( G \) is compact, we will see in Exercise 7 that \( G \) possesses a bi-invariant metric.

If \( G \) has a bi-invariant metric, the inner product that the metric determines on \( \mathcal{G} \) satisfies the following relation: For any \( U, V, X \in  \mathcal{G} \) ,

(3)

\[
\langle \left\lbrack  {U, X}\right\rbrack  , V\rangle  =  - \langle U,\left\lbrack  {V, X}\right\rbrack  \rangle .
\]

Before proving the relation above, we need some preliminary facts about Lie groups.

For any \( a \in  G \) , let \( {R}_{{a}^{-1}}{L}_{a} : G \rightarrow  G \) be the inner automorphism of \( G \) determined by \( a \) . Such a mapping is a diffeomorphism that keeps \( e \) fixed. Thus, the differential \( d\left( {{R}_{{a}^{-1}}{L}_{a}}\right)  = {Ad}\left( a\right)  : \mathcal{G} \rightarrow  \mathcal{G} \) is a linear map (in fact, it is a homomorphism of the Lie algebra, but we do not need this fact). Explicitly,

\[
{Ad}\left( a\right) Y = d{R}_{{a}^{-1}}d{L}_{a}Y = d{R}_{{a}^{-1}}Y,\;\text{ for all }Y \in  \mathcal{G}.
\]

Let \( {x}_{t} \) be the flow of \( X \in  \mathcal{G} \) . Then, from Proposition 5.4 of Chapter 0,

\[
\left\lbrack  {Y, X}\right\rbrack   = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}\frac{1}{t}\left( {d{x}_{t}\left( Y\right)  - Y}\right)
\]

On the other hand, since \( X \) is left invariant, \( {L}_{y} \circ  {x}_{t} = {x}_{t} \circ  {L}_{y} \) , giving

\[
{x}_{t}\left( y\right)  = {x}_{t}\left( {{L}_{y}\left( e\right) }\right)  = {L}_{y}\left( {{x}_{t}\left( e\right) }\right)  = y{x}_{t}\left( e\right)  = {R}_{{x}_{t}\left( e\right) }\left( y\right) .
\]

Therefore, \( d{x}_{t} = d{R}_{{x}_{t}\left( e\right) } \) , and

\[
\left\lbrack  {Y, X}\right\rbrack   = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}\frac{1}{t}\left( {d{R}_{{x}_{t}\left( e\right) }\left( Y\right)  - Y}\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}\frac{1}{t}\left( {{Ad}\left( {{x}_{t}^{-1}\left( e\right) }\right) Y - Y}\right) .
\]

Let us now return to the proof of (3). Let \( \langle \) , \( \rangle {beabi} - {invariant} \) metric on a Lie group \( G \) . Then for any \( X, U, V \in  \mathcal{G} \) ,

\[
\langle U, V\rangle  = \left\langle  {d{R}_{{x}_{t}\left( e\right) } \circ  d{L}_{{x}_{t}^{-1}\left( e\right) }U, d{R}_{{x}_{t}\left( e\right) } \circ  d{L}_{{x}_{t}^{-1}\left( e\right) }V}\right\rangle   =
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {d{R}_{{x}_{t}\left( e\right) }U, d{R}_{{x}_{t}\left( e\right) }V}\right\rangle  .
\]

Differentiating the expression above with respect to \( t \) , recalling that \( \langle \) , \( \rangle {isbilinear},{andsetting}t = 0 \) in the expression obtained, we conclude that

\[
0 = \langle \left\lbrack  {U, X}\right\rbrack  , V\rangle  + \langle U,\left\lbrack  {V, X}\right\rbrack  \rangle ,
\]

which is the equation (3).

The important point about the relation above is that it characterizes the bi-invariant metrics of \( G \) , in the following sense. If a positive bilinear form \( \langle \) , \( {\rangle }_{e} \) defined on \( \mathcal{G} \) satisfies the relation (3), then the Riemannian metric defined on \( G \) by (2) is bi-invariant. It is not difficult to prove this fact but we will not go into the proof here.
