nodes.label: Example 2.7
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.7 EXAMPLE. The product metric. Let \( {M}_{1} \) and \( {M}_{2} \) be Riemannian manifolds and consider the cartesian product \( {M}_{1} \times  {M}_{2} \) with the product structure. Let \( {\pi }_{1} : {M}_{1} \times  {M}_{2} \rightarrow  {M}_{1} \) and \( {\pi }_{2} : {M}_{1} \times  {M}_{2} \rightarrow  {M}_{2} \) be the natural projections. Introduce on \( {M}_{1} \times  {M}_{2} \) a Riemannian metric as follows:

\[
\langle u, v{\rangle }_{\left( p, q\right) } = {\left\langle  d{\pi }_{1} \cdot  u, d{\pi }_{1} \cdot  v\right\rangle  }_{p} + {\left\langle  d{\pi }_{2} \cdot  u, d{\pi }_{2} \cdot  v\right\rangle  }_{q},
\]

\[
\text{ for all }\left( {p, q}\right)  \in  {M}_{1} \times  {M}_{2}, u, v \in  {T}_{\left( p, q\right) }\left( {{M}_{1} \times  {M}_{2}}\right) \text{ . }
\]

It is easy to verify that this is really a Riemannian metric on the product. For example, the torus \( {S}^{1} \times  \cdots  \times  {S}^{1} = {T}^{n} \) has a Riemannian structure obtained by choosing the induced Riemannian metric from \( {\mathbf{R}}^{2} \) on the circle \( {S}^{1} \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{2} \) and then taking the product metric. The torus \( {T}^{n} \) with this metric is called the flat torus.

We are now going to show how a Riemannian metric can be used to calculate the lengths of curves.

nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.9 Definition. A vector field \( V \) along a curve c: \( I \rightarrow  M \) is a differentiable mapping that associates to every \( t \in  I \) a tangent vector \( V\left( t\right)  \in  {T}_{c\left( t\right) }M \) . To say that \( V \) is differentiable means that for any differentiable function \( f \) on \( M \) , the function \( t \rightarrow  V\left( t\right) f \) is a differentiable function on \( I \) .

The vector field \( {dc}\left( \frac{d}{dt}\right) \) , denoted by \( \frac{dc}{dt} \) , is called the velocity field (or tangent vector field) ofc. Observe that a vector field along \( c \) cannot necessarily be extended to a vector field on an open set of \( M \) .

The restriction of a curve \( c \) to a closed interval \( \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack   \subset  I \) is called a segment. If \( M \) is a Riemannian manifold, we define the length of a segment by

\[
{\ell }_{a}^{b}\left( c\right)  = {\int }_{a}^{b}{\left\langle  \frac{dc}{dt},\frac{dc}{dt}\right\rangle  }^{1/2}{dt}.
\]

Let us now prove a theorem on the existence of Riemannian metrics.

nodes.label: Proposition 2.10
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 2.10 Proposition. A differentiable manifold \( M \) (Hausdorff with countable basis) has a Riemannian metric.
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.10 Proposition. A differentiable manifold \( M \) (Hausdorff with countable basis) has a Riemannian metric.

nodes.proof:
Let \( \left\{  {f}_{\alpha }\right\} \) be a differentiable partition of unity on \( M \) subordinate to a covering \( \left\{  {V}_{\alpha }\right\} \) of \( M \) by coordinate neighborhoods. This means (See Chap. 0, Sec. 5) that \( \left\{  {V}_{\alpha }\right\} \) is a locally finite covering (i.e., any point of \( M \) has a neighborhood \( U \) such that \( U \cap  {V}_{\alpha } \neq  \phi \) at most for a finite number of indices) and \( \left\{  {f}_{\alpha }\right\} \) is a family of differentiable functions on \( M \) satisfying:

1) \( {f}_{\alpha } \geq  0,{f}_{\alpha } = 0 \) on the complement of the closed set \( {\bar{V}}_{\alpha } \) .

2) \( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }{f}_{\alpha }\left( p\right)  = 1 \) for all \( p \) on \( M \) .

It is clear that we can define a Riemannian metric \( \langle ,{\rangle }^{\alpha } \) on each \( {V}_{\alpha } \) : the metric induced by the system of local coordinates. Let us then set \( \langle u, v{\rangle }_{p} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }{f}_{\alpha }\left( p\right) \langle u, v{\rangle }_{p}^{\alpha } \) for all \( p \in  M, u, v \in  {T}_{p}M \) . It is easy to verify that this construction defines a Riemannian metric on \( M \) .

To conclude this chapter, we are going to show how a Riemannian metric permits us to define a notion of volume on a given oriented manifold \( {M}^{n} \) .

As usual we need some preliminary facts. Let \( p \in  M \) and let \( \mathbf{x} : U \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  M \) be a parametrization about \( p \) which belongs to a family of parametrizations consistent with the orientation of \( M \) (we say that such parametrizations are positive). Consider a positive orthonormal basis \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n}}\right\} \) of \( {T}_{p}M \) and write \( {X}_{i}\left( p\right)  = \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}}\left( p\right) \) in the basis \( \left\{  {e}_{i}\right\}   : {X}_{i}\left( p\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{ij}}{a}_{ij}{e}_{j} \) . Then

\[
{g}_{ik}\left( p\right)  = \left\langle  {{X}_{i},{X}_{k}}\right\rangle  \left( p\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j\ell }}{a}_{ij}{a}_{k\ell }\left\langle  {{e}_{j},{e}_{\ell }}\right\rangle   = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{a}_{ij}{a}_{kj}.
\]

Since the volume \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {{X}_{1}\left( p\right) ,\ldots ,{X}_{n}\left( p\right) }\right) \) of the parallelepiped formed by the vectors \( {X}_{1}\left( p\right) ,\ldots ,{X}_{n}\left( p\right) \) in \( {T}_{p}M \) is equal to \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {{e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n}}\right)  = \) 1 multiplied by the determinant of the matrix \( \left( {a}_{ij}\right) \) , we obtain

\[
\operatorname{vol}\left( {{X}_{1}\left( p\right) ,\ldots ,{X}_{n}\left( p\right) }\right)  = \det \left( {a}_{ij}\right)  = \sqrt{\det \left( {g}_{ij}\right) }\left( p\right) .
\]

If \( \mathbf{y} : V \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  M \) is another positive parametrization about \( p \) , with \( {Y}_{i}\left( p\right)  = \frac{\partial }{\partial {y}_{i}}\left( p\right) \) and \( {h}_{ij}\left( p\right)  = \left\langle  {{Y}_{i},{Y}_{j}}\right\rangle  \left( p\right) \) , we obtain

(4)

\[
\sqrt{\det \left( {g}_{ij}\right) }\left( p\right)  = \operatorname{vol}\left( {{X}_{1}\left( p\right) ,\ldots ,{X}_{n}\left( p\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= J\operatorname{vol}\left( {{Y}_{1}\left( p\right) ,\ldots ,{Y}_{n}\left( p\right) }\right)  = J\sqrt{\det \left( {h}_{ij}\right) }\left( p\right) ,
\]

where \( J = \det \left( \frac{\partial {x}_{i}}{\partial {y}_{j}}\right)  = \det \left( {d{\mathbf{y}}^{-1} \circ  d\mathbf{x}}\right) \left( p\right)  > 0 \) is the determinant of the derivative of the change of coordinates.

Now let \( R \subset  M \) be a region (an open connected subset), whose closure is compact. We suppose that \( R \) is contained in a coordinate neighborhood \( x\left( U\right) \) with a positive parametrization \( x : U \rightarrow  M \) , and that the boundary of \( {x}^{-1}\left( R\right)  \subset  U \) has measure zero in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) (observe that the notion of measure zero in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is invariant by diffeomorphism). Let us define the volume \( \operatorname{vol}\left( R\right) \) of \( R \) by the integral in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \)

(5)

\[
\operatorname{vol}\left( R\right)  = {\int }_{{\mathbf{x}}^{-1}\left( R\right) }\sqrt{\det \left( {g}_{ij}\right) }d{x}_{1}\ldots d{x}_{n}.
\]

The expression above is well-defined. Indeed, if \( R \) is contained in another coordinate neighborhood \( y\left( V\right) \) with a positive parametrization \( y : V \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  M \) , we obtain from the change of variable theorem for multiple integrals, (using the same notation as in (4),

\[
{\int }_{{x}^{-1}\left( R\right) }\sqrt{\det \left( {g}_{ij}\right) }d{x}_{1}\ldots d{x}_{n}
\]

\[
= {\int }_{{y}^{-1}\left( R\right) }\sqrt{\det {h}_{ij}}d{y}_{1}\ldots d{y}_{n} = \operatorname{vol}\left( R\right) ,
\]

which proves that the definition given by (5) does not depend on the choice of the coordinate system (here the hypothesis of the ori-entability of \( M \) enters by guaranteeing that vol \( \left( R\right) \) does not change sign).

nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.11 REMARK. The reader familiar with differential forms will note that equation (4) implies that the integrand in the formula for the volume in expression (5) is a positive differential form of degree \( n \) , which is usually called a volume form (or volume element) \( \nu \) on \( M \) . In order to define the volume of a compact region \( R \) , which is not contained in a coordinate neighborhood it is necessary to consider a partition of unity \( \left\{  {\varphi }_{i}\right\} \) subordinate to a (finite) covering of \( R \) consisting of coordinate neighborhoods \( \mathbf{x}\left( {U}_{i}\right) \) and to take

\[
\operatorname{vol}\left( R\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{\int }_{{x}_{i}^{-1}\left( R\right) }{\varphi }_{i}\nu
\]

It follows immediately that the expression above does not depend on the choice of the partition of unity.

4. A function \( g : \mathbf{R} \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) given by \( g\left( t\right)  = {yt} + x,\;t, x, y \in  \mathbf{R},\;y > \) 0 , is called a proper affine function. The subset of all such functions with respect to the usual composition law forms a Lie group \( G \) . As a differentiable manifold \( G \) is simply the upper half-plane \( \left\{  {\left( {x, y}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{2};y > 0}\right\} \) with the differentiable structure induced from \( {\mathbf{R}}^{2} \) . (b) Putting \( \left( {x, y}\right)  = z = x + {iy}, i = \sqrt{-1} \) , the transformation \( z \rightarrow  {z}^{\prime } = \frac{{az} + b}{{cz} + d}, a, b, c, d \in  \mathbf{R},{ad} - {bc} = 1 \) is an isometry of \( G \) .

\[

\]

nodes.content:
## 1. Introduction

A fundamental event in the development of differential geometry was the introduction, in 1917, of the Levi-Civita parallelism (see Levi-Civita [LC]). For the case of surfaces in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) , an equivalent idea can be described in the following manner. Let \( S \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) be a surface and let \( c : I \rightarrow  S \) be a parametrized curve in \( S \) , with \( V : I \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) a vector field along \( c \) tangent to \( S \) . The vector \( \frac{dV}{dt}\left( t\right) , t \in  I \) , does not in general belong to the tangent plane of \( S,{T}_{c\left( t\right) }S \) . The concept of differentiating a vector field is not therefore an "intrinsic" geometric notion on \( S \) . To remedy this state of affairs we consider, instead of the usual derivative \( \frac{dV}{dt}\left( t\right) \) , the orthogonal projection of \( \frac{dV}{dt}\left( t\right) \) on \( {T}_{c\left( t\right) }S \) . This orthogonally projected vector we call the covariant derivative and denote it by \( \frac{DV}{dt}\left( t\right) \) . The covariant derivative of \( V \) is the derivative of \( V \) as seen from the "viewpoint of \( S \) ".

A basic point is that the covariant derivative depends only on the first fundamental form of \( S \) and is therefore a concept which can be considered within Riemannian geometry. In particular, the notion of covariant derivative permits us to take the derivative of the velocity vector of \( c \) , which gives the acceleration of the curve \( c \) in \( S \) . It is possible to show that curves with zero acceleration are precisely the geodesics of \( S \) and that the Gaussian curvature of \( S \) can be expressed in terms of the notion of the covariant derivative.

We say that a vector field \( V \) along \( c \) is parallel if \( \frac{DV}{dt} \equiv  0 \) . Conversely, starting from the notion of parallelism it is possible to recover the notion of covariant derivative (Cf. Exercise 1 of this chapter). These notions are then equivalent to each other.

Although nowadays it is preferable to start from the notion of covariant derivative, historically the idea of parallelism came first. For surfaces in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) , parallelism can be introduced in the following manner. Consider a family of planes tangent to \( S \) along the curve c. This family determines a surface \( E \) , enveloping these tangent planes, which possesses the property that it will be tangent to \( S \) along the curve \( c \) and whose Gaussian curvature \( K \equiv  0 \) . (Cf. M. do Carmo [dC 2] pp. 195-197). It is not difficult to show that the parallelism along \( c \) , defined through the vanishing of the covariant derivative is the same whether considered relative to \( S \) or relative to \( E \) . On the other hand, surfaces of zero curvature can be shown to be locally isometric to a plane. Since parallelism is invariant by isometry, we can perform it "euclideanly" in the isometric image of \( E \) and then bring it back to \( S \) . This was the construction used classically to define parallelism. (M. do Carmo [dC 2] p. 244). It will turn out that it is preferable, technically, to work with the covariant derivative.

The notion of covariant derivative has many important consequences. It makes it clear that the two basic ideas of geodesic and curvature can be defined in more general situations than that of Riemannian manifolds. To this end it suffices that one be able to define a notion of derivation of vector fields with certain properties (which nowadays we call an affine connection, Cf. Definition 2.1 of this chapter). This has stimulated the creation of many different "geometric structures" (on differentiable manifolds) more general than Riemannian geometry. In the same way as metric Euclidean geometry is a particular case of affine geometry and more generally of projective geometry, Riemannian geometry is a particular case of more general geometric structures.

We are not going to enter into the details of these developments. Our interest in affine connections rests in the fact (Cf. Theorem 3.6 of this chapter) that a choice of a Riemannian metric on a manifold \( M \) uniquely determines a certain affine connection on \( M \) . We are then able, in this fashion, to differentiate vector fields on \( M \) .

nodes.content:
2.1 Definition. An affine connection \( \nabla \) on a differentiable manifold \( M \) is a mapping

\[
\nabla  : \mathcal{X}\left( M\right)  \times  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right)  \rightarrow  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right)
\]

which is denoted by \( \left( {X, Y}\right) \overset{\nabla }{ \rightarrow  }{\nabla }_{X}Y \) and which satisfies the following properties :

i) \( {\nabla }_{{fX} + {gY}}Z = f{\nabla }_{X}Z + g{\nabla }_{Y}Z \) .

ii) \( {\nabla }_{X}\left( {Y + Z}\right)  = {\nabla }_{X}Y + {\nabla }_{X}Z \) .

iii) \( {\nabla }_{X}\left( {fY}\right)  = f{\nabla }_{X}Y + X\left( f\right) Y \)

in which \( X, Y, Z \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) and \( f, g \in  \mathcal{D}\left( M\right) \) .

nodes.label: Proposition 2.2
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.2 PROPOSITION. Let \( M \) be a differentiable manifold with an affine connection \( \nabla \) . There exists a unique correspondence which associates to a vector field \( V \) along the differentiable curve c: \( I \rightarrow  M \) another vector field \( \frac{DV}{dt} \) along \( c \) , called the covariant derivative of \( V \) along \( c \) , such that:

a) \( \frac{D}{dt}\left( {V + W}\right)  = \frac{DV}{dt} + \frac{DW}{dt} \) .

b) \( \frac{D}{dt}\left( {fV}\right)  = \frac{df}{dt}V + f\frac{DV}{dt} \) , where \( W \) is a vector field along \( c \) and \( f \) is a differentiable function on \( I \) .

c) If \( V \) is induced by a vector field \( Y \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) , i.e., \( V\left( t\right)  = \; Y\left( {c\left( t\right) }\right) \) , then \( \frac{DV}{dt} = {\nabla }_{{dc}/{dt}}Y \) .

Let us suppose initially that there exists a correspondence satisfying (a),(b) and (c). Let \( \mathbf{x} : U \subset \; {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  M \) be a system of coordinates with \( c\left( I\right)  \cap  \mathbf{x}\left( U\right)  \neq  \phi \) and \( \operatorname{let}\left( {{x}_{1}\left( t\right) ,{x}_{2}\left( t\right) ,\ldots ,{x}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) be the local expression of \( c\left( t\right) , t \in  I \) . Let \( {X}_{i} = \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}} \) . Then we can express the field \( V \) locally as \( V = \; \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{v}^{j}{X}_{j}, j = 1,\ldots , n \) , where \( {v}^{j} = {v}^{j}\left( t\right) \) and \( {X}_{j} = {X}_{j}\left( {c\left( t\right) }\right) \) .

By a) and b), we have

\[
\frac{DV}{dt} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}\frac{d{v}^{j}}{dt}{X}_{j} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{v}^{j}\frac{D{X}_{j}}{dt}.
\]

By c) and (i) of Definition 2.1,

\[
\frac{D{X}_{j}}{dt} = {\nabla }_{{dc}/{dt}}{X}_{j} = {\nabla }_{\left( \sum \frac{d{x}_{i}}{dt}{X}_{i}\right) }{X}_{j}
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}\frac{d{x}_{i}}{dt}{\nabla }_{{X}_{i}}{X}_{j},\;i, j = 1,\ldots , n.
\]

Therefore,

(1)

\[
\frac{DV}{dt} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}\frac{d{v}^{j}}{dt}{X}_{j} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i, j}}\frac{d{x}_{i}}{dt}{v}^{j}{\nabla }_{{X}_{i}}{X}_{j}.
\]

The expression (1) shows us that if there is a correspondence satisfying the conditions of Proposition 2.2, then such a correspondence is unique.

To show existence, define \( \frac{DV}{dt} \) in \( \mathbf{x}\left( U\right) \) by (1). It is easy to verify that (1) possesses the desired properties. If \( \mathbf{y}\left( W\right) \) is another coordinate neighborhood, with \( \mathbf{y}\left( W\right)  \cap  \mathbf{x}\left( U\right)  \neq  \phi \) and we define \( \frac{DV}{dt} \) in \( \mathbf{y}\left( W\right) \) by \( \left( 1\right) \) , the definitions agree in \( \mathbf{y}\left( W\right)  \cap  \mathbf{x}\left( U\right) \) , by the uniqueness of \( \frac{DV}{dt} \) in \( \mathbf{x}\left( U\right) \) . It follows that the definition can be extended over all of \( M \) , and this concludes the proof.

The last line of (c) makes sense, since \( {\nabla }_{X}Y\left( p\right) \) depends on the value of \( X\left( p\right) \) and the value \( Y \) along a curve, tangent to \( X \) at \( p \) . In effect, part (iii) of Definition 2.1 allows us to show that the notion of affine connection is actually a local notion (cf. Rem. 5.7 of Chap. 0). Choosing a system of coordinates \( \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right) \) about \( p \) and writing

\[
X = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{x}_{i}{X}_{i},\;Y = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{y}_{j}{Xj},
\]

where \( {X}_{i} = \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}} \) , we have

\[
{\nabla }_{X}Y = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{x}_{i}{\nabla }_{{X}_{i}}\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{y}_{j}{X}_{j}}\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{ij}}{x}_{i}{y}_{j}{\nabla }_{{X}_{i}}{X}_{j} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{ij}}{x}_{i}{X}_{i}\left( {y}_{j}\right) {X}_{j}.
\]

Setting \( {\nabla }_{{X}_{i}}{X}_{j} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{k}{\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}{X}_{k} \) , we conclude that the \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} \) are differentiable functions and that

\]

nodes.proof:
Suppose that the theorem was proved for the case in which \( c\left( I\right) \) is contained in a local coordinate neighborhood. By compactness, for any \( {t}_{1} \in  I \) , the segment \( c\left( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{o},{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack  \right)  \subset  M \) can be covered by a finite number of coordinate neighborhoods, in each of which \( V \) can be defined, by hypothesis. From uniqueness, the definitions coincide when the intersections are not empty, thus allowing the definition of \( V \) along all of \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{o},{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack \) .

We have only, therefore, to prove the theorem when \( c\left( I\right) \) is contained in a coordinate neighborhood \( \mathbf{x}\left( U\right) \) of a system of coordinates \( \mathbf{x} : U \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  M \) . Let \( {\mathbf{x}}^{-1}\left( {c\left( t\right) }\right)  = \left( {{x}_{1}\left( t\right) ,\ldots ,{x}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) be the local expression for \( c\left( t\right) \) and let \( {V}_{o} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{v}_{o}^{j}{X}_{j} \) , where \( {X}_{j} = \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{j}}\left( {c\left( {t}_{o}\right) }\right) \) .

Suppose that there exists a vector field \( V \) in \( \mathbf{x}\left( U\right) \) which is parallel along \( c \) with \( V\left( {t}_{o}\right)  = {V}_{o} \) . Then \( V = \sum {v}^{j}{X}_{j} \) satisfies

\[
0 = \frac{DV}{dt} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}\frac{d{v}^{j}}{dt}{X}_{j} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i, j}}\frac{d{x}_{i}}{dt}{v}^{j}\nabla {X}_{i}{X}_{j}.
\]

Putting \( {\nabla }_{{X}_{i}}{X}_{j} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{k}{\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}{X}_{k} \) , and replacing \( j \) with \( k \) in the first sum, we obtain

\[
\frac{DV}{dt} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{k}\left\{  {\frac{d{v}^{k}}{dt} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i, j}}{v}^{j}\frac{d{x}_{i}}{dt}{\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}}\right\}  {X}_{k} = 0.
\]

The system of \( n \) differential equations in \( {v}^{k}\left( t\right) \) ,

(2)

\[
0 = \frac{d{v}^{k}}{dt} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i, j}}{\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}{v}^{j}\frac{d{x}_{i}}{dt},\;k = 1,\ldots , n,
\]

possesses a unique solution satisfying the initial conditions \( {v}^{k}\left( {t}_{o}\right)  = \; {v}_{o}^{k} \) . It then follows that, if \( V \) exists, it is unique. Moreover, since the system is linear, any solution is defined for all \( t \in  I \) , which then proves the existence (and uniqueness ) of \( V \) with the desired properties.

nodes.content:
3.6 Theorem. (Levi-Civita). Given a Riemannian manifold \( M \) , there exists a unique affine connection \( \nabla \) on \( M \) satisfying the conditions:

a) \( \nabla \) is symmetric.

b) \( \nabla \) is compatible with the Riemannian metric.
nodes.content_excerpt:
3.6 Theorem. (Levi-Civita). Given a Riemannian manifold \( M \) , there exists a unique affine connection \( 
abla \) on \( M \) satisfying the conditions: a) \(

nodes.proof:
Suppose initially the existence of such a \( \nabla \) . Then

(6)

\[
X\langle Y, Z\rangle  = \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Z}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {Y,{\nabla }_{X}Z}\right\rangle  ,
\]

(7)

\[
Y\langle Z, X\rangle  = \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Y}Z, X}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {Z,{\nabla }_{Y}X}\right\rangle  ,
\]

(8)

\[
Z\langle X, Y\rangle  = \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}X, Y}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {X,{\nabla }_{Z}Y}\right\rangle  .
\]

Adding (6) and (7) and subtracting (8), we have, using the symmetry of \( \nabla \) , that

\[
X\langle Y, Z\rangle  + Y\langle Z, X\rangle  - Z\langle X, Y\rangle
\]

\[
= \langle \left\lbrack  {X, Z}\right\rbrack  , Y\rangle  + \langle \left\lbrack  {Y, Z}\right\rbrack  , X\rangle  + \langle \left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  , Z\rangle  + 2\left\langle  {Z,{\nabla }_{Y}X}\right\rangle  .
\]

Therefore

(9)

\[
\langle Z,{\nabla }_{Y}X\rangle  = \frac{1}{2}\{ X\langle Y, Z\rangle  + Y\langle Z, X\rangle  - Z\langle X, Y\rangle
\]

\[
- \langle \left\lbrack  {X, Z}\right\rbrack  , Y\rangle  - \langle \left\lbrack  {Y, Z}\right\rbrack  , X\rangle  - \langle \left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  , Z\rangle \}
\]

The expression (9) shows that \( \nabla \) is uniquely determined from the metric \( \langle \) , \( \rangle {.Hence},{ifitexists},{itwillbeunique}. \)

To prove existence, define \( \nabla \) by (9). It is easy to verify that \( \nabla \) is well-defined and that it satisfies the desired conditions.

nodes.label: Remark 3.7
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
3.7 REMARK. The connection given by the theorem will be referred to, from now on, as the Levi-Civita (or Riemannian) connection on M.

Let us conclude this chapter by writing part of what was shown above in a coordinate system \( \left( {U,\mathbf{x}}\right) \) . It is customary to call the functions \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} \) defined on \( U \) by \( {\nabla }_{{X}_{i}}{X}_{j} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{k}{\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}{X}_{k} \) , the coefficients of the connection \( \nabla \) on \( U \) or the Christoffel symbols of the connection. From (9) it follows that

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{\ell }{\Gamma }_{ij}^{\ell }{g}_{\ell k} = \frac{1}{2}\left\{  {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}}{g}_{jk} + \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{j}}{g}_{ki} - \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{k}}{g}_{ij}}\right\}  ,
\]

where \( {g}_{ij} = \left\langle  {{X}_{i},{X}_{j}}\right\rangle \) .

Since the matrix \( \left( {g}_{km}\right) \) admits an inverse \( \left( {g}^{km}\right) \) , we obtain that

(10)

\[
{\Gamma }_{ij}^{m} = \frac{1}{2}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{k}\left\{  {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}}{g}_{jk} + \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{j}}{g}_{ki} - \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{k}}{g}_{ij}}\right\}  {g}^{km}.
\]

The equation (10) is a classical expression for the Christoffel symbols of the Riemannian connection in terms of the \( {g}_{ij} \) (given by the metric).

Observe that for the Euclidean space \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) , we have \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} = 0 \) .

In terms of the Christoffel symbols, the covariant derivative has the classical expression

\[
\frac{DV}{dt} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{k}\left\{  {\frac{d{v}^{k}}{dt} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i, j}}{\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}{v}^{j}\frac{d{x}_{i}}{dt}}\right\}  {X}_{k}
\]

which follows from (1). Observe that \( \frac{DV}{dt} \) differs from the usual derivative in Euclidean space by terms which involve the Christoffel symbols. Therefore, in Euclidean spaces the covariant derivative coincides with the usual derivative.

nodes.title: 3.2. The geodesic flow

nodes.label: Definition 2.1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.1 Definition. A parametrized curve \( \gamma  : I \rightarrow  M \) is a geodesic at \( {t}_{o} \in  I \) if \( \frac{D}{dt}\left( \frac{d\gamma }{dt}\right)  = 0 \) at the point \( {t}_{o} \) ; if \( \gamma \) is a geodesic at \( t \) , for all \( t \in  I \) , we say that \( \gamma \) is a geodesic. If \( \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack   \subset  I \) and \( \gamma  : I \rightarrow  M \) is a geodesic, the restriction of \( \gamma \) to \( \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack \) is called a geodesic segment joining \( \gamma \left( a\right) \) to \( \gamma \left( b\right) \) .

At times, by abuse of language, we refer to the image \( \gamma \left( I\right) \) , of a geodesic \( \gamma \) , as a geodesic.

If \( \gamma  : I \rightarrow  M \) is a geodesic, then

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\left\langle  {\frac{d\gamma }{dt},\frac{d\gamma }{dt}}\right\rangle   = 2\left\langle  {\frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\gamma }{dt},\frac{d\gamma }{dt}}\right\rangle   = 0,
\]

that is, the length of the tangent vector \( \frac{d\gamma }{dt} \) is constant. We assume, from now on, that \( \left| \frac{d\gamma }{dt}\right|  = c \neq  0 \) , that is, we exclude the geodesics which reduce to points. The arc length \( s \) of \( \gamma \) , starting from a fixed origin, say \( t = {t}_{o} \) , is then given by

\[
s\left( t\right)  = {\int }_{{t}_{o}}^{t}\left| \frac{d\gamma }{dt}\right| {dt} = c\left( {t - {t}_{o}}\right) .
\]

Therefore, the parameter of a geodesic is proportional to arc length. When the parameter is actually arc length, that is, \( c = 1 \) , we say that the geodesic \( \gamma \) is normalized.

nodes.content: 2.3 LEMMA. There exists a unique vector field \( G \) on \( {TM} \) whose trajectories are of the form \( t \rightarrow  \left( {\gamma \left( t\right) ,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right) \) , where \( \gamma \) is a geodesic on \( M \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.3 LEMMA. There exists a unique vector field \( G \) on \( {TM} \) whose trajectories are of the form \( t \rightarrow \left( {\gamma \left( t\right) ,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right) \) , where \( \gamma \) is a geodesic on \( M \) .

nodes.proof:
We shall first prove the uniqueness of \( G \) , supposing its existence. Consider a system of coordinates \( \left( {U,\mathbf{x}}\right) \) on \( M \) . From the hypothesis, the trajectories of \( G \) on \( {TU} \) are given by \( t \rightarrow  \left( {\gamma \left( t\right) ,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right) \) where \( \gamma \) is a geodesic. It follows that \( t \rightarrow  \left( {\gamma \left( t\right) ,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a solution of the system of differential equations \( \left( {1}^{\prime }\right) \) . From the uniqueness of the trajectories of such a system, we conclude that if \( G \) exists, then it is unique.

To prove the existence of \( G \) , define it locally by the system \( \left( {1}^{\prime }\right) \) . Using the uniqueness, we conclude that \( G \) is well-defined on TM.

nodes.content:
Proposition 2.7 permits us to introduce the concept of the exponential map in the following manner. Let \( p \in  M \) and let \( \mathcal{U} \subset  {TM} \) be an open set given by Proposition 2.7. Then the map exp: \( \mathcal{U} \rightarrow  M \) given by

\[
\exp \left( {q, v}\right)  = \gamma \left( {1, q, v}\right)  = \gamma \left( {\left| v\right| , q,\frac{v}{\left| v\right| }}\right) ,\;\left( {q, v}\right)  \in  \mathcal{U},
\]

is called the exponential map on \( \mathcal{U} \) .

It is clear that exp is differentiable. In most of the applications, we shall utilize the restriction of exp to an open subset of the tangent space \( {T}_{q}M \) , that is, we define

\[
{\exp }_{q} : {B}_{\varepsilon }\left( 0\right)  \subset  {T}_{q}M \rightarrow  M
\]

by \( {\exp }_{q}\left( v\right)  = \exp \left( {q, v}\right) \) . Here, and in what follows, we denote by \( {B}_{\varepsilon }\left( 0\right) \) an open ball with center at the origin 0 of \( {T}_{q}M \) and of radius \( \varepsilon \) . It is easy to verify that \( {\exp }_{q} \) is differentiable and that \( {\exp }_{q}\left( 0\right)  = q \) .

Geometrically, \( {\exp }_{q}\left( v\right) \) is a point of \( M \) obtained by going out the length equal to \( \left| v\right| \) , starting from \( q \) , along a geodesic which passes through \( q \) with velocity equal to \( \frac{v}{\left| v\right| } \) .

nodes.label: Example 2.11
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.11 EXAMPLE. Let \( M = {S}^{n} \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) be the unit sphere of dimension \( n \) . As we saw in Exercise 4(b) of Chapter 2, the great circles of \( {S}^{n} \) , parametrized by arc length, are geodesics. We are going to show that all of the geodesics of \( {S}^{n} \) are great circles parametrized proportionally to arc length. Indeed, given \( p \in  {S}^{n} \) and a unit vector \( v \in  {T}_{p}{S}^{n} \) , the intersection with \( {S}^{n} \) of the plane that contains the origin of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) , the point \( p \) , and the vector \( v \) , is a great circle that can be parametrized as the geodesic through \( p \) with velocity \( v \) . From the uniqueness of Proposition 2.5, the statement follows.

Given a point \( \left( {p, v}\right)  \in  {TM} \) , the point \( {\exp }_{p}v \in  M \) is obtained by running along the geodesic \( \gamma \left( {t, p,\frac{v}{\left| v\right| }}\right) \) a length equal to \( \left| v\right| \) , starting from \( p \) . In the case at hand, it is clear that \( {\exp }_{p} \) is defined over the entire tangent space, and can be described in the following way: \( {\exp }_{p} \) transforms \( {B}_{\pi }\left( 0\right) \) injectively into \( {S}^{n} - \{ q\} \) , where \( q \) is the antipodal point to \( p \) ; the boundary of \( {B}_{\pi }\left( 0\right) \) is transformed to \( q \) ; the open annulus \( {B}_{2\pi }\left( 0\right)  - \overline{{B}_{\pi }\left( 0\right) } \) is transformed injectively onto \( {S}^{n} - \{ p, q\} \) ; the boundary of \( {B}_{2\pi }\left( 0\right) \) collapses to \( p \) , etc. (Fig. 1).

Observe that if we consider the Riemannian manifold \( {S}^{n} - \{ q\} ,{\exp }_{p} \) will be defined only on \( {B}_{\pi }\left( 0\right)  \subset  {T}_{p}\left( {{S}^{n}-\{ q\} }\right) \) .

nodes.label: Definition 3.1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 3.1 Definition. A piecewise differentiable curve is a continuous mapping \( c : \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) of a closed interval \( \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack   \subset  \mathbf{R} \) into \( M \) satisfying the following condition: there exists a partition \( a = \; {t}_{o} < {t}_{1} < \ldots  < {t}_{k - 1} < {t}_{k} = b \) of \( \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack \) such that the restrictions \( {\left. c\right| }_{\left\lbrack  {t}_{i},{t}_{i + 1}\right\rbrack  },\;i = 0,\ldots , k - 1 \) , are differentiable. We say that \( c \) joins the points \( c\left( a\right) \) and \( c\left( b\right) .c\left( {t}_{i}\right) \) is called a vertex of \( c \) , and the angle formed by \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  {t}_{i}^{ + }}}{c}^{\prime }\left( t\right) \) with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  {t}_{i}^{ - }}}{c}^{\prime }\left( t\right) \) is called the vertex angle at \( c\left( {t}_{i}\right) \) ; here \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  {t}_{i}^{ + }}}\left( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  {t}_{i}^{ - }}}\right) \) signifies that \( t \) approaches \( {t}_{i} \) through values above (below) that of \( {t}_{i} \) .

nodes.label: Definition 3.3
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
3.3 Definition. Let \( A \) be a connected set in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{2}, U \subset  A \subset  \bar{U}, U \) open, such that the boundary \( \partial A \) of \( A \) is a piecewise differentiable curve with vertex angles different from \( \pi \) . A parametrized surface in \( M \) is a differentiable mapping \( s : A \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{2} \rightarrow  M \) . (Observe that to say that \( s \) is differentiable on \( A \) means that there exists an open set \( U \supset  A \) to which \( s \) can be extended differentiably. The condition on the vertex angles of \( A \) is necessary to ensure that the differential of \( s \) does not depend on the given extension.)

A vector field \( V \) along \( s \) is a mapping which associates to each \( q \in  A \) a vector \( V\left( q\right)  \in  {T}_{s\left( q\right) }M \) , and which is differentiable in the following sense: if \( f \) is a differentiable function on \( M \) , then the mapping \( q \rightarrow  V\left( q\right) f \) is differentiable.

Let \( \left( {u, v}\right) \) be cartesian coordinates on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{2} \) . For \( {v}_{o} \) fixed, the mapping \( u \rightarrow  s\left( {u,{v}_{o}}\right) \) , where \( u \) belongs to a connected component of \( A \cap  \left\{  {v = {v}_{o}}\right\} \) , is a curve in \( M \) , and \( {ds}\left( \frac{\partial }{\partial u}\right) \) , which we indicate by \( \frac{\partial s}{\partial u} \) , is a vector field along this curve. This defines \( \frac{\partial s}{\partial u} \) for all \( \left( {u, v}\right)  \in  A \) and \( \frac{\partial s}{\partial u} \) is a vector field along \( s \) . The vector field \( \frac{\partial s}{\partial v} \) is defined analogously.

If \( V \) is a vector field along \( s : A \rightarrow  M \) , let us define the covariant derivative \( \frac{DV}{\partial u} \) and \( \frac{DV}{\partial v} \) in the following way. \( \frac{DV}{\partial u}\left( {u,{v}_{o}}\right) \) is the covariant derivative along the curve \( u \rightarrow  s\left( {u,{v}_{o}}\right) \) of the restriction of \( V \) to this curve. This defines \( \frac{DV}{\partial u}\left( {u, v}\right) \) for all \( \left( {u, v}\right)  \in  A \) . \( \frac{DV}{\partial v} \) is defined analogously.

nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
3.4 LEMMA. (symmetry). If \( M \) is a differentiable manifold with a symmetric connection and \( s : A \rightarrow  M \) is a parametrized surface then:

\[
\frac{D}{\partial v}\frac{\partial s}{\partial u} = \frac{D}{\partial u}\frac{\partial s}{\partial v}
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.4 LEMMA. (symmetry). If \( M \) is a differentiable manifold with a symmetric connection and \( s : A \rightarrow M \) is a parametrized surface then: \[ \frac{D}{\partial v}\frac{\partial s}{\partial u} = \frac{D}{\partial u}\frac{\partial s}{\partial v} \]

nodes.proof:
Let \( \mathbf{x} : V \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  M \) be a system of coordinates in a neighborhood of a point of \( s\left( A\right) \) . We can write

\[
{\mathbf{x}}^{-1} \circ  s\left( {u, v}\right)  = \left( {{x}^{1}\left( {u, v}\right) ,\ldots ,{x}^{n}\left( {u, v}\right) }\right) .
\]

Therefore

\[
\frac{D}{\partial v}\left( \frac{\partial s}{\partial u}\right)  = \frac{D}{\partial v}\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}\frac{\partial {x}^{i}}{\partial u}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}}\right)
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}\frac{{\partial }^{2}{x}^{i}}{\partial v\partial u}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}\frac{\partial {x}^{i}}{\partial u}{\nabla }_{{\sum }_{j}\left( {\partial {x}^{j}/\partial v}\right) \partial /\partial {x}^{j}}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}\frac{{\partial }^{2}{x}^{i}}{\partial v\partial u}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i, j}}\frac{\partial {x}^{i}}{\partial u}\frac{\partial {x}^{j}}{\partial v}{\nabla }_{\partial /\partial {x}^{j}}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}.
\]

From the symmetry of the connection, \( {\nabla }_{\partial /\partial {x}^{j}}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}} = {\nabla }_{\partial /\partial {x}^{i}}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{j}} \) . Hence calculating \( \frac{D}{\partial u}\left( \frac{\partial s}{\partial v}\right) \) we obtain the same expression as above, which proves the lemma.

\[
\left\langle  {{\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{v}\left( v\right) ,{\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{v}\left( w\right) }\right\rangle   = \langle v, w\rangle .
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.5 LEMMA. (Gauss). Let \( p \in M \) and let \( v \in {T}_{p}M \) such that \( {\exp }_{p}v \) is defined. Let \( w \in {T}_{p}M \approx {T}_{v}\left( {{T}_{p}M}\right) \) . Then (2) \[ \left\langle {{\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{v}\left( v\right) ,{\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{v}\left( w\right) }\right\rangle = \langle v, w\rangle . \]

nodes.proof:
Let \( w = {w}_{T} + {w}_{N} \) , where \( {w}_{T} \) is parallel to \( v \) and \( {w}_{N} \) is normal to \( v \) . Since \( d{\exp }_{p} \) is linear and, by the definition of \( {\exp }_{p} \) ,

\[
\left\langle  {{\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{v}\left( v\right) ,{\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{v}\left( {w}_{T}\right) }\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {v,{w}_{T}}\right\rangle  ,
\]

it suffices to prove (2) for \( w = {w}_{N} \) . It is clear that we can assume \( {w}_{N} \neq  0 \) .

Since \( {\exp }_{p}v \) is defined, there exists \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) such that \( {\exp }_{p}u \) is defined for

\[
u = {tv}\left( s\right) ,\;0 \leq  t \leq  1,\; - \varepsilon  < s < \varepsilon ,
\]

where \( v\left( s\right) \) is a curve in \( {T}_{p}M \) with \( v\left( 0\right)  = v,{v}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = {w}_{N} \) and \( \left| {v\left( s\right) }\right|  = \) const. We can, therefore, consider the parametrized surface

\[
f : A \rightarrow  M,\;A = \{ \left( {t, s}\right) ;0 \leq  t \leq  1, - \varepsilon  < s < \varepsilon \}
\]

given by

\[
f\left( {t, s}\right)  = {\exp }_{p}{tv}\left( s\right) .
\]

Observe that the curves \( t \rightarrow  f\left( {t,{s}_{o}}\right) \) are geodesics (see Fig. 2).

To prove (2) for \( w = {w}_{N} \) , observe first that

(3)

\[
\langle \frac{\partial f}{\partial s},\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\rangle \left( {1,0}\right)  = \langle {\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{v}\left( {w}_{N}\right) ,{\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{v}\left( v\right) \rangle .
\]

In addition, for all \( \left( {t, s}\right) \) , we have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left\langle  {\frac{\partial f}{\partial s},\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s},\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {\frac{\partial f}{\partial s},\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}}\right\rangle  .
\]

The last term of the expression above is zero, since \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \) is the tangent vector of a geodesic. From the symmetry of the connection, the first term of the sum is transformed into

\[
\left\langle  {\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s},\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {\frac{D}{\partial s}\frac{\partial f}{\partial t},\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}}\right\rangle   = \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial }{\partial s}\left\langle  {\frac{\partial f}{\partial t},\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}}\right\rangle   = 0.
\]

It follows that \( \left\langle  {\frac{\partial f}{\partial s},\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}}\right\rangle \) is independent of \( t \) . Since

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {t,0}\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}{\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{tv}t{w}_{N} = 0,
\]

we conclude that \( \left\langle  {\frac{\partial f}{\partial s},\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}}\right\rangle  \left( {1,0}\right)  = 0 \) , which together with (3) proves the lemma.

nodes.content: It is convenient to use the following terminology. If \( {\exp }_{p} \) is a diffeomorphism of a neighborhood \( V \) of the origin in \( {T}_{p}M,{\exp }_{p}V = \; U \) is called a normal neighborhood of \( p \) . If \( {B}_{\varepsilon }\left( 0\right) \) is such that \( \overline{{B}_{\varepsilon }\left( 0\right) } \subset \; V \) , we call \( {\exp }_{p}{B}_{\varepsilon }\left( 0\right)  = {B}_{\varepsilon }\left( p\right) \) the normal ball (or geodesic ball) with center \( p \) and radius \( \varepsilon \) . From the Gauss lemma, the boundary of a normal ball is a hypersurface (submanifold of codimension 1) in \( M \) orthogonal to the geodesics that start from \( p \) ; it is denoted by \( {S}_{\varepsilon }\left( p\right) \) and called the normal sphere (or geodesic sphere) at \( p \) . The geodesics in \( {B}_{\varepsilon }\left( p\right) \) that begin at \( p \) are referred to as radial geodesics.

nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 3.6 Proposition. Let \( p \in  M, U \) a normal neighborhood of \( p \) , and \( B \subset  U \) a normal ball of center \( p \) . Let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  B \) be a geodesic segment with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p \) . If \( c : \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) is any piecewise differentiable curve joining \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) to \( \gamma \left( 1\right) \) then \( \ell \left( \gamma \right)  \leq  \ell \left( c\right) \) and if equality holds then \( \gamma \left( \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack  \right)  = c\left( \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack  \right) \) .

Let \( \gamma : \left\lbrack {0,1}\right\rbrack \rightarrow B \) be a geodesic segment with \( \gamma \left( 0\right) = p \) . If \( c : \left\lbrack {0,1}\right\rbrack \rightarrow M \) is any piecewise differentiable curve joining \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) to \( \gamma \left( 1\right...

nodes.proof:
Suppose initially that \( c\left( \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack  \right)  \subset  B \) . Since \( {\exp }_{p} \) is a diffeomorphism on \( U \) , the curve \( c\left( t\right) \) , for \( t \neq  0 \) , can be written uniquely as \( {\exp }_{p}\left( {r\left( t\right)  \cdot  v\left( t\right) }\right)  = f\left( {r\left( t\right) , t}\right) \) where \( t \rightarrow  v\left( t\right) \) is a curve in \( {T}_{p}M \) with \( \left| {v\left( t\right) }\right|  = 1 \) and \( r : (0,1\rbrack  \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) is a positive piecewise differentiable function (we can suppose that if \( {t}_{1} \in  (0,1\rbrack \) then \( c\left( {t}_{1}\right)  \neq  p \) ; otherwise, ignore the interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{1}}\right) ) \) . It follows that, except for a finite number of points,

\[
\frac{dc}{dt} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial r}{r}^{\prime }\left( t\right)  + \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}.
\]

From the Gauss lemma, \( \left\langle  {\frac{\partial f}{\partial r},\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}}\right\rangle   = 0 \) . Since \( \left| \frac{\partial f}{\partial r}\right|  = 1 \) ,

(1)

\[
{\left| \frac{dc}{dt}\right| }^{2} = {\left| {r}^{\prime }\left( t\right) \right| }^{2} + {\left| \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\right| }^{2} \geq  {\left| {r}^{\prime }\left( t\right) \right| }^{2}
\]

and so

(2)

\[
{\int }_{\varepsilon }^{1}\left| \frac{dc}{dt}\right| {dt} \geq  {\int }_{\varepsilon }^{1}\left| {{r}^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right| {dt} \geq  {\int }_{\varepsilon }^{1}{r}^{\prime }\left( t\right) {dt} = r\left( 1\right)  - r\left( \varepsilon \right) .
\]

Taking \( \varepsilon  \rightarrow  0 \) we obtain \( \ell \left( c\right)  \geq  \ell \left( \gamma \right) \) , because \( r\left( 1\right)  = \ell \left( \gamma \right) \) .

It is clear that if the inequality (1), or the second inequality (2), is strict then \( \ell \left( c\right)  > \ell \left( \gamma \right) \) . If \( \ell \left( c\right)  = \ell \left( \gamma \right) \) , then \( \left| \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\right|  = 0 \) , that is, \( v\left( t\right)  = \) const., and \( \left| {{r}^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right|  = {r}^{\prime }\left( t\right)  > 0 \) . It follows that \( c \) is a monotonic reparametrization of \( \gamma \) , hence \( c\left( \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack  \right)  = \gamma \left( \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack  \right) \) .

If \( c\left( \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack  \right) \) is not contained in \( B \) , consider the first point \( {t}_{1} \in \; \left( {0,1}\right) \) for which \( c\left( {t}_{1}\right) \) belongs to the boundary of \( B \) . If \( \rho \) is the radius of the geodesic ball \( B \) , we have:

\[
\ell \left( c\right)  \geq  {\ell }_{\left\lbrack  0,{t}_{1}\right\rbrack  }\left( c\right)  \geq  \rho  > \ell \left( \gamma \right) .
\]

nodes.label: Theorem 3.7
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 3.7 Theorem. For any \( p \in  M \) there exist a neighborhood \( W \) of \( p \) and a number \( \delta  > 0 \) , such that, for every \( q \in  W,{\exp }_{q} \) is a diffeomorphism on \( {B}_{\delta }\left( 0\right)  \subset  {T}_{q}M \) and \( {\exp }_{q}\left( {{B}_{\delta }\left( 0\right) }\right)  \supset  W \) , that is, \( W \) is a normal neighborhood of each of its points.
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.7 Theorem. For any \( p \in M \) there exist a neighborhood \( W \) of \( p \) and a number \( \delta > 0 \) , such that, for every \( q \in W,{\exp }_{q} \) is a diffeomorphism on \( {B}_{\delta }\left( 0\right) \subset {T}_{q}M \) and \( {\exp }_{q}\left( {{B}_{\delta }\left( 0\right) }\right) \supset W \) , that is, \( W \) is a normal neighborhood of each of its points.

nodes.proof:
Let \( \varepsilon  > 0, V \) and \( \mathcal{U} \) as in Proposition 2.7. Define \( F : \mathcal{U} \rightarrow \; M \times  M \) by \( F\left( {q, v}\right)  = \left( {q,{\exp }_{q}v}\right) \) . Recall that \( \mathcal{U} \subset  {TU} \) , where \( U \) is the domain of a system of coordinates \( \mathbf{x} \) at \( p \) , with \( V \subset  \mathbf{x}\left( U\right) \) . Consider, around \( F\left( {p,0}\right)  = \left( {p, p}\right)  \in  M \times  M \) the system of coordinates \( \left( {U \times  U;\left( {\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}}\right) }\right) \) . Thus, the matrix of \( d{F}_{\left( p,0\right) } \) is

\[
\left( \begin{array}{ll} I & I \\  0 & I \end{array}\right)
\]

because \( {\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{o} = I \) . It follows that \( F \) is a local diffeomorphism in a neighborhood of \( \left( {p,0}\right) \) . This means that there exists a neighborhood \( {\mathcal{U}}^{\prime } \subset  \mathcal{U} \) of \( \left( {p,0}\right) \) in \( {TM} \) such that \( F \) maps \( {\mathcal{U}}^{\prime } \) diffeomorphically onto a neighborhood \( {W}^{\prime } \) of \( \left( {p, p}\right) \) in \( M \times  M \) . It is possible to choose \( {\mathcal{U}}^{\prime } \) of the form

\[
{\mathcal{U}}^{\prime } = \left\{  {\left( {q, v}\right) ;q \in  {V}^{\prime }, v \in  {T}_{q}M,\left| v\right|  < \delta }\right\}  ,
\]

where \( {V}^{\prime } \subset  V \) is a neighborhood of \( p \) in \( M \) . Now choose a neighborhood \( W \subset  M \) of \( p \) such that \( W \times  W \subset  {W}^{\prime } \) . We claim that \( W \) and \( \delta \) , so obtained, satisfy the assertion of the Proposition.

Indeed, if \( q \in  W \) and \( {B}_{\delta }\left( 0\right)  \subset  {T}_{q}M \) then, since \( F \) is a diffeomorphism on \( {\mathcal{U}}^{\prime } \) , we get

\[
F\left( {\{ q\}  \times  {B}_{\delta }\left( 0\right) }\right)  \supset  \{ q\}  \times  W.
\]

From the definition of \( F,{\exp }_{q}\left( {{B}_{\delta }\left( 0\right) }\right)  \supset  W \) .

nodes.content:
3.8 REMARK. From the proposition above and the minimizing property of geodesics, it follows that given two points \( {q}_{1},{q}_{2} \in  W \) there exists a unique minimizing geodesic \( \gamma \) of length \( < \delta \) joining \( {q}_{1} \) to \( {q}_{2} \) . The proof shows, moreover, that \( \gamma \) depends differentiably on \( \left( {{q}_{1},{q}_{2}}\right) \) in the following sense: given \( \left( {{q}_{1},{q}_{2}}\right) \) there exists a unique \( v \in \; {T}_{{q}_{1}}M \) (given by \( {F}^{-1}\left( {{q}_{1},{q}_{2}}\right)  = \left( {{q}_{1}, v}\right) \) ) that depends differentiably on \( \left( {{q}_{1},{q}_{2}}\right) \) and is such that \( {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = v \) .

It is customary to call \( W \) a totally normal neighborhood of \( p \in  M \) .

nodes.label: Corollary 3.9
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 3.9 Corollary. If a piecewise differentiable curve \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) , with parameter proportional to arc length, has length less or equal to the length of any other piecewise differentiable curve joining \( \gamma \left( a\right) \) to \( \gamma \left( b\right) \) then \( \gamma \) is a geodesic. In particular, \( \gamma \) is regular.
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.9 Corollary. If a piecewise differentiable curve \( \gamma : \left\lbrack {a, b}\right\rbrack \rightarrow M \) , with parameter proportional to arc length, has length less or equal to the length of any other piecewise differentiable curve joining \( \gamma \left( a\right) \) to \( \gamma \left( b\right) \) then \( \gamma \) is a geodesic. In particular, \( \gamma \) is regular.

nodes.proof: Let \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack \) and let \( W \) be a totally normal neighborhood of \( \gamma \left( t\right) \) . There exists a closed interval \( I \subset  \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack \) , with non-empty interior, \( t \in  I \) , such that \( \gamma \left( I\right)  \subset  W \) ; the restriction \( {\gamma }_{I} : I \rightarrow  W \) is then a piecewise differentiable curve joining two points of a normal ball. From the hypothesis and from Proposition 3.6, \( \ell \left( {\gamma }_{I}\right) \) is equal to the length of a radial geodesic joining these two points. Again, from Proposition 3.6, and from the fact that \( {\gamma }_{I} \) is parametrized proportionally to arc length, \( {\gamma }_{I} \) is a geodesic on \( I \) , and therefore at \( t \) .

nodes.label: Example 3.10
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
3.10 EXAMPLE. Let \( G \) be the upper half-plane, that is, \( G = \; \left\{  {\left( {x, y}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{2};y > 0}\right\} \) with the Riemannian metric \( {g}_{11} = {g}_{22} = \; \frac{1}{{y}^{2}},{g}_{12} = {g}_{21} = 0 \)

We are going to show that the segment \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  G, a > 0 \) , of the \( y \) axis, given by \( \gamma \left( t\right)  = \left( {0, t}\right) \) is the image of a geodesic. In fact, for any arc \( c : \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  G \) given by \( c\left( t\right)  = \left( {x\left( t\right) , y\left( t\right) }\right) \) with \( c\left( a\right)  = \left( {0, a}\right) \) and \( c\left( b\right)  = \left( {0, b}\right) \) , we have that

\[
\ell \left( c\right)  = {\int }_{a}^{b}\left| \frac{dc}{dt}\right| {dt} = {\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{{\left( \frac{dx}{dt}\right) }^{2} + {\left( \frac{dy}{dt}\right) }^{2}}\frac{dt}{y}
\]

\[
\geq  {\int }_{a}^{b}\left| \frac{dy}{dt}\right| \frac{dt}{y} \geq  {\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{dy}{y} = \ell \left( \gamma \right) .
\]

It follows that \( \gamma \) minimizes arc length for piecewise differentiable curves, and from Corollary 3.9, that the image of \( \gamma \) is a geodesic.

It is easy to see that the isometries of \( G \) (cf. Exercise 4 of Chap. 1)

\[
z \rightarrow  \frac{{az} + b}{{cz} + d},\;z = x + {iy},\;{ad} - {bc} = 1,
\]

transform the \( {0y} \) axis into (upper) semi-circles or rays \( x = {x}_{o}, y > 0 \) . These curves are, therefore, geodesics of \( G \) . Indeed, they are all of the geodesics of \( G \) , since for each \( p \in  G \) and any direction in \( {T}_{p}G \) there passes such a circle with center on the \( {0x} \) axis (Fig. 3; in the special case that a direction is normal to \( {0x} \) , the circle degenerates to a ray normal to \( {0x} \) ).

nodes.label: Definition 3.4-extra-1

nodes.content:
## 4. Convex neighborhoods

We saw in Theorem 3.7 (Cf. Remark 3.8) that any point \( p \in  M \) possesses a totally normal neighborhood, that is, a neighborhood \( W \) and a number \( \delta  > 0 \) such that any two points \( {q}_{1},{q}_{2} \in  W \) can be joined by a minimizing geodesic of length \( < \delta \) . However, such a geodesic may not lie completely in \( W \) . We say that a subset \( S \subset  M \) is strongly convex if for any two points \( {q}_{1},{q}_{2} \) in the closure \( \bar{S} \) of \( S \) there exists unique minimizing geodesic \( \gamma \) joining \( {q}_{1} \) with \( {q}_{2} \) whose interior is contained in \( S \) . Now we are going to prove that the radius of a totally normal ball can be chosen in such a way that the ball is strongly convex.

nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
4.1 LEMMA. For any \( p \in  M \) there exists a number \( c > 0 \) such that any geodesic in \( M \) that is tangent at \( q \in  M \) to the geodesic sphere

\( {S}_{r}\left( p\right) \) of radius \( r < c \) stays out of the geodesic ball \( {B}_{r}\left( p\right) \) for some neighborhood of \( q \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 4.1 LEMMA. For any \( p \in M \) there exists a number \( c > 0 \) such that any geodesic in \( M \) that is tangent at \( q \in M \) to the geodesic sphere \( {S}_{r}\left( p\right) \) of radius \( r < c \) stays out of the geodesic ball \( {B}_{r}\left( p\right) \) for some neighborhood of \( q \) .

nodes.proof:
Let \( W \) be a totally normal neighborhood of \( p \) . Using the lemma of homogeneity, we can suppose, by conveniently restricting the interval of definition, that all of the geodesics of \( W \) have velocity one. We can, therefore, restrict ourselves to the unit tangent bundle \( {T}_{1}W \) given by

\[
{T}_{1}W = \left\{  {\left( {q, v}\right) ;q \in  W, v \in  {T}_{q}M,\left| v\right|  = 1}\right\}  .
\]

Let \( \gamma  : I \times  {T}_{1}W \rightarrow  M, I = \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right) \) , be the differentiable mapping such that \( t \rightarrow  \gamma \left( {t, q, v}\right) \) is the geodesic that at the instant \( t = 0 \) passes through \( q \) with velocity \( v,\left| v\right|  = 1 \) . Define \( u\left( {t, q, v}\right)  = {\exp }_{p}^{-1}\left( {\gamma \left( {t, q, v}\right) }\right) \) and

\[
F : I \times  {T}_{1}W \rightarrow  R,\;F\left( {t, q, v}\right)  = {\left| u\left( t, q, v\right) \right| }^{2}.
\]

\( F \) measures the square of the "distance" from \( p \) to a point that is moving along the geodesic \( \gamma \) (Fig. 4). It is clear that \( u \) and \( F \) are differentiable, and that

\[
\frac{\partial F}{\partial t} = 2\left\langle  {\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}, u}\right\rangle
\]

\[
\frac{{\partial }^{2}F}{\partial {t}^{2}} = 2\left\langle  {\frac{{\partial }^{2}u}{\partial {t}^{2}}, u}\right\rangle   + 2{\left| \frac{\partial u}{\partial t}\right| }^{2}.
\]

Now let \( r > 0 \) be chosen so that

\[
\mathop{\exp }\limits_{p}{B}_{r}\left( 0\right)  = {B}_{r}\left( p\right)  \subset  W
\]

If a geodesic \( \gamma \) is tangent to the geodesic sphere \( {S}_{r}\left( p\right) \) at the point \( q = \gamma \left( {0, q, v}\right) \) , then, from the Gauss lemma,

\[
\left\langle  {\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}\left( {0, q, v}\right) , u\left( {0, q, v}\right) }\right\rangle   = 0,
\]

that is, \( \frac{\partial F}{\partial t}\left( {0, q, v}\right)  = 0 \) . If we show that, for \( r \) sufficiently small, the critical point \( \left( {0, q, v}\right) \) of \( F \) is a strict minimum point, we have proven the lemma.

![019eafa4-c1ab-71ca-a069-1af7cc3160f3_90_303_88_1277_1136_0.jpg](images/019eafa4-c1ab-71ca-a069-1af7cc3160f3_90_303_88_1277_1136_0.jpg)

Figure 4

For this it suffices to observe that for \( q = p \) , we have \( u\left( {t, p, v}\right)  = {tv} \) and, therefore

\[
\frac{{\partial }^{2}F}{\partial {t}^{2}}\left( {0, p, v}\right)  = 2{\left| v\right| }^{2} = 2.
\]

It follows that there exists a neighborhood \( V \subset  W \) of \( p \) such that \( \frac{{\partial }^{2}F}{\partial {t}^{2}}\left( {0, q, v}\right)  > 0 \) , for all \( q \in  V \) and all \( v \in  {T}_{q}M,\left| v\right|  = 1 \) . Let \( c > 0 \) be such that

\[
{\exp }_{p}{B}_{c}\left( 0\right)  \subset  V\text{ . }
\]

From what was previously proved, any geodesic in \( {B}_{c}\left( p\right) \) that is tangent to the geodesic sphere of radius \( r < c \) at the point \( \gamma \left( {0, q, v}\right) \) produces a strict local minimum for \( F \) at \( \left( {0, q, v}\right) \) . It follows that, in a neighborhood of \( q \) , the points of \( \gamma \) stay outside of the ball \( {B}_{r}\left( p\right) \) .

nodes.content: 4.2 Proposition. (Convex neighborhoods). For any \( p \in  M \) there exists a number \( \beta  > 0 \) such that the geodesic ball \( {B}_{\beta }\left( p\right) \) is strongly convex.
nodes.content_excerpt: 4.2 Proposition. (Convex neighborhoods). For any \( p \in M \) there exists a number \( \beta > 0 \) such that the geodesic ball \( {B}_{\beta }\left( p\right) \) is strongly convex.

nodes.proof:
Let \( c \) be the number given in Lemma 4.1. Choose \( \delta  > 0 \) and \( W \) in Theorem 3.7 in such a way that \( \delta  < \frac{c}{2} \) . Take \( \beta  < \delta \) such that \( {B}_{\beta }\left( p\right)  \subset  W \) . We shall prove that \( {B}_{\beta }\left( p\right) \) is strongly convex. Let \( {q}_{1},{q}_{2} \in  {B}_{\beta }\left( p\right) \) and let \( \gamma \) be the (unique) geodesic of length \( < {2\delta } < c \) joining \( {q}_{1} \) to \( {q}_{2} \) . It is clear that \( \gamma \) is contained in \( {B}_{c}\left( p\right) \) (Fig. 5).

![019eafa4-c1ab-71ca-a069-1af7cc3160f3_91_552_460_688_666_0.jpg](images/019eafa4-c1ab-71ca-a069-1af7cc3160f3_91_552_460_688_666_0.jpg)

If the interior of \( \gamma \) is not contained in \( {B}_{\beta }\left( p\right) \) , then there exists a point \( m \) in the interior of \( \gamma \) where the maximum distance \( r \) from \( p \) to \( \gamma \) is attained. The points of \( \gamma \) in a neighborhood of \( m \) remain in the closure of \( {B}_{r}\left( p\right) \) . Since \( m \in  {B}_{c}\left( p\right) \) this contradicts Lemma 4.1 and proves the proposition.

nodes.label: Exercise 1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
1. (Geodesics of a surface of revolution). Denote by \( \left( {u, v}\right) \) the cartesian coordinates of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{2} \) . Show that the function \( \varphi  : U \subset \; {\mathbf{R}}^{2} \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) given by \( \varphi \left( {u, v}\right)  = \left( {f\left( v\right) \cos u, f\left( v\right) \sin u, g\left( v\right) }\right) \) ,

\[
U = \left\{  {\left( {u, v}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{2} : {u}_{o} < u < {u}_{1};{v}_{o} < v < {v}_{1}}\right\}  ,
\]

where \( f \) and \( g \) are differentiable functions, with \( {f}^{\prime }{\left( v\right) }^{2} + \; {g}^{\prime }{\left( v\right) }^{2} \neq  0 \) and \( f\left( v\right)  \neq  0 \) , is an immersion. The image \( \varphi \left( U\right) \) is the surface generated by the rotation of the curve \( \left( {f\left( v\right) , g\left( v\right) }\right) \) around the axis \( {0z} \) and is called a surface of revolution \( S \) . The image by \( \varphi \) of the curves \( u = \) constant and \( v = \) constant are called meridians and parallels, respectively, of \( S \) .

a) Show that the induced metric in the coordinates \( \left( {u, v}\right) \) is given by

\[
{g}_{11} = {f}^{2},\;{g}_{12} = 0,\;{g}_{22} = {\left( {f}^{\prime }\right) }^{2} + {\left( {g}^{\prime }\right) }^{2}.
\]

b) Show that local equations of a geodesic \( \gamma \) are

\[
\frac{{d}^{2}u}{d{t}^{2}} + \frac{{2f}{f}^{\prime }}{{f}^{2}}\frac{du}{dt}\frac{dv}{dt} = 0
\]

\[
\frac{{d}^{2}v}{d{t}^{2}} - \frac{f{f}^{\prime }}{{\left( {f}^{\prime }\right) }^{2} + {\left( {g}^{\prime }\right) }^{2}}{\left( \frac{du}{dt}\right) }^{2} + \frac{{f}^{\prime }{f}^{\prime \prime } + {g}^{\prime }{g}^{\prime \prime }}{\left( {f}^{\prime 2} + {\left( {g}^{\prime }\right) }^{2}\right. }{\left( \frac{dv}{dt}\right) }^{2} = 0.
\]

c) Obtain the following geometric meaning of the equations above: the second equation is, except for meridians and parallels, equivalent to the fact that the "energy" \( {\left| {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) \right| }^{2} \) of a geodesic is constant along \( \gamma \) ; the first equation signifies that if \( \beta \left( t\right) \) is the oriented angle, \( \beta \left( t\right)  < \pi \) , of \( \gamma \) with a parallel \( P \) intersecting \( \gamma \) at \( \gamma \left( t\right) \) , then

\[
r\cos \beta  = \text{ const. }
\]

where \( r \) is the radius of the parallel \( P \) (the equation above is called Clairaut's relation).

d) Use Clairaut's relation to show that a geodesic of the paraboloid

\[
\left( {f\left( v\right)  = v, g\left( v\right)  = {v}^{2},0 < v < \infty , - \varepsilon  < u < {2\pi } + \varepsilon }\right) ,
\]

which is not a meridian, intersects itself an infinite number of times(Fig. 6).

2. It is possible to introduce a Riemannian metric in the tangent bundle \( {TM} \) of a Riemannian manifold \( M \) in the following manner. Let \( \left( {p, v}\right)  \in  {TM} \) and \( V, W \) be tangent vectors in \( {TM} \) at \( \left( {p, v}\right) \) . Choose curves in \( {TM} \)

\[
\alpha  : t \rightarrow  \left( {p\left( t\right) , v\left( t\right) }\right) ,\beta  : s \rightarrow  \left( {q\left( s\right) , w\left( s\right) }\right) ,
\]

with \( p\left( 0\right)  = q\left( 0\right)  = p, v\left( 0\right)  = w\left( 0\right)  = v \) , and \( V = {\alpha }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) , W = \; {\beta }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) . Define an inner product on \( {TM} \) by

\[
\langle V, W{\rangle }_{\left( p, v\right) } = \langle {d\pi }\left( V\right) ,{d\pi }\left( W\right) {\rangle }_{p} + {\left\langle  \frac{Dv}{dt}\left( 0\right) ,\frac{Dw}{ds}\left( 0\right) \right\rangle  }_{p},
\]

![019eafa4-c1ab-71ca-a069-1af7cc3160f3_93_599_156_606_609_0.jpg](images/019eafa4-c1ab-71ca-a069-1af7cc3160f3_93_599_156_606_609_0.jpg)

Figure 6. Geodesics of a paraboloid.

where \( {d\pi } \) is the differential of \( \pi  : {TM} \rightarrow  M \) .

a) Prove that this inner product is well-defined and introduces a Riemannian metric on \( {TM} \) .

b) A vector at \( \left( {p, v}\right)  \in  {TM} \) that is orthogonal (for the metric above) to the fiber \( {\pi }^{-1}\left( p\right)  \approx  {T}_{p}M \) is called a horizontal vector. A curve

\[
t \rightarrow  \left( {p\left( t\right) , v\left( t\right) }\right)
\]

in \( {TM} \) is horizontal if its tangent vector is horizontal for all \( t \) . Prove that the curve

\[
t \rightarrow  \left( {p\left( t\right) , v\left( t\right) }\right)
\]

is horizontal if and only if the vector field \( v\left( t\right) \) is parallel along \( p\left( t\right) \) in \( M \) .

c) Prove that the geodesic field is a horizontal vector field (i.e., it is horizontal at every point).

d) Prove that the trajectories of the geodesic field are geodesics on \( {TM} \) in the metric above.

Hint: Let \( \widetilde{\alpha }\left( t\right)  = \left( {\alpha \left( t\right) , v\left( t\right) }\right) \) be a curve in \( {TM} \) . Show that \( \ell \left( \widetilde{\alpha }\right)  \geq  \ell \left( \alpha \right) \) and that the inequality is verified if \( v \) is parallel along \( \alpha \) . Consider a trajectory of the geodesic flow passing through \( \left( {p, v}\right) \) which is locally of the form \( \bar{\gamma }\left( t\right)  = \left( {\gamma \left( t\right) ,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right) \) , where \( \gamma \left( t\right) \) is a geodesic on \( M \) . Choose convex neighborhoods \( W \subset  {TM} \) of \( \left( {p, v}\right) \) and \( V \subset  M \) of \( p \) such that \( \pi \left( W\right)  = V \) . Take two points \( {Q}_{1} = \left( {{q}_{1},{v}_{1}}\right) ,{Q}_{2} = \left( {{q}_{2},{v}_{2}}\right) \) in \( \bar{\gamma } \cap  W \) . If \( \bar{\gamma } \) is not a geodesic, there exists a curve \( \bar{\alpha } \) in \( W \) passing through \( {Q}_{1} \) and \( {Q}_{2} \) such that \( \ell \left( \bar{\alpha }\right)  < \ell \left( \bar{\gamma }\right)  = \ell \left( \gamma \right) \) . Let \( \alpha  = \pi \left( \bar{\alpha }\right) \) ; since \( \ell \left( \alpha \right)  \leq  \ell \left( \bar{\alpha }\right) \) , this contradicts the fact that \( \gamma \) is a geodesic.

e) A vector at \( \left( {p, v}\right)  \in  {TM} \) is called vertical if it is tangent to the fiber \( {\pi }^{-1}\left( p\right)  \approx  {T}_{p}M \) . Show that:

\[
\langle W, W{\rangle }_{\left( p, v\right) } = \langle {d\pi }\left( W\right) ,{d\pi }\left( W\right) {\rangle }_{p},\;\text{ if }W\text{ is horizontal, }
\]

\[
\langle W, W{\rangle }_{\left( p, v\right) } = \langle W, W{\rangle }_{p},\;\text{ if }W\text{ is vertical, }
\]

where we are identifying the tangent space to the fiber with \( {T}_{p}M \) .

3. Let \( G \) be a Lie group, \( \mathcal{G} \) its Lie algebra and let \( X \in  \mathcal{G} \) (see Example 2.6, Chap. 1). The trajectories of \( X \) determine a mapping \( \varphi  : \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)  \rightarrow  G \) with \( \varphi \left( 0\right)  = e,{\varphi }^{\prime }\left( t\right)  = X\left( {\varphi \left( t\right) }\right) \) .

a) Prove that \( \varphi \left( t\right) \) is defined for all \( t \in  \mathbf{R} \) and that \( \varphi \left( {t + s}\right)  = \varphi \left( t\right)  \cdot  \varphi \left( s\right) ,(\varphi  : \mathbf{R} \rightarrow  G \) is then called a 1- parameter subgroup of \( G \) ).

Hint: Let \( \varphi \left( {t}_{o}\right)  = y,{t}_{o} \in  \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right) \) . Show that, from the left invariance, \( t \rightarrow  {y}^{-1}\varphi \left( t\right) , t \in  \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right) \) , is also an integral curve of \( X \) passing through \( e \) for \( t = {t}_{o} \) . By uniqueness, \( \varphi {\left( {t}_{o}\right) }^{-1}\varphi \left( t\right)  = \; \varphi \left( {t - {t}_{o}}\right) \) , hence \( \varphi \) can be extended out from \( {t}_{o} \) in an interval of radius \( \varepsilon \) . This shows that \( \varphi \left( t\right) \) is defined for all \( t \in  \mathbf{R} \) . In addition \( \varphi {\left( {t}_{o}\right) }^{-1} = \varphi \left( {-{t}_{o}}\right) \) and, since \( {t}_{o} \) is arbitrary, we obtain \( \varphi \left( {t + s}\right)  = \varphi \left( t\right)  \cdot  \varphi \left( s\right) . \)

b) Prove that if \( G \) has a bi-invariant metric \( \langle \) , \( \rangle {thenthe} \) geodesics of \( G \) that start from \( e \) are 1-parameter subgroups of \( G \) .

Hint: Use the relation (see Eq. (9) of Chap. 2)

\[
2\left\langle  {X,{\nabla }_{Z}Y}\right\rangle   = Z\langle X, Y\rangle  + Y\langle X, Z\rangle  - X\langle Y, Z\rangle
\]

\[
+ \langle Z,\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  \rangle  + \langle Y,\left\lbrack  {X, Z}\right\rbrack  \rangle  - \langle X,\left\lbrack  {Y, Z}\right\rbrack  \rangle
\]

and the fact that the metric is left invariant to prove that \( \left\langle  {X,{\nabla }_{Y}Y}\right\rangle   = \langle Y,\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  \rangle \) , where \( X, Y \) and \( Z \) are left invariant fields. Use also the fact that the bi-invariance of \( \langle \) , \( \rangle {implies} \) that

\[
\langle \left\lbrack  {U, X}\right\rbrack  , V\rangle  =  - \langle U,\left\lbrack  {V, X}\right\rbrack  \rangle ,\;X, U, V \in  \mathcal{G}.
\]

It follows that \( {\nabla }_{Y}Y = 0 \) , for all \( Y \in  \mathcal{G} \) . Thus 1-parameter subgroups are geodesics. By uniqueness, geodesics are 1-parameter subgroups.

nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
5. Let \( M \) be a Riemannian manifold and \( X \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) . Let \( p \in  M \) and let \( U \subset  M \) be a neighborhood of \( p \) . Let \( \varphi  : \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)  \times  U \rightarrow  M \) be a differentiable mapping such that for any \( q \in  U \) the curve \( t \rightarrow  \varphi \left( {t, q}\right) \) is a trajectory of \( X \) passing through \( q \) at \( t = 0 \) ( \( U \) and \( \varphi \) are given by the fundamental theorem for ordinary differential equations, Cf. Theorem 2.2). \( X \) is called a Killing field (or an infinitesimal isometry) if, for each \( {t}_{o} \in  \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right) \) , the mapping \( \varphi \left( {{t}_{o},}\right)  : U \subset  M \rightarrow  M \) is an isometry.

Prove that:

a) A vector vield \( v \) on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) may be seen as a map \( v : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \; {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) ; we say that the field is linear if \( v \) is a linear map. A linear field on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) , defined by a matrix \( A \) , is a Killing field if and only if \( A \) is anti-symmetric.

b) Let \( X \) be a Killing field on \( M, p \in  M \) , and let \( U \) be a normal neighborhood of \( p \) on \( M \) . Assume that \( p \) is a unique point of \( U \) that satisfies \( X\left( p\right)  = 0 \) . Then, in \( U, X \) is tangent to the geodesic spheres centered at \( p \) .

c) Let \( X \) be a differentiable vector field on \( M \) and let \( f : M \rightarrow \; N \) be an isometry. Let \( Y \) be a vector field on \( N \) defined by \( Y\left( {f\left( p\right) }\right)  = d{f}_{p}\left( {X\left( p\right) }\right) , p \in  M \) . Then \( Y \) is a Killing field if and only if \( X \) is also a Killing vector field.

d) \( X \) is Killing \( \Leftrightarrow  \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Y}X, Z}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}X, Y}\right\rangle   = 0 \) for all \( Y, Z \in \; \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) (the equation above is called the Killing equation).

Hint for \( \Rightarrow \) : By continuity, it suffices to prove the equation above for points \( q \in  U \) where \( X\left( q\right)  \neq  0 \) . If this is the case, let \( S \subset  U \) be a submanifold of \( U \) , passing through \( q \) , normal to \( X\left( q\right)  \neq  0 \) at \( q \) , with \( \dim S = \dim M - 1 \) . Let \( \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n - 1}}\right) \) be coordinates in a neighborhood \( V \subset  S \) of \( q \) such that \( \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n - 1}, t}\right) \) are coordinates in a neighborhood \( V \times  \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)  \subset  U \) and \( X = \frac{\partial }{\partial t} \) . Putting \( {X}_{i} = \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}} \) , obtain

\[
\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{{X}_{j}}X,{X}_{i}}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{{X}_{i}}X,{X}_{j}}\right\rangle   = X\left\langle  {{X}_{i},{X}_{j}}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {\left\lbrack  {X,{X}_{i}}\right\rbrack  ,{X}_{j}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
- \left\langle  {\left\lbrack  {X,{X}_{j}}\right\rbrack  ,{X}_{i}}\right\rangle   = \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left\langle  {{X}_{i},{X}_{j}}\right\rangle   = 0,
\]

where in the last equality the fact was used that \( X \) is a Killing field.

e) Let \( X \) be a Killing field on \( M \) with \( X\left( q\right)  \neq  0, q \in  M \) . Then there exists a system of coordinates \( \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right) \) in a neighborhood of \( q \) , so that the coefficients \( {g}_{ij} \) of the metric in this system coordinates do not depend on \( {x}_{n} \) .

6. Let \( X \) be a Killing field (Cf. Exercise 5) on a connected Riemannian manifold \( M \) . Assume that there exists a point \( q \in  M \) such that \( X\left( q\right)  = 0 \) and \( {\nabla }_{Y}X\left( q\right)  = 0 \) , for all \( Y\left( q\right)  \in  {T}_{q}M \) . Prove that \( X \equiv  0 \) .

Hint: Show that, for all \( t \) , the local isometry \( \varphi \left( {t,}\right)  : U \subset  M \rightarrow \; M \) generated by the field \( X \) (Cf. Exercise 5) leaves the point \( q \) fixed and its differential at \( q \) , as a linear map of \( {T}_{q}M \) , is the identity. For this, observe that \( d{\varphi }_{t} : {T}_{q}M \rightarrow  {T}_{q}M \) for all \( t \) . In addition, \( \left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  \left( q\right)  = \left( {{\nabla }_{X}Y - {\nabla }_{Y}X}\right) \left( q\right)  = 0 \) , by hypothesis. Since

\[
0 = \left\lbrack  {Y, X}\right\rbrack  \left( q\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}\frac{1}{t}\left\lbrack  {d{\varphi }_{t} - \mathrm{{Id}}}\right\rbrack  \left( Y\right)  = {\left. \frac{d}{dt}\left( d{\varphi }_{t}\right) \right| }_{t = 0}
\]

nodes.label: Exercise 11
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
†11. Let \( M \) be an oriented Riemannian manifold. Let \( \nu \) be a differential form of degree \( n = \dim M \) defined in the following way:

\[
\nu \left( {{v}_{1},\ldots ,{v}_{n}}\right) \left( p\right)  =  \pm  \sqrt{\det \left( \left\langle  {{v}_{i},{v}_{j}}\right\rangle  \right) }
\]

\[
= \text{ orient. vol. }\left\{  {{v}_{1},\ldots ,{v}_{n}}\right\}  ,\;p \in  M\text{ , }
\]

where \( {v}_{1},\ldots ,{v}_{n} \in  {T}_{p}\left( M\right) \) are linearly independent, and the oriented volume is affected by the sign + or - depending on whether or not the basis \( \left\{  {{v}_{1},\ldots ,{v}_{n}}\right\} \) belongs to the orientation of \( M;\nu \) is called the volume element of \( M \) . For a vector field \( X \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) define the interior product \( i\left( X\right) \nu \) of \( X \) with \( \nu \) as the \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -form:

\[
i\left( X\right) \nu \left( {{Y}_{2},\ldots ,{Y}_{n}}\right)  = \nu \left( {X,{Y}_{2},\ldots ,{Y}_{n}}\right) ,{Y}_{2},\ldots ,{Y}_{n} \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) .
\]

Prove that

\[
d\left( {i\left( X\right) \nu }\right)  = \operatorname{div}{X\nu }
\]

Hint: Let \( p \in  M \) and let \( {E}_{i} \) be a geodesic frame at \( p \) . Write \( X \) as a sum, \( X = \sum {f}_{i}{E}_{i} \) and let \( {\omega }_{i} \) be differential forms of degree one defined on a neighborhood of \( p \) by \( {\omega }_{i}\left( {E}_{j}\right)  = {\delta }_{ij} \) . Show that \( {\omega }_{i} \land  \ldots  \land  {\omega }_{n} \) is a volume form \( \nu \) on \( M \) . Next put \( {\theta }_{i} = {\omega }_{1} \land  \ldots  \land  {\widehat{\omega }}_{i} \land  \ldots  \land  {\omega }_{n} \) , where \( {\widehat{\omega }}_{i} \) signifies that the factor \( {\widehat{\omega }}_{i} \) is not present. Prove that \( i\left( X\right) \nu  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{\left( -1\right) }^{i + 1}{f}_{i}{\theta }_{i} \) . It then follows that

\[
d\left( {i\left( X\right) \nu }\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{\left( -1\right) }^{i + 1}d{f}_{i} \land  {\theta }_{i} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{\left( -1\right) }^{i + 1}{f}_{i} \land  d{\theta }_{i}
\]

\[
= \left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{E}_{i}\left( {f}_{i}\right) }\right) \nu  + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{\left( -1\right) }^{i + 1}{f}_{i} \land  d{\theta }_{i}.
\]

But \( d{\theta }_{i} = 0 \) at \( p \) , since

\[
d{\omega }_{k}\left( {{E}_{i},{E}_{j}}\right)  = {E}_{i}{\omega }_{k}\left( {E}_{j}\right)  - {E}_{j}{\omega }_{k}\left( {E}_{i}\right)  - {\omega }_{k}\left( \left\lbrack  {{E}_{i},{E}_{j}}\right\rbrack  \right)
\]

\[
= {\omega }_{k}\left( {{\nabla }_{{E}_{i}}{E}_{j} - {\nabla }_{{E}_{j}}{E}_{i}}\right) .
\]

Therefore

\[
d\left( {i\left( X\right) \nu }\right) \left( p\right)  = \left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{E}_{i}\left( {f}_{i}\right) \left( p\right) }\right) \nu  = \operatorname{div}X\left( p\right) \nu
\]

and since \( p \) is arbitrary, this completes the proof.

Remark. The result obtained implies that the notion of the divergence of \( X \) makes sense on an oriented differentiable manifold on which a "volume element" has been chosen, that is, an \( n \) -form \( \nu \) which takes positive values on positive bases.

†12. (Theorem of E. Hopf). Let \( M \) be a compact orientable Riemannian manifold which is also connected. Let \( f \) be a differentiable function on \( M \) with \( {\Delta f} \geq  0 \) . Then \( f = \) const. In particular, the harmonic functions on \( M \) , that is, those for which \( {\Delta f} = 0 \) , are constant.

Hint: Take grad \( f = X \) . Using Stokes theorem and the result of exercise 11, obtain

\[
{\int }_{M}\bigtriangleup {f\nu } = {\int }_{M}\operatorname{div}{X\nu } = {\int }_{M}d\left( {i\left( X\right) \nu }\right)  = {\int }_{\partial M}i\left( X\right) \nu  = 0.
\]

Since \( {\Delta f} \geq  0 \) , we have \( {\Delta f} = 0 \) . Using again Stokes theorem on \( {f}^{2}/2 \) , and the result of exercise 9(b), we obtain

\[
0 = {\int }_{M}\bigtriangleup \left( {{f}^{2}/2}\right) \nu  = {\int }_{M}f\bigtriangleup {f\nu } + {\int }_{M}{\left| \operatorname{grad}f\right| }^{2}\nu
\]

\[
= {\int }_{M}{\left| \operatorname{grad}f\right| }^{2}\nu
\]

which together with the connectedness of \( M \) , implies that \( f = \) const..
