nodes.content:
14. (Liouville’s Theorem). Prove that if \( G \) is the geodesic field on \( {TM} \) then \( \operatorname{div}G = 0 \) . Conclude from this that the geodesic flow preserves the volume of \( {TM} \) .

Hint: Let \( p \in  M \) and consider a system \( \left( {{u}_{1},\ldots ,{u}_{n}}\right) \) of normal coordinates at \( p \) . Such coordinates are defined in a normal neighborhood \( U \) of \( p \) by considering an orthonormal basis \( \left\{  {e}_{i}\right\} \) of \( {T}_{p}M \) and taking \( \left( {{u}_{1},\ldots ,{u}_{n}}\right) , q = {\exp }_{p}\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{u}_{i}{e}_{i}}\right) \) , \( i = 1,\ldots , n \) , as coordinates of \( q \) . In such a coordinate system, \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}\left( p\right)  = 0 \) , since the geodesics that pass through \( p \) are given by linear equations. Therefore if \( X = \sum {x}_{i}\frac{\partial }{\partial {u}_{i}} \) , then \( \operatorname{div}X\left( p\right)  = \sum \frac{\partial {x}_{i}}{\partial {u}_{i}}. \)

Now let \( \left( {u}_{i}\right) \) be normal coordinates in a neighborhood \( U \subset  M \) around \( p \in  M \) and let \( \left( {{u}_{i},{v}_{j}}\right) , v = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{v}_{j}\frac{\partial }{\partial {u}_{j}}, i, j = \; 1,\ldots , n \) , be coordinates on \( {TM} \) . Calculate the volume element of the natural metric of \( {TM} \) at \( \left( {q, v}\right) , q \in  U, v \in  {T}_{q}M \) , and show that it is the volume element of the product metric on \( U \times \; U \) at the point \( \left( {q, q}\right) \) (See Exercise 2(e)). Since the divergence of \( G \) only depends on the volume element (see Exercise 11), and \( G \) is horizontal, we can calculate \( \operatorname{div}G \) in the product metric. Observe that in the coordinates \( \left( {{u}_{i},{v}_{j}}\right) \) we have

\[
G\left( {u}_{i}\right)  = {v}_{i},\;G\left( {v}_{j}\right)  =  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{ik}}{\Gamma }_{ik}^{j}{v}_{i}{v}_{k},\;k = 1,\ldots , n.
\]

Since the Christoffel symbols of the product metric on \( U \times  U \) vanish at \( \left( {p, p}\right) \) , we obtain finally, at \( p \) ,

\[
\operatorname{div}G = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}\frac{\partial {v}_{i}}{\partial {u}_{i}} - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}\frac{\partial }{\partial {v}_{j}}\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{ik}}{\Gamma }_{ik}^{j}{v}_{i}{v}_{k}}\right)  = 0.
\]

nodes.title: 4.1. Introduction
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry

nodes.label: Remark 4.1-extra-1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
## 1. Introduction

The notion of curvature in a Riemannian manifold was introduced by Riemann (See Riemann [Ri]) in a rather geometric manner, which we are now going to describe. Let \( p \) be a point of a Riemannian manifold \( M \) and let \( \sigma  \subset  {T}_{p}M \) be a two dimensional subspace of the tangent space \( {T}_{p}M \) of \( M \) at \( p \) . Consider the set of geodesics that start at \( p \) and are tangent to \( \sigma \) . The segments of such geodesics in a normal neighborhood \( U \subset  M \) of \( p \) determine a submanifold of dimension two \( S \subset  M \) (with our present notation, \( S \) is the image of \( {\exp }_{p} \) restricted to \( \sigma  \cap  {\exp }_{p}^{-1}\left( U\right) ) \) . \( S \) has a metric induced from the inclusion. Since Gauss had proved that the curvature of a surface can be expressed in terms of its metric, so Riemann could speak of the curvature of \( S \) at \( p \) , and indicate it by \( K\left( {p,\sigma }\right) \) ,(nowadays, \( K\left( {p,\sigma }\right) \) is called the sectional curvature of \( M \) at \( p \) with respect to \( \sigma ) \) . This was the curvature considered by Riemann in [Ri]. It is a natural generalization of the Gaussian curvature of surfaces and it is clear that if \( M = {R}^{n}, K\left( {p,\sigma }\right)  = 0 \) for all \( p \) and all \( \sigma \) .

Riemann did not indicate a way to calculate the sectional curvature starting with the metric of \( M \) ; that was done a few years later by Christoffel (see Christoffel [Cf]; Cf. also Eq. (2) of this chapter). Indeed, all the work of Riemann contains just one formula, namely, an expression for the metric for which \( K\left( {p,\sigma }\right) \) is constant, for all \( p \) and \( \sigma \) , and even this formula was presented without proof. (The formula of Riemann will be presented in Exercise 1(c) of Chap. 8.)

As frequently happens in mathematics, a "workable" formulation of the concept of curvature required a long time for its development. When such a formulation finally appeared it had the advantage of being easy to use to prove theorems but it had the disadvantage of being so far removed from the initial intuitive concept that it looked as if it were some kind of arbitrary creation.

This chapter presents a definition of curvature that, intuitively, measures the amount that a Riemannian manifold deviates from being Euclidean (Cf. Def. 2.1). In Chapter 6, we are going to show that the notion of sectional curvature (Cf. Def. 3.2) obtained by starting with this definition of curvature generalizes the notion of Gaussian curvature for surfaces, and coincides with the concept introduced by Riemann.

nodes.title: 4.2. Curvature
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry

nodes.label: Definition 2.1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.1 Definition. The curvature \( R \) of a Riemannian manifold \( M \) is a correspondence that associates to every pair \( X, Y \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) a mapping \( R\left( {X, Y}\right)  : \mathcal{X}\left( M\right)  \rightarrow  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) given by

\[
\begin{matrix} R\left( {X, Y}\right) Z = {\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{X}Z - {\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{Y}Z + {\nabla }_{\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }Z,\;Z \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) , \end{matrix}
\]

where \( \nabla \) is the Riemannian connection of \( M \) .

Observe that if \( M = {R}^{n} \) , then \( R\left( {X, Y}\right) Z = 0 \) for all \( X, Y, Z \in \; \mathcal{X}\left( {R}^{n}\right) \) . In fact, if the vector field \( Z \) is given by \( Z = \left( {{z}_{1},\ldots ,{z}_{n}}\right) \) , with the components of \( Z \) coming from the natural coordinates of \( {R}^{n} \) , we obtain

\[
{\nabla }_{X}Z = \left( {X{z}_{1},\ldots , X{z}_{n}}\right)
\]

hence

\[
{\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{X}Z = \left( {{YX}{z}_{1},\ldots ,{YX}{z}_{n}}\right)
\]

which implies that

\[
R\left( {X, Y}\right) Z = {\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{X}Z - {\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{Y}Z + {\nabla }_{\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }Z = 0,
\]

as was stated. We are able, therefore, to think of \( R \) as a way of measuring how much \( M \) deviates from being Euclidean.

Another way of viewing definition 2.1 is to consider a system of coordinates \( \left\{  {x}_{i}\right\} \) around \( p \in  M \) . Since \( \left\lbrack  {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}},\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{j}}}\right\rbrack   = 0 \) , we obtain

\[
R\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}},\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{j}}}\right) \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{k}} = \left( {{\nabla }_{\partial /\partial {x}_{j}}{\nabla }_{\partial /\partial {x}_{i}} - {\nabla }_{\partial /\partial {x}_{i}}{\nabla }_{\partial /\partial {x}_{j}}}\right) \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{k}},
\]

that is, the curvature measures the non-commutativity of the covariant derivative.

These interpretations, are, however, more or less formal. In this chapter we advise the reader to get used to the formal properties of curvature, postponing until Chapter 6 the proof of a more geometric interpretation of curvature. Let us remark also that a frequently encountered definition of curvature in the literature differs from definition 2.1 by a sign.

nodes.label: Proposition 2.2
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.2 Proposition. The curvature \( R \) of a Riemannian manifold has the following properties:

(i) \( R \) is bilinear in \( \mathcal{X}\left( M\right)  \times  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) , that is,

\[
R\left( {f{X}_{1} + g{X}_{2},{Y}_{1}}\right)  = {fR}\left( {{X}_{1},{Y}_{1}}\right)  + {gR}\left( {{X}_{2},{Y}_{1}}\right) ,
\]

\[
R\left( {{X}_{1}, f{Y}_{1} + g{Y}_{2}}\right)  = {fR}\left( {{X}_{1},{Y}_{1}}\right)  + {gR}\left( {{X}_{1},{Y}_{2}}\right) ,
\]

\[
f, g \in  \mathcal{D}\left( M\right) ,\;{X}_{1},{X}_{2},{Y}_{1},{Y}_{2} \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) .
\]

(ii) For any \( X, Y \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) , the curvature operator \( R\left( {X, Y}\right) \) : \( \mathcal{X}\left( M\right)  \rightarrow  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) is linear, that is,

\[
R\left( {X, Y}\right) \left( {Z + W}\right)  = R\left( {X, Y}\right) Z + R\left( {X, Y}\right) W
\]

\[
R\left( {X, Y}\right) {fZ} = {fR}\left( {X, Y}\right) Z
\]

\[
f \in  \mathcal{D}\left( M\right) ,\;Z, W \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right)
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.2 Proposition. The curvature \( R \) of a Riemannian manifold has the following properties: (i) \( R \) is bilinear in \( \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \times \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) , that is, \[ R\left( {f{X}_{1} + g{X}_{2},{Y}_{1}}\right) = {fR}\left( {{X}_{1},{Y}_{1}}\right) + {gR}\left( {{X}_{2},{Y}_{1}}\right) , \] \[ R\left( {{X}_{1}, f{Y}_{1} + g{Y}_{2}}\right) = {fR}\left( {{X}_{1},{Y}_{1}}\right) +...

nodes.proof:
Let us verify (ii) only, leaving (i) as an exercise for the reader. The first part of (ii) is obvious. As for the second, we have

\[
{\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{X}\left( {fZ}\right)  = {\nabla }_{Y}\left( {f{\nabla }_{X}Z + \left( {Xf}\right) Z}\right)  = f{\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{X}Z + \left( {Yf}\right) \left( {{\nabla }_{X}Z}\right)
\]

\[
+ \left( {Xf}\right) \left( {{\nabla }_{Y}Z}\right)  + \left( {Y\left( {Xf}\right) }\right) Z.
\]

Therefore,

\[
{\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{X}\left( {fZ}\right)  - {\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{Y}\left( {fZ}\right)
\]

\[
= f\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{X} - {\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{Y}}\right) Z + \left( {\left( {{YX} - {XY}}\right) f}\right) Z,
\]

hence

\[
R\left( {X, Y}\right) {fZ} = f{\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{X}Z - f{\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{Y}Z + \left( {\left\lbrack  {Y, X}\right\rbrack  f}\right) Z + f{\nabla }_{\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }Z
\]

\[
+ \left( {\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  f}\right) Z = {fR}\left( {X, Y}\right) Z
\]

nodes.label: Remark 2.3
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 2.3 REMARK. An analysis of the proof above shows that the necessity of the appearance of the term \( {\nabla }_{\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }Z \) in the definition of the curvature is connected to the fact that we want the mapping \( R\left( {X, Y}\right)  : \mathcal{K}\left( M\right)  \rightarrow  \mathcal{K}\left( M\right) \) to be linear (see the next Rem. 2.6).

nodes.content:
2.4 Proposition. (Bianchi Identity).

\[
R\left( {X, Y}\right) Z + R\left( {Y, Z}\right) X + R\left( {Z, X}\right) Y = 0.
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.4 Proposition. (Bianchi Identity). \[ R\left( {X, Y}\right) Z + R\left( {Y, Z}\right) X + R\left( {Z, X}\right) Y = 0. \]

nodes.label: Proposition 2.5
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.5 Proposition. (a) \( \left( {X, Y, Z, T}\right)  + \left( {Y, Z, X, T}\right)  + \left( {Z, X, Y, T}\right)  = 0 \)

(b) \( \left( {X, Y, Z, T}\right)  =  - \left( {Y, X, Z, T}\right) \)

(c) \( \left( {X, Y, Z, T}\right)  =  - \left( {X, Y, T, Z}\right) \)

(d) \( \left( {X, Y, Z, T}\right)  = \left( {Z, T, X, Y}\right) \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.5 Proposition. (a) \( \left( {X, Y, Z, T}\right) + \left( {Y, Z, X, T}\right) + \left( {Z, X, Y, T}\right) = 0 \) (b) \( \left( {X, Y, Z, T}\right) = - \left( {Y, X, Z, T}\right) \) (c) \( \left( {X, Y, Z, T}\right) = - \left( {X, Y, T, Z}\right) \) (d) \( \left( {X, Y, Z, T}\right) = \left( {Z, T, X, Y}\right) \) .

nodes.proof:
(a) is just the Bianchi identity again;

(b) follows directly from Definition 2.1;

(c) is equivalent to \( \left( {X, Y, Z, Z}\right)  = 0 \) , whose proof follows:

\[
\left( {X, Y, Z, Z}\right)  = \langle {\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{X}Z - {\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{Y}Z + {\nabla }_{\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }Z, Z\rangle .
\]

But

\[
\langle {\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{X}Z, Z\rangle  = Y\langle {\nabla }_{X}Z, Z\rangle  - \langle {\nabla }_{X}Z,{\nabla }_{Y}Z\rangle ,
\]

and

\[
\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }Z, Z}\right\rangle   = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  \langle Z, Z\rangle .
\]

Hence

\[
\left( {X, Y, Z, Z}\right)  = Y\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}Z, Z}\right\rangle   - X\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Y}Z, Z}\right\rangle   + \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  \langle Z, Z\rangle
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}Y\left( {X\langle Z, Z\rangle }\right)  - \frac{1}{2}X\left( {Y\langle Z, Z\rangle }\right)
\]

\[
+ \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  \langle Z, Z\rangle  =  - \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  \langle Z, Z\rangle
\]

\[
+ \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  \langle Z, Z\rangle  = 0
\]

which proves (c).

In order to prove (d), we use (a), and write:

\[
\left( {X, Y, Z, T}\right)  + \left( {Y, Z, X, T}\right)  + \left( {Z, X, Y, T}\right)  = 0,
\]

\[
\left( {Y, Z, T, X}\right)  + \left( {Z, T, Y, X}\right)  + \left( {T, Y, Z, X}\right)  = 0,
\]

\[
\left( {Z, T, X, Y}\right)  + \left( {T, X, Z, Y}\right)  + \left( {X, Z, T, Y}\right)  = 0,
\]

\[
\left( {T, X, Y, Z}\right)  + \left( {X, Y, T, Z}\right)  + \left( {Y, T, X, Z}\right)  = 0.
\]

Summing the equations above, we obtain

\[
2\left( {Z, X, Y, T}\right)  + 2\left( {T, Y, Z, X}\right)  = 0
\]

and, therefore,

\[
\left( {Z, X, Y, T}\right)  = \left( {Y, T, Z, X}\right)
\]

nodes.label: Remark 2.6
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 2.6 REMARK. The equation (1), which depends on the linearity of the operator \( R \) , shows that the value of \( R\left( {X, Y}\right) Z \) at the point \( p \) depends uniquely on the values of \( X, Y, Z \) at \( p \) and the values of the functions \( {R}_{ijk}^{\ell } \) at \( p \) . Observe that this contrasts with the behavior of the covariant derivative (See Rem. 2.3, Chap. 2), the reason being that the covariant derivative is not linear in all of its arguments. In general, entities, such as the curvature, that are linear, are called tensors on \( M \) (more details will be given in Section 5).

In what follows it is convenient to use the following notation. Given a vector space \( V \) , we denote by \( \left| {x \land  y}\right| \) the expression

\[
\sqrt{{\left| x\right| }^{2}{\left| y\right| }^{2}-\langle x, y{\rangle }^{2}}
\]

which represents the area of a two-dimensional parallelogram determined by the pair of vectors \( x, y \in  V \) .

nodes.content:
3.1 Proposition. Let \( \sigma  \subset  {T}_{p}M \) be a two-dimensional subspace of the tangent space \( {T}_{p}M \) and let \( x, y \in  \sigma \) be two linearly independent vectors. Then

\[
K\left( {x, y}\right)  = \frac{\left( x, y, x, y\right) }{{\left| x \land  y\right| }^{2}}
\]

does not depend on the choice of the vectors \( x, y \in  \sigma \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.1 Proposition. Let \( \sigma \subset {T}_{p}M \) be a two-dimensional subspace of the tangent space \( {T}_{p}M \) and let \( x, y \in \sigma \) be two linearly independent vectors. Then \[ K\left( {x, y}\right) = \frac{\left( x, y, x, y\right) }{{\left| x \land y\right| }^{2}} \] does not depend on the choice of the vectors \( x, y \in \sigma \) .

nodes.proof:
To avoid calculating, we observe that we can pass from the basis \( \{ x, y\} \) of \( \sigma \) to any other basis \( \left\{  {{x}^{\prime },{y}^{\prime }}\right\} \) by iterating the following elementary transformations:

(a) \( \{ x, y\}  \rightarrow  \{ y, x\} \) ,

(b) \( \{ x, y\}  \rightarrow  \{ {\lambda x}, y\} \) ,

(c) \( \{ x, y\}  \rightarrow  \{ x + {\lambda y}, y\} \) .

It is easy to see that \( K\left( {x, y}\right) \) is invariant by such transformations and that completes the proof.

nodes.label: Lemma 3.3
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
3.3 LEMMA. Let \( V \) be a vector space of dimension \( \geq  2 \) , provided with an inner product \( \langle  \cdot  , \cdot  \rangle \) . Let \( R : V \times  V \times  V \rightarrow  V \) and \( {R}^{\prime } : V \times \; V \times  V \rightarrow  V \) be tri-linear mappings such that conditions (a),(b),(c) and (d) of Proposition 2.5 are satisfied by

\[
\left( {x, y, z, t}\right)  = \langle R\left( {x, y}\right) z, t\rangle ,\;{\left( x, y, z, t\right) }^{\prime } = \left\langle  {{R}^{\prime }\left( {x, y}\right) z, t}\right\rangle  .
\]

If \( x, y \) are two linearly independent vectors, we may write,

\[
K\left( \sigma \right)  = \frac{\left( x, y, x, y\right) }{{\left| x \land  y\right| }^{2}},\;{K}^{\prime }\left( \sigma \right)  = \frac{{\left( x, y, x, y\right) }^{\prime }}{{\left| x \land  y\right| }^{2}},
\]

where \( \sigma \) is the bi-dimensional subspace generated by \( x \) and \( y \) . If for all \( \sigma  \subset  V, K\left( \sigma \right)  = {K}^{\prime }\left( \sigma \right) \) , then \( R = {R}^{\prime } \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.3 LEMMA. Let \( V \) be a vector space of dimension \( \geq 2 \) , provided with an inner product \( \langle \cdot , \cdot \rangle \) . Let \( R : V \times V \times V \rightarrow V \) and \( {R}^{\prime } : V \times \; V \times V \rightarrow V \) be tri-linear mappings such that conditions (a),(b),(c) and (d) of Proposition 2.5 are satisfied by \[ \left( {x, y, z, t}\right) = \langle R\left( {x, y}\right) z, t\r...

nodes.proof:
It suffices to prove that \( \left( {x, y, z, t}\right)  = {\left( x, y, z, t\right) }^{\prime } \) for any \( x, y, z, t \in  V \) . Observe first that, by hypothesis, we have \( \left( {x, y, x, y}\right)  = \; {\left( x, y, x, y\right) }^{\prime } \) , for all \( x, y \in  V \) . Then

\[
\left( {x + z, y, x + z, y}\right)  = {\left( x + z, y, x + z, y\right) }^{\prime },
\]

hence

\[
\left( {x, y, x, y}\right)  + 2\left( {x, y, z, y}\right)  + \left( {z, y, z, y}\right)
\]

\[
= {\left( x, y, x, y\right) }^{\prime } + 2{\left( x, y, z, y\right) }^{\prime } + {\left( z, y, z, y\right) }^{\prime }
\]

and, therefore

\[
\left( {x, y, z, y}\right)  = {\left( x, y, z, y\right) }^{\prime },
\]

for all \( x, y, z \in  V \) .

Using what we have just proved, we obtain

\[
\left( {x, y + t, z, y + t}\right)  = {\left( x, y + t, z, y + t\right) }^{\prime },
\]

hence

\[
\left( {x, y, z, t}\right)  + \left( {x, t, z, y}\right)  = {\left( x, y, z, t\right) }^{\prime } + {\left( x, t, z, y\right) }^{\prime },
\]

which can be written further as

\[
\left( {x, y, z, t}\right)  - {\left( x, y, z, t\right) }^{\prime } = \left( {y, z, x, t}\right)  - {\left( y, z, x, t\right) }^{\prime }.
\]

It follows that, the expression \( \left( {x, y, z, t}\right)  - {\left( x, y, z, t\right) }^{\prime } \) is invariant by cyclic permutations of the first three elements. Therefore, by (a) of Proposition 2.5, we have

\[
3\left\lbrack  {\left( {x, y, z, t}\right)  - {\left( x, y, z, t\right) }^{\prime }}\right\rbrack   = 0,
\]

hence

\[
\left( {x, y, z, t}\right)  = {\left( x, y, z, t\right) }^{\prime }
\]

for all \( x, y, z, t \in  V \) .

nodes.content:
3.4 LEMMA. Let \( M \) be a Riemannian manifold and \( p \) a point of \( M \) . Define a tri-linear mapping \( {R}^{\prime } : {T}_{p}M \times  {T}_{p}M \times  {T}_{p}M \rightarrow  {T}_{p}M \) by

\[
\langle {R}^{\prime }\left( {X, Y, W}\right) , Z\rangle  = \langle X, W\rangle \langle Y, Z\rangle  - \langle Y, W\rangle \langle X, Z\rangle ,
\]

for all \( X, Y, W, Z \in  {T}_{p}M \) . Then \( M \) has constant sectional curvature equal to \( {K}_{o} \) if and only if \( R = {K}_{o}{R}^{\prime } \) , where \( R \) is the curvature of \( M \) .

Observe that \( {R}^{\prime } \) satisfies the properties (a), (b), (c) and (d) of Proposition 2.5. Since

\[
{\left( X, Y, X, Y\right) }^{\prime } = \langle X, X\rangle \langle Y, Y\rangle  - \langle X, Y{\rangle }^{2},
\]

we have that, for all pairs of vectors \( X, Y \in  {T}_{p}M \) ,

\[

\]

\[
R\left( {X, Y, W, Z}\right)  = {K}_{o}{R}^{\prime }\left( {X, Y, W, Z}\right) ,
\]

nodes.content:
3.5 COROLLARY. Let \( M \) be a Riemannian manifold, \( p \) a point of \( M \) and \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n}}\right\}  , n = \dim M \) , an orthonormal basis of \( {T}_{p}M \) . Define \( {R}_{{ijk}\ell } = \left\langle  {R\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{j}}\right) {e}_{k},{e}_{\ell }}\right\rangle  , i, j, k,\ell  = 1,\ldots , n \) . Then \( K\left( {p,\sigma }\right)  = {K}_{o} \) for all \( \sigma  \subset  {T}_{p}M \) , if and only if

\[
{R}_{ijkl} = {K}_{o}\left( {{\delta }_{ik}{\delta }_{jl} - {\delta }_{il}{\delta }_{jk}}\right) ,
\]

where

\[
{\delta }_{ij} = \left\{  \begin{array}{ll} 1, & \text{ if }i = j \\  0, & i \neq  j \end{array}\right.
\]

In other words, \( K\left( {p,\sigma }\right)  = {K}_{o} \) for all \( \sigma  \subset  {T}_{p}M \) if and only if \( {R}_{ijij} = \; - {R}_{ijji} = {K}_{o} \) for all \( i \neq  j \) , and \( {R}_{{ijk}\ell } = 0 \) in the other cases.

nodes.title: 4. Ricci curvature and scalar curvature
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry

nodes.label: Definition 4-extra-1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
## 4. Ricci curvature and scalar curvature

Certain combinations of sectional curvature appear with such frequency that they deserve special names.

Let \( x = {z}_{n} \) be a unit vector in \( {T}_{p}M \) ; we take an orthonormal basis \( \left\{  {{z}_{1},{z}_{2},\ldots ,{z}_{n - 1}}\right\} \) of the hyperplane in \( {T}_{p}M \) orthogonal to \( x \) and consider the following averages:

\[
{\operatorname{Ric}}_{p}\left( x\right)  = \frac{1}{n - 1}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}\left\langle  {R\left( {x,{z}_{i}}\right) x,{z}_{i}}\right\rangle  ,\;i = 1,2,\ldots , n - 1,
\]

\[
K\left( p\right)  = \frac{1}{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{p}\left( {z}_{j}\right)  = \frac{1}{n\left( {n - 1}\right) }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{ij}}\left\langle  {R\left( {{z}_{i},{z}_{j}}\right) {z}_{i},{z}_{j}}\right\rangle  ,
\]

\[
j = 1,\ldots , n.
\]

We are going to prove that the expressions above do not depend on the choice of the corresponding orthonormal basis; these expressions are called the Ricci curvature in the direction \( x \) and the scalar curvature at \( p \) , respectively.

To prove these facts, we give an intrinsic characterization of the expressions above. First, define a bilinear form on \( {T}_{p}M \) as follows: let \( x, y \in  {T}_{p}M \) and put

\[
Q\left( {x, y}\right)  = \text{ trace of the mapping }z \mapsto  R\left( {x, z}\right) y\text{ . }
\]

\( Q \) is obviously bilinear. Choosing \( x \) a unit vector and then completing it to an orthonormal basis \( \left\{  {{z}_{1},\ldots ,{z}_{n - 1},{z}_{n} = x}\right\} \) of \( {T}_{p}M \) we have

\[
Q\left( {x, y}\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}\left\langle  {R\left( {x,{z}_{i}}\right) y,{z}_{i}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}\left\langle  {R\left( {y,{z}_{i}}\right) x,{z}_{i}}\right\rangle   = Q\left( {y, x}\right) ,
\]

that is, \( Q \) is symmetric and \( Q\left( {x, x}\right)  = \left( {n - 1}\right) {\operatorname{Ric}}_{p}\left( x\right) \) ; this proves that \( {\operatorname{Ric}}_{p}\left( x\right) \) is intrinsically defined.

On the other hand, the bilinear form \( Q \) on \( {T}_{p}M \) corresponds to a linear self-adjoint mapping \( K \) , given by

\[
\langle K\left( x\right) , y\rangle  = Q\left( {x, y}\right) .
\]

Taking an orthonormal basis \( \left\{  {{z}_{1},\ldots ,{z}_{n}}\right\} \) , we have

\[
\text{ Trace of }K = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}\left\langle  {K\left( {z}_{j}\right) ,{z}_{j}}\right\rangle   = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}Q\left( {{z}_{j},{z}_{j}}\right)
\]

\[
= \left( {n - 1}\right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{p}\left( {z}_{j}\right)  = n\left( {n - 1}\right) K\left( p\right) ,
\]

which proves the statement.

The bilinear form \( \frac{1}{n - 1}Q \) is, at times, called the Ricci tensor.

As usual we should express what was done above in a coordinate system \( \left( {x}_{i}\right) \) . Let \( {X}_{i} = \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}},{g}_{ij} = \left\langle  {{X}_{i},{X}_{j}}\right\rangle \) , and \( {g}^{ij} \) the inverse matrix of \( {g}_{ij} \) (i.e., \( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{k}{g}_{ik}{g}^{k\ell } = {\delta }_{i}^{\ell } \) ). Then the coefficients of the bilinear form \( \frac{1}{n - 1}Q \) in the basis \( \left\{  {X}_{i}\right\} \) are given by

\[
\frac{1}{n - 1}{R}_{ik} = \frac{1}{n - 1}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{R}_{ijk}^{j} = \frac{1}{n - 1}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{sj}}{R}_{ijks}{g}^{sj}.
\]

We observe now that if \( A : {T}_{p}M \rightarrow  {T}_{p}M \) is a linear self-adjoint mapping and \( B : {T}_{p}M \times  {T}_{p}M \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) is the associated bilinear form, i.e., \( B\left( {X, Y}\right)  = \langle A\left( X\right) , Y\rangle \) , then the trace of \( A \) is equal to \( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{ik}}B\left( {{X}_{i},{X}_{k}}\right) {g}^{ik} \) . Thus, the scalar curvature in the coordinate system \( \left( {x}_{i}\right) \) is given by

\[
K = \frac{1}{n\left( {n - 1}\right) }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{ik}}{R}_{ik}{g}^{ik}.
\]

nodes.proof:
The proof is a long calculation. Choose a system of coordinates \( \left( {U,\mathbf{x}}\right) \) based at \( p \in  M \) . Let \( V = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{v}^{i}{X}_{i} \) , where \( {v}^{i} = {v}^{i}\left( {s, t}\right) \) e \( {X}_{i} = \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}} \) . Then

\[
\frac{D}{\partial s}V = \frac{D}{\partial s}\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{v}^{i}{X}_{i}}\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{v}^{i}\frac{D}{\partial s}{X}_{i} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}\frac{\partial {v}^{i}}{\partial s}{X}_{i},
\]

and

\[
\frac{D}{\partial t}\left( {\frac{D}{\partial s}V}\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{v}^{i}\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{D}{\partial s}{X}_{i} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}\frac{\partial {v}^{i}}{\partial t}\frac{D}{\partial s}{X}_{i}
\]

\[
+ \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}\frac{\partial {v}^{i}}{\partial s}\frac{D}{\partial t}{X}_{i} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}\frac{{\partial }^{2}{v}^{i}}{\partial t\partial s}{X}_{i}
\]

Therefore, interchanging the roles of \( s \) and \( t \) in the expression above, and subtracting, we obtain

\[
\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{D}{\partial s}V - \frac{D}{\partial s}\frac{D}{\partial t}V = \sum {v}^{i}\left( {\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{D}{\partial s}{X}_{i} - \frac{D}{\partial s}\frac{D}{\partial t}{X}_{i}}\right) .
\]

Let us now calculate \( \frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{D}{\partial s}{X}_{i} \) . Put

\[
f\left( {s, t}\right)  = \left( {{x}_{1}\left( {s, t}\right) ,\ldots ,{x}_{n}\left( {s, t}\right) }\right) .
\]

Then \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial s} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}\frac{\partial {x}_{j}}{\partial s}{X}_{j} \) and \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{k}\frac{\partial {x}_{k}}{\partial t}{X}_{k} \) . Thus, we have

\[
\frac{D}{\partial s}{X}_{i} = {\nabla }_{{\sum }_{j}\left( {\partial {x}_{j}/\partial s}\right) {X}_{j}}\left( {X}_{i}\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}\frac{\partial {x}_{j}}{\partial s}{\nabla }_{{X}_{j}}{X}_{i}
\]

and

\[
\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{D}{\partial s}{X}_{i} = \frac{D}{\partial t}\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}\frac{\partial {x}_{j}}{\partial s}{\nabla }_{{X}_{j}}{X}_{i}}\right)
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}\frac{{\partial }^{2}{x}_{j}}{\partial t\partial s}{\nabla }_{{X}_{j}}{X}_{i} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}\frac{\partial {x}_{j}}{\partial s}{\nabla }_{{\sum }_{k}\left( {\partial {x}_{k}/\partial t}\right) {X}_{k}}\left( {{\nabla }_{{X}_{j}}{X}_{i}}\right)
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}\frac{{\partial }^{2}{x}_{j}}{\partial t\partial s}{\nabla }_{{X}_{j}}{X}_{i} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{jk}}\frac{\partial {x}_{j}}{\partial s}\frac{\partial {x}_{k}}{\partial t}{\nabla }_{{X}_{k}}{\nabla }_{{X}_{j}}{X}_{i},
\]

or

\[
\left( {\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{D}{\partial s} - \frac{D}{\partial s}\frac{D}{\partial t}}\right) {X}_{i} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{jk}}\frac{\partial {x}_{j}}{\partial s}\frac{\partial {x}_{k}}{\partial t}\left( {{\nabla }_{{X}_{k}}{\nabla }_{{X}_{j}}{X}_{i} - {\nabla }_{{X}_{j}}{\nabla }_{{X}_{k}}{X}_{i}}\right) .
\]

Joining everything together, we finally get

\[
\left( {\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{D}{\partial s} - \frac{D}{\partial s}\frac{D}{\partial t}}\right) V = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{ijk}}{v}^{i}\frac{\partial {x}_{j}}{\partial s}\frac{\partial {x}_{k}}{\partial t}R\left( {{X}_{j},{X}_{k}}\right) {X}_{i}
\]

\[
= R\left( {\frac{\partial f}{\partial s},\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}}\right) V
\]

nodes.title: 4.5. Tensors on Riemannian manifolds
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry

nodes.label: Definition 5.1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
5.1 DEFINITION. A tensor \( T \) of order \( r \) on a Riemannian manifold is a multilinear mapping

\[
T : \underset{r\;\text{ factors }}{\underbrace{\mathcal{X}\left( M\right)  \times  \cdots  \times  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) }} \rightarrow  \mathcal{D}\left( M\right) .
\]

This means that given \( {Y}_{1},\ldots ,{Y}_{r} \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) , T\left( {{Y}_{1},\ldots ,{Y}_{r}}\right) \) , is a differentiable function on \( M \) , and that \( T \) is linear in each argument, that is,

\[
T\left( {{Y}_{1},\ldots ,{fX} + {gY},\ldots ,{Y}_{r}}\right)  = {fT}\left( {{Y}_{1},\ldots , X,\ldots ,{Y}_{r}}\right)
\]

\[
+ {gT}\left( {{Y}_{1},\ldots , Y,\ldots ,{Y}_{r}}\right) ,
\]

for all \( X, Y \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) , f, g \in  \mathcal{D}\left( M\right) \) .

A tensor \( T \) is a pointwise object in a sense that we now explain. Fix a point \( p \in  M \) and let \( U \) be a neighborhood of \( p \) in \( M \) on which it is possible to define vector fields \( {E}_{1}\ldots ,{E}_{n} \in  \mathcal{X}\left( {M}^{n}\right) \) , in such a fashion that at each \( q \in  U \) , the vectors \( \left\{  {{E}_{i}\left( q\right) }\right\}  , i = 1,\ldots , n \) , form a basis of \( {T}_{q}M \) ; we say, in this case, that \( \left\{  {E}_{i}\right\} \) is a moving frame on \( U \) . Let

\[
{Y}_{1} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i}_{1}}{y}_{{i}_{1}}{E}_{{i}_{1}},\ldots ,{Y}_{r} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i}_{r}}{y}_{{i}_{r}}{E}_{{i}_{r}},\;{i}_{1},\ldots ,{i}_{r} = 1,\ldots , n,
\]

be the restrictions to \( U \) of the vector fields \( {Y}_{1},\ldots ,{Y}_{r} \) , expressed in the moving frame \( \left\{  {E}_{i}\right\} \) . By linearity,

\[
T\left( {{Y}_{1},\ldots ,{Y}_{r}}\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{{i}_{1},\ldots ,{i}_{r}}}{y}_{{i}_{1}}\ldots {y}_{{i}_{r}}T\left( {{E}_{{i}_{1}},\ldots ,{E}_{{i}_{r}}}\right) .
\]

The functions \( T\left( {{E}_{{i}_{1}},\ldots ,{E}_{{i}_{r}}}\right)  = {T}_{{i}_{1}\ldots {i}_{r}} \) on \( U \) are called the components of \( T \) in the frame \( \left\{  {E}_{i}\right\} \) .

The expression above implies that the value of \( T\left( {{Y}_{1},\ldots ,{Y}_{r}}\right) \) at a point \( p \in  M \) depends only on the values at \( p \) of the components of \( T \) , and the values of \( {Y}_{1},\ldots ,{Y}_{r} \) at \( p \) . It is in this sense that we say that \( T \) is a pointwise object.

5.2 EXAMPLE. The curvature tensor

R : \mathcal{X}\left( M\right)  \times  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right)  \times  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right)  \times  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right)  \rightarrow  \mathcal{D}\left( M\right)

\[

\]

It is easy to verify that \( R \) is a tensor of order 4, whose components in the frame \( \left\{  {{X}_{i} = \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}_{i}}}\right\} \) associated with the system of coordinates \( \left( {x}_{i}\right) \) is

\[
R\left( {{X}_{i},{X}_{j},{X}_{k},{X}_{\ell }}\right)  = {R}_{{ijk}\ell }.
\]

nodes.label: Remark 5.5
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
5.5 REMARK. It is possible to define the notion of a tensor on a differentiable manifold which does not have a Riemannian metric. In this case, it is necessary to distinguish the covariant tensors (which we have already defined) from the contravariant tensors (which can be defined in an analogous manner, using in place of \( \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) its dual \( {\mathcal{X}}^{ * }\left( M\right) ) \) . On a Riemannian manifold this is unnecessary, because the Riemannian metric associates to each \( X \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) a unique element \( \omega  \in  {\mathcal{X}}^{ * }\left( M\right) \) given by

\[
\omega \left( Y\right)  = \langle X, Y\rangle ,\;\text{ for all }\;Y \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) .
\]

Such a correspondence allows us to identify the contravariant tensors with the covariant tensors. For reasons of economy, we restrict ourselves to covariant tensors.

nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
5.7 Definition. Let \( T \) be a tensor of order \( r \) . The covariant differential \( \nabla T \) of \( T \) is a tensor of order \( \left( {r + 1}\right) \) given by

\[
\nabla T\left( {{Y}_{1},\ldots ,{Y}_{r}, Z}\right)  = Z\left( {T\left( {{Y}_{1},\ldots ,{Y}_{r}}\right) }\right)  - T\left( {{\nabla }_{Z}{Y}_{1},\ldots ,{Y}_{r}}\right)
\]

\[
- \cdots  - T\left( {{Y}_{1},\ldots ,{Y}_{r - 1},{\nabla }_{Z}{Y}_{r}}\right)
\]

For each \( Z \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) , the covariant derivative \( {\nabla }_{Z}T \) of \( T \) relative to \( Z \) is a tensor of order \( r \) given by

\[
{\nabla }_{Z}T\left( {{Y}_{1},\ldots ,{Y}_{r}}\right)  = \nabla T\left( {{Y}_{1},\ldots ,{Y}_{r}, Z}\right) .
\]

We are going to show that, in a convenient frame, the definition of the covariant derivative of a tensor \( T \) relative to \( Z \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) becomes quite natural. For this, let \( p \in  M \) and let \( \alpha  : \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)  \rightarrow  M \) be a differentiable curve with \( \alpha \left( 0\right)  = p,{\alpha }^{\prime }\left( t\right)  = Z\left( {\alpha \left( t\right) }\right) \) . Let \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n}}\right\} \) be a basis of \( {T}_{p}M \) and let \( {e}_{i}\left( t\right) \) be the parallel transport of \( {e}_{i} \) along \( \alpha  = \alpha \left( t\right) \) , for \( i = 1,\ldots , n \) . Let \( {T}_{{i}_{1}\ldots {i}_{r}}\left( t\right) \) be the components, in the basis \( \left\{  {{e}_{i}\left( t\right) }\right\} \) , of the restriction \( T\left( {\alpha \left( t\right) }\right) \) of \( T \) to the curve \( \alpha \) . Then, by the definition of \( {\nabla }_{Z}T \) ,

\[
\left( {{\nabla }_{Z}T}\right) \left( {{e}_{{i}_{1}}\left( t\right) ,\ldots ,{e}_{{i}_{r}}\left( t\right) }\right)  = \frac{d}{dt}{T}_{{i}_{1}\ldots {i}_{r}}\left( t\right)  - T\left( {{\nabla }_{Z}{e}_{{i}_{1}}\left( t\right) ,\ldots ,{e}_{{i}_{r}}\left( t\right) }\right) \tag{t}
\]

\[
\left. {-\cdots  - T\left( {{e}_{{i}_{1}}\left( t\right) ,\ldots ,{\nabla }_{Z}{e}_{{i}_{r}}\left( t\right) }\right) }\right) .
\]

Since \( {\nabla }_{Z}{e}_{i}\left( t\right)  = 0 \) , we have, by linearity,

\[
{\left( {\nabla }_{Z}T\right) }_{{i}_{1}\ldots {i}_{r}} = \left( {{\nabla }_{Z}T}\right) \left( {{e}_{{i}_{1}}\left( t\right) ,\ldots ,{e}_{{i}_{r}}\left( t\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{d}{dt}{T}_{{i}_{1}\ldots {i}_{r}}.
\]

In other words, in this frame, the components of the covariant derivative of \( T \) are the usual derivatives of the components of \( T \) .

nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
5.8 EXAMPLE. The covariant differential of the metric tensor is the zero tensor. Indeed, for all \( X, Y, Z \in  \mathcal{K}\left( M\right) \) ,

\[
\nabla G\left( {X, Y, Z}\right)  = Z\langle X, Y\rangle  - \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}X, Y}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {X,{\nabla }_{Z}Y}\right\rangle   = 0,
\]

because \( \nabla \) is the Riemannian connection.

nodes.label: Example 5.9
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
5.9 EXAMPLE. Let \( X \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) . Identify \( X \) with the tensor that associates to the vector field \( Y \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) the function \( \langle X, Y\rangle \) (See Rem. 5.6). The covariant derivative of the tensor \( X \) relative to the vector field \( Z \in  \mathcal{K}\left( M\right) \) is such that, for all \( Y \in  \mathcal{K}\left( M\right) \) ,

\[
{\nabla }_{Z}X\left( Y\right)  = \nabla X\left( {Y, Z}\right)  = Z\left( {X\left( Y\right) }\right)  - X\left( {{\nabla }_{Z}Y}\right)
\]

\[
= Z\langle X, Y\rangle  - \left\langle  {X,{\nabla }_{Z}Y}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}X, Y}\right\rangle  .
\]

We conclude thus that the tensor \( {\nabla }_{Z}X \) can be identified with the vector field \( {\nabla }_{Z}X \) . This justifies the notation adopted, and shows that the covariant derivative of tensors is a generalization of the covariant derivative of vector fields.

1. Let \( G \) be a Lie group with a bi-invariant metric \( \langle \) , \( \rangle .{Let} \; X, Y, Z \in  \mathcal{K}\left( G\right) \) be unit left invariant vector fields on \( G \) .

a) Show that \( {\nabla }_{X}Y = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack \) .

Hint: Use the symmetry of the connection and the fact that \( {\nabla }_{X}X = 0 \) (Cf. Exercise 3 of Chap. 3).

b) Conclude from (a) that \( R\left( {X, Y}\right) Z = \frac{1}{4}\left\lbrack  {\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  , Z}\right\rbrack \) .

c) Prove that, if \( X \) and \( Y \) are orthonormal, the sectional curvature \( K\left( \sigma \right) \) of \( G \) with respect to the plane \( \sigma \) generated by \( X \) and \( Y \) is given by

\[
K\left( \sigma \right)  = \frac{1}{4}\parallel \left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  {\parallel }^{2}.
\]

Therefore, the sectional curvature \( K\left( \sigma \right) \) of a Lie group with bi-invariant metric is non-negative and is zero if and only if \( \sigma \) is generated by vectors \( X, Y \) which commute, that is, such that \( \left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack   = 0. \)

2. Let \( X \) be a Killing field (See Exercise 5 of Chap. 3) on a Riemannian manifold \( M \) . Define a mapping \( {A}_{X} : \mathcal{X}\left( M\right)  \rightarrow  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) by \( {A}_{X}\left( Z\right)  = {\nabla }_{Z}X, Z \in  \mathcal{K}\left( M\right) \) . Consider the function \( f : M \rightarrow  R \) given by \( f\left( q\right)  = \langle X, X{\rangle }_{q}, q \in  M \) . Let \( p \in  M \) be a critical point of \( f \) (that is, \( d{f}_{p} = 0 \) ). Prove that for any \( Z \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) , at \( p \)

a) \( \left\langle  {{A}_{X}\left( Z\right) , X}\right\rangle  \left( p\right)  = 0 \) .

b) \( \left\langle  {{A}_{X}\left( Z\right) ,{A}_{X}\left( Z\right) }\right\rangle  \left( p\right)  = \frac{1}{2}{Z}_{p}\left( {Z\langle X, X\rangle }\right)  + \langle R\left( {X, Z}\right) X, Z\rangle \) . Hint for (b): Put \( S = \frac{1}{2}{ZZ}\langle X, X\rangle  - \langle R\left( {X, Z}\right) X, Z\rangle \) .

Using the Killing equation \( \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}X, X}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}X, Z}\right\rangle   = 0 \) (cf. Exercise 5 of Chap. 3), we obtain

\[
S = \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{\left\lbrack  X, Z\right\rbrack  }X, Z}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}X,{\nabla }_{Z}Z}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{Z}, Z}\right\rangle  .
\]

Using the Killing equation again, we obtain

\[
S =  - \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}X,{\nabla }_{X}Z}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}X,{\nabla }_{Z}X}\right\rangle
\]

\[
+ \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}X,{\nabla }_{X}Z}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}X,{\nabla }_{Z}Z}\right\rangle
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}X,{\nabla }_{Z}X}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}X,{\nabla }_{Z}Z}\right\rangle  .
\]

Because of the Killing equation at \( p,{\nabla }_{X}X\left( p\right)  = 0 \) , and we conclude the assertion.

Let \( E \subset  {T}_{p}M \) be orthogonal to \( X\left( p\right) \) . Use the previous exercise to show that \( A : E \rightarrow  E \) is an antisymmetric isomorphism. This implies that \( \dim E = \dim M - 1 \) is even, which is a contradiction; thus \( X\left( p\right)  = 0 \) .

4. Let \( M \) be a Riemannian manifold with the following property: given any two points \( p, q \in  M \) , the parallel transport from \( p \) to \( q \) does not depend on the curve that joins \( p \) to \( q \) . Prove that the curvature of \( M \) is identically zero, that is, for all \( X, Y, Z \in \; \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) , R\left( {X, Y}\right) Z = 0 \) .

Hint: Consider a parametrized surface \( f : U \subset  {R}^{2} \rightarrow  M \) , where

\[
U = \left\{  {\left( {s, t}\right)  \in  {R}^{2}; - \varepsilon  < t < 1 + \varepsilon , - \varepsilon  < s < 1 + \varepsilon ,\varepsilon  > 0}\right\}
\]

and \( f\left( {s,0}\right)  = f\left( {0,0}\right) \) , for all \( s \) . Let \( {V}_{o} \in  {T}_{f\left( {0,0}\right) }\left( M\right) \) and define a field \( V \) along \( f \) by: \( V\left( {s,0}\right)  = {V}_{o} \) and, if \( t \neq  0, V\left( {s, t}\right) \) is the parallel transport of \( {V}_{o} \) along the curve \( t \rightarrow  f\left( {s, t}\right) \) . Then, from Lemma 4.1,

\[
\frac{D}{\partial s}\frac{D}{\partial t}V = 0 = \frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{D}{\partial s}V + R\left( {\frac{\partial f}{\partial t},\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}}\right) V.
\]

Since parallel transport does not depend on the curve chosen, \( V\left( {s,1}\right) \) is the parallel transport of \( V\left( {0,1}\right) \) along the curve \( s \rightarrow \; f\left( {s,1}\right) \) , hence \( \frac{D}{\partial s}V\left( {s,1}\right)  = 0 \) . Thus,

\[
{R}_{f\left( {0,1}\right) }\left( {\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\left( {0,1}\right) ,\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {0,1}\right) }\right) V\left( {0,1}\right)  = 0.
\]

Use the arbitrariness of \( f \) and \( {V}_{o} \) to conclude what is required.

7. Prove the 2nd Bianchi Identity:

\[
\nabla R\left( {X, Y, Z, W, T}\right)  + \nabla R\left( {X, Y, W, T, Z}\right)  + \nabla R\left( {X, Y, T, Z, W}\right)  = 0
\]

for all \( X, Y, Z, W, T \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) .

Hint: Since the objects involved are all tensors, it suffices to prove the equality at a point \( p \in  M \) . Choose a geodesic frame \( \left\{  {e}_{i}\right\} \) based at \( p \) (See Exercise 7 of Chap. 3). In this frame \( {\nabla }_{{e}_{i}}{e}_{j}\left( p\right)  = 0 \) , hence

\[
\nabla R\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{j},{e}_{k},{e}_{\ell },{e}_{h}}\right)  = {e}_{h}\left\langle  {R\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{j}}\right) {e}_{k},{e}_{\ell }}\right\rangle   = {e}_{h}\left\langle  {R\left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{\ell }}\right) {e}_{i},{e}_{j}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{{e}_{h}}{\nabla }_{{e}_{\ell }}{\nabla }_{{e}_{k}}{e}_{i} - {\nabla }_{{e}_{h}}{\nabla }_{{e}_{k}}{\nabla }_{{e}_{\ell }}{e}_{i} + {\nabla }_{{e}_{h}}{\nabla }_{\left\lbrack  {e}_{k},{e}_{\ell }\right\rbrack  }{e}_{i},{e}_{j}}\right\rangle  .
\]

Therefore, using the Jacobi identity for the bracket, we find

\[
\nabla R\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{j},{e}_{k},{e}_{\ell },{e}_{h}}\right)  + \nabla R\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{j},{e}_{\ell },{e}_{h},{e}_{k}}\right)
\]

\[
+ \nabla R\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{j},{e}_{h},{e}_{k},{e}_{\ell }}\right)  = R\left( {{e}_{\ell },{e}_{h},{\nabla }_{{e}_{k}}{e}_{i},{e}_{j}}\right)
\]

\[
+ R\left( {{e}_{h},{e}_{k},{\nabla }_{{e}_{\ell }}{e}_{i},{e}_{j}}\right)  + R\left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{\ell },{\nabla }_{{e}_{h}}{e}_{i},{e}_{j}}\right)  = 0,
\]

since each one of the summands vanishes at \( p \) . The general case follows by linearity.

8. (Schur’s Theorem). Let \( {M}^{n} \) be a connected Riemannian manifold with \( n \geq  3 \) . Suppose that \( M \) is isotropic, that is, for each \( p \in  M \) , the sectional curvature \( K\left( {p,\sigma }\right) \) does not depend on \( \sigma  \subset  {T}_{p}M \) . Prove that \( M \) has constant sectional curvature, that is, \( K\left( {p,\sigma }\right) \) also does not depend on \( p \) .

Hint: Define a tensor \( {R}^{\prime } \) of order 4 by

\[
{R}^{\prime }\left( {W, Z, X, Y}\right)  = \langle W, X\rangle \langle Z, Y\rangle  - \langle Z, X\rangle \langle W, Y\rangle .
\]

If \( K\left( {p,\sigma }\right)  = K \) does not depend on \( \sigma \) , by Lemma 3.4, \( R = K{R}^{\prime } \) . Therefore, for all \( U \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) ,{\nabla }_{U}R = \left( {UK}\right) {R}^{\prime } \) . Using the 2nd Bianchi identity (see Exercise 7):

\[
\nabla R\left( {W, Z, X, Y, U}\right)  + \nabla R\left( {W, Z, Y, U, X}\right)
\]

\[
+ \nabla R\left( {W, Z, U, X, Y}\right)  = 0,
\]

we obtain, for all \( X, Y, W, Z, U \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) ,

\[
0 = \left( {UK}\right) \left( {\langle W, X\rangle \langle Z, Y\rangle -\langle Z, X\rangle \langle W, Y\rangle }\right)
\]

\[
+ \left( {XK}\right) \left( {\langle W, Y\rangle \langle Z, U\rangle  - \langle Z, Y\rangle \langle W, U\rangle }\right)
\]

\[
+ \left( {YK}\right) \left( {\langle W, U\rangle \langle Z, X\rangle -\langle Z, U\rangle \langle W, X\rangle }\right) .
\]

Fix \( p \in  M \) . Because \( n \geq  3 \) , it is possible, fixing \( X \) at \( p \) , to choose \( Y \) and \( Z \) at \( p \) such that \( \langle X, Y\rangle  = \langle Y, Z\rangle  = \langle Z, X\rangle  = 0 \) , \( \langle Z, Z\rangle  = 1 \) . Put \( U = Z \) at \( p \) . The relation above yields, for all \( W \)

\[
\langle \left( {XK}\right) Y - \left( {YK}\right) X, W\rangle  = 0.
\]

Since \( X \) and \( Y \) are linearly independent at \( p \) , we conclude that \( {XK} = 0 \) for all \( X \in  {T}_{p}M \) . Thus \( K = \) const.

9. Prove that the scalar curvature \( K\left( p\right) \) at \( p \in  M \) is given by

\[
K\left( p\right)  = \frac{1}{{\omega }_{n - 1}}{\int }_{{S}^{n - 1}}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{p}\left( x\right) d{S}^{n - 1},
\]

where \( {\omega }_{n - 1} \) is the area of the sphere \( {S}^{n - 1} \) in \( {T}_{p}M \) and \( d{S}^{n - 1} \) is the area elements on \( {S}^{n - 1} \) .

Hint: Use the following general argument on quadratic forms. Consider an orthonormal basis \( {e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n} \) in \( {T}_{p}M \) such that if \( x = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{x}_{i}{e}_{i} \)

\[
{\operatorname{Ric}}_{p}\left( x\right)  = \sum {\lambda }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2},\;{\lambda }_{i}\text{ real. }
\]

Because \( \left| x\right|  = 1 \) , the vector \( \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right)  = \nu \) is a unit normal vector on \( {S}^{n - 1} \) . Denoting \( V = \left( {{\lambda }_{1}{x}_{1},\ldots ,{\lambda }_{n}{x}_{n}}\right) \) , and using Stokes Theorem, we obtain

\[
\frac{1}{{\omega }_{n - 1}}{\int }_{{S}^{n - 1}}\left( {\sum {\lambda }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}}\right) d{S}^{n - 1} = \frac{1}{{\omega }_{n - 1}}{\int }_{{S}^{n - 1}}\langle V,\nu \rangle d{S}^{n - 1}
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{{\omega }_{n - 1}}{\int }_{{B}^{n}}\operatorname{div}{Vd}{B}^{n}
\]

where \( {B}^{n} \) is the unit ball whose boundary is \( {S}^{n - 1} = \partial {B}^{n} \) . Noting that vol \( {B}^{n}/{\omega }_{n} = 1/n \) , we conclude that

\[
\frac{1}{{\omega }_{n - 1}}{\int }_{{S}^{n - 1}}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{p}\left( x\right) d{S}^{n - 1} = \frac{1}{n}\operatorname{div}V = \frac{\sum {\lambda }_{i}}{n}
\]

\[
= \frac{\sum {\operatorname{Ric}}_{p}\left( {e}_{i}\right) }{n} = K\left( p\right) .
\]

10. (Einstein manifolds). A Riemannian manifold \( {M}^{n} \) is called an Einstein manifold if, for all \( X, Y \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) ,\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, Y}\right)  = \; \lambda \langle X, Y\rangle \) , where \( \lambda  : M \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) is a real valued function. Prove that:

a) If \( {M}^{n} \) is connected and Einstein, with \( n \geq  3 \) , then \( \lambda \) is constant on \( M \) .

b) If \( {M}^{3} \) is a connected Einstein manifold then \( {M}^{3} \) has constant sectional curvature.

Hint for (a): Consider a geodesic orthonormal frame \( \left\{  {e}_{i}\right\} \) , \( i = 1,\ldots , n \geq  3 \) , at a point \( p \in  M \) (see Exercise 7 of Chap. 3). The 2nd Bianchi identity (see Exercise 7) at \( p \) can be written

(*)

\[
{e}_{s}\left( {R}_{\text{ hijk }}\right)  + {e}_{j}\left( {R}_{\text{ hiks }}\right)  + {e}_{k}\left( {R}_{\text{ hish }}\right)  = 0,
\]

where \( {R}_{hijk} \) are the components of the curvature tensor in this frame and we take into account that \( {\nabla }_{{e}_{i}}{e}_{j}\left( p\right)  = 0 \) . Observe that \( \left\langle  {{e}_{i},{e}_{k}}\right\rangle   = {g}_{ik} = {\delta }_{ik} = {\delta }^{ik} \) . Multiplying (*) by \( {\delta }_{ik}{\delta }_{hj} \) and summing on \( i, k, h, j \) , we obtain: for the first part,

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{ikjh}}{\delta }_{hj}{\delta }_{ik}{e}_{s}\left( {R}_{hijk}\right)  = {e}_{s}\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{ikjh}}{\delta }_{hj}{\delta }_{ik}{R}_{hijk}}\right)
\]

\[
= {e}_{s}\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{hj}}{\delta }_{hj}{R}_{hj}}\right)  = {e}_{s}\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{hj}}{\delta }_{hj}\left( {\lambda {\delta }_{hj}}\right) }\right)  = n{e}_{s}\left( \lambda \right)
\]

for the second part,

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{ikjh}}{\delta }_{hj}{\delta }_{ik}{e}_{j}\left( {R}_{hiks}\right)  =  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{jh}}{\delta }_{hj}{e}_{j}\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{ik}}{\delta }_{ik}{R}_{hisk}}\right)
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{jh}}{\delta }_{hj}{e}_{j}\left( {\lambda {\delta }_{hs}}\right)  =  - {e}_{s}\left( \lambda \right)
\]

Exercises 109 and for the third part,

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{ikjh}}{\delta }_{hj}{\delta }_{ik}{e}_{k}\left( {R}_{hiks}\right)  =  - {e}_{s}\left( \lambda \right)
\]

Therefore,(*) implies that, for all \( s,\left( {n - 2}\right) {e}_{s}\left( \lambda \right)  = 0 \) . From the arbitrariness of \( p,\lambda \) is constant on \( M \) .

nodes.title: 5.2. The Jacobi equation
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry

nodes.label: Definition 2.1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.1 Definition. Let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) be a geodesic in \( M \) . A vector field \( J \) along \( \gamma \) is said to be a Jacobi field if it satisfies the Jacobi equation (1), for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack \) .

A Jacobi field is determined by its initial conditions \( J\left( 0\right) \) , \( \frac{DJ}{dt}\left( 0\right) \) . Indeed, let \( {e}_{1}\left( t\right) ,\ldots ,{e}_{n}\left( t\right) \) be parallel, orthonormal fields along \( \gamma \) . We shall write:

\[
J\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}\left( t\right) {e}_{i}\left( t\right) ,\;{a}_{ij} = \left\langle  {R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) ,{e}_{i}\left( t\right) }\right) {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) ,{e}_{j}\left( t\right) }\right\rangle  ,
\]

112 Jacobi fields

\[
i, j = 1,\ldots , n = \dim M.
\]

Then

\[
\frac{{D}^{2}J}{d{t}^{2}} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}^{\prime \prime }\left( t\right) {e}_{i}\left( t\right)
\]

and

\[
R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }, J}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime } = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}\left\langle  {R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }, J}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime },{e}_{j}}\right\rangle  {e}_{j}
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{ij}}{f}_{i}\left\langle  {R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime },{e}_{i}}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime },{e}_{j}}\right\rangle  {e}_{j} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{ij}}{f}_{i}{a}_{ij}{e}_{j}.
\]

Therefore, the equation (1) is equivalent to the system

\[
{f}_{j}^{\prime \prime }\left( t\right)  + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{a}_{ij}\left( t\right) {f}_{i}\left( t\right)  = 0,\;j = 1,\ldots , n,
\]

which is a linear system of the second order. Hence, given the initial conditions \( J\left( 0\right) ,\frac{DJ}{dt}\left( 0\right) \) , there exists a \( {C}^{\infty } \) solution of the system, defined on \( \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack \) . There exist, therefore, \( {2n} \) linearly independent Jacobi fields along \( \gamma \) .

2.3 EXAMPLE. (Jacobi fields on manifolds of constant curvature). Let \( M \) be a Riemannian manifold of constant sectional curvature \( K \) , and let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) be a normalized geodesic on \( M \) . Further let \( J \) be a Jacobi field along \( \gamma \) , normal to \( {\gamma }^{\prime } \) . We claim that from the fact that \( \left| {\gamma }^{\prime }\right|  = 1 \) and from Lemma 3.4 of Chapter 4, it follows that

\[
R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }, J}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime } = {KJ}.
\]

Indeed, for all vector fields \( T \) along \( \gamma \) we have

\[
\left\langle  {R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }, J}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime }, T}\right\rangle   = K\left\{  {\left\langle  {{\gamma }^{\prime },{\gamma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle  \langle J, T\rangle  - \left\langle  {{\gamma }^{\prime }, T}\right\rangle  \left\langle  {J,{\gamma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle  }\right\}
\]

\[
= K\langle J, T\rangle
\]

which was asserted.

As a result, the Jacobi equation can be written as

(2)

\[
\frac{{D}^{2}J}{d{t}^{2}} + {KJ} = 0.
\]

Let \( w\left( t\right) \) be a parallel field along \( \gamma \) with \( \left\langle  {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) , w\left( t\right) }\right\rangle   = 0 \) and \( \left| {w\left( t\right) }\right|  = \) 1. It is easy to verify that

\[
J\left( t\right)  = \left\{  \begin{array}{ll} \frac{\sin \left( {t\sqrt{K}}\right) }{\sqrt{K}}w\left( t\right) , & \text{ if }K > 0, \\  {tw}\left( t\right) , & \text{ if }K = 0, \\  \frac{\sinh \left( {t\sqrt{-K}}\right) }{\sqrt{-K}}w\left( t\right) , & \text{ if }K < 0, \end{array}\right.
\]

is a solution of (2) with initial conditions \( J\left( 0\right)  = 0,{J}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = w\left( 0\right) \) .

As we saw previously, given \( p \in  M, v \in  {T}_{p}M \) , and \( w \in \; {T}_{v}\left( {{T}_{p}M}\right) \) , we can construct a Jacobi field along the geodesic \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) , given by \( \gamma \left( t\right)  = {\exp }_{p}{tv} \) . For that, we consider the parametrized surface given by \( f\left( {t, s}\right)  = {\exp }_{p}{tv}\left( s\right) \) , where \( v\left( s\right) \) is a curve in \( {T}_{p}M \) with \( v\left( 0\right)  = v,{v}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = w \) , and take \( J\left( t\right)  = \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {t,0}\right) \) . Notice that \( J\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) .

We are going to show that this is essentially the only way of constructing Jacobi fields along \( \gamma \left( t\right) \) with \( J\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) . More precisely, we have the following proposition.

2.11 REMARK. The expression (6) essentially contains the relation between geodesics and curvature, mentioned in the beginning of this chapter. Indeed, considering the parametrized surface

\[
f\left( {t, s}\right)  = {\exp }_{p}{tv}\left( s\right) ,\;t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\delta }\right\rbrack  ,\;s \in  \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right) ,
\]

where \( \delta \) is chosen so small that \( {\exp }_{p}{tv}\left( s\right) \) is defined, and \( v\left( s\right) \) is a curve in \( {T}_{p}M \) with \( \left| {v\left( s\right) }\right|  = 1, v\left( 0\right)  = v,{v}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = w \) , we see that the rays \( t \rightarrow  {tv}\left( s\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\delta }\right\rbrack \) , that start from the origin 0 of \( {T}_{p}M \) , deviate from the ray \( t \rightarrow  {tv}\left( 0\right) \) with the velocity

\[
\left| {\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial s}{tv}\left( s\right) }\right) \left( 0\right) }\right|  = \left| {tw}\right|  = t
\]

On the other hand,(6) tells us that the geodesics \( t \rightarrow  {\exp }_{p}\left( {{tv}\left( s\right) }\right) \) deviate from the geodesic \( \gamma \left( t\right)  = {\exp }_{p}{tv}\left( 0\right) \) with a velocity that differs from \( t \) by a term of the third order in \( t \) , given by \( - \frac{1}{6}K\left( {p,\sigma }\right) {t}^{3} \) . This tells us that, locally, the geodesics spread apart less than the rays in \( {T}_{p}M \) , if \( {K}_{p}\left( \sigma \right)  > 0 \) , and that they spread apart more than the rays in \( {T}_{p}M \) , if \( {K}_{p}\left( \sigma \right)  < 0 \) . Actually, for \( t \) small, the value \( K\left( {p,\sigma }\right) {t}^{3} \) furnishes an approximation for the extent of this spread with an error of order \( {t}^{3} \) .

3.1 Definition. Let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) be a geodesic. The point \( \gamma \left( {t}_{o}\right) \) is said to be conjugate to \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) along \( \gamma ,{t}_{o} \in  (0, a\rbrack \) , if there exists a Jacobi field \( J \) along \( \gamma \) , not identically zero, with \( J\left( 0\right)  = 0 = J\left( {t}_{o}\right) \) . The maximum number of such linearly independent fields is called the multiplicity of the conjugate point \( \gamma \left( {t}_{o}\right) \) .

Observe that if \( \gamma \left( {t}_{o}\right) \) is conjugate to \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) , then \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) is conjugate to \( \gamma \left( {t}_{o}\right) \) .

nodes.content: 3.2 REMARK. If the dimension of \( M \) is \( n \) , there exist exactly \( n \) linearly independent Jacobi fields along the geodesic \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) , which are zero at \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) . This follows from the fact, easily checked, that the Jacobi fields \( {J}_{1},\ldots ,{J}_{k} \) with \( {J}_{i}\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) are linearly independent if and only if \( {J}_{1}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,\ldots ,{J}_{k}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) are linearly independent. In addition, the Jacobi field \( J\left( t\right)  = t{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) \) never vanishes for \( t \neq  0 \) (see Rem. 2.2). From this we deduce that the multiplicity of a conjugate point never exceeds \( n - 1 \) .

nodes.content: 3.3 EXAMPLE. Let \( {S}^{n} = \left\{  {x \in  {R}^{n + 1};\left| x\right|  = 1}\right\} \) . In this example, we assume a fact which will be proved in the next chapter, namely, the sectional curvatures of \( {S}^{n} \) are all equal to one. The Jacobi field on \( {S}^{n} \) given in example 2.3, that is, \( J\left( t\right)  = \left( {\sin t}\right) w\left( t\right) \) , satisfies the condition \( J\left( 0\right)  = J\left( \pi \right)  = 0 \) . Therefore, along any geodesic \( \gamma \) of \( {S}^{n} \) , the antipodal point \( \gamma \left( \pi \right) \) to \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) is conjugate to \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) . It is trivial to verify that there exists \( n - 1 \) such fields that are linearly independent, that is, the multiplicity of \( \gamma \left( \pi \right) \) as a conjugate point of \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) is \( n - 1 \) .

3.4 Definition. The set of (first) conjugate points to the point \( p \in  M \) , for all the geodesics that start at \( p \) , is called the conjugate locus of \( p \) and is denoted by \( C\left( p\right) \) .

On \( {S}^{n}, C\left( p\right)  = \{  - p\} \) , for all \( p \) . The case of \( {S}^{n} \) , however, is not typical. A more typical example is given by the ellipsoid, where \( C\left( p\right) \) is, in general, a curve with four singular points (see Fig. 4 of Chap. 13); Cf. Braunmühl, A., "Geodätische Linien auf dreiachsigen Flächen 2-Grades", Math. Ann., 20 (1882), 557-586.

nodes.proof:
The point \( q = \gamma \left( {t}_{o}\right) \) is a conjugate point of \( p \) along \( \gamma \) if and only if there exists a non-zero Jacobi field \( J \) along \( \gamma \) with \( J\left( 0\right)  = \; J\left( {t}_{o}\right)  = 0 \) . Let \( v = {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) and \( w = {J}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) . From Corollary 2.5, \( J\left( t\right)  = {\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{tv}\left( {tw}\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack \) . Observe that \( J \) is non-zero if and only if \( w \neq  0 \) . Therefore, \( q = \gamma \left( {t}_{o}\right) \) is conjugate to \( p \) if and only if

\[
0 = J\left( {t}_{o}\right)  = {\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{{t}_{o}v}\left( {{t}_{o}w}\right) ,\;w \neq  0,
\]

that is, if and only if, \( {t}_{o}v \) is a critical point of \( {\exp }_{v} \) . The first assertion is therefore proved.

The multiplicity of \( q \) is equal to the number of linearly independent Jacobi fields \( {J}_{1},\ldots ,{J}_{k} \) which are zero at 0 and at \( {t}_{o} \) . As is easy to verify, the fields \( {J}_{1},\ldots ,{J}_{k} \) are linearly independent if and only if \( {J}_{1}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,\ldots ,{J}_{k}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) are linearly independent in \( {T}_{p}M \) . From the

118 Jacobi fields construction above, the multiplicity of \( q \) is equal to the dimension of the kernel of \( {\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{{t}_{o}v} \) .

\]

Integrating this last equation in \( t \) , we obtain finally

\[

\]

nodes.proof:
Let \( \mathcal{J} \) be the space of Jacobi fields \( J \) with \( J\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) . Define a mapping \( \Theta  : \mathcal{J} \rightarrow  {T}_{\gamma \left( a\right) }M \) by

\[
\Theta \left( J\right)  = J\left( a\right) ,\;J \in  \mathcal{J}.
\]

Since \( \gamma \left( a\right) \) is not conjugate to \( \gamma \left( 0\right) ,\Theta \) is injective. Indeed, if \( {J}_{1} \neq  {J}_{2} \) with \( {J}_{1}\left( a\right)  = {J}_{2}\left( a\right) \) , we should have \( {J}_{1} - {J}_{2} \) , a non-zero

Exercises Jacobi field, with \( \left( {{J}_{1} - {J}_{2}}\right) \left( 0\right)  = 0 \) , which contradicts the fact that \( \gamma \left( a\right) \) is not conjugate to \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) .

Since \( \Theta \) is linear, it follows from injectivity and the fact that \( \dim \mathcal{J} = \dim {T}_{\gamma \left( a\right) }M \) that \( \Theta \) is an isomorphism. Hence there exists \( {\bar{J}}_{1} \in  \mathcal{J} \) with \( {\bar{J}}_{1}\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) and \( {\bar{J}}_{1}\left( a\right)  = {V}_{2} \) .

By an analogous argument, there exists a Jacobi field \( {\bar{J}}_{2} \) along \( \gamma \) with \( {\bar{J}}_{2}\left( a\right)  = 0,{\bar{J}}_{2}\left( 0\right)  = {V}_{1} \) . The desired field is now given by \( J = {\bar{J}}_{1} + {\bar{J}}_{2} \) . Uniqueness is clear.

4. Let \( b < 0 \) and let \( M \) be a manifold with constant negative sectional curvature equal to \( b \) . Let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) be a normalized geodesic, and let \( v \in  {T}_{\gamma \left( \ell \right) }M \) such that \( \left\langle  {v,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( \ell \right) }\right\rangle   = 0 \) and \( \left| v\right|  = 1 \) . Since \( M \) has negative curvature, \( \gamma \left( \ell \right) \) is not conjugate to \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) (see Exercise 3). Show that the Jacobi field \( J \) along \( \gamma \) determined by \( J\left( 0\right)  = 0, J\left( \ell \right)  = v \) is given by

\[
J\left( t\right)  = \frac{\sinh \left( {t\sqrt{-b}}\right) }{\sinh \left( {\ell \sqrt{-b}}\right) }w\left( t\right) ,
\]

where \( w\left( t\right) \) is the parallel transport along \( \gamma \) of the vector

\[
w\left( 0\right)  = \frac{{u}_{o}}{\left| {u}_{o}\right| },\;{u}_{o} = {\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{\ell {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }^{-1}\left( v\right)
\]

and where \( {u}_{o} \) is considered as a vector \( {T}_{\gamma \left( 0\right) }M \) by the identification \( {T}_{\gamma \left( 0\right) }M \approx  {T}_{\ell {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\left( {{T}_{\gamma \left( 0\right) }M}\right) \) .

Hint: From example 2.3, the Jacobi field \( {J}_{1} \) along \( \gamma \) satisfying \( {J}_{1}\left( 0\right)  = 0,{J}_{1}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = \frac{{u}_{o}}{\left| {u}_{o}\right| } \) , is given by

\[
{J}_{1}\left( t\right)  = \frac{\sinh t\sqrt{-b}}{\sqrt{-b}}w\left( t\right) .
\]

In addition, from Corollary 2.5,

\[
{J}_{1}\left( \ell \right)  = {\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{\ell {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\left( {\ell w\left( 0\right) }\right) .
\]

It follows that

\[
J\left( \ell \right)  = v = {\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{\ell {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\left( {u}_{o}\right)  = {J}_{1}\left( \ell \right) \frac{\left| {u}_{o}\right| }{\ell }.
\]

Therefore,

\[
J\left( t\right)  = {J}_{1}\left( t\right) \frac{\left| {u}_{o}\right| }{\ell } = \frac{\sinh t\sqrt{-b}}{\sqrt{-b}}w\left( t\right) \frac{\left| {u}_{o}\right| }{\ell }.
\]

In addition, since

\[
1 = \left| v\right|  = \left| {J\left( \ell \right) }\right|  = \frac{\sinh \ell \sqrt{-b}}{\sqrt{-b}}\frac{\left| {u}_{o}\right| }{\ell },
\]

we have

\[
\frac{\left| {u}_{o}\right| }{\ell } = {\left( \frac{\sinh \ell \sqrt{-b}}{\sqrt{-b}}\right) }^{-1}
\]

which implies what was asserted.

6. Let \( M \) be a Riemannian manifold of dimension two (in this case we say that \( M \) is a surface). Let \( {B}_{\delta }\left( p\right) \) be a normal ball around the point \( p \in  M \) and consider the parametrized surface

\[
f\left( {\rho ,\theta }\right)  = {\exp }_{p}{\rho v}\left( \theta \right) ,\;0 < \rho  < \delta ,\; - \pi  < \theta  < \pi ,
\]

where \( v\left( \theta \right) \) is a circle of radius \( \delta \) in \( {T}_{p}M \) parametrized by the central angle \( \theta \) .

a) Show that \( \left( {\rho ,\theta }\right) \) are coordinates in an open set \( U \subset  M \) formed by the open ball \( {B}_{\delta }\left( p\right) \) minus the ray \( {\exp }_{p}\left( {-{\rho v}\left( 0\right) }\right) 0 < \rho  < \delta \) . Such coordinates are called polar coordinates at \( \mathbf{p} \) .

b) Show that the coefficients \( {g}_{ij} \) of the Riemannian metric in these coordinates are:

\[
{g}_{12} = 0,\;{g}_{11} = {\left| \frac{\partial f}{\partial \rho }\right| }^{2} = {\left| v\left( \theta \right) \right| }^{2} = 1,\;{g}_{22} = {\left| \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta }\right| }^{2}.
\]

c) Show that, along the geodesic \( f\left( {\rho ,0}\right) \) , we have

\[
{\left( \sqrt{{g}_{22}}\right) }_{\rho \rho } =  - K\left( p\right) \rho  + R\left( \rho \right) ,\;\text{ where }\;\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\rho  \rightarrow  0}}\frac{R\left( \rho \right) }{\rho } = 0
\]

and \( K\left( p\right) \) is the sectional curvature of \( M \) at \( p \) .

d) Prove that

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\rho  \rightarrow  0}}\frac{{\left( \sqrt{{g}_{22}}\right) }_{\rho \rho }}{\sqrt{{g}_{22}}} =  - K\left( p\right)
\]

This last expression is the value of the Gaussian curvature of \( M \) at \( p \) given in polar coordinates (Cf., for example, M. do Carmo [dC 2] p. 288). This fact from the theory of surfaces, and (d) shows that, in dimension two, the sectional curvature coincides with the Gaussian curvature. In the next chapter, we shall give a more direct proof of this fact.

nodes.title: 6.2. The second fundamental form
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry

nodes.label: Definition 6.2-extra-1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
The Riemannian connection on \( \bar{M} \) will be denoted by \( \bar{\nabla } \) . If \( X \) and \( Y \) are local vector fields on \( M \) , and \( \bar{X},\overrightarrow{Y} \) are local extensions to \( \bar{M} \) , define

\[
{\nabla }_{X}Y = {\left( {\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}\bar{Y}\right) }^{T}.
\]

It is easy to verify that this is the Riemannian connection relative to the metric induced on \( M \) (Cf. Exercise 3 of Chap. 2).

We want to define the second fundamental form of the immersion \( f : M \rightarrow  \bar{M} \) . To do this, it is convenient to introduce beforehand the following definition. If \( X, Y \) are local vector fields on \( M \) ,

\[
B\left( {X, Y}\right)  = {\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}\bar{Y} - {\nabla }_{X}Y
\]

is a local vector field on \( \bar{M} \) normal to \( M.B\left( {X, Y}\right) \) does not depend on the extensions \( \bar{X},\bar{Y} \) . Indeed, if \( {\bar{X}}_{1} \) is another extension of \( X \) , we have

\[
\left( {{\overline{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}\overline{Y} - {\nabla }_{X}Y}\right)  - \left( {{\overline{\nabla }}_{{\bar{X}}_{1}}\overline{Y} - {\nabla }_{X}Y}\right)  = {\overline{\nabla }}_{\bar{X} - {\bar{X}}_{1}}\overline{Y},
\]

which vanishes on \( M \) , because \( \bar{X} - {\bar{X}}_{1} = 0 \) on \( M \) ; using what was proved, it follows that if \( {\bar{Y}}_{1} \) is another extension of \( Y \) ,

\[
\left( {{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}\bar{Y} - {\nabla }_{X}Y}\right)  - \left( {{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}{\bar{Y}}_{1} - {\nabla }_{X}Y}\right)  = {\bar{\nabla }}_{X}\left( {\bar{Y} - {\bar{Y}}_{1}}\right)  = 0,
\]

because \( \widetilde{Y} - {\bar{Y}}_{1} = 0 \) on \( M \) .

Therefore \( B\left( {X, Y}\right) \) is well-defined. In what follows, let us denote by \( \mathcal{X}{\left( U\right) }^{ \bot  } \) the differentiable vector fields on \( U \) that are normal to \( f\left( U\right)  \approx  U \) .

nodes.label: Proposition 2.1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.1 Proposition. If \( X, Y \in  \mathcal{X}\left( U\right) \) , the mapping \( B : \mathcal{X}\left( U\right)  \times \; \mathcal{X}\left( U\right)  \rightarrow  \mathcal{X}{\left( U\right) }^{ \bot  } \) given by

\[
B\left( {X, Y}\right)  = {\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}\bar{Y} - {\nabla }_{X}Y
\]

is bilinear and symmetric.
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.1 Proposition. If \( X, Y \in \mathcal{X}\left( U\right) \) , the mapping \( B : \mathcal{X}\left( U\right) \times \; \mathcal{X}\left( U\right) \rightarrow \mathcal{X}{\left( U\right) }^{ \bot } \) given by \[ B\left( {X, Y}\right) = {\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}\bar{Y} - {\nabla }_{X}Y \] is bilinear and symmetric.

nodes.proof:
From the properties of linearity of a connection, it is immediate that \( B \) is additive in \( X \) and \( Y \) and that

\[
B\left( {{fX}, Y}\right)  = {fB}\left( {X, Y}\right) , f \in  \mathcal{D}\left( U\right) .
\]

It remains to show that

\[
B\left( {X,{fY}}\right)  = {fB}\left( {X, Y}\right) , f \in  \mathcal{D}\left( U\right) .
\]

Denoting the extension of \( f \) to \( \bar{U} \) by \( \bar{f} \) , we have

\[
B\left( {X,{fY}}\right)  = {\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}\left( {\bar{f}\bar{Y}}\right)  - {\nabla }_{X}\left( {fY}\right)
\]

\[
= \bar{f}{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}\bar{Y} - f{\nabla }_{X}Y + \bar{X}\left( \bar{f}\right) \bar{Y} - X\left( f\right) Y.
\]

Since \( f = \bar{f},\bar{X}\left( \bar{f}\right)  = X\left( f\right) \) , and \( Y = \bar{Y} \) on \( M \) , we conclude that the last two cancel, leaving,

\[
B\left( {X,{fY}}\right)  = {fB}\left( {X, Y}\right)
\]

as we claimed.

To show that \( B \) is symmetric, we use the symmetry of the Riemannian connection, obtaining

\[
B\left( {X, Y}\right)  = {\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}\bar{Y} - {\nabla }_{X}Y = {\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{Y}}\bar{X} + \left\lbrack  {\bar{X},\bar{Y}}\right\rbrack   - {\nabla }_{Y}X - \left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  .
\]

Since, \( \left\lbrack  {\bar{X},\bar{Y}}\right\rbrack   = \left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack \) on \( M \) , we conclude that \( B\left( {X, Y}\right)  = \; B\left( {Y, X}\right) \) .

Because \( B \) is bilinear, we see by writing \( B \) in a system of coordinates, that the value \( B\left( {X, Y}\right) \left( p\right) \) depends only on the values \( X\left( p\right) \) and \( Y\left( p\right) \) .

nodes.content:
Now we are in a position to define the second fundamental form. Let \( p \in  M \) and \( \eta  \in  {\left( {T}_{p}M\right) }^{ \bot  } \) . The mapping \( {H}_{\eta } : {T}_{p}M \times  {T}_{p}M \rightarrow \) R given by

\[
{H}_{\eta }\left( {x, y}\right)  = \langle B\left( {x, y}\right) ,\eta \rangle ,\;x, y \in  {T}_{p}M,
\]

is, by Proposition 2.1, a symmetric bilinear form.

2.2 Definition. The quadratic form \( {\Pi }_{\eta } \) defined on \( {T}_{p}M \) by

\[
{\Pi }_{\eta }\left( x\right)  = {H}_{\eta }\left( {x, x}\right)
\]

is called the second fundamental form of \( f \) at \( p \) along the normal vector \( \eta \) .

Sometimes the expression second fundamental form is also used to designate the mapping \( B \) which at every point \( p \in  M \) is a symmetric bilinear mapping, taking values in \( {\left( {T}_{p}M\right) }^{ \bot  } \) .

nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.3 Proposition. Let \( p \in  M, x \in  {T}_{p}M \) and \( \eta  \in  {\left( {T}_{p}M\right) }^{ \bot  } \) . Let \( N \) be a local extension of \( \eta \) normal to \( M \) . Then

\[
{S}_{\eta }\left( x\right)  =  - {\left( {\widetilde{\nabla }}_{x}N\right) }^{T}.
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.3 Proposition. Let \( p \in M, x \in {T}_{p}M \) and \( \eta \in {\left( {T}_{p}M\right) }^{ \bot } \) . Let \( N \) be a local extension of \( \eta \) normal to \( M \) . Then \[ {S}_{\eta }\left( x\right) = - {\left( {\widetilde{\nabla }}_{x}N\right) }^{T}. \]

nodes.proof:
Let \( y \in  {T}_{p}M \) and let \( X, Y \) be local extensions of \( x, y \) , respectively, which are tangent to \( M \) . Then \( \langle N, Y\rangle  = 0 \) , and therefore

\[
\left\langle  {{S}_{\eta }\left( x\right) , y}\right\rangle   = \langle B\left( {X, Y}\right) \left( p\right) , N\rangle  = \left\langle  {{\bar{\nabla }}_{X}Y - {\nabla }_{X}Y, N}\right\rangle  \left( p\right)
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {{\bar{\nabla }}_{X}Y, N}\right\rangle  \left( p\right)  =  - \left\langle  {Y,{\bar{\nabla }}_{X}N}\right\rangle  \left( p\right)  = \left\langle  {-{\bar{\nabla }}_{x}N, y}\right\rangle  ,
\]

for all \( y \in  {T}_{p}M \) .

nodes.label: Example 2.4
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.4 EXAMPLE. Consider the particular case in which the codi-mension of the immersion is 1, i.e., \( f : {M}^{n} \rightarrow  {\bar{M}}^{n + 1};f\left( M\right)  \subset  \bar{M} \) is then called a hypersurface. (Observe that a hypersurface can have self-intersections).

Let \( p \in  M \) and \( \eta  \in  {\left( {T}_{p}M\right) }^{ \bot  },\left| \eta \right|  = 1 \) . Since \( {S}_{\eta } : {T}_{p}M \rightarrow \; {T}_{p}M \) is symmetric, there exists an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n}}\right\} \) of \( {T}_{p}M \) with real eigenvalues \( {\lambda }_{1},\ldots ,{\lambda }_{n} \) , i.e., \( {S}_{\eta }\left( {e}_{i}\right)  = \; {\lambda }_{i}{e}_{i},1 \leq  i \leq  n \) . If \( M \) and \( \bar{M} \) are both orientable and oriented (i.e., orientations are chosen on \( M \) and \( \bar{M} \) ) then the vector \( \eta \) is uniquely determined if we require that both \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n}}\right\} \) is a basis in the orientation of \( M \) , and \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n},\eta }\right\} \) is a basis in the orientation of \( \bar{M} \) . In this case, we say that the \( {e}_{i} \) are principal directions and that the \( {\lambda }_{i} = {k}_{i} \) are principal curvatures of \( f \) . The symmetric functions of \( {\lambda }_{1},\ldots ,{\lambda }_{n} \) are invariants of the immersion. For example: \( \det \left( {S}_{\eta }\right)  = {\lambda }_{1}\ldots {\lambda }_{n} \) is called the Gauss-Kronecker curvature of \( f \) and \( \frac{1}{n}\left( {{\lambda }_{1} + \cdots  + {\lambda }_{n}}\right) \) is called the mean curvature of \( f \) .

An important case occurs when \( \bar{M} = {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) . Here, we can give an interesting geometric interpretation of \( {S}_{\eta } \) . To begin with, let \( N \) be a local extension of \( \eta \) , which is a unit vector field normal to \( M \) . Let \( {S}_{1}^{n} = \left\{  {x \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1};\left| x\right|  = 1}\right\} \) be the unit sphere in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) and define the Gauss spherical mapping, \( g : {M}^{n} \rightarrow  {S}_{1}^{n} \) , by translating the origin of the field \( N \) to the origin of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) and taking

\[
g\left( q\right)  = \text{ endpoint of the translation of }N\left( q\right) \text{ . }
\]

Since \( {T}_{q}M \) and \( {T}_{g\left( q\right) }{S}_{1}^{n} \) are parallel, we can identify them, and see that \( d{g}_{q} : {T}_{q}M \rightarrow  {T}_{q}M \) is given by

\[
d{g}_{q}\left( x\right)  = \frac{d}{dt}{\left( N \circ  c\left( t\right) \right) }_{t = 0} = {\bar{\nabla }}_{x}N = {\left( {\bar{\nabla }}_{x}N\right) }^{T} =  - {S}_{\eta }\left( x\right) ,
\]

where \( c : \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)  \rightarrow  M \) is a curve with \( c\left( 0\right)  = q,{c}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = x \) , and we have used the fact that \( \langle N, N\rangle  = 1 \) to guarantee that \( {\bar{\nabla }}_{x}N = {\left( {\bar{\nabla }}_{x}N\right) }^{T} \) . It follows that \( - {S}_{\eta } \) is the derivative of the Gauss spherical mapping.

The Gauss mapping has important topological implications. As an example, we shall prove the following fact: Let \( {M}^{n}, n \geq \) 2, be a connected, compact, orientable manifold. If there exists an immersion \( f : {M}^{n} \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) with non-vanishing Gauss-Kronecker curvature at every point of \( M \) , then \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}_{1}^{n} \) . The proof depends on the properties of covering spaces (see for example, M. do Carmo \( \left\lbrack  {dC2}\right\rbrack  §{5.6}) \) . The fact that \( \det \left( {d{g}_{p}}\right)  \neq  0 \) , for the Gauss mapping, tells us that \( g : M \rightarrow  {S}_{1}^{n} \) is a local diffeomorphism. Since \( M \) is compact, \( g \) is a covering map, and because \( {S}_{1}^{n} \) is simply connected, \( g \) is a diffeomorphism.

We now relate the curvature of \( M \) with the curvature of \( \bar{M} \) and the second fundamental forms. If \( x, y \in  {T}_{p}M \subset  {T}_{p}\bar{M} \) , are linearly independent, denote by \( K\left( {x, y}\right) \) and \( \bar{K}\left( {x, y}\right) \) the sectional curvatures of \( M \) and \( \bar{M} \) , respectively, in the plane generated by \( x \) and \( y \) . Another proof of the next theorem will come up in Section 3 of this chapter.
