nodes.content:
2.5 THEOREM. (Gauss). Let \( p \in  M \) and let \( x, y \) be orthonormal vectors in \( {T}_{p}M \) . Then

(1)

\[
K\left( {x, y}\right)  - \bar{K}\left( {x, y}\right)  = \langle B\left( {x, x}\right) , B\left( {y, y}\right) \rangle  - {\left| B\left( x, y\right) \right| }^{2}.
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.5 THEOREM. (Gauss). Let \( p \in M \) and let \( x, y \) be orthonormal vectors in \( {T}_{p}M \) . Then (1) \[ K\left( {x, y}\right) - \bar{K}\left( {x, y}\right) = \langle B\left( {x, x}\right) , B\left( {y, y}\right) \rangle - {\left| B\left( x, y\right) \right| }^{2}. \]

nodes.proof:
Let \( X, Y \) be local orthogonal extensions of \( x, y \) , respectively, which are tangent to \( M \) ; we denote the local extensions to \( \bar{M} \) of \( X \) , \( Y \) by \( \bar{X},\bar{Y} \) . Then

\[
K\left( {x, y}\right)  - \bar{K}\left( {x, y}\right)
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{X}X - {\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{Y}X - \left( {{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{Y}}{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}\bar{X} - {\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{Y}}\bar{X}}\right) , Y}\right\rangle  \left( p\right)
\]

\[
+ \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }X - {\bar{\nabla }}_{\left\lbrack  \bar{X},\bar{Y}\right\rbrack  }\bar{X}, Y}\right\rangle  \left( p\right) .
\]

Observe, first of all, that the last term is zero, because

\[
\langle {\nabla }_{\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }X - {\overline{\nabla }}_{\left\lbrack  \overline{X},\overline{Y}\right\rbrack  }\overline{X}, Y\rangle \left( p\right)  =  - \langle {\left( {\overline{\nabla }}_{\left\lbrack  \overline{X},\overline{Y}\right\rbrack  }\overline{X}\right) }^{N}, Y\rangle \left( p\right)  = 0.
\]

On the other hand, if we denote by \( {E}_{1},\ldots ,{E}_{m}, m = \dim \bar{M} - \dim M \) , local orthonormal fields which are normal to \( M \) , we have

\[
B\left( {X, Y}\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{H}_{i}\left( {X, Y}\right) {E}_{i},\;{H}_{i} = {H}_{{E}_{i}},\;i = 1,\ldots , m.
\]

Therefore, at \( p \) ,

\[
{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{Y}}{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}\bar{X} = {\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{Y}}\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{H}_{i}\left( {X, X}\right) {E}_{i} + {\nabla }_{X}X}\right)
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}\left\{  {{H}_{i}\left( {X, X}\right) {\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{Y}}{E}_{i} + \bar{Y}{H}_{i}\left( {X, X}\right) {E}_{i}\}  + {\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{Y}}{\nabla }_{X}X.}\right.
\]

Hence, at \( p \) ,

(2)

\[
\left\langle  {{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{Y}}{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}\bar{X}, Y}\right\rangle   =  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{H}_{i}\left( {X, X}\right) {H}_{i}\left( {Y, Y}\right)  + \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{X}X, Y}\right\rangle  .
\]

Similarly,(3)

\[
\left\langle  {{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{Y}}\bar{X}, Y}\right\rangle   =  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{H}_{i}\left( {X, Y}\right) {H}_{i}\left( {X, Y}\right)  + \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{Y}X, Y}\right\rangle  .
\]

Using (2) and (3), we obtain (1).

Let \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n}}\right\} \) be an orthonormal basis of \( {T}_{p}M \) in which \( {S}_{\eta } = S \) is diagonal, that is, \( S\left( {e}_{i}\right)  = {\lambda }_{i}{e}_{i}, i = 1,\ldots , n \) , where \( {\lambda }_{1},\ldots ,{\lambda }_{n} \) are the eigenvalues of \( S \) . Then \( H\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{i}}\right)  = {\lambda }_{i} \) and \( H\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{j}}\right)  = 0 \) , if \( i \neq  j \) . Therefore (1) can be written

(4)

\[
K\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{j}}\right)  - \bar{K}\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{j}}\right)  = {\lambda }_{i}{\lambda }_{j}.
\]

In this case, the previous Remark shows that the Gaussian curvature coincides with the sectional curvature of the surface, and implies the famous Theorem Egregium of Gauss, which asserts that the Gaussian curvature of \( {M}^{2} \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) is an invariant under isometries.

nodes.content:
2.8 EXAMPLE. (curvature of \( {S}^{n} \) ). We are going to show that the sectional curvature of the unit sphere \( {S}^{n} \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) is a constant equal to 1 .

For this, orient \( {S}^{n} \) by the inward pointing unit normal \( N\left( x\right)  =  - x \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1},\left| x\right|  = 1 \) . The Gauss mapping is then equal to \( \left( {-i}\right) \) , where \( i \) is the identity of \( {S}^{n} \) . It follows then that the selfadjoint operator associated to \( {H}_{N} \) has all of its eigenvalues equal to 1. This means that for all \( p \in  {S}^{n} \) , every \( v \in  {T}_{p}{S}^{n} \) is an eigenvector. Using the expression (4), we conclude that all sectional curvatures of \( {S}^{n} \) are equal to 1, as we have claimed.

nodes.content: An immersion \( f : M \rightarrow  \bar{M} \) is said to be geodesic at \( p \in  M \) if for every \( \eta  \in  {\left( {T}_{p}M\right) }^{ \bot  } \) the second fundamental form \( {H}_{\eta } \) is identically zero at \( p \) . An immersion \( f \) is called totally geodesic if it is geodesic for all \( p \in  M \) . The reason for this terminology is given by the next proposition.

nodes.label: Proposition 2.9
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 2.9 Proposition. An immersion \( f : M \rightarrow  \bar{M} \) is geodesic at \( p \in  M \) if and only if every geodesic \( \gamma \) of \( M \) starting from \( p \) is a geodesic of \( \bar{M} \) at \( p \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.9 Proposition. An immersion \( f : M \rightarrow \bar{M} \) is geodesic at \( p \in M \) if and only if every geodesic \( \gamma \) of \( M \) starting from \( p \) is a geodesic of \( \bar{M} \) at \( p \) .

nodes.proof:
Let \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p \) and \( {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = x \) . Let \( N \) be a local extension, normal to \( M \) , of a vector \( \eta \) normal to \( M \) at \( p \) , and let \( X \) be a local extension of \( {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) \) to a tangent field on \( M \) . Since \( \langle X, N\rangle  = 0 \) , we obtain, at \( p \) ,

\[
{H}_{\eta }\left( {x, x}\right)  = \left\langle  {{S}_{\eta }\left( x\right) , x}\right\rangle   =  - \left\langle  {{\widetilde{\nabla }}_{X}N, X}\right\rangle
\]

\[
=  - X\langle N, X\rangle  + \left\langle  {N,{\bar{\nabla }}_{X}X}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {N,{\bar{\nabla }}_{X}X}\right\rangle  .
\]

It follows that \( f \) is geodesic at \( p \) if and only if, for all \( x \in  {T}_{p}M \) , the geodesic \( \gamma \) of \( M \) that is tangent to \( x \) at \( p \) satisfies the condition: \( {\bar{\nabla }}_{X}X\left( p\right) \) does not have a normal component. Therefore \( f \) is geodesic at \( p \) if and only if every geodesic \( \gamma \) of \( M \) starting from \( p \) is a geodesic of \( \bar{M} \) at \( p \) .

nodes.content:
2.10 Definition. An immersion \( f : M \rightarrow  \bar{M} \) is called minimal if for every \( p \in  M \) and every \( \eta  \in  {\left( {T}_{p}M\right) }^{ \bot  } \) the trace of \( {S}_{\eta } = 0 \) .

Choosing an orthonormal frame \( {E}_{1},\ldots ,{E}_{m} \) of vectors in \( \mathcal{X}{\left( U\right) }^{ \bot  } \) , where \( U \) is a neighborhood of \( p \) in which \( f \) is an embedding, we can write, at \( p \) ,

\[
B\left( {x, y}\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{H}_{i}\left( {x, y}\right) {E}_{i},\;x, y \in  {T}_{p}M,\;i = 1,\ldots , m,
\]

where \( {H}_{i} = {H}_{{E}_{i}} \) . It is not hard to verify that the normal vector given by

\[
H = \frac{1}{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}\left( {\operatorname{trace}{S}_{i}}\right) {E}_{i}
\]

where \( {S}_{i} = {S}_{{E}_{i}} \) , does not depend on the chosen frame \( {E}_{i} \) . The vector \( H \) is called the mean curvature vector of \( f \) . It is clear that \( f \) is minimal if and only if \( H\left( p\right)  = 0 \) , for all \( p \in  M \) .

nodes.title: 6.3. The fundamental equations
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry

nodes.label: Definition 6.3-extra-1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
Given an isometric immersion \( f : {M}^{n} \rightarrow  {\bar{M}}^{n + m} \) , we have at each \( p \in  M \) the decomposition

\[
{T}_{p}\bar{M} = {T}_{p}M \oplus  {\left( {T}_{p}M\right) }^{ \bot  },
\]

which varies differentiably with \( p \) . This means that, locally, the portion of the tangent bundle \( T\bar{M} \) which sits over \( M \) can be decomposed into the direct sum of the tangent bundle \( {TM} \) and the normal bundle \( T{M}^{ \bot  } \) . In what follows, we shall systematically use Latin letters \( X, Y, Z \) , etc., to denote differentiable vector fields tangent to \( M \) and Greek letters \( \xi ,\eta ,\zeta \) , etc., to indicate differentiable vector fields normal to \( M \) .

Given \( X \) and \( \eta \) , we saw that the tangent component of \( {\bar{\nabla }}_{X}\eta \) is given by \( {\left( {\bar{\nabla }}_{X}\eta \right) }^{T} =  - {S}_{\eta }\left( X\right) \) . We plan now to study the normal component of \( {\bar{\nabla }}_{X}\eta \) , which will be called the normal connection \( {\nabla }^{ \bot  } \) of the immersion. Explicitly,

(5)

\[
{\nabla }_{X}^{ \bot  }\eta  = {\left( {\overline{\nabla }}_{X}\eta \right) }^{N} = {\overline{\nabla }}_{X}\eta  - {\left( {\overline{\nabla }}_{X}\eta \right) }^{T} = {\overline{\nabla }}_{X}\eta  + {S}_{\eta }\left( X\right) .
\]

It is easy to verify that the normal connection \( {\nabla }^{ \bot  } \) has all of the usual properties of a connection, that is, it is linear in \( X \) , additive in \( \eta \) , and

\[
{\nabla }_{X}^{ \bot  }\left( {f\eta }\right)  = f{\nabla }_{X}^{ \bot  }\eta  + X\left( f\right) \eta ,\;f \in  \mathcal{D}\left( M\right) .
\]

In a similar way as in the case of the tangent bundle, we can introduce for the normal connection \( {\nabla }^{ \bot  } \) , a notion of curvature in the normal bundle which is called the normal curvature \( {R}^{ \bot  } \) of the immersion and is defined by

\[
{R}^{ \bot  }\left( {X, Y}\right) \eta  = {\nabla }_{Y}^{ \bot  }{\nabla }_{X}^{ \bot  }\eta  - {\nabla }_{X}^{ \bot  }{\nabla }_{Y}^{ \bot  }\eta  + {\nabla }_{\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }^{ \bot  }\eta .
\]

Everything about immersions occurs as if the geometry decomposes into two geometries: the geometry of the tangent bundle and the geometry of the normal bundle. These geometries are related by the second fundamental form of the immersion by means of expressions that generalize the classical equations of Gauss and Codazzi in the theory of surfaces. The objective of this section is to establish these relations.

nodes.label: Proposition 3.1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
3.1 Proposition. The following equations are valid: (a) Gauss equation

\[
\langle \bar{R}\left( {X, Y}\right) Z, T\rangle  = \langle R\left( {X, Y}\right) Z, T\rangle
\]

\[
- \langle B\left( {Y, T}\right) , B\left( {X, Z}\right) \rangle  + \langle B\left( {X, T}\right) , B\left( {Y, Z}\right) \rangle .
\]

(b) Ricci equation

\[
\langle \bar{R}\left( {X, Y}\right) \eta ,\zeta \rangle  - \langle {R}^{ \bot  }\left( {X, Y}\right) \eta ,\zeta \rangle  = \langle \left\lbrack  {{S}_{\eta },{S}_{\zeta }}\right\rbrack  X, Y\rangle ,
\]

where \( \left\lbrack  {{S}_{\eta },{S}_{\zeta }}\right\rbrack \) denotes the operator \( {S}_{\eta } \circ  {S}_{\zeta } - {S}_{\zeta } \circ  {S}_{\eta } \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.1 Proposition. The following equations are valid: (a) Gauss equation \[ \langle \bar{R}\left( {X, Y}\right) Z, T\rangle = \langle R\left( {X, Y}\right) Z, T\rangle \] \[ - \langle B\left( {Y, T}\right) , B\left( {X, Z}\right) \rangle + \langle B\left( {X, T}\right) , B\left( {Y, Z}\right) \rangle . \] (b) Ricci equation \[ \langle \bar{R}\left( {X, Y}\right) \eta ,\zeta \rangle - \langle {R}^{ \bot }\left( {X, Y...

nodes.proof:
Observe that \( {\bar{\nabla }}_{X}Y = {\nabla }_{X}Y + B\left( {X, Y}\right) \) . Since

\[
\bar{R}\left( {X, Y}\right) Z = {\bar{\nabla }}_{Y}{\bar{\nabla }}_{X}Z - {\bar{\nabla }}_{X}{\bar{\nabla }}_{Y}Z + {\bar{\nabla }}_{\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }Z
\]

\[
= {\bar{\nabla }}_{Y}\left( {{\nabla }_{X}Z + B\left( {X, Z}\right) }\right)  - {\bar{\nabla }}_{X}\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}Z + B\left( {Y, Z}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
+ {\nabla }_{\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }Z + B\left( {\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  , Z}\right)
\]

we have

\[
\bar{R}\left( {X, Y}\right) Z = R\left( {X, Y}\right) Z + B\left( {Y,{\nabla }_{X}Z}\right)  + {\nabla }_{Y}^{ \bot  }B\left( {X, Z}\right)
\]

(6)

\[
- {S}_{B\left( {X, Z}\right) }Y - B\left( {X,{\nabla }_{Y}Z}\right)  - {\nabla }_{X}^{ \bot  }B\left( {Y, Z}\right)
\]

\[
+ {S}_{B\left( {Y, Z}\right) }X + B\left( {\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  , Z}\right) .
\]

Taking the inner product of (6) with \( T \) , since the normal terms vanish, we obtain finally

\[
\langle \bar{R}\left( {X, Y}\right) Z, T\rangle  = \langle R\left( {X, Y}\right) Z, T\rangle  - \left\langle  {{S}_{B\left( {X, Z}\right) }Y, T}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {{S}_{B\left( {Y, Z}\right) }X, T}\right\rangle
\]

\[
= \langle R\left( {X, Y}\right) Z, T\rangle  - \langle B\left( {Y, T}\right) , B\left( {X, Z}\right) \rangle
\]

\[
+ \langle B\left( {X, T}\right) , B\left( {Y, Z}\right) \rangle
\]

which is the Gauss equation.

To get the Ricci equation, we calculate

\[
\bar{R}\left( {X, Y}\right) \eta  = {\bar{\nabla }}_{Y}{\bar{\nabla }}_{X}\eta  - {\bar{\nabla }}_{X}{\bar{\nabla }}_{Y}\eta  + {\bar{\nabla }}_{\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }\eta
\]

\[
= {\bar{\nabla }}_{Y}\left( {{\nabla }_{X}^{ \bot  }\eta  - {S}_{\eta }X}\right)  - {\bar{\nabla }}_{X}\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}^{ \bot  }\eta  - {S}_{\eta }Y}\right)
\]

\[
+ {\nabla }_{\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }^{ \bot  }\eta  - {S}_{\eta }\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
= {R}^{ \bot  }\left( {X, Y}\right) \eta  - {S}_{{\nabla }_{X}^{ \bot  }\eta }Y - {\nabla }_{Y}\left( {{S}_{\eta }X}\right)  - B\left( {{S}_{\eta }X, Y}\right)
\]

\[
+ {S}_{{\nabla }_{Y}^{ \bot  }\eta }X + {\nabla }_{X}\left( {{S}_{\eta }Y}\right)  + B\left( {X,{S}_{\eta }Y}\right)  - {S}_{\eta }\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  .
\]

Multiplying the expression by \( \zeta \) and observing that \( \langle B\left( {X, Y}\right) ,\eta \rangle  = \; \left\langle  {{S}_{\eta }X, Y}\right\rangle \) , we obtain

\[
\langle \bar{R}\left( {X, Y}\right) \eta ,\zeta \rangle  = \left\langle  {{R}^{ \bot  }\left( {X, Y}\right) \eta ,\zeta }\right\rangle   - \langle B\left( {{S}_{\eta }X, Y}\right) ,\zeta \rangle  + \left\langle  {B\left( {X,{S}_{\eta }Y}\right) ,\zeta }\right\rangle
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {{R}^{ \bot  }\left( {X, Y}\right) \eta ,\zeta }\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {\left( {{S}_{\eta }{S}_{\zeta } - {S}_{\zeta }{S}_{\eta }}\right) X, Y}\right\rangle
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {{R}^{ \bot  }\left( {X, Y}\right) \eta ,\zeta }\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {\left\lbrack  {{S}_{\eta },{S}_{\zeta }}\right\rbrack  X, Y}\right\rangle  ,
\]

which is Ricci's equation.

nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 3.2 REMARK. Theorem 2.5 of this chapter is a special case of Gauss' equation.
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.2 REMARK. Theorem 2.5 of this chapter is a special case of Gauss' equation.

nodes.label: Remark 3.3
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
3.3 REMARK. We say that the normal bundle of an immersion is flat if \( {R}^{ \bot  } = 0 \) . Assume that the ambient space \( \bar{M} \) has constant sectional curvature. Then the Ricci equation can be written as

\[
\left\langle  {{R}^{ \bot  }\left( {X, Y}\right) \eta ,\zeta }\right\rangle   =  - \left\langle  {\left\lbrack  {{S}_{\eta },{S}_{\zeta }}\right\rbrack  X, Y}\right\rangle  .
\]

It follows that \( {R}^{ \bot  } = 0 \) if and only if \( \left\lbrack  {{S}_{\eta },{S}_{\zeta }}\right\rbrack   = 0 \) for all \( \eta ,\zeta \) , that is, if and only if for all \( p \in  M \) there exists a basis of \( {T}_{p}M \) which diagonalizes all of the \( {S}_{\eta } \) simultaneously.

The Gauss and Ricci equations are algebraic expressions that relate the curvatures of the tangent and normal bundles, respectively, with the second fundamental form of the immersion. A nonalgebraic relation is given by the Codazzi equation, for which we need to "differentiate" the second fundamental form considered as a tensor.

Given an isometric immersion, let us denote the space of differentiable vector fields normal to \( M \) by \( \mathcal{X}{\left( M\right) }^{ \bot  } \) . The second fundamental form of the immersion can then be considered as a tensor

\[
B : \mathcal{X}\left( M\right)  \times  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right)  \times  \mathcal{X}{\left( M\right) }^{ \bot  } \rightarrow  \mathbf{R}
\]

defined by

\[
B\left( {X, Y,\eta }\right)  = \langle B\left( {X, Y}\right) ,\eta \rangle
\]

The definition of covariant derivative extends to tensors of this type in a natural way:

\[
\left( {{\bar{\nabla }}_{X}B}\right) \left( {Y, Z,\eta }\right)  = X\left( {B\left( {Y, Z,\eta }\right) }\right)  - B\left( {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Z,\eta }\right)
\]

\[
- B\left( {Y,{\nabla }_{X}Z,\eta }\right)  - B\left( {Y, Z,{\nabla }_{X}^{ \bot  }\eta }\right) .
\]

nodes.label: Proposition 3.4
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
3.4 Proposition. (Codazzi’s equation). With the notation above,

\[
\langle \overline{R}\left( {X, Y}\right) Z,\eta \rangle  = \left( {{\overline{\nabla }}_{Y}B}\right) \left( {X, Z,\eta }\right)  - \left( {{\overline{\nabla }}_{X}B}\right) \left( {Y, Z,\eta }\right) .
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.4 Proposition. (Codazzi’s equation). With the notation above, \[ \langle \overline{R}\left( {X, Y}\right) Z,\eta \rangle = \left( {{\overline{\nabla }}_{Y}B}\right) \left( {X, Z,\eta }\right) - \left( {{\overline{\nabla }}_{X}B}\right) \left( {Y, Z,\eta }\right) . \]

nodes.proof:
Observe, to begin with, that

\[
\left( {{\bar{\nabla }}_{X}B}\right) \left( {Y, Z,\eta }\right)  = X\langle B\left( {Y, Z}\right) ,\eta \rangle  - \left\langle  {B\left( {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Z}\right) ,\eta }\right\rangle
\]

\[
- \left\langle  {B\left( {Y,{\nabla }_{X}Z}\right) ,\eta }\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {B\left( {Y, Z}\right) ,{\nabla }_{X}^{ \bot  }\eta }\right\rangle
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}^{ \bot  }\left( {B\left( {Y, Z}\right) }\right) ,\eta }\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {B\left( {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Z}\right) ,\eta }\right\rangle
\]

\[
- \langle B\left( {Y,{\nabla }_{X}Z}\right) ,\eta \rangle
\]

Consider now expression (6) in the proof of Proposition 3.1, and multiply both sides of (6) by \( \eta \) . We obtain, taking into account the remark above,

\[
\langle \bar{R}\left( {X, Y}\right) Z,\eta \rangle  = \left\langle  {B\left( {Y,{\nabla }_{X}Z}\right) ,\eta }\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Y}^{ \bot  }B\left( {X, Z}\right) ,\eta }\right\rangle
\]

\[
- \left\langle  {B\left( {X,{\nabla }_{Y}Z}\right) ,\eta }\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}^{ \bot  }B\left( {Y, Z}\right) ,\eta }\right\rangle
\]

\[
+ \langle B\left( {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Z}\right) ,\eta \rangle  - \langle B\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}X, Z}\right) \eta \rangle
\]

\[
=  - \left( {{\bar{\nabla }}_{X}B}\right) \left( {Y, Z,\eta }\right)  + \left( {{\bar{\nabla }}_{Y}B}\right) \left( {X, Z,\eta }\right)
\]

which is Codazzi's equation.

nodes.label: Remark 3.5
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
3.5 REMARK. If the ambient space \( \bar{M} \) has constant sectional curvature, the Codazzi equation reduces to

\[
\left( {{\bar{\nabla }}_{X}B}\right) \left( {Y, Z,\eta }\right)  = \left( {{\bar{\nabla }}_{Y}B}\right) \left( {X, Z,\eta }\right) .
\]

If, in addition, the codimension of the immersion is \( 1,{\nabla }_{X}^{ \bot  }\eta  = 0 \) , hence

\[
{\bar{\nabla }}_{X}B\left( {Y, Z,\eta }\right)  = X\left\langle  {{S}_{\eta }\left( Y\right) , Z}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {{S}_{\eta }\left( {{\nabla }_{X}Y}\right) , Z}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {{S}_{\eta }\left( Y\right) ,{\nabla }_{X}Z}\right\rangle
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}\left( {{S}_{\eta }\left( Y\right) }\right) , Z}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {{S}_{\eta }\left( {{\nabla }_{X}Y}\right) , Z}\right\rangle  .
\]

Therefore, in this case, the Codazzi equation can be written

\[
{\nabla }_{X}\left( {{S}_{\eta }\left( Y\right) }\right)  - {\nabla }_{Y}\left( {{S}_{\eta }\left( X\right) }\right)  = {S}_{\eta }\left( \left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  \right)
\]

The importance of the equations of Gauss, Codazzi, and Ricci is that, in the case in which the ambient space has constant sectional curvature, they play an analogous role to that of the compatibility equations in the local theory of surfaces (Cf. M. do Carmo [dC 2], pp. 235-236). Indeed, the compatibility equations in surface theory are only special cases of the Gauss and Codazzi equations obtained in this section. In the present case, it is possible to state an analogous theorem to the fundamental theorem of local surface theory (cf. loc. cit. p. 236). We refer the reader to the article of K. Tenenblat, "On isometric immersions of Riemannian manifolds", Boletim da Soc. Bras. de Mat. vol. 2 (1971), 23-36. A very nice discussion on the subject can be found in the article of H. Jacobowitz, "The Gauss-Codazzi equations", Tensor N.S., 39 (1982), 15-22.

nodes.label: Exercise 1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
1. Let \( {M}_{1} \) and \( {M}_{2} \) be Riemannian manifolds, and consider the product \( {M}_{1} \times  {M}_{2} \) , with the product metric. Let \( {\nabla }^{1} \) be the Riemannian connection of \( {M}_{1} \) and let \( {\nabla }^{2} \) be the Riemannian connection of \( {M}_{2} \) .

10. Let \( f : {M}^{n} \rightarrow  {\bar{M}}^{n + k} \) be an isometric immersion and let \( {S}_{\eta } \) : \( {TM} \rightarrow  {TM} \) be the operator associated to the second fundamental form of \( f \) along the normal field \( \eta \) . Consider \( {S}_{\eta } \) as a tensor of order 2 given by \( {S}_{\eta }\left( {X, Y}\right)  = \left\langle  {{S}_{\eta }\left( X\right) , Y}\right\rangle \) , \( X, Y \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) . Observe that saying the operator \( {S}_{\eta } \) is selfadjoint is equivalent to saying that the tensor \( {S}_{\eta } \) is symmetric, that is, \( {S}_{\eta }\left( {X, Y}\right)  = {S}_{\eta }\left( {Y, X}\right) \) . Prove that for all \( V \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) , the tensor \( {\nabla }_{V}{S}_{\eta } \) is symmetric.

Hint: Differentiating \( \left\langle  {{S}_{\eta }X, Y}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {X,{S}_{\eta }Y}\right\rangle \) with respect to \( V \) , we obtain

\[
\langle {\nabla }_{V}\left( {{S}_{\eta }X}\right) , Y\rangle  + \langle {S}_{\eta }X,{\nabla }_{V}Y\rangle  = \langle {\nabla }_{V}X,{S}_{\eta }Y\rangle  + \langle X,{\nabla }_{V}\left( {{S}_{\eta }Y}\right) \rangle .
\]

Using the fact that

\[
\langle \left( {{\nabla }_{V}{S}_{\eta }}\right) X), Y\rangle  = \langle {\nabla }_{V}\left( {{S}_{\eta }X}\right) , Y\rangle  - \langle {S}_{\eta }\left( {{\nabla }_{V}X}\right) , Y\rangle
\]

and the previous expression, we obtain easily that

\[
\langle \left( {{\nabla }_{V}{S}_{\eta }}\right) X, Y\rangle  = \langle X,\left( {{\nabla }_{V}{S}_{\eta }}\right) Y\rangle .
\]

11. Let \( f : {\bar{M}}^{n + 1} \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) be a differentiable function. Define the Hessian, Hess \( f \) of \( f \) at \( p \in  \bar{M} \) as the linear operator

Hess \( f : {T}_{p}\bar{M} \rightarrow  {T}_{p}\bar{M},\;\left( {\text{ Hess }f}\right) Y = {\bar{\nabla }}_{Y}\operatorname{grad}f,\;Y \in  {T}_{p}\bar{M}, \) where \( \bar{\nabla } \) is the Riemannian connection of \( \bar{M} \) . Let \( a \) be a regular value of \( f \) and let \( {M}^{\underline{n}} \subset  {\bar{M}}^{n + 1} \) be the hypersuperface in \( M \) defined by \( M = \{ p \in  \bar{M};f\left( p\right)  = a\} \) . Prove that: a) The Laplacian \( \bar{\Delta }f \) is given by

\[
\bar{\Delta }f = \text{ trace Hess }f\text{ . }
\]

b) If \( X, Y \in  \mathcal{X}\left( \bar{M}\right) \) , then

\[
\langle \left( {\operatorname{Hess}f}\right) Y, X\rangle  = \langle Y,\left( {\operatorname{Hess}f}\right) X\rangle .
\]

Conclude that Hess \( f \) is self-adjoint, hence determines a symmetric bilinear form on \( {T}_{p}\bar{M}, p \in  \bar{M} \) , given by \( \left( {\operatorname{Hess}f}\right) \left( {X, Y}\right)  = \langle \left( {\operatorname{Hess}f}\right) X, Y\rangle , X, Y \in  {T}_{p}\bar{M} \) .

c) The mean curvature \( H \) of \( M \subset  \bar{M} \) is given by

\[
{nH} =  - \operatorname{div}\left( \frac{\operatorname{grad}f}{\left| \operatorname{grad}f\right| }\right)
\]

Hint: Take an orthonormal frame \( {E}_{1},\ldots ,{E}_{n},{E}_{n + 1} = \frac{\operatorname{grad}f}{\left| \operatorname{grad}f\right| } \; = \eta \) in a neighborhood of \( p \in  M \) in \( \bar{M} \) and use the definition of divergence in Exercise 8, Chapter 3, to obtain

\[
{nH} = \operatorname{trace}{S}_{\eta } = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left\langle  {{S}_{\eta }\left( {E}_{i}\right) ,{E}_{i}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
=  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left\langle  {{\bar{\nabla }}_{{E}_{i}}\eta ,{E}_{i}}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {{\bar{\nabla }}_{\eta }\eta ,\eta }\right\rangle   = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{{n + 1}}\left\langle  {{\bar{\nabla }}_{{E}_{i}}\eta ,{E}_{i}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
=  - {\operatorname{div}}_{\bar{M}}\eta  =  - \operatorname{div}\left( \frac{\operatorname{grad}f}{\left| \operatorname{grad}f\right| }\right) .
\]

d) Observe that every embedded hypersurface \( {M}^{n} \subset \; {\widetilde{M}}^{n + 1} \) is locally the inverse image of a regular value. Conclude from (c) that the mean curvature \( H \) of such a hypersuperface is given by

\[
H =  - \frac{1}{n}\operatorname{div}N
\]

where \( N \) is an appropriate local extension of the unit normal vector field on \( {M}^{n} \subset  {\bar{M}}^{n + 1} \) .

nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
12. (Singularities of a Killing field). Let \( X \) be a Killing vector field on a Riemannian manifold \( M \) . Let \( N = \{ p \in  M;X\left( p\right)  = \) 0\}. Prove that:

a) If \( p \in  N \) , and \( V \subset  M \) is a normal neighborhood of \( p \) , with \( q \in  N \cap  V \) , then the radial geodesic segment \( \gamma \) joining \( p \) to \( q \) is contained in \( N \) . Conclude that \( \gamma  \cap  V \subset  N \) .

b) If \( p \in  N \) , there exists a neighborhood \( V \subset  M \) of \( p \) such that \( V \cap  N \) is a submanifold of \( M \) (this implies that every connected component of \( N \) is a submanifold of M).

Hint: Proceed by induction, using (a). If \( p \) is isolated, nothing has to be done. In the contrary case, let \( V \subset  M \) be a normal neighborhood of \( p \) such that there exists \( {q}_{1} \in  V \cap  N \) and consider the radial geodesic \( {\gamma }_{1} \) joining \( p \) to \( {q}_{1} \) . If \( V \cap  N = {\gamma }_{1} \) , by (a), the proof is complete. Otherwise, let \( {q}_{2} \in  V \cap  N - \left\{  {\gamma }_{1}\right\} \) and let \( {\gamma }_{2} \) be the radial geodesic joining \( p \) to \( {q}_{2} \) . Let \( Q \subset  {T}_{p}M \) be the subspace generated by the vectors \( {\exp }_{p}^{-1}\left( {q}_{1}\right) \) and \( {\exp }_{p}^{-1}\left( {q}_{2}\right) \) and let \( {N}_{2} = {\exp }_{p}\left( {Q \cap  {\exp }_{p}^{-1}\left( V\right) }\right) \) . Show that for all \( t \in  \mathbf{R} \) , the restriction of the differential \( {\left( d{X}_{t}\right) }_{p} \) of the flow \( {X}_{t} : M \rightarrow  M \) , to \( Q \) , is the identity; conclude now that \( {N}_{2} \subset  V \cap  N \) . Proceed in this way until the dimension of \( {T}_{p}M \) is exhausted.

c) The codimension, as a submanifold of \( M \) , of a connected component \( {N}_{k} \) of \( N \) is even. Assume the following fact: if a sphere has a non-vanishing differentiable vector field on it then its dimension must be odd (for a proof, see Armstrong, [Ar], p. 198).

Hint: Let \( {E}_{p} = {\left( {T}_{p}{N}_{k}\right) }^{ \bot  } \) and let \( V \subset  M \) be a normal neighborhood of \( p \) . Set \( {N}_{k}^{ \bot  } = {\exp }_{p}\left( {{E}_{p} \cap  {\exp }_{p}^{-1}\left( V\right) }\right) \) . Since, for all \( t,{\left( d{X}_{t}\right) }_{p} : {E}_{p} \rightarrow  {E}_{p} \) , we have that \( X \) is tangent to \( {N}_{k}^{ \bot  } \) . On the other hand, \( X \neq  0 \) is tangent to the geodesic spheres of \( {N}_{k}^{ \bot  } \) with center \( p \) . From the theorem mentioned above, the dimension of such a sphere is odd. Hence \( \dim {N}_{k}^{ \bot  } = \dim {E}_{p} \) is even.

nodes.label: Definition 7.1-extra-1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: In this chapter, we begin the study of the relations between local and global properties. First, we define the natural "habitat" of global properties, namely, a complete Riemannian manifold \( M \) , as a manifold in which the geodesics are defined for all values of their parameter (Cf. Def. 2.2). Formally, this means that for any \( p \in  M \) , \( {\exp }_{p} \) is defined on all of \( {T}_{p}M \) ; intuitively, this means that the manifold does not have any holes or boundaries.

nodes.title: 7.2. Complete manifolds; Hopf-Rinow Theorem

nodes.label: Definition 2.1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 2.1 Definition. A Riemannian manifold \( M \) is said to be extendible if there exists a Riemannian manifold \( {M}^{\prime } \) such that \( M \) is isometric to a proper open subset of \( {M}^{\prime } \) . In the opposite case, \( M \) is called non-extendible.
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.1 Definition. A Riemannian manifold \( M \) is said to be extendible if there exists a Riemannian manifold \( {M}^{\prime } \) such that \( M \) is isometric to a proper open subset of \( {M}^{\prime } \) . In the opposite case, \( M \) is called non-extendible.

nodes.label: Definition 2.2
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 2.2 Definition. A Riemannian manifold \( M \) is (geodesically) complete if for all \( p \in  M \) , the exponential map, \( {\exp }_{p} \) , is defined for all \( v \in  {T}_{p}M \) , i.e., if any geodesic \( \gamma \left( t\right) \) starting from \( p \) is defined for all values of the parameter \( t \in  \mathbf{R} \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.2 Definition. A Riemannian manifold \( M \) is (geodesically) complete if for all \( p \in M \) , the exponential map, \( {\exp }_{p} \) , is defined for all \( v \in {T}_{p}M \) , i.e., if any geodesic \( \gamma \left( t\right) \) starting from \( p \) is defined for all values of the parameter \( t \in \mathbf{R} \) .

nodes.label: Proposition 2.3
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 2.3 Proposition. If \( M \) is complete then \( M \) is non-extendible.
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.3 Proposition. If \( M \) is complete then \( M \) is non-extendible.

nodes.proof: Suppose that \( M \subset  {M}^{\prime } \) is isometric to a proper open subset of a Riemannian manifold \( {M}^{\prime } \) . Because \( {M}^{\prime } \) is connected, the boundary \( \partial M \) of \( M \) in \( {M}^{\prime } \) is non-empty. Let \( p \in  \partial M \) and let \( {U}^{\prime } \subset  {M}^{\prime } \) be a normal neighborhood of \( p \) in \( {M}^{\prime } \) . Let \( q \in  {U}^{\prime } \cap  M \) and let \( \widetilde{\gamma }\left( t\right) \) be a geodesic in \( {M}^{\prime } \) with \( \widetilde{\gamma }\left( 0\right)  = p,\widetilde{\gamma }\left( 1\right)  = q \) . Then \( \gamma \left( t\right)  = \widetilde{\gamma }\left( {1 - t}\right) \) , \( \left| t\right|  < \delta \) , is a geodesic in \( M \) with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = q \) . This geodesic is not defined for some \( t \leq  1 \) , which contradicts the fact that \( M \) is complete.

nodes.content: 2.4 Definition. The distance \( d\left( {p, q}\right) \) is defined by \( d\left( {p, q}\right)  = \) infimum of the lengths of all curves \( {f}_{p, q} \) , where \( {f}_{p, q} \) is a piecewise differentiable curve joining \( p \) to \( q \) .

nodes.label: Proposition 2.5
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.5 PROPOSITION. With the distance \( d, M \) is a metric space, that is:

1) \( d\left( {p, r}\right)  \leq  d\left( {p, q}\right)  + d\left( {q, r}\right) \) ,

2) \( d\left( {p, q}\right)  = d\left( {q, p}\right) \) ,

3) \( d\left( {p, q}\right)  \geq  0 \) , and \( d\left( {p, q}\right)  = 0 \Leftrightarrow  p = q \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.5 PROPOSITION. With the distance \( d, M \) is a metric space, that is: 1) \( d\left( {p, r}\right) \leq d\left( {p, q}\right) + d\left( {q, r}\right) \) , 2) \( d\left( {p, q}\right) = d\left( {q, p}\right) \) , 3) \( d\left( {p, q}\right) \geq 0 \) , and \( d\left( {p, q}\right) = 0 \Leftrightarrow p = q \) .

nodes.proof: (1), (2) and two of the assertions of (3) are immediate consequences of the definition of the infimum. It remains to show that if \( d\left( {p, q}\right)  = 0 \) then \( p = q \) . Suppose to the contrary, and take a normal ball \( {B}_{r}\left( p\right) \) that does not contain \( q \) . Since \( d\left( {p, q}\right)  = 0 \) , there exists a curve \( c \) joining \( p \) to \( q \) of length less than \( r \) . But the segment of \( c \) contained in \( {B}_{r}\left( p\right) \) certainly has length greater than or equal to \( r \) , by Proposition 3.6 of Chapter 3, and that is a contradiction.

2.8 THEOREM. (Hopf and Rinow [HR]). Let \( M \) be a Riemannian manifold and let \( p \in  M \) . The following assertions are equivalent:

sec. 2] Complete manifolds; Hopf-Rinow Theorem 147

a) \( {\exp }_{p} \) is defined on all of \( {T}_{p}\left( M\right) \) .

In addition, any of the statements above implies that

f) For any \( q \in  M \) there exists a geodesic \( \gamma \) joining \( p \) to \( q \) with \( \ell \left( \gamma \right)  = d\left( {p, q}\right) . \)

Let \( d\left( {p, q}\right)  = r \) , and let \( {B}_{\delta }\left( p\right) \) be a normal ball at \( p \) , with \( {S}_{\delta }\left( p\right)  = S \) the boundary of \( {B}_{\delta }\left( p\right) \) . Let \( {x}_{o} \) be a point where the continuous function \( d\left( {q, x}\right) , x \in  S \) , attains a minimum. Then \( {x}_{o} = {\exp }_{p}{\delta v} \) , where \( v \in  {T}_{p}M \) and \( \left| v\right|  = 1 \) . Let \( \gamma \) be a geodesic given by \( \gamma \left( s\right)  = {\exp }_{p}{sv} \) (See Fig. 1). We are going to show that \( \gamma \left( r\right)  = q \) .

![019eafac-0959-75f1-800b-ea58ccc72a58_61_281_1097_1228_539_0.jpg](images/019eafac-0959-75f1-800b-ea58ccc72a58_61_281_1097_1228_539_0.jpg)

Figure 1

To prove this fact, consider the equation

(1)

\[
d\left( {\gamma \left( s\right) , q}\right)  = r - s
\]

and let \( A = \{ s \in  \left\lbrack  {0, r}\right\rbrack  ;\left( 1\right) \) is valid \( \} .A \) is not empty, since (1) is true for \( s = 0 \) . In addition, \( A \) is closed in \( \left\lbrack  {0, r}\right\rbrack \) . Let \( {s}_{o} \in  A \) . We are going to show that if \( {s}_{o} < r \) , then (1) is valid for \( {s}_{o} + {\delta }^{\prime } \) , where \( {\delta }^{\prime } > 0 \) is sufficiently small. This implies that \( \sup A = r \) ; since \( A \) is closed then \( r \in  A \) , which shows that \( \gamma \left( r\right)  = q \) .

In order to prove that (1) is true for \( {s}_{o} + {\delta }^{\prime } \) , let \( {B}_{{\delta }^{\prime }}\left( {\gamma \left( {s}_{o}\right) }\right) \) be a normal ball at \( \gamma \left( {s}_{o}\right) \) , with \( {S}^{\prime } = \partial {B}_{\delta \prime }\left( {\gamma \left( {s}_{o}\right) }\right) \) its boundary and let \( {x}_{o}^{\prime } \) be a point where \( d\left( {x, q}\right) , x \in  {S}^{\prime } \) has a minimum. It suffices to show that \( {x}_{o}^{\prime } = \gamma \left( {{s}_{o} + {\delta }^{\prime }}\right) \) . Indeed, if \( {x}_{o}^{\prime } = \gamma \left( {{s}_{o} + {\delta }^{\prime }}\right) \) , since

\[
d\left( {\gamma \left( {s}_{o}\right) , q}\right)  = {\delta }^{\prime } + \min d\left( {x, q}\right)  = {\delta }^{\prime } + d\left( {{x}_{o}^{\prime }, q}\right)
\]

and

\[
d\left( {\gamma \left( {s}_{o}\right) , q}\right)  = r - {s}_{o},
\]

we have

(2)

\[
r - {s}_{o} = {\delta }^{\prime } + d\left( {{x}_{o}^{\prime }, q}\right)  = {\delta }^{\prime } + d\left( {\gamma \left( {{s}_{o} + {\delta }^{\prime }}\right) , q}\right) ,
\]

or that

\[
d\left( {\gamma \left( {{s}_{o} + {\delta }^{\prime }}\right) , q}\right)  = r - \left( {{s}_{o} + {\delta }^{\prime }}\right) ,
\]

which is (1) for \( {s}_{o} + {\delta }^{\prime } \) .

To prove finally that \( \gamma \left( {{s}_{o} + {\delta }^{\prime }}\right)  = {x}_{o}^{\prime } \) , observe that, by the triangle inequality and by the first equality of (2),

\[
d\left( {p,{x}_{o}^{\prime }}\right)  \geq  d\left( {p, q}\right)  - d\left( {q,{x}_{o}^{\prime }}\right)  = r - \left( {r - {s}_{o} - {\delta }^{\prime }}\right)  = {s}_{o} + {\delta }^{\prime }.
\]

On the other hand, the broken curve joining \( p \) to \( {x}_{o}^{\prime } \) , that goes from \( p \) to \( \gamma \left( {s}_{o}\right) \) by the geodesic \( \gamma \) , and from \( \gamma \left( {s}_{o}\right) \) to \( {x}_{o}^{\prime } \) by the geodesic ray, has length equal to \( {s}_{o} + {\delta }^{\prime } \) . Hence \( d\left( {p,{x}_{o}^{\prime }}\right)  = {s}_{o} + {\delta }^{\prime } \) , and such a curve, by Corollary 3.9 of Chapter 3, is a geodesic. In particular, the curve is not broken, hence \( \gamma \left( {{s}_{o} + {\delta }^{\prime }}\right)  = {x}_{o}^{\prime } \) . This concludes the proof that a) \( \Rightarrow \) f).

a) \( \Rightarrow \) b). Let \( A \subset  M \) be closed and bounded. Since \( A \) is bounded, \( A \subset  B \) , where \( B \) is a ball with center \( p \) in the metric \( d \) . By (f), there exists a ball \( {B}_{r}\left( 0\right)  \subset  {T}_{p}M \) , such that \( B \subset  {\exp }_{p}\overline{{B}_{r}\left( 0\right) } \) . Being the continuous image of a compact set, \( {\exp }_{p}\overline{{B}_{r}\left( 0\right) } \) is compact. Hence, \( A \) is a closed set contained in a compact set, and is therefore compact. b) \( \Rightarrow \) c). It suffices to observe that a subset \( \left\{  {p}_{n}\right\} \) formed by a Cauchy sequence is bounded, therefore, has compact closure by (b). Thus \( \left\{  {p}_{n}\right\} \) contains a convergent subsequence and, being Cauchy, converges.

c) \( \Rightarrow \) d). Suppose that \( M \) is not geodesically complete. Then some normalized geodesic \( \gamma \) of \( M \) is defined for \( s < {s}_{o} \) and is not defined for \( {s}_{o} \) . Let \( \left\{  {s}_{n}\right\} \) be a convergent sequence, converging to \( {s}_{o} \) with \( {s}_{n} < {s}_{o} \) . Given \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there exists an index \( {n}_{o} \) such that if \( n, m > {n}_{o} \) then \( \left| {{s}_{n} - {s}_{m}}\right|  < \varepsilon \) . It follows that

\[
d\left( {\gamma \left( {s}_{n}\right) ,\gamma \left( {s}_{m}\right) }\right)  \leq  \left| {{s}_{n} - {s}_{m}}\right|  < \varepsilon
\]

and hence the sequence \( \left\{  {\gamma \left( {s}_{n}\right) }\right\} \) is a Cauchy sequence in \( M \) . Since \( M \) is complete in the metric \( d,\left\{  {\gamma \left( {s}_{n}\right) }\right\}   \rightarrow  {p}_{o} \in  M \) .

Let \( \left( {W,\delta }\right) \) be a totally normal neighborhood of \( {p}_{o} \) . Choose \( {n}_{1} \) such that if \( n, m > {n}_{1} \) , then \( \left| {{s}_{m} - {s}_{n}}\right|  < \delta \) and \( \gamma \left( {s}_{n}\right) ,\gamma \left( {s}_{m}\right) \) belong to \( W \) . Then, there exists a unique geodesic \( g \) whose length is less than \( \delta \) joining \( \gamma \left( {s}_{n}\right) \) to \( \gamma \left( {s}_{m}\right) \) . It is clear that \( g \) coincides with \( \gamma \) , wherever \( \gamma \) is defined. Since \( {\exp }_{\gamma \left( {s}_{n}\right) } \) is a diffeomorphism on \( {B}_{\delta }\left( 0\right) \) and \( {\exp }_{\gamma \left( {s}_{n}\right) }\left( {{B}_{\delta }\left( 0\right) }\right)  \supset  W, g \) extends \( \gamma \) beyond \( {s}_{0} \) .

d) \( \Rightarrow \) a). Obvious.

b) \( \Leftrightarrow \) e). General topology.

nodes.content: 3.1 THEOREM. (Hadamard). nodes.content: 3.3 LEMMA. Let \( M \) be a complete Riemannian manifold and let \( f : M \rightarrow  N \) be a local diffeomorphism onto a Riemannian manifold \( N \) which has the following property: for all \( p \in  M \) and for all \( v \in  {T}_{p}M \) , we have \( \left| {d{f}_{p}\left( v\right) }\right|  \geq  \left| v\right| \) . Then \( f \) is a covering map.
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.3 LEMMA. Let \( M \) be a complete Riemannian manifold and let \( f : M \rightarrow N \) be a local diffeomorphism onto a Riemannian manifold \( N \) which has the following property: for all \( p \in M \) and for all \( v \in {T}_{p}M \) , we have \( \left| {d{f}_{p}\left( v\right) }\right| \geq \left| v\right| \) . Then \( f \) is a covering map.

nodes.proof:
By a general property of covering spaces (Cf. M. do Carmo, [dC2], p. 383), it suffices to show that \( f \) has the path lifting property for curves in \( N \) , that is, given a differentiable curve \( c : \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  N \) and a point \( q \in  M \) with \( f\left( q\right)  = c\left( 0\right) \) , there exists a curve \( \bar{c} : \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) with \( \bar{c}\left( 0\right)  = q \) and \( f \circ  \bar{c} = c \) .

To prove what is required, observe that, since \( f \) is a local diffeomorphism at \( q \) , there exists an \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) such that it is possible to define \( \bar{c} : \left\lbrack  {0,\varepsilon }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) with \( \bar{c}\left( 0\right)  = q \) and \( f \circ  \bar{c} = c \) ; that is, \( c \) can be lifted to a small interval starting from \( q \) . Because \( f \) is a local diffeomorphism over all of \( M \) , the set of values \( A \subset  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) , such that \( c \) can be lifted on \( A \) starting from \( q \) , is an open interval on the right; that is, \( A = \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{o}}\right) \) . If we can show that \( {t}_{o} \in  A \) , we shall have \( A \) open and closed in \( \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) , therefore \( A = \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) and \( c \) can be lifted on the entire interval.

To show that \( {t}_{o} \in  A \) , let \( \left\{  {t}_{n}\right\}  , n = 1,\ldots \) , be an increasing sequence in \( A \) with \( \lim {t}_{n} = {t}_{o} \) . Then the sequence \( \left\{  {\bar{c}\left( {t}_{n}\right) }\right\} \) is contained in a compact set \( K \subset  M \) . Indeed, if this were not the case, since \( M \) is complete, the distance from \( \bar{c}\left( {t}_{n}\right) \) to \( \bar{c}\left( 0\right) \) would be arbitrarily large. However, by hypothesis,

\[
{\ell }_{0,{t}_{n}}\left( c\right)  = {\int }_{o}^{{t}_{n}}\left| \frac{dc}{dt}\right| {dt} = {\int }_{0}^{{t}_{n}}\left| {d{f}_{\widetilde{C}\left( t\right) }\left( \frac{d\bar{c}}{dt}\right) }\right| {dt}
\]

\[
\geq  {\int }_{0}^{{t}_{n}}\left| \frac{d\bar{c}}{dt}\right| {dt} \geq  d\left( {\bar{c}\left( {t}_{n}\right) ,\bar{c}\left( 0\right) }\right)
\]

implying that the length of \( c \) between 0 and \( {t}_{o} \) is arbitrarily large, which is absurd, and proves the assertion.

Since \( \left\{  {\bar{c}\left( {t}_{n}\right) }\right\}   \subset  K, n = 1,\ldots \) , there exists an accumulation point \( r \in  M \) of \( \left\{  {\bar{c}\left( {t}_{n}\right) }\right\} \) . Let \( V \) be a neighborhood of \( r \) such that \( f \mid  V \) is a diffeomorphism. Then \( c\left( {t}_{o}\right)  \in  f\left( V\right) \) and, by continuity, there exists an interval \( I \subset  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack  ,{t}_{o} \in  I \) , such that \( c\left( I\right)  \subset  f\left( V\right) \) . Choose an index \( n \) such that \( \bar{c}\left( {t}_{n}\right)  \in  V \) and consider the lifting \( g \) of \( c \) on \( I \) passing through \( r \) . The liftings \( g \) and \( \bar{c} \) coincide on \( \lbrack 0,{t}_{n}) \cap  I \) , because \( f \mid  V \) is bijective. Therefore, \( g \) is an extension of \( \bar{c} \) to \( I \) , hence \( \bar{c} \) is defined at \( {t}_{o} \) and \( {t}_{o} \in  A \) .

nodes.content: 3.4 REMARK. The above proof gives a little more than what is stated. Call a point \( p \) of a complete Riemannian manifold \( M \) a pole if it has the property that it has no conjugate points. Any point of a complete manifold \( M \) with non-positive sectional curvature is a pole of \( M \) . However, poles can exist in non-compact manifolds which have positive sectional curvature (See Exercise 13). What we have just proved is the following general fact. If a complete simply connected Riemannian manifold \( M \) has a pole, then \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . \( n = \dim M \) .

nodes.content:
4. Consider the universal covering

\[
\pi  : M \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{2} - \{ \left( {0,0}\right) \}
\]

of the Euclidean plane minus the origin. Introduce the covering metric on \( M \) (Cf. Exercise 2). Show that \( M \) is not complete and not extendible, and that the Hopf-Rinow theorem is not true for \( M \) (this shows that the definition of non-extendibility, though natural, is not a satisfactory one).

Hint: The single difficult point is to prove that \( M \) is nonextendible. Suppose to the contrary, that is, \( M \subset  {M}^{\prime } \) , is an isometry and \( M \neq  {M}^{\prime } \) . Let \( {p}^{\prime } \in  {M}^{\prime } \) be a point in the boundary of \( M \) and let \( {W}^{\prime } \subset  {M}^{\prime } \) be a convex neighborhood of \( {p}^{\prime } \) .

If we prove that \( {W}^{\prime } - \left\{  {p}^{\prime }\right\}   \subset  M \) , we obtain a contradiction, since then \( \pi \left( {{W}^{\prime } - \left\{  {p}^{\prime }\right\}  }\right)  = U \) is a neighborhood of \( \left( {0,0}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{2} \) and considering the closed circle in \( U \) with center at \( \left( {0,0}\right) \) we can lift the closed circle into \( M \) , which is impossible.

To prove that \( {W}^{\prime } - \left\{  {p}^{\prime }\right\}   \subset  M \) , observe first that through any point \( p \in  M \) passes a unique geodesic in \( M \) that cannot be extended for all values of \( t \in  \mathbf{R} \) . Let \( x \in  {W}^{\prime } \cap  M \) and join \( x \) to \( {p}^{\prime } \) by a geodesic \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) of \( {M}^{\prime } - \widetilde{\gamma } \) coincides initially with a geodesic of \( M \) and therefore is the unique geodesic passing through \( x \) which cannot be extended for all values of \( t \) . From uniqueness and from the fact that \( {p}^{\prime } \) is a point of the boundary it follows that all the points of \( \widetilde{\gamma } \cap  W \) , except \( {p}^{\prime } \) , belong to \( M \) , because \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) approaches the boundary of \( M \) arbitrarily close. Finally, if \( z \in  {W}^{\prime } \) and \( z \notin  \widetilde{\gamma } \) , the geodesic joining \( z \) to \( x \) is, from the uniqueness above, entirely in \( M \) , hence \( z \in  M \) .

nodes.section_title: 8.2. Theorem of Cartan on the determination of the metric by means of the curvature
nodes.content:
Let \( M \) and \( \widetilde{M} \) be two Riemannian manifolds of dimension \( n \) and let \( p \in  M \) and \( \widetilde{p} \in  \widetilde{M} \) . Choose a linear isometry \( i : {T}_{p}\left( M\right)  \rightarrow  {T}_{\widetilde{p}}\left( \widetilde{M}\right) \) . Let \( V \subset  M \) be a normal neighborhood of \( p \) such that \( {\exp }_{\widetilde{p}} \) is defined at \( i \circ  {\exp }_{p}^{-1}\left( V\right) \) . Define a mapping \( f : V \rightarrow  \widetilde{M} \) by

\[
f\left( q\right)  = {\exp }_{\bar{p}} \circ  i \circ  {\exp }_{p}^{-1}\left( q\right) ,\;q \in  V.
\]

For all \( q \in  V \) there exists a unique normalized geodesic \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0, t}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p,\gamma \left( t\right)  = q \) . Denote by \( {P}_{t} \) the parallel transport along \( \gamma \) from \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) to \( \gamma \left( t\right) \) . Define \( {\phi }_{t} : {T}_{q}\left( M\right)  \rightarrow  {T}_{f\left( q\right) }\left( \bar{M}\right) \) by

\[
{\phi }_{t}\left( v\right)  = {\widetilde{P}}_{t} \circ  i \circ  {P}_{t}^{-1}\left( v\right) ,\;v \in  {T}_{q}\left( M\right) ,
\]

where \( {\widetilde{P}}_{t} \) is the parallel transport along the normalized geodesic \( \widetilde{\gamma } : \left\lbrack  {0, t}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \widetilde{M} \) given by \( \widetilde{\gamma }\left( 0\right)  = \widetilde{p},{\widetilde{\gamma }}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = i\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) . Finally, denote by \( R \) and \( \widetilde{R} \) the curvatures of \( M \) and \( \widetilde{M} \) , respectively.

nodes.proof:
Let \( q \in  V \) and let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) be a normalized geodesic with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p,\gamma \left( \ell \right)  = q \) . Let \( v \in  {T}_{q}\left( M\right) \) and let \( J \) be a Jacobi field along \( \gamma \) given by \( J\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) and \( J\left( \ell \right)  = v \) . Let \( {e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n} = {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) be an orthonormal basis of \( {T}_{p}\left( M\right) \) and let \( {e}_{i}\left( t\right) , i = 1,\ldots , n \) , be the parallel transport of \( {e}_{i} \) along \( \gamma \) . Writing

\[
J\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{y}_{i}\left( t\right) {e}_{i}\left( t\right)
\]

and using the Jacobi equation, we conclude that

\[
{y}_{j}^{\prime \prime } + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}\left\langle  {R\left( {{e}_{n},{e}_{i}}\right) {e}_{n},{e}_{j}}\right\rangle  {y}_{i} = 0,\;j = 1,\ldots , n.
\]

Now, let \( \widetilde{\gamma } : \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \widetilde{M} \) be a normalized geodesic given by \( \widetilde{\gamma }\left( 0\right)  = \widetilde{p},{\widetilde{\gamma }}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = i\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) . Let \( \widetilde{J}\left( t\right) \) be the field along \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) given by

\[
\widetilde{J}\left( t\right)  = {\phi }_{t}\left( {J\left( t\right) }\right) ,\;t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack
\]

Let \( {\widetilde{e}}_{j}\left( t\right)  = {\phi }_{t}\left( {{e}_{j}\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Then, from the linearity of \( {\phi }_{t} \) ,

\[
\widetilde{J}\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{y}_{i}\left( t\right) {\widetilde{e}}_{i}\left( t\right) .
\]

Since, by hypothesis,

\[
\left\langle  {R\left( {{e}_{n},{e}_{i}}\right) {e}_{n},{e}_{j}}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {\widetilde{R}\left( {{\widetilde{e}}_{n},{\widetilde{e}}_{i}}\right) {\widetilde{e}}_{n},{\widetilde{e}}_{j}}\right\rangle  ,
\]

we have that

\[
{y}_{j}^{\prime \prime } + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}\left\langle  {\widetilde{R}\left( {{\widetilde{e}}_{n},{\widetilde{e}}_{i}}\right) {\widetilde{e}}_{n},{\widetilde{e}}_{j}}\right\rangle  {y}_{i} = 0,\;j = 1,\ldots , n.
\]

It follows that \( \widetilde{J} \) is a Jacobi field along \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) with \( \widetilde{J}\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) . Since parallel transport is an isometry, \( \left| {\widetilde{J}\left( \ell \right) }\right|  = \left| {J\left( \ell \right) }\right| \) . If we show that

\[
\widetilde{J}\left( \ell \right)  = d{f}_{q}\left( v\right)  = d{f}_{q}\left( {J\left( \ell \right) }\right) ,
\]

we have completed the proof.

Since \( \widetilde{J}\left( t\right)  = {\phi }_{t}\left( {J\left( t\right) }\right) \) , we have that \( {\widetilde{J}}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = i\left( {{J}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) . On the other hand, since \( J\left( t\right) \) and \( \widetilde{J}\left( t\right) \) are Jacobi fields which vanish at \( t = 0 \) , we have from Corollary 2.5 of Chapter 5

\[
J\left( t\right)  = {\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{t{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\left( {t{J}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\widetilde{J}\left( t\right)  = {\left( d{\exp }_{\widetilde{p}}\right) }_{t{\widetilde{\gamma }}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\left( {t{\widetilde{J}}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) .
\]

Therefore,

\[
\widetilde{J}\left( \ell \right)  = {\left( d{\exp }_{\widetilde{p}}\right) }_{\ell {\widetilde{\gamma }}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\ell i\left( {{J}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= {\left( d{\exp }_{\widetilde{p}}\right) }_{\ell {\bar{\gamma }}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) } \circ  i \circ  {\left( {\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{\ell {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) }^{-1}\left( {J\left( \ell \right) }\right)  = d{f}_{q}\left( {J\left( \ell \right) }\right) ,
\]

which proves what was asserted.

\[
\langle u, v{\rangle }_{p} = f\left( p\right) \langle \langle u, v\rangle {\rangle }_{p}.
\]

For example, the metric (1) of \( {H}^{n} \) is conformal to the usual metric of Euclidean space \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) .

nodes.label: Theorem 4.1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
4.1 THEOREM. Let \( {M}^{n} \) be a complete Riemannian manifold with constant sectional curvature \( K \) . Then the universal covering \( \widetilde{M} \) of \( M \) , with the covering metric, is isometric to:

a) \( {H}^{n} \) , if \( K =  - 1 \) ,

\[
\text{ b) }{\mathbf{R}}^{n}\text{ , if }K = 0\text{ , }
\]

c) \( {S}^{n} \) , if \( K = 1 \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 4.1 THEOREM. Let \( {M}^{n} \) be a complete Riemannian manifold with constant sectional curvature \( K \) . Then the universal covering \( \widetilde{M} \) of \( M \) , with the covering metric, is isometric to: a) \( {H}^{n} \) , if \( K = - 1 \) , \[ \text{ b) }{\mathbf{R}}^{n}\text{ , if }K = 0\text{ , } \] c) \( {S}^{n} \) , if \( K = 1 \) .

nodes.proof:
\( \widetilde{M} \) is a simply connected, complete Riemannian manifold, with constant sectional curvature \( K \) . Let us consider, in the first place, the cases (a) and (b) and denote, for convenience, \( {H}^{n} \) as well as \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) by \( \bigtriangleup \) . Fix points \( p \in  \bigtriangleup ,\widetilde{p} \in  \widetilde{M} \) and a linear isometry \( i : {T}_{p}\left( \bigtriangleup \right)  \rightarrow  {T}_{\widetilde{p}}\left( \widetilde{M}\right) \) . Consider the map:

\[
f = {\exp }_{\widetilde{p}} \circ  i \circ  {\exp }_{p}^{-1} : \bigtriangleup  \rightarrow  \widetilde{M}.
\]

Since \( \Delta \) and \( \widetilde{M} \) are complete with non-positive sectional curvature, \( f \) is well-defined. From the Theorem of Cartan, \( f \) is a local isometry. From Lemma 3.3 of Chap. 7, \( f \) is a diffeomorphism and this proves (a) and (b).

For the case (c), fix, once more, points \( p \in  {S}^{n},\widetilde{p} \in  \widetilde{M} \) and a linear isometry \( i : {T}_{p}\left( {S}^{n}\right)  \rightarrow  {T}_{\widetilde{p}}\left( \widetilde{M}\right) \) . Let \( q \in  {S}^{n} \) be the antipodal point of \( p \) and define

\[
f = {\exp }_{\widetilde{p}} \circ  i \circ  {\exp }_{p}^{-1} : {S}^{n} - \{ q\}  \rightarrow  \widetilde{M}.
\]

From the Theorem of Cartan, \( f \) is a local isometry. Now choose a point \( {p}^{\prime } \in  {S}^{n};{p}^{\prime } \neq  p,{p}^{\prime } \neq  q \) . Set \( {\widetilde{p}}^{\prime } = f\left( {p}^{\prime }\right) ,{i}^{\prime } = d{f}_{{p}^{\prime }} \) and define

\[
{f}^{\prime } = {\exp }_{{\bar{p}}^{\prime }} \circ  {i}^{\prime } \circ  {\exp }_{{p}^{\prime }}^{-1} : {S}^{n} - \left\{  {q}^{\prime }\right\}   \rightarrow  \widetilde{M},
\]

where \( {q}^{\prime } \) is the antipodal point of \( {p}^{\prime } \) .

Observe that \( {S}^{n} - \left( {\{ q\}  \cup  \left\{  {q}^{\prime }\right\}  }\right)  = W \) is connected, \( {p}^{\prime } \in  W \) , and

\[
f\left( {p}^{\prime }\right)  = {\widetilde{p}}^{\prime } = {f}^{\prime }\left( {p}^{\prime }\right) ,\;d{f}_{{p}^{\prime }} = {i}^{\prime } = d{f}_{{p}^{\prime }}^{\prime }.
\]

It follows from Lemma 4.2, that \( f = {f}^{\prime } \) on \( W \) . As a consequence, we can define a map \( g : {S}^{n} \rightarrow  \widetilde{M} \) by

\[
g\left( r\right)  = \left\{  \begin{array}{ll} f\left( r\right) , & \text{ if }r \in  {S}^{n} - \{ q\} \\  {f}^{\prime }\left( r\right) , & \text{ if }r \in  {S}^{n} - \left\{  {q}^{\prime }\right\}  . \end{array}\right.
\]

It is clear that \( g \) is a local isometry, therefore a local diffeomorphism. By the compactness of \( {S}^{n}, g \) is a covering map, and since \( \widetilde{M} \) is simply connected, \( g \) is a diffeomorphism (see M. do Carmo [dC 2] §5.6). Therefore \( g \) is an isometry.

nodes.content: 4.2 LEMMA. Let \( {f}_{i} : M \rightarrow  N, i = 1,2 \) , be two local isometries of the (connected) Riemannian manifold \( M \) to the Riemannian manifold \( N \) . Suppose that there exists a point \( p \in  M \) such that \( d{f}_{1}\left( p\right)  = {f}_{2}\left( p\right) \) and \( {\left( d{f}_{l}\right) }_{p} = {\left( d{f}_{2}\right) }_{p} \) . Then \( {f}_{1} = {f}_{2} \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 4.2 LEMMA. Let \( {f}_{i} : M \rightarrow N, i = 1,2 \) , be two local isometries of the (connected) Riemannian manifold \( M \) to the Riemannian manifold \( N \) . Suppose that there exists a point \( p \in M \) such that \( d{f}_{1}\left( p\right) = {f}_{2}\left( p\right) \) and \( {\left( d{f}_{l}\right) }_{p} = {\left( d{f}_{2}\right) }_{p} \) . Then \( {f}_{1} = {f}_{2} \) .

nodes.proof:
Let \( V \) be a normal neighborhood of \( p \) such that the restrictions \( {f}_{1}\left| {V\text{ and }{f}_{2}}\right| V \) are diffeomorphisms. Let \( \varphi  = \; {f}_{1}^{-1} \circ  {f}_{2} : V \rightarrow  V \) . Then \( \varphi \left( p\right)  = p \) and \( d{\varphi }_{p} \) is the identity. If \( q \in  V \) , there exists a unique \( v \in  {T}_{p}M \) with \( {\exp }_{p}\left( v\right)  = q \) . It follows that \( \varphi \left( q\right)  = q \) , hence \( {f}_{1} = {f}_{2} \) on \( V \) . Since \( M \) is connected, any point \( r \in  M \) can be joined to \( p \) by a path \( \alpha  : \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M,\alpha \left( 0\right)  = p \) , \( \alpha \left( 1\right)  = r \) . Let

\[
A = \left\{  {t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack  ;{f}_{1}\left( {\alpha \left( t\right) }\right)  = {f}_{2}\left( {\alpha \left( t\right) }\right) \text{ and }{\left( d{f}_{1}\right) }_{\alpha \left( t\right) } = {\left( d{f}_{2}\right) }_{\alpha \left( t\right) }}\right\}  .
\]

From the preceding, \( \sup A \) is positive. If \( \sup A = {t}_{o} \neq  1 \) , we repeat the argument above for the point \( \alpha \left( {t}_{o}\right) \) , obtaining a contradiction. Therefore \( \sup A = 1 \) , hence \( {f}_{1}\left( r\right)  = {f}_{2}\left( r\right) \) , for all \( r \in  M \) .

nodes.label: Definition 8.4-extra-2
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
We say that a group \( G \) acts (on the left) on a set \( M \) if there exists a map of \( G \times  M \) onto \( M \) , denoted by

\[
G \times  M \ni  \left( {g, x}\right)  \rightarrow  {gx} \in  M
\]

such that

\[
{ex} = x,\;\left( {{g}_{1}{g}_{2}}\right) x = {g}_{1}\left( {{g}_{2}x}\right)
\]

where \( e = \) the identity of \( G, x \in  M \) and \( {g}_{1},{g}_{2} \in  G \) . We say that \( G \) acts freely (i.e., without fixed points) on \( M \) if \( {gx} = x \) implies \( g = e \) . The orbit of a point \( x \in  M \) is the set

\[
{Gx} = \{ {gx};g \in  G\} .
\]

The action of \( G \) is said to be transitive if \( {Gx} = M \) . The set of all orbits is denoted by \( M/G \) ; there exists a natural projection \( \pi  : M \rightarrow \; M/G \) given by \( \pi \left( x\right)  = {Gx} \) . When \( M \) has some additional structure (topological, differentiable, etc.), it is convenient to consider \( G \) as a group of isomorphisms (homeomorphisms, diffeomorphisms, etc.) of the structure under consideration.

If \( M \) is a topological space, we say that the group \( G \) (of homeomorphisms of \( M \) ) acts in a totally discontinuous manner if every \( x \in  M \) has a neighborhood \( U \) such that \( g\left( U\right)  \cap  U = \phi \) , for all \( g \in  G, g \neq  e \) . In this case, the projection \( \pi  : M \rightarrow  M/G \) (where \( M/G \) has the quotient topology) is a regular covering map and \( G \) is the group of covering transformations (See Massey [Ma], Prop. 8.2, p. 165).

nodes.proof: Consider the universal covering \( p : \widetilde{M} \rightarrow  M \) , and provide \( \widetilde{M} \) with the covering metric, that is, the metric such that \( p \) is a local isometry. Let \( \Gamma \) be the group of covering transformations of the covering \( p \) . Then \( \Gamma \) is a subgroup of the group of isometries of \( \widetilde{M} \) and acts on \( \widetilde{M} \) in a totally discontinuous manner. Therefore it is possible to introduce on \( \widetilde{M}/\Gamma \) the Riemannian metric induced by \( \pi  : \widetilde{M} \rightarrow  \widetilde{M}/\Gamma \) . Since the covering \( p \) is regular, given \( \widetilde{x},\widetilde{y} \in  \widetilde{M} \) then \( p\left( \widetilde{x}\right)  = p\left( \widetilde{y}\right) \) if and only if \( \Gamma \widetilde{x} = \Gamma \widetilde{y} \) which is equivalent to \( \pi \left( \widetilde{x}\right)  = \pi \left( \widetilde{y}\right) \) . The equivalence classes given by \( p \) and \( \pi \) on \( \widetilde{M} \) are, therefore, the same, and this induces a bijection \( \xi  : M \rightarrow  \widetilde{M}/\Gamma \) such that \( \pi  = \xi  \circ  p \) . Since \( \pi \) and \( p \) are local isometries, \( \xi \) is a local isometry as well, and being a bijection, is an isometry of \( M \) onto \( \widetilde{M}/\Gamma \) .

nodes.proof: The orthogonal group \( 0\left( {{2m} + 1}\right) \) is the (transitive) group of isometries of \( {S}^{n} \) . Let \( \Gamma \) be a subgroup that acts in a totally discontinuous manner on \( {S}^{n} \) . If \( \gamma  \in  \Gamma \) has determinant +1, there exists an eigenvalue of \( \gamma \) equal to 1 . Then \( \gamma \) has a fixed point, which implies that \( \gamma  = e \) . If \( \widetilde{\gamma } \in  \Gamma \) has determinant -1, then \( {\widetilde{\gamma }}^{2} \) has determinant 1, therefore \( {\widetilde{\gamma }}^{2} = e \) . As a consequence, the eigenvalues of \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) are 1 or -1 . If 1 is an eigenvalue of \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) , then \( \widetilde{\gamma } = e \) , which contradicts the fact that \( \det \widetilde{\gamma } =  - 1 \) . As a result \( \widetilde{\gamma } =  - e \) , hence, \( \Gamma  = \{ e, - e\} \) . Using now Proposition 4.3 we obtain that \( {M}^{n} \) is either \( {S}^{n} \) , if \( \Gamma  = \{ e\} \) , or \( {P}^{n} \) , if \( \Gamma  = \{ e, - e\} \) .

nodes.label: Proposition 4.5
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 4.5 Proposition. Every compact orientable surface of genus \( p > 1 \) can be provided with a metric of constant negative curvature.
nodes.content_excerpt: 4.5 Proposition. Every compact orientable surface of genus \( p > 1 \) can be provided with a metric of constant negative curvature.

nodes.proof:
In the hyperbolic plane \( {H}^{2} \) take a closed geodesic polygon \( P \) with \( {4p} \) sides of equal lengths. By a well known process of identifying the sides, \( P \) can be identified with a topological surface \( {M}^{2} \) (See Massey [Ma], Chap. 1). Let \( \Gamma \) be the subgroup of isometries of \( {H}^{2} \) generated by the isometries that identify the sides of \( P \) . It is possible to show that the transforms of \( P \) by \( \Gamma \) "tile \( {H}^{2} \) without any gaps" if and only if the sum \( \alpha \) of the interior angles at the vertices of \( P \) is equal to \( {2\pi } \) (for a simple proof see Roger Fenn,"What is the geometry of a surface?", American Math. Monthly, Feb. 1983); in this case, \( {M}^{2} = {H}^{2}/\Gamma \) has a metric of constant curvature equal to -1 . We assert that it is possible to find a polygon \( P \) which satisfies the condition \( \alpha  = {2\pi } \) , which will conclude the proof of the proposition.

To prove what is required, observe that by the Gauss-Bonnet Theorem (see M. do Carmo [dC 2], p. 274), we obtain that

\[
\alpha  =  - A + {2\pi }\left( {{2p} - 1}\right) ,
\]

where \( A \) is the area of \( P \) in the hyperbolic metric. Therefore, on the one hand, if the polygon \( P \) is arbitrarily small, \( \alpha \) is arbitrarily close to \( {2\pi }\left( {{2p} - 1}\right) \) . On the other hand, we can enlarge the area \( A \) of polygon \( P \) in such a way that \( \alpha \) is arbitrarily small. It follows that, by continuously deforming \( P \) , there exists a geodesic polygon such that \( \alpha  = {2\pi } \) .

nodes.label: Definition 8.5-extra-1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.section_title: 8.5. Isometries of the hyperbolic space; Theorem of Liouville
nodes.content:
A map \( f : U \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) of an open set \( U \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is called conformal if the (non-oriented) angles of intersecting curves are preserved, that is, if the (non-oriented) angle of any two vectors \( {v}_{1} \) and \( {v}_{2} \) at \( p \in  U \) is equal to the angle formed by \( d{f}_{p}\left( {v}_{1}\right) \) with \( d{f}_{p}\left( {v}_{2}\right) \) . The principal objective of this section is to show that the isometries of the upper half-space \( {H}^{n} \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) with the metric \( \frac{{\delta }_{ij}}{{x}_{n}^{2}} \) (cf. Section 2) are the restrictions to \( {H}^{n} \) of conformal transformations of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) that map \( {H}^{n} \) onto \( {H}^{n} \) . To prove this theorem, we have to describe the conformal transformations of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) .

For the case of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{2} \) , which we identify with the complex plane C, it is well-known that the conformal transformations are holomorphic or anti-holomorphic functions (anti-holomorphic means that the complex conjugate function is holomorphic) with non-zero derivatives. In this regard, the Riemann mapping theorem guarantees that given two simply connected proper open sets in the plane, there exists a conformal mapping taking one into the other.

For the case of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n}, n > 2 \) , the situation is radically different, and the fact that \( f \) is a conformal transformation imposes strong restrictions on \( f \) . This is contained in the Theorem of Liouville below, for which we require some considerations.

First, observe that a necessary and sufficient condition so that \( f : U \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is conformal is that for all \( p \in  U \) and for all pairs of vectors \( {v}_{1},{v}_{2} \) at \( p \) it is true that:

(3)

\[
\left\langle  {d{f}_{p}\left( {v}_{1}\right) , d{f}_{p}\left( {v}_{2}\right) }\right\rangle   = {\lambda }^{2}\left( p\right) \left\langle  {{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}\right\rangle  ,\;{\lambda }^{2} \neq  0.
\]

Indeed, if (3) is satisfied, \( {\left| d{f}_{p}\left( v\right) \right| }^{2} = {\lambda }^{2}{\left| v\right| }^{2} \) , for every vector \( v \) at \( p \) , hence

(4)

\[
\cos \mathcal{X}\left( {d{f}_{p}\left( {v}_{1}\right) , d{f}_{p}\left( {v}_{2}\right) }\right)  = \cos \mathcal{X}\left( {{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}\right) ,
\]

that is, the (non-oriented) angles are preserved. Conversely, (4) implies that \( d{f}_{p} \) takes a triangle with vertex at \( p \) into a similar triangle with vertex at \( f\left( p\right) \) . Therefore \( {\left| d{f}_{p}\left( v\right) \right| }^{2} = {\lambda }^{2}{\left| v\right| }^{2} \) , for every \( v \) at \( p \) ; applying this last relation to the sum of vectors \( u + v \) we obtain (3).

The positive function \( \lambda  : U \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) defined in (3) will be called the coefficient of conformality of \( f \) .

nodes.label: Example 5.1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.section_title: 8.5. Isometries of the hyperbolic space; Theorem of Liouville
nodes.content:
5.1 Example.. It is clear that an isometry of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) (orthogonal linear transformation followed by a translation) is a conformal transformation of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) with coefficient of conformality \( \lambda  \equiv  1 \) . The linear transformation \( f\left( p\right)  = {\lambda I}\left( p\right) , p \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) , where \( I \) is the identity matrix and \( \lambda  = \) const. \( > 0 \) , is evidently a conformal transformation with coefficient of conformality \( \lambda ;f \) is called a dilatation. As a last example, we are going to show that the inversion with respect to the unit sphere centered at \( {p}_{o} \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) , defined by

(5)

\[
f\left( p\right)  = \frac{p - {p}_{o}}{{\left| p - {p}_{o}\right| }^{2}} + {p}_{o},\;p \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} - \left\{  {p}_{o}\right\}  ,
\]

is a conformal transformation.

Geometrically, \( f \) takes \( p \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} - \left\{  {p}_{o}\right\} \) into a point \( f\left( p\right) \) which is on the line through \( p \) and \( {p}_{o} \) , at a distance \( \left| {f\left( p\right)  - {p}_{o}}\right|  = \frac{1}{\left| p - {p}_{o}\right| } \) from \( {p}_{o} \) . Therefore \( f \) keeps fixed the sphere of radius 1 around \( {p}_{o} \) , and permutes the interior region with the exterior of such a sphere; in particular, \( {f}^{2} = \) identity.

To see that \( f \) is conformal, observe that, if \( v \) is a vector at \( p \) ,

\[
d{f}_{p}\left( v\right)  = \frac{v{\left| p - {p}_{o}\right| }^{2} - 2\left\langle  {v, p - {p}_{o}}\right\rangle  \left( {p - {p}_{o}}\right) }{{\left| p - {p}_{o}\right| }^{4}},
\]

therefore

\[
{\left| d{f}_{p}\left( v\right) \right| }^{2} = \frac{\langle v, v\rangle }{{\left| p - {p}_{o}\right| }^{4}} + \frac{\left( {4\langle v, p - {p}_{o}{\rangle }^{2} - 4\langle v, p - {p}_{o}{\rangle }^{2}}\right) {\left| p - {p}_{o}\right| }^{2}}{{\left| p - {p}_{o}\right| }^{8}}
\]

\[
= \frac{\langle v, v\rangle }{{\left| p - {p}_{o}\right| }^{4}},
\]

that is, the inversion (5) is a conformal transformation with coefficient of conformality \( \lambda  = \frac{1}{{\left| p - {p}_{o}\right| }^{2}} \) .
