nodes.content: 5.2 THEOREM. (Liouville). Let \( f : U \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{n}, n \geq  3 \) , be a conformal transformation of an open set \( U \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . Then \( f \) is the restriction to \( U \) of a composition of isometries, dilatations or inversions, at most one of each.
nodes.content_excerpt: 5.2 THEOREM. (Liouville). Let \( f : U \rightarrow {\mathbf{R}}^{n}, n \geq 3 \) , be a conformal transformation of an open set \( U \subset {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . Then \( f \) is the restriction to \( U \) of a composition of isometries, dilatations or inversions, at most one of each.

nodes.proof:
Let \( {a}_{1} = \left( {1,0,\ldots ,0}\right) ,\ldots ,{a}_{n} = \left( {0,0,\ldots ,0,1}\right) \) be the canonical basis of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) and \( \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right) \) the cartesian coordinates of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) relative to this basis. Let \( {e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n} \) be parallel differentiable vector fields on \( U \) , such that at each point of \( U,\left\langle  {{e}_{i},{e}_{j}}\right\rangle   = {\delta }_{ij} \) . If \( \lambda \) is the coefficient of conformality of \( f \) , we can write

(6)

\[
\left\langle  {{{df}\left( {e}_{i}\right) },{{df}\left( {e}_{k}\right) }}\right\rangle   = {\lambda }^{2}{\delta }_{ik},\;i, k = 1,\ldots , n.
\]

Let \( {d}^{2}f \) be the second differential of \( f \) ; that is, \( d{f}^{2} = {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \times \; {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is a symmetric bilinear map with values in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) and such that, in the canonical basis, \( {d}^{2}f\left( {{a}_{i},{a}_{j}}\right)  = \frac{{\partial }^{2}f}{\partial {x}_{i}\partial {x}_{j}} \) . Taking the indices \( i, j, k \) distinct and differentiating (6), we obtain:

\[
\left\langle  {{d}^{2}f\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{j}}\right) ,{df}\left( {e}_{k}\right) }\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {{df}\left( {e}_{i}\right) ,{d}^{2}f\left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{j}}\right) }\right\rangle   = 0,
\]

\[
\left\langle  {{d}^{2}f\left( {{e}_{j},{e}_{k}}\right) ,{df}\left( {e}_{i}\right) }\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {{df}\left( {e}_{j}\right) ,{d}^{2}f\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{k}}\right) }\right\rangle   = 0
\]

\[
\left\langle  {{d}^{2}f\left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{i}}\right) ,{df}\left( {e}_{j}\right) }\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {{df}\left( {e}_{k}\right) ,{d}^{2}f\left( {{e}_{j},{e}_{i}}\right) }\right\rangle   = 0.
\]

Summing the first two equations above and subtracting the third, we have

\[
\left\langle  {{d}^{2}f\left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{j}}\right) ,{df}\left( {e}_{i}\right) }\right\rangle   = 0,\;\text{ if }i, j, k\text{ are distinct. }
\]

Fixing \( k, j \) and letting \( i \) vary in the remaining \( \left( {n - 2}\right) \) indices, we conclude that \( {d}^{2}f\left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{j}}\right) \) belongs to the plane generated by \( {df}\left( {e}_{j}\right) \) and \( {df}\left( {e}_{k}\right) \) . Therefore,

\[
{d}^{2}f\left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{j}}\right)  = {\mu df}\left( {e}_{k}\right)  + {\nu df}\left( {e}_{j}\right) ,
\]

in which, since \( \left\langle  {{df}\left( {e}_{k}\right) ,{df}\left( {e}_{k}\right) }\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {{df}\left( {e}_{j}\right) ,{df}\left( {e}_{j}\right) }\right\rangle   = {\lambda }^{2} \) ,

\[
\mu  = \frac{\left\langle  {d}^{2}f\left( {e}_{k},{e}_{j}\right) , df\left( {e}_{k}\right) \right\rangle  }{{\lambda }^{2}} = \frac{{\lambda d\lambda }\left( {e}_{j}\right) }{{\lambda }^{2}} = \frac{{d\lambda }\left( {e}_{j}\right) }{\lambda },
\]

\[
\nu  = \frac{{d\lambda }\left( {e}_{k}\right) }{\lambda }
\]

that is,

(7)

\[
{d}^{2}f\left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{j}}\right)  = \frac{1}{\lambda }\left( {{df}\left( {e}_{k}\right) {d\lambda }\left( {e}_{j}\right)  + {df}\left( {e}_{j}\right) {d\lambda }\left( {e}_{k}\right) }\right) .
\]

It will be convenient, in what follows, to put \( \rho  = \frac{1}{\lambda } \) . We are going to calculate the second differential \( {d}^{2}\left( {\rho f}\right) \) . Because \( d\left( {\rho f}\right)  = \; {d\rho f} + {\rho df} \) , we obtain, using (7),(8)

\[
{d}^{2}\left( {\rho f}\right) \left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{j}}\right)  = {d}^{2}\rho \left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{j}}\right) f + \rho {d}^{2}f\left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{j}}\right)  + {d\rho }\left( {e}_{k}\right) {df}\left( {e}_{j}\right)
\]

\[
+ {d\rho }\left( {e}_{j}\right) {df}\left( {e}_{k}\right)  = {d}^{2}\rho \left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{j}}\right) f + \frac{1}{\lambda }{d}^{2}f\left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{j}}\right)
\]

\[
- \frac{1}{{\lambda }^{2}}\left\{  {{d\lambda }\left( {e}_{k}\right) {df}\left( {e}_{j}\right)  + {d\lambda }\left( {e}_{j}\right) {df}\left( {e}_{k}\right) }\right\}   = {d}^{2}\rho \left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{j}}\right) f.
\]

We claim that \( {d}^{2}\rho \left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{j}}\right)  = 0 \) , for \( k \neq  j \) . To see this, calculate the third differential \( {d}^{3}\left( {\rho f}\right) \) , that is, the symmetric trilinear mapping, \( {d}^{3}\left( {\rho f}\right)  : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \times  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \times  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) with values in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) and such that, in the canonical basis, \( {d}^{3}\left( {\rho f}\right) \left( {{a}_{i},{a}_{j},{a}_{k}}\right)  = \frac{{\partial }^{3}\left( {\rho f}\right) }{\partial {x}_{i}\partial {x}_{j}\partial {x}_{k}} \) . Using (8), we obtain

\[
{d}^{3}\left( {\rho f}\right) \left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{j},{e}_{i}}\right)  = {d}^{3}\rho \left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{j},{e}_{i}}\right) f + {d}^{2}\rho \left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{j}}\right) {df}\left( {e}_{i}\right) .
\]

In the expression above, the first member and the first part of the second member are symmetric in the three indices \( i, j, k \) . Therefore, the same thing happens with the second part of the second member. We conclude that

\[
{d}^{2}\rho \left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{j}}\right) {df}\left( {e}_{i}\right)  = {d}^{2}\rho \left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{i}}\right) {df}\left( {e}_{j}\right) .
\]

Since \( {df}\left( {e}_{i}\right) \) and \( {df}\left( {e}_{j}\right) \) are linearly independent and \( i, j, k \) are distinct but arbitrary indices, we obtain that \( {d}^{2}\rho \left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{j}}\right)  = 0 \) , for all \( j \neq  k \) , as we have asserted.

Now observe that, fixing \( p \in  U \) , we can choose the vector fields \( {e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n} \) in such a way that they form an orthonormal basis previously given at \( p \) . Therefore the relation \( {d}^{2}\rho \left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{j}}\right)  = 0 \) is valid at \( p \) for every orthonormal basis at \( p \) and, because \( p \) is arbitrary, the same thing happens on \( U \) . Since \( {d}^{2}\rho \) is a symmetric bilinear form and

\[
0 = {d}^{2}\rho \left( {\frac{{e}_{j} + {e}_{k}}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{{e}_{j} - {e}_{k}}{\sqrt{2}}}\right)  = \frac{1}{2}\left\{  {{d}^{2}\rho \left( {{e}_{j},{e}_{j}}\right)  - {d}^{2}\rho \left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{k}}\right) }\right\}  ,
\]

we conclude that \( {d}^{2}\rho \left( {{e}_{j},{e}_{j}}\right)  = {d}^{2}\rho \left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{k}}\right) \) , for all \( j \neq  k \) .

In summary, for every \( p \in  U \) and for any orthonormal basis \( {e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n} \) at \( p \) , we have that \( {d}^{2}\rho \left( {{e}_{j},{e}_{k}}\right)  = \sigma {\delta }_{jk} \) . Taking, in particular, the canonical basis, we have

(9)

\[
\frac{{\partial }^{2}\rho }{\partial {x}_{i}\partial {x}_{j}} = \sigma {\delta }_{ij}
\]

Calculating the derivative of both of the members of (9), we conclude that \( \left( {i \neq  j}\right) \)

\[
\frac{\partial \sigma }{\partial {x}_{i}} = \frac{{\partial }^{3}\rho }{\partial {x}_{i}\partial {x}_{j}\partial {x}_{j}} = \frac{{\partial }^{3}\rho }{\partial {x}_{j}\partial {x}_{i}\partial {x}_{j}} = 0,
\]

that is, \( \sigma  = \) const.

First we are going to consider the case \( \sigma  = \) const. \( \neq  0 \) and show that Eq. (9) implies that(10)\( \rho  = \frac{\sigma }{2}\sum {x}_{i}^{2} + \sigma \sum {b}_{i}{x}_{i} + c,\;{b}_{i} \) and \( c \) constants.

Indeed, from \( \frac{{\partial }^{2}\rho }{\partial {x}_{i}^{2}} = \sigma \) we conclude that

\[
\frac{\partial \rho }{\partial {x}_{i}} = \sigma {x}_{i} + \sigma {b}_{i}
\]

where \( {b}_{i} \) is a function that does not depend on \( {x}_{i} \) ; since \( \frac{{\partial }^{2}\rho }{\partial {x}_{i}\partial {x}_{j}} = 0 \) , \( {b}_{i} \) also does not depend on \( {x}_{j}, j \neq  i \) . Therefore \( {b}_{i} \) is a constant, and

\[
\rho  = \frac{1}{2}\sigma {x}_{i}^{2} + \sigma {b}_{i}{x}_{i} + {\varphi }_{i},
\]

where \( {\varphi }_{i} \) does not depend on \( {x}_{i} \) . Because \( \frac{\partial \rho }{\partial {x}_{j}} = \frac{\partial {\varphi }_{i}}{\partial {x}_{j}}, j \neq  i \) , we conclude that

\[
{\varphi }_{i} = \frac{1}{2}\sigma {x}_{j}^{2} + \sigma {b}_{j}{x}_{j} + {\varphi }_{ij},
\]

where \( {\varphi }_{ij} \) does not depend on \( {x}_{i} \) and on \( {x}_{j} \) . Proceeding inductively, we obtain (10), as claimed.

Therefore, if \( \sigma  \neq  0 \) , we can write (10) in the form

\[
\frac{1}{\lambda } = \rho  = {a}_{1}{\left| p - {p}_{o}\right| }^{2} + {k}_{1},\;{a}_{1} = \frac{\sigma }{2}\;\text{ and }{k}_{1} = \text{ const. },{p}_{o} \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n}.
\]

The proof will be complete, for the case \( \sigma  \neq  0 \) , if we show that \( {k}_{1} = 0 \) . Because, considering the inversion \( g : U \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) :

\[
g\left( p\right)  = \frac{p - {p}_{o}}{{\left| p - {p}_{o}\right| }^{2}} + {p}_{o}
\]

and taking the composition \( h = g \circ  {f}^{-1} \) , we have that \( h \) is a conformal transformation whose coefficient of conformality is

\[
{a}_{1}{\left| p - {p}_{o}\right| }^{2}\frac{1}{{\left| p - {p}_{o}\right| }^{2}} = {a}_{1}.
\]

Therefore, \( h \) is an isometry followed by a dilatation, hence \( f = {h}^{-1} \circ  g \) is an inversion followed by a dilatation, followed by an isometry.

Now we are going to prove that \( {k}_{1} = 0 \) . Observe that applying to \( {f}^{-1} \) the above argument, we obtain

\[
\lambda  = {a}_{2}{\left| f\left( p\right)  - {q}_{o}\right| }^{2} + {k}_{2},\;{a}_{2}\text{ and }{k}_{2}\text{ const. }
\]

hence

(11)

\[
\left( {{a}_{1}{\left| p - {p}_{o}\right| }^{2} + {k}_{1}}\right) \left( {{a}_{2}{\left| f\left( p\right)  - {q}_{o}\right| }^{2} + {k}_{2}}\right)  = 1.
\]

Equation (11) shows that (the intersection with \( U \) of) a sphere of center \( {p}_{o} \) is mapped by \( f \) into a sphere of center \( {q}_{o} \) . Since \( f \) preserves angles, the radii of the first sphere are mapped into radii of the second. Let \( p\left( s\right) ,0 \leq  s \leq  {s}_{o} \) , be a segment of a radius of the first sphere contained in \( U \) , where \( s \) is the arc length, and let \( f \circ  p\left( s\right) \) be its image. The length of the image segment is given by

\[
{\int }_{0}^{{s}_{o}}\left| {{df}\left( \frac{dp}{ds}\right) }\right| {ds} = {\int }_{0}^{{s}_{o}}\frac{ds}{{a}_{1}{\left| p\left( s\right)  - {p}_{o}\right| }^{2} + {k}_{1}} = \left| {f\left( {p\left( {s}_{o}\right) }\right)  - f(p\left( 0\right) }\right| .
\]

If \( {k}_{1} \neq  0,\left| {f\left( {p\left( {s}_{o}\right) }\right)  - f\left( {p\left( 0\right) }\right) }\right| \) is a transcendental function of \( \left| {p\left( {s}_{o}\right)  - {p}_{o}}\right| \) . On the other hand, Eq. (11) implies that such a function is algebraic. This contradiction shows that \( {k}_{1} = 0 \) .

It remains to consider the case \( \sigma  = 0 \) . In this situation,

\[
\rho  = \frac{1}{\lambda } = \sum {a}_{i}{x}_{i} + {c}_{1} = {A}_{1}\left( x\right)  + {c}_{1},\;{c}_{1} = \text{ const. },
\]

where we write, for convenience, \( \sum {a}_{i}{x}_{i} = {A}_{1}\left( x\right) , x = \; \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right) \) . In a similar manner as before, applying the initial argument to \( {f}^{-1} \) , we obtain

\( \left( {11}^{\prime }\right) \)

\[
\left( {{A}_{1}\left( x\right)  + {c}_{1}}\right) \left( {{A}_{2}\left( {f\left( x\right) }\right)  + {c}_{2}}\right)  = 1.
\]

Equation \( \left( {11}^{\prime }\right) \) shows that (the intersection with \( U \) of) a hyperplane parallel to \( {A}_{1} = 0 \) is taken by \( f \) into a hyperplane parallel to \( {A}_{2} = 0 \) . Because \( f \) preserves angles, a line perpendicular to the hyperplane \( {A}_{1} = 0 \) is taken by \( f \) into a line (perpendicular to the hyperplane \( \left. {{A}_{2} = 0}\right) \) . Considering a segment \( p\left( s\right) ,0 \leq  s \leq  {s}_{o} \) , of such a line, parametrized by arc length \( s \) , we obtain, in an analogous manner as before, that

\[
\left| {f\left( {p\left( {s}_{o}\right) }\right)  - f\left( {p\left( 0\right) }\right) }\right|  = {\int }_{0}^{{s}_{o}}\frac{ds}{{A}_{1}\left( {p\left( s\right) }\right)  + {c}_{1}}.
\]

The expression above contradicts \( \left( {11}^{\prime }\right) \) , except if the linear expression \( {A}_{1}\left( {p\left( s\right) }\right) \) were zero.

We conclude that if \( \sigma  = 0,\lambda  = \) const. In this case, the lengths of tangent vectors are multiplied by a constant \( \lambda \) and, as is easy to verify, \( f \) is an isometry, followed by a dilatation. This concludes the case \( \sigma  = 0 \) and the proof of Liouville’s Theorem.

nodes.content: 5.3 THEOREM. The isometries of \( {H}^{n} \) are the restrictions to \( {H}^{n} \subset \; {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) of the conformal transformations of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) that take \( {H}^{n} \) onto itself.
nodes.content_excerpt: 5.3 THEOREM. The isometries of \( {H}^{n} \) are the restrictions to \( {H}^{n} \subset \; {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) of the conformal transformations of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) that take \( {H}^{n} \) onto itself.

nodes.proof:
Suppose first that \( n \geq  3 \) . Let \( f : {H}^{n} \rightarrow  {H}^{n} \) be an isometry in the metric \( {g}_{ij} \) . Then, by Liouville’s Theorem, \( f \) extends to a conformal map of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) with the metric \( {\delta }_{ij} \) . Since \( {H}^{n} \) is complete in the metric \( {g}_{ij}, f \) maps \( {H}^{n} \) onto \( {H}^{n} \) .

Conversely, let \( f : {H}^{n} \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {H}^{n} \) be a conformal transformation of \( {H}^{n} \) onto \( {H}^{n} \) and let \( {e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n} \) be an orthonormal basis, in the metric \( {g}_{ij} \) , at a point \( p \in  {H}^{n} \) . Since \( {g}_{ij} = \frac{{\delta }_{ij}}{{x}_{n}^{2}} \) and \( f \) is conformal, there exists a \( {\lambda }^{2} > 0 \) such that \( \left\langle  {d{f}_{p}\left( {e}_{i}\right) , d{f}_{p}\left( {e}_{j}\right) }\right\rangle   = {\lambda }^{2}{\delta }_{ij} \) , where \( \langle \) , \( \rangle {istheinnerproductinthemetric}{g}_{ij} \) . Therefore, the basis \( \left\{  \frac{d{f}_{p}\left( {e}_{i}\right) }{\lambda }\right\} \) is orthonormal at \( f\left( p\right) \) , and by Corollary 2.3 of Cartan’s Theorem, there exists an isometry \( g \) of \( {H}^{n} \) taking \( p \) to \( f\left( p\right) \) , with \( {dg}\left( {e}_{i}\right)  = \frac{{df}\left( {e}_{i}\right) }{\lambda } \) . From what was proven in the first part, \( g \) is conformal. Hence \( h = {g}^{-1} \circ  f \) is the restriction to \( {H}^{n} \) of a conformal mapping of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) which takes \( {H}^{n} \) onto \( {H}^{n} \) , leaving \( p \) fixed and satisfying \( d{h}_{p} = {\lambda I} \) .

The proof will be concluded if we show that \( h = \) identity. In other words, we must show that if a conformal map \( h \) of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) takes \( {H}^{n} \) onto \( {H}^{n} \) , leaving a point \( p \in  {H}^{n} \) fixed and satisfying \( d{h}_{p} = \) multiple of the identity, then \( h \) is the identity.

To see this, let \( P \) be a hyperplane passing through \( p \) . From Liouville’s theorem, \( h\left( P\right) \) is a hyperplane or a sphere passing through \( p \) . Because \( d{h}_{p} \) is a multiple of the identity, \( P \) and \( h\left( P\right) \) are tangent at \( P \) . Because \( h \) takes the boundary \( \partial {H}^{n} \) of \( {H}^{n} \) into itself, and \( h \) is conformal, the angle of \( P \) with \( \partial {H}^{n} \) is the same as the angle of \( h\left( P\right) \) with \( \partial {H}^{n} \) .

We claim that \( h\left( P\right)  = P \) . To see this, consider a straight line \( {r}_{1} \) passing through \( p \) and perpendicular to \( \partial {H}^{n} \) , and let \( {q}_{1} = \; {r}_{1} \cap  \partial {H}^{n} \) . Since the image \( h\left( {r}_{1}\right) \) of \( {r}_{1} \) is a circle or a line, and makes the same angle with \( \partial {H}^{n} \) that \( {r}_{1} \) does, it is clear that \( h\left( {r}_{1}\right)  = {r}_{1} \) . Hence \( h\left( {q}_{1}\right)  = {q}_{1} \) . This shows that if \( P \) is perpendicular to \( \partial {H}^{n} \) , then \( h\left( P\right)  = P \) . If \( P \) is not perpendicular to \( \partial {H}^{n} \) , let \( r \) be a line contained in \( P \) . Again, \( h\left( r\right) \) is a circle or a line. In order that \( h\left( r\right) \) be a circle, making the same angle \( \alpha \) with \( \partial {H}^{n} \) that \( r \) makes with \( \partial {H}^{n} \) , it is necessary that \( {q}_{1} \in  h\left( r\right) \) (See Fig. 2), which contradicts the fact that \( h\left( {q}_{1}\right)  = {q}_{1} \) . Hence \( h\left( r\right) \) is a line, \( h\left( r\right)  = r \) , and because \( r \) is an arbitrary line in \( P, h\left( P\right)  = P \) , as we have claimed.

![019eafac-0959-75f1-800b-ea58ccc72a58_90_278_407_1214_609_0.jpg](images/019eafac-0959-75f1-800b-ea58ccc72a58_90_278_407_1214_609_0.jpg)

Figure 2

It follows that \( h \) cannot be an inversion (since the image of some plane will be a sphere) or an isometry distinct from the identity. From Liouville’s Theorem, \( h \) is a dilatation. Because \( h \) takes \( {H}^{n} \) onto \( {H}^{n}, h \) is the identity.

For \( n = 2 \) , the argument above does not apply. However, a simple calculation (cf. Exercise 4 of Chap. 1) shows that the conformal transformations of the form:

(12)

\[
f\left( z\right)  = \frac{{az} + b}{{cz} + d},\;z \in  {H}^{2} \subset  \mathbf{C},\;a, b, c, d \in  \mathbf{R},\;{ad} - {bc} \neq  0
\]

(observe that \( f \) maps \( {H}^{2} \) onto \( {H}^{2} \) ) are isometries of \( {H}^{2} \) with the metric \( {g}_{ij} \) . Moreover it is not difficult to show that for a fixed point \( {p}_{o} \in  {H}^{2} \) and unit vector \( {v}_{o} \) at \( {p}_{o} \) , there exists a transformation \( f \) of the form (12) which takes an arbitrary point \( p \in  {H}^{2} \) and a unit vector \( v \) at \( p \) into \( {p}_{o} \) and \( {v}_{o} \) , respectively (it suffices to observe that \( p \) and \( v \) are determined by three parameters which is the number of parameters of \( f \) ). Since there exists a unique isometry of \( {H}^{2} \) which takes \( \left( {p, v}\right) \) into \( \left( {{p}_{o},{v}_{o}}\right) \) , we conclude that all isometries of \( {H}^{2} \) are of the form (12). This completes the proof of the case \( n = 2 \) and of Theorem 5.3.

nodes.label: Exercise 1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
1. Consider, on a neighborhood in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n}, n > 2 \) the metric

\[
{g}_{ij} = \frac{{\delta }_{ij}}{{F}^{2}}
\]

where \( F \neq  0 \) is a function of \( \left( {{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . Denote by \( {F}_{i} = \frac{\partial F}{\partial {x}_{i}},{F}_{ij} = \frac{{\partial }^{2}F}{\partial {x}_{i}\partial {x}_{j}} \) , etc.

a) Show that a necessary and sufficient condition for the metric to have constant curvature \( K \) is

(*)

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} {F}_{ij} = 0,\;i \neq  j, \\  F\left( {{F}_{jj} + {F}_{ii}}\right)  = K + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\left( {F}_{i}\right) }^{2}. \end{array}\right.
\]

b) Use (*) to prove that the metric \( {g}_{ij} \) has constant curvature \( K \) if and only if

\[
F = {G}_{1}\left( {x}_{1}\right)  + {G}_{2}\left( {x}_{2}\right)  + \cdots  + {G}_{n}\left( {x}_{n}\right) ,
\]

where

\[
{G}_{i}\left( {x}_{i}\right)  = a{x}_{i}^{2} + {b}_{i}{x}_{i} + {c}_{i}
\]

and

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}\left( {4{c}_{i}a - {b}_{i}^{2}}\right)  = K.
\]

c) Put \( a = K/4,{b}_{i} = 0,{c}_{i} = 1/n \) and obtain the formula of Riemann (See [Ri])(**)

\[
{g}_{ij} = \frac{{\delta }_{ij}}{{\left( 1 + \frac{K}{4}\sum {x}_{i}^{2}\right) }^{2}}
\]

for a metric \( {g}_{ij} \) of constant curvature \( K \) . If \( K < 0 \) the metric \( {g}_{ij} \) is defined in a ball of radius \( \sqrt{\frac{4}{-K}} \) .

d) If \( K > 0 \) , the metric (**) is defined on all of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . Show that such a metric on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) is not complete.

3. (Another model of the hyperbolic space). Consider on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) the quadratic form

\[
Q\left( {{x}_{o},{x}_{1},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right)  =  - {\left( {x}_{o}\right) }^{2} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\left( {x}_{i}\right) }^{2},
\]

\[
\left( {{x}_{o},\ldots ,{x}_{n}}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1}.
\]

With the pseudo-Riemannian metric \( \left( ,\right) \) induced by \( Q \) (Cf. Exercise 9, Chap. 2), \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) will be denoted by \( {L}^{n + 1} \) (The Lorentzian space). Denote by \( {H}_{k}^{n}, k =  - \frac{1}{{r}^{2}} \) , the connected component corresponding to \( {x}_{o} > 0 \) of the regular surface of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) given by \( Q\left( x\right)  =  - {r}^{2}, r > 0 \) . (Geometrically \( Q\left( x\right)  =  - {r}^{2} \) is a hyperboloid of two sheets and \( {H}_{k}^{n} \) is the sheet contained in the half-space \( {x}_{o} > 0 \) .)

a) Show that for all \( x \in  {H}_{k}^{n} \) , the vector \( \eta  = \frac{x}{r} \) is normal to the tangent space \( {T}_{x}\left( {H}_{k}^{n}\right) \) .

b) Prove that \( \left( {\eta ,\eta }\right)  =  - 1 \) , and that it is possible to choose a basis \( {b}_{o},\ldots ,{b}_{n} \) of \( {L}^{n + 1} \) with \( {b}_{o} = \eta ,\left( {{b}_{i},{b}_{j}}\right)  = {\delta }_{ij} \) , \( \left( {{b}_{i},{b}_{o}}\right)  = 0, i, j = 1,\ldots , n \) . (Use the fact that the index of a quadratic form does not depend on the basis chosen to represent it.) Conclude that the metric induced by \( {L}^{n + 1} \) on \( {H}_{k}^{n} \) is Riemannian.

c) Use the pseudo-Riemannian connection \( \bar{\nabla } \) of \( {L}^{n + 1} \) (Cf. Exercise 9, Chap. 2) to show that \( {S}_{\eta } = \left( {-\frac{1}{r}}\right) I \) , where \( I \) is the identity map. Conclude that \( B\left( {X, Y}\right)  = \frac{\eta }{r}\left( {X, Y}\right) \) , and use the Gauss formula to show that the sectional curvature of \( {H}_{k}^{n} \) is constant and equal \( k =  - \frac{1}{{r}^{2}} \) .

d) Let \( 0\left( {1, n + 1}\right) \) be the subgroup of linear transformations of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) which preserve the metric \( \left( ,\right) \) . Show that the elements of \( 0\left( {1, n + 1}\right) \) with det \( > 0 \) are isometries of

\( {H}_{k}^{n} \) and that given \( X, Y \in  {H}_{k}^{n} \) and orthonormal bases \( \left\{  {v}_{i}\right\}   \in  {T}_{X}\left( {H}_{k}^{n}\right) \) and \( \left\{  {w}_{i}\right\}   \in  {T}_{Y}\left( {H}_{k}^{n}\right) , i = 1,\ldots , n \) , the restriction to \( {H}_{k}^{n} \) of the "linear" transformation which takes

\[
\frac{X}{r} \rightarrow  \frac{Y}{r}\;\text{ and }\;{v}_{i} \rightarrow  {w}_{i}
\]

is an isometry of \( {H}_{k}^{n} \) . Conclude then that \( {H}_{k}^{n} \) has constant curvature (which we already know from (c)) and that \( {H}_{k}^{n} \) is complete.

e) Show that \( {H}_{-1}^{n} \) is isometric to the hyperbolic space \( {H}^{n} \) .

f) Show that the symmetries of \( {H}_{k}^{n} \) with respect to the plane \( P \) which passes through the origin of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) and contains the \( {x}_{o} \) -axis are isometries of \( {H}_{k}^{n} \) . Conclude that all of the geodesics of \( {H}_{n}^{k} \) which pass through \( \left( {r,0,\ldots ,0}\right) \) are obtained as intersections \( {H}_{k}^{n} \cap  P \) .

nodes.content:
5. (Connections of conformal metrics) Let \( M \) be a differentiable manifold. Two Riemannian metrics \( g \) and \( \bar{g} \) on \( M \) are conformal if there exists a positive function \( \mu  : M \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) such that \( \bar{g}\left( {X, Y}\right)  = {\mu g}\left( {X, Y}\right) \) , for all \( X, Y \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) . Let \( \nabla \) and \( \bar{\nabla } \) be the Riemannian connections of \( g \) and \( \bar{g} \) , respectively. Prove that

\[
{\bar{\nabla }}_{X}Y = {\nabla }_{X}Y + S\left( {X, Y}\right)
\]

where \( S\left( {X, Y}\right)  = \frac{1}{2\mu }\{ \left( {X\mu }\right) Y + \left( {Y\mu }\right) X - g\left( {X, Y}\right) \operatorname{grad}\mu \} \) and \( \operatorname{grad}\mu \) is calculated in the metric \( g \) , that is,

\[
X\left( \mu \right)  = g\left( {X,\operatorname{grad}\mu }\right) .
\]

Hint: Since \( \bar{\nabla } \) is obviously symmetric, it suffices to show that \( \bar{\nabla } \) is compatible with \( \bar{g} \) , that is, that

\[
X\left( {\bar{g}\left( {Y, Z}\right) }\right)  = \bar{g}\left( {{\bar{\nabla }}_{X}Y, Z}\right)  + \bar{g}\left( {Y,{\bar{\nabla }}_{X}Z}\right) .
\]

But the first member of the equality above is

\[
X\left( {{\mu g}\left( {Y, Z}\right) }\right)  = X\left( \mu \right) g\left( {Y, Z}\right)  + {\mu g}\left( {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Z}\right)  + {\mu g}\left( {Y,{\nabla }_{X}Z}\right) ,
\]

and the second is

\[
{\mu g}\left( {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Z}\right)  + {\mu g}\left( {Y,{\nabla }_{X}Z}\right)
\]

\[
+ \mu \{ g\left( {S\left( {X, Y}\right) , Z}\right)  + g\left( {Y, S\left( {X, Z}\right) }\right) \}
\]

Therefore, it is enough to prove that

\[
X\left( \mu \right) g\left( {Y, Z}\right)  = \mu \{ g\left( {S\left( {X, Y}\right) , Z}\right)  + g\left( {Y, S\left( {X, Z}\right) }\right) \} ,
\]

which follows from a direct calculation.

nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
6. (Umbilic hypersurfaces of the hyperbolic space). Let \( \left( {{M}^{n + 1}, g}\right) \) be a manifold with a Riemannian metric \( g \) and let \( \nabla \) be its Riemannian connection. We say an immersion \( x : {N}^{n} \rightarrow  {M}^{n + 1} \) is (totally) umbilic if for all \( p \in  N \) , the second fundamental form \( B \) of \( x \) at \( p \) satisfies

\[
\langle B\left( {X, Y}\right) ,\eta \rangle \left( p\right)  = \lambda \left( p\right) \;\langle X, Y\rangle \;,\;\lambda \left( p\right)  \in  \mathbf{R},
\]

for all \( X, Y \in  \mathcal{K}\left( N\right) \) and for a given unit field \( \eta \) normal to \( x\left( N\right) \) ; here we are using \( \langle \) , \( \rangle {todenotethemetricgonMand} \) the metric induced by \( x \) on \( N \) .

a) Show that if \( {M}^{n + 1} \) has constant sectional curvature, \( \lambda \) does not depend on \( p \) .

Hint: Let \( T, X, Y \in  \mathcal{X}\left( N\right) \) . The given condition implies that

\[
- \left\langle  {\nabla {x}^{\eta }, Y}\right\rangle   = \lambda \langle X, Y\rangle \;\text{ and }\; - \left\langle  {\nabla {T}^{\eta }, Y}\right\rangle   = \lambda \langle T, Y\rangle .
\]

Differentiate the first equation with respect to \( T \) and the second with respect to \( X \) , obtaining, for all \( Y \) ,

\[
\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{T}{\nabla }_{X}\eta  - {\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{T}\eta , Y}\right\rangle
\]

\[
=  - \left\langle  {T\left( \lambda \right) X - X\left( \lambda \right) T + {\nabla }_{\left\lbrack  X, T\right\rbrack  }\eta , Y}\right\rangle  .
\]

Use the fact that \( M \) has constant sectional curvature to conclude that \( T\left( \lambda \right) X - X\left( \lambda \right) T = 0 \) . Because \( T \) and \( X \) can be chosen linearly independently, this implies that \( X\left( \lambda \right)  = 0 \) , for all \( X \in  \mathcal{X}\left( N\right) \) ; therefore \( \lambda  = \) const.

b) Use Exercise 5 to show that if we change the metric \( g \) to a metric \( \bar{g} = {\mu g} \) , conformal to \( g \) , the immersion \( x : {N}^{n} \rightarrow \; \left( {{M}^{n + 1},\bar{g}}\right) \) continues being umbilic, that is, if (using the notation of Exercise 5) \( {\left\langle  \nabla {x}^{\eta }, Y\right\rangle  }_{g} =  - \lambda \langle X, Y{\rangle }_{g} \) , then

\[
{\left\langle  {\overline{\nabla }}_{X}\left( \frac{\eta }{\sqrt{\mu }}\right) , Y\right\rangle  }_{\widetilde{g}} = \frac{-{2\lambda \mu } + \eta \left( \mu \right) }{{2\mu }\sqrt{\mu }}{\left\langle  X, Y\right\rangle  }_{\bar{g}}.
\]

c) Take \( {M}^{n + 1} = {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) with the euclidean metric. Show that if \( x : {N}^{n} \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) is umbilic, then \( x\left( N\right) \) is contained in an \( n \) -plane or an \( n \) -sphere in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) .

Hint: For (a), \( \lambda  = \) constant. If \( \lambda  = 0,\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}\eta , Y}\right\rangle   = 0 \) for all \( X, Y \in  \mathcal{X}\left( N\right) \) and all \( \eta  \in  \mathcal{X}{\left( N\right) }^{ \bot  } \) . It follows that \( x\left( N\right) \) is contained in an affine \( n \) -plane in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) . If \( \lambda  \neq  0 \) , consider the map \( y : N \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) given by

\[
y\left( p\right)  = x\left( p\right)  - \frac{\eta \left( p\right) }{\lambda },\;p \in  N.
\]

Let \( T, Y \in  \mathcal{X}\left( N\right) \) . Observe that

\[
\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{T}y, Y}\right\rangle   = \langle T, Y\rangle  - \frac{1}{\lambda }\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{T}\eta , Y}\right\rangle   = 0.
\]

It follows that \( y\left( N\right) \) reduces to a point, call it \( {x}_{o} \) , and that \( x \) satisfies

\[
{\left| x\left( p\right)  - {x}_{o}\right| }^{2} = 1/{\lambda }^{2},
\]

that is, \( x\left( N\right) \) is contained in a sphere of center \( {x}_{o} \) and radius \( 1/\lambda \) .

d) Use (b) and (c) to establish that the umbilic hypersurfaces of the hyperbolic space, in the upper half-space model \( {H}^{n + 1} \) , are the intersections with \( {H}^{n + 1} \) of \( n \) -planes or \( n \) - spheres of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) . Therefore, the umbilic hypersurfaces of the hyperbolic space are the geodesic spheres, the horo-spheres and the hyperspheres. Conclude that such hyper-surfaces have constant sectional curvature.

e) Calculate the mean curvature and the sectional curvature of the umbilic hypersurfaces of the hyperbolic space.

Hint: Consider the model of \( {H}^{n} \) as the upper half-space. Let \( \sum  = S \cap  {H}^{n} \) be the intersection of \( {H}^{n} \) with a Euclidean \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) - sphere \( S \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) of radius 1 and center in \( {H}^{n} \) . Since \( \sum \) is umbilic, all of the directions are principal, and it is enough to calculate the curvature of the curves of intersection of \( \sum \) with the \( {x}_{1}{x}_{n} \) -plane. Use the expression obtained in part (b) of this exercise to establish that the mean curvature of \( \sum \) (in the metric of \( {H}^{n} \) ) is equal to 1 if \( S \) is tangent to \( \partial {H}^{n} \) , is equal to \( \cos \alpha \) if \( S \) makes an angle \( \alpha \) with \( \partial {H}^{n} \) , and is equal to the "height" of the Euclidean center of \( S \) relative to \( \partial {H}^{n} \) , if \( S \subset  {H}^{n} \) . To calculate the sectional curvature, use the Gauss formula.

8. (Riemannian submersions). A differentiable mapping \( f : {\bar{M}}^{n + k} \rightarrow  {M}^{n} \) is called submersion if \( f \) is surjective, and for all \( \bar{p} \in  \bar{M}, d{f}_{\bar{p}} : {T}_{\bar{p}}\bar{M} \rightarrow  {T}_{f\left( p\right) }M \) has rank \( n \) . In this case, for all \( p \in  M \) , the fiber \( {f}^{-1}\left( p\right)  = {F}_{p} \) is a submanifold of \( \bar{M} \) and a tangent vector of \( \bar{M} \) , tangent to some \( {F}_{p}, p \in  M \) , is called a vertical vector of the submersion. If, in addition, \( \bar{M} \)

and \( M \) have Riemannian metrics, the submersion \( f \) is said to be Riemannian if, for all \( p \in  \bar{M}, d{f}_{p} : {T}_{p}\bar{M} \rightarrow  {T}_{f\left( p\right) }M \) preserves lengths of vectors orthogonal to \( {F}_{p} \) . Show that:

a) If \( {M}_{1} \times  {M}_{2} \) is the Riemannian product, then the natural projections \( {\pi }_{i} : {M}_{1} \times  {M}_{2} \rightarrow  {M}_{i}, i = 1,2 \) , are Riemannian submersions.

b) If the tangent bundle \( {TM} \) is given the Riemannian metric as in Exercise 2 of Chap. 3, then the projection \( \pi  : {TM} \rightarrow \; M \) is a Riemannian submersion.

9. (Connection of a Riemannian submersion). Let \( f : \bar{M} \rightarrow  M \) be a Riemannian submersion. A vector \( \bar{x} \in  {T}_{\bar{p}}\bar{M} \) is horizontal if it is orthogonal to the fiber. The tangent space \( {T}_{\bar{p}}\bar{M} \) then admits a decomposition \( {T}_{\bar{p}}\bar{M} = {\left( {T}_{\bar{p}}\bar{M}\right) }^{h} \oplus  {\left( {T}_{\bar{p}}\bar{M}\right) }^{v} \) , where \( {\left( {T}_{\bar{p}}\bar{M}\right) }^{h} \) and \( {\left( {T}_{\bar{p}}\bar{M}\right) }^{v} \) denote the subspaces of horizontal and vertical vectors, respectively. If \( X \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) , the horizontal lift \( \bar{X} \) of \( X \) is the horizontal field defined by \( d{f}_{\bar{p}}\left( {\bar{X}\left( \bar{p}\right) }\right)  = X\left( {f\left( p\right) }\right) \) .

a) Show that \( \bar{X} \) is differentiable.

b) Let \( \nabla \) and \( \bar{\nabla } \) be the Riemannian connections of \( M \) and \( \bar{M} \) respectively. Show that

\[
{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}\bar{Y} = \overline{\left( {\nabla }_{X}Y\right) } + \frac{1}{2}{\left\lbrack  \bar{X},\bar{Y}\right\rbrack  }^{v},\;X, Y \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) ,
\]

where \( {Z}^{v} \) is the vertical component of \( Z \) .

c) \( {\left\lbrack  \bar{X},\bar{Y}\right\rbrack  }^{v}\left( \bar{p}\right) \) depends only on \( \widehat{\bar{X}}\left( \bar{p}\right) \) and \( \bar{Y}\left( \bar{p}\right) \) .

Hint for (b): Let \( X, Y, Z \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) . Let \( T \in  \mathcal{X}\left( \bar{M}\right) \) be a vertical field. Observe that:

\[
\langle \bar{X}, T\rangle  = \langle \bar{Y}, T\rangle  = \langle \bar{Z}, T\rangle  = 0,\;\bar{X}\langle \bar{Y},\bar{Z}\rangle  = X\langle Y, Z\rangle
\]

\[
{df}\left\lbrack  {\bar{X}, T}\right\rbrack   = 0,\;\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack   = \left\lbrack  {{df}\bar{X},{df}\bar{Y}}\right\rbrack   = {df}\left\lbrack  {\bar{X},\bar{Y}}\right\rbrack  \;\text{ and }
\]

\[
T\langle \bar{X},\bar{Y}\rangle  = 0
\]

Conclude that \( \langle \left\lbrack  {\bar{X},\bar{Y}}\right\rbrack  ,\bar{Z}\rangle  = \langle \left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  , Z\rangle ,\left\langle  {\left\lbrack  {\bar{X}, T}\right\rbrack  ,\bar{Y}}\right\rangle   = 0 \) and use the formula for the Riemannian connection as a function of the metric to obtain

\[
\left\langle  {{\overline{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}\overline{Y},\bar{Z}}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Z}\right\rangle  ,\;2\left\langle  {{\overline{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}\overline{Y}, T}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {T,\left\lbrack  {\overline{X},\overline{Y}}\right\rbrack  }\right\rangle  ,
\]

which implies (b).

Hint for (c): Use the fact that

\[
\left\langle  {\left\lbrack  {\overline{X},\overline{Y}}\right\rbrack  , T}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {{\overline{\nabla }}_{\overline{X}}\overline{Y} - {\overline{\nabla }}_{\overline{Y}}\overline{X}, T}\right\rangle  .
\]

10. (Curvature of a Riemannian submersion). Let \( f : \bar{M} \rightarrow  M \) be a Riemannian submersion. Let \( X, Y, Z, W \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) ,\bar{X},\bar{Y},\bar{Z},\bar{W} \) be their horizontal lifts, and let \( R \) and \( \bar{R} \) be the curvature tensors of \( M \) and \( \bar{M} \) respectively. Prove that:

\[
\text{ (a) }\left\langle  {\bar{R}\left( {\bar{X},\bar{Y}}\right) \bar{Z},\bar{W}}\right\rangle   = \langle R\left( {X, Y}\right) Z, W\rangle  - \frac{1}{4}\left\langle  {{\left\lbrack  \bar{X},\bar{Z}\right\rbrack  }^{v},{\left\lbrack  \bar{Y},\bar{W}\right\rbrack  }^{v}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
+ \frac{1}{4}\left\langle  {{\left\lbrack  \bar{Y},\bar{Z}\right\rbrack  }^{v},{\left\lbrack  \bar{X},\bar{W}\right\rbrack  }^{v}}\right\rangle   - \frac{1}{2}\left\langle  {{\left\lbrack  \bar{Z},\bar{W}\right\rbrack  }^{v},{\left\lbrack  \bar{X},\bar{Y}\right\rbrack  }^{v}}\right\rangle
\]

b) \( K\left( \sigma \right)  = \widetilde{K}\left( \bar{\sigma }\right)  + \frac{3}{4}{\left| {\left\lbrack  \widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y}\right\rbrack  }^{v}\right| }^{2} \geq  \widetilde{K}\left( \bar{\sigma }\right) \) ,

where \( \sigma \) is the plane generated by the orthonormal vectors \( X, Y \in  \mathcal{X}\left( M\right) \) and \( \bar{\sigma } \) is the plane generated by \( \bar{X},\bar{Y} \) .

Hint for \( \left( a\right) \) : We shall use the notation of Exercise 9. Observe that \( \bar{X}\left\langle  {{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{Y}}\bar{Z},\bar{W}}\right\rangle   = X\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Y}Z, W}\right\rangle \) . Therefore

\[
\left\langle  {{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{Y}}\bar{Z},\bar{W}}\right\rangle   = \bar{X}\left\langle  {{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{Y}}\bar{Z},\bar{W}}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{Y}}\bar{Z},{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}\bar{W}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{Y}Z, W}\right\rangle   - \frac{1}{4}\left\langle  {{\left\lbrack  \overrightarrow{Y},\overrightarrow{Z}\right\rbrack  }^{v},{\left\lbrack  \overrightarrow{X},\overrightarrow{W}\right\rbrack  }^{v}}\right\rangle  .
\]

On the other hand, if \( T \in  \mathcal{X}\left( \bar{M}\right) \) is vertical,

\[
\left\langle  {{\overline{\nabla }}_{T}\overline{X},\overline{Y}}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {{\overline{\nabla }}_{\overline{X}}T,\overline{Y}}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {\left\lbrack  {T,\overline{X}}\right\rbrack  ,\overline{Y}}\right\rangle   =  - \left\langle  {T,{\overline{\nabla }}_{\overline{X}}\overline{Y}}\right\rangle  .
\]

Therefore,

\[
\left\langle  {{\bar{\nabla }}_{\left\lbrack  \bar{X},\bar{Y}\right\rbrack  }\bar{Z},\bar{W}}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {{\bar{\nabla }}_{{\left\lbrack  \bar{X},\bar{Y}\right\rbrack  }^{h}}\bar{Z},\bar{W}}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {{\bar{\nabla }}_{{\left\lbrack  \bar{X},\bar{Y}\right\rbrack  }^{v}}\bar{Z},\bar{W}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {{\widetilde{\nabla }}_{\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }Z, W}\right\rangle   - \frac{1}{2}\left\langle  {{\left\lbrack  \widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y}\right\rbrack  }^{v},{\left\lbrack  \widetilde{Z},\widetilde{W}\right\rbrack  }^{v}}\right\rangle  .
\]

Putting the above together, we obtain (a).

11. (The complex projective space). Let

\[
{\mathbf{C}}^{n + 1} - \{ 0\}  = \left\{  {\left( {{z}_{o},\ldots ,{z}_{n}}\right)  = Z \neq  0,{z}_{j} = {x}_{j} + i{y}_{j}, j = 0,\ldots , n}\right\}
\]

be the set of all non-zero \( \left( {n + 1}\right) \) -tuples of complex numbers \( {z}_{j} \) . Define an equivalence relation on \( {\mathbf{C}}^{n + 1} - \{ 0\}  : Z = \; \left( {{z}_{o},\ldots ,{z}_{n}}\right)  \sim  W = \left( {{w}_{o},\ldots ,{w}_{n}}\right) \) if \( {z}_{j} = \lambda {w}_{j},\lambda  \in  \mathbf{C},\lambda  \neq  0 \) . The equivalence class of \( Z \) will be denoted by \( \left\lbrack  Z\right\rbrack  ( = \) the complex line passing through the origin and through \( Z \) ). The set of such classes is called, by analogy with the real case, the complex projective space \( {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{C}\right) \) of complex dimension \( n \) .

a) Show that \( {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{C}\right) \) has a differentiable structure of a manifold of real dimension \( {2n} \) and that \( {P}^{1}\left( \mathbf{C}\right) \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \) .

b) Let \( \left( {Z, W}\right)  = {z}_{o}{\bar{w}}_{o} + \cdots  + {z}_{n}{\bar{w}}_{n} \) be the hermitian product on \( {\mathbf{C}}^{n + 1} \) , where the bar denotes complex conjugation. Identify \( {\mathbf{C}}^{n + 1} \approx  {\mathbf{R}}^{{2n} + 2} \) by putting \( {z}_{j} = {x}_{j} + i{y}_{j} = \; \left( {{x}_{j},{y}_{j}}\right) \) . Show that

\[
{S}^{{2n} + 1} = \left\{  {N \in  {\mathbf{C}}^{n + 1} \approx  {\mathbf{R}}^{{2n} + 2};\left( {N, N}\right)  = 1}\right\}
\]

is the unit sphere in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{{2n} + 2} \) .

c) Show that the equivalence relation \( \sim \) induces on \( {S}^{{2n} + 1} \) the following equivalence relation: \( Z \sim  W \) if \( {e}^{i\theta }Z = W \) . Establish that there exists a differentable map (the Hopf fibering) \( f : {S}^{{2n} + 1} \rightarrow  {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{C}\right) \) such that

\[
{f}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  Z\right\rbrack  \right)
\]

\[
= \left\{  {{e}^{i\theta }N \in  {S}^{{2n} + 1}, N \in  \left\lbrack  Z\right\rbrack   \cap  {S}^{{2n} + 1},0 \leq  \theta  \leq  {2\pi }}\right\}
\]

\[
= \left\lbrack  Z\right\rbrack   \cap  {S}^{{2n} + 1}\text{ . }
\]

d) Show that \( f \) is a submersion.

12. (Curvature of the complex projective space). Define a Riemannian metric on \( {\mathbf{C}}^{n + 1} - \{ 0\} \) in the following way: If \( Z \in  {\mathbf{C}}^{n + 1} - \{ 0\} \) and \( V, W \in  {T}_{Z}\left( {{\mathbf{C}}^{n + 1}-\{ 0\} }\right) \) ,

\[
\langle V, W{\rangle }_{Z} = \frac{\operatorname{Real}\left( {V, W}\right) }{\left( Z, Z\right) }.
\]

Observe that the metric \( \langle \) , \( \rangle {restrictedto}{S}^{{2n} + 1} \subset  {\mathbf{C}}^{n + 1} - \{ 0\} \) coincides with the metric induced from \( {\mathbf{R}}^{{2n} + 2} \) .

a) Show that, for all \( 0 \leq  \theta  \leq  {2\pi },{e}^{i\theta } : {S}^{{2n} + 1} \rightarrow  {S}^{{2n} + 1} \) is an isometry, and that, therefore, it is possible to define a Riemannian metric on \( {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{C}\right) \) in such a way that the submersion \( f \) is Riemannian.

b) Show that, in this metric, the sectional curvature of \( {P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{C}\right) \) is given by

\[
K\left( \sigma \right)  = 1 + 3{\cos }^{2}\varphi
\]

where \( \sigma \) is generated by the orthonormal pair \( X, Y \) , \( \cos \varphi  = \left\langle  {\bar{X}, i\bar{Y}}\right\rangle \) , and \( \bar{X},\bar{Y} \) are the horizontal lifts of

\( X \) and \( Y \) , respectively. In particular, \( 1 \leq  K\left( \sigma \right)  \leq  4 \) .

Hint for \( \left( b\right) \) : Let \( Z \) be the position vector describing \( {S}^{{2n} + 1} \) . Since \( {\left( \frac{d}{d\theta }{e}^{i\theta }Z\right) }_{\theta  = 0} = {iZ},{iZ} \in  {T}_{Z}\left( {S}^{{2n} + 1}\right) \) and is vertical. Let \( \bar{\nabla } \) be the Riemannian connection of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{{2n} + 2} \approx  {\mathbf{C}}^{n + 1} \) and \( X, Y \in \; \underline{\mathcal{X}}\left( {{P}^{n}\left( \mathbf{C}\right) }\right) \) . Take \( \alpha  : \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)  \rightarrow  {S}^{{2n} + 1} \) with \( \alpha \left( 0\right)  = Z,{\alpha }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = \) X. Then

\[
{\left. {\left( {\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}iZ\right) }_{Z} = \frac{d}{dt}iZ \circ  \alpha \left( t\right) )\right| }_{t = 0}
\]

\[
= {\left. \frac{d}{dt}i\alpha \left( t\right) \right| }_{t = 0} = i{\alpha }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = i\bar{X}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\left\langle  {\left\lbrack  {\bar{X},\bar{Y}}\right\rbrack  ,{iZ}}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {{\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{X}}\bar{Y} - {\bar{\nabla }}_{\bar{Y}}\bar{X},{iZ}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
=  - \langle i\bar{X},\bar{Y}\rangle  + \langle i\bar{Y},\bar{X}\rangle  = 2\cos \varphi
\]

Now use Exercise 10 (b).

14. (Geometric characterization of locally symmetric spaces). Let \( M \) be a Riemannian manifold. A local symmetry at \( p \in  M \) is a map \( \sigma  : {B}_{\varepsilon }\left( p\right)  \rightarrow  {B}_{\varepsilon }\left( p\right) \) of a normal geodesic ball centered at \( p \) such that \( \sigma \left( {\gamma \left( t\right) }\right)  = \gamma \left( {-t}\right) \) , where \( \gamma \) is a radial geodesic \( \left( {\gamma \left( 0\right)  = p}\right) \) of \( {B}_{\varepsilon }\left( p\right) \) . Prove that: \( M \) is locally symmetric \( \Leftrightarrow \) every local symmetry is an isometry.

Hint \( \Rightarrow \) : Consider a geodesic frame \( {e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n} \) in the ball \( {B}_{\varepsilon }\left( p\right) \) (Cf. Exercise 7 of Chap. 3) and put \( {R}_{{ijk}\ell } = R\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{j},{e}_{k},{e}_{\ell }}\right) \) . Since \( \nabla R = 0,{R}_{{ijk}\ell } \) is constant along the geodesics which start from \( p \) . Let \( i : {T}_{p}M \rightarrow  {T}_{p}M \) be a linear isometry given by \( i\left( v\right)  =  - v, v \in  {T}_{p}M \) , and observe that \( \sigma  = {\exp }_{p} \circ  i \circ  {\exp }_{p}^{-1} \) . Use Cartan’s Theorem to establish that \( \sigma \) is an isometry.

Hint \( \Leftarrow \) : Let \( p \in  M \) and \( Z \in  {T}_{p}\left( M\right) \) . Consider a geodesic \( \gamma  : \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)  \rightarrow  M \) with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = Z \) . Take an orthonormal basis \( {e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n} \) in \( {T}_{p}M \) , and obtain, by parallel transport, a frame \( {e}_{1}\left( t\right) ,\ldots ,{e}_{n}\left( t\right) \) along \( \gamma \) . Put \( {R}_{{ijk}\ell }\left( t\right)  = \; R\left( {{e}_{i}\left( t\right) ,{e}_{j}\left( t\right) ,{e}_{k}\left( t\right) ,{e}_{\ell }\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Then

\[
\left( {{\nabla }_{Z}R}\right) \left( p\right)  = {\left. \frac{d}{dt}{R}_{{ijk}\ell }\right| }_{t = 0}
\]

\[
= \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}\frac{{R}_{{ijk}\ell }\left( t\right)  - {R}_{{ijk}\ell }\left( {-t}\right) }{2t} = 0
\]

where, in the last equality, we use that \( \sigma \) is an isometry and we also use the last exercise. Since \( p \) and \( Z \) are arbitrary, \( \nabla R = 0 \) .

nodes.label: Definition 2.1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.section_title: 9.2. Formulas for the first and second variations of energy
nodes.content:
2.1 DEFINITION. Let \( c : \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) be a piecewise differentiable curve in a manifold \( M \) . A variation of \( c \) is a continuous mapping \( f : \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) such that:

a) \( f\left( {0, t}\right)  = c\left( t\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack \) ,

b) there exists a subdivision of \( \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack \) by points \( 0 = {t}_{o} < {t}_{1} < \; \cdots  < {t}_{k + 1} = a \) , such that the restriction of \( f \) to each \( \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)  \times \; \left\lbrack  {{t}_{i},{t}_{i + 1}}\right\rbrack  , i = 0,1,\ldots , k \) , is differentiable.

A variation is said to be proper if

\[
f\left( {s,0}\right)  = c\left( 0\right) \;\text{ and }\;f\left( {s, a}\right)  = c\left( a\right) ,
\]

for all \( s \in  \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right) \) . If \( f \) is differentiable, the variation is said to be differentiable.

For each \( s \in  \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right) \) , the parametrized curve \( {f}_{s} : \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) given by \( {f}_{s}\left( t\right)  = f\left( {s, t}\right) \) is called a curve in the variation. In this way, a variation determines a family \( {f}_{s}\left( t\right) \) of neighboring curves of \( {f}_{o}\left( t\right)  = c\left( t\right) \) , and a variation is proper if and only if the curves of this family have the same initial point \( c\left( 0\right) \) and the same endpoint \( c\left( a\right) \) .

It is customary to call the parametrized differentiable curve given by \( {f}_{t}\left( s\right)  = f\left( {s, t}\right) , t \) fixed, a transversal curve of the variation. The velocity vector of a transversal curve at \( s = 0 \) , defined by \( V\left( t\right)  = \; \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {0, t}\right) \) , is a (piecewise differentiable) vector field along \( c\left( t\right) \) and is called the variational field of \( f \) (Fig. 1).

Since \( c\left( \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack  \right)  \subset  M \) is compact it is possible to find a \( \delta  > 0 \) such that \( {\exp }_{c\left( t\right) }, t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack \) , is well-defined for all \( v \in  {T}_{c\left( t\right) }M \) , with \( \left| v\right|  < \delta \) . Indeed, for each \( c\left( t\right) \) consider a totally normal neighborhood \( {W}_{t} \) of \( c\left( t\right) \) and the number \( {\delta }_{t} > 0 \) associated to this neighborhood (Theor. 3.7, Chap. 3). The union \( \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{t}{W}_{t} \) covers the compact set \( c\left( \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack  \right) \) and, therefore, a finite number of the \( {W}_{t} \) ’s, say \( {W}_{1},\ldots ,{W}_{n} \) , still cover \( c\left( \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack  \right) \) . Taking \( \delta  = \min \left( {{\delta }_{1},\ldots ,{\delta }_{n}}\right) \) , where \( {\delta }_{i} > 0 \) is the number corresponding to the neighborhoods \( {W}_{i}, i = 1,\ldots , n \) , we see that this \( \delta \) satisfies the conditions of the assertion that was made.

Consider \( N = \mathop{\max }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack  }}\left| {V\left( t\right) }\right| ,\varepsilon  < \frac{\delta }{N} \) and define \( f\left( {s, t}\right)  = \; {\exp }_{c\left( t\right) }{sV}\left( t\right) , s \in  \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack  . \)

By the choice of \( \varepsilon \) , the map \( f : \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) is well-defined. In addition, since

\[
{\exp }_{c\left( t\right) }{sV}\left( t\right)  = \gamma \left( {1, c\left( t\right) ,{sV}\left( t\right) }\right)
\]

and the geodesic \( \gamma \left( {1, c\left( t\right) ,{sV}\left( t\right) }\right) \) depends differentiably on the initial conditions, the map \( f \) is piecewise differentiable. It is easy to verify that \( f\left( {0, t}\right)  = c\left( t\right) \) .

Finally, the variational field of \( f \) is given by:

\[
{\left. \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( 0, t\right)  = \frac{d}{ds}\left( {\exp }_{c\left( t\right) }sV\left( t\right) \right) \right| }_{s = 0} = {\left( d{\exp }_{c\left( t\right) }\right) }_{o}V\left( t\right)  = V\left( t\right) ,
\]

and it is clear that, from the definition of \( f \) , if \( V\left( 0\right)  = V\left( a\right)  = 0 \) then \( f \) is proper.

2.3 LEMMA. Let \( p, q \in  M \) and let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) be a minimizing geodesic joining \( p \) to \( q \) . Then, for all curves \( c : \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) joining \( p \) to \( q \) ,

\[
E\left( \gamma \right)  \leq  E\left( c\right)
\]

with equality holding if and only if \( c \) is a minimizing geodesic.
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.3 LEMMA. Let \( p, q \in M \) and let \( \gamma : \left\lbrack {0, a}\right\rbrack \rightarrow M \) be a minimizing geodesic joining \( p \) to \( q \) . \]

which proves the first assertion. If the equality holds, we have \( {\left( L\left( c\right) \right) }^{2} = {aE}\left( c\right) \) , which implies that the parameter of \( c \) is proportional to arc length, and \( L\left( \gamma \right)  = L\left( c\right) \) , which implies that \( c \) is clearly a minimizing geodesic (see Corollary 3.9 of Chapter 3). The converse is obvious.

2.4 Proposition. (Formula for the first variation of the energy of a curve). Let \( c : \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) be a piecewise differentiable curve and let \( f : \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) be a variation of \( c \) . If \( E : \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) is the energy of \( f \) then

\[

By definition,

\]

\[

\]

\[
= {\left. 2\left\langle  \frac{\partial f}{\partial s},\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\right\rangle  \right| }_{{t}_{i}}^{{t}_{i + 1}} - 2{\int }_{{t}_{i}}^{{t}_{i + 1}}\left\langle  {\frac{\partial f}{\partial s},\frac{D}{dt}\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}}\right\rangle  {dt}.
\]

Therefore,

(2)

\[

\]

Putting \( s = 0 \) in (2), this yields (1).

nodes.proof:
If \( c \) is a geodesic, \( \frac{D}{dt}\frac{dc}{dt} = 0 \) and \( c \) is regular. Therefore if \( f \) is proper, \( V\left( 0\right)  = V\left( a\right)  = 0 \) , and all the terms of (1) are zero. Conversely, suppose that \( \frac{dE}{ds}\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) , for all proper variations of \( c \) . Let \( V\left( t\right)  = g\left( t\right) \frac{D}{dt}\frac{dc}{dt} \) , where \( g : \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) is a piecewise differentiable function with \( g\left( t\right)  > 0 \) if \( t \neq  {t}_{i} \) and \( g\left( {t}_{i}\right)  = 0, i = 0,1,\ldots , k + 1 \) . Construct a variation of \( c \) having \( V\left( t\right) \) as variational field. Then, since

\[
\frac{1}{2}\frac{dE}{ds}\left( 0\right)  =  - {\int }_{o}^{a}g\left( t\right) \left\langle  {\frac{D}{dt}\frac{dc}{dt},\frac{D}{dt}\frac{dc}{dt}}\right\rangle  {dt} = 0,
\]

we have \( \frac{D}{dt}\frac{dc}{dt} = 0 \) on each interval \( \left( {{t}_{i},{t}_{i + 1}}\right) \) , that is, \( c \) is a geodesic on each \( \left( {{t}_{i},{t}_{i + 1}}\right) , i = 0,1,\ldots , k \) .

To see what happens at the points \( {t}_{i} \) , consider another variational field \( \bar{V}\left( t\right) \) such that \( \bar{V}\left( 0\right)  = \bar{V}\left( a\right)  = 0 \) and if \( t \neq  0, a \) , \( \bar{V}\left( {t}_{i}\right)  = \frac{dc}{dt}\left( {t}_{i}^{ + }\right)  - \frac{dc}{dt}\left( {t}_{i}^{ - }\right) \) . Then, using the fact that \( c \) is a geodesic on \( \left( {{t}_{i},{t}_{i + 1}}\right) \) , we obtain

\[
0 = \frac{1}{2}\frac{dE}{ds}\left( 0\right)
\]

\[
=  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\left\langle  {\frac{dc}{dt}\left( {t}_{i}^{ + }\right)  - \frac{dc}{dt}\left( {t}_{i}^{ - }\right) ,\frac{dc}{dt}\left( {t}_{i}^{ + }\right)  - \frac{dc}{dt}\left( {t}_{i}^{ - }\right) }\right\rangle
\]

\[
=  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}{\left| \frac{dc}{dt}\left( {t}_{i}^{ + }\right)  - \frac{dc}{dt}\left( {t}_{i}^{ - }\right) \right| }^{2},
\]

or that \( c \) is of class \( {C}^{1} \) at each \( {t}_{i} \) . Since \( \frac{D}{dt}\frac{dc}{dt} = 0 \) at \( {t}_{i}, c \) satisfies the equation for geodesics on \( \left( {0, a}\right) \) . By the uniqueness of the solutions to ordinary differential equations, \( c \in  {C}^{\infty } \) and, therefore, \( c \) is a geodesic.

2.6 REMARK. Proposition 2.5 furnishes a characterization of geodesics as critical points of the energy for all proper variations.

It is in this sense that geodesics can be thought of as solutions to a variational problem. Observe that, in contrast to previous characterizations, such a characterization is not local but involves the behavior of the geodesic as a whole.

nodes.content:
2.7 REMARK. There is a certain analogy between the first variation of a proper variation and the usual derivative of a function defined on a differentiable manifold. It is natural to think of the set \( {\Omega }_{p, q} \) of piecewise differentiable curves \( c \) , joining two points \( p \) and \( q \) of \( M \) , as a manifold, a tangent vector at the point \( c \) being a piecewise differentiable vector field \( V \) along \( c \) which vanishes at the extremities of \( c \) . The energy \( E \) is then a differentiable function on such a manifold, and \( \frac{dE}{ds}\left( 0\right) \) is the derivative of \( E \) in the direction of \( V \) ; geodesics joining \( p \) to \( q \) are critical points of the function \( E \) .

The difficulty with this point of view is that the tangent space of such a manifold at a point \( c \) (that is, the set of piecewise differentiable vector fields along \( c \) ) does not have finite dimension. Thus the impossibility of finding local parametrizations of this manifold by means of open subsets of \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . This tangent space, nevertheless, is a vector space (infinite dimensional) and this suggests the possibility of having manifolds with infinitely many dimensions. Such manifolds can indeed be constructed but will not be treated further here. The interested reader can consult Palais, R., "Morse theory on Hilbert manifolds", Topology 2 (1963), 299-340, for more information.

Because \( \frac{dE}{ds}\left( 0\right) \) is zero for every proper variation of a geodesic, our next information on the energy of neighboring curves is given by \( \frac{{d}^{2}E}{d{s}^{2}}\left( 0\right) \) , which we are going to calculate.

Taking the derivative of (2), we obtain

\[
\frac{1}{2}\frac{{d}^{2}E}{d{s}^{2}} = {\left. \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{k}\left\langle  \frac{D}{ds}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s},\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\right\rangle  \right| }_{{t}_{i}}^{{t}_{i + 1}} + {\left. \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{k}\left\langle  \frac{\partial f}{\partial s},\frac{D}{ds}\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\right\rangle  \right| }_{{t}_{i}}^{{t}_{i + 1}}

\]

Putting \( s = 0 \) in the expression above, we obtain that the first and the third terms are zero, since \( f \) is proper and \( \gamma \) is a geodesic. In addition, because

\[
\frac{D}{ds}\frac{D}{dt}\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \frac{D}{dt}\frac{D}{ds}\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + R\left( {\frac{\partial f}{\partial t},\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}}\right) \frac{\partial f}{\partial t},
\]

\[

\]

\[

\]

Putting all these facts together, we obtain (3).

= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{k}\left\{  {{\int }_{{t}_{i}}^{{t}_{i + 1}}\frac{d}{dt}\left\langle  {V,\frac{DV}{dt}}\right\rangle  {dt}}\right.
\]

Therefore

\[
\frac{1}{2}{E}^{\prime \prime }\left( 0\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{k}\left\{  {{\int }_{{t}_{i}}^{{t}_{i + 1}}\left( {\left\langle  {{V}^{\prime },{V}^{\prime }}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }, V}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime }, V}\right\rangle  }\right) {dt}}\right\}
\]

\[
- \left\langle  {\frac{D}{ds}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s},\frac{d\gamma }{dt}}\right\rangle  \left( {0,0}\right)  + \left\langle  {\frac{D}{ds}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s},\frac{d\gamma }{dt}}\right\rangle  \left( {0, a}\right)
\]

\[
= {\int }_{0}^{a}\left\{  {\left\langle  {{V}^{\prime },{V}^{\prime }}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }, V}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime }, V}\right\rangle  }\right\}  {dt}
\]

\[
- \left\langle  {\frac{D}{ds}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s},{\gamma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle  \left( {0,0}\right)  + \left\langle  {\frac{D}{ds}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s},{\gamma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle  \left( {0, a}\right) .
\]

For reasons which will be clear later, it is convenient to write

\[
{\int }_{0}^{a}\left\{  {\left\langle  {{V}^{\prime },{V}^{\prime }}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }, V}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime }, V}\right\rangle  }\right\}  {dt} = {I}_{a}\left( {V, V}\right) .
\]

Observe that, if the variation is proper, \( {I}_{a}\left( {V, V}\right)  = \frac{1}{2}{E}^{\prime \prime }\left( 0\right) \) depends only on \( V \) . In the general case, we have(6)

\[
\frac{1}{2}{E}^{\prime \prime }\left( 0\right)  = {I}_{a}\left( {V, V}\right)  - \left\langle  {\frac{D}{ds}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s},{\gamma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle  \left( {0,0}\right)  + \left\langle  {\frac{D}{ds}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s},{\gamma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle  \left( {0, a}\right) .
\]

nodes.label: Theorem 3.1

nodes.section_title: 9.3. The theorems of Bonnet-Myers and of Synge-Weinstein
nodes.content:
3.1 THEOREM. (Bonnet [Bo], Myers [My]). Let \( {M}^{n} \) be a complete Riemannian manifold. Suppose that the Ricci curvature of \( M \) satisfies

\[
{\operatorname{Ric}}_{p}\left( v\right)  \geq  \frac{1}{{r}^{2}} > 0
\]

for all \( p \in  M \) and for all \( v \in  {T}_{p}\left( M\right) \) . Then \( M \) is compact and the diameter \( \operatorname{diam}\left( M\right)  \leq  {\pi r} \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.1 THEOREM. (Bonnet [Bo], Myers [My]). Let \( {M}^{n} \) be a complete Riemannian manifold. Suppose that the Ricci curvature of \( M \) satisfies \[ {\operatorname{Ric}}_{p}\left( v\right) \geq \frac{1}{{r}^{2}} > 0 \] for all \( p \in M \) and for all \( v \in {T}_{p}\left( M\right) \) . Then \( M \) is compact and the diameter \( \operatorname{diam}\left( M\right) \leq {\pi r} \) .

nodes.proof:
Let \( p \) and \( q \) be any two points in \( M \) . Since \( M \) is complete, there exists a minimizing geodesic \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) joining \( p \) to \( q \) . It is enough to show that the length \( \ell \left( \gamma \right)  \leq  {\pi r} \) , because then \( M \) is bounded and complete, therefore compact; in addition, since \( d\left( {p, q}\right)  \leq  {\pi r} \) , for any \( p, q \in  M \) , it follows that \( \operatorname{diam}\left( M\right)  \leq  {\pi r} \) , as asserted.

Suppose, to the contrary, that \( \ell \left( \gamma \right)  = \ell  > {\pi r} \) . Let us consider parallel fields \( {e}_{1}\left( t\right) ,\ldots ,{e}_{n - 1}\left( t\right) \) along \( \gamma \) which are orthonormal, for each \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) , and belong to the orthogonal complement of \( {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) \) . Let \( {e}_{n}\left( t\right)  = \frac{{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) }{\ell } \) and let \( {V}_{j} \) be a vector field along \( \gamma \) given by

\[
{V}_{j}\left( t\right)  = \left( {\sin {\pi t}}\right) {e}_{j}\left( t\right) ,\;j = 1,\ldots , n - 1.
\]

It is clear that \( {V}_{j}\left( 0\right)  = {V}_{j}\left( 1\right)  = 0 \) , therefore \( {V}_{j} \) generates a proper variation of \( \gamma \) , whose energy we denote by \( {E}_{j} \) .

Using the formula for the second variation of energy and the fact that \( {e}_{j} \) is parallel, we obtain

\[
\frac{1}{2}{E}_{j}^{\prime \prime }\left( 0\right)  =  - {\int }_{0}^{1}\left\langle  {{V}_{j},{V}_{j}^{\prime \prime } + R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime },{V}_{j}}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle  {dt}
\]

\[
= {\int }_{0}^{1}{\sin }^{2}{\pi t}\left( {{\pi }^{2} - {\ell }^{2}K\left( {{e}_{n}\left( t\right) ,{e}_{j}\left( t\right) }\right) }\right) {dt},
\]

where \( K\left( {{e}_{n}\left( t\right) ,{e}_{j}\left( t\right) }\right) \) is the sectional curvature at \( \gamma \left( t\right) \) with respect to the plane generated by \( {e}_{n}\left( t\right) ,{e}_{j}\left( t\right) \) . Summing on \( j \) and using the definition of the Ricci curvature, we get

\[
\frac{1}{2}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{{n - 1}}{E}_{j}^{\prime \prime }\left( 0\right)
\]

\[
= {\int }_{0}^{1}\left\{  {{\sin }^{2}{\pi t}\left( {\left( {n - 1}\right) {\pi }^{2} - \left( {n - 1}\right) {\ell }^{2}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{\gamma \left( t\right) }\left( {{e}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) }\right) }\right\}  {dt}.
\]

Since \( {\operatorname{Ric}}_{\gamma \left( t\right) }\left( {{e}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right)  \geq  \frac{1}{{r}^{2}} \) and \( \ell  > {\pi r} \) , we have

\[
\left( {n - 1}\right) {\ell }^{2}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{\gamma \left( t\right) }\left( {{e}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right)  > \left( {n - 1}\right) {\pi }^{2},
\]

hence

\[
\frac{1}{2}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{{n - 1}}{E}_{j}^{\prime \prime }\left( 0\right)  < {\int }_{0}^{1}{\sin }^{2}{\pi t}\left( {\left( {n - 1}\right) {\pi }^{2} - \left( {n - 1}\right) {\pi }^{2}}\right) {dt} = 0.
\]

As a result there exists an index \( j \) such that \( {E}_{j}^{\prime \prime }\left( 0\right)  < 0 \) , which, by Lemma 2.3, contradicts the fact that \( \gamma \) is minimizing. Therefore \( \ell  \leq  {\pi r} \) .

nodes.content:
3.2 Corollary. Let \( M \) be a complete Riemannian manifold with \( {\operatorname{Ric}}_{p}\left( v\right)  \geq  \delta  > 0 \) , for all \( p \in  M \) and all \( v \in  {T}_{p}\left( M\right) \) . Then, the universal cover of \( M \) is compact. In particular, the fundamental group \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) is finite.

Because, introducing on the universal cover \( \pi  : \widetilde{M} \rightarrow  M \) the covering metric (that is, the metric such that \( \pi \) is a local isometry), we conclude that \( \widetilde{M} \) is complete and that its Ricci curvature satisfies \( {\widetilde{\mathrm{{Ric}}}}_{p} \geq  \delta  > 0 \) . From the theorem, \( \widetilde{M} \) is compact. Hence the number of sheets of the covering is finite; since that is the number of elements in the fundamental group \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) of \( M \) , we conclude that \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) is finite.

3.4 REMARK. The hypothesis \( K \geq  \delta  > 0 \) cannot be relaxed to \( K > 0 \) . Indeed, the paraboloid

\[
\left\{  {\left( {x, y, z}\right)  \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{3};z = {x}^{2} + {y}^{2}}\right\}
\]

has curvature \( K > 0 \) , but is complete and non-compact.

nodes.content: 3.6 REMARK. The estimate for the diameter given by Theorem 3.1 cannot be improved. Indeed, the unit sphere \( {S}^{n} \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + 1} \) has constant sectional curvature equal to 1 (therefore its Ricci curvature also is a constant equal to 1) and \( \operatorname{diam}\left( {S}^{n}\right)  = \pi \) . A surprising theorem is that this example is unique in the following sense: Let \( {M}^{n} \) be complete with \( {\operatorname{Ric}}_{p}\left( v\right)  \geq  1/{r}^{2} \) , for all \( p \in  M \) and all \( v \in  {T}_{p}M \) ; if \( \operatorname{diam}\left( M\right)  = {\pi r} \) , then \( {M}^{n} \) is isometric to the sphere \( {S}^{n} \) of curvature \( 1/{r}^{2} \) (see S.Y. Cheng,"Eigenvalues comparison theorems and its geometric applications", Math. Z. 143 (1975), 289-297 and, for another proof, K. Shiohama, "A sphere theorem for manifolds of positive Ricci curvature", Trans. A.M.S. 275 (1983), 811-819).

nodes.content: 3.7 THEOREM. (Weinstein [We 2] and Synge [Sy]). Let \( f \) be an isometry of a compact oriented Riemannian manifold \( {M}^{n} \) . Suppose that \( M \) has positive sectional curvature and that \( f \) preserves the orientation of \( M \) if \( n \) is even, and reverses it if \( n \) is odd. Then \( f \) has a fixed point, i.e., there exists \( p \in  M \) with \( f\left( p\right)  = p \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.7 THEOREM. (Weinstein [We 2] and Synge [Sy]). Let \( f \) be an isometry of a compact oriented Riemannian manifold \( {M}^{n} \) . Suppose that \( M \) has positive sectional curvature and that \( f \) preserves the orientation of \( M \) if \( n \) is even, and reverses it if \( n \) is odd. Then \( f \) has a fixed point, i.e., there exists \( p \in M \) with \( f\left( p\right) = p \) .

nodes.proof:
Suppose, to the contrary, that \( f\left( q\right)  \neq  q \) for all \( q \in  M \) . Let \( p \in  M \) such that \( d\left( {p, f\left( p\right) }\right) \) attains a minimum. Since \( M \) is complete, there exists a normalized minimizing geodesic \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) , joining \( p \) to \( f\left( p\right) \) , that is, \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p,\gamma \left( \ell \right)  = f\left( p\right) \) .

Let \( \bar{A} = P \circ  d{f}_{p} : {T}_{p}\left( M\right)  \rightarrow  {T}_{p}\left( M\right) \) , where \( P \) is the parallel transport along \( \gamma \) from \( f\left( p\right)  = \gamma \left( \ell \right) \) to \( p \) . Then \( \widetilde{A} \) is an isometry. We are going to show that

\[
{\left( f \circ  \gamma \right) }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( \ell \right)
\]

In fact, consider the geodesic \( f \circ  \gamma \) which joins \( f\left( p\right) \) to \( {f}^{2}\left( p\right) \) . Let \( {p}^{\prime } = \gamma \left( {t}^{\prime }\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \neq  0,{t}^{\prime } \neq  \ell \) , and \( f\left( {p}^{\prime }\right)  = f \circ  \gamma \left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) .

Since \( f \) is an isometry, \( d\left( {p,{p}^{\prime }}\right)  = d\left( {f\left( p\right) , f\left( {p}^{\prime }\right) }\right) \) and, from the triangle inequality (see Fig. 2),

\[
d\left( {{p}^{\prime }, f\left( {p}^{\prime }\right) }\right)  \leq  d\left( {{p}^{\prime }, f\left( p\right) }\right)  + d\left( {f\left( p\right) , f\left( {p}^{\prime }\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= d\left( {{p}^{\prime }, f\left( p\right) }\right)  + d\left( {p,{p}^{\prime }}\right)
\]

\[
= d\left( {p, f\left( p\right) }\right) \text{ . }
\]

![019eafb3-a904-7162-90c5-5ccd2f5d76bf_18_434_305_964_315_0.jpg](images/019eafb3-a904-7162-90c5-5ccd2f5d76bf_18_434_305_964_315_0.jpg)

## Figure 2

Because \( d\left( {p, f\left( p\right) }\right) \) is a minimum,

\[
d\left( {{p}^{\prime }, f\left( {p}^{\prime }\right) }\right)  = d\left( {{p}^{\prime }, f\left( p\right) }\right)  + d\left( {f\left( p\right) , f\left( {p}^{\prime }\right) }\right) .
\]

Therefore, the curve formed by \( \gamma \) and \( f \circ  \gamma \) is a geodesic, hence

\[
{\left( f \circ  \gamma \right) }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( \ell \right)
\]

as we have asserted.

It follows that \( \widetilde{A} \) leaves \( {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) fixed, since

\[
\widetilde{A}\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right)  = P \circ  d{f}_{p}\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right)  = P\left( {{\left( f \circ  \gamma \right) }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right)  = P\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( \ell \right) }\right)  = {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) .
\]

Let \( A \) be the restriction of \( \widetilde{A} \) to the orthogonal complement of \( {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) . Then \( A \) is orthogonal on \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n - 1} \) and, since \( P \) is an isometry which preserves orientation,

\[
\det A = \det \widetilde{A} = \det \left( {P \circ  d{f}_{p}}\right)  = {\left( -1\right) }^{n},
\]

where in the last equality we use the hypothesis on \( f \) and the fact that \( P \) preserves orientation. From the lemma, \( A \) leaves a vector invariant. Let \( {e}_{1}\left( t\right) \) be a unit parallel field along \( \gamma \) such that, for each \( t,{e}_{1}\left( t\right) \) belongs to the orthogonal complement of \( {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) \) and \( {e}_{1}\left( 0\right) \) is invariant by \( A \) .

Let \( \beta \left( s\right) , s \in  \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right) \) , be a geodesic such that \( \beta \left( 0\right)  = p \) and \( {\beta }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = {e}_{1}\left( 0\right) \) . Because \( P \circ  d{f}_{p}\left( {{e}_{1}\left( 0\right) }\right)  = {e}_{1}\left( 0\right) \) , we have

\[
d{f}_{p}\left( {{e}_{1}\left( 0\right) }\right)  = {e}_{1}\left( \ell \right) ,
\]

sec.3] Bonnet-Myers, Synge-Weinstein Theorems

that is, the geodesic \( f \circ  \beta \) is such that \( f \circ  \beta \left( 0\right)  = f\left( p\right) \) and \( {\left( f \circ  \beta \right) }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = \; {e}_{1}\left( \ell \right) \) .

Let \( h \) be a variation of \( \gamma \) given by

\[
h\left( {s, t}\right)  = {\exp }_{\gamma \left( t\right) }\left( {s{e}_{1}\left( t\right) }\right) ,\;s \in  \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right) ,\;t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack  .
\]

Observe that, since \( h\left( {s,0}\right)  = \beta \left( s\right) \) , then (see Fig. 3)

\[
h\left( {s,\ell }\right)  = {\exp }_{f\left( p\right) }\left( {s{e}_{1}\left( \ell \right) }\right)  = \left( {f \circ  \beta }\right) \left( s\right) .
\]

![019eafb3-a904-7162-90c5-5ccd2f5d76bf_19_270_797_1228_440_0.jpg](images/019eafb3-a904-7162-90c5-5ccd2f5d76bf_19_270_797_1228_440_0.jpg)

Figure 3

Therefore,

\[
V\left( t\right)  = {\left. \frac{\partial }{\partial s}\mathop{\exp }\limits_{{\gamma \left( t\right) }}\left( s{e}_{1}\left( t\right) \right) \right| }_{s = 0} = {e}_{1}\left( t\right) ,
\]

hence \( \frac{{D}^{2}V}{d{t}^{2}} = 0 \) . Using the formula for the second variation (see Remark 2.9) and the fact that \( \frac{\partial h}{\partial s}\left( {0, t}\right)  = {e}_{1}\left( t\right) \) , we obtain

\[
\frac{1}{2}\frac{{d}^{2}E}{d{s}^{2}}\left( 0\right)  =  - {\int }_{0}^{\ell }\left\langle  {V\left( t\right) , R\left( {\frac{d\gamma }{dt}, V}\right) \frac{d\gamma }{dt}}\right\rangle  {dt}
\]

\[
+ \left\langle  {\frac{d\gamma }{dt},\frac{D}{ds}\frac{\partial h}{\partial s}}\right\rangle  \left( {0,\ell }\right)  - \left\langle  {\frac{d\gamma }{dt},\frac{D}{ds}\frac{\partial h}{\partial s}}\right\rangle  \left( {0,0}\right)
\]

\[
=  - {\int }_{0}^{\ell }K\left( {{e}_{1}\left( t\right) ,\frac{d\gamma }{dt}}\right) {dt}.
\]

Because the sectional curvature is positive,

\[
\frac{1}{2}\frac{{d}^{2}E}{d{s}^{2}}\left( 0\right)  < 0,
\]

and therefore \( \frac{dE}{ds} \) is strictly decreasing on a neighborhood of zero. This shows that there exists a curve \( c \) in the variation, such that \( {\left( \ell \left( c\right) \right) }^{2} \leq  \ell E\left( c\right)  < \ell E\left( \gamma \right)  = \ell {\left( \gamma \right) }^{2} \) . Since the curves in the variation join \( q \) to \( f\left( q\right) \) , we obtain a contradiction to the fact that \( d\left( {p, f\left( p\right) }\right) \) is a minimum.

nodes.proof:
If \( n \) is even, \( \det \left( {A - {\lambda I}}\right) \) is a real polynomial in \( \lambda \) of odd degree \( \left( { = n - 1}\right) \) . Therefore, \( A \) has a real eigenvalue. Since \( A \) is orthogonal, such eigenvalues are of the form \( \pm  1 \) . Since the product of the complex eigenvalues of \( A \) is non-negative, and \( \det A = 1 \) , at least one of the eigenvalues of \( A \) equals 1 . This proves the lemma in this case.

If \( n \) is odd, \( \det A =  - 1 \) . Because the product of the complex eigenvalues is non-negative, there is at least one pair of real eigenvalues, one of which is positive, hence equal to 1 .

3.10 Corollary. (Synge). Let \( {M}^{n} \) be a compact manifold with positive sectional curvature.

a) If \( {M}^{n} \) is orientable and \( n \) is even, then \( M \) is simply connected.

b) If \( n \) is odd, then \( {M}^{n} \) is orientable.
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.10 Corollary. (Synge). Let \( {M}^{n} \) be a compact manifold with positive sectional curvature. a) If \( {M}^{n} \) is orientable and \( n \) is even, then \( M \) is simply connected. b) If \( n \) is odd, then \( {M}^{n} \) is orientable.

nodes.proof:
a) Let \( \pi  : \widetilde{M} \rightarrow  M \) be the universal covering of \( M \) . Introduce on \( \widetilde{M} \) the covering metric, and orient \( \widetilde{M} \) in such a way that \( \pi \) preserves the orientation. Because \( M \) is compact and has positive curvature, we must have \( K \geq  \delta  > 0 \) . From the fact that \( \pi \) is a local isometry, the same curvature condition holds on \( \widetilde{M} \) . Since \( \widetilde{M} \) is complete, by Corollary 3.3, \( \widetilde{M} \) is compact. Let \( k : \widetilde{M} \rightarrow  \widetilde{M} \) be a covering transformation of \( \widetilde{M} \) , that is, \( \pi  \circ  k = \pi \) (see Massey [Ma], p. 159). Then \( k \) is an isometry of \( \widetilde{M} \) which, from the way that we oriented \( \widetilde{M} \) , preserves the orientation. Because \( n \) is even, we can use the theorem to conclude that \( k \) has a fixed point. But a covering transformation which has a fixed point is the identity. It follows that the group of covering transformations of \( \widetilde{M} \) (which is isomorphic to the fundamental group of \( M \) ; see Massey [Ma], p. 163) reduces to the identity. Therefore \( M \) is simply connected.

b) Suppose that \( M \) is not orientable, and consider the ori-entable double cover \( \bar{M} \) of \( M \) (see Exercise 12 of Chap.0). We introduce on \( \bar{M} \) the covering metric. Since \( \bar{M} \) is the double cover of

3. Prove the following generalization of the Theorem of Bonnet-Myers: Let \( {M}^{n} \) be a complete Riemannian manifold. Suppose that there exist constants \( a > 0 \) and \( c \geq  0 \) such that for all pairs of points in \( {M}^{n} \) and for all minimizing geodesics \( \gamma \left( s\right) \) , parametrized by arc length \( s \) , joining these points, we have

\[
\operatorname{Ric}\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) }\right)  \geq  a + \frac{df}{ds},\;\text{ along }\gamma ,
\]

where \( f \) is a function of \( s \) , satisfying \( \left| {f\left( s\right) }\right|  \leq  c \) along \( \gamma \) . Then \( {M}^{n} \) is compact.

Calculate an estimate for the diameter of \( {M}^{n} \) , and observe that if \( f \equiv  0 \) and \( c = 0 \) , we obtain the Theorem of Bonnet-Myers.

The theorem above has application to Relativity, see G.J. Galloway, "A generalization of Myers' Theorem and an application to relativistic cosmology", J. Diff. Geometry, 14 (1979), 105- 116.

4. Let \( {M}^{n} \) be an orientable Riemannian manifold with positive curvature and even dimension. Let \( \gamma \) be a closed geodesic in \( M \) , that is, \( \gamma \) is an immersion of the circle \( {S}^{1} \) in \( M \) that is geodesic at all of its points. Prove that \( \gamma \) is homotopic to a closed curve whose length is strictly less than that of \( \gamma \) .

Hint: The parallel transport along the closed curve \( \gamma \) leaves a vector orthogonal to \( \gamma \) invariant (this comes from the ori-entability of \( M \) and the fact that the dimension is even). Therefore there exists a vector field \( V\left( t\right) \) parallel along the closed curve \( \gamma \) . Calculate \( {E}_{V}^{\prime \prime }\left( 0\right) \) and show that it is strictly negative. Therefore, close to \( \gamma \) , there exists a closed curve of length smaller than that of \( \gamma \) .
