nodes.label: Remark 10.1-extra-1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
## 1. Introduction

Let \( M \) be a Riemannian manifold. As we saw in Chapter 5, if \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) is a normalized geodesic and \( J \) is a Jacobi field along \( \gamma \) with \( J\left( 0\right)  = 0,\left| {{J}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right|  = 1 \) and \( \left\langle  {{J}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right\rangle   = 0 \) , then

\[
\left| {J\left( t\right) }\right|  = t - \frac{K}{6}{t}^{3} + R,\;\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}\frac{R}{{t}^{3}} = 0,
\]

where \( K \) is the sectional curvature at \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) with respect to the plane generated by \( {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) and \( {J}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) . Therefore, if \( t \) is small, the smaller \( K \) is, the larger \( \left| {J\left( t\right) }\right| \) will be. Consider now another Riemannian manifold \( \widetilde{M} \) , a geodesic \( \widetilde{\gamma } : \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \widetilde{M} \) and a Jacobi field \( \widetilde{J} \) along \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) satisfying: \( \widetilde{J}\left( 0\right)  = 0,\left| {{\widetilde{J}}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right|  = 1,\left\langle  {{\widetilde{J}}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,{\widetilde{\gamma }}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right\rangle   = 0 \) . Suppose that

\[
\widetilde{K}\left( {{\widetilde{\gamma }}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,{\widetilde{J}}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right)  \geq  K\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,{J}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) .
\]

It follows from the expression above that, for small \( t,\left| {\widetilde{J}\left( t\right) }\right|  \leq  \left| {J\left( t\right) }\right| \) .

The Theorem of Rauch, which we intend to prove in this chapter, furnishes conditions so that the inequality above is valid without the restriction that \( t \) be small. More precisely, the theorem asserts (see the statement in Section 2) that if \( \widetilde{\gamma } : \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \widetilde{M} \) does not have conjugate points and

\[
\widetilde{K}\left( {{\widetilde{\gamma }}^{\prime }\left( t\right) ,\widetilde{J}\left( t\right) }\right)  \geq  K\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) , J\left( t\right) }\right) ,\;t \in  \left( {0,\ell }\right) ,
\]

then \( \left| {\widetilde{J}\left( t\right) }\right|  \leq  \left| {J\left( t\right) }\right| \) .

Rauch's Theorem is one of the basic facts in Riemannian Geometry. Intuitively, it expresses the plausible fact that as the curvature grows, lengths shorten.

In dimension two, such a theorem is an easy consequence of the classical theorem of Sturm on ordinary differential equations. In fact, in this case, the Jacobi equations for \( J = f{e}_{2},\widetilde{J} = \widetilde{f}{\widetilde{e}}_{2}\left( {{e}_{2}\left( t\right) }\right. \) and \( {\widetilde{e}}_{2}\left( t\right) \) are unit parallel vector fields along and normal to the geodesics \( \gamma \left( t\right) \) and \( \widetilde{\gamma }\left( t\right) \) , respectively) can be written:

\[
{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( t\right)  + K\left( t\right) f\left( t\right)  = 0,\;f\left( 0\right)  = 0,\;t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack  ,
\]

\[
{\widetilde{f}}^{\prime \prime }\left( t\right)  + \widetilde{K}\left( t\right) \widetilde{f}\left( t\right)  = 0,\;\widetilde{f}\left( 0\right)  = 0,\;t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack  .
\]

Sturm’s Theorem asserts that if \( {f}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = {\widetilde{f}}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  > 0,\widetilde{f}\left( t\right)  \neq  0 \) on \( (0,\ell \rbrack \) , and \( \widetilde{K}\left( t\right)  \geq  K\left( t\right) \) , then \( \widetilde{f}\left( t\right)  \leq  f\left( t\right) \) (see Fig. 1 and Exercise 5 of this chapter).

![019eafb3-a904-7162-90c5-5ccd2f5d76bf_25_305_974_1188_417_0.jpg](images/019eafb3-a904-7162-90c5-5ccd2f5d76bf_25_305_974_1188_417_0.jpg)

## Figure 1

In dimension higher than two, the proof is much less simple, and a presentation of the theorem was made for the first time in 1951 by Rauch [R 1] (for another exposition, see Rauch [R 3]). The proof that we present in Section 2 is an elaboration due to various mathematicians in the fifties, among whom we should mention Ambrose and Singer.

In Section 3 we make an application of the ideas in the Rauch Theorem to the theory of isometric immersions. In Section 4, we introduce the notion of focal point, which generalizes the idea of conjugate point, and we extend the Theorem of Rauch to this situation. The last two sections are not used in the rest of the book and can be omitted on a first reading.

2.2 LEMMA. (The Index Lemma). Let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) be a geodesic without conjugate points to \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) in the interval \( (0, a\rbrack \) . Let \( J \) be a Jacobi field along \( \gamma \) , with \( \left\langle  {J,{\gamma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle   = 0 \) , and let \( V \) be a piecewise differentiable vector field along \( \gamma \) , with \( \left\langle  {V,{\gamma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle   = 0 \) . Suppose that \( J\left( 0\right)  = V\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) and that \( J\left( {t}_{o}\right)  = V\left( {t}_{o}\right) ,{t}_{o} \in  (0, a\rbrack \) . Then

\[
{I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {J, J}\right)  \leq  {I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {V, V}\right)
\]

and equality occurs if and only if \( V = J \) on \( \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{o}}\right\rbrack \) .

nodes.proof:
The vector space \( \mathcal{J} \) of Jacobi fields \( J \) along \( \gamma \) with \( J\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) and \( \left\langle  {J,{\gamma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle   = 0 \) has dimension \( n - 1 \) , where \( n = \dim M \) . Let \( \left\{  {{J}_{1},\ldots ,{J}_{n - 1}}\right\} \) be a basis for this space. Then \( J = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{\alpha }_{i}{J}_{i} \) , \( i = 1,\ldots , n - 1 \) , where the \( {\alpha }_{i} \) are constants. Since there are no conjugate points in the interval \( (0, a\rbrack \) , for all \( t \neq  0 \) , the vectors \( {J}_{1}\left( t\right) ,\ldots ,{J}_{n - 1}\left( t\right) \) form a basis of the orthogonal complement of \( {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) \) in \( {T}_{\gamma \left( t\right) }\left( M\right) \) . Therefore, for \( t \neq  0 \) , we can write

\[
V\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}\left( t\right) {J}_{i}\left( t\right)
\]

where \( {f}_{i} \) are piecewise differentiable functions on \( (0, a\rbrack \) . We are going to show that \( {f}_{i} \) can be extended continuously and differentiably to \( t = 0 \) , that is, \( {f}_{i} \) is piecewise differentiable on \( \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack \) .

For this, use Lemma 2.1 to write \( {J}_{i}\left( t\right)  = t{A}_{i}\left( t\right) \) . Then \( {A}_{i}\left( 0\right)  = {J}_{i}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) , hence the \( {A}_{i}\left( 0\right) \) are linearly independent. Therefore, the \( {A}_{i}\left( t\right) \) are linearly independent for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack \) , and we can write \( V\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{g}_{i}\left( t\right) {A}_{i}\left( t\right) \) where the \( {g}_{i} \) are piecewise differentiable functions on \( \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack \) and \( {g}_{i}\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) . Applying Lemma 2.1 again, we have that \( {g}_{i}\left( t\right)  = t{h}_{i}\left( t\right) \) , where the \( {h}_{i}\left( t\right) \) are piecewise differentiable on \( \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack \) . Since we have \( {f}_{i}\left( t\right)  = {h}_{i}\left( t\right) \) , for \( t \neq  0 \) , the claim is proved.

We are going to show that, on the interior of each subinterval where \( {f}_{i} \) is differentiable,

\[
\left\langle  {{V}^{\prime },{V}^{\prime }}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }, V}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime }, V}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}^{\prime }{J}_{i},\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}^{\prime }{J}_{j}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
+ \frac{d}{dt}\left\langle  {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}{J}_{i},\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}{J}_{j}^{\prime }}\right\rangle
\]

Indeed, since

\[
R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }, V}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime } = R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime },\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}{J}_{i}}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime } = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime },{J}_{i}}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime } =  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}{J}_{i}^{\prime \prime },
\]

we have

\[
\left\langle  {{V}^{\prime },{V}^{\prime }}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }, V}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime }, V}\right\rangle
\]

\[
= \langle \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}^{\prime }{J}_{i} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}{J}_{i}^{\prime },\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}^{\prime }{J}_{j} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}{J}_{j}^{\prime }\rangle  - \langle R({\gamma }^{\prime }, V){\gamma }^{\prime }, V\rangle
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}^{\prime }{J}_{i},\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}^{\prime }{J}_{j}}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}^{\prime }{J}_{i},\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}{J}_{j}^{\prime }}\right\rangle
\]

\[
+ \langle \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}{J}_{i}^{\prime },\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}^{\prime }{J}_{j}\rangle  + \langle \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}{J}_{i}^{\prime },\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}{J}_{j}^{\prime }\rangle
\]

\[
+ \langle \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}{J}_{i}^{\prime \prime },\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}{J}_{j}\rangle .
\]

On the other hand,

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\left\langle  {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}{J}_{i},\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}{J}_{j}^{\prime }}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}^{\prime }{J}_{i} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}{J}_{i}^{\prime },\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}{J}_{j}^{\prime }}\right\rangle
\]

\[
+ \langle \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}{J}_{i},\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}^{\prime }{J}_{j}^{\prime } + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}{J}_{j}^{\prime \prime }\rangle
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}^{\prime }{J}_{i},\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}{J}_{j}^{\prime }}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}{J}_{i}^{\prime },\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}{J}_{j}^{\prime }}\right\rangle
\]

\[
+ \langle \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}{J}_{i},\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}{J}_{j}^{\prime \prime }\rangle  + \langle \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}{J}_{i},\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}^{\prime }{J}_{j}^{\prime }\rangle .
\]

Therefore, to prove (1), it suffices to show that

(2)

\[
\left\langle  {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}{J}_{i}^{\prime },\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}^{\prime }{J}_{j}}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}{J}_{i},\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}^{\prime }{J}_{j}^{\prime }}\right\rangle  .
\]

To prove (2), we write

\[
h\left( t\right)  = \left\langle  {{J}_{i}^{\prime },{J}_{j}}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {{J}_{i},{J}_{j}^{\prime }}\right\rangle  ;
\]

since \( h\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) and

\[
{h}^{\prime }\left( t\right)  = \left\langle  {{J}_{i}^{\prime \prime },{J}_{j}}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {{J}_{i}^{\prime },{J}_{j}^{\prime }}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {{J}_{i}^{\prime },{J}_{j}^{\prime }}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {{J}_{i},{J}_{j}^{\prime \prime }}\right\rangle
\]

\[
=  - \left\langle  {R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime },{J}_{i}}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime },{J}_{j}}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {{J}_{i}, R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime },{J}_{j}}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle   = 0
\]

we conclude that \( h\left( t\right)  \equiv  0 \) . By distributivity, we then obtain (2), which concludes the proof of (1).

Applying (1) to \( V \) and \( J \) , we obtain sucessively:

\[
{I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {V, V}\right)  = \left\langle  {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}{J}_{i},\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}{J}_{j}^{\prime }}\right\rangle  \left( {t}_{o}\right)  + {\int }_{0}^{{t}_{o}}\left\langle  {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}^{\prime }{J}_{i},\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{f}_{j}^{\prime }{J}_{j}}\right\rangle  {dt}
\]

\[
{I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {J, J}\right)  = \left\langle  {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{\alpha }_{i}{J}_{i},\mathop{\sum }\limits_{j}{\alpha }_{j}{J}_{j}^{\prime }}\right\rangle  \left( {t}_{o}\right)
\]

Because \( J\left( {t}_{o}\right)  = V\left( {t}_{o}\right) \) , we have that \( {\alpha }_{i} = {f}_{i}\left( {t}_{o}\right) \) , hence

(3)

\[
{I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {V, V}\right)  = {I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {J, J}\right)  + {\int }_{0}^{{t}_{o}}{\left| \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}^{\prime }{J}_{i}\right| }^{2}{dt}.
\]

It follows from (3) that \( {I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {V, V}\right)  \geq  {I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {J, J}\right) \) , which proves the first part of the lemma. If \( {I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {V, V}\right)  = {I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {J, J}\right) \) , then \( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{f}_{i}^{\prime }{J}_{i} = 0 \) . Because the \( {J}_{i} \) are linearly independent for \( t \neq  0 \) , we conclude, by continuity, that \( {f}_{i}^{\prime } = 0 \) , for all \( i \) and for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{o}}\right\rbrack \) . Therefore, \( {f}_{i} = \) const., and since \( {f}_{i}\left( {t}_{o}\right)  = {\alpha }_{i} \) , we have that \( {f}_{i}\left( t\right)  = {\alpha }_{i} \) , that is, \( V = J \) , as claimed.

2.3 THEOREM. (Rauch). Let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {M}^{n} \) and \( \widetilde{\gamma } : \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\widetilde{M}}^{n + k} \) , \( k \geq  0 \) , be geodesics with the same velocity (i.e., \( \left| {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right|  = \left| {{\widetilde{\gamma }}^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right| \) ), and let \( J \) and \( \widetilde{J} \) be Jacobi fields along \( \gamma \) and \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) , respectively, such that

\[
J\left( 0\right)  = \widetilde{J}\left( 0\right)  = 0,\;\left\langle  {{J}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {{\widetilde{J}}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,{\widetilde{\gamma }}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right\rangle  ,
\]

\[
\left| {{J}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right|  = \left| {{\widetilde{J}}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right|
\]

Assume that \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) does not have conjugate points on \( (0, a\rbrack \) and that, for all \( t \) and all \( x \in  {T}_{\gamma \left( t\right) }\left( M\right) ,\widetilde{x} \in  {T}_{\widetilde{\gamma }\left( t\right) }\left( \widetilde{M}\right) \) , we have

\[
\widetilde{K}\left( {\widetilde{x},{\widetilde{\gamma }}^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right)  \geq  K\left( {x,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right) ,
\]

where \( K\left( {x, y}\right) \) denotes the sectional curvature with respect to the plane generated by \( x \) and \( y \) . Then

\[
\left| \widetilde{J}\right|  \leq  \left| J\right| \text{ . }
\]

In addition, if for some \( {t}_{o} \in  (0, a\rbrack \) , we have \( \left| {\widetilde{J}\left( {t}_{o}\right) }\right|  = \left| {J\left( {t}_{o}\right) }\right| \) , then \( \widetilde{K}\left( {\widetilde{J}\left( t\right) ,{\widetilde{\gamma }}^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right)  = K\left( {J\left( t\right) ,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right) \) , for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{o}}\right\rbrack \) .

nodes.proof:
Observe that, from Proposition 3.6 of Chapter 5, the condition \( \left\langle  {{J}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {{\widetilde{J}}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,{\widetilde{\gamma }}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right\rangle \) is equivalent (with \( J\left( 0\right)  = \widetilde{J}\left( 0\right)  = \) 0) to the condition \( \left\langle  {J,{\gamma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {\widetilde{J},{\widetilde{\gamma }}^{\prime }}\right\rangle \) . In addition, since

\[
\left\langle  {J,{\gamma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle  {\gamma }^{\prime } = \left\langle  {{J}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right\rangle  t{\gamma }^{\prime } + \left\langle  {J\left( 0\right) ,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right\rangle  {\gamma }^{\prime },
\]

the tangential components of \( J \) and \( \widetilde{J} \) have, by hypothesis, the same length. Therefore, we can suppose that

\[
\left\langle  {J,{\gamma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle   = 0 = \left\langle  {\widetilde{J},{\widetilde{\gamma }}^{\prime }}\right\rangle  .
\]

If \( \left| {{J}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right|  = \left| {{\widetilde{J}}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right|  = 0 \) , then \( \left| J\right|  = \left| \widetilde{J}\right|  = 0 \) . In the contrary case, we put \( {\left| J\left( t\right) \right| }^{2} = v\left( t\right) \) and \( {\left| \widetilde{J}\left( t\right) \right| }^{2} = \widetilde{v}\left( t\right) \) . Since \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) does not have any conjugate points on \( (0, a\rbrack ,\frac{v\left( t\right) }{\bar{v}\left( t\right) } \) is well-defined for \( t \in  (0, a\rbrack \) . From L'Hospital's rule,

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}\frac{v\left( t\right) }{\widetilde{v}\left( t\right) } = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}\frac{{v}^{\prime \prime }\left( t\right) }{{\widetilde{v}}^{\prime \prime }\left( t\right) } = \frac{{\left| {J}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \right| }^{2}}{{\left| {\widetilde{J}}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \right| }^{2}} = 1.
\]

Therefore, to prove that \( \left| \widetilde{J}\right|  \leq  \left| J\right| \) , it is enough to prove that \( \frac{d}{dt}\left( \frac{v\left( t\right) }{\widetilde{v}\left( t\right) }\right)  \geq  0 \) . This is equivalent to proving that \( {v}^{\prime }\widetilde{v} \geq  v{\widetilde{v}}^{\prime } \) .

To prove what we want, fix \( {t}_{o} \in  (0, a\rbrack \) . If \( v\left( {t}_{o}\right)  = 0 \) we have that

\[
{v}^{\prime }\left( {t}_{o}\right)  = 2\left\langle  {{J}^{\prime }\left( {t}_{o}\right) , J\left( {t}_{o}\right) }\right\rangle   = 0,
\]

and the inequality is satisfied trivially. Suppose, therefore, that \( v\left( {t}_{o}\right)  \neq  0 \) . Put

\[
U\left( t\right)  = \frac{1}{v\left( {t}_{o}\right) }J\left( t\right) ,\;\widetilde{U}\left( t\right)  = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\widetilde{v}\left( {t}_{o}\right) }}\widetilde{J}\left( t\right) ,
\]

and observe that

\[
\frac{{v}^{\prime }\left( {t}_{o}\right) }{v\left( {t}_{o}\right) } = \frac{2\left\langle  {{J}^{\prime }\left( {t}_{o}\right) , J\left( {t}_{o}\right) }\right\rangle  }{\left\langle  J\left( {t}_{o}\right) , J\left( {t}_{o}\right) \right\rangle  } = 2\left\langle  {{U}^{\prime }\left( {t}_{o}\right) , U\left( {t}_{o}\right) }\right\rangle   = \langle U, U{\rangle }^{\prime }\left( {t}_{o}\right)
\]

\[
= {\int }_{0}^{{t}_{o}}\langle U, U{\rangle }^{\prime \prime }{dt} = 2{\int }_{0}^{{t}_{o}}\left\{  {\left\langle  {{U}^{\prime },{U}^{\prime }}\right\rangle   - \left\langle  {U, R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }, U}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle  }\right\}  {dt}
\]

\[
= 2{I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {U, U}\right) \text{ . }
\]

Similarly,

\[
\frac{{\widetilde{v}}^{\prime }\left( {t}_{o}\right) }{\widetilde{v}\left( {t}_{o}\right) } = 2{I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {\widetilde{U},\widetilde{U}}\right)
\]

By the arbitrariness of \( {t}_{o} \) , it suffices, therefore, to prove that \( {I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {\widetilde{U},\widetilde{U}}\right)  \leq  {I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {U, U}\right) \) to complete the proof of the inequality.

For this, let \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n}}\right\} \) and \( \left\{  {{\widetilde{e}}_{1},\ldots ,{\widetilde{e}}_{n + k}}\right\} \) be parallel orthonormal bases along \( \gamma \) and \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) , respectively, such that:

\[
{e}_{1}\left( t\right)  = {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) /\left| {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right| ,\;{e}_{2}\left( {t}_{o}\right)  = U\left( {t}_{o}\right) ,
\]

\[
{\widetilde{e}}_{1}\left( t\right)  = {\widetilde{\gamma }}^{\prime }\left( t\right) /\left| {{\widetilde{\gamma }}^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right| ,\;{\widetilde{e}}_{2}\left( {t}_{o}\right)  = \widetilde{U}\left( {t}_{o}\right) .
\]

To each vector field \( V\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{g}_{i}\left( t\right) {e}_{i}\left( t\right) \) along \( \gamma \) associate the field \( {\phi V} \) along \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) given by

\[
\left( {\phi V}\right) \left( t\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{g}_{i}\left( t\right) {\widetilde{e}}_{i}\left( t\right) .
\]

The map \( \phi \) defined above satisfies the following properties:

(4)

\[
\left\langle  {\phi {V}_{1},\phi {V}_{2}}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {{V}_{1},{V}_{2}}\right\rangle
\]

(5)

\[
{\left( \phi V\right) }^{\prime } = \phi \left( {V}^{\prime }\right) .
\]

It follows, from the hypothesis on the curvature and the fact that the geodesics have the same velocity, that

\[
{I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {\phi \left( U\right) ,\phi \left( U\right) }\right)  \leq  {I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {U, U}\right) .
\]

Observe now that \( \widetilde{U} \) and \( \phi \left( U\right) \) are vector fields along \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) which satisfy the hypothesis of Lemma 2.2, and that \( \widetilde{U} \) is a Jacobi field. From Lemma 2.2,

\[
{I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {\widetilde{U},\widetilde{U}}\right)  \leq  {I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {\phi \left( U\right) ,\phi \left( U\right) }\right)  \leq  {I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {U, U}\right) ,
\]

which proves the inequality in the Theorem.

Suppose now that \( \left| {J\left( {t}_{o}\right) }\right|  = \left| {\widetilde{J}\left( {t}_{o}\right) }\right| \) , for some \( {t}_{o} \in  (0, a\rbrack \) . For all \( t \neq  0 \) , we have \( {I}_{t}\left( {\widetilde{U},\widetilde{U}}\right)  \leq  {I}_{t}\left( {U, U}\right) \) , and, therefore, \( {v}^{\prime }\widetilde{v}\left( t\right)  \geq \; v{\widetilde{v}}^{\prime }\left( t\right) \) . Since \( \left| {J\left( {t}_{o}\right) }\right|  = \left| {\widetilde{J}\left( {t}_{o}\right) }\right| \) , it follows that

\[
{v}^{\prime }\widetilde{v}\left( t\right)  = v{\widetilde{v}}^{\prime }\left( t\right) ,\;t \in  \left( {0,{t}_{o}}\right\rbrack
\]

hence the inequalities above are equalities for \( t \in  \left( {0,{t}_{o}}\right\rbrack \) , i.e.,

\[
{I}_{t}\left( {\phi \left( U\right) ,\phi \left( U\right) }\right)  = {I}_{t}\left( {U, U}\right) ,\;t \in  \left( {0,{t}_{o}}\right\rbrack  .
\]

Since \( \phi \) satisfies (4) and (5), we conclude from the equality above and from the hypothesis on the curvature that \( K\left( {J\left( t\right) ,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right)  = \; \widetilde{K}\left( {\widetilde{J}\left( t\right) ,{\widetilde{\gamma }}^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right) \) , for \( t \in  \left( {0,{t}_{o}}\right\rbrack \) , hence, by continuity, for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{o}}\right\rbrack \) , as has been asserted.

2.4 Proposition. Suppose that the sectional curvature \( K \) of a Riemannian manifold \( M \) satisfies the inequality

\[
0 < L \leq  K \leq  H,
\]

where \( H \) and \( L \) are constants. Let \( \gamma \) be geodesic in \( M \) . Then the distance \( d \) along \( \gamma \) between two consecutive conjugate points of \( \gamma \) satisfies

\[
\frac{\pi }{\sqrt{H}} \leq  d \leq  \frac{\pi }{\sqrt{L}}
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.4 Proposition. Suppose that the sectional curvature \( K \) of a Riemannian manifold \( M \) satisfies the inequality \[ 0 < L \leq K \leq H, \] where \( H \) and \( L \) are constants. Let \( \gamma \) be geodesic in \( M \) . Then the distance \( d \) along \( \gamma \) between two consecutive conjugate points of \( \gamma \) satisfies \[ \frac{\pi }{\sqrt{H}} \leq d \leq \frac{\pi }{\sqrt{L}} \]

nodes.proof:
To get the inequality \( d \geq  \pi /\sqrt{H} \) , it suffices to compare the manifold \( {M}^{n} \) with the sphere \( {S}^{n}\left( H\right) \) of curvature \( H \) . Let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow \; M \) be a normalized geodesic in \( M \) with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p \) , and let \( J \) be a Jacobi field along \( \gamma \) with \( J\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) and \( \left\langle  {J,{\gamma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle   = 0 \) . Choose a point \( \widetilde{p} \in  {S}^{n}\left( H\right) \) and a normalized geodesic \( \widetilde{\gamma } : \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {S}^{n}\left( H\right) \) with \( \widetilde{\gamma }\left( 0\right)  = \widetilde{p} \) . Let \( \widetilde{J} \) be a Jacobi field along \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) with \( \widetilde{J}\left( 0\right)  = 0,\left\langle  {\widetilde{J},{\widetilde{\gamma }}^{\prime }}\right\rangle   = 0 \) , \( \left| {{\widetilde{J}}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right|  = \left| {{J}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right| \) . Since \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) does not have conjugate points in the interval \( \left( {0,\pi /\sqrt{H}}\right) \) , by Rauch’s Theorem, \( \left| {J\left( t\right) }\right|  \geq  \left| {\widetilde{J}\left( t\right) }\right|  > 0, t \in \; \left( {0,\pi /\sqrt{H}}\right) \) . Therefore, the distance \( d \) from \( p \) to its first conjugate point satisfies \( d \geq  \pi /\sqrt{H} \) .

To obtain the inequality \( d \leq  \pi /\sqrt{L} \) , we make an analogous comparison with the sphere \( {S}^{n}\left( L\right) \) of dimension \( n \) and constant curvature \( L \) . If \( d > \pi /\sqrt{L} \) , Rauch’s Theorem applies, hence \( {S}^{n}\left( L\right) \) has all its conjugate points after \( \pi /\sqrt{L} \) , which is absurd. Therefore \( d \leq  \pi /\sqrt{L} \) .

2.5 Proposition. Let \( {M}^{n} \) and \( {\widetilde{M}}^{n} \) be Riemannian manifolds and suppose that for all \( p \in  M,\widetilde{p} \in  \widetilde{M},\sigma  \subset  {T}_{p}M,\widetilde{\sigma } \subset  {T}_{\widetilde{p}}\widetilde{M} \) , we have that \( {\widetilde{K}}_{\widetilde{p}}\left( \widetilde{\sigma }\right)  \geq  {K}_{p}\left( \sigma \right) \) . Let \( p \in  M,\widetilde{p} \in  \widetilde{M} \) and fix a linear isometry \( i : {T}_{p}M \rightarrow  {T}_{\widetilde{p}}\widetilde{M} \) . Let \( r > 0 \) be such that the restriction \( {\exp }_{p}\left| {{B}_{r}\left( 0\right) \text{ is a diffeomorphism and }{\exp }_{\widetilde{p}}}\right| {\widetilde{B}}_{r}\left( 0\right) \) is non-singular. Let \( c : \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\exp }_{p}\left( {{B}_{r}\left( 0\right) }\right)  \subset  M \) be a differentiable curve and define a curve \( \widetilde{c} : \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\exp }_{\widetilde{p}}\left( {{\widetilde{B}}_{r}\left( 0\right) }\right)  \subset  \widetilde{M} \) by

\[
\widetilde{c}\left( s\right)  = {\exp }_{\bar{p}} \circ  i \circ  {\exp }_{p}^{-1}\left( {c\left( s\right) }\right) ,\;s \in  \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack  .
\]

Then \( \ell \left( c\right)  \geq  \ell \left( \widetilde{c}\right) \) .

Consider the curve \( \bar{c}\left( s\right)  = {\exp }_{p}^{-1}c\left( s\right) \) in \( {T}_{p}M \) . For \( s \) fixed, consider the radial geodesic \( {\gamma }_{s}\left( t\right)  = {\exp }_{p}t\bar{c}\left( s\right) \) . The mapping

\[
f\left( {t, s}\right)  = {\gamma }_{s}\left( t\right) ,\;0 \leq  s \leq  a,\;0 \leq  t \leq  1,
\]

is a parametrized surface (see Fig. 2). Therefore, for all \( s,\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {t, s}\right)  = \; {J}_{s}\left( t\right) \) is a Jacobi field along \( {\gamma }_{s} \) , with \( {J}_{s}\left( 0\right)  = 0,{J}_{s}\left( 1\right)  = \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {1, s}\right)  = \; {c}^{\prime }\left( s\right) \) . In addition,

\[
{\left. \frac{D{J}_{s}}{dt}\left( 0\right)  = \frac{D}{dt}\left\{  {\left( d{\exp }_{p}\right) }_{t\bar{c}\left( s\right) }\left( t{\bar{c}}^{\prime }\left( s\right) \right) \right\}  \right| }_{t = o} = {\bar{c}}^{\prime }\left( s\right) .
\]

\[
\widetilde{f}\left( {t, s}\right)  = {\exp }_{\widetilde{p}}\operatorname{ti}\left( {\bar{c}\left( s\right) }\right)  = {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{s}\left( t\right) ,
\]

and observe that \( {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{s} \) is a geodesic. Then the Jacobi field \( {\widetilde{J}}_{s}\left( t\right)  = \; \frac{\partial \bar{f}}{\partial s}\left( {t, s}\right) \) satisfies

\[
{\widetilde{J}}_{s}\left( 0\right)  = 0,\;{\widetilde{J}}_{s}\left( 1\right)  = {\widetilde{c}}^{\prime }\left( s\right) ,\;\frac{D{\widetilde{J}}_{s}}{dt}\left( 0\right)  = i{\bar{c}}^{\prime }\left( s\right) .
\]

Because \( i \) is an isometry,

\[
\left| {{J}_{s}\left( 0\right) }\right|  = \left| {{\widetilde{J}}_{s}\left( 0\right) }\right|  = 0,\;\left| {{J}_{s}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right|  = \left| {{\widetilde{J}}_{s}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right|
\]

and

\[
\left\langle  {{\widetilde{J}}_{s}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,{\widetilde{\gamma }}_{s}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {i{\widetilde{c}}^{\prime }\left( s\right) , i{\gamma }_{s}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right\rangle
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {{\overrightarrow{c}}^{\prime }\left( s\right) ,{\gamma }_{s}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {{J}_{s}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,{\gamma }_{s}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right\rangle  .
\]

We can, therefore, apply Rauch's Theorem and conclude that

\[
\left| {{\widetilde{c}}^{\prime }\left( s\right) }\right|  = \left| {{\widetilde{J}}_{s}\left( 1\right) }\right|  \leq  \left| {{J}_{s}\left( 1\right) }\right|  = \left| {{c}^{\prime }\left( s\right) }\right| ,
\]

hence, by integration, \( \ell \left( c\right)  \geq  \ell \left( \widetilde{c}\right) \) .

2.6 REMARK. The methods used in Rauch's Theorem can be employed to obtain an upper bound for the volume of a normal ball in a Riemannian manifold whose Ricci curvature is bounded below. More precisely, let \( M \) be a complete Riemannian manifold such that \( {\operatorname{Ric}}_{M} \geq  H \) , and let \( {B}_{r}\left( p\right)  \subset  M,{B}_{r}\left( \widetilde{p}\right)  \subset  \widetilde{M}\left( H\right) \) be normal balls of radius \( r \) , where \( \widetilde{M}\left( H\right) \) is the complete, simply connected manifold, of constant sectional curvature \( H \) . Then

\[
\operatorname{vol}\left( {{B}_{r}\left( p\right) }\right)  \leq  \operatorname{vol}{B}_{r}\left( \widetilde{p}\right)
\]

and, if the equality is satisfied, \( {\operatorname{Ric}}_{M}\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right)  \equiv  H \) , for all \( t < r \) and all normalized radial geodesics \( \gamma \left( t\right) \) in \( {B}_{r}\left( p\right) \) (see Bishop and Crittenden, Geometry of Manifolds, Academic Press, 1964, p. 256 and K. Tenenblat, On the Rauch comparison theorem for volumes, Bol. Soc. Bras. Mat. 4 (1973), 31-39).

It is curious to observe that, in contrast to Rauch's Theorem, the theorem above does not extend to the case \( {\operatorname{Ric}}_{M} \leq  L \) ; a counterexample is described in the article cited above, by K. Tenenblat.

2.7 REMARK. The relation between the Ricci curvature and the volume can be extended to the following global theorem: With the same notation as in Remark 2.6, suppose that \( {\operatorname{Ric}}_{M} \geq  H \) and denote the corresponding volumes by \( {V}_{r} = \operatorname{vol}{B}_{r}\left( p\right) \) and \( {\widetilde{V}}_{r} = \operatorname{vol}{B}_{r}\left( \widetilde{p}\right) \) , where \( r \) is now an arbitrary positive real number. Then for all \( R \geq  r > 0 \) , we have

\[
{V}_{r}/{\widetilde{V}}_{r} \geq  {V}_{R}/{\widetilde{V}}_{R}.
\]

In addition, the equality occurs for \( R \leq  \operatorname{diam}\left( M\right) \) if and only if \( {B}_{R}\left( p\right)  \subset  M \) is isometric to the ball \( {B}_{R}\left( \widetilde{p}\right)  \subset  \widetilde{M}\left( H\right) \) . For a proof, see J. Eschenburg "Comparison theorems and hypersurfaces", Manuscripta Math. 59 (1987), 295-323. This reference contains an exposition of comparison theorems from a point of view different than that presented here; in particular, the theorem above is used to establish the uniqueness theorem mentioned in Remark 3.6 of Chapter 9.

3.1 THEOREM. (J.D. Moore,[Mo]). Let \( \bar{M} \) be a complete simply connected, Riemannian manifold, whose sectional curvature satisfies

\[
\bar{K} \leq  b \leq  0.
\]

Let \( M \) be a compact Riemannian manifold whose sectional curvature satisfies \( K - \bar{K} \leq   - b \) . If \( \dim \bar{M} < 2\dim M \) , there does not exist an isometric immersion \( f : M \rightarrow  \bar{M} \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.1 THEOREM. (J.D. Moore,[Mo]). Let \( \bar{M} \) be a complete simply connected, Riemannian manifold, whose sectional curvature satisfies \[ \bar{K} \leq b \leq 0. \] Let \( M \) be a compact Riemannian manifold whose sectional curvature satisfies \( K - \bar{K} \leq - b \) . If \( \dim \bar{M} < 2\dim M \) , there does not exist an isometric immersion \( f : M \rightarrow \bar{M} \) .

nodes.proof:
We suppose that such an immersion exists, and obtain a contradiction. Choose a point \( \bar{p} \in  \bar{M},\bar{p} \notin  f\left( M\right) \) , and let \( q \in  M \) be such that

\[
d\left( {f\left( q\right) ,\bar{p}}\right)  \geq  d\left( {f\left( p\right) ,\bar{p}}\right) ,\;\text{ for all }\;p \in  M.
\]

Let \( U \subset  M \) be a neighborhood of \( q \) in which \( f \) is an embedding, and identify \( U \) with \( f\left( U\right) \) . Let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \bar{M} \) be the normalized minimizing geodesic in \( \bar{M} \) , with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = \bar{p},\gamma \left( \ell \right)  = q \) . Using the formula for the first variation, we see that \( \gamma \) is perpendicular to \( U \) at \( q \) .

For all \( v \in  {T}_{q}M,\left| v\right|  = 1 \) , consider a curve \( c\left( s\right) \) in \( U \) with \( c\left( 0\right)  = q,{c}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = v, s \in  \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right) \) . Let \( \widetilde{c}\left( s\right)  = {\exp }_{\bar{p}}^{-1}\left( {c\left( s\right) }\right) \) . Then, the parametrized surface

\[
f\left( {t, s}\right)  = {\exp }_{\bar{p}}\frac{t}{\ell }\widetilde{c}\left( s\right) ,\;t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack  , s \in  \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)
\]

generates a Jacobi field \( V\left( t\right)  = \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {t,0}\right) \) with \( V\left( 0\right)  = 0, V\left( \ell \right)  = v \) (Fig. 3). Observe that the radial geodesics \( {\gamma }_{s} : t \rightarrow  f\left( {t, s}\right) \) in this variation are shorter than \( \gamma \) .

3.3 LEMMA. (Otsuki). Let \( B : {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \times  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {R}^{k} \) be a symmetric bilinear form such that, for some \( b \leq  0 \) ,

\[
\langle B\left( {v, v}\right) , B\left( {w, w}\right) \rangle  - \parallel B\left( {v, w}\right) {\parallel }^{2} \leq   - b,
\]

\[
\parallel B\left( {v, v}\right) \parallel  > \sqrt{-b}
\]

for all orthonormal pairs \( v, w \in  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) . Then \( k \geq  n \) .

nodes.proof:
We suppose that \( k < n \) and obtain a contradiction. Let \( S \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) be the unit sphere and consider the map \( f : S \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) , given by

\[
f\left( v\right)  = \langle B\left( {v, v}\right) , B\left( {v, v}\right) \rangle .
\]

Let \( v \in  S \) be a point where \( f \) assumes a minimum. Then taking the curve \( v\left( t\right)  = v\cos t + w\sin t \) in \( S, t \in  \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right) \) , we have

(8)

\[
0 = d{f}_{v}\left( w\right)  = {\left. 2\left\langle  \frac{d}{dt}B\left( v\left( t\right) , v\left( t\right) \right) \right\rangle  \right| }_{t = 0}, B\left( {v, v}\right) \rangle
\]

\[
= 2\left\langle  {{2B}\left( {{v}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) , v}\right) , B\left( {v, v}\right) }\right\rangle   = 4\langle B\left( {w, v}\right) , B\left( {v, v}\right) \rangle ,
\]

and, since \( {v}^{\prime \prime }\left( 0\right)  =  - v \) ,

\[
0 \leq  {d}^{2}{f}_{v}\left( {w, w}\right)  = 4\left\langle  {B\left( {{v}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) , v}\right) ,{2B}\left( {{v}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) , v}\right) }\right\rangle
\]

\[
+ 4\left\langle  {B\left( {{v}^{\prime \prime }\left( 0\right) , v}\right) , B\left( {v, v}\right) }\right\rangle   + 4\left\langle  {B\left( {w,{v}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) , B\left( {v, v}\right) }\right\rangle
\]

\[
= 8\parallel B\left( {w, v}\right) {\parallel }^{2} - 4\langle B\left( {v, v}\right) , B\left( {v, v}\right) \rangle
\]

\[
+ 4\langle B\left( {w, w}\right) , B\left( {v, v}\right) \rangle
\]

Consider now the map \( L : {T}_{v}S \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{k} \) , given by

\[
L\left( w\right)  = B\left( {v, w}\right) .
\]

The equation (8) above yields that \( \langle L\left( w\right) , B\left( {v, v}\right) \rangle  = 0 \) , hence \( \dim L\left( {{T}_{v}S}\right)  \leq  k - 1 \) . Because \( k < n \) , the kernel of \( L \) has dimension at least 1, hence there exists \( {w}_{o} \neq  0,{w}_{o} \bot  v \) , with \( L\left( {w}_{o}\right)  = 0 = B\left( {v,{w}_{o}}\right) . \)

Introducing \( {w}_{o} \) in equation (9), we obtain

\[
0 \leq  \langle B\left( {{w}_{o},{w}_{o}}\right) , B\left( {v, v}\right) \rangle  - \langle B\left( {v, v}\right) , B\left( {v, v}\right) \rangle .
\]

By the hypothesis of the Lemma, we conclude that

\[
0 \leq  \left\langle  {B\left( {{w}_{o},{w}_{o}}\right) , B\left( {v, v}\right) }\right\rangle   - \parallel B\left( {v, v}\right) {\parallel }^{2}
\]

\[
< \langle B\left( {{w}_{o},{w}_{o}}\right) , B\left( {v, v}\right) \rangle  - {\left( \sqrt{-b}\right) }^{2} \leq   - b - {\left( \sqrt{-b}\right) }^{2} = 0,
\]

which produces the contradiction.

nodes.content: 3.7 REMARK. Essentially the same proof that we used in Theorem 3.1 can serve as a proof of the following theorem of S.S. Chern and N. Kuiper, "Some theorems on the isometric embedding of compact Riemannian manifolds in euclidean spaces", Ann. of Math. 56 (1952),422-430: Suppose that \( {M}^{n} \) is compact and that, for each point \( p \in  M \) there exists a subspace of dimension \( m,{V}^{m} \subset  {T}_{p}M \) , such that the sectional curvature with respect to the planes contained in \( V \) are non-positive. If \( k < m \) , there does not exist an isometric immersion \( f : {M}^{n} \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{n + k} \) . The historical importance of the article of Chern-Kuiper is that they stressed the fundamental fact that the existence of an isometric immersion \( f : {M}^{n} \rightarrow  {\bar{M}}^{n + k} \) implies a relation between the nullity of the second fundamental form of \( f \) and the nullity of an intrinsic operator on \( M \) defined from the curvature of \( M \) . For more details see M. Dajczer,[Da].

ii) \( {J}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  + {\dot{S}}_{{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\left( {J\left( 0\right) }\right)  \in  {\left( {T}_{p}N\right) }^{ \bot  } \) , where \( {S}_{{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) } \) is the linear operator on \( {T}_{p}N \) given by the second fundamental form of \( N \subset  M \) .

Conversely, if \( J \) is a Jacobi field along the geodesic \( \gamma \) with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p \in  N,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  \in  {\left( {T}_{p}N\right) }^{ \bot  } \) , satisfying (i) and (ii), then there exists a variation \( f \) of \( \gamma \) satisfying (1) and (2), whose variational field is \( J \) .

\[
J\left( 0\right)  = {\left. \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( 0,0\right)  = \frac{d}{ds}\left( \alpha \left( s\right) \right) \right| }_{s = 0} \in  {T}_{p}N,
\]

which verifies (i). To prove (ii), let \( v \in  {T}_{p}N \) be an arbitrary vector. We shall show that

(10)

\[
\left\langle  {{J}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  + {S}_{{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\left( {J\left( 0\right) }\right) , v}\right\rangle   = 0.
\]

Indeed,

\[
\left\langle  {\frac{DJ}{dt}\left( 0\right) , v}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {\frac{D}{dt}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {0,0}\right) , v}\right\rangle
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {\frac{D}{ds}\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\left( {0,0}\right) , v}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {\frac{DA}{ds}\left( 0\right) , v}\right\rangle  .
\]

Since \( A\left( s\right) \) is a vector field along \( \alpha \left( s\right) \) with \( {\alpha }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = J\left( 0\right) \) , we have

\[
\frac{DA}{ds}\left( 0\right)  = {\left. {\bar{\nabla }}_{J\left( 0\right) }A\left( s\right) \right| }_{s = 0}
\]

where \( \bar{\nabla } \) is the covariant derivative of \( M \) . Therefore,

\[
\left\langle  {\frac{DA}{ds}\left( 0\right) , v}\right\rangle   = {\left. \left\langle  {\left( {\bar{\nabla }}_{J\left( 0\right) }A\left( s\right) \right) }^{T}, v\right\rangle  \right| }_{s = 0}
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {-{S}_{A\left( 0\right) }\left( {J\left( 0\right) }\right) , v}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {-{S}_{{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\left( {J\left( 0\right) }\right) , v}\right\rangle  ,
\]

which implies (10) and verifies (ii).

To prove the converse, let \( s \rightarrow  \alpha \left( s\right) \) be a curve in \( N \) with \( \alpha \left( 0\right)  = p,{\alpha }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = J\left( 0\right) \) . We can choose a vector field \( W \) along \( \alpha \) such that \( W\left( 0\right)  = {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) and \( \frac{DW}{ds}\left( 0\right)  = \frac{DJ}{dt}\left( 0\right) \) . Write \( W\left( s\right)  = V\left( s\right)  + U\left( s\right) \) , where

\[
V\left( s\right)  \in  {\left( {T}_{\alpha \left( s\right) }\left( N\right) \right) }^{ \bot  },\;U\left( s\right)  \in  {T}_{\alpha \left( s\right) }\left( N\right) ,
\]

and define \( f\left( {s, t}\right)  = {\exp }_{\alpha \left( s\right) }\left( {{tV}\left( s\right) }\right) \) . We show that \( f \) is the variation of \( \gamma \) which satisfies (1) and (2) and whose variational field is \( J \) .

In fact, for all \( s \) , the curve

\[
t \mapsto  {f}_{s}\left( t\right)  = {\exp }_{\alpha \left( s\right) }{tV}\left( s\right)
\]

is a geodesic. In addition,

\[
{f}_{s}\left( 0\right)  = \alpha \left( s\right)  \in  N
\]

and

\[
A\left( s\right)  = \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\left( {s,0}\right)  = {\left( d{\exp }_{\alpha \left( s\right) }\right) }_{o}\left( {V\left( s\right) }\right)  = V\left( s\right)  \in  {\left( {T}_{\alpha \left( s\right) }\left( N\right) \right) }^{ \bot  }.
\]

It remains to show that \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {0, t}\right)  = J\left( t\right) \) . It is enough to verify that \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {0,0}\right)  = J\left( 0\right) \) and \( \frac{D}{dt}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {0,0}\right)  = \frac{DJ}{dt}\left( 0\right) \) . Because

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {0,0}\right)  = {\alpha }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = J\left( 0\right)
\]

and

\[
\frac{D}{dt}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {0,0}\right)  = \frac{D}{ds}\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\left( {0,0}\right)  = \frac{DV}{ds}\left( 0\right)  = \frac{DW}{ds}\left( 0\right)  - \frac{DU}{ds}\left( 0\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{DJ}{dt}\left( 0\right)  - \frac{DU}{ds}\left( 0\right) ,
\]

it suffices to show that \( \frac{DU}{ds}\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) . But \( J\left( t\right) \) and \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {0, t}\right) \) satisfy:

\[
\frac{DJ}{dt}\left( 0\right)  + {S}_{{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\left( {J\left( 0\right) }\right)  \in  {\left( {T}_{p}N\right) }^{ \bot  }
\]

\[
\frac{D}{dt}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {0,0}\right)  + {S}_{{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\left( {\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {0,0}\right) }\right)  \in  {\left( {T}_{p}N\right) }^{ \bot  },
\]

where the second assertion comes from the first part of the Lemma. Since \( J\left( 0\right)  = \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {0,0}\right) \) , we can conclude that

\[
\frac{DU}{ds}\left( 0\right)  = \frac{DJ}{dt}\left( 0\right)  - \frac{D}{dt}\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {0,0}\right)  \in  {\left( {T}_{p}N\right) }^{ \bot  }.
\]

On the other hand, \( U\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) and \( U\left( s\right)  \in  {T}_{\alpha \left( s\right) }\left( N\right) \) . Therefore, given \( v \in  {\left( {T}_{p}N\right) }^{ \bot  } \) and a vector field \( v\left( s\right) \) along \( \alpha \left( s\right) \) with \( v\left( 0\right)  = v \) and \( v\left( s\right)  \in  {\left( {T}_{\alpha \left( s\right) }\left( N\right) \right) }^{ \bot  } \) , we have

\[
0 = {\left. \frac{d}{ds}\langle U\left( s\right) , v\left( s\right) \rangle \right| }_{s = 0} = \left\langle  {\frac{DU}{ds}\left( 0\right) , v}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {U\left( 0\right) ,\frac{Dv}{ds}\left( 0\right) }\right\rangle
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {\frac{DU}{ds}\left( 0\right) , v}\right\rangle  \text{ . }
\]

From the arbitrariness of \( v \) , this implies that \( \frac{DU}{ds}\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) , which proves the assertion, and concludes the proof.

nodes.content: 4.2 Definition. Let \( N \subset  M \) be a submanifold of a Riemannian manifold \( M \) . The point \( q \in  M \) is called a focal point of \( N \) if there exists a geodesic \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) , with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p \in  N,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  \in  {\left( {T}_{p}N\right) }^{ \bot  } \) , \( \gamma \left( \ell \right)  = q \) , and a non-zero Jacobi field \( J \) along \( \gamma \) , satisfying (i),(ii) and with \( J\left( \ell \right)  = 0 \) .

To obtain a characterization of the focal points in terms of the exponential map, we introduce the following notation. Let \( T\left( M\right) \) be the tangent bundle of \( M,\pi  : T\left( M\right)  \rightarrow  M \) its projection onto \( M \) . Denote this statement by \( T\left( M\right)  \rightarrow  M \) . Similarly, \( T\left( N\right)  \rightarrow  N \) denotes the tangent bundle \( T\left( N\right) \) and its projection onto \( N, T{\left( N\right) }^{ \bot  } \rightarrow  N \) denotes the normal bundle of the immersion \( N \subset  M \) and its projection onto \( N \) (a point of \( T{\left( N\right) }^{ \bot  } \) is a pair \( \left( {p, n}\right) \) , where \( p \in  N \) , \( n \in  {\left( {T}_{p}N\right) }^{ \bot  } \) ). Remember that the exponential mapping can be thought of as a map \( \exp  : T\left( M\right)  \rightarrow  M \) , defined by

\[
\exp \left( {p, v}\right)  = {\exp }_{p}\left( v\right) .
\]

Since \( T{\left( N\right) }^{ \bot  } \rightarrow  N \) is contained in the restriction of \( T\left( M\right)  \rightarrow \; M \) to \( N \subset  M \) , the exponential map can be restricted to \( T{\left( N\right) }^{ \bot  } \) ; this restriction will be denoted by

\[
{\exp }^{ \bot  } : T{\left( N\right) }^{ \bot  } \rightarrow  M.
\]

Observe that \( \dim T{\left( N\right) }^{ \bot  } = \dim M \) .

nodes.content: 4.4 Proposition. The point \( q \in  M \) is a focal point of \( N \subset  M \) if and only if it is a critical value of \( {\exp }^{ \bot  } \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 4.4 Proposition. The point \( q \in M \) is a focal point of \( N \subset M \) if and only if it is a critical value of \( {\exp }^{ \bot } \) .

nodes.proof:
From Lemma 4.1, there exists a geodesic \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) , with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p \in  N,\gamma \left( \ell \right)  = q \) , \( {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  \in  {\left( {T}_{p}N\right) }^{ \bot  } \) and a variation \( f : \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) of \( \gamma \) satisfying (1) and (2) and with \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {0,\ell }\right)  = 0 \) . It follows that

\[
w\left( s\right)  = \left( {\alpha \left( s\right) ,\ell A\left( s\right) }\right) ,\;A\left( s\right)  = \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\left( {s,0}\right) ,\;\alpha \left( s\right)  = {f}_{s}\left( 0\right) ,
\]

is a curve in \( T{\left( N\right) }^{ \bot  } \) such that:

\[
{\exp }^{ \bot  }\left( {w\left( s\right) }\right)  = {\exp }_{\alpha \left( s\right) }\ell A\left( s\right)  = f\left( {s,\ell }\right) ,
\]

\[
{\exp }^{ \bot  }\left( {w\left( 0\right) }\right)  = q
\]

and

\[
{\left( d{\exp }^{ \bot  }\right) }_{w\left( 0\right) }\left( {{w}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right)  = \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {0,\ell }\right)  = 0.
\]

Then \( w\left( 0\right) \) is a critical point of \( {\exp }^{ \bot  } \) , with \( {\exp }^{ \bot  }\left( {w\left( 0\right) }\right)  = q \) .

Conversely, suppose that \( q \) is a critical value of \( {\exp }^{ \bot  } \) . Then there exist \( {w}_{o},{w}_{o}^{\prime } \) such that \( {\exp }^{ \bot  }\left( {w}_{o}\right)  = q \) and \( {\left( d{\exp }^{ \bot  }\right) }_{{w}_{o}}\left( {w}_{o}^{\prime }\right)  = 0 \) . Let \( w\left( s\right)  = \left( {\sigma \left( s\right) ,\ell V\left( s\right) }\right) \) be a curve in \( T{\left( N\right) }^{ \bot  } \) , with \( w\left( 0\right)  = {w}_{o} \) and \( {w}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = {w}_{o}^{\prime } \) . Since \( q = {\exp }_{\sigma \left( 0\right) }\left( {\ell V\left( 0\right) }\right) \) , there exists a geodesic \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) such that \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = \sigma \left( 0\right) ,\gamma \left( \ell \right)  = q,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = V\left( 0\right) \) . Consider the variation of \( \gamma \) given by

\[
f\left( {s, t}\right)  = {\exp }_{\sigma \left( s\right) }{tV}\left( s\right) .
\]

\( f \) satisfies the conditions (1) and (2). In fact,

\[
f\left( {s,0}\right)  = {\exp }_{\sigma \left( s\right) }\left( 0\right)  = \sigma \left( s\right)  \in  N,
\]

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\left( {s,0}\right)  = {\left( d{\exp }_{\sigma \left( s\right) }\right) }_{o}\left( {V\left( s\right) }\right)  = V\left( s\right)  \in  {\left( {T}_{\sigma \left( s\right) }\left( N\right) \right) }^{ \bot  }.
\]

From the lemma, \( J\left( t\right)  = \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( {0, t}\right) \) is a Jacobi field satisfying (i) and (ii), with

\[
J\left( \ell \right)  = {\left. \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\left( 0,\ell \right)  = \frac{\partial }{\partial s}{\exp }_{\sigma \left( s\right) }\ell V\left( s\right) \right| }_{s = 0}
\]

\[
= {\left. \frac{d}{ds}{\exp }^{ \bot  }w\left( s\right) \right| }_{s = 0} = {\left( d{\exp }^{ \bot  }\right) }_{{w}_{o}}\left( {w}_{o}^{\prime }\right)  = 0,
\]

and therefore, \( q \) is a focal point of \( N \) .

4.6 EXAMPLE. Let \( {N}^{2} \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) be a regular surface in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) . The connected components of the focal set \( F\left( N\right)  \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) are called the "focal surfaces" (or surfaces of centers) in classical differential geometry. In general such subsets are not regular surfaces and can degenerate to points or curves. For example, if \( {N}^{2} \) is a sphere \( {S}^{2} \) , then \( F\left( {S}^{2}\right) \) is the center of \( {S}^{2} \) ; if \( {N}^{2} \) is the right circular cylinder \( C, F\left( C\right) \) is the axis of \( C \) . A way of constructing, geometrically, the focal points of \( {N}^{2} \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) is the following.

Let \( \mathbf{x} : U \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{2} \rightarrow  N \subset  {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) be a parametrization of \( N \) at \( p \in  N \) . If we denote by \( \left( {{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}\right) \) the coordinates of \( U \) and by \( n = \; n\left( {{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}\right) \) a unit normal field on \( \mathbf{x}\left( U\right)  \subset  N \) , we can write the map \( {\exp }^{ \bot  } : T{\left( U\right) }^{ \bot  } \rightarrow  {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) as

\[
{\exp }^{ \bot  }\left( {\left( {{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}\right) , t}\right)  = \mathbf{x}\left( {{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}\right)  + {tn},\;t \in  \mathbf{R}.
\]

The basis of the tangent space \( {T}_{\left( p, tn\right) }\left( {T{\left( N\right) }^{ \bot  }}\right)  \approx  {\mathbf{R}}^{3} \) associated to this parametrization is

\[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{x}}{\partial {u}_{1}},\frac{\partial \mathbf{x}}{\partial {u}_{2}}, n
\]

In this basis, the linear map \( d{\exp }^{ \bot  } \) is given by the matrix

\[
d{\exp }^{ \bot  } = \left( \begin{matrix} \left\langle  {\frac{\partial x}{\partial {u}_{1}} + t\frac{\partial n}{\partial {u}_{1}},\frac{\partial x}{\partial {u}_{1}}}\right\rangle  & \left\langle  {\frac{\partial x}{\partial {u}_{2}} + t\frac{\partial n}{\partial {u}_{2}},\frac{\partial x}{\partial {u}_{1}}}\right\rangle  & \left\langle  {n,\frac{\partial x}{\partial {u}_{1}}}\right\rangle  \\  \left\langle  {\frac{\partial x}{\partial {u}_{1}} + t\frac{\partial n}{\partial {u}_{1}},\frac{\partial x}{\partial {u}_{2}}}\right\rangle  & \left\langle  {\frac{\partial x}{\partial {u}_{2}} + t\frac{\partial n}{\partial {u}_{2}},\frac{\partial x}{\partial {u}_{2}}}\right\rangle  & \left\langle  {n,\frac{\partial x}{\partial {u}_{2}}}\right\rangle  \\  \left\langle  {\frac{\partial x}{\partial {u}_{1}} + t\frac{\partial n}{\partial {u}_{1}}, n}\right\rangle  & \left\langle  {\frac{\partial x}{\partial {u}_{2}} + t\frac{\partial n}{\partial {u}_{2}}, n}\right\rangle  & \left\langle  {n, n}\right\rangle   \end{matrix}\right)
\]

\[
= \left( \begin{matrix} \frac{{g}_{ij} - t\left\langle  {\frac{{\partial }^{2}\mathbf{x}}{\partial {u}_{i}\partial {u}_{j}}, n}\right\rangle  }{\mathbf{B}} & 0 \\  \mathbf{B} & 1 \end{matrix}\right)
\]

where the matrix \( B \) is not important in what follows. By Proposition 4.4, \( x + {tn} \) is a focal point of \( N \) if and only if the matrix above is singular. Because the coefficients of the second fundamental form \( {H}_{n} \) in the basis \( \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}}{\partial {u}_{1}},\frac{\partial \mathbf{x}}{\partial {u}_{2}} \) are given by

\[
{h}_{ij} = {H}_{n}\left( {\frac{\partial \mathbf{x}}{\partial {u}_{i}},\frac{\partial \mathbf{x}}{\partial {u}_{j}}}\right)  = \left\langle  {B\left( {\frac{\partial \mathbf{x}}{\partial {u}_{i}},\frac{\partial \mathbf{x}}{\partial {u}_{j}}}\right) , n}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {\frac{{\partial }^{2}\mathbf{x}}{\partial {u}_{i}\partial {u}_{j}}, n}\right\rangle  ,
\]

we conclude that the matrix above is singular if and only if the matrix

\[
\left( {{g}_{ij} - t{h}_{ij}}\right)
\]

is singular. It is possible to choose the parametrization \( x \) in such a way that at \( p,\left( {g}_{ij}\right) \) is the identity matrix. Therefore, \( x + {tn} \) is a focal point if and only if \( \frac{1}{t} \) is an eigenvalue of \( \left( {h}_{ij}\right) \) , that is, \( \frac{1}{t} \) is one of the principal curvatures of \( {N}^{2} \) at \( p \) .

In summary, to construct a connected component of \( F\left( N\right) \) , fix a principal curvature \( {k}_{i} \) and mark on the normal at each \( p \in  N \) , in the direction given by \( n\left( p\right) \) , a length equal to \( 1/{k}_{i}\left( p\right) \) (this point is the center of the osculating circle in the normal section of \( N \) in the principal direction \( {e}_{i} \) , which justifies the name "surface of centers").

nodes.label: Exercise 1

nodes.content:
1. (Klingenberg’s Lemma). Let \( M \) be a complete Riemannian manifold with sectional curvature \( K \leq  {K}_{o} \) , where \( {K}_{o} \) is a positive constant. Let \( p, q \in  M \) and let \( {\gamma }_{o} \) and \( {\gamma }_{1} \) be two distinct geodesics joining \( p \) to \( q \) with \( \ell \left( {\gamma }_{o}\right)  \leq  \ell \left( {\gamma }_{1}\right) \) . Assume that \( {\gamma }_{o} \) is homotopic to \( {\gamma }_{1} \) , that is, there exists a continuous family of curves \( {\alpha }_{t}, t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) such that \( {\alpha }_{o} = {\gamma }_{o} \) and \( {\alpha }_{1} = {\gamma }_{1} \) . Prove that there exists \( {t}_{o} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) such that

\[
\ell \left( {\gamma }_{o}\right)  + \ell \left( {\alpha }_{{t}_{o}}\right)  \geq  \frac{2\pi }{\sqrt{{K}_{o}}}
\]

(Thus, the given homotopy has to pass through a "long" curve. Fig. 6).

![019eafb3-a904-7162-90c5-5ccd2f5d76bf_50_556_847_680_855_0.jpg](images/019eafb3-a904-7162-90c5-5ccd2f5d76bf_50_556_847_680_855_0.jpg)

Figure 6

Hint: Assume \( \ell \left( {\gamma }_{o}\right)  < \frac{\pi }{\sqrt{{K}_{o}}} \) (otherwise, we have nothing to prove). From Rauch’s Theorem, \( {\exp }_{p} : {T}_{p}M \rightarrow  M \) has no critical point in the open ball \( B \) of radius \( \pi /\sqrt{{K}_{o}} \) centered at \( p \) . For \( t \) small, it is possible to lift the curve \( {\alpha }_{t} \) to the tangent space \( {T}_{p}M \) , i.e., there exists a curve \( {\widetilde{\alpha }}_{t} \) in \( {T}_{p}M \) , joining \( {\exp }_{p}^{-1}\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) to \( {\exp }_{p}^{-1}\left( q\right)  = \widetilde{q} \) , such that \( {\exp }_{p} \circ  {\widetilde{\alpha }}_{t} = {\alpha }_{t} \) . It is clear that it is not possible to do the same for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) , since \( {\alpha }_{1} \) cannot be lifted keeping the endpoints fixed.

We conclude that for all \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) there exists a \( t\left( \varepsilon \right) \) such that \( {\alpha }_{t\left( \varepsilon \right) } \) can be lifted to \( {\widetilde{\alpha }}_{t\left( \varepsilon \right) } \) and \( {\widetilde{\alpha }}_{t\left( \varepsilon \right) } \) contains points with distance \( < \varepsilon \) from the boundary \( \partial B \) of \( B \) . In the contrary case, for some \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , all lifts \( {\widetilde{\alpha }}_{t} \) are at the distance \( \geq  \varepsilon \) from \( \partial B \) ; the set of \( t \) ’s for which it is possible to lift \( {\alpha }_{t} \) will then be open and closed and \( {\alpha }_{1} \) could be lifted, which is a contradiction. Therefore, for all \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , we have

\[
\ell \left( {\gamma }_{o}\right)  + \ell \left( {\alpha }_{t\left( \varepsilon \right) }\right)  \geq  \frac{2\pi }{\sqrt{{K}_{o}}} - {2\varepsilon }.
\]

Now choose a sequence \( \left\{  {\varepsilon }_{n}\right\}   \rightarrow  0 \) , and consider a convergent subsequence of \( \left\{  {t\left( {\varepsilon }_{n}\right) }\right\}   \rightarrow  {t}_{o} \) . Then there exists a curve \( {\alpha }_{{t}_{o}} \) with

\[
\ell \left( {\gamma }_{o}\right)  + \ell \left( {\alpha }_{{t}_{o}}\right)  \geq  \frac{2\pi }{\sqrt{{K}_{o}}}
\]

nodes.content:
5. (The Sturm Comparison Theorem). In this exercise we present a direct proof of Rauch's Theorem in dimension two, without using material from the present chapter. We will indicate a proof of the Theorem of Sturm mentioned in the Introduction to the chapter.

Let

\[
{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( t\right)  + K\left( t\right) f\left( t\right)  = 0,\;f\left( 0\right)  = 0,\;t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack  ,
\]

\[
{\widetilde{f}}^{\prime \prime }\left( t\right)  + \widetilde{K}\left( t\right) \bar{f}\left( t\right)  = 0,\;\widetilde{f}\left( 0\right)  = 0,\;t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack  ,
\]

be two ordinary differential equations. Suppose that \( \widetilde{K}\left( t\right)  \geq \; K\left( t\right) \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack \) , and that \( {f}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = {\widetilde{f}}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = 1 \) .

![019eafb3-a904-7162-90c5-5ccd2f5d76bf_53_461_174_703_934_0.jpg](images/019eafb3-a904-7162-90c5-5ccd2f5d76bf_53_461_174_703_934_0.jpg)

Figure 8

a) Show that for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack \) ,

(1)

\[
0 = {\int }_{0}^{t}\left\{  {\widetilde{f}\left( {{f}^{\prime \prime } + {Kf}}\right)  - f\left( {{\widetilde{f}}^{\prime \prime } + \widetilde{K}\widetilde{f}}\right) }\right\}  {dt}
\]

\[
= {\left\lbrack  \widetilde{f}{f}^{\prime } - f{\widetilde{f}}^{\prime }\right\rbrack  }_{o}^{t} + {\int }_{0}^{t}\left( {K - \widetilde{K}}\right) f\widetilde{f}{dt}.
\]

Conclude from this that the first zero of \( f \) does not occur before the first zero of \( \widetilde{f} \) (that is, if \( \widetilde{f}\left( t\right)  > 0 \) on \( \left( {0,{t}_{o}}\right) \) and \( f\left( {t}_{o}\right)  = 0 \) , then \( f\left( t\right)  > 0 \) on \( \left. \left( {0,{t}_{o}}\right) \right) \) .

Hint: From the initial condition, \( f\left( t\right) \) is positive in a neighborhood of zero. Assume that \( f\left( {t}_{1}\right)  = 0,{t}_{1} < {t}_{o} \) . Then \( {f}^{\prime }\left( {t}_{1}\right)  < 0 \) , \( f\left( {t}_{1}\right)  > 0 \) , and this contradicts (1).

b) Suppose that \( \widetilde{f}\left( t\right)  > 0 \) on \( (0,\ell \rbrack \) . Use (1) and the fact that \( f\left( t\right)  > 0 \) on \( (0,\ell \rbrack \) to show that \( f\left( t\right)  \geq  \widetilde{f}\left( t\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack \) , and that the equality is verified for \( t = {t}_{1} \in  (0,\ell \rbrack \) if and only if \( K\left( t\right)  = \bar{K}\left( t\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack \) .

Verify that this is the Theorem of Rauch in dimension two.

Hint: From (1) conclude that \( {f}^{\prime }/f \geq  {\widetilde{f}}^{\prime }/\widetilde{f} \) , that is, \( {\left( \log f\right) }^{\prime } \geq \; {\left( \log \widetilde{f}\right) }^{\prime } \) . Let \( 0 < {t}_{o} \leq  t \leq  \ell \) . Integrating the last inequality from \( {t}_{o} \) to \( t \) , we obtain

\[
\log f\left( t\right)  - \log f\left( {t}_{o}\right)  \geq  \log \widetilde{f}\left( t\right)  - \log \widetilde{f}\left( {t}_{o}\right) ,
\]

that is,

\[
f\left( t\right) /\widetilde{f}\left( t\right)  \geq  f\left( {t}_{o}\right) /\widetilde{f}\left( {t}_{o}\right) ,\;\text{ for all }\;{t}_{o} \in  (0,\ell \rbrack .
\]

Now observe that

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{{t}_{o} \rightarrow  0}}\left( {f\left( {t}_{o}\right) /\widetilde{f}\left( {t}_{o}\right) }\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{{t}_{o} \rightarrow  0}}\left( {{f}^{\prime }\left( {t}_{o}\right) /{\widetilde{f}}^{\prime }\left( {t}_{o}\right) }\right)  = 1,
\]

hence the desired inequality. For equality, go back to (1).

nodes.content:
6. (The Oscillation Theorem of Sturm). What follows is a slight generalization of Sturm's Comparison Theorem. We present the theorem in geometric form.

Let \( {M}^{2} \) be a complete Riemannian manifold of dimension 2, and let \( \gamma  : \lbrack 0,\infty ) \rightarrow  {M}^{2} \) be a geodesic. Let \( J\left( t\right) \) be a Jacobi field along \( \gamma \) with \( J\left( 0\right)  = J\left( {t}_{o}\right)  = 0,{t}_{o} \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) , and \( J\left( t\right)  \neq  0 \) , \( t \in  \left( {0,{t}_{o}}\right) \) . Then \( J \) is a field normal to \( \gamma \) and can be written \( J\left( t\right)  = f\left( t\right) {e}_{2}\left( t\right) \) , where \( {e}_{2}\left( t\right) \) is the parallel transport of a unit vector \( {e}_{2} \in  {T}_{\gamma \left( 0\right) }\left( M\right) \) with \( {e}_{2} \bot  {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) . Because \( J \) is a Jacobi field,

\[
{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( t\right)  + K\left( t\right) f\left( t\right)  = 0,
\]

where \( K \) is the Gaussian curvature of \( {M}^{2} \) . Assume that

\[
K\left( t\right)  \leq  L\left( t\right)
\]

where \( L \) is a differentiable function on \( \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) . Prove that any solution of the equation

\[
{\widetilde{f}}^{\prime \prime }\left( t\right)  + L\left( t\right) \widetilde{f}\left( t\right)  = 0
\]

has a zero on \( \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{o}}\right\rbrack \) , that is, there exists \( {t}_{1} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{o}}\right\rbrack \) with \( \widetilde{f}\left( {t}_{1}\right)  = \) 0.

Hint: Suppose that \( \widetilde{f}\left( t\right)  \neq  0 \) for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{o}}\right\rbrack \) . Using expression (1) of the last exercise, we obtain

(2)

\[
{\int }_{0}^{{t}_{o}}\left( {K - L}\right) f\widetilde{f}{dt} + \widetilde{f}\left( {t}_{o}\right) {f}^{\prime }\left( {t}_{o}\right)  - \widetilde{f}\left( 0\right) {f}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = 0.
\]

Suppose, for example, that \( \widetilde{f}\left( t\right)  > 0 \) and \( f\left( t\right)  < 0 \) in \( \left( {0,{t}_{o}}\right) \) . Then \( {f}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  < 0 \) and \( {f}^{\prime }\left( {t}_{o}\right)  > 0 \) . This contradicts (2). The other cases are treated in the same way.

7. (Kneser’s criterion for points conjugate in surfaces). Let \( {M}^{2} \) be a complete Riemannian manifold of dimension two and let \( \gamma  : \lbrack 0,\infty ) \rightarrow  {M}^{2} \) be a geodesic with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p \) . Let \( K\left( s\right) \) be the Gaussian curvature of \( {M}^{2} \) along \( \gamma \) . Assume that:

(3)

\[
{\int }_{t}^{\infty }K\left( s\right) {ds} \leq  \frac{1}{4\left( {t + 1}\right) },\;\text{ for all }\;t \geq  0,
\]

in the sense that the integral converges and has the bound indicated.

a) Define

\[
\omega \left( t\right)  = {\int }_{t}^{\infty }K\left( s\right) {ds} + \frac{1}{4\left( {t + 1}\right) },
\]

and show that \( {\omega }^{\prime }\left( t\right)  + {\left( \omega \left( t\right) \right) }^{2} \leq   - K\left( t\right) \) .

b) For \( t \geq  0 \) , put \( {\omega }^{\prime }\left( t\right)  + {\left( \omega \left( t\right) \right) }^{2} =  - L\left( t\right) \) (hence \( L\left( t\right)  \geq  K\left( t\right) \) ) and define

\[
\widetilde{f}\left( t\right)  = \exp \left( {{\int }_{0}^{t}\omega \left( s\right) {ds}}\right) ,\;t \geq  0.
\]

Show that

\[
{\widetilde{f}}^{\prime \prime }\left( t\right)  + L\left( t\right) \widetilde{f}\left( t\right)  = 0,\;\widetilde{f}\left( 0\right)  = 1.
\]

c) Observe that \( \widetilde{f}\left( t\right)  > 0 \) and use the oscillation theorem of Sturm (Exercise 6) to show that there does not exist a Jacobi field \( J\left( s\right) \) on \( \gamma \left( s\right) \) with \( J\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) and \( J\left( {s}_{o}\right)  = 0 \) , for some \( {s}_{o} \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) . Therefore the condition (3) implies that there do not exist conjugate points to \( p \) along \( \gamma \) .

nodes.content: In general, given a symmetric bilinear form \( B \) over a vector space \( \mathcal{V} \) , we define the index of \( B \) as the the maximal dimension of all subspaces of \( \mathcal{V} \) on which the quadratic form associated to \( B \) is negative definite. The nullity of \( B \) is defined to be the dimension of the subspace of \( \mathcal{V} \) formed by the elements \( V \in  \mathcal{V} \) such that \( B\left( {V, W}\right)  = 0 \) , for all \( W \in  \mathcal{V} \) ; such a subspace is called the null space of \( B \) . We say that \( B \) is degenerate if its nullity is strictly positive.

nodes.content: 2.2 Index Theorem. (Morse). The index of the form \( {I}_{a} \) is finite and equals the number of points \( \gamma \left( t\right) ,0 < t < a \) , conjugate to \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) , each counted with its multiplicity.
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.2 Index Theorem. (Morse). The index of the form \( {I}_{a} \) is finite and equals the number of points \( \gamma \left( t\right) ,0 < t < a \) , conjugate to \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) , each counted with its multiplicity.

nodes.proof:
It is convenient to introduce the following notation. If \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack \) , denote by \( {\gamma }_{t} \) the restriction of \( \gamma \) to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {0, t}\right\rbrack \) ; the corresponding index form will be denoted by \( {I}_{t} \) , and the index of \( {I}_{t} \) will be denoted by \( i\left( t\right) \) . In this manner, we define a function \( i : \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbf{N} \) , whose behavior we wish to study.

Recalling that the subdivision (which is supposed fixed) of \( \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack \) by the points \( {t}_{j}, j = 0,\ldots , k \) , was chosen in a way that \( \gamma  \mid  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{j - 1},{t}_{j}}\right\rbrack \) is a minimizing geodesic, we conclude that \( i\left( t\right) \) is zero in a neighborhood of 0 . In addition, \( i\left( t\right) \) is non-decreasing, that is, if \( \bar{t} > t \) , then \( i\left( \bar{t}\right)  \geq  i\left( t\right) \) . In fact, by the definition of \( i\left( t\right) \) , there exists a subspace \( \mathcal{U} \subset  \mathcal{V}\left( {0, t}\right) \) such that \( {I}_{t} \) is negative definite on \( \mathcal{U} \) and \( \dim \mathcal{U} = i\left( t\right) \) . Every element \( V \in  \mathcal{U} \) can be extended to an element \( \bar{V} \in  \mathcal{V}\left( {0,\bar{t}}\right) \) by defining \( \bar{V} = 0 \) on \( \left\lbrack  {t,\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . It is clear that \( {I}_{t}\left( {V, V}\right)  = {I}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{V},\bar{V}}\right) \) . From the definition of the index-, \( i\left( \bar{t}\right)  \geq  i\left( t\right) \) , as has been claimed.

To obtain other properties of \( i\left( t\right) \) we proceed in the following manner. First, observe that, from the definition, \( i\left( t\right) \) does not depend on the choice of normal subdivision of \( \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack \) ; we can, therefore, choose such subdivisions in a way that \( t \in  \left( {{t}_{j - 1},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . Next, we observe that the index of \( {I}_{t} \) is the index of the restriction of \( {I}_{t} \) to the subspace \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ - }\left( {0, t}\right) \) ; such a restriction will be again denoted by \( {I}_{t} \) . Then, as each element of \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ - }\left( {0, t}\right) \) is determined by its value at the points \( \gamma \left( {t}_{1}\right) ,\ldots ,\gamma \left( {t}_{j - 1}\right) \) , we have that \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ - }\left( {0, t}\right) \) is isomorphic to a direct sum

\[
{\mathcal{V}}^{ - }\left( {0, t}\right)  = {T}_{\gamma \left( {t}_{1}\right) }M \oplus  \cdots  \oplus  {T}_{\gamma \left( {t}_{j - 1}\right) }M = {S}_{j}.
\]

It follows, by letting \( t \) vary on \( \left( {{t}_{j - 1},{t}_{j}}\right) \) , that the spaces \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ - }\left( {0, t}\right) \) are isomorphic to each other and isomorphic to \( {S}_{j} \) . We can, therefore, consider the quadratic forms \( {I}_{t} \) as a family of quadratic forms on a fixed space \( {S}_{j} \) . In addition, since the elements of \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ - }\left( {0, t}\right) \) are "broken" Jacobi fields, it follows from (2) that \( {I}_{t} \) depends continuously on \( t \in  \left( {{t}_{j - 1},{t}_{j}}\right) \) .

We can now obtain more information about \( i\left( t\right) \) which will be gathered together in the lemmas below.

2.7 LEMMA. If \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) is sufficiently small, \( i\left( {t - \varepsilon }\right)  = i\left( t\right) \) .

Proof of Lemma 2.7. Since \( i\left( t\right) \) is non-decreasing, \( i\left( t\right)  \geq  i\left( {t - \varepsilon }\right) \) , for all \( \varepsilon \) . On the other hand, if \( {I}_{t} \) is negative definite on a subspace \( \bar{S} \subset \; {S}_{j} \) , with \( \dim \left( \widetilde{S}\right)  = i\left( t\right) \) , then, by continuity of \( {I}_{t} \) , there exists \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) such that \( {I}_{t - \varepsilon } \) is still negative definite on \( \bar{S} \) , hence \( i\left( {t - \varepsilon }\right)  \geq  i\left( t\right) \) . Therefore \( i\left( t\right)  = i\left( {t - \varepsilon }\right) \) .

Now let \( d \) be the nullity of \( {I}_{t} \) ; observe that \( d = 0 \) if \( \gamma \left( t\right) \) is not conjugate to \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) .

2.8 LEMMA. If \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) is sufficiently small, \( i\left( {t + \varepsilon }\right)  = i\left( t\right)  + d \) .

Proof of Lemma 2.8. We show first that \( i\left( {t + \varepsilon }\right)  \leq  i\left( t\right)  + d \) . Indeed, because \( \dim \left( {S}_{j}\right)  = n\left( {j - 1}\right) ,{I}_{t} \) is positive definite on a subspace of dimension \( n\left( {j - 1}\right)  - i\left( t\right)  - d \) . By continuity, \( {I}_{t + \varepsilon } \) is still positive definite on this subspace, for \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) sufficiently small. Therefore

\[
i\left( {t + \varepsilon }\right)  \leq  n\left( {j - 1}\right)  - \{ n\left( {j - 1}\right)  - i\left( t\right)  - d\}  = i\left( t\right)  + d.
\]

To prove the inequality in the other direction, it is necessary to use the Index Lemma (Lemma 2.2 of Chap. 10). Let \( V \in  {S}_{j} \) , with \( V\left( {{t}_{j - 1} \neq  0}\right. \) , and denote by \( {V}_{{t}_{o}} \) the "broken" Jacobi field which coincides with \( V\left( {t}_{i}\right) \) at \( {t}_{i}, i = 1,\ldots , j - 1 \) , and which vanishes at the point \( {t}_{o} \in  \left( {{t}_{j - 1},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . We claim that

\[
{I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {{V}_{{t}_{o}},{V}_{{t}_{o}}}\right)  > {I}_{{t}_{o} + \varepsilon }\left( {{V}_{{t}_{o} + \varepsilon },{V}_{{t}_{o} + \varepsilon }}\right)
\]

In fact, if we denote by \( {W}_{{t}_{o}} \) (see Fig. 1) the vector field defined along \( \gamma \left( \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{o} + \varepsilon }\right\rbrack  \right) \) by:

\[
{W}_{{t}_{o}}\left( t\right)  = {V}_{{t}_{o}}\left( t\right) ,\;t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{o}}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
{W}_{{t}_{o}}\left( t\right)  = 0,\;t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{o},{t}_{o} + \varepsilon }\right\rbrack  ,
\]

we have, from the Index Lemma,

\[
{I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {{V}_{{t}_{o}},{V}_{{t}_{o}}}\right)  = {I}_{{t}_{o} + \varepsilon }\left( {{W}_{{t}_{o}},{W}_{{t}_{o}}}\right)  > {I}_{{t}_{o} + \varepsilon }\left( {{V}_{{t}_{o} + \varepsilon },{V}_{{t}_{o} + \varepsilon }}\right) ,
\]

where the last inequality is strict, since \( {W}_{{t}_{o}} \) is not a Jacobi field. This proves the assertion made.

![019eafb3-a904-7162-90c5-5ccd2f5d76bf_61_260_1477_1326_667_0.jpg](images/019eafb3-a904-7162-90c5-5ccd2f5d76bf_61_260_1477_1326_667_0.jpg)

Therefore, if \( V \in  {S}_{j} \) and \( {I}_{t}\left( {V, V}\right)  \leq  0 \) , then \( {I}_{t + \varepsilon }\left( {V, V}\right)  < 0 \) . Hence, if \( {I}_{t} \) is negative definite on a subspace \( \bar{S} \subset  {S}_{j},{I}_{t + \varepsilon } \) will still be negative definite on the direct sum of \( \bar{S} \) with the null space of \( {I}_{t} \) . Therefore

\[
i\left( {t + \varepsilon }\right)  \geq  i\left( t\right)  + d,
\]

which, together with the previous inequality implies that \( i\left( {t + \varepsilon }\right)  = \; i\left( t\right)  + d \) .

The information which we obtained about \( i\left( t\right) \) allows us to describe \( i\left( t\right) \) as a function which is zero in a neighborhood of the origin, is continuous on the left and has "step" type discontinuities at the conjugate points to \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) , the step being exactly equal to the multiplicity of the conjugate point (see Fig. 2). But this is precisely the statement of the Index Theorem.

nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 2.3 Proposition. An element \( V \in  \mathcal{V} \) belongs to the null space of \( {I}_{a} \) if and only if \( V \) is a Jacobi field along \( \gamma \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.3 Proposition. An element \( V \in \mathcal{V} \) belongs to the null space of \( {I}_{a} \) if and only if \( V \) is a Jacobi field along \( \gamma \) .

nodes.proof:
First observe that we have the following expression for \( {I}_{a} \) (Compare Rem. 2.10 of Chap. 9):

(2)

\[
{I}_{a}\left( {V, W}\right)  =  - {\int }_{0}^{a}\left\langle  {{V}^{\prime \prime } + R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }, V}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime }, W}\right\rangle  {dt}
\]

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{{k - 1}}\left\langle  {\frac{DV}{dt}\left( {t}_{j}^{ + }\right)  - \frac{DV}{dt}\left( {t}_{j}^{ - }\right) , W\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right\rangle  .
\]

If \( V \) is a Jacobi field, then by (2), \( V \) is in the null space of \( {I}_{a} \) .

Conversely, suppose that \( {I}_{a}\left( {V, W}\right)  = 0 \) for all \( W \in  \mathcal{V} \) . Let \( 0 = {t}_{o} < {t}_{1} < \cdots  < {t}_{k - 1} < {t}_{k} = a \) be a subdivision of \( \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack \) such that the restriction \( V \mid  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{j - 1},{t}_{j}}\right\rbrack \) is differentiable, \( j = 1,\ldots , k \) . Let \( f : \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) be a differentiable function with \( f\left( t\right)  > 0 \) , for \( t \neq  {t}_{j} \) and \( f\left( {t}_{j}\right)  = 0, j = 0,\ldots , k \) . Define \( W \) by

\[
W\left( t\right)  = f\left( t\right) \left( {{V}^{\prime \prime } + R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }, V}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime }}\right) .
\]

Then

\[
0 = {I}_{a}\left( {V, W}\right)  =  - {\int }_{0}^{a}f\left( t\right) {\begin{Vmatrix}{V}^{\prime \prime } + R\left( {\gamma }^{\prime }, V\right) {\gamma }^{\prime }\end{Vmatrix}}^{2}{dt}.
\]

It follows that the integrand is zero, and therefore the restriction \( V \mid  \left( {{t}_{j - 1},{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a Jacobi field. To see what happens at each \( {t}_{j} \) , choose \( T \in  \mathcal{V} \) in such a way that

\[
T\left( {t}_{j}\right)  = \frac{DV}{dt}\left( {t}_{j}^{ + }\right)  - \frac{DV}{dt}\left( {t}_{j}^{ - }\right) ,\;j = 1,\ldots , k - 1.
\]

Since

\[
0 = {I}_{a}\left( {V, T}\right)  =  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{{k - 1}}{\begin{Vmatrix}\frac{DV}{dt}\left( {t}_{j}^{ + }\right)  - \frac{DV}{dt}\left( {t}_{j}^{ - }\right) \end{Vmatrix}}^{2},
\]

we conclude that \( V \) is of class \( {C}^{1} \) at each \( {t}_{j} \) . By the uniqueness of the solution to an ordinary differential equation, \( V \) is \( {C}^{\infty } \) . Therefore \( V \) is a Jacobi field.

Since each point of \( M \) is contained in a totally normal neighborhood and \( \gamma \left( \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack  \right) \) is compact, we can choose a subdivision

\[
0 = {t}_{0} < {t}_{1} < \cdots  < {t}_{k - 1} < {t}_{k} = a
\]

of \( \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack \) such that each \( \gamma  \mid  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{j - 1},{t}_{j}}\right\rbrack  , j = 1,\ldots , k \) , is contained in a totally normal neighborhood. Thus each \( \gamma  \mid  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{j - 1},{t}_{j}}\right\rbrack \) is a minimizing geodesic and doesn't contain any conjugate points. In what follows, such a subdivision will be called normal and will be fixed until mention to the contrary.

Let \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ - }\left( {0, a}\right)  = {\mathcal{V}}^{ - } \) be the vector subspace of \( \mathcal{V} \) formed from the fields \( V \) such that \( V \mid  \left( {{t}_{i - 1},{t}_{i}}\right) , i = 1,\ldots , k \) , is a Jacobi field; \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ - } \) has finite dimension. Let \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ + } \) be the subspace of \( \mathcal{V} \) consisting of vector fields \( W \) such that \( W\left( {t}_{1}\right)  = W\left( {t}_{2}\right)  = \cdots  = W\left( {t}_{k - 1}\right)  = 0 \) .
