nodes.label: Proposition 2.5
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 2.5 Proposition. \( \mathcal{V} \) is a direct sum \( \mathcal{V} = {\mathcal{V}}^{ + } \oplus  {\mathcal{V}}^{ - } \) , and the subspaces \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ + } \) and \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ - } \) are orthogonal with respect to \( {I}_{a} \) . In addition, \( {I}_{a} \) restricted to \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ + } \) is positive definite.
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.5 Proposition. \( \mathcal{V} \) is a direct sum \( \mathcal{V} = {\mathcal{V}}^{ + } \oplus {\mathcal{V}}^{ - } \) , and the subspaces \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ + } \) and \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ - } \) are orthogonal with respect to \( {I}_{a} \) . In addition, \( {I}_{a} \) restricted to \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ + } \) is positive definite.

nodes.proof:
Given \( V \in  \mathcal{V} \) , let \( W \) be a vector field in \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ - } \) given by \( W\left( {t}_{j}\right)  = \; V\left( {t}_{j}\right) \) ; because \( \gamma  \mid  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{j - 1},{t}_{j}}\right\rbrack \) does not have any conjugate points, such a \( W \) exists and is unique. Hence \( V - W \in  {\mathcal{V}}^{ + } \) and, therefore \( \mathcal{V} = {\mathcal{V}}^{ + } \oplus  {\mathcal{V}}^{ - } \) . In addition, if \( X \in  {\mathcal{V}}^{ - } \) and \( Y \in  {\mathcal{V}}^{ + } \) , we have

\[
{I}_{a}\left( {X, Y}\right)  =  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{{k - 1}}\left\langle  {0,\frac{DX}{dt}\left( {t}_{j}^{ + }\right)  - \frac{DX}{dt}\left( {t}_{j}^{ - }\right) }\right\rangle   = 0,
\]

that is, \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ + } \) and \( {\mathcal{V}}^{ - } \) are orthogonal, relative to \( {I}_{a} \) . This proves the first part of Proposition 2.5.

Since \( \gamma  \mid  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{j - 1},{t}_{j}}\right\rbrack  , j = 1,\ldots , k \) , are minimizing geodesics, they have less energy than any other paths between their endpoints. Therefore, if \( V \in  {\mathcal{V}}^{ + } \) , then \( {I}_{a}\left( {V, V}\right)  \geq  0 \) .

It remains to show that \( {I}_{a}\left( {V, V}\right)  > 0 \) if \( V \in  {\mathcal{V}}^{ + } - \{ 0\} \) . Suppose, to the contrary, that \( {I}_{a}\left( {V, V}\right)  = 0 \) with \( V \in  {\mathcal{V}}^{ + }, V \neq  0 \) . We are going to show that this implies that \( V \) belongs to the null space of \( {I}_{a} \) . Indeed, if \( W \in  {\mathcal{V}}^{ - } \) , then \( {I}_{a}\left( {V, W}\right)  = 0 \) , from the orthogonality above. If \( W \in  {\mathcal{V}}^{ + } \) , consider the inequality

\[
0 \leq  {I}_{a}\left( {V + {cW}, V + {cW}}\right)  = {2c}{I}_{a}\left( {V, W}\right)  + {c}^{2}{I}_{a}\left( {W, W}\right) ,
\]

valid for all real \( c \) . This says that there exist real numbers \( A \geq  0 \) and \( B \) such that \( A{c}^{2} + {2Bc} \geq  0 \) for all \( c \in  \mathbf{R} \) , which is only possible when \( B = 0 \) , that is, \( {I}_{a}\left( {V, W}\right)  = 0 \) . Therefore \( V \) belongs to the null space of \( {I}_{a} \) . Since the null space consists of Jacobi fields and \( V \) vanishes at \( {t}_{j} \) , we conclude that \( V = 0 \) , which is a contradiction and ends the proof.

nodes.label: Lemma 2.8
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 2.8 LEMMA. If \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) is sufficiently small, \( i\left( {t + \varepsilon }\right)  = i\left( t\right)  + d \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.8 LEMMA. If \( \varepsilon > 0 \) is sufficiently small, \( i\left( {t + \varepsilon }\right) = i\left( t\right) + d \) .

nodes.proof:
We show first that \( i\left( {t + \varepsilon }\right)  \leq  i\left( t\right)  + d \) . Indeed, because \( \dim \left( {S}_{j}\right)  = n\left( {j - 1}\right) ,{I}_{t} \) is positive definite on a subspace of dimension \( n\left( {j - 1}\right)  - i\left( t\right)  - d \) . By continuity, \( {I}_{t + \varepsilon } \) is still positive definite on this subspace, for \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) sufficiently small. Therefore

\[
i\left( {t + \varepsilon }\right)  \leq  n\left( {j - 1}\right)  - \{ n\left( {j - 1}\right)  - i\left( t\right)  - d\}  = i\left( t\right)  + d.
\]

To prove the inequality in the other direction, it is necessary to use the Index Lemma (Lemma 2.2 of Chap. 10). Let \( V \in  {S}_{j} \) , with \( V\left( {{t}_{j - 1} \neq  0}\right. \) , and denote by \( {V}_{{t}_{o}} \) the "broken" Jacobi field which coincides with \( V\left( {t}_{i}\right) \) at \( {t}_{i}, i = 1,\ldots , j - 1 \) , and which vanishes at the point \( {t}_{o} \in  \left( {{t}_{j - 1},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . We claim that

\[
{I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {{V}_{{t}_{o}},{V}_{{t}_{o}}}\right)  > {I}_{{t}_{o} + \varepsilon }\left( {{V}_{{t}_{o} + \varepsilon },{V}_{{t}_{o} + \varepsilon }}\right)
\]

In fact, if we denote by \( {W}_{{t}_{o}} \) (see Fig. 1) the vector field defined along \( \gamma \left( \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{o} + \varepsilon }\right\rbrack  \right) \) by:

\[
{W}_{{t}_{o}}\left( t\right)  = {V}_{{t}_{o}}\left( t\right) ,\;t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{o}}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
{W}_{{t}_{o}}\left( t\right)  = 0,\;t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{o},{t}_{o} + \varepsilon }\right\rbrack  ,
\]

we have, from the Index Lemma,

\[
{I}_{{t}_{o}}\left( {{V}_{{t}_{o}},{V}_{{t}_{o}}}\right)  = {I}_{{t}_{o} + \varepsilon }\left( {{W}_{{t}_{o}},{W}_{{t}_{o}}}\right)  > {I}_{{t}_{o} + \varepsilon }\left( {{V}_{{t}_{o} + \varepsilon },{V}_{{t}_{o} + \varepsilon }}\right) ,
\]

where the last inequality is strict, since \( {W}_{{t}_{o}} \) is not a Jacobi field. This proves the assertion made.

![019eafb3-a904-7162-90c5-5ccd2f5d76bf_61_260_1477_1326_667_0.jpg](images/019eafb3-a904-7162-90c5-5ccd2f5d76bf_61_260_1477_1326_667_0.jpg)

Therefore, if \( V \in  {S}_{j} \) and \( {I}_{t}\left( {V, V}\right)  \leq  0 \) , then \( {I}_{t + \varepsilon }\left( {V, V}\right)  < 0 \) . Hence, if \( {I}_{t} \) is negative definite on a subspace \( \bar{S} \subset  {S}_{j},{I}_{t + \varepsilon } \) will still be negative definite on the direct sum of \( \bar{S} \) with the null space of \( {I}_{t} \) . Therefore

\[
i\left( {t + \varepsilon }\right)  \geq  i\left( t\right)  + d,
\]

which, together with the previous inequality implies that \( i\left( {t + \varepsilon }\right)  = \; i\left( t\right)  + d \) .

nodes.content: 2.9 COROLLARY. (Jacobi). Let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) be a geodesic segment on \( M \) such that \( \gamma \left( a\right) \) is not conjugate to \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) . Then \( \gamma \) has no conjugate points on \( \left( {0, a}\right) \) if and only if for all proper variations of \( \gamma \) there exists a \( \delta  > 0 \) such that \( E\left( s\right)  < E\left( \delta \right) \) for \( 0 < \left| s\right|  < \delta \) . In particular, if \( \gamma \) is minimizing, \( \gamma \) has no conjugate points on \( \left( {0, a}\right) \) .

nodes.label: Remark 2.12
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
2.12 REMARK. The fact that the index and the nullity of \( I \) are finite reflect the fundamental fact that the "infinite dimensional manifold" \( {\Omega }_{p, q} = \Omega \) mentioned in Remark 2.7 of Chapter 9 can be replaced, under certain conditions, by a finite dimensional manifold. This was the original point of view of Morse to prove his theorem. For some applications (cf. the Sphere Theorem, Prop. 3.1), it is convenient to have this construction in mind which can be summarized in the following way. (For more details, see Milnor [Mi], pp. 88-92).

Let \( {\Omega }^{c} \) (resp. \( {\overset{ \circ  }{\Omega }}^{c} \) ) be the subset of \( \Omega \) formed by curves in \( \Omega \) of energy \( \leq  c \) (resp. \( < c \) ). It is clear that the curves in \( {\Omega }^{c} \) are contained in a compact subset \( S \subset  M \) . Let \( \delta  > 0 \) be such that given two points of \( S \) at a distance less than \( \delta \) , there exists a unique minimizing geodesic joining these two points. Suppose that the curves in \( {\Omega }^{c} \) are defined on \( \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) and subdivide \( \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) by the points \( {t}_{i}, i = 0,\ldots , k \) , in such a way that \( \left| {{t}_{i} - {t}_{i - 1}}\right|  < \frac{{\delta }^{2}}{c} \) . Let \( B \subset  {\Omega }^{c} \) (resp. \( B \subset  {\overset{ \circ  }{\Omega }}^{c} \) ) be the set of geodesics broken at \( {t}_{i} \) , that is, \( w \in  B \) if \( w\left( 0\right)  = p, w\left( 1\right)  = q \) , and the restriction \( w \mid  \left( {{t}_{i - 1},{t}_{i}}\right)  = {w}_{i} \) is a geodesic joining \( w\left( {t}_{i - 1}\right) \) to \( w\left( {t}_{i}\right) \) . Such a geodesic is entirely determined by the points \( w\left( {t}_{i}\right) \) since

\[
{L}^{2}\left( {w}_{i}\right)  = \left( {{t}_{i} - {t}_{i - 1}}\right) E\left( {w}_{i}\right)  < {\delta }^{2}.
\]

The correspondence

\[
w \rightarrow  \left( {w\left( {t}_{1}\right) ,\ldots , w\left( {t}_{k - 1}\right) }\right)  \in  M \times  \cdots  \times  M,\;w \in  \overset{ \circ  }{B},
\]

is bijective and takes \( B \) into an open subset of \( M \times  \cdots  \times  M \) . This allows us to introduce a differentiable structure (of finite dimension) on \( \overset{ \circ  }{B} \) . Observe that the tangent space \( {T}_{w}\left( \overset{ \circ  }{B}\right) \) to a broken geodesic \( w \) corresponds to the set of Jacobi fields along \( w \) , broken at \( {t}_{i} \) . It is possible to show that there exists a homotopy \( {h}_{s} : {\overset{ \circ  }{\Omega }}^{c} \rightarrow  {\overset{o}{\Omega }}^{c}, s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) with \( {h}_{o} = \) ident. and \( {h}_{1} : {\overset{ \circ  }{\Omega }}^{c} \rightarrow  \overset{ \circ  }{B} \) , that is, \( \overset{ \circ  }{B} \) is a "deformation retract" of \( {\widetilde{\Omega }}^{c} \) .

Restricting the energy \( E \) to a function \( \bar{E} \) on \( \overset{ \circ  }{B} \) , one verifies that the geodesics \( \gamma \) of \( {\overset{ \circ  }{\Omega }}^{c} \) are in the manifold \( \overset{ \circ  }{B} \) and are precisely the critical points of \( \bar{E} \) . In addition, the index and the nullity of \( I \) at \( \gamma \) coincide with the index and the nullity, respectively, of the hessian of \( \bar{E} \) at \( \gamma \) , since from Corollary 2.6 they coincide with the index and the nullity, respectively, of \( I \) restricted to the broken Jacobi fields along \( \gamma \) .

In this way, for many purposes, we can substitute the set \( {\overset{ \circ  }{\Omega }}^{c} \) by its finite dimensional approximation \( B \) .

Prove the following version of the Theorem of Bonnet-Myers: If \( M \) is complete and the sectional curvature \( K \) satisfies \( K \geq \; \delta  > 0 \) , then \( M \) is compact and \( \operatorname{diam}M \leq  \pi /\sqrt{\delta } \) , using the Comparison Theorem of Rauch and the Jacobi theorem.

Hint: Comparing \( M \) with a sphere of curvature \( \delta \) , conclude, from Rauch’s Theorem, that the first conjugate point to \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) along a normalized geodesic \( \gamma  : \lbrack 0,\infty ) \rightarrow  M \) does not occur after \( \gamma \left( {\pi /\sqrt{\delta }}\right) \) . Therefore a geodesic of length larger than \( \pi /\sqrt{\delta } \) contains conjugate points. By Jacobi's theorem, such a geodesic does not minimize.

2. Prove the following inequality on real functions (Wirtinger's inequality). Let \( f : \left\lbrack  {0,\pi }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) be a real function of class \( {C}^{2} \) such that \( f\left( 0\right)  = f\left( \pi \right)  = 0 \) . Then

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{f}^{2}{dt} \leq  {\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\left( {f}^{\prime }\right) }^{2}{dt}
\]

and equality occurs if and only if \( f\left( t\right)  = c\sin t \) , where \( c \) is a constant. (In the next exercise, we use this fact to prove an interesting geometric fact).

Hint: A geometric solution is the following. Consider a normalized geodesic \( \gamma \) joining the antipodal points \( p \) and \( - p \) of a unit sphere \( {S}^{2} \) . Let \( v\left( t\right) \) be a parallel field along \( \gamma \) , with \( \left\langle  {v,{\gamma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle   = 0 \) , \( \left| v\right|  = 1 \) . Set \( V = {fv} \) and calculate the second variation for the variational vector \( V \) , obtaining

\[
{I}_{\pi }\left( {V, V}\right)  = {\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\left( {f}^{\prime }\right) }^{2}{dt} - {\int }_{0}^{\pi }{f}^{2}{dt}.
\]

By the Morse index theorem, \( {I}_{\pi }\left( {V, V}\right)  \geq  0 \) , which establishes the inequality. For the equality, use the fact that \( {I}_{\pi }\left( {V, V}\right)  = 0 \) implies that \( V \) is a Jacobi field. (For another proof, using Fourier series, see W. Blaschke, Kreis and Kugel, Chelsea, New York, 1949, p. 105).

3. Let \( {M}^{n} \) be a complete simply connected Riemannian manifold. Suppose that for each point \( p \in  M \) , the locus \( C\left( p\right) \) of (first) conjugate points of \( p \) reduces to a unique point \( q \neq  p \) and that \( d\left( {p, C\left( p\right) }\right)  = \pi \) . Prove that, if the sectional curvature \( K \) of \( M \) satisfies \( K \leq  1 \) , then \( M \) is isometric to the sphere \( {S}^{n} \) with constant curvature 1.

Hint: Let \( J \) be a Jacobi field along a normalized geodesic \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,\pi }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) joining \( p \) to \( q \) with \( J\left( 0\right)  = J\left( \pi \right)  = 0,\left\langle  {J,{\gamma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle   = 0. \) Choosing fields \( {e}_{1},{e}_{2},\ldots ,{e}_{n - 1},{\gamma }^{\prime } \) which are parallel and orthonormal along \( \gamma \) , we can write \( J = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{{n - 1}}{a}_{i}{e}_{i} \) . Then, letting \( K\left( t\right)  = K\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }, J}\right) \) , using integration by parts and Exercise 2, we have

\[
0 = {I}_{\pi }\left( {J, J}\right)  =  - {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\left\langle  {{J}^{\prime \prime } + R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }, J}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime }, J}\right\rangle  {dt}
\]

\[
=  - {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{a}_{i}^{\prime \prime }{a}_{i}}\right) {dt} - {\int }_{0}^{\pi }K\left( t\right) \left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{a}_{i}^{2}}\right) {dt}
\]

\[
= {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{\left( {a}_{i}^{\prime }\right) }^{2}{dt} - {\int }_{0}^{\pi }K\left( t\right) \left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{a}_{i}^{2}}\right) {dt}
\]

\[
\geq  \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{a}_{i}^{2}\left( {1 - K\left( t\right) }\right) {dt} \geq  0.
\]

It follows that \( K\left( t\right)  \equiv  1 \) .

nodes.content_excerpt: 6. A line in a complete Riemannian manifold is a geodesic \[ \gamma : \left( {-\infty ,\infty }\right) \rightarrow M \] which minimizes the arc length between any two of its points. Show that if the sectional curvature \( K \) of \( M \) is strictly positive, \( M \) does not have any lines. By an example show that the theorem is false if \( K \geq 0 \) .

nodes.content:
## 2. Existence of closed geodesics

We denote by \( \pi  : \widetilde{M} \rightarrow  M \) the universal covering of a complete Riemannian manifold \( M \) with the covering metric and denote by \( A\left( \widetilde{M}\right) \) the group of covering transformations of \( \widetilde{M} \) (covering auto-morphisms). Observe that the elements in \( A\left( \widetilde{M}\right) \) , different from the identity, are isometries of \( \widetilde{M} \) , which have no fixed points, and that \( A\left( M\right) \) is isomorphic to \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {M;p}\right) , p \in  M \) (cf. Massey [Ma]). We should say that this isomorphism depends on the choice of the point \( \widetilde{p} \in  \widetilde{M} \) , with \( \pi \left( \widetilde{p}\right)  = p \) , and associates to each \( g \in  {\pi }_{1}\left( {M;p}\right) \) an isometry \( {\alpha }_{\widetilde{p}} \in  A\left( \widetilde{M}\right) \) defined in the following way: If \( \widetilde{q} \in  \widetilde{M} \) , join \( \widetilde{q} \) to \( \widetilde{p} \) by a path \( \widetilde{\sigma } \) , put \( \pi \left( \widetilde{\sigma }\right)  = \sigma \) and \( \beta  = {\sigma g}{\sigma }^{-1} \) , where, by abuse of notation, we also denote by \( g \) a path in the class \( g \) . In what follows, if \( \beta  : \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) is a path in \( M,{\widetilde{\beta }}_{\widetilde{q}}\left( 1\right) \) will denote the endpoint of the lifting to \( \widetilde{M} \) of \( \beta \) starting from \( \widetilde{q} \) . Taking \( \beta  = {\sigma g}{\sigma }^{-1} \) , we define

\[
{\alpha }_{\widetilde{p}}\left( \widetilde{q}\right)  = {\widetilde{\beta }}_{\widetilde{q}}\left( 1\right) .
\]

2.1 Definition. A set \( \mathcal{L} \) of closed paths in \( M \) is called a free homotopy class if given \( f \in  \mathcal{L} \) and \( g : I \rightarrow  M \) such that there exists a homotopy

\[
F : I \times  I \rightarrow  M, F\left( {0, t}\right)  = f\left( t\right) , F\left( {1, t}\right)  = g\left( t\right) , F\left( {s,0}\right)  = F\left( {s,1}\right) ,
\]

then \( g \in  \mathcal{L} \) . The set of such classes will be denoted by \( {C}_{1}\left( M\right) \) .

nodes.label: Theorem 2.2
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 2.2 THEOREM. (Cartan). If \( M \) is compact and \( \mathcal{L} \in  {C}_{1}\left( M\right) \) is not the constant class, then there exists a closed geodesic of \( M \) in the class \( \mathcal{L} \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.2 THEOREM. (Cartan). If \( M \) is compact and \( \mathcal{L} \in {C}_{1}\left( M\right) \) is not the constant class, then there exists a closed geodesic of \( M \) in the class \( \mathcal{L} \) .

nodes.proof:
Let \( d \) be the infimum of the lengths of piecewise differentiable curves belonging to \( \mathcal{L} \) . Since \( \mathcal{L} \) is not trivial, \( d > 0 \) . Let \( {\gamma }_{j} \) be a sequence of piecewise differentiable curves belonging to \( \mathcal{L} \) such that \( \ell \left( {\gamma }_{j}\right)  \rightarrow  d \) . We can suppose that \( {\gamma }_{j} \) is a broken geodesic defined on the interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) parametrized proportionally to arc length. Let \( L = \sup \ell \left( {\gamma }_{j}\right) \) . Then

\[
d\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {t}_{1}\right) ,{\gamma }_{j}\left( {t}_{2}\right) }\right)  \leq  {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\left| {{\gamma }_{j}^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right| {dt} \leq  L\left( {{t}_{2} - {t}_{1}}\right) ,
\]

for all \( {t}_{1} \leq  {t}_{2} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . Therefore the set \( \left\{  {\gamma }_{j}\right\} \) is equicontinuous. Since \( M \) is compact, there exists a subsequence of \( {\gamma }_{j} \) , which we denote again by \( {\gamma }_{j} \) , which converges uniformly to a continuous closed curve \( {\gamma }_{o} : \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) .

Now let \( 0 = {t}_{o} < {t}_{1} < \cdots  < {t}_{k} = 1 \) be a partition of the interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) such that \( {\gamma }_{o}{ \mid  }_{\left\lbrack  {t}_{i - 1},{t}_{i}\right\rbrack  }, i = 1,\ldots , k \) , is contained in a totally normal neighborhood. Let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) be a piecewise differentiable curve such that \( {\gamma }^{i} = {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  {t}_{i - 1},{t}_{i}\right\rbrack  } \) is the unique geodesic segment which joins the points \( {\gamma }_{o}\left( {t}_{i - 1}\right) \) and \( {\gamma }_{o}\left( {t}_{i}\right) \) . It is clear that \( \gamma  \in  \mathcal{L} \) , hence \( \ell \left( \gamma \right)  \geq  d \) . We are going to show that \( \ell \left( \gamma \right)  = d \) .

Suppose that \( \ell \left( \gamma \right)  > d \) and let \( \varepsilon  = \frac{\ell \left( \gamma \right)  - d}{{2k} + 1} \) . There exists an integer \( j \) such that

\[
\ell \left( {\gamma }_{j}\right)  - d < \varepsilon \;\mathrm{{and}}\;d\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( t\right) ,{\gamma }_{o}\left( t\right) }\right)  < \varepsilon ,\;\mathrm{{for}}\;\mathrm{{all}}\;t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack  .
\]

Denoting by \( {\gamma }_{j}^{i} = {\left. {\gamma }_{j}\right| }_{\left\lbrack  {t}_{i - 1},{t}_{i}\right\rbrack  } \) , we have

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\left( {\ell \left( {\gamma }_{j}^{i}\right)  + {2\varepsilon }}\right)  = \ell \left( {\gamma }_{j}\right)  + {2k\varepsilon } < d + \left( {{2k} + 1}\right) \varepsilon
\]

\[
= \ell \left( \gamma \right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\ell \left( {\gamma }^{i}\right)
\]

Therefore, there exists an integer \( i,1 \leq  i \leq  k \) , such that

\[
\ell \left( {\gamma }_{j}^{i}\right)  + {2\varepsilon } < \ell \left( {\gamma }^{i}\right) ,
\]

which contradicts the fact that \( {\gamma }^{i} \) is minimizing and proves that \( \ell \left( \gamma \right)  = d \) .

We parametrize \( \gamma \) by arc length. Then \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0, d}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) is a broken geodesic which has minimum length in the class \( \mathcal{L} \) . We are going to show that \( \gamma \) is regular at the point \( {p}_{i} = \gamma \left( {t}_{i}\right) \) , for all \( i = \; 0,\ldots , k \) .

Suppose to the contrary and let \( B \) be a convex ball centered at \( {p}_{i} \) . Choose points \( {q}_{1} \) and \( {q}_{2} \) in \( \gamma  \cap  B \) in a way that the geodesic triangle \( {p}_{i}{q}_{1}{q}_{2} \) is homotopic to a point (see Fig. 2). Then the closed curve constituted by the minimizing geodesic \( {q}_{1}{q}_{2} \) and by the arc of \( \gamma \) between \( {q}_{1} \) and \( {q}_{2} \) that does not contain \( {p}_{i} \) is in the class \( \mathcal{L} \) and has length smaller than \( \gamma \) , which is a contradiction.

nodes.label: Remark 2.3
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 2.3 REMARK. If \( M \) is not compact, the theorem is false, as shown by the example of Fig 3. The surface in Fig. 3 represents a surface of revolution generated by a curve which is asymptotic to the axis of revolution. Since there exist curves of arbitrarily small length in the free homotopy classes which are non-trivial, such classes do not contain curves of minimum length.

nodes.label: Remark 2.4
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 2.4 REMARK. If \( M \) is simply connected (and compact), the existence of a closed geodesic in \( M \) , although true, is a more difficult problem. Indeed, the problem of determining the number and the nature of the closed geodesics on a Riemannian manifold is one of the most celebrated chapters in Geometry. A good reference on this topic is Klingenberg [Kℓ 4].

nodes.label: Proposition 2.6
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 2.6 Proposition. Let \( M \) be a compact Riemannian manifold and \( \alpha \) a covering transformation of \( \widetilde{M} \) , considered with the covering metric. Then \( \alpha \) is a translation of \( \widetilde{M} \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.6 Proposition. Let \( M \) be a compact Riemannian manifold and \( \alpha \) a covering transformation of \( \widetilde{M} \) , considered with the covering metric. Then \( \alpha \) is a translation of \( \widetilde{M} \) .

nodes.proof:
Let \( \widetilde{p} \in  \widetilde{M} \) and let \( g \in  {\pi }_{1}\left( {M;p}\right) , p = \pi \left( \widetilde{p}\right) \) , the element corresponding to \( \alpha \) under the isomorphism mentioned in the introduction of this Section. We can assume \( \alpha  \neq \) ident. By Cartan’s Theorem, there exists a closed geodesic \( \gamma \) of \( M \) in the free homotopy class determined by \( g \) . Choose a point \( q \in  \gamma \) . Then \( \gamma \) is homotopic to the closed path \( {\sigma g}{\sigma }^{-1} \) , where \( \sigma \) is a path joining \( p \) to \( q \) . Let \( \widetilde{q} = {\widetilde{\sigma }}_{\widetilde{p}}\left( 1\right) \) , that is, \( \widetilde{q} \) is the endpoint of the lifting of \( \sigma \) starting from \( \widetilde{p} \) . Let \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) be the lift of \( \gamma \) starting from \( \widetilde{q} \) ; we are going to show that \( \alpha \) leaves \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) invariant.

For this, let \( {\alpha }_{\widetilde{q}} \in  A\left( \widetilde{M}\right) \) be the isometry corresponding to the class \( \left\lbrack  \gamma \right\rbrack   \in  {\pi }_{1}\left( {M;q}\right) \) and the point \( \widetilde{q} \) , in the isomorphism indicated above. We claim that \( {\alpha }_{\widetilde{q}} = \alpha \) . In fact, since \( \gamma \) is homotopic to \( {\sigma g}{\sigma }^{-1} \) , its lift starting from \( \widetilde{q} \) has the same endpoint, that is,

\[
\alpha \left( \widetilde{q}\right)  = {\alpha }_{\widetilde{q}}\left( \widetilde{q}\right) .
\]

Therefore, \( \widetilde{q} \) is a fixed point of \( \alpha  \circ  {\alpha }_{\widetilde{q}}^{-1} \) , and the claim made follows easily.

It follows that if \( \widetilde{\gamma }\left( s\right) \) is a point of the lift of \( \gamma \) starting from \( \widetilde{q} \) , we have, by uniqueness of lifting,

\[
\alpha \left( {\widetilde{\gamma }\left( s\right) }\right)  = {\alpha }_{\widetilde{q}}\left( {\widetilde{\gamma }\left( s\right) }\right)  \in  \gamma ,
\]

which shows that \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) is invariant by \( \alpha \) , and proves the Proposition.

A geodesic triangle \( T \) in a Riemannian manifold \( M \) is a set formed by three segments of minimizing normalized geodesics (called sides of the triangle)

\[
{\gamma }_{1} : \left\lbrack  {0,{\ell }_{1}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M,\;{\gamma }_{2} : \left\lbrack  {0,{\ell }_{2}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M,\;{\gamma }_{3} : \left\lbrack  {0,{\ell }_{3}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M,
\]

in such a way that \( {\gamma }_{i}\left( {\ell }_{i}\right)  = {\gamma }_{i + 1}\left( 0\right) , i = 1,2 \) and \( {\gamma }_{3}\left( {\ell }_{3}\right)  = {\gamma }_{1}\left( 0\right) \) . The endpoints of the geodesic segments are called vertices of \( T \) . The angle

\[
\pounds \left( {-{\gamma }_{i}^{\prime }\left( {\ell }_{i}\right) ,{\gamma }_{i + 1}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) , i = 1,2,
\]

or

\[
\chi \left( {-{\gamma }_{3}^{\prime }\left( {\ell }_{3}\right) ,{\gamma }_{1}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) ,
\]

is called the (interior) angle of the corresponding vertex.

3.1 LEMMA. Let \( \widetilde{M} \) be a complete simply connected Riemannian manifold, with curvature \( K \leq  0 \) . Let \( a, b \) and \( c \) be three points of \( \widetilde{M} \) . Such points determine a unique geodesic triangle \( T \) in \( \widetilde{M} \) with vertices \( a, b, c \) . Let \( \alpha ,\beta \) and \( \gamma \) be the angles of the vertices \( a, b \) , \( c \) , respectively, and let \( A, B, C \) be the lengths of the sides opposite the vertices \( a, b, c \) , respectively. Then

(i) \( {A}^{2} + {B}^{2} - {2AB}\cos \gamma  \leq  {C}^{2}\;\left( { < {C}^{2}\text{ , if }K < 0}\right) \)

(ii) \( \alpha  + \beta  + \gamma  \leq  \pi \;\left( { < \pi \text{ , if }K < 0}\right) \) .

nodes.proof:
Let \( {\gamma }_{A},{\gamma }_{B},{\gamma }_{C} \) be the geodesics of lengths \( \ell \left( {\gamma }_{A}\right)  = A \) , \( \ell \left( {\gamma }_{B}\right)  = B,\ell \left( {\gamma }_{C}\right)  = C \) which form the sides of \( T \) . Let \( {\Gamma }_{A} = \; {\exp }_{c}^{-1}\left( {\gamma }_{A}\right) ,{\Gamma }_{B} = {\exp }_{c}^{-1}\left( {\gamma }_{B}\right) \) and \( {\Gamma }_{C} = {\exp }_{c}^{-1}\left( {\gamma }_{C}\right) \) be curves in \( {T}_{c}\left( \bar{M}\right) \) . Since \( {\gamma }_{A} \) and \( {\gamma }_{B} \) are radial geodesics issuing from the origin \( c \) , we have

\[
A = \ell \left( {\gamma }_{A}\right)  = \ell \left( {\Gamma }_{A}\right) ,\;B = \ell \left( {\gamma }_{B}\right)  = \ell \left( {\Gamma }_{B}\right) .
\]

In addition, denoting by \( {\Gamma }_{o} \) the segment of the straight line in \( {T}_{c}\left( \widetilde{M}\right) \) that joins the endpoints of \( {\Gamma }_{C} \) , we have that \( \ell \left( {\Gamma }_{o}\right)  \leq  \ell \left( {\Gamma }_{C}\right) \) (see Fig 4) and

\[
\ell {\left( {\Gamma }_{o}\right) }^{2} = {A}^{2} + {B}^{2} - {2AB}\cos \gamma .
\]

Since \( K \leq  0 \) and \( {T}_{c}\left( \widetilde{M}\right) \) has zero curvature, we can apply Proposition 2.5 of Chapter 10 (application of Rauch's Theorem) and obtain that

\[
\ell \left( {\Gamma }_{C}\right)  \leq  \ell \left( {\gamma }_{C}\right) \;\left( { < ,\text{ if }K < 0}\right) .
\]

It follows that

\[
\left. {{A}^{2} + {B}^{2} - {2AB}\cos \gamma  \leq  \ell {\left( {\Gamma }_{C}\right) }^{2} \leq  \ell {\left( {\gamma }_{C}\right) }^{2} = {C}^{2}\;\left( { < ,\mathrm{{if}}K < 0}\right) ,}\right.
\]

Figure 4

which proves (i).

To prove (ii), let us observe that

\[
C = d\left( {a, b}\right) ,\;B = d\left( {a, c}\right) ,\;A = d\left( {b, c}\right)
\]

and, therefore, each length \( A, B \) or \( C \) is bounded by the sum of the other two. We can then consider in the Euclidean space \( {T}_{c}\left( \widetilde{M}\right) \) , a triangle whose sides have lengths \( A, B \) and \( C \) . Denoting the opposite angles of this triangle by \( {\alpha }^{\prime },{\beta }^{\prime } \) and \( {\gamma }^{\prime } \) , respectively, we obtain from (i),

\[
\alpha  \leq  {\alpha }^{\prime },\;\beta  \leq  {\beta }^{\prime },\;\gamma  \leq  {\gamma }^{\prime }\;\left( { < ,\;\text{ if }K < 0}\right) .
\]

Since \( {\alpha }^{\prime } + {\beta }^{\prime } + {\gamma }^{\prime } = \pi \) ,(ii) follows.

nodes.content: 3.2 THEOREM. (Preissman [Pr]) If \( M \) is a compact Riemannian manifold with negative curvature, then any abelian subgroup of the fundamental group \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) , different from the identity, is infinite cyclic.
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.2 THEOREM. (Preissman [Pr]) If \( M \) is a compact Riemannian manifold with negative curvature, then any abelian subgroup of the fundamental group \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) , different from the identity, is infinite cyclic.

nodes.proof: Let \( H \subset  {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) be an abelian subgroup with \( H \neq  \{ e\} \) . By Proposition 2.9 and by Lemmas 3.3 and 3.4, there exists a unique geodesic \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) which is invariant under all the elements of \( H \) . By Lemma 3.5, \( H \) is cyclic infinite.

nodes.label: Lemma 3.3
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 3.3 LEMMA. If \( K < 0 \) and \( f : \widetilde{M} \rightarrow  \widetilde{M} \) is a translation along the geodesic \( \widetilde{\gamma }, f \neq \) id., then \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) is the unique geodesic left invariant by \( f \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.3 LEMMA. If \( K < 0 \) and \( f : \widetilde{M} \rightarrow \widetilde{M} \) is a translation along the geodesic \( \widetilde{\gamma }, f \neq \) id., then \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) is the unique geodesic left invariant by \( f \) .

nodes.proof:
Suppose that \( f \) leaves invariant two geodesics \( {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{1} \) and \( {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{2} \) . Since \( f \) does not have fixed points, \( {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{1} \cap  {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{2} = \phi \) ; otherwise, \( {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{1} \cap  {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{2} \) has at least two points, which contradicts the simple connectivity of \( \widetilde{M} \) . Let \( {\widetilde{p}}_{1} \in  {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{1},{\widetilde{p}}_{2} \in  {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{2} \) , and let \( {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{3} \) be the minimizing geodesic joining \( {\widetilde{p}}_{1} \) to \( {\widetilde{p}}_{2} \) . Consider the "geodesic quadrilateral" \( {\widetilde{p}}_{1}, f\left( {\widetilde{p}}_{1}\right) \) , \( {\widetilde{p}}_{2}, f\left( {\widetilde{p}}_{2}\right) \) in \( \widetilde{M} \) (Fig. 5) and denote its (interior) angles by \( \alpha ,\pi  - {\alpha }^{\prime } \) (adjacent to the side \( {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{1} \) ), \( \beta ,\pi  - {\beta }^{\prime } \) (adjacent to the side \( {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{2} \) ). Since \( f \) is an isometry, \( \alpha  = {\alpha }^{\prime } \) and \( \beta  = {\beta }^{\prime } \) . Therefore, the sum of the interior angles of such a quadrilateral is equal to \( {2\pi } \) . Now divide this quadrilateral into two triangles \( {T}_{1} \) and \( {T}_{2} \) and denote by \( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i} \) the sum of the interior angles of the triangle \( {T}_{i}, i = 1,2 \) . It is clear that, at each vertex, the sum of the angles of the triangles which meet there is greater than or equal to the angle of the quadrilateral at this vertex. Therefore \( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{1} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{2} \geq  {2\pi } \) . It follows that one of the two triangles has its sum of interior angles \( \geq  \pi \) , which contradicts Lemma 3.1 (ii).

nodes.content: 3.5 LEMMA. If all the elements of a non-trivial subgroup \( H \subset \; {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) , considered as isometries of \( \widetilde{M} \) , leave invariant a fixed geodesic \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) , then \( H \) is infinite cyclic.

nodes.proof: Fix a point \( \widetilde{p} \in  \widetilde{\gamma } \) as origin and consider the map \( \theta  : H \rightarrow  \mathbf{R} \) given by \( \theta \left( h\right)  =  \pm  d\left( {\bar{p}, h\left( \widetilde{p}\right) }\right) \) , where the sign - or + is used acordingly as \( h\left( \widetilde{p}\right) \) is "before" or "after" \( \widetilde{p} \) , respectively, in the orientation of \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) . Since the elements of \( H \) are isometries which leave \( \bar{\gamma } \) invariant, \( \theta \) is a homomorphism of \( H \) into the additive group of the reals \( \mathbf{R} \) . \( \theta \) is an injective homomorphism; otherwise, \( {h}_{1}\left( \widetilde{p}\right)  = {h}_{2}\left( \widetilde{p}\right) \) , with \( {h}_{1} \neq  {h}_{2} \) , hence \( \widetilde{p} \) would be a fixed point of \( {h}_{1}{h}_{2}^{-1} \) . Therefore, \( H \) is a additive subgroup of \( \mathbf{R} \) . But any additive subgroup of \( \mathbf{R} \) is either dense in R or infinite cyclic. Since the isometries of \( H \) operate in a totally discontinuous way, \( H \) is not dense. Hence \( H \) is infinite cyclic.

nodes.label: Example 3.6
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 3.6 EXAMPLE. Let \( N \) be a surface of genus two and let \( M = N \times  {S}^{1} \) be the product manifold of \( N \) with a circle \( {S}^{1} \) . Then \( M \) does not carry a metric of negative curvature. Indeed, if \( C \subset  {\pi }_{1}\left( N\right) \) is a cyclic subgroup, then \( C \oplus  \mathbf{Z} \subset  {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) is an abelian subgroup which is not cyclic.

nodes.label: Lemma 3.9
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 3.9 LEMMA. If \( M \) is complete, \( K \leq  0 \) , and there exists a geodesic invariant under the elements of \( A\left( \widetilde{M}\right) \) , then \( M \) is not compact.
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.9 LEMMA. If \( M \) is complete, \( K \leq 0 \) , and there exists a geodesic invariant under the elements of \( A\left( \widetilde{M}\right) \) , then \( M \) is not compact.

nodes.proof:
Let \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) be the geodesic invariant under the elements of \( A\left( \widetilde{M}\right) \) . Fix a point \( \widetilde{p} \in  \widetilde{\gamma } \) , a real number \( t > 0 \) , and consider the normalized geodesic \( \widetilde{\beta } : \left\lbrack  {0, t}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \widetilde{M},\bar{\beta }\left( 0\right)  = \widetilde{p} \) , perpendicular to \( \bar{\gamma } \) at \( \widetilde{p} \) . Let \( \beta  = \pi  \circ  \widetilde{\beta },\gamma  = \pi  \circ  \widetilde{\gamma }, p = \pi \left( \widetilde{p}\right) \) , and \( {\alpha }_{t} \) be a minimizing geodesic in \( M \) joining \( \beta \left( t\right) \) to \( p \) . We are going to show that the length \( \ell \left( {\alpha }_{t}\right)  = t \) .

Let \( {\widetilde{\alpha }}_{t} \) be the lift of \( {\alpha }_{t} \) starting from \( \widetilde{\beta }\left( t\right) \) . Since \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) is invariant, the endpoint of \( {\widetilde{\alpha }}_{t} \) belongs to \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) . (see Fig. 6). Since \( K \leq  0 \) , by

Lemma 3.1 (i), \( \ell \left( {\widetilde{\alpha }}_{t}\right)  \geq  \ell \left( \widetilde{\beta }\right) \) . On the other hand,

\[
\ell \left( {\widetilde{\alpha }}_{t}\right)  = \ell \left( {\alpha }_{t}\right)  \leq  \ell \left( \beta \right)  = \ell \left( \widetilde{\beta }\right)  = t,
\]

hence \( \ell \left( {\alpha }_{t}\right)  = t \) , as was claimed.

Since \( t \) is arbitrary, \( M \) is not bounded, which concludes the proof of Lemma 3.9.

nodes.label: Theorem 3.10
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content: 3.10 Theorem. (Byers,[By]). If \( M \) is compact, \( K < 0 \) , and \( H \) is a solvable subgroup of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) , H \neq  \{ e\} \) , then \( H \) is infinite cyclic. In addition, \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) does not have a cyclic subgroup of finite index.
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.10 Theorem. (Byers,[By]). If \( M \) is compact, \( K < 0 \) , and \( H \) is a solvable subgroup of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) , H \neq \{ e\} \) , then \( H \) is infinite cyclic. In addition, \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) does not have a cyclic subgroup of finite index.

nodes.proof:
Since \( H \) is solvable, there exists a finite sequence of subgroups

\[
H = {H}_{0} \supset  {H}_{1} \supset  \cdots  \supset  {H}_{k - 1} \supset  {H}_{k} = \{ e\}
\]

such that \( {H}_{i + 1} \) is normal in \( {H}_{i} \) and \( {H}_{i}/{H}_{i + 1} \) is abelian. Then \( {H}_{k - 1} \) is abelian, hence, by Preissman's Theorem, infinite cyclic.

Let \( g \in  {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) be a generator of \( {H}_{k - 1} \) and let \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) be the geodesic in \( \widetilde{M} \) invariant under \( g \) . Let \( a \in  {H}_{k - 2} \) and \( b \in  {H}_{k - 1} \) . Since \( {a}^{-1}{b}^{-1}{ab} \in  {H}_{k - 1} \) , we have, for some integer \( n \) ,

\[
{a}^{-1}{b}^{-1}{ab} = {g}^{n}.
\]

It follows that

\[
{a}^{-1}{b}^{-1}{ab}\left( \widetilde{\gamma }\right)  = {g}^{n}\left( \widetilde{\gamma }\right)  = \widetilde{\gamma }.
\]

Since \( b \in  {H}_{k - 1}, b\left( \widetilde{\gamma }\right)  = \widetilde{\gamma } \) . Therefore \( {b}^{-1}a\left( \widetilde{\gamma }\right)  = a\left( \widetilde{\gamma }\right) \) , that is, \( {b}^{-1} \) leaves invariant the geodesic \( a\left( \widetilde{\gamma }\right) \) . By uniqueness, \( a\left( \widetilde{\gamma }\right)  = \widetilde{\gamma } \) . Therefore, all the elements of \( {H}_{k - 2} \) leave \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) invariant. By Lemma 3.5, \( {H}_{k - 2} \) is infinite cyclic.

Repeating the argument above a finite number of times, we conclude that \( H \) is infinite cyclic, which proves the first statement of the theorem.

To prove the final assertion, suppose that there exists a subgroup \( H \subset  {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) , cyclic and of finite index. Let \( g \) be a generator of \( H \) and let \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) be the geodesic of \( \widetilde{M} \) invariant under \( g \) . Let \( a \in  {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right)  - H \) . Since \( H \) has finite index, there exist integers \( m \) and \( n \) such that \( {a}^{n} = {g}^{m} \) . Therefore

\[
{a}^{n}\left( \widetilde{\gamma }\right)  = {g}^{m}\left( \widetilde{\gamma }\right)  = \widetilde{\gamma }.
\]

By uniqueness, \( a\left( \widetilde{\gamma }\right)  = \widetilde{\gamma } \) , for all \( a \in  {\pi }_{1}\left( m\right)  - H \) . It follows that every element of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) leaves invariant the geodesic \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) . By Lemma 3.5, \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) is infinite cyclic, which contradicts Theorem 3.8.

nodes.title: 13.2. The cut locus
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry

nodes.label: Definition 13.2-extra-1
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
### 2.The cut locus

Let \( M \) be a complete Riemannian manifold, let \( p \in  M \) be a point of \( M \) , and let \( \gamma  : \lbrack 0,\infty ) \rightarrow  M \) be a normalized geodesic with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p \) . We know that if \( t > 0 \) is sufficiently small, \( d\left( {\gamma \left( 0\right) ,\gamma \left( t\right) }\right)  = t \) , that is, \( \gamma \left( \left\lbrack  {0, t}\right\rbrack  \right) \) is a minimizing geodesic. In addition, if \( \gamma \left( \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack  \right) \) is not minimizing, the same is true for all \( t > {t}_{1} \) . By continuity, the set of numbers \( t > 0 \) for which \( d\left( {\gamma \left( 0\right) ,\gamma \left( t\right) }\right)  = t \) is of the form \( \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) or \( \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) . In the first case, \( \gamma \left( {t}_{0}\right) \) is called the cut point of \( p \) along \( \gamma \) ; in the second case, we say that such a cut point does not exist.

We define the cut locus of \( p \) denoted by \( {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \) , as the union of the cut points of \( p \) along all of the geodesics that start from \( p \) .

nodes.content: 2.1 REMARK. The cut locus, for surfaces, was introduced under the name of "ligne de partage" by H. Poincaré in 1905 [Po]. For Riemannian manifolds, the cut locus was introduced by J. H. C. Whitehead in 1935, [Wh], in which he proved some of the properties that we present in this section (see pp. 700-704 of [Wh]). The interest in the cut locus was revived in 1959 when Klingenberg showed in \( \left\lbrack  {\mathrm{K}\ell 1}\right\rbrack \) that its introduction is useful in improving the "pinching" of the sphere theorem.

2.2 PROPOSITION. Suppose that \( \gamma \left( {t}_{0}\right) \) is the cut point of \( p = \gamma \left( 0\right) \) along \( \gamma \) . Then:

a) either \( \gamma \left( {t}_{0}\right) \) is the first conjugate point of \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) along \( \gamma \) ,

b) or there exists a geodesic \( \sigma  \neq  \gamma \) from \( p \) to \( \gamma \left( {t}_{0}\right) \) such that \( \ell \left( \sigma \right)  = \ell \left( \gamma \right) \) .

Conversely, if (a) or (b) is satisfied, then there exists \( \widetilde{t} \) in \( \left( {0,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) such that \( \gamma \left( \widetilde{t}\right) \) is the cut point of \( p \) along \( \gamma \) .

nodes.proof:
Let \( {t}_{o} \) satisfy the condition asserted, and let \( \left\{  {{t}_{o} + {\varepsilon }_{i}}\right\} \) be a sequence, in which \( {\varepsilon }_{i} > 0 \) and \( \left\{  {\varepsilon }_{i}\right\}   \rightarrow  0 \) . Consider a sequence of minimizing geodesics \( {\sigma }_{i} \) joining \( p \) to \( \gamma \left( {{t}_{o} + {\varepsilon }_{i}}\right) \) and let \( \left\{  {{\sigma }_{i}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right\}   \in  {T}_{p}M \) be its corresponding sequence of tangent vectors at \( p \) . Since the sphere in \( {T}_{p}M \) is compact, we can suppose, taking a subsequence, if necessary, that \( \left\{  {{\sigma }_{i}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right\} \) converges. Therefore there exists a geodesic \( \sigma \) such that \( {\sigma }_{i}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  \rightarrow  {\sigma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) . By continuity, \( \sigma \) is a minimizing geodesic joining \( p \) to \( \gamma \left( {t}_{o}\right) \) , that is, \( \ell \left( \sigma \right)  = \ell \left( \gamma \right) \) . If \( \sigma  \neq  \gamma \) , the assertion (b) is verified. If \( \sigma  = \gamma \) , we are going to show that (a) holds. Since \( \gamma \) is minimizing up to \( \gamma \left( {t}_{0}\right) \) , it suffices to show that \( d{\exp }_{p} \) is singular at \( {t}_{o}{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) .

Suppose therefore that \( {\sigma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) and that \( d{\exp }_{p} \) is not singular at \( {t}_{o}{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) . Then there exists a neighborhood \( U \) of \( {t}_{o}{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) where \( {\exp }_{p} \) is a diffeomorphism (Fig. 1). By definition of \( {\sigma }_{j},\gamma \left( {{t}_{o} + }\right. \; \left. {\varepsilon }_{j}\right)  = {\sigma }_{j}\left( {{t}_{o} + {\varepsilon }_{j}^{\prime }}\right) \) , where \( {\varepsilon }_{j}^{\prime } \leq  {\varepsilon }_{j} \) , because \( {\sigma }_{j} \) is minimizing. Take \( {\varepsilon }_{j} \) sufficiently small so that \( \left( {{t}_{o} + {\varepsilon }_{j}^{\prime }}\right) {\sigma }_{j}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) and \( \left( {{t}_{o} + {\varepsilon }_{j}}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) belong to \( U \) . Then

\[
{\exp }_{p}\left( {{t}_{o} + {\varepsilon }_{j}}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = \gamma \left( {{t}_{o} + {\varepsilon }_{j}}\right)
\]

\[
= {\sigma }_{j}\left( {{t}_{o} + {\varepsilon }_{j}^{\prime }}\right)  = {\exp }_{p}\left( {{t}_{o} + {\varepsilon }_{j}^{\prime }}\right) {\sigma }_{j}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,
\]

hence \( \left( {{t}_{o} + {\varepsilon }_{j}}\right) {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = \left( {{t}_{o} + {\varepsilon }_{j}^{\prime }}\right) {\sigma }_{j}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) , that is, \( {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = {\sigma }_{j}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) , which contradicts the definition of \( {t}_{o} \) , and concludes the proof of the first part of the proposition.

Conversely, if (a) holds, since a geodesic does not minimize distance after the first conjugate point, (see Corollary 2.9 to the Index Theorem, Chap. 11), the cut point of \( p \) along \( \gamma \) occurs at \( \gamma \left( \widetilde{t}\right) \) , \( \widetilde{t} \leq  {t}_{o}. \)

Suppose now that (b) holds. Let \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) be sufficiently small so that \( \sigma \left( {{t}_{o} - \varepsilon }\right) \) and \( \gamma \left( {{t}_{o} + \varepsilon }\right) \) are both contained in a totally normal neighborhood of \( \gamma \left( {t}_{o}\right) \) , and consider the unique minimizing geodesic \( \tau \) which joins \( \sigma \left( {{t}_{o} - \varepsilon }\right) \) to \( \gamma \left( {{t}_{o} + \varepsilon }\right) \) (Fig. 2). The curve \( {p\sigma }\left( {{t}_{o} - \varepsilon }\right)  \cup  \tau \) has arc length strictly less than \( {t}_{o} + \varepsilon \) . Therefore, the cut point of \( p \) along \( \gamma \) occurs at \( \gamma \left( \widetilde{t}\right) ,\widetilde{t} \leq  {t}_{o} \) .

nodes.content: 2.6′REMARK. A compact Riemannian manifold \( M \) for which the cut locus \( {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \) of any point \( p \in  M \) reduces to a unique point is called a wiedersehen manifold. There is a theorem due to L. Green [Gn] to the effect that wiedersehen surfaces (dim \( M = 2 \) ) are isometric to the sphere. This theorem was generalized, recently, by M. Berger and J. Kazdan [Be, pp. 236-246] to the case in which \( \dim M \) is even, and by C.T. Yang [Yg] to the case in which \( \dim M \) is odd. For an exposition of these questions, see Kazdan [Ka].

nodes.proof:
Consider sequences \( {\gamma }_{i}\left( 0\right)  \rightarrow  \gamma \left( 0\right) \) and \( {\gamma }_{i}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  \rightarrow  {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) , and let \( {\gamma }_{i}\left( {t}_{o}^{i}\right) \) and \( \gamma \left( {t}_{o}\right) \) be the cut points of \( {\gamma }_{i}\left( 0\right) \) and \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) along \( {\gamma }_{i} \) and \( \gamma \) , respectively, where \( {t}_{o}^{i},{t}_{o} \in  R \cup  \{ \infty \} \) . We have to prove that \( \lim {t}_{o}^{i} = {t}_{o} \) .

First let us prove that \( \lim \sup {t}_{o}^{i} \leq  {t}_{o} \) . If \( {t}_{o} = \infty \) , there is nothing to prove. Let then \( {t}_{o} < \infty \) and let \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) . Observe that there do not exist infinitely many indices \( j \) such that \( {t}_{o} + \varepsilon  < {t}_{o}^{j} \) . Otherwise,

\[
d\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( 0\right) ,{\gamma }_{j}\left( {{t}_{o} + \varepsilon }\right) }\right)  = {t}_{o} + \varepsilon
\]

and, by continuity of \( d, d\left( {\gamma \left( 0\right) ,\gamma \left( {{t}_{o} + \varepsilon }\right) }\right)  = {t}_{o} + \varepsilon \) , which contradicts the fact that \( \gamma \left( {t}_{o}\right) \) is a cut point of \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) along \( \gamma \) . Therefore \( \lim \sup {t}_{o}^{i} \leq  {t}_{o} + \varepsilon \) , for all \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , which proves the claim made.

Now let \( \bar{t} = \liminf {t}_{o}^{i} \) . Since

\[
\overline{t} = \liminf {t}_{o}^{i} \leq  \limsup {t}_{o}^{i} \leq  {t}_{o},
\]

it suffices to show that \( \bar{t} \geq  {t}_{o} \) to complete the proof.

For this, suppose \( \bar{t} < \infty \) (if \( \bar{t} = \infty \) nothing need be proved), and consider a subsequence of the sequence \( {t}_{o}^{j} \) , again denoted by \( {t}_{o}^{j} \) , which converges to \( \bar{t} \) . Because an accumulation point of conjugate points is a conjugate point, if for any such subsequence, the points \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {t}_{o}^{j}\right) \) are conjugate to \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( 0\right) \) along \( {\gamma }_{j} \) , then \( \gamma \left( \bar{t}\right) \) is conjugate to \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) along \( \gamma \) , hence \( \bar{t} \geq  {t}_{o} \) , and we have concluded the proof.

Suppose, therefore, that there exists a subsequence \( {t}_{o}^{j} \rightarrow  \bar{t} \) in which, for all \( j,{\gamma }_{j}\left( {t}_{o}^{j}\right) \) is not conjugate to \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( 0\right) \) along \( {\gamma }_{j} \) . By Proposition 2.2, there exist geodesics \( {\sigma }_{j} \neq  {\gamma }_{j} \) with

\[
{\sigma }_{j}\left( 0\right)  = {\gamma }_{j}\left( 0\right) ,\;{\sigma }_{j}\left( {t}_{o}^{j}\right)  = {\gamma }_{j}\left( {t}_{o}^{j}\right) ,\;\ell \left( {\sigma }_{j}\right)  = \ell \left( {\gamma }_{j}\right) .
\]

Taking, if necessary, a subsequence, we can suppose that \( {\sigma }_{j} \rightarrow  \sigma \) , where \( \sigma \) is a geodesic joining \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) to \( \gamma \left( \bar{t}\right) \) . If \( \sigma  \neq  \gamma \) , by Proposition 2.2, we have \( {t}_{o} \leq  \bar{t} \) , as required. If \( \sigma  = \gamma \) , then, by a similar argument as in Proposition 2.2, we show that \( \gamma \left( \bar{t}\right) \) is conjugate to \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) , hence \( \bar{t} \geq  {t}_{o} \) .

nodes.content: 2.10 COROLLARY. For all \( p \in  M \) , \( {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \) is closed; in particular, if \( M \) is compact, \( {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \) is compact.
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.10 COROLLARY. For all \( p \in M \) , \( {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \) is closed; in particular, if \( M \) is compact, \( {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \) is compact.

nodes.proof:
It is easy to verify that

\[
{C}_{m}\left( p\right)  = \left\{  {\gamma \left( t\right) ;t = f\left( {p,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) }\right\}  ,
\]

where \( \gamma  : \lbrack 0,\infty ) \rightarrow  M \) is a normalized geodesic with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p \) and \( f \) is the function of Proposition 2.9. Therefore, if \( q \) is an accumulation point of \( {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \) , there exists a sequence \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {t}_{j}\right) \) , with \( {t}_{j} = f\left( {p,{\gamma }_{j}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) , such that \( \lim {\gamma }_{j}\left( {t}_{j}\right)  = q \) . Passing to a subsequence, if necessary, the sequence \( {\gamma }_{j}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) converges to a unit vector \( v \) . Let \( \gamma \) be the geodesic with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = v \) . Then, since \( f \) is continuous,

\[
q = \lim {\gamma }_{j}\left( {t}_{j}\right)  = \lim {\gamma }_{j}\left( {f\left( {p,{\gamma }_{j}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= \mathop{\lim }\limits_{j}{\exp }_{p}\left( {f\left( {p,{\gamma }_{j}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) {\gamma }_{j}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right)  = {\exp }_{p}\left( {f\left( {p,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= \gamma \left( {f\left( {p,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) }\right)  \in  {C}_{m}\left( p\right) ,
\]

which shows that \( {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \) is closed.

nodes.content: 2.11 COROLLARY. Suppose that \( M \) is complete and that there exists \( p \in  M \) which has a cut point for every geodesic starting from p. Then \( M \) is compact.
nodes.content_excerpt: 2.11 COROLLARY. Suppose that \( M \) is complete and that there exists \( p \in M \) which has a cut point for every geodesic starting from p. Then \( M \) is compact.

nodes.proof:
Observe that

\[
M =  \cup  \{ \gamma \left( t\right) ;t \leq  f\left( {p,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) \}
\]

for all geodesics \( \gamma \) of \( M \) with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p \) . The hypothesis of the corollary and the continuity of \( f \) imply that \( f \) is bounded. Therefore \( M \) is bounded and the theorem follows from the Hopf-Rinow Theorem.

The hypothesis of the corollary and the continuity of \( f \) imply that \( f \) is bounded. Therefore \( M \) is bounded and the theorem follows from the Hopf-Rinow Theorem.

2.12 Proposition. Let \( p \in  M \) . Suppose that there exists a point \( q \in  {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \) which realizes the distance from \( p \) to \( {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \) . Then:

a) either there exists a minimizing geodesic \( \gamma \) from \( p \) to \( q \) along which \( q \) is conjugate to \( p \) ,

b) or there exist exactly two minimizing geodesics \( \gamma \) and \( \sigma \) from \( p \) to \( q \) ; in addition, \( {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( \ell \right)  =  - {\sigma }^{\prime }\left( \ell \right) ,\ell  = d\left( {p, q}\right) \) .

Suppose that there exists a point \( q \in {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \) which realizes the distance from \( p \) to \( {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \) . Then: a) either there exists a minimizing geodesic \( \gamma \) from \( p \) to \( q \) along which \( q \) is conjugate to \( p \) , b) or there exist exactly two minimizing geodesics \( \gamma \) and \( \sigma \) from \( p \) to \( q...

nodes.proof:
Let \( \gamma \) be a minimizing geodesic joining \( p \) to \( q \) . By Proposition 2.2, either \( q \) is conjugate to \( p \) along \( \gamma \) , and (a) holds, or there exists another minimizing geodesic \( \sigma  \neq  \gamma \) , joining \( p \) to \( q \) with \( \ell \left( \sigma \right)  = \ell \left( \gamma \right) \) . Suppose then that \( q \) is not conjugate to \( p \) along \( \gamma \) and \( \sigma \) , and that \( {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( \ell \right)  \neq   - {\sigma }^{\prime }\left( \ell \right) \) , from which we are going to derive a contradiction. In particular, this shows that, in this situation, there can be only two such geodesics.

Because \( {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( \ell \right)  \neq   - {\sigma }^{\prime }\left( \ell \right) \) , there exists \( V \in  {T}_{q}\left( M\right) \) such that

\[
\langle V,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( \ell \right) \rangle  < 0,\;\langle V,{\sigma }^{\prime }\left( \ell \right) \rangle  < 0.
\]

Let \( \tau  : \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)  \rightarrow  M \) be a curve with \( \tau \left( 0\right)  = q,{\tau }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = V \) . Since \( q \) is not conjugate to \( p \) along \( \gamma \) , there exists a neighborhood \( U \subset  {T}_{p}M \) of \( \ell {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) where \( {\exp }_{p} \) is a diffeomorphism. Let \( v : \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right)  \rightarrow \; U \) be a curve such that \( {\exp }_{p}v\left( s\right)  = \tau \left( s\right) , s \in  \left( {-\varepsilon ,\varepsilon }\right) \) , and let \( {\gamma }_{s}\left( t\right)  = \; {\exp }_{p}\frac{t}{\ell }v\left( s\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack \) , be a variation of \( \gamma \) (see Fig. 5). By the formula for the first variation,

\[
{\left. \frac{d}{ds}\ell \left( {\gamma }_{s}\right) \right| }_{s = 0} = \left\langle  {V,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( \ell \right) }\right\rangle   < 0.
\]

Because \( q \) is not conjugate to \( p \) along \( \sigma \) , we obtain in an analogous manner a variation \( {\sigma }_{s}\left( t\right) \) of \( \sigma \) such that:

\[
{\left. \frac{d}{ds}\left( \ell \left( {\sigma }_{s}\right) \right) \right| }_{s = 0} = \left\langle  {V,{\sigma }^{\prime }\left( \ell \right) }\right\rangle   < 0
\]

\[
{\sigma }_{s}\left( \ell \right)  = \tau \left( s\right)
\]

Therefore, if \( s > 0 \) is sufficiently small, \( \ell \left( {\gamma }_{s}\right)  < \ell \left( \gamma \right) \) and \( \ell \left( {\sigma }_{s}\right)  < \ell \left( \sigma \right) . \)

If \( \ell \left( {\gamma }_{s}\right)  = \ell \left( {\sigma }_{s}\right) \) , from Proposition 2.2, \( \tau \left( s\right)  = {\gamma }_{s}\left( \ell \right) \) is a cut point of \( p \) . Since

\[
d\left( {p,{\gamma }_{s}\left( \ell \right) }\right)  = \ell \left( {\gamma }_{s}\right)  < d\left( {p,{C}_{m}\left( p\right) }\right) ,
\]

this contradicts the fact that \( q \) realizes the distance from \( p \) to \( {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \) . If \( \ell \left( {\gamma }_{s}\right)  < \ell \left( {\sigma }_{s}\right) ,{\sigma }_{s} \) is not minimizing, hence there exists a cut point \( {\sigma }_{s}\left( \widetilde{t}\right) ,\widetilde{t} < \ell \) , of \( p \) along \( {\sigma }_{s} \) . But this contradicts again the fact that \( q \) realizes the distance from \( p \) to \( {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \) . The case \( \ell \left( {\gamma }_{s}\right)  > \ell \left( {\sigma }_{s}\right) \) is similar.

b) there exists a closed geodesic \( \gamma \) in \( M \) , whose length is less than that of any other closed geodesic in \( M \) , and which is such that

\[
i\left( M\right)  = \frac{1}{2}\ell \left( \gamma \right) .
\]

By the Theorem of Bonnet-Myers (Theor. 3.1 of Chap. 9), M is compact. Since \( {T}_{1}M \) is compact, it follows from Proposition 2.9 that there exists \( p \in  M \) such that \( d\left( {p,{C}_{m}\left( p\right) }\right)  = \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{r \in  M}}d\left( {r,{C}_{m}\left( r\right) }\right) \) . Because \( {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \) is compact, there exists \( q \in  {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \) such that \( q \) assumes the distance from \( p \) to \( {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \) .

If \( q \) is conjugate to \( p, d\left( {p, q}\right)  \geq  \pi /\sqrt{{K}_{\max }} \) from Proposition 2.4 of Chapter 10. If \( q \) is not conjugate to \( p \) , there exists, by Proposition 2.12, two minimizing geodesics \( \mu \) and \( \sigma \) from \( p \) to \( q \) , with \( {\mu }^{\prime }\left( \ell \right)  =  - {\sigma }^{\prime }\left( \ell \right) ,\ell  = d\left( {p, q}\right) \) . Since \( q \in  {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \) , we have that \( p \in  {C}_{m}\left( q\right) \) and, by its very definition, \( p \) realizes the distance from \( q \) to \( {C}_{m}\left( q\right) \) . It follows that \( {\mu }^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  =  - {\sigma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) , hence \( \mu \) and \( \sigma \) form a closed geodesic \( \gamma \) which, clearly, satisfies (b).

nodes.content_excerpt: 3.1 Proposition. (Klingenberg [Kℓ2]). Let \( {M}^{n}, n \geq 3 \) , be a simply connected, compact Riemannian manifold, such that 1/4 < \( K \leq 1 \) . Then, \( i\left( M\right) \geq \pi \) .

nodes.proof:
Suppose \( i\left( M\right)  < \pi \) . From Proposition 2.13, there exists a closed geodesic \( \gamma \) in \( M \) of length \( \ell  = \ell \left( \gamma \right)  < \; {2\pi } \) .

From the Corollary 2.10 of Chap. 11, the set of conjugate points to \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) along \( \gamma \) is discrete. Choose an \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) satisfying the following conditions \( \left( {{B}_{a}\left( q\right) }\right. \) denotes the open ball with center \( q \) and radius \( a \) ):

1) \( \gamma \left( {\ell  - \varepsilon }\right) \) is not conjugate to \( p = \gamma \left( 0\right) \) along \( \gamma \) ;

2) \( {\exp }_{p} \) is a diffeomorphism on \( {B}_{2\varepsilon }\left( p\right) \) ;

3) \( {3\varepsilon } < {2\pi } - \pi /\sqrt{\widetilde{K}} \) , where \( \widetilde{K} = \mathop{\inf }\limits_{M}K \) ;

4) \( {3\varepsilon } < {2\pi } - \ell \) ;

5) \( {5\varepsilon } < {2\pi } \) .

From Sard’s Theorem, there exists a regular value \( q \in \; {B}_{\varepsilon }\left( {\gamma \left( {\ell  - \varepsilon }\right) }\right) \) of \( {\exp }_{p} \) . By (1), it is possible to choose \( q \) in such a way that \( q = {\gamma }_{1}\left( t\right) \) , where \( {\gamma }_{1} \) is a geodesic starting from \( p \) with \( {3\varepsilon } < \ell \left( {\gamma }_{1}\right)  < \ell \) (v. Fig. 7).

![019eafb3-a904-7162-90c5-5ccd2f5d76bf_94_246_357_1287_832_0.jpg](images/019eafb3-a904-7162-90c5-5ccd2f5d76bf_94_246_357_1287_832_0.jpg)

Figure 7

Let \( {\gamma }_{o} \) be a minimizing geodesic joining \( p \) to \( q \) . Then by (2),

\[
\ell \left( {\gamma }_{o}\right)  \leq  d\left( {p,\gamma \left( {\ell  - \varepsilon }\right) }\right)  + d\left( {\gamma \left( {\ell  - \varepsilon }\right) , q}\right)  \leq  {2\varepsilon }
\]

hence \( {\gamma }_{o} \neq  {\gamma }_{1} \) .

Consider the space \( {\Omega }_{p, q}^{c} \) of Remark 2.12 of Chapter 11 and its finite dimensional approximation \( B \) . Because \( q \) is a regular value of \( {\exp }_{p} \) , all of the critical points in \( {\Omega }_{p, q}^{c} \) are non-degenerate. From the fact that \( M \) is simply connected, there exists a homotopy \( {\gamma }_{s} \) between \( {\gamma }_{o} \) and \( {\gamma }_{1} \) , keeping fixed the points \( p \) and \( q \) . Since \( B \) is a deformation retract of \( {\Omega }_{p, q}^{c} \) , the homotopy \( {\gamma }_{s} \) (which is a curve in \( {\Omega }_{p, q}^{c} \) ) is deformed to a curve in \( B \) . From the remark after Lemma 3.3, for all \( \delta  > 0,{\gamma }_{s} \) can be deformed by a homotopy \( {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{s} \) from \( {\gamma }_{o} \) to \( {\gamma }_{1} \) in such a way that the curve of larger length \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) of \( {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{s} \) satisfies the following condition: \( \ell \left( \widetilde{\gamma }\right)  < a + \delta \) , where \( a = \max \left\{  {\ell \left( {\gamma }_{o}\right) ,\ell \left( {\gamma }_{1}\right) ,\ell \left( \sigma \right) }\right\} \) and \( \sigma \) is the geodesic of larger length with index \( \sigma  < 2 \) in \( {\Omega }_{p, q}^{c} \) .

Put \( \delta  = \varepsilon \) . We have already seen that \( \ell \left( {\gamma }_{o}\right)  \leq  {2\varepsilon } \) and that \( \ell \left( {\gamma }_{1}\right)  < \ell  < {2\pi } - {3\varepsilon } \) , by (4). To estimate \( \ell \left( \sigma \right) \) , apply Lemma 3.2 to the case in which \( \widetilde{M} \) is a sphere with curvature \( \widetilde{K} = \mathop{\inf }\limits_{M}K > 1/4 \) obtaining

index \( \widetilde{\sigma } \leq \) index \( \sigma  < 2 \) .

Since \( \widetilde{\sigma } \) is a geodesic on \( {S}^{n}, n \geq  3 \) , it follows from the Morse Index Theorem that if \( \ell \left( \sigma \right)  > \pi /\sqrt{\widetilde{K}} \) then index \( \widetilde{\sigma } \geq  2 \) . Therefore, by \( \left( 3\right) ,\ell \left( \sigma \right)  \leq  \pi /\sqrt{\widetilde{K}} < {2\pi } - {3\varepsilon } \) . It follows then, by (5), that

\[
\ell \left( \widetilde{\gamma }\right)  < a + \varepsilon  < {2\pi } - {3\varepsilon } + \varepsilon  = {2\pi } - {2\varepsilon }.
\]

On the other hand, the Lemma of Klingenberg (see Exercise 1 of Chap. 10) yields that in the homotopy \( {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{s} \) there exists a curve \( {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{{s}_{o}} \) with \( \ell \left( {\gamma }_{o}\right)  + \ell \left( {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{{s}_{o}}\right)  \geq  {2\pi } \) . It follows that

\[
\ell \left( \widetilde{\gamma }\right)  \geq  \ell \left( {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{{s}_{o}}\right)  \geq  {2\pi } - \ell \left( {\gamma }_{o}\right)  \geq  {2\pi } - {2\varepsilon }
\]

which contradicts the fact above that \( \ell \left( \widetilde{\gamma }\right)  < {2\pi } - {2\varepsilon } \) , and shows that the hypothesis \( i\left( M\right)  < \pi \) untenable. This completes the proof of Proposition 3.1.

3.2 LEMMA. Let \( M \) and \( \bar{M} \) be Riemannian manifolds of the same dimension and such that their sectional curvatures \( K \) and \( \widetilde{K} \) , respectively, satisfy \( \sup \widetilde{K} \leq  \inf K \) . Consider a geodesic \( \sigma  : \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) , \( \sigma \left( 0\right)  = p \) , and fix a point \( \widetilde{p} \in  \widetilde{M} \) . Let \( i : {T}_{p}M \rightarrow  {T}_{\widetilde{p}}\widetilde{M} \) be a linear isometry and let \( \widetilde{\sigma } : \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \widetilde{M} \) be given by

\[
\widetilde{\sigma }\left( t\right)  = {\exp }_{\widetilde{p}}t\left( {i{\sigma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right) ,\;t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\ell }\right\rbrack
\]

Then index \( \sigma  \geq \) index \( \widetilde{\sigma } \) .

nodes.proof:
Let \( \widetilde{W} \) be a piecewise differentiable vector field along \( \widetilde{\sigma } \) . Define, as usual (Cf. Chap. 10), a vector field \( W \) along \( \sigma \) by

\[
W\left( t\right)  = {\phi }^{-1}\left( \widetilde{W}\right) \left( t\right)  = {P}_{t} \circ  {i}^{-1} \circ  {\widetilde{P}}_{t}^{-1}\left( {\widetilde{W}\left( t\right) }\right) ,
\]

where, for example, \( {P}_{t} \) is the parallel transport along \( \sigma \) from 0 to \( t \) . It is clear that (Cf. Eq. (4) of Chap. 10)

\[
\left\langle  {W,{\sigma }^{\prime }}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {\widetilde{W},{\widetilde{\sigma }}^{\prime }}\right\rangle  ,\;\left| {W\left( t\right) }\right|  = \left| {\widetilde{W}\left( t\right) }\right| ,\;\left\langle  {{W}^{\prime },{W}^{\prime }}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {{\widetilde{W}}^{\prime },{\widetilde{W}}^{\prime }}\right\rangle  .
\]

Because \( \sup \widetilde{K} \leq  \inf K \) , we conclude that \( I\left( {W, W}\right)  \leq  I\left( {\widetilde{W},\widetilde{W}}\right) \) . Therefore, if \( I\left( {\widetilde{W},\widetilde{W}}\right)  < 0 \) , we have that \( I\left( {W, W}\right)  < 0 \) , which proves the lemma.

3.3 LEMMA. Let \( {M}^{n} \) be a differentiable manifold and let \( f : {M}^{n} \rightarrow \; R \) be a differentiable function whose critical points are all nondegenerate. Given \( p, q \in  M \) and a differentiable curve \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p,\gamma \left( 1\right)  = q \) , let \( a = \max \{ f\left( p\right) , f\left( q\right) \} \) , and put

\[
{M}^{a} = \{ x \in  M;f\left( x\right)  \leq  a\} ,
\]

\( b = \mathop{\max }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack  }}\left( {f \circ  \gamma \left( t\right) }\right) \) . Assume that \( {f}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack  \right) \) is compact and does not contain any critical points of index zero or one. Then, for all \( \delta  > 0,\gamma \) is homotopic, keeping endpoints fixed, to a curve \( \bar{\gamma } \) such that \( \widetilde{\gamma }\left( \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack  \right)  \subset  {M}^{a + \delta } \) .

nodes.proof:
Choose a Riemannian metric on \( M \) . We use, in the course of the proof, the following fact (cf. Milnor [Mi], p. 12). If \( {f}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}\right\rbrack  \right) \) is compact and does not contain critical points of \( f \) , using the vector field grad \( f \) (which vanishes exactly at the critical points of \( f \) ), we obtain a map \( h : {M}^{{a}_{2}} \rightarrow  {M}^{{a}_{1}} \) , which is a deformation retract, that is, \( h \mid  {M}^{{a}_{1}} = \) identity, and there exists a homotopy \( {h}_{s} : {M}^{{a}_{2}} \rightarrow  {M}^{{a}_{2}} \) , \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) , such that \( {h}_{o} = \) identity and \( {h}_{1} = h \) .

Let \( b \) be as in the statement. We can suppose \( b > a \) ; otherwise, there is nothing to prove. Let \( {p}_{1},\ldots ,{p}_{k} \) be the critical points of \( f \) in \( {M}^{b} - {M}^{a} \) , with values \( f\left( {p}_{i}\right)  = {c}_{i}, i = 1,\ldots , k \) . Since the critical points are isolated, we can perturb \( f \) on \( {M}^{b} - {M}^{a} \) in such a way that all the \( {c}_{i} \) ’s are distinct. Suppose therefore that \( b \geq  {c}_{1} > {c}_{2} > \cdots  > {c}_{k} > a. \)

If \( b \) is not a critical value of \( f,{f}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {{c}_{1} + \varepsilon , b}\right\rbrack  \right) \) does not contain critical points of \( f \) for sufficiently small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) . From the remark above, there exists a deformation retract \( {h}_{1} : {M}^{b} \rightarrow  {M}^{{c}_{1} + \varepsilon } \) and the curve \( {\gamma }_{1} = {h}_{1} \circ  \gamma \) is in \( {M}^{{c}_{1} + \varepsilon } \) . If \( b = {c}_{1} \) is a critical value of \( f \) , we proceed in the following way.

By hypothesis, \( {p}_{1} \) has index \( \lambda  \geq  2 \) . Let \( H \) be a neighborhood of \( {p}_{1} \) where \( f \) can be written in the form

\[
f = {\mathrm{c}}_{1} + {x}_{1}^{2} + \cdots  + {x}_{n - \lambda }^{2} - {y}_{1}^{2} - \cdots  - {y}_{\lambda }^{2}.
\]

Suppose that \( H \) and \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) are sufficiently small so that \( {M}^{{c}_{1} + \varepsilon } - \; \left( {{M}^{{c}_{1} - \varepsilon } \cup  H}\right) \) does not contain critical points. Then, using the vector field grad \( f \) we obtain a deformation retract \( {\bar{h}}_{1} : {M}^{{c}_{1} + \varepsilon } \rightarrow  {M}^{{c}_{1} - \varepsilon } \cup  H \) . Let \( {\bar{\gamma }}_{1} = {\bar{h}}_{1} \circ  \gamma  \subset  {M}^{{c}_{1} - \varepsilon } \cup  H \) .

Now let \( L \) be the set of points of \( H \) such that \( {y}_{1} = {y}_{2} = \cdots  = \; {y}_{\lambda } = 0 \) (see Fig. 6). Since

\[
\dim {\bar{\gamma }}_{1}^{\prime } + \dim L \leq  1 + n - 2 < \dim M
\]

it is possible, by transversality, to perturb \( {\bar{\gamma }}_{1} \) in such a way that \( {\bar{\gamma }}_{1}\left( \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack  \right)  \cap  L = \phi \) ; such a perturbation can be done in \( H \) , in a way that fixes the endpoints of \( {\bar{\gamma }}_{1} \) . Since, for points not in \( L \) , the trajectories of grad \( f \) go away from the critical point \( {p}_{1} \) , there exists a deformation retract \( {h}_{2} : {M}^{{c}_{1} - \varepsilon } \cup  \left( {H - L}\right)  \rightarrow  {M}^{{c}_{1} - \varepsilon } \) . It is clear that \( {\gamma }_{2} = {h}_{2} \circ  {\bar{\gamma }}_{1} \subset  {M}^{{c}_{1} - \varepsilon }. \)

Proceeding inductively, we obtain \( {\gamma }_{j} \subset  {M}^{{c}_{k} - \varepsilon } \) . Given \( \delta  > \) 0, there do not exist critical points in \( {M}^{{c}_{k} - \varepsilon } - {M}^{a + \delta } \) and we can obtain a deformation retract \( {h}_{j + 1} : {M}^{{c}_{k} - \varepsilon } \rightarrow  {M}^{a + \delta } \) . It is clear that \( \widetilde{\gamma } = {h}_{j + 1} \circ  {\gamma }_{j} \subset  {M}^{a + \delta } \) , as required.

With the same argument, we see that if there are critical points of index zero or one in \( {f}^{-1}\left( {\left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack  \text{ and }c}\right. \) is the largest value of such critical points, then \( \gamma \) is homotopic to a curve \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) with \( \widetilde{\gamma }\left( \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack  \right)  \subset \; {M}^{c + \delta } \) .

nodes.content: 3.4 Proposition. If the sectional curvature \( K \) of a compact ori-entable even dimensional Riemannian manifold \( {M}^{n} \) satisfies \( 0 < \; K \leq  1 \) , then \( i\left( M\right)  \geq  \pi \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 3.4 Proposition. If the sectional curvature \( K \) of a compact ori-entable even dimensional Riemannian manifold \( {M}^{n} \) satisfies \( 0 < \; K \leq 1 \) , then \( i\left( M\right) \geq \pi \) .

nodes.proof:
By compactness, there exist points \( p, q \in  M \) such that:

\[
q \in  {C}_{m}\left( p\right) \text{ and }d\left( {p, q}\right)  = i\left( M\right) .
\]

Supposing that \( d\left( {p, q}\right)  < \pi \) , we are going to obtain a contradiction.

If \( p \) is conjugate to \( q \) , it follows from Proposition 2.4 of Chap. 10 that \( d\left( {p, q}\right)  \geq  \pi \) , which contradicts the hypothesis. Therefore \( p \) is not conjugate to \( q \) and, by Proposition 2.12 and 2.13, there exists a closed geodesic \( \gamma \) passing through \( p = \gamma \left( 0\right) \) and \( q \) , and such that \( \ell \left( \gamma \right)  < {2\pi } \) . The parallel transport along the closed curve \( \gamma \) leaves invariant a vector \( V \) orthogonal to \( \gamma \) (cf. Lemma 3.8 of Chap. 9). Calculating the second variation \( {E}_{V}^{\prime \prime }\left( 0\right) \) for such \( V \) , we see that it is strictly negative. Therefore there exists a variation through regular closed curves \( {\gamma }_{s}\left( t\right) \) of \( \gamma , s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\varepsilon }\right\rbrack \) , such that \( \ell \left( {\gamma }_{s}\right)  < \ell \left( \gamma \right) \) for all \( s \neq  0 \) (the fact that \( M \) has even dimension plays a crucial role here).

Let \( {q}_{s} \) be a point of \( {\gamma }_{s} \) at a maximum distance from \( {\gamma }_{s}\left( 0\right) \) (see Fig 8). Since \( d\left( {{\gamma }_{s}\left( 0\right) ,{q}_{s}}\right)  < d\left( {p, q}\right) \) , there exists a unique minimizing geodesic \( {\sigma }_{s} \) joining \( {q}_{s} = {\sigma }_{s}\left( 0\right) \) to \( {\gamma }_{s}\left( 0\right) \) . Because \( q \) is the unique point of \( \gamma \) which is at maximum distance from \( p \) , \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{s \rightarrow  0}}{\sigma }_{s}\left( 0\right)  = q \) . In addition, by local compactness of the tangent bundle, there exists in \( {T}_{q}\left( M\right) \) an accumulation point \( w \) of the vectors \( {\sigma }_{s}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) . By continuity, the geodesic \( \sigma \left( t\right)  = {\exp }_{q}{tw} \) is a minimizing geodesic joining \( q \) to \( p \) . On the other hand, let \( {\sigma }_{s, t} \) be a minimizing geodesic joining \( {\gamma }_{s}\left( 0\right) \) to a point \( {\gamma }_{s}\left( t\right) \) , close to \( {q}_{s} \) . Then \( {\sigma }_{s, t} \) is a variation of \( {\sigma }_{s} \) and, applying the formula for the first variation, we conclude that \( {\sigma }_{s}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) is orthogonal to \( {\gamma }_{s}^{\prime } \) at \( {q}_{s} \) , for all \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\varepsilon }\right\rbrack \) ; therefore \( {\sigma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) is orthogonal to \( {\gamma }^{\prime } \) at \( q \) . It follows that there exist three minimizing geodesics joining \( p \) to \( q \) . Since \( p \) is not conjugate to \( q \) , this contradicts Proposition 2.12.

nodes.content: 3.5 REMARK. From Synge's theorem (see Chap. 9, Cor. 3.10), the manifolds which satisfy the hypotheses of Proposition 3.4 are simply connected. On the other hand, a simply connected manifold is ori-entable; otherwise, it has a two-sheeted covering (see Exercise 12 of Chap. 0), which contradicts the fact it is simply connected. Therefore, the hypothesis of orientability in Proposition 4 is equivalent to the assumption that \( M \) be simply connected.

nodes.content: 4.1 LEMMA. (Berger [Br 1]). Let \( M \) be a compact Riemannian manifold, and let \( p, q \in  M \) be such that \( d\left( {p, q}\right)  = \operatorname{diam}M \) . Then, for all \( W \in  {T}_{p}M \) , there exists a minimizing geodesic \( \gamma \) from \( p = \gamma \left( 0\right) \) to \( q \) with \( \left\langle  {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) , W}\right\rangle   \geq  0 \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 4.1 LEMMA. (Berger [Br 1]). Let \( M \) be a compact Riemannian manifold, and let \( p, q \in M \) be such that \( d\left( {p, q}\right) = \operatorname{diam}M \) . Then, for all \( W \in {T}_{p}M \) , there exists a minimizing geodesic \( \gamma \) from \( p = \gamma \left( 0\right) \) to \( q \) with \( \left\langle {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) , W}\right\rangle \geq 0 \) .

nodes.proof:
Let \( \lambda \left( t\right)  = {\exp }_{p}{tW} \) and let \( {\gamma }_{t} : \left\lbrack  {0,\ell \left( {\gamma }_{t}\right) }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) be a minimizing geodesic such that \( {\gamma }_{t}\left( 0\right)  = \lambda \left( t\right) ,{\gamma }_{t}\left( {\ell \left( {\gamma }_{t}\right) }\right)  = q \) . Suppose, first, that for each integer \( n \) there exists a \( {t}_{n},0 \leq  {t}_{n} \leq  \frac{1}{n} \) , such that \( \left\langle  {{\gamma }_{{t}_{n}}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,{\lambda }^{\prime }\left( {t}_{n}\right) }\right\rangle   \geq  0 \) . Passing to a subsequence, if necessary, the sequence \( {\gamma }_{{t}_{n}} \) converges to a minimizing geodesic \( \gamma \) which satisfies

\[
0 \leq  \left\langle  {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,{\lambda }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) , W}\right\rangle  ,
\]

and the proof would be finished.

Suppose now that there exists an \( n \) such that for all \( t,0 \leq \; t \leq  1/n,\left\langle  {{\gamma }_{t}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,{\lambda }^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right\rangle   < 0 \) holds. We are going to show that this leads to a contradiction.

Consider a totally normal neighborhood \( U \) of \( \lambda \left( t\right) \) , and let \( {q}_{o} \in  U \) be a point of \( {\gamma }_{t} \) . Let \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) be sufficiently small, \( s \in  \left( {t - \varepsilon , t + \varepsilon }\right) \) and let \( {\sigma }_{s} \) be a minimizing geodesic joining \( {q}_{o} \) to \( \lambda \left( s\right) \) (see Fig. 9). Using the formula for the first variation of energy, we obtain

\[
{\left. \frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{ds}E\left( {\sigma }_{s}\right) \right| }_{s = t} =  - \left\langle  {{\gamma }_{t}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,{\lambda }^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right\rangle   > 0.
\]

Therefore, for \( s < t, d\left( {{q}_{o},\lambda \left( s\right) }\right)  < d\left( {{q}_{o},\lambda \left( t\right) }\right) \) holds, hence

\[
d\left( {q,\lambda \left( s\right) }\right)  < d\left( {q,{q}_{o}}\right)  + d\left( {{q}_{o},\lambda \left( s\right) }\right)  < d\left( {q,{q}_{o}}\right)
\]

\[
+ d\left( {{q}_{o},\lambda \left( t\right) }\right)  = d\left( {q,\lambda \left( t\right) }\right) .
\]

On the other hand, since \( p \) is at a maximum distance from \( q \) , \( d\left( {q,\lambda \left( t\right) }\right)  \leq  d\left( {q,\lambda \left( 0\right) }\right) \) , which furnishes the desired contradiction.

nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
4.2 LEMMA. Let \( {M}^{n} \) be a compact, simply connected Riemannian manifold whose sectional curvature \( K \) satisfies

\[
\frac{1}{4} < \delta  \leq  K \leq  1
\]

and let \( p, q \in  M \) be such that \( d\left( {p, q}\right)  = \operatorname{diam}\left( M\right) \) . Then

\[
M = {B}_{\rho }\left( p\right)  \cup  {B}_{\rho }\left( q\right)
\]

where \( {B}_{r}\left( p\right)  \subset  M \) denotes the open geodesic ball of radius \( r \) and center \( p \in  M \) and \( \rho \) is such that \( \pi /2\sqrt{\delta } < \rho  < \pi \) .
