Then \[ M = {B}_{\rho }\left( p\right) \cup {B}_{\rho }\left( q\right) \] where \( {B}_{r}\left( p\right) \subset M \) denotes the open geodesic ba...

nodes.proof:
By the estimate of the injectivity radius of Section 3, \( {B}_{p}\left( p\right) \) does not contain points of the cut locus of \( p \) . Therefore \( {B}_{\rho }\left( p\right) \) is diffeomorphic, through the exponential map, to an Euclidean ball, and the same thing happens for \( {B}_{\rho }\left( q\right) \) . It is at this point that the estimate \( i\left( M\right)  \geq  \pi \) enters, in a crucial manner, in the Sphere Theorem.

Suppose that there exists \( r \in  M \) such that \( d\left( {p, r}\right)  \geq  \rho \) , \( d\left( {q, r}\right)  \geq  \rho \) . Then we are going to obtain a contradiction. We can assume that \( d\left( {p, r}\right)  \geq  d\left( {q, r}\right)  \geq  \rho \) .

A minimizing geodesic from \( q \) to \( r \) intersects \( \partial \left( {{B}_{\rho }\left( q\right) }\right) \) in a point \( {q}^{\prime } \notin  {B}_{\rho }\left( p\right) \) ; otherwise,

\[
d\left( {r,{q}^{\prime }}\right)  > d\left( {r,{B}_{\rho }\left( p\right) }\right)  \geq  d\left( {r,{B}_{\rho }\left( q\right) }\right)  = d\left( {r,{q}^{\prime }}\right) ,
\]

which is absurd. On the other hand, from the Theorem of Bonnet-Myers, \( \operatorname{diam}\left( M\right)  \leq  \pi /\sqrt{\delta } < {2\rho } \) . Therefore, if \( {q}^{\prime \prime } \) is a point of intersection of the minimizing geodesic from \( q \) to \( p \) with \( \partial {B}_{\rho }\left( q\right) \) , then \( {q}^{\prime \prime } \in  {B}_{\rho }\left( p\right) \) , since,

\[
d\left( {p,{q}^{\prime \prime }}\right)  = d\left( {p, q}\right)  - d\left( {q,{q}^{\prime \prime }}\right)  < {2\rho } - \rho  = \rho .
\]

Since \( \partial {B}_{\rho }\left( q\right) \) is path connected (because \( {B}_{\rho }\left( q\right) \) is homeomorphic to an Euclidean ball), it follows that \( \partial {B}_{\rho }\left( p\right)  \cap  \partial {B}_{\rho }\left( q\right)  \neq  \phi \) , hence there exists \( {r}_{o} \in  M \) such that \( d\left( {{r}_{o}, p}\right)  = d\left( {{r}_{o}, q}\right)  = \rho \) . The desired contradiction obtains from the existence of such an \( {r}_{o} \) .

Consider a minimizing geodesic \( \lambda \) joining \( p \) to \( {r}_{o} \) . By Berger’s Lemma, there exists a minimizing geodesic \( \gamma \) from \( p \) to \( q \) with \( \left\langle  {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) ,{\lambda }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\right\rangle   \geq  0 \) (Fig. 10). Let \( s \) be a point of \( \gamma \) such that \( d\left( {p, s}\right)  = \rho \) . Apply Rauch’s Theorem to this situation (see Proposition 2.5 of Chap. 10), comparing \( {M}^{n} \) with a sphere \( {S}^{n} \) of constant curvature \( \delta \) . Since the angle \( \lambda {r}_{o}{ps} \leq  \pi /2 \) and \( d\left( {{r}_{o}, s}\right) \) is less than or equal to the length of any curve in \( M \) joining \( {r}_{o} \) to \( s \) , we conclude that

\[
d\left( {{r}_{o}, s}\right)  \leq  \pi /2\sqrt{\delta }.
\]

Since \( d\left( {{r}_{o}, p}\right)  = d\left( {{r}_{o}, q}\right)  = \rho \) , and there exists a point \( s \) of \( \gamma \) with \( d\left( {{r}_{o}, s}\right)  < \rho \) , the distance from \( {r}_{o} \) to \( \gamma \) is realized by a point

\( {s}_{o} \) in the interior of \( \gamma \) . The minimizing geodesic from \( {r}_{o} \) to \( {s}_{o} \) is orthogonal to \( \gamma \) , and

\[
d\left( {{r}_{o},\gamma }\right)  = d\left( {{r}_{o},{s}_{o}}\right)  \leq  \pi /2\sqrt{\delta }.
\]

Since \( d\left( {p, q}\right)  \leq  \pi /\sqrt{\delta } \) , we have that either \( d\left( {p,{s}_{o}}\right)  \leq  \pi /2\sqrt{\delta } \) or \( d\left( {q,{s}_{o}}\right)  \leq  \pi /2\sqrt{\delta } \) . In either of the two cases, we obtain the desired contradiction. Consider the case \( d\left( {p,{s}_{o}}\right)  \leq  \pi /2\sqrt{\delta } \) , the other case being analogous. In this case, since \( d\left( {{r}_{o},{s}_{o}}\right)  \leq  \pi /2\sqrt{\delta } \) and the angle * * \( p{s}_{o}{r}_{o} = \pi /2 \) , we have, by the comparison the Theorem of Rauch cited above, \( d\left( {p,{r}_{o}}\right)  \leq  \pi /2\sqrt{\delta } < \rho \) , which contradicts the fact that \( d\left( {p,{r}_{o}}\right)  = \rho \) , and concludes the proof.

nodes.label: Lemma 4.3
nodes.document_title: Manfredo P. do Carmo - Riemannian Geometry
nodes.content:
4.3 LEMMA. Under the conditions of Lemma 4.2, on each geodesic of length \( \rho \) starting from \( p \) there exists a unique point \( m \) such that

\[
d\left( {p, m}\right)  = d\left( {q, m}\right)  < \rho .
\]

Similarly, on each geodesic starting from \( q \) of length \( \rho \) there exists a unique point \( n \) equidistant from \( p \) and \( q \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 4.3 LEMMA. Under the conditions of Lemma 4.2, on each geodesic of length \( \rho \) starting from \( p \) there exists a unique point \( m \) such that \[ d\left( {p, m}\right) = d\left( {q, m}\right) < \rho . \] Similarly, on each geodesic starting from \( q \) of length \( \rho \) there exists a unique point \( n \) equidistant from \( p \) and \( q \) .

nodes.proof:
Let \( \gamma \left( s\right) \) be a geodesic with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p \) and consider the difference

\[
d\left( {q,\gamma \left( s\right) }\right)  - d\left( {p,\gamma \left( s\right) }\right)  = f\left( s\right) .
\]

The function \( f \) is evidently continuous and \( f\left( 0\right)  = d\left( {q, p}\right)  > 0 \) . Let \( {s}_{o} \) be such that \( \gamma \left( {s}_{o}\right) \) is the cut point of \( p \) along \( \gamma \) . Then by the estimate of Klingenberg (Prop. 3.l, or Prop. 3.4 for the even dimensional case), \( d\left( {p,\gamma \left( {s}_{o}\right) }\right)  \geq  \pi  > \rho \) . From Lemma 4.2, \( d\left( {q,\gamma \left( {s}_{o}\right) }\right)  < \rho \) . Therefore,

\[
f\left( {s}_{o}\right)  = d\left( {q,\gamma \left( {s}_{o}\right) }\right)  - d\left( {p,\gamma \left( {s}_{o}\right) }\right)  < 0.
\]

It follows that \( f \) vanishes for some \( {s}_{1} \in  \left( {0,{s}_{o}}\right) \) ; that is, there exists \( m = \gamma \left( {s}_{1}\right) \) satisfying the claim.

To prove uniqueness, suppose that there exists \( {m}_{1} \neq  {m}_{2} \) . both equidistant from \( p \) and \( q \) . We can assume that \( {m}_{1} \) is between \( p \) and \( {m}_{2} \) . Then

\[
d\left( {q,{m}_{2}}\right)  = d\left( {p,{m}_{2}}\right)  = d\left( {p,{m}_{1}}\right)  + d\left( {{m}_{1},{m}_{2}}\right)  = d\left( {q,{m}_{1}}\right)  + d\left( {{m}_{1},{m}_{2}}\right) .
\]

Let \( {\sigma }_{1} \) be the (unique) minimizing geodesic joining \( q \) to \( {m}_{1} \) . By the equality above, \( {\sigma }_{1} \) coincides with \( \gamma \) , hence \( q \) belongs to \( \gamma \) . Since \( d\left( {p,{m}_{1}}\right)  = d\left( {q,{m}_{1}}\right) , d\left( {p,{m}_{2}}\right)  = d\left( {q,{m}_{2}}\right) \) and \( {m}_{1} \neq  {m}_{2} \) , we conclude that \( p = q \) , which contradicts the hypothesis. The situation for the point \( q \) is entirely analogous.

nodes.content: THEOREM 0.3. Let \( \left( {M,{g}_{0}}\right) \) be a closed Riemannian 3-manifold. Suppose that there is no embedded, locally separating \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) contained \( {}^{2} \) in \( M \) . Then there is a Ricci flow with surgery defined for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) with initial metric \( \left( {M,{g}_{0}}\right) \) . The set of discontinuity times for this Ricci flow with surgery is a discrete subset of \( \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) . The topological change in the 3-manifold as one crosses a surgery time is a connected sum decomposition together with removal of connected components, each of which is diffeomorphic to one of \( {S}^{2} \times  {S}^{1},\mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) , the non-orientable 2-sphere bundle over \( {S}^{1} \) , or a manifold admitting a metric of constant positive curvature.

nodes.content: THEOREM 0.4. Let \( M \) be a closed 3-manifold whose fundamental group is a free product of finite groups and infinite cyclic groups \( {}^{3} \) . Let \( {g}_{0} \) be any Riemannian metric on \( M \) . Then \( M \) admits no locally separating \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) , so that there is a Ricci flow with surgery defined for all positive time with \( \left( {M,{g}_{0}}\right) \) as initial metric as described in Theorem 0.3. This Ricci flow with surgery becomes extinct after some time \( T < \infty \) , in the sense that the manifolds \( {M}_{t} \) are empty for all \( t \geq  T \) .

nodes.content:
COROLLARY 0.5. Let \( \left( {{M}_{0},{g}_{0}}\right) \) be a connected Riemannian manifold with no locally separating \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) . Let \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) be a Ricci flow with surgery defined for \( 0 \leq  t < \infty \) with \( \left( {{M}_{0},{g}_{0}}\right) \) as initial manifold. Then the following four conditions are equivalent:

(1) \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) becomes extinct after a finite time, i.e., \( {M}_{T} = \varnothing \) for all \( T \) sufficiently large,

(2) \( {M}_{0} \) is diffeomorphic to a connected sum of three-dimensional spherical space-forms and \( {S}^{2} \) -bundles over \( {S}^{1} \) ,

(3) the fundamental group of \( {M}_{0} \) is a free product of finite groups and infinite cyclic groups,

(4) no prime \( {}^{4} \) factor of \( {M}_{0} \) is acyclic, i.e., every prime factor of \( {M}_{0} \) has either non-trivial \( {\pi }_{2} \) or non-trivial \( {\pi }_{3} \) .

nodes.proof: Repeated application of Theorem 0.3 shows that (1) implies (2). The implication (2) implies (3) is immediate from van Kampen's theorem. The fact that (3) implies (1) is Theorem 0.4. This shows that (1), (2) and (3) are all equivalent. Since three-dimensional spherical space-forms and \( {S}^{2} \) -bundles over \( {S}^{1} \) are easily seen to be prime,(2) implies (4). Thus, it remains only to see that (4) implies (3). We consider a manifold \( M \) satisfying (4), a prime factor \( P \) of \( M \) , and universal covering \( \widetilde{P} \) of \( P \) . First suppose that \( {\pi }_{2}\left( P\right)  = {\pi }_{2}\left( \widetilde{P}\right) \) is trivial. Then, by hypothesis \( {\pi }_{3}\left( P\right)  = {\pi }_{3}\left( \widetilde{P}\right) \) is non-trivial. By the Hurewicz theorem this means that \( {H}_{3}\left( \widetilde{P}\right) \) is non-trivial, and hence that \( \widetilde{P} \) is a compact, simply connected three-manifold. It follows that \( {\pi }_{1}\left( P\right) \) is finite. Now suppose that \( {\pi }_{2}\left( P\right) \) is non-trivial. Then \( P \) is not diffeomorphic to \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) . Since \( P \) is prime and contains no locally separating \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) , it follows that \( P \) contains no embedded \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) . Then by the sphere theorem there is an embedded 2-sphere in \( P \) that is homotopically non-trivial. Since \( P \) is prime, this sphere cannot separate, so cutting \( P \) open along it produces a connected manifold \( {P}_{0} \) with two boundary 2-spheres. Since \( {P}_{0} \) is prime, it follows that \( {P}_{0} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  I \) and hence \( P \) is diffeomorphic to a 2-sphere bundle over the circle.

nodes.label: Remark 0.6
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
REMARK 0.6. (i) The use of the sphere theorem is unnecessary in the above argument for what we actually prove is that if every prime factor of \( M \) has non-trivial \( {\pi }_{2} \) or non-trivial \( {\pi }_{3} \) , then the Ricci flow with surgery with \( \left( {M,{g}_{0}}\right) \) as initial metric becomes extinct after a finite time. In fact, the sphere theorem for closed 3-manifolds follows from the results here.

(ii) If the initial manifold is simpler then all the time-slices are simpler: If \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) is a Ricci flow with surgery whose initial manifold is prime, then every time-slice is a disjoint union of connected components, all but at most one being diffeomorphic to a 3-sphere and if there is one not diffeomorphic to a 3-sphere, then it is diffeomorphic to the initial manifold. If the initial manifold is a simply connected manifold \( {M}_{0} \) , then every component of every time-slice \( {M}_{T} \) must be simply connected, and thus a posteriori every time-slice is a disjoint union of manifolds diffeomorphic to the 3-sphere. Similarly, if the initial manifold has finite fundamental group, then every connected component of every time-slice is either simply connected or has the same fundamental group as the initial manifold.

(iii) The conclusion of this result is a natural generalization of Hamilton's conclusion in analyzing the Ricci flow on manifolds of positive Ricci curvature in [29]. Namely, under appropriate hypotheses, during the evolution process of Ricci flow with surgery the manifold breaks into components each of which disappears in finite time. As a component disappears at some finite time, the metric on that component is well enough controlled to show that the disappearing component admits a non-flat, homogeneous Riemannian metric of non-negative sectional curvature, i.e., a metric locally isometric to either a round \( {S}^{3} \) or to a product of a round \( {S}^{2} \) with the usual metric on \( \mathbb{R} \) . The existence of such a metric on a component immediately gives the topological conclusion of Theorem 0.1 for that component, i.e., that it is diffeomorphic to a 3-dimensional spherical space-form, to \( {S}^{2} \times  {S}^{1} \) to a nonorientable 2-sphere bundle over \( {S}^{1} \) , or to \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) . The biggest difference between these two results is that Hamilton's hypothesis is geometric (positive Ricci curvature) whereas Perelman's is homotopy theoretic (information about the fundamental group).

(iv) It is also worth pointing out that it follows from Corollary 0.5 that the manifolds that satisfy the four equivalent conditions in that corollary are exactly the closed, connected, 3-manifolds that admit a Riemannian metric of positive scalar curvature, cf, [62] and [26].

nodes.content: 2.1. Volume and injectivity radius. One important general concept that is used throughout is the notion of a manifold being non-collapsed at a point. Suppose that we have a point \( x \) in a complete Riemannian \( n \) -manifold. Then we say that the manifold is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed at \( x \) provided that the following holds: For any \( r \) such that the norm of the Riemann curvature tensor, \( \left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \) , is \( \leq  {r}^{-2} \) at all points of the metric ball, \( B\left( {x, r}\right) \) , of radius \( r \) centered at \( x \) , we have \( \operatorname{Vol}B\left( {x, r}\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}^{n} \) . There is a relationship between this notion and the injectivity radius of \( M \) at \( x \) . Namely, if \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right|  \leq  {r}^{-2} \) on \( B\left( {x, r}\right) \) and if \( B\left( {x, r}\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed then the injectivity radius of \( M \) at \( x \) is greater than or equal to a positive constant that depends only on \( r \) and \( \kappa \) . The advantage of working with the volume non-collapsing condition is that, unlike for the injectivity radius, there is a simple equation for the evolution of volume under Ricci flow.

nodes.content: The first is the soul theorem for manifolds of non-negative sectional curvature. A soul is a compact, totally geodesic submanifold. The entire manifold is diffeomorphic to the total space of a vector bundle over any of its souls. If a non-compact \( n \) -manifold has positive sectional curvature, then any soul for it is a point, and in particular, the manifold is diffeomorphic to Euclidean space. In addition, the distance function \( f \) from a soul has the property that, for every \( t > 0 \) , the pre-image \( {f}^{-1}\left( t\right) \) is homeomorphic to an \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -sphere and the pre-image under this distance function of any non-degenerate interval \( I \subset  {\mathbb{R}}^{ + } \) is homeomorphic to \( {S}^{n - 1} \times  I \) .

nodes.content: Another important result is the splitting theorem, which says that, if a complete manifold of non-negative sectional curvature has a geodesic line (an isometric copy of \( \mathbb{R} \) ) that is distance minimizing between every pair of its points, then that manifold is a metric product of a manifold of one lower dimension and \( \mathbb{R} \) . In particular, if a complete \( n \) -manifold of non-negative sectional curvature has two ends, then it is a metric product \( {N}^{n - 1} \times  \mathbb{R} \) where \( {N}^{n - 1} \) is a compact manifold.

nodes.content: 2.3. Canonical neighborhoods. Much of the analysis of the geometry of Ricci flows revolves around the notion of canonical neighborhoods. Fix some \( \epsilon  > 0 \) sufficiently small. There are two types of non-compact canonical neighborhoods: \( \epsilon \) -necks and \( \epsilon \) -caps. An \( \epsilon \) -neck in a Riemannian 3-manifold \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) centered at a point \( x \in  M \) is a submanifold \( N \subset  M \) and a diffeomorphism \( \psi  : {S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)  \rightarrow  N \) such that \( x \in  \psi \left( {{S}^{2}\times \{ 0\} }\right) \) and such that the pullback of the rescaled metric, \( {\psi }^{ * }\left( {R\left( x\right) g}\right) \) , is within \( \epsilon \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology of the product of the round metric of scalar curvature 1 on \( {S}^{2} \) with the usual metric on the interval \( \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) . (Throughout, \( R\left( x\right) \) denotes the scalar curvature of \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) at the point \( x \) .) An \( \epsilon \) -cap is a non-compact submanifold \( \mathcal{C} \subset  M \) with the property that a neighborhood \( N \) of infinity in \( \mathcal{C} \) is an \( \epsilon \) -neck, such that every point of \( N \) is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( M \) , and such that the core, \( \mathcal{C} \smallsetminus  \bar{N} \) , of the \( \epsilon \) -cap is diffeomorphic to either a 3-ball or a punctured \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) . It will also be important to consider \( \epsilon \) -caps that, after rescaling to make \( R\left( x\right)  = 1 \) for some point \( x \) in the cap, have bounded geometry (bounded diameter, bounded ratio of the curvatures at any two points, and bounded volume). If \( C \) represents the bound for these quantities, then we call the cap a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. See FIG. 1. An \( \epsilon \) -tube in \( M \) is a submanifold of \( M \) diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) which is a union of \( \epsilon \) -necks and with the property that each point of the \( \epsilon \) -tube is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( M \) .

The \( C \) -component is a compact, connected Riemannian manifold of positive sectional curvature diffeomorphic to either \( {S}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) with the property that rescaling the metric by \( R\left( x\right) \) for any \( x \) in the component produces a Riemannian manifold whose diameter is at most \( C \) , whose sectional curvature at any point and in any 2-plane direction is between \( {C}^{-1} \) and \( C \) , and whose volume is between \( {C}^{-1} \) and \( C \) . nodes.title: 3. Background material from Ricci flow
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture

nodes.label: Definition 3-extra-1
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
Hamilton [29] introduced the Ricci flow equation,

\[
\frac{\partial g\left( t\right) }{\partial t} =  - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {g\left( t\right) }\right) .
\]

This is an evolution equation for a one-parameter family of Riemannian metrics \( g\left( t\right) \) on a smooth manifold \( M \) . The Ricci flow equation is weakly parabolic and is strictly parabolic modulo the 'gauge group', which is the group of diffeomorphisms of the underlying smooth manifold. One should view this equation as a non-linear, tensor version of the heat equation. From it, one can derive the evolution equation for the Riemannian metric tensor, the Ricci tensor, and the scalar curvature function. These are all parabolic equations. For example, the evolution equation for scalar curvature \( R\left( {x, t}\right) \) is

(0.1)

\[
\frac{\partial R}{\partial t}\left( {x, t}\right)  = {\Delta R}\left( {x, t}\right)  + 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( x, t\right) \right| }^{2},
\]

illustrating the similarity with the heat equation. (Here \( \bigtriangleup \) is the Laplacian with non-positive spectrum.)

3.2. Gradient shrinking solitons. Suppose that \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) is a complete Riemannian manifold, and suppose that there is a constant \( \lambda  > 0 \) with the property that

\[
\operatorname{Ric}\left( g\right)  = {\lambda g}
\]

In this case, it is easy to see that there is a Ricci flow given by

\[
g\left( t\right)  = \left( {1 - {2\lambda t}}\right) g.
\]

In particular, all the metrics in this flow differ by a constant factor depending on time and the metric is a decreasing function of time. These are called shrinking solitons. Examples are compact manifolds of constant positive Ricci curvature.

There is a closely related, but more general, class of examples: the gradient shrinking solitons. Suppose that \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) is a complete Riemannian manifold, and suppose that there is a constant \( \lambda  > 0 \) and a function \( f : M \rightarrow \; \mathbb{R} \) satisfying

\[
\operatorname{Ric}\left( g\right)  = {\lambda g} - {\operatorname{Hess}}^{g}f.
\]

In this case, there is a Ricci flow which is a shrinking family after we pull back by the one-parameter family of diffeomorphisms generated by the time-dependent vector field \( \frac{1}{1 - {2\lambda t}}{\nabla }_{g}f \) . An example of a gradient shrinking soliton is the manifold \( {S}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) with the family of metrics being the product of the shrinking family of round metrics on \( {S}^{2} \) and the constant family of standard metrics on \( \mathbb{R} \) . The function \( f \) is \( {s}^{2}/4 \) where \( s \) is the Euclidean parameter on \( \mathbb{R} \) .

nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
A generalized 3-dimensional Ricci flow consists of a smooth manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) of dimension 4 (the space-time) together with a time function \( \mathbf{t} : \mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) and a smooth vector field \( \chi \) . These are required to satisfy:

(1) Each \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) has a neighborhood of the form \( U \times  J \) , where \( U \) is an open subset in \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) and \( J \subset  \mathbb{R} \) is an interval, in which \( \mathbf{t} \) is the projection onto \( J \) and \( \chi \) is the unit vector field tangent to the one-dimensional foliation \( \{ u\}  \times  J \) pointing in the direction of increasing t. We call \( {\mathbf{t}}^{-1}\left( t\right) \) the \( t \) time-slice. It is a smooth 3-manifold.

(2) The image \( \mathbf{t}\left( \mathcal{M}\right) \) is a connected interval \( I \) in \( \mathbb{R} \) , possibly infinite. The boundary of \( \mathcal{M} \) is the pre-image under \( \mathbf{t} \) of the boundary of \( I \) .

(3) The level sets \( {\mathbf{t}}^{-1}\left( t\right) \) form a codimension-one foliation of \( \mathcal{M} \) , called the horizontal foliation, with the boundary components of \( \mathcal{M} \) being leaves.

(4) There is a metric \( G \) on the horizontal distribution, i.e., the distribution tangent to the level sets of \( \mathbf{t} \) . This metric induces a Riemannian metric on each \( t \) time-slice, varying smoothly as we vary the time-slice. We define the curvature of \( G \) at a point \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) to be the curvature of the Riemannian metric induced by \( G \) on the time-slice \( {M}_{t} \) at \( x \) .

(5) Because of the first property the integral curves of \( \chi \) preserve the horizontal foliation and hence the horizontal distribution. Thus, we can take the Lie derivative of \( G \) along \( \chi \) . The Ricci flow equation is then

\[
{\mathcal{L}}_{\chi }\left( G\right)  =  - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( G\right) .
\]

Locally in space-time the horizontal metric is simply a smoothly varying family of Riemannian metrics on a fixed smooth manifold and the evolution equation is the ordinary Ricci flow equation. This means that the usual formulas for the evolution of the curvatures as well as much of the analytic analysis of Ricci flows still hold in this generalized context. In the end, a Ricci flow with surgery is a more singular type of space-time, but it will have an open dense subset which is a generalized Ricci flow, and all the analytic estimates take place in this open subset.

nodes.content:
4.1. The reduced length function. In Chapter 6 we come to the first of Perelman's major contributions. Let us first describe it in the context of an ordinary 3-dimensional Ricci flow, but viewing the Ricci flow as a horizontal metric on a space-time which is the manifold \( M \times  I \) , where \( I \) is the interval of definition of the flow. Suppose that \( I = \lbrack 0, T) \) and fix \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  M \times  \left( {0, T}\right) \) . We consider paths \( \gamma \left( \tau \right) ,0 \leq  \tau  \leq  \bar{\tau } \) , in space-time with the property that for every \( \tau  \leq  \bar{\tau } \) we have \( \gamma \left( \tau \right)  \in  M \times  \{ t - \tau \} \) and \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = x \) . These paths are said to be parameterized by backward time. See FIG. 2. The \( \mathcal{L} \) -length of such a path is given by

\[
\mathcal{L}\left( \gamma \right)  = {\int }_{0}^{\bar{\tau }}\sqrt{\tau }\left( {R\left( {\gamma \left( \tau \right) }\right)  + {\left| {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( \tau \right) \right| }^{2}}\right) {d\tau },
\]

where the derivative on \( \gamma \) refers to the spatial derivative. There is also the closely related reduced length

\[
\ell \left( \gamma \right)  = \frac{\mathcal{L}\left( \gamma \right) }{2\sqrt{\tau }}.
\]

There is a theory for the functional \( \mathcal{L} \) analogous to the theory for the usual energy function \( {}^{6} \) . In particular, there is the notion of an \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic, and the reduced length as a function on space-time \( {\ell }_{\left( x, t\right) } : M \times  \lbrack 0, t) \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) . One establishes a crucial monotonicity for this reduced length along \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesics. Then one defines the reduced volume

\[
{\widetilde{V}}_{\left( x, t\right) }\left( {U\times \{ \bar{t}\} }\right)  = {\int }_{U\times \{ \bar{t}\} }{\bar{\tau }}^{-3/2}{e}^{-{\ell }_{\left( x, t\right) }\left( {q,\bar{\tau }}\right) }d{\operatorname{vol}}_{g(\bar{\tau }}\left( q\right) ,
\]

where, as before \( \bar{\tau } = t - \bar{t} \) . Because of the monotonicity of \( {\ell }_{\left( x, t\right) } \) along \( \mathcal{L} \) - geodesics, the reduced volume is also non-increasing under the flow (forward in \( \bar{\tau } \) and hence backward in time) of open subsets along \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesics. This is the fundamental tool which is used to establish non-collapsing results which in turn are essential in proving the existence of geometric limits.

nodes.section_title: 5. The standard solution and the surgery process
nodes.content:
5.1. The standard solution. In preparing the way for defining the surgery process, we must construct a metric on the 3-ball that we shall glue in when we perform surgery. This we do in Chapter 12. We fix a non-negatively curved, rotationally symmetric metric on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) that is isometric near infinity to \( {S}^{2} \times  \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) where the metric on \( {S}^{2} \) is the round metric of scalar curvature 1, and outside this region has positive sectional curvature, see FIG. 4. Any such metric will suffice for the gluing process, and we fix one and call it the standard metric. It is important to understand Ricci flow with the standard metric as initial metric. Because of the special nature of this metric (the rotational symmetry and the asymptotic nature at infinity), it is fairly elementary to show that there is a unique solution of bounded curvature on each time-slice to the Ricci flow equation with the standard metric as the initial metric; this flow is defined for \( 0 \leq  t < 1 \) ; and for any \( T < 1 \) outside of a compact subset \( X\left( T\right) \) the restriction of the flow to \( \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) is close to the evolving round cylinder. Using the length function, one shows that the Ricci flow is non-collapsed, and that the bounded curvature and bounded distance result applies to it. This allows one to prove that every point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in this flow has one of the following types of neighborhoods:

(1) \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {{C}_{2},\epsilon }\right) \) -cap, where \( {C}_{2} < \infty \) is a given universal constant depending only on \( \epsilon \) .

(2) \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck.

(3) \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is the center of an evolving \( \epsilon \) -neck whose initial slice is at time zero.

These form the second source of models for canonical neighborhoods in a Ricci flow with surgery. Thus, we shall set \( C = C\left( \epsilon \right)  = \max \left( {{C}_{1}\left( \epsilon \right) ,{C}_{2}\left( \epsilon \right) }\right) \) and we shall find \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhoods in Ricci flows with surgery.

nodes.section_title: 5. The standard solution and the surgery process
nodes.content: 5.2. Ricci flows with surgery. Now it is time to introduce the notion of a Ricci flow with surgery. To do this we formulate an appropriate notion of 4-dimensional space-time that allows for the surgery operations. We define space-time to be a 4-dimensional Hausdorff singular space with a time function \( \mathbf{t} \) with the property that each time-slice is a compact, smooth 3-manifold, but level sets at different times are not necessarily diffeomorphic. Generically space-time is a smooth 4-manifold, but there are exposed regions at a discrete set of times. Near a point in the exposed region space-time is a 4-manifold with boundary. The singular points of space-time are the boundaries of the exposed regions. Near these, space-time is modeled on the product of \( {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \) with the square \( \left( {-1,1}\right)  \times  \left( {-1,1}\right) \) , the latter having a topology in which the open sets are, in addition to the usual open sets, open subsets of \( \left( {0,1}\right)  \times  \lbrack 0,1) \) , see FIG. 5 . There is a natural notion of smooth functions on space-time. These are smooth in the usual sense on the open subset of non-singular points. Near the singular points, and in the local coordinates described above, they are required to be pull-backs from smooth functions on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \times  \left( {-1,1}\right)  \times  \left( {-1,1}\right) \) under the natural map. Space-time is equipped with a smooth vector field \( \chi \) with \( \chi \left( \mathbf{t}\right)  = 1 \) .

nodes.content:
We shall study Ricci flows with surgery defined for \( 0 \leq  t < T < \infty \) whose associated generalized Ricci flows satisfy the following properties:

(1) The initial metric is normalized, meaning that for the metric at time zero the norm of the Riemann curvature is bounded above by 1 and the volume of any ball of radius 1 is at least half the volume of the unit ball in Euclidean space.

(2) The curvature of the flow is pinched toward positive.

(3) There is \( \kappa  > 0 \) so that the associated generalized Ricci flow is \( \kappa \) - non-collapsed on scales at most \( \epsilon \) , in the sense that we require only that balls of radius \( r \leq  \epsilon \) be \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed.

(4) There is \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) such that any point of space-time at which the scalar curvature is \( \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) has a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood.

nodes.content:
Now we are ready to describe the surgery procedure. It depends on our choice of standard solution on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) and on a choice of \( \delta  > 0 \) sufficiently small. For each \( \epsilon \) -horn in \( \Omega \) whose boundary is contained in \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) , fix a point of curvature \( {\left( h\left( \delta ,\rho ,{r}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-2} \) and fix a strong \( \delta \) -neck centered at this point. Then we cut the \( \epsilon \) -horn open along the central 2-sphere \( S \) of this neck and remove the end of the \( \epsilon \) -horn that is cut off by \( S \) . Then we glue in a ball of a fixed radius around the tip from the standard solution, after scaling the metric on this ball by \( {\left( h\left( \delta ,\rho ,{r}_{0}\right) \right) }^{2} \) . To glue these two metrics together we must use a partition of unity near the 2-spheres that are matched. There is also a delicate point that we first bend in the metrics slightly so as to achieve positive curvature near where we are gluing. This is an idea due to Hamilton, and it is needed in order to show that the condition of curvature pinching toward positive is preserved. In addition, we remove all components of \( \Omega \) that do not contain any points of \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) .

This operation produces a new compact 3-manifold. One continues the Ricci flow with surgery by letting this Riemannian manifold at time \( T \) evolve under the Ricci flow. See FIG. 6.

nodes.section_title: 1. Riemannian metrics and the Levi-Civita connection
nodes.content:
DEFINITION 1.1. Let \( M \) be an \( n \) -dimensional manifold. A Riemannian metric \( g \) on \( M \) is a smooth section of \( {T}^{ * }M \otimes  {T}^{ * }M \) defining a positive definite symmetric bilinear form on \( {T}_{p}M \) for each \( p \in  M \) . In local coordinates \( \left( {{x}^{1},\ldots ,{x}^{n}}\right) \) , one has a natural local basis \( \left\{  {{\partial }_{1},\ldots ,{\partial }_{n}}\right\} \) for \( {TM} \) , where \( {\partial }_{i} = \; \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}} \) . The metric tensor \( g = {g}_{ij}d{x}^{i} \otimes  d{x}^{j} \) is represented by a smooth matrix-valued function

\[
{g}_{ij} = g\left( {{\partial }_{i},{\partial }_{j}}\right) .
\]

The pair \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) is a Riemannian manifold. We denote by \( \left( {g}^{ij}\right) \) the inverse of the matrix \( \left( {g}_{ij}\right) \) .

Using a partition of unity, one can easily see that any manifold admits a Riemannian metric. A Riemannian metric on \( M \) allows us to measure lengths of smooth paths in \( M \) and hence to define a distance function by setting \( d\left( {p, q}\right) \) equal to the infimum of the lengths of smooth paths from \( p \) to \( q \) . This makes \( M \) a metric space. For a point \( p \) in a Riemannian manifold \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) and for \( r > 0 \) we denote the metric ball of radius \( r \) centered at \( p \) in \( M \) by \( B\left( {p, r}\right) \) or by \( {B}_{g}\left( {p, r}\right) \) if the metric needs specifying or emphasizing. It is defined by

\[
B\left( {p, r}\right)  = \{ q \in  M \mid  d\left( {p, q}\right)  < r\} .
\]

nodes.section_title: 1. Riemannian metrics and the Levi-Civita connection
nodes.content:
THEOREM 1.2. Given a Riemannian metric \( g \) on \( M \) , there uniquely exists a torsion-free connection on \( {TM} \) making \( g \) parallel, i.e., there is a unique

\( \mathbb{R} \) -linear mapping \( \nabla  : \Gamma \left( {TM}\right)  \rightarrow  \Gamma \left( {{T}^{ * }M \otimes  {TM}}\right) \) satisfying the Leibnitz formula

\[
\nabla \left( {fX}\right)  = {df} \otimes  X + f\nabla X
\]

and the following two additional conditions for all vector fields \( X \) and \( Y \) :

- (g orthogonal) \( d\left( {g\left( {X, Y}\right) }\right)  = g\left( {\nabla X, Y}\right)  + g\left( {X,\nabla Y}\right) \) ;

- (Torsion-free) \( {\nabla }_{X}Y - {\nabla }_{Y}X - \left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack   = 0 \) (where, as is customary, we denote \( \nabla Y\left( X\right) \) by \( {\nabla }_{X}Y \) ).

We call the above connection the Levi-Civita connection of the metric and \( \nabla X \) the covariant derivative of \( X \) . On a Riemannian manifold we always use the Levi-Civita connection.

In local coordinates \( \left( {{x}^{1},\ldots ,{x}^{n}}\right) \) the Levi-Civita connection \( \nabla \) is given by the \( {\nabla }_{{\partial }_{i}}\left( {\partial }_{j}\right)  = {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}{\partial }_{k} \) , where the Christoffel symbols \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} \) are the smooth functions

(1.1)

\[
{\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} = \frac{1}{2}{g}^{kl}\left( {{\partial }_{i}{g}_{lj} + {\partial }_{j}{g}_{il} - {\partial }_{l}{g}_{ij}}\right) .
\]

Note that the above two additional conditions for the Levi-Civita connection \( \nabla \) correspond respectively to

- \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} = {\Gamma }_{ji}^{k} \) , - \( {\partial }_{k}{g}_{ij} = {g}_{lj}{\Gamma }_{ki}^{l} + {g}_{il}{\Gamma }_{kj}^{l} \) .

The covariant derivative extends to all tensors. In the special case of a function \( f \) we have \( \nabla \left( f\right)  = {df} \) . Note that there is a possible confusion between this and the notation in the literature, since one often sees \( \nabla f \) written for the gradient of \( f \) , which is the vector field dual to \( {df} \) . We always use \( \nabla f \) to mean \( {df} \) , and we will denote the gradient of \( f \) by \( {\left( \nabla f\right) }^{ * } \) ,

The covariant derivative allows us to define the Hessian of a smooth function at any point, not just a critical point. Let \( f \) be a smooth real-valued function on \( M \) . We define the Hessian of \( f \) , denoted Hess \( \left( f\right) \) , as follows:

(1.2)

\[
\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \left( {X, Y}\right)  = X\left( {Y\left( f\right) }\right)  - {\nabla }_{X}Y\left( f\right) .
\]

LEMMA 1.3. The Hessian is a contravariant, symmetric two-tensor, i.e., for vector fields \( X \) and \( Y \) we have

\[
\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \left( {X, Y}\right)  = \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \left( {Y, X}\right)
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \left( {{\phi X},{\psi Y}}\right)  = {\phi \psi }\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \left( {X, Y}\right)
\]

for all smooth functions \( \phi ,\psi \) . Other formulas for the Hessian are

\[
\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \left( {X, Y}\right)  = \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}\left( {\nabla f}\right) , Y}\right\rangle   = {\nabla }_{X}\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}\left( f\right) }\right)  = {\nabla }^{2}f\left( {X, Y}\right) .
\]

Also, in local coordinates we have

\[
\operatorname{Hess}{\left( f\right) }_{ij} = {\partial }_{i}{\partial }_{j}f - \left( {{\partial }_{k}f}\right) {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}.
\]

nodes.proof:
The proof of symmetry is direct from the torsion-free assumption:

\[
\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \left( {X, Y}\right)  - \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \left( {Y, X}\right)  = \left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  \left( f\right)  - \left( {{\nabla }_{X}Y - {\nabla }_{Y}X}\right) \left( f\right)  = 0.
\]

The fact that \( \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \) is a tensor is also established by direct computation. The equivalence of the various formulas is also immediate:

(1.3)

\[
\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}\left( {\nabla f}\right) , Y}\right\rangle   = X\left( {\langle \nabla f, Y\rangle }\right)  - \left\langle  {\nabla f,{\nabla }_{X}Y}\right\rangle
\]

\[
= X\left( {Y\left( f\right) }\right)  - {\nabla }_{X}Y\left( f\right)  = \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \left( {X, Y}\right) .
\]

Since \( {df} = \left( {{\partial }_{r}f}\right) d{x}^{r} \) and \( \nabla \left( {d{x}^{k}}\right)  =  - {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}d{x}^{i} \otimes  d{x}^{j} \) , it follows that

\[
\nabla \left( {df}\right)  = \left( {{\partial }_{i}{\partial }_{j}f - \left( {{\partial }_{k}f}\right) {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}}\right) d{x}^{i} \otimes  d{x}^{j}.
\]

It is direct from the definition that

\[
\operatorname{Hess}{\left( f\right) }_{ij} = \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \left( {{\partial }_{i},{\partial }_{j}}\right)  = {\partial }_{i}{\partial }_{j}f - \left( {{\partial }_{k}f}\right) {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}.
\]

The Laplacian \( \bigtriangleup f \) is defined as the trace of the Hessian: That is to say, in local coordinates near \( p \) we have

\[
\bigtriangleup f\left( p\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{ij}}{g}^{ij}\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \left( {{\partial }_{i},{\partial }_{j}}\right) .
\]

Thus, if \( \left\{  {X}_{i}\right\} \) is an orthonormal basis for \( {T}_{p}M \) then

(1.4)

\[
\bigtriangleup f\left( p\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \left( {{X}_{i},{X}_{i}}\right) .
\]

Notice that this is the form of the Laplacian that is non-negative at a local minimum, and consequently has a non-positive spectrum.

nodes.content:
DEFINITION 1.4. The Riemann curvature tensor of \( M \) is the \( \left( {1,3}\right) \) -tensor on \( M \) ,

\[
\mathcal{R}\left( {X, Y}\right) Z = {\nabla }_{X, Y}^{2}Z - {\nabla }_{Y, X}^{2}Z = {\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{Y}Z - {\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{X}Z - {\nabla }_{\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }Z,
\]

where \( {\nabla }_{X, Y}^{2}Z = {\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{Y}Z - {\nabla }_{{\nabla }_{X}Y}Z \) .

In local coordinates the curvature tensor can be represented as

\[
\mathcal{R}\left( {{\partial }_{i},{\partial }_{j}}\right) {\partial }_{k} = {R}_{ij}{}^{l}{}_{k}{\partial }_{l},
\]

where

\[
{R}_{ij}{}^{l}{}_{k} = {\partial }_{i}{\Gamma }_{jk}^{l} - {\partial }_{j}{\Gamma }_{ik}^{l} + {\Gamma }_{jk}^{s}{\Gamma }_{is}^{l} - {\Gamma }_{ik}^{s}{\Gamma }_{js}^{l}.
\]

Using the metric tensor \( g \) , we can change \( \mathcal{R} \) to a \( \left( {0,4}\right) \) -tensor as follows:

\[
\mathcal{R}\left( {X, Y, Z, W}\right)  = g\left( {\mathcal{R}\left( {X, Y}\right) W, Z}\right) .
\]

(Notice the change of order in the last two variables.) Notice that we use the same symbol and the same name for both the \( \left( {1,3}\right) \) tensor and the \( \left( {0,4}\right) \) tensor; which one we are dealing with in a given context is indicated by the index structure or the variables to which the tensor is applied. In local coordinates, the Riemann curvature tensor can be represented as

\[
\mathcal{R}\left( {{\partial }_{i},{\partial }_{j},{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{l}}\right)  = {R}_{ijkl}
\]

\[
= {g}_{ks}{R}_{ij}{}^{s}{}_{l}
\]

\[
= {g}_{ks}\left( {{\partial }_{i}{\Gamma }_{jl}^{s} - {\partial }_{j}{\Gamma }_{il}^{s} + {\Gamma }_{jl}^{t}{\Gamma }_{it}^{s} - {\Gamma }_{il}^{t}{\Gamma }_{jt}^{s}}\right) .
\]

CLAIM 1.5. The Riemann curvature tensor \( \mathcal{R} \) satisfies the following properties:

- (Symmetry) \( {R}_{ijkl} =  - {R}_{jikl},{R}_{ijkl} =  - {R}_{ijlk},{R}_{ijkl} = {R}_{klij} \) .

- (1st Bianchi identity) The sum of \( {R}_{ijkl} \) over the cyclic permutation of any three indices vanishes.

- (2nd Bianchi identity) \( {R}_{{ijkl}, h} + {R}_{{ijlh}, k} + {R}_{{ijhk}, l} = 0 \) , where

\[
{R}_{{ijkl}, h} = {\left( {\nabla }_{{\partial }_{h}}\mathcal{R}\right) }_{ijkl}.
\]

nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
DEFINITION 1.6. The sectional curvature of a 2-plane \( P \subset  {T}_{p}M \) is defined as

\[
K\left( P\right)  = \mathcal{R}\left( {X, Y, X, Y}\right) ,
\]

where \( \{ X, Y\} \) is an orthonormal basis of \( P \) . We say that \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) has positive sectional curvature (resp., negative sectional curvature) if \( K\left( P\right)  > 0 \) (resp., \( K\left( P\right)  < 0) \) for every 2-plane \( P \) . There are analogous notions of non-negative and non-positive sectional curvature.

In local coordinates, suppose that \( X = {X}^{i}{\partial }_{i} \) and \( Y = {Y}^{i}{\partial }_{i} \) . Then we have

\[
K\left( P\right)  = {R}_{ijkl}{X}^{i}{Y}^{j}{X}^{k}{Y}^{l}.
\]

A Riemannian manifold is said to have constant sectional curvature if \( K\left( P\right) \) is the same for all \( p \in  M \) and all 2-planes \( P \subset  {T}_{p}M \) . One can show that a manifold \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) has constant sectional curvature \( \lambda \) if and only if

\[
{R}_{ijkl} = \lambda \left( {{g}_{ik}{g}_{jl} - {g}_{il}{g}_{jk}}\right) .
\]

Of course, the sphere of radius \( r \) in \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) has constant sectional curvature \( 1/{r}^{2} \) , \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) with the Euclidean metric has constant sectional curvature 0, and the hyperbolic space \( {\mathbb{H}}^{n} \) , which in the Poincaré model is given by the unit disk with the metric

\[
\frac{4\left( {d{x}_{1}^{2} + \cdots  + d{x}_{n}^{2}}\right) }{{\left( 1 - {\left| x\right| }^{2}\right) }^{2}},
\]

or in the upper half-space model with coordinates \( \left( {{x}^{1},\ldots ,{x}^{n}}\right) \) is given by

\[
\frac{d{s}^{2}}{{\left( {x}^{n}\right) }^{2}},
\]

has constant sectional curvature -1 . In all three cases we denote the constant curvature metric by \( {g}_{\mathrm{{st}}} \) .

nodes.label: Definition 1.7
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
DEFINITION 1.7. Using the metric, one can replace the Riemann curvature tensor \( \mathcal{R} \) by a symmetric bilinear form \( \mathrm{{Rm}} \) on \( { \land  }^{2}{TM} \) . In local coordinates let \( \varphi  = {\varphi }^{ij}{\partial }_{i} \land  {\partial }_{j} \) and \( \psi  = {\psi }^{kl}{\partial }_{k} \land  {\partial }_{l} \) be local sections of \( { \land  }^{2}{TM} \) . The formula for \( \mathrm{{Rm}} \) is

\[
\operatorname{Rm}\left( {\varphi ,\psi }\right)  = {R}_{ijkl}{\varphi }^{ij}{\psi }^{kl}.
\]

We call Rm the curvature operator. We say \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) has positive curvature operator if \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {\varphi ,\varphi }\right)  > 0 \) for any non-zero 2-form \( \varphi  = {\varphi }^{ij}{\partial }_{i} \land  {\partial }_{j} \) and has non-negative curvature operator if \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {\varphi ,\varphi }\right)  \geq  0 \) for any \( \varphi  \in  { \land  }^{2}{TM} \) .

If the curvature operator is a positive (resp., non-negative) operator then the manifold is positively (resp., non-negatively) curved.

nodes.content:
DEFINITION 1.8. The Ricci curvature tensor, denoted Ric or \( {\operatorname{Ric}}_{g} \) when it is necessary to specify the metric, is a symmetric contravariant two-tensor. In local coordinates it is defined by

\[
\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, Y}\right)  = {g}^{kl}R\left( {X,{\partial }_{k}, Y,{\partial }_{l}}\right) .
\]

The value of this tensor at \( p \in  M \) is given by \( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}R\left( {X\left( p\right) ,{e}_{i}, Y\left( p\right) ,{e}_{i}}\right) \) where \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n}}\right\} \) is an orthonormal basis of \( {T}_{p}M \) . Clearly Ric is a symmetric bilinear form on \( {TM} \) , given in local coordinates by

\[
\operatorname{Ric} = {\operatorname{Ric}}_{ij}d{x}^{i} \otimes  d{x}^{j},
\]

where \( {\operatorname{Ric}}_{ij} = \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{\partial }_{i},{\partial }_{j}}\right) \) . The scalar curvature is defined by:

\[
R = {R}_{g} = {\operatorname{tr}}_{g}\operatorname{Ric} = {g}^{ij}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{ij}.
\]

We will say that \( \operatorname{Ric} \geq  k\left( {\text{ or } \leq  k}\right) \) if all the eigenvalues of Ric are \( \geq  k \) (or \( \leq  k) \) .

THEOREM 1.11. (Uniformization Theorem) If \( \left( {{M}^{n}, g}\right) \) is a complete, simply-connected Riemannian manifold of constant sectional curvature \( \lambda \) , then:

(1) If \( \lambda  = 0 \) , then \( {M}^{n} \) is isometric to Euclidean \( n \) -space.

(2) If \( \lambda  > 0 \) there is a diffeomorphism \( \phi  : M \rightarrow  {S}^{n} \) such that \( g = \; {\lambda }^{-1}{\phi }^{ * }\left( {g}_{\mathrm{{st}}}\right) \) where \( {g}_{\mathrm{{st}}} \) is the usual metric on the unit sphere in \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n + 1} \) .

(3) If \( \lambda  < 0 \) there is a diffeomorphism \( \phi  : M \rightarrow  {\mathbb{H}}^{n} \) such that \( g = \; {\left| \lambda \right| }^{-1}{\phi }^{ * }\left( {g}_{\mathrm{{st}}}\right) \) where \( {g}_{\mathrm{{st}}} \) is the Poincaré metric of constant curvature -1 on \( {\mathbb{H}}^{n} \) .

DEFINITION 1.14. Let \( \left( {N, g}\right) \) be a Riemannian manifold. We define the open cone over \( \left( {N, g}\right) \) to be the manifold \( N \times  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) with the metric \( \widetilde{g} \) defined as follows: For any \( \left( {x, s}\right)  \in  N \times  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) we have

\[
\widetilde{g}\left( {x, s}\right)  = {s}^{2}g\left( x\right)  + d{s}^{2}.
\]

Fix local coordinates \( \left( {{x}^{1},\ldots ,{x}^{n}}\right) \) on \( N \) . Let \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k};1 \leq  i, j, k \leq  n \) , be the Christoffel symbols for the Levi-Civita connection on \( N \) . Set \( {x}^{0} = s \) . In the local coordinates \( \left( {{x}^{0},{x}^{1},\ldots ,{x}^{n}}\right) \) for the cone we have the Christoffel symbols \( {\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{ij}^{k},0 \leq  i, j, k \leq  n \) , for \( \widetilde{g} \) . The relation between the metrics gives the following relations between the two sets of Christoffel symbols:

\[
{\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{ij}^{k} = {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k};\;1 \leq  i, j, k \leq  n,
\]

\[
{\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{ij}^{0} =  - s{g}_{ij};\;1 \leq  i, j \leq  n,
\]

\[
{\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{i0}^{j} = {\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{0i}^{j} = {s}^{-1}{\delta }_{i}^{j};\;1 \leq  i, j \leq  n,
\]

\[
{\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{i0}^{0} = 0;\;0 \leq  i \leq  n
\]

\[
{\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{00}^{i} = 0;\;0 \leq  i \leq  n.
\]

Denote by \( {\mathcal{R}}_{g} \) the curvature tensor for \( g \) and by \( {\mathcal{R}}_{\widetilde{g}} \) the curvature tensor for \( \widetilde{g} \) . Then the above formulas lead directly to:

\[
{\mathcal{R}}_{\widetilde{g}}\left( {{\partial }_{i},{\partial }_{j}}\right) \left( {\partial }_{0}\right)  = 0;\;0 \leq  i, j \leq  n,
\]

\[
{\mathcal{R}}_{\widetilde{g}}\left( {{\partial }_{i},{\partial }_{j}}\right) \left( {\partial }_{i}\right)  = {\mathcal{R}}_{g}\left( {{\partial }_{i},{\partial }_{j}}\right) \left( {\partial }_{i}\right)  + {g}_{ii}{\partial }_{j} - {g}_{ji}{\partial }_{i}\;1 \leq  i, j \leq  n.
\]

nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
DEFINITION 1.17. Let \( I \) be an open interval. A smooth curve \( \gamma  : I \rightarrow  M \) is called a geodesic if \( {\nabla }_{\dot{\gamma }}\dot{\gamma } = 0 \) .

In local coordinates, we write \( \gamma \left( t\right)  = \left( {{x}^{1}\left( t\right) ,\ldots ,{x}^{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) and this equation becomes

\[
0 = {\nabla }_{\dot{\gamma }}\dot{\gamma }\left( t\right)  = \left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{k}\left( {{\ddot{x}}^{k}\left( t\right)  + {\dot{x}}^{i}\left( t\right) {\dot{x}}^{j}\left( t\right) {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}\left( {\gamma \left( t\right) }\right) }\right) {\partial }_{k}}\right) .
\]

This is a system of \( {2}^{nd} \) order ODE’s. The local existence, uniqueness and smoothness of a geodesic through any point \( p \in  M \) with initial velocity vector \( v \in  {T}_{p}M \) follow from the classical ODE theory. Given any two points in a complete manifold, a standard limiting argument shows that there is a rectifiable curve of minimal length between these points. Any such curve is a geodesic. We call geodesics that minimize the length between their endpoints minimizing geodesics.

We have the classical theorem showing that on a complete manifold all geodesics are defined for all time (see Theorem 16 of Chapter 5 on p. 137 of [57]).

Proposition 1.20. Suppose that \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) is a minimal geodesic. Then for any \( t < 1 \) the restriction of \( \gamma \) to \( \left\lbrack  {0, t}\right\rbrack \) is the unique minimal geodesic between its endpoints and there are no conjugate points on \( \gamma \left( {\lbrack 0,1}\right) ) \) , i.e., there is no non-zero Jacobi field along \( \gamma \) vanishing at any \( t \in  \lbrack 0,1) \) .

We shall sketch the proof. For more details see Proposition 19 and Lemma 14 of Chapter 5 on pp. 139 and 140 of [57].

Fix \( 0 < {t}_{0} < 1 \) . Suppose that there were a different geodesic \( \mu  : \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) from \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) to \( \gamma \left( {t}_{0}\right) \) , whose length was at most that of \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  0,{t}_{0}\right\rbrack  } \) . The fact that \( \mu \) and \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  0,{t}_{0}\right\rbrack  } \) are distinct means that \( {\mu }^{\prime }\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \neq  {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) . Then the curve formed by concatenating \( \mu \) with \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  {t}_{0},1\right\rbrack  } \) is a curve from \( \gamma \left( 0\right) \) to \( \gamma \left( 1\right) \) whose length is at most that of \( \gamma \) . But this concatenated curve is not smooth at \( \mu \left( {t}_{0}\right) \) , and hence it is not a geodesic, and in particular there is a curve with shorter length (a minimal geodesic) between these points. This is contrary to our assumption that \( \gamma \) was minimal.

nodes.content:
DEFINITION 1.22. For any \( p \in  M \) , we can define the exponential map at \( p,{\exp }_{p} \) . It is defined on an open neighborhood \( {O}_{p} \) of the origin in \( {T}_{p}M \) and is defined by \( {\exp }_{p}\left( v\right)  = {\gamma }_{v}\left( 1\right) \) , the endpoint of the unique geodesic \( {\gamma }_{v} : \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) starting from \( p \) with initial velocity vector \( v \) . We always take \( {O}_{p} \subset  {T}_{p}M \) to be the maximal domain on which \( {\exp }_{p} \) is defined, so that \( {O}_{p} \) is a star-shaped open neighborhood of \( 0 \in  {T}_{p}M \) . By the Hopf-Rinow Theorem, if \( M \) is complete, then the exponential map is defined on all of \( {T}_{p}M \) .

By the inverse function theorem there exists \( {r}_{0} = {r}_{0}\left( {p, M}\right)  > 0 \) , such that the restriction of \( {\exp }_{p} \) to the ball \( {B}_{g \mid  {T}_{p}M}\left( {0,{r}_{0}}\right) \) in \( {T}_{p}M \) is a diffeomorphism onto \( {B}_{g}\left( {p,{r}_{0}}\right) \) . Fix \( g \) -orthonormal linear coordinates on \( {T}_{p}M \) . Transferring these coordinates via \( {\exp }_{p} \) to coordinates on \( B\left( {p,{r}_{0}}\right) \) gives us Gaussian normal coordinates on \( B\left( {p,{r}_{0}}\right)  \subset  M \) .

Suppose now that \( M \) is complete, and fix a point \( p \in  M \) . For every \( q \in  M \) , there is a length-minimizing path from \( p \) to \( q \) . When parameterized at constant speed equal to its length, this path is a geodesic with domain interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . Consequently, \( {\exp }_{p} : {T}_{p}M \rightarrow  M \) is onto. The differential of the exponential mapping is given by Jacobi fields: Let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) be a geodesic from \( p \) to \( q \) , and let \( X \in  {T}_{p}M \) be \( {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) \) . Then the exponential mapping at \( p \) is a smooth map from \( {T}_{p}\left( M\right)  \rightarrow  M \) sending \( X \) to \( q \) . Fix \( Z \in \; {T}_{p}M \) . Then there is a unique Jacobi field \( {Y}_{Z} \) along \( \gamma \) with \( {\nabla }_{X}{Y}_{Z}\left( 0\right)  = Z \) . The association \( Z \mapsto  {Y}_{Z}\left( 1\right)  \in  {T}_{q}M \) is a linear map from \( {T}_{p}\left( M\right)  \rightarrow  {T}_{q}M \) . Under the natural identification of \( {T}_{p}M \) with the tangent plane to \( {T}_{p}M \) at the point \( Z \) , this linear mapping is the differential of \( {\exp }_{p} : {T}_{p}M \rightarrow  M \) at the point \( X \in  {T}_{p}M \) .

nodes.content:
DEFINITION 1.26. The injectivity radius \( \mathop{\operatorname{inj}}\limits_{M}\left( p\right) \) of \( M \) at \( p \) is the supremum of the \( r > 0 \) for which the restriction of \( {\exp }_{p} : {T}_{p}M \rightarrow  M \) to the ball \( B\left( {0, r}\right) \) of radius \( r \) in \( {T}_{p}M \) is a diffeomorphism into \( M \) . Clearly, \( {\operatorname{inj}}_{M}\left( p\right) \) is the distance in \( {T}_{p}M \) from 0 to the frontier of \( {U}_{p} \) . It is also the distance in \( M \) from \( p \) to the cut locus \( {\mathcal{C}}_{p} \) .

Suppose that \( {\operatorname{inj}}_{M}\left( p\right)  = r \) . There are two possibilities: Either there is a broken, closed geodesic through \( p \) , broken only at \( p \) , of length \( {2r} \) , or there is a geodesic \( \gamma \) of length \( r \) emanating from \( p \) whose endpoint is a conjugate point along \( \gamma \) . The first case happens when the exponential mapping is not one-to-one of the closed ball of radius \( r \) in \( {T}_{p}M \) , and the second happens when there is a tangent vector in \( {T}_{p}M \) of length \( r \) at which \( {\exp }_{p} \) is not a local diffeomorphism.

LEMMA 1.27. The Laplacian operator acting on scalar functions on \( M \) is given in local coordinates by

\[
\bigtriangleup  = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\det \left( g\right) }}{\partial }_{i}\left( {{g}^{ij}\sqrt{\det \left( g\right) }{\partial }_{j}}\right) .

nodes.content_excerpt: LEMMA 1.27. The Laplacian operator acting on scalar functions on \( M \) is given in local coordinates by \[ \bigtriangleup = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\det \left( g\right) }}{\partial }_{i}\left( {{g}^{ij}\sqrt{\det \left( g\right) }{\partial }_{j}}\right) . \]

nodes.proof:
Let us compute the derivative at a point \( p \) . We have

\[
\frac{1}{\sqrt{\det \left( g\right) }}{\partial }_{i}\left( {{g}^{ij}\sqrt{\det \left( g\right) }{\partial }_{j}}\right) f = {g}^{ij}{\partial }_{i}{\partial }_{j}f + {\partial }_{i}{g}^{ij}{\partial }_{j}f + \frac{1}{2}{g}^{ij}{\partial }_{i}\operatorname{Tr}\left( \widetilde{g}\right) {\partial }_{j}f,
\]

where \( \widetilde{g} = g{\left( p\right) }^{-1}g \) . On the other hand from the definition of the Laplacian, Equation (1.4), and Equation (1.3) we have

\[
\bigtriangleup f = {g}^{ij}\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \left( {{\partial }_{i},{\partial }_{j}}\right)  = {g}^{ij}\left( {{\partial }_{i}{\partial }_{j}\left( f\right)  - {\nabla }_{{\partial }_{i}}{\partial }_{j}f}\right)  = {g}^{ij}{\partial }_{i}{\partial }_{j}f - {g}^{ij}{\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}{\partial }_{k}f.
\]

Thus, to prove the claim it suffices to show that

\[
{g}^{ij}{\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} =  - \left( {{\partial }_{i}{g}^{ik} + \frac{1}{2}{g}^{ik}\operatorname{Tr}\left( {{\partial }_{i}\widetilde{g}}\right) }\right) .
\]

From the definition of the Christoffel symbols we have

\[
{g}^{ij}{\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} = \frac{1}{2}{g}^{ij}{g}^{kl}\left( {{\partial }_{i}{g}_{jl} + {\partial }_{j}{g}_{il} - {\partial }_{l}{g}_{ij}}\right) .
\]

Of course, \( {g}^{ij}{\partial }_{i}{g}_{jl} =  - {\partial }_{i}{g}^{ij}{g}_{jl} \) , so that \( {g}^{ij}{g}^{kl}{\partial }_{i}{g}_{jl} =  - {\partial }_{i}{g}^{ik} \) . It follows by symmetry that \( {g}^{ij}{g}^{jl}{\partial }_{j}{g}_{il} =  - {\partial }_{i}{g}^{ik} \) . The last term is clearly \( - \frac{1}{2}{g}^{ik}\operatorname{Tr}\left( {{\partial }_{i}\widetilde{g}}\right) \) .

nodes.label: Remark 1.29
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
REMARK 1.29. The statement that \( \bigtriangleup f \leq  \frac{n - 1}{f} \) in the sense of distributions (or equivalently in the weak sense) means that for any non-negative test function \( \phi \) , that is to say for any compactly supported \( {C}^{\infty } \) -function \( \phi \) , we have

\[
{\int }_{M}f\bigtriangleup {\phi d}\operatorname{vol} \leq  {\int }_{M}\left( \frac{n - 1}{f}\right) {\phi d}\operatorname{vol}.
\]

Since the triangle inequality implies that \( \left| {f\left( x\right)  - f\left( y\right) }\right|  \leq  d\left( {x, y}\right) \) , it follows that \( f \) is Lipschitz, and hence that the restriction of \( \nabla f \) to any compact subset of \( M \) is an \( {L}^{2} \) one-form. Integration by parts then shows that

\[
{\int }_{M}f\bigtriangleup {\phi d}\operatorname{vol} =  - {\int }_{M}\langle \nabla f,\nabla \phi \rangle d\operatorname{vol}.
\]

Since \( \left| {\nabla f}\right|  = 1 \) and \( \bigtriangleup f \) is the mean curvature of the geodesic sphere \( \partial B\left( {x, r}\right) ,\operatorname{Ric}\left( {v, v}\right) \) measures the difference of the mean curvature between the standard Euclidean sphere and the geodesic sphere in the direction \( v \) . Another important geometric object is the shape operator associated to \( f \) , denoted \( S \) . By definition it is the Hessian of \( f \) ; i.e., \( S = {\nabla }^{2}f = \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \) .

\]

THEOREM 1.34. (Relative Volume Comparison, Bishop-Gromov 1964- 1980) Suppose \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) is a Riemannian manifold. Fix a point \( p \in  M \) , and suppose that \( B\left( {p, R}\right) \) has compact closure in \( M \) . Suppose that for some \( k \geq  0 \) we have \( \operatorname{Ric} \geq   - \left( {n - 1}\right) k \) on \( B\left( {p, R}\right) \) . Recall that \( {H}_{k}^{n} \) is the simply connected, complete manifold of constant curvature \( - k \) and \( {q}_{k} \in  {H}_{k}^{n} \) is a point. Then

\[
\frac{\operatorname{Vol}B\left( {p, r}\right) }{\operatorname{Vol}{B}_{{H}_{k}^{n}}B\left( {{q}_{k}, r}\right) }
\]

is a non-increasing function of \( r \) for \( r < R \) , whose limit as \( r \rightarrow  0 \) is 1 . In particular, if the Ricci curvature of \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) is \( \geq  0 \) on \( B\left( {p, R}\right) \) , then \( \operatorname{Vol}B\left( {p, r}\right) /{r}^{n} \) is a non-increasing function of \( r \) for \( r < R \) .

nodes.label: Definition 2.2
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
DEFINITION 2.2. Suppose that \( \lambda  : \lbrack 0,\infty ) \rightarrow  M \) is a minimizing geodesic ray with initial point \( p \) . For each \( t \geq  0 \) we consider \( {B}_{\lambda , t}\left( x\right)  = d\left( {\lambda \left( t\right) , x}\right)  - t \) . This is a family of functions satisfying \( \left| {{B}_{\lambda , t}\left( x\right)  - {B}_{\lambda , t}\left( y\right) }\right|  \leq  d\left( {x, y}\right) \) . Since \( \lambda \) is a minimizing geodesic, \( {B}_{\lambda , t}\left( p\right)  = 0 \) for all \( t \) . It follows that \( {B}_{\lambda , t}\left( x\right)  \geq \; - d\left( {x, p}\right) \) for all \( x \in  M \) . Thus, the family of functions \( {B}_{\lambda , t} \) is pointwise bounded below. The triangle inequality shows that for each \( x \in  M \) the function \( {B}_{\lambda , t}\left( x\right) \) is a non-increasing function of \( t \) . It follows that, for each \( x \in  M,\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  \infty }}{B}_{\lambda , t}\left( x\right) \) exists. We denote this limit by \( {B}_{\lambda }\left( x\right) \) . This is the Busemann function for \( \lambda \) .

Clearly, \( {B}_{\lambda }\left( x\right)  \geq   - d\left( {x,\lambda \left( 0\right) }\right) \) . By equicontinuity \( {B}_{\lambda }\left( x\right) \) is a continuous function of \( x \) and in fact a Lipschitz function satisfying \( \left| {{B}_{\lambda }\left( x\right)  - {B}_{\lambda }\left( y\right) }\right|  \leq \; d\left( {x, y}\right) \) for all \( x, y \in  X \) . Clearly \( {B}_{\lambda }\left( {\lambda \left( s\right) }\right)  =  - s \) for all \( s \geq  0 \) . Since \( {B}_{\lambda } \) is Lipschitz, \( \nabla {B}_{\lambda } \) is well-defined as an \( {L}^{2} \) -vector field.

nodes.label: Proposition 2.3
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content: Proposition 2.3. Suppose that \( M \) is complete and of non-negative Ricci curvature. Then, for any minimizing geodesic ray \( \lambda \) , the Busemann function \( {B}_{\lambda } \) satisfies \( \Delta {B}_{\lambda } \leq  0 \) in the weak sense.
nodes.content_excerpt: Proposition 2.3. Suppose that \( M \) is complete and of non-negative Ricci curvature. Then, for any minimizing geodesic ray \( \lambda \) , the Busemann function \( {B}_{\lambda } \) satisfies \( \Delta {B}_{\lambda } \leq 0 \) in the weak sense.

nodes.proof:
First notice that since \( {B}_{\lambda } \) is Lipschitz, \( \nabla {B}_{\lambda } \) is an \( {L}^{2} \) -vector field on \( M \) . That is to say, \( {B}_{\lambda } \in  {W}_{\text{ loc }}^{1,2} \) , i.e., \( {B}_{\lambda } \) locally has one derivative in \( {L}^{2} \) . Hence, there is a sequence of \( {C}^{\infty } \) -functions \( {f}_{n} \) converging to \( {B}_{\lambda } \) in \( {W}_{loc}^{1,2} \) . Let \( \varphi \) be a test function (i.e., a compactly supported \( {C}^{\infty } \) -function). Integrating by parts yields

\[
- {\int }_{M}\left\langle  {\nabla {f}_{n},\nabla \varphi }\right\rangle  d\operatorname{vol} = {\int }_{M}{f}_{n}\bigtriangleup {\varphi d}\operatorname{vol}.
\]

Using the fact that \( {f}_{n} \) converges to \( {B}_{\lambda } \) in \( {W}_{loc}^{1,2} \) and taking limits yields

\[
- {\int }_{M}\left\langle  {\nabla {B}_{\lambda },\nabla \varphi }\right\rangle  d\operatorname{vol} = {\int }_{M}{B}_{\lambda }\bigtriangleup {\varphi d}\operatorname{vol}.
\]

Thus, to prove the proposition we need only show that if \( \varphi \) is a nonnegative test function, then

\[
- {\int }_{M}\left\langle  {\nabla {B}_{\lambda },\nabla \varphi }\right\rangle  d\operatorname{vol} \leq  0.
\]

For a proof of this see Proposition 1.1 and its proof on pp. 7 and 8 in [61].

We set \( \left| {s}_{xy}\right|  = d\left( {x, y}\right) \) and call it the length of the side. We denote by \( {\angle }_{a} \) the angle of the triangle at \( a \) , i.e., the angle at \( a \) between the geodesic rays \( {s}_{ab} \) and \( {s}_{ac} \) .

nodes.content:
THEOREM 2.4. (Length comparison) Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a manifold of nonnegative curvature. Suppose that \( \bigtriangleup  = \bigtriangleup \left( {a, b, c}\right) \) is a triangle in \( M \) and let \( {\bigtriangleup }^{\prime } = \bigtriangleup \left( {{a}^{\prime },{b}^{\prime },{c}^{\prime }}\right) \) be a Euclidean triangle.

(1) Suppose that the corresponding sides of \( \bigtriangleup \) and \( {\bigtriangleup }^{\prime } \) have the same lengths. Then the angle at each vertex of \( {\bigtriangleup }^{\prime } \) is no larger than the corresponding angle of \( \bigtriangleup \) . Furthermore, for any \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) less than \( \left| {s}_{ab}\right| \) and \( \left| {s}_{ac}\right| \) respectively, let \( x \) , resp. \( {x}^{\prime } \) , be the point on \( {s}_{ab} \) , resp. \( {s}_{{a}^{\prime }{b}^{\prime }} \) , at distance \( \alpha \) from a, resp. \( {a}^{\prime } \) , and let \( y \) , resp. \( {y}^{\prime } \) , be the point on \( {s}_{ac} \) , resp. \( {s}_{{a}^{\prime }{c}^{\prime }} \) , at distance \( \beta \) from a, resp. \( {a}^{\prime } \) . Then \( d\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  d\left( {{x}^{\prime },{y}^{\prime }}\right) . \)

(2) Suppose that \( \left| {s}_{ab}\right|  = \left| {s}_{{a}^{\prime }{b}^{\prime }}\right| \) , that \( \left| {s}_{ac}\right|  = \left| {s}_{{a}^{\prime }{c}^{\prime }}\right| \) and that \( {\angle }_{a} = {\angle }_{{a}^{\prime }} \) . Then \( \left| {s}_{{b}^{\prime }{c}^{\prime }}\right|  \geq  \left| {s}_{bc}\right| \) .

COROLLARY 2.6. Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a complete Riemannian manifold of nonnegative curvature. Let \( p, a, b, c \) be four points in \( M \) and let \( \alpha ,\beta ,\gamma \) be minimizing geodesic arcs from the point \( p \) to \( a, b, c \) respectively. Let \( T\left( {apb}\right) \) , \( T\left( {bpc}\right) \) and \( T\left( {cpa}\right) \) be the triangles in \( M \) made out of these minimizing geodesics and minimizing geodesics between \( a, b, c \) . Let \( T\left( {{a}^{\prime }{p}^{\prime }{b}^{\prime }}\right) , T\left( {{b}^{\prime }{p}^{\prime }{c}^{\prime }}\right) \) and \( T\left( {{c}^{\prime }{p}^{\prime }{a}^{\prime }}\right) \) be planar triangles with the same side lengths. Then

\[

\]

nodes.content: A subset \( X \) of a Riemannian manifold \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) is said to be totally convex if every geodesic segment with endpoints in \( X \) is contained in \( X \) . Thus, a point \( p \) in \( M \) is totally convex if and only if there is no broken geodesic arc in \( M \) broken exactly at \( x \) .

nodes.label: Theorem 2.7
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content: THEOREM 2.7. (Cheeger-Gromoll, see [8] and [10]) Suppose that \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) is a connected, complete, non-compact Riemannian manifold of non-negative sectional curvature. Then \( M \) contains a soul \( S \subset  M \) . By definition a soul is a compact, totally geodesic, totally convex submanifold (automatically of positive codimension). Furthermore, \( M \) is diffeomorphic to the total space of the normal bundle of the \( S \) in \( M \) . If \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) has positive curvature, then any soul for it is a point, and consequently \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) .

LEMMA 2.9. Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a complete, non-compact Riemannian manifold of non-negative sectional curvature and let \( p \in  M \) . For every \( \epsilon  > 0 \) there is a compact subset \( K = K\left( {p,\epsilon }\right)  \subset  M \) such that for all points \( q \notin  K \) , if \( \gamma \) and \( \mu \) are minimizing geodesics from \( p \) to \( q \) , then the angle that \( \gamma \) and \( \mu \) make at \( q \) is less than \( \epsilon \) .

See FIG. 2.

nodes.proof:
The proof is by contradiction. Fix \( 0 < \epsilon  < 1 \) sufficiently small so that \( \cos \left( {\epsilon /2}\right)  < 1 - {\epsilon }^{2}/{12} \) . Suppose that there is a sequence of points \( {q}_{n} \) tending to infinity such that for each \( n \) there are minimizing geodesics \( {\gamma }_{n} \) and \( {\mu }_{n} \) from \( p \) to \( {q}_{n} \) making angle at least \( \epsilon \) at \( {q}_{n} \) . For each \( n \) let \( {d}_{n} = d\left( {p,{q}_{n}}\right) \) . By passing to a subsequence we can suppose that for all \( n \) and \( m \) the cosine of the angle at \( p \) between \( {\gamma }_{n} \) and \( {\gamma }_{m} \) at least \( 1 - {\epsilon }^{2}/{24} \) , and the cosine of the angle at \( p \) between \( {\mu }_{n} \) and \( {\mu }_{m} \) is at least \( 1 - {\epsilon }^{2}/{24} \) . We can also assume that for all \( n \geq  1 \) we have \( {d}_{n + 1} \geq  \left( {{100}/{\epsilon }^{2}}\right) {d}_{n} \) . Let \( {\delta }_{n} = d\left( {{q}_{n},{q}_{n + 1}}\right) \) . Applying the first Toponogov property at \( p \) , we see that \( {\delta }_{n}^{2} \leq  {d}_{n}^{2} + {d}_{n + 1}^{2} - 2{d}_{n}{d}_{n + 1}\left( {1 - {\epsilon }^{2}/{24}}\right) \) . Applying the same property at \( {q}_{n} \) we have

\[
{d}_{n + 1}^{2} \leq  {d}_{n}^{2} + {\delta }_{n}^{2} - 2{d}_{n}{\delta }_{n}\cos \left( \theta \right) ,
\]

where \( \theta  \leq  \pi \) is the angle at \( {q}_{n} \) between \( {\gamma }_{n} \) and a minimal geodesic joining \( {q}_{n} \) to \( {q}_{n + 1} \) . Thus,

\[
\cos \left( \theta \right)  \leq  \frac{{d}_{n} - {d}_{n + 1}\left( {1 - {\epsilon }^{2}/{24}}\right) }{{\delta }_{n}}.
\]

By the triangle inequality (and the fact that \( \epsilon  < 1 \) ) we have \( {\delta }_{n} \geq  \left( {{99}/\epsilon }\right) {d}_{n} \) and \( {\delta }_{n} \geq  {d}_{n + 1}\left( {1 - \left( {{\epsilon }^{2}/{100}}\right) }\right) \) . Thus,

\[
\cos \left( \theta \right)  \leq  {\epsilon }^{2}/{99} - \left( {1 - {\epsilon }^{2}/{24}}\right) /\left( {1 - \left( {{\epsilon }^{2}/{100}}\right) }\right)  <  - \left( {1 - {\epsilon }^{2}/{12}}\right) .
\]

This implies that \( \cos \left( {\pi  - \theta }\right)  > \left( {1 - {\epsilon }^{2}/{12}}\right) \) , which implies that \( \pi  - \theta  < \epsilon /2 \) . That is to say, the angle at \( {q}_{n} \) between \( {\gamma }_{n} \) and a shortest geodesic from \( {q}_{n} \) to \( {q}_{n + 1} \) is between \( \pi  - \epsilon /2 \) and \( \pi \) . By symmetry, the same is true for the angle between \( {\mu }_{n} \) and the same shortest geodesic from \( {q}_{n} \) to \( {q}_{n + 1} \) . Thus, the angle between \( {\gamma }_{n} \) and \( {\mu }_{n} \) at \( {q}_{n} \) is less than \( \epsilon \) , contradicting our assumption.

nodes.proof: Given \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) and \( p \in  M \) as in the statement of the corollary, choose a constant \( R < \infty \) such that any two minimal geodesics from \( p \) to a point \( q \) with \( d\left( {p, q}\right)  \geq  R/2 \) make an angle at most \( \pi /6 \) at \( q \) . Now following [57] p. 335, it is possible to find a smooth unit vector field \( X \) on \( U = M - \overline{B\left( {p, R/2}\right) } \) with the property that \( f\left( \cdot \right)  = d\left( {p, \cdot  }\right) \) is increasing along any integral curve for \( X \) at a rate bounded below by \( \cos \left( {\pi /3}\right) \) . In particular, for any \( s \geq  R \) each integral curve of \( X \) crosses the level set \( {f}^{-1}\left( s\right) \) in a single point. Using this vector field we see that for any \( s,{s}^{\prime } > R \) , the pre-image \( {f}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {s,{s}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack  \right) \) is homeomorphic to \( {f}^{-1}\left( s\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {s,{s}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) and that the end \( {f}^{-1}\left( {\lbrack s,\infty }\right) ) \) is homeomorphic to \( {f}^{-1}\left( s\right)  \times  \lbrack s,\infty ) \) .

nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content: COROLLARY 2.11. Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a complete, non-compact Riemannian n-manifold of positive curvature. Then for any point \( p \in  M \) there is a constant \( R = R\left( p\right) \) such that for any \( s < {s}^{\prime } \) with \( R \leq  s \) both \( {f}^{-1}\left( {s,{s}^{\prime }}\right) \) and \( {f}^{-1}\left( {s,\infty }\right) \) are homotopy equivalent to \( {S}^{n - 1} \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: COROLLARY 2.11. Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a complete, non-compact Riemannian n-manifold of positive curvature. Then for any point \( p \in M \) there is a constant \( R = R\left( p\right) \) such that for any \( s < {s}^{\prime } \) with \( R \leq s \) both \( {f}^{-1}\left( {s,{s}^{\prime }}\right) \) and \( {f}^{-1}\left( {s,\infty }\right) \) are homotopy equivalent to \( {S}^{n - 1} \) .

nodes.proof: Given \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) and \( p \) , fix \( R < \infty \) sufficiently large so that Corollary 2.10 holds. Since \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) it has only one end and hence the level sets \( {f}^{-1}\left( s\right) \) for \( s \geq  R \) are connected. Given any compact subset \( K \subset  M \) there is a larger compact set \( B \) (a ball) such that \( M \smallsetminus  B \) has trivial fundamental group and trivial homology groups \( {H}_{i} \) for \( i < n - 1 \) . Hence for any subset \( Z \subset  M \smallsetminus  B \) , the inclusion of \( Z \rightarrow  M \smallsetminus  K \) induces the trivial map on \( {\pi }_{1} \) and on \( {H}_{i} \) for \( i < n - 1 \) . Clearly, for any \( R \leq  s < b \) the inclusion \( {f}^{-1}\left( {b,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  {f}^{-1}\left( {s,\infty }\right) \) is a homotopy equivalence. Thus, it must be the case that \( {f}^{-1}\left( {b,\infty }\right) \) has trivial fundamental group and \( {H}_{i} \) for \( i < n - 1 \) . Hence, the same is true for \( {f}^{-1}\left( {s,\infty }\right) \) for any \( s \geq  R \) . Lastly, since \( {f}^{-1}\left( {s,\infty }\right) \) is connected and simply connected ( hence orientable) and has two ends, it follows by the non-compact form of Poincaré duality that \( {H}_{n - 1}\left( {{f}^{-1}\left( {s,\infty }\right) }\right)  \cong  \mathbb{Z} \) . Hence, by the Hurewicz theorem \( {f}^{-1}\left( {s,\infty }\right) \) is homotopy equivalent to \( {S}^{n - 1} \) for any \( s \geq  R \) . Of course, it is also true for \( R \leq  s \leq  {s}^{\prime } \) that \( {f}^{-1}\left( {s,{s}^{\prime }}\right) \) is homotopy equivalent to \( {S}^{n - 1} \) .

nodes.label: Definition 2.12
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content: DEFINITION 2.12. Let \( M \) be a connected manifold. Consider the inverse system of spaces indexed by the compact, codimension-0 submanifolds \( K \subset  M \) , where the space associated to \( K \) is the finite set \( {\pi }_{0}\left( {M \smallsetminus  K}\right) \) with the discrete topology. The inverse limit of this inverse system is the space of ends of \( M \) . It is a compact space. An end of \( M \) is a point of the space of ends. An end \( \mathcal{E} \) determines a complementary component of each compact, codimension-0 submanifold \( K \subset  M \) , called a neighborhood of the end. Conversely, by definition these neighborhoods are cofinal in the set of all neighborhoods of the end. A sequence \( \left\{  {x}_{n}\right\} \) in \( M \) converges to the end \( \mathcal{E} \) if it is eventually in every neighborhood of the end. In fact, what we are doing is defining a topology on the union of \( M \) and its space of ends that makes this union a compact, connected Hausdorff space which is a compactification of \( M \) .

nodes.content: Now suppose that \( M \) has a Riemannian metric \( g \) . Then we can distinguish between ends at finite and infinite distance. An end is at finite distance if there is a rectifiable path of finite length to the end. Otherwise, the end is at infinite distance. If an end is at finite distance we have the notion of the distance from a point \( x \in  M \) to the end. It is the infimum of the lengths of rectifiable paths from \( x \) to the end. This distance is always positive. Also, notice that the Riemannian manifold is complete if and only if has no end at finite distance.

nodes.content: LEMMA 2.14. Any complete Riemannian manifold \( X \) of non-negative Ricci curvature containing a minimizing line is isometric to a product \( N \times  \mathbb{R} \) for some Riemannian manifold \( N \) .
