Proposition 4.1. Let \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 \leq  t < T \) , be a Ricci flow with \( M \) a compact \( n \) -dimensional manifold. Denote by \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) \) the minimum value of the scalar curvature of \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Then:

- \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) \) is a non-decreasing function of \( t \) .

- If \( {R}_{\min }\left( 0\right)  \geq  0 \) , then

\[
{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \geq  {R}_{\min }\left( 0\right) \left( \frac{1}{1 - \frac{2t}{n}{R}_{\min }\left( 0\right) }\right) ,
\]

in particular,

\[
T \leq  \frac{n}{2{R}_{\min }\left( 0\right) }.
\]

- If \( {R}_{\min }\left( 0\right)  < 0 \) , then

\[
{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \geq   - \frac{n\left| {{R}_{\min }\left( 0\right) }\right| }{{2t}\left| {{R}_{\min }\left( 0\right) }\right|  + n}.
\]

nodes.proof:
According to Equation (3.7), the evolution equation for \( R \) is

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}R\left( {x, t}\right)  = {\Delta R}\left( {x, t}\right)  + 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( x, t\right) \right| }^{2}.
\]

Since \( M \) is compact, the function \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) \) is continuous but may not be \( {C}^{1} \) at points where the minimum of the scalar curvature is achieved at more than one point.

The first thing to notice is the following:

\[
\text{ CLAIM 4.2. If }R\left( {x, t}\right)  = {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) \text{ , then }\left( {\partial R/\partial t}\right) \left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  \frac{2}{n}{R}^{2}\left( {x, t}\right) \text{ . }
\]

Proof. This is immediate from the evolution equation for \( R \) , the fact that if \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  = {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) \) , then \( {\Delta R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  0 \) , and the fact that \( R \) is the trace of Ric which implies by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality that \( {\left| R\right| }^{2} \leq \; n{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\right| }^{2} \) .

Now it follows that:

CLAIM 4.3.

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\left( {{R}_{\min }\left( t\right) }\right)  \geq  \frac{2}{n}{R}_{\min }^{2}\left( t\right)
\]

where, at times \( t \) where \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) \) is not smooth, this inequality is interpreted as an inequality for the forward difference quotients.

Proof. This is immediate from the first statement in Proposition 2.23.

It follows immediately from Claim 4.3 and Lemma 2.22 that \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) \) is a non-decreasing function of \( t \) . This establishes the first item and also the second item in the case when \( {R}_{\min }\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) .

Suppose that \( {R}_{\min }\left( 0\right)  \neq  0 \) . Consider the function

\[
S\left( t\right)  = \frac{-1}{{R}_{\min }\left( t\right) } - \frac{2t}{n} + \frac{1}{{R}_{\min }\left( 0\right) }.
\]

Clearly, \( S\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) and \( {S}^{\prime }\left( t\right)  \geq  0 \) (in the sense of forward difference quotients), so that by Lemma 2.22 we have \( S\left( t\right)  \geq  0 \) for all \( t \) . This means that

(4.1)

\[
\frac{1}{{R}_{\min }\left( t\right) } \leq  \frac{1}{{R}_{\min }\left( 0\right) } - \frac{2t}{n}
\]

provided that \( {R}_{\min } \) is not ever zero on the interval \( \left\lbrack  {0, t}\right\rbrack \) . If \( {R}_{\min }\left( 0\right)  > 0 \) , then by the first item, \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  > 0 \) for all \( t \) for which the flow is defined, and the inequality in the second item of the proposition is immediate from Equation (4.1). The third inequality in the proposition also follows easily from Equation (4.1) when \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  < 0 \) . But if \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \geq  0 \) , then the third item is obvious.

nodes.content: LEMMA 4.5. Let \( Z \) be a closed convex subset in a finite-dimensional real vector space \( V \) . Let \( \psi \) be a smooth vector field defined on an open neighborhood of \( Z \) in \( V \) . Then \( \psi \) preserves \( Z \) if and only if every integral curve \( \gamma  : \lbrack 0, a) \rightarrow  V \) for \( \psi \) with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  \in  Z \) has \( \gamma \left( t\right)  \in  Z \) for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, a) \) . nodes.proof:
The bound on the Riemann curvature follows directly from Lemma 6.1 on page 207 of [14] and the definition of normalized initial conditions. Once we know that the Riemann curvature is bounded by 2 on \( \left\lbrack  {0,{2}^{-4}}\right\rbrack \) , there is an \( 0 < {r}_{0} \) depending on \( n \) such that for every \( x \in  M \) and every \( r \leq  {r}_{0} \) we have \( B\left( {x,0,{r}_{0}r}\right)  \subset  B\left( {x, t, r}\right)  \subset  B\left( {x,0,1}\right) \) . Also, from the bound on the Riemann curvature and the evolution equation for volume given in Equation (3.7), we see that there is \( A < \infty \) such that \( {\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( {B\left( {x,0, s}\right) }\right)  \geq  {A}^{-1}{\operatorname{Vol}}_{0}\left( {B\left( {x,0, s}\right) }\right) \) . Putting this together we see that

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( {B\left( {x, t, r}\right)  \geq  {A}^{-1}\left( {{\omega }_{n}/2}\right) {r}_{0}^{n}{r}^{n}.}\right.
\]

This proves the result.

\]

Proposition 4.17. Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a Riemannian manifold and let \( \mathcal{V} \) be a tensor bundle. Suppose that \( \bar{U} \) is a compact, connected, smooth submanifold of \( M \) of codimension 0 . Consider a one-parameter family of sections \( \mathcal{T}\left( {x, t}\right) \) defined for \( 0 \leq  t \leq  T \) , of \( \mathcal{V} \) . Suppose that \( \mathcal{T} \) evolves according to the equation

\[
\frac{\partial \mathcal{T}}{\partial t} = \Delta \mathcal{T} + \psi \left( \mathcal{T}\right)
\]

for some smooth, fiberwise vector field \( \psi \left( \mathcal{T}\right) \) defined on \( \mathcal{V} \) . Suppose that \( s : \mathcal{V} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) is a function satisfying the following properties:

(1) For each \( x \in  M \) the restriction \( {s}_{x} \) to the fiber \( {V}_{x} \) of \( \mathcal{V} \) over \( x \) is a convex function.

(2) For any \( A \) satisfying \( {s}_{x}\left( A\right)  \geq  0 \) the vector \( \psi \left( A\right) \) is contained in the tangent cone of the convex set \( \left\{  {y \mid  {s}_{x}\left( y\right)  \geq  {s}_{x}\left( A\right) }\right. \) at the point \( A \) .

Suppose also that there is \( {x}_{0} \in  \operatorname{int}\left( \bar{U}\right) \) with \( s\left( {\mathcal{T}\left( {{x}_{0},0}\right) }\right)  > 0 \) . Then \( s\left( {\mathcal{T}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right)  > 0 \) for all \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  \operatorname{int}\left( \bar{U}\right)  \times  (0, T\rbrack \) .

\[

\]

Consider the tensor bundle \( \mathcal{V} \oplus  \mathbb{R} \) over \( M \) . We define

\[
{Z}_{x} = \left\{  {\left( {\mathcal{T}, h}\right)  \in  {V}_{x} \oplus  \mathbb{R} \mid  {s}_{x}\left( \mathcal{T}\right)  \geq  h \geq  0}\right\}  .
\]

The union over all \( x \in  M \) of the \( {Z}_{x} \) defines a closed convex subset \( \mathcal{Z} \subset  \mathcal{V} \oplus  \mathbb{R} \) which is invariant under parallel translation since \( s \) is. We consider the family of sections \( \left( {\mathcal{T}\left( {x, t}\right) , h\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) ,0 \leq  t \leq  T \) , of \( \mathcal{V} \oplus  \mathbb{R} \) . These evolve by

\[
\frac{d\left( {\mathcal{T}\left( {x, t}\right) , h\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) }{dt} = \left( {\Delta \mathcal{T}\left( {x, t}\right) ,{\Delta h}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right)  + \widetilde{\psi }\left( {\mathcal{T}\left( {x, t}\right) , h\left( {x, t}\right) }\right)
\]

where \( \widetilde{\psi }\left( {\mathcal{T}, h}\right)  = \left( {\psi \left( \mathcal{T}\right) ,0}\right) \) . Clearly, by our hypotheses, the vector field \( \widetilde{\psi } \) preserves the convex set \( \mathcal{Z} \) . Applying the local version of the maximum principle (Theorem 4.9), we conclude that \( \mathcal{T}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  h\left( {x, t}\right) \) for all \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in \; \bar{U} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) .

The result then follows immediately from Theorem 4.16.

nodes.label: Theorem 4.18
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.section_title: 4. The strong maximum principle for curvature
nodes.content: THEOREM 4.18. Let \( \left( {U, g\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 \leq  t \leq  T \) , be a 3-dimensional Ricci flow with non-negative sectional curvature with \( U \) connected but not necessarily complete and with \( T > 0 \) . If \( R\left( {p, T}\right)  = 0 \) for some \( p \in  U \) , then \( \left( {U, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is flat for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: THEOREM 4.18. Let \( \left( {U, g\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 \leq t \leq T \) , be a 3-dimensional Ricci flow with non-negative sectional curvature with \( U \) connected but not necessarily complete and with \( T > 0 \) . If \( R\left( {p, T}\right) = 0 \) for some \( p \in U \) , then \( \left( {U, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is flat for every \( t \in \left\lbrack {0, T}\right\rbrack \) .

nodes.proof:
We suppose that there is \( p \in  U \) with \( R\left( {p, T}\right)  = 0 \) . Since all the metrics in the flow are of non-negative sectional curvature, if the flow does not consist entirely of flat manifolds, then there is \( \left( {q, t}\right)  \in  U \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) with \( R\left( {q, t}\right)  > 0 \) . Clearly, by continuity, we can assume \( t < T \) . By restricting to the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {t, T}\right\rbrack \) and shifting by \( - t \) we can arrange that \( t = 0 \) . Let \( V \) be a compact, connected smooth submanifold with boundary whose interior contains \( q \) and \( p \) . Let \( h\left( {y,0}\right) \) be a smooth non-negative function with support in \( V \) , positive at \( q \) , such that \( R\left( {y,0}\right)  \geq  h\left( {y,0}\right) \) for all \( y \in  V \) . Let \( h\left( {y, t}\right) \) be the solution to the heat equation on \( V \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) that vanishes on \( \partial V \) . Of course, \( h\left( {y, T}\right)  > 0 \) for all \( y \in  \operatorname{int}\left( V\right) \) . Also, from Equation (3.7) we have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {R - h}\right)  = \Delta \left( {R - h}\right)  + 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\right| }^{2},
\]

so that \( \left( {R - h}\right) \left( {y,0}\right)  \geq  0 \) on \( \left( {V\times \{ 0\} }\right)  \cup  \left( {\partial V \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack  }\right) \) . It follows from the maximum principle that \( \left( {R - h}\right)  \geq  0 \) on all of \( V \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . In particular, \( R\left( {p, T}\right)  \geq  h\left( {p, T}\right)  > 0 \) . This is a contradiction, establishing the theorem.

nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture

nodes.content: COROLLARY 4.19. Fix \( T > 0 \) . Suppose that \( \left( {U, g\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 \leq  t \leq  T \) , is a Ricci flow such that for each \( t \) , the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {U, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a (not necessarily complete) connected, 3-manifold of non-negative sectional curvature. Suppose that \( \left( {U, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is not flat and that for some \( p \in  M \) the Ricci curvature at \( \left( {p, T}\right) \) has a zero eigenvalue. Then for each \( t \in  (0, T\rbrack \) the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {U, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) splits locally as a product of a surface of positive curvature and a line, and under this local splitting the flow is locally the product of a Ricci flow on the surface and the trivial flow on the line.

Suppose that \( \left( {U, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is not flat and that for some \( p \in M \) the R...

nodes.proof:
First notice that it follows from Theorem 4.18 that because \( \left( {U, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is not flat, we have \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  > 0 \) for every \( \left( {y, t}\right)  \in  U \times  (0, T\rbrack \) .

We consider the function \( s \) on \( {\operatorname{Sym}}^{2}\left( {{ \land  }^{2}{T}_{y}^{ * }U}\right) \) that associates to each endomorphism the sum of the smallest two eigenvalues. Then \( {s}_{y} \) is the minimum of the traces on 2-dimensional subsets in \( { \land  }^{2}{T}_{y}U \) . Thus, \( s \) is a convex function, and the subset \( \mathcal{S} = {s}^{-1}\left( {\lbrack 0,\infty }\right) ) \) is a convex subset. Clearly, this subset is invariant under parallel translation. By the computations in the proof of Corollary 4.15 it is invariant under the vector field \( \psi \left( \mathcal{T}\right) \) . The hypothesis of the corollary tells us that \( s\left( {p, T}\right)  = 0 \) . Suppose that \( s\left( {q, t}\right)  > 0 \) for some \( \left( {q, t}\right)  \in  U \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . Of course, by continuity we can take \( t < T \) . Shift the time parameter so that \( t = 0 \) , and fix a compact connected, codimension- 0 submanifold \( V \) containing \( p, q \) in its interior. Then by Theorem 4.17 \( s\left( {y, T}\right)  > 0 \) for all \( y \in  \operatorname{int}\left( V\right) \) and in particular \( s\left( {p, T}\right)  > 0 \) . This is a contradiction, and we conclude that \( s\left( {q, t}\right)  = 0 \) for all \( \left( {q, t}\right)  \in  U \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) .

Since we have already established that each \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  > 0 \) for all \( \left( {y, t}\right)  \in \; U \times  (0, T\rbrack \) , so that \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {y, t}\right) \) is not identically zero, this means that for all \( y \in  U \) and all \( t \in  (0, T\rbrack \) , the null space of the operator \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {y, t}\right) \) is a 2-dimensional subspace of \( { \land  }^{2}{T}_{y}U \) . This 2-dimensional subspace is dual to a line in \( {T}_{x}M \) . Thus, we have a one-dimensional distribution (a line bundle in the tangent bundle) \( \mathcal{D} \) in \( U \times  (0, T\rbrack \) with the property that the sectional curvature \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {y, t}\right) \) vanishes on any 2-plane containing the line \( \mathcal{D}\left( {y, t}\right) \) . The fact that the sectional curvature of \( g\left( t\right) \) vanishes on all two-planes in \( {T}_{y}M \) containing \( \mathcal{D}\left( {y, t}\right) \) means that its eigenvalues are \( \{ \lambda ,0,0\} \) where \( \lambda  > 0 \) is the sectional curvature of the \( g\left( t\right) \) -orthogonal 2-plane to \( \mathcal{D}\left( {y, t}\right) \) . Hence \( \mathcal{R}\left( {V\left( {y, t}\right) ,\cdot ,\cdot , \cdot  }\right)  = 0. \)

Locally in space and time, there is a unique (up to sign) vector field \( V\left( {y, t}\right) \) that generates \( \mathcal{D} \) and satisfies \( {\left| V\left( y, t\right) \right| }_{g\left( t\right) }^{2} = 1 \) . We wish to show that this local vector field is invariant under parallel translation and time translation; cf. Lemma 8.2 in [30]. Fix a point \( x \in  M \) , a direction \( X \) at \( x \) , and a time \( t \) . Let \( \widetilde{V}\left( {y, t}\right) \) be a parallel extension of \( V\left( {x, t}\right) \) along a curve \( C \) passing through \( x \) in the \( X \) -direction, and let \( \widetilde{W}\left( {y, t}\right) \) be an arbitrary parallel vector field along \( C \) . Since the sectional curvature is non-negative, we have \( \mathcal{R}\left( {\widetilde{V},\widetilde{W},\widetilde{V},\widetilde{W}}\right) \left( y\right)  \geq  0 \) for all \( y \in  C \) ; furthermore, this expression vanishes at \( x \) . Hence, its first variation vanishes at \( x \) . That is to say

\[
\nabla \left( {\mathcal{R}\left( {\widetilde{V},\widetilde{W},\widetilde{V},\widetilde{W}}\right) }\right) \left( {x, t}\right)  = \left( {\nabla \mathcal{R}}\right) \left( {\widetilde{V},\widetilde{W},\widetilde{V},\widetilde{W}}\right)
\]

vanishes at \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) . Since this is true for all \( \widetilde{W} \) , it follows that the null space of the quadratic form \( \nabla \mathcal{R}\left( {x, t}\right) \) contains the null space of \( \mathcal{R}\left( {x, t}\right) \) , and thus

\[
\left( {\nabla \mathcal{R}}\right) \left( {V\left( {x, t}\right) ,\cdot ,\cdot , \cdot  }\right)  = 0.
\]

Now let us consider three parallel vector fields \( {\widetilde{W}}_{1},{\widetilde{W}}_{2} \) , and \( {\widetilde{W}}_{3} \) along \( C \) . We compute \( 0 = {\nabla }_{X}\left( {\mathcal{R}\left( {V\left( {y, t}\right) ,{\widetilde{W}}_{1}\left( {y, t}\right) ,{\widetilde{W}}_{2}\left( {y, t}\right) ,{\widetilde{W}}_{3}\left( {y, t}\right) }\right) }\right) \) . (Notice that while the \( {\widetilde{W}}_{i} \) are parallel along \( C, V\left( {y, t}\right) \) is defined to be the vector field spanning \( \mathcal{D}\left( {y, t}\right) \) rather than a parallel extension of \( V\left( {x, t}\right) \) .) Given the above result we find that

\[
0 = 2\mathcal{R}\left( {{\nabla }_{X}V\left( {x, t}\right) ,{\widetilde{W}}_{1}\left( {x, t}\right) ,{\widetilde{W}}_{2}\left( {x, t}\right) ,{\widetilde{W}}_{3}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) .
\]

Since this is true for all triples of vector fields \( {\widetilde{W}}_{i}\left( {x, t}\right) \) , it follows that \( {\nabla }_{X}V\left( {x, t}\right) \) is a real multiple of \( V\left( {x, t}\right) \) . But since \( {\left| V\left( y, t\right) \right| }_{g\left( t\right) }^{2} = 1 \) , we see that \( {\nabla }_{X}V\left( {x, t}\right) \) is orthogonal to \( V\left( {x, t}\right) \) . We conclude that \( {\nabla }_{X}V\left( {x, t}\right)  = 0 \) . Since \( x \) and \( X \) are general, this shows that the local vector field \( V\left( {x, t}\right) \) is invariant under the parallel translation associated to the metric \( g\left( t\right) \) .

It follows that locally \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a Riemannian product of a surface of positive curvature with a line. Under this product decomposition, the curvature is the pullback of the curvature of the surface. Hence, by Equation (3.5), under Ricci flow on the 3-manifold, the time derivative of the curvature at time \( t \) also decomposes as the pullback of the time derivative of the curvature of the surface under Ricci flow on the surface. In particular, \( \left( {\partial \mathcal{R}/\partial t}\right) \left( {V,\cdot ,\cdot , \cdot  }\right)  = 0 \) . It now follows easily that \( \partial V\left( {x, t}\right) /\partial t = 0 \) .

This completes the proof that the unit vector field in the direction \( \mathcal{D}\left( {x, t}\right) \) is invariant under parallel translation and under time translation. Thus, there is a local Riemannian splitting of the 3-manifold into a surface and a line, and this splitting is invariant under the Ricci flow. This completes the proof of the corollary.

In the complete case, this local product decomposition globalizes in some cover; see Lemma 9.1 in [30].

COROLLARY 4.20. Suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 \leq  t \leq  T \) , is a Ricci flow of complete, connected Riemannian 3-manifolds with \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  0 \) for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) and with \( T > 0 \) . Suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is not flat and that for some \( x \in  M \) the endomorphism \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, T}\right) \) has a zero eigenvalue. Then \( M \) has a cover \( \widetilde{M} \) such that, denoting the induced family of metrics on this cover by \( \widetilde{g}\left( t\right) \) , we have that \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) }\right) \) splits as a product

\[
\left( {N, h\left( t\right) }\right)  \times  \left( {\mathbb{R}, d{s}^{2}}\right)
\]

where \( \left( {N, h\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a surface of positive curvature for all \( 0 < t \leq  T \) . The Ricci flow is a product of the Ricci flow \( \left( {N, h\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 \leq  t \leq  T \) , with the trivial flow on \( \mathbb{R} \) .

nodes.content: REMARK 4.21. Notice that there are only four possibilities for the cover required by the corollary. It can be trivial, or a normal \( \mathbb{Z} \) -cover, or it can be a two-sheeted cover or a normal infinite dihedral group cover. In the first two cases, there is a unit vector field on \( M \) parallel under \( g\left( t\right) \) for all \( t \) spanning the null direction of Ric. In the last two cases, there is no such vector field, only a non-orientable line field.

nodes.content: Proposition 4.22. Suppose that \( \left( {U, g\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 \leq  t \leq  T \) , is a 3-dimensional Ricci flow with non-negative sectional curvature, with \( U \) being connected but not necessarily complete and \( T > 0 \) . Then \( \left( {U, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is flat for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) .

nodes.proof:
If \( \left( {U, g\left( T\right) }\right) \) is flat, then by Theorem 4.18 for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {U, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is flat.

We must rule out the possibility that \( \left( {U, g\left( T\right) }\right) \) is non-flat. Suppose that \( \left( {U, g\left( T\right) }\right) \) is an open subset in a non-flat cone. According to Proposition 1.15, for each \( x \in  U \) the Riemann curvature tensor of \( \left( {U, g\left( T\right) }\right) \) at \( x \) has a 2-dimensional null space in \( { \land  }^{2}{T}_{x}U \) . Since we are assuming that \( \left( {U, g\left( T\right) }\right) \) is not flat, the third eigenvalue of the Riemann curvature tensor is not identically zero. Restricting to a smaller open subset if necessary, we can assume that the third eigenvalue is never zero. By the computations in Proposition 1.15, the non-zero eigenvalue is not constant, and in fact it scales by \( {s}^{-2} \) in the terminology of that proposition, as we move along the cone lines. Of course, the 2-dimensional null-space for the Riemann curvature tensor at each point is equivalent to a line field in the tangent bundle of the manifold. Clearly, that line field is the line field along the cone lines. Corollary 4.19 says that since the Riemann curvature of \( \left( {U, g\left( T\right) }\right) \) has a 2-dimensional null-space in \( { \land  }^{2}{T}_{x}U \) at every point \( x \in  U \) , the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {U, g\left( T\right) }\right) \) locally splits as a Riemannian product of a line with a surface of positive curvature, and the 2-dimensional null-space for the Riemann curvature tensor is equivalent to the line field in the direction of the second factor. Along these lines the non-zero eigenvalue of the curvature is constant. This is a contradiction and establishes the result.

THEOREM 4.23. Suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 \leq  t < T \) , is a Ricci flow with \( M \) being a compact 3-dimensional manifold. If \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( {x,0}\right)  \geq  0 \) for all \( x \in  M \) , then either \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( {x, t}\right)  > 0 \) for all \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  M \times  \left( {0, T}\right) \) or \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( {x, t}\right)  = 0 \) for all \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  M \times  \lbrack 0, T) \) . Suppose that \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( {x, t}\right)  > 0 \) for some \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) and that the flow is maximal in the sense that there is no \( {T}^{\prime } > T \) and an extension of the given flow to a flow defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}^{\prime }}\right) \) . For each \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) , let \( \lambda \left( {x, t}\right) \) , resp. \( \nu \left( {x, t}\right) \) , denote the largest, resp. smallest, eigenvalue of \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) \) on \( { \land  }^{2}{T}_{x}M \) . Then as \( t \) tends to \( T \) the Riemannian manifolds \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) are becoming round in the sense that

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  T}}\frac{\mathop{\max }\limits_{{x \in  M}}\lambda \left( {x, t}\right) }{\mathop{\min }\limits_{{x \in  M}}\nu \left( {x, t}\right) } = 1.
\]

Furthermore, for any \( x \in  M \) the largest eigenvalue \( \lambda \left( {x, t}\right) \) tends to \( \infty \) as \( t \) tends to \( T \) , and rescaling \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) by \( \lambda \left( {x, t}\right) \) produces a family of Riemannian manifolds converging smoothly as \( t \) goes to \( T \) to a compact round manifold. In particular, the underlying smooth manifold supports a Riemannian metric of constant positive curvature so that the manifold is diffeomorphic to a 3-dimensional spherical space-form.

Let \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 \leq  t < T \) , be the maximal Ricci flow with initial manifold \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) . Since \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( {x,0}\right)  > 0 \) for all \( x \in  M \) , it follows from Theorem 4.23 that \( T < \infty \) and that as \( t \) tends to \( T \) the metrics \( g\left( t\right) \) converge smoothly to a round metric. Since all the manifolds \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) are isometric up to diffeomorphism and a constant conformal factor, this implies that all the \( g\left( t\right) \) are of constant positive curvature.

The last statement is a standard consequence of the fact that the manifold has constant positive curvature.

THEOREM 4.26. Let \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 \leq  t < T \) , be a Ricci flow with \( M \) a compact 3-manifold. Assume that for every \( x \in  M \) the smallest eigenvalue of \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x,0}\right) \) , denoted \( \nu \left( {x,0}\right) \) , is at least -1 . Set \( X\left( {x, t}\right)  = \max \left( {-\nu \left( {x, t}\right) ,0}\right) \) . Then we have:

(1) \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  \frac{-6}{{4t} + 1} \) , and

(2) for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) for which \( 0 < X\left( {x, t}\right) \) ,

\[
R\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  {2X}\left( {x, t}\right) \left( {\log X\left( {x, t}\right)  + \log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - 3}\right) .
\]

For any fixed \( t \) , the limit as \( X \) goes to 0 from above of

\[
X\left( {\log \left( X\right)  + \log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - 3}\right)
\]

is zero, so that it is natural to interpret this expression to be zero when \( X = 0 \) . Of course, when \( X\left( {x, t}\right)  = 0 \) all the eigenvalues of \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) \) are nonnegative so that \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  0 \) as well. Thus, with this interpretation of the expression in part 2 of the theorem, it remains valid even when \( X\left( {x, t}\right)  = 0 \) .

nodes.proof:
First note that by Proposition 4.1, if \( {R}_{\min }\left( 0\right)  \geq  0 \) , then the same is true for \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) \) for every \( t > 0 \) and thus the first inequality stated in the theorem is clearly true. If \( {R}_{\min }\left( 0\right)  < 0 \) , the first inequality stated in the theorem follows easily from the last inequality in Proposition 4.1.

We turn now to the second inequality in the statement of the theorem. Consider the tensor bundle \( \mathcal{V} = {\operatorname{Sym}}^{2}\left( {{ \land  }^{2}{T}^{ * }M}\right) \) . Then the curvature operator, written in the evolving frame \( \mathcal{T}\left( {x, t}\right) \) , is a one-parameter family of smooth sections of this bundle, evolving by

\[
\frac{\partial \mathcal{T}}{\partial t} = \Delta \mathcal{T} + \psi \left( \mathcal{T}\right)
\]

We consider two subsets of \( \mathcal{V} \) . There are two solutions to

\[
x\left( {\log \left( x\right)  + \left( {\log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - 3}\right)  =  - 3/\left( {1 + t}\right) .}\right.
\]

One is \( x = 1/\left( {1 + t}\right) \) ; let \( \xi \left( t\right)  > 1/\left( {1 + t}\right) \) be the other. We set \( S\left( \mathcal{T}\right)  = \operatorname{tr}\left( \mathcal{T}\right) \) , so that \( R = {2S} \) , and we set \( X\left( \mathcal{T}\right)  = \max \left( {-\nu \left( \mathcal{T}\right) ,0}\right) \) . Define

\[
{\mathcal{Z}}_{1}\left( t\right)  = \left\{  {\mathcal{T} \in  \mathcal{V} \mid  S\left( \mathcal{T}\right)  \geq   - \frac{3}{\left( 1 + t\right) }}\right\}
\]

\[
{\mathcal{Z}}_{2}\left( t\right)  = \left\{  {\mathcal{T} \in  \mathcal{V} \mid  S\left( \mathcal{T}\right)  \geq  {f}_{t}\left( {X\left( \mathcal{T}\right) }\right) ,\;\text{ if }\;X\left( \mathcal{T}\right)  \geq  \xi \left( t\right) }\right\}
\]

where \( {f}_{t}\left( x\right)  = x\left( {\log x + \log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - 3}\right) \) . Then we define

\[
\mathcal{Z}\left( t\right)  = {\mathcal{Z}}_{1}\left( t\right)  \cap  {\mathcal{Z}}_{2}\left( t\right) .
\]

CLAIM 4.28. For each \( x \in  M \) and each \( t \geq  0 \) , the fiber \( Z\left( {x, t}\right) \) of \( \mathcal{Z}\left( t\right) \) over \( x \) is a convex subset of \( {\operatorname{Sym}}^{2}\left( {{ \land  }^{2}{T}^{ * }M}\right) \) .

Proof. First consider the function \( {f}_{t}\left( x\right)  = x\left( {\log \left( x\right)  + \log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - 3}\right) \) on the interval \( \lbrack \xi \left( t\right) ,\infty ) \) . Direct computation shows that \( {f}^{\prime }\left( x\right)  > 0 \) and \( {f}^{\prime \prime }\left( x\right)  > \) 0 on this interval. Hence, for every \( t \geq  0 \) the region \( \mathcal{C}\left( t\right) \) in the \( S - X \) plane, defined by \( S \geq   - 3/\left( {1 + t}\right) \) and in addition by \( S \geq  {f}_{t}\left( X\right) \) when \( X \geq  \xi \left( t\right) \) , is convex and has the property that if \( \left( {S, X}\right)  \in  \mathcal{C}\left( t\right) \) then so is \( \left( {S,{X}^{\prime }}\right) \) for all \( {X}^{\prime } \leq  X \) . (See FIG. 1). By definition an element \( \mathcal{T} \in  \mathcal{V} \) is contained in \( \mathcal{Z}\left( t\right) \) if and only if \( \left( {S\left( \mathcal{T}\right) , X\left( \mathcal{T}\right)  \in  \mathcal{C}\left( t\right) }\right. \) . Now fix \( t \geq  0 \) and suppose that \( {\mathcal{T}}_{1} \) and \( {\mathcal{T}}_{2} \) are elements of \( {\operatorname{Sym}}^{2}\left( {{ \land  }^{2}{T}^{ * }{M}_{x}}\right) \) such that setting \( {S}_{i} = \operatorname{tr}\left( {\mathcal{T}}_{i}\right) \) and \( {X}_{i} = X\left( {\mathcal{T}}_{i}\right) \) we have \( \left( {{S}_{i},{X}_{i}}\right)  \in  \mathcal{C}\left( t\right) \) for \( i = 1,2 \) . Then we consider \( \mathcal{T} = s{\mathcal{T}}_{1} + \left( {1 - s}\right) {\mathcal{T}}_{2} \) for some \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . Let \( S = \operatorname{tr}\left( \mathcal{T}\right) \) and \( X = X\left( \mathcal{T}\right) \) . Since \( \mathcal{C}\left( t\right) \) is convex, we know that \( \left( {s{S}_{1} + \left( {1 - s}\right) {S}_{2}, s{X}_{1} + \left( {1 - s}\right) {X}_{2}}\right)  \in  \mathcal{C}\left( t\right) \) , so that \( \mathcal{T} \in  \mathcal{Z}\left( t\right) \) . Clearly, \( S = s{S}_{1} + \left( {1 - s}\right) {S}_{2} \) , so that we conclude that \( \left( {S,\left( {s{X}_{1} + \left( {1 - s}\right) {X}_{2}}\right) }\right)  \in  \mathcal{C}\left( t\right) \) . But since \( \nu \) is a convex function, \( X \) is a concave function, i.e., \( X \leq  s{X}_{1} + \left( {1 - s}\right) {X}_{2} \) . Hence \( \left( {S, X}\right)  \in  \mathcal{C}\left( t\right) \) .

CLAIM 4.29. \( \mathcal{T}\left( {x,0}\right)  \in  Z\left( {x,0}\right) \) for all \( x \in  M \) .

Proof. Note that by the hypothesis of the theorem the trace of \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x,0}\right) \) is at least -3 so \( \left( {S\left( {x,0}\right) , X\left( {x,0}\right) }\right)  \in  \mathcal{C}\left( 0\right) \) for all \( x \in  M \) . On the other hand, if \( 0 < X\left( {x,0}\right) \) , then since \( X\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  1 \) we have \( S\left( {x,0}\right)  \geq   - {3X}\left( {x,0}\right)  \geq \; X\left( {\log X - 3}\right) \) . This completes the proof that \( \mathcal{T}\left( {x,0}\right)  \in  \mathcal{C}\left( 0\right) \) for all \( x \in  M \) .

CLAIM 4.30. The vector field \( \psi \left( \mathcal{T}\right)  = {\mathcal{T}}^{2} + {\mathcal{T}}^{\sharp } \) preserves the family \( \mathcal{Z}\left( t\right) \) of convex sets.

Proof. We denote the eigenvalues of \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) \) by \( \lambda \left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  \mu \left( {x, t}\right)  \geq \; \nu \left( {x, t}\right) \) . Fix \( x \in  M \) and let \( \gamma \left( t\right) ,{t}_{0} \leq  t \leq  T \) , be an integral curve for \( \psi \) with \( \gamma \left( {t}_{0}\right)  \in  Z\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \) . We wish to show that \( \gamma \left( t\right)  \in  Z\left( {x, t}\right) \) for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0}, T}\right\rbrack \) . The function \( S\left( t\right)  = S\left( {\gamma \left( t\right) }\right) \) satisfies

\[
\frac{dS}{dt} = {\lambda }^{2} + {\mu }^{2} + {\nu }^{2} + {\lambda \mu } + {\lambda \nu } + {\mu \nu } = \frac{1}{2}\left( {{\left( \lambda  + \mu \right) }^{2} + {\left( \lambda  + \nu \right) }^{2} + {\left( \mu  + \nu \right) }^{2}}\right) .
\]

By Cauchy-Schwarz we have

\[
{\left( \lambda  + \mu \right) }^{2} + {\left( \lambda  + \nu \right) }^{2} + {\left( \mu  + \nu \right) }^{2}) \geq  \frac{4{S}^{2}}{3} \geq  \frac{2{S}^{2}}{3}.
\]

Since \( \gamma \left( {t}_{0}\right)  \in  Z\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \) we have \( S\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \geq   - 3/\left( {1 + {t}_{0}}\right) \) . It then follows that

(4.2)

\[
S\left( t\right)  \geq   - 3/\left( {1 + t}\right) \;\text{ for all }\;t \geq  {t}_{0}.
\]

Now let us consider the evolution of \( X\left( t\right)  = X\left( {\gamma \left( t\right) }\right) \) . Assume that we are at a point \( t \) for which \( X\left( t\right)  > 0 \) . For this computation we set \( Y =  - \mu \) .

\[
\frac{dX}{dt} =  - \frac{d\nu }{dt} =  - {\nu }^{2} - {\mu \lambda } =  - {X}^{2} + {Y\lambda }
\]

\[
\frac{dS}{dt} = \frac{d\left( {\nu  + \mu  + \lambda }\right) }{dt} = {\nu }^{2} + {\mu }^{2} + {\lambda }^{2} + {\mu \lambda } + {\nu \lambda } + {\nu \mu }
\]

\[
= {X}^{2} + {Y}^{2} + {\lambda }^{2} + {XY} - \lambda \left( {X + Y}\right) .
\]

Putting this together yields

(4.3)

\[
X\frac{dS}{dt} - \left( {S + X}\right) \frac{dX}{dt} = {X}^{3} + I,
\]

where \( I = X{Y}^{2} + {\lambda Y}\left( {Y - X}\right)  + {\lambda }^{2}\left( {X - Y}\right) \) .

Claim 4.31. \( I \geq  0 \) .

Proof. First we consider the case when \( Y \leq  0 \) . This means that \( \mu  \geq  0 \) and hence that \( \lambda  \geq  0 \) . Since by definition \( X \geq  0 \) , we have \( X \geq  Y \) . This immediately gives \( I \geq  0 \) . Now let us consider the case when \( Y > 0 \) which means that \( \nu  \leq  \mu  < 0 \) . In this case, we have

\[
I = {Y}^{3} + \left( {X - Y}\right) \left( {{\lambda }^{2} - {\lambda Y} + {Y}^{2}}\right)  > 0
\]

since \( X \geq  Y \) and \( {\lambda }^{2} - {\lambda Y} + {Y}^{2} = {\left( \lambda  - \frac{Y}{2}\right) }^{2} + \frac{3{Y}^{2}}{4} > 0 \) .

The above claim and Equation (4.3) immediately imply that

(4.4)

\[
X\frac{dS}{dt} - \left( {S + X}\right) \frac{dX}{dt} \geq  {X}^{3}.
\]

Set \( W = \frac{S}{X} - \log X \) , then rewriting Equation (4.4) in terms of \( W \) gives

(4.5)

\[
\frac{dW}{dt} \geq  X
\]

Now suppose that \( \gamma \left( t\right)  \notin  Z\left( {x, t}\right) \) for some \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0}, T}\right\rbrack \) . Let \( {t}_{1} < T \) be maximal subject to the condition that \( \gamma \left( t\right)  \in  Z\left( {x, t}\right) \) for all \( {t}_{0} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{1} \) . Of course, \( \gamma \left( {t}_{1}\right)  \in  \partial Z\left( {x,{t}_{1}}\right) \) which implies that \( \left( {S\left( {t}_{1}\right) , X\left( {t}_{1}\right) }\right)  \in  \partial \mathcal{C}\left( {t}_{1}\right) \) . There are two possibilities: either \( S\left( {t}_{1}\right)  =  - 3/\left( {1 + {t}_{1}}\right) \) and \( X\left( {t}_{1}\right)  < \xi \left( {t}_{1}\right) \) or \( X\left( {t}_{1}\right)  \geq  \xi \left( {t}_{1}\right)  > 1/\left( {1 + {t}_{1}}\right) \) and \( S\left( {t}_{1}\right)  = {f}_{{t}_{1}}\left( {X\left( {t}_{1}\right) }\right) \) . But Equation (4.2) implies that \( S\left( t\right)  \geq   - 3/\left( {1 + t}\right) \) for all \( t \) . Hence, if the first case holds then \( \gamma \left( t\right)  \in  Z\left( {x, t}\right) \) for \( t \) in some interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) with \( {t}_{1}^{\prime } > {t}_{1} \) . This contradicts the maximality of \( {t}_{1} \) . Thus, it must be the case that \( X\left( {t}_{1}\right)  \geq  \xi \left( {t}_{1}\right) \) . But then \( X\left( t\right)  > \frac{1}{1 + t} \) for all \( t \) sufficiently close to \( {t}_{1} \) . Hence, by Equation (4.5) we have

\[
\frac{dW}{dt}\left( t\right)  \geq  X\left( t\right)  > \frac{1}{1 + t}
\]

for all \( t \) sufficiently close to \( {t}_{1} \) . Also, since \( S\left( {t}_{1}\right)  = {f}_{{t}_{1}}\left( {X\left( {t}_{1}\right) }\right) \) , we have \( W\left( {t}_{1}\right)  = \log \left( {1 + {t}_{1}}\right)  - 3 \) . It follows immediately that \( W\left( t\right)  \geq  \log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - 3 \) for all \( t > {t}_{1} \) sufficiently close to \( {t}_{1} \) . This proves that \( S\left( t\right)  \geq  {f}_{t}\left( {X\left( t\right) }\right) \) for all \( t \geq  {t}_{1} \) sufficiently close to \( {t}_{1} \) , again contradicting the maximality of \( {t}_{1} \) .

This contradiction proves that \( \psi \) preserves the family \( \mathcal{Z}\left( t\right) \) .

By Theorem 4.8, the previous three claims imply that \( \mathcal{T}\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  \mathcal{Z}\left( t\right) \) for all \( x \in  M \) and all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) . That is to say, \( S\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq   - 3/\left( {1 + t}\right) \) and \( S\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  {f}_{t}\left( {X\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) whenever \( X\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  \xi \left( t\right) \) . For \( X \in  \left\lbrack  {1/\left( {1 + t}\right) ,\xi \left( t\right) }\right\rbrack \) we have \( {f}_{t}\left( X\right)  \leq   - 3/\left( {1 + t}\right) \) , and thus in fact \( S\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  {f}_{t}\left( {X\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) as long as \( X\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  1/\left( {1 + t}\right) \) . On the other hand, if \( 0 < X\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  1/\left( {1 + t}\right) \) then \( {f}_{t}\left( {X\left( {x, t}\right) }\right)  <  - {3X}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  S\left( {x, t}\right) \) . On the other hand, since \( X\left( {x, t}\right) \) is the negative of the smallest eigenvalue of \( \mathcal{T}\left( {x, t}\right) \) and \( S\left( {x, t}\right) \) is the trace of this matrix, we have \( S\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq   - {3X}\left( {x, t}\right) \) . Thus, \( S\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  {f}_{t}\left( {X\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) in this case as well. This completes the proof of Theorem 4.26.

nodes.content: CLAIM 4.30. The vector field \( \psi \left( \mathcal{T}\right)  = {\mathcal{T}}^{2} + {\mathcal{T}}^{\sharp } \) preserves the family \( \mathcal{Z}\left( t\right) \) of convex sets.
nodes.content_excerpt: CLAIM 4.30. The vector field \( \psi \left( \mathcal{T}\right) = {\mathcal{T}}^{2} + {\mathcal{T}}^{\sharp } \) preserves the family \( \mathcal{Z}\left( t\right) \) of convex sets.

nodes.proof:
We denote the eigenvalues of \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) \) by \( \lambda \left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  \mu \left( {x, t}\right)  \geq \; \nu \left( {x, t}\right) \) . Fix \( x \in  M \) and let \( \gamma \left( t\right) ,{t}_{0} \leq  t \leq  T \) , be an integral curve for \( \psi \) with \( \gamma \left( {t}_{0}\right)  \in  Z\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \) . We wish to show that \( \gamma \left( t\right)  \in  Z\left( {x, t}\right) \) for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0}, T}\right\rbrack \) . The function \( S\left( t\right)  = S\left( {\gamma \left( t\right) }\right) \) satisfies

\[
\frac{dS}{dt} = {\lambda }^{2} + {\mu }^{2} + {\nu }^{2} + {\lambda \mu } + {\lambda \nu } + {\mu \nu } = \frac{1}{2}\left( {{\left( \lambda  + \mu \right) }^{2} + {\left( \lambda  + \nu \right) }^{2} + {\left( \mu  + \nu \right) }^{2}}\right) .
\]

By Cauchy-Schwarz we have

\[
{\left( \lambda  + \mu \right) }^{2} + {\left( \lambda  + \nu \right) }^{2} + {\left( \mu  + \nu \right) }^{2}) \geq  \frac{4{S}^{2}}{3} \geq  \frac{2{S}^{2}}{3}.
\]

Since \( \gamma \left( {t}_{0}\right)  \in  Z\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \) we have \( S\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \geq   - 3/\left( {1 + {t}_{0}}\right) \) . It then follows that

(4.2)

\[
S\left( t\right)  \geq   - 3/\left( {1 + t}\right) \;\text{ for all }\;t \geq  {t}_{0}.
\]

Now let us consider the evolution of \( X\left( t\right)  = X\left( {\gamma \left( t\right) }\right) \) . Assume that we are at a point \( t \) for which \( X\left( t\right)  > 0 \) . For this computation we set \( Y =  - \mu \) .

\[
\frac{dX}{dt} =  - \frac{d\nu }{dt} =  - {\nu }^{2} - {\mu \lambda } =  - {X}^{2} + {Y\lambda }
\]

\[
\frac{dS}{dt} = \frac{d\left( {\nu  + \mu  + \lambda }\right) }{dt} = {\nu }^{2} + {\mu }^{2} + {\lambda }^{2} + {\mu \lambda } + {\nu \lambda } + {\nu \mu }
\]

\[
= {X}^{2} + {Y}^{2} + {\lambda }^{2} + {XY} - \lambda \left( {X + Y}\right) .
\]

Putting this together yields

(4.3)

\[
X\frac{dS}{dt} - \left( {S + X}\right) \frac{dX}{dt} = {X}^{3} + I,
\]

where \( I = X{Y}^{2} + {\lambda Y}\left( {Y - X}\right)  + {\lambda }^{2}\left( {X - Y}\right) \) .

Claim 4.31. \( I \geq  0 \) .

Proof. First we consider the case when \( Y \leq  0 \) . This means that \( \mu  \geq  0 \) and hence that \( \lambda  \geq  0 \) . Since by definition \( X \geq  0 \) , we have \( X \geq  Y \) . This immediately gives \( I \geq  0 \) . Now let us consider the case when \( Y > 0 \) which means that \( \nu  \leq  \mu  < 0 \) . In this case, we have

\[
I = {Y}^{3} + \left( {X - Y}\right) \left( {{\lambda }^{2} - {\lambda Y} + {Y}^{2}}\right)  > 0
\]

since \( X \geq  Y \) and \( {\lambda }^{2} - {\lambda Y} + {Y}^{2} = {\left( \lambda  - \frac{Y}{2}\right) }^{2} + \frac{3{Y}^{2}}{4} > 0 \) .

The above claim and Equation (4.3) immediately imply that

(4.4)

\[
X\frac{dS}{dt} - \left( {S + X}\right) \frac{dX}{dt} \geq  {X}^{3}.
\]

Set \( W = \frac{S}{X} - \log X \) , then rewriting Equation (4.4) in terms of \( W \) gives

(4.5)

\[
\frac{dW}{dt} \geq  X
\]

Now suppose that \( \gamma \left( t\right)  \notin  Z\left( {x, t}\right) \) for some \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0}, T}\right\rbrack \) . Let \( {t}_{1} < T \) be maximal subject to the condition that \( \gamma \left( t\right)  \in  Z\left( {x, t}\right) \) for all \( {t}_{0} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{1} \) . Of course, \( \gamma \left( {t}_{1}\right)  \in  \partial Z\left( {x,{t}_{1}}\right) \) which implies that \( \left( {S\left( {t}_{1}\right) , X\left( {t}_{1}\right) }\right)  \in  \partial \mathcal{C}\left( {t}_{1}\right) \) . There are two possibilities: either \( S\left( {t}_{1}\right)  =  - 3/\left( {1 + {t}_{1}}\right) \) and \( X\left( {t}_{1}\right)  < \xi \left( {t}_{1}\right) \) or \( X\left( {t}_{1}\right)  \geq  \xi \left( {t}_{1}\right)  > 1/\left( {1 + {t}_{1}}\right) \) and \( S\left( {t}_{1}\right)  = {f}_{{t}_{1}}\left( {X\left( {t}_{1}\right) }\right) \) . But Equation (4.2) implies that \( S\left( t\right)  \geq   - 3/\left( {1 + t}\right) \) for all \( t \) . Hence, if the first case holds then \( \gamma \left( t\right)  \in  Z\left( {x, t}\right) \) for \( t \) in some interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) with \( {t}_{1}^{\prime } > {t}_{1} \) . This contradicts the maximality of \( {t}_{1} \) . Thus, it must be the case that \( X\left( {t}_{1}\right)  \geq  \xi \left( {t}_{1}\right) \) . But then \( X\left( t\right)  > \frac{1}{1 + t} \) for all \( t \) sufficiently close to \( {t}_{1} \) . Hence, by Equation (4.5) we have

\[
\frac{dW}{dt}\left( t\right)  \geq  X\left( t\right)  > \frac{1}{1 + t}
\]

for all \( t \) sufficiently close to \( {t}_{1} \) . Also, since \( S\left( {t}_{1}\right)  = {f}_{{t}_{1}}\left( {X\left( {t}_{1}\right) }\right) \) , we have \( W\left( {t}_{1}\right)  = \log \left( {1 + {t}_{1}}\right)  - 3 \) . It follows immediately that \( W\left( t\right)  \geq  \log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - 3 \) for all \( t > {t}_{1} \) sufficiently close to \( {t}_{1} \) . This proves that \( S\left( t\right)  \geq  {f}_{t}\left( {X\left( t\right) }\right) \) for all \( t \geq  {t}_{1} \) sufficiently close to \( {t}_{1} \) , again contradicting the maximality of \( {t}_{1} \) .

This contradiction proves that \( \psi \) preserves the family \( \mathcal{Z}\left( t\right) \) .

THEOREM 4.32. Fix \( a \geq  0 \) . Let \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) , a \leq  t < T \) , be a Ricci flow with \( M \) a compact 3-manifold. Suppose the eigenvalues of \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) \) are \( \lambda \left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  \mu \left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  \nu \left( {x, t}\right) \) and set \( X\left( {x, t}\right)  = \max \left( {-\nu \left( {x, t}\right) ,0}\right) \) . Assume that for every \( x \in  M \) we have

\[
R\left( {x, a}\right)  \geq  \frac{-6}{{4a} + 1}
\]

and

\[
R\left( {x, a}\right)  \geq  {2X}\left( {x, a}\right) \left( {\log X\left( {x, a}\right)  + \log \left( {1 + a}\right)  - 3}\right) ,
\]

where the second inequality holds whenever \( X\left( {x, a}\right)  > 0 \) . Then for all \( a \leq \; t < T \) and all \( x \in  M \) we have:

(4.6)

\[
R\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  \frac{-6}{{4t} + 1}.
\]

(4.7)

\[
R\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  {2X}\left( {x, t}\right) \left( {\log X\left( {x, t}\right)  + \log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - 3}\right) \;\text{ if }X\left( {x, t}\right)  > 0.
\]

Once again it is natural to interpret the right-hand side of the second inequality to be zero when \( X\left( {x, t}\right)  = 0 \) . With this convention, the second inequality remains true even when \( X\left( {x, t}\right)  = 0 \) .

nodes.proof: By rescaling we can assume that for all \( x \in  M \) all the eigenvalues of \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x,0}\right) \) have absolute value \( \leq  1 \) . This implies that \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) satisfies the hypothesis of Theorem 4.26. Our first goal is to show that \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x,0}\right)  \geq  0 \) for all \( x \in  M \) . Suppose that this is not true; then there is a point \( x \) with \( X\left( {x,0}\right)  > 0 \) . Consider \( A = X\left( {x,0}\right) /R\left( {x,0}\right) \) . For each \( t < T \) let \( {x}_{t} \in  M \) be the image of \( x \) under the isometry from \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) to \( \left( {M, c\left( t\right) g\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Then \( X\left( {{x}_{t}, t}\right)  = {c}^{-1}\left( t\right) X\left( {x,0}\right) \) and \( X\left( {{x}_{t}, t}\right) /R\left( {{x}_{t}, t}\right)  = A \) . Since \( c\left( t\right) \) tends to 0 as \( t \) approaches \( T \) , this contradicts Theorem 4.26. Now, according to Theorem 4.18 either all \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) are flat or \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right)  > 0 \) for all \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  M \times  \left( {0, T}\right) \) . But if the \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) are all flat, then the flow is trivial and hence the diameters of the \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) do not go to zero as \( t \) approaches \( T \) , contradicting the hypothesis. Hence, \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right)  > 0 \) for all \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  M \times  \left( {0, T}\right) \) . According to Theorem 4.23 this means that as the singularity develops the metrics are converging to round. By the shrinking soliton hypothesis, this implies that all the metrics \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 < t < T \) , are in fact round. Of course, it then follows that \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) is round.

nodes.proof:
Apply the differential form of the Harnack inequality to

\[
\chi  =  - \nabla \left( {\log R}\right) /2 =  - \nabla R/{2R},
\]

and divide by \( R \) . The result is

\[
{R}^{-1}\left( {\partial R/\partial t}\right)  - {\left| \nabla \left( \log R\right) \right| }^{2} + \frac{\operatorname{Ric}\left( {\nabla \left( {\log R}\right) ,\nabla \left( {\log R}\right) }\right) }{2R} \geq  0.
\]

Since \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( {A, A}\right) /R \leq  {\left| A\right| }^{2} \) , it follows that

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {\log R}\right)  - \frac{{\left| \nabla \left( \log R\right) \right| }^{2}}{2} \geq  0.
\]

Let \( d \) be the \( g\left( {t}_{1}\right) \) -distance from \( {x}_{1} \) to \( {x}_{2} \) and let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {{t}_{1},{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) be a \( g\left( {t}_{1}\right) \) -geodesic from \( {x}_{1} \) to \( {x}_{2} \) , parameterized at speed \( d/\left( {{t}_{2} - {t}_{1}}\right) \) . Then let \( \mu \left( t\right)  = \left( {\gamma \left( t\right) , t}\right) \) be a path in space-time. We compute

\[
\log \left( \frac{R\left( {{x}_{2},{t}_{2}}\right) }{R\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right) }\right)  = {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\frac{d}{dt}\log (R\left( {\mu \left( t\right) }\right) {dt}
\]

\[
= {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\frac{\frac{\partial R}{\partial t}\left( {\mu \left( t\right) }\right) }{R\left( {\mu \left( t\right) }\right) } + \left\langle  {\nabla \left( {\log R}\right) \left( {\mu \left( t\right) }\right) ,\frac{d\mu }{dt}\left( {\mu \left( t\right) }\right) {dt}}\right.
\]

\[
\geq  {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\frac{1}{2}{\left| \nabla \left( \log R\right) \left( \mu \left( t\right) \right) \right| }^{2} - \left| {\nabla \left( {\log R}\right) \left( {\mu \left( t\right) }\right) }\right|  \cdot  \left| \frac{d\gamma }{dt}\right| {dt}
\]

\[
\geq   - \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}{\left| \frac{d\gamma }{dt}\right| }^{2}{dt}
\]

where the last inequality comes by completing the square. Since \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq \) 0, we have \( {\left| d\gamma /dt\right| }_{g\left( t\right) } \leq  {\left| d\gamma /dt\right| }_{g\left( {t}_{1}\right) } \) , and thus

\[
\log \left( \frac{R\left( {{x}_{2},{t}_{2}}\right) }{R\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right) }\right)  \geq   - \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}{\left| \frac{d\gamma }{dt}\right| }_{g\left( {t}_{1}\right) }^{2}{dt}.
\]

Since \( \gamma \) is a \( g\left( {t}_{1}\right) \) -geodesic, this latter expression is

\[
- \frac{{d}_{g\left( {t}_{1}\right) }^{2}\left( {{x}_{1},{x}_{2}}\right) }{2\left( {{t}_{2} - {t}_{1}}\right) }\text{ . }
\]

nodes.content: DEFINITION 5.1. Let \( \left( {U, g}\right) \) be a Riemannian manifold. Let \( \delta  > 0 \) be given. We say that \( p \in  U \) is a \( \delta \) -regular point if for every \( {r}^{\prime } < \delta \) the metric ball \( B\left( {p,{r}^{\prime }}\right) \) has compact closure in \( U \) . Equivalently, \( p \) is \( \delta \) -regular if the exponential mapping at \( p \) is defined on the open ball of radius \( \delta \) centered at the origin in \( {T}_{p}U \) , i.e., if each geodesic ray emanating from \( p \) extends to a geodesic defined on \( \lbrack 0,\delta ) \) . We denote by \( {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {U, g}\right) \) the subset of \( \delta \) -regular points in \( \left( {U, g}\right) \) . For any \( x \in  {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {U, g}\right) \) we denote by \( {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {U, g, x}\right) \) the connected component of \( {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {U, g}\right) \) containing \( x \) .

nodes.content:
DEFINITION 5.3. For each \( k \) let \( \left( {{U}_{k},{g}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) \) be a based, connected Riemannian manifold. A geometric limit of the sequence \( {\left\{  {U}_{k},{g}_{k},{x}_{k}\right\}  }_{k = 0}^{\infty } \) is a based, connected Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{U}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) with the extra data:

(1) An increasing sequence \( {V}_{k} \subset  {U}_{\infty } \) of connected open subsets of \( {U}_{\infty } \) whose union is \( {U}_{\infty } \) and which satisfy the following for all \( k \) :

(a) the closure \( {\bar{V}}_{k} \) is compact,

(b) \( {\bar{V}}_{k} \subset  {V}_{k + 1} \) ,

(c) \( {V}_{k} \) contains \( {x}_{\infty } \) .

(2) For each \( k \geq  0 \) a smooth embedding \( {\varphi }_{k} : \left( {{V}_{k},{x}_{\infty }}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{U}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) \) with the properties that:

(a) \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{\varphi }_{k}^{ * }{g}_{k} = {g}_{\infty } \) , where the limit is in the uniform \( {C}^{\infty } \) - topology on compact subsets of \( {U}_{\infty } \) .

(b) For any \( \delta  > 0 \) and any \( R < \infty \) for all \( k \) sufficiently large, \( {x}_{k} \in  {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{U}_{k},{g}_{k}}\right) \) and for any \( \ell  \geq  k \) the image \( {\varphi }_{\ell }\left( {V}_{k}\right) \) contains \( B\left( {{x}_{\ell }, R}\right)  \cap  {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{U}_{\ell },{g}_{\ell },{x}_{\ell }}\right) . \)

We also say that the sequence converges geometrically to \( \left( {{U}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) if there exist \( \left( {{V}_{k},{\varphi }_{k}}\right) \) as required in the above definition. We also say that \( \left( {{U}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) is the geometric limit of the sequence.

More generally, given \( \left( {{U}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , a sequence of open subsets and \( {\left\{  {V}_{k}\right\}  }_{k = 1}^{\infty } \) satisfying (1) above, and smooth maps \( {\varphi }_{k} : {V}_{k} \rightarrow  {U}_{k} \) satisfying (2a) above, we say that \( \left( {{U}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) is a partial geometric limit of the sequence.

REMARK 5.4. Conditions (1) and (2a) in the definition above also appear in the definition in the case of complete limits. It is Condition (2b) that is extra in this incomplete case. It says that once \( k \) is sufficiently large then the image \( {\varphi }_{\ell }\left( {V}_{k}\right) \) contains all points satisfying two conditions: they are at most a given bounded distance from \( {x}_{\ell } \) , and also they are at least a fixed distance from the boundary of \( {U}_{\ell } \) .

Notice that if the \( \left( {{U}_{k},{g}_{k}}\right) \) have uniformly bounded volume by, say, \( V \) , then any geometric limit has volume \( \leq  V \) .

nodes.label: Lemma 5.5
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content: LEMMA 5.5. The geometric limit of a sequence \( \left( {{U}_{k},{g}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) \) is unique up to based isometry.
nodes.content_excerpt: LEMMA 5.5. The geometric limit of a sequence \( \left( {{U}_{k},{g}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) \) is unique up to based isometry.

nodes.proof:
Suppose that \( \left( {{U}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) and \( \left( {{U}_{\infty }^{\prime },{g}_{\infty }^{\prime },{x}_{\infty }^{\prime }}\right) \) are geometric limits. Let \( \left\{  {{V}_{k},{\varphi }_{k}}\right\} \) and \( \left\{  {{V}_{k}^{\prime },{\varphi }_{k}^{\prime }}\right\} \) be the sequences of open subsets and maps as required by the definition of the limit.

Fix \( k \) . Since \( {V}_{k} \) is connected and has compact closure, there are \( R < \infty \) and \( \delta  > 0 \) such that \( {V}_{k} \subset  B\left( {{x}_{\infty }, R}\right)  \cap  {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{U}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) . Let \( x \) be contained in the closure of \( {V}_{k} \) . Then by the triangle inequality the closed ball \( \overline{B\left( {x,\delta /3}\right) } \) is contained in \( B\left( {{x}_{\infty }, R + \delta }\right)  \cap  {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta /2}\left( {{U}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) . Since the union of these closed balls as \( x \) ranges over \( {\bar{V}}_{k} \) is a compact set, for all \( \ell \) sufficiently large, the restriction of \( {\varphi }_{\ell }^{ * }{g}_{\ell } \) to the union of these balls is close to the restriction of \( {g}_{\infty } \) to the same subset. In particular, for all \( \ell \) sufficiently large and any \( x \in  {V}_{k} \) we see that \( {\varphi }_{\ell }\left( {B\left( {x,\delta /3}\right) }\right) \) contains \( B\left( {{\varphi }_{\ell }\left( x\right) ,\delta /4}\right) \) . Thus, for all \( \ell \) sufficiently large \( {\varphi }_{\ell }\left( {V}_{k}\right)  \subset  B\left( {{x}_{\ell }, R + {2\delta }}\right)  \cap  {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta /4}\left( {{U}_{\ell },{g}_{\ell },{x}_{\ell }}\right) \) . This implies that, for given \( k \) , for all \( \ell \) sufficiently large \( {\varphi }_{\ell }\left( {V}_{k}\right)  \subset  {\varphi }_{\ell }^{\prime }\left( {V}_{\ell }^{\prime }\right) \) . Of course, \( {\left( {\varphi }_{\ell }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1} \circ  {\varphi }_{\ell }\left( {x}_{\infty }\right)  = {x}_{\infty }^{\prime } \) . Fix \( k \) and pass to a subsequence of \( \ell \) , such that as \( \ell  \rightarrow  \infty \) , the compositions \( {\left( {\varphi }_{\ell }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1} \circ  \left( {\left. {\varphi }_{\ell }\right| }_{{V}_{k}}\right)  : {V}_{k} \rightarrow  {U}_{\infty }^{\prime } \) converge to a basepoint preserving isometric embedding of \( {V}_{k} \) into \( {U}_{\infty }^{\prime } \) . Clearly, as we pass from \( k \) to \( {k}^{\prime } > k \) and take a further subsequence of \( \ell \) these limiting isometric embeddings are compatible. Their union is then a base-point preserving isometric embedding of \( {U}_{\infty } \) into \( {U}_{\infty }^{\prime } \) .

The last thing we need to see is that the embedding of \( {U}_{\infty } \) into \( {U}_{\infty }^{\prime } \) constructed in the previous paragraph is onto. For each \( n \) we have \( {\bar{V}}_{n}^{\prime } \subset \; {V}_{n + 1}^{\prime } \) . Since \( {\bar{V}}_{n}^{\prime } \) is compact and connected, it follows that there are \( R < \infty \) and \( \delta  > 0 \) (depending on \( n \) ) such that \( {\bar{V}}_{n}^{\prime } \subset  B\left( {{x}_{\infty }^{\prime }, R}\right)  \cap  {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{V}_{n + 1},{g}_{\infty }^{\prime },{x}_{\infty }^{\prime }}\right) \) . Since \( {V}_{n + 1}^{\prime } \) has compact closure in \( {U}_{\infty }^{\prime } \) , as \( \ell \) tends to \( \infty \) the metrics \( {\left( {\varphi }_{\ell }^{\prime }\right) }^{ * }{g}_{\ell } \) converge uniformly on \( {V}_{n + 1} \) to \( {\left. {g}_{\infty }^{\prime }\right| }_{{V}_{n + 1}} \) . This means that there are \( {R}^{\prime } < \infty \) and \( {\delta }^{\prime } > 0 \) (depending on \( n \) ) such that for all \( \ell \) sufficiently large, \( {\varphi }_{\ell }^{\prime }\left( {V}_{n}\right)  \subset \; B\left( {{x}_{k},{R}^{\prime }}\right)  \cap  {\operatorname{Reg}}_{{\delta }^{\prime }}\left( {{U}_{\ell },{g}_{\ell },{x}_{\ell }}\right) \) . This implies that for all \( k \) sufficiently large and any \( \ell  \geq  k \) the image \( {\varphi }_{\ell }^{\prime }\left( {V}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) is contained in the image of \( {\varphi }_{\ell }\left( {V}_{k}\right) \) . Hence, for all \( k \) sufficiently large and any \( \ell  \geq  k \) we have \( {V}_{n}^{\prime } \subset  {\left( {\varphi }_{\ell }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\left( {{\varphi }_{\ell }\left( {V}_{k}\right) }\right) \) . Hence, the isometric embedding \( {U}_{\infty } \rightarrow  {U}_{\infty }^{\prime } \) constructed above contains \( {V}_{n}^{\prime } \) . Since this is true for every \( n \) , it follows that this isometric embedding is in fact an isometry \( {U}_{\infty } \rightarrow  {U}_{\infty }^{\prime } \) .

nodes.content:
THEOREM 5.6. Suppose that \( {\left\{  \left( {U}_{k},{g}_{k},{x}_{k}\right) \right\}  }_{k = 1}^{\infty } \) is a sequence of based, connected, n-dimensional Riemannian manifolds. In addition, suppose the following:

(1) There is \( \delta  > 0 \) such that \( {x}_{k} \in  {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{U}_{k},{g}_{k}}\right) \) for all \( k \) .

(2) For each \( R < \infty \) and \( \delta  > 0 \) there is a constant \( V\left( {R,\delta }\right)  < \infty \) such that \( \operatorname{Vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{k}, R}\right)  \cap  {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{U}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) }\right)  \leq  V\left( {R,\delta }\right) \) for all \( k \) sufficiently large.

(3) For each non-negative integer \( \ell \) , each \( \delta  > 0 \) , and each \( R < \infty \) , there is a constant \( C\left( {\ell ,\delta , R}\right) \) such that for every \( k \) sufficiently large we have

\[
\left| {{\nabla }^{\ell }\operatorname{Rm}\left( {g}_{k}\right) }\right|  \leq  C\left( {\ell ,\delta , R}\right)
\]

on all of \( B\left( {{x}_{k}, R}\right)  \cap  {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{U}_{k},{g}_{k}}\right) \) .

(4) For every \( R < \infty \) there are \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) and \( \kappa  > 0 \) such that for every \( k \) sufficiently large, for every \( \delta  \leq  {r}_{0} \) and every \( x \in  B\left( {{x}_{k}, R}\right)  \cap \; {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{U}_{k},{g}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) \) the volume of the metric ball \( B\left( {x,\delta }\right)  \subset  {U}_{k} \) is at least \( \kappa {\delta }^{n} \) .

Then, after passing to a subsequence, there exists a based Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{U}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) that is a geometric limit of the sequence \( {\left\{  \left( {U}_{k},{g}_{k},{x}_{k}\right) \right\}  }_{k = 1}^{\infty } \) .

(2) For each \( R < \infty \) and \( \delta > 0 \) there is a co...

nodes.proof:
Fix \( R < \infty \) and \( \delta  > 0 \) . Let

\[
X\left( {\delta , R}\right)  = B\left( {{x}_{k}, R}\right)  \cap  {\operatorname{Reg}}_{2\delta }\left( {{U}_{k},{g}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) .
\]

From the non-collapsing assumption and the curvature bound assumption if follows from Theorem 1.36 that there is a uniform positive lower bound (independent of \( k \) ) to the injectivity radius of every point in \( X\left( {\delta , R}\right) \) . Fix \( 0 < {\delta }^{\prime } \leq  \min \left( {{r}_{0},\delta /2}\right) \) much less than this injectivity radius. We also choose \( {\delta }^{\prime } > 0 \) sufficiently small so that any ball of radius \( 2{\delta }^{\prime } \) in \( B\left( {{x}_{k}, R + \delta }\right)  \cap \; {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{U}_{k},{g}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) \) is geodesically convex. (This is possible because of the curvature bound.) We cover \( X\left( {\delta , R}\right) \) by balls \( {B}_{1}^{\prime },\ldots ,{B}_{N}^{\prime } \) of radii \( {\delta }^{\prime }/2 \) centered at points of \( X\left( {\delta , R}\right) \) with the property that the sub-balls of radius \( {\delta }^{\prime }/4 \) are disjoint. We denote by \( {B}_{i}^{\prime } \subset  {B}_{i} \subset  {\widetilde{B}}_{i} \) the metric balls with the same center and radii \( {\delta }^{\prime }/2,{\delta }^{\prime } \) , and \( 2{\delta }^{\prime } \) respectively. Notice that each of the balls \( {\widetilde{B}}_{i} \) is contained in \( B\left( {{x}_{k}, R + \delta }\right)  \cap  {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{U}_{k},{g}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) \) . Because \( {\delta }^{\prime } \leq  {r}_{0} \) , because Vol \( B\left( {{x}_{k}, R + \delta }\right) \) is bounded independent of \( k \) , and because the concentric balls of radius \( {\delta }^{\prime }/4 \) are disjoint, there is a uniform bound (independent of \( k) \) to the number of such balls. Passing to a subsequence we can assume that the number of balls in these coverings is the same for all \( k \) . We number them \( {\widetilde{B}}_{1},\ldots ,{\widetilde{B}}_{N} \) . Next, using the exponential mapping at the central point, identify each of these balls with the ball of radius \( 2{\delta }^{\prime } \) in \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . By passing to a further subsequence we can arrange that the metrics on each \( {\widetilde{B}}_{i} \) converge uniformly. (This uses the fact that the concentric balls of radius \( {2\delta } \geq  4{\delta }^{\prime } \) are embedded in the \( {U}_{k} \) by the exponential mapping.) Now we pass to a further subsequence so that the distance between the centers of the balls converges, and so that for any pair \( {\widetilde{B}}_{i} \) and \( {\widetilde{B}}_{j} \) for which the limiting distance between their centers is less than \( 4{\delta }^{\prime } \) , the overlap functions in the \( {U}_{k} \) also converge. The limits of the overlap functions defines a limiting equivalence relation on \( \mathop{\coprod }\limits_{i}{\widetilde{B}}_{i} \) .

This allows us to form a limit manifold \( {\widehat{U}}_{\infty } \) . It is the quotient of the disjoint union of the \( {\widetilde{B}}_{i} \) with the limit metrics under the limit equivalence relation. We set \( \left( {{U}_{\infty }\left( {\delta , R}\right) ,{g}_{\infty }\left( {\delta , R}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }\left( {\delta , R}\right) }\right) \) equal to the submanifold of \( {\widehat{U}}_{\infty } \) that is the union of the sub-balls \( {B}_{i} \subset  {\widetilde{B}}_{i} \) of radii \( {\delta }^{\prime } \) . A standard argument using partitions of unity and the geodesic convexity of the balls \( {\widetilde{B}}_{i} \) shows that, for all \( k \) sufficiently large, there are smooth embeddings \( {\varphi }_{k}\left( {\delta , R}\right)  : {U}_{\infty }\left( {\delta , R}\right)  \rightarrow  B\left( {{x}_{k}, R + \delta }\right)  \cap  {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{U}_{k},{g}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) \) sending \( {x}_{\infty }\left( {\delta , R}\right) \) to \( {x}_{k} \) and converging as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) , uniformly in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology on each \( {B}_{i} \) , to the identity. Furthermore, the images of each of these maps contains \( B\left( {{x}_{k}, R}\right)  \cap  {\operatorname{Reg}}_{2\delta }\left( {{U}_{k},{g}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) \) ; compare [6]. Also, the pull-backs under these embeddings of the metrics \( {g}_{k} \) converge uniformly to \( {g}_{\infty }\left( {\delta , R}\right) \) .

Repeat the process with \( R \) replaced by \( {2R} \) and \( \delta  = {\delta }_{1} \) replaced by \( {\delta }_{2} \leq  {\delta }_{1}/2 \) . This produces

\[
\left( {{U}_{\infty }\left( {{\delta }_{2},{2R}}\right) ,{g}_{\infty }\left( {{\delta }_{2},{2R}}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }\left( {{\delta }_{2},{2R}}\right) }\right)
\]

and, for all \( k \) sufficiently large, embeddings \( {\varphi }_{k}\left( {{\delta }_{2},{2R}}\right) \) of this manifold into

\[
B\left( {{x}_{k},{2R} + {\delta }_{2}}\right)  \cap  {\operatorname{Reg}}_{{\delta }_{2}}\left( {{U}_{k},{g}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) .
\]

Hence, the image of these embeddings contains the images of the original embeddings. The compositions \( {\left( {\varphi }_{k}\left( {\delta }_{2},2R\right) \right) }^{-1} \circ  {\varphi }_{k}\left( {\delta , R}\right) \) converge to an isometric embedding

\[
\left( {{U}_{\infty }\left( {\delta , R}\right) ,{g}_{\infty }\left( {\delta , R}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }\left( {\delta , R}\right) }\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{U}_{\infty }\left( {{\delta }_{2},{2R}}\right) ,{g}_{\infty }\left( {{\delta }_{2},{2R}}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }\left( {{\delta }_{2},{2R}}\right) }\right) .
\]

Repeating this construction infinitely often produces a based Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{U}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) which is written as an increasing union of open subsets \( {V}_{k} = {U}_{\infty }\left( {{\delta }_{k},{2}^{k}R}\right) \) , where the \( {\delta }_{k} \) tend to zero as \( k \) tends to \( \infty \) . For each \( k \) the open subset \( {V}_{k} \) has compact closure contained in \( {V}_{k + 1} \) . By taking a subsequence of the original sequence we have maps \( {\varphi }_{k} : {V}_{k} \rightarrow  {U}_{k} \) so that (2a) in the definition of geometric limits holds. Condition (2b) clearly holds by construction.

nodes.content:
LEMMA 5.7. Suppose that we have a sequence of n-dimensional balls \( \left( {{B}_{k},{h}_{k}}\right) \) of radius \( r \) in Riemannian n-manifolds. Suppose that for each \( \ell \) there is a constant \( C\left( \ell \right) \) such that for every \( k \) , we have \( \left| {{\nabla }^{\ell }\operatorname{Rm}\left( {h}_{k}\right) }\right|  \leq  C\left( \ell \right) \) throughout \( {B}_{k} \) . Suppose also that for each \( n \) the exponential mapping from the tangent space at the center of \( {B}_{k} \) induces a diffeomorphism from a ball in the tangent space onto \( {B}_{k} \) . Then choosing an isometric identification of the tangent spaces at the central points of the \( {B}_{k} \) with \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) and pulling back the metrics \( {h}_{k} \) via the exponential mapping to metrics \( {\widetilde{h}}_{k} \) on the ball \( B \) of radius \( r \) in \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) gives us a family of metrics on \( B \) that, after passing to a subsequence, converge in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology, uniformly on compact subsets of B, to a limit.

The basic point in proving this lemma is to 'find the right gauge,' which in this case means find local coordinates so that the metric tensor is controlled by the curvature. The correct local coordinates are the Gaussian coordinates centered at the center of the ball.

THEOREM 5.9. Let \( {\left\{  \left( {M}_{k},{g}_{k},{x}_{k}\right) \right\}  }_{k = 1}^{\infty } \) be a sequence of connected, based Riemannian manifolds. Suppose that:

(1) For every \( A < \infty \) the ball \( B\left( {{x}_{k}, A}\right) \) has compact closure in \( {M}_{k} \) for all \( k \) sufficiently large.

(2) For each integer \( \ell  \geq  0 \) and each \( A < \infty \) there is a constant \( C = \; C\left( {\ell , A}\right) \) such that for each \( {y}_{k} \in  B\left( {{x}_{k}, A}\right) \) we have

\[
\left| {{\nabla }^{\ell }\operatorname{Rm}\left( {g}_{k}\right) \left( {y}_{k}\right) }\right|  \leq  C
\]

for all \( k \) sufficiently large.

(3) Suppose also that there is a constant \( \delta  > 0 \) with \( \mathop{\operatorname{inj}}\limits_{\left( {M}_{k},{g}_{k}\right) }\left( {x}_{k}\right)  \geq  \delta \) for all \( k \) sufficiently large.

Then after passing to a subsequence there is a geometric limit which is a complete Riemannian manifold.

By the curvature bounds, it follows from the Bishop-Gromov theorem (Theorem 1.34) that for each \( A < \infty \) there is a uniform bound to the volumes of the balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k}, A}\right) \) for all \( k \) sufficiently large. It also follows from the same result that the uniform lower bound on the injectivity radius at the central point implies that for each \( A < \infty \) there is a uniform lower bound for the injectivity radius on the entire ball \( B\left( {{x}_{k}, A}\right) \) , again for \( k \) sufficiently large. Given these two facts, it follows immediately from Theorem 5.6 that there is a geometric limit.

Since, for every \( A < \infty \) , the \( B\left( {{x}_{k}, A}\right) \) have compact closure in \( {M}_{k} \) for all \( k \) sufficiently large, it follows that for every \( A < \infty \) the ball \( B\left( {{x}_{\infty }, A}\right) \) has compact closure in \( {M}_{\infty } \) . This means that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) is complete.

nodes.proof:
Let \( A = \max \left( {{\delta }^{-2}, C\left( {0,\delta }\right) }\right) \) , where \( C\left( {0,\delta }\right) \) is the constant given in the second condition in Theorem 5.9. Rescale, replacing the Riemannian metric \( {g}_{k} \) by \( A{g}_{k} \) . Of course, the first condition of Theorem 5.9 still holds as does the second with different constants, and we have \( \left| {{\operatorname{Rm}}_{A{g}_{k}}\left( {y}_{k}\right) }\right|  \leq  1 \) for all \( {y}_{k} \in  {B}_{A{g}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},\sqrt{A}\delta }\right) \) . Also, \( \operatorname{Vol}{B}_{A{g}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},\sqrt{A}\delta }\right)  \geq  \kappa {\left( \sqrt{A}\delta \right) }^{n} \) . Thus, by the Bishop-Gromov inequality (Theorem 1.34), we have \( {\operatorname{Vol}}_{A{g}_{k}}B\left( {{x}_{k},1}\right)  \geq  \kappa /\Omega \) where

\[
\Omega  = \frac{V\left( {\sqrt{A}\delta }\right) }{{\left( \sqrt{A}\delta \right) }^{n}V\left( 1\right) },
\]

and \( V\left( a\right) \) is the volume of the ball of radius \( a \) in hyperbolic \( n \) -space (the simply connected \( n \) -manifold of constant curvature -1 ). Since \( \sqrt{A}\delta  \geq  1 \) , this proves that, for all \( k \) sufficiently large, the absolute values of the sectional curvatures of \( A{g}_{k} \) on \( {B}_{A{g}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},1}\right) \) are bounded by 1 and that \( {\operatorname{Vol}}_{A{g}_{k}}B\left( {{x}_{k},1}\right) \) is bounded below by a positive constant independent of \( k \) . According to Theorem 1.36 these conditions imply that there is \( r > 0 \) , such that for all \( k \) sufficiently large, the injectivity radius of \( \left( {{M}_{k}, A{g}_{k}}\right) \) at \( {x}_{k} \) is at least \( r \) . Hence, for all \( k \) sufficiently large, the injectivity radius at \( {x}_{k} \) of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}}\right) \) is bounded below by \( r/\sqrt{A} \) . This means that the original sequence of manifolds satisfies the third condition in Theorem 5.9. Invoking this theorem gives the result.

Fix a compact subset \( K \subset  {M}_{\infty } \) and a compact sub-interval \( I \subset  \left( {{T}^{\prime }, T}\right) \) . Then under these hypothesis, Shi's theorem can be used to show that the curvatures of the \( {g}_{k}\left( {K, I}\right) \) are uniformly bounded \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology. The basic computation done by Hamilton in [33] shows that after passing to a further subsequence, the Ricci flows \( {g}_{k}\left( {K, I}\right) \) converge uniformly in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to a limit flow on \( K \times  I \) . A standard diagonalization argument allows us to pass to a further subsequence so that the pullbacks \( {\widetilde{\varphi }}_{k}^{ * }{G}_{k} \) converge uniformly in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology on every compact subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left( {{T}^{\prime }, T}\right) \) . Of course, the limit satisfies the Ricci flow equation.

Let \( {\left\{  \left( {\mathcal{M}}_{k},{G}_{k},{x}_{k}\right) \right\}  }_{k = 1}^{\infty } \) be a sequence of based, generalized Ricci flows. Suppose that \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{k}\right)  = 0 \) for all \( k \) , and denote by \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}}\right) \) the 0 time-slice of \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{k},{G}_{k}}\right) \) . (1) the ball \( {B}_{{g}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},0, A}\right) \) has compact closure in \( {M}_{k} \) ,

(2) there is an embedding \( {B}_{{g}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},0, A}\right)  \times  I \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{k} \) compatible with time and with the vector field,

(3) the norms of the Riemann curvature of \( {G}_{k} \) on the image of the embedding in the previous item are bounded by \( C\left( {A, I}\right) \) , and

nodes.content:
## 3. Gromov-Hausdorff convergence

Let us begin with the notion of the Gromov-Hausdorff distance between based metric spaces of finite diameter. Let \( Z \) be a metric space. We define the Hausdorff distance between subsets of \( Z \) as follows: \( {d}_{H}^{Z}\left( {X, Y}\right) \) is the infimum of all \( \delta  \geq  0 \) such that \( X \) is contained in the \( \delta \) -neighborhood of \( Y \) and \( Y \) is contained in the \( \delta \) -neighborhood of \( X \) . For metric spaces \( X \) and \( Y \) we define the Gromov-Hausdorff distance between them, denoted \( {D}_{GH}\left( {X, Y}\right) \) , to be the infimum over all metric spaces \( Z \) and isometric embeddings \( f : X \rightarrow \; Z \) and \( g : Y \rightarrow  Z \) of the Hausdorff distance between \( f\left( X\right) \) and \( g\left( Y\right) \) . For pointed metric spaces \( \left( {X, x}\right) \) and \( \left( {Y, y}\right) \) of finite diameter, we define the Gromov-Hausdorff distance between them, denoted \( {D}_{GH}\left( {\left( {X, x}\right) ,\left( {Y, y}\right) }\right) \) , to be the infimum of \( {D}_{H}^{Z}\left( {f\left( X\right) , g\left( Y\right) }\right) \) over all triples \( \left( {\left( {Z, z}\right) , f, g}\right) \) where \( \left( {Z, z}\right) \) is a pointed metric space and \( f : \left( {X, x}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {Z, z}\right) \) and \( g : \left( {Y, y}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {Z, z}\right) \) are base-point preserving isometries.

nodes.proof:
Suppose \( {D}_{GH}\left( {\left( {X, x}\right) ,\left( {Y, y}\right) }\right)  = a \) and \( {D}_{GH}\left( {\left( {Y, y}\right) ,\left( {Z, z}\right) }\right)  = b \) . Fix any \( \delta  > 0 \) . Then there is a metric \( {d}_{1} \) on \( X \vee  Y \) such that \( {d}_{1} \) extends the metrics on \( X, Y \) and the \( \left( {a + \delta }\right) \) -neighborhood of \( X \) is all of \( X \vee  Y \) as is the \( \left( {a + \delta }\right) \) -neighborhood of \( Y \) . Similarly, there is a metric \( {d}_{2} \) on \( Y \vee  Z \) with the analogous properties (with \( b \) replacing \( a \) ). Take a \( \delta \) -net \( \left( {L, y}\right)  \subset  \left( {Y, y}\right) \) , and define

\[
d\left( {{x}^{\prime },{z}^{\prime }}\right)  = \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{\ell  \in  L}}d\left( {{x}^{\prime },\ell }\right)  + d\left( {\ell ,{z}^{\prime }}\right) .
\]

We claim that \( d\left( {{x}^{\prime },{z}^{\prime }}\right)  > 0 \) unless \( {x}^{\prime } = {z}^{\prime } \) is the common base point. The reason is that if \( \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{\ell  \in  L}}d\left( {{x}^{\prime },\ell }\right)  = 0 \) , then by the triangle inequality, any sequence of \( {\ell }_{n} \in  L \) with \( d\left( {{x}^{\prime },{\ell }_{n}}\right) \) converging to zero is a Cauchy sequence, and hence is eventually constant. This means that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( {x}^{\prime } = {\ell }_{n} \in  L \cap  X \) and hence \( {x}^{\prime } \) is the common base point. Similarly for \( {z}^{\prime } \) .

A straightforward computation shows that the function \( d \) above, together with the given metrics on \( X \) and \( Z \) , define a metric on \( X \vee  Z \) with the property that the \( \left( {a + b + {3\delta }}\right) \) -neighborhood of \( X \) is all of \( X \vee  Z \) and likewise for \( Z \) . Since we can do this for any \( \delta  > 0 \) , we conclude that \( {D}_{GH}\left( {\left( {X, x}\right) ,\left( {Z, z}\right) }\right)  \leq  a + b. \)

DEFINITION 5.19. We say that a sequence of based metric spaces \( \left( {{X}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) \) of uniformly bounded diameter converges in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to a based metric space \( \left( {Y, y}\right) \) of finite diameter if

\[

\]
