nodes.proof: By the triangle inequality for Gromov-Hausdorff distance, it follows from the hypothesis of the lemma that \( {D}_{GH}\left( {\left( {Y, y}\right) ,\left( {{Y}^{\prime },{y}^{\prime }}\right) }\right)  = 0 \) . Fix \( \delta  > 0 \) . Since \( {D}_{GH}\left( {\left( {Y, y}\right) ,\left( {{Y}^{\prime },{y}^{\prime }}\right) }\right)  = 0 \) , for any \( n > 0 \) and finite \( \left( {1/n}\right) \) -net \( {L}_{n} \subset  Y \) containing \( y \) there is an embedding \( {\varphi }_{n} : {L}_{n} \rightarrow  {Y}^{\prime } \) sending \( y \) to \( {y}^{\prime } \) such that the image is a \( 2/n \) -net in \( {Y}^{\prime } \) and such that the map from \( {L}_{n} \) to its image is a \( \left( {1 + \delta }\right) \) -bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism. Clearly, we can suppose that in addition the \( {L}_{n} \) are nested: \( {L}_{n} \subset  {L}_{n + 1} \subset  \cdots \) . Since \( {Y}^{\prime } \) is compact and \( {L}_{n} \) is finite, and we can pass to a subsequence so that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{\left. {\varphi }_{k}\right| }_{{L}_{n}} \) converges to a map \( {\psi }_{n} : {L}_{n} \rightarrow  {Y}^{\prime } \) which is a \( \left( {1 + \delta }\right) \) -bi-Lipschitz map onto its image which is a \( 2/n \) net in \( {Y}^{\prime } \) . By a standard diagonalization argument, we can arrange that \( {\left. {\psi }_{n + 1}\right| }_{{L}_{n}} = {\psi }_{n} \) for all \( n \) . The \( \left\{  {\psi }_{n}\right\} \) then define an embedding \( { \cup  }_{n}{L}_{n} \rightarrow  {Y}^{\prime } \) that is a \( \left( {1 + \delta }\right) \) -bi-Lipschitz map onto its image which is a dense subset of \( {Y}^{\prime } \) . Clearly, using the compactness of \( {Y}^{\prime } \) this map extends to a \( \left( {1 + \delta }\right) \) -bi-Lipschitz embedding \( {\psi }_{\delta } : \left( {Y, y}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{Y}^{\prime },{y}^{\prime }}\right) \) onto a dense subset of \( {Y}^{\prime } \) . Since \( Y \) is also compact, this image is in fact all of \( {Y}^{\prime } \) . That is to say, \( {\psi }_{\delta } \) is a \( \left( {1 + \delta }\right) \) -bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism \( \left( {Y, y}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{Y}^{\prime },{y}^{\prime }}\right) \) . Now perform this construction for a sequence of \( {\delta }_{n} \rightarrow  0 \) and \( \left( {1 + {\delta }_{n}}\right) \) -bi-Lipschitz homeomorphisms \( {\psi }_{{\delta }_{n}} : \left( {Y, y}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{Y}^{\prime },{y}^{\prime }}\right) \) . These form an equicontinuous family so that by passing to a subsequence we can extract a limit \( \psi  : \left( {Y, y}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{Y}^{\prime },{y}^{\prime }}\right) \) . Clearly, this limit is an isometry.

nodes.content: DEFINITION 5.27. A length space is a connected metric space \( \left( {X, d}\right) \) such that for any two points \( x, y \) there is a rectifiable arc \( \gamma \) with endpoints \( x \) and \( y \) and with the length of \( \gamma \) equal to \( d\left( {x, y}\right) \) .

nodes.content: THEOREM 5.28. Suppose that \( \left( {{X}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) \) is a sequence of based length spaces. Then there is a based length space \( \left( {X, x}\right) \) that is the limit in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense of a subsequence of the \( \left( {{X}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) \) if for every \( \delta  > 0 \) and \( R < \infty \) there is an \( N < \infty \) such that \( N\left( {\delta , R,{X}_{k}}\right)  \leq  N \) for all \( k \) . On the other hand, if the sequence \( \left( {{X}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) \) has a Gromov-Hausdorff limit, then for every \( \delta  > 0 \) and \( R < \infty \) the \( N\left( {\delta , R,{X}_{k}}\right) \) are bounded independent of \( k \) .

We define the Tits cone of \( M \) at \( p \) , denoted \( \mathcal{T}\left( {M, p}\right) \) , to be the cone over \( {S}_{\infty }\left( {M, p}\right) \) , i.e., the quotient of the space \( {S}_{\infty }\left( {M, p}\right)  \times  \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) where all points \( \left( {x,0}\right) \) are identified (becoming the cone point). The cone metric on this space is given as follows: Let \( \left( {{x}_{1},{a}_{1}}\right) \) and \( \left( {{x}_{2},{a}_{2}}\right) \) be points of \( {S}_{\infty }\left( {M, p}\right)  \times  \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) . Then the distance between their images in the cone is determined by

\[
{d}^{2}\left( {\left\lbrack  {{x}_{1},{a}_{1}}\right\rbrack  ,\left\lbrack  {{x}_{2},{a}_{2}}\right\rbrack  }\right)  = {a}_{1}^{2} + {a}_{2}^{2} - 2{a}_{1}{a}_{2}\cos \left( {{\theta }_{\infty }\left( {{x}_{1},{x}_{2}}\right) }\right) .
\]

It is an easy exercise to show that the Tits cone of \( M \) at \( p \) is in fact independent of the choice of \( p \) . From the previous claim, it follows that the Tits cone of \( M \) is locally compact and complete.

nodes.content: Proposition 5.31. Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a non-negatively curved, complete, non-compact Riemannian manifold of dimension \( k \) . Fix a point \( p \in  M \) and let \( {\left\{  {x}_{n}\right\}  }_{n = 1}^{\infty } \) be a sequence tending to infinity in \( M \) . Let \( {\lambda }_{n} = {d}^{2}\left( {p,{x}_{n}}\right) \) and consider the sequence of based Riemannian manifolds \( \left( {M,{g}_{n}, p}\right) \) , where \( {g}_{n} = {\lambda }_{n}^{-1}g \) . Then there is a subsequence converging in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense. Any Gromov-Hausdorff limit \( \left( {X,{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) of a subsequence \( \left( {X,{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) is isometric to the Tits cone \( \mathcal{T}\left( {M, p}\right) \) with base point the cone point.

Let \( {\lambda }_{n} = {d}^{2}\left( {p,{x}_{n}}\right) \) and consider the sequence of based Riemannian manifolds \( \left( {M,{g}_{n}, p}\ri...

nodes.proof:
Let \( c \) be the cone point of \( \mathcal{T}\left( {M, p}\right) \) , and denote by \( d \) the distance function on \( \mathcal{T}\left( {M, p}\right) \) . Consider the ball \( B\left( {c, R}\right)  \subset  \mathcal{T}\left( {M, p}\right) \) . Since \( {S}_{\infty }\left( {M, p}\right) \) is the metric completion of the quotient space of minimal geodesic rays emanating from \( p \) , for any \( \delta  > 0 \) there is a \( \delta \) -net \( L \subset  B\left( {c, R}\right) \) consisting of the cone point together with points of the form \( \left( {\left\lbrack  \gamma \right\rbrack  , t}\right) \) where \( \gamma \) is a minimal geodesic ray emanating from \( p \) and \( t > 0 \) . We define a map from \( {\psi }_{n} : L \rightarrow  \left( {M,{g}_{n}}\right) \) by sending the cone point to \( p \) and sending \( \left( {\left\lbrack  \gamma \right\rbrack  , t}\right) \) to the point at \( {g}_{n} \) -distance \( t \) from \( p \) along \( \gamma \) . Clearly, \( {\psi }_{n}\left( L\right) \) is contained in \( {B}_{{g}_{n}}\left( {p, R}\right) \) . From the second item of Theorem 2.4 and the monotonicity of angles it follows that the map \( {\psi }_{n} : L \rightarrow  \left( {M,{g}_{n}}\right) \) is a distance non-decreasing map; i.e., \( {\psi }_{n}^{ * }\left( {{g}_{n} \mid  {\psi }_{n}\left( L\right) }\right)  \geq  {\left. d\right| }_{L} \) . On the other hand, by the monotonicity, \( {\psi }_{n + 1}^{ * }\left( {{g}_{n + 1} \mid  {\psi }_{n + 1}\left( L\right) }\right)  \leq  {\psi }_{n}^{ * }\left( {{g}_{n} \mid  {\psi }_{n}\left( L\right) }\right) \) and this non-increasing sequence of metrics converges to \( {\left. d\right| }_{L} \) . This proves that for any \( \delta  > 0 \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the embedding \( {\psi }_{n} \) is a \( \left( {1 + \delta }\right) \) -bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism.

It remains to show that for any \( \eta  > 0 \) the images \( {\psi }_{n}\left( L\right) \) are eventually \( \left( {\delta  + \eta }\right) \) -nets in \( {B}_{{g}_{n}}\left( {p, R}\right) \) . Suppose not. Then after passing to a subsequence, for each \( n \) we have a point \( {x}_{n} \in  {B}_{{g}_{n}}\left( {p, R}\right) \) whose distance from \( {\psi }_{n}\left( L\right) \) is at least \( \delta  + \eta \) . In particular, \( {d}_{{g}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n}, p}\right)  \geq  \delta \) . Consider a sequence of minimal geodesic rays \( {\mu }_{n} \) connecting \( p \) to the \( {x}_{n} \) . Since the \( g \) -length of \( {\mu }_{n} \) is at least \( {n\delta } \) , by passing to a further subsequence, we can arrange that the \( {\mu }_{n} \) converge to a minimal geodesic ray \( \gamma \) emanating from \( p \) . By passing to a further subsequence if necessary, we arrange that \( {d}_{{g}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n}, p}\right) \) converges to \( r > 0 \) . Now consider the points \( {\widetilde{x}}_{n} \) on \( \gamma \) at \( g \) -distance \( \sqrt{{\lambda }_{n}}r \) from \( p \) . Clearly, from the second item of Theorem 2.4 and the fact that the angle at \( p \) between the \( {\mu }_{n} \) and \( \mu \) tends to zero as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) we have \( {d}_{{g}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n},{\widetilde{x}}_{n}}\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) . Hence, it suffices to show that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( {\widetilde{x}}_{n} \) is within \( \delta \) of \( {\psi }_{n}\left( L\right) \) to obtain a contradiction. Consider the point \( z = \left( {\left\lbrack  \mu \right\rbrack  , r}\right)  \in  \mathcal{T}\left( {M, p}\right) \) . There is a point \( \ell  = \left( {\left\lbrack  \gamma \right\rbrack  ,{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \in  L \) within distance \( \delta \) of \( z \) in the metric \( d \) . Let \( {\widetilde{y}}_{n} \in  M \) be the point in \( M \) at \( g \) -distance \( \sqrt{{\lambda }_{n}}{t}^{\prime } \) along \( \gamma \) . Of course, \( {\widetilde{y}}_{n} = {\psi }_{n}\left( \ell \right) \) . Then \( {d}_{{g}_{n}}\left( {{\widetilde{x}}_{n},{\widetilde{y}}_{n}}\right)  \rightarrow  d\left( {\ell , z}\right)  < \delta \) . Hence, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( {d}_{{g}_{n}}\left( {{\widetilde{x}}_{n},{\widetilde{y}}_{n}}\right)  < \delta \) . This proves that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {\widetilde{x}}_{n} \) is within \( \delta \) of \( {\psi }_{n}\left( L\right) \) and hence for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {x}_{n} \) is within \( \delta  + \eta \) of \( {\psi }_{n}\left( L\right) \) .

We have established that for every positive \( \delta ,\eta \) and every \( R < \infty \) there is a finite \( \delta \) -net \( L \) in \( \left( {\mathcal{T}\left( {M, p}\right) , c}\right) \) and, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, an \( \left( {1 + \delta }\right) \) -bi-Lipschitz embedding \( {\psi }_{n} \) of \( L \) into \( \left( {M,{g}_{n}, p}\right) \) with image a \( \delta  + \eta \) - net for \( \left( {M,{g}_{n}, p}\right) \) . This proves that the sequence \( \left( {M,{g}_{n}, p}\right) \) converges in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to \( \mathcal{T}\left( {M, p}\right) , c)) \) .

nodes.content: DEFINITION 5.32. Let \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{k},{G}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) \) be a sequence of based, generalized Ricci flows. We suppose that \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{k}\right)  = 0 \) for all \( n \) . We set \( {Q}_{k} \) equal to \( R\left( {x}_{k}\right) \) . We denote by \( \left( {{Q}_{k}{\mathcal{M}}_{k},{Q}_{k}{G}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) \) the family of generalized flows that have been rescaled so that \( {R}_{{Q}_{k}{G}_{k}}\left( {x}_{k}\right)  = 1 \) . Suppose that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{Q}_{k} = \infty \) and that after passing to a subsequence there is a geometric limit of the sequence \( \left( {{Q}_{k}{\mathcal{M}}_{k},{Q}_{k}{G}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) \) which is a Ricci flow defined for \( - T < t \leq  0 \) . Then we call this limit a blow-up limit of the original based sequence. In the same fashion, if there is a geometric limit for a subsequence of the zero time-slices of the \( \left( {{Q}_{k}{\mathcal{M}}_{k},{Q}_{k}{G}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) \) , then we call this limit the blow-up limit of the 0 time-slices.

nodes.content: THEOREM 5.33. Let \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{k},{G}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) \) be a sequence of generalized Ricci flows of dimension 3, each of which has time interval of definition contained in \( \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) and each of which has curvature pinched toward positive. Suppose that \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {x}_{k}\right) \) tends to infinity as \( k \) tends to infinity. Let \( {t}_{k} = \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{k}\right) \) and let \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{k}^{\prime },{G}_{k}^{\prime },{x}_{k}}\right) \) be the result of shifting time by \( - {t}_{k} \) so that \( {\mathbf{t}}^{\prime }\left( {x}_{k}\right)  = 0 \) . Then any blow-up limit of the sequence \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{k},{G}_{k}^{\prime },{x}_{k}}\right) \) has non-negative Riemann curvature. Similarly, any blow-up limit of the zero time-slices of this sequence has non-negative curvature.

nodes.proof:
Let us consider the case of the geometric limit of the zero time-slice first. Let \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) be a blow-up limit of the zero time-slices in the sequence. Let \( {V}_{k} \subset  {M}_{\infty } \) and \( {\varphi }_{k} : {V}_{k} \rightarrow  {\left( {M}_{k}\right) }_{0} \) be as in the definition of the geometric limit. Let \( y \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{\infty } \) be a point and let \( \lambda \left( y\right)  \geq  \mu \left( y\right)  \geq  \nu \left( y\right) \) be the eigenvalues of the Riemann curvature operator for \( {g}_{\infty } \) at \( y \) . Let \( \left\{  {y}_{k}\right\} \) be a sequence in \( {Q}_{k}{\mathcal{M}}_{k}^{\prime } \) converging to \( y \) , in the sense that \( {y}_{k} = {\varphi }_{k}\left( y\right) \) for all \( k \) sufficiently large. Then

\[
\lambda \left( y\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}{Q}_{k}^{-1}\lambda \left( {y}_{k}\right)
\]

\[
\mu \left( y\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}{Q}_{k}^{-1}\mu \left( {y}_{k}\right) ,
\]

\[
\nu \left( y\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}{Q}_{k}^{-1}\nu \left( {y}_{k}\right) .
\]

Since by Equation (4.6) we have \( R\left( {y}_{k}\right)  \geq   - 6 \) for all \( k \) and since by hypothesis \( {Q}_{k} \) tends to infinity as \( n \) does, it follows that \( R\left( y\right)  \geq  0 \) . Thus if \( \lambda \left( y\right)  = 0 \) , then \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( y\right)  = 0 \) and the result is established at \( y \) . Hence, we may assume that \( \lambda \left( y\right)  > 0 \) , which means that \( \lambda \left( {y}_{k}\right) \) tends to infinity as \( k \) does. If \( \nu \left( {y}_{k}\right) \) remains bounded below as \( k \) tends to infinity, then \( {Q}_{k}^{-1}\nu \left( {y}_{k}\right) \) converges to a limit which is \( \geq  0 \) , and consequently \( {Q}_{k}^{-1}\mu \left( {y}_{k}\right)  \geq  {Q}_{k}^{-1}\nu \left( {y}_{k}\right) \) has a nonnegative limit. Thus, in this case the Riemann curvature of \( {g}_{\infty } \) at \( y \) is nonnegative. On the other hand, if \( \nu \left( {y}_{k}\right) \) goes to \( - \infty \) as \( k \) does, then according to Equation (4.7) the ratio of \( X\left( {y}_{k}\right) /R\left( {y}_{k}\right) \) goes to zero. Since \( {Q}_{k}^{-1}R\left( {y}_{k}\right) \) converges to the finite limit \( R\left( y\right) \) , the product \( {Q}_{k}^{-1}X\left( {y}_{k}\right) \) converges to zero as \( k \) goes to infinity. This means that \( \nu \left( y\right)  = 0 \) and consequently that \( \mu \left( y\right)  \geq  0 \) . Thus, once again we have non-negative curvature for \( {g}_{\infty } \) at \( y \) .

The argument in the case of a geometric limit flow is identical.

nodes.content: THEOREM 5.35. Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a complete, connected manifold of nonnegative sectional curvature. Let \( \left\{  {x}_{n}\right\} \) be a sequence of points going off to infinity, and suppose that we can find scaling factors \( {\lambda }_{n} > 0 \) such that the based Riemannian manifolds \( \left( {M,{\lambda }_{n}g,{x}_{n}}\right) \) have a geometric limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) . Suppose that there is a point \( p \in  M \) such that \( {\lambda }_{n}{d}^{2}\left( {p,{x}_{n}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) . Then, after passing to a subsequence, minimizing geodesic arcs \( {\gamma }_{n} \) from \( {x}_{n} \) to \( p \) converge to a minimizing geodesic ray in \( {M}_{\infty } \) . This minimizing geodesic ray is part of a minimizing geodesic line \( \ell \) in \( {M}_{\infty } \) . In particular, there is a Riemannian product decomposition \( {M}_{\infty } = N \times  \mathbb{R} \) with the property that \( \ell \) is \( \{ x\}  \times  \mathbb{R} \) for some \( x \in  N \) .

nodes.proof:
Let \( {d}_{n} \) be the distance from \( p \) to \( {x}_{n} \) . Consider minimizing geodesic arcs \( {\gamma }_{n} \) from \( p \) to \( {x}_{n} \) . By passing to a subsequence we can assume that tangent directions at \( p \) of these arcs converge. Hence, for every \( 0 < \; \delta  < 1 \) there is \( N \) such that for all \( n, m \geq  N \) the angle between \( {\gamma }_{n} \) and \( {\gamma }_{m} \) at \( p \) is less than \( \delta \) . For any \( n \) we can choose \( m\left( n\right) \) such that \( {d}_{m\left( n\right) )} \geq \; {d}_{n}\left( {1 + 1/\delta }\right) \) . Let \( {\mu }_{n} \) be a minimizing geodesic from \( {x}_{n} \) to \( {x}_{m\left( n\right) } \) . Now applying the Toponogov comparison (first part of Theorem 2.4) and the usual law of cosines in Euclidean space, we see that the distance \( d \) from \( {x}_{n} \) to \( {x}_{m\left( n\right) } \) satisfies

\[
{d}_{m\left( n\right) } - {d}_{n} \leq  d \leq  \sqrt{{d}_{n}^{2} + {d}_{m\left( n\right) }^{2} - 2{d}_{n}{d}_{m\left( n\right) }\cos \left( \delta \right) }.
\]

Let \( {\theta }_{n} = {\angle }_{{x}_{n}^{\prime }} \) of the Euclidean triangle \( \bigtriangleup \left( {{x}_{n}^{\prime },{p}^{\prime },{x}_{m\left( n\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) with \( \left| {s}_{{x}_{n}^{\prime }{p}^{\prime }}\right|  = \; {d}_{n},\left| {s}_{{x}_{n}^{\prime }{x}_{m\left( n\right) }^{\prime }}\right|  = d \) and \( \left| {s}_{{p}^{\prime }{x}_{m\left( n\right) }^{\prime }}\right|  = {d}_{m\left( n\right) } \) . Then for any \( \alpha  < {d}_{n} \) and \( \beta  < d \) let \( x \) and \( y \) be the points on \( {s}_{{x}_{n}p} \) and on \( {s}_{{x}_{n}{x}_{m\left( n\right) }} \) at distances \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) respectively from \( {x}_{n} \) . Given this, according to the Toponogov comparison result (first part of Theorem 2.4), we have

\[
d\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  \sqrt{{\alpha }^{2} + {\beta }^{2} - {2\alpha \beta }\cos \left( {\theta }_{n}\right) }.
\]

The angle \( {\theta }_{n} \) satisfies:

\[
{d}_{n}^{2} + {d}^{2} - 2{d}_{n}d\cos \left( {\theta }_{n}\right)  = {d}_{m\left( n\right) }^{2}.
\]

Thus,

\[
\cos \left( {\theta }_{n}\right)  = \frac{{d}_{n}^{2} + {d}^{2} - {d}_{m\left( n\right) }^{2}}{2{d}_{n}d}
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{2{d}_{n}^{2} - 2{d}_{n}{d}_{m\left( n\right) }\cos \left( \delta \right) }{2{d}_{n}d}
\]

\[
= \frac{{d}_{n}}{d} - \frac{{d}_{m\left( n\right) }}{d}\cos \left( \delta \right)
\]

\[
\leq  \delta  - \left( {1 - \delta }\right) \cos \left( \delta \right) .
\]

Since \( \delta  \rightarrow  0 \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) , it follows that given any \( \delta  > 0 \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( 1 + \cos \left( {\theta }_{n}\right)  < \delta \) .

We are assuming the based Riemannian manifolds \( {\left\{  \left( M,{\lambda }_{n}g,{x}_{n}\right) \right\}  }_{n = 1}^{\infty } \) converge to a geometric limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , and that \( {d}_{{\lambda }_{n}{g}_{n}}\left( {p,{x}_{n}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) , so that the lengths of the \( {\gamma }_{n} \) tend to infinity in the metrics \( {\lambda }_{n}{g}_{n} \) . This also means that the lengths of \( {\mu }_{n} \) , measured in the metrics \( {\lambda }_{n}{g}_{n} \) , tend to infinity. Thus, by passing to a subsequence we can assume that each of these families, \( \left\{  {\gamma }_{n}\right\} \) and \( \left\{  {\mu }_{n}\right\} \) , of minimizing geodesic arcs converges to a minimizing geodesic arc, which we denote \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) and \( \widetilde{\mu } \) , respectively, in \( {M}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( {x}_{\infty } \) . The above computation shows that the angle between these arcs is \( \pi \) and hence that their union is a geodesic, say \( \ell \) . The same computation shows that \( \ell \) is minimizing.

The existence of the minimizing geodesic line \( \ell \) together with the fact that the sectional curvatures of the limit are \( \geq  0 \) implies by Lemma 2.14 that the limit manifold is a Riemannian product \( N \times  \mathbb{R} \) in such a way that \( \ell \) is of the form \( \{ x\}  \times  \mathbb{R} \) for some \( x \in  N \) .

Let \( 0 \leq  {\tau }_{1} < {\tau }_{2} \) be given and let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},{\tau }_{2}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathcal{M} \) be a continuous map. We say that \( \gamma \) is parameterized by backward time provided that \( \gamma \left( \tau \right)  \in  {M}_{T - \tau } \) for all \( \tau  \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},{\tau }_{2}}\right\rbrack \) .

nodes.label: Definition 6.2
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
DEFINITION 6.2. Let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},{\tau }_{2}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathcal{M},0 \leq  {\tau }_{1} < {\tau }_{2} \) , be a \( {C}^{1} \) -path parameterized by backward time. We define \( {X}_{\gamma }\left( \tau \right) \) to be the horizontal projection of the tangent vector \( {d\gamma }\left( \tau \right) /{d\tau } \) , so that \( {d\gamma }/{d\tau } =  - \chi  + {X}_{\gamma }\left( \tau \right) \) with \( {X}_{\gamma }\left( \tau \right)  \in  \mathcal{H}T\mathcal{M} \) . We define the \( \mathcal{L} \) -length of \( \gamma \) to be

\[
\mathcal{L}\left( \gamma \right)  = {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{{\tau }_{2}}\sqrt{\tau }\left( {R\left( {\gamma \left( \tau \right) }\right)  + {\left| {X}_{\gamma }\left( \tau \right) \right| }^{2}}\right) {d\tau },
\]

where the norm of \( {X}_{\gamma }\left( \tau \right) \) is measured using the metric \( {G}_{T - \tau } \) on \( \mathcal{H}T\mathcal{M} \) . When \( \gamma \) is clear from the context, we write \( X \) for \( {X}_{\gamma } \) ; see FIG. 2 from the Introduction.

nodes.label: Example 6.3
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
EXAMPLE 6.3. Suppose that our generalized Ricci flow is a constant family of Euclidean metrics on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . That is to say, \( g\left( t\right)  = {g}_{0} \) is the usual Euclidean metric. Then we have \( R\left( {\gamma \left( \tau \right) }\right)  \equiv  0 \) . Using the change of variables \( s = \sqrt{\tau } \) , we have

\[
\mathcal{L}\left( \gamma \right)  = \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}}^{\sqrt{{\tau }_{2}}}{\left| A\left( s\right) \right| }^{2}{ds}
\]

which is the standard energy functional in Riemannian geometry for the path \( \gamma \left( s\right) \) . The minimizers for this functional are the maps \( s \mapsto  \left( {\alpha \left( s\right) , T - {s}^{2}}\right) \) where \( \alpha \left( s\right) \) is a straight line in \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) parameterized at constant speed. Written in the \( \tau \) variables the minimizers are

\[
\gamma \left( \tau \right)  = \left( {x + \sqrt{\tau }v, T - \tau }\right) ,
\]

straight lines parameterized at speed varying linearly with \( \sqrt{\tau } \) .

nodes.label: Lemma 6.4
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
LEMMA 6.4. The Euler-Lagrange equation for critical paths for the \( \mathcal{L} \) -length is

(6.3)

\[
{\nabla }_{X}X - \frac{1}{2}\nabla R + \frac{1}{2\tau }X + 2\operatorname{Ric}{\left( X, \cdot  \right) }^{ * } = 0.
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: LEMMA 6.4. The Euler-Lagrange equation for critical paths for the \( \mathcal{L} \) -length is (6.3) \[ {\nabla }_{X}X - \frac{1}{2}\nabla R + \frac{1}{2\tau }X + 2\operatorname{Ric}{\left( X, \cdot \right) }^{ * } = 0. \]

nodes.proof:
First, let us suppose that the generalized Ricci flow is an ordinary Ricci flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Let \( {\gamma }_{u}\left( \tau \right)  = \gamma \left( {\tau , u}\right) \) be a family of curves parameterized by backward time. Let

\[
\widetilde{Y}\left( {\tau , u}\right)  = \frac{\partial \gamma }{\partial u}.
\]

Then \( \widetilde{X}\left( {\tau , u}\right)  = {X}_{{\gamma }_{u}}\left( {\tau , u}\right) \) and \( \widetilde{Y}\left( {\tau , u}\right) \) are the coordinate vector fields along the surface obtained by taking the projection of \( \gamma \left( {\tau , u}\right) \) into \( M \) . Thus, \( \left\lbrack  {\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y}}\right\rbrack   = 0 \) . We denote by \( X \) and \( Y \) the restrictions of \( \widetilde{X} \) and \( \widetilde{Y} \) , respectively to \( {\gamma }_{0} \) . We have

\[
{\left. \frac{d}{du}\mathcal{L}\left( {\gamma }_{u}\right) \right| }_{u = 0} = {\left. \frac{d}{du}\left( {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{{\tau }_{2}}\sqrt{\tau }\left( R\left( {\gamma }_{u}\left( \tau \right) \right)  + {\left| \widetilde{X}\left( \tau , u\right) \right| }^{2}\right) d\tau \right) \right| }_{u = 0}
\]

\[
= {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{{\tau }_{2}}\sqrt{\tau }\left( {\langle \nabla R, Y\rangle  + 2\left\langle  {\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}\widetilde{X}}\right) {\left| {}_{u = 0}, X\rangle )d\tau .\right| }_{X}}\right\rangle  }\right) {d\tau }.
\]

On the other hand, since \( \partial g/\partial \tau  = 2 \) Ric and since \( \left\lbrack  {\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y}}\right\rbrack   = 0 \) , we have

\[
2\frac{d}{d\tau }\left( {\sqrt{\tau }\langle Y, X{\rangle }_{g\left( {T - \tau }\right) }}\right)  = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}\langle Y, X\rangle  + 2\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}Y, X}\right\rangle   + 2\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle  {Y,{\nabla }_{X}X}\right\rangle
\]

\[
+ 4\sqrt{\tau }\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, X}\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}\langle Y, X\rangle  + 2\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle  {\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}\widetilde{X}}\right) {\left. \right| }_{u = 0}, X}\right\rangle   + 2\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle  {Y,{\nabla }_{X}X}\right\rangle
\]

\[
+ 4\sqrt{\tau }\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, X}\right) .
\]

Using this we obtain(6.4)

\[
{\left. \frac{d}{du}\mathcal{L}\left( {\gamma }_{u}\right) \right| }_{u = 0} = {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{{\tau }_{2}}\left( {2\frac{d}{d\tau }\left\lbrack  {\left( \sqrt{\tau }\right) \langle Y, X\rangle }\right\rbrack   - \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}\langle Y, X\rangle }\right.
\]

\[
\left. {+\sqrt{\tau }\left( {\langle \nabla R, Y\rangle  - 2\left\langle  {Y,{\nabla }_{X}X}\right\rangle   - 4\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, Y}\right) }\right) }\right) {d\tau }
\]

\[
= 2\sqrt{\tau }\langle Y, X\rangle { \mid  }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{{\tau }_{2}}
\]

\[
+ {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{{\tau }_{2}}\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle  {Y,\left( {\nabla R - \frac{1}{\tau }X - 2{\nabla }_{X}X - 4\operatorname{Ric}{\left( X, \cdot  \right) }^{ * }}\right) }\right\rangle  {d\tau }.
\]

Now we drop the assumption that the generalized Ricci flow is an ordinary Ricci flow. Still we can partition the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},{\tau }_{2}}\right\rbrack \) into finitely many sub-intervals with the property that the restriction of \( {\gamma }_{0} \) to each of the sub-intervals is contained in a patch of space-time on which the generalized Ricci flow is isomorphic to an ordinary Ricci flow. The above argument then applies to each of the sub-intervals. Adding up Equation (6.4) over these sub-intervals shows that the same equation for the first variation of length for the entire family \( {\gamma }_{u} \) holds.

We consider a variation \( \gamma \left( {\tau , u}\right) \) with fixed endpoints, so that \( Y\left( {\tau }_{1}\right)  = \; Y\left( {\tau }_{2}\right)  = 0 \) . Thus, the condition that \( \gamma \) be a critical path for the \( \mathcal{L} \) -length is that the integral expression vanish for all variations \( Y \) satisfying \( Y\left( {\tau }_{1}\right)  = \; Y\left( {\tau }_{2}\right)  = 0 \) . Equation (6.4) holds for all such \( Y \) if and only if \( \gamma \) satisfies Equation (6.3).

DEFINITION 6.7. Let \( \gamma \) be a curve parameterized by backward time. Then \( \gamma \) is an \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic if it is a critical point of the \( \mathcal{L} \) -length. Equation (6.3) is the \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic equation.

Written with respect to the variable \( s = \sqrt{\tau } \) the \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic equation becomes

(6.5)

\[
{\nabla }_{A\left( s\right) }A\left( s\right)  - 2{s}^{2}\nabla R + {4s}\operatorname{Ric}{\left( A\left( s\right) , \cdot  \right) }^{ * } = 0.
\]

Notice that in this form the ODE is regular even at \( s = 0 \) .

nodes.content: Lemma 6.8. Let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,{\tau }_{2}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathcal{M} \) be an \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic. Then \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\tau  \rightarrow  0}}\sqrt{\tau }{X}_{\gamma }\left( \tau \right) \) exists. The \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic \( \gamma \) is completely determined by this limit (and by \( {\tau }_{2} \) ).

nodes.label: Lemma 6.10
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
LEMMA 6.10. \( Y\left( \tau \right) \) satisfies the \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi equation:

(6.6)

\[
{\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{X}Y + \mathcal{R}\left( {Y, X}\right) X - \frac{1}{2}{\nabla }_{Y}\left( {\nabla R}\right)
\]

\[
+ \frac{1}{2\tau }{\nabla }_{X}Y + 2\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) {\left( X, \cdot  \right) }^{ * } + 2\operatorname{Ric}{\left( {\nabla }_{X}Y, \cdot  \right) }^{ * } = 0.
\]

This is a second-order linear equation for \( Y \) . Supposing that \( {\tau }_{1} > 0 \) , there is a unique horizontal vector field \( Y \) along \( \gamma \) solving this equation, vanishing at \( {\tau }_{1} \) with a given first-order derivative along \( \gamma \) at \( {\tau }_{1} \) . Similarly, there is a unique solution \( Y \) to this equation, vanishing at \( {\tau }_{2} \) and with a given first-order derivative at \( {\tau }_{2} \) .

nodes.proof:
Given a family \( \gamma \left( {\tau , u}\right) \) of \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesics, then from Lemma 6.4 we have

\[
{\nabla }_{\widetilde{X}}\widetilde{X} = \frac{1}{2}\nabla R\left( \gamma \right)  - \frac{1}{2\tau }\widetilde{X} - 2\operatorname{Ric}{\left( \widetilde{X}, \cdot  \right) }^{ * }.
\]

Differentiating this equation in the \( u \) -direction along the curve \( u = 0 \) yields

\[
{\left. {\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{\widetilde{X}}\widetilde{X}\right| }_{u = 0} = \frac{1}{2}{\nabla }_{Y}\left( {\nabla R}\right)  - {\left. \frac{1}{2\tau }{\nabla }_{Y}\left( \widetilde{X}\right) \right| }_{u = 0} - {\left. 2{\nabla }_{Y}{\left( \operatorname{Ric}\left( \widetilde{X}, \cdot  \right) \right) }^{ * }\right| }_{u = 0}.
\]

Of course, we have

\[
{\left. {\nabla }_{Y}\left( \operatorname{Ric}{\left( \widetilde{X}, \cdot  \right) }^{ * }\right) \right| }_{u = 0} = \left( {{\nabla }_{Y}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) {\left( X, \cdot  \right) }^{ * } + \operatorname{Ric}{\left( {\nabla }_{Y}\widetilde{X}{\left| {}_{u = 0}, \cdot  \right| }^{ * }\right) }^{ * }.
\]

Plugging this in, interchanging the orders of differentiation on the left-hand side, using \( {\nabla }_{\widetilde{Y}}\widetilde{X} = {\nabla }_{\widetilde{X}}\widetilde{Y} \) , and restricting to \( u = 0 \) , yields the equation given in the statement of the lemma. This equation is a regular, second-order linear equation for all \( \tau  > 0 \) , and hence is determined by specifying the value and first derivative at any \( \tau  > 0 \) .

Equation (6.6) is obtained by applying \( {\nabla }_{Y} \) to Equation (6.3) and exchanging orders of differentiation. The result, Equation (6.6), is a second-order differential equation for \( Y \) that makes no reference to an extension of \( \gamma \left( \tau \right) \) to an entire family of curves.

nodes.content: DEFINITION 6.11. A field \( Y\left( \tau \right) \) along an \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic is called an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field if it satisfies the \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi equation, Equation (6.6), and if it vanishes at \( {\tau }_{1} \) . For any horizontal vector field \( Y \) along \( \gamma \) we denote by \( \operatorname{Jac}\left( Y\right) \) the expression on the left-hand side of Equation (6.6).

nodes.content:
LEMMA 6.12. Let \( \gamma \) be an \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic defined on \( \left\lbrack  {0,{\tau }_{2}}\right\rbrack \) and let \( Y\left( \tau \right) \) be an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field along \( \gamma \) . Then

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\tau  \rightarrow  0}}\sqrt{\tau }{\nabla }_{X}Y
\]

exists. Furthermore, \( Y\left( \tau \right) \) is completely determined by this limit.
nodes.content_excerpt: LEMMA 6.12. Let \( \gamma \) be an \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic defined on \( \left\lbrack {0,{\tau }_{2}}\right\rbrack \) and let \( Y\left( \tau \right) \) be an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field along \( \gamma \) . Then \[ \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\tau \rightarrow 0}}\sqrt{\tau }{\nabla }_{X}Y \] exists. Furthermore, \( Y\left( \tau \right) \) is completely determined by this limit.

nodes.proof:
We use the variable \( s = \sqrt{\tau } \) , and let \( A\left( s\right) \) be the horizontal component of \( {d\gamma }/{ds} \) . Then differentiating the \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic equation written with respect to this variable we see

\[
{\nabla }_{A}{\nabla }_{A}Y =  - \mathcal{R}\left( {Y, A}\right) A + 2{s}^{2}{\nabla }_{Y}\left( {\nabla R}\right)  - {4s}\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {A, \cdot  }\right)  - {4s}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {{\nabla }_{A}Y, \cdot  }\right) .
\]

Hence, for each tangent vector \( Z \) , there is a unique solution to this equation with the two initial conditions \( Y\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) and \( {\nabla }_{A}Y\left( 0\right)  = Z \) .

On the other hand, from Equation (6.1) we have \( {\nabla }_{X}\left( Y\right)  = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\tau }}{\nabla }_{A}\left( Y\right) \) , so that

\[
\sqrt{\tau }{\nabla }_{X}\left( Y\right)  = \frac{1}{2}{\nabla }_{A}\left( Y\right) .
\]

Proposition 6.13. Suppose that \( \gamma \) is a minimizing \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic. Then, for any vector field \( Y \) along \( \gamma \) , vanishing at both endpoints, and any family \( {\gamma }_{u} \) of curves parameterized by backward time with \( {\gamma }_{0} = \gamma \) and with the \( u \) - derivative of the family at \( u = 0 \) being the vector field \( Y \) along \( \gamma \) , we have

\[
\frac{{d}^{2}}{d{u}^{2}}\mathcal{L}{\left. \left( {\gamma }_{u}\right) \right| }_{u = 0} =  - {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{{\tau }_{2}}2\sqrt{\tau }\langle \operatorname{Jac}\left( Y\right) , Y\rangle {d\tau }.
\]

This quantity vanishes if and only if \( Y \) is an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field.

From the equation in Lemma 6.14, the equality of the second variation of \( \mathcal{L} \) -length at \( u = 0 \) and the integral is immediate from the fact that \( Y\left( {\tau }_{2}\right)  = 0 \) . It follows immediately that, if \( Y \) is an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field vanishing at \( {\tau }_{2} \) , then the second variation of the length vanishes at \( u = 0 \) . Conversely, suppose given a family \( {\gamma }_{u} \) with \( {\gamma }_{0} = \gamma \) with the property that the second variation of length vanishes at \( u = 0 \) , and that the vector field \( Y = {\left. \left( \partial \gamma /\partial u\right) \right| }_{u = 0} \) along \( \gamma \) vanishes at the end points. It follows that the integral also vanishes. Since \( \gamma \) is a minimizing \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic, for any variation \( W \) , vanishing at the endpoints, the first variation of the length vanishes and the second variation of length is non-negative. That is to say,

\[
- {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{{\tau }_{2}}2\sqrt{\tau }\langle \operatorname{Jac}\left( W\right) , W\rangle {d\tau } \geq  0
\]

for all vector fields \( W \) along \( \gamma \) vanishing at the endpoints. Hence, the restriction to the space of vector fields along \( \gamma \) vanishing at the endpoints of the symmetric bilinear form

\]

is positive semi-definite. Since \( B\left( {Y, Y}\right)  = 0 \) , it follows that \( B\left( {Y, \cdot  }\right)  = 0 \) ; that is to say, \( \operatorname{Jac}\left( Y\right)  = 0 \) .

nodes.proof:
Given \( {Y}_{1} \) and \( {Y}_{2} \) along \( \gamma \) we construct a two-parameter family of curves parameterized by backward time as follows. Let \( \gamma \left( {\tau ,{u}_{1}}\right) \) be the value at \( {u}_{1} \) of the geodesic through \( \gamma \left( \tau \right) \) with tangent vector \( {Y}_{1}\left( \tau \right) \) . This defines a family of curves parameterized by backward time, the family being parameterized by \( {u}_{1} \) sufficiently close to 0 . We extend \( {Y}_{1} \) and \( X \) to vector fields on this entire family by defining them to be \( \partial /\partial {u}_{1} \) and the horizontal projection of \( \partial /\partial \tau \) , respectively. Now we extend the vector field \( {Y}_{2} \) along \( \gamma \) to a vector field on this entire one-parameter family of curves. We do this so that \( {Y}_{2}\left( {{\tau }_{2},{u}_{1}}\right)  = {Y}_{1}\left( {{\tau }_{2},{u}_{1}}\right) \) . Now given this extension \( {Y}_{2}\left( {\tau ,{u}_{1}}\right) \) we define a two-parameter family of curves parameterized by backward time by setting \( \gamma \left( {\tau ,{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}\right) \) equal to the value at \( {u}_{2} \) of the geodesic through \( \gamma \left( {\tau ,{u}_{1}}\right) \) in the direction \( {Y}_{2}\left( {\tau ,{u}_{1}}\right) \) . We then extend \( {Y}_{1},{Y}_{2} \) , and \( X \) over this entire family by letting them be \( \partial /\partial {u}_{1},\partial /\partial {u}_{2} \) , and the horizontal projection of \( \partial /\partial \tau \) , respectively. Applying Lemma 6.14 and using the fact that \( {Y}_{i}\left( \bar{\tau }\right)  = 0 \) we conclude that

\[
{\left. \frac{\partial }{\partial {u}_{1}}\frac{\partial }{\partial {u}_{2}}\mathcal{L}\left( \gamma \right) \right| }_{{u}_{1} = {u}_{2} = 0} =  - {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{{\tau }_{2}}2\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle  {\operatorname{Jac}\left( {Y}_{1}\right) ,{Y}_{2}}\right\rangle  {d\tau }
\]

and symmetrically that

\[
{\left. \frac{\partial }{\partial {u}_{2}}\frac{\partial }{\partial {u}_{1}}\mathcal{L}\left( \gamma \right) \right| }_{{u}_{1} = {u}_{2} = 0} =  - {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{{\tau }_{2}}2\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle  {\operatorname{Jac}\left( {Y}_{2}\right) ,{Y}_{1}}\right\rangle  {d\tau }.
\]

Since the second cross-partials are equal, the corollary follows.

DEFINITION 6.17. We define the domain of definition of \( \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x} \) , denoted \( {\mathcal{D}}_{x} \) , to be the subset of \( {T}_{x}{M}_{T - {\tau }_{1}} \times  \left( {{\tau }_{1},\infty }\right) \) consisting of all pairs \( \left( {Z,\tau }\right) \) for which \( \tau  > {\tau }_{1} \) is in the maximal domain of definition of \( {\gamma }_{Z} \) . Then we define \( \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x} : {\mathcal{D}}_{x} \rightarrow  \mathcal{M} \) by setting \( \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x}\left( {Z,\tau }\right)  = {\gamma }_{Z}\left( \tau \right) \) for all \( \left( {Z,\tau }\right)  \in  {\mathcal{D}}_{x} \) . (See FIG. 1.) We define the map \( \widetilde{L} : {\mathcal{D}}_{x} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) by \( \widetilde{L}\left( {Z,\tau }\right)  = \mathcal{L}\left( {\left. {\gamma }_{Z}\right| }_{\left\lbrack  {\tau }_{1},\tau \right\rbrack  }\right) \) . Lastly, for any \( \tau  > {\tau }_{1} \) we denote by \( \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x}^{\tau } \) the restriction of \( \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x} \) to the slice

\[
{\mathcal{D}}_{x}^{\tau } = {\mathcal{D}}_{x} \cap  \left( {{T}_{x}{M}_{T - {\tau }_{1}}\times \{ \tau \} }\right) ,
\]

which is the domain of definition of \( \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x}^{\tau } \) . We also denote by \( {\widetilde{L}}^{\tau } \) the restriction of \( \widetilde{L} \) to this slice. We will implicitly identify \( {\mathcal{D}}_{x}^{\tau } \) with a subset of \( {T}_{x}{M}_{T - {\tau }_{1}}. \)

Suppose that the associated \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic \( {\gamma }_{Z} \) minimizes \( \mathcal{L} \) -length between its endpoints, \( x \) and \( {\gamma }_{Z}\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \) , and that \( {d}_{Z}\mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x}^{\bar{\tau }} \) is an isomorphism. \[

Lemma 6.22. Suppose that \( Z \in  {\mathcal{D}}_{x}^{\tau } \) . Then for any \( \widetilde{Y} \in  {T}_{x}{M}_{T - {\tau }_{1}} = \; {T}_{Z}\left( {\mathcal{D}}_{x}^{\tau }\right) \) we have

\[
\left\langle  {\nabla {\widetilde{L}}^{\tau },\widetilde{Y}}\right\rangle   = 2\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle  {X\left( \tau \right) ,{d}_{Z}\left( {\mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x}^{\tau }}\right) \left( \widetilde{Y}\right) }\right\rangle  .
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: Lemma 6.22. Suppose that \( Z \in {\mathcal{D}}_{x}^{\tau } \) . Then for any \( \widetilde{Y} \in {T}_{x}{M}_{T - {\tau }_{1}} = \; {T}_{Z}\left( {\mathcal{D}}_{x}^{\tau }\right) \) we have \[ \left\langle {\nabla {\widetilde{L}}^{\tau },\widetilde{Y}}\right\rangle = 2\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle {X\left( \tau \right) ,{d}_{Z}\left( {\mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x}^{\tau }}\right) \left( \widetilde{Y}\right) }\right\rangle . \]

nodes.proof:
Since \( {\mathcal{D}}_{x}^{\tau } \) is an open subset of \( {T}_{x}\left( {M}_{T - {\tau }_{1}}\right) \) , it follows that for any \( \widetilde{Y} \in  {T}_{x}\left( {M}_{T - {\tau }_{1}}\right) \) there is a one-parameter family \( {\gamma }_{u}\left( {\tau }^{\prime }\right)  = \gamma \left( {{\tau }^{\prime }, u}\right) \) of \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesics, defined for \( {\tau }_{1} \leq  {\tau }^{\prime } \leq  \tau \) , starting at \( x \) with \( \gamma \left( {\cdot ,0}\right)  = {\gamma }_{Z} \) and with \( \frac{\partial }{\partial u}\left( {\sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}X\left( {\tau }_{1}\right) }\right)  = \widetilde{Y} \) . (Again, when \( {\tau }_{1} = 0 \) , this equation is interpreted to mean \( \frac{\partial }{\partial u}\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{{\tau }^{\prime } \rightarrow  0}}\left( {\sqrt{{\tau }^{\prime }}X\left( {{\tau }^{\prime }, u}\right) }\right)  = \widetilde{Y} \) .) Let \( Y\left( {\tau }^{\prime }\right)  = {\left. \frac{\partial }{\partial u}\left( \gamma \left( {\tau }^{\prime }, u\right) \right) \right| }_{u = 0} \) be the corresponding \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field along \( {\gamma }_{Z} \) . Since \( \gamma \left( {{\tau }_{1}, u}\right)  = x \) for all \( u \) , we have \( Y\left( {\tau }_{1}\right)  = 0 \) . Since \( \gamma \left( {\cdot , u}\right) \) is an \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic for all \( u \) , according to Equation (6.4), and in the case \( {\tau }_{1} = 0 \) , using the fact that \( \sqrt{\tau }X\left( {\tau }^{\prime }\right) \) approaches a finite limit as \( \tau  \rightarrow  0 \) , we have

\[
{\left. \frac{d}{du}\mathcal{L}\left( {\gamma }_{u}\right) \right| }_{u = 0} = 2\sqrt{\tau }\langle X\left( \tau \right) , Y\left( \tau \right) \rangle .
\]

By Lemma 6.19 we have \( Y\left( \tau \right)  = {d}_{Z}\mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x}^{\tau }\left( \widetilde{Y}\right) \) . Thus,

\[
\left\langle  {\nabla {\widetilde{L}}^{\tau },\widetilde{Y}}\right\rangle   = {\left. \frac{d}{du}\mathcal{L}\left( {\gamma }_{u}\right) \right| }_{u = 0} = 2\sqrt{\tau }\langle X\left( \tau \right) , Y\left( \tau \right) \rangle  = 2\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle  {X\left( \tau \right) ,{d}_{Z}\left( {\mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x}^{\tau }}\right) \left( \widetilde{Y}\right) }\right\rangle  .
\]

nodes.content:
DEFINITION 6.25. The injectivity set \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}}_{x} \subset  {\mathcal{D}}_{x} \subset  \left( {{T}_{x}{M}_{T - {\tau }_{1}} \times  \left( {{\tau }_{1},\infty }\right) }\right) \) is the subset of all \( \left( {Z,\tau }\right)  \in  {\mathcal{D}}_{x} \) with the following properties:

(1) The map \( \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x}^{\tau } \) is a local diffeomorphism near \( Z \) from \( {T}_{x}\left( {M}_{T - {\tau }_{1}}\right) \) to \( {M}_{T - \tau } \) .

(2) There is a neighborhood \( \mathcal{Z} \) of \( Z \) in \( {\mathcal{D}}_{x}^{\tau } \) such that for every \( {Z}^{\prime } \in  \mathcal{Z} \) the \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic \( {\left. {\gamma }_{{Z}^{\prime }}\right| }_{\left\lbrack  {\tau }_{1},\tau \right\rbrack  } \) is the unique minimizing path parameterized by backward time for the \( \mathcal{L} \) -length. That is to say, the \( \mathcal{L} \) -length of \( {\left. {\gamma }_{{Z}^{\prime }}\right| }_{\left\lbrack  {\tau }_{1},\tau \right\rbrack  } \) is less than the \( \mathcal{L} \) -length of any other path parameterized by backward time between the same endpoints.

For any \( \tau  > {\tau }_{1} \) , we set \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}}_{x}\left( \tau \right)  \subset  {T}_{x}{M}_{T - {\tau }_{1}} \) equal to the slice of \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}}_{x} \) at \( \tau \) , i.e., \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}}_{x}\left( \tau \right) \) is determined by the equation

\[
{\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}}_{x}\left( \tau \right)  \times  \{ \tau \}  = {\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}}_{x} \cap  \left( {{T}_{x}{M}_{T - {\tau }_{1}}\times \{ \tau \} }\right) .
\]

It is clear from the definition that \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}}_{x} \subset  {\mathcal{D}}_{x} \) is an open subset and hence \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}}_{x} \) is an open subset of \( {T}_{x}{M}_{T - {\tau }_{1}} \times  \left( {{\tau }_{1},\infty }\right) \) . Of course, this implies that \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}}_{x}\left( \tau \right) \) is an open subset of \( {\mathcal{D}}_{x}^{\tau } \) for every \( \tau  > {\tau }_{1} \) .

We consider the differential of \( \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x} \) at any \( \left( {Z,\tau }\right)  \in  {\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}}_{x} \) . By construction the restriction of this differential to \( {T}_{x}{M}_{T - {\tau }_{1}} \) is a local isomorphism onto \( \mathcal{H}T\mathcal{M} \) at the image point. On the other hand, the differential of \( \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x} \) in the \( \tau \) direction is \( {\gamma }_{Z}^{\prime }\left( \tau \right) \) , whose ’vertical’ component is \( - \chi \) . By the inverse function theorem this shows that \( \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x} \) is a local diffeomorphism at \( \left( {Z,\tau }\right) \) , and its image is an open subset of \( \mathcal{M} \) . The uniqueness in Condition 2 of Definition 6.25 immediately implies that the restriction of \( \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x} \) to \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}}_{x} \) is one-to-one, and hence that it is a global diffeomorphism onto its image \( {\mathcal{U}}_{x} \) .

Since for every \( \left( {Z,\tau }\right)  \in  {\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}}_{x} \) the \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic \( {\left. {\gamma }_{Z}\right| }_{\left\lbrack  {\tau }_{1},\tau \right\rbrack  } \) is \( \mathcal{L} \) -minimizing, we see that \( {\left. {L}_{x} \circ  \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x}\right| }_{{\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}}_{x}} = {\left. \widetilde{L}\right| }_{{\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}}_{x}} \) and that \( {L}_{x} : {\mathcal{U}}_{x} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) is a smooth function.

nodes.proof:
For \( Z \in  {\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}}_{x}\left( {\bar{\tau }}^{\prime }\right) \) , we shall show that: (i) the \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic \( {\left. {\gamma }_{{Z}^{\prime }}\right| }_{\left\lbrack  {\tau }_{1},\bar{\tau }\right\rbrack  } \) is the unique minimizing \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic from \( x \) to \( {\gamma }_{Z}\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \) , and (ii) the differential \( {d}_{Z}\mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x}^{\bar{\tau }} \) is an isomorphism. Given these two conditions, it follows from the definition that \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}}_{x}\left( {\bar{\tau }}^{\prime }\right) \) is contained in \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}}_{x}\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \) .

We will show that the \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic \( {\left. {\gamma }_{Z}\right| }_{\left\lbrack  {\tau }_{1},\bar{\tau }\right\rbrack  } \) is the unique minimizing \( \mathcal{L} \) - geodesic to its endpoint. If there is an \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic \( {\gamma }_{1} \) , distinct from \( {\left. {\gamma }_{Z}\right| }_{\left\lbrack  {\tau }_{1},\bar{\tau }\right\rbrack  } \) , from \( x \) to \( {\gamma }_{Z}\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \) whose \( \mathcal{L} \) -length is at most that of \( {\left. {\gamma }_{Z}\right| }_{\left\lbrack  {\tau }_{1},\bar{\tau }\right\rbrack  } \) , then there is a broken path \( {\gamma }_{1} * {\gamma }_{Z}{ \mid  }_{\left\lbrack  \bar{\tau },{\bar{\tau }}^{\prime }\right\rbrack  } \) parameterized by backward time whose \( \mathcal{L} \) -length is at most that of \( {\gamma }_{Z} \) . Since this latter path is not smooth, its \( \mathcal{L} \) -length cannot be the minimum, which is a contradiction.

Now suppose that \( {d}_{Z}\mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x}^{\bar{\tau }} \) is not an isomorphism. The argument is similar to the one above, using a non-zero \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field vanishing at both endpoints rather than another geodesic. Let \( {\tau }_{2}^{\prime } \) be the first \( \tau \) for which \( {d}_{Z}\mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x}^{\tau } \) is not an isomorphism. According to Lemma 6.23, \( {\tau }_{1} < {\tau }_{2}^{\prime } \leq  \bar{\tau } \) . Since \( \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x}^{{\tau }_{2}^{\prime }} \) is not a local diffeomorphism at \( \left( {Z,{\tau }_{2}^{\prime }}\right) \) , by Lemma 6.19 there is a non-zero \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field \( Y \) along \( {\left. {\gamma }_{Z}\right| }_{\left\lbrack  {\tau }_{1},{\tau }_{2}^{\prime }\right\rbrack  } \) vanishing at both ends. Since \( {\left. {\gamma }_{Z}\right| }_{\left\lbrack  {\tau }_{1},{\tau }_{2}^{\prime }\right\rbrack  } \) is \( \mathcal{L} \) -minimizing, according to Proposition 6.13, the second variation of the length of \( {\left. {\gamma }_{Z}\right| }_{\left. {\tau }_{1},{\tau }_{2}^{\prime }\right\rbrack  } \) in the \( Y \) -direction vanishes, in the sense that if \( \gamma \left( {u,\tau }\right) \) is any one-parameter family of paths parameterized by backward time from \( x \) to \( {\gamma }_{Z}\left( {\tau }_{2}^{\prime }\right) \) with \( {\left. \left( \partial \gamma /\partial u\right) \right| }_{u = 0} = Y \) , then

\[
{\left. \frac{{\partial }^{2}\mathcal{L}\left( {\gamma }_{u}\right) }{\partial {u}^{2}}\right| }_{u = 0} = 0.
\]

Extend \( Y \) to a horizontal vector field \( \widehat{Y} \) along \( {\gamma }_{Z} \) by setting \( \widehat{Y}\left( \tau \right)  = 0 \) for all \( \tau  \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{2}^{\prime },\bar{\tau }}\right\rbrack \) . Of course, the extended horizontal vector field \( \widehat{Y} \) is not \( {C}^{2} \) at \( {\tau }_{2}^{\prime } \) since \( Y \) , being a non-zero \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field, does not vanish to second order there. This is the first-order variation of the family \( \widehat{\gamma }\left( {u,\tau }\right) \) that agrees with \( \gamma \left( {u,\tau }\right) \) for all \( \tau  \leq  {\tau }_{2}^{\prime } \) and has \( \widehat{\gamma }\left( {u,\tau }\right)  = {\gamma }_{Z}\left( \tau \right) \) for all \( \tau  \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{2}^{\prime },\bar{\tau }}\right\rbrack \) . Of course, the second-order variation of this extended family at \( u = 0 \) agrees with the second-order variation of the original family at \( u = 0 \) , and hence vanishes. But according to Proposition 6.13 this means that \( \widehat{Y} \) is an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field, which is absurd since it is not a \( {C}^{2} \) -vector field.

nodes.content: Proposition 6.31. Let \( \gamma \) be a minimizing \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic defined for \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},\bar{\tau }}\right\rbrack \) . Proof. According to Lemma 6.14 we have

\[
{\left. \frac{{d}^{2}}{d{u}^{2}}\mathcal{L}\right| }_{0} = 2\sqrt{\tau }Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) {\left( \langle \widetilde{Y}\left( \bar{\tau }, u\right) ,\widetilde{X}\left( \bar{\tau }, u\right) \rangle \right| }_{0} - {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{{\tau }_{2}}2\sqrt{\tau }\langle \operatorname{Jac}\left( Y\right) , Y\rangle {d\tau }.
\]

We plug in Equation 6.6 for \( \operatorname{Jac}\left( Y\right) \) and this makes the integrand

\[
\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Y}\left( {\nabla R}\right) , Y}\right\rangle   + 2\sqrt{\tau }\langle \mathcal{R}\left( {Y, X}\right) Y, X\rangle  - 2\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{X}Y, Y}\right\rangle
\]

\[
- \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Y}\right\rangle   - 4\sqrt{\tau }\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {X, Y}\right)  - 4\sqrt{\tau }\operatorname{Ric}\left( {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Y}\right) .
\]

The first term is \( \sqrt{\tau }\operatorname{Hess}\left( R\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right) \) . Let us deal with the third and fourth terms. According to the previous claim, we have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau }\left( {2\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Y}\right\rangle  }\right)  = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Y}\right\rangle   + 2\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{X}Y, Y}\right\rangle
\]

\[
+ 2\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}Y,{\nabla }_{X}Y}\right\rangle   + 4\sqrt{\tau }\operatorname{Ric}\left( {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Y}\right)  + 2\sqrt{\tau }\left( {{\nabla }_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right) .
\]

This allows us to replace the two terms under consideration by

\[
- \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {2\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Y}\right\rangle  }\right)  + 2\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}Y,{\nabla }_{X}Y}\right\rangle
\]

\[
+ 4\sqrt{\tau }\operatorname{Ric}\left( {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Y}\right)  + 2\sqrt{\tau }\left( {{\nabla }_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right) .
\]

Integrating the total derivative out of the integrand and canceling terms leaves the integrand as

\[
\sqrt{\tau }\operatorname{Hess}\left( R\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right)  + 2\sqrt{\tau }\langle \mathcal{R}\left( {Y, X}\right) Y, X\rangle
\]

\[
+ 2\sqrt{\tau }{\left| {\nabla }_{X}Y\right| }^{2} - 4\sqrt{\tau }\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {X, Y}\right)  + 2\sqrt{\tau }\left( {{\nabla }_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right) ,
\]

and makes the boundary term (the one in front of the integral) equal to

\[
2\sqrt{\bar{\tau }}\left( {Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \left\langle  {\widetilde{Y}\left( {\bar{\tau }, u}\right) ,\widetilde{X}\left( {\bar{\tau }, u}\right) }\right\rangle  {\left. \right| }_{0} - \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) , Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) }\right\rangle  }\right)
\]

\[
= 2\sqrt{\bar{\tau }}\left\langle  {X\left( \bar{\tau }\right) ,{\nabla }_{Y}\widetilde{Y}\left( {\bar{\tau }, u}\right) { \mid  }_{0}}\right\rangle  .
\]

This completes the proof of the proposition.

CLAIM 6.34. Let \( \gamma \left( \tau \right) \) be a curve parameterized by backward time. Let \( Y \) be a horizontal vector field along \( \gamma \) and let \( X \) be the horizontal component of \( \partial \widetilde{\gamma }/\partial \tau \) . Then

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau }\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Y}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}Y,{\nabla }_{X}Y}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{X}Y, Y}\right\rangle
\]

\[
+ 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Y}\right) ) + \left( {{\nabla }_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right) )
\]

nodes.proof:
Proof. We can break \( \frac{\partial }{\partial \tau }\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Y}\right\rangle \) into two parts: the first assumes that the metric is constant and the second deals with the variation with \( \tau \) of the metric. The first contribution is the usual formula

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau }{\left\langle  {\nabla }_{X}Y, Y\right\rangle  }_{G\left( {T - {\tau }_{0}}\right) } = {\left\langle  {\nabla }_{X}Y,{\nabla }_{X}Y\right\rangle  }_{G\left( {T - {\tau }_{0}}\right) } + {\left\langle  {\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{X}Y, Y\right\rangle  }_{G\left( {T - {\tau }_{0}}\right) }.
\]

This gives us the first two terms of the right-hand side of the equation in the claim.

We show that the last two terms in that equation come from differentiating the metric with respect to \( \tau \) . To do this recall that in local coordinates, writing the metric \( G\left( {T - \tau }\right) \) as \( {g}_{ij} \) , we have

\[
\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Y}\right\rangle   = {g}_{ij}\left( {{X}^{k}{\partial }_{k}{Y}^{i} + {\Gamma }_{kl}^{i}{X}^{k}{Y}^{l}}\right) {Y}^{j}.
\]

There are two contributions coming from differentiating the metric with respect to \( \tau \) . The first is when we differentiate \( {g}_{ij} \) . This leads to

\[
2{\operatorname{Ric}}_{ij}\left( {{X}^{k}{\partial }_{k}{Y}^{i} + {\Gamma }_{kl}^{i}{X}^{k}{Y}^{l}}\right) {Y}^{j} = 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Y}\right\rangle  .
\]

The other contribution is from differentiating the Christoffel symbols. This yields

\[
{g}_{ij}\frac{\partial {\Gamma }_{kl}^{i}}{\partial \tau }{X}^{k}{Y}^{l}{Y}^{j}.
\]

Differentiating the formula \( {\Gamma }_{kl}^{i} = \frac{1}{2}{g}^{si}\left( {{\partial }_{k}{g}_{sl} + {\partial }_{l}{g}_{sk} - {\partial }_{s}{g}_{kl}}\right) \) leads to

\[
{g}_{ij}\frac{\partial {\Gamma }_{kl}^{i}}{\partial \tau } =  - 2{\operatorname{Ric}}_{ij}{\Gamma }_{kl}^{i} + {g}_{ij}{g}^{si}\left( {{\partial }_{k}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{sl} + {\partial }_{l}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{sk} - {\partial }_{s}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{kl}}\right)
\]

\[
=  - 2{\operatorname{Ric}}_{ij}{\Gamma }_{kl}^{i} + {\partial }_{k}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{jl} + {\partial }_{l}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{jk} - {\partial }_{j}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{kl}.
\]

Thus, we have

\[
{g}_{ij}\frac{\partial {\Gamma }_{kl}^{i}}{\partial \tau }{X}^{k}{Y}^{l}{Y}^{j} = \left( {-2{\operatorname{Ric}}_{ij}{\Gamma }_{kl}^{i} + {\partial }_{k}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{jl}}\right) ){X}^{k}{Y}^{l}{Y}^{j}
\]

\[
= \left( {{\nabla }_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right) .
\]

This completes the proof of the claim.

\leq  \frac{{d}^{2}}{d{u}^{2}}\mathcal{L}\left( {\gamma }_{u}\right)  - 2\sqrt{\bar{\tau }}{\left\langle  {\nabla }_{Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) }\widetilde{Y}\left( \bar{\tau }, u\right) { \mid  }_{0}, X\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \right\rangle  }^{ * }
\]

\[
= {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{\bar{\tau }}\sqrt{\tau }\left\lbrack  {\operatorname{Hess}\left( R\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right)  + 2\langle \mathcal{R}\left( {Y, X}\right) Y, X\rangle }\right.
\]

\[
- 4\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {X, Y}\right)  + 2\left( {{\nabla }_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right)
\]

\[
\left. {+2{\left| {\nabla }_{X}Y\right| }^{2}}\right\rbrack  {d\tau }
\]

Equation (6.9) and the fact that \( {\left| Y\left( \tau \right) \right| }^{2} = {\left| Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \right| }^{2}\frac{{\left( \sqrt{\tau } - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) }^{2}}{{\left( \sqrt{\bar{\tau }} - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) }^{2}} \) , give

\[
\operatorname{Hess}\left( {L}^{\bar{\tau }}\right) \left( {Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) , Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\leq  {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{\bar{\tau }}\sqrt{\tau }\left\lbrack  {\operatorname{Hess}\left( R\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right)  + 2\langle \mathcal{R}\left( {Y, X}\right) Y, X\rangle  - 4\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {X, Y}\right) }\right.
\]

\[
\left. {+2\left( {{\nabla }_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right)  + 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( Y, \cdot  \right) \right| }^{2}}\right\rbrack  {d\tau }
\]

\[
+ {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{\bar{\tau }}\left\lbrack  {\frac{{\left| Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \right| }^{2}}{2\sqrt{\tau }{\left( \sqrt{\bar{\tau }} - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) }^{2}} - \frac{2}{\left( \sqrt{\tau } - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) }\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right) }\right\rbrack  {d\tau }
\]

Using the definition of \( H\left( {X, Y}\right) \) given in Equation (6.12), allows us to write

\[
\operatorname{Hess}\left( {L}^{\bar{\tau }}\right) \left( {Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) , Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\leq   - {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{\bar{\tau }}\sqrt{\tau }H\left( {X, Y}\right) {d\tau }
\]

\[
+ {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{\bar{\tau }}\left\lbrack  {\sqrt{\tau }\left( {-2\left( {{\nabla }_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right)  - 2\frac{\partial \operatorname{Ric}}{\partial \tau }\left( {Y, Y}\right)  + 4{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( Y, \cdot  \right) \right| }^{2}}\right) }\right.
\]

\[
+ \frac{{\left| Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \right| }^{2}}{2\sqrt{\tau }{\left( \sqrt{\bar{\tau }} - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) }^{2}} - \left( {\frac{2}{\left( \sqrt{\tau } - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) } + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}}\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right) \rbrack {d\tau }.
\]

To simplify further, we compute, using Equation (6.9),

\[
\frac{d}{d\tau }\left( {\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y\left( \tau \right) , Y\left( \tau \right) }\right) }\right)  = \frac{\partial \operatorname{Ric}}{\partial \tau }\left( {Y, Y}\right)  + 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {{\nabla }_{X}Y, Y}\right)  + \left( {{\nabla }_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{\partial \operatorname{Ric}}{\partial \tau }\left( {Y, Y}\right)  + \left( {{\nabla }_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right)
\]

\[
+ \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }\left( {\sqrt{\tau } - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}}\right) }\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right)  - 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( Y, \cdot  \right) \right| }^{2}.
\]

Consequently, we have

\[
\frac{d\left( {2\sqrt{\tau }\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y\left( \tau \right) , Y\left( \tau \right) }\right) }\right) }{d\tau }
\]

\[
= 2\sqrt{\tau }\left( {\frac{\partial \operatorname{Ric}}{\partial \tau }\left( {Y, Y}\right)  + \left( {{\nabla }_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Y}\right)  - 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( Y, \cdot  \right) \right| }^{2}}\right)
\]

\[
+ \left( {\frac{2}{\left( \sqrt{\tau } - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) } + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}}\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right) .
\]

Using this, and the fact that \( Y\left( {\tau }_{1}\right)  = 0 \) , gives

(6.13) \( \operatorname{Hess}\left( {L}_{x}^{\bar{\tau }}\right) \left( {Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) , Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) }\right) \)

\[
\leq   - {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{\bar{\tau }}\left( {\sqrt{\tau }H\left( {X, Y}\right)  - \frac{d}{d\tau }\left( {2\sqrt{\tau }\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right) }\right)  - \frac{{\left| Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \right| }^{2}}{2\sqrt{\tau }{\left( \sqrt{\bar{\tau }} - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) }^{2}}}\right) {d\tau }
\]

\[
= \frac{{\left| Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \right| }^{2}}{\sqrt{\bar{\tau }} - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}} - 2\sqrt{\bar{\tau }}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) , Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) }\right)  - {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{\bar{\tau }}\sqrt{\tau }H\left( {X, Y}\right) {d\tau }.
\]

This proves Inequality (6.11). Now we examine when equality holds in this expression. Given an adapted vector field \( Y\left( \tau \right) \) along \( \gamma \) , let \( \mu \left( v\right) \) be a geodesic through \( \gamma \left( {\bar{\tau },0}\right) \) with tangent vector \( Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \) . Then there is a one-parameter family \( \mu \left( {\tau , v}\right) \) of minimizing \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesics with the property that \( \mu \left( {\bar{\tau }, v}\right)  = \mu \left( v\right) \) . Let \( {\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime }\left( {\tau , v}\right) \) be \( \partial \mu \left( {\tau , v}\right) /\partial v \) . It is an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field with \( {\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime }\left( {\bar{\tau },0}\right)  = Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \) . Since \( {L}_{x} \circ  \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{x} = \widetilde{L} \) , we see that

\[
\frac{{d}^{2}}{d{v}^{2}}\mathcal{L}\left( {\mu }_{v}\right) {\left| {}_{v = 0} = \frac{{d}^{2}}{d{u}^{2}}{L}_{x}^{\bar{\tau }}\left( \mu \left( u\right) \right) \right| }_{0}.
\]

Hence, the assumption that we have equality in (6.11) implies that

\[
\frac{{d}^{2}}{d{v}^{2}}\mathcal{L}\left( {\mu }_{v}\right) {\left| {}_{v = 0} = \frac{{d}^{2}}{d{u}^{2}}\mathcal{L}\left( {\widetilde{\gamma }}_{u}\right) \right| }_{0}.
\]

Now we extend this one-parameter family to a two-parameter family \( \mu \left( {\tau , u, v}\right) \) so that \( \partial \mu \left( {\tau ,0,0}\right) /\partial v = {\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime } \) and \( \partial \mu \left( {\tau ,0,0}\right) /\partial u = Y\left( \tau \right) \) . Let \( w \) be the variable \( u - v \) , and let \( \widetilde{W} \) be the tangent vector in this coordinate direction, so that \( \widetilde{W} = \widetilde{Y} - {\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime } \) . We denote by \( W \) the restriction of \( \widetilde{W} \) to \( {\gamma }_{0,0} = {\gamma }_{Z} \) . By Remark 6.15 the second partial derivative of the length of this family in the \( u \) -direction at \( u = v = 0 \) agrees with the second derivative of the length of the original family \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) in the \( u \) -direction.

Claim 6.42.

\[
{\left. \frac{\partial }{\partial v}\frac{\partial }{\partial w}\mathcal{L}\left( \mu \right) \right| }_{u = v = 0} = {\left. \frac{\partial }{\partial w}\frac{\partial }{\partial v}\mathcal{L}\left( \mu \right) \right| }_{v = w = 0} = 0.
\]

Proof. Of course, the second cross-partials are equal. By Lemma 6.14 we have

\[
{\left. \frac{\partial }{\partial v}\frac{\partial }{\partial w}\mathcal{L}\left( \mu \right) \right| }_{v = w = 0} = 2\sqrt{\tau }{\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime }\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \langle \widetilde{W}\left( \bar{\tau }\right) , X\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \rangle  - {\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{\bar{\tau }}2\sqrt{\tau }\left\langle  {\operatorname{Jac}\left( {\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime }\right) , W}\right\rangle  {d\tau }.
\]

Since \( W\left( \bar{\tau }\right)  = 0 \) and since \( {\nabla }_{{\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime }}\left( \widetilde{W}\right)  = {\nabla }_{W}\left( {\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime }\right) \) , we see that the boundary term in the above expression vanishes. The integral vanishes since \( {\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime } \) is an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field.

If Inequality (6.11) is an equality, then

\[
{\left. \frac{{\partial }^{2}}{\partial {v}^{2}}\mathcal{L}\left( \mu \right) \right| }_{u = v = 0} = {\left. \frac{{\partial }^{2}}{\partial {u}^{2}}\mathcal{L}\left( \mu \right) \right| }_{u = v = 0}.
\]

We write \( \partial /\partial u = \partial /\partial v + \partial /\partial w \) . Expanding the right-hand side and canceling the common terms gives

\[
0 = \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial v}\frac{\partial }{\partial w} + \frac{\partial }{\partial w}\frac{\partial }{\partial v} + \frac{{\partial }^{2}}{\partial {w}^{2}}}\right) {\left. \mathcal{L}\left( \mu \right) \right| }_{u = v = 0}.
\]

The previous claim tells us that the first two terms on the right-hand side of this equation vanish, and hence we conclude

\[
{\left. \frac{{\partial }^{2}}{\partial {w}^{2}}\mathcal{L}\left( \mu \right) \right| }_{u = v = 0} = 0.
\]

Since \( W \) vanishes at both endpoints this implies, according to Proposition 6.13, that \( \widetilde{W}\left( {\tau ,0,0}\right)  = 0 \) for all \( \tau \) , or in other words \( Y\left( \tau \right)  = {\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime }\left( {\tau ,0,0}\right) \) for all \( \tau \) . Of course by construction \( {\widetilde{Y}}^{\prime }\left( {\tau ,0,0}\right) \) is an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field. This shows that equality holds only if the adapted vector field \( Y\left( \tau \right) \) is also an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field.

Conversely, if the adapted vector field \( Y\left( \tau \right) \) is also an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field, then inequality between the second variations at the beginning of the proof is an equality. In the rest of the argument we dealt only with equalities. Hence, in this case Inequality (6.11) is an equality.

This shows that we have equality in (6.11) if and only if the adapted vector field \( Y\left( \tau \right) \) is also an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field.

(6.15)

\[
H\left( X\right)  =  - \frac{\partial R}{\partial \tau } - \frac{1}{\tau }R - 2\langle \nabla R, X\rangle  + 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) ,
\]

where \( X \) is the horizontal projection of \( {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( \tau \right) \) . Furthermore, Inequality (6.14) is an equality if and only if for every \( Y \in  {T}_{q}\left( {M}_{T - \bar{\tau }}\right) \) the unique adapted vector field \( Y\left( \tau \right) \) along \( \gamma \) satisfying \( Y\left( \bar{\tau }\right)  = Y \) is an \( \mathcal{L} \) -Jacobi field. In this case

\[
\operatorname{Ric} + \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\bar{\tau }}}\operatorname{Hess}\left( {L}_{x}^{\bar{\tau }}\right)  = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\bar{\tau }}\left( {\sqrt{\bar{\tau }} - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}}\right) }G\left( {T - \bar{\tau }}\right) .
\]

Suppose that \( q \in {\mathcal{U}}_{x}\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \) , that \( Z \in {\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}}_{x}\left( \bar{\tau }\right) \) is the preimage of \( q \) and that \( {\gamma }_{Z} \) is the \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic determined by \( Z \) . Then (6.14) \[ \bigtriangleup {L}_{x}^{\bar{\tau }}\left( q\right) \leq \frac{n}{\sqrt{\bar{\tau }} - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}} - 2\sqrt{\bar{\tau }...

nodes.proof:
Proof. Choose an orthonormal basis \( \left\{  {Y}_{\alpha }\right\} \) for \( {T}_{q}\left( {M}_{T - \bar{\tau }}\right) \) . For each \( \alpha \) , extend \( \left\{  {Y}_{\alpha }\right\} \) to an adapted vector field along the \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic \( {\gamma }_{Z} \) by solving

\[
{\nabla }_{X}{Y}_{\alpha } = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\tau }\left( {\sqrt{\tau } - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}}\right) }{Y}_{\alpha } - \operatorname{Ric}{\left( {Y}_{\alpha }, \cdot  \right) }^{ * }.
\]

As in Equation (6.10), we have

\[
\frac{d}{d\tau }\left\langle  {{Y}_{\alpha },{Y}_{\beta }}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}{Y}_{\alpha },{Y}_{\beta }}\right\rangle   + \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{X}{Y}_{\beta },{Y}_{\alpha }}\right\rangle   + 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {{Y}_{\alpha },{Y}_{\beta }}\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }\left( {\sqrt{\tau } - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}}\right) }\left\langle  {{Y}_{\alpha },{Y}_{\beta }}\right\rangle  .
\]

By integrating we get

\[
\left\langle  {{Y}_{\alpha },{Y}_{\beta }}\right\rangle  \left( \tau \right)  = \frac{{\left( \sqrt{\tau } - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) }^{2}}{{\left( \sqrt{\tau } - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) }^{2}}{\delta }_{\alpha \beta }.
\]

To simplify the notation we set

\[
I\left( \tau \right)  = \frac{\sqrt{\bar{\tau }} - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}}{\sqrt{\tau } - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}}
\]

and \( {W}_{\alpha }\left( \tau \right)  = I\left( \tau \right) {Y}_{\alpha }\left( \tau \right) \) . Then \( {\left\{  {W}_{\alpha }\left( \tau \right) \right\}  }_{\alpha } \) form an orthonormal basis at \( \tau \) . Consequently, summing Inequality (6.13) over \( \alpha \) gives

(6.16)

\[
\Delta {L}_{x}^{\bar{\tau }}\left( q\right)  \leq  \frac{n}{\sqrt{\bar{\tau }} - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}} - 2\sqrt{\bar{\tau }}R\left( q\right)  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }{\int }_{{\tau }_{1}}^{\bar{\tau }}\sqrt{\tau }H\left( {X,{Y}_{\alpha }}\right) {d\tau }.
\]

To establish Inequality (6.14) it remains to prove the following claim.

CLAIM 6.44.

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }H\left( {X,{Y}_{\alpha }}\right)  = \frac{{\left( \sqrt{\tau } - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) }^{2}}{{\left( \sqrt{\tau } - \sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}\right) }^{2}}H\left( X\right) .
\]

Proof. To prove the claim we sum Equation (6.12) giving

\[
{I}^{2}\left( \tau \right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }H\left( {X,{Y}_{\alpha }}\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }H\left( {X,{W}_{\alpha }}\right)
\]

\[
=  - \bigtriangleup R + 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  + 4\mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }\left( {{\nabla }_{{W}_{\alpha }}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {{W}_{\alpha }, X}\right)
\]

\[
- 2\mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }{\operatorname{Ric}}_{\tau }\left( {{W}_{\alpha },{W}_{\alpha }}\right)  + 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\right| }^{2} - \frac{1}{\tau }R - 4\langle \nabla R, X\rangle .
\]

Taking the trace of the second Bianchi identity, we get

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }\left( {{\nabla }_{{W}_{\alpha }}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {{W}_{\alpha }, X}\right)  = \frac{1}{2}\langle \nabla R, X\rangle .
\]

In addition by Equation (3.7), recalling that \( \partial R/\partial \tau  =  - \partial R/\partial t \) , we have

\[
\frac{\partial R}{\partial \tau } =  - \bigtriangleup R - 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\right| }^{2}.
\]

On the other hand,

\[
\frac{\partial R}{\partial \tau } = \partial \left( {{g}^{ij}{R}_{ij}}\right) /\partial \tau  =  - 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\right| }^{2} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }\frac{\partial \operatorname{Ric}}{\partial \tau }\left( {{W}_{\alpha },{W}_{\alpha }}\right) ,
\]

and so \( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }\frac{\partial \operatorname{Ric}}{\partial \tau }\left( {{W}_{\alpha },{W}_{\alpha }}\right)  =  - \bigtriangleup R \) . Putting all this together gives

\[
{I}^{2}\left( \tau \right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }H\left( {X,{Y}_{\alpha }}\right)  = H\left( X\right) .
\]

Clearly, Inequality (6.14) follows immediately from Inequality (6.16) and the claim. The last statement of Proposition 6.43 follows directly from the last statement of Proposition 6.37 and Lemma 6.41. This completes the proof of Proposition 6.43.

Proposition 6.59. Given constants \( \epsilon  > 0,{\bar{\tau }}_{0} < \infty ,{l}_{0} < \infty \) , and \( {C}_{0} < \infty \) , there are constants \( C < \infty \) and \( 0 < \delta  < \epsilon \) depending only on the given constants such that the following holds. Let \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) be a generalized Ricci flow and let \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) be a point with \( \mathbf{t}\left( x\right)  = T - {\tau }_{1} \) . Let \( y \in  \mathcal{M} \) be a point with \( \mathbf{t}\left( y\right)  = t = T - \bar{\tau } \) where \( {\tau }_{1} + \epsilon  \leq  \bar{\tau } \leq  {\bar{\tau }}_{0} \) . Suppose that there is a minimizing \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic \( \gamma \) from \( x \) to \( y \) with \( l\left( \gamma \right)  \leq  {l}_{0} \) . Suppose that the ball \( B\left( {y, t,\epsilon }\right) \) has compact closure in \( {M}_{t} \) and that \( \widetilde{P}\left( {y,\epsilon ,\epsilon }\right)  \subset  \mathcal{M} \) exists and that the sectional curvatures of the restriction of \( G \) to this submanifold are bounded by \( {C}_{0} \) . Lastly, suppose that for every point of the form \( z \in  \widetilde{P}\left( {y,\delta ,\delta }\right) \) there is a minimizing \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic from \( x \) to \( z \) with \( \left| \operatorname{Ric}\right| \) and \( \left| {\nabla R}\right| \) bounded by \( {C}_{0} \) along this geodesic. Then for all \( \left( {b,{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \in  B\left( {y, t,\delta }\right)  \times  \left( {t - \delta , t + \delta }\right) \) we have

\[
\left| {{l}_{x}\left( y\right)  - {l}_{x}\left( {\iota \left( {b,{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right) }\right|  \leq  C\sqrt{{d}_{t}{\left( y, b\right) }^{2} + {\left| t - {t}^{\prime }\right| }^{2}}.
\]

Proof. (of Proposition 6.59) Let \( {\delta }_{2} \) and \( {C}_{3} \) be the constants as in Lemma 6.62 associated to \( \epsilon /2,{\bar{\tau }}_{0},{C}_{0} \) , and \( {l}_{0} \) . We shall choose \( C \geq  {C}_{3} \) and \( \delta  \leq  {\delta }_{2} \) so that by Lemma 6.62 we will automatically have

\[
{l}_{x}\left( {\iota \left( {b,{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right)  \leq  {l}_{x}\left( y\right)  + {C}_{3}\sqrt{{d}_{{t}_{0}}{\left( y, b\right) }^{2} + {\left| {t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }\right| }^{2}}
\]

\]

for all \( \iota \left( {b,{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \in  P\left( {y,\delta ,\delta }\right) \) . It remains to choose \( C \) and \( \delta \) so that

\[
{l}_{x}\left( y\right)  \leq  {l}_{x}\left( {\iota \left( {b,{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right)  + C\sqrt{{d}_{{t}_{0}}{\left( y, b\right) }^{2} + {\left| {t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }\right| }^{2}}.
\]

Let \( {\delta }_{2}^{\prime } \) and \( {C}_{3}^{\prime } \) be the constants given by Lemma 6.62 for the following set of input constants: \( {C}_{0}^{\prime } = {C}_{0},{\bar{\tau }}_{0} \) replaced by \( {\bar{\tau }}_{0}^{\prime } = {\bar{\tau }}_{0} + \epsilon /2 \) , and \( {l}_{0} \) replaced by \( {l}_{0}^{\prime } = {l}_{0} + \sqrt{2}{C}_{3}{\delta }_{2} \) , and \( \epsilon \) replaced by \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } = \epsilon /4 \) . Then set \( C = \max \left( {2{C}_{3}^{\prime },{C}_{3}}\right) \) .

Let \( z = \iota \left( {b,{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \in  \widetilde{P}\left( {y,\delta ,\delta }\right) \) .

CLAIM 6.65. For \( \delta \) sufficiently small (how small depends on \( {\delta }_{2} \) and \( {\delta }_{2}^{\prime } \) ) we have \( B\left( {z,{t}^{\prime },\epsilon /4}\right)  \subset  B\left( {y,{t}_{0},\epsilon }\right) \) .

Proof. Since \( \left| {{t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }}\right|  < \delta  \leq  {\delta }_{2} \) , and by construction \( {\delta }_{2} < {\delta }_{0} \) , it follows that for any \( c \in  B\left( {y,{t}_{0},\epsilon }\right) \) we have \( {d}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {b, c}\right)  \leq  2{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {b, c}\right) \) . Since \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y, b}\right)  < \; \delta  \leq  \epsilon /4 \) , the result is immediate from the triangle inequality.

By the above and the fact that \( \delta  \leq  \epsilon /4 \) , the sectional curvatures on \( \widetilde{P}\left( {z,\epsilon /4,\epsilon /4}\right) \) are bounded by \( {C}_{0} \) . By Lemma 6.62 there is a curve parameterized by backward time from \( x \) to \( z \) whose \( l \) -length is at most \( {l}_{0}^{\prime } \) . Thus the \( l \) -length of any minimizing \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic from \( x \) to \( z \) is at most \( {l}_{0}^{\prime } \) . By assumption we have a minimizing \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic with the property that Ric and \( \left| {\nabla R}\right| \) are bounded by \( {C}_{0} \) along the \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic.

Of course, \( {t}_{0} - \delta  < {t}^{\prime } < {t}_{0} + \delta \) , so that \( {\tau }_{1} + \epsilon /2 < T - {t}^{\prime } \leq  {\bar{\tau }}_{0} + \epsilon /4 \) . This means that Lemma 6.62 applies to show that for very \( w = \iota \left( {c, t}\right)  \in \; \widetilde{P}\left( {z,{\delta }_{2}^{\prime },{\delta }_{2}^{\prime }}\right) \) , we have

\[
{l}_{x}\left( w\right)  \leq  {l}_{x}\left( z\right)  + {C}_{3}^{\prime }\sqrt{{d}_{{t}^{\prime }}{\left( b, c\right) }^{2} + {\left| t - {t}^{\prime }\right| }^{2}}.
\]

The proof is then completed by showing the following:

CLAIM 6.66. \( y \in  \widetilde{P}\left( {z,{\delta }_{2}^{\prime },{\delta }_{2}^{\prime }}\right) \) .

Proof. By construction \( \left| {{t}^{\prime } - {t}_{0}}\right|  < \delta  \leq  {\delta }_{2}^{\prime } \) . Also, \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y, b}\right)  < \delta  \leq  {\delta }_{2}^{\prime }/2 \) . Since \( {d}_{{t}_{0}} \leq  2{d}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) , we have \( {d}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {y, b}\right)  < {\delta }_{2}^{\prime } \) the claim is then immediate.

It follows immediately that

\[
{l}_{x}\left( y\right)  \leq  {l}_{x}\left( z\right)  + {C}_{3}^{\prime }\sqrt{{d}_{{t}^{\prime }}{\left( b, y\right) }^{2} + {\left| {t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }\right| }^{2}}
\]

\[
\leq  {l}_{x}\left( z\right)  + 2{C}_{3}^{\prime }\sqrt{{d}_{{t}_{0}}{\left( b, y\right) }^{2} + {\left| {t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }\right| }^{2}}
\]

\[
\leq  {l}_{x}\left( z\right)  + C\sqrt{{d}_{{t}_{0}}{\left( b, y\right) }^{2} + {\left| {t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }\right| }^{2}}.
\]

This completes the proof of Proposition 6.59.

(6.18)
