Fix \( \tau \) and take a sequence of \( {\tau }_{0} \rightarrow  \infty \) , allowing us to take \( c \rightarrow  1 \) , and apply the previous proposition. This gives the first inequality and gives the lower bound for \( \partial {l}_{x}/\partial \tau \) in the second inequality.

To establish the upper bound in the second inequality we consider the path that is the concatenation of a minimal \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic \( \gamma \) from \( x \) to \( \left( {q,\tau }\right) \) followed by the path \( \mu \left( {\tau }^{\prime }\right)  = \left( {q,{\tau }^{\prime }}\right) \) for \( {\tau }^{\prime } \geq  \tau \) . Then

\[
{l}_{x}\left( {\gamma  * {\left. \mu \right| }_{\left\lbrack  \tau ,{\tau }_{1}\right\rbrack  }}\right)  = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{{\tau }_{1}}}\left( {\mathcal{L}\left( \gamma \right)  + {\int }_{\tau }^{{\tau }_{1}}\sqrt{{\tau }^{\prime }}R\left( {q,{\tau }^{\prime }}\right) d{\tau }^{\prime }}\right) .
\]

Differentiating at \( {\tau }_{1} = \tau \) gives

\[
{\left. \frac{\partial {l}_{x}\left( {\gamma  * \mu }\right) }{\partial \tau }\right| }_{{\tau }_{1} = \tau } =  - \frac{1}{4{\tau }^{3/2}}\mathcal{L}\left( \gamma \right)  + \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\tau }}\sqrt{\tau }R\left( {q,\tau }\right)
\]

\[
=  - \frac{{l}_{x}\left( {q,\tau }\right) }{2\tau } + \frac{R\left( {q,\tau }\right) }{2}.
\]

By the first inequality in this statement, we have

\[
- \frac{{l}_{x}\left( {q,\tau }\right) }{2\tau } + \frac{R\left( {q,\tau }\right) }{2} \leq  \frac{{l}_{x}\left( {q,\tau }\right) }{\tau }.
\]

Since \( {l}_{x}\left( {q,{\tau }^{\prime }}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{l}\left( {\gamma  * {\left. \mu \right| }_{\left\lbrack  \tau ,{\tau }^{\prime }\right\rbrack  }}\right) \) for all \( {\tau }^{\prime } \geq  \tau \) , this establishes the claimed upper bound for \( \partial {l}_{x}/\partial \tau \) .

nodes.label: Theorem 9.11

nodes.section_title: 9.2. The asymptotic gradient shrinking soliton for \( \kappa \) -solutions
nodes.content:
THEOREM 9.11. Let \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) , - \infty  < t \leq  0 \) , be a \( \kappa \) -solution of dimension \( n \) . Fix \( x = \left( {p,0}\right)  \in  M \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) . Suppose that \( {\left\{  {\bar{\tau }}_{k}\right\}  }_{k = 1}^{\infty } \) is a sequence tending to \( \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) . Then, after replacing \( \left\{  {\bar{\tau }}_{k}\right\} \) by a subsequence, the following holds. For each \( k \) denote by \( {M}_{k} \) the manifold \( M \) , by \( {g}_{k}\left( t\right) \) the family of metrics \( {g}_{{\bar{\tau }}_{k}}\left( t\right) \) on \( {M}_{k} \) , and by \( {q}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) the point \( q\left( {\bar{\tau }}_{k}\right) \) . The sequence of pointed flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) ,\left( {{q}_{k}, - 1}\right) }\right) \) defined for \( t \in  \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) converges smoothly to a non-flat based Ricci flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,\left( {{q}_{\infty }, - 1}\right) }\right) \) defined

for \( t \in  \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) . This limiting Ricci flow satisfies the gradient shrinking soliton equation in the sense that there is a smooth function \( f : {M}_{\infty } \times  \left( {-\infty ,0}\right)  \rightarrow \; \mathbb{R} \) such that for every \( t \in  \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) we have

(9.2)

\[
{\operatorname{Ric}}_{{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) } + {\operatorname{Hess}}^{{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( {f\left( t\right) }\right)  + \frac{1}{2t}{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right)  = 0.
\]

Furthermore, \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) has non-negative curvature operator, is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed, and satisfies \( \partial {R}_{{g}_{\infty }}\left( {x, t}\right) /\partial t \geq  0 \) for all \( x \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and all \( t < 0 \) .

See FIG. 1.

nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture

nodes.content: REMARK 9.12. We are not claiming that the gradient shrinking soliton is a \( \kappa \) -solution (or more precisely an extension forward in time of a time-shifted version of a \( \kappa \) -solution) because we are not claiming that the time-slices have bounded curvature operator. Indeed, we do not know if this is true in general. We shall establish below (see Corollary 9.50 and Corollary 9.53) that in the case \( n = 2,3 \) , the gradient shrinking soliton does indeed have time-slices of bounded curvature, and hence is an extension of a \( \kappa \) -solution. We are also not claiming at this point that the limiting flow is a gradient shrinking soliton in the sense that there is a one-parameter family of diffeomorphisms \( {\varphi }_{t} : {M}_{\infty } \rightarrow  {M}_{\infty }, t < 0 \) , with the property that \( \left| t\right| {\varphi }_{t}^{ * }{g}_{\infty }\left( {-1}\right)  = {g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) \) and with the property that the \( {\varphi }_{t} \) are generated by the gradient vector field of a function. We shall also establish this result in dimensions 2 and 3 later in this chapter.

nodes.content:
Lemma 9.21. For any \( t \in  \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) we have

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{\left| {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}\right| }_{{h}_{k}}^{2}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {h}_{k}\right)  = {\left| \nabla {l}_{\infty }\right| }_{{g}_{\infty }}^{2}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {g}_{\infty }\right)
\]

in the sense of distributions on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \{ t\} \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: Lemma 9.21. For any \( t \in \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) we have \[ \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow \infty }}{\left| {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}\right| }_{{h}_{k}}^{2}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {h}_{k}\right) = {\left| \nabla {l}_{\infty }\right| }_{{g}_{\infty }}^{2}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {g}_{\infty }\right) \] in the sense of distributions on \( {M}_{\infty } \times \{ t\} \) .

nodes.proof:
It suffices to fix \( 0 < {\tau }_{0} < \left| t\right| \) . The inequality in one direction \( \left(  \geq  \right) \) is a general result. Here is the argument. Since the \( {\left| {\nabla }^{{g}_{k}}{l}_{{x}_{k}}\right| }_{{g}_{k}} \) are uniformly essentially bounded on every \( B\left( {{x}_{k}, - {\tau }_{0}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-T, - {\tau }_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , the \( {\left| {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}\right| }_{{h}_{k}} \) are uniformly essentially bounded on \( B\left( {{x}_{\infty }, - {\tau }_{0}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-T, - {\tau }_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . (Of course, \( {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k} = d{l}_{k} = \nabla {l}_{k} \) .) Since the \( {h}_{k} \) converge uniformly on compact sets to \( {g}_{\infty } \) , it is clear that

(9.6)

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}\left( {{\left| {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}\right| }_{{h}_{k}}^{2}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {h}_{k}\right)  - {\left| \nabla {l}_{k}\right| }_{{g}_{\infty }}^{2}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {g}_{\infty }\right) }\right)  = 0
\]

in the sense of distributions on \( M \times  \{ t\} \) . Since the \( {l}_{k} \) converge uniformly on compact subsets to \( {l}_{\infty } \) , it follows immediately from Fatou’s lemma that

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{\left| \nabla {l}_{k}\right| }_{{g}_{\infty }}^{2}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {g}_{\infty }\right)  \geq  {\left| \nabla {l}_{\infty }\right| }_{{g}_{\infty }}^{2}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {g}_{\infty }\right)
\]

in the sense of distributions on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \{ t\} \) . Thus, we have the following inequality of distributions:

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{\left| {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}\right| }_{{h}_{k}}^{2}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {h}_{k}\right)  \geq  {\left| \nabla {l}_{\infty }\right| }_{{g}_{\infty }}^{2}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {g}_{\infty }\right) .
\]

We need to establish the opposite inequality which is not a general result, but rather relies on the bounds on \( {\bigtriangleup }^{{g}_{k}}{l}_{{x}_{k}} \) (or equivalently on \( {\bigtriangleup }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k} \) ) given in the second inequality in Theorem 7.13. We must show that for each \( t \leq   - {\tau }_{0} \) and for any \( \varphi \) , a non-negative, smooth function with compact support in \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \{ t\} \) , we have

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{\int }_{M\times \{ t\} }\varphi \left( {{\left| {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}\right| }_{{h}_{k}}^{2}\operatorname{dvol}\left( {h}_{k}\right)  - {\left| \nabla {l}_{\infty }\right| }_{{g}_{\infty }}^{2}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {g}_{\infty }\right) }\right)  \leq  0.
\]

First, notice that since, on the support of \( \varphi \) , the metrics \( {h}_{k} \) converge uniformly in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to \( {g}_{\infty } \) and since \( {\left| {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}\right| }_{{h}_{k}}^{2} \) and \( {\left| \nabla {l}_{\infty }\right| }_{{g}_{\infty }}^{2} \) are essentially bounded on the support of \( \varphi \) , we have

(9.7)

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{\int }_{M\times \{ t\} }\varphi \left( {{\left| {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}\right| }_{{h}_{k}}^{2}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {h}_{k}\right)  - {\left| \nabla {l}_{\infty }\right| }_{{g}_{\infty }}^{2}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {g}_{\infty }\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{\int }_{M\times \{ t\} }\varphi \left( {{\left| {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}\right| }_{{h}_{k}}^{2} - {\left| \nabla {l}_{\infty }\right| }_{{h}_{k}}^{2}}\right) d\operatorname{vol}\left( {h}_{k}\right)
\]

\[
= \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{\int }_{M\times \{ t\} }\left\langle  {{\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k} - \nabla {l}_{\infty }}\right\rangle  ,\varphi {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}{\rangle }_{{h}_{k}}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {h}_{k}\right)
\]

\[
+ {\int }_{M\times \{ t\} }{\left\langle  {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k} - \nabla {l}_{\infty }),\varphi \nabla {l}_{\infty }\right\rangle  }_{{h}_{k}}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {h}_{k}\right) .
\]

We claim that, in the limit, the last term in this expression vanishes. Using the fact that the \( {h}_{k} \) converge uniformly in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to \( {g}_{\infty } \) on the support of \( \varphi \) , and \( \left| {\nabla {l}_{\infty }}\right| \) is bounded on this support we can rewrite the last term as

(9.8)

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{\int }_{M\times \{ t\} }{\left\langle  \nabla \left( {l}_{k} - {l}_{\infty }\right) ,\varphi \nabla {l}_{\infty }\right\rangle  }_{{g}_{\infty }}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {g}_{\infty }\right) .
\]

Since \( {l}_{k} - {l}_{\infty } \) goes to zero weakly in \( {W}^{1,2} \) on the support of \( \varphi \) whereas \( {l}_{\infty } \) is an element of \( {W}^{1,2} \) of this compact set, we see that the expression given in (9.8) vanishes and hence that

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{\int }_{M\times \{ t\} }{\left\langle  {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}\left( {l}_{k} - {l}_{\infty }\right) ,\varphi \nabla {l}_{\infty }\right\rangle  }_{{h}_{k}}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {h}_{k}\right)  = 0.
\]

It remains to consider the first term in the last expression in Equation (9.7). (This is where we shall need the differential inequality for the \( {\bigtriangleup }^{{g}_{k}}{l}_{{x}_{k}} \) .) Since the \( {l}_{k} \) converge uniformly to \( {l}_{\infty } \) on the support of \( \varphi \) , we can choose positive constants \( {\epsilon }_{k} \) tending to 0 as \( k \) tends to \( \infty \) so that \( {l}_{\infty } - {l}_{k} + {\epsilon }_{k} > 0 \) on the support of \( \varphi \) . We can rewrite

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{\int }_{M\times \{ t\} }\left\langle  {\left( {{\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k} - \nabla {l}_{\infty }}\right) ,\varphi {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}}\right\rangle  {h}_{k}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {h}_{k}\right)
\]

\[
= \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{\int }_{M\times \{ t\} }\left\langle  {{\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}\left( {{l}_{k} - {l}_{\infty } - {\epsilon }_{k}}\right) ,\varphi {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}{\rangle }_{{h}_{k}}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {h}_{k}\right) .}\right.
\]

nodes.label: Claim 9.22
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.section_title: 9.2. The asymptotic gradient shrinking soliton for \( \kappa \) -solutions
nodes.content:
CLAIM 9.22.

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{\int }_{M\times \{ t\} }{\left\langle  {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}\left( {l}_{k} - {l}_{\infty } - {\epsilon }_{k}\right) ,\varphi {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}\right\rangle  }_{{h}_{k}}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {h}_{k}\right)  \leq  0.
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: CLAIM 9.22. \[ \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow \infty }}{\int }_{M\times \{ t\} }{\left\langle {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}\left( {l}_{k} - {l}_{\infty } - {\epsilon }_{k}\right) ,\varphi {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}\right\rangle }_{{h}_{k}}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {h}_{k}\right) \leq 0. \]

nodes.proof:
Since \( \varphi \) is a compactly supported, non-negative smooth function, it follows from Theorem 7.13 that we have the following inequality of distributions:

\[
\varphi {\bigtriangleup }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k} \leq  \frac{\varphi }{2}\left( {{\left| {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}\right| }_{{h}_{k}}^{2} - {R}_{{h}_{k}} - \frac{{l}_{k} - n}{\tau }}\right) .
\]

(Here \( {R}_{{h}_{k}} \) is the scalar curvature of \( {h}_{k} \) .) That is to say, for any non-negative \( {C}^{\infty } \) -function \( f \) we have

\[
{\int }_{M\times \{ t\} } - {\left\langle  {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k},{\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}\left( \varphi  \cdot  f\right) \right\rangle  }_{{h}_{k}}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {h}_{k}\right)
\]

\[
\leq  {\int }_{M\times \{ t\} }\frac{\varphi f}{2}\left( {{\left| {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}\right| }_{{h}_{k}}^{2} - {R}_{{h}_{k}} - \frac{{l}_{k} - n}{\tau }}\right) d\operatorname{vol}\left( {h}_{k}\right) .
\]

We claim that the same inequality holds as long as \( f \) is a non-negative, locally Lipschitz function. The point is that given such a function \( f \) , we can find a sequence of non-negative \( {C}^{\infty } \) -functions \( {f}_{k} \) on the support of \( \varphi \) (by say mollifying \( f \) ) that converge to \( f \) strongly in the \( {W}^{1,2} \) -norm on the support of \( \varphi \) . The sought-after inequality holds for every \( {f}_{k} \) . Since both sides of the inequality are continuous in the \( {W}^{1,2} \) -norm of the function, the result holds for the limit function \( f \) as well.

Now we apply this with \( f \) being the non-negative locally Lipschitz function \( {l}_{\infty } - {l}_{k} + {\epsilon }_{k} \) . We conclude that

\[
{\int }_{M\times \{ t\} }{\left\langle  {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}\left( \varphi \left( {l}_{k} - {l}_{\infty } - {\epsilon }_{k}\right) \right) ,{\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}\right\rangle  }_{{h}_{k}}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {h}_{k}\right)
\]

\[
\leq  {\int }_{M\times \{ t\} }\frac{\varphi \left( {{l}_{\infty } - {l}_{k} + {\epsilon }_{k}}\right) }{2}\left( {{\left| {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}\right| }_{{h}_{k}}^{2} - {R}_{{h}_{k}} - \frac{{l}_{k} - n}{\tau }}\right) d\operatorname{vol}\left( {h}_{k}\right) .
\]

Now taking the limit as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) , we see that the right-hand side of this inequality tends to zero since \( \left( {{l}_{\infty } - {l}_{k} + {\epsilon }_{k}}\right) \) tends uniformly to zero on the support of \( \varphi \) and \( {\left| {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}\right| }_{{h}_{k}}^{2},{R}_{k} \) and \( {l}_{k} \) are all uniformly essentially bounded on the support of \( \varphi \) . Thus, the term

\[
{\int }_{M\times \{ t\} }\left\langle  {{\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}\left( {\varphi \left( {{l}_{k} - {l}_{\infty } - {\epsilon }_{k}}\right) }\right) ,{\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k}}\right\rangle  {h}_{k}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {h}_{k}\right)
\]

has a limsup \( \leq  0 \) as \( k \) tends to \( \infty \) . Now we expand

\[
{\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}\left( {\varphi \left( {{l}_{k} - {l}_{\infty } - {\epsilon }_{k}}\right) }\right)  = {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}\left( \varphi \right) \left( {{l}_{k} - {l}_{\infty } - {\epsilon }_{k}}\right)  + \varphi {\nabla }^{{h}_{k}}\left( {{l}_{k} - {l}_{\infty } - {\epsilon }_{k}}\right) .
\]

The first term on the right-hand side converges to zero as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) since \( {l}_{k} - {l}_{\infty } - {\epsilon }_{k} \) tends uniformly to zero on the support of \( \varphi \) . This completes the proof of the claim.

nodes.content:
LEMMA 9.23. Consider the distribution

\[
\mathcal{D} = \frac{\partial {l}_{\infty }}{\partial \tau } + {\left| \nabla {l}_{\infty }\right| }^{2} - R + \frac{n}{2\tau } - \bigtriangleup {l}_{\infty }
\]

on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) . Then \( \mathcal{D} \) extends to a continuous linear functional on the space of compactly supported \( {W}^{1,2} \) -functions on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) . Furthermore, if \( \psi \) is a non-negative Lipschitz function on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) with compact support, then \( \mathcal{D}\left( \psi \right)  \leq  0 \) .

Then \( \mathcal{D} \) extends to a continuous linear functional on the space of compactly supported \( {W}^{1,2} \) -functions on \( {M}_{\infty } \times \...

nodes.proof:
Clearly, since the \( {l}_{k} \) converge uniformly on compact subsets of \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) to \( {l}_{\infty } \) and the metrics \( {h}_{k} \) converge smoothly to \( {g}_{\infty } \) , uniformly on compact sets, it follows that the \( {\bigtriangleup }^{{h}_{k}}{l}_{k} \) converge in the weak sense to \( \bigtriangleup {l}_{\infty } \) and similarly, the \( \partial {l}_{k}/\partial \tau \) converge in the weak sense to \( \partial {l}_{\infty }/\partial \tau \) . Hence, by taking limits from Theorem 7.13, using Lemma 9.21, we see that

(9.9)

\[
\mathcal{D} = \frac{\partial {l}_{\infty }}{\partial \tau } + {\left| \nabla {l}_{\infty }\right| }^{2} - R + \frac{n}{2\tau } - \Delta {l}_{\infty } \geq  0
\]

in the weak sense on \( M \times  \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) .

Since \( R \) and \( \frac{n}{2\tau } \) are \( {C}^{\infty } \) -functions, it is clear that the distributions given by these terms extend to continuous linear functionals on the space of compactly supported \( {W}^{1,2} \) -functions. Similarly, since \( {\left| \nabla {l}_{\infty }\right| }^{2} \) is an element of \( {L}_{\mathrm{{loc}}}^{\infty } \) , it also extends to a continuous linear functional on compactly supported \( {W}^{1,2} \) -functions. Since \( \left| {\partial {l}_{\infty }/\partial \tau }\right| \) is an locally essentially bounded function,

\( \partial {l}_{\infty }/\partial \tau \) extends to a continuous functional on the space of compactly supported \( {W}^{1,2} \) functions. Lastly, we consider \( \bigtriangleup {l}_{\infty } \) . As we have seen, the value of the associated distribution on \( \varphi \) is given by

\[
{\int }_{M \times  \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) } - {\left\langle  \nabla \varphi ,\nabla {l}_{\infty }\right\rangle  }_{{g}_{\infty }}d\operatorname{vol}\left( {g}_{\infty }\right) {d\tau }.
\]

Since \( \left| {\nabla {l}_{\infty }}\right| \) is a locally essentially bounded function, this expression also extends to a continuous linear functional on compactly supported \( {W}^{1,2} \) - functions.

Lastly, if \( \psi \) is an element of \( {W}^{1,2} \) with compact support and hence can be approximated in the \( {W}^{1,2} \) -norm by non-negative smooth functions. The last statement is now immediate from Equation (9.9).

nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.section_title: 9.2. The asymptotic gradient shrinking soliton for \( \kappa \) -solutions
nodes.content:
COROLLARY 9.24. The functional

\[
\varphi  \mapsto  \mathcal{D}\left( {{e}^{-{l}_{\infty }}\varphi }\right)
\]

is a distribution and its value on any non-negative, compactly supported \( {C}^{\infty } \) -function \( \varphi \) is \( \geq  0 \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: COROLLARY 9.24. The functional \[ \varphi \mapsto \mathcal{D}\left( {{e}^{-{l}_{\infty }}\varphi }\right) \] is a distribution and its value on any non-negative, compactly supported \( {C}^{\infty } \) -function \( \varphi \) is \( \geq 0 \) .

nodes.proof: If \( \varphi \) is a compactly supported non-negative \( {C}^{\infty } \) -function, then \( {e}^{-{l}_{\infty }}\varphi \) is a compactly supported non-negative Lipschitz function. Hence, this result is an immediate consequence of the previous corollary.

nodes.label: Lemma 9.25
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.section_title: 9.2. The asymptotic gradient shrinking soliton for \( \kappa \) -solutions
nodes.content:
LEMMA 9.25. There is a constant \( {c}_{1} > 0 \) depending only on the dimension \( n \) such that for any \( p, q \in  {M}_{k} \) we have

\[
{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {p,\tau }\right)  \geq   - {l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {q,\tau }\right)  - 1 + {c}_{1}\frac{{d}_{g\left( {-\tau }\right) }^{2}\left( {p, q}\right) }{\tau }.
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: LEMMA 9.25. There is a constant \( {c}_{1} > 0 \) depending only on the dimension \( n \) such that for any \( p, q \in {M}_{k} \) we have \[ {l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {p,\tau }\right) \geq - {l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {q,\tau }\right) - 1 + {c}_{1}\frac{{d}_{g\left( {-\tau }\right) }^{2}\left( {p, q}\right) }{\tau }. \]

nodes.proof:
Since both sides of this inequality and also Ricci flow are invariant if the metric and time are simultaneously rescaled, it suffices to consider the case when \( \tau  = 1 \) . Also, since \( {\mathcal{U}}_{x}\left( 1\right) \) is a dense subset, it suffices to assume that \( p, q \in  {\mathcal{U}}_{x}\left( 1\right) \) . Also, by symmetry, we can suppose that \( {l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {q,1}\right)  \leq  {l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {p,1}\right) . \)

Let \( {\gamma }_{1} \) and \( {\gamma }_{2} \) be the minimizing \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesics from \( x \) to \( \left( {p,1}\right) \) and \( \left( {q,1}\right) \) respectively. We define a function \( f : {M}_{k} \times  {M}_{k} \times  \lbrack 0,\infty ) \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) by

\[
f\left( {a, b,\tau }\right)  = {d}_{{g}_{k}\left( {-\tau }\right) }\left( {a, b}\right) .
\]

Since \( {\gamma }_{1}\left( 0\right)  = {\gamma }_{2}\left( 0\right) \) we have

(9.10)

\[
{d}_{{g}_{k}\left( {-1}\right) }\left( {p, q}\right)  = f\left( {p, q,1}\right)
\]

\[
= {\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{d}{d\tau }f\left( {{\gamma }_{1}\left( \tau \right) ,{\gamma }_{2}\left( \tau \right) ,\tau }\right) {d\tau }
\]

\[
= {\int }_{0}^{1}\left( {\frac{\partial f}{\partial \tau }\left( {{\gamma }_{1}\left( \tau \right) ,{\gamma }_{2}\left( \tau \right) ,\tau }\right) +\langle \nabla {f}_{a},{\gamma }_{1}^{\prime }\left( \tau \right) \rangle }\right.
\]

\[
\left. {+\left\langle  {\nabla {f}_{b},{\gamma }_{2}^{\prime }\left( \tau \right) }\right\rangle  }\right) {d\tau }
\]

where \( {\nabla }_{a}f \) and \( {\nabla }_{b}f \) refer respectively to the gradient of \( f \) with respect to the first copy of \( {M}_{k} \) in the domain and the second copy of \( {M}_{k} \) in the domain. Of course, \( \left| {\nabla {f}_{a}}\right|  = 1 \) and \( \left| {\nabla {f}_{b}}\right|  = 1 \) .

By Corollary 6.29, \( {\gamma }_{1}^{\prime }\left( \tau \right)  = \nabla {l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {{\gamma }_{1}\left( \tau \right) ,\tau }\right) \) and \( {\gamma }_{2}^{\prime }\left( \tau \right)  = \nabla {l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {{\gamma }_{2}\left( \tau \right) ,\tau }\right) \) . Since \( R \geq  0 \) we have

\[
{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {{\gamma }_{1}\left( \tau \right) ,\tau }\right)  = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\tau }}{\mathcal{L}}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {\left. {\gamma }_{1}\right| }_{\left\lbrack  0,\tau \right\rbrack  }\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\tau }}{\mathcal{L}}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {\gamma }_{1}\right)  = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {p,1}\right) .
\]

Symmetrically, we have

\[
{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {{\gamma }_{2}\left( \tau \right) ,\tau }\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {q,1}\right) .
\]

From this inequality, Corollary 9.10, and the fact that \( R \geq  0 \) , we have

(9.11)

\[
\left| \left\langle  {\nabla {f}_{a}\left( {{\gamma }_{1}\left( \tau \right) ,{\gamma }_{2}\left( \tau \right) ,\tau }\right) ,{\gamma }_{1}^{\prime }\left( \tau \right) }\right\rangle  \right|  \leq  \left| {{\gamma }_{1}^{\prime }\left( \tau \right) }\right|  = \left| {\nabla {l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {{\gamma }_{1}\left( \tau \right) ,\tau }\right) }\right|
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{\sqrt{3}}{{\tau }^{3/4}}\sqrt{{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {p,1}\right) }
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{\sqrt{3}}{{\tau }^{3/4}}\sqrt{{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {p,1}\right)  + 1}
\]

Symmetrically, we have

(9.12)

\[
\left| \left\langle  {\nabla {f}_{b}\left( {{\gamma }_{1}\left( \tau \right) ,{\gamma }_{2}\left( \tau \right) ,\tau }\right) ,{\gamma }_{2}^{\prime }\left( \tau \right) }\right\rangle  \right|  \leq  \frac{\sqrt{3}}{{\tau }^{3/4}}\sqrt{{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {q,1}\right) } \leq  \frac{\sqrt{3}}{{\tau }^{3/4}}\sqrt{{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {q,1}\right)  + 1}.
\]

It follows from Corollary 9.10 that for any \( p \) , we have

\[
\left| {\nabla \left( \sqrt{{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {p,\tau }\right) }\right) }\right|  \leq  \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{\tau }}.
\]

Set \( {r}_{0}\left( \tau \right)  = {\tau }^{3/4}{\left( {l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( q,1\right)  + 1\right) }^{-1/2} \) . For any \( {p}^{\prime } \in  {B}_{{g}_{k}}\left( {{\gamma }_{1}\left( \tau \right) ,\tau ,{r}_{0}\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) integrating gives

\[
{l}_{{x}_{k}}^{1/2}\left( {{p}^{\prime },\tau }\right)  \leq  {l}_{{x}_{k}}^{1/2}\left( {{\gamma }_{1}\left( \tau \right) ,\tau }\right)  + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{\tau }}{r}_{0}\left( \tau \right)  \leq  \left( {{\tau }^{-1/4} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}{\tau }^{1/4}}\right) \sqrt{{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {p,1}\right)  + 1},
\]

where in the last inequality we have used the fact that \( 1 \leq  {l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {q,1}\right)  + 1 \leq \; {l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {p,1}\right)  + 1 \) . Again using Corollary 9.10 we have

\[
R\left( {{p}^{\prime },\tau }\right)  \leq  \frac{3}{\tau }{\left( {\tau }^{-1/4} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}{\tau }^{1/4}\right) }^{2}\left( {{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {p,1}\right)  + 1}\right) .
\]

Now consider \( {q}^{\prime } \in  {B}_{{g}_{k}\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{\gamma }_{2}\left( \tau \right) ,\tau ,{r}_{0}\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) . Similarly to the above computations, we have

\[
{l}_{{x}_{k}}^{1/2}\left( {{q}^{\prime },\tau }\right)  \leq  {l}_{{x}_{k}}^{1/2}\left( {q,1}\right)  + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{\tau }}{r}_{0}\left( \tau \right) ,
\]

so that

\[
{l}_{{x}_{k}}^{1/2}\left( {{q}^{\prime },\tau }\right)  \leq  \left( {{\tau }^{-1/4} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}{\tau }^{1/4}}\right) \sqrt{{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {q,1}\right)  + 1},
\]

and

\[
\left| {\operatorname{Ric}\left( {{q}^{\prime },\tau }\right)  \leq  R\left( {{q}^{\prime },\tau }\right)  \leq  \frac{3}{\tau }{\left( {\tau }^{-1/4} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}{\tau }^{1/4}\right) }^{2}\left( {{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {q,1}\right)  + 1}\right) .}\right|
\]

We set

\[
K = \frac{3}{\tau }{\left( {\tau }^{-1/4} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}{\tau }^{1/4}\right) }^{2}\left( {{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {q,1}\right)  + 1}\right) .
\]

Now, noting that \( \partial /\partial \tau \) here is \( - \partial /\partial t \) of Proposition 3.21, we apply Proposition 3.21 to see that

\[
\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau }f\left( {{\gamma }_{1}\left( \tau \right) ,{\gamma }_{2}\left( \tau \right) ,\tau }\right) }\right|  \leq  2\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {\frac{2}{3\left( {n - 1}\right) }K{r}_{0}\left( \tau \right)  + {r}_{0}{\left( \tau \right) }^{-1}}\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {{C}_{1}{\tau }^{-3/4} + {C}_{2}{\tau }^{-1/4} + {C}_{3}{\tau }^{1/4}}\right) \sqrt{{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {q,1}\right)  + 1}
\]

where \( {C}_{1},{C}_{2},{C}_{3} \) are constants depending only on the dimension \( n \) .

Now plugging Equation (9.11) and (9.12) and the above inequality into Equation (9.10) we see that

\[
{d}_{g\left( {-1}\right) }\left( {p, q}\right)  \leq  {\int }_{0}^{1}\left( {\left( {{C}_{1}{\tau }^{-3/4} + {C}_{2}{\tau }^{-1/4} + {C}_{3}{\tau }^{1/4}}\right) \sqrt{{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {q,1}\right)  + 1}}\right.
\]

\[
\left. {+\sqrt{3}{\tau }^{-3/4}\sqrt{{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {q,1}\right)  + 1} + \sqrt{3}{\tau }^{-3/4}\sqrt{{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {p,1}\right)  + 1}}\right) {d\tau }.
\]

This implies that

\[
{d}_{g\left( {-1}\right) }\left( {p, q}\right)  \leq  C\left( {\sqrt{{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {q,1}\right)  + 1} + \sqrt{{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {p,1}\right)  + 1}}\right) ,
\]

for some constant depending only on the dimension. Thus, since we are assuming that \( {l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {p,1}\right)  \geq  {l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {q,1}\right) \) we have

\[
{d}_{g\left( {-1}\right) }^{2}\left( {p, q}\right)  \leq  {C}^{2}\left( {3\left( {{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {p,1}\right)  + 1}\right)  + \left( {{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {q,1}\right)  + 1}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\leq  4{C}^{2}\left( {{l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {p,1}\right)  + 1 + {l}_{{x}_{k}}\left( {q,1}\right) }\right) ,
\]

for some constant \( C < \infty \) depending only on the dimension. The result now follows immediately.

Lemma 9.33. Let \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 \leq  t \leq  T \) , be an n-dimensional Ricci flow, and let \( f : M \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) be a smooth function. As usual set \( \tau  = T - t \) . Then the function

\[
u = {\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}{e}^{-f}
\]

satisfies the conjugate heat equation

\[
- \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} - \bigtriangleup u + {Ru} = 0,
\]

if and only if we have

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + {\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + R - \frac{n}{2\tau } = 0.
\]

Assuming that \( u \) satisfies the conjugate heat equation, then setting

\[
v = \left\lbrack  {\tau \left( {2\bigtriangleup f - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + R}\right)  + f - n}\right\rbrack  u,
\]

\[
- \frac{\partial v}{\partial t} - \bigtriangleup v + {Rv} =  - {2\tau }{\left| {\operatorname{Ric}}_{g} + {\operatorname{Hess}}^{g}\left( f\right)  - \frac{1}{2\tau }g\right| }^{2}u.
\]

LEMMA 9.37. Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a Riemannian manifold and let \( p \in  M \) and \( r > 0 \) be given. Suppose that \( B\left( {p,{2r}}\right) \) has compact closure in \( M \) and suppose that \( f : B\left( {p,{2r}}\right)  \times  ( - {2r},0\rbrack  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) is a continuous, bounded function with \( f\left( {p,0}\right)  > 0 \) . Then there is a point \( \left( {q, t}\right)  \in  B\left( {p,{2r}}\right)  \times  ( - {2r},0\rbrack \) with the following properties:

(1) \( f\left( {q, t}\right)  \geq  f\left( {p,0}\right) \) .

(2) Setting \( \alpha  = f\left( {p,0}\right) /f\left( {q, t}\right) \) we have \( d\left( {p, q}\right)  \leq  {2r}\left( {1 - \alpha }\right) \) and \( t \geq \; - {2r}\left( {1 - \alpha }\right) \) .

(3) \( f\left( {{q}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  < {2f}\left( {q, t}\right) \) for all \( \left( {{q}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \in  B\left( {q,{\alpha r}}\right)  \times  (t - {\alpha r}, t\rbrack \) .

nodes.proof:
Consider sequences of points \( {x}_{0} = \left( {p,0}\right) ,{x}_{1} = \left( {{p}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right) ,\ldots ,{x}_{j} = \; \left( {{p}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) in \( B\left( {p,{2r}}\right)  \times  ( - {2r},0\rbrack \) with the following properties:

(1) \( f\left( {x}_{i}\right)  \geq  {2f}\left( {x}_{i - 1}\right) \) .

(2) Setting \( {r}_{i} = {rf}\left( {x}_{0}\right) /f\left( {x}_{i - 1}\right) \) , then \( {r}_{i} \leq  {2}^{i - 1}r \) , and we have that

\[
{x}_{i} \in  B\left( {{p}_{i - 1},{r}_{i}}\right)  \times  \left( {{t}_{i - 1} - {r}_{i},{t}_{i - 1}}\right\rbrack  .
\]

Of course, there is exactly one such sequence with \( j = 0 \) : it has \( {x}_{0} = \; \left( {p,0}\right) \) . Suppose we have such a sequence defined for some \( j \geq  0 \) . If follows immediately from the properties of the sequence that \( f\left( {{p}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {2}^{j}f\left( {p,0}\right) \) , that

\[
{t}_{j} \geq   - r\left( {1 + {2}^{-1} + \cdots  + {2}^{1 - j}}\right) ,
\]

and that \( {r}_{j + 1} \leq  {2}^{-j}r \) . It also follows immediately from the triangle inequality that \( d\left( {p,{p}_{j}}\right)  \leq  r\left( {1 + {2}^{-1} + \cdots  + {2}^{1 - j}}\right) \) . This means that

\[
B\left( {{p}_{j},{r}_{j + 1}}\right)  \times  \left( {{t}_{j} - {r}_{j + 1},{t}_{j}}\right\rbrack   \subset  B\left( {p,{2r}}\right)  \times  ( - {2r},0\rbrack .
\]

Either the point \( {x}_{j} \) satisfies the conclusion of the lemma, or we can find \( {x}_{j + 1} \in  B\left( {{p}_{j},{r}_{j + 1}}\right)  \times  \left( {{t}_{j} - {r}_{j + 1},{t}_{j}}\right\rbrack \) with \( f\left( {x}_{j + 1}\right)  \geq  {2f}\left( {x}_{j}\right) \) . In the latter case we extend our sequence by one term. This shows that either the process terminates at some \( j \) , in which case \( {x}_{j} \) satisfies the conclusion of the lemma, or it continues indefinitely. But it cannot continue indefinitely since \( f \) is bounded on \( B\left( {p,{2r}}\right)  \times  ( - {2r},0\rbrack \) .

nodes.label: Proposition 9.39
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
Proposition 9.39. Suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) , - \infty  < t < 0 \) , is a \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed Ricci flow of dimension \( {}^{1}n \leq  3 \) . Suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a complete, non-compact, non-flat Riemannian manifold with non-negative curvature operator for each \( t \) . Suppose that \( \partial R\left( {q, t}\right) /\partial t \geq  0 \) for all \( q \in  M \) and all \( t < 0 \) . Fix \( p \in  M \) . Suppose that there is a sequence of points \( {p}_{i} \in  M \) going to infinity with the property that

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{i \rightarrow  \infty }}R\left( {{p}_{i}, - 1}\right) {d}_{g\left( {-1}\right) }^{2}\left( {p,{p}_{i}}\right)  = \infty .
\]

Then there is a sequence of points \( {q}_{i} \in  M \) tending to infinity such that, setting \( {Q}_{i} = R\left( {{q}_{i}, - 1}\right) \) , we have \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{i \rightarrow  \infty }}{d}^{2}\left( {p,{q}_{i}}\right) {Q}_{i} = \infty \) . Furthermore, setting \( {g}_{i}\left( t\right)  = {Q}_{i}g\left( {{Q}_{i}^{-1}\left( {t + 1}\right)  - 1}\right) \) , the sequence of based flows

\[
\left( {M,{g}_{i}\left( t\right) ,\left( {{q}_{i}, - 1}\right) }\right) , - \infty  < t \leq   - 1,
\]

converges smoothly to \( \left( {{N}^{n - 1}, h\left( t\right) }\right)  \times  \left( {\mathbb{R}, d{s}^{2}}\right) \) , a product Ricci flow defined for \( - \infty  < t \leq   - 1 \) with \( \left( {{N}^{n - 1}, h\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) being non-flat and of bounded, nonnegative curvature.

Suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a complete, non-compact, non-flat Riemannian manifold with non-negative curvature operator for each \( t \) . Suppose that \( \partial R\left( {q, t}\right) /\partial t \geq 0 \) for...

nodes.proof:
Take a sequence \( {p}_{i} \in  M \) such that

\[
{d}_{g\left( {-1}\right) }^{2}\left( {p,{p}_{i}}\right) R\left( {{p}_{i}, - 1}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty
\]

as \( i \rightarrow  \infty \) . We set \( {d}_{i} = {d}_{g\left( {-1}\right) }\left( {p,{p}_{i}}\right) \) and we set \( {B}_{i} = B\left( {{p}_{i}, - 1,{d}_{i}/2}\right) \) , and we let \( f : {B}_{i} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) be the square root of the scalar curvature. Since \( \left( {M, g\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) is complete, \( {B}_{i} \) has compact closure in \( M \) , and consequently \( f \) is a bounded continuous function on \( {B}_{i} \) . Applying Corollary 9.38 to \( \left( {{B}_{i}, g\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) and \( f \) , we conclude that there is a point \( {q}_{i} \in  {B}_{i} \) with the following properties:

(1) \( R\left( {{q}_{i}, - 1}\right)  \geq  R\left( {{p}_{i}, - 1}\right) \) .

(2) \( {B}_{i}^{\prime } = B\left( {{q}_{i}, - 1,\left( {{d}_{i}R{\left( {p}_{i}, - 1\right) }^{1/2}}\right) /\left( {{4R}{\left( {q}_{i},{t}_{i}\right) }^{1/2}}\right)  \subset  B\left( {{p}_{i}, - 1,{d}_{i}/2}\right) }\right. \) .

(3) \( R\left( {{q}^{\prime }, - 1}\right)  \leq  {4R}\left( {{q}_{i}, - 1}\right) \) for all \( \left( {{q}^{\prime }, - 1}\right)  \in  {B}_{i}^{\prime } \) .

Since \( {d}_{g\left( {-1}\right) }\left( {p,{q}_{i}}\right)  \geq  {d}_{i}/2 \) , it is also the case that \( {d}_{g\left( {-1}\right) }^{2}\left( {p,{q}_{i}}\right) R\left( {{q}_{i}, - 1}\right) \) tends to infinity as \( i \) tends to infinity. Because of our assumption on the time derivative of \( R \) , it follows that \( R\left( {{q}^{\prime }, t}\right)  \leq  {4R}\left( {{q}_{i}, - 1}\right) \) for all \( {q}^{\prime } \in  {B}_{i}^{\prime } \) and for all \( t \leq   - 1 \) .

Set \( {Q}_{i} = R\left( {{q}_{i}, - 1}\right) \) . Let \( {M}_{i} = M \) , and set \( {x}_{i} = \left( {{q}_{i}, - 1}\right) \) . Lastly, set \( {g}_{i}\left( t\right)  = {Q}_{i}g\left( {{Q}_{i}^{-1}\left( {t + 1}\right)  - 1}\right) \) . We consider the based Ricci flows

\[
\left( {{M}_{i},{g}_{i}\left( t\right) ,{x}_{i}}\right) , - \infty  < t \leq   - 1.
\]

We see that \( {R}_{{g}_{i}}\left( {{q}^{\prime }, t}\right)  \leq  4 \) for all

\[
\left( {{q}^{\prime }, t}\right)  \in  {B}_{{g}_{i}}\left( {{q}_{i}, - 1,{d}_{i}R{\left( {p}_{i}, - 1\right) }^{1/2}/4}\right)  \times  ( - \infty , - 1\rbrack .
\]

Since the original Ricci flows are \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed, the same is true for the rescaled flows. Since \( {d}_{i}R{\left( {p}_{i}, - 1\right) }^{1/2}/4 \rightarrow  \infty \) , by Theorem 5.15 there is a geometric limit flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,\left( {{q}_{\infty }, - 1}\right) }\right) \) defined for \( t \in  ( - \infty , - 1\rbrack \) . Of course, by taking limits we see that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed, its scalar curvature is bounded above by 4 , and its curvature operator is non-negative. It follows that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) has bounded curvature.

To complete the proof we show that the Ricci flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) splits as a product of a line with a Ricci flow of one lower dimension. By construction \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) is the geometric limit constructed from \( \left( {M, g\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) in the following manner. We have a sequence of points \( {q}_{i} \) tending to infinity in \( M \) and constants \( {\lambda }_{i} = R\left( {{q}_{i}, - 1}\right) \) with the property that \( {\lambda }_{i}{d}_{g\left( {-1}\right) }^{2}\left( {p,{q}_{i}}\right) \) tending to infinity such that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) is the geometric limit of \( \left( {M,{\lambda }_{i}g\left( {-1}\right) ,{q}_{i}}\right) \) . Thus, according to Theorem 5.35, the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) splits as a Riemannian product with a line. If the dimension of \( {M}_{\infty } \) is 2, then this is a contradiction: We have that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) splits as the Riemannian product of a line and a one-manifold and hence is flat, but \( R\left( {{q}_{\infty }, - 1}\right)  = 1 \) . Suppose that the dimension of \( {M}_{\infty } \) is 3 . Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) splits as a product with a line, it follows from the maximum principle (Corollary 4.19) that the entire flow splits as a product with a line, and the Ricci flow on the surface has strictly positive curvature.

nodes.label: Definition 9.41

nodes.content: DEFINITION 9.41. Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be an \( n \) -dimensional complete Riemannian manifold and fix \( \kappa  > 0 \) . We say that \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed if for every \( p \in  M \) and any \( r > 0 \) , if \( \left| {\mathrm{{Rm}}}_{g}\right|  \leq  {r}^{-2} \) on \( B\left( {p, r}\right) \) then Vol \( B\left( {p, r}\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}^{n} \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: DEFINITION 9.41. Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be an \( n \) -dimensional complete Riemannian manifold and fix \( \kappa > 0 \) . We say that \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed if for every \( p \in M \) and any \( r > 0 \) , if \( \left| {\mathrm{{Rm}}}_{g}\right| \leq {r}^{-2} \) on \( B\left( {p, r}\right) \) then Vol \( B\left( {p, r}\right) \geq \kappa {r}^{n} \) .

nodes.label: Theorem 9.42
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
THEOREM 9.42. Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a complete, non-flat Riemannian manifold of bounded non-negative curvature of dimension 2 or 3. Suppose that the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed. Lastly, suppose that there is a \( {C}^{2} \) -function \( f : M \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) such that

\[
{\operatorname{Ric}}_{g} + {\operatorname{Hess}}^{g}\left( f\right)  = \frac{1}{2}g.
\]

Then there is a Ricci flow \( \left( {M, G\left( t\right) }\right) , - \infty  < t < 0 \) , with \( G\left( {-1}\right)  = g \) and with \( \left( {M, G\left( t\right) }\right) \) isometric to \( \left( {M,\left| t\right| g}\right) \) for every \( t < 0 \) . In addition, \( \left( {M, G\left( t\right) }\right) \) is of one of the following three types:

(1) The flow \( \left( {M, G\left( t\right) }\right) , - \infty  < t < 0 \) , is a shrinking family of compact, round (constant positive curvature) manifolds.

(2) The flow \( \left( {M, G\left( t\right) }\right) , - \infty  < t < 0 \) , is a product of a shrinking family of round 2-spheres with the real line.

(3) \( \left( {M, G\left( t\right) }\right) \) is isomorphic to the quotient family of metrics of the product of a shrinking family of round 2-spheres and the real line under the action of an isometric involution.

nodes.proof: The manifold \( \left( {M, G\left( t\right) }\right) \) given in Equation (9.19) is equivalent up to diffeomorphism and scaling by \( \left| t\right| \) to \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) . If the dimension of \( M \) is 3 , then according to Hamilton's pinching toward positive curvature result (Theorem 4.23), the Ricci flow becomes singular in finite time and as it becomes singular the metric approaches constant curvature in the sense that the ratio of the largest sectional curvature to the smallest goes to 1. But this ratio is invariant under scaling and diffeomorphism, so that it must be the case that for each \( t \) , all the sectional curvatures of the metric \( G\left( t\right) \) are equal; i.e., for each \( t \) the metric \( G\left( t\right) \) is round. If the dimension of \( M \) is 2, then the results go back to Hamilton in [31]. According to Proposition 5.21 on p. 118 of \( \left\lbrack  \mathbf{{13}}\right\rbrack  , M \) is a shrinking family of constant positive curvature surfaces, which must be either \( {S}^{2} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) . This completes the analysis in the compact case.

nodes.content: COROLLARY 9.44. Suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a \( \kappa \) -solution of dimension 3 with a compact asymptotic gradient shrinking soliton. Then the Ricci flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is isomorphic to a time-shifted version of its asymptotic gradient shrinking soliton.
nodes.content_excerpt: COROLLARY 9.44. Suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a \( \kappa \) -solution of dimension 3 with a compact asymptotic gradient shrinking soliton. Then the Ricci flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is isomorphic to a time-shifted version of its asymptotic gradient shrinking soliton.

nodes.proof:
We suppose that the compact asymptotic gradient shrinking soliton is the limit of the \( \left( {M,{g}_{{\tau }_{n}}\left( t\right) ,\left( {{q}_{n}, - 1}\right) }\right) \) for some sequence of \( {\tau }_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) . Since by the discussion in the compact case, this limit is of constant positive curvature, it follows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( M \) is diffeomorphic to the limit manifold and the metric \( {g}_{{\tau }_{n}}\left( {-1}\right) \) is close to a metric of constant positive curvature. In particular, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( \left( {M,{g}_{{\tau }_{n}}\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) is compact and of strictly positive curvature. Furthermore, as \( n \rightarrow  \infty ,{\tau }_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) and Riemannian manifolds \( \left( {M,{g}_{{\tau }_{n}}\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) become closer and closer to round in the sense that the ratio of its largest sectional curvature to its smallest sectional curvature goes to 1. Since this is a scale invariant ratio, the same is true for the sequence of Riemannian manifolds \( \left( {M, g\left( {-{\tau }_{n}}\right) }\right) \) . In the case when the dimension of \( M \) is 3, by Hamilton’s pinching toward round result or Ivey’s theorem (see Theorem 4.23), this implies that the \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) are all exactly round.

This proves that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a shrinking family of round metrics. The only invariants of such a family are the diffeomorphism type of \( M \) and the time \( \Omega \) at which the flow becomes singular. Of course, \( M \) is diffeomorphic to its asymptotic soliton. Hence, the only remaining invariant is the singular time, and hence \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is equivalent to a time-shifted version of its asymptotic soliton.

It follows immediately that \( n = 3 \) . Let \( \widetilde{f} \) be the lifting of \( f \) to this one- or two-sheeted covering. Let \( Y \) be a unit tangent vector in the direction of the one-manifold. Then it follows from Equation (9.18) that the value of the Hessian of \( \widetilde{f} \) of \( \left( {Y, Y}\right) \) is 1 . If the flat one-manifold factor is a circle then there can be no such function \( \widetilde{f} \) . Hence, it follows that the one- or two-sheeted covering is a product of an evolving surface with a constant copy of \( \mathbb{R} \) . Since \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed and of bounded curvature, \( \left( {M, G\left( t\right) }\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed and each time-slice has positive bounded curvature. These statements are also true for the flow of surfaces.

nodes.content:
PROPOSITION 9.46. There is no 2- or 3-dimensional Ricci flow satisfying the hypotheses of Theorem 9.42 with \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) non-compact and of positive curvature.

We suppose that we have \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) as in Theorem 9.42 with \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) being non-compact and of positive curvature. Let \( n \) be the dimension of \( M \) , so that \( n \) is either 2 or 3 . Taking the trace of the gradient shrinking soliton equation yields

\[
R + \bigtriangleup f - \frac{n}{2} = 0,
\]

and consequently that

\[
{dR} + d\left( {\bigtriangleup f}\right)  = 0.
\]

Using Lemma 1.10 we rewrite this equation as

(9.20)

\[
{dR} + \bigtriangleup \left( {df}\right)  - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {\nabla f, \cdot  }\right)  = 0.
\]

On the other hand, taking the divergence of the gradient shrinking soliton equation and using the fact that \( {\nabla }^{ * }g = 0 \) gives

\[
{\nabla }^{ * }\operatorname{Ric} + {\nabla }^{ * }\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right)  = 0.
\]

Of course,

\[
{\nabla }^{ * }\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right)  = {\nabla }^{ * }\left( {\nabla \nabla f}\right)  = \left( {{\nabla }^{ * }\nabla }\right) \nabla f = \bigtriangleup \left( {df}\right) ,
\]

so that

\[
\Delta \left( {df}\right)  =  - {\nabla }^{ * }\operatorname{Ric}.
\]

Plugging this into Equation 9.20 gives

\[
{dR} - {\nabla }^{ * }\operatorname{Ric} - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {\nabla f, \cdot  }\right)  = 0.
\]

Now invoking Lemma 1.9 we have

(9.21)

\[
{dR} = 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {\nabla f, \cdot  }\right) .
\]

Fix a point \( p \in  M \) . Let \( \gamma \left( s\right) ;0 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s} \) , be a shortest geodesic (with respect to the metric \( g \) ), parameterized at unit speed, emanating from \( p \) , and set \( X\left( s\right)  = {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) \) .

CLAIM 9.47. There is a constant \( C \) independent of the choice of \( \gamma \) and of \( \bar{s} \) such that

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) {ds} \leq  C.
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: CLAIM 9.47. There is a constant \( C \) independent of the choice of \( \gamma \) and of \( \bar{s} \) such that \[ {\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) {ds} \leq C. \]

nodes.proof:
Since the curvature is bounded, clearly it suffices to assume that \( \bar{s} >  > 1 \) . Since \( \gamma \) is length-minimizing and parameterized at unit speed, it follows that it is a local minimum for the energy functional \( E\left( \gamma \right)  = \; \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}{\left| {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) \right| }^{2}{ds} \) among all paths with the same end points. Thus, letting \( {\gamma }_{u}\left( s\right)  = \gamma \left( {s, u}\right) \) be a one-parameter family of variations (fixed at the endpoints) with \( {\gamma }_{0} = \gamma \) and with \( {\left. d\gamma /du\right| }_{u = 0} = Y \) , we see

\[
0 \leq  {\delta }_{Y}^{2}E\left( {\gamma }_{u}\right)  = {\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}{\left| {\nabla }_{X}Y\right| }^{2} + \langle \mathcal{R}\left( {Y, X}\right) Y, X\rangle {ds}.
\]

We conclude that

(9.22)

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\langle  - \mathcal{R}\left( {Y, X}\right) Y, X\rangle {ds} \leq  {\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}{\left| {\nabla }_{X}Y\right| }^{2}{ds}.
\]

Fix an orthonormal basis \( {\left\{  {E}_{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{n} \) at \( p \) with \( {E}_{n} = X \) , and let \( {\widetilde{E}}_{i} \) denote the parallel translation of \( {E}_{i} \) along \( \gamma \) . (Of course, \( {\widetilde{E}}_{n} = X \) .) Then, for \( i \leq  n - 1 \) , we define

\[
{Y}_{i} = \left\{  \begin{array}{ll} s{\widetilde{E}}_{i} & \text{ if }0 \leq  s \leq  1, \\  {\widetilde{E}}_{i} & \text{ if }1 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s} - 1, \\  \left( {\bar{s} - s}\right) {E}_{i} & \text{ if }\bar{s} - 1 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s}. \end{array}\right.
\]

Adding up Equation (9.22) for each \( i \) gives

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{{n - 1}}{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\left\langle  {\mathcal{R}\left( {{Y}_{i}, X}\right) {Y}_{i}, X}\right\rangle  {ds} \leq  \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{{n - 1}}{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}{\left| {\nabla }_{X}{Y}_{i}\right| }^{2}{ds}.
\]

Of course, since the \( {\widetilde{E}}_{i} \) are parallel along \( \gamma \) , we have

\[
{\left| {\nabla }_{X}{Y}_{i}\right| }^{2} = \left\{  \begin{array}{ll} 1 & \text{ if }0 \leq  s \leq  1, \\  0 & \text{ if }1 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s} - 1, \\  1 & \text{ if }\bar{s} - 1 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s}, \end{array}\right.
\]

so that

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{{n - 1}}{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}{\left| {\nabla }_{X}{Y}_{i}\right| }^{2} = 2\left( {n - 1}\right) .
\]

On the other hand,

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{{n - 1}}\left\langle  {\mathcal{R}\left( {{Y}_{i}, X}\right) \left( {Y}_{i}\right) , X}\right\rangle   = \left\{  \begin{array}{ll} {s}^{2}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) & \text{ if }0 \leq  s \leq  1, \\  \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) & \text{ if }1 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s} - 1, \\  {\left( \bar{s} - s\right) }^{2}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) & \text{ if }\bar{s} - 1 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s}. \end{array}\right.
\]

Since the curvature is bounded and \( \left| X\right|  = 1 \) , we see that

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\left( {1 - {s}^{2}}\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) {ds} + {\int }_{\bar{s} - 1}^{\bar{s}}{\left( \bar{s} - s\right) }^{2}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)
\]

is bounded independent of \( \gamma \) and of \( \bar{s} \) . This concludes the proof of the claim.

nodes.proof:
Let \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) be a 2-dimensional Ricci flow satisfying all the hypotheses of Proposition 9.39 except possibly non-compactness. It then follows from Corollary 9.40 that \( M \) is compact. This proves the first item.

Now suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is an asymptotic soliton for a \( \kappa \) -solution of dimension 2. If \( \left( {M, g\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) does not have bounded curvature, then there is a sequence \( {p}_{i} \rightarrow  \infty \) so that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{i \rightarrow  \infty }}R\left( {{p}_{i}, - 1}\right)  = \infty \) . By this and Theorem 9.11 the Ricci flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) satisfies all the hypotheses of Proposition 9.39. But this contradicts Corollary 9.40. We conclude that \( \left( {M, g\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) has bounded curvature. According to Corollary 9.49 this means that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is compact. Results going back to Hamilton in [31] imply that this compact asymptotic shrinking soliton is a shrinking family of compact, round surfaces. For example, this result is contained in Proposition 5.21 on p. 118 of [13]. This proves the second item.

Now suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a 2-dimensional \( \kappa \) -solution. By the second item any asymptotic gradient shrinking soliton for this \( \kappa \) -solution is compact. It follows that \( M \) is compact. We know that as \( t \) goes to \( - \infty \) the Riemannian surfaces \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) are converging to compact, round surfaces. Extend the flow forward from 0 to a maximal time \( \Omega  < \infty \) . By Theorem 5.64 on p. 149 of [13] the surfaces \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) are also becoming round as \( t \) approaches \( \Omega \) from below. Also, according to Proposition 5.39 on p. 134 of [13] the entropy of the flow is weakly monotone decreasing and is strictly decreasing unless the flow is a gradient shrinking soliton. But we have seen that the limits at both \( - \infty \) and \( \Omega \) are round manifolds, and hence of the same entropy. It follows that the \( \kappa \) -solution is a shrinking family of compact, round surfaces.

nodes.content: CLAIM 9.51. The scalar curvature of \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) is equal to 1.
nodes.content_excerpt: CLAIM 9.51. The scalar curvature of \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) is equal to 1.

nodes.proof: Since the shrinking family of round 2-spheres \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h\left( t\right) }\right) \) exists for all \( - \infty  < t < 0 \) , it follows that the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) is at most 1. On the other hand, since the scalar curvature is increasing along the gradient flow lines of \( f \) , the infimum of the scalar curvature of \( \left( {M, g}\right) ,{R}_{\text{ inf }} \) , is positive. Thus, the infimum of the scalar curvature of \( \left( {M, G\left( t\right) }\right) \) is \( {R}_{\text{ inf }}/\left| t\right| \) and goes to infinity as \( \left| t\right| \) approaches 0 . Thus, the infimum of the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h\left( t\right) }\right) \) goes to infinity as \( t \) approaches zero. This means that the shrinking family of 2-spheres becomes singular as \( t \) approaches zero, and consequently the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) is equal to 1 .

nodes.proof:
If an asymptotic gradient shrinking soliton \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) of a 3- dimensional \( \kappa \) -solution does not have strictly positive curvature, then according to Corollary 4.20, \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) has a covering that splits as a product of a 2-dimensional Ricci flow and a line. The 2-dimensional Ricci flow satisfies all the hypotheses of Proposition 9.39 except possibly compactness, and hence by Corollary 9.50 it is a shrinking family of round surfaces. In this case, it is clear that each time-slice of \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) has bounded curvature.

Now we consider the remaining case when \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) has strictly positive curvature. Assume that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) has unbounded curvature. Then there is a sequence of points \( {p}_{i} \) tending to infinity in \( M \) such that \( R\left( {{p}_{i}, t}\right) \) tends to infinity. By Corollary 9.52 we can replace the points \( {p}_{i} \) by points \( {q}_{i} \) with \( {Q}_{i} = \; R\left( {{q}_{i}, t}\right)  \geq  R\left( {{p}_{i}, t}\right) \) so that the based Riemannian manifolds \( \left( {M,{Q}_{i}g\left( t\right) ,{q}_{i}}\right) \) converge to a product of a round surface \( \left( {N, h\left( t\right) }\right) \) with \( \mathbb{R} \) . The surface \( N \) is either diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) . Since \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) has positive curvature, by Theorem 2.7, it is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) , and hence it contains no embedded \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) . It follows that \( \left( {N, h\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a round 2-sphere.

Fix \( \epsilon  > 0 \) sufficiently small as in Proposition 2.19. Then the limiting statement means that, for every \( i \) sufficiently large, there is an \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) centered at \( {q}_{i} \) with scale \( {Q}_{i}^{-1/2} \) . This contradicts Proposition 2.19, establishing that for each \( t < 0 \) the curvature of \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is bounded.

nodes.proof:
Let \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , - \infty  < t < 0 \) , be an asymptotic gradient shrinking soliton for \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) . According to Corollary 9.53, this soliton is a \( \kappa \) -solution, implying that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) is a complete Riemannian manifold of bounded, non-negative curvature. Suppose that \( B\left( {p, - 1, r}\right)  \subset  {M}_{\infty } \) is a metric ball and \( \left| {\operatorname{Rm}}_{{g}_{\infty }}\right| \left( {x, - 1}\right)  \leq  {r}^{-2} \) for all \( x \in  B\left( {p, - 1, r}\right) \) . Since \( \partial {R}_{{g}_{\infty }}\left( {x, t}\right) /\partial t \geq  0 \) , it follows that \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  3{r}^{-2} \) on \( B\left( {p, - 1, r}\right)  \times  ( - 1 - \; \left. {{r}^{2}, - 1}\right\rbrack \) , and hence that \( \left| {\operatorname{Rm}}_{{g}_{\infty }}\right|  \leq  3{r}^{-2} \) on this same region. Since the Ricci flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed, it follows that \( \operatorname{Vol}B\left( {p, - 1, r/\sqrt{3}}\right)  \geq \; \kappa {\left( r/\sqrt{3}\right) }^{3} \) . Hence, \( \operatorname{Vol}, B\left( {p, - 1, r}\right)  \geq  \left( {\kappa /3\sqrt{3}}\right) {r}^{3} \) . This proves that the manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) is \( {\kappa }^{\prime } \) -non-collapsed for some \( {\kappa }^{\prime } > 0 \) depending only on \( \kappa \) . On the other hand, according to Theorem 9.11 there is a function \( f\left( {\cdot , - 1}\right) \) from \( {M}_{\infty } \) to \( \mathbb{R} \) satisfying the gradient shrinking soliton equation at the time-slice -1 . Thus, Theorem 9.42 applies to \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) to produce a Ricci flow \( G\left( t\right) , - \infty  < t < 0 \) , of one of the three types listed in that theorem and with \( G\left( {-1}\right)  = {g}_{\infty }\left( {-1}\right) \) .

Now we must show that \( G\left( t\right)  = {g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) \) for all \( t < 0 \) . In the first case when \( {M}_{\infty } \) is compact, this is clear by uniqueness of the Ricci flow in the compact case. Suppose that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty }, G\left( t\right) }\right) \) is of the second type listed in Theorem 9.42. Then \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) is a product of a round 2-sphere and the real line. By Corollary 4.20 this implies that the entire flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) splits as the product of a flow of compact 2-spheres and the real line. Again by uniqueness in the compact case, this family of 2-spheres must be a shrinking family of round 2-spheres. In the third case, one passes to a finite sheeted covering of the second type, and applies the second case.

Since we have already established that it has a metric of constant positive curvature, it must be diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \) , and hence isometric to a round sphere. (In higher dimensions one can prove that \( {S}_{\infty }\left( {M, p}\right) \) is simply connected, and hence isometric to a round sphere.)

nodes.content: Proposition 9.58. There is a \( {\kappa }_{0} > 0 \) such that any non-round 3- dimensional \( \kappa \) -solution is a \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution.
nodes.content_excerpt: Proposition 9.58. There is a \( {\kappa }_{0} > 0 \) such that any non-round 3- dimensional \( \kappa \) -solution is a \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution.

nodes.proof:
Let \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) be a non-round 3-dimensional \( \kappa \) -solution. By Corollary 9.44 since \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is not a family of round manifolds, the asymptotic soliton for the \( \kappa \) -solution cannot be compact. Thus, according to Corollary 9.42 there are only two possibilities for the asymptotic soliton \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) - either \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is the product of a round 2-sphere of Gaussian curvature \( 1/2\left| t\right| \) with a line or has a two-sheeted covering by such a product. In fact, there are three possibilities: \( {S}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or the twisted \( \mathbb{R} \) -bundle over \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) whose total space is diffeomorphic to the complement of a point in \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

Fix a point \( x = \left( {p,0}\right)  \in  M \times  \{ 0\} \) . Let \( {\bar{\tau }}_{k} \) be a sequence converging to \( \infty \) , and \( {q}_{k} \in  M \) a point with \( {l}_{x}\left( {{q}_{k},{\bar{\tau }}_{k}}\right)  \leq  3/2 \) . The existence of an asymptotic soliton means that, possibly after passing to a subsequence, there is a gradient shrinking soliton \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) and a ball \( B \) of radius 1 in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-1}\right) }\right) \) centered at a point \( {q}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and a sequence of embeddings \( {\psi }_{k} : B \rightarrow  M \) such that \( {\psi }_{k}\left( {q}_{\infty }\right)  = {q}_{k} \) and such that the map

\[
B \times  \left\lbrack  {-2, - 1}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \times  \left\lbrack  {-2{\bar{\tau }}_{k}, - {\bar{\tau }}_{k}}\right\rbrack
\]

given by \( \left( {b, t}\right)  \mapsto  \left( {{\psi }_{k}\left( b\right) ,{\bar{\tau }}_{k}t}\right) \) has the property that the pullback of \( {\bar{\tau }}_{k}^{-1}g\left( {{\bar{\tau }}_{k}t}\right) \) converges smoothly and uniformly as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) to the restriction of \( {g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) \) to \( B \times  \left\lbrack  {-2, - 1}\right\rbrack \) . Let \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) }\right) \) be this rescaling of the \( \kappa \) -solution by \( {\tau }_{k} \) . Then the embeddings \( {\psi }_{k} \times  \mathrm{{id}} : B \times  ( - 2, - 1\rbrack  \rightarrow  \left( {{M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {-2, - 1}\right\rbrack  }\right. \) converge as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) to a one-parameter family of isometries. That is to say, the image \( {\psi }_{k}\left( {B \times  \left\lbrack  {-2, - 1}\right\rbrack  }\right)  \subset  {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {-2, - 1}\right\rbrack \) is an almost isometric embedding. Since the reduced length from \( x \) to \( \left( {{\psi }_{k}\left( a\right) , - 1}\right) \) is at most \( 3/2 \) , from the invariance of reduced length under rescalings (see Corollary 6.74) it follows that the reduced length function on \( {\psi }_{k}\left( {B\times \{  - 2\} }\right) \) is bounded independent of \( k \) . Similarly, the volume of \( {\psi }_{k}\left( {B\times \{  - 2\} }\right) \) is bounded independent of \( k \) . This means the reduced volume of \( {\psi }_{k}\left( {B\times \{  - 2\} }\right) \) in \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) }\right) \) is bounded independent of \( k \) . Now according to Theorem 8.1 this implies that \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) }\right) \) is \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -non-collapsed at \( \left( {p,0}\right) \) on scales \( \leq  \sqrt{2} \) for some \( {\kappa }_{0} \) depending only on the geometry of the three possibilities for \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , - 2 \leq  t \leq   - 1 \) . Being \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -non-collapsed is invariant under rescalings, so that it follows immediately that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -non-collapsed on scales \( \leq  \sqrt{2{\bar{\tau }}_{k}} \) . Since this is true for all \( k \) , it follows that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -non-collapsed on all scales at \( \left( {p,0}\right) \) .

This result holds of course for every \( p \in  M \) , showing that at \( t = 0 \) the flow is \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -non-collapsed. To prove this result at points of the form \( \left( {p, t}\right)  \in  M \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) we simply shift the original \( \kappa \) -solution upward by \( \left| t\right| \) and remove the part of the flow at positive time. This produces a new \( \kappa \) - solution and the point in question has been shifted to the time-zero slice, so that we can apply the previous results.

## 6. Asymptotic volume

Let \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) be an \( n \) -dimensional \( \kappa \) -solution. For any \( t \leq  0 \) and any point \( p \in  M \) we consider \( \left( {\operatorname{Vol}{B}_{g\left( t\right) }\left( {p, r}\right) }\right) /{r}^{n} \) . According to the Bishop-Gromov Theorem (Theorem 1.34), this is a non-increasing function of \( r \) . We define the asymptotic volume \( {\mathcal{V}}_{\infty }\left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) , or \( {\mathcal{V}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) \) if the flow is clear from the context, to be the limit as \( r \rightarrow  \infty \) of this function. Clearly, this limit is independent of \( p \in  M \) .

nodes.content: THEOREM 9.59. For \( {}^{3} \) any \( \kappa  > 0 \) and any \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) the asymptotic volume \( {\mathcal{V}}_{\infty }\left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is identically zero.
nodes.content_excerpt: THEOREM 9.59. For \( {}^{3} \) any \( \kappa > 0 \) and any \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) the asymptotic volume \( {\mathcal{V}}_{\infty }\left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is identically zero.

nodes.proof:
The proof is by induction on the dimension \( n \) of the solution. For \( n = 2 \) by Corollary 9.50 there are only compact \( \kappa \) -solutions, which clearly have zero asymptotic volume. Suppose that we have established the result for \( n - 1 \geq  2 \) and let us prove it for \( n \) .

According to Proposition 9.39 there is a sequence of points \( {p}_{n} \in  M \) tending to infinity such that setting \( {Q}_{n} = R\left( {{p}_{n},0}\right) \) the sequence of Ricci flows

\[
\left( {M,{Q}_{n}g\left( {{Q}_{n}^{-1}t}\right) ,\left( {{q}_{n},0}\right) }\right)
\]

converges geometrically to a limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,\left( {{q}_{\infty },0}\right) }\right) \) , and this limit splits off a line: \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right)  = \left( {N, h\left( t\right) }\right)  \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Since the ball of radius \( R \) about a point \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  N \times  \mathbb{R} \) is contained in the product of the ball of radius \( R \) in \( N \) centered at \( x \) and an interval of length \( {2R} \) , it follows that \( \left( {N, h\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a \( \kappa /2 \) -ancient solution. Hence, by induction, for every \( t \) , the asymptotic volume of \( \left( {N, h\left( t\right) }\right) \) is zero, and hence so is that of \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) .

nodes.content: Proposition 9.60. Fix the dimension \( n \) . For every \( \nu  > 0 \) there is \( A < \infty \) such that the following holds. Suppose that \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) }\right) , - {t}_{k} \leq  t \leq  0 \) , is a sequence of (not necessarily complete) n-dimensional Ricci flows of nonnegative curvature operator. Suppose in addition we have points \( {p}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) and radii \( {r}_{k} > 0 \) with the property that for each \( k \) the ball \( B\left( {{p}_{k},0,{r}_{k}}\right) \) has compact closure in \( {M}_{k} \) . Then \( \operatorname{Vol}B\left( {{p}_{k},0, A/\sqrt{{Q}_{k}}}\right)  < \nu {\left( A/\sqrt{{Q}_{k}}\right) }^{n} \) for all \( k \) sufficiently large.

nodes.proof:
Suppose that the result fails for some \( \nu  > 0 \) . Then there is a sequence \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) }\right) , - {t}_{k} \leq  t \leq  0 \) , of \( n \) -dimensional Ricci flows, points \( {p}_{k} \in \; {M}_{k} \) , and radii \( {r}_{k} \) as in the statement of the lemma such that for every \( A < \infty \) there is an arbitrarily large \( k \) with \( \operatorname{Vol}B\left( {{p}_{k},0, A/\sqrt{{Q}_{k}}}\right)  \geq  \nu {\left( A/\sqrt{{Q}_{k}}\right) }^{n} \) . Pass to a subsequence so that for each \( A < \infty \) we have

\[
\operatorname{Vol}B\left( {{p}_{k},0, A/\sqrt{{Q}_{k}}}\right)  \geq  \nu {\left( A/\sqrt{{Q}_{k}}\right) }^{n}
\]

for all \( k \) sufficiently large. Consider now the flows \( {h}_{k}\left( t\right)  = {Q}_{k}{g}_{k}\left( {{Q}_{k}^{-1}t}\right) \) , defined for \( - {Q}_{k}{t}_{k} \leq  t \leq  0 \) . Then for every \( A < \infty \) for all \( k \) sufficiently large we have \( {R}_{{h}_{k}}\left( {q, t}\right)  \leq  4 \) for all \( q \in  {B}_{{h}_{k}}\left( {{p}_{k},0, A}\right) \) and all \( t \in  \left( {-{t}_{k}{Q}_{k},0}\right\rbrack \) . Also, for every \( A < \infty \) for all \( k \) sufficiently large we have \( \operatorname{Vol}B\left( {{p}_{k},0, A}\right)  \geq  \nu {A}^{n} \) . According to Theorem 5.15 we can then pass to a subsequence that has a geometric limit which is an ancient flow of complete Riemannian manifolds. Clearly, the time-slices of the limit have non-negative curvature operator, and the scalar curvature is bounded (by 4) and is equal to 1 at the base point of the limit. Also, the asymptotic volume \( \mathcal{V}\left( 0\right)  \geq  \nu \) .

---

\( {}^{3} \) This theorem and all the other results of this section are valid in all dimensions. Our proofs use Theorem 9.56 and Proposition 9.39 which are also valid in all dimensions but which we proved only in dimensions 2 and 3 . Thus, while we state the results of this section for all dimensions, strictly speaking we give proofs only for dimensions 2 and 3. These are the only cases we need in what follows.

CLAIM 9.61. Suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is an ancient Ricci flow such that for each \( t \leq  0 \) the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is complete and has bounded, non-negative curvature operator. Let \( \mathcal{V}\left( t\right) \) be the asymptotic volume of the manifold \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) .

(1) The asymptotic volume \( \mathcal{V}\left( t\right) \) is a non-increasing function of \( t \) .

(2) If \( \mathcal{V}\left( t\right)  = V > 0 \) then every metric ball \( B\left( {x, t, r}\right) \) has volume at least \( V{r}^{n} \) .

nodes.proof:
We begin with the proof of the first item. Fix \( a < b \leq  0 \) . By hypothesis there is a constant \( K < \infty \) such that the scalar curvature of \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is bounded by \( \left( {n - 1}\right) K \) . By the Harnack inequality (Corollary 4.39) the scalar curvature of \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is bounded by \( \left( {n - 1}\right) K \) for all \( t \leq  0 \) . Hence, since the \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) have non-negative curvature, we have \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( {p, t}\right)  \leq  \left( {n - 1}\right) K \) for all \( p \) and \( t \) . Set \( A = 4\left( {n - 1}\right) \sqrt{\frac{2K}{3}} \) . Then by Corollary 3.26 we have

\[
{d}_{a}\left( {{p}_{0},{p}_{1}}\right)  \leq  {d}_{b}\left( {{p}_{0},{p}_{1}}\right)  + A\left( {b - a}\right) .
\]

This means that for any \( r > 0 \) we have

\[
B\left( {{p}_{0}, b, r}\right)  \subset  B\left( {{p}_{0}, a, r + A\left( {b - a}\right) }\right) .
\]

On the other hand, since \( d\mathrm{{Vol}}/{dt} =  - {Rd}\mathrm{{Vol}} \) , it follows that, in the case of non-negative curvature, the volume of any open set is non-increasing in time. Consequently,

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{g\left( b\right) }B\left( {{p}_{0}, b, r}\right)  \leq  {\operatorname{Vol}}_{g\left( a\right) }B\left( {{p}_{0}, a, r + A\left( {b - a}\right) }\right) ,
\]

and hence

\[
\frac{{\operatorname{Vol}}_{g\left( b\right) }B\left( {{p}_{0}, b, r}\right) }{{r}^{n}} \leq  \frac{{\operatorname{Vol}}_{g\left( a\right) }B\left( {{p}_{0}, a, r + A\left( {b - a}\right) }\right) }{{\left( r + A\left( b - a\right) \right) }^{n}}\frac{{\left( r + A\left( b - a\right) \right) }^{n}}{{r}^{n}}.
\]

Taking the limit as \( r \rightarrow  \infty \) gives

\[
\mathcal{V}\left( b\right)  \leq  \mathcal{V}\left( a\right) .
\]

The second item of the claim is immediate from the Bishop-Gromov inequality (Theorem 1.34).

Suppose that the result fails for some \( \nu  > 0 \) . Then there is a sequence \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) }\right) \) of \( n \) -dimensional Ricci flows, complete, with bounded non-negative curvature operator and points \( {p}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) , constants \( {r}_{k} > 0 \) , and points \( {q}_{k} \in  B\left( {{p}_{k},0,{r}_{k}}\right) \) such that:

(1) Vol \( B\left( {{p}_{k},0,{r}_{k}}\right)  \geq  \nu {r}_{k}^{n} \) , and

(2) setting \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{q}_{k},0}\right) \) we have \( {r}_{k}^{2}{Q}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) .

Using Lemma 9.37 we can find points \( {q}_{k}^{\prime } \in  B\left( {{p}_{k},0,2{r}_{k}}\right) \) and constants \( {s}_{k} \leq \; {r}_{k} \) , such that setting \( {Q}_{k}^{\prime } = R\left( {{q}_{k}^{\prime },0}\right) \) we have \( {Q}_{k}^{\prime }{s}_{k}^{2} = {Q}_{k}{r}_{k}^{2} \) and \( R\left( {q,0}\right)  < 4{Q}_{k}^{\prime } \) for all \( q \in  B\left( {{q}_{k}^{\prime },0,{s}_{k}}\right) \) . Of course, \( {Q}_{k}^{\prime }{s}_{k}^{2} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) . Since \( {d}_{0}\left( {{p}_{k},{q}_{k}^{\prime }}\right)  < \; 2{r}_{k} \) , we have \( B\left( {{p}_{k},0,{r}_{k}}\right)  \subset  B\left( {{q}_{k}^{\prime },0,3{r}_{k}}\right) \) so that

\[
\operatorname{Vol}B\left( {{q}_{k}^{\prime },0,3{r}_{k}}\right)  \geq  \operatorname{Vol}B\left( {{p}_{k},0,{r}_{k}}\right)  \geq  \nu {r}_{k}^{n} = \left( {\nu /{3}^{n}}\right) {\left( 3{r}_{k}\right) }^{n}.
\]

Since the sectional curvatures of \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) are non-negative, it follows from the Bishop-Gromov inequality (Theorem 1.34) that \( \operatorname{Vol}B\left( {{q}_{k}^{\prime },0, s}\right)  \geq \; \left( {\nu /{3}^{n}}\right) {s}^{n} \) for any \( s \leq  {s}_{k} \) .

Of course, by Corollary 4.39, we have \( R\left( {q, t}\right)  < 4{Q}_{k}^{\prime } \) for all \( t \leq  0 \) and all \( q \in  B\left( {{q}_{k}^{\prime },0,{s}_{k}}\right) \) . Now consider the sequence of based, rescaled flows

\[
\left( {{M}_{k},{Q}_{k}^{\prime }g\left( {{Q}_{k}^{\prime  - 1}t}\right) ,\left( {{q}_{k}^{\prime },0}\right) }\right) \text{ . }
\]

In these manifolds all balls centered at \( \left( {{q}_{k}^{\prime },0}\right) \) of radii at most \( \sqrt{{Q}_{k}}{s}_{k} \) are \( \left( {\nu /{3}^{n}}\right) \) non-collapsed. Also, the curvatures of these manifolds are nonnegative and the scalar curvature is bounded by 4. It follows that by passing to a subsequence we can extract a geometric limit. Since \( {Q}_{k}^{\prime }{s}_{k}^{2} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) the asymptotic volume of this limit is at least \( \nu /{3}^{n} \) . But this geometric limit is a \( \nu /{3}^{n} \) -non-collapsed ancient solution with non-negative curvature operator with scalar curvature bounded by 4 . This contradicts Theorem 9.59.

Let \( K\left( A\right)  = C\left( {\nu /{}^{n}}\right) \) , where \( C \) is the constant provided by the previous corollary. The result is immediate from the previous corollary.

nodes.proof: Let \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) ,\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right) }\right) \) be a sequence of based 3-dimensional \( \kappa \) -solutions with \( R\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right)  = 1 \) for all \( k \) . The immediate consequence of Lemma 9.65 and Corollary 4.39 is the following. For every \( r < \infty \) there is a constant \( C\left( r\right)  < \infty \) such that \( R\left( {q, t}\right)  \leq  C\left( r\right) \) for all \( q \in  B\left( {{p}_{k},0, r}\right) \) and for all \( t \leq  0 \) . Of course, since, in addition, the elements in the sequence are \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed, by Theorem 5.15 this implies that there is a subsequence of the \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) ,\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right) }\right) \) that converges geometrically to an ancient flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,\left( {{p}_{\infty },0}\right) }\right) \) . Being a geometric limit of \( \kappa \) -solutions, this limit is complete and \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed, and each time-slice is of nonnegative curvature. Also, it is not flat since, by construction, \( R\left( {{p}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1 \) . Of course, it also follows from the limiting procedure that \( \partial R\left( {q, t}\right) /\partial t \geq  0 \) for every \( \left( {q, t}\right)  \in  {M}_{\infty } \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) . Thus, according to Corollary 9.53 the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) has bounded curvature for each \( t \leq  0 \) . Hence, the limit is a \( \kappa \) -solution. This completes the proof of Theorem 9.64.
