nodes.proof:
Fix a based 3-dimensional \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) ,\left( {p,0}\right) }\right) \) . By Theorem 9.56 we have

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{q \in  M}}{d}_{0}{\left( p, q\right) }^{2}R\left( {q,0}\right)  = \infty .
\]

Let \( q \) be a closest point to \( p \) satisfying

\[
{d}_{0}{\left( p, q\right) }^{2}R\left( {q,0}\right)  = 1
\]

We set \( d = {d}_{0}\left( {p, q}\right) \) , and we set \( Q = R\left( {q,0}\right) \) . Of course, \( {d}^{2}Q = 1 \) . We carry this notation and these assumptions through the next five claims. The goal of these claims is to show that \( R\left( {{q}^{\prime },0}\right) \) is uniformly bounded for \( {q}^{\prime } \) near \( \left( {p,0}\right) \) so that in fact the distance \( d \) from the point \( q \) to \( p \) is uniformly bounded from below by a positive constant (see Claim 9.69 for a more precise statement). Once we have this the lemma will follow easily. To establish this uniform bound requires a sequence of claims.

nodes.proof:
Suppose not. Then there is a sequence \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) ,\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right) }\right) \) of based 3-dimensional \( \kappa \) -solutions with \( R\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right)  = 1 \) , points \( {q}_{k} \) in \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) closest to \( {p}_{k} \) satisfying \( {d}_{k}^{2}R\left( {{q}_{k},0}\right)  = 1 \) , where \( {d}_{k} = {d}_{0}\left( {{p}_{k},{q}_{k}}\right) \) , and points \( {q}_{k}^{\prime } \in  B\left( {{q}_{k},0,2{d}_{k}}\right) \) with

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{\left( 2{d}_{k}\right) }^{2}R\left( {{q}_{k}^{\prime },0}\right)  = \infty .
\]

Then according to Corollary 9.62 for every \( \nu  > 0 \) for all \( k \) sufficiently large, we have

(9.27)

\[
\operatorname{Vol}B\left( {{q}_{k},0,2{d}_{k}}\right)  < \nu {\left( 2{d}_{k}\right) }^{3}.
\]

Therefore, by passing to a subsequence, we can assume that for each \( \nu  > 0 \)

(9.28)

\[
\operatorname{Vol}B\left( {{q}_{k},0,2{d}_{k}}\right)  < \nu {\left( 2{d}_{k}\right) }^{3}
\]

for all \( k \) sufficiently large. Let \( {\omega }_{3} \) be the volume of the unit ball in \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) . Then for all \( k \) sufficiently large, \( \operatorname{Vol}B\left( {{q}_{k},0,2{d}_{k}}\right)  < \left\lbrack  {{\omega }_{3}/2}\right\rbrack  {\left( 2{d}_{k}\right) }^{3} \) . Since the sectional curvatures of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) are non-negative, by the Bishop-Gromov inequality (Theorem 1.34), it follows that for every \( k \) sufficiently large there is \( {r}_{k} < 2{d}_{k} \) such that

(9.29)

\[
\operatorname{Vol}B\left( {{q}_{k},0,{r}_{k}}\right)  = \left\lbrack  {{\omega }_{3}/2}\right\rbrack  {r}_{k}^{3}.
\]

Of course, because of Equation (9.28) we see that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{r}_{k}/{d}_{k} = 0 \) . Then, according to Corollary 9.63, for all \( q \in  {M}_{k} \) , we have

\[
{\left( {r}_{k} + {d}_{{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\left( {q}_{k}, q\right) \right) }^{2}R\left( {q,0}\right)  \leq  K\left( {{d}_{{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\left( {{q}_{k}, q}\right) /{r}_{k}}\right) ,
\]

where \( K \) is as given in Corollary 9.63. Form the sequence \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}^{\prime }\left( t\right) ,\left( {{q}_{k},0}\right) }\right) \) , where \( {g}_{k}^{\prime }\left( t\right)  = {r}_{k}^{-2}{g}_{k}\left( {{r}_{k}^{2}t}\right) \) . This is a sequence of based Ricci flows. For each \( A < \infty \) we have

\[
{\left( 1 + A\right) }^{2}{R}_{{g}_{k}^{\prime }}\left( {q,0}\right)  \leq  K\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( q \in  {B}_{{g}_{k}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\left( {{q}_{k},0, A}\right) \) . Hence, by the consequence of Hamilton’s Harnack inequality (Corollary 4.39)

\[
{R}_{{g}_{k}^{\prime }}\left( {q, t}\right)  \leq  K\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( \left( {q, t}\right)  \in  {B}_{{g}_{k}^{\prime }\left( 0\right) }\left( {{q}_{k},0, A}\right)  \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) . Using this and the fact that all the flows are \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed, Theorem 5.15 implies that, after passing to a subsequence, the sequence \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}^{\prime }\left( t\right) ,\left( {{q}_{k},0}\right) }\right) \) converges geometrically to a limiting Ricci flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,\left( {{q}_{\infty },0}\right) }\right) \) consisting of non-negatively curved, complete manifolds \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed on all scales (though possibly with unbounded curvature).

Furthermore, Equation (9.29) passes to the limit to give

(9.30)

\[
\operatorname{Vol}{B}_{{g}_{\infty }}\left( {{q}_{\infty },0,1}\right)  = {\omega }_{3}/2\text{ . }
\]

Since \( {r}_{k}/{d}_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) and since \( {R}_{{g}_{k}}\left( {{q}_{k},0}\right)  = {d}_{k}^{-2} \) , we see that \( {R}_{{g}_{\infty }}\left( {{q}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 0 \) . By the strong maximum principle for scalar curvature (Theorem 4.18), this implies that the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is flat. But Equation (9.30) tells us that this limit is not \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) . Since it is complete and flat, it must be a quotient of \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) by an action of a non-trivial group of isometries acting freely and properly discontinuously. But the quotient of \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) by any non-trivial group of isometries acting freely and properly discontinuously has zero asymptotic volume. [Proof: It suffices to prove the claim in the special case when the group is infinite cyclic. The generator of this group has an axis \( \alpha \) on which it acts by translation and on the orthogonal subspace its acts by an isometry. Consider the circle in the quotient that is the image of \( \alpha \) , and let \( {L}_{\alpha } \) be its length. The volume of the ball of radius \( r \) about \( {L}_{\alpha } \) is \( \pi {r}^{2}{L}_{\alpha } \) . Clearly then, for any \( p \in  \alpha \) , the volume of the ball of radius \( r \) about \( p \) is at most \( \pi {L}_{\alpha }{r}^{2} \) . This proves that the asymptotic volume of the quotient is zero.]

We have now shown that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) has zero curvature and zero asymptotic volume. But this implies that it is not \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed on all scales, which is a contradiction. This contradiction completes the proof of Claim 9.66.

nodes.proof:
Let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0, d}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) be a \( g\left( 0\right) \) -geodesic from \( p \) to \( q \) , parameterized at unit speed. Denote by \( {\ell }_{t}\left( \gamma \right) \) the length of \( \gamma \) under the metric \( g\left( t\right) \) . We have \( {d}_{t}\left( {p, q}\right)  \leq  {\ell }_{t}\left( \gamma \right) \) . We estimate \( {\ell }_{t}\left( \gamma \right) \) using the fact that \( \left| \operatorname{Ric}\right|  \leq  {CQ} \) on the image of \( \gamma \) at all times.

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{\ell }_{{t}_{0}}\left( \gamma \right)  = {\left. \frac{d}{dt}\left( {\int }_{0}^{d}\sqrt{{\left\langle  {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) ,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) \right\rangle  }_{g\left( t\right) }}ds\right) \right| }_{t = {t}_{0}}
\]

\[
= {\int }_{0}^{d}\frac{-{\operatorname{Ric}}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) ,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) }\right) }{\sqrt{{\left\langle  {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) ,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) \right\rangle  }_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }}}{ds}
\]

\[
\geq   - {CQ}{\int }_{0}^{d}{\left| {\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) \right| }_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }{ds} =  - {CQ}{\ell }_{{t}_{0}}\left( \gamma \right) .
\]

Integrating yields

\[
{\ell }_{-t}\left( \gamma \right)  \leq  {e}^{CQt}{\ell }_{0}\left( \gamma \right)  = {e}^{CQt}{Q}^{-1/2}.
\]

(Recall \( {d}^{2}Q = 1 \) .) Plugging in \( t = c{Q}^{-1} \) gives us

\[
{d}_{-c{Q}^{-1}}\left( {p, q}\right)  \leq  {\ell }_{-c{Q}^{-1}}\left( \gamma \right)  \leq  {e}^{cC}{Q}^{-1/2}.
\]

Setting \( \widetilde{C} = {e}^{cC} \) completes the proof of the claim.

Then \( {R}_{{G}^{\prime }}\left( {{q}^{\prime },0}\right)  \leq  C \) for all \( {q}^{\prime } \in \; {B}_{{G}^{\prime }}\left( {q,0,2}\right) \) . Consequently, \( {R}_{{G}^{\prime }}\left( {{q}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \leq  C \) for all \( {q}^{\prime } \in  {B}_{{G}^{\prime }}\left( {q,0,2}\right) \) and all \( {t}^{\prime } \leq  0 \) . Thus, by Shi’s derivative estimates (Theorem 3.28)applied with \( T = \) 2 and \( r = 2 \) , there is a universal constant \( {C}_{1} \) such that for all \( - 1 \leq  {t}^{\prime } \leq  0 \) ,

\[

\]

where the Laplacian is taken with respect to the metric \( {G}^{\prime } \) . Rescaling by \( {Q}^{-1} \) we see that for all \( - {Q}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  0 \) we have

\[
\left| {\bigtriangleup {\operatorname{Rm}}_{G}\left( {q, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {C}_{1}{Q}^{2},
\]

where the Laplacian is taken with respect to the metric \( G \) . Since the metric is non-negatively curved, by Corollary 4.39 we have \( 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( q, t\right) \right| }^{2} \leq  2{Q}^{2} \) for all \( t \leq  0 \) . From these two facts we conclude from the flow equation (3.7) that there is a constant \( 1 < {C}^{\prime \prime } < \infty \) with the property that \( \partial R/\partial t\left( {q, t}\right)  \leq  {C}^{\prime \prime }{Q}^{2} \) for all \( - {Q}^{-1} < t \leq  0 \) . Thus for any \( 0 < c < 1 \) , we have \( Q = R\left( {q,0}\right)  \leq \; c{C}^{\prime \prime }Q + R\left( {q, - c{Q}^{-1}}\right)  \leq  c{C}^{\prime \prime }Q + {e}^{\left( {\widetilde{C}}^{2}\left( c\right) /2c\right) } \) . Now we take \( c = {\left( 2{C}^{\prime \prime }\right) }^{-1} \) and \( \widetilde{C} = \widetilde{C}\left( c\right) \) . Plugging these values into the previous inequality yields

\[
Q \leq  2{e}^{\left( {\widetilde{C}}^{2}{C}^{\prime \prime }\right) }.
\]

DEFINITION 9.72. Fix constants \( 0 < \epsilon  < 1/2 \) and \( C < \infty \) . Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a Riemannian 3-manifold. A \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap in \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) is an open submani-fold \( \left( {\mathcal{C},{\left. g\right| }_{\mathcal{C}}}\right) \) together with an open submanifold \( N \subset  \mathcal{C} \) with the following properties:

(1) \( \mathcal{C} \) is diffeomorphic either to an open 3-ball or to a punctured \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

(2) \( N \) is an \( \epsilon \) -neck with compact complement in \( \mathcal{C} \) .

(3) \( \bar{Y} = \mathcal{C} \smallsetminus  N \) is a compact submanifold with boundary. Its interior, \( Y \) , is called the core of \( \mathcal{C} \) . The frontier of \( Y \) , which is \( \partial \bar{Y} \) , is a central 2-sphere of an \( \epsilon \) -neck contained in \( \mathcal{C} \) .

(4) The scalar curvature \( R\left( y\right)  > 0 \) for every \( y \in  \mathcal{C} \) and

\[
\operatorname{diam}\left( {\mathcal{C},{\left. g\right| }_{\mathcal{C}}}\right)  < C{\left( \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{y \in  \mathcal{C}}}R\left( y\right) \right) }^{-1/2}.
\]

(5) \( \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x, y \in  \mathcal{C}}}\left\lbrack  {R\left( y\right) /R\left( x\right) }\right\rbrack   < C \) .

(6) Vol \( \mathcal{C} < C{\left( \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{y \in  \mathcal{C}}}R\left( y\right) \right) }^{-3/2} \) .

(7) For any \( y \in  Y \) let \( {r}_{y} \) be defined so that \( \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{y}^{\prime } \in  B\left( {y,{r}_{y}}\right) }}R\left( {y}^{\prime }\right)  = {r}_{y}^{-2} \) . Then for each \( y \in  Y \) , the ball \( B\left( {y,{r}_{y}}\right) \) lies in \( \mathcal{C} \) and indeed has compact closure in \( \mathcal{C} \) . Furthermore,

\[
{C}^{-1} < \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{y \in  Y}}\frac{\operatorname{Vol}B\left( {y,{r}_{y}}\right) }{{r}_{y}^{3}}.
\]

(8) Lastly,

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{y \in  \mathcal{C}}}\frac{\left| \nabla R\left( y\right) \right| }{R{\left( y\right) }^{3/2}} < C
\]

and

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{y \in  \mathcal{C}}}\frac{\left| \bigtriangleup R\left( y\right)  + 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\right| }^{2}\right| }{R{\left( y\right) }^{2}} < C.
\]

REMARK 9.73. If the ball \( B\left( {y,{r}_{y}}\right) \) meets the complement of the core of \( \mathcal{C} \) , then it contains a point whose scalar curvature is close to \( R\left( x\right) \) , and hence \( {r}_{y} \) is bounded above by, say \( {2R}{\left( x\right) }^{-1} \) . Since \( \epsilon  < 1/2 \) , using the fact that \( y \) is contained in the core of \( \mathcal{C} \) it follows that \( B\left( {y,{r}_{y}}\right) \) is contained in \( \mathcal{C} \) and has compact closure in \( \mathcal{C} \) .

Implicitly, we always orient the \( \epsilon \) -neck structure on \( N \) so that the closure of its negative end meets the core of \( \mathcal{C} \) . See FIG. 1 in the Introduction.

DEFINITION 9.75. Fix a positive constant \( C \) . A compact connected Riemannian manifold \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) is called a \( C \) -component if:

(1) \( M \) is diffeomorphic to either \( {S}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

(2) \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) has positive sectional curvature.

(3)

\[
{C}^{-1} < \frac{\mathop{\inf }\limits_{P}K\left( P\right) }{\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{y \in  M}}R\left( y\right) }
\]

where \( P \) varies over all 2-planes in \( {TX} \) (and \( K\left( P\right) \) denotes the sectional curvature in the \( P \) -direction).

(4)

\[
{C}^{-1}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{y \in  M}}\left( {R{\left( y\right) }^{-1/2}}\right)  < \operatorname{diam}\left( M\right)  < C\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{y \in  M}}\left( {R{\left( y\right) }^{-1/2}}\right) .
\]

DEFINITION 9.76. Fix \( \epsilon  > 0 \) . Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a compact, connected 3- manifold. Then \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) is within \( \epsilon \) of round in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology if there exist a constant \( R > 0 \) , a compact manifold \( \left( {Z,{g}_{0}}\right) \) of constant curvature +1, and a diffeomorphism \( \varphi  : Z \rightarrow  M \) with the property that the pull-back under \( \varphi \) of \( {Rg} \) is within \( \epsilon \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology of \( {g}_{0} \) .

Notice that both of these notions are scale invariant notions.

Definition 9.77. Fix \( C < \infty \) and \( \epsilon  > 0 \) . For any Riemannian manifold \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) , an open neighborhood \( U \) of a point \( x \in  M \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood if one of the following holds:

(1) \( U \) is an \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) centered at \( x \) .

(2) \( U \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap in \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) whose core contains \( x \) .

(3) \( U \) is a \( C \) -component of \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) .

(4) \( U \) is an \( \epsilon \) -round component of \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) .

Whether or not a point \( x \in  M \) has a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood in \( M \) is a scale invariant notion.

DEFINITION 9.78. Fix constants \( C < \infty \) and \( \epsilon  > 0 \) . Let \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) be a generalized Ricci flow. An evolving \( \epsilon \) -neck defined for an interval of normalized time of length \( {t}^{\prime } > 0 \) centered at a point \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) with \( \mathbf{t}\left( x\right)  = t \) is an embedding \( \psi  : {S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \overset{ \cong  }{ \rightarrow  }N \subset  {M}_{t} \) with \( x \in  \psi \left( {{S}^{2}\times \{ 0\} }\right) \) satisfying the following properties:

(1) There is an embedding \( N \times  \left( {t - R{\left( x\right) }^{-1}{t}^{\prime }, t}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathcal{M} \) compatible with time and the vector field.

(2) The pullback under \( \psi \) of the one-parameter family of metrics on \( N \) determined by restricting \( R\left( x\right) G \) to the image of this embedding is within \( \epsilon \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology of the standard family \( \left( {h\left( t\right) , d{s}^{2}}\right) \) on the interval \( - {t}^{\prime } < t \leq  0 \) , where \( h\left( t\right) \) is the round metric of scalar curvature \( 1/\left( {1 - t}\right) \) on \( {S}^{2} \) and \( d{s}^{2} \) is the usual Euclidean metric on the interval (see Definition 2.16 for the notion of two families of metrics being close).

A strong \( \epsilon \) -neck is the image of an evolving \( \epsilon \) -neck which is defined for an interval of normalized time of length 1.

Both of these notions are scale invariant notions.

Let \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) be a generalized Ricci flow. Let \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) be a point with \( \mathbf{t}\left( x\right)  = t \) . We say that an open neighborhood \( U \) of \( x \) in \( {M}_{t} \) is a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood of \( x \) if one of the following holds:

(1) \( U \) is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) centered at \( x \) .

(2) \( U \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap in \( {M}_{t} \) whose core contains \( x \) .

(3) \( U \) is a \( C \) -component of \( {M}_{t} \) .

(4) \( U \) is an \( \epsilon \) -round component of \( {M}_{t} \) .

Whether or not a point \( x \) in a generalized Ricci flow has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood is a scale invariant notion.

Proposition 9.79. The following holds for any \( \epsilon  < 1/4 \) and any \( C < \; \infty \) . Let \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) be a generalized Ricci flow and let \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) be a point with \( \mathbf{t}\left( x\right)  = t. \)

(1) Suppose that \( U \subset  {M}_{t} \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood for \( x \) . Then for any horizontal metric \( {G}^{\prime } \) sufficiently close to \( {\left. G\right| }_{U} \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology, \( \left( {\left. U,{G}^{\prime }\right| }_{U}\right) \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood for any \( {x}^{\prime } \in  U \) sufficiently close to \( x \) .

(2) Suppose that in \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) there is an evolving \( \epsilon \) -neck \( U \) centered at \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) defined for an interval of normalized time of length \( a > 1 \) . Then any Ricci flow on

\[
U \times  \left( {t - {aR}{\left( x, t\right) }^{-1}, t}\right\rbrack
\]

sufficiently close in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology to the pullback of \( G \) contains a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) .

(3) Given \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) and \( \left( {{C}^{\prime },{\epsilon }^{\prime }}\right) \) with \( {C}^{\prime } > C \) and \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > \epsilon \) there is \( \delta  > 0 \) such that the following holds. Suppose that \( R\left( x\right)  \leq  2 \) . Let \( \left( {U, g}\right) \) be a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood of \( x \) then for any metric \( {g}^{\prime } \) within \( \delta \) of \( g \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology \( \left( {U,{g}^{\prime }}\right) \) contains a \( \left( {{C}^{\prime },{\epsilon }^{\prime }}\right) \) -neighborhood of \( x \) .

(4) Suppose that \( g\left( t\right) , - 1 < t \leq  0 \) , is a one-parameter family of metrics on \( \left( {U, g}\right) \) that is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( \left( {x,0}\right) \) and \( {R}_{g}\left( {x,0}\right)  = 1 \) . Then any one-parameter family \( {g}^{\prime }\left( t\right) \) within \( \delta \) in the \( {C}^{\lbrack 1/\epsilon \rbrack } \) -topology of \( g \) with \( {R}_{{g}^{\prime }}\left( {x,0}\right)  = 1 \) is a strong \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) -neck.

nodes.proof:
Since \( \epsilon  < 1/4 \) , the diameter of \( \left( {U, g}\right) \) , the volume of \( \left( {U, g}\right) \) , the supremum over \( x \in  U \) of \( R\left( x\right) \) , the supremum over \( x \) and \( y \) in \( U \) of \( R\left( y\right) /R\left( x\right) \) , and the infimum over all 2-planes \( P \) in \( \mathcal{H}{TU} \) of \( K\left( P\right) \) are all continuous functions of the horizontal metric \( G \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology.

Let us consider the first statement. Suppose \( \left( {U,{\left. G\right| }_{U}}\right) \) is a \( C \) -component or an \( \epsilon \) -round component. Since the defining inequalities are strict, and, as we just remarked, the quantities in these inequalities vary continuously with the metric in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology, the result is clear in this case.

Let us consider the case when \( U \subset  {M}_{t} \) is an \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( x \) . Let \( \psi  : {S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)  \rightarrow  U \) be the map giving the \( \epsilon \) -neck structure. Then for all horizontal metrics \( {G}^{\prime } \) sufficiently close to \( G \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology, the same map \( \psi \) determines an \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( x \) for the structure \( \left( {\left. U,{G}^{\prime }\right| }_{U}\right) \) . Now let us consider moving \( x \) to a nearby point \( {x}^{\prime } \) , say \( {x}^{\prime } \) is the image of \( \left( {a, s}\right)  \in  {S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) . We pre-compose \( \psi \) by a map which is the product of the identity in the \( {S}^{2} \) -factor with a diffeomorphism \( \alpha \) on \( \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) that is the identity near the ends and moves 0 to \( s \) . As \( {x}^{\prime } \) approaches \( x, s \) tends to zero, and hence we can choose \( \alpha \) so that it tends to the identity in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology. Thus, for \( {x}^{\prime } \) sufficiently close to \( x \) , this composition will determine an \( \epsilon \) -neck structure centered at \( {x}^{\prime } \) . Lastly, let us consider the case when \( \left( {U,{\left. G\right| }_{U}}\right) \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core \( Y \) contains \( x \) . Let \( {G}^{\prime } \) be a horizontal metric sufficiently close to \( {\left. G\right| }_{U} \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology. Let \( N \subset  U \) be the \( \epsilon \) -neck \( U \smallsetminus  \bar{Y} \) . We have just seen that \( \left( {\left. N,{G}^{\prime }\right| }_{N}\right) \) is an \( \epsilon \) -neck. Similarly, if \( {N}^{\prime } \subset  U \) is an \( \epsilon \) -neck with central 2-sphere \( \partial \bar{Y} \) , then \( \left( {{N}^{\prime },{\left. {G}^{\prime }\right| }_{{N}^{\prime }}}\right) \) is an \( \epsilon \) -neck if \( {G}^{\prime } \) is sufficiently close to \( G \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology.

Thus, Conditions (1),(2), and (3) in the definition of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap hold for \( \left( {U,{G}_{U}^{\prime }}\right) \) . Since the curvature, volume and diameter inequalities in Conditions (4),(5), and (6) are strict, they also hold for \( {g}^{\prime } \) . To verify that Condition (7) holds for \( {G}^{\prime } \) , we need only remark that \( {r}_{y} \) is a continuous function of the metric. Lastly, since the derivative inequalities for the curvature in Condition (8) are strict inequalities and \( {\epsilon }^{-1} > 4 \) , if these inequalities hold for all horizontal metrics \( {G}^{\prime } \) sufficiently close to \( G \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology. This completes the examination of all cases and proves the first statement.

The second statement is proved in the same way using the fact that if \( {g}^{\prime }\left( t\right) \) is sufficiently close to \( g \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology and if \( {x}^{\prime } \) is sufficiently close to \( x \) , then \( {R}_{{g}^{\prime }}{\left( {x}^{\prime }\right) }^{-1} < a{R}_{g}{\left( x\right) }^{-1} \) .

Now let us turn to the third statement. The result is clear for \( \epsilon \) -necks. Also, since \( R\left( x\right)  \leq  2 \) the result is clear for \( \epsilon \) -round components and \( C \) - components as well. Lastly, we consider a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap \( U \) whose core \( Y \) contains \( x \) . Clearly, since \( R\left( x\right) \) is bounded above by 2, for \( \delta  > 0 \) sufficiently small, any metric \( {g}^{\prime } \) within \( \delta \) of \( g \) will satisfy the diameter, volume and curvature and the derivative of the curvature inequalities with \( {C}^{\prime } \) replacing \( C \) . Let \( N \) be the \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {U, g}\right) \) containing the end of \( U \) . Assuming that \( \delta \) is sufficiently small, let \( {N}^{\prime } \) be the image of \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},2{\left( {\epsilon }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1} - {\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) . Then \( \left( {{N}^{\prime },{g}^{\prime }}\right) \) becomes an \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) -neck structure once we shift the parameter in the \( s \) -direction by \( {\epsilon }^{-1} - {\left( {\epsilon }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1} \) . We let \( {U}^{\prime } = \bar{Y} \cup  {N}^{\prime } \) . Clearly, the \( \epsilon \) -neck with central 2-sphere \( \partial \bar{Y} \) will also determine an \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) -neck with the same central 2- sphere provided that \( \delta  > 0 \) is sufficiently small. Thus, for \( \delta  > 0 \) sufficiently small, for any \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) the result of this operation is a \( \left( {{C}^{\prime },{\epsilon }^{\prime }}\right) \) -cap with the same core.

The fourth statement is immediate.

nodes.label: Definition 9.81
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
DEFINITION 9.81. An \( \epsilon \) -tube \( \mathcal{T} \) in a Riemannian 3-manifold \( M \) is a sub-manifold diffeomorphic to the product of \( {S}^{2} \) with a non-degenerate interval with the following properties:

(1) Each boundary component \( S \) of \( \mathcal{T} \) is the central 2-sphere of an \( \epsilon \) -neck \( N\left( S\right) \) in \( M \) .

(2) \( \mathcal{T} \) is a union of \( \epsilon \) -necks and the closed half \( \epsilon \) -necks whose boundary sphere is a component of \( \partial \mathcal{T} \) . Furthermore, the central 2-sphere of each of the \( \epsilon \) -necks is isotopic in \( \mathcal{T} \) to the \( {S}^{2} \) -factors of the product structure.

An open \( \epsilon \) -tube is one without boundary. It is a union of \( \epsilon \) -necks with the central spheres that are isotopic to the 2-spheres of the product structure.

A \( C \) -capped \( \epsilon \) -tube in \( M \) is a connected submanifold that is the union of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap \( \mathcal{C} \) and an open \( \epsilon \) -tube where the intersection of \( \mathcal{C} \) with the \( \epsilon \) -tube is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) and contains an end of the \( \epsilon \) -tube and an end of the cap. A doubly \( C \) -capped \( \epsilon \) -tube in \( M \) is a closed, connected submanifold of \( M \) that is the union of two \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -caps \( {\mathcal{C}}_{1} \) and \( {\mathcal{C}}_{2} \) and an open \( \epsilon \) -tube. Furthermore, we require (i) that the cores \( {Y}_{1} \) and \( {Y}_{2} \) of \( {\mathcal{C}}_{1} \) and \( {\mathcal{C}}_{2} \) have disjoint closures,(ii) that the union of either \( {\mathcal{C}}_{i} \) with the \( \epsilon \) -tube is a capped \( \epsilon \) -tube and \( {\mathcal{C}}_{1} \) and \( {\mathcal{C}}_{2} \) contain the opposite ends of the \( \epsilon \) -tube. There is one further closely related notion, that of an \( \epsilon \) -fibration. By definition an \( \epsilon \) -fibration is a closed, connected manifold that fibers over the circle with fibers \( {S}^{2} \) that is also a union of \( \epsilon \) -necks with the property that the central 2-sphere of each neck is isotopic to a fiber of the fibration structure. We shall not see this notion again until the appendix, but because it is clearly closely related to the notion of an \( \epsilon \) -tube, we introduce it here.

PROPOSITION 9.83. Let \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) be a 3-dimensional \( \kappa \) -solution. Then one of the following holds:

(1) For every \( t \leq  0 \) the manifold \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) has positive curvature.

(2) \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is the product of an evolving family of round \( {S}^{2} \) ’s with a line.

(3) \( M \) is diffeomorphic to a line bundle over \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) , and there is a finite covering of \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is a flow as in (2).

nodes.proof: Suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) does not have positive curvature for some \( t \) . Then, by the application of the strong maximum principle given in Corollary 4.20, there is a covering \( \widetilde{M} \) of \( M \) , with either one or two sheets, such that \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) }\right) \) is the product of an evolving family of round surfaces with a flat 1-manifold (either a circle or the real line). Of course, the covering must be a \( \kappa \) -solution. In the case in which \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) }\right) \) is isometric to the product of an evolving family of round surfaces and a circle, that circle has a fixed length, say \( L < \infty \) . Since the curvature of the surface in the \( t \) time-slice goes to zero as \( t \rightarrow   - \infty \) , we see that the flow is not \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed on all scales for any \( \kappa  > 0 \) . Thus, \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) has either a trivial cover or a double cover isometric to the product of a shrinking family of round surfaces with \( \mathbb{R} \) . If the round surface is \( {S}^{2} \) , then we have established the result. If the round surface is \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) a further double covering is a product of round 2-spheres with \( \mathbb{R} \) . This proves the proposition.

LEMMA 9.84. Let \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) be a non-compact 3-dimensional \( \kappa \) -solution of positive curvature and let \( p \in  M \) . Then there is \( {D}^{\prime } < \infty \) , possibly depending on \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) and \( p \) , such that every point of

\[
M \times  \{ 0\}  \smallsetminus  B\left( {p,0,{D}^{\prime }R{\left( p,0\right) }^{-1/2}}\right)
\]

is the center of an evolving \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) defined for an interval of normalized time of length 2. Furthermore, there is \( {D}_{1}^{\prime } < \infty \) such that for any point \( x \in  B\left( {p,0,{D}^{\prime }R{\left( p,0\right) }^{-1/2}}\right) \) and any 2-plane \( {P}_{x} \) in \( {T}_{x}M \) we have \( {\left( {D}_{1}^{\prime }\right) }^{-1} < K\left( {P}_{x}\right) /R\left( {p,0}\right)  < {D}_{1}^{\prime } \) where \( K\left( {P}_{x}\right) \) denotes the sectional curvature in the direction of the 2-plane \( {P}_{x} \) .

nodes.proof:
Given \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) and \( p \) , suppose that no such \( {D}^{\prime } < \infty \) exists. Because the statement is scale invariant, we can arrange that \( R\left( {p,0}\right)  = 1 \) . Then we can find a sequence of points \( {p}_{k} \in  M \) with \( {d}_{0}\left( {p,{p}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) such that no \( {p}_{k} \) is the center of an evolving \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) defined for an interval of normalized time of length 2. By passing to a subsequence we can assume that one of two possibilities holds: either \( {d}_{0}^{2}\left( {p,{p}_{k}}\right) R\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) or \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{d}_{0}^{2}\left( {p,{p}_{k}}\right) R\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right)  = \ell  < \infty \) . In the first case, set \( {\lambda }_{k} = \; R\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right) \) and consider the based flows \( \left( {M,{\lambda }_{k}g\left( {{\lambda }_{k}^{-1}t}\right) ,\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right) }\right) \) . According to Theorem 9.64, after passing to a subsequence there is a geometric limit. Thus, by Theorem 5.35 and Corollary 4.19 the limit splits as a product of a 2-dimensional \( \kappa \) -solution and \( \mathbb{R} \) . By Corollary 9.50 it follows that the limit is the standard round evolving cylinder. This implies that for all \( k \) sufficiently large \( \left( {{p}_{k},0}\right) \) is the center of an evolving \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) defined for an interval of normalized time of length 2. This contradiction establishes the existence of \( {D}^{\prime } \) as required in this case.

Now suppose that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{d}_{0}^{2}\left( {p,{p}_{k}}\right) R\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right)  = \ell  < \infty \) . Of course, since \( {d}_{0}\left( {p,{p}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) , it must be the case that \( R\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) . Set \( {Q}_{k} = \; R\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right) \) . By passing to a subsequence we can arrange that \( {d}_{0}^{2}\left( {p,{p}_{k}}\right) {Q}_{k} < \; \ell  + 1 \) for all \( k \) . Consider the \( \kappa \) -solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) }\right)  = \left( {M,{Q}_{k}g\left( {{Q}_{k}^{-1}t}\right) }\right) \) . For each \( k \) we have \( p \in  {B}_{{g}_{k}}\left( {{p}_{k},0,\ell  + 1}\right) \) , and \( {R}_{{g}_{k}}\left( {p,0}\right)  = {Q}_{k}^{-1} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) . This contradicts Lemma 9.65, and completes the proof of the existence of \( D \) as required in this case as well.

The existence of \( {D}_{1}^{\prime } \) is immediate since the closure of the ball is compact and the manifold has positive curvature.

nodes.content:
Proposition 9.85. For any \( 0 < \epsilon \) sufficiently small there are constants \( D = D\left( \epsilon \right)  < \infty \) and \( {D}_{1} = {D}_{1}\left( \epsilon \right)  < \infty \) such that the following holds for any non-compact 3-dimensional \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) of positive curvature. Let \( p \in  M \) be a soul of \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) . Then:

(1) Every point in \( M \smallsetminus  B\left( {p,0,{DR}{\left( p,0\right) }^{-1/2}}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Furthermore, for any \( x \in  B\left( {p,0,{DR}{\left( p,0\right) }^{-1/2}}\right) \) and any 2-plane \( {P}_{x} \) in \( {T}_{x}M \) we have

\[
{D}_{1}^{-1} < K\left( {P}_{x}\right) /R\left( {p,0}\right)  < {D}_{1}.
\]

\( {Also}, \)

\[
{D}_{1}^{-3/2}R{\left( p,0\right) }^{-3/2} < \operatorname{Vol}\left( {B\left( {p,0,{DR}{\left( p,0\right) }^{-1/2}}\right)  < {D}_{1}^{3/2}R{\left( p,0\right) }^{-3/2}.}\right.
\]

(2) Let \( f \) denote the distance function from \( p \) . For any \( \epsilon \) -neck \( N \subset \; \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) , the middle two-thirds of \( N \) is disjoint from \( p \) , and the central 2-sphere \( {S}_{N} \) of \( N \) is (topologically) isotopic in \( M \smallsetminus  \{ p\} \) to \( {f}^{-1}\left( a\right) \) for any \( a > 0 \) . In particular, given two disjoint central 2- spheres of \( \epsilon \) -necks in \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) the region of \( M \) bounded by these 2-spheres is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) .

nodes.proof:
First suppose that no \( D \) exists so that the first statement holds. Then there is a sequence of such solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) }\right) \) , with \( {p}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) being a soul of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) and points \( {q}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) with \( {d}_{0}^{2}\left( {{p}_{k},{q}_{k}}\right) R\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) such that \( {q}_{k} \) is not the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) . By rescaling we can assume that \( R\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right)  = 1 \) for all \( k \) , and hence that \( {d}_{0}\left( {{p}_{k},{q}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) . Then, according to Theorem 9.64, by passing to a subsequence we can assume that there is a geometric limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,\left( {{p}_{\infty },0}\right) }\right) \) with \( R\left( {{p}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1 \) . By Lemma A.10, provided that \( \epsilon \) is sufficiently small for all \( k \) the soul \( \left( {{p}_{k},0}\right) \) is not the center of a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck in \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Hence, invoking part 4 of Proposition 9.79 and using the fact that \( R\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right)  = \) 1 for all \( k \) and hence \( R\left( {{p}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1 \) , we see that \( \left( {{p}_{\infty },0}\right) \) is not the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Since the manifolds \( {M}_{k} \) are non-compact and have metrics of positive curvature, they are diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) and in particular, do not contain embedded copies of \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) . Thus, the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a non-compact \( \kappa \) -solution containing no embedded copy of \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) . Thus, by Proposition 9.83 either it is positively curved or it is a Riemannian product \( {S}^{2} \) times \( \mathbb{R} \) . In the second case every point is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. Since we have seen that the point \( \left( {{p}_{\infty },0}\right) \) is not the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck, it follows that the limit is a positively curved \( \kappa \) -solution.

Then according to the previous lemma there is \( {D}^{\prime } \) , which depends only on \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) and \( {p}_{\infty } \) , such that every point outside \( B\left( {{p}_{\infty },0,{D}^{\prime }}\right) \) is the center of an evolving \( \epsilon /2 \) -neck defined for an interval of normalized time of length 2.

Since \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) ,\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right) }\right) \) converge geometrically to \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,\left( {{p}_{\infty },0}\right) }\right) \) , by part 2 of Proposition 9.79 for any \( L < \infty \) , for all \( k \) sufficiently large, all points of

\[
B\left( {{p}_{k},0, L}\right)  \smallsetminus  B\left( {{p}_{k},0,2{D}^{\prime }}\right)
\]

are centers of strong \( \epsilon \) -necks in \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) }\right) \) . In particular, for all \( k \) sufficiently large, \( {d}_{0}\left( {{p}_{k},{q}_{k}}\right)  > L \) . Let \( {L}_{k} \) be a sequence tending to infinity as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) . Passing to a subsequence, we can suppose that every point of \( \left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},0,{L}_{k}}\right)  \smallsetminus  B\left( {{p}_{k},0,2{D}^{\prime }}\right) }\right)  \subset  {M}_{k} \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) . Of course, for all \( k \) sufficiently large, \( {q}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \smallsetminus  B\left( {{p}_{k},0,2{D}^{\prime }}\right) ) \) . By Corollary 9.80 the subset of points in \( {M}_{k} \times  \{ 0\} \) that are centers of strong \( \epsilon \) -necks is an open set. Thus, replacing \( {q}_{k} \) with another point if necessary, we can suppose that \( {q}_{k} \) is a closest point to \( {p}_{k} \) contained in \( {M}_{k} \smallsetminus  B\left( {{p}_{k},0,2{D}^{\prime }}\right) \) with the property that \( {q}_{k} \) is not the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. Then \( {q}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \smallsetminus  B\left( {{p}_{k},0,{L}_{k}}\right) \) and \( \left( {{q}_{k},0}\right) \) is in the closure of the set of points in \( {M}_{k} \) that are centers of strong \( \epsilon \) -necks in \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) }\right) \) , and hence by part 3 of Proposition 9.79 each \( \left( {{q}_{k},0}\right) \) is the center of a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck in \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) }\right) \) .

Let \( {\gamma }_{k} \) be a minimizing geodesic connecting \( \left( {{p}_{k},0}\right) \) to \( \left( {{q}_{k},0}\right) \) , and let \( {\mu }_{k} \) be a minimizing geodesic ray from \( \left( {{q}_{k},0}\right) \) to infinity. Set \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{q}_{k},0}\right) \) . Since \( \left( {{q}_{k},0}\right) \) is the center of a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck, from Lemma 2.20 we see that, provided that \( \epsilon \) is sufficiently small, the \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( {q}_{k} \) separates \( p \) from \( \infty \) , so that \( {\gamma }_{k} \) and \( {\mu }_{k} \) exit this \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck at opposite ends. According to

Theorem 9.64, after passing to a subsequence, the based, rescaled flows

\[
\left( {{M}_{k},{Q}_{k}g\left( {{Q}_{k}^{-1}t}\right) ,\left( {{q}_{k},0}\right) }\right)
\]

converge geometrically to a limit. Let \( \left( {{q}_{\infty },0}\right) \) be the base point of the resulting limit. By part 3 of Proposition 9.79, it is the center of a \( {4\epsilon } \) -neck in the limit.

Unbounded curvature at bounded distance contradicts Lemma 9.65, and this establishes the claim.

If the non-compact \( \kappa \) -solution has positive curvature, then the corollary follows immediately from Proposition 9.85 and Corollary 9.71. If the \( \kappa \) - solution is the product of an evolving round \( {S}^{2} \) with the line, then every point of the zero time-slice is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck for every \( \epsilon  > 0 \) so that the zero time-slice of the solution is a strong \( \epsilon \) -tube. Suppose the solution is double covered by the product of an evolving round 2-sphere and the line. Let \( \iota \) be the involution and take the product coordinates so that \( {S}^{2} \times  \{ 0\} \) is the invariant 2-sphere of \( \iota \) in the zero time-slice. Then any point in the zero time-slice at distance at least \( 3{\epsilon }^{-1} \) from \( P = \left( {{S}^{2}\times \{ 0\} }\right) /\iota \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. Furthermore, an appropriate neighborhood of \( P \) in the time zero slice is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains the \( 3{\epsilon }^{-1} \) neighborhood of \( P \) . The derivative bounds in this case come from the fact that the metric is close in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology to the standard evolving flow. This proves the corollary in this case and hence completes the proof.

THEOREM 9.89. There is \( {\bar{\epsilon }}_{3} > 0 \) such that for every \( 0 < \epsilon  \leq  {\bar{\epsilon }}_{3} \) there is \( {C}_{1} = {C}_{1}\left( \epsilon \right)  < \infty \) such that one of the following holds for any \( \kappa  > 0 \) and any compact 3-dimensional \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) .

(1) The manifold \( M \) is compact and of constant positive sectional curvature.

(2) The diameter of \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is less than \( {C}_{1} \cdot  {\left( \mathop{\max }\limits_{{x \in  M}}R\left( x,0\right) \right) }^{-1/2} \) , and \( M \) is diffeomorphic to either \( {S}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

(3) \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is a double \( {C}_{1} \) -capped strong \( \epsilon \) -tube.

nodes.proof:
First notice that if \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is not of strictly positive curvature, then the universal covering of \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is a Riemannian product \( {S}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , and hence \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is either non-compact or finitely covered by the product flow on \( {S}^{2} \times  {S}^{1} \) . The former case is ruled out since we are assuming that \( M \) is compact and the latter case is ruled out because such flows are not \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed for any \( \kappa  > 0 \) . We conclude that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is of positive curvature. This implies that the fundamental group of \( M \) is finite. If there were an embedded \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) in \( M \) with trivial normal bundle, that \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) could not separate (since the Euler characteristic of \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) is 1, it is not the boundary of a compact 3-manifold). But a non-separating surface in \( M \) induces a surjective homomorphism of \( {H}_{1}\left( M\right) \) onto \( \mathbb{Z} \) . We conclude from this that \( M \) does not contain an embedded \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) with trivial normal bundle.

We assume that \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is not round so that by Proposition 9.58 there is a universal \( {\kappa }_{0} > 0 \) such that \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is a \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution. Let \( {C}_{0}\left( \epsilon \right) \) be the constant from Corollary 9.88.

CLAIM 9.90. Assuming that \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is compact but not of constant positive sectional curvature, for each \( \epsilon  > 0 \) there is \( {C}_{1} \) such that if the diameter of \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is greater than \( {C}_{1}{\left( \mathop{\max }\limits_{{x \in  M}}R\left( x,0\right) \right) }^{-1/2} \) , then every point of \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is either contained in the core of \( \left( {{C}_{0}\left( \epsilon \right) ,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap or is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) .

Proof. Suppose that for some \( \epsilon  > 0 \) there is no such \( {C}_{1} \) . We take a sequence of constants \( {C}_{k}^{\prime } \) that diverges to \( + \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) and a sequence \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) ,\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right) }\right) \) of based \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solutions such that the diameter of \( \left( {{M}_{k},0}\right) \) is greater than \( {C}_{k}^{\prime }{R}^{-1/2}\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right) \) and yet \( \left( {{p}_{k},0}\right) \) is not contained in the core of a \( \left( {{C}_{0}\left( \epsilon \right) ,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap nor is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. We scale \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) }\right) \) by \( R\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right) \) . This allows us to assume that \( R\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right)  = 1 \) for all \( k \) . According to Theorem 9.64, after passing to a subsequence we can assume these based \( \kappa \) -solutions converge to a based \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,\left( {{p}_{\infty },0}\right) }\right) \) . Since the diameters of the \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) go to infinity, \( {M}_{\infty } \) is non-compact. According to Corollary 9.88 the point \( {p}_{\infty } \) is either the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck, or is contained in the core of a \( \left( {{C}_{0}\left( \epsilon \right) ,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. Since \( R\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right)  = 1 \) for all \( k \) , it follows from parts 1 and 4 of Proposition 9.79 that for all \( k \) sufficiently large, \( \left( {{p}_{k},0}\right) \) is either the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) }\right) \) or is contained in the core of a \( \left( {{C}_{0}\left( \epsilon \right) ,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. This is a contradiction, proving the claim.

Now it follows from Proposition A. 25 that if the diameter of \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is greater than \( {C}_{1}{\left( \mathop{\max }\limits_{{x \in  M}}R\left( x,0\right) \right) }^{-1/2} \) and if it is not of constant positive curvature, then \( M \) is diffeomorphic to either \( {S}^{3},\mathbb{R}{P}^{3},\mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) or is an \( {S}^{2} \) -fibration over \( {S}^{1} \) . On the other hand, since \( M \) is compact of positive curvature its fundamental group is finite, see Theorem 4.1 on p. 154 of [57]. This rules out the last two cases. This implies that when \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) has diameter greater than \( {C}_{1}{\left( \mathop{\max }\limits_{{x \in  M}}R\left( x,0\right) \right) }^{-1/2} \) and is not of constant positive curvature, it is a double \( {C}_{0} \) -capped \( \epsilon \) -tube.

We must consider the case when \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is not of constant positive curvature and its diameter is less than or equal to \( {C}_{1}{\left( \mathop{\max }\limits_{{x \in  M}}R\left( x,0\right) \right) }^{-1/2} \) . Since \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is not round, by Corollary 9.44 its asymptotic soliton is not compact. Thus, by Theorem 9.42 its asymptotic soliton is either \( {S}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or is double covered by this product. This means that for \( t \) sufficiently negative the diameter of \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is greater than \( {C}_{1}{\left( \mathop{\max }\limits_{{x \in  M}}R\left( x,0\right) \right) }^{-1/2} \) . Invoking the previous result for this negative time tells us that \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

Proposition 9.91. Let \( {\bar{\epsilon }}_{2} \) and \( {\bar{\epsilon }}_{3} \) be as in Corollary 9.88 and Theorem 9.89, respectively. For each \( 0 < \epsilon  \leq  \min \left( {{\bar{\epsilon }}_{2},{\bar{\epsilon }}_{3}}\right) \) let \( {C}_{1} = {C}_{1}\left( \epsilon \right) \) be as in Theorem 9.89. There is \( {C}_{2} = {C}_{2}\left( \epsilon \right)  < \infty \) such that for any \( \kappa  > 0 \) and any compact \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) the following holds. If \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is not of constant positive curvature and if \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is of diameter less than \( {C}_{1}{\left( \mathop{\max }\limits_{{x \in  M}}R\left( x,0\right) \right) }^{-1/2} \) , then for any \( x \in  M \) we have

\[
{C}_{2}^{-1}R{\left( x,0\right) }^{-3/2} < \operatorname{Vol}\left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right)  < {C}_{2}R{\left( x,0\right) }^{-3/2}.
\]

In addition, for any \( y \in  M \) and any 2-plane \( {P}_{y} \) in \( {T}_{y}M \) we have

\[
{C}_{2}^{-1} < \frac{K\left( {P}_{y}\right) }{R\left( {x,0}\right) } < {C}_{2}
\]

where \( K\left( {P}_{y}\right) \) is the sectional curvature in the \( {P}_{y} \) -direction.

For a round \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) we have \( R\left( {x,0}\right)  = \; R\left( {y,0}\right) \) for all \( x, y \in  M \) , and the volume of \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is bounded above by a constant times \( R{\left( x,0\right) }^{-3/2} \) . There is no universal lower bound to the volume in terms of the curvature. The lower bound takes the form \( {C}_{2}{\left| {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \right| }^{-1}R{\left( x,0\right) }^{-3/2} \) , where \( \left| {{\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) }\right| \) is the order of the fundamental group \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) .

THEOREM 9.93. There is \( \bar{\epsilon } > 0 \) such that the following is true for any \( 0 < \epsilon  < \bar{\epsilon } \) . There is \( C = C\left( \epsilon \right) \) such that for any \( \kappa  > 0 \) and any \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) one of the following holds.

(1) \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is round for all \( t \leq  0 \) . In this case \( M \) is diffeomorphic to the quotient of \( {S}^{3} \) by a finite subgroup of \( {SO}\left( 4\right) \) acting freely.

(2) \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is compact and of positive curvature. For any \( x, y \in  M \) and any 2-plane \( {P}_{y} \) in \( {T}_{y}M \) we have

\[
{C}^{-1/2}R{\left( x,0\right) }^{-1} < \operatorname{diam}\left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right)  < {CR}{\left( x,0\right) }^{-1/2},
\]

\[
{C}^{-1}R{\left( x,0\right) }^{-3/2} < \operatorname{Vol}\left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right)  < {CR}{\left( x,0\right) }^{-3/2},
\]

\[
{C}^{-1}R\left( {x,0}\right) \; < K\left( {P}_{y}\right) \; < {CR}\left( {x,0}\right) .
\]

In this case \( M \) is diffeomorphic either to \( {S}^{3} \) or to \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

(3) \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is of positive curvature and is a double \( C \) -capped strong \( \epsilon \) -tube, and in particular \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{3} \) or to \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

(4) \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is of positive curvature and is a \( C \) -capped strong \( \epsilon \) -tube and \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) .

(5) \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is isometric to the quotient of the product of a round \( {S}^{2} \) and \( \mathbb{R} \) by a free, orientation-preserving involution. It is a \( C \) -capped strong \( \epsilon \) -tube and is diffeomorphic to a punctured \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

(6) \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is isometric to the product of a round \( {S}^{2} \) and \( \mathbb{R} \) and is a strong \( \epsilon \) -tube.

(7) \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is isometric to a product \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , where the metric on \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) is of constant Gaussian curvature.

In particular, in all cases except the first two and the last one, all points of \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) are either contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap or are the centers of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) .

Lastly, in all cases we have

(9.33)

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{p \in  M, t \leq  0}}\frac{\left| \nabla R\left( p, t\right) \right| }{R{\left( p, t\right) }^{3/2}} < C,
\]

(9.34)

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{p \in  M, t \leq  0}}\frac{\left| \partial R\left( p, t\right) /\partial t\right| }{R{\left( p, t\right) }^{2}} < C.
\]

nodes.proof: The limiting manifold \( {M}_{\infty } \) cannot contain an embedded \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) with trivial normal bundle. Hence, by the previous corollary, the point \( \left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right) \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood in the limiting flow. If the limiting \( \kappa \) -solution is round, then for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( {x}_{n} \) is contained in a component of the zero time-slice that is \( \epsilon \) -round. If \( \left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right) \) is contained in a \( C \) -component of the zero time-slice of the limiting \( \kappa \) -solution, then for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {x}_{n} \) is contained in a \( C \) -component of the zero time-slice of \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Suppose that \( \left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in the limiting flow. This neck extends backwards in the limiting solution some amount past an interval of normalized time of length 1 , where by continuity it is an evolving \( \epsilon \) -neck defined backwards for an interval of normalized time of length greater than 1. Then by part 2 of Proposition 9.79, any family of metrics on this neck sufficiently close to the limiting metric will determine a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. This implies that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( {x}_{n} \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) . Lastly, if \( \left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right) \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap in the limiting flow, then by part 1 of Proposition 9.79 for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( {x}_{n} \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap in \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) .

nodes.label: Definition 10.1
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
DEFINITION 10.1. Let \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) be a generalized 3-dimensional Ricci flow whose domain of definition is contained in \( \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) . For each \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) , let \( \nu \left( x\right) \) be the smallest eigenvalue of \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( x\right) \) on \( { \land  }^{2}{T}_{x}{M}_{\mathbf{t}\left( x\right) } \) , as measured with respect to a \( G\left( x\right) \) -orthonormal basis for the horizontal space at \( x \) , and set \( X\left( x\right)  = \max \left( {0, - \nu \left( x\right) }\right) \) . We say that \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) has curvature pinched toward positive if, for all \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) , if the following two inequalities hold:

\[
R\left( x\right)  \geq  \frac{-6}{1 + 4\mathbf{t}\left( x\right) },
\]

\[
R\left( x\right)  \geq  {2X}\left( x\right) \left( {\log X\left( x\right)  + \log \left( {1 + \mathbf{t}\left( x\right) }\right)  - 3}\right) ,\;\text{ if }0 < X\left( x\right) .
\]

THEOREM 10.2. Fix \( 0 < \epsilon  \leq  {\epsilon }_{0} \) and \( C < \infty \) . Then for each \( A < \infty \) there are \( {D}_{0} < \infty \) and \( D < \infty \) depending on \( A,\epsilon \) and \( C \) such that the following holds. Suppose that \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) is a generalized 3-dimensional Ricci flow whose interval of definition is contained in \( \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) , and suppose that \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) . Set \( t = \mathbf{t}\left( x\right) \) . We suppose that these data satisfy the following:

(1) \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) has curvature pinched toward positive.

(2) Every point \( y \in  \mathcal{M} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  \geq  {4R}\left( x\right) \) and \( \mathbf{t}\left( y\right)  \leq  t \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood.

\[
\text{ If }R\left( x\right)  \geq  {D}_{0}\text{ , then }R\left( y\right)  \leq  {DR}\left( x\right) \text{ for all }y \in  B\left( {x, t,{AR}{\left( x\right) }^{-1/2}}\right) \text{ . }
\]

nodes.content:
CLAIM 10.4. For every \( n \) sufficiently large, there is a sub-geodesic \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) of \( {\gamma }_{n} \) with end points \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) and \( {y}_{n}^{\prime } \) such that the following hold:

(1) The length of \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) is bounded independent of \( n \) .

(2) \( R\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) is bounded independent of \( n \) .

(3) \( R\left( {y}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) tends to infinity as \( n \) tends to infinity.

(4) \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) is contained in a strong \( \epsilon \) -tube \( {T}_{n} \) that is the union of a balanced chain of strong \( \epsilon \) -necks centered at points of \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) . The first element in this chain is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck \( N\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) centered at \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) . The last element is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck containing \( {y}_{n}^{\prime } \) .

(5) For every \( x \in  {T}_{n} \) , we have \( R\left( x\right)  > 3 \) and \( x \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in the flow \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n}^{\prime },{G}_{n}^{\prime }}\right) \) .

nodes.proof:
The first item is immediate since, for all \( n \) , the geodesic \( {\gamma }_{n} \) has \( {G}_{n} \) -length at most \( {A}_{0}{Q}_{n}^{-1/2} \) and hence \( {G}_{n}^{\prime } \) -length at most \( {A}_{0} \) . Suppose that we have a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap \( \mathcal{C} \) whose core \( Y \) contains a point of \( {\gamma }_{n} \) . Let \( N \) be the \( \epsilon \) -neck that is the complement of the closure of \( Y \) in \( \mathcal{C} \) , and let \( \widehat{Y} \) be the union of \( Y \) and the closed negative half of \( N \) . We claim that \( \widehat{Y} \) contains either \( {z}_{n} \) or \( {y}_{n} \) . By Corollary A.8, since \( Y \) contains a point of \( {\gamma }_{n} \) , the intersection of \( \widehat{Y} \) with \( {\gamma }_{n} \) is a subinterval containing one of the end points of \( {\gamma }_{n} \) , i.e., either \( {z}_{n} \) or \( {y}_{n} \) . This means that any point \( w \) which is contained in a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains a point of \( {\gamma }_{n} \) must satisfy one of the following:

\[
R\left( w\right)  < {CR}\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \text{ or }R\left( w\right)  > {C}^{-1}R\left( {y}_{n}^{\prime }\right) .
\]

We pass to a subsequence so that \( R\left( {y}_{n}\right) /R\left( {z}_{n}\right)  > 4{C}^{2} \) for all \( n \) , and we pass to a subinterval \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) of \( {\gamma }_{n} \) with endpoints \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) and \( {y}_{n}^{\prime } \) such that:

(1) \( R\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right)  = {2CR}\left( {z}_{n}\right) \) .

(2) \( R\left( {y}_{n}^{\prime }\right)  = {\left( 2C\right) }^{-1}R\left( {y}_{n}\right) \) .

(3) \( R\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right)  \leq  R\left( w\right)  \leq  R\left( {y}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) for all \( w \in  {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) .

Clearly, with these choices \( R\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) is bounded independent of \( n \) and \( R\left( {y}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) tends to infinity as \( n \) tends to infinity. Also, no point of \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. Since every point of \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood, it follows that every point of \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) - neck. It now follows from Proposition A. 19 that there is a balanced \( \epsilon \) -chain consisting of strong \( \epsilon \) -necks centered at points of \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) whose union contains \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) . (Even if the 2-spheres of these necks do not separate the zero time-slice of \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n}^{\prime } \) , as we build the balanced \( \epsilon \) -chain as described in Proposition A. 19 the new necks we add can not meet the negative end of \( N\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) since the geodesic \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) is minimal.) We can take the first element in the balanced chain to be a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck \( N\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) centered at \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) , and the last element to be a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck \( {N}_{n}^{ + } \) containing \( {y}_{n}^{\prime } \) . The union of this chain is \( {T}_{n} \) . (See FIG. 1.)

![019eafd8-fdc6-7b80-ae12-d1283dd2df0a_92_487_243_845_648_0.jpg](images/019eafd8-fdc6-7b80-ae12-d1283dd2df0a_92_487_243_845_648_0.jpg)

Figure 1. Limiting tube.

Next, we show that every point of \( {T}_{n} \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) . We must rule out the possibility that there is a point of \( {T}_{n} \) that is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. Since \( {T}_{n} \) is a union of \( \epsilon \) -necks centered at points of \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) we see that every point \( w \in  {T}_{n} \) has

\[
\left( {{3C}/2}\right) R\left( {z}_{n}\right)  < R\left( w\right)  < \left( {2/{3C}}\right) R\left( {y}_{n}\right) .
\]

This tells us that no point of \( {T}_{n} \) is contained in a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains a point of \( {\gamma }_{n} \) . Thus, to complete the argument we need only see that if there is a point of \( {T}_{n} \) contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap, then the core of that \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap also contains a point of \( {\gamma }_{n} \) . The scalar curvature inequality implies that both \( {z}_{n} \) and \( {y}_{n} \) are outside \( {T}_{n} \) . This means that \( {\gamma }_{n} \) traverses \( {T}_{n} \) from one end to the other. Let \( {w}_{ - } \) , resp. \( {w}_{ + } \) , be the point of \( {\gamma }_{n} \) that lies in the frontier of \( {T}_{n} \) contained in the closure of the \( N\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) , resp. \( {N}_{n}^{ + } \) . Since the scalar curvatures at these two points of \( \gamma \) satisfy the weak version of the above inequalities, we see that there are strong \( \epsilon \) -necks \( N\left( {w}_{ - }\right) \) and \( N\left( {w}_{ + }\right) \) centered at them. Let \( {\widehat{T}}_{n} \) be the union of \( {T}_{n}, N\left( {w}_{ - }\right) \) and \( N\left( {w}_{ + }\right) \) . It is also a strong \( \epsilon \) -tube, and every point \( \widehat{w} \) of \( {\widehat{T}}_{n} \) satisfies

\[
\text{ (1.1) }{CR}\left( {z}_{n}\right)  < R\left( \widehat{w}\right)  < \left( {0.9}\right) {C}^{-1}R\left( {y}_{n}\right) \text{ . }
\]

Thus, \( {z}_{n} \) and \( {y}_{n} \) are disjoint from \( {\widehat{T}}_{n} \) and hence \( \gamma \) crosses \( {\widehat{T}}_{n} \) from one end to the other.

Now suppose that \( {T}_{n} \) meets the core \( Y \) of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap \( \mathcal{C} \) . Consider the boundary \( S \) of the closure of \( Y \) . If it is disjoint from \( {T}_{n} \) then \( {T}_{n} \) is contained in the core \( Y \) . For large \( n \) this is inconsistent with the fact that the ratio of the scalar curvature at the endpoints of \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) goes to infinity. Thus, we are left to consider the case when \( S \) contains a point of the tube \( {T}_{n} \) . In this case \( S \) is completely contained in \( {\widehat{T}}_{n} \) and by Corollary A.3, \( S \) is isotopic to the 2-spheres of the product decomposition of \( {\widehat{T}}_{n} \) . Hence, \( S \) meets a point of \( {\gamma }_{n} \) and consequently the core \( Y \) contains a point of \( {\gamma }_{n} \) . But we have already seen that this is not possible.

Lastly, we must show that \( R\left( x\right)  > 3 \) for every \( x \in  {T}_{n} \) . We have just seen that every \( x \in  {T}_{n} \) is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck. If \( x \) is contained in the \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) or \( {y}_{n}^{\prime } \) , then since \( R\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right)  \geq  4 \) and \( R\left( {y}_{n}^{\prime }\right)  \geq  4 \) , clearly \( R\left( x\right)  > 3 \) . We must consider the case when \( x \) is not contained in either of these \( \epsilon \) -necks. In this case the central 2-sphere \( {S}_{x} \) of the \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( x \) is contained in the compact submanifold of \( {T}_{n}^{\prime } \) bounded by the central 2-spheres of the necks centered at \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) and \( {y}_{n}^{\prime } \) . These 2-spheres are disjoint and by Condition 4 in Proposition A.11 each is a homotopically non-trivial 2-sphere in \( {T}_{n}^{\prime } \) . Hence, the compact manifold with their disjoint union as boundary is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) and, again according to Condition 4 of Proposition A.11, \( {S}_{x} \) is isotopic to the 2-sphere factor in this product decomposition. Since the intersection of \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) with this submanifold is an arc spanning from one boundary component to the other, \( {S}_{x} \) must meet \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) , in say \( w \) . By construction, since \( w \in  {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) we have \( R\left( w\right)  \geq  4 \) . This implies that \( R\left( x\right)  > 3 \) . This completes the proof of the claim.

Since \( {T}_{n} \) is a union of \( \epsilon \) -necks centered at points of \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) we see that every point \( w \in  {T}_{n} \) has

\[
\left( {{3C}/2}\right) R\left( {z}_{n}\right)  < R\left( w\right)  < \left( {2/{3C}}\right) R\left( {y}_{n}\right) .
\]

This tells us that no point of \( {T}_{n} \) is contained in a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains a point of \( {\gamma }_{n} \) . Thus, to complete the argument we need only see that if there is a point of \( {T}_{n} \) contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap, then the core of that \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap also contains a point of \( {\gamma }_{n} \) . The scalar curvature inequality implies that both \( {z}_{n} \) and \( {y}_{n} \) are outside \( {T}_{n} \) . This means that \( {\gamma }_{n} \) traverses \( {T}_{n} \) from one end to the other. Let \( {w}_{ - } \) , resp. \( {w}_{ + } \) , be the point of \( {\gamma }_{n} \) that lies in the frontier of \( {T}_{n} \) contained in the closure of the \( N\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) , resp. \( {N}_{n}^{ + } \) . Since the scalar curvatures at these two points of \( \gamma \) satisfy the weak version of the above inequalities, we see that there are strong \( \epsilon \) -necks \( N\left( {w}_{ - }\right) \) and \( N\left( {w}_{ + }\right) \) centered at them. Let \( {\widehat{T}}_{n} \) be the union of \( {T}_{n}, N\left( {w}_{ - }\right) \) and \( N\left( {w}_{ + }\right) \) . It is also a strong \( \epsilon \) -tube, and every point \( \widehat{w} \) of \( {\widehat{T}}_{n} \) satisfies

\[
\text{ (1.1) }{CR}\left( {z}_{n}\right)  < R\left( \widehat{w}\right)  < \left( {0.9}\right) {C}^{-1}R\left( {y}_{n}\right) \text{ . }
\]

Thus, \( {z}_{n} \) and \( {y}_{n} \) are disjoint from \( {\widehat{T}}_{n} \) and hence \( \gamma \) crosses \( {\widehat{T}}_{n} \) from one end to the other.

Now suppose that \( {T}_{n} \) meets the core \( Y \) of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap \( \mathcal{C} \) . Consider the boundary \( S \) of the closure of \( Y \) . If it is disjoint from \( {T}_{n} \) then \( {T}_{n} \) is contained in the core \( Y \) . For large \( n \) this is inconsistent with the fact that the ratio of the scalar curvature at the endpoints of \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) goes to infinity. Thus, we are left to consider the case when \( S \) contains a point of the tube \( {T}_{n} \) . In this case \( S \) is completely contained in \( {\widehat{T}}_{n} \) and by Corollary A.3, \( S \) is isotopic to the 2-spheres of the product decomposition of \( {\widehat{T}}_{n} \) . Hence, \( S \) meets a point of \( {\gamma }_{n} \) and consequently the core \( Y \) contains a point of \( {\gamma }_{n} \) . But we have already seen that this is not possible.

Lastly, we must show that \( R\left( x\right)  > 3 \) for every \( x \in  {T}_{n} \) . We have just seen that every \( x \in  {T}_{n} \) is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck. If \( x \) is contained in the \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) or \( {y}_{n}^{\prime } \) , then since \( R\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right)  \geq  4 \) and \( R\left( {y}_{n}^{\prime }\right)  \geq  4 \) , clearly \( R\left( x\right)  > 3 \) . We must consider the case when \( x \) is not contained in either of these \( \epsilon \) -necks. In this case the central 2-sphere \( {S}_{x} \) of the \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( x \) is contained in the compact submanifold of \( {T}_{n}^{\prime } \) bounded by the central 2-spheres of the necks centered at \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) and \( {y}_{n}^{\prime } \) . These 2-spheres are disjoint and by Condition 4 in Proposition A.11 each is a homotopically non-trivial 2-sphere in \( {T}_{n}^{\prime } \) . Hence, the compact manifold with their disjoint union as boundary is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) and, again according to Condition 4 of Proposition A.11, \( {S}_{x} \) is isotopic to the 2-sphere factor in this product decomposition. Since the intersection of \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) with this submanifold is an arc spanning from one boundary component to the other, \( {S}_{x} \) must meet \( {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) , in say \( w \) . By construction, since \( w \in  {\gamma }_{n}^{\prime } \) we have \( R\left( w\right)  \geq  4 \) . This implies that \( R\left( x\right)  > 3 \) . This completes the proof of the claim.

nodes.proof:
The curvature on \( N\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) is bounded independent of \( n \) . Consider a point \( w \) near the end of \( N\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) that separates \( {y}_{n}^{\prime } \) from \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) . It is also the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck \( N\left( w\right) \) . By Proposition A.11 and our assumption that \( \epsilon  \leq  \bar{\epsilon }\left( {10}^{-2}\right) \) , the scalar curvature on \( N\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right)  \cup  N\left( w\right) \) is between \( \left( {0.9}\right) R\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) and (1.1) \( R\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) . Since, by construction, the negative end of \( N\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) contains an end of \( {T}_{n} \) , this implies that

\[
N\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right)  \cup  N\left( w\right)  \supset  B\left( {{z}_{n}^{\prime },{7R}{\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1}/4}\right)  \cap  {T}_{n},
\]

so that we see that \( {A}_{1} \geq  7{\epsilon }^{-1}\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}R{\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) }^{-1/2}/4 > {3R}{\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}{\epsilon }^{-1}/2 \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large. Obviously then \( {U}_{n} \) contains \( N\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) .

nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content: CLAIM 10.6. For any \( \delta  > 0 \) there is a uniform bound, independent of \( n \) , for the curvature on \( {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{U}_{n},{g}_{n}^{\prime }}\right) \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: CLAIM 10.6. For any \( \delta > 0 \) there is a uniform bound, independent of \( n \) , for the curvature on \( {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{U}_{n},{g}_{n}^{\prime }}\right) \) .

nodes.proof:
To prove this it suffices to show that given \( \delta  > 0 \) there is \( A < {A}_{1} \) such that \( {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{U}_{n},{g}_{n}^{\prime }}\right)  \subset  B\left( {{z}_{n}^{\prime }, A}\right) \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large. Of course, if we establish this for every \( \delta  > 0 \) sufficiently small, then it follows for all \( \delta  > 0 \) . First of all, by Corollary A. 5 and Lemma A.2, the fact that \( \epsilon  \leq  \bar{\epsilon }\left( {10}^{-2}\right) \) implies that any point \( w \) with the property that the strong \( \epsilon \) -neighborhood centered at \( w \) contains \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) is contained in the ball of radius (1.1) \( R{\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1} < {A}_{1} \) centered at \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) . Thus, it suffices to consider points \( {w}_{n} \) in \( {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{U}_{n},{g}_{n}^{\prime }}\right) \) with the property that the strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( {w}_{n} \) does not contain \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) . Fix such a \( {w}_{n} \) . Take a path \( {\mu }_{n}\left( s\right) \) starting at \( {w}_{n} \) moving in the \( s \) -direction at unit speed measured in the \( s \) -coordinate of the \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( {w}_{n} \) away from \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) and ending at the frontier of this neck. Let \( {u}_{1} \) be the final point of this path. The rescaled version of Lemma A. 9 implies that the forward difference quotient for the distance from \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) satisfies

\[
\left( {0.99}\right) R{\left( {w}_{n}\right) }^{-1/2} \leq  \frac{d}{ds}d\left( {{z}_{n}^{\prime },{\mu }_{n}\left( s\right) }\right)  \leq  \left( {1.01}\right) R{\left( {w}_{n}\right) }^{-1/2}.
\]

Of course, since we are working in an \( \epsilon \) -neck we also have

\[
\left( {1 - \epsilon }\right) R{\left( {w}_{n}\right) }^{-1/2} \leq  \frac{d\left( {d\left( {{w}_{n},{\mu }_{n}\left( s\right) }\right) }\right) }{ds} \leq  \left( {1 + \epsilon }\right) R{\left( {w}_{n}\right) }^{-1/2}.
\]

We continue the path \( {\mu }_{n} \) moving in the \( s \) -direction of a neck centered at \( {u}_{1} \) . Applying Lemma A. 9 again both to the distance from \( {w}_{n} \) and the distance from \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) yields:

\[
\left( {0.99}\right) R{\left( {u}_{1}\right) }^{-1/2} \leq  \frac{d\left( {d\left( {{z}_{n}^{\prime },{\mu }_{n}\left( s\right) }\right) }\right) }{ds} \leq  \left( {1.01}\right) R{\left( {u}_{1}\right) }^{-1/2},
\]

\[
\left( {0.99}\right) R{\left( {u}_{1}\right) }^{-1/2} \leq  \frac{d\left( {d\left( {{w}_{n},{\mu }_{n}\left( s\right) }\right) }\right) }{ds} \leq  \left( {1.01}\right) R{\left( {u}_{1}\right) }^{-1/2}
\]

on this part of the path \( {\mu }_{n} \) . We repeat this process as many times as necessary until we reach a point \( {w}_{n}^{\prime } \in  {U}_{n} \) at distance \( \delta /2 \) from \( {w}_{n} \) . This is possible since the ball of radius \( \delta \) centered at \( {w}_{n} \) is contained in \( {U}_{n} \) . By the difference quotient inequalities, it follows that \( d\left( {{z}_{n}^{\prime },{w}_{n}^{\prime }}\right)  - d\left( {{z}_{n}^{\prime },{w}_{n}}\right)  > \; \delta /4 \) . Since \( {w}_{n}^{\prime } \in  {U}_{n} \) and consequently that \( d\left( {{z}_{n}^{\prime },{w}_{n}^{\prime }}\right)  < {A}_{1} \) . It follows that \( d\left( {{z}_{n}^{\prime },{w}_{n}}\right)  \leq  {A}_{1} - \delta /4 \) . This proves that, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{U}_{n},{g}_{n}^{\prime }}\right)  \subset  B\left( {{z}_{n}^{\prime },{A}_{1} - \delta /4}\right) \) , and consequently that the curvature on \( {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{U}_{n},{g}_{n}^{\prime }}\right) \) is bounded independent of \( n \) .

nodes.content: Proposition 10.7. The geometric limit \( \left( {{U}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{z}_{\infty }}\right) \) is an incomplete Riemannian 3-manifold of finite diameter. There is a diffeomorphism \( \psi \) from \( {U}_{\infty } \) to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) . There is a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( {z}_{\infty } \) whose central 2-sphere \( {S}^{2}\left( {z}_{\infty }\right) \) maps under \( \psi \) to a 2-sphere isotopic to a 2-sphere factor in the product decomposition. The scalar curvature is bounded at one end of \( {U}_{\infty } \) but tends to infinity at the other end, the latter end which is denoted \( \mathcal{E} \) . Let \( {\mathcal{U}}_{\infty } \subset  {U}_{\infty } \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) be the open subset consisting of all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) for which \( - R{\left( x\right) }^{-1} < t \leq  0 \) . We have a generalized Ricci flow on \( {\mathcal{U}}_{\infty } \) which is a partial geometric limit of a subsequence of the generalized Ricci flows \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n}^{\prime },{G}_{n}^{\prime },{z}_{n}^{\prime }}\right) \) . In particular, the zero time-slice of the limit flow is \( \left( {{U}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) . The Riemannian curvature is non-negative at all points of the limiting smooth flow on \( {\mathcal{U}}_{\infty } \) . Every point \( x \in  {U}_{\infty } \times  \{ 0\} \) which is not separated from \( \mathcal{E} \) by \( {S}^{2}\left( {z}_{\infty }\right) \) is the center of an evolving \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck \( N\left( x\right) \) defined for an interval of normalized time of length \( 1/2 \) . Furthermore, the central 2-sphere of \( N\left( x\right) \) is isotopic to the 2-sphere factor of \( {U}_{\infty } \) under the diffeomorphism \( \psi \) (see FIG. 1).
