nodes.proof:
Let \( {V}_{1} \subset  {V}_{2} \subset  \cdots  \subset  {U}_{\infty } \) be the open subsets and \( {\varphi }_{n} : {V}_{n} \rightarrow  {U}_{n} \) be the maps having all the properties stated in Definition 5.3 so as to exhibit \( \left( {{U}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{z}_{\infty }}\right) \) as the geometric limit of the \( \left( {{U}_{n},{g}_{n}^{\prime },{z}_{n}^{\prime }}\right) \) .

Since the \( {U}_{n} \) are all contained in \( B\left( {{z}_{n}^{\prime },{A}_{1}}\right) \) , it follows that any point of \( {U}_{\infty } \) is within \( {A}_{1} \) of the limiting base point \( {z}_{\infty } \) . This proves that the diameter of \( {U}_{\infty } \) is bounded.

For each \( n \) there is the \( \epsilon \) -neck \( N\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) centered at \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) contained in \( {U}_{n} \) . The middle two-thirds, \( {N}_{n}^{\prime } \) , of this neck has closure contained in \( {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{U}_{n},{g}_{n}}\right) \) for some \( \delta  > 0 \) independent of \( n \) (in fact, restricting to \( n \) sufficiently large, \( \delta \) can be taken to be approximately equal to \( R{\left( {z}_{\infty }\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1}/3 \) ). This means that for some \( n \) sufficiently large and for all \( m \geq  n \) , the image \( {\varphi }_{m}\left( {V}_{n}\right)  \subset  {U}_{m} \) contains \( {N}_{m}^{\prime } \) . For any fixed \( n \) as \( m \) tends to infinity the metrics \( {\left. {\varphi }_{m}^{ * }{g}_{m}\right| }_{{V}_{n}} \) converge uniformly in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to \( {\left. {g}_{\infty }\right| }_{{V}_{n}} \) . Thus, it follows from Proposition 9.79 that for all \( m \) sufficiently large, \( {\varphi }_{m}^{-1}\left( {N}_{m}^{\prime }\right) \) is a \( {3\epsilon }/2 \) -neck centered at \( {z}_{\infty } \) . We fix such a neck \( {N}^{\prime }\left( {z}_{\infty }\right)  \subset  {U}_{\infty } \) . Let \( S\left( {z}_{\infty }\right) \) be the central 2-sphere of \( {N}^{\prime }\left( {z}_{\infty }\right) \) . For each \( n \) sufficiently large, \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( {S\left( {z}_{\infty }\right) }\right) \) separates \( {U}_{n} \) into two components, one, say \( {W}_{n}^{ - } \) contained in \( N\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) and the other, \( {W}_{n}^{ + } \) containing all of \( {U}_{n} \smallsetminus  N\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) . It follows that \( S\left( {z}_{\infty }\right) \) separates \( {U}_{\infty } \) into two components, one, denoted \( {W}_{\infty }^{ - } \) , where the curvature is bounded (and where, in fact, the curvature is close to \( R\left( {z}_{\infty }\right) \) ) and the other, denoted \( {W}_{\infty }^{ + } \) , where it is unbounded.

CLAIM 10.8. Any point \( q \in  {W}_{\infty }^{ + } \) is the center of a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck in \( {U}_{\infty } \) .

Proof. Fix a point \( q \in  {W}_{\infty }^{ + } \) . For all \( n \) sufficiently large let \( {q}_{n} = {\varphi }_{n}\left( q\right) \) . Then for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( {q}_{n} \in  {W}_{n}^{ + } \) and \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}R\left( {q}_{n}\right)  = R\left( q\right) \) . This means that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( \left. {R\left( {y}_{n}^{\prime }\right)  >  > R\left( {q}_{n}\right) }\right) \) , and hence the \( {3\epsilon }/2 \) - neck centered at \( {q}_{n} \in  {U}_{n} \) is disjoint from \( N\left( {y}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) . Thus, by the rescaled version of Corollary A.5, the distance from the \( {3\epsilon }/2 \) -neck centered at \( {q}_{n} \) to \( N\left( {y}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) is bounded below by \( \left( {0.99}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1}R{\left( {q}_{n}\right) }^{-1/2}/4 \geq  {\epsilon }^{-1}R{\left( {q}_{\infty }\right) }^{-1/2}/{12} \) . Also, since \( {q}_{n} \in  {W}_{n} \) , this \( {3\epsilon }/2 \) -neck \( {N}^{\prime }\left( {q}_{n}\right) \) centered at \( {q}_{n} \) does not extend past the 2-sphere at \( {s}^{-1}\left( {-3{\epsilon }^{-1}/4}\right) \) in the \( \epsilon \) -neck \( N\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) . It follows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, this \( {3\epsilon }/2 \) -neck has compact closure contained in \( {\operatorname{Reg}}_{\delta }\left( {{U}_{n},{g}_{n}}\right) \) for some \( \delta \) independent of \( n \) , and hence there is \( m \) such that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {N}^{\prime }\left( {q}_{n}\right) \) is contained in the image \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( {V}_{m}\right) \) . Again using the fact that \( {\varphi }_{n}^{ * }\left( {{g}_{n}{ \mid  }_{{V}_{m}}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to \( {\left. {g}_{\infty }\right| }_{{V}_{m}} \) as \( n \) tends to infinity, we see, by Proposition 9.79 that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {\varphi }_{n}^{-1}\left( {N}_{m}\right) \) contains a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck in \( {U}_{\infty } \) centered at \( q \) .

It now follows from Proposition A. 21 that \( {W}_{\infty }^{ + } \) is contained in a \( {2\epsilon } \) -tube \( {T}_{\infty } \) that is contained in \( {U}_{\infty } \) . Furthermore, the frontier of \( {W}_{\infty }^{ + } \) in \( {T}_{\infty } \) is the 2-sphere \( S\left( {z}_{\infty }\right) \) which is isotopic to the central 2-spheres of the \( {2\epsilon } \) -necks making up \( {T}_{\infty } \) . Hence, the closure \( {\bar{W}}_{\infty }^{ + } \) of \( {W}_{\infty }^{ + } \) is a \( {2\epsilon } \) -tube with boundary \( S\left( {z}_{\infty }\right) \) . In particular, \( {\bar{W}}_{\infty }^{ + } \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \lbrack 0,1) \) .

Now we consider the closure \( {\bar{W}}_{\infty }^{ - } \) of \( {W}_{\infty }^{ - } \) . Since the closure of each \( {W}_{n}^{ - } \) is the closed negative half of the \( \epsilon \) -neck \( N\left( {z}_{n}^{\prime }\right) \) and the curvatures of the \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) have a finite, positive limit, the limit \( {\bar{W}}_{\infty }^{ - } \) is diffeomorphic to a product \( {S}^{2} \times  ( - 1,0\rbrack \) . Hence, \( {U}_{\infty } \) is the union of \( {\bar{W}}_{\infty }^{ + } \) and \( {\bar{W}}_{\infty }^{ - } \) along their common boundary. It follows immediately that \( {U}_{\infty } \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) .

CLAIM 10.9. The curvature is bounded in a neighborhood of one end of \( {U}_{\infty } \) and goes to infinity at the other end.

Proof. A neighborhood of one end of \( {U}_{\infty } \) , the end \( {\bar{W}}_{\infty }^{ - } \) , is the limit of the negative halves of \( \epsilon \) -necks centered at \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) . Thus, the curvature is bounded on this neighborhood, and in fact is approximately equal to \( R\left( {z}_{\infty }\right) \) . Let \( {x}_{k} \) be any sequence of points in \( {U}_{\infty } \) tending to the other end. We show that \( R\left( {x}_{k}\right) \) tends to \( \infty \) as \( k \) does. The point is that since the sequence is tending to the end, the distance from \( {x}_{k} \) to the end of \( {U}_{\infty } \) is going to zero. Yet, each \( {x}_{k} \) is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( {U}_{\infty } \) . The only way this is possible is if the scales of these \( \epsilon \) -necks are converging to zero as \( k \) goes to infinity. This is equivalent to the statement that \( R\left( {x}_{k}\right) \) tends to \( \infty \) as \( k \) goes to infinity.

The next step in the proof of Proposition 10.7 is to extend the flow backwards a certain amount. As stated in the proposition, the amount of backward time that we can extend the flow is not uniform over all of \( {U}_{\infty } \) , but rather depends on the curvature of the point at time zero.

CLAIM 10.10. For each \( x \in  {U}_{n} \subset  {M}_{n} \) there is a flow line in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) through \( x \) defined on the time-interval \( \left( {-R{\left( x\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . Furthermore, the scalar curvature at any point of this flow line is less than or equal to the scalar curvature at \( x \) .

Proof. Since \( x \in  {U}_{n} \subset  {T}_{n} \) , there is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) centered at \( x \) . Both statements follow immediately from that.

Let \( X \subset  {U}_{\infty } \) be an open submanifold with compact closure and set

\[
{t}_{0}\left( X\right)  = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  X}}\left( {-{R}_{{g}_{\infty }}{\left( x\right) }^{-1}}\right) .
\]

Then for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {\varphi }_{n} \) is defined on \( X \) and the scalar curvature of the flow \( {g}_{n}\left( t\right) \) on \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( X\right)  \times  \left( {{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) is uniformly bounded independent of \( n \) . Thus, according to Proposition 5.14, by passing to a subsequence we can arrange that there is a limiting flow defined on \( X \times  \left( {{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) . Let \( {\mathcal{U}}_{\infty } \subset  {U}_{\infty } \times \; ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) consist of all pairs \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with the property that \( - {R}_{{g}_{\infty }}{\left( x,0\right) }^{-1} < t \leq \) 0 . Cover \( {\mathcal{U}}_{\infty } \) by countably many such boxes of the type \( X \times  \left( {-{t}_{0}\left( X\right) ,0}\right\rbrack \) as described above, and take a diagonal subsequence. This allows us to pass to a subsequence so that the limiting flow exists (as a generalized Ricci flow) on \( {\mathcal{U}}_{\infty } \) .

CLAIM 10.11. The curvature of the generalized Ricci flow on \( {\mathcal{U}}_{\infty } \) is nonnegative.

Proof. This claim follows from the fact that the original sequence \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) consists of generalized flows whose curvatures are pinched toward positive in the weak sense given in Equation (10.1) and the fact that \( {Q}_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) . (See Theorem 5.33.)

This completes the proof that all the properties claimed in Proposition 10.7 hold for the geometric limit \( \left( {{U}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{z}_{\infty }}\right) \) . This completes the proof of that proposition.

nodes.proof: A neighborhood of one end of \( {U}_{\infty } \) , the end \( {\bar{W}}_{\infty }^{ - } \) , is the limit of the negative halves of \( \epsilon \) -necks centered at \( {z}_{n}^{\prime } \) . Thus, the curvature is bounded on this neighborhood, and in fact is approximately equal to \( R\left( {z}_{\infty }\right) \) . Let \( {x}_{k} \) be any sequence of points in \( {U}_{\infty } \) tending to the other end. We show that \( R\left( {x}_{k}\right) \) tends to \( \infty \) as \( k \) does. The point is that since the sequence is tending to the end, the distance from \( {x}_{k} \) to the end of \( {U}_{\infty } \) is going to zero. Yet, each \( {x}_{k} \) is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( {U}_{\infty } \) . The only way this is possible is if the scales of these \( \epsilon \) -necks are converging to zero as \( k \) goes to infinity. This is equivalent to the statement that \( R\left( {x}_{k}\right) \) tends to \( \infty \) as \( k \) goes to infinity.

nodes.content: CLAIM 10.13. There is a minimizing geodesic ray to \( \mathcal{E} \) from each \( x \in  {U}_{\infty } \) with \( R\left( x\right)  \geq  2{Q}_{\infty } \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: CLAIM 10.13. There is a minimizing geodesic ray to \( \mathcal{E} \) from each \( x \in {U}_{\infty } \) with \( R\left( x\right) \geq 2{Q}_{\infty } \) .

nodes.proof: Fix \( x \) with \( R\left( x\right)  \geq  2{Q}_{\infty } \) and fix a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck \( {N}_{x} \) centered at \( x \) . Let \( {S}_{x}^{2} \) be the central 2-sphere of this neck. Take a sequence of points \( {q}_{n} \) tending to the end \( \mathcal{E} \) , each being closer to the end than \( x \) in the sense that \( {S}_{x}^{2} \) does not separate any \( {q}_{n} \) from the end \( \mathcal{E} \) . We claim that there is a minimizing geodesic from \( x \) to each \( {q}_{n} \) . The reason is that by Lemma A. 7 any minimizing sequence of arcs from \( x \) to \( {q}_{n} \) cannot exit from the minus end of \( {N}_{x} \) nor the plus end of a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( {q}_{n} \) . Consider a sequence of paths from \( x \) to \( {q}_{n} \) minimizing the distance. Hence these paths all lie in a fixed compact subset of \( {U}_{n} \) . After replacing the sequence by a subsequence, we can pass to a limit, which is clearly a minimizing geodesic from \( x \) to \( {q}_{n} \) . Consider minimizing geodesics \( {\mu }_{n} \) from \( x \) to \( {q}_{n} \) . The same argument shows that, after passing to a subsequence, the \( {\mu }_{n} \) converge to a minimizing geodesic ray from \( x \) to \( \mathcal{E} \) .

nodes.content:
CLAIM 10.14. (1) Any minimizing geodesic ray from \( x \) to the end \( \mathcal{E} \) is a shortest ray from \( x \) to the end \( \mathcal{E} \) , and conversely any shortest ray from \( x \) to the end \( \mathcal{E} \) is a minimizing geodesic ray.

(2) The length of a shortest ray from \( x \) to \( \mathcal{E} \) is the distance (see Section 4 of Chapter 2) from \( x \) to \( \mathcal{E} \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: CLAIM 10.14. (1) Any minimizing geodesic ray from \( x \) to the end \( \mathcal{E} \) is a shortest ray from \( x \) to the end \( \mathcal{E} \) , and conversely any shortest ray from \( x \) to the end \( \mathcal{E} \) is a minimizing geodesic ray. (2) The length of a shortest ray from \( x \) to \( \mathcal{E} \) is the distance (see Section 4 of Chapter 2) from \( x \) to \( \mathcal{E} \) .

nodes.proof:
The implication in (1) in one direction is clear: If \( \gamma \) is a ray from \( x \) to the end \( \mathcal{E} \) , and for some \( y \in  \gamma \) the segment on \( \gamma \) from \( x \) to \( y \) is not minimizing, then there is a shorter geodesic segment \( \mu \) from \( x \) to \( y \) . The union of this together with the ray on \( \gamma \) from \( y \) to the end is a shorter ray from \( x \) to the end.

Let us establish the opposite implication. Suppose that \( \gamma \) is a minimizing geodesic ray from \( x \) to the end \( \mathcal{E} \) and that there is a \( \delta  > 0 \) and a shortest geodesic ray \( {\gamma }^{\prime } \) from \( x \) to the end \( \mathcal{E} \) with \( \left| {\gamma }^{\prime }\right|  = \left| \gamma \right|  - \delta \) . As we have just seen, \( {\gamma }^{\prime } \) is a minimizing geodesic ray. Take a sequence of points \( {q}_{i} \) tending to the end \( \mathcal{E} \) and let \( {S}_{i}^{2} \) be the central 2-sphere in the \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( {q}_{i} \) . Of course, for all \( i \) sufficiently large, both \( {\gamma }^{\prime } \) and \( \gamma \) must cross \( {S}_{i}^{2} \) . Since the scalar curvature tends to infinity at the end \( \mathcal{E} \) , it follows from Lemma A. 4 that for all \( i \) sufficiently large, the extrinsic diameter of \( {S}_{i}^{2} \) is less than \( \delta /3 \) . Let \( {p}_{i} \) be a point of intersection of \( \gamma \) with \( {S}_{i}^{2} \) . For all \( i \) sufficiently large the length \( {d}_{i} \) of the sub-ray in \( \gamma \) from \( {p}_{i} \) to the end \( \mathcal{E} \) is at most \( \delta /3 \) . Let \( {p}_{i}^{\prime } \) be a point of intersection of \( {\gamma }^{\prime } \) with \( {S}_{i}^{2} \) and let \( {d}_{i}^{\prime } \) be the length of the ray in \( {\gamma }^{\prime } \) from \( {p}_{i}^{\prime } \) to the end \( \mathcal{E} \) . Let \( \lambda \) be the sub-geodesic of \( \gamma \) from \( x \) to \( {p}_{i} \) and \( {\lambda }^{\prime } \) the sub-geodesic of \( {\gamma }^{\prime } \) from \( x \) to \( {p}_{i}^{\prime } \) . Let \( \beta \) be a minimizing geodesic from \( {p}_{i}^{\prime } \) to \( {p}_{i} \) . Of course, \( \left| \beta \right|  < \delta /3 \) so that by the minimality of \( \lambda \) and \( {\lambda }^{\prime } \) we have

\[
- \delta /3 < \left| \lambda \right|  - \left| {\lambda }^{\prime }\right|  < \delta /3
\]

Since \( \left| {\lambda }^{\prime }\right|  + {d}_{i}^{\prime } = \left| \lambda \right|  + {d}_{i} - \delta \) , we have

\[
{2\delta }/3 \leq  {d}_{i} - {d}_{i}^{\prime }.
\]

This is absurd since \( {d}_{i}^{\prime } > 0 \) and \( {d}_{i} < \delta /3 \) .

(2) follows immediately from (1) and the definition.

nodes.content: DEFINITION 10.17. We say that two minimizing geodesic rays limiting to \( \mathcal{E} \) are equivalent if one is contained in the other. From the unique continuation of geodesics it is easy to see that this generates an equivalence relation. An equivalence class is a direction at \( \mathcal{E} \) , and the set of equivalence classes is the set of directions at \( \mathcal{E} \) .

LEMMA 10.21. For all \( \gamma , s,\mu ,{s}^{\prime } \) as in the previous definition we have

\[
0 \leq  \theta \left( {\gamma , s,\mu ,{s}^{\prime }}\right)  \leq  \pi
\]

Furthermore, \( \theta \left( {\gamma , s,\mu ,{s}^{\prime }}\right) \) is a non-increasing function of \( s \) when \( \gamma ,\mu ,{s}^{\prime } \) are held fixed, and symmetrically it is a non-increasing function of \( {s}^{\prime } \) when \( \gamma , s,\mu \) are held fixed. In particular, fixing \( \gamma \) and \( \mu \) , the function \( \theta \left( {\gamma , s,\mu ,{s}^{\prime }}\right) \) is nondecreasing as \( s \) and \( {s}^{\prime } \) tend to zero. Thus, there is a well-defined limit as \( s \) and \( {s}^{\prime } \) go to zero, denoted \( \theta \left( {\gamma ,\mu }\right) \) . This limit is greater than or equal to \( \theta \left( {\gamma , s,\mu ,{s}^{\prime }}\right) \) for all \( s \) and \( {s}^{\prime } \) for which the latter is defined. We have \( 0 \leq  \theta \left( {\gamma ,\mu }\right)  \leq  \pi \) . The angle \( \theta \left( {\gamma ,\mu }\right)  = 0 \) if and only if \( \gamma \) and \( \mu \) are equivalent. Furthermore, if \( \gamma \) is equivalent to \( {\gamma }^{\prime } \) and \( \mu \) is equivalent to \( {\mu }^{\prime } \) , then \( \theta \left( {\gamma ,\mu }\right)  = \; \theta \left( {{\gamma }^{\prime },{\mu }^{\prime }}\right) \) .

nodes.proof:
By restricting \( \gamma \) and \( \mu \) to slightly smaller rays, we can assume that each is the unique shortest ray from its endpoint to the end \( \mathcal{E} \) . Let \( x \) , resp., \( y \) be the endpoint of \( \gamma \) , resp., \( \mu \) . Now let \( {q}_{n} \) be any sequence of points in \( {U}_{\infty } \) limiting to the end \( \mathcal{E} \) , and consider minimizing geodesic rays \( {\gamma }_{n} \) from \( {q}_{n} \) to \( x \) and \( {\mu }_{n} \) from \( {q}_{n} \) to \( y \) , each parameterized by the distance from \( {q}_{n} \) . By passing to a subsequence we can assume that each of the sequences \( \left\{  {\gamma }_{n}\right\} \) and \( \left\{  {\mu }_{n}\right\} \) converge to a minimizing geodesic ray, which by uniqueness, implies that the first sequence limits to \( \gamma \) and the second to \( \mu \) . For \( s,{s}^{\prime } \) sufficiently small, let \( {\theta }_{n}\left( {s,{s}^{\prime }}\right) \) be the angle at \( {\widetilde{q}}_{n} \) of the Euclidean triangle \( {\alpha }_{n}{\widetilde{q}}_{n}{\beta }_{n} \) , where \( \left| {{\alpha }_{n}{\widetilde{q}}_{n}}\right|  = d\left( {{\gamma }_{n}\left( s\right) ,{q}_{n}}\right) ,\left| {{\beta }_{n}{\widetilde{q}}_{n}}\right|  = d\left( {{\mu }_{n}\left( {s}^{\prime }\right) ,{q}_{n}}\right) \) and \( \left| {{\alpha }_{n}{\beta }_{n}}\right|  = d\left( {{\gamma }_{n}\left( s\right) ,{\mu }_{n}\left( {s}^{\prime }\right) }\right) \) . Clearly, for fixed \( s \) and \( {s}^{\prime } \) sufficiently small, \( {\theta }_{n}\left( {s,{s}^{\prime }}\right) \) converges as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) to \( \theta \left( {\gamma , s,\mu ,{s}^{\prime }}\right) \) . By the Toponogov property (Theorem 2.4) for manifolds with non-negative curvature, for each \( n \) the function \( {\theta }_{n}\left( {s,{s}^{\prime }}\right) \) is a non-increasing function of each variable, when the other is held fixed. This property then passes to the limit, giving the first statement in the lemma.

By the monotonicity, \( \theta \left( {\gamma ,\mu }\right)  = 0 \) if and only if for all \( s,{s}^{\prime } \) sufficiently small we have \( \theta \left( {\gamma , s,\mu ,{s}^{\prime }}\right)  = 0 \) , which means one of \( \gamma \) and \( \mu \) is contained in the other.

It is obvious that the last statement holds.

It follows that \( \theta \left( {\gamma ,\mu }\right) \) yields a well-defined function on the set of pairs of directions at \( \mathcal{E} \) . It is clearly a symmetric, non-negative function which is positive off of the diagonal. The next lemma shows that it is a metric by establishing the triangle inequality for \( \theta \) .

nodes.proof:
It suffices to prove that given any subsequence of the original sequence, the result holds for a further subsequence. So let us replace the given sequence by a subsequence. Recall that for each \( 0 < r < R < \infty \) we have \( {A}_{\mathcal{E}}\left( {r, R}\right)  \subset  {C}_{\mathcal{E}}^{\prime } \) , the compact annulus which is the image of \( \bar{X}\left( \mathcal{E}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {r, R}\right\rbrack \) . The statement about the non-compact spaces converging in the Gromov-Hausdorff topology, means that for each compact subspace \( K \) of \( {C}_{\mathcal{E}}^{\prime } \) containing the base point, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, there are compact subspaces \( {K}_{n} \subset  \left( {{U}_{\infty },{\lambda }_{n}{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) containing \( {x}_{n} \) with the property that the \( \left( {{K}_{n},{x}_{n}}\right) \) converge in the Gromov-Hausdorff topology to \( \left( {K, x}\right) \) (see Section D of Chapter 3, p. 39, of [25]).

Because of this, it suffices to fix \( 0 < r < 1 < R < \infty \) arbitrarily and prove the convergence result for \( {A}_{\mathcal{E}}\left( {r, R}\right) \) . Since the Gromov-Hausdorff distance from a compact pointed metric space to a \( \delta \) -net in it containing the base point is at most \( \delta \) , it suffices to prove that for \( \delta  > 0 \) there is a \( \delta \) -net \( \left( {\mathcal{N}, h}\right) \) in \( {A}_{\mathcal{E}}\left( {r, R}\right) \) , with \( \left( {\left\lbrack  \gamma \right\rbrack  ,1}\right)  \in  \mathcal{N} \) such that for all \( n \) sufficiently large there are embeddings \( {\varphi }_{n} \) of \( \mathcal{N} \) into \( {A}_{n}\left( {r, R}\right)  = {\bar{B}}_{{\lambda }_{n}{g}_{\infty }}\left( {\mathcal{E}, R}\right)  \smallsetminus  {B}_{{\lambda }_{n}{g}_{\infty }}\left( {\mathcal{E}, r}\right) \) with the following four properties:

(1) \( {\varphi }_{n}^{ * }\left( {{\lambda }_{n}{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) converge to \( h \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) ,

(2) \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( {\left\lbrack  \gamma \right\rbrack  ,1}\right)  = {x}_{n} \) ,

(3) \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( \mathcal{N}\right) \) is a \( \delta \) -net in \( {A}_{n}\left( {r, R}\right) \) , and

(4) denoting the cone point by \( c \in  {C}_{\mathcal{E}} \) , if \( d\left( {p, c}\right)  = r \) then \( d\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( p\right) ,\mathcal{E}}\right)  = \; r \) .

According to Corollary 10.28 there is a \( \delta \) -net \( \mathcal{N} \subset  {A}_{\mathcal{E}}\left( {r, R}\right) \) consisting of points \( \left( {{\ell }_{i},{s}_{i}}\right) \) where the \( {\ell }_{i} \) are realizable directions and \( r < {s}_{i} < R \) . Add \( \left( {\left\lbrack  \gamma \right\rbrack  ,1}\right) \) to \( \mathcal{N} \) if necessary so that we can assume that \( \left( {\left\lbrack  \gamma \right\rbrack  ,1}\right)  \in  \mathcal{N} \) . Let \( {\gamma }_{i} \) be a minimizing geodesic realizing \( {\ell }_{i} \) and let \( {d}_{i} \) be its length.

Fix \( n \) sufficiently large so that \( {\lambda }_{n}^{-1/2}R \leq  {d}_{i} \) for all \( i \) . We define \( {\varphi }_{n} : \mathcal{N} \rightarrow \; {A}_{n}\left( {r, R}\right) \) as follows. For any \( {a}_{i} = \left( {\left\lbrack  {\gamma }_{i}\right\rbrack  ,{s}_{i}}\right)  \in  \mathcal{N} \) we let \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( {a}_{i}\right)  = {\gamma }_{i}\left( {{\lambda }_{n}^{-1/2}{s}_{i}}\right) \) . (Since \( {\lambda }_{n}^{-1/2}s \leq  {\lambda }_{n}^{-1/2}R \leq  {d}_{i} \) , the geodesic \( {\gamma }_{i} \) is defined at \( {\lambda }_{n}^{-1/2}{s}_{i} \) .) This defines the embeddings \( {\varphi }_{n} \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large. Notice that

\[
{d}_{{g}_{\infty }}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( {{\ell }_{i},{s}_{i}}\right) ,{\varphi }_{n}\left( {{\ell }_{j},{s}_{j}}\right) }\right)  = {\lambda }_{n}^{-1}{s}_{i}^{2} + {\lambda }_{n}^{-1}{s}_{j}^{2} - 2{\lambda }_{n}^{-1}{s}_{i}{s}_{j}{\theta }_{ij}\left( {{\lambda }_{n}^{-1/2}{s}_{i},{\lambda }_{n}^{-1/2}{s}_{j}}\right) ,
\]

or equivalently

\[
{d}_{{\lambda }_{n}{g}_{\infty }}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( {{\ell }_{i},{s}_{i}}\right) ,{\varphi }_{n}\left( {{\ell }_{j},{s}_{j}}\right) }\right)  = {s}_{i}^{2} + {s}_{j}^{2} - 2{s}_{i}{s}_{j}{\theta }_{ij}\left( {{\lambda }_{n}^{-1/2}{s}_{i},{\lambda }_{n}^{-1/2}{s}_{j}}\right) .
\]

Here, \( {\theta }_{ij}\left( {{\lambda }_{n}^{-1/2}{s}_{i},{\lambda }_{n}^{-1/2}{s}_{j}}\right) \) is the comparison angle between the point at distance \( {\lambda }_{n}^{-1/2}{s}_{i} \) along \( {\gamma }_{i} \) , the point \( p \) , and the point at distance \( {\lambda }_{n}^{-1/2}{s}_{j} \) along \( {\gamma }_{j} \) . ( Because of the convergence result on angles (Lemma 10.21), for all \( i \) and \( j \) we have

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}{d}_{{\lambda }_{n}{g}_{\infty }}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( {{\ell }_{i},{s}_{i}}\right) ,{\varphi }_{n}\left( {{\ell }_{j},{s}_{j}}\right) }\right)  = {s}_{i}^{2} + {s}_{j}^{2} - 2{s}_{i}{s}_{j}\cos \left( {\theta \left( {{\gamma }_{i},{\gamma }_{j}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= {d}_{{g}_{\mathcal{E}}}\left( {\left( {{\ell }_{i},{s}_{i}}\right) ,\left( {{\ell }_{j},{s}_{j}}\right) }\right) .
\]

This establishes the existence of the \( {\varphi }_{n} \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large satisfying the first condition. Clearly, from the definition \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( {\left\lbrack  \gamma \right\rbrack  ,1}\right)  = {x}_{n} \) , and for all \( p \in  \mathcal{N} \) we have \( d\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( p\right) ,\mathcal{E}}\right)  = d\left( {p, c}\right) \) .

It remains to check that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( \mathcal{N}\right) \) is a \( \delta \) -net in \( {A}_{n}\left( {r, R}\right) \) . For \( n \) sufficiently large let \( z \in  {A}_{n}\left( {r, R}\right) \) and let \( {\gamma }_{z} \) be a minimizing geodesic ray from \( z \) to \( \mathcal{E} \) parameterized by the distance from the end. Set \( {d}_{n} = {d}_{{\lambda }_{n}{g}_{\infty }}\left( {z,\mathcal{E}}\right) \) , so that \( r \leq  {d}_{n} \leq  R \) . Fix \( n \) sufficiently large so that \( {\lambda }_{n}^{-1/2}R < {d}_{i} \) for all \( i \) . The point \( \left( {\left\lbrack  {\gamma }_{z}\right\rbrack  ,{d}_{n}}\right)  \in  {C}_{\mathcal{E}} \) is contained in \( {A}_{\mathcal{E}}\left( {r, R}\right) \) and hence there is an element \( a = \left( {\left\lbrack  {\gamma }_{i}\right\rbrack  ,{s}_{i}}\right)  \in  \mathcal{N} \) within distance \( \delta \) of \( \left( {\left\lbrack  {\gamma }_{z}\right\rbrack  ,{d}_{n}}\right) \) in \( {C}_{\mathcal{E}} \) . Since \( {s}_{i} \leq  R,{\lambda }_{n}^{-1/2}{s}_{i} \leq  {d}_{i} \) and hence \( x = {\gamma }_{i}\left( {{\lambda }_{n}^{-1/2}{s}_{i}}\right) \) is defined. By Corollary 10.26 we have

\[
{d}_{{\lambda }_{n}{g}_{\infty }}\left( {x, z}\right)  \leq  {d}_{{g}_{\mathcal{E}}}\left( {\left( {\left\lbrack  \gamma \right\rbrack  ,{d}_{n}}\right) ,\left( {\left\lbrack  {\gamma }_{i}\right\rbrack  ,{s}_{i}}\right) }\right)  \leq  \delta .
\]

This completes the proof that for \( n \) sufficiently large the image \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( \mathcal{N}\right) \) is a \( \delta \) -net in \( {A}_{n}\left( {r, R}\right) \) .

This shows that the \( \left( {{U}_{\infty },{\lambda }_{n}{g}_{\infty },{x}_{n}}\right) \) converge in the Gromov-Hausdorff topology to \( \left( {{C}_{\mathcal{E}}^{\prime },{g}_{\mathcal{E}},\left( {\left\lbrack  \gamma \right\rbrack  ,1}\right) }\right) \) .

nodes.content: REMARK 10.30. Notice that since the manifolds \( \left( {{U}_{\infty },{\lambda }_{n}{g}_{\infty },{x}_{n}}\right) \) are not complete, there can be more than one Gromov-Hausdorff limit. For example we could take the full cone as a limit. Indeed, the cone is the only Gromov-Hausdorff limit that is complete as a metric space.

nodes.proof:
Since there is a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n} \) , according to Proposition A.11 the distance \( {\lambda }_{n}^{-1/2} \) from \( {x}_{n} \) to \( \mathcal{E} \) is at least \( R{\left( {x}_{n}\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1}/2 = \; {\left( {\lambda }_{n}^{\prime }\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1}/2 \) . Thus,

\[
{\rho }_{n}^{-1} = {\lambda }_{n}/{\lambda }_{n}^{\prime } \leq  4{\epsilon }^{2}.
\]

On the other hand, suppose that \( {\rho }_{n} = {\lambda }_{n}^{\prime }/{\lambda }_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) . Rescale by \( {\lambda }_{n}^{\prime } \) so that \( R\left( {x}_{n}\right)  = 1 \) . The distance from \( {x}_{n} \) to \( \mathcal{E} \) is \( \sqrt{{\rho }_{n}} \) . Then by Lemma A. 4 with respect to this metric there is a sphere of diameter at most \( {2\pi } \) through \( {x}_{n} \) that separates all points at distance at most \( \sqrt{{\rho }_{n}} - {\epsilon }^{-1} \) from \( \mathcal{E} \) from all points at distance at least \( \sqrt{{\rho }_{n}} + {\epsilon }^{-1} \) from \( \mathcal{E} \) . Now rescale the metric by \( {\rho }_{n} \) . In the rescaled metric there is a 2-sphere of diameter at most \( {2\pi }/\sqrt{{\rho }_{n}} \) through \( {x}_{n} \) that separates all points at distance at most \( 1 - {\epsilon }^{-1}/\sqrt{{\rho }_{n}} \) from \( \mathcal{E} \) from all points at distance at least \( 1 + {\epsilon }^{-1}/\sqrt{{\rho }_{n}} \) from \( \mathcal{E} \) . Taking the Gromov-Hausdorff limit of these spaces, we see that the base point \( {x}_{\infty } \) separates all points of distance less than 1 from \( \mathcal{E} \) from all points of distance greater than 1 from \( \mathcal{E} \) . This is impossible since the Gromov-Hausdorff limit is a cone that is not the cone on a single point.

nodes.content:
THEOREM 11.1. Fix canonical neighborhood constants \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) , and non-collapsing constants \( r > 0,\kappa  > 0 \) . Let \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n},{x}_{n}}\right) \) be a sequence of based generalized 3-dimensional Ricci flows. We set \( {t}_{n} = \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right) \) and \( {Q}_{n} = R\left( {x}_{n}\right) \) . We denote by \( {M}_{n} \) the \( {t}_{n} \) time-slice of \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . We suppose that:

(1) Each \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) either has a time interval of definition contained in \( \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) and has curvature pinched toward positive, or has nonnegative curvature.

(2) Every point \( {y}_{n} \in  \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) with \( \mathbf{t}\left( {y}_{n}\right)  \leq  {t}_{n} \) and with \( R\left( {y}_{n}\right)  \geq \; {4R}\left( {x}_{n}\right) \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood.

(3) \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}{Q}_{n} = \infty \) .

(4) For each \( A < \infty \) the following holds for all \( n \) sufficiently large. The ball \( B\left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) has compact closure in \( {M}_{n} \) and the flow is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed on scales \( \leq  r \) at each point of \( B\left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) .

(5) There is \( \mu  > 0 \) such that for every \( A < \infty \) the following holds for all \( n \) sufficiently large. For every \( {y}_{n} \in  B\left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) the maximal flow line through \( {y}_{n} \) extends backwards for a time at least \( \mu {\left( \max \left( {Q}_{n}, R\left( {y}_{n}\right) \right) \right) }^{-1} \) .

Then, after passing to a subsequence and shifting the times of each of the generalized flows so that \( {t}_{n} = 0 \) for every \( n \) , there is a geometric limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) of the sequence \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{n}}\right) \) of based Riemannian manifolds. This limit is a complete 3-dimensional Riemannian manifold of bounded, non-negative curvature. Furthermore, for some \( {t}_{0} > 0 \) which depends on the curvature bound for \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) and on \( \mu \) , there is a geometric limit Ricci flow defined on \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , - {t}_{0} \leq  t \leq  0 \) , with \( {g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right)  = {g}_{\infty } \) .

LEMMA 11.2. Let \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) be a generalized 3-dimensional Ricci flow. Suppose that \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) and that any \( z \in  \mathcal{M} \) with \( R\left( z\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Suppose \( z \in  \mathcal{M} \) and \( \mathbf{t}\left( z\right)  = {t}_{0} \) . Set

\[
r = \frac{1}{{2C}\sqrt{\max \left( {R\left( z\right) ,{r}_{0}^{-2}}\right) }}
\]

and

\[
{\Delta t} = \frac{1}{{16C}\left( {R\left( z\right)  + {r}_{0}^{-2}}\right) }.
\]

Suppose that \( {r}^{\prime } \leq  r \) and that \( \left| {{t}^{\prime } - {t}_{0}}\right|  \leq  {\Delta t} \) and let \( I \) be the interval with endpoints \( {t}_{0} \) and \( {t}^{\prime } \) . Suppose that there is an embedding of \( j : B\left( {z,{t}_{0},{r}^{\prime }}\right)  \times \) I into \( \mathcal{M} \) compatible with time and with the vector field. Then \( R\left( y\right)  \leq \; 2\left( {R\left( z\right)  + {r}_{0}^{-2}}\right) \) for all \( y \) in the image of \( j \) .

\[
R\left( y\right)  \leq  \frac{16}{9}\left( {R\left( z\right)  + {r}_{0}^{-2}}\right) .
\]

Let \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,{s}_{0}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  B\left( {z,{t}_{0}, r}\right) \) be a path of length \( {s}_{0} < r \) connecting \( z = \gamma \left( 0\right) \) to \( y = \gamma \left( {s}_{0}\right) \) . We take \( \gamma \) parameterized by arc length. For any \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{s}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) let \( R\left( s\right)  = R\left( {\gamma \left( s\right) }\right) \) . According to the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption at any point where \( R\left( s\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) we have \( \left| {{R}^{\prime }\left( s\right) }\right|  \leq  C{R}^{3/2}\left( s\right) \) . Let \( J \subset  \left\lbrack  {0,{s}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) be the closed subset consisting of \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{s}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) for which \( R\left( s\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . There are three possibilities. If \( {s}_{0} \notin  J \) then \( R\left( y\right)  \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) and we have established Inequality (11.1). If \( J = \left\lbrack  {0,{s}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , then we have \( \left| {{R}^{\prime }\left( s\right) }\right|  \leq  C{R}^{3/2}\left( s\right) \) for all \( s \) in \( J \) . Using this differential inequality and the fact that the interval has length at most \( \frac{1}{{2C}\sqrt{R\left( z\right) }} \) , we see that \( R\left( y\right)  \leq  {16R}\left( z\right) /9 \) , again establishing Inequality (11.1). The last possibility is that \( J \neq  \left\lbrack  {0,{s}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) but \( {s}_{0} \in  J \) . We restrict attention to the maximal interval of \( J \) containing \( {s}_{0} \) . This interval has length at most \( \frac{{r}_{0}}{2C} \) and at its initial point \( R \) takes the value \( {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . For every \( s \) in this interval by our assumptions we again have the inequality \( \left| {{R}^{\prime }\left( s\right) }\right|  \leq  C{R}^{3/2}\left( s\right) \) ; it follows immediately that \( R\left( y\right)  \leq  {16}{r}_{0}^{-2}/9 \) . This establishes Inequality (11.1) in all cases.

Now consider the vertical path \( j\left( {\{ y\}  \times  I}\right) \) . Let \( R\left( t\right)  = R\left( {j\left( {y, t}\right) }\right) \) . Again by the strong canonical neighborhood assumption \( \left| {{R}^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right|  \leq  C{R}^{2}\left( t\right) \) at all points where \( R\left( t\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . Consider the closed subset \( K \) of \( I \) where \( R\left( t\right)  \geq \; {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . There are three cases to consider: \( {t}^{\prime } \notin  K,{t}^{\prime } \in  K \neq  I \) , or \( K = I \) . In the first case, \( R\left( {y,{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) and we have established the result. In the second case, let \( {K}^{\prime } \) be the maximal subinterval of \( K \) containing \( {t}^{\prime } \) . On the interval \( {K}^{\prime } \) we have \( \left| {{R}^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right|  \leq  C{R}^{2}\left( t\right) \) and at one endpoint \( R\left( t\right)  = {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . Since this interval has length at most \( {r}_{0}^{2}/{16C} \) , it follows easily that \( R\left( {t}^{\prime }\right)  \leq  {16}{r}_{0}^{-2}/{15} \) , establishing the result. In the last case where \( K = I \) , then, by what we established above, the initial condition is \( R\left( {t}_{0}\right)  = R\left( y\right)  \leq  {16}\left( {R\left( z\right)  + {r}_{0}^{-2}}\right) /9 \) , and the differential inequality \( \left| {{R}^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right|  \leq  C{R}^{2}\left( t\right) \) holds for all \( t \in  I \) . Since the length of \( I \) is at most \( \frac{1}{{16C}\left( {R\left( y\right)  + {r}_{0}^{-2}}\right) } \) we see directly that \( R\left( {t}^{\prime }\right)  \leq  2\left( {R\left( z\right)  + {r}_{0}^{-2}}\right) \) , completing the proof in this case as well.

Let \( q \in  {M}_{\infty } \) be a point with \( {R}_{{g}_{\infty }}\left( q\right)  > 4 \) . Then for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( q \in  {V}_{n} \) , so that \( {q}_{n} = {\varphi }_{n}\left( q\right) \) is defined, and \( {R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {q}_{n}\right)  > 4 \) . Thus, \( {q}_{n} \) has an \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood, \( {U}_{n} \) , in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) ; and, since \( R\left( {q}_{n}\right)  > 4 \) for all \( n \) , there is a uniform bound to the distance from any point of \( {U}_{n} \) to \( {q}_{n} \) . Thus, there exists \( m \) such that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( {V}_{m}\right) \) contains \( {U}_{n} \) . Clearly as \( n \) goes to infinity the Riemannian metrics \( {\left. {\varphi }_{n}^{ * }\left( {G}_{n}\right) \right| }_{{\varphi }_{n}^{-1}\left( {U}_{m}\right) } \) converge smoothly to \( {\left. {g}_{\infty }\right| }_{{\varphi }_{n}^{-1}\left( {U}_{n}\right) } \) . Thus, by Proposition 9.79 for all \( n \) sufficiently large the restriction of \( {g}_{\infty } \) to \( {\varphi }_{n}^{-1}\left( {U}_{n}\right) \) contains a \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -canonical neighborhood of \( q \) .

nodes.content: CLAIM 11.7. The limit Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature.
nodes.content_excerpt: CLAIM 11.7. The limit Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature.

nodes.proof:
Suppose that \( y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) has the property that \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( y\right) \) has a zero eigenvalue. Fix \( A < \infty \) greater than \( {d}_{{g}_{\infty }}\left( {{x}_{\infty }, y}\right) \) . Then applying Corollary 4.19 to the limit flow on \( B\left( {{x}_{\infty },0, A}\right)  \times  ( - t\left( A\right) ,0\rbrack \) , we see that the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {B\left( {{x}_{\infty },0, A}\right) ,{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) is locally a Riemannian product of a compact surface of positive curvature with a one-manifold. Since this is true for every \( A < \infty \) sufficiently large, the same is true for \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) . Hence \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) has a one- or two-sheeted covering that is a global Riemannian product of a compact surface and one-manifold. Clearly, in this case the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) is bounded.

If \( {M}_{\infty } \) is compact, then it is clear that the curvature is bounded.

It remains to consider the case where \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) is non-compact and of strictly positive curvature. Since any point of curvature greater than 4 has a \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -canonical neighborhood, and since \( {M}_{\infty } \) is non-compact, it follows that the only possible canonical neighborhoods for \( x \in  {M}_{\infty } \) are a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( x \) or \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -cap whose core contains \( x \) . Each of these canonical neighborhoods contains a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck. Thus, if \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) has unbounded and positive Riemann curvature or equivalently, it has unbounded scalar curvature, then it has \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -canonical neighborhoods of arbitrarily small scale, and hence \( {2\epsilon } \) -necks of arbitrarily small scale. But this contradicts Proposition 2.19. It follows from this contradiction that the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) is bounded.

THEOREM 11.8. Suppose that \( {\left\{  \left( {\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n},{x}_{n}\right) \right\}  }_{n = 1}^{\infty } \) is a sequence of generalized 3-dimensional Ricci flows satisfying the hypotheses of Theorem 11.1. Suppose in addition that there is \( {T}_{0} \) with \( 0 < {T}_{0} \leq  \infty \) such that the following holds. For any \( T < {T}_{0} \) , for each \( A < \infty \) , and all \( n \) sufficiently large, there is an embedding \( B\left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right)  \times  \left( {{t}_{n} - T{Q}_{n}^{-1},{t}_{n}}\right\rbrack \) into \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) compatible with time and with the vector field and at every point of the image the generalized flow is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed on scales \( \leq  r \) . Then, after shifting the times of the generalized flows so that \( {t}_{n} = 0 \) for all \( n \) and passing to a subsequence there is a geometric limit Ricci flow

\[
\left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) , - {T}_{0} < t \leq  0,
\]

for the rescaled generalized flows \( \left( {{Q}_{n}{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n},{x}_{n}}\right) \) . This limit flow is complete and of non-negative curvature. Furthermore, the curvature is locally bounded in time. If in addition \( {T}_{0} = \infty \) , then it is a \( \kappa \) -solution.

In Theorem 11.1 we proved that, after passing to a subsequence, there is a geometric limit Ricci flow, complete of bounded non-negative curvature,

\[
\left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) , - {t}_{0} \leq  t \leq  0,
\]

nodes.content: REMARK 11.9. Let us point out the differences between this result and Theorem 11.1. The hypotheses of this theorem include all the hypotheses of Theorem 11.1. The main difference between the conclusions is that in Theorem 11.1 the amount of backward time for which the limit flow is defined depends on the curvature bound for the final time-slice of the limit (as well as how far back the flows in the sequence are defined). This amount of backward time tends to zero as the curvature of the final time-slice limit tends to infinity. Here, the amount of backward time for which the limit flow is defined depends only on how far backwards the flows in the sequence are defined.

nodes.proof:
The argument is by contradiction, so we suppose that there is a \( T < {T}_{0} \) as in the statement of the proposition. Then the geometric limit flow on \( ( - T,0\rbrack \) is complete of non-negative curvature and with the curvature locally bounded in time. First suppose that the scalar curvature is bounded by, say \( Q < \infty \) . Fix \( {T}^{\prime } < T \) . The Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {T}^{\prime }\right) }\right) \) is complete of non-negative curvature with the scalar curvature, and hence the norm of the Riemann curvature, bounded by \( Q \) . Thus, for any \( A < \infty \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the norm of the Riemann curvature of \( {Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( {-{T}^{\prime }}\right) \) on \( {B}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n}, - T, A}\right) \) is bounded above by \( {2Q} \) . Also, arguing as in the proof of Theorem 11.1 we see that any point \( y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) with \( R\left( {y, - {T}^{\prime }}\right)  > 4 \) has a \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Hence, applying Lemma 11.2 as in the argument in the proof of Corollary 11.3 shows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, every point in \( {B}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n}, - {T}^{\prime }, A}\right) \) has a uniform size parabolic neighborhood on which the Riemann curvature is uniformly bounded, where both the time interval in the parabolic neighborhood and the curvature bound on this neighborhood depend only on \( C \) and the curvature bound on \( Q \) for the limit flow. According to Hamilton's result (Proposition 5.14) this implies that, by passing to a further subsequence, we can extend the limit flow backward beyond \( - {T}^{\prime } \) a uniform amount of time, say \( {2\delta } \) . Taking \( {T}^{\prime } > T - \delta \) then gives the desired extension under the condition that the scalar curvature is bounded on \( ( - T,0\rbrack \) .

It remains to show that, provided that \( T < {T}_{0} \) , the scalar curvature of the limit flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , - T < t \leq  0 \) , is bounded. To establish this we need a couple of preliminary results.

nodes.proof:
Let us begin with:

CLAIM 11.12. Let \( Q \) be an upper bound on \( R\left( {x,0}\right) \) for all \( x \in  {M}_{\infty } \) . Then for any points \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and any \( t \in  ( - T,0\rbrack \) we have

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {d}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  + {16}\sqrt{\frac{Q}{3}}T.
\]

Proof. Fix \( - {t}_{0} \in  ( - T,0\rbrack \) . Then for any \( \epsilon  > 0 \) sufficiently small, by the Harnack inequality (the second result in Theorem 4.37) we have

\[
\frac{\partial R}{\partial t}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq   - \frac{R\left( {x, t}\right) }{t + T - \epsilon }.
\]

Taking the limit as \( \epsilon  \rightarrow  0 \) gives

\[
\frac{\partial R}{\partial t}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq   - \frac{R\left( {x, t}\right) }{t + T},
\]

and hence, fixing \( x \) ,

\[
\frac{{dR}\left( {x, t}\right) }{R\left( {x, t}\right) } \geq  \frac{-{dt}}{\left( t + T\right) }.
\]

Integrating from \( - {t}_{0} \) to 0 shows that

\[
\log \left( {R\left( {x,0}\right) }\right)  - \log \left( {R\left( {x, - {t}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  \log \left( {T - {t}_{0}}\right)  - \log \left( T\right) ,
\]

and since \( R\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  Q \) , this implies

\[
R\left( {x, - {t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  Q\frac{T}{T - {t}_{0}}.
\]

Recalling that \( n = 3 \) and that the curvature is non-negative we see that

\[
\operatorname{Ric}\left( {x, - {t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \left( {n - 1}\right) \frac{QT}{2}\frac{1}{T - {t}_{0}}.
\]

Hence by Corollary 3.26, for all \( - {t}_{0} \in  ( - T,0\rbrack \) we have that

\[
{\operatorname{dist}}_{-{t}_{0}}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {\operatorname{dist}}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  + 8{\int }_{-{t}_{0}}^{0}\sqrt{\frac{QT}{3\left( {T + t}\right) }} \leq  {\operatorname{dist}}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  + {16}\sqrt{\frac{Q}{3}}T.
\]

It follows immediately from this claim that any compact subset \( X \subset  {M}_{\infty } \) has uniformly bounded diameter under all the metrics \( {g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) , - T < t \leq  0 \) .

By the hypothesis of the lemma there is a constant \( {C}^{\prime } < \infty \) such that for each \( t \in  ( - T,0\rbrack \) there is \( {y}_{t} \in  X \) with \( {R}_{{g}_{\infty }}\left( {{y}_{t}, t}\right)  \leq  {C}^{\prime } \) . Suppose that the conclusion of the lemma does not hold. Then there is a sequence \( {t}_{m} \rightarrow   - T \) as \( m \rightarrow  \infty \) and points \( {z}_{m} \in  X \) such that \( {R}_{{g}_{\infty }}\left( {{z}_{m},{t}_{m}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( m \rightarrow  \infty \) . In this case, possibly after redefining the constant \( {C}^{\prime } \) , we can also assume that there is a point \( {y}_{m} \) such that \( 2 \leq  R\left( {{y}_{m},{t}_{m}}\right)  \leq  {C}^{\prime } \) . Since the sequence \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n},{x}_{n}}\right) \) converges smoothly to \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) for \( t \in  ( - T,0\rbrack \) , it follows that for each \( m \) there are sequences \( {\left\{  {y}_{m, n} \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{n}\right\}  }_{n = 1}^{\infty } \) and \( \left\{  {{z}_{m, n} \in  }\right. \; {\left. {\mathcal{M}}_{n}\right\}  }_{n = 1}^{\infty } \) with \( \mathbf{t}\left( {y}_{m, n}\right)  = \mathbf{t}\left( {z}_{m, n}\right)  = {t}_{m} \) converging to \( \left( {{y}_{m},{t}_{m}}\right) \) and \( \left( {{z}_{m},{t}_{m}}\right) \) respectively. Thus, for all \( m \) there is \( {n}_{0} = {n}_{0}\left( m\right) \) such that for all \( n \geq  {n}_{0} \) we have:

(1) \( 1 \leq  {R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {y}_{m, n}\right)  \leq  2{C}^{\prime } \) ,

(2) \( {R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {z}_{m, n}\right)  \geq  {R}_{{g}_{\infty }}\left( {{z}_{m},{t}_{m}}\right) /2 \) ,

(3) \( {d}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {\left( {y}_{m, n}\right) ,\left( {z}_{m, n}\right) }\right)  \leq  2{\operatorname{diam}}_{{g}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{m}\right) }\left( X\right) \) .

It follows from the third condition and the fact that \( X \) has uniformly bounded diameter under all the metrics \( {g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) \) for \( t \in  ( - T,0\rbrack \) , that the distance \( {d}_{{Q}_{m, n}{G}_{m, n}}\left( {{z}_{m, n},{y}_{m, n}}\right) \) is bounded independent of \( m \) and \( n \) as long as \( n \geq  {n}_{0} \) . Because of the fact that \( {R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {y}_{m, n}\right)  \geq  1 = R\left( {x}_{n}\right) \) , it follows that any point \( z \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) with \( \mathbf{t}\left( {z}_{m}\right)  \leq  {t}_{m} \) and with \( R\left( z\right)  \geq  {4R}\left( {y}_{m, n}\right) \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. This then contradicts Theorem 10.2 and completes the proof of the lemma.

Clearly, this argument will be enough to handle the case when \( {M}_{\infty } \) is compact. The case when \( {M}_{\infty } \) is non-compact uses additional results.

nodes.content: LEMMA 11.13. Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a complete, connected, non-compact manifold of non-negative sectional curvature and let \( {x}_{0} \in  M \) be a point. Then there is \( D > 0 \) , such that for any \( y \in  M \) with \( d\left( {{x}_{0}, y}\right)  = d \geq  D \) , there is \( x \in  M \) with \( d\left( {y, x}\right)  = d \) and with \( d\left( {{x}_{0}, x}\right)  > {3d}/2 \) .

nodes.proof: Suppose that the result is false for \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) and \( x \in  M \) . Then there is a sequence \( {y}_{n} \in  M \) with the following property. Let \( {d}_{n} = d\left( {x,{y}_{n}}\right) \) . Then \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}{d}_{n} = \infty \) and yet \( B\left( {{y}_{n},{d}_{n}}\right)  \subset  B\left( {x,3{d}_{n}/2}\right) \) for every \( n \) . Let \( {\gamma }_{n} \) be a minimal geodesic from \( x \) to \( {y}_{n} \) . By passing to a subsequence we arrange that the \( {\gamma }_{n} \) converge to a minimal geodesic ray \( \gamma \) from \( x \) to infinity in \( M \) . In particular, the angle at \( x \) between \( {\gamma }_{n} \) and \( \gamma \) tends to zero as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) . Let \( {w}_{n} \) be the point on \( \gamma \) at distance \( {d}_{n} \) from \( x \) , and let \( {\alpha }_{n} = d\left( {{y}_{n},{w}_{n}}\right) \) . Because \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) has non-negative curvature, by Corollary 2.5, \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}{\alpha }_{n}/{d}_{n} = 0 \) . In particular, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( {\alpha }_{n} < {d}_{n} \) . This implies that there is a point \( {z}_{n} \) on the sub-ray of \( \gamma \) with endpoint \( {w}_{n} \) at distance \( {d}_{n} \) from \( {y}_{n} \) . By the triangle inequality, \( d\left( {{w}_{n},{z}_{n}}\right)  \geq  {d}_{n} - {\alpha }_{n} \) . Since \( \gamma \) is a minimal geodesic ray, \( d\left( {z,{z}_{n}}\right)  = d\left( {z,{w}_{n}}\right)  + d\left( {{w}_{n},{z}_{n}}\right)  \geq  2{d}_{n} - {\alpha }_{n} \) . Since \( {\alpha }_{n}/{d}_{n} \rightarrow  0 \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) , it follows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( d\left( {z,{z}_{n}}\right)  > 3{d}_{n}/2 \) . This contradiction proves the lemma.

nodes.proof:
Let \( \mathcal{C} \) be a \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -canonical neighborhood of \( y \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Since \( R\left( {y, t}\right) \) can be arbitrarily large, we can assume that \( d \gg  {2CR}{\left( y\right) }^{-1/2} \) , which is a bound on the diameter of \( \mathcal{C} \) . This implies that minimal \( g\left( t\right) \) -geodesics \( {\gamma }_{{x}_{\infty }} \) and \( {\gamma }_{z} \) connecting \( y \) to \( {x}_{\infty } \) and to \( z \) , respectively, must exit from \( \mathcal{C} \) . Let \( a \) be a point on \( {\gamma }_{{x}_{\infty }} \cap  \mathcal{C} \) close to the complement of \( \mathcal{C} \) . Let \( b \) be a point at the same \( g\left( t\right) \) -distance from \( y \) on \( {\gamma }_{z} \) . In the case that \( \mathcal{C} \) is a cap or that it is a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck and \( {\gamma }_{{x}_{\infty }} \) and \( {\gamma }_{z} \) exit from the same end, then \( {d}_{t}\left( {b, y}\right) /{d}_{t}\left( {a, y}\right)  < {4\pi \epsilon } \) . This means that the angle \( \theta \) of the Euclidean triangle with these side lengths at the point corresponding to \( y \) satisfies

\[
\cos \left( \theta \right)  \geq  1 - \frac{{\left( 4\pi \epsilon \right) }^{2}}{2}.
\]

![019eafda-8952-787d-9673-43fe715df5d3_18_449_248_906_592_0.jpg](images/019eafda-8952-787d-9673-43fe715df5d3_18_449_248_906_592_0.jpg)

Figure 1. Minimal geodesics in necks and caps.

Recall that \( Q \) is the maximum value of \( R\left( {x,0}\right) \) , and that by Claim 11.12 we have

\[
d \leq  {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{\infty }, y}\right)  \leq  d + {16}\sqrt{\frac{Q}{3}}T,
\]

with the same inequalities holding with \( {d}_{t}\left( {z, y}\right) \) replacing \( {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{\infty }, y}\right) \) . Also, by construction \( d \geq  {32}\sqrt{\frac{Q}{3}}T \) . We set \( {a}_{0} = {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{\infty }, y}\right) \) and \( {a}_{1} = {d}_{t}\left( {z, y}\right) \) . Then by the Toponogov property we have

\[
{d}_{t}{\left( x, z\right) }^{2} \leq  {a}_{0}^{2} + {a}_{1}^{2} - 2{a}_{0}{a}_{1}\left( {1 - \frac{{\left( 4\pi \epsilon \right) }^{2}}{2}}\right)  = {\left( {a}_{0} - {a}_{1}\right) }^{2} + {\left( 4\pi \epsilon \right) }^{2}{a}_{0}{a}_{1}.
\]

Since \( \left| {{a}_{0} - {a}_{1}}\right|  \leq  d/2 \) and \( {a}_{0},{a}_{1} \leq  {3d}/2 \) and \( \epsilon  < 1/{8\pi } \) , it follows that \( {d}_{t}\left( {x, z}\right)  < d \) . Since distances do not increase under the flow, it follows that \( {d}_{0}\left( {x, z}\right)  < d \) . This contradicts the fact that \( {d}_{0}\left( {x, z}\right)  = d \) .

Since \( y \) is the center of a \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -neck \( N \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) and minimal \( g\left( t\right) \) -geodesics from \( y \) to \( z \) and to \( {x}_{\infty } \) exit out of opposite ends of \( N \) , it follows that \( B\left( {y, t,{4\pi R}{\left( y, t\right) }^{-1/2}}\right) \) separates \( {x}_{\infty } \) and \( z \) . Since the curvature of the time-slices is non-negative, the Ricci flow does not increase distances. Hence, \( B\left( {y,0,{4\pi R}{\left( y, t\right) }^{-1/2}}\right) \) separates \( z \) from \( {x}_{\infty } \) . (Notice that since \( d > {4\pi R}{\left( y, t\right) }^{-1/2} \) , neither \( z \) nor \( {x}_{\infty } \) lies in this ball.) Thus, if \( R\left( {y, t}\right) \) is unbounded as \( t \rightarrow   - T \) then arbitrarily small \( g\left( 0\right) \) -balls centered at \( y \) separate \( z \) and \( {x}_{\infty } \) . Since \( y \) is distinct from \( {x}_{\infty } \) and \( z \) , this is clearly impossible.

nodes.content: COROLLARY 11.16. Suppose there is a geometric limit flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) of a subsequence defined on \( ( - T,0\rbrack \) for some \( T < \infty \) . Suppose that the limit flow is complete of non-negative curvature with the curvature locally bounded in time. Then for every \( A < \infty \) the scalar curvature \( {R}_{{g}_{\infty }}\left( {y, t}\right) \) is uniformly bounded for all \( \left( {y, t}\right)  \in  B\left( {{x}_{\infty },0, A}\right)  \times  ( - T,0\rbrack \) .

nodes.proof:
First we pass to a subsequence so that a geometric limit flow

\[
\left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right) }\right)
\]

exists on \( ( - T,0\rbrack \) . We let \( Q \) be the upper bound for \( R\left( {x,0}\right) \) for all \( x \in  {M}_{\infty } \) . We now divide the argument into two cases: (i) \( {M}_{\infty } \) is compact, and (ii) \( {M}_{\infty } \) is non-compact.

Suppose that \( {M}_{\infty } \) is compact. By Proposition 4.1 we know that

\[
\mathop{\min }\limits_{{x \in  {M}_{\infty }}}\left( {{R}_{{g}_{\infty }}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right)
\]

is a non-decreasing function of \( t \) . Since \( {R}_{{g}_{\infty }}\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1 \) , it follows that for each \( t \in  ( - T,0\rbrack \) , we have \( \mathop{\min }\limits_{{x \in  {M}_{\infty }}}R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  1 \) , and hence there is a point \( {x}_{t} \in  {M}_{\infty } \) with \( R\left( {{x}_{t}, t}\right)  \leq  1 \) . Now we can apply Lemma 11.11 to see that the scalar curvature of \( {g}_{\infty } \) is bounded on all of \( {M}_{\infty } \times  ( - T,0\rbrack \) .

If \( {M}_{\infty } \) is non-compact, choose \( D \) as in Claim 11.14. According to that claim every point in the boundary of \( B\left( {{x}_{\infty },0, D}\right) \) has bounded curvature under \( {g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) \) for all \( t \in  ( - T,0\rbrack \) . In particular, for each \( t \in  ( - T,0\rbrack \) the minimum of \( R\left( {x, t}\right) \) over \( \bar{B}\left( {{x}_{\infty },0, D}\right) \) is bounded independent of \( t \) . Now apply Lemma 11.11 to the closure of \( B\left( {{x}_{\infty },0, D}\right) \) . We conclude that the curvature of \( B\left( {{x}_{\infty },0, D}\right) \) is uniformly bounded for all \( {g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) \) for all \( t \in  ( - T,0\rbrack \) . In particular, \( R\left( {{x}_{\infty }, t}\right) \) is uniformly bounded for all \( t \in  ( - T,0\rbrack \) .

Now for any \( A < \infty \) we apply Lemma 11.11 to the compact subset \( \bar{B}\left( {{x}_{\infty },0, A}\right) \) to conclude that the curvature is uniformly bounded on \( B\left( {{x}_{\infty },0, A}\right)  \times  ( - T,0\rbrack \) . This completes the proof of the corollary.

nodes.content: CLAIM 11.17. For each \( A < \infty \) and for all \( n \) sufficiently large, there are \( \delta  > 0 \) with \( \delta  \leq  {T}_{0} - T \) and a bound, independent of \( n \) , on the scalar curvature of the restriction of \( {Q}_{n}{G}_{n} \) to \( {B}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n},0, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-\left( {T + \delta }\right) ,0}\right\rbrack \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: CLAIM 11.17. For each \( A < \infty \) and for all \( n \) sufficiently large, there are \( \delta > 0 \) with \( \delta \leq {T}_{0} - T \) and a bound, independent of \( n \) , on the scalar curvature of the restriction of \( {Q}_{n}{G}_{n} \) to \( {B}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n},0, A}\right) \times \left\lbrack {-\left( {T + \delta }\right) ,0}\right\rbrack \) .

nodes.proof:
Fix \( A < \infty \) and let \( K \) be the bound for the scalar curvature of \( {g}_{\infty } \) on \( B\left( {{x}_{\infty },0,{2A}}\right)  \times  ( - T,0\rbrack \) from Corollary 11.16. Lemma 11.2 shows that there are \( \delta  > 0 \) and a bound in terms of \( K \) and \( C \) on the scalar curvature of the restriction of \( {Q}_{n}{G}_{n} \) to \( {B}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n},0, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-\left( {T + \delta }\right) ,0}\right\rbrack \) .

Since the scalar curvature is bounded, by the assumption that either the curvature is pinched toward positive or the Riemann curvature is nonnegative, this implies that the sectional curvatures of \( {Q}_{n}{G}_{n} \) are also uniformly bounded on the products \( {B}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n},0, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-\left( {T + \delta }\right) ,0}\right\rbrack \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large. Consequently, it follows that by passing to a further subsequence we can arrange that the \( - T \) time-slices of the \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n},{x}_{n}}\right) \) converge to a limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-T}\right) }\right) \) . This limit manifold satisfies the hypothesis of Proposition 2.19 and hence, by that proposition, it has bounded sectional curvature. This means that there is a \( \delta  > 0 \) such that for all \( n \) sufficiently large and for any \( A < \infty \) the scalar curvatures (and hence the Riemann curvatures) of the restriction of \( {Q}_{n}{G}_{n} \) to \( {B}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n},0, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-\left( {T + \delta }\right) ,0}\right\rbrack \) are bounded independent of \( n \) . This allows us to pass to a further subsequence for which there is a geometric limit defined on \( ( - \left( {T + \delta /2}\right) , - T\rbrack \) . This geometric limit is complete of bounded, non-negative curvature. Hence, we have now constructed a limit flow on \( ( - \left( {T + \delta /2}\right) ,0\rbrack \) with the property that for each \( t \in  ( - \left( {T + \delta /2}\right) ,0\rbrack \) the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is complete and of bounded non-negative curvature. (We still don't know whether the entire flow is of bounded curvature.) But now invoking Hamilton's Harnack inequality (Theorem 4.37), we see that the curvature is bounded on \( \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) . Since we already know it is bounded in \( ( - T + \delta /2, - T\rbrack \) , this completes the proof of the proposition.

nodes.content:
Assumptions 11.18. (a) The singular times form a discrete subset of \( \mathbb{R} \) , and each time slice of the flow at a non-singular time is a compact 3-manifold.

(b) The time interval of definition of the generalized Ricci flow \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) is contained in \( \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) and its curvature is pinched toward positive.

(c) There are \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) and \( C < \infty \) , such that any point \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) with \( R\left( x\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. In particular, for every \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) with \( R\left( x\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) the following two inequalities hold:

\[
\left| \frac{\partial R\left( x\right) }{\partial t}\right|  < C{R}^{2}\left( x\right)
\]

\[
\left| {\nabla R\left( x\right) }\right|  < C{R}^{3/2}\left( x\right) .
\]

nodes.label: Theorem 11.19
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.section_title: 11.3. Incomplete smooth limits at singular times
nodes.content:
THEOREM 11.19. Suppose that \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) is a generalized Ricci flow defined for \( 0 \leq  t < T < \infty \) satisfying Assumptions 11.18. Let \( {T}^{ - } < T \) be such that there is a diffeomorphism \( \rho  : {M}_{{T}^{ - }} \times  \left\lbrack  {{T}^{ - }, T}\right)  \rightarrow  {\mathbf{t}}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {{T}^{ - }, T}\right) \right) \) compatible with time and with the vector field. Set \( M = {M}_{{T}^{ - }} \) and let \( g\left( t\right) ,{T}^{ - } \leq  t < T \) , be the family of metrics \( {\rho }^{ * }G\left( t\right) \) on \( M \) . Let \( \Omega  \subset  M \) be the subset defined by

\[
\Omega  = \left\{  {x \in  M \mid  \mathop{\liminf }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  T}}{R}_{g}\left( {x, t}\right)  < \infty }\right\}  .
\]

Then \( \Omega  \subset  M \) is an open subset and there is a Riemannian metric \( g\left( T\right) \) with the following properties:

(1) As \( t \rightarrow  T \) the metrics \( {\left. g\left( t\right) \right| }_{\Omega } \) limit to \( g\left( T\right) \) uniformly in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology on every compact subset of \( \Omega \) .

(2) The scalar curvature \( R\left( {g\left( T\right) }\right) \) is a proper function from \( \Omega  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) and is bounded below.

(3) Let

\[
\widehat{\mathcal{M}} = \mathcal{M}{ \cup  }_{\Omega  \times  \left\lbrack  {{T}^{ - }, T}\right) }\left( {\Omega  \times  \left\lbrack  {{T}^{ - }, T}\right\rbrack  }\right)
\]

Then the generalized Ricci flow \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) extends to a generalized Ricci flow \( \left( {\widehat{\mathcal{M}},\widehat{G}}\right) \) .

(4) Every end of a connected component of \( \Omega \) is contained in a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -tube.

(5) Any \( x \in  \Omega  \times  \{ T\} \) with \( R\left( x\right)  > {r}_{0}^{-2} \) has a strong \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -canonical neighborhood in \( \widehat{\mathcal{M}} \) .

nodes.content: LEMMA 11.21. Suppose that \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) is a generalized Ricci flow defined for \( 0 \leq  t < T < \infty \) satisfying the three assumptions given in 11.18. Let \( {T}^{\prime } < \; T \) be as in the previous theorem, set \( M = {M}_{{T}^{ - }} \) , and let \( g\left( t\right) \) be the family of metrics on \( M \) and let \( \Omega  \subset  M \) , each being as defined in the previous theorem. Then \( \Omega  \subset  M \) is an open subset of \( M \) . Furthermore, the restriction of the family \( g\left( t\right) \) to \( \Omega \) converges in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology, uniformly on compact sets of \( \Omega \) , to a Riemannian metric \( g\left( T\right) \) . Lastly, \( R\left( {g\left( T\right) }\right) \) is a proper function, bounded below, from \( \Omega \) to \( \mathbb{R} \) .

nodes.proof:
We pull back \( G \) to \( M \times  \left\lbrack  {{T}^{ - }, T}\right) \) in order to define a Ricci flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) ,{T}^{ - } \leq  t < T \) . Suppose that \( x \in  \Omega \) . Then there is a sequence \( {t}_{n} \rightarrow  T \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) such that \( R\left( {x,{t}_{n}}\right) \) is bounded above, independent of \( n \) , by say \( Q \) . For all \( n \) sufficiently large we have \( T - {t}_{n} \leq  \frac{1}{{16C}\left( {{Q}^{2} + {r}_{0}^{-2}}\right) } \) . Fix such an \( n \) . Then, according to Lemma 11.2, there is \( r > 0 \) such that \( R\left( {y, t}\right) \) is uniformly bounded for \( y \in  B\left( {x,{t}_{n}, r}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{n}, T}\right) \) . This means that \( B\left( {x,{t}_{n}, r}\right)  \subset  \Omega \) , proving that \( \Omega \) is open in \( M \) .

Furthermore, since \( R\left( {y, t}\right) \) is bounded on \( B\left( {x,{t}_{n}, r}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{n}, T}\right) \) , it follows from the curvature pinching toward positive hypothesis that \( \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {y, t}\right) }\right| \) is bounded on \( B\left( {x,{t}_{n}, r}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{n}, T}\right) \) . Now applying Theorem 3.28 we see that in fact Rm is bounded in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology on \( B\left( {x,{t}_{n}, r}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {\left( {{t}_{n} + T}\right) /2, T}\right) \) . The same is of course also true for Ric and hence for \( \frac{\partial g}{\partial t} \) in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology. It then follows that there is a continuous extension of \( g \) to \( B\left( {x,{t}_{n}, r}\right)  \times \; \left\lbrack  {{t}_{n}, T}\right\rbrack \) . Since this is true for every \( x \in  \Omega \) we see that \( g\left( t\right) \) converges in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology, uniformly on compact subsets of \( \Omega \) , to \( g\left( T\right) \) .

Lastly, let us consider the function \( R\left( {g\left( T\right) }\right) \) on \( \Omega \) . Since the metric \( g\left( T\right) \) is a smooth metric on \( \Omega \left( T\right) \) , this is a smooth function. Clearly, by the curvature pinching toward positive hypothesis, this function is bounded below. We must show that it is proper. Since \( M \) is compact, it suffices to show that if \( {x}_{n} \) is a sequence in \( \Omega  \subset  M \) converging to a point \( x \in  M \smallsetminus  \Omega \) then \( R\left( {{x}_{n}, T}\right) \) is unbounded. Suppose that \( R\left( {{x}_{n}, T}\right) \) is bounded independent of \( n \) . It follows from Lemma 11.2 that there is a positive constant \( {\Delta t} \) such that \( R\left( {{x}_{n}, t}\right) \) is uniformly bounded for all \( n \) and all \( t \in  \lbrack T - {\Delta t}, T) \) , and hence, by the same result, there is \( r > 0 \) such that \( R\left( {{y}_{n}, t}\right) \) is bounded for all \( n \) , all \( {y}_{n} \in  B\left( {{x}_{n}, T - {\Delta t}, r}\right) \) , and all \( t \in  \lbrack T - {\Delta t}, T) \) . Since the \( {x}_{n} \rightarrow  x \in  M \) , it follows that, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( x \in  B\left( {{x}_{n}, T - {\Delta t}, r}\right) \) , and hence \( R\left( {x, t}\right) \) is uniformly bounded as \( t \rightarrow  T \) . This contradicts the fact that \( x \notin  \Omega \) .

nodes.content:
DEFINITION 11.22. Let

\[
\widehat{\mathcal{M}} = \mathcal{M}{ \cup  }_{\Omega  \times  \left\lbrack  {{T}^{ - }, T}\right) }\left( {\Omega  \times  \left\lbrack  {{T}^{ - }, T}\right\rbrack  }\right)
\]

Since both \( \mathcal{M} \) and \( \Omega  \times  \left\lbrack  {{T}^{ - }, T}\right\rbrack \) have the structure of space-times and the time functions and vector fields agree on the overlap, \( \widehat{\mathcal{M}} \) inherits the structure of a space-time. Let \( {G}^{\prime }\left( t\right) ,{T}^{ - } \leq  t \leq  T \) , be the smooth family of metrics on \( \Omega \) . The horizontal metrics, \( G \) , on \( \mathcal{M} \) and this family of metrics on \( \Omega \) agree on the overlap and hence define a horizontal metric \( \widehat{G} \) on \( \widehat{\mathcal{M}} \) . Clearly, this metric satisfies the Ricci flow equation, so that \( \left( {\widehat{\mathcal{M}},\widehat{G}}\right) \) is a generalized Ricci flow extending \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) . We call this the maximal extension of \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) to time \( T \) . Notice that even though the time-slices \( {M}_{t} \) of \( \mathcal{M} \) are compact, it will not necessarily be the case that the time-slice \( \Omega \) is complete.

LEMMA 11.23. For any \( x \in  \Omega  \times  \{ T\} \) with \( R\left( {x, T}\right)  > {r}_{0}^{-2} \) one of the following holds:

(1) \( \left( {x, T}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck in \( \left( {\widehat{\mathcal{M}},\widehat{G}}\right) \) .

(2) There is a \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -cap in \( \left( {\Omega \left( T\right) ,\widehat{G}\left( T\right) }\right) \) whose core contains \( \left( {x, T}\right) \) .

(3) There is a \( {2C} \) -component of \( \Omega \left( T\right) \) that contains \( \left( {x, T}\right) \) .

(4) There is a \( {2\epsilon } \) -round component of \( \Omega \left( T\right) \) that contains \( \left( {x, T}\right) \) .

nodes.proof:
We fix \( x \in  \Omega \left( T\right) \) with \( R\left( {x, T}\right)  > {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . First notice that for all \( t < T \) sufficiently close to \( T \) we have \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  > {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . Thus, for all such \( t \) the point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood in \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right)  \subset \; \left( {\widehat{\mathcal{M}},\widehat{G}}\right) \) . Furthermore, since \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  T}}R\left( {x, t}\right)  = R\left( {x, T}\right)  < \infty \) , for all \( t < T \) sufficiently close to \( T \) , there is a constant \( D < \infty \) such that for any point \( y \) contained in a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood containing \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) , we have \( {D}^{-1}R\left( {x, T}\right)  \leq  R\left( {y, t}\right)  \leq  {DR}\left( {x, T}\right) \) . Again assuming that \( t < T \) is sufficiently close to \( T \) , by Lemma 11.2 there is \( {D}^{\prime } < \infty \) depending only on \( D, t \) , and \( {r}_{0} \) such that the curvature \( R\left( {y, T}\right) \) satisfies \( {\left( {D}^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}R\left( {x, T}\right)  \leq \; R\left( {y, T}\right)  \leq  {D}^{\prime }R\left( {x, T}\right) \) . By Lemma 11.21 this implies that there is a compact subset \( K \subset  \Omega \left( T\right) \) containing all the \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhoods for \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) . The same lemma implies that the metrics \( {\left. G\left( t\right) \right| }_{K} \) converge uniformly in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to \( {\left. G\left( T\right) \right| }_{K} \) . If there is a sequence of \( t \) converging to \( T \) for which the canonical neighborhood of \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) is an \( \epsilon \) -round component, resp. a \( C \) -component, then \( \left( {y, T}\right) \) is contained in a \( {2\epsilon } \) -round, resp. a \( {2C} \) - component of \( \widehat{\Omega } \) . If there is a sequence of \( {t}_{n} \) converging to \( T \) so that each \( \left( {y,{t}_{n}}\right) \) has a canonical neighborhood \( {\mathcal{C}}_{n} \) which is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains \( \left( {y,{t}_{n}}\right) \) , then by Proposition 9.79, since these caps are all contained in a fixed compact subset \( K \) and since the \( {\left. G\left( {t}_{n}\right) \right| }_{K} \) converge uniformly in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to \( {\left. G\left( T\right) \right| }_{K} \) , it follows that for any \( n \) sufficiently large, the metric \( G\left( T\right) \) restricted to \( {\mathcal{C}}_{n} \) contains a \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -cap \( \mathcal{C} \) whose core contains \( \left( {y, T}\right) \) .

Now we examine the case of strong \( \epsilon \) -necks.

nodes.content: CLAIM 11.24. Fix a point \( x \in  \Omega \) . Suppose that there is a sequence \( {t}_{n} \rightarrow  T \) such that for every \( n \) , the point \( \left( {x,{t}_{n}}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \widehat{\mathcal{M}} \) . Then \( \left( {x, T}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck in \( \widehat{\mathcal{M}} \) .

nodes.proof:
By an overall rescaling we can assume that \( R\left( {x, T}\right)  = 1 \) . For each \( n \) let \( {N}_{n} \subset  \Omega \) and let \( {\psi }_{n} : {S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)  \rightarrow  {N}_{n} \times  \{ t\} \) be a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( \left( {x,{t}_{n}}\right) \) . Let \( B = B\left( {x, T,2{\epsilon }^{-1}/3}\right) \) . Clearly, for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( B \subset  {N}_{n} \) . Thus, for each point \( y \in  B \) and each \( n \) there is a flow line through \( y \) defined on the interval \( \left( {{t}_{n} - R{\left( x,{t}_{n}\right) }^{-1},{t}_{n}}\right. \) ]. Since the \( {t}_{n} \rightarrow  T \) and since \( R\left( {x,{t}_{n}}\right)  \rightarrow  R\left( {x, T}\right)  = 1 \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) , it follows that there is a flow line through \( y \) defined on \( (T - 1, T\rbrack \) .

Consider the maps

\[
{\alpha }_{n} : B \times  ( - 1,0\rbrack  \rightarrow  \widehat{\mathcal{M}}
\]

that send \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) to the value at time \( {t}_{n} - {tR}{\left( x,{t}_{n}\right) }^{-1} \) of the flow line through \( y \) . Pulling back the metric \( R\left( {x,{t}_{n}}\right) \widehat{G} \) by \( {\alpha }_{n} \) produces the restriction of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck structure to \( B \) . The maps \( {\alpha }_{n} \) converge uniformly in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to the map \( \alpha  : B \times  ( - 1,0\rbrack  \rightarrow  \widehat{M} \) defined by sending \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) to the value of the flowline through \( \left( {y, T}\right) \) at the time \( T - t \) . Hence, the sequence of metrics \( {\alpha }_{n}^{ * }\left( {R\left( {x,{t}_{n}}\right) }\right) \widehat{G} \) on \( B \times  ( - 1,0\rbrack \) converges uniformly on compact subsets of \( B \times  ( - 1,0\rbrack \) in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to the family \( {\alpha }^{ * }\left( \widehat{G}\right) \) . Then, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the image \( {\psi }_{n}\left( {{S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1}/2,{\epsilon }^{-1}/2}\right) }\right) \) is contained in \( B \) and has compact closure in \( B \) . Since the family of metrics \( {\psi }_{n}^{ * }\widehat{G} \) on \( B \) converge smoothly to \( {\psi }^{ * }\widehat{G} \) , it follows that for every \( n \) sufficiently large, the restriction of \( {\psi }_{n} \) to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1}/2,{\epsilon }^{-1}/2}\right) \) gives the coordinates showing that the restriction of the family of metrics \( {\psi }^{ * }\left( \widehat{G}\right) \) to the image \( {\psi }_{n}\left( {{S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1}/2,{\epsilon }^{-1}/2}\right) }\right) \) is a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck at time \( T \) .

DEFINITION 11.25. A strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn in \( \left( {\Omega , g\left( T\right) }\right) \) is a submanifold of \( \Omega \) diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \lbrack 0,1) \) with the following properties:

(2) Every point of the image of this map is the center of a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) - neck in \( \left( {\widehat{\mathcal{M}},\widehat{G}}\right) \) .

(3) The image of the boundary \( {S}^{2} \times  \{ 0\} \) is the central sphere of a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck.

DEFINITION 11.26. A strong double \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn in \( \left( {\Omega , g\left( T\right) }\right) \) is a component of \( \Omega \) diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) with the property that every point of this component is the center of a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck in \( \widehat{\mathcal{M}} \) . This means that a strong double \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn is a \( {2\epsilon } \) -tube and hence is a component of \( \Omega \) diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {-1,1}\right) \) . Notice that each end of a strong double \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn contains a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn.

For any \( {C}^{\prime } < \infty \) , a \( {C}^{\prime } \) -capped \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn in \( \left( {\Omega , g\left( T\right) }\right) \) is a component of \( \Omega \) that is a the union of a the core of a \( \left( {{C}^{\prime },{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -cap and a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn. Such a component is diffeomorphic to an open 3-ball or to a punctured \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .
