LEMMA 11.28. Suppose that \( 0 < \rho  < {r}_{0} \) and that \( {\Omega }^{0} \) is a component of \( \Omega \) which contains no point of \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) . Then one of the following holds:

(1) \( {\Omega }^{0} \) is a strong double \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn and is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) .

(2) \( {\Omega }^{0} \) is a \( {2C} \) -capped \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn and is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) or to a punctured \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

(3) \( {\Omega }^{0} \) is a compact component and is the union of the cores of two \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -caps and a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -tube. It is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{3},\mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

(4) \( {\Omega }^{0} \) is a compact \( {2\epsilon } \) -round component and is diffeomorphic to a compact manifold of constant positive curvature.

(5) \( {\Omega }^{0} \) is a compact component that fibers over \( {S}^{1} \) with fibers \( {S}^{2} \) .

(6) \( {\Omega }^{0} \) is a compact \( {2C} \) -component and is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{3} \) or to \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

Therefore, by Lemma 11.23 \( \left( {x, T}\right) \) has a \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Of course, this entire neighborhood is contained in \( \widehat{\mathcal{M}} \) and hence is contained in \( {\Omega }^{0} \) (or, more precisely, in the case of strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -necks in the union of maximum backward flow lines ending at points of \( {\Omega }^{0} \) ). If the canonical neighborhood of \( \left( {x, T}\right)  \in  {\Omega }^{0} \) is a \( {2C} \) -component or is a \( {2\epsilon } \) -round component, then of course \( {\Omega }^{0} \) is that \( {2C} \) - component or \( {2\epsilon } \) -round component. Otherwise, each point of \( {\Omega }^{0} \) is either the center of a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck or contained in the core of a \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -cap. We have chosen \( {2\epsilon } \) sufficiently small so that the result follows from Proposition A.25.

LEMMA 11.30. Let \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) be a generalized 3-dimensional Ricci flow defined for \( 0 \leq  t < T < \infty \) satisfying Assumptions 11.18. Fix \( 0 < \rho  < {r}_{0} \) .

![019eafda-8952-787d-9673-43fe715df5d3_27_421_245_967_1082_0.jpg](images/019eafda-8952-787d-9673-43fe715df5d3_27_421_245_967_1082_0.jpg)

Figure 3. Components of \( \Omega \) disjoint from \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) .

Let \( {\Omega }^{0}\left( \rho \right) \) be the union of all components of \( \Omega \) containing points of \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) . Then \( {\Omega }^{0}\left( \rho \right) \) has finitely many components and is a union of a compact set and finitely many strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -horns each of which is disjoint from \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) and has its boundary contained in \( {\Omega }_{\rho /{2C}} \) .

Components of \( \Omega \) disjoint from \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) . Let \(...

nodes.proof:
Since \( R : \Omega  \times  \{ T\}  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) is a proper function bounded below, \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) is compact. Hence, there are only finitely many components of \( \Omega \) containing points of \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) . Let \( {\Omega }^{0} \) be a non-compact component of \( \Omega \) containing a point of \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) , and let \( \mathcal{E} \) be an end of \( {\Omega }^{0} \) . Let

\[
X = \left\{  {x \in  {\Omega }^{0} \mid  R\left( x\right)  \geq  2{C}^{2}{\rho }^{-2}}\right\}  .
\]

Then \( X \) is a closed set and contains a neighborhood of the end \( \mathcal{E} \) . Since \( {\Omega }^{0} \) contains a point of \( {\Omega }_{\rho },{\Omega }^{0} \smallsetminus  X \) is non-empty. Let \( {X}_{0} \) be the connected component of \( X \) that contains a neighborhood of \( \mathcal{E} \) . This is a closed, connected set every point of which has a \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Since \( {X}_{0} \) includes an end of \( {\Omega }^{0} \) , no point of \( {X}_{0} \) can be contained in an \( \epsilon \) -round component nor in a \( C \) -component. Hence, every point of \( {X}_{0} \) is either the center of a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck or is contained in the core of a \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -cap. Since \( {2\epsilon } \) is sufficiently small to invoke Proposition A.21, the latter implies that \( {X}_{0} \) is contained either in a \( {2\epsilon } \) -tube which is a union of strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -necks centered at points of \( {X}_{0} \) or \( {X}_{0} \) is contained in a \( {2C} \) -capped \( {2\epsilon } \) -tube where the core of the cap contains a point of \( {X}_{0} \) . \( \left( {X}_{0}\right. \) cannot be contained in a double capped \( {2\epsilon } \) -tube since the latter is compact.) In the second case, since this capped tube contains an end of \( {\Omega }^{0} \) , it is in fact equal to \( {\Omega }^{0} \) . Since a point of \( {X}_{0} \) is contained in the core of the \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -cap, the curvature of this point is at most \( 2{C}^{2}{\rho }^{-2} \) and hence the curvature at any point of the cap is at least \( {2C}{\rho }^{-2} > {\rho }^{-2} \) . This implies that the cap is disjoint from \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) . Of course, any \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at a point of \( {X}_{0} \) has curvature at least \( {C}^{2}{\rho }^{-2} \) and hence is also disjoint from \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) . Hence, if \( {\Omega }^{0} \) is a \( {2C} \) -capped \( {2\epsilon } \) -tube and there is a point of \( {X}_{0} \) in the core of the cap, then this component is disjoint from \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) , which is a contradiction. Thus, \( {X}_{0} \) is contained in a \( {2\epsilon } \) -tube made up of strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -necks centered at points of \( {X}_{0} \) .

This proves that \( {X}_{0} \) is contained in a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -tube, \( Y \) , every point of which has curvature \( \geq  {C}^{2}{\rho }^{-2} \) . Since \( {X}_{0} \) is closed but not the entire component \( {\Omega }^{0} \) , it follows that \( {X}_{0} \) has a frontier point \( y \) . Of course, \( R\left( y\right)  = \; 2{C}^{2}{\rho }^{-2} \) . Let \( N \) be the strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( y \) and let \( {S}_{N}^{2} \) be its central 2-sphere. Clearly, every \( {y}^{\prime } \in  {S}_{N}^{2} \) satisfies \( R\left( {y}^{\prime }\right)  \leq  4{C}^{2}{\rho }^{-2} \) , so that \( {S}_{N}^{2} \) is contained in \( {\Omega }_{\rho /{2C}} \) . Let \( {Y}^{\prime } \subset  Y \) be the complementary component of \( {S}_{N}^{2} \) in \( Y \) that contains a neighborhood of the end \( \mathcal{E} \) . Then the closure of \( {Y}^{\prime } \) is the required strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn containing a neighborhood of \( \mathcal{E} \) , disjoint from \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) and with boundary contained in \( {\Omega }_{\rho /{2C}} \) .

The last thing to see is that there are only finitely many such ends in a given component \( {\Omega }^{0} \) . First suppose that the boundary 2-sphere of one of the \( {2\epsilon } \) -horns is homotopically trivial in \( {\Omega }^{0} \) . Then this 2-sphere separates \( {\Omega }^{0} \) into two components, one of which is compact, and hence \( {\Omega }^{0} \) has only one boundary component. Thus, we can assume that all the boundary 2-spheres of the \( {2\epsilon } \) -horns are homotopically non-trivial. Suppose that two of these \( {2\epsilon } \) -horns containing different ends of \( {\Omega }^{0} \) have non-empty intersection. Let \( N \) be the \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck whose central 2-sphere is the boundary of one of the \( {2\epsilon } \) -horns. Then the boundary of the other \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn is also contained in \( N \) . This means that the union of the two \( {2\epsilon } \) -horns and \( N \) is a component of \( \Omega \) . Clearly, this component has exactly two ends. Thus, we can assume that all the \( {2\epsilon } \) -horns with boundary in \( {\Omega }_{\rho /{2C}} \) are disjoint. If two of the \( {2\epsilon } \) -horns have boundary components that are topologically parallel in \( {\Omega }^{0} \cap  {\Omega }_{\rho /{2C}} \) (meaning that they are the boundary components of a compact submanifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  I \) ), then \( {\Omega }^{0} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) and has only two ends. By compactness of \( {\Omega }_{\rho /{2C}} \) , there can only be finitely many disjoint \( {2\epsilon } \) -horns with non-parallel, homotopically non-trivial boundaries in \( {\Omega }^{0} \cap  {\Omega }_{\rho /{2C}} \) . This completes the proof of the fact that each component of \( {\Omega }_{\rho /{2C}} \) has only finitely many ends.

This completes the proof of Theorem 11.19.

THEOREM 11.31. Fix \( \rho  > 0 \) . Then for any \( \delta  > 0 \) there is an \( 0 < h = \; h\left( {\delta ,\rho }\right)  \leq  \min \left( {\rho  \cdot  \delta ,\rho /{2C}}\right) \) , implicitly depending on \( r \) and \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) which are fixed, such that for any generalized Ricci flow \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) defined for \( 0 \leq  t < \; T < \infty \) satisfying Assumptions 11.18 and for any \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn \( \mathcal{H} \) of \( \left( {\Omega , g\left( T\right) }\right) \) with boundary contained in \( {\Omega }_{\rho /{2C}} \) , every point \( x \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( {x, T}\right)  \geq  {h}^{-2} \) is the center of a strong \( \delta \) -neck in \( \left( {\widehat{\mathcal{M}},\widehat{G}}\right) \) contained in \( \mathcal{H} \) . Furthermore, there is a point \( y \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  = {h}^{-2} \) with the property that the central 2-sphere of the \( \delta \) -neck centered at \( y \) cuts off an end of the \( \mathcal{H} \) disjoint from \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) . See FIG. 4.

![019eafda-8952-787d-9673-43fe715df5d3_29_468_986_855_334_0.jpg](images/019eafda-8952-787d-9673-43fe715df5d3_29_468_986_855_334_0.jpg)

nodes.proof:
The proof of the first statement is by contradiction. Fix \( \rho  > 0 \) and \( \delta  > 0 \) and suppose that there is no \( 0 < h \leq  \min \left( {\rho  \cdot  \delta ,\rho /{2C}}\right) \) as required. Then there is a sequence of generalized Ricci flows \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) defined for \( 0 \leq  t < {T}_{n} < \infty \) satisfying Assumptions 11.18 and points \( {x}_{n} \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) with \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right)  = {T}_{n} \) contained in \( {2\epsilon } \) -horns \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) in \( {\Omega }_{n} \) with boundary contained in \( {\left( {\Omega }_{n}\right) }_{\rho /{2C}} \) with \( {Q}_{n} = R\left( {x}_{n}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) but such that no \( {x}_{n} \) is the center of a strong \( \delta \) -neck in \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) . Form the maximal extensions, \( \left( {{\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n},{\widehat{G}}_{n}}\right) \) , to time \( T \) of the \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) .

CLAIM 11.32. The sequence \( \left( {{\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n},{\widehat{G}}_{n},{x}_{n}}\right) \) satisfies the five hypotheses of Theorem 11.1.

Proof. By our assumptions, hypotheses (1) and (3) of Theorem 11.1 hold for this sequence. Also, we are assuming that any point \( y \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Since \( R\left( {x}_{n}\right)  = \; {Q}_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) this means that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, any point \( y \in  {\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  \geq  R\left( {x}_{n}\right) \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. This establishes hypothesis (2) in the statement of Theorem 11.1.

Next, we have:

CLAIM 11.33. For any \( A < \infty \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the ball \( B\left( {{x}_{n},0, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) is contained in the \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) and has compact closure in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) .

Proof. Any point \( z \in  \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) has scalar curvature at most \( {16}{C}^{2}{\rho }^{-2} \) and there is a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( z \) . This means that for all \( y \) with \( {d}_{{G}_{n}}\left( {z, y}\right)  < {\epsilon }^{-1}\rho /{2C} \) we have \( R\left( y\right)  \leq  {32}{C}^{2}{\rho }^{-2} \) . Hence, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( {d}_{{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n}, z}\right)  > {\epsilon }^{-1}\rho /{2C} \) , and thus \( {d}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n}, z}\right)  > {Q}_{n}^{1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1}\rho /{2C} \) . This implies that, given \( A < \infty \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( z \notin  {B}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n},0, A}\right) \) . Since this is true for all \( z \in  \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) , it follows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {B}_{{Q}_{n},{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n},0, A}\right)  \subset  {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) . Next, we must show that, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, this ball has compact closure. That is to say, we must show that for every \( A \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large the distance from \( {x}_{n} \) to the end of the horn \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) is greater than \( A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2} \) . If not, then since the curvature at the end of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) goes to infinity for each \( n \) , this sequence would violate Theorem 10.2.

Because \( B\left( {{x}_{n},0, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) is contained in a \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn, it is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed on scales \( \leq  r \) for a universal \( \kappa  > 0 \) and \( r > 0 \) . Also, because every point in the horn is the center of a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck, for every \( n \) sufficiently large and every \( y \in  B\left( {{x}_{n},0, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) the flow is defined on an interval through \( y \) defined for backward time \( R{\left( y\right) }^{-1} \) .

This completes the proof that all the hypotheses of Theorem 11.1 hold and establishes Claim 11.32.

We form a new sequence of generalized Ricci flows from the \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) by translating by \( - {T}_{n} \) , so that the final time-slice is at \( {\mathbf{t}}_{n} = 0 \) , where \( {\mathbf{t}}_{n} \) is the time function for \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) .

Theorem 11.1 implies that, after passing to a subsequence, there is a limit flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right) }\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack  ) \) defined for some \( {t}_{0} > 0 \) for the sequence \( \left( {{Q}_{n}{\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n},{Q}_{n}{\widehat{G}}_{n},{x}_{n}}\right) \) . Because of the curvature pinching toward positive assumption, by Theorem 5.33, the limit Ricci flow has non-negative sectional curvature. Of course, \( R\left( {x}_{\infty }\right)  = 1 \) so that the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is non-flat.

CLAIM 11.34. \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is isometric to the product \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h}\right)  \times  \left( {\mathbb{R}, d{s}^{2}}\right) \) , where \( h \) is a metric of non-negative curvature on \( {S}^{2} \) and \( d{s}^{2} \) is the usual Euclidean metric on the real line.

Proof. Because of the fact that the \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) have curvature pinched toward positive, and since \( {Q}_{n} \) tend to \( \infty \) as \( n \) tends to infinity, it follows that the geometric limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) has non-negative curvature. In \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) take a minimizing geodesic ray \( {\alpha }_{n} \) from \( {x}_{n} \) to the end of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) and a minimizing geodesic \( {\beta }_{n} \) from \( {x}_{n} \) to \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) . As we have seen, the lengths of both \( {\alpha }_{n} \) and \( {\beta }_{n} \) tend to \( \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) . By passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the \( {\alpha }_{n} \) converge to a minimizing geodesic ray \( \alpha \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) and that the \( {\beta }_{n} \) converge to a minimizing geodesic ray \( \beta \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) . Since, for all \( n \) , the union of \( {\alpha }_{n} \) and \( {\beta }_{n} \) forms a piecewise smooth ray in \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) meeting the central 2-sphere of a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n} \) in a single point and at this point crossing from one side of this 2-sphere to the other, the union of \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) forms a proper, piecewise smooth map of \( \mathbb{R} \) to \( {M}_{\infty } \) that meets the central 2-sphere of a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{\infty } \) in a single point and crosses from one side to the other at the point. This means that \( {M}_{\infty } \) has at least two ends. Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) has non-negative curvature, according to Theorem 2.13, this implies that \( {M}_{\infty } \) is a product of a surface with \( \mathbb{R} \) . Since \( M \) has nonnegative curvature, the surface has non-negative curvature. Since \( M \) has positive curvature at least at one point, the surface is diffeomorphic to the 2-sphere.

According to Theorem 11.1, after passing to a subsequence there is a limit flow defined on some interval of the form \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) for \( {t}_{0} > 0 \) . Suppose that, after passing to a subsequence there is a limit flow defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) for some \( 0 < T < \infty \) . It follows that for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) , the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is of non-negative curvature and has two ends. Again by Theorem 2.13, this implies that for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a Riemannian product of a metric of non-negative curvature on \( {S}^{2} \) with \( \mathbb{R} \) . Thus, by Corollary 4.19 the Ricci flow is a product of a Ricci flow \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h\left( t\right) }\right) \) with the trivial flow on \( \left( {\mathbb{R}, d{s}^{2}}\right) \) . It now follows from Corollary 4.14 that for every \( t \in  ( - T,0\rbrack \) the curvature of \( {g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) \) on \( {S}^{2} \) is positive.

Let \( {M}_{n} \) be the zero time-slice of \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) is the geometric limit of the \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{n}}\right) \) , there is an exhaustive sequence \( {x}_{\infty } \in \; {V}_{1} \subset  {V}_{2} \subset  \cdots \) of open subsets of \( {M}_{\infty } \) with compact closure and embeddings \( {\varphi }_{n} : {V}_{n} \rightarrow  {M}_{n} \) sending \( {x}_{\infty } \) to \( {x}_{n} \) such that \( {\varphi }_{n}^{ * }\left( {{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) converges in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology, uniformly on compact sets, to \( {g}_{\infty } \) .

CLAIM 11.35. For any \( z \in  {M}_{\infty } \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( z \in  {V}_{n} \) , so that \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) \) is defined. Furthermore, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, there is a backward flow line through \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) \) in the generalized Ricci flow \( \left( {{Q}_{n}{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\right) \) defined on the interval \( \left( {-T - \left( {{R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}^{-1}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) ,0}\right) /2}\right) ,0}\right) \) . The scalar curvature is bounded above on this entire flow line by \( R\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) ,0}\right) \) .

Proof. Of course, for any compact subset \( K \subset  {M}_{\infty } \) and any \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( K \subset  {V}_{n} \) , and there is an embedding \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack   \subset \; {Q}_{n}{\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) compatible with time and the vector field. The map \( {\varphi }_{n} \) defines a map \( {Q}_{n}^{-1}{\varphi }_{n} : K \times  \left\lbrack  {-{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Since the scalar curvature of the limit is positive, and hence bounded away from zero on the compact set \( K \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) and since \( {Q}_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \) tends to infinity, the following is true: For any compact subset \( K \subset  M \) and any \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the scalar curvature of \( {G}_{n} \) on the image \( {Q}_{n}^{-1}{\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) is greater than \( {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , and hence for all \( n \) sufficiently large, every point in \( {Q}_{n}^{-1}{\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times \; \left\lbrack  {-{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Since having a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood is invariant under rescaling, it follows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, every point of \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood.

Next we claim that, for all \( n \) sufficiently large and for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , the point \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. We have already seen that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Of course, since \( {M}_{\infty } \) is non-compact, for \( n \) sufficiently large, the canonical neighborhood of \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) must either be a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap or a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. We shall rule out the possibility of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap, at least for all \( n \) sufficiently large.

To do this, take \( K \) to be a neighborhood of \( \left( {z,0}\right) \) in the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) with the topology of \( {S}^{2} \times  I \) and with the metric being the product of a positively curved metric on \( {S}^{2} \) with the Euclidean metric on \( I \) . We take \( K \) to be sufficiently large to contain the \( {2C} \) -ball centered at \( \left( {z,0}\right) \) . Because the limit flow is the product of a positively curved flow on \( {S}^{2} \) with the trivial flow on \( \mathbb{R} \) , the flow is distance decreasing. Thus, for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) the subman-ifold \( K \times  \{ t\} \) contains the ball in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) centered at \( \left( {z, t}\right) \) of radius \( {2C} \) . For every \( n \) sufficiently large, consider the submanifolds \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) of \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Since the metrics \( {\varphi }_{n}^{ * }{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) \) are converging uniformly for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) to the product flow on \( K \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large and any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , this submanifold contains the \( C \) -ball centered at \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) in \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Furthermore, the maximal curvature two-plane at any point of \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) is almost tangent to the \( {S}^{2} \) -direction of \( K \) . Hence, by Lemma A. 2 the central 2-sphere of any \( \epsilon \) -neck contained \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) is almost parallel to the \( {S}^{2} \) -factors in the product structure on \( K \) at every point. This implies that the central 2-sphere of any such \( \epsilon \) -neck is isotopic to the \( {S}^{2} \) -factor of \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) . Suppose that \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap \( \mathcal{C} \) . Then \( \mathcal{C} \) is contained in \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) . Consider the \( \epsilon \) -neck \( N \subset  \mathcal{C} \) that is the complement of the core of \( \mathcal{C} \) . Its central 2-sphere, \( \sum \) , is isotopic in \( K \) to the 2-sphere factor of \( K \) , but this is absurd since \( \sum \) bounds a 3-ball in the \( \mathcal{C} \) . This contradiction shows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large and all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , it is not possible for \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) to be contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. The only other possibility is that for all \( n \) sufficiently large and all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) the point \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) .

Fix \( n \) sufficiently large. Since, for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , the point \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck, it follows from Definition 9.78 that for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) we have \( R\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right)  \leq  R\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) ,0}\right) \) (this follows from the fact that the partial derivative in the time-direction of the scalar curvature of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck of scale one is positive and bounded away from 0 \( ) \) . It also follows from Definition 9.78 that the flow near \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , - {t}^{\prime }}\right) \) extends backwards to time

\[
- {t}^{\prime } - {R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}^{-1}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( {z,{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right)  <  - {t}^{\prime } - {R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}^{-1}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( {z,0}\right) }\right) ,
\]

with the same inequality for scalar curvature holding for all \( t \) in this extended interval. Applying this for \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) but sufficiently close to \( T \) establishes the last statement in the claim, and completes the proof of the claim.

Let \( {Q}_{0} \) be the upper bound of the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) . By the previous claim, \( {Q}_{0} \) is also an upper bound for the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right) \) for any \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) . Applying Theorem 11.1 to the flows

\[
\left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) , - {t}^{\prime } - {Q}_{0}^{-1}/2 < t \leq   - {t}^{\prime },
\]

we conclude that there is \( {t}_{0} \) depending only on the bound of the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right) \) , and hence depending only on \( {Q}_{0} \) , such that, after passing to a subsequence the limit flow exists for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime } - {t}_{0}, - {t}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) . Since the limit flow already exists on \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , we conclude that, for this further subsequence, the limit flow exists on \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime } - {t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) . Now apply this with \( {t}^{\prime } = T - {t}_{0}/2 \) . This proves that if, after passing to a subsequence, there is a limit flow defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) , then, after passing to a further subsequence there is a limit flow defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T - {t}_{0}/2,0}\right\rbrack \) where \( {t}_{0} \) depends only on \( {Q}_{0} \) , and in particular, is independent of \( T \) . Repeating this argument with \( T + \left( {{t}_{0}/2}\right) \) replacing \( T \) , we pass to a further subsequence so that the limit flow is defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T - {t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) . Repeating this inductively, we can find a sequence of subsequences so that for the \( n \) subsequence the limit flow is defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T - n{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) . Taking a diagonal subsequence produces a subsequence for which the limit is defined on \( ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) .

The limit flow is the product of a flow on \( {S}^{2} \) of positive curvature defined for \( t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) and the trivial flow on \( \mathbb{R} \) . Now, invoking Hamilton’s result (Corollary 9.50), we see that the ancient solution of positive curvature on \( {S}^{2} \) must be a shrinking round \( {S}^{2} \) . This means that the limit flow is the product of the shrinking round \( {S}^{2} \) with \( \mathbb{R} \) , and implies that for all \( n \) sufficiently large there is a strong \( \delta \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n} \) . This contradiction proves the existence of \( h \) as required.

Now let us establish the last statement in Theorem 11.31. The subset of \( \mathcal{H} \) consisting of all \( z \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( z\right)  \leq  {\rho }^{-2} \) is compact (since \( R \) is a proper function), and disjoint from any \( \delta \) -neck of scale \( h \) since \( h < \rho /{2C} \) . On the other hand, for any point \( z \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( z\right)  \leq  {\rho }^{-2} \) take a minimal geodesic from \( z \) to the end of \( \mathcal{H} \) . There must be a point \( y \) on this geodesic with \( R\left( y\right)  = {h}^{-2} \) . The \( \delta \) -neck centered at \( y \) is disjoint from \( z \) (since \( h < \rho /{2C} \) ) and hence this neck separates \( z \) from the end of \( \mathcal{H} \) . It now follows easily that there is a point \( y \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  = {h}^{-2} \) and such that the central 2-sphere of the \( \delta \) -neck centered at \( y \) divides \( \mathcal{H} \) into two pieces with the non-compact piece disjoint from \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) .

nodes.proof:
By our assumptions, hypotheses (1) and (3) of Theorem 11.1 hold for this sequence. Also, we are assuming that any point \( y \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Since \( R\left( {x}_{n}\right)  = \; {Q}_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) this means that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, any point \( y \in  {\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  \geq  R\left( {x}_{n}\right) \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. This establishes hypothesis (2) in the statement of Theorem 11.1.

Next, we have:

CLAIM 11.33. For any \( A < \infty \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the ball \( B\left( {{x}_{n},0, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) is contained in the \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) and has compact closure in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) .

Proof. Any point \( z \in  \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) has scalar curvature at most \( {16}{C}^{2}{\rho }^{-2} \) and there is a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( z \) . This means that for all \( y \) with \( {d}_{{G}_{n}}\left( {z, y}\right)  < {\epsilon }^{-1}\rho /{2C} \) we have \( R\left( y\right)  \leq  {32}{C}^{2}{\rho }^{-2} \) . Hence, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( {d}_{{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n}, z}\right)  > {\epsilon }^{-1}\rho /{2C} \) , and thus \( {d}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n}, z}\right)  > {Q}_{n}^{1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1}\rho /{2C} \) . This implies that, given \( A < \infty \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( z \notin  {B}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n},0, A}\right) \) . Since this is true for all \( z \in  \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) , it follows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {B}_{{Q}_{n},{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n},0, A}\right)  \subset  {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) . Next, we must show that, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, this ball has compact closure. That is to say, we must show that for every \( A \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large the distance from \( {x}_{n} \) to the end of the horn \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) is greater than \( A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2} \) . If not, then since the curvature at the end of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) goes to infinity for each \( n \) , this sequence would violate Theorem 10.2.

Because \( B\left( {{x}_{n},0, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) is contained in a \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn, it is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed on scales \( \leq  r \) for a universal \( \kappa  > 0 \) and \( r > 0 \) . Also, because every point in the horn is the center of a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck, for every \( n \) sufficiently large and every \( y \in  B\left( {{x}_{n},0, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) the flow is defined on an interval through \( y \) defined for backward time \( R{\left( y\right) }^{-1} \) .

This completes the proof that all the hypotheses of Theorem 11.1 hold and establishes Claim 11.32.

nodes.proof:
Because of the fact that the \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) have curvature pinched toward positive, and since \( {Q}_{n} \) tend to \( \infty \) as \( n \) tends to infinity, it follows that the geometric limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) has non-negative curvature. In \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) take a minimizing geodesic ray \( {\alpha }_{n} \) from \( {x}_{n} \) to the end of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) and a minimizing geodesic \( {\beta }_{n} \) from \( {x}_{n} \) to \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) . As we have seen, the lengths of both \( {\alpha }_{n} \) and \( {\beta }_{n} \) tend to \( \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) . By passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the \( {\alpha }_{n} \) converge to a minimizing geodesic ray \( \alpha \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) and that the \( {\beta }_{n} \) converge to a minimizing geodesic ray \( \beta \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) . Since, for all \( n \) , the union of \( {\alpha }_{n} \) and \( {\beta }_{n} \) forms a piecewise smooth ray in \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) meeting the central 2-sphere of a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n} \) in a single point and at this point crossing from one side of this 2-sphere to the other, the union of \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) forms a proper, piecewise smooth map of \( \mathbb{R} \) to \( {M}_{\infty } \) that meets the central 2-sphere of a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{\infty } \) in a single point and crosses from one side to the other at the point. This means that \( {M}_{\infty } \) has at least two ends. Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) has non-negative curvature, according to Theorem 2.13, this implies that \( {M}_{\infty } \) is a product of a surface with \( \mathbb{R} \) . Since \( M \) has nonnegative curvature, the surface has non-negative curvature. Since \( M \) has positive curvature at least at one point, the surface is diffeomorphic to the 2-sphere.

According to Theorem 11.1, after passing to a subsequence there is a limit flow defined on some interval of the form \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) for \( {t}_{0} > 0 \) . Suppose that, after passing to a subsequence there is a limit flow defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) for some \( 0 < T < \infty \) . It follows that for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) , the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is of non-negative curvature and has two ends. Again by Theorem 2.13, this implies that for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a Riemannian product of a metric of non-negative curvature on \( {S}^{2} \) with \( \mathbb{R} \) . Thus, by Corollary 4.19 the Ricci flow is a product of a Ricci flow \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h\left( t\right) }\right) \) with the trivial flow on \( \left( {\mathbb{R}, d{s}^{2}}\right) \) . It now follows from Corollary 4.14 that for every \( t \in  ( - T,0\rbrack \) the curvature of \( {g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) \) on \( {S}^{2} \) is positive.

Let \( {M}_{n} \) be the zero time-slice of \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) is the geometric limit of the \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{n}}\right) \) , there is an exhaustive sequence \( {x}_{\infty } \in \; {V}_{1} \subset  {V}_{2} \subset  \cdots \) of open subsets of \( {M}_{\infty } \) with compact closure and embeddings \( {\varphi }_{n} : {V}_{n} \rightarrow  {M}_{n} \) sending \( {x}_{\infty } \) to \( {x}_{n} \) such that \( {\varphi }_{n}^{ * }\left( {{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) converges in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology, uniformly on compact sets, to \( {g}_{\infty } \) .

Of course, for any compact subset \( K \subset  {M}_{\infty } \) and any \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( K \subset  {V}_{n} \) , and there is an embedding \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack   \subset \; {Q}_{n}{\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) compatible with time and the vector field. The map \( {\varphi }_{n} \) defines a map \( {Q}_{n}^{-1}{\varphi }_{n} : K \times  \left\lbrack  {-{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Since the scalar curvature of the limit is positive, and hence bounded away from zero on the compact set \( K \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) and since \( {Q}_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \) tends to infinity, the following is true: For any compact subset \( K \subset  M \) and any \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the scalar curvature of \( {G}_{n} \) on the image \( {Q}_{n}^{-1}{\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) is greater than \( {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , and hence for all \( n \) sufficiently large, every point in \( {Q}_{n}^{-1}{\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times \; \left\lbrack  {-{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Since having a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood is invariant under rescaling, it follows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, every point of \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood.

Next we claim that, for all \( n \) sufficiently large and for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , the point \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. We have already seen that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Of course, since \( {M}_{\infty } \) is non-compact, for \( n \) sufficiently large, the canonical neighborhood of \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) must either be a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap or a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. We shall rule out the possibility of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap, at least for all \( n \) sufficiently large.

To do this, take \( K \) to be a neighborhood of \( \left( {z,0}\right) \) in the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) with the topology of \( {S}^{2} \times  I \) and with the metric being the product of a positively curved metric on \( {S}^{2} \) with the Euclidean metric on \( I \) . We take \( K \) to be sufficiently large to contain the \( {2C} \) -ball centered at \( \left( {z,0}\right) \) . Because the limit flow is the product of a positively curved flow on \( {S}^{2} \) with the trivial flow on \( \mathbb{R} \) , the flow is distance decreasing. Thus, for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) the subman-ifold \( K \times  \{ t\} \) contains the ball in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) centered at \( \left( {z, t}\right) \) of radius \( {2C} \) . For every \( n \) sufficiently large, consider the submanifolds \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) of \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Since the metrics \( {\varphi }_{n}^{ * }{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) \) are converging uniformly for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) to the product flow on \( K \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large and any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , this submanifold contains the \( C \) -ball centered at \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) in \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Furthermore, the maximal curvature two-plane at any point of \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) is almost tangent to the \( {S}^{2} \) -direction of \( K \) . Hence, by Lemma A. 2 the central 2-sphere of any \( \epsilon \) -neck contained \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) is almost parallel to the \( {S}^{2} \) -factors in the product structure on \( K \) at every point. This implies that the central 2-sphere of any such \( \epsilon \) -neck is isotopic to the \( {S}^{2} \) -factor of \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) . Suppose that \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap \( \mathcal{C} \) . Then \( \mathcal{C} \) is contained in \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) . Consider the \( \epsilon \) -neck \( N \subset  \mathcal{C} \) that is the complement of the core of \( \mathcal{C} \) . Its central 2-sphere, \( \sum \) , is isotopic in \( K \) to the 2-sphere factor of \( K \) , but this is absurd since \( \sum \) bounds a 3-ball in the \( \mathcal{C} \) . This contradiction shows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large and all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , it is not possible for \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) to be contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. The only other possibility is that for all \( n \) sufficiently large and all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) the point \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) .

Fix \( n \) sufficiently large. Since, for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , the point \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck, it follows from Definition 9.78 that for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) we have \( R\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right)  \leq  R\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) ,0}\right) \) (this follows from the fact that the partial derivative in the time-direction of the scalar curvature of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck of scale one is positive and bounded away from 0 \( ) \) . It also follows from Definition 9.78 that the flow near \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , - {t}^{\prime }}\right) \) extends backwards to time

\[
- {t}^{\prime } - {R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}^{-1}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( {z,{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right)  <  - {t}^{\prime } - {R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}^{-1}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( {z,0}\right) }\right) ,
\]

with the same inequality for scalar curvature holding for all \( t \) in this extended interval. Applying this for \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) but sufficiently close to \( T \) establishes the last statement in the claim, and completes the proof of the claim.

nodes.label: Definition 12.1
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
DEFINITION 12.1. A standard initial metric is a metric \( {g}_{0} \) on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) with the following properties:

(i) \( {g}_{0} \) is a complete metric.

(ii) \( {g}_{0} \) has non-negative sectional curvature at every point.

(iii) \( {g}_{0} \) is invariant under the usual \( {SO}\left( 3\right) \) -action on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) .

(iv) there is a compact ball \( B \subset  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) so that the restriction of the metric \( {g}_{0} \) to the complement of this ball is isometric to the product \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h}\right)  \times  \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{ + }, d{s}^{2}}\right) \) where \( h \) is the round metric of scalar curvature 1 on \( {S}^{2} \) .

(v) \( {g}_{0} \) has constant sectional curvature \( 1/4 \) near the origin. (This point will be denoted \( p \) and is called the tip of the initial metric.)

See FIG. 1.

Actually, one can work with an alternative weaker version of the fourth condition, namely:

(iv \( {}^{\prime } \) ) \( {g}_{0} \) is asymptotic at infinity in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to the product of the round metric \( {h}_{0} \) on \( {S}^{2} \) of scalar curvature 1 with the usual metric \( d{s}^{2} \) on the real line. By this we mean that if \( {x}_{n} \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) is any sequence converging to infinity, then the based Riemannian manifolds \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3},{g}_{0},{x}_{n}}\right) \) converge smoothly to \( \left( {{S}^{2},{h}_{0}}\right)  \times  \left( {\mathbb{R}, d{s}^{2}}\right) \) . But we shall only use standard initial metrics as given in Definition 12.1.

nodes.proof:
We construct our Riemannian manifold as follows. Fix Euclidean coordinates \( \left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}}\right) \) on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{4} \) . Let \( y = f\left( s\right) \) be a function defined for \( s \geq  0 \) and satisfying:

(1) \( f \) is \( {C}^{\infty } \) on \( \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) .

(2) \( f\left( s\right)  > 0 \) for all \( s > 0 \) .

(3) \( {f}^{\prime \prime }\left( s\right)  \leq  0 \) for all \( s > 0 \) .

(4) There is \( {s}_{1} > 0 \) such that \( f\left( s\right)  = \sqrt{2} \) for all \( s \geq  {s}_{1} \) .

(5) There is \( {s}_{0} > 0 \) such that \( f\left( s\right)  = \sqrt{{4s} - {s}^{2}} \) for all \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{s}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) .

Given such a function \( f \) , consider the graph

\[
\Gamma  = \left\{  {\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{1}}\right)  \mid  {x}_{0} \geq  0\text{ and }{x}_{1} = f\left( {x}_{0}\right) }\right\}
\]

in the \( \left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{1}}\right) \) -plane. We define \( \sum \left( f\right) \) by rotating \( \Gamma \) about the \( {x}_{0} \) -axis in four-space:

\[
\sum \left( f\right)  = \left\{  {\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}}\right)  \mid  {x}_{0} \geq  0\text{ and }{x}_{1}^{2} + {x}_{2}^{2} + {x}_{3}^{2} = f{\left( {x}_{0}\right) }^{2}}\right\}  .
\]

Because of the last condition on \( f \) , there is a neighborhood of \( 0 \in  \sum \left( f\right) \) that is isometric to a neighborhood of the north pole in the 3-sphere of radius 2. Because of this and the first item, we see that \( \sum \left( f\right) \) is a smooth submanifold of \( {\mathbb{R}}^{4} \) . Hence, it inherits a Riemannian metric \( {g}_{0} \) . Because of the fourth item, a neighborhood of infinity of \( \left( {\sum \left( f\right) ,{g}_{0}}\right) \) is isometric to \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h}\right)  \times  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) , and in particular, \( \left( {\sum \left( f\right) ,{g}_{0}}\right) \) is complete. Clearly, the rotation action of \( {S0}\left( 3\right) \) on \( \sum \left( f\right) \) , induced by the orthogonal action on the last three coordinates in \( {\mathbb{R}}^{4} \) , is an isometric action with the origin as the only fixed point. It is also clear that \( \sum \left( f\right) \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) by a diffeomorphism that send the \( {SO}\left( 3\right) \) action to the standard one on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) .

It remains to compute the sectional curvatures of \( {g}_{0} \) . Let \( q \in  \sum \left( f\right) \) be a point distinct from the fixed point of the \( {SO}\left( 3\right) \) -action. Direct computation shows that the tangent plane to the 2-dimensional \( {SO}\left( 3\right) \) -orbit through \( q \) is a principal direction for the curvature, and the sectional curvature on this tangent two-plane is given by

\[
\frac{1}{f{\left( q\right) }^{2}\left( {1 + {f}^{\prime }{\left( q\right) }^{2}}\right) }.
\]

On the subspace in \( { \land  }^{2}{T}_{q}\sum \left( f\right) \) perpendicular to the line given by this two-plane, the curvature is constant with eigenvalue

\[
\frac{-{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( q\right) }{f\left( q\right) {\left( 1 + {f}^{\prime }{\left( q\right) }^{2}\right) }^{2}}\text{ . }
\]

Under our assumptions about \( f \) , it is clear that \( \sum \left( f\right) \) has non-negative curvature and has constant sectional curvature \( 1/4 \) near the origin. It remains to choose the function \( f \) satisfying items (1) - (5) above.

Consider the function \( h\left( s\right)  = \left( {2 - s}\right) /\sqrt{{4s} - {s}^{2}} \) . This function is integrable from 0 and the definite integral from zero to \( s \) is equal to \( \sqrt{{4s} - {s}^{2}} \) . Let \( \lambda \left( s\right) \) be a non-increasing \( {C}^{\infty } \) -function defined on \( \left\lbrack  {0,1/2}\right\rbrack \) , with \( \lambda \) identically one near 0 and identically equal to 0 near \( 1/2 \) . We extend \( \lambda \) to be identically 1 for \( s < 0 \) and identically 0 for \( s > 1/2 \) . Clearly,

\[
{\int }_{0}^{2}h\left( s\right) \lambda \left( {s - 3/2}\right) {ds} > {\int }_{0}^{3/2}h\left( s\right) {ds} > \sqrt{2}
\]

and

\[
{\int }_{0}^{2}h\left( s\right) \lambda \left( s\right) {ds} < {\int }_{0}^{1/2}h\left( s\right)  < \sqrt{2}.
\]

Hence, for some \( {s}_{0} \in  \left( {1/2,3/2}\right) \) we have

\[
{\int }_{0}^{2}h\left( s\right) \lambda \left( {s - {s}_{0}}\right) {ds} = \sqrt{2}.
\]

We define

\[
f\left( s\right)  = {\int }_{0}^{s}h\left( \sigma \right) \lambda \left( {\sigma  - {s}_{0}}\right) {d\sigma }.
\]

It is easy to see that \( f \) satisfies all the above conditions.

The following lemma is clear from the construction.

nodes.content: DEFINITION 12.4. A partial standard Ricci flow is a Ricci flow \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) defined for \( 0 \leq  t < T \) , such that \( g\left( 0\right)  = {g}_{0} \) and such that the curvature is locally bounded in time. We say that a partial standard Ricci flow is a standard Ricci flow if it has the property that \( T \) is maximal in the sense that there is no extension of the flow to a flow with curvature locally bounded in time defined on an time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}^{\prime }}\right) \) with \( {T}^{\prime } > T \) .

THEOREM 12.5. There is a standard Ricci flow defined for some positive amount of time. Let \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 \leq  t < T \) , be a standard Ricci flow. Then the following hold.

(1) (Uniqueness): If \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3},{g}^{\prime }\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 \leq  t < {T}^{\prime } \) , is a standard Ricci flow, then \( {T}^{\prime } = T \) and \( {g}^{\prime }\left( t\right)  = g\left( t\right) \) .

(2) (Time Interval): \( T = 1 \) .

(3) (Positive curvature): For each \( t \in  \left( {0,1}\right) \) the metric \( g\left( t\right) \) on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) is complete of strictly positive curvature.

(4) (SO(3)-invariance): For each \( t \in  \lbrack 0,1) \) the metric \( g\left( t\right) \) is invariant under the \( {SO}\left( 3\right) \) -action on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) .

(5) (Asymptotics at \( \infty \) ): For any \( {t}_{0} < 1 \) and any \( \epsilon  > 0 \) there is a compact subset \( X \) of \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) such that for any \( x \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \smallsetminus  X \) the restriction of the standard flow to an appropriate neighborhood of \( x \) for time \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) is within \( \epsilon \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology of the product Ricci flow \( \left( {{S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) }\right) , h\left( t\right)  \times  d{s}^{2},0 \leq  t \leq  {t}_{0} \) , where \( h\left( t\right) \) is the round metric with scalar curvature \( 1/\left( {1 - t}\right) \) on \( {S}^{2} \) .

(6) (Non-collapsing): There are \( r > 0 \) and \( \kappa  > 0 \) such that \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed on scales less than \( r \) for all \( 0 \leq  t < 1 \) .

nodes.content:
## 3. Existence of a standard flow

For any \( R < \infty \) , denote by \( {B}_{R} \subset  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) , the ball of radius \( R \) about the origin in the metric \( {g}_{0} \) . For \( R \geq  {A}_{0} + 1 \) , a neighborhood of the boundary of this ball is isometric to \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h}\right)  \times  \left( {\left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack  , d{s}^{2}}\right) \) . Thus, in this case, we can double the ball, gluing the boundary to itself by the identity, forming a manifold we denote by \( {S}_{R}^{3} \) . The doubled metric will be a smooth Riemannian metric \( {g}_{R} \) on \( {S}_{R}^{3} \) . Let \( p \in  {S}_{R}^{3} \) be the image of the origin in the first copy of \( {B}_{R} \) . Now take a sequence, \( {R}_{n} \) , tending to infinity to construct based Riemannian manifolds \( \left( {{S}_{{R}_{n}}^{3},{g}_{{R}_{n}}, p}\right) \) that converge geometrically to \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3},{g}_{0}, p}\right) \) . For each \( n \) , let \( \left( {{S}_{{R}_{n}}^{3},{g}_{{R}_{n}}\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 \leq  t < {T}_{n} \) be maximal Ricci flow with \( \left( {{S}_{{R}_{n}}^{3},{g}_{{R}_{n}}}\right) \) as initial metric. The maximum principle applied to Equation (3.7), \( \partial R/\partial t = \; \bigtriangleup R + {\left| \mathrm{{Ric}}\right| }^{2} \) , then implies by Proposition 2.23 that the maximum of \( R \) at time \( t,{R}_{\max }\left( t\right) \) obeys the inequality \( \partial {R}_{\max }/\partial t \leq  {R}_{\max }{\left( t\right) }^{2} \) , and integrating this inequality (i.e., invoking Lemma 2.22) one finds positive constants \( {t}_{0} \) and \( {Q}_{0} \) such that for each \( n \) , the norm of the scalar curvature of \( {g}_{{R}_{n}}\left( t\right) \) are bounded by \( {Q}_{0} \) on the interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,\max \left( {{t}_{0},{T}_{n}}\right) }\right) \) . By Corollary 4.14, for each \( n \) the sectional curvature of the flow \( \left( {{S}_{{R}_{n}}^{3},{g}_{{R}_{n}}\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 \leq  t < {T}_{n} \) is non-negative, and hence the sectional curvature of this flow is also bounded by \( {Q}_{0} \) on \( \left\lbrack  {0,\max \left( {{t}_{0},{T}_{n}}\right) }\right) \) . It now follows from Proposition 4.12 and the fact that the \( {T}_{n} \) are maximal that \( {T}_{n} > {t}_{0} \) for all \( n \) . Since the Riemann curvatures of the \( \left( {{S}_{{R}_{n}}^{3},{g}_{{R}_{n}}\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 \leq  t < {t}_{0} \) , are bounded independent of \( n \) , and since the \( \left( {{S}_{{R}_{n}}^{3},{g}_{{R}_{n}}, p}\right) \) converge geometrically to \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3},{g}_{0}, p}\right) \) , it follows from Theorem 5.15 that there is a geometric limiting flow defined on \( \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Since this flow is the geometric limit of flows of uniformly bounded curvature, it has uniformly bounded curvature. Taking a maximal extension of this flow to one of locally bounded curvature gives a standard flow.

nodes.label: Lemma 12.6
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.section_title: 12.4. Completeness, positive curvature, and asymptotic behavior
nodes.content: LEMMA 12.6. For each \( {t}_{0} \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) is complete and of positive curvature.
nodes.content_excerpt: LEMMA 12.6. For each \( {t}_{0} \in \lbrack 0, T) \) the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) is complete and of positive curvature.

nodes.proof:
Fix \( {t}_{0} \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) . By hypothesis \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( t\right) }\right) ,0 \leq  t \leq  {t}_{0} \) has bounded curvature. Hence, there is a constant \( C < \infty \) such that \( g\left( 0\right)  \leq \; {Cg}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) , so that for any points \( x, y \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) , we have \( {d}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  \sqrt{C}{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, y}\right) \) . Since \( g\left( 0\right) \) is complete, this implies that \( g\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) is also complete.

Now let us show that \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) has non-negative curvature. Here, the argument is the analogue of the proof of Corollary 4.14 with one additional step, the use of a function \( \varphi \) to localize the argument. Suppose this is false, i.e., suppose that there is \( x \in  M \) with \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \) having an eigenvalue less than zero. Since the restriction of the flow to \( \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) is complete and of bounded curvature, according to \( \left\lbrack  \mathbf{{33}}\right\rbrack \) for any constants \( C < \infty \) and \( \eta  > 0 \) and any compact subset \( K \subset  M \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) there is \( \epsilon  > 0 \) and a function \( \varphi  : M \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) with the following properties:

(1) \( {\left. \varphi \right| }_{K} \leq  \eta \) .

(2) \( \varphi  \geq  \epsilon \) everywhere.

(3) For each \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) the restriction of \( \varphi \) to \( M \times  \{ t\} \) goes to infinity at infinity in the sense that for any \( A < \infty \) the pre-image \( {\varphi }^{-1}(\left\lbrack  {0, A}\right\rbrack   \cap \; \left( {M\times \{ t\} }\right) \) is compact.

(4) On all of \( M \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) we have \( \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \bigtriangleup }\right) \varphi  \geq  {C\varphi } \) .

Recall from Section 5 of Chapter 3 is the curvature tensor written with respect to an evolving orthonormal frame \( \left\{  {F}_{\alpha }\right\} \) for the tangent bundle. Consider the symmetric, horizontal two-tensor \( \widehat{\mathcal{T}} = \mathcal{T} + {\varphi g} \) . Let \( \widehat{\mu }\left( {x, t}\right) \) denote the smallest eigenvalue of this symmetric two-tensor at \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) . Clearly, since the curvature is bounded, it follows from the third property of \( \varphi \) that for each \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) the restriction of \( \widehat{\mu } \) to \( M \times  \{ t\} \) goes to infinity at infinity in \( M \) . In particular, the subset of \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  M \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) with the property that \( \widehat{\mu }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \widehat{\mu }\left( {y, t}\right) \) for all \( y \in  M \) is a compact subset of \( M \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . It follows from Proposition 2.23 that \( f\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\min }\limits_{{x \in  M}}\widehat{\mu }\left( {x, t}\right) \) is a continuous function of \( t \) . Choosing \( \eta  > 0 \) sufficiently small and \( K \) to include \( \left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \) , then \( \widehat{\mathcal{T}} \) will have a negative eigenvalue at \( \left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Clearly, it has only positive eigenvalues on \( M \times  \{ 0\} \) . Thus, there is \( 0 < {t}_{1} < {t}_{0} \) so that \( \widehat{\mathcal{T}} \) has only positive eigenvalues on \( M \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{1}}\right) \) but has a zero eigenvalue at \( \left( {y,{t}_{1}}\right) \) for some \( y \in  M \) . That is to say, \( \mathcal{T} \geq   - {\varphi g} \) on \( M \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack \) . Diagonalizing \( \mathcal{T} \) at any point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( t \leq  {t}_{1} \) , all its eigenvalues are at least \( - \varphi \left( {x,{t}_{1}}\right) \) . It follows immediately that on \( M \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack \) the smallest eigenvalue of the symmetric form \( {\mathcal{T}}^{2} + {\mathcal{T}}^{\# } \) is bounded below by \( {2\varphi } \) . Thus, choosing \( C \geq  4 \) we see that for \( t \leq  {t}_{1} \) every eigenvalue of \( {\mathcal{T}}^{2} + {\mathcal{T}}^{\# } \) is at least \( - {C\varphi }/2 \) .

We compute the evolution equation using the formula in Lemma 4.13 for the evolution of \( \mathcal{T} \) in an evolving orthonormal frame:

\[
\frac{\partial \widehat{\mathcal{I}}}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{I}}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial t}g - {2\varphi }\operatorname{Ric}\left( g\right)
\]

\[
= \Delta \mathcal{T} + {\mathcal{T}}^{2} + {\mathcal{T}}^{\# } + \frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial t}g - {2\varphi }\operatorname{Ric}\left( g\right)
\]

\[
= \bigtriangleup \widehat{\mathcal{T}} + {\mathcal{T}}^{2} + {\mathcal{T}}^{\# } + \left( {\frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial t} - \bigtriangleup \varphi }\right) g - {2\varphi }\operatorname{Ric}\left( g\right)
\]

\[
\geq  \bigtriangleup \widehat{T} + {\mathcal{T}}^{2} + {\mathcal{T}}^{\# } + \varphi \left( {{Cg} - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( g\right) }\right) .
\]

Since every eigenvalue of \( {\mathcal{T}}^{2} + {\mathcal{T}}^{\# } \) on \( M \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack \) is at least \( - {C\varphi }/2 \) , it follows that on \( M \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack \) ,

\[
\frac{\partial \widehat{\mathcal{T}}}{\partial t} \geq  \bigtriangleup \widehat{\mathcal{T}} + \varphi \left( {{Cg}/2 - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( g\right) }\right) .
\]

Once again assuming that \( C \) is sufficiently large, we see that for any \( t \leq  {t}_{1} \) ,

\[
\frac{\partial \widehat{\mathcal{T}}}{\partial t} \geq  \bigtriangleup \widehat{T}.
\]

Thus, at any local minimum \( x \in  M \) for \( \widehat{\mu }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) , we have

\[
\frac{\partial \widehat{\mu }}{\partial t} \geq  0
\]

This immediately implies by Proposition 2.23 that \( \psi \left( t\right)  = \mathop{\min }\limits_{{x \in  M}}\widehat{\mu }\left( {x, t}\right) \) is a non-decreasing function of \( t \) . Since its value at \( t = 0 \) is at least \( \epsilon  > 0 \) and its value at \( {t}_{1} \) is zero, this is a contradiction. This establishes that the solution has non-negative curvature everywhere. Indeed, by Corollary 4.20 it has strictly positive curvature for every \( t > 0 \) .

nodes.content:
LEMMA 12.9. With \( X \) and its dual \( {X}^{ * } \) evolving by the above equations, set \( V = \nabla {X}^{ * } \) , so that \( V \) is a contravariant two-tensor. In local coordinates we have \( V = {V}_{ij}d{x}^{i} \otimes  d{x}^{j} \) with

\[
{V}_{ij} = {\left( {\nabla }_{i}X\right) }_{j} = {g}_{jk}{\left( {\nabla }_{i}X\right) }^{k}.
\]

This symmetric two-tensor satisfies

(12.3)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}V = \bigtriangleup V - \left( {2{R}_{k}{}^{rl}{}_{j}{V}_{rl} + {\operatorname{Ric}}_{k}^{l}{V}_{lj} + {\operatorname{Ric}}_{j}^{l}{V}_{kl}}\right) d{x}^{k} \otimes  d{x}^{j}.
\]

nodes.proof:
The computation is routine, if complicated. We make the computation at a point \( \left( {p, t}\right) \) of space-time. We fix local \( g\left( t\right) \) -Gaussian coordinates \( \left( {{x}^{1},\ldots ,{x}^{n}}\right) \) centered at \( p \) for space, so that the Christoffel symbols vanish at \( \left( {p, t}\right) \) .

We compute

(12.4)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}V = \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {\nabla {X}^{ * }}\right)  =  - \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\Gamma }_{kj}^{l}}\right) {X}_{l}^{ * }d{x}^{k} \otimes  d{x}^{j} + \nabla \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{X}^{ * }}\right)
\]

\[
= \left( {-{\nabla }^{l}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{kj} + {\nabla }_{k}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{j}^{l} + {\nabla }_{j}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{k}^{l}}\right) {X}_{l}^{ * }d{x}^{k} \otimes  d{x}^{j}
\]

\[
+ \nabla \left( {\Delta {X}^{ * } - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, \cdot  }\right) }\right) .
\]

We have

\[
\nabla \left( {\bigtriangleup {X}^{ * }}\right)  = \nabla \left( \left( {{g}^{rs}\left( {{\nabla }_{r}{\nabla }_{s}\left( {X}^{ * }\right)  - {\Gamma }_{rs}^{l}{\nabla }_{l}{X}^{ * }}\right) }\right) \right.
\]

\[
= {g}^{rs}\left( {\nabla \left( {{\nabla }_{r}{\nabla }_{s}\left( {X}^{ * }\right)  - {\Gamma }_{rs}^{l}{\nabla }_{l}{X}^{ * }}\right) }\right) .
\]

Let us recall the formula for commuting \( \nabla \) and \( {\nabla }_{r} \) . The following is immediate from the definitions.

CLAIM 12.11. For any tensor \( \phi \) we have

\[
\nabla \left( {{\nabla }_{r}\phi }\right)  = {\nabla }_{r}\left( {\nabla \phi }\right)  + d{x}^{k} \otimes  \operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{r}}\right) \left( \phi \right)  - {\nabla }_{r}\left( {d{x}^{l}}\right)  \otimes  {\nabla }_{l}\left( \phi \right) .
\]

Applying this to our formula gives

\[
\nabla \left( {\bigtriangleup {X}^{ * }}\right)  = {g}^{rs}\left( {{\nabla }_{r}\nabla {\nabla }_{s}{X}^{ * } + d{x}^{k} \otimes  \operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{r}}\right) \left( {{\nabla }_{s}{X}^{ * }}\right) }\right.
\]

\[
\left. {-{\nabla }_{r}\left( {d{x}^{l}}\right)  \otimes  {\nabla }_{l}{\nabla }_{s}{X}^{ * } - \nabla \left( {{\Gamma }_{rs}^{l}{\nabla }_{l}{X}^{ * }}\right) }\right) .
\]

Now we apply the same formula to commute \( \nabla \) and \( {\nabla }_{s} \) . The result is

\[
\nabla \left( {\bigtriangleup {X}^{ * }}\right)  = {g}^{rs}\left( {{\nabla }_{r}{\nabla }_{s}\nabla {X}^{ * } + {\nabla }_{r}\left( {d{x}^{k} \otimes  \operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{s}}\right) {X}^{ * } - {\nabla }_{s}d{x}^{l} \otimes  {\nabla }_{l}{X}^{ * }}\right. }\right.
\]

\[
+ d{x}^{k} \otimes  \operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{r}}\right) \left( {{\nabla }_{s}{X}^{ * }}\right)
\]

\[
\left. {-{\nabla }_{r}\left( {d{x}^{l}}\right)  \otimes  {\nabla }_{l}{\nabla }_{s}{X}^{ * } - \nabla \left( {{\Gamma }_{rs}^{l}{\nabla }_{l}{X}^{ * }}\right) }\right) .
\]

Now we expand

\[
{\nabla }_{r}\left( {d{x}^{k} \otimes  \operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{s}}\right) {X}^{ * } - {\nabla }_{s}d{x}^{l} \otimes  {\nabla }_{l}{X}^{ * }}\right)
\]

\[
= {\nabla }_{r}\left( {d{x}^{k}}\right)  \otimes  \operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{s}}\right) {X}^{ * } + d{x}^{k} \otimes  {\nabla }_{r}\left( {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{s}}\right) }\right) {X}^{ * }
\]

\[
+ d{x}^{k} \otimes  \operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{s}}\right) {\nabla }_{r}{X}^{ * } - {\nabla }_{r}{\nabla }_{s}d{x}^{l} \otimes  {\nabla }_{l}{X}^{ * } - {\nabla }_{s}d{x}^{l} \otimes  {\nabla }_{r}{\nabla }_{l}{X}^{ * }.
\]

Invoking the fact that the Christoffel symbols vanish at the point of spacetime where we are making the computation, this above expression simplifies to

\[
{\nabla }_{r}\left( {d{x}^{k} \otimes  \operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{s}}\right) {X}^{ * } - {\nabla }_{s}d{x}^{l} \otimes  {\nabla }_{l}{X}^{ * }}\right)
\]

\[
= d{x}^{k} \otimes  {\nabla }_{r}\left( {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{s}}\right) }\right) {X}^{ * } + d{x}^{k} \otimes  \operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{s}}\right) {\nabla }_{r}{X}^{ * } - {\nabla }_{r}{\nabla }_{s}d{x}^{l} \otimes  {\nabla }_{l}{X}^{ * }.
\]

Also, expanding and using the vanishing of the Christoffel symbols we have

\[
- \nabla \left( {{\Gamma }_{rs}^{l}{\nabla }_{l}{X}^{ * }}\right)  =  - d{\Gamma }_{rs}^{l} \otimes  {\nabla }_{l}{X}^{ * } - {\Gamma }_{rs}^{l}\nabla {\nabla }_{l}{X}^{ * }
\]

\[
=  - d{\Gamma }_{rs}^{l} \otimes  {\nabla }_{l}{X}^{ * }.
\]

Plugging these computations into the equation above and using once more the vanishing of the Christoffel symbols gives

\[
\nabla \left( {\bigtriangleup {X}^{ * }}\right)
\]

\[
= \bigtriangleup \left( {\nabla {X}^{ * }}\right)  + {g}^{rs}\left( {d{x}^{k} \otimes  {\nabla }_{r}\left( {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{s}}\right) }\right) {X}^{ * } + d{x}^{k} \otimes  \operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{s}}\right) {\nabla }_{r}{X}^{ * }}\right.
\]

\[
\left. {-{\nabla }_{r}{\nabla }_{s}d{x}^{l} \otimes  {\nabla }_{l}{X}^{ * } + d{x}^{k} \otimes  \operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{r}}\right) \left( {{\nabla }_{s}{X}^{ * }}\right)  - d{\Gamma }_{rs}^{l} \otimes  {\nabla }_{l}{X}^{ * }}\right) .
\]

Now by the symmetry of \( {g}^{rs} \) we can amalgamate the second and fourth terms on the right-hand side to give

\[
\nabla \left( {\bigtriangleup {X}^{ * }}\right)  = \bigtriangleup \left( {\nabla {X}^{ * }}\right)  + {g}^{rs}\left( {d{x}^{k} \otimes  {\nabla }_{r}\left( {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{s}}\right) }\right) {X}^{ * }}\right.
\]

\[
+ {2d}{x}^{k} \otimes  \operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{s}}\right) {\nabla }_{r}{X}^{ * } - {\nabla }_{r}{\nabla }_{s}d{x}^{l} \otimes  {\nabla }_{l}{X}^{ * }
\]

\[
\left. {-d{\Gamma }_{rs}^{l} \otimes  {\nabla }_{l}{X}^{ * }}\right)
\]

We expand

\[
\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{s}}\right) {\nabla }_{r}{X}^{ * } =  - {R}_{ks}{}^{l}{}_{j}{V}_{rl}d{x}^{j}.
\]

Also we have (again using the vanishing of the Christoffel symbols)

\[
- {\nabla }_{r}{\nabla }_{s}d{x}^{l} - d{\Gamma }_{rs}^{l} = {\nabla }_{r}{\Gamma }_{ks}^{l}d{x}^{k} - {\partial }_{k}{\Gamma }_{rs}^{l}d{x}^{k}
\]

\[
= {R}_{rk}{}^{l}{}_{s}d{x}^{k}.
\]

Lastly,

\[
{\nabla }_{r}\left( {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{k},{\partial }_{s}}\right) }\right) {X}^{ * } =  - {\left( {\nabla }_{r}R\right) }_{ks}^{l}{}_{j}^{l}{X}_{l}^{ * }d{x}^{j}.
\]

Plugging all this in and raising indices yields

\[
\nabla \left( {\bigtriangleup {X}^{ * }}\right)  = \bigtriangleup \left( {\nabla {X}^{ * }}\right)  - {g}^{rs}{\left( {\nabla }_{r}R\right) }_{ks}{}^{l}{}_{j}{X}_{l}^{ * }d{x}^{k} \otimes  d{x}^{j} - 2{R}_{k}{}^{rl}{}_{j}{V}_{rl}d{x}^{k} \otimes  d{x}^{j}
\]

\[
+ {g}^{rs}{R}_{rk}{}^{l}{}_{s}{V}_{lj}d{x}^{k} \otimes  d{x}^{j}
\]

\[
= \bigtriangleup \left( {\nabla {X}^{ * }}\right)  - {g}^{rs}{\left( {\nabla }_{r}R\right) }_{ks}{}^{j}{}_{l}{X}_{j}^{ * }d{x}^{k} \otimes  d{x}^{l} - 2{R}_{k}{}^{rl}{}_{j}{V}_{rl}d{x}^{k} \otimes  d{x}^{j}
\]

\[
- {\operatorname{Ric}}_{k}^{l}{V}_{lj}d{x}^{k} \otimes  d{x}^{j}
\]

Thus, we have

\[
\nabla \left( {\bigtriangleup {X}^{ * }}\right)  - \nabla \left( {\operatorname{Ric}{\left( X, \cdot  \right) }^{ * }}\right)
\]

\[
= \bigtriangleup \left( {\nabla {X}^{ * }}\right)  - {g}^{rs}{\left( {\nabla }_{r}R\right) }_{ks}{}^{l}{}_{j}{X}_{l}^{ * }d{x}^{k} \otimes  d{x}^{j} - 2{R}_{k}{}^{rl}{}_{j}{V}_{rl}d{x}^{k} \otimes  d{x}^{j}
\]

\[
- \left( {{\operatorname{Ric}}_{k}^{l}{V}_{lj} + {\nabla }_{k}{\left( \operatorname{Ric}\right) }_{j}^{l}{X}_{l}^{ * } + {\operatorname{Ric}}_{j}^{l}{V}_{kl}}\right) d{x}^{k} \otimes  d{x}^{j},
\]

and consequently, plugging back into Equation (12.4), and canceling the two like terms appearing with opposite sign, we have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}V = \left( {-{\nabla }^{l}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{kj} + {\nabla }_{j}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{k}^{l}}\right) {X}_{l}^{ * }d{x}^{k} \otimes  d{x}^{j} + \bigtriangleup \left( {\nabla {X}^{ * }}\right)
\]

\[
- {g}^{rs}{\left( {\nabla }_{r}R\right) }_{ks}{}^{l}{}_{j}{X}_{l}^{ * }d{x}^{k} \otimes  d{x}^{j} - 2{R}_{k}{}^{rl}{}_{j}{V}_{rl}d{x}^{k} \otimes  d{x}^{j}
\]

\[
- \left( {{\operatorname{Ric}}_{k}^{l}{V}_{lj} + {\operatorname{Ric}}_{j}^{l}{V}_{kl}}\right) d{x}^{k} \otimes  d{x}^{j}
\]

The last thing we need to see in order to complete the proof is that

\[

\]

REMARK 12.10. The covariant derivative acts on one-forms \( \omega \) in such a way that the following equation holds:

\[
\langle \nabla \left( \omega \right) ,\xi \rangle  = \langle \omega ,\nabla \left( \xi \right) \rangle
\]

for every vector field \( \xi \) . This means that in local coordinates we have

\[
{\nabla }_{{\partial }_{r}}\left( {d{x}^{k}}\right)  =  - {\Gamma }_{rl}^{k}d{x}^{l}.
\]

Similarly, the Riemann curvature acts on one-forms \( \omega \) satisfying

\[
\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\xi }_{1},{\xi }_{2}}\right) \left( \omega \right) \left( \xi \right)  =  - \omega \left( {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\xi }_{1},{\xi }_{2}}\right) \left( \xi \right) }\right) .
\]

Recall that in local coordinates

\[
{R}_{ijkl} = \left\langle  {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{i},{\partial }_{j}}\right) \left( {\partial }_{l}\right) ,{\partial }_{k}}\right\rangle  .
\]

Thus, we have

\[
\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{\partial }_{i},{\partial }_{j}}\right) \left( {d{x}^{k}}\right)  =  - {g}^{ka}{R}_{ijal}d{x}^{l} =  - {R}_{ij}{}^{k}{}_{l}d{x}^{l},
\]

where as usual we use the inverse metric tensor to raise the index.

Also, notice that \( \bigtriangleup {X}_{i} - {\operatorname{Ric}}_{ik}{X}^{k} =  - {\bigtriangleup }_{d}{X}_{i} \) , where by \( {\bigtriangleup }_{d} \) we mean the Laplacian associated to the operator \( d \) from vector fields to one-forms with values in the vector field. Since

\[
- \left( {{d\delta } + {\delta d}}\right) {X}_{i} =  - {\nabla }_{i}\left( {-{\nabla }^{k}{X}_{k}}\right)  - \left( {-{\nabla }^{k}}\right) \left( {{\nabla }_{k}{X}_{i} - {\nabla }_{i}{X}_{k}}\right)
\]

\[
= {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }^{k}{X}_{k} + {\nabla }^{k}{\nabla }_{k}{X}_{i} - {\nabla }^{k}{\nabla }_{i}{X}_{k}
\]

\[
= {R}_{i}{}^{k}{}_{k}{}^{j}{X}_{j} + {\nabla }^{k}{\nabla }_{k}{X}_{i} = \bigtriangleup {X}_{i} - {\operatorname{Ric}}_{i}^{j}{X}_{j}.
\]

nodes.proof:
By the asymptotic condition, there is a compact subset \( X \subset  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) such that for any point \( p \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \smallsetminus  X \) and for any \( t \leq  {t}_{0} \) we have \( R\left( {p, t}\right)  < \; 2/\left( {1 - t}\right) \) . Since \( C \geq  2 \) , for all \( t \) for which \( \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3}}}R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  2/\left( {1 - t}\right) \) , we also have

\[
R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \frac{C}{1 - {Ct}}.
\]

Consider the complementary subset of \( t \) , that is to say the subset of \( \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) for which there is \( x \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) with \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  > C/\left( {1 - {Ct}}\right) \) . This is an open subset of \( \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , and hence is a disjoint union of relatively open intervals. Let \( \left\{  {{t}_{1} < {t}_{2}}\right\} \) be the endpoints of one such interval. If \( {t}_{1} \neq  0 \) , then clearly \( {R}_{\max }\left( {t}_{1}\right)  = C/\left( {1 - C{t}_{1}}\right) \) . Since \( C \geq  \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3}}}R\left( {x,0}\right) \) , this is also true if \( {t}_{1} = 0 \) . For every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{1},{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) the maximum of \( R \) on the \( t \) time-slice is achieved, and the subset of \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{1},{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) of all points where maxima are achieved is compact. Furthermore, at any maximum point we have \( \partial R/\partial t \leq  {R}^{2} \) . Hence, according to Proposition 2.23 for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{1},{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) we have

\[
{R}_{\max }\left( t\right)  \leq  G\left( t\right)
\]

where \( {G}^{\prime }\left( t\right)  = {G}^{2}\left( t\right) \) and \( G\left( {t}_{1}\right)  = C/\left( {1 - C{t}_{1}}\right) \) . It is easy to see that

\[
G\left( t\right)  = \frac{C}{1 - {Ct}}
\]

This shows that for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{1},{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) we have \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \frac{C}{1 - {Ct}} \) , completing the proof of the claim.
