6.1. From Ricci flow to Ricci-DeTurck flow. Let \( \left( {{M}^{n}, g\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in \; \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0}, T}\right\rbrack \) , be a solution of the Ricci flow and let \( {\psi }_{t} : M \rightarrow  M, t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{T}_{1}}\right\rbrack \) be a solution of the harmonic map flow

(12.8)

\[
\frac{\partial {\psi }_{t}}{\partial t} = {\bigtriangleup }_{g\left( t\right) , g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }{\psi }_{t},\;{\psi }_{{t}_{0}} = \text{ Id. }
\]

Here, \( {\bigtriangleup }_{g\left( t\right) , g\left( {t}_{0}\right) } \) is the Laplacian for maps from the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) to the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . In local coordinates \( \left( {x}^{i}\right) \) on the domain \( M \) and \( \left( {y}^{\alpha }\right) \) on the target \( M \) , the harmonic map flow (12.8) can be written as

(12.9)

\[
\text{ 12.9) }\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - {\bigtriangleup }_{g\left( t\right) }}\right) {\psi }^{\alpha }\left( {x, t}\right)  = {g}^{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) {\Gamma }_{\beta \gamma }^{\alpha }\left( {\psi \left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \frac{\partial {\psi }^{\beta }\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial {x}^{i}}\frac{\partial {\psi }^{\gamma }\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial {x}^{j}}
\]

where \( {\Gamma }_{\beta \gamma }^{\alpha } \) are the Christoffel symbols of \( g\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) . Suppose \( \psi \left( {x, t}\right) \) is a bounded smooth solution of (12.9) with \( {\psi }_{{t}_{0}} = \mathrm{{Id}} \) . Then \( \psi \left( t\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{T}_{1}}\right\rbrack \) are dif-feomorphisms when \( {T}_{1} > {t}_{0} \) is sufficiently close to \( {t}_{0} \) . For any such \( {T}_{1} \) and for \( {t}_{0} \leq  t \leq  {T}_{1} \) , define \( \widehat{g}\left( t\right)  = {\left( {\psi }_{t}^{-1}\right) }^{ * }g\left( t\right) \) . Then \( \widehat{g}\left( t\right) \) satisfies the following equation:

(12.10)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\widehat{g}}_{ij} =  - 2{\widehat{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{ij} + {\widehat{\nabla }}_{i}{W}_{j}\left( t\right)  + {\widehat{\nabla }}_{j}{W}_{i}\left( t\right) \;\widehat{h}\left( 0\right)  = h\left( 0\right) ,
\]

where \( {\widehat{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{ij} \) and \( {\widehat{\nabla }}_{i} \) are the Ricci curvature and Levi-Civita connection of \( \widehat{g}\left( t\right) \) respectively and \( W\left( t\right) \) is the time-dependent 1-form defined by

\[
W{\left( t\right) }_{j} = {\widehat{g}}_{jk}\left( t\right) {\widehat{g}}^{pq}\left( t\right) \left( {{\widehat{\Gamma }}_{pq}^{k}\left( t\right)  - {\Gamma }_{pq}^{k}\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) .
\]

Here, \( {\widehat{\Gamma }}_{pq}^{k}\left( t\right) \) denotes the Christoffel symbols of the metric \( \widehat{g}\left( t\right) \) and \( {\Gamma }_{pq}^{k}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) denotes the Christoffel symbols of the metric \( g\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) . (See, for example,([65] Lemma 2.1).) We call a solution to this flow equation a Ricci-DeTurck flow (see [16], or [13] Chapter 3 for details). In local coordinates we have(12.11)

\[
\frac{\partial {\widehat{g}}_{ij}}{\partial t} = {\widehat{g}}^{kl}{\nabla }_{k}{\nabla }_{l}{\widehat{g}}_{ij} - {\widehat{g}}^{kl}g{\left( {t}_{0}\right) }_{ip}{\widehat{g}}^{pq}{R}_{jkql}\left( {g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right)  - {\widehat{g}}^{kl}g{\left( {t}_{0}\right) }_{jp}{\widehat{g}}^{pq}{R}_{ikql}\left( {g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
+ \frac{1}{2}{\widehat{g}}^{kl}{\widehat{g}}^{pq}\left\lbrack  \begin{matrix} {\nabla }_{i}{\widehat{g}}_{pk}{\nabla }_{j}{\widehat{g}}_{ql} + 2{\nabla }_{k}{\widehat{g}}_{jp}{\nabla }_{q}{\widehat{g}}_{il} \\   - 2{\nabla }_{k}{\widehat{g}}_{jp}{\nabla }_{l}{\widehat{g}}_{iq} - 2{\nabla }_{j}{\widehat{g}}_{pk}{\nabla }_{l}{\widehat{g}}_{iq} - 2{\nabla }_{i}{\widehat{g}}_{pk}{\nabla }_{l}{\widehat{g}}_{jq} \end{matrix}\right\rbrack  ,
\]

where \( \nabla \) is the Levi-Civita connection of \( g\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) . This is a strictly parabolic equation.

nodes.content: CLAIM 12.17. For any fixed \( t \) the function \( r : {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) is a function only of \( \widehat{r} \) . Considered as a function of two variables, \( r\left( {\widehat{r}, t}\right) \) is a smooth function defined for \( \widehat{r} \geq  0 \) . It is an odd function of \( \widehat{r} \) . nodes.proof:
Write the metric \( g\left( t\right)  = {g}_{ij}d{x}^{i}d{x}^{j} \) and let

(12.13)

\[
{x}^{1} = \widehat{r}\cos {\theta }^{1},\;{x}^{2} = \widehat{r}\sin {\theta }^{1}\cos {\theta }^{2},\ldots ,{x}^{n} = \sin {\theta }^{1}\cdots \sin {\theta }^{n - 1}.
\]

We compute \( f\left( {r, t}\right) \) by restricting attention to the ray \( \widehat{r} = {x}^{1} \) and \( {\theta }^{1} = \cdots  = \; {\theta }^{n - 1} = 0 \) , i.e., \( {x}^{2} = \cdots  = {x}^{n} = 0 \) . Then

\[
g\left( t\right)  = {g}_{11}\left( {\widehat{r},0,\ldots ,0, t}\right) d{\widehat{r}}^{2} + {g}_{22}\left( {\widehat{r},0,\ldots ,0, t}\right) {\widehat{r}}^{2}{d\sigma }.
\]

Both \( {g}_{11} \) and \( {g}_{22} \) are positive smooth and even in \( \widehat{r} \) . Thus \( \sqrt{{g}_{11}\left( {\widehat{r},0,\ldots ,0, t}\right) } \) is a positive smooth function defined for all \( \left( {\widehat{r}, t}\right) \) and is invariant under the involution \( \widehat{r} \mapsto   - \widehat{r} \) . Hence its restriction to \( \widehat{r} \geq  0 \) is an even function. Since

\[
r = {\int }_{0}^{\widehat{r}}\sqrt{{g}_{11}\left( {\widehat{s},0,\ldots ,0, t}\right) }d\widehat{s} = \widehat{r}{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{g}_{11}\left( {\widehat{r}s,0,\ldots ,0, t}\right) }{ds},
\]

we see that \( r\left( {\widehat{r}, t}\right) \) is of the form \( \widehat{r} \cdot  \phi \left( {\widehat{r}, t}\right) \) where \( \phi \left( {\widehat{r}, t}\right) \) is an even smooth function. This shows that \( r\left( {\widehat{r}, t}\right) \) is an odd function. It is also clear from this formula that \( \partial r/\partial \widehat{r} > 0 \) .

Since, for each \( {t}_{0} \) , the function \( r\left( {\widehat{r},{t}_{0}}\right) \) is an increasing function of \( \widehat{r} \) , it can be inverted to give a function \( \widehat{r}\left( {r,{t}_{0}}\right) \) . In Equation (12.12), we have chosen to write \( f \) as a function of \( r \) and \( t \) , rather than a function of \( \widehat{r} \) and t. We look for rotationally symmetric solutions to Equation (12.8), i.e., solutions of the form:

(12.14)

\[

\]

\[

\]

When we say that such a function is smooth we mean that for each \( n, m \geq  0 \) we have a continuous function \( {f}_{nm}\left( {w, t}\right) \) defined for all \( w \geq  0 \) satisfying:(1)

\[
{f}_{00} = f
\]

(2)

\[
\frac{\partial {f}_{nm}}{\partial t} = {f}_{n\left( {m + 1}\right) },\;\text{ and }
\]

\[

LEMMA 12.18. (a) Suppose that \( f\left( {w, t}\right) \) is a smooth function defined for \( w \geq  0 \) . Define \( \phi \left( {r, t}\right)  = f\left( {{r}^{2}, t}\right) \) . Then \( \phi \left( {r, t}\right) \) is a smooth function defined for all \( r \in  \mathbb{R} \) . Now fix \( k \) and let \( \widehat{r} : {\mathbb{R}}^{k} \rightarrow  \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) be the usual radial coordinate. Then we have a smooth family of smooth functions on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{k} \) defined by

\[
\widehat{\phi }\left( {{x}^{1},\ldots ,{x}^{k}, t}\right)  = \phi \left( {\widehat{r}\left( {{x}^{1},\ldots ,{x}^{k}}\right) , t}\right)  = f\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}{\left( {x}^{i}\right) }^{2}, t}\right) .
\]

(b) If \( \psi \left( {r, t}\right) \) is a smooth function defined for \( r \geq  0 \) and if it is even in the sense that its Taylor expansion to all orders along the line \( r = 0 \) involves only even powers of \( r \) , then there is a smooth function \( f\left( {w, t}\right) \) defined for \( w \geq  0 \) such that \( \psi \left( {r, t}\right)  = f\left( {{r}^{2}, t}\right) \) . In particular, for any \( k \geq  2 \) the function \( \widehat{\psi }\left( {\left( {{x}^{1},\ldots ,{x}^{k}}\right) , t}\right)  = \psi \left( {r\left( {{x}^{1},\ldots ,{x}^{k}}\right) , t}\right) \) is a smooth family of smooth functions on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{k} \) .

nodes.proof:
Item (a) is obvious, and item (b) is obvious away from \( r = 0 \) . We establish item (b) along the line \( r = 0 \) . Consider the Taylor theorem with remainder of order \( {2N} \) in the \( r \) -direction for \( \psi \left( {r, t}\right) \) at a point \( \left( {0, t}\right) \) . By hypothesis it takes the form

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}{c}_{i}\left( t\right) {w}^{2i} + {w}^{{2N} + 1}R\left( {w, t}\right) .
\]

Now we replace \( w \) by \( \sqrt{r} \) to obtain

\[
f\left( {r, t}\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}{c}_{i}{r}^{i} + {\sqrt{r}}^{{2N} + 1}R\left( {\sqrt{r}, t}\right) .
\]

Applying the usual chain rule and taking limits as \( r \rightarrow  {0}^{ + } \) we see that \( f\left( {r, t}\right) \) is \( N \) times differentiable along the line \( r = 0 \) . Since this is true for every \( N < \infty \) , the result follows.

Notice that an even function \( f\left( {r, t}\right) \) defined for \( r \geq  0 \) extends to a smooth function on the entire plane invariant under \( r \mapsto   - r \) . When we say a function \( f\left( {r, t}\right) \) defines a smooth family of smooth functions on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) we mean that, under the substitution \( \widehat{f}\left( {\left( {{x}^{1},\ldots ,{x}^{n}}\right) , t}\right)  = f\left( {r\left( {{x}^{1},\ldots ,{x}^{n}}\right) , t}\right) \) , the function \( \widehat{f} \) is a smooth function on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) for each \( t \) .

We shall also consider odd functions \( f\left( {r, t}\right) \) , i.e., smooth functions defined for \( r \geq  0 \) whose Taylor expansion in the \( r \) -direction along the line \( r = 0 \) involves only odd powers of \( r \) . These do not define smooth functions on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . On the other hand, by the same argument as above with the Taylor expansion one sees that they can be written as \( {rg}\left( {r, t}\right) \) where \( g \) is even, and hence define smoothly varying families of smooth functions on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Notice also that the product of two odd functions \( {f}_{1}\left( {r, t}\right) {f}_{2}\left( {r, t}\right) \) is an even function and hence this product defines a smoothly varying family of smooth function on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) .

7.1. The properties of \( r \) as a function of \( \widehat{r} \) and \( t \) . We shall make a change of variables and write the harmonic map flow equation in terms of \( r \) and \( \theta \) . For this we need some basic properties of \( r \) as a function of \( \widehat{r} \) and \( t \) . Recall that we are working on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) with its usual Euclidean coordinates \( \left( {{x}^{1},\ldots ,{x}^{n}}\right) \) . We shall also employ spherical coordinates \( \widehat{r},{\theta }^{1},\ldots ,{\theta }^{n - 1} \) . (We denote the fixed radial coordinate on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) by \( \widehat{r} \) to distinguish it from the varying radial function \( r = r\left( t\right) \) that measures the distance from the tip in the metric \( g\left( t\right) \) .)

COROLLARY 12.19. \( {r}^{2}\left( {\widehat{r}, t}\right) \) is a smoothly varying family of smooth functions on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Also, \( \widehat{r} \) is a smooth function of \( \left( {r, t}\right) \) defined for \( r \geq  0 \) and odd in \( r \) . In particular, any smooth even function of \( r \) is a smooth even function of \( \widehat{r} \) and thus defines a smooth function on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Moreover, there is a smooth function \( \xi \left( {w, t}\right) \) such that \( d\left( {\log r}\right) /{dt} = {r}^{-1}\left( {{dr}/{dt}}\right)  = \xi \left( {{r}^{2}, t}\right) \) .

For future reference we define

(12.15)

\[
B\left( {w, t}\right)  = \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{w}\xi \left( {u, t}\right) {du}.
\]

Then \( B\left( {{r}^{2}, t}\right) \) is a smooth function even in \( r \) and hence, as \( t \) varies, defines a smoothly varying family of smooth functions on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Notice that

\[
\frac{\partial B\left( {{r}^{2}, t}\right) }{\partial r} = {\left. 2r\frac{\partial B}{\partial w}\left( w, t\right) \right| }_{w = {r}^{2}} = {2r}\left( {\frac{1}{2}\xi \left( {{r}^{2}, t}\right) }\right)  = \frac{dr}{dt}.
\]

(1) \( {e}^{\widetilde{h}\left( {{r}^{2}, t}\right) } \) is asymptotic to \( \frac{1}{\left( {1 - t}\right) r} \) .

(2) \( \widetilde{h}\left( {{r}^{2}, t}\right) \) is asymptotic to \( - \log r \) .

(3) \( \frac{\partial \widetilde{h}}{\partial w}\left( {{r}^{2}, t}\right) \) is asymptotic to \( - \frac{1}{2{r}^{2}} \) .

(4) \( {r}^{-1}\frac{\partial r}{\partial t} \) is asymptotic to \( \frac{C}{r} \) .

(5) \( \frac{\partial B\left( {{r}^{2}, t}\right) }{\partial r} \) is asymptotic to \( C \) .

(6) \( \left| {G\left( {\widetilde{\rho },{r}^{2}, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {C}_{ * } < \infty \) where \( {C}_{ * } = {C}_{ * }\left( {\sup \{ \left| \widetilde{\rho }\right| ,\widetilde{h}\} }\right) \) is a constant depending only on \( \sup \{ \left| \widetilde{\rho }\right| ,\widetilde{h}\} \) .

nodes.label: Proposition 12.24
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.section_title: 12.7. Solution of the harmonic map flow
nodes.content:
PROPOSITION 12.24. For any \( {t}_{0} \geq  0 \) for which there is a standard solution \( g\left( t\right) \) defined on \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{1}}\right\rbrack \) with \( {t}_{0} < {T}_{1} \) , there is \( T > {t}_{0} \) and a solution to Equation (12.19) with initial condition \( \widetilde{\rho }\left( {r,{t}_{0}}\right)  = 0 \) defined on the time-interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0}, T}\right\rbrack \) .

At this point to simplify the notation we shift time by \( - {t}_{0} \) so that our initial time is 0, though our initial metric is not \( {g}_{0} \) but rather is the \( {t}_{0} \) time-slice of the standard solution we are considering, so that now \( {t}_{0} = 0 \) and our initial condition is \( \widetilde{\rho }\left( {r,0}\right)  = 0 \) .

Let \( x = \left( {{x}^{1},\ldots ,{x}^{n + 2}}\right) \) and \( y = \left( {{y}^{1},\ldots ,{y}^{n + 2}}\right) \) be two points in \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n + 1} \) and

\[
H\left( {x, y, t}\right)  = \frac{1}{{\left( 4\pi t\right) }^{\left( {n + 2}\right) /2}}{e}^{-\frac{{\left| x - y\right| }^{2}}{4t}}
\]

be the heat kernel. We solve (12.19) by successive approximation [47].

Define

\[
F\left( {x,\widetilde{\rho },\nabla \widetilde{\rho }, t}\right)  = \nabla \left\lbrack  {\left( {n - 1}\right) \widetilde{h} - B}\right\rbrack   \cdot  \nabla \widetilde{\rho } + {\left| \nabla \widetilde{\rho }\right| }^{2} + G\left( {\widetilde{\rho }, x, t}\right) .
\]

Let \( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{0}\left( {x, t}\right)  = 0 \) and for \( i \geq  1 \) we define \( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} \) by

(12.20)

\[
{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} = {\int }_{0}^{t}{\int }_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2}}H\left( {x, y, t - s}\right) F\left( {y,{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1},\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}, t}\right) {dyds}
\]

which solves

(12.21)

\[
\frac{\partial {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}}{\partial t} = \bigtriangleup {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} + F\left( {x,{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1},\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}, t}\right) \;{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}\left( {x,0}\right)  = 0.
\]

To show the existence of \( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} \) by induction, it suffices to prove the following statement: For any \( i \geq  1 \) , if \( \left| {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}\right| ,\left| {\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}}\right| \) are bounded, then \( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} \) exists and \( \left| {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}\right| ,\left| {\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}}\right| \) are bounded. Assume \( \left| {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}\right|  \leq  {C}_{1},\left| {\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}}\right|  \leq  {C}_{2} \) are bounded on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) ; then it follows from Claim 12.23 that \( G\left( {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1},\mathbf{x}, t}\right) \) is bounded on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) ,

\[
\left| {G\left( {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}, x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {C}_{ * }\left( {{C}_{1},\widetilde{h}}\right) ,
\]

and also because of Claim 12.23 both \( \left| {\nabla B}\right| \) and \( \left| {\nabla \widetilde{h}}\right| \) are bounded on all of \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , it follows that \( F\left( {x,{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1},\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}, t}\right) \) is bounded:

\[
\left| {F\left( {x,{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1},\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  \left\lbrack  {\left( {n - 1}\right) \sup \left| {\nabla \widetilde{h}}\right|  + \sup \left| {\nabla B}\right| }\right\rbrack  {C}_{2} + {C}_{2}^{2} + {C}_{ * }\left( {{C}_{1},\widetilde{h}}\right) .
\]

Clearly, the last expression is bounded by a constant \( {C}_{3} \) depending only on the previous bounds. Hence \( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} \) exists.

The bounds on \( \left| {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}\right| \) and \( \left| {\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}}\right| \) follow from the estimates

\[
\left| {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}\right|  \leq  {\int }_{0}^{t}{\int }_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2}}H\left( {x, y, t - s}\right) {C}_{3}{dyds} \leq  {C}_{3}t,
\]

and

\[
\left| {\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}}\right|  = \left| {{\int }_{0}^{t}{\int }_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2}}\left\lbrack  {{\nabla }_{x}H\left( {x, y, t - s}\right) }\right\rbrack  F\left( {y,{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1},\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}, t}\right) {dyds}}\right|
\]

\[
\leq  {\int }_{0}^{t}{\int }_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2}}\left| {{\nabla }_{x}H\left( {x, y, t - s}\right) }\right| {C}_{3}{dyds}
\]

\[
= {\int }_{0}^{t}{\int }_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2}}\frac{1}{{\left( 4\pi \left( t - s\right) \right) }^{\left( {n + 2}\right) /2}}{e}^{-\frac{{\left| x - y\right| }^{2}}{4\left( {t - s}\right) }}\frac{\left| x - y\right| }{2\left( {t - s}\right) }{C}_{3}{dyds}
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{\left( {n + 2}\right) {C}_{3}}{\sqrt{\pi }}{\int }_{0}^{t}\frac{1}{\sqrt{t - s}}{ds} = \frac{2\left( {n + 2}\right) {C}_{3}}{\sqrt{\pi }}\sqrt{t}
\]

Assuming, as we shall, that \( T \leq  \min \left\{  {\frac{{C}_{3}}{{C}_{1}},\frac{\pi {C}_{2}^{2}}{4{\left( n + 2\right) }^{2}{C}_{3}^{2}}}\right\} \) , then for \( 0 \leq  t \leq  T \) we have for all \( i \) ,

(12.22)

\[
\left| {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}\right|  \leq  {C}_{1}\;\text{ and }\;\left| {\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}}\right|  \leq  {C}_{2}.
\]

We prove the convergence of \( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} \) to a solution of (12.19) via proving that it is a Cauchy sequence in \( {C}^{1} \) -norm. Note that \( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} - {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1} \) satisfies

(12.23)

\[
\frac{\partial \left( {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} - {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}}\right) }{\partial t} = \bigtriangleup \left( {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} - {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}}\right)
\]

\[
+ F\left( {x,{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1},\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}, t}\right)  - F\left( {x,{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 2},\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 2}, t}\right)
\]

with

\[
\left( {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} - {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}}\right) \left( {x,0}\right)  = 0,
\]

where

\[
F\left( {x,{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1},\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}, t}\right)  - F\left( {x,{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 2},\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 2}, t}\right)
\]

\[
= \left\lbrack  {\left( {n - 1}\right) \nabla \widetilde{h} - \nabla B + \nabla \left( {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1} + {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 2}}\right) }\right\rbrack   \cdot  \nabla \left( {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1} - {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 2}}\right)
\]

\[
+ G\left( {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1},\mathbf{x}, t}\right)  - G\left( {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 2},\mathbf{x}, t}\right) .
\]

By lengthy but straightforward calculations one can verify the Lipschitz property of \( G\left( {\widetilde{\rho },\mathbf{x}, t}\right) \) ,

\[
\left| {G\left( {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1},\mathbf{x}, t}\right)  - G\left( {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 2},\mathbf{x}, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {C}_{\& }\left( {{C}_{1},{C}_{2},\widetilde{f},{\widetilde{f}}_{0}}\right)  \cdot  \left| {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1} - {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 2}}\right| .
\]

This and (12.22) implies

(12.24)

\[
\left| {F\left( {x,{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1},\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}, t}\right)  - F\left( {x,{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 2},\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 2}, t}\right) }\right|
\]

\[
\leq  {C}_{4} \cdot  \left| {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1} - {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 2}}\right|  + {C}_{5} \cdot  \left| {\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1} - \nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 2}}\right|
\]

where \( {C}_{4} = {C}_{\& }\left( {{C}_{1},{C}_{2},\widetilde{f},{\widetilde{f}}_{0}}\right) \) and \( {C}_{5} = \left\lbrack  {\left( {n - 1}\right) \sup \left| {\nabla \widetilde{f}}\right|  + \sup \left| {\nabla B}\right|  + 2{C}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) .

Let

\[
{A}_{i}\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{0 \leq  s \leq  t, x \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2}}}\left| {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} - {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}}\right| \left( {x, s}\right) ,
\]

\[
{B}_{i}\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{0 \leq  s \leq  t, x \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2}}}\left| {\nabla \left( {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} - {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}}\right) }\right| \left( {x, s}\right) .
\]

From Equations (12.23) and (12.24) we can estimate \( \left| {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} - {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}}\right| \) and \( \left| {\nabla \left( {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} - {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}}\right) }\right| \) in the same way as we estimate \( \left| {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}\right| \) and \( \left| {\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}}\right| \) above; we conclude

\[
{A}_{i}\left( t\right)  \leq  \left\lbrack  {{C}_{4}{A}_{i - 1}\left( t\right)  + {C}_{5}{B}_{i - 1}\left( t\right) }\right\rbrack   \cdot  t
\]

\[
{B}_{i}\left( t\right)  \leq  \frac{2\left( {n + 2}\right) \left\lbrack  {{C}_{4}{A}_{i - 1}\left( t\right)  + {C}_{5}{B}_{i - 1}\left( t\right) }\right\rbrack  }{\sqrt{\pi }} \cdot  \sqrt{t}.
\]

Let \( {C}_{6} = \max \left\{  {{C}_{4},{C}_{5}}\right\} \) ; then we get

\[
{A}_{i}\left( t\right)  + {B}_{i}\left( t\right)  \leq  \left( {{C}_{6}t + \frac{2\left( {n + 2}\right) {C}_{6}\sqrt{t}}{\sqrt{\pi }}}\right)  \cdot  \left( {{A}_{i - 1}\left( t\right)  + {B}_{i - 1}\left( t\right) }\right) .
\]

Now suppose that \( T \leq  {T}_{2} \) where \( {T}_{2} \) satisfies \( {C}_{6}{T}_{2} + \frac{2\left( {n + 2}\right) {C}_{6}\sqrt{{T}_{2}}}{\sqrt{\pi }} = \frac{1}{2} \) ; then for all \( t \leq  T \) we have

\[
{A}_{i}\left( t\right)  + {B}_{i}\left( t\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{2}\left( {{A}_{i - 1}\left( t\right)  + {B}_{i - 1}\left( t\right) }\right) .
\]

This proves that \( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} \) is a Cauchy sequence in \( {C}^{1}\left( {\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2}\right) \) . Let \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{i \rightarrow   + \infty }}{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} = {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty } \) . Then \( \nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} \rightarrow  \nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty } \) and \( F\left( {x,{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1},\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}, t}\right)  \rightarrow  F\left( {x,{\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty },\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty }, t}\right) \) uniformly. Hence we get from (12.20),

(12.25)

\[
{\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty } = {\int }_{0}^{t}{\int }_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2}}H\left( {x, y, t - s}\right) F\left( {y,{\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty },\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty }, t}\right) {dyds}.
\]

The next argument is similar to the argument in [47], p.21. The function \( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} \) is a smooth solution of (12.21) with \( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}\left( {x,0}\right)  = 0 \) . Also, both \( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i} \) and \( F\left( {x,{\widetilde{\rho }}_{{i}_{1}},\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i - 1}, t}\right) \) are uniformly bounded on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . Thus, by Theorems 1.11 on p. 211 and 12.1 on p. 223 of [46], for any compact \( K \subset  {\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2} \) and any \( 0 < {t}_{ * } < T \) , there is \( {C}_{7} \) and \( \alpha  \in  \left( {0,1}\right) \) independent of \( i \) such that

\[
\left| {\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}\left( {x, t}\right)  - \nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}\left( {y, s}\right) }\right|  \leq  {C}_{7} \cdot  \left( {{\left| x - y\right| }^{\alpha } + {\left| t - s\right| }^{\alpha /2}}\right)
\]

where \( x, y \in  K \) and \( 0 \leq  t < s \leq  {t}_{ * } \) .

Letting \( i \rightarrow  \infty \) we get

(12.26)

\[
\left| {\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  - \nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty }\left( {y, s}\right) }\right|  \leq  {C}_{7} \cdot  \left( {{\left| x - y\right| }^{\alpha } + {\left| t - s\right| }^{\alpha /2}}\right) .
\]

Hence \( \nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty } \in  {C}^{\alpha ,\alpha /2} \) . That is to say \( \nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty } \) is \( \alpha \) -Hölder continuous in space and \( \alpha /2 \) -Hölder continuous in time. From (12.25) we conclude that \( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty } \) is a solution of (12.19) on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) with \( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty }\left( {x,0}\right)  = 0 \) .

7.5. The asymptotic behavior of the solutions. In the rest of this subsection we study the asymptotic behavior of solution \( \widetilde{\rho }\left( {x, t}\right) \) as \( x \rightarrow  \infty \) . First we prove inductively that there is a constant \( \lambda \) and \( {T}_{3} \) such that, provided that \( T \leq  {T}_{3} \) , for \( x \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2}, t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , we have

(12.27)

\[
\left| {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  \frac{\lambda }{{\left( 1 + \left| x\right| \right) }^{2}}\;\text{ and }\;\left| {\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  \frac{\lambda }{{\left( 1 + \left| x\right| \right) }^{2}}.
\]

Clearly, since \( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{0} = 0 \) , these estimates hold for \( i = 0 \) . It follows from (12.22) and Claim 12.23 that there is a constant \( {C}_{8} \) independent of \( i \) such that

\[
\left| {G\left( {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i},\mathbf{x}, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  \frac{{C}_{8}}{{\left( 1 + \left| x\right| \right) }^{2}}
\]

\[
\left\lbrack  {\left( {n - 1}\right) \left| {\nabla \widetilde{h}}\right|  + \left| {\nabla B}\right| }\right\rbrack  \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {C}_{8}.
\]

Now we assume these estimates hold for \( i \) . Then for \( 0 \leq  t \leq  T \) we have

\[
\left| {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|
\]

\[
\leq  {\int }_{0}^{t}{\int }_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2}}H\left( {x, y, t - s}\right) \left\lbrack  {\frac{{C}_{8}\lambda }{{\left( 1 + \left| y\right| \right) }^{2}} + \frac{{\lambda }^{2}}{{\left( 1 + \left| y\right| \right) }^{2}} + \frac{{C}_{8}}{{\left( 1 + \left| y\right| \right) }^{2}}}\right\rbrack  {dyds}
\]

\[
= {\int }_{0}^{t}{\int }_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2}}\frac{1}{{\left( 4\pi \left( t - s\right) \right) }^{\left( {n + 2}\right) /2}}{e}^{-\frac{{\left| x - y\right| }^{2}}{4\left( {t - s}\right) }}\left\lbrack  \frac{{C}_{8}\lambda  + {\lambda }^{2} + {C}_{8}}{{\left( 1 + \left| y\right| \right) }^{2}}\right\rbrack  {dyds}
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {{C}_{8}\lambda  + {\lambda }^{2} + {C}_{8}}\right)  \cdot  \frac{C\left( n\right) t}{{\left( 1 + \left| x\right| \right) }^{2}}.
\]

Also, we have

\[
\left| {\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{i}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {\int }_{0}^{t}{\int }_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2}}\left| {{\nabla }_{x}H\left( {x, y, t - s}\right) }\right| \left\lbrack  \frac{{C}_{8}\lambda  + {\lambda }^{2} + {C}_{8}}{{\left( 1 + \left| y\right| \right) }^{2}}\right\rbrack  {dyds}
\]

\[
= {\int }_{0}^{t}{\int }_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n + 2}}\frac{\left| x - y\right| }{2\left( {t - s}\right) }\frac{1}{{\left( 4\pi \left( t - s\right) \right) }^{\left( {n + 2}\right) /2}}{e}^{-\frac{{\left| x - y\right| }^{2}}{4\left( {t - s}\right) }}\left\lbrack  \frac{{C}_{8}\lambda  + {\lambda }^{2} + {C}_{8}}{{\left( 1 + \left| y\right| \right) }^{2}}\right\rbrack  {dyds}
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {{C}_{8}\lambda  + {\lambda }^{2} + {C}_{8}}\right)  \cdot  \frac{C\left( n\right) \sqrt{t}}{{\left( 1 + \left| x\right| \right) }^{2}}.
\]

If we choose \( {T}_{3} \) such that

\[
\left( {{C}_{8}\lambda  + {\lambda }^{2} + {C}_{8}}\right)  \cdot  C\left( n\right) {T}_{3} \leq  \lambda \;\text{ and }\;\left( {{C}_{8}\lambda  + {\lambda }^{2} + {C}_{8}}\right)  \cdot  C\left( n\right) \sqrt{{T}_{3}} \leq  \lambda ,
\]

then (12.27) hold for all \( i \) . From the definition of \( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty } \) we conclude that

(12.28)

\[
\left| {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  \frac{\lambda }{{\left( 1 + \left| x\right| \right) }^{2}}\text{ and }\left| {\nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  \frac{\lambda }{{\left( 1 + \left| x\right| \right) }^{2}}.
\]

Recall that \( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty } \) is a solution of the following linear equation (in \( v \) ):

\[
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = {\Delta v} + \nabla \left\lbrack  {\left( {n - 1}\right) \widetilde{h} - B}\right\rbrack   \cdot  \nabla v + G\left( {{\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty },\mathbf{x}, t}\right) ,
\]

\[
v\left( {x,0}\right)  = 0.
\]

From (12.26) and Claim 12.23 we know that \( \nabla \left\lbrack  {\left( {n - 1}\right) \widetilde{h} - B + {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) has \( {C}^{\alpha ,\alpha /2} \) -Hölder-norm bounded (this means \( \alpha \) -Hölder norm in space and the \( \alpha /2 \) -Hölder norm in time). By some lengthy calculations we get

\[
{\left| G\left( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty },\mathbf{x}, t\right) \right| }_{{C}^{\alpha ,\alpha /2}} \leq  \frac{{C}_{9}}{{\left( 1 + \left| x\right| \right) }^{2}}.
\]

By local Schauder estimates for parabolic equations we conclude

\[
{\left| {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty }\right| }_{{C}^{2 + \alpha ,1 + \alpha /2}} \leq  \frac{{C}_{10}}{{\left( 1 + \left| x\right| \right) }^{2}}.
\]

Using this estimate one can further show by calculation that

\[
{\left. \left| \nabla \nabla \left\lbrack  \left( n - 1\right) \widetilde{f} - B + {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty }\right\rbrack  \right| \right| }_{{C}^{\alpha ,\alpha /2}} \leq  {C}_{11}
\]

\[
{\left| \nabla G\left( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty },\mathbf{x}, t\right) \right| }_{{C}^{\alpha ,\alpha /2}} \leq  \frac{{C}_{12}}{{\left( 1 + \left| x\right| \right) }^{2}}.
\]

By local high order Schauder estimates for parabolic equations we conclude

\[
{\left| \nabla {\widetilde{\rho }}_{\infty }\right| }_{{C}^{2 + \alpha ,1 + \alpha /2}} \leq  \frac{{C}_{13}}{{\left( 1 + \left| x\right| \right) }^{2}}.
\]

We have proved the following:

Proposition 12.26. Let \( {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right) \) and \( {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) ,0 \leq  t \leq  T \) , be two bounded solutions of the Ricci-DeTurck flow on complete and non-compact manifold \( {M}^{n} \) with initial metric \( {g}_{1}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  = {g}_{2}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  = g \) . Suppose that for some \( 1 < C < \; \infty \) we have

\[
{C}^{-1}g \leq  {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  \leq  {Cg}
\]

\[
{C}^{-1}g \leq  {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right)  \leq  {Cg}
\]

Suppose that in addition we have

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right) \end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{2}\left( M\right) , g} \leq  C
\]

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{2}\left( M\right) , g} \leq  C.
\]

Lastly, suppose there is an exhaustive sequence of compact, smooth sub-manifolds of \( {\Omega }_{k} \subset  M \) , i.e., \( {\Omega }_{k} \subset  \operatorname{int}{\Omega }_{k + 1} \) and \( \cup  {\Omega }_{k} = M \) such that \( {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right) \) and \( {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \) have the same sequential asymptotic behavior at \( \infty \) in the sense that for any \( \epsilon  > 0 \) , there is a \( {k}_{0} \) arbitrarily large with

\[
{\left| {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \right| }_{{C}^{1}\left( {\partial {\Omega }_{{k}_{0}}}\right) , g} \leq  \epsilon .
\]

Then \( {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  = {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \) .

Letting \( \widetilde{\nabla } \) be the covariant derivative determined by \( g \) , then, using the Ricci-DeTurck flow (12.11) for \( {\widehat{g}}_{1} \) and \( {\widehat{g}}_{2} \) , we can make the following estimate for an appropriate constant \( D \) depending on \( g \) . (In these formulas all norms and inner products are with respect to the background metric \( g \) .)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \right| }^{2}
\]

\[
= 2\left\langle  {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {{\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) }\right) ,{\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) }\right\rangle
\]

\[
\leq  2\left\langle  {{\widehat{g}}_{1}^{\alpha \beta }{\widetilde{\nabla }}_{\alpha }{\widetilde{\nabla }}_{\beta }\left( {{\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) }\right) ,\left( {{\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) }\right) }\right\rangle
\]

\[
+ D{\left| {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \right| }_{g}^{2} + D\left| {\widetilde{\nabla }\left( {{\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) }\right) }\right| \left| {{\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) }\right|
\]

\[
\leq  {\widehat{g}}_{1}^{\alpha \beta }{\widetilde{\nabla }}_{\alpha }{\widetilde{\nabla }}_{\beta }\left( {\left| {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \right| }^{2}\right)
\]

\[
- 2{\widehat{g}}_{1}^{\alpha \beta }\left\langle  {{\widetilde{\nabla }}_{\beta }\left( {{\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) }\right) ,{\widetilde{\nabla }}_{\alpha }\left( {{\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) }\right) }\right\rangle
\]

\[
+ D{\left| {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \right| }^{2} + D\left| {\widetilde{\nabla }\left( {{\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) }\right) }\right| \left| {{\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) }\right|
\]

\[
\leq  {\widehat{g}}_{1}^{\alpha \beta }{\widetilde{\nabla }}_{\alpha }{\widetilde{\nabla }}_{\beta }\left( {\left| {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \right| }^{2}\right)  - 2{C}^{-1}{\left| \widetilde{\nabla }\left( {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \right) \right| }^{2}
\]

\[
+ D{\left| {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \right| }^{2} + {C}^{-1}{\left| \widetilde{\nabla }\left( {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \right) \right| }^{2} + \frac{{D}^{2}}{4{C}^{-1}}{\left| {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \right| }^{2},
\]

where the last inequality comes from completing the square to replace the last term in the previous expression. Thus, we have proved

(12.29)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \right| }_{g}^{2} \leq  2{\widehat{g}}_{1}^{\alpha \beta }{\widetilde{\nabla }}_{\alpha }{\widetilde{\nabla }}_{\beta }{\left| {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \right| }_{g}^{2}
\]

\[
+ {C}_{15}{\left| {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \right| }_{g}^{2}
\]

pointwise on \( {\Omega }_{k} \) with \( {C}_{15} \) a constant that depends only on \( n, C \) and \( g \) .

Suppose that \( {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  \neq  {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \) for some \( t \) . Then there is a point \( {x}_{0} \) such that \( {\left| {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( {x}_{0}, t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( {x}_{0}, t\right) \right| }_{g}^{2} > {\epsilon }_{0} \) for some \( {\epsilon }_{0} > 0 \) .

We choose a \( {k}_{0} \) sufficiently large that \( {x}_{0} \in  {\Omega }_{{k}_{0}} \) and for all \( {t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0}, T}\right\rbrack \) we have

(12.30)

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  \partial {\Omega }_{b}}}{\left| {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( x,{t}^{\prime }\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( x,{t}^{\prime }\right) \right| }_{g}^{2} \leq  \epsilon
\]

where \( \epsilon  > 0 \) is a constant to be chosen later.

Recall we have the initial condition \( {\left| {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( 0\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( 0\right) \right| }_{g}^{2} = 0 \) . Using Equation (12.29) and applying the maximum principle to \( {\left| {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \right| }_{g}^{2} \) ) on the domain \( {\Omega }_{{k}_{0}} \) , we get

\[
{e}^{-{C}_{15}t}{\left| {\widehat{g}}_{1}\left( t\right)  - {\widehat{g}}_{2}\left( t\right) \right| }_{g}^{2}\left( x\right)  \leq  \epsilon \;\text{ for all }x \in  {\Omega }_{{k}_{0}}.
\]

This is a contradiction if we choose \( \epsilon  \leq  {\epsilon }_{0}{e}^{-{C}_{15}T} \) . This contradiction establishes the proposition.

THEOREM 12.28. Fix \( 0 < \epsilon  < 1 \) . Then there is \( r > 0 \) such that for any point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) in the standard flow with \( R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {r}^{-2} \) the following hold.

(1) \( {t}_{0} > {r}^{2} \) .

(2) \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) has a strong canonical \( \left( {C\left( \epsilon \right) ,\epsilon }\right) \) -neighborhood. If this canonical neighborhood is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) , then the strong neck extends to an evolving neck defined for backward rescaled time \( \left( {1 + \epsilon }\right) \) .

nodes.proof:
Take an increasing sequence of times \( {t}_{n}^{\prime } \) converging to \( T \) . Since the curvature of \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is locally bounded in time, for each \( n \) , there is a bound on the scalar curvature on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{n}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) . Hence, there is a finite upper bound \( {R}_{n} \) on \( R\left( {x, t}\right) \) for all points \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( t \leq  {t}_{n}^{\prime } \) for which the conclusion of the theorem does not hold. (There clearly are such points since the conclusion of the theorem fails for all \( \left( {x,0}\right) \) .) Pick \( \left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{n} \leq  {t}_{n}^{\prime } \) , with \( R\left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right)  \geq  {R}_{n}/2 \) and such that the conclusion of the theorem does not hold for \( \left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right) \) . To prove the theorem we must show that \( {\overline{\lim }}_{n \rightarrow  \infty }R\left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right)  < \infty \) . Suppose the contrary. By passing to a subsequence we can suppose that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}R\left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right)  = \infty \) . We set \( {Q}_{n} = R\left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right) \) . We claim that all the hypotheses of Theorem 11.8 apply to the sequence \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( t\right) ,\left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right) }\right) \) . First, we show that all the hypotheses of Theorem 11.1 (except the last) hold. Since \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) has non-negative curvature all these flows have curvature pinched toward positive. By Proposition 12.13 there are \( r > 0 \) and \( \kappa  > 0 \) so that all these flows are \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed on scales \( \leq  r \) . By construction if \( t \leq  {t}_{n} \) and \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  > 2{Q}_{n} \geq  {R}_{n} \) then the point \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) has a strong canonical \( \left( {C\left( \epsilon \right) ,\epsilon }\right) \) -neighborhood. We are assuming that \( {Q}_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) in order to achieve the contradiction. Since all time-slices are complete, all balls of finite radius have compact closure.

Lastly, we need to show that the extra hypothesis of Theorem 11.8 (which includes the last hypothesis of Theorem 11.1) is satisfied. This is clear since \( {t}_{n} \rightarrow  T \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( {Q}_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) . Applying Theorem 11.8 we conclude that after passing to a subsequence there is a limiting flow which is a \( \kappa \) -solution. Clearly, this and Corollary 9.95 imply that for all sufficiently large \( n \) (in the subsequence) the neighborhood as required by the theorem exists. This contradicts our assumption that none of the points \( \left( {{x}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right) \) have these neighborhoods. This contradiction proves the result.

nodes.label: Theorem 12.29
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.section_title: 12.8. Completion of the proof of uniqueness
nodes.content: THEOREM 12.29. For the standard flow, \( T = 1 \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: THEOREM 12.29. For the standard flow, \( T = 1 \) .

nodes.proof:
We have already seen in Corollary 12.8 that \( T \leq  1 \) . Suppose now that \( T < 1 \) . Take \( {T}_{0} < T \) sufficiently close to \( T \) . Then according to Proposition 12.7 there is a compact subset \( X \subset  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) such that restriction of the flow to \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3} \smallsetminus  X}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to the standard evolving flow on \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,\infty }\right) ,\left( {1 - t}\right) {h}_{0} \times  d{s}^{2} \) , where \( {h}_{0} \) is the round metric of scalar curvature 1 on \( {S}^{2} \) . In particular, \( R\left( {x,{T}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + \epsilon }\right) {\left( 1 - {T}_{0}\right) }^{-1} \) for all \( x \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \smallsetminus  X \) . Because of Theorem 12.28 and the definition of \( \left( {C\left( \epsilon \right) ,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhoods, it follows that at any point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  {r}^{-2} \) , where \( r > 0 \) is the constant given in Theorem 12.28, we have \( \partial R/\partial t\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C\left( \epsilon \right) {R}^{2}\left( {x, t}\right) \) . Thus, provided that \( T - {T}_{0} \) is sufficiently small, there is a uniform bound to \( R\left( {x, t}\right) \) for all \( x \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \smallsetminus  X \) and all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{T}_{0}, T}\right) \) . Using Theorem 3.29 and the fact that the standard flow is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed implies that the restrictions of the metrics \( g\left( t\right) \) to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \smallsetminus  X \) converge smoothly to a limiting Riemannian metric \( g\left( T\right) \) on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \smallsetminus  X \) . Fix a non-empty open subset \( \Omega  \subset  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \smallsetminus  X \) with compact closure. For each \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) let \( V\left( t\right) \) be the volume of \( \left( {\Omega ,{\left. g\left( t\right) \right| }_{\Omega }}\right) \) . Of course, \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  T}}V\left( t\right)  = {\operatorname{Vol}}_{g\left( T\right) }\Omega  > 0. \)

Since the limiting metric \( g\left( T\right) \) exists in a neighborhood of infinity and has bounded curvature there, if the limit metric \( g\left( T\right) \) exists on all of \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) , then we can extend the flow keeping the curvature bounded. This contradicts the maximality of our flow subject to the condition that the curvature be locally bounded in time. Consequently, there is a point \( x \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) for which the limit metric \( g\left( T\right) \) does not exist. This means that \( {\overline{\lim }}_{t \rightarrow  T}R\left( {x, t}\right)  = \infty \) . That is to say, there is a sequence of \( {t}_{n} \rightarrow  T \) such that setting \( {Q}_{n} = R\left( {x,{t}_{n}}\right) \) , we have \( {Q}_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \) tends to infinity. By Theorem 12.28 the second hypothesis in the statement of Theorem 11.1 holds for the sequence \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( t\right) ,\left( {x,{t}_{n}}\right) }\right) \) . All the other hypotheses of this theorem as well as the extra hypothesis in Theorem 11.8 obviously hold for this sequence. Thus, according to Theorem 11.8 the based flows \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3},{Q}_{n}g\left( {{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime } + {t}_{n}}\right) ,\left( {x,0}\right) }\right) \) converge smoothly to a \( \kappa \) -solution. Since the asymptotic volume of any \( \kappa \) -solution is zero (see Theorem 9.59), we see that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the following holds:

CLAIM 12.30. For any \( \epsilon  > 0 \) , there is \( A < \infty \) such that for all \( n \) sufficiently large we have

\[
\operatorname{Vol}{B}_{{Q}_{n}g}\left( {x,{t}_{n}, A}\right)  < \epsilon {A}^{3}.
\]

Rescaling, we see that for all \( n \) sufficiently large we have

\[
\operatorname{Vol}{B}_{g}\left( {x,{t}_{n}, A/\sqrt{{Q}_{n}}}\right)  < \epsilon {\left( A/\sqrt{{Q}_{n}}\right) }^{3}.
\]

Since the curvature of \( g\left( {t}_{n}\right) \) is non-negative and since the \( {Q}_{n} \) tend to \( \infty \) , it follows from the Bishop-Gromov Inequality (Theorem 1.34) that for any \( 0 < A < \infty \) and any \( \epsilon  > 0 \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large we have

\[
\operatorname{Vol}{B}_{g}\left( {x,{t}_{n}, A}\right)  < \epsilon {A}^{3}.
\]

On the other hand, since \( \Omega \) has compact closure, there is an \( {A}_{1} < \infty \) with \( \Omega  \subset  B\left( {x,0,{A}_{1}}\right) \) . Since the curvature of \( g\left( t\right) \) is non-negative for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , it follows from Lemma 3.14 that the distance is a non-increasing function of \( t \) , so that for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) we have \( \Omega  \subset  B\left( {x, t,{A}_{1}}\right) \) . Applying the above, for any \( \epsilon  > 0 \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large we have

\[
\operatorname{Vol}\left( {\Omega , g\left( {t}_{n}\right) }\right)  \leq  {\operatorname{Vol}}_{g}B\left( {x,{t}_{n},{A}_{1}}\right)  < \epsilon {\left( {A}_{1}\right) }^{3}.
\]

But this contradicts the fact that

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}\operatorname{Vol}\left( {\Omega , g\left( {t}_{n}\right) }\right)  = \operatorname{Vol}\left( {\Omega , g\left( T\right) }\right)  > 0.
\]

This contradiction proves that \( T = 1 \) .

nodes.content_excerpt: Proposition 12.31. There is a constant \( c > 0 \) such that for all \( \left( {p, t}\right) \) in the standard solution we have \[ R\left( {p, t}\right) \geq \frac{c}{1 - t} \]

nodes.proof:
First, let us show that there is not a limiting metric \( g\left( 1\right) \) defined on all of \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) . This does not immediately contradict the maximality of the flow because we are assuming only that the flow is maximal subject to having curvature locally bounded in time. Assume that a limiting metric \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( 1\right) }\right) \) exists. First, notice that from the canonical neighborhood assumption and Lemma 11.2 we see that the curvature of \( g\left( T\right) \) must be unbounded at spatial infinity. On the other hand, by Proposition 9.79 every point of \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( 1\right) }\right) \) of curvature greater than \( {R}_{0} \) has a \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Hence, since \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( 1\right) }\right) \) has unbounded curvature, it then has \( {2\epsilon } \) -necks of arbitrarily small scale. This contradicts Proposition 2.19. (One can also rule this possibility out by direct computation using the spherical symmetry of the metric.) This means that there is no limiting metric \( g\left( 1\right) \) .

The next step is to see that for any \( p \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) we have \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  1}}R\left( {p, t}\right)  = \infty \) . Let \( \Omega  \subset  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) be the subset of \( x \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) for which \( \mathop{\liminf }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  1}}R\left( {x, t}\right)  < \infty \) . We suppose that \( \Omega  \neq  \varnothing \) . According to Theorem 11.19 the subset \( \Omega \) is open and the metrics \( {\left. g\left( t\right) \right| }_{\Omega } \) converge smoothly to a limiting metric \( {\left. g\left( 1\right) \right| }_{\Omega } \) . On the other hand, we have just seen that there is not a limit metric \( g\left( 1\right) \) defined everywhere. This means that there is \( p \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  1}}R\left( {p, t}\right)  = \infty \) .

Take a sequence \( {t}_{n} \) converging to 1 and set \( {Q}_{n} = R\left( {p,{t}_{n}}\right) \) . By Theorem 11.8 we see that, possibly after passing to a subsequence, the based flows \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3},{Q}_{n}g\left( {{t}^{\prime } - {t}_{n}}\right) ,\left( {p,0}\right) }\right) \) converge to a \( \kappa \) -solution. Then by Theorem 9.59 for any \( \epsilon  > 0 \) there is \( A < \infty \) such that \( \operatorname{Vol}{B}_{{Q}_{n}g}\left( {p,{t}_{n}, A}\right)  < \epsilon {A}^{3} \) , and hence after rescaling we have \( \operatorname{Vol}{B}_{g}\left( {p,{t}_{n}, A/\sqrt{{Q}_{n}}}\right)  < \epsilon {\left( A/\sqrt{{Q}_{n}}\right) }^{3} \) . By the Bishop-Gromov inequality (Theorem 1.34) it follows that for any \( 0 < A < \infty \) , any \( \epsilon  > 0 \) and for all \( n \) sufficiently large, we have \( \operatorname{Vol}{B}_{g}\left( {p,{t}_{n}, A}\right)  < \epsilon {A}^{3} \) . Take a non-empty subset \( {\Omega }^{\prime } \subset  \Omega \) with compact closure. Of course, \( \operatorname{Vol}\left( {{\Omega }^{\prime }, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) converges to \( \operatorname{Vol}\left( {{\Omega }^{\prime }, g\left( T\right) }\right)  > 0 \) as \( t \rightarrow  T \) . Then there is \( A < \infty \) such that for each \( n \) , the subset \( {\Omega }^{\prime } \) is contained in the ball \( B\left( {{p}_{0},{t}_{n}, A}\right) \) . This is a contradiction since it implies that for any \( \epsilon  > 0 \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large we have \( \operatorname{Vol}\left( {{\Omega }^{\prime }, g\left( t\right) }\right)  < \epsilon {A}^{3} \) . This completes the proof that for every \( p \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) we have \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  1}}R\left( {p, t}\right)  = \infty \) .

Fix \( \epsilon  > 0 \) sufficiently small and set \( C = C\left( \epsilon \right) \) . Then for every \( \left( {p, t}\right) \) with \( R\left( {p, t}\right)  \geq  {r}^{-2} \) we have

\[
\left| {\frac{dR}{dt}\left( {p, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  C{R}^{2}\left( {p, t}\right) .
\]

Fix \( {t}_{0} = 1 - 1/2{r}^{2}C \) . Since the flow has curvature locally bounded in time, there is \( {2C} \leq  {C}^{\prime } < \infty \) such that \( R\left( {p,{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  1/\left( {{C}^{\prime }\left( {1 - {t}_{0}}\right) }\right. \) for all \( p \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) . Since \( R\left( {p,{t}_{0}}\right)  = 1/{C}^{\prime }\left( {1 - {t}_{0}}\right) \) , for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},1}\right) \) we have

\[
R\left( {p, t}\right)  < \max \left( {{\left\lbrack  \left( {C}^{\prime } - C\right) \left( 1 - {t}_{0}\right) \right\rbrack  }^{-1},{\left\lbrack  {r}^{-2} - C\left( 1 - {t}_{0}\right) \right\rbrack  }^{-1}}\right) .
\]

This means that \( R\left( {p, t}\right) \) is uniformly bounded as \( t \rightarrow  1 \) , contradicting what we just established. This shows that for \( t \geq  1 - 1/2{r}^{2}C \) the result holds. For \( t \leq  1 - 1/2{r}^{2}C \) there is a positive lower bound on the scalar curvature, and hence the result is immediate for these \( t \) as well.

THEOREM 12.32. For any \( \epsilon  > 0 \) there is \( {C}^{\prime }\left( \epsilon \right)  < \infty \) such that for any point \( x \) in the standard solution one of the following holds (see FIG. 2).

(1) \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {{C}^{\prime }\left( \epsilon \right) ,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap.

(2) \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is the center of an evolving \( \epsilon \) -neck \( N \) whose initial time-slice is \( t = 0 \) , and this time-slice is disjoint from the surgery cap.

(3) \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is the center of an evolving \( \epsilon \) -neck defined for rescaled time \( 1 + \epsilon \) .

nodes.content: REMARK 12.33. At first glance it may seem impossible for a point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in the standard solution to be the center of an evolving \( \epsilon \) -neck defined for rescaled time \( 1 + \epsilon \) since the standard solution itself is only defined for time 1. But this is indeed possible. The reason is because the scale referred to for an evolving neck centered at \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is \( R{\left( x, t\right) }^{-1/2} \) . As \( t \) approaches \( 1, R\left( {x, t}\right) \) goes to infinity, so that rescaled time 1 at \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is an arbitrarily small time interval measured in the scale of the standard solution.

Suppose that we have a sequence of generalized Ricci flows \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) , points \( {x}_{n} \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) with \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right)  = 0 \) , neighborhoods \( {U}_{n} \) of \( {x}_{n} \) in the zero time-slice of \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) , and a constant \( 0 < \theta  < 1 \) . Then for all \( n \) sufficiently large, and any point \( {y}_{n} \) in the image of \( {\rho }_{n} \) , one of the following holds:

(1) \( {y}_{n} \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {{C}^{\prime }\left( \epsilon \right) ,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap.

(2) \( {y}_{n} \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck.

(3) \( {y}_{n} \) is the center of an evolving \( \epsilon \) -neck whose initial time-slice is at time 0 .

## 1. Notation and the statement of the result

In this chapter we describe the surgery process. For this chapter we fix:

(1) A \( \delta \) -neck \( \left( {N, g}\right) \) centered at a point \( {x}_{0} \) . We denote by \( \rho  : {S}^{2} \times \; \left( {-{\delta }^{-1},{\delta }^{-1}}\right)  \rightarrow  N \) the diffeomorphism that gives the \( \delta \) -neck structure.

(2) Standard initial conditions \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3},{g}_{0}}\right) \) .

We denote by \( {h}_{0} \times  d{s}^{2} \) the metric on \( {S}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) which is the product of the round metric \( {h}_{0} \) on \( {S}^{2} \) of scalar curvature 1 and the Euclidean metric \( d{s}^{2} \) on \( \mathbb{R} \) . We denote by \( {N}^{ - } \subset  N \) the image \( \rho \left( {\left( {-{\delta }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack   \times  {S}^{2}}\right) \) and we denote by \( s : {N}^{ - } \rightarrow  \left( {-{\delta }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) the composition \( {\rho }^{-1} \) followed by the projection to the second factor.

Recall that the standard initial metric \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3},{g}_{0}}\right) \) is invariant under the standard \( {SO}\left( 3\right) \) -action on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) . We let \( {p}_{0} \) denote the origin in \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) . It is the fixed point of this action and is called the tip of the standard initial metric. Recall from Lemma 12.3 that there are \( {A}_{0} > 0 \) and an isometry

\[
\psi  : \left( {{S}^{2}\times ( - \infty ,4\rbrack ,{h}_{0} \times  d{s}^{2}}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3} \smallsetminus  B\left( {{p}_{0},{A}_{0}}\right) ,{g}_{0}}\right) .
\]

The composition of \( {\psi }^{-1} \) followed by projection onto the second factor defines a map \( {s}_{1} : {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \smallsetminus  B\left( {{p}_{0},{A}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow  ( - \infty ,4\rbrack \) . Lastly, there is \( 0 < {r}_{0} < {A}_{0} \) such that on \( B\left( {{p}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) the metric \( {g}_{0} \) is of constant sectional curvature \( 1/4 \) . We extend the map \( {s}_{1} \) to a continuous map \( {s}_{1} : {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \rightarrow  \left( {-\infty ,4 + {A}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) defined by \( {s}_{1}\left( x\right)  = {A}_{0} + 4 - {d}_{{g}_{0}}\left( {p, x}\right) \) . This map is an isometry along each radial geodesic ray emanating from \( {p}_{0} \) . It is smooth except at \( {p}_{0} \) and sends \( {p}_{0} \) to \( 4 + {A}_{0} \) . The pre-images of \( {s}_{1} \) on \( \left( {-\infty ,4 + {A}_{0}}\right) \) are 2-spheres with round metrics of scalar curvature at least 1 .

The surgery process is a local one defined on the \( \delta \) -neck \( \left( {N, g}\right) \) . The surgery process replaces \( \left( {N, g}\right) \) by a smooth Riemannian manifold \( \left( {\mathcal{S},\widetilde{g}}\right) \) . The underlying smooth manifold \( \mathcal{S} \) is obtained by gluing together \( \rho \left( {{S}^{2} \times  }\right. \; \left. \left( {-{\delta }^{-1},4}\right) \right) \) and \( B\left( {{p}_{0},{A}_{0} + 4}\right) \) by identifying \( \rho \left( {x, s}\right) \) with \( \psi \left( {x, s}\right) \) for all \( x \in  {S}^{2} \) and all \( s \in  \left( {0,4}\right) \) . The functions \( s \) on \( {N}^{ - } \) and \( {s}_{1} \) agree on their overlap and hence together define a function \( s : \mathcal{S} \rightarrow  \left( {-{\delta }^{-1},4 + {A}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , a function smooth except at \( {p}_{0} \) . In order to define the metric \( \widetilde{g} \) we must make some universal choices. We fix once and for all two bump functions \( \alpha  : \left\lbrack  {1,2}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) , which is required to be identically 1 near 1 and identically 0 near 2 , and \( \beta  : \left\lbrack  {4 + {A}_{0} - {r}_{0},4 + {A}_{0}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) , which is required to be identically 1 near \( 4 + {A}_{0} - {r}_{0} \) and identically 0 on \( \left\lbrack  {4 + {A}_{0} - {r}_{0}/2,{A}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . These functions are chosen once and for all and are independent of \( \delta \) and \( \left( {N, g}\right) \) . Next we set \( \eta  = \sqrt{1 - \delta } \) . The purpose of this choice is the following:

THEOREM 13.2. There are constants \( {C}_{0}, q,{R}_{0} < \infty \) and \( {\delta }_{0}^{\prime } > 0 \) such that the following hold for the result \( \left( {\mathcal{S},\widetilde{g}}\right) \) of surgery on \( \left( {N, g}\right) \) provided that \( R\left( {x}_{0}\right)  \geq  {R}_{0},0 < \delta  \leq  {\delta }_{0}^{\prime } \) . Define \( f\left( s\right) \) as above with the constants \( {C}_{0},\delta \) and then use \( f \) to define surgery on a \( \delta \) -neck \( N \) to produce \( \left( {\mathcal{S},\widetilde{g}}\right) \) . Then the following hold.

- Fix \( t \geq  0 \) . For any \( p \in  N \) , let \( X\left( p\right)  = \max \left( {0, - \nu \left( p\right) }\right) \) , where \( \nu \left( p\right) \) is the smallest eigenvalue of \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( p\right) \) . Suppose that for all \( p \in  N \) we have:

(1) \( R\left( p\right)  \geq  \frac{-6}{1 + {4t}} \) , and

(2) \( R\left( p\right)  \geq  {2X}\left( p\right) \left( {\log X\left( p\right)  + \log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - 3}\right) \) , whenever \( 0 < X\left( p\right) \) . Then the curvature of \( \left( {\mathcal{S},\widetilde{g}}\right) \) satisfies the same equations at every point of \( \mathcal{S} \) with the same value of \( t \) .

nodes.content: DEFINITION 14.1. By a space-time we mean a paracompact Hausdorff space \( \mathcal{M} \) with a continuous function \( \mathbf{t} : \mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) , called time. We require that the image of \( \mathbf{t} \) be an interval \( I \) , finite or infinite with or without endpoints, in \( \mathbb{R} \) . The interval \( I \) is called the time-interval of definition of space-time. The initial point of \( I \) , if there is one, is the initial time and the final point of \( I \) , if there is one, is the final time. The level sets of \( \mathbf{t} \) are called the time-slices of space-time, and the preimage of the initial (resp., final) point of \( I \) is the initial (resp., final) time-slice.

nodes.label: Definition 14.2
nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
DEFINITION 14.2. A surgery space-time is a space-time \( \mathcal{M} \) equipped with a maximal atlas of charts covering \( \mathcal{M} \) , each chart being of one of the three types listed above, with the overlap functions being diffeomorphisms preserving the functions \( \mathbf{t} \) and the vector fields \( \chi \) . The points with neighborhoods of the first type are called smooth points, those with neighborhoods of the second type but not the first type are called exposed points, and all the other points are called singular points. Notice that the union of the set of smooth points and the set of exposed points forms a smooth manifold with boundary (possibly disconnected). Each component of the boundary of this manifold is contained in a single time-slice. The union of those components contained in a time distinct from the initial time and the final time is called the exposed region. and the boundary points of the closure of the exposed region form the set of the singular points of \( \mathcal{M} \) . (Technically, the exposed points are singular, but we reserve this word for the most singular points.) An \( \left( {n + 1}\right) \) -dimensional surgery space-time is by definition of homogeneous dimension \( n + 1 \) .

By construction, the local smooth functions \( \mathbf{t} \) are compatible on the overlaps and hence fit together to define a global smooth function \( \mathbf{t} : \mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) , called the time function. The level sets of this function are called the time-slices of the space-time, and \( {\mathbf{t}}^{-1}\left( t\right) \) is denoted \( {M}_{t} \) . Similarly, the tangent bundles of the various charts are compatible under the overlap diffeomor-phisms and hence glue together to give a global smooth tangent bundle on space-time. The smooth sections of this vector bundle, the smooth vector fields on space time, act as derivations on the smooth functions on spacetime. The tangent bundle of an \( \left( {n + 1}\right) \) -dimensional surgery space-time is a vector bundle of dimension \( n + 1 \) . Also, by construction the local vector fields \( \chi \) are compatible and hence glue together to define a global vector field, denoted \( \chi \) . The vector field and time function satisfy

\[
\chi \left( \mathbf{t}\right)  = 1
\]

At the manifold points (including the exposed points) it is a usual vector field. Along the exposed region and the initial time-slice the vector field points into the manifold; along the final time-slice it points out of the manifold.

nodes.content: DEFINITION 14.3. Let \( \mathcal{M} \) be a surgery space-time. Given a space \( K \) and an interval \( J \subset  \mathbb{R} \) we say that an embedding \( K \times  J \rightarrow  \mathcal{M} \) is compatible with time and the vector field if: (i) the restriction of \( \mathbf{t} \) to the image agrees with the projection onto the second factor and (ii) for each \( x \in  X \) the image of \( \{ x\}  \times  J \) is the integral curve for the vector field \( \chi \) . If in addition \( K \) is a subset of \( {M}_{t} \) we require that \( t \in  J \) and that the map \( K \times  \{ t\}  \rightarrow  {M}_{t} \) be the identity. Clearly, by the uniqueness of integral curves for vector fields, two such embeddings agree on their common interval of definition, so that, given \( K \subset  {M}_{t} \) there is a maximal interval \( {J}_{K} \) containing \( t \) such that such an embedding is defined on \( K \times  {J}_{K} \) . In the special case when \( K = \{ x\} \) for a point \( x \in  {M}_{t} \) we say that such an embedding is the maximal flow line through \( x \) . The embedding of the maximal interval through \( x \) compatible with time and the vector field \( \chi \) is called the domain of definition of the flow line through \( x \) . For a more general subset \( K \subset  {M}_{t} \) there is an embedding \( K \times  J \) compatible with time and the vector field \( \chi \) if and only if, for every \( x \in  K \) , the interval \( J \) is contained in the domain of definition of the flow line through \( x \) .

nodes.content: LEMMA 14.5. Let \( \mathcal{M} \) be an \( \left( {n + 1}\right) \) -dimensional surgery space-time, and fix \( t \) . The restriction of the smooth structure on \( \mathcal{M} \) to the time-slice \( {M}_{t} \) induces the structure of a smooth n-manifold on this time-slice. That is to say, we have a smooth embedding of \( {M}_{t} \rightarrow  \mathcal{M} \) . This smooth embedding identifies the tangent bundle of \( {M}_{t} \) with a codimension-1 subbundle of the restriction of tangent bundle of \( \mathcal{M} \) to \( {M}_{t} \) . This subbundle is complementary to the line field spanned by \( \chi \) . These codimension-1 sub-bundle along the various time-slices fit together to form a smooth, codimension-1 subbundle of the tangent bundle of space-time.

nodes.label: Definition 14.7

nodes.content:
DEFINITION 14.7. By a horizontal metric \( G \) on a surgery space-time \( \mathcal{M} \) we mean a \( {C}^{\infty } \) metric on \( \mathcal{H}T\mathcal{M} \) . For each \( t \) , the horizontal metric \( G \) induces a Riemannian metric, denoted \( G\left( t\right) \) , on the time-slice \( {M}_{t} \) . Associated to a horizontal metric \( G \) we have the horizontal covariant derivative, denoted \( \nabla \) . This is a pairing between horizontal vector fields

\[
X \otimes  Y \mapsto  {\nabla }_{X}Y
\]

On each time slice \( {M}_{t} \) it is the usual Levi-Civita connection associated to the Riemannian metric \( G\left( t\right) \) . Given a function \( F \) on space-time, by its gradient \( \nabla F \) we mean its horizontal gradient. The value of this gradient at a point \( q \in  {M}_{t} \) is the usual \( G\left( t\right) \) -gradient of \( {\left. F\right| }_{{M}_{t}} \) . In particular, \( \nabla F \) is a smooth horizontal vector field on space-time. The horizontal metric \( G \) on spacetime has its (horizontal) curvatures \( {\mathrm{{Rm}}}_{G} \) . These are smooth symmetric endomorphisms of the second exterior power of \( \mathcal{H}T\mathcal{M} \) . The value of \( {\operatorname{Rm}}_{G} \) at a point \( q \in  {M}_{t} \) is simply the usual Riemann curvature operator of \( G\left( t\right) \) at the point \( q \) . Similarly, we have the (horizontal) Ricci curvature \( \operatorname{Ric} = {\operatorname{Ric}}_{G} \) , a section of the symmetric square of the horizontal cotangent bundle, and the (horizontal) scalar curvature denoted \( R = {R}_{G} \) . The reason for working in \( \mathcal{H}T\mathcal{M} \) rather than individually in each slice is to emphasize the fact that all these horizontal quantities vary smoothly over the surgery space-time.

Suppose that \( t \in  I \) is not the final time and suppose that \( U \subset  {M}_{t} \) is an open subset with compact closure. Then there is \( \epsilon  > 0 \) and an embedding \( {i}_{U} : U \times  \lbrack t, t + \epsilon ) \subset  \mathcal{M} \) compatible with time and the vector field. Of course, two such embeddings agree on their common domain of definition. Notice also that for each \( {t}^{\prime } \in  \lbrack t, t + \epsilon ) \) the restriction of the map \( {i}_{U} \) to \( U \times  \left\{  {t}^{\prime }\right\} \) induces a diffeomorphism from \( U \) to an open subset \( {U}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) of \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . It follows that the local flow generated by the vector field \( \chi \) preserves the horizontal subbundle. Hence, the vector field \( \chi \) acts by Lie derivative on the sections of \( \mathcal{H}T\left( \mathcal{M}\right) \) and on all associated bundles (for example the symmetric square of the dual bundle).

nodes.content:
EXAMPLE 14.10. One example of a Ricci flow with surgery is \( \mathcal{M} = \; {M}_{0} \times  \lbrack 0, T) \) with time function \( \mathbf{t} \) and the vector field \( \chi \) coming from the second factor. In this case the Lie derivative \( {\mathcal{L}}_{\chi } \) agrees with the usual partial derivative in the time direction, and hence our generalized Ricci flow equation is the usual Ricci flow equation. This shows that an ordinary Ricci flow is indeed a Ricci flow with surgery.

The next lemma gives an example of a Ricci flow with surgery where the topology of the time-slices changes.

LEMMA 14.11. Suppose that we have manifolds \( {M}_{1} \times  (a, b\rbrack \) and \( {M}_{2} \times  \lbrack b, c) \) and compact, smooth codimension-0 submanifolds \( {\Omega }_{1} \subset  {M}_{1} \) and \( {\Omega }_{2} \subset  {M}_{2} \) with open neighborhoods \( {U}_{1} \subset  {M}_{1} \) and \( {U}_{2} \subset  {M}_{2} \) respectively. Suppose we have a diffeomorphism \( \psi  : {U}_{1} \rightarrow  {U}_{2} \) carrying \( {\Omega }_{1} \) onto \( {\Omega }_{2} \) . Let \( {\left( {M}_{1} \times  \left( a, b\right) \right) }_{0} \) be the subset obtained by removing \( \left( {{M}_{1} \smallsetminus  {\Omega }_{1}}\right)  \times  \{ b\} \) from \( {M}_{1} \times  (a, b\rbrack \) . Form the topological space

\[
\mathcal{M} = {\left( {M}_{1} \times  (a, b\rbrack \right) }_{0} \cup  {M}_{2} \times  \lbrack b, c)
\]

where \( {\Omega }_{1} \times  \{ b\} \) in \( {\left( {M}_{1} \times  \left( a, b\right\rbrack  \right) }_{0} \) is identified with \( {\Omega }_{2} \times  \{ b\} \) using the restriction of \( \psi \) to \( {\Omega }_{1} \) . Then \( \mathcal{M} \) naturally inherits the structure of a surgery space-time where the time function restricts to \( {\left( {M}_{1}\times (a, b\rbrack \right) }_{0} \) and to \( {M}_{2} \times  \lbrack b, c) \) to be the projection onto the second factor and the vector field \( \chi \) agrees with the vector fields coming from the second factor on each of \( {\left( {M}_{1} \times  \left( a, b\right\rbrack  \right) }_{0} \) and \( {M}_{2} \times  \lbrack b, c) \) .

Lastly, given Ricci flows \( \left( {{M}_{1},{g}_{1}\left( t\right) }\right) , a < t \leq  b \) , and \( \left( {{M}_{2},{g}_{2}\left( t\right) }\right) , b \leq \; t < c \) , if \( \psi  : \left( {{U}_{1},{g}_{1}\left( b\right) }\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{U}_{2},{g}_{2}\left( b\right) }\right) \) is an isometry, then these families fit together to form a smooth horizontal metric \( G \) on \( \mathcal{M} \) satisfying the Ricci flow equation, so that \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) is a Ricci flow with surgery.

nodes.proof:
As the union of Hausdorff spaces along closed subsets, \( \mathcal{M} \) is a Hausdorff topological space. The time function is the one induced from the projections onto the second factor. For any point outside the \( b \) time-slice there is the usual smooth coordinate coming from the smooth manifold \( {M}_{1} \times  \left( {a, b}\right) \) (if \( t < b \) ) or \( {M}_{2} \times  \left( {b, c}\right) \) (if \( t > b \) ). At any point of \( \left( {{M}_{2} \smallsetminus  {\Omega }_{2}}\right)  \times  \{ b\} \) there is the smooth manifold with boundary coordinate patch coming from \( {M}_{2} \times  \lbrack b, c) \) . For any point in \( \operatorname{int}\left( {\Omega }_{1}\right)  \times  \{ b\} \) we have the smooth manifold structure obtained from gluing (int \( \left( {\Omega }_{1}\right) ) \times  (a, b\rbrack \) to \( \operatorname{int}\left( {\Omega }_{2}\right)  \times  \lbrack b, c) \) along the \( b \) time-slice by \( \psi \) . Thus, at all these points we have neighborhoods on which our data determine a smooth manifold structure. Lastly, let us consider a point \( x \in  \partial {\Omega }_{1} \times  \{ b\} \) . Choose local coordinates \( \left( {{x}^{1},\ldots ,{x}^{n}}\right) \) for a neighborhood \( {V}_{1} \) of \( x \) such that \( {\Omega }_{1} \cap  {V}_{1} = \left\{  {{x}^{n} \leq  0}\right\} \) . We can assume that \( \psi \) is defined on all of \( {V}_{1} \) . Let \( {V}_{2} = \psi \left( {V}_{1}\right) \) and take the local coordinates on \( {V}_{2} \) induced from the \( {x}^{i} \) on \( {V}_{1} \) . Were we to identify \( {V}_{1} \times  (a, b\rbrack \) with \( {V}_{2} \times  \lbrack b, c) \) along the \( b \) time-slice using this map, then this union would be a smooth manifold. There is a neighborhood of the point \( \left( {x, b}\right)  \in  \mathcal{M} \) which is obtained from the smooth manifold \( {V}_{1} \times  (a, b\rbrack { \cup  }_{\psi }{V}_{2} \times  \lbrack b, c) \) by inducing a new topology where the open subsets are, in addition to the usual ones, any open subset of the form \( \left\{  {{x}^{n} > 0}\right\}   \times  \left\lbrack  {b,{b}^{\prime }}\right) \) where \( b < {b}^{\prime } \leq  c \) . This then gives the coordinate charts of the third type near the points of \( \partial {\Omega }_{2} \times  \{ b\} \) . Clearly, since the function \( \mathbf{t} \) and the vector field \( \partial /\partial t \) are smooth on \( {V}_{1} \times  (a, b\rbrack { \cup  }_{\psi }{V}_{2} \times  \lbrack b, c) \) , we see that these objects glue together to form smooth objects on \( \mathcal{M} \) .

Given the Ricci flows \( {g}_{1}\left( t\right) \) and \( {g}_{2}\left( t\right) \) as in the statement, they clearly determine a (possibly singular) horizontal metric on \( \mathcal{M} \) . This horizontal metric is clearly smooth except possibly along the \( b \) time-slice. At any point of \( \left( {{M}_{2} \smallsetminus  {\Omega }_{2}}\right)  \times  \{ b\} \) we have a one-sided smooth family, which means that on this set the horizontal metric is smooth. At a point of \( \operatorname{int}\left( {\Omega }_{2}\right)  \times  \{ b\} \) , the fact that the metrics fit together smoothly is an immediate consequence of Proposition 3.12. At a point \( x \in  \partial {\Omega }_{2} \times  \{ b\} \) we have neighborhoods \( {V}_{2} \subset  {M}_{2} \) of \( x \) and \( {V}_{1} \subset  {M}_{1} \) of \( {\psi }^{-1}\left( x\right) \) that are isometrically identified by \( \psi \) . Hence, again by Proposition 3.12 we see that the Ricci flows fit together to form a smooth family of metrics on \( {V}_{1} \times  (a, b\rbrack { \cup  }_{\psi }{V}_{2} \times  \lbrack b, c) \) . Hence, the induced horizontal metric on \( \mathcal{M} \) is smooth near this point.

REMARK 14.16. For \( \epsilon  > 0 \) sufficiently small, an \( \epsilon \) -round component satisfies the first condition in the above definition for some \( \kappa  > 0 \) depending only on the order of the fundamental group of the underlying manifold, but there is no universal \( \kappa  > 0 \) that works for all \( \epsilon \) -round manifolds. Fixing an integer \( N \) let \( {\mathcal{C}}_{N} \) be the class of closed 3-manifolds with the property that any finite free factor of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) has order at most \( N \) . Then any \( \epsilon \) - round component of any time-slice of any Ricci flow \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) whose initial conditions consist of a manifold in \( {\mathcal{C}}_{N} \) will have fundamental group of order at most \( N \) and hence will satisfy the first condition in the above definition for some \( \kappa  > 0 \) depending only on \( N \) .

We also have the notion of the curvature being pinched toward positive, analogous to the notions for Ricci flows and generalized Ricci flows.

DEFINITION 14.17. Let \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) be a 3-dimensional Ricci flow with surgery, whose time domain of definition is contained in \( \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) . For any \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) we denote the eigenvalues of \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( x\right) \) by \( \lambda \left( x\right)  \geq  \mu \left( x\right)  \geq  \nu \left( x\right) \) and we set \( X\left( x\right)  = \max \left( {0, - \nu \left( x\right) }\right) \) . We say that its curvature is pinched toward positive if the following hold for every \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) :

(1) \( R\left( x\right)  \geq  \frac{-6}{1 + 4\mathbf{t}\left( x\right) } \) .

(2) \( R\left( x\right)  \geq  {2X}\left( x\right) \left( {\log X\left( x\right)  + \log \left( {1 + \mathbf{t}\left( x\right) }\right)  - 3}\right) \) , whenever \( 0 < X\left( x\right) \) .

Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a Riemannian manifold and let \( T \geq  0 \) . We say that \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) has curvature pinched toward positive up to time \( T \) if the above two inequalities hold for all \( x \in  M \) with \( \mathbf{t}\left( x\right) \) replaced by \( T \) .

Lastly, we extend the notion of canonical neighborhoods to the context of Ricci flows with surgery.

nodes.content:
DEFINITION 14.18. Fix constants \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) and a constant \( r \) . We say that a Ricci flow with surgery \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) satisfies the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( r \) if every point \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) with \( R\left( x\right)  \geq  {r}^{-2} \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood in \( \mathcal{M} \) . In all cases except that of the strong \( \epsilon \) -neck, the strong canonical neighborhood of \( x \) is a subset of the time-slice containing \( x \) , and the notion of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood has exactly the same meaning as in the case of an ordinary Ricci flow. In the case of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( x \) this means that there is an embedding \( \left( {{S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) }\right)  \times  \left( {\mathbf{t}\left( x\right)  - R{\left( x\right) }^{-1},\mathbf{t}\left( x\right) \rbrack  \rightarrow  \mathcal{M}\text{ , mapping }\left( {{q}_{0},0}\right) }\right. \) to \( x \) , where \( {q}_{0} \) is the basepoint of \( {S}^{2} \) , an embedding compatible with time and the vector field, such that the pullback of \( G \) is a Ricci flow on \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) which, when the time is shifted by \( - \mathbf{t}\left( x\right) \) and then the flow is rescaled by \( R\left( x\right) \) , is within \( \epsilon \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology of the standard evolving round cylinder \( \left( {{S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) ,{h}_{0}\left( t\right)  \times  d{s}^{2}}\right) , - 1 < t \leq  0 \) , where the scalar curvature of the \( {h}_{0}\left( t\right) \) is \( 1 - t \) .

Notice that if \( x \) is an exposed point or sufficiently close to an exposed point, then \( x \) cannot be the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck.

PROPOSITION 15.2. There is \( 0 < \beta  < 1/2 \) such that the following holds for any \( \epsilon  < 1 \) . Suppose we have an isometric embedding of \( N \times  \left\{  {-{t}_{0}}\right\} \) with \( {N}^{\prime } \times  \left\{  {-{t}_{0}}\right\} \) and the strong

\( {\beta \epsilon }/2 \) -neck structure on \( {N}^{\prime } \times  \left( {-{t}_{1}, - {t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) is centered at the image of \( \left( {x, - {t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . Then the union

\]

with the induced one-parameter family of metrics contains a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( \left( {x,0}\right) \) .
