nodes.proof:
By supposition, for each \( b \) there is a point \( x \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) at which the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption fails for the parameter \( {r}_{a} \) . We call points at which this condition fails counterexample points. Of course, since \( {r}_{a} \leq  {r}_{i} \) and since the restriction of \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) },{g}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) to \( {\mathbf{t}}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{i}}\right) \right) \) satisfies the hypothesis of the proposition, we see that any counterexample point \( x \) has \( \mathbf{t}\left( x\right)  \geq  {T}_{i} \) . Take a sequence \( {x}_{n} = {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) of counterexample points with \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n + 1}\right)  \leq  \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right) \) for all \( n \) that minimizes \( \mathbf{t} \) among all counterexample points in the sense that for any \( \xi  > 0 \) and for any counterexample point \( x \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) eventually \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right)  < \mathbf{t}\left( x\right)  + \xi \) . Let \( {t}^{\prime } = {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right) \) . Clearly, \( {t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{T}_{i},{T}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) , and by construction the restriction of \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) },{G}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) to \( {\mathbf{t}}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {0,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \right) \) satisfies the \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {r}_{a} \) . Since the surgery times are discrete, there is \( {t}^{\prime \prime } = {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime \prime } \) with \( {t}^{\prime } < {t}^{\prime \prime } \leq  {T}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) and a diffeomorphism \( \psi  = {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) } : {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right)  \rightarrow  {\mathbf{t}}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \right) \) compatible with time and the vector field. We view \( {\psi }^{ * }{G}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) as a one-parameter family of metrics \( g\left( t\right)  = {g}_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( t\right) \) on \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \) . By passing to a subsequence we can arrange that \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right)  \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \) for all \( n \) . Thus, for each \( n \) there are \( {y}_{n} = {y}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \in  {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) and \( {t}_{n} \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \) with \( \psi \left( {{y}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right)  = {x}_{n} \) . Since \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is a compact 3-manifold, by passing to a further subsequence we can assume that \( {y}_{n} \rightarrow  {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . Of course, \( {t}_{n} \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}{x}_{n} = {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b,\right) } \) .

We claim that, for all \( b \) sufficiently large, the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {r}_{a} \) fails at \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . Notice that since \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is the limit of a sequence where the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -neighborhood assumption fails, the points in the sequence converging to \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) have scalar curvature at least \( {r}_{a}^{-2} \) . It follows that \( R\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right)  \geq  {r}_{a}^{-2} \) . Suppose that \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) satisfies the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {r}_{a} \) . This means that there is a neighborhood \( U = {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) of \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) which is a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood of \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . According to Definition 9.78 there are four possibilities. The first two we consider are that \( \left( {U, g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) }\right) \) is an \( \epsilon \) -round component or a \( C \) -component. In either of these cases, since the defining inequalities given in Definition 9.76 and 9.75 are strong inequalities, all metrics on \( U \) sufficiently close to \( g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) - topology satisfy these same inequalities. But as \( n \) tends to \( \infty \) , the metrics \( {\left. g\left( {t}_{n}\right) \right| }_{U} \) converge in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to \( {\left. g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \right| }_{U} \) . Thus, in these two cases, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the metrics \( g\left( {t}_{n}\right) \) on \( U \) are \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood metrics of the same type as \( {\left. g\left( {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }\right) \right| }_{U} \) . Hence, in either of these cases, for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood of the same type as \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) , contrary to our assumption about the sequence \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) .

Now suppose that there is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . This is to say that \( \left( {U, g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) }\right) \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . By Proposition 9.79, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( \left( {U, g\left( {t}_{n}\right) }\right) \) is also a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap with the same core. This core contains \( {y}_{n} \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, showing that \( {x}_{n} \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap for all \( n \) sufficiently large.

Now let us consider the remaining case when \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. In this case we have an embedding

\[
{\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} : {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \times  \left( {{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - {R}^{-1}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) ,{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) }
\]

compatible with time and the vector field and a diffeomorphism \( {f}_{\left( a, b\right) } : {S}^{2} \times \; \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)  \rightarrow  {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) such that

\[
{\left( {f}_{\left( a, b\right) } \times  \mathrm{{Id}}\right) }^{ * }{\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }}^{ * }\left( {R\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) {G}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right)
\]

is \( \epsilon \) -close in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology to the evolving product metric

\[
{h}_{0}\left( t\right)  \times  d{s}^{2}, - 1 < t \leq  0,
\]

where \( {h}_{0}\left( t\right) \) is a round metric of scalar curvature \( 1/\left( {1 - t}\right) \) on \( {S}^{2} \) and \( d{s}^{2} \) is the Euclidean metric on the interval. Here, there are two subcases to consider.

(i) \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) extends backward past \( {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - {R}^{-1}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) .

(ii) There is a flow line through a point \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) that is defined on the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - {R}^{-1}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) ,{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) but with the value of the flow line at \( {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - {R}^{-1}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) an exposed point.

Let us consider the first subcase. The embedding \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) extends forward in time because of the diffeomorphism \( {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) } : {M}_{{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime },{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime \prime }}\right)  \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) and, by assumption, \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) extends backward in time some amount. Thus, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, we can use these extensions of \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) to define an embedding \( {\psi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } : {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \times  \left( {\mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }\right)  - {R}^{-1}\left( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }\right) ,\mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }\right) \rbrack  \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right. \) compatible with time and the vector field. Furthermore, since the \( {\psi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) converge in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) as \( n \) tends to infinity, the Riemannian metrics \( {\left( {f}_{\left( a, b\right) } \times  \mathrm{{Id}}\right) }^{ * }{\psi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }^{ * }\left( {R\left( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }\right) {G}_{a, b}}\right) \) converge in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to the pullback \( {\left( {f}_{\left( a, b\right) } \times  \mathrm{{Id}}\right) }^{ * }{\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }}^{ * }\left( {R\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) {G}_{a, b}}\right) \) . Clearly then, for fixed \( \left( {a, b}\right) \) and for all \( n \) sufficiently large the pullbacks of the rescalings of these metrics by \( R\left( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }\right) \) are within \( \epsilon \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology of the standard evolving flow \( {h}_{0}\left( t\right)  \times  d{s}^{2}, - 1 < t \leq  0 \) , on the product of \( {S}^{2} \) with the interval. Under these identifications the points \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) correspond to points

\[
\left( {{p}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) },{s}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }}\right)  \in  {S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)
\]

where \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}{s}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } = 0 \) . The last thing we do is to choose diffeomorphisms \( {\varphi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } : \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) that are the identity near both ends, such that \( {\varphi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) carries 0 to \( {s}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) and such that the \( {\varphi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) converge to the identity in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology for fixed \( \left( {a, b}\right) \) as \( n \) tends to infinity. Then, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the composition

\[
{S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \overset{\operatorname{Id} \times  {\varphi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }}{ \rightarrow  }{S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \overset{{f}_{\left( a, b\right) }}{ \rightarrow  }U\overset{{\psi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }}{ \rightarrow  }{\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) }
\]

is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) . This shows that for any \( b \) for which the first subcase holds, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, there is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) .

Now suppose that the second subcase holds for all \( b \) . Here, unlike all previous cases, we shall have to let \( b \) vary and we shall prove the result only for \( b \) sufficiently large. We shall show that for all \( b \) sufficiently large, \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. This will establish the result by contradiction, for as we showed in the previous case, if \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap, then the same is true for the \( {x}_{n} \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, contrary to our assumption.

For the moment fix \( b \) . Set \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } = {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - {R}_{{G}_{\left( a, b\right) }}{\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) }^{-1} \) . Since, by supposition the embedding \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) does not extend backwards past \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) , it must be the case that \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is a surgery time and furthermore that there is a surgery cap \( {\mathcal{C}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) at this time with the property that there is a point \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) such that \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\left( {{y}_{\left( a, b\right) }, t}\right) \) converges to a point \( {z}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {\mathcal{C}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) as \( t \) tends to \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) from above. (See FIG. 1.) We denote by \( {p}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) the tip of \( {\mathcal{C}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) , and we denote by \( {\bar{h}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) the scale of the surgery at time \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) .

Since the statement that \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap is a scale invariant statement, we are free to replace \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) },{G}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) with \( \left( {{\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{\left( a, b\right) },{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) , which has been rescaled to make \( {\bar{h}}_{\left( a, b\right) } = 1 \) and shifted in time so that \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } = 0 \) . We denote the new time function by \( \widetilde{\mathbf{t}} \) . (Notice that this rescaling and time-shifting is different from what we usually do. Normally, when we have a base point like \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) we rescale to make its scalar curvature 1 and we shift time to make it be at time 0 . Here we have rescaled based on the scale of the surgery cap rather than \( R\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) .) We set \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } = \; {R}_{{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) and we set \( {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } = \widetilde{\mathbf{t}}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) . Since the initial time of the strong \( \epsilon \) -neck is zero, \( {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } = {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1} \) . We denote the flow line backward in time from \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) by \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( \widetilde{t}\right) ,0 \leq  \widetilde{t} \leq  {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } \) , so that \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }\right)  = {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . Since \( {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck, by our choice of \( \epsilon \) , it follows from Lemma A. 2 and rescaling that \( R\left( {\psi \left( {{y}_{\left( a, b\right) },\widetilde{t}}\right) }\right) \) is within \( \left( {0.01}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) of \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }/\left( {1 + {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - \widetilde{t}}\right) }\right) \) for all \( t \in  \left( {0,{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) . By taking limits as \( t \) approaches 0, we see that \( {R}_{{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\left( {z}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) is within \( \left( {0.01}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) of \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }/2 \) . Let \( D \) be the universal constant given in Lemma 12.3, so that the scalar curvature at any point of the standard initial metric is at least \( {D}^{-1} \) and at most \( D \) . It follows from the third item in Theorem 13.2 that, since we have rescaled to make the surgery scale 1, for all \( b \) sufficiently large the scalar curvature on the surgery \( {\mathcal{C}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is at least \( {\left( 2D\right) }^{-1} \) and at most \( {2D} \) . In particular, for all \( b \) sufficiently large

\[
{\left( 2D\right) }^{-1} \leq  {R}_{\widetilde{G}\left( {a, b}\right) }\left( {z}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right)  \leq  {2D}.
\]

Together with the above estimate relating \( {R}_{{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\left( {z}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) and \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) , this gives

(17.1)

\[
{\left( 5D\right) }^{-1} \leq  {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \leq  {5D}.
\]

Since the flow line from \( {z}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) to \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) lies in the closure of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck of scale \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1/2} \) , the scalar curvature is less than \( {6D} \) at every point of this flow line. According to Proposition 12.31 there is \( {\theta }_{1} < 1 \) (depending only on \( D \) ) such that \( R\left( {q, t}\right)  \geq  {8D} \) for all \( \left( {q, t}\right) \) in the standard solution with \( t \geq  {\theta }_{1} \) .

![019eafdb-e076-77f6-81c2-3ca4f7500935_41_452_584_887_382_0.jpg](images/019eafdb-e076-77f6-81c2-3ca4f7500935_41_452_584_887_382_0.jpg)

Figure 1. A strong neck with initial time in a surgery cap.

By the fifth property of Theorem 12.5 there is \( {A}^{\prime }\left( {\theta }_{1}\right)  < \infty \) such that in the standard flow, \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right) \) contains \( B\left( {{p}_{0},{\theta }_{1}, A/2}\right) \) for every \( A \geq  {A}^{\prime }\left( {\theta }_{1}\right) \) . We set \( A \) equal to the maximum of \( {A}^{\prime }\left( {\theta }_{1}\right) \) and

\[
3\left( {\left( {1.2}\right) \sqrt{5D}{\epsilon }^{-1} + \left( {1.1}\right) \left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right)  + C\sqrt{5D}}\right) .
\]

Now for any \( \bar{\delta } > 0 \) for all \( b \) sufficiently large, we have \( {\delta }_{\left( a, b\right) } \leq  {\delta }^{\prime \prime }\left( {A,{\theta }_{1},\bar{\delta }}\right) \) , where \( {\delta }^{\prime \prime }\left( {A,{\theta }_{1},\bar{\delta }}\right) \) is the constant given in Proposition 16.13.

CLAIM 17.3. Suppose \( b \) is sufficiently large so that \( {\delta }_{\left( a, b\right) } \leq  {\delta }^{\prime \prime }\left( {A,{\theta }_{1},{\bar{\delta }}_{0}}\right) \) , where \( {\bar{\delta }}_{0} \) is the constant given in Definition 16.12. Then \( {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } \leq  {\theta }_{1} \) .

Proof. In this proof we shall fix \( \left( {a, b}\right) \) , so we drop these indices from the notation. Consider \( s \leq  {\theta }_{1} \) maximal so that there is an embedding

\[
\psi  = {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) } : B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right)  \times  \lbrack 0, s) \rightarrow  {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{\left( a, b\right) }
\]

compatible with time and the vector field. First suppose that \( s < {\theta }_{1} \) . Then according to Proposition 16.5 either the entire ball \( B\left( {p,0, A}\right) \) disappears at time \( s \) or \( s \) is the final time of the time interval of definition for the flow \( \left( {{\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{\left( a, b\right) },{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) . Since we have the flow line from \( z \in  B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right) \) extending to time \( {\widetilde{t}}^{\prime } = {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } \) , in either case this implies that \( {\widetilde{t}}^{\prime } < s \) , proving that \( {t}^{\prime } < {\theta }_{1} \) in this case.

Now suppose that \( s = {\theta }_{1} \) . By the choice of \( {\theta }_{1} \) , for the standard solution the scalar curvature at every \( \left( {q,{\theta }_{1}}\right) \) is at least \( {8D} \) . Since \( {\delta }_{\left( a, b\right) } \leq  {\delta }^{\prime \prime }\left( {A,{\theta }_{1},{\bar{\delta }}_{0}}\right) \) , by the definition of \( {\bar{\delta }}_{0} \) given in Definition 16.12 and by Proposition 16.5 the scalar curvature of the pullback of the metric under \( \psi \) is within a factor of 2 of the scalar curvature of the rescaled standard solution. Hence, the scalar curvature along the flow line \( \left( {z, t}\right) \) through \( z \) limits to at least \( {8D} \) as \( t \) tends to \( {\theta }_{1} \) . Since the scalar curvature on \( \left( {z, t}\right) \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{\widetilde{t}}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) is bounded above by \( {6D} \) , it follows that \( {\widetilde{t}}^{\prime } < {\theta }_{1} \) in this case as well. This completes the proof of the claim.

Thus, we have maps

\[
{\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) } : B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{\left( a, b\right) }
\]

compatible with time and the vector field, with the property that for each \( \delta  > 0 \) , for all \( b \) sufficiently large the pullback under this map of \( {\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is within \( \delta \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\delta \right\rbrack  } \) -topology of the restriction of the standard solution. Let \( {w}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) be the result of flowing \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) backward to time 0 .

CLAIM 17.4. For all \( b \) sufficiently large, \( {w}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right) \times \{ 0\} }\right) \) .

Proof. First notice that, by our choice of \( \epsilon \) , every point in the 0 time-slice of the closure of the strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is within distance (1.1) \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1}{\epsilon }^{-1} \) of \( {w}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . In particular,

\[
{d}_{{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\left( {{w}_{\left( a, b\right) },{y}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right)  < \left( {1.1}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1}.
\]

Since \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is contained in the surgery cap and the scale of the surgery at this time is \( 1,{y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is within distance \( {A}_{0} + 5 \) of \( {p}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . Hence, by the triangle inequality and Inequality (17.1), we have

\[
{d}_{{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\left( {{w}_{\left( a, b\right) },{p}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right)  < \left( {1.1}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1} + \left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right)
\]

\[
< \left( {1.1}\right) \sqrt{5D}{\epsilon }^{-1} + \left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) \text{ . }
\]

For \( b \) sufficiently large, the image \( {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right) }\right) \) contains the ball of radius \( \left( {0.95}\right) A \) centered at \( {p}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . Since by our choice of \( A \) we have \( \left( {0.95}\right) A > \) (1.1) \( \sqrt{5D}{\epsilon }^{-1} + \left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) \) , the claim follows.

We define \( {q}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right) \) so that \( {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {{q}_{\left( a, b\right) },0}\right)  = {w}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . Of course,

\[
{\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {{q}_{\left( a, b\right) },{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right)  = {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }.
\]

If follows from the above computation that for all \( b \) sufficiently large we have

\[
{d}_{0}\left( {{q}_{\left( a, b\right) },{p}_{0}}\right)  < \left( {1.15}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1} + \left( {1.05}\right) \left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) .
\]

Since the standard flow has non-negative curvature, it is a distance nonincreasing flow. Therefore,

\[
{d}_{{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\left( {{q}_{\left( a, b\right) },{p}_{0}}\right)  < \left( {1.15}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1} + \left( {1.05}\right) \left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) .
\]

Suppose that a point \( \left( {q,{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) in the standard solution were the center of a \( {\beta \epsilon }/3 \) -neck, where \( \beta \) is the constant from Proposition 15.2. Of course, for all \( b \) sufficiently large, \( R\left( {q,{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right)  > \left( {0.99}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . Since \( \beta  < 1/2 \) and \( \epsilon  < \sqrt{5D}\left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) /2 \) and \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \leq  {5D} \) , it follows from the above distance estimate that this neck would contain \( \left( {{p}_{0},{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) . But this is impossible: since \( \left( {{p}_{0},{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) is an isolated fixed point of an isometric \( {SO}\left( 3\right) \) -action on the standard flow, all the sectional curvatures at \( \left( {{p}_{0},{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) are equal, and this is in contradiction with estimates on the sectional curvatures at any point of an \( \epsilon \) -neck given in Lemma A.2. We can then conclude from Theorem 12.32 that for all \( b \) sufficiently large, the point \( \left( {{p}_{0},{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C\left( {{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right) ,{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right) \) -cap \( {Y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) in the \( {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } \) time-slice of the standard solution. Now note that for all \( b \) sufficiently large, the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{q}_{\left( a, b\right) },{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) is at least \( \left( {0.99}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) , since the scalar curvature of \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is equal to \( {Q}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . This implies that the diameter of \( {Y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is at most

\[
\text{ (1.01) }{\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1/2}C\left( {{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right)  < \left( {1.1}\right) \sqrt{5D}C\left( {{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right) \text{ . }
\]

Since \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right) \) contains \( B\left( {{p}_{0},{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }, A/2}\right) \) , and since \( C > C\left( {{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right) \) , it follows from the definition of \( A \) , the above distance estimate, and the triangle inequality that for all \( b \) sufficiently large \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right)  \times  \left\{  {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }\right\} \) contains \( {Y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) .

Since \( C > C\left( {{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right)  + 1 \) and since for \( b \) sufficiently large \( {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) }^{ * }{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is arbitrarily close to the restriction of the standard solution metric, it follows from Theorem 12.32 and Proposition 9.79 that for all \( b \) sufficiently large, the image \( {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {Y}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . As we have already remarked, this contradicts the assumption that no \( {x}_{n} \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood.

This completes the proof in the last case and establishes Lemma 17.2.

nodes.content: CLAIM 17.6. For all a sufficiently large, every point \( \widetilde{x} \in  \left( {{\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a},{\widetilde{G}}_{a}}\right) \) with \( R\left( \widetilde{x}\right)  > 1 \) and \( \mathbf{t}\left( \widetilde{x}\right)  = 0 \) has a \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -canonical neighborhood.
nodes.content_excerpt: CLAIM 17.6. For all a sufficiently large, every point \( \widetilde{x} \in \left( {{\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a},{\widetilde{G}}_{a}}\right) \) with \( R\left( \widetilde{x}\right) > 1 \) and \( \mathbf{t}\left( \widetilde{x}\right) = 0 \) has a \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -canonical neighborhood.

nodes.proof:
Assume that \( \widetilde{x} \in  \widetilde{\mathcal{M}} \) has \( R\left( \widetilde{x}\right)  > 1 \) . Suppose that \( \widetilde{x} \) is an exposed point. If \( a \) is sufficiently large, then \( {\delta }_{b\left( a\right) } \) is arbitrarily close to zero and hence by the last item in Theorem 13.2 and the structure of the standard initial condition, we see that \( \widetilde{x} \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -cap.

Suppose now that \( \widetilde{x} \) is not an exposed point. Then we can take a sequence of points \( {\widetilde{y}}_{n} \in  {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a} \) all lying on the flow line for the vector field through \( \widetilde{x} \) converging to \( \widetilde{x} \) with \( \mathbf{t}\left( {\widetilde{y}}_{n}\right)  < 0 \) . Of course, for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( R\left( {\widetilde{y}}_{n}\right)  > 1 \) , which implies that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {\widetilde{y}}_{n} \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Passing to a subsequence, we can arrange that all of these canonical neighborhoods are of the same type. If they are all \( \epsilon \) -round components, all \( C \) -components, or all \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -caps whose cores contain \( {y}_{n} \) , then by taking limits and arguing as in the proof of Lemma 11.23 we see that \( \widetilde{x} \) has a strong \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -canonical neighborhood of the same type. On the other hand, if \( {\widetilde{y}}_{n} \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck for all \( n \) , then according to Claim 11.24, the limit point \( \widetilde{x} \) is the center of a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck.

Since we have chosen \( \epsilon  > 0 \) sufficiently small so that Theorem 11.8 applies with \( \epsilon \) replaced by \( {2\epsilon } \) , applying this theorem shows that we can pass to a subsequence and take a smooth limiting flow of a subsequence of the rescaled flows \( \left( {{\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a},{\widetilde{G}}_{a}}\right) \) based at \( {\widetilde{x}}_{a} \) and defined for all \( t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) . Because the \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{a},{G}_{a}}\right) \) all have curvature pinched toward positive and since \( R\left( {x}_{a}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( a \) tends to infinity, this result says that the limiting flow has non-negative, bounded curvature and is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed on all scales. That is to say, the limiting flow is a \( \kappa \) -solution. By Corollary 9.95 this contradicts the fact that the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption fails at \( {x}_{a} \) for every \( a \) . This contradiction shows that in the second case there is a subsequence of the \( a \) such that \( {x}_{a} \) has a strong canonical neighborhood and completes the proof of the second case.

nodes.proof:
Suppose the result does not hold. Then there are \( {A}^{\prime },{D}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime } < \infty \) and we can pass to a subsequence (in \( a \) ) such that the hypotheses of the lemma hold for every \( a \) but no \( {x}_{a} \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. The essential point of the argument is to show that in the units of the surgery scale the elapsed time between the surgery time and 0 is less than 1 and the distance from the point \( {z}_{a} \) to the tip of the surgery cap is bounded independent of \( a \) .

By Lemma 12.3, the fact that the scalar curvature at \( {z}_{a} \) is bounded by \( {D}^{\prime } \) implies that for all \( a \) sufficiently large the scale \( {\bar{h}}_{a} \) of the surgery at time \( - {t}_{a} \) satisfies

(17.2)

\[
{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} \geq  {\left( 2{D}^{\prime }D\right) }^{-1}.
\]

(Recall that we are working in the rescaled flow \( \left( {{\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a},{\widetilde{G}}_{a}}\right) \) .)

Now we are ready to show that the elapsed time is bounded less than 1 in the surgery scale.

CLAIM 17.8. There is \( {\theta }_{1} < 1 \) , depending on \( {D}^{\prime } \) and \( {t}^{\prime } \) , such that for all a sufficiently large we have \( {t}_{a} < {\theta }_{1}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} \) .

Proof. We consider two cases: either \( {t}_{a} \leq  {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2}/2 \) or \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2}/2 < {t}_{a} \) . In the first case, the claim is obviously true with \( {\theta }_{1} \) anything greater than \( 1/2 \) and less than 1. In the second case, the curvature everywhere along the flow line is at most \( {D}^{\prime } < \left( {2{t}_{a}{D}^{\prime }}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \leq  \left( {2{t}^{\prime }{D}^{\prime }}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) . Using Proposition 12.31 fix \( 1/2 < {\theta }_{1} < 1 \) so that every point of the standard solution \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( t \geq  \left( {2{\theta }_{1} - 1}\right) \) satisfies \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  6{t}^{\prime }{D}^{\prime } \) . Notice that \( {\theta }_{1} \) depends only on \( {D}^{\prime } \) and \( {t}^{\prime } \) . If \( {t}_{a} < {\theta }_{1}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} \) , then the claim holds for this value of \( {\theta }_{1} < 1 \) . Suppose \( {t}_{a} \geq  {\theta }_{1}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} \) , so that \( - {t}_{a} + \left( {2{\theta }_{1} - 1}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} < 0 \) . For all \( a \) sufficiently large we have \( {\delta }_{a} \leq  {\delta }_{0}^{\prime \prime }\left( {{A}_{0} + 5,{\theta }_{1},{\bar{\delta }}_{0}}\right) \) where \( {\bar{\delta }}_{0} \) is the constant from Definition 16.12 and \( {\delta }_{0}^{\prime \prime } \) is the constant from Proposition 16.5. This means that the scalar curvatures at corresponding points of the rescaled standard solution and the evolution of the surgery cap (up to time 0) in \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a} \) differ by at most a factor of two. Thus, for these \( a \) , we have \( R\left( {{y}_{a},\left( {-{t}_{a} + \left( {2{\theta }_{1} - 1}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2}}\right) }\right)  \geq  3\left( {{t}^{\prime }{D}^{\prime }}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) from the definition of \( {\bar{\delta }}_{0} \) and Proposition 16.5. But this is impossible since \( - {t}_{a}\left( {2{\theta }_{1} - 1}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} < 0 \) and \( 3{t}^{\prime }{D}^{\prime }/{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} \geq  3{t}_{a}{D}^{\prime }/{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} > {D}^{\prime } \) as \( {t}_{a} > {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2}/2 \) . Hence, \( R\left( {{y}_{a},\left( {-{t}_{a} + \left( {2{\theta }_{1} - 1}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a}^{2}}\right) }\right)  \leq  2{t}_{a}{D}^{\prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \leq  2{t}^{\prime }{D}^{\prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) . This contradiction shows that if \( a \) is sufficiently large then \( {t}_{a} < {\theta }_{1}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{2} \) .

We pass to a subsequence so that \( {t}_{a}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) converges to some \( \theta  \leq  {\theta }_{1} \) . We define \( \widetilde{C} \) to be the maximum of \( C \) and \( 3{\epsilon }^{-1}{\beta }^{-1} \) . Now, using part 5 of Theorem 12.5 we set \( {A}^{\prime \prime } \geq  \left( {9\widetilde{C} + 3{A}^{\prime }}\right) \sqrt{{2D}{D}^{\prime }} + 6\left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) \) sufficiently large so that in the standard flow \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0,{A}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \) contains \( B\left( {{p}_{0}, t,{A}^{\prime \prime }/2}\right) \) for any \( t \leq  \left( {{\theta }_{1} + 1}\right) /2 \) . This constant is chosen only to depend on \( {\theta }_{1},{A}^{\prime } \) , and \( C \) . As \( a \) tends to infinity, \( {\delta }_{a} \) tends to zero which means, by Proposition 16.5, that for all \( a \) sufficiently large there is an embedding

\[
{\rho }_{a} : B\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a},{A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{a},0}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a}
\]

compatible with time and the vector field such that (after translating by \( {t}_{a} \) to make the flow start at time 0 and scaling by \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) ) the restriction of \( {\widetilde{G}}_{a} \) to this image is close in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to the restriction of the standard flow to \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0,{A}^{\prime \prime }}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right\rbrack \) . The image \( {\rho }_{a}\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a}}\right) \) is the tip \( {p}_{a} \) of the surgery cap \( {\mathcal{C}}_{a} \) in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{a} \) . Thus, for all \( a \) sufficiently large the image \( {\rho }_{a}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a},{A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}}\right) \times \{ 0\} }\right) \) contains the \( {A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}/3 \) -neighborhood of the image \( {\rho }_{a}\left( {{p}_{0},0}\right) \) of the tip of the surgery cap under the flow forward to time 0. By our choice of \( {A}^{\prime \prime } \) , and Equation (17.2), this means that for all \( a \) sufficiently large \( {\rho }_{a}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a},{A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}}\right)  \times  \left\{  {-{t}_{a}}\right\}  }\right) \) contains the \( \left( {3\widetilde{C} + {A}^{\prime }}\right)  + 2\left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a} \) - neighborhood of \( {p}_{a} = {\rho }_{a}\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a}}\right) \) . Notice also that, since the standard solution has positive curvature and hence the distance between points is nonincreasing in time by Lemma 3.14, the distance at time 0 between \( {\rho }_{a}\left( {{p}_{0},0}\right) \) and \( {y}_{a} \) is less than \( 2\left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) {\bar{h}}_{a} \) . By the triangle inequality, we conclude that for all \( a \) sufficiently large, \( {\rho }_{a}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a},{A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}}\right) \times \{ 0\} }\right) \) contains the \( 3\widetilde{C} \) - neighborhood of \( {x}_{a} \) . Since the family of metrics on

\[
{\rho }_{a}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{0}, - {t}_{a},{A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{a},0}\right\rbrack  }\right) \}
\]

(after time-shifting by \( {t}_{a} \) and rescaling by \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) ) are converging smoothly to the ball \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0,{A}^{\prime \prime }}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {0,\theta }\right\rbrack \) in the standard flow, for all \( a \) sufficiently large, the flow from time \( - {t}_{a} \) to 0 on the \( 3\widetilde{C} \) -neighborhood of \( {x}_{a} \) is, after rescaling by \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) , very nearly isometric to the restriction of the standard flow from time 0 to \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a} \) on the \( 3\widetilde{C}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-1} \) -neighborhood of some point \( {q}_{a} \) in the standard flow. Of course, since the scalar curvature of \( {x}_{a} \) is \( 1, R\left( {{q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right) \) in the standard flow is close to \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) . Hence, by Theorem 12.32 there is a neighborhood \( X \) of \( \left( {{q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right) \) in the standard solution that either is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap, or is an evolving \( {\beta \epsilon }/3 \) -neck centered at \( \left( {{q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right) \) . In the latter case either the evolving neck is defined for backward time \( \left( {1 + {\beta \epsilon }/3}\right) \) or its initial time-slice is the zero time-slice and this initial time-slice lies at distance at least 1 from the surgery cap. Of course, \( X \) is contained in the \( {CR}{\left( {q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}\right) }^{-1/2} \) -neighborhood of \( \left( {{q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right) \) in the standard solution. Since \( \widetilde{C} \geq  C \) and \( R\left( {{q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right) \) is close to \( {\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2} \) , the neighborhood \( X \) is contained in the \( 2\widetilde{C}{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-1} \) -neighborhood of \( \left( {{q}_{a},{\bar{h}}_{a}^{-2}{t}_{a}}\right) \) in the standard solution. Hence, after rescaling, the corresponding neighborhood of \( {x}_{a} \) is contained in the \( 3\widetilde{C} \) -neighborhood of \( {x}_{a} \) . If either of the first two cases in Theorem 12.32 occurs for a subsequence of \( a \) tending to infinity, then by Lemma 9.79 and the fact that \( \widetilde{C} > \max \left( {C,{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) , we see that there is a subsequence of \( a \) for which \( {x}_{a} \) either is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap or is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck.

We must examine further the last case. We suppose that for every \( a \) this last case holds. Then for all \( a \) sufficiently large we have an \( {\beta \epsilon }/3 \) -neck \( {N}_{a} \) in the zero time-slice of \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a} \) centered at \( {x}_{a} \) . It is an evolving neck and there is an embedding \( \psi  : {N}_{a} \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{a},0}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{a} \) compatible with time and the vector field so that the initial time-slice \( \psi \left( {{N}_{a} \times  \left\{  {-{t}_{a}}\right\}  }\right) \) is in the surgery time-slice \( {M}_{-{t}_{a}} \) and is disjoint from the surgery cap, so in fact it is contained in the continuing region at time \( - {t}_{a} \) . As we saw above, the image of the central 2-sphere \( \psi \left( {{S}_{a}^{2} \times  \left\{  {-{t}_{a}}\right\}  }\right) \) lies at distance at most \( {A}^{\prime \prime }{\bar{h}}_{a} \) from the tip of the surgery cap \( {p}_{a} \) (where, recall, \( {A}^{\prime \prime } \) is a constant independent of \( a \) ). The 2-sphere, \( {\sum }_{a} \) , along which we do surgery, creating the surgery cap with \( {p}_{a} \) as its tip, is the central 2-sphere of a strong \( {\delta }_{b\left( a\right) } \) -neck. As \( a \) tends to infinity the surgery control parameter \( {\delta }_{b\left( a\right) } \) tends to zero. Thus, for \( a \) sufficiently large this strong \( {\delta }_{b\left( a\right) } \) -neck will contain a strong \( {\beta \epsilon }/2 \) - neck \( {N}^{\prime } \) centered at \( \psi \left( {{x}_{a}, - {t}_{a}}\right) \) . Since we know that the continuing region at time \( - {t}_{a} \) contains a \( {\beta \epsilon }/3 \) -neck centered at \( \left( {{x}_{a}, - {t}_{a}}\right) \) , it follows that \( {N}^{\prime } \) is also contained in \( {C}_{-{t}_{a}} \) . That is to say, \( {N}^{\prime } \) is contained in the negative half of the \( {\delta }_{b\left( a\right) } \) -neck centered at \( {\sum }_{a} \) . Now we are in the situation of Proposition 15.2. Applying this result tells us that \( {x}_{a} \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck.

This completes the proof that for all \( a \) sufficiently large, \( {x}_{a} \) has a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood in contradiction to our assumption. This contradiction completes the proof of Lemma 17.7.

Let \( \left( {{M}_{t}, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) be the \( t \) time-slice of \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) . If \( {t}_{0} \) is not a surgery time, then \( \operatorname{Vol}\left( t\right)  = \operatorname{Vol}\left( {{M}_{t}, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a smooth function of \( t \) near \( {t}_{0} \) and

\[
\frac{d\operatorname{Vol}}{dt}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  =  - {\int }_{{M}_{{t}_{0}}}{Rd}\operatorname{vol},
\]

so that, because of the curvature pinching toward positive hypothesis, we have \( \frac{d\mathrm{{Vol}}}{dt}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \leq  6\mathrm{{Vol}}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) . If \( {t}_{0} \) is a surgery time, then either \( {M}_{{t}_{0}} \) has fewer connected components than \( {M}_{{t}_{0}^{ - }} \) or we do a surgery in an \( \epsilon \) -horn of \( {M}_{{t}_{0}^{ - }} \) . In the latter case we remove the end of the \( \epsilon \) -horn, which contains the positive half of a \( \bar{\delta }\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) -neck of scale \( h\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) . We then sew in a ball with volume at most \( \left( {1 + \epsilon }\right) K{h}^{3}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) , where \( K < \infty \) is the universal constant given in Lemma 12.3. Since \( h\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \leq  {\bar{\delta }}^{2}\left( {t}_{0}\right) r\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \leq  {\delta }_{0}^{2}r\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) and since we have chosen \( \bar{\delta }\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \leq  {\delta }_{0} < \; {K}^{-1} \) , it follows that this operation lowers volume by at least \( {\delta }^{-1}{h}^{2}\left( {t}_{0}\right) /2 \) . Since \( \bar{\delta }\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \geq  \bar{\delta }\left( {T}_{i + 1}\right)  > 0 \) and the canonical neighborhood parameter \( r \) at time \( {t}_{0} \) is at least \( {r}_{i + 1} > 0 \) , it follows that \( h\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \geq  h\left( {T}_{i + 1}\right)  > 0 \) . Thus, each surgery at time \( {t}_{0} \leq  {T}_{i + 1} \) along a 2-sphere removes at least a fixed amount of volume depending on \( \bar{\delta }\left( {T}_{i + 1}\right) \) and \( {r}_{i + 1} \) . Since under Ricci flow the volume grows at most exponentially, we see that there is a bound depending only on \( \bar{\delta }\left( {T}_{i + 1}\right) ,{T}_{i + 1},{r}_{i + 1} \) and \( \operatorname{Vol}\left( {{M}_{0}, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) on the number of 2-sphere surgeries that we can do in this time interval. On the other hand, the number of components at any time \( t \) is at most \( {N}_{0} + S\left( t\right)  - D\left( t\right) \) where \( {N}_{0} \) is the number of connected components of \( {M}_{0}, S\left( t\right) \) is the number of 2-sphere surgeries performed in the time interval \( \lbrack 0, t) \) and \( D\left( t\right) \) is the number of connected components removed by surgeries at times in the interval \( \lbrack 0, t) \) . Hence, there is a bound on the number of components in terms of \( {N}_{0} \) and \( S\left( T\right) \) that can be removed by surgery in the interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) . Since the initial conditions are normalized, \( {N}_{0} \) is bounded by the volume of \( \left( {{M}_{0}, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) . This completes the proof of the result.

DEFINITION 18.4. Let \( X \) be a compact 3-manifold (possibly disconnected). An embedded 2-sphere in \( X \) is said to be homotopically essential if the inclusion of the 2-sphere into \( X \) is not homotopic to a point map of the 2-sphere to \( X \) . More generally, let \( F = \left\{  {{\sum }_{1},\ldots ,{\sum }_{n}}\right\} \) be a family of disjointly embedded 2-spheres in \( X \) . We say that the family is homotopically essential if

(i) each 2-sphere in the family is homotopically essential, and

(ii) for any \( 1 \leq  i < j \leq  n \) , the inclusion of \( {\sum }_{i} \) into \( X \) is not homotopic in \( X \) to the inclusion of \( {\sum }_{j} \) into \( X \) .

Notice that if \( F = \left\{  {{\sum }_{1},\ldots ,{\sum }_{n}}\right\} \) is a homotopically essential family of disjointly embedded 2-spheres in \( X \) , then any subset \( F \) is also homotopically essential.

nodes.proof:
Proof. Clearly, without loss of generality we can assume that \( X \) is connected. If \( F \) is a homotopically essential family of 2-spheres in \( X \) , then by van Kampen's theorem, see p. 40 of [38], there is an induced graph of groups decomposition of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( X\right) \) with all the edge groups being trivial. Since the family is homotopically essential, it follows that the group associated with each vertex of order 1 and each vertex of order 2 is a non-trivial group. The rank of the first homology of the graph underlying the graph of groups, denoted \( k \) , is bounded above by the rank of \( {H}_{1}\left( X\right) \) . Furthermore, by the theory of graphs of groups there is a free product decomposition of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( X\right) \) with the free factors being the vertex groups and then \( k \) infinite cyclic factors. Denote by \( {V}_{i} \) the number of vertices of order \( i \) and by \( E \) the number of edges of the graph. The number \( E \) is the number of 2-spheres in the family \( F \) . An elementary combinatorial argument shows that

\[
2{V}_{1} + {V}_{2} \geq  E + 3\left( {1 - k}\right) .
\]

Thus, there is a free product decomposition of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( X\right) \) with at least \( E + 3\left( {1 - k}\right) \) non-trivial free factors. Since \( k \) is bounded by the rank of \( {H}_{1}\left( X\right) \) , applying Lemma 18.3 and using the fact that the fundamental group of a compact manifold is finitely presented establishes the result.

nodes.proof:
Proof. Clearly, for any \( {t}_{0} \) we have \( s\left( t\right)  = s\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) for \( t \geq  {t}_{0} \) sufficiently close to \( {t}_{0} \) . Also, if \( t \) is not a surgery time, then \( s\left( t\right)  = s\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) for all \( {t}^{\prime } < t \) and sufficiently close to \( t \) . According to Proposition 15.3, if \( t \) is a surgery time then for \( {t}^{\prime } < t \) but sufficiently close to it, the manifold \( {M}_{t} \) is obtained from \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) by doing surgery on a finite number of 2-spheres and removing certain components of the result. We divide the operations into three types: (i) surgery along homotopically trivial 2-spheres in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) ,(ii) surgery along homo-topically non-trivial 2-spheres in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) ,(iii) removal of components. Clearly, the first operation does not change the invariant \( s \) since it simply creates a manifold that is the disjoint union of a manifold homotopy equivalent to the original manifold with a collection of homotopy 3-spheres. Removal of components will not increase the invariant. The last operation to consider is surgery along a homotopically non-trivial 2-sphere. Let \( {F}_{t} \) be a homotopi-cally essential family of disjointly embedded 2-spheres in \( {M}_{t} \) . This family of 2-spheres in \( {M}_{t} \) can be deformed to miss the 3-disks (the surgery caps) in \( {M}_{t} \) that we sewed in doing the surgery at time \( t \) along a homotopically nontrivial 2-sphere. After deforming the spheres in the family \( {F}_{t} \) away from the surgery caps, they produce a disjoint family \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) of 2 -spheres in the manifold \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) , for \( {t}^{\prime } < t \) but \( {t}^{\prime } \) sufficiently close to \( t \) . Each 2-sphere in \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) is disjoint from the homotopically essential 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) along which we do surgery at time \( t \) . Let \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) be the family \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \cup  \left\{  {S}_{0}\right\} \) . We claim that \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is a homotopically essential family in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) .

First, suppose that one of the spheres \( \sum \) in \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is homotopically trivial in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . Of course, we are in the case when the surgery 2-sphere is homotopically essential, so \( \sum \) is not \( {S}_{0} \) and hence is the image of one of the 2-spheres in \( {F}_{t} \) . Since \( \sum \) is homotopically trivial, it is the boundary of a homotopy 3-ball \( B \) in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . If \( B \) is disjoint from the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) , then it exists in \( {M}_{t} \) and hence \( \sum \) is homotopically trivial in \( {M}_{t} \) , which is not possible from the assumption about the family \( {F}_{t} \) . If \( B \) meets the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) , then since the spheres in the family \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) are disjoint, it follows that \( B \) contains the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) . This is not possible since in this case \( {S}_{0} \) would be homotopically trivial in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) , contrary to assumption.

We also claim that no distinct members of \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) are homotopic. For suppose that two of the members \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) are homotopic. It cannot be the case that one of \( \sum \) or \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) is the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) since, in that case, the other one would be homotopically trivial after surgery, i.e., in \( {M}_{t} \) . The 2- spheres \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) are the boundary components of a submanifold \( A \) in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) homotopy equivalent to \( {S}^{2} \times  I \) . If \( A \) is disjoint from the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) , then \( A \) exists in \( {M}_{t} \) and \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) are homotopic in \( {M}_{t} \) , contrary to assumption. Otherwise, the surgery sphere \( {S}_{0} \) must be contained in \( A \) . Every 2-sphere in \( A \) is either homotopically trivial in \( A \) or is homotopic in \( A \) to either boundary component. If \( {S}_{0} \) is homotopically trivial in \( A \) , then it would be homotopically trivial in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) and this contradicts our assumption. If \( {S}_{0} \) is homotopic in \( A \) to each of \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) , then each of \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) is homo-topically trivial in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) , contrary to assumption. This shows that the family \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is homotopically essential. It follows immediately that doing surgery on a homotopically non-trivial 2-sphere strictly decreases the invariant \( s \) .

nodes.document_title: John Morgan and Gang Tian - Ricci Flow and the Poincare Conjecture
nodes.content:
PROPOSITION 18.9. Let \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) be a Ricci flow with surgery satisfying the conclusion of Theorem 15.9. Then there is some time \( {T}_{1} < \infty \) such that every component of \( {M}_{T} \) for any \( T \geq  {T}_{1} \) has trivial \( {\pi }_{2} \) . For every \( T \geq  {T}_{1} \) , each component of \( {M}_{T} \) either has finite fundamental group, and hence has a homotopy 3-sphere as universal covering, or has contractible universal covering.

If \( M \) is a connected 3-manifold with \( {\pi }_{2}\left( M\right)  = 0 \) , then the universal covering, \( \widetilde{M} \) , of \( M \) is a 2-connected 3-manifold. The covering \( \widetilde{M} \) is compact if and only if \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) is finite. In this case \( \widetilde{M} \) is a homotopy 3-sphere. If \( \widetilde{M} \) is non-compact then \( {H}_{3}\left( \widetilde{M}\right)  = 0 \) , so that all its homology groups and hence, by the Hurewicz theorem, all its homotopy groups vanish. It follows from the Whitehead theorem that \( \widetilde{M} \) is contractible in this case. This proves the last assertion in the proposition modulo the first assertion.

The proof of the first assertion of this proposition occupies the rest of this subsection. By the above discussion we see that the proposition holds unless there is a path of components \( \mathcal{X} \) defined for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{T}_{0},\infty }\right) \) with the property that every time-slice has non-trivial \( {\pi }_{2} \) . We must rule out this possibility. To achieve this we introduce the area functional.

LEMMA 18.10. Let \( X \) be a compact Riemannian manifold with \( {\pi }_{2}\left( X\right)  \neq \) 0 . Then there is a positive number \( {e}_{0} = {e}_{0}\left( X\right) \) with the following two properties:

(1) Any map \( f : {S}^{2} \rightarrow  X \) with area less than \( {e}_{0} \) is homotopic to a point map.

(2) There is a minimal 2-sphere \( f : {S}^{2} \rightarrow  X \) , which is a branched immersion, with the property that the area of \( f\left( {S}^{2}\right)  = {e}_{0} \) and with the property that \( f \) is not homotopic to a point map.

Proof. The first statement is Theorem 3.3 in [59]. As for the second, following Sacks-Uhlenbeck, for any \( \alpha  > 1 \) we consider the perturbed energy \( {E}_{\alpha } \) given by

\[
{E}_{\alpha }\left( s\right)  = {\int }_{{S}^{2}}{\left( 1 + {\left| ds\right| }^{2}\right) }^{\alpha }{da}.
\]

According to [59] this energy functional is Palais-Smale on the space of \( {H}^{1,{2\alpha }} \) maps and has an absolute minimum among homotopically non-trivial maps, realized by a map \( {s}_{\alpha } : {S}^{2} \rightarrow  X \) . We consider a decreasing sequence of \( \alpha \) tending to 1 and the minimizers \( {s}_{\alpha } \) among homotopically non-trivial maps. According to [59], after passing to a subsequence, there is a weak limit which is a strong limit on the complement of a finite set of points in \( {S}^{2} \) . This limit extends to a harmonic map of \( {S}^{2} \rightarrow  M \) , and its energy is less than or equal to the limit of the \( \alpha \) -energies of \( {s}_{\alpha } \) . If the result is homotopically non-trivial then it realizes a minimum value of the usual energy among all homotopically non-trivial maps, for were there a homotopically non-trivial map of smaller energy, it would have smaller \( {E}_{\alpha } \) energy than \( {s}_{\alpha } \) for all \( \alpha \) sufficiently close to 1. Of course if the limit is a strong limit, then the map is homotopically non-trivial, and the proof is complete.

We must examine the case when the limit is truly a weak limit. Let \( {s}_{n} \) be a sequence as above with a weak limit \( s \) . If the limit is truly a weak limit, then there is bubbling. Let \( x \in  {S}^{2} \) be a point where the limit \( s \) is not a strong limit. Then according to [59] pre-composing with a sequence of conformal dilations \( {\rho }_{n} \) centered at this point leads to a sequence of maps \( {s}_{n}^{\prime } \) converging uniformly on compact subsets of \( {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \) to a non-constant harmonic map \( {s}^{\prime } \) that extends over the one-point compactification \( {S}^{2} \) . The energy of this limiting map \( {s}^{\prime } \) is at most the limit of the \( \alpha \) -energies of the \( {s}_{\alpha } \) . If \( {s}^{\prime } \) is homotopically non-trivial, then, arguing as before, we see that it realizes the minimum energy among all homotopically non-trivial maps, and once again we have completed the proof. We rule out the possibility that \( {s}^{\prime } \) is homotopically trivial. Let \( \alpha \) be the area, or equivalently the energy, of \( {s}^{\prime } \) . Let \( D \subset  {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \) be a disk centered at the origin which contains three-quarters of the energy of \( {s}^{\prime } \) (or equivalently three-quarters of the area of \( {s}^{\prime } \) ), and let \( {D}^{\prime } \) be the complementary disk to \( D \) in \( {S}^{2} \) . For all \( n \) sufficiently large the area of \( {s}_{n}^{\prime } \mid  D \) minus the area of \( {s}_{n}^{\prime } \mid  {D}^{\prime } \) is at least \( \alpha /3 \) . The restrictions of \( {s}_{n}^{\prime } \) on \( \partial D \) are converging smoothly to \( {s}^{\prime } \mid  \partial {D}^{\prime } \) . Let \( {D}_{n} \subset  {S}^{2} \) be \( {\rho }_{n}^{-1}\left( D\right) \) . Then the area of \( {s}_{n} \mid  {D}_{n} \) equals the area of \( {s}_{n}^{\prime } \mid  D \) and hence is at least the area of \( {s}^{\prime } \mid  {D}^{\prime } \) plus \( \alpha /4 \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large. Also, as \( n \) tends to infinity the image \( {s}_{n}\left( {D}_{n}\right) \) converges smoothly, after reparameterization, to \( {s}^{\prime }\left( {\partial D}\right) \) . Thus, for all \( n \) large, we can connect \( {s}_{n}\left( {\partial {D}_{n}}\right) \) to \( {s}^{\prime }\left( {\partial {D}^{\prime }}\right) \) by an annulus \( {A}_{n} \) contained in a small neighborhood of \( {s}^{\prime }\left( {\partial {D}^{\prime }}\right) \) and whose area tends to 0 as \( n \) goes to infinity. For all \( n \) sufficiently large, the resulting 2-sphere \( {\sum }_{n} \) made out of \( {s}_{n} \mid  \left( {{S}^{2} \smallsetminus  {D}_{n}}\right)  \cup  {A}_{n} \cup  {S}^{\prime }\left( {D}^{\prime }\right) \) is homotopic to \( s\left( {S}^{2}\right) \) since \( {s}^{\prime } \) is homotopically trivial. Also, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the area of \( {\sum }_{n} \) is less than the area of \( {s}_{n} \) minus \( \alpha /5 \) . Reparameterizing this 2-sphere by a conformal map leads to a homotopically non-trivial map of energy less than the area of \( {s}_{n} \) minus \( \alpha /5 \) . Since as \( n \) tends to infinity, the limsup of the areas of the \( {s}_{n} \) converge to at most \( {e}_{0} \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large we have constructed a homotopically non-trivial map of energy less than \( {e}_{0} \) , which contradicts the fact that the minimal \( \alpha \) energy for a homotopically non-trivial map tends to \( {e}_{0} \) as \( \alpha \) tends to 1 .

Of course, any minimal energy map of \( {S}^{2} \) into \( M \) is conformal because there is no non-trivial holomorphic quadratic differential on \( {S}^{2} \) . It follows that such a map is a branched immersion.

(Of course, since \( f\left( {S}^{2}\right) \) is minimal, the determinant of its second fundamental form is \( - {\left| A\right| }^{2}/2 \) .) nodes.proof: Proof. Let \( M \) be as in the statement of the corollary. Let \( g \) be a normalized metric on \( M \) , and let \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) be the Ricci flow with surgery defined for all time with \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) as initial conditions. According to Proposition 18.9 there is \( T < \infty \) such that every component of \( {M}_{T} \) has trivial \( {\pi }_{2} \) . Thus, by the analysis above, we see that there must be surgeries that kill elements in \( {\pi }_{2} \) : either the removal of a component with non-trivial \( {\pi }_{2} \) or surgery along a homotopically non-trivial 2-sphere. We consider the first such surgery in \( M \) . The only components with non-trivial \( {\pi }_{2} \) that can be removed by surgery are \( {S}^{2} \) -bundles over \( {S}^{1} \) and \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) . Since each of these has homotopi-cally non-trivially embedded 2-spheres, if the first surgery killing an element in \( {\pi }_{2} \) is removal of such a component, then, because all the earlier 2-sphere surgeries are along homotopically trivial 2-spheres, the homotopically nontrivial embedded 2-sphere in this component deforms back to an embedded, homotopically non-trivial 2-sphere in \( M \) . The other possibility is that the first time an element in \( {\pi }_{2}\left( M\right) \) is killed it is by surgery along a homotopically non-trivial 2-sphere. Once again, using the fact that all previous surgeries are along homotopically trivial 2-spheres, deform this 2-sphere back to \( M \) producing a homotopically non-trivial 2-sphere in \( M \) .

nodes.content: REMARK 18.15. Notice that it follows from the list of disappearing components that the only ones with non-trivial \( {\pi }_{2} \) are those based on the geometry \( {S}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) ; that is to say,2-sphere bundles over \( {S}^{1} \) and \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) . Thus, once we have reached the level \( {T}_{0} \) after which all 2-sphere surgeries are performed on homotopically trivial 2-spheres the only components that can have non-trivial \( {\pi }_{2} \) are components of these types. Thus, for example if the original manifold has no \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) prime factors and no non-separating 2-spheres, then when we reach time \( {T}_{0} \) we have done a connected sum decomposition into components each of which has trivial \( {\pi }_{2} \) . Each of these components is either covered by a contractible 3-manifold or by a homotopy 3-sphere, depending on whether its fundamental group has infinite or finite order.

nodes.proof: An element in \( {\pi }_{2}\left( {{\Lambda M}, * }\right) \) is represented by a map \( {S}^{2} \times  {S}^{1} \rightarrow  M \) that sends \( \{ \mathrm{{pt}}\}  \times  {S}^{1} \) to \( {x}_{0} \) . Hence, this map factors through the quotient of \( {S}^{2} \times  {S}^{1} \) obtained by collapsing \( \{ \mathrm{{pt}}\}  \times  {S}^{1} \) to a point. The resulting quotient space is homotopy equivalent to \( {S}^{2} \vee  {S}^{3} \) , and a map of this space into \( M \) sending the wedge point to \( {x}_{0} \) is, up to homotopy, the same as an element of \( {\pi }_{2}\left( {M,{x}_{0}}\right)  \oplus  {\pi }_{3}\left( {M,{x}_{0}}\right) \) . But we are assuming that \( {\pi }_{2}\left( {M,{x}_{0}}\right)  = 0 \) . The first statement follows. For the second, notice that since \( {\pi }_{2}\left( {M,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is trivial, \( {\pi }_{3}\left( {M,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is identified with \( {H}_{3} \) of the universal covering \( \widetilde{M} \) of \( M \) . Hence, for any map of \( {S}^{2} \) into the component of \( {\Lambda M} \) containing the trivial loops, the resulting map \( {S}^{2} \times  {S}^{1} \rightarrow  M \) lifts to \( \widetilde{M} \) . The corresponding element in \( {\pi }_{3}\left( {M,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is the image of the fundamental class of \( {S}^{2} \times  {S}^{1} \) in \( {H}_{3}\left( \widetilde{M}\right)  = {\pi }_{3}\left( M\right) . \)

nodes.content: DEFINITION 18.17. Fix a homotopically trivial loop \( \gamma  \in  {\Lambda M} \) . We set \( A\left( \gamma \right) \) equal to the infimum of the areas of any spanning disks for \( \gamma \) , where by definition a spanning disk is a Lipschitz map \( {D}^{2} \rightarrow  M \) whose boundary is, up to reparameterization, \( \gamma \) . Notice that \( A\left( \gamma \right) \) is a continuous function of \( \gamma \) in \( {\Lambda M} \) . Also, notice that \( A\left( \gamma \right) \) is invariant under reparameterization of the curve \( \gamma \) . Now suppose that \( \Gamma  : {S}^{2} \rightarrow  {\Lambda M} \) is given with the image consisting of homotopically trivial loops. We define \( W\left( \Gamma \right) \) to be equal to the maximum over all \( c \in  {S}^{2} \) of \( A\left( {\Gamma \left( c\right) }\right) \) . More generally, given a homotopy class \( \xi  \in  {\pi }_{2}\left( {{\Lambda M}, * }\right) \) we define \( W\left( \xi \right) \) to be equal to the infimum over all (not necessarily based) maps \( \Gamma  : {S}^{2} \rightarrow  {\Lambda M} \) into the component of \( {\Lambda M} \) consisting of homotopically trivial loops representing \( \xi \) of \( W\left( \Gamma \right) \) .

Proposition 18.18. Suppose that \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) is a Ricci flow with surgery as in Theorem 15.9. Let \( \mathcal{X} \) be a path of components of \( \mathcal{M} \) defined for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack \) with \( {\pi }_{2}\left( {\mathcal{X}\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right)  = 0 \) . Suppose that \( \xi  \in  {\pi }_{3}\left( {X\left( {t}_{0}\right) , * }\right) \) is a non-trivial element. Then the function \( {W}_{\xi }\left( t\right) \) satisfies the following inequality in the sense of forward difference quotients:

\[
\frac{d{W}_{\xi }\left( t\right) }{dt} \leq   - {2\pi } - \frac{1}{2}{R}_{\min }\left( t\right) {W}_{\xi }\left( t\right) .
\]

Also, for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack \) that is not a surgery time the function \( {W}_{\xi }\left( t\right) \) is continuous at \( t \) . Lastly, if \( t \) is a surgery time then

\[
{W}_{\xi }\left( t\right)  \leq  \mathop{\liminf }\limits_{{{t}^{\prime } \rightarrow  {t}^{ - }}}{W}_{\xi }\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) .
\]

nodes.proof:
Since \( t \) is not a surgery time, a family \( \Gamma \left( t\right)  : {S}^{2} \rightarrow  \Lambda \mathcal{X}\left( t\right) \) is also a family \( \Gamma \left( {t}^{\prime }\right)  : {S}^{2} \rightarrow  \Lambda \mathcal{X}\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) for all nearby \( {t}^{\prime } \) . The minimal spanning disks for the elements of \( \Gamma \left( t\right) \left( x\right) \) are also spanning disks in the nearby \( \mathcal{X}\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) and their areas vary continuously with \( t \) . But the maximum of the areas of these disks is an upper bound for \( {W}_{\xi }\left( t\right) \) . This immediately implies that \( {W}_{\xi }\left( t\right) \) is upper semi-continuous at \( t \) .

The result for lower semi-continuity is the same as in the case of 2-spheres. Given a time \( t \) distinct from a surgery time and a family \( \Gamma  : {S}^{2} \rightarrow \; \Lambda \mathcal{X}\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) for a time \( {t}^{\prime } \) near \( t \) we can view the family \( \Gamma \) as a map to \( \Lambda \mathcal{X}\left( t\right) \) . The areas of all minimal spanning disks for the loops represented by points \( \Gamma \) measured in \( \mathcal{X}\left( t\right) \) are at most \( \left( {1 + \eta \left( \left| {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right| \right) }\right) \) times their areas measured in \( \mathcal{X}\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) , where \( \eta \left( \left| {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right| \right) \) is a function going to zero as \( \left| {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right| \) goes to zero. This immediately implies the lower semi-continuity at the non-surgery time \( t \) .

nodes.proof: We choose \( \zeta \) smaller than the injectivity radius of \( \left( {X, g}\right) \) . Then any pair of points at distance less than \( \zeta \) apart are joined by a unique geodesic of length less than \( \zeta \) . Furthermore, the geodesic varies smoothly with the points. Given a map \( \Gamma  : {S}^{2} \rightarrow  {\Lambda X} \) such that every loop of the form \( \Gamma \left( c\right) \) has length at most \( \zeta \) , we consider the map \( f : {S}^{2} \rightarrow  X \) defined by \( f\left( c\right)  = \Gamma \left( c\right) \left( {x}_{0}\right) \) , where \( {x}_{0} \) is the base point of the circle. Then we can join each point \( \Gamma \left( c\right) \left( x\right) \) to \( \Gamma \left( c\right) \left( {x}_{0}\right) \) by a geodesic of length at most \( \zeta \) to fill out a map of the disk \( \widehat{\Gamma }\left( c\right)  : {D}^{2} \rightarrow  X \) . This disk is smooth except at the point \( \Gamma \left( c\right) \left( {x}_{0}\right) \) . The disks \( \widehat{\Gamma }\left( c\right) \) fit together as \( c \) varies to make a continuous family of disks parameterized by \( {S}^{2} \) or equivalently a map \( {S}^{2} \times  {D}^{2} \) into \( X \) whose boundary is the family of loops \( \Gamma \left( c\right) \) . Now shrinking the loops \( \Gamma \left( c\right) \) across the disks \( \widehat{\Gamma }\left( c\right) \) to \( \Gamma \left( c\right) \left( {x}_{0}\right) \) shows that the family \( \Gamma \) is homotopic to a 2-sphere family of constant loops at different points of \( X \) . Since we are assuming that \( {\pi }_{2}\left( X\right) \) is trivial, this means the family of loops is in fact trivial as an element of \( {\pi }_{2}\left( {{\Lambda X}, * }\right) \) , which means that the original element \( \xi  \in  {\pi }_{3}\left( X\right) \) is trivial.

## 1. Curve-shrinking

Given \( \Gamma \) , the idea for constructing the one-parameter family \( \widetilde{\Gamma }\left( t\right) \) required by Proposition 18.24 is to evolve an appropriate approximation \( \widetilde{\Gamma }\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) of \( \Gamma \) by the curve-shrinking flow. Suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) ,{t}_{0} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{1} \) , is a Ricci flow of compact manifolds and that \( c : {S}^{1} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) is a family of parameterized, immersed \( {C}^{2} \) -curves. We denote by \( x \) the parameter on the circle. Let \( X\left( {x, t}\right) \) be the tangent vector \( \partial c\left( {x, t}\right) /\partial x \) and let \( S\left( {x, t}\right)  = X\left( {x, t}\right) /\left( {\left| X\left( x, t\right) \right| }_{g\left( t\right) }\right) \) be the unit tangent vector to \( c \) . We denote by \( s \) the arc length parameter on \( c \) . We set \( H\left( {x, t}\right)  = {\nabla }_{S\left( {x, t}\right) }S\left( {x, t}\right) \) , the curvature vector of \( c \) with respect to the metric \( g\left( t\right) \) . We define the curve-shrinking flow by

\[
\frac{\partial c\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t} = H\left( {x, t}\right) ,
\]

where \( c\left( {x, t}\right) \) is a one-parameter family of curves and \( H\left( {x, t}\right) \) is the curvature vector of the curve \( c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at the point \( x \) with respect to the metric \( g\left( t\right) \) . We denote by \( k\left( {x, t}\right) \) the curvature function: \( k\left( {x, t}\right)  = {\left| H\left( x, t\right) \right| }_{g\left( t\right) } \) . We shall often denote the one-parameter family of curves by \( c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) . Notice that if \( c\left( {x, t}\right) \) is a curve-shrinking flow and if \( x\left( y\right) \) is a reparameterization of the domain circle, then \( {c}^{\prime }\left( {y, t}\right)  = c\left( {x\left( y\right) , t}\right) \) is also a curve-shrinking flow.

nodes.proof:
Proof. According to results of Hildebrandt and Morrey, [40] and [52], for each \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack \) , there is a smooth minimal disk spanning \( c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) . Fix \( {t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1}}\right) \) and consider a smooth minimal disk \( D \rightarrow  \left( {M, g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) }\right) \) spanning \( c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) . It is immersed, see [37] or [27]. The family \( c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) for \( t \) near \( {t}^{\prime } \) is an isotopy of \( c\left( {\cdot ,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) . We can extend this to an ambient isotopy \( {\varphi }_{t} : M \rightarrow  M \) with \( {\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }} = \) Id. We impose coordinates \( \left\{  {x}_{\alpha }\right\} \) on \( D \) ; we let \( {h}_{\alpha \beta }\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) be the metric induced on \( {\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) \) by \( g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) , and we let \( {da} \) be the area form induced by the Euclidean coordinates on \( D \) . We compute

\[
{\left. \frac{d}{dt}\right| }_{t = {t}^{\prime }}\operatorname{Area}\left( {{\varphi }_{t}\left( D\right) }\right)  = {\left. \frac{d}{dt}\right| }_{t = {t}^{\prime }}{\int }_{{\varphi }_{t}\left( D\right) }\sqrt{\det \left( {h}_{\alpha \beta }\right) \left( t\right) }{da}.
\]

Of course,

\[
{\left. \frac{d}{dt}\right| }_{t = {t}^{\prime }}{\int }_{{\varphi }_{t}\left( D\right) }\sqrt{\det \left( {{h}_{\alpha \beta }\left( t\right) }\right) }{da} =  - {\int }_{{\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) }\left( {\operatorname{Tr}{\operatorname{Ric}}^{T}}\right) \sqrt{\det \left( {{h}_{\alpha \beta }\left( t\right) }\right) }{da}
\]

\[
+ {\int }_{{\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) }\operatorname{div}{\left( \frac{\partial {\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}}{dt}\right) }^{T}\sqrt{\det \left( {{h}_{\alpha \beta }\left( t\right) }\right) }{da}.
\]

Here, \( {\operatorname{Ric}}^{T} \) denotes the restriction of the Ricci curvature of \( g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) to the tangent planes of \( {\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) \) and \( \frac{\partial {\left( {\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\right) }^{T}}{\partial t} \) is the component of \( {\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) tangent to \( {\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) \) . Setting \( \widehat{A} \) equal to the second fundamental form of \( {\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) \) , using the fact that \( {\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) \) is minimal and arguing as in the proof of Claim 18.12, we have

\[
- {\int }_{{\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) }\left( {\operatorname{Tr}{\operatorname{Ric}}^{T}}\right) \sqrt{\det \left( {{h}_{\alpha \beta }\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) }\right) }{da}
\]

\[
=  - {\int }_{{\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) }{K}_{{\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) }{da} - \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) }\left( {{\left| \widehat{A}\right| }^{2} + R}\right) {da}
\]

\[
\leq   - {\int }_{{\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) }{K}_{{\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) }\sqrt{\det \left( {{h}_{\alpha \beta }\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) }\right) }{da} - \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Area}\left( {{\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) }\right) \mathop{\min }\limits_{{x \in  M}}\left\{  {R\left( {x,{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right\}  .
\]

Integration by parts shows that

\[
{\int }_{{\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) }\operatorname{div}{\left( \frac{\partial {\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}}{dt}\right) }^{T}\sqrt{\det \left( {{h}_{\alpha \beta }\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) }\right) }{da} =  - {\int }_{{\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {\partial D}\right) }\left( {\left. \frac{d{\varphi }_{t}}{dt}\right| }_{t = {t}^{\prime }}\right)  \cdot  {nds},
\]

where \( n \) is the inward pointing normal vector to \( {\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) \) along \( {\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {\partial D}\right) \) . Of course, by definition, if the variation along the boundary is given by the curve-shrinking flow, then along \( {\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {\partial D}\right) \) we have

\[
\left( {\left. \frac{d{\varphi }_{t}}{dt}\right| }_{t = {t}^{\prime }}\right)  \cdot  n = {k}_{\text{ geod }}.
\]

Thus, we have

\[
{\left. \frac{d}{dt}\right| }_{t = {t}^{\prime }}{\int }_{{\varphi }_{t}\left( D\right) }\sqrt{\det \left( {{h}_{\alpha \beta }\left( t\right) }\right) }{da}
\]

\[
\leq   - {\int }_{{\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) }{K}_{{\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) }{da} - {\int }_{{\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {\partial D}\right) }{k}_{\text{ geod }}{ds} - \frac{1}{2}{R}_{\min }\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \operatorname{Area}\left( {{\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) }\right) .
\]

Of course, the Gauss-Bonnet theorem allows us to rewrite this as

\[
{\left. \frac{d}{dt}\right| }_{t = {t}^{\prime }}{\int }_{{\varphi }_{t}\left( D\right) }\sqrt{\det \left( {{h}_{\alpha \beta }\left( t\right) }\right) }{da} \leq   - {2\pi } - \frac{1}{2}{R}_{\min }\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \operatorname{Area}\left( {{\varphi }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( D\right) }\right) .
\]

Let \( \psi \left( t\right) \) be the solution to the ODE

\[
{\psi }^{\prime }\left( t\right)  =  - {2\pi } - \frac{1}{2}{R}_{\min }\left( t\right) \psi \left( t\right)
\]

with \( \psi \left( {t}^{ - }\right)  = A\left( {t}^{ - }\right) \) . The following is immediate from the previous lemma and Lemma 2.22.
