nodes.content: LEMMA 19.46. There is no \( x \) for which \( {D}_{x} \) is an embedded arc with both endpoints on \( {c}_{0} \) and otherwise disjoint from \( \partial A \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: LEMMA 19.46. There is no \( x \) for which \( {D}_{x} \) is an embedded arc with both endpoints on \( {c}_{0} \) and otherwise disjoint from \( \partial A \) .

nodes.proof:
Proof. Suppose that there were such a \( {D}_{x} \) . Then \( {D}_{x} \) separates \( A \) into two components, one of which, \( B \) , is a topological disk. Let \( {c}_{0}^{\prime } \) be the intersection of \( {c}_{0} \) with \( B \) . We consider two cases: Case (i): \( l\left( {c}_{0}^{\prime }\right)  \leq  1 \) and Case (ii): \( l\left( {c}_{0}^{\prime }\right)  > 1 \) .

Let us show that the first case is not possible. Since \( {D}_{x} \) is a geodesic and \( {D}_{x} \) is perpendicular to \( {c}_{0} \) at one end, the total turning around the boundary of \( B \) is at most

\[
{3\pi }/2 + {\int }_{{c}_{0}^{\prime }}{k}_{\text{ geod }}{ds} < {3\pi }/2 + \delta ,
\]

where the last inequality uses the fact that the length of \( {c}_{0}^{\prime } \) is at most 1 . On the other hand, \( {\int }_{B}{Kda} < \mu \) , and \( \mu  < 1/{20} < \left( {\pi /2}\right)  - \delta \) . This contradicts the Gauss-Bonnet theorem.

Now let us consider the second case. Let \( J \) be the subinterval of \( {c}_{0}^{\prime } \) with one end point being \( x \) and with the length of \( J \) being 1 . We orient \( J \) so that \( x \) is its initial point. We set \( {X}_{J} = J \cap  X \) . We define \( {S}_{{X}_{J}}\left( B\right)  \subset  {S}_{{X}_{J}} \) as follows. For each \( y \in  {X}_{J} \) we let \( {f}_{B}\left( y\right) \) be the minimum of \( {\delta }^{\prime } \) and the distance along \( {D}_{y} \) to the first point (excluding \( y \) ) of \( {D}_{y} \) contained in \( \partial B \) and let \( {D}_{y}\left( B\right) \) be the sub-geodesic of \( {D}_{y} \) of this length starting at \( y \) . Then \( {S}_{{X}_{J}}\left( B\right)  \subset  {S}_{{X}_{J}} \) is the union over \( y \in  {X}_{J} \) of \( \left\lbrack  {0,{f}_{B}\left( y\right) }\right\rbrack \) . Clearly, the exponential mapping defines an immersion of \( {S}_{{X}_{J}}\left( B\right) \) into \( B \) . We need to replace \( {X}_{J} \) by a slightly smaller subset in order to make the exponential mapping be an embedding. To do this we shall remove bases of a maximal focusing triangles in \( B \) .

First notice that for each \( y \in  {X}_{J} \) the exponential mapping is an embedding on \( {D}_{y}\left( B\right) \) . The reason is that the image of \( {D}_{y}\left( B\right) \) is a geodesic contained in the ball \( B \) . Lemma 19.45 then shows that this geodesic is embedded. This leads to:

CLAIM 19.47. For any component \( c \) of \( {X}_{J} \) , the restriction of the exponential mapping to \( {S}_{c}\left( B\right)  = \left( {c \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{\delta }^{\prime }}\right) }\right)  \cap  {S}_{{X}_{J}}\left( B\right) \) is an embedding.

Proof. Since the geodesics that make up \( {S}_{c}\left( B\right) \) have length at most \( {\delta }^{\prime } < 1/{10} \) and since the curvature of the annulus is bounded above by 1, the restriction of the exponential mapping to \( {S}_{c}\left( B\right) \) is a local diffeomorphism. The restriction to each \( \{ y\}  \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{f}_{B}\left( y\right) }\right\rbrack \) is an embedding onto \( {D}_{y}\left( B\right) \) . If the restriction of the exponential mapping to \( {S}_{c}\left( B\right) \) is not an embedding, then there are \( y \neq  {y}^{\prime } \) in \( c \) such that the geodesics \( {D}_{y}\left( B\right) \) and \( {D}_{{y}^{\prime }}\left( B\right) \) meet. When they meet, they meet at a positive angle and by the Gauss-Bonnet theorem this angle is less than \( \mu  + \delta \) . Thus, all the geodesics starting at points sufficiently close to \( {y}^{\prime } \) and between \( y \) and \( {y}^{\prime } \) along \( c \) must also meet \( {D}_{y}\left( B\right) \) . Of course, if a sequence of \( {D}_{{y}_{i}}\left( B\right) \) meet \( {D}_{y}\left( B\right) \) , then the same is true for the limit. It now follows that \( {D}_{{y}^{\prime \prime }}\left( B\right) \) meets \( {D}_{y}\left( B\right) \) for all \( {y}^{\prime \prime } \) between \( y \) and \( {y}^{\prime } \) . This contradicts the fact that \( {D}_{y}\left( B\right) \) is embedded.

CLAIM 19.48. Any focusing triangle for \( J \) must contain a component of \( J \smallsetminus  {X}_{J} \) . If \( \left\{  {\mathcal{I}}_{n}\right\} \) is an infinite sequence of focus triangles for \( J \) , then, after passing to a subsequence, there is a limiting focusing triangle for J.

Proof. The first statement is immediate from Claim 19.47. Since \( X \cap  J \) is compact, it is clear that after passing to a subsequence each of the sequence of left-hand sides and the sequence of right-hand sides converge to a geodesic arc orthogonal to \( J \) at points of \( X \) . Furthermore, these limiting geodesics meet in a point at distance at most \( {\delta }^{\prime } \) from the end of each. The only thing remaining to show is that the limiting left- and right-hand sides do not begin at the same point of \( X \) . This is clear since each focusing triangle contains one of the finitely many components of \( J \smallsetminus  {X}_{J} \) .

Using Claim 19.48 we see that if there is a focusing triangle for \( J \) there is a first point \( {x}_{1} \) in \( {X}_{J} \) whose associated geodesic contains the left-hand side of a focusing triangle for \( J \) . Then since the base length of any focusing triangle is bounded by a fixed constant, invoking again Claim 19.48, that there is a focusing triangle \( {\mathcal{T}}_{1} \) for \( J \) that has left-hand side contained in the geodesic \( {D}_{{x}_{1}} \) and has a maximal base among all such focusing triangles, maximal in the sense that the base of this focusing triangle contains the base of any other focusing triangle with left-hand side contained in \( {D}_{{x}_{1}} \) . Denote its base by \( {\xi }_{1} \) and denote the right-hand endpoint of \( {\xi }_{1} \) by \( {y}_{1} \) . For the triangle we take the geodesic arcs to the first point of intersection measured along \( {D}_{{y}_{1}} \) . Set \( {J}_{1} = \overline{J \smallsetminus  \xi } \) , and repeat the process for \( {J}_{1} \) . If there is a focusing triangle for \( {J}_{1} \) we find the first left-hand side of such focusing triangles and then find the maximal focusing triangle \( {\mathcal{T}}_{2} \) with this left-hand side.

CLAIM 19.49. The interior of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{2} \) is disjoint from the interior of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{1} \) .

Proof. Since by construction the interiors of the bases of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{1} \) and \( {\mathcal{T}}_{2} \) are disjoint, if the interior of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{2} \) meets \( {\mathcal{T}}_{1} \) , then one of the sides of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{2} \) crosses the interior of one of the sides of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{1} \) . But since \( {\mathcal{T}}_{1} \) is a maximal focusing triangle with its left-hand side, neither of the sides of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{2} \) can cross the interior of the left-hand side of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{1} \) . If one of the sides of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{2} \) crosses the interior of the right-hand side of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{1} \) , then the right-hand side of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{1} \) is the left-hand side of a focusing triangle for \( {J}_{1} \) . Since by construction the left-hand side of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{2} \) is the first such, this means that the left-hand side of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{2} \) is the right-hand side of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{1} \) . This means that the right-hand side of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{2} \) terminates when it meets the right-hand side of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{1} \) and hence the right-hand side of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{2} \) ends the first time that it meets the right-hand side of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{1} \) and hence does not cross it.

We continue in this way constructing focusing triangles for \( J \) with disjoint interiors. Since each focusing triangle for \( J \) contains a component of \( J \smallsetminus  {X}_{J} \) , and as there are only finitely many such components, this process must terminate after a finite number of steps. Let \( {\mathcal{T}}_{1},\ldots ,{\mathcal{T}}_{k} \) be the focusing triangles so constructed, and denote by \( {\xi }_{i} \) the base of \( {\mathcal{T}}_{i} \) . Let \( {X}_{J}^{\prime } = {X}_{J} \smallsetminus  { \cup  }_{i = 1}^{k}{\xi }_{i} \)

DEFINITION 19.50. We call the triangles \( {\mathcal{T}}_{1},\ldots ,{\mathcal{T}}_{k} \) constructed above, the maximal set of focusing triangles for \( J \) relative to \( B \) .

CLAIM 19.51. The length of \( {X}_{J}^{\prime } \) is at least \( 1 - {2\delta } - \mu \) .

Proof. Since the interiors of the \( {\mathcal{T}}_{i} \) are disjoint, according to Corollary 19.44, we have \( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}l\left( {\xi }_{i}\right)  < \delta  + \mu \) . We also know by Remark 19.36 that the length of \( {X}_{J} \) is at least \( \left( {1 - \delta }\right) \) . Putting these together gives the result.

We define \( {S}_{{X}_{J}^{\prime }}\left( B\right) \) to be the intersection of \( {S}_{{X}_{J}}\left( B\right) \) with \( {S}_{{X}_{J}^{\prime }} \) .

CLAIM 19.52. The restriction of the exponential mapping to \( {S}_{{X}_{J}^{\prime }}\left( B\right) \) is an embedding.

Proof. Suppose that we have distinct points \( {x}^{\prime },{y}^{\prime } \) in \( {X}_{J}^{\prime } \) such that \( {D}_{{x}^{\prime }}\left( B\right)  \cap  {D}_{{y}^{\prime }}\left( B\right)  \neq  \varnothing \) . We assume that \( {x}^{\prime } < {y}^{\prime } \) in the orientation on \( J \) .

Then there is a focusing triangle for \( J \) whose base is the sub-arc of \( J \) with endpoints \( {x}^{\prime } \) and \( {y}^{\prime } \) , and hence the left-hand side of the focusing triangle is contained in \( {D}_{{x}^{\prime }}\left( B\right) \) . Since \( {x}^{\prime } \) is not a point of \( { \cup  }_{i}{\xi }_{i} \) either it lies between two of them, say \( {\xi }_{j} \) and \( {\xi }_{j + 1} \) or it lies between the initial point \( x \) of \( J \) and the initial point of \( {\xi }_{1} \) or it lies between the last \( {\xi }_{n} \) and the final point of \( J \) .

But \( {x}^{\prime } \) cannot lie before \( {\xi }_{1} \) , for this would contradict the construction which took as the left-hand endpoint of \( {\xi }_{1} \) the first point of \( J \) whose geodesic contained the left-hand side of a focusing triangle for \( J \) . Similarly, \( {x}^{\prime } \) cannot lie between \( {\xi }_{j} \) and \( {\xi }_{j + 1} \) for any \( j \) since the left-hand endpoint of \( {\xi }_{j + 1} \) is the first point at or after the right-hand endpoint of \( {\xi }_{j} \) whose geodesic contains the left-hand side of a focusing triangle for \( J \) . Lastly, \( {x}^{\prime } \) cannot lie to the right of the last \( {\xi }_{k} \) , for then we would not have finished the inductive construction.

We pull back the metric of \( A \) to the \( {S}_{{X}_{J}^{\prime }}\left( B\right) \) by the exponential mapping. Since this pullback metric is at least \( {\left( 1 - \delta \right) }^{2} \) times the product of the metric on \( {X}_{J}^{\prime } \) induced from \( {c}_{0} \) and the usual metric on the interval, and since the map on this subset is an embedding, we see that the area of the region of the annulus which is the image under the exponential mapping of this subset is at least

\[
{\left( 1 - \delta \right) }^{2}{\int }_{{X}_{J}^{\prime }}{f}_{B}\left( x\right) {ds}
\]

where \( s \) is arc length along \( {X}_{J}^{\prime } \) . Of course, the area of this subset is at most \( \mu \) . This means that, setting \( Z \) equal to the subset of \( {X}_{J}^{\prime }\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) \) given by

\[
Z = \left\{  {z \in  {X}_{J}^{\prime } \mid  {f}_{B}\left( z\right)  < {\delta }^{\prime }}\right\}  ,
\]

the total length of \( {X}_{J}^{\prime } \smallsetminus  Z \) satisfies

\[
l\left( {{X}_{J}^{\prime } \smallsetminus  Z}\right)  \leq  {\left( 1 - \delta \right) }^{-2}{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\mu  < \frac{1}{10},
\]

where the last inequality is an immediate consequence of our choice of \( \mu \) . Thus, the length of \( Z \) is at least \( \left( {{0.9} - {2\delta } - \mu }\right)  \geq  {0.87} \) . Let \( {\partial }_{ + }{S}_{Z}\left( B\right) \) be the union of the final endpoints (as opposed to the initial points) of the \( {D}_{x}\left( B\right) \) as \( x \) ranges over \( Z \) . Of course, since \( {f}_{B}\left( z\right)  < {\delta }^{\prime } \) for all \( z \in  Z \) , it must be the case that the exponential mapping embeds \( {\partial }_{ + }{S}_{Z}\left( B\right) \) into \( \partial B \) . Furthermore, the total length of the image of \( {\partial }_{ + }{S}_{Z}\left( B\right) \) is at least \( \left( {1 - \delta }\right) l\left( Z\right)  \geq  {0.86} \) . The boundary of \( B \) is made up of two pieces: \( {D}_{x} \) and an arc on \( {c}_{0} \) . But the length of \( {D}_{x} \) is at most \( {\delta }^{\prime } < 1/{20} \) so that not all of \( {\partial }_{ + }{S}_{Z}\left( B\right) \) can be contained in \( {D}_{x} \) . Thus, there is \( z \in  Z \) , distinct from \( x \) such that \( {D}_{z} \) has both endpoints in \( {c}_{0} \) . It then follows that all points of \( Z \) that are separated (along \( J \) ) from \( x \) by \( z \) have the same property. Since the length of \( Z \) is at least 0.86, it follows that there is a point \( z \in  X \) at least distance 0.85 along \( J \) from \( x \) with the property that \( {D}_{z} \) has both endpoints in \( {c}_{0} \) . The complementary component of \( {D}_{z} \) in \( A \) , denoted \( {B}^{\prime } \) , is a disk that is contained in \( B \) and the length of \( {B}^{\prime } \cap  {c}_{0} \) is at least 0.85 less than the length of \( B \cap  {c}_{0} \) .

The length of \( {B}^{\prime } \cap  {c}_{0} \) cannot be less than 1, for that gives a contradiction. But if the length of \( {B}^{\prime } \cap  {c}_{0} \) is greater than 1, we now repeat this construction replacing \( B \) by \( {B}^{\prime } \) . Continuing in this way we eventually we cut down the length of \( B \cap  {c}_{0} \) to be less than 1 and hence reach a contradiction.

It then follows that all points of \( Z \) that are separated (along \( J \) ) from \( x \) by \( z \) have the same property. Since the length of \( Z \) is at least 0.86, it follows that there is a point \( z \in  X \) at least distance 0.85 along \( J \) from \( x \) with the property that \( {D}_{z} \) has both endpoints in \( {c}_{0} \) . The complementary component of \( {D}_{z} \) in \( A \) , denoted \( {B}^{\prime } \) , is a disk that is contained in \( B \) and the length of \( {B}^{\prime } \cap  {c}_{0} \) is at least 0.85 less than the length of \( B \cap  {c}_{0} \) .

The length of \( {B}^{\prime } \cap  {c}_{0} \) cannot be less than 1, for that gives a contradiction. But if the length of \( {B}^{\prime } \cap  {c}_{0} \) is greater than 1, we now repeat this construction replacing \( B \) by \( {B}^{\prime } \) . Continuing in this way we eventually we cut down the length of \( B \cap  {c}_{0} \) to be less than 1 and hence reach a contradiction.

nodes.content: LEMMA 19.53. For any \( x \in  X \) there is no sub-geodesic of \( {D}_{x} \) that is an embedded loop in \( A \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: LEMMA 19.53. For any \( x \in X \) there is no sub-geodesic of \( {D}_{x} \) that is an embedded loop in \( A \) .

nodes.proof: Proof. We have already treated the case when the loop bounds a disk. Now we need to treat the case when the loop is homotopically non-trivial in \( A \) . Let \( {D}_{x}^{\prime } \subset  {D}_{x} \) be the minimal compact sub-geodesic containing \( x \) that is not an embedded arc. Let int \( B \) be the complementary component of \( {D}_{x}^{\prime } \) in \( A \) that contains \( {c}_{0} \smallsetminus  \{ x\} \) . There is a natural compactification of int \( B \) as a disk and an immersion of this disk into \( A \) , an immersion that is two-to-one along the shortest sub-geodesic of \( {D}_{x}^{\prime } \) from \( x \) to the point of intersection of \( {D}_{x} \) with itself. We do exactly the same construction as before. Take a sub-arc \( J \) of length 1 with \( x \) as an endpoint and construct \( {S}_{{X}_{J}}\left( B\right) \) consisting of the union of the sub-geodesics of \( {D}_{z} \) , for \( z \in  J \cap  X \) that do not cross the boundary of \( B \) . We then construct a sequence of maximal focusing triangles along \( J \) relative to \( B \) just as in the previous case. In this way we construct a subset \( Z \) of \( X \cap  J \) of total length at least 0.87 with the property that for every \( z \in  Z \) the final end of \( {D}_{z}^{\prime }\left( B\right) \) lies in \( \partial B \) . Furthermore, the length of the arcs that these final ends sweep out is at least 0.86 . Hence, since the total length of the part of the boundary of \( B \) coming from \( {D}_{x}^{\prime } \) is at most \( 2{\delta }^{\prime } < {0.2} \) , there must be a \( z \in  Z \) for which \( {D}_{z}\left( B\right) \) has both ends in \( {c}_{0} \) . This puts us back in the case ruled out in Lemma 19.46.

LEMMA 19.58. Let \( \left( {W, h\left( t\right) }\right) ,{t}_{0} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{1} \) , be a Ricci flow and fix \( \Theta  < \infty \) . Then there exist constants \( \delta  > 0 \) and \( 0 < {r}_{0} \leq  1 \) depending only on the curvature bound for the ambient Ricci flow and \( \Theta \) such that the following holds. Let \( c\left( {x, t}\right) ,{t}_{0} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{1} \) , be a curve-shrinking flow with \( c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) immersed for each \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1}}\right\rbrack \) and with the total curvature of \( c\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) \) being at most \( \Theta \) . Suppose that there is \( 0 < r \leq  {r}_{0} \) and at a time \( {t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1} - \delta {r}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) such that the length of \( c\left( {\cdot ,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) is at least \( r \) and the total curvature of \( c\left( {\cdot ,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) on any sub-arc of length \( r \) is at most \( \delta \) . Then for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) the curvature \( k \) satisfies

\[
{k}^{2} \leq  \frac{2}{\left( t - {t}^{\prime }\right) }.
\]

nodes.proof:
The rest of this section is devoted to the proof of this lemma. In [2] such a local estimate was established when the ambient manifold was Euclidean space and the curve in question is a graph. A related result for hypersurfaces that are graphs appears in [19]. The passage from Euclidean space to a general Ricci flow is straightforward, but it is more delicate to use the bound on total curvature on initial sub-arcs of length \( r \) to show that in appropriate coordinates the evolving curve can be written as an evolving graph, so that the analysis in [2] can be applied.

We fix \( \delta  > 0 \) sufficiently small. We fix \( {t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{1} - \delta {r}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) for which the hypotheses of the lemma hold. The strategy of the proof is to first restrict to the maximum subinterval of \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) of \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) on which \( k \) is bounded by \( \sqrt{2/\left( {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) } \) . If \( {t}_{2} < {t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2} \) , then \( k \) achieves the bound \( \sqrt{2/\left( {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) } \) at time \( {t}_{2} \) . We show that in fact on this subinterval \( k \) never achieves the bound. The result then follows. To show that \( k \) never achieves the bound, we show that on a possibly smaller interval of time \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{3}}\right\rbrack \) with \( {t}_{3} \leq  {t}_{2} \) we can write the restriction of the curve-shrinking flow to any interval whose length at time \( {t}^{\prime } \) is \( \left( {0.9}\right) r \) as a family of graphs in a local coordinate system so that the function \( f \) (of arc and time) defining the graph has derivative along the arc bounded in norm by \( 1/2 \) . We take \( {t}_{3} \leq  {t}_{2} \) maximal with respect to these conditions. Then with both the bound on \( k \) and the bound on the derivative of \( f \) one shows that the spatial derivative of \( f \) never reaches \( 1/2 \) and also that the curves do not move too much so that they always remain in the coordinate patch. The only way that this can happen is that if \( {t}_{2} = {t}_{3} \) , that is to say, on the entire time interval where we have the curvature bound, we also can write the curve-shrinking flow as a flow of graphs with small spatial derivatives. Then it is convenient to replace the curve-shrinking flow by an equivalent flow, introduced in [2], called the graph flow. Applying a simple maximum principle argument to this flow we see that \( k \) never achieves the value \( \sqrt{2/\left( {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) } \) on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) and hence the curvature estimate \( k < \sqrt{2/\left( {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) } \) holds throughout the interval \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) .

8.1. A bound for \( \int {kds} \) . Recall that \( k \) is the norm of the curvature vector \( {\nabla }_{S}S \) , and in particular, \( k \geq  0 \) . For any sub-arc \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) of \( c\left( {\cdot ,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) at time \( {t}^{\prime } \) we let \( {\gamma }_{t} \) be the result at time \( t \) of applying the curve-shrinking flow to \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . The purpose of this subsection is to show that \( {\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{kds} \) is small for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) and all initial arcs \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) of length at most \( r \) .

CLAIM 19.59. There is a constant \( {D}_{0} < \infty \) , depending only on \( \Theta \) and the curvature bound of the ambient Ricci flow such that for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) and every sub-arc \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) whose length is at most \( r \) , we have \( {\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{kds} < {D}_{0} \) and \( l\left( {\gamma }_{t}\right)  \leq  {D}_{0}r \) , where \( l\left( {\gamma }_{t}\right) \) is the length of \( {\gamma }_{t} \) .

Proof. This is immediate from Corollary 19.10 applied to all of \( c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) .

Now we fix \( {t}_{2} \leq  {t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2} \) maximal subject to the condition that \( k\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq \; \sqrt{\frac{2}{t - {t}^{\prime }}} \) for all \( x \) and all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) . If \( {t}_{2} < {t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2} \) then there is \( x \) with \( k\left( {x,{t}_{2}}\right)  = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\left( {t}_{2} - {t}^{\prime }\right) }}. \)

Now consider a curve \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) of length \( r \) . From the integral estimate in the previous claim and the assumed pointwise estimate on \( k \) , we see that

\[
{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{k}^{2}{ds} \leq  \mathop{\max }\limits_{{x \in  {\gamma }_{t}}}k\left( {x, t}\right) {\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{kds} < \sqrt{\frac{2}{t - {t}^{\prime }}} \cdot  {D}_{0}.
\]

Using Equation (19.8), it follows easily that, provided that \( \delta  > 0 \) is sufficiently small, the length of \( {\gamma }_{t} \) is at least \( \left( {0.9}\right) r \) for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) , and more generally for any subinterval \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) of \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) and for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) the length of the corresponding interval \( {\gamma }_{t}^{\prime } \) is at least (0.9) times the length of \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) . We introduce a cut-off function on \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) as follows. First, fix a smooth function \( \psi  : \left\lbrack  {-1/2,1/2}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) which is identically zero on \( \left\lbrack  {-{0.50}, - {0.45}}\right\rbrack \) and on \( \left\lbrack  {{0.45},{0.50}}\right\rbrack \) , and is identically 1 on \( \left\lbrack  {-3/8,3/8}\right\rbrack \) . There is a constant \( {D}^{\prime } \) such that \( \left| {\psi }^{\prime }\right|  \leq  {D}^{\prime } \) and \( \left| {\psi }^{\prime \prime }\right|  \leq  {D}^{\prime } \) . Now we fix the midpoint \( {x}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) and define the signed distance from \( \left( {{x}_{0}, t}\right) \) , denoted

\[
s : {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbb{R}
\]

as follows:

\[
s\left( {x, t}\right)  = {\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}\left| {X\left( {y, t}\right) }\right| {dy}.
\]

We define the cut-off function

\[
\varphi \left( {x, t}\right)  = \psi \left( \frac{s\left( {x, t}\right) }{r}\right) .
\]

CLAIM 19.60. There is a constant \( {D}_{1} \) depending only on the curvature bound for the ambient Ricci flow such that for any sub-arc \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) of length \( r \) , defining \( \varphi \left( {x, t}\right) \) as above, for all \( x \in  {\gamma }_{t} \) and all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) we have

\[
\left| \frac{\partial \varphi \left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right|  \leq  \frac{{D}_{1}}{r\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}} + {D}_{1}.
\]

Proof. Clearly,

\[
\frac{\partial \varphi \left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t} = {\psi }^{\prime }\left( \frac{s\left( {x, t}\right) }{r}\right)  \cdot  \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial s\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}.
\]

We know that \( \left| {\psi }^{\prime }\right|  \leq  {D}^{\prime } \) so that

\[
\left| \frac{\partial \varphi \left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right|  \leq  \frac{{D}^{\prime }}{r}\left| \frac{\partial s\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right| .
\]

On the other hand,

\[
s\left( {x, t}\right)  = {\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}\left| {X\left( {y, t}\right) }\right| {dy}
\]

so that

\[
\left| \frac{\partial s\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right|  = \left| {{\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}\frac{\partial \left| {X\left( {y, t}\right) }\right| }{\partial t}{dy}}\right| ,
\]

By Lemma 19.6 we have

\[
\frac{\partial \left| {X\left( {y, t}\right) }\right| }{\partial y}{dy} = \left( {-\operatorname{Ric}\left( {S\left( {y, t}\right) , S\left( {y, t}\right) }\right)  - {k}^{2}\left( {y, t}\right) }\right) {ds},
\]

so that there is a constant \( D \) depending only on the bound of the sectional curvatures of the ambient Ricci flow with

\[
\left| \frac{\partial s\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right|  \leq  {\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}\left( {D + {k}^{2}}\right) {ds} \leq  {Dl}\left( {\gamma }_{t}\right)  + {\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}{k}^{2}\left( {y, t}\right) {ds}\left( {y, t}\right) ,
\]

and hence by Claim 19.59

\[
\left| \frac{\partial s\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right|  \leq  D{D}_{0}r + {\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}{k}^{2}\left( {y, t}\right) {ds}\left( {y, t}\right) .
\]

Using the fact that \( {k}^{2} \leq  2/\left( {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) \) , we have

\[
{\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}{k}^{2}\left( {y, t}\right) {ds}\left( {y, t}\right)  \leq  \sqrt{\frac{2}{t - {t}^{\prime }}}{\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}{kds} \leq  \frac{\sqrt{2}{D}_{0}}{\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}}.
\]

Putting all this together, we see that there is a constant \( {D}_{1} \) such that

\[
\left| \frac{\partial \varphi \left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right|  \leq  {D}_{1}\left( {\frac{1}{r\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}} + 1}\right) .
\]

CLAIM 19.61. There is a constant \( {D}_{2} \) depending only on the curvature bound of the ambient Ricci flow and \( \Theta \) and a constant \( {D}_{3} \) depending only on the curvature bound of the ambient Ricci flow, such that for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) and any sub-arc \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) of length \( r \) , we have

\[
\left| {\frac{d}{dt}{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{\varphi kds}}\right|  \leq  {D}_{2}\left( {1 + \frac{1}{r\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}}}\right)  + \frac{{D}_{2}}{{r}^{2}} + {D}_{3}{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{\varphi kds}.
\]

Proof. We have

\[
\left| {\frac{d}{dt}{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{\varphi kds}}\right|  \leq  \left| {{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}\frac{\partial \varphi \left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}{kds}}\right|  + \left| {{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}\varphi \frac{\partial \left( {kds}\right) }{\partial t}}\right| .
\]

Using Claim 19.60 for the first term and Claim 19.8 and arguing as in the proof of Lemma 19.9 for the second term, we have

\[
\left| {\frac{d}{dt}{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{\varphi kds}}\right|  \leq  {D}_{1}\left( {1 + \frac{1}{r\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}}}\right) {\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{kds} + \left| {{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}\varphi {k}^{\prime \prime }{ds}}\right|  + {\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{C}_{1}^{\prime }{\varphi kds},
\]

where \( {C}_{1}^{\prime } \) depends only on the ambient curvature bound. We bound the first term by

\[
{D}_{1}{D}_{0}\left( {\frac{1}{r\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}} + 1}\right) ,
\]

where \( {D}_{0} \) is the constant depending on \( \Theta \) and the ambient curvature bound from Claim 19.59. Since the ends of \( {\gamma }_{t} \) are at distance at least \( \left( {0.45}\right) r \) from \( {x}_{0} \) all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) , we see that for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) ,

\[
{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}\varphi {k}^{\prime \prime } = {\int }_{c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\varphi {k}^{\prime \prime }.
\]

Integrating by parts we have

\[
{\int }_{c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\varphi {k}^{\prime \prime }{ds} = {\int }_{c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }{\varphi }^{\prime \prime }{kds},
\]

where the prime here refers to the derivative along \( c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) with respect to arc length. Of course \( \left| {\varphi }^{\prime \prime }\right|  \leq  \frac{{D}^{\prime }}{{r}^{2}} \) . Thus, we see that

\[
\left| {{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}\varphi {k}^{\prime \prime }{ds}}\right|  \leq  \frac{{D}^{\prime }}{{r}^{2}}{\int }_{c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }{kds} \leq  \frac{{D}^{\prime }{D}_{0}}{{r}^{2}}.
\]

Putting all this together, we have

\[
\left| {\frac{d}{dt}{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{\varphi kds}}\right|  \leq  {D}_{2}\left( {1 + \frac{1}{r\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}}}\right)  + \frac{{D}_{2}}{{r}^{2}} + {D}_{3}{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{\varphi kds}
\]

for \( {D}_{2} = {D}_{0}\max \left( {{D}^{\prime },{D}_{1}}\right) \) and \( {D}_{3} = {C}_{1}^{\prime } \) . This gives the required estimate.

COROLLARY 19.62. For any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) and any sub-arc \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) of length \( r \) we have

\[
{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{\varphi kds} \leq  {D}_{4}\sqrt{\delta }
\]

for a constant \( {D}_{4} \) that depends only on the sectional curvature bound of the ambient Ricci flow and \( \Theta \) .

Proof. This is immediate from the previous result by integrating from \( {t}^{\prime } \) to \( {t}_{2} \leq  {t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2} \) , and using the fact that \( \delta  < 1 \) and \( r < 1 \) , and using the fact that

\[
{\int }_{{\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}}{\varphi kds} \leq  {\int }_{{\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}}{kds} < \delta
\]

since \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) has length at most \( r \) .

This gives:

COROLLARY 19.63. For \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \subset  c\left( {\cdot ,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) a sub-arc of length at most \( r \) and for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) , we have

\[
{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{kds} \leq  2{D}_{4}\sqrt{\delta }.
\]

For any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) and any sub-arc \( J \subset  c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) of length at most \( r/2 \) with respect to the metric \( h\left( t\right) \) , we have

\[
{\int }_{J}k\left( {x, t}\right) {ds}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  2{D}_{4}\sqrt{\delta }.
\]

Proof. We divide an interval \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \subset  c\left( {\cdot ,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) of length at most \( r \) into two subintervals \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) and \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime \prime } \) of lengths at most \( r/2 \) . Let \( {\widehat{\gamma }}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) and \( {\widehat{\gamma }}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime \prime } \) be intervals of length \( r \) containing \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) and \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime \prime } \) respectively as middle subintervals. We then apply the previous corollary to \( {\widehat{\gamma }}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) and \( {\widehat{\gamma }}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime \prime } \) using the fact that \( {\varphi k} \geq  0 \) everywhere and \( {\varphi k} = k \) on the middle subintervals of \( {\widehat{\gamma }}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) and \( {\widehat{\gamma }}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime \prime } \) . For an interval \( J \subset  {\gamma }_{t} \) of length \( r/2 \) , according to Lemma 19.10 the length of \( {\left. {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}\right| }_{J} \) with respect to the metric \( h\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) is at most \( r \) , and hence this case follows from the previous case.

8.2. Writing the curve flow as a graph. Now we restrict attention to \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) , the maximal interval in \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) where \( {k}^{2} \leq  2/\left( {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) \) . Let \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) be an arc of length \( r \) in \( c\left( {\cdot ,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) and let \( {x}_{0} \) be the central point of \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . Denote \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {x}_{0}\right)  = p \in  W \) . We take the \( h\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) -exponential mapping from \( {T}_{p}W \rightarrow  W \) . This map will be a local diffeomorphism out to a distance determined by the curvature of \( h\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) . For an appropriate choice of the ball (depending on the ambient curvature bound) the metric on the ball induced by pulling back \( h\left( t\right) \) for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) will be within \( \delta \) in the \( {C}^{1} \) -topology to the Euclidean metric \( {h}^{\prime } = h{\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) }_{p} \) . By this we mean that

(1) \( \left| {\langle X, Y{\rangle }_{h\left( t\right) }-\langle X, Y{\rangle }_{{h}^{\prime }}}\right|  < \delta {\left| X\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }}{\left| Y\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \) for all tangent vectors in the coordinate system, and

(2) viewing the connection \( \Gamma \) as a bilinear map on the coordinate space with values in the coordinate space we have \( {\left| \Gamma \left( X, Y\right) \right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} < \; \delta {\left| X\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }}{\left| Y\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \)

We choose \( 0 < {r}_{0} \leq  1 \) so that it is much smaller than this distance, and hence \( r \) is also much smaller than this distance. We lift to the ball in \( {T}_{p}W \) .

We fix orthonormal coordinates with respect to the metric \( {h}^{\prime } \) so that the tangent vector of \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {x}_{0}\right) \) points in the positive \( {x}^{1} \) -direction. Using these coordinates we decompose the coordinate patch as a product of an interval in the \( {x}^{1} \) -direction and an open ball, \( B \) , spanned by the remaining Euclidean coordinates. From now on we shall work in this coordinate system using this product structure. To simplify the notation in the coming computations, we rename the \( {x}^{1} \) -coordinate the \( z \) -coordinate. Ordinary derivatives of a function \( \alpha \) with respect to \( z \) are written \( {\alpha }_{z} \) . When we write norms and inner products without indicating the metric we implicitly mean that the metric is \( h\left( t\right) \) . When we use the Euclidean metric on these coordinates we denote it explicitly. Next, we wish to understand how \( {\gamma }_{t} \) moves in the Euclidean coordinates under the curve-shrinking flow. Since we have \( {\left| {\nabla }_{S}S\right| }_{h} = k \) , it follows that \( {\left| {\nabla }_{S}S\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \leq  \sqrt{1 + \delta }k \leq  2/\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }} \) , and hence, integrating tells us that for any \( x \in  {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) we have

\[
{\left| {\gamma }_{t}\left( x\right)  - {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( x\right) \right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \leq  4\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }} \leq  4\sqrt{\delta }r.
\]

This shows that for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) , the curve \( {\gamma }_{t} \) is contained in the coordinate patch that we are considering. This computation also implies that the \( z \) -coordinate of \( {\gamma }_{t} \) changes by at most \( 4\sqrt{\delta }r \) over this time interval.

Because the total curvature of \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is small and the metric is close to the Euclidean metric, it follows that the tangent vector at every point of \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is close to the positive \( z \) -direction. This means that we can write \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) as a graph of a function \( f \) from a subinterval in the \( z \) -line to \( Y \) with \( {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} < {2\delta } \) . By continuity, there is \( {t}_{3} \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) such that all the curves \( {\gamma }_{t} \) are written as graphs of functions (over subintervals of the \( z \) -axis that depend on \( t \) ) with \( {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \leq  1/{10} \) . That is to say, we have an open subset \( U \) of the product of the \( z \) -axis with \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{3}}\right\rbrack \) , and the evolving curves define a map \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) from \( U \) into the coordinate system, where the slices at constant time are graphs \( z \mapsto  \left( {z, f\left( {z, t}\right) }\right) \) and are the curves \( {\gamma }_{t} \) . Using the coordinates \( \left( {z, t}\right) \) gives a new flow of curves by moving in the \( t \) -direction. This new flow is called the graph flow. It is a reparameterization of the curve shrinking flow in such a way that the \( z \) -coordinate is preserved. We denote by \( Z = Z\left( {z, t}\right) \) the image under the differential of the map \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) of the tangent vector in the \( z \) -direction and by \( Y\left( {z, t}\right) \) the image under the differential of \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) of the tangent vector in the \( t \) -direction. Notice that \( Z \) is the tangent vector along the parameterized curves in the graph flow. Since we are now using a different parameterization of the curves from the one determined by the curve-shrinking flow, the tangent vector \( Z \) has the same direction but not necessarily the same length as the tangent vector \( X \) from the curve-shrinking parameterization. Also, notice that in the Euclidean norm we have \( {\left| Z\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }}^{2} = 1 + {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }}^{2} \) . It follows that on \( U \) we have

\[
\left( {1 - \delta }\right) \left( {1 + {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }}^{2}}\right)  \leq  {\left| Z\left( z, t\right) \right| }_{h\left( t\right) }^{2} \leq  \left( {1 + \delta }\right) \left( {1 + {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }}^{2}}\right) .
\]

In particular, because of our restriction to the subset where \( {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \leq  1/{10} \) we have \( \left( {1 - \delta }\right)  \leq  {\left| Z\left( z, t\right) \right| }_{h\left( t\right) }^{2} \leq  \left( {1.01}\right) \left( {1 + \delta }\right) \) .

Now we know that \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is a graph of a function \( f\left( {z,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) defined on some interval \( I \) along the \( z \) -axis. Let \( {I}^{\prime } \) be the subinterval of \( I \) centered in \( I \) with \( {h}^{\prime } \) -length (0.9) times the \( {h}^{\prime } \) -length of \( I \) . By the above estimate on \( \left| Z\right| \) it follows that the restriction of \( {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }} \) to \( {I}^{\prime } \) has length between \( \left( {0.8}\right) r \) and \( r \) , and also that the \( {h}^{\prime } \) -length of \( {I}^{\prime } \) is between \( \left( {0.8}\right) r \) and \( r \) . The above estimate means that, provided that \( \delta  > 0 \) is sufficiently small, for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{3}}\right\rbrack \) there is a subinterval of \( {\gamma }_{t} \) that is the graph of a function defined on all of \( {I}^{\prime } \) . We now restrict attention to the family of curves parameterized by \( {I}^{\prime } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{3}}\right\rbrack \) . For every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{3}}\right\rbrack \) the curve \( {\left. {\gamma }_{t}\right| }_{{I}^{\prime }} \) has length between \( \left( {0.8}\right) r \) and \( r \) . The curve-shrinking flow is not defined on this product because under the curve-shrinking flow the \( z \) -coordinate of any given point is not constant. But the graph flow defined above, and studied in [2] (in the case of Euclidean background metric), is defined on \( {I}^{\prime } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{3}}\right\rbrack \) since this flow preserves the \( z \) -coordinate. The time partial derivative in the curve-shrinking flow is given by

(19.10)

\[
{\nabla }_{S}S = \frac{{\nabla }_{Z}Z}{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}} - \frac{1}{{\left| Z\right| }^{4}}\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}Z, Z}\right\rangle  Z.
\]

The time partial derivative in the graph-flow is given by \( Y = \partial \widetilde{\gamma }/\partial t \) . The tangent vector \( Y \) is characterized by being \( {h}^{\prime } \) -orthogonal to the \( z \) -axis and differing from \( {\nabla }_{S}S \) by a functional multiple of \( Z \) .

CLAIM 19.64.

\[
Y = \frac{{\nabla }_{Z}Z-\langle \Gamma \left( {Z, Z}\right) ,{\partial }_{z}{\rangle }_{{h}^{\prime }}Z}{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}} = {\nabla }_{S}S + \left( {\frac{\left\langle  {\nabla }_{Z}Z, Z\right\rangle  }{{\left| Z\right| }^{4}} - \frac{{\left\langle  \Gamma \left( Z, Z\right) ,{\partial }_{z}\right\rangle  }_{{h}^{\prime }}}{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}}}\right) Z.
\]

Proof. In our Euclidean coordinates, \( Z = \left( {1,{f}_{z}}\right) \) so that \( {\nabla }_{Z}Z = \; \left( {0,{f}_{zz}}\right)  + \Gamma \left( {Z, Z}\right) \) . Thus,

\[
{\left\langle  {\nabla }_{Z}Z,{\partial }_{z}\right\rangle  }_{{h}^{\prime }} = {\left\langle  \Gamma \left( Z, Z\right) ,{\partial }_{z}\right\rangle  }_{{h}^{\prime }}.
\]

Since \( {\left\langle  Z,{\partial }_{z}\right\rangle  }_{{h}^{\prime }} = 1 \) , it follows that

\[
\frac{{\nabla }_{Z}Z - {\left\langle  \Gamma \left( Z, Z\right) ,{\partial }_{z}\right\rangle  }_{{h}^{\prime }}Z}{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}}
\]

is \( {h}^{\prime } \) -orthogonal to the \( z \) -axis and hence is a multiple of \( Y \) . Since it differs by a multiple of \( Z \) from \( {\nabla }_{S}S \) , it follows that it is \( Y \) . This gives the first equation; the second follows from this and Equation (19.10).

To simplify the notation we set

\[
\psi \left( Z\right)  = \frac{{\left\langle  \Gamma \left( Z, Z\right) ,{\partial }_{z}\right\rangle  }_{{h}^{\prime }}}{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}}.
\]

Notice that from the conditions on \( \Gamma \) and \( {h}^{\prime } \) it follows immediately that \( \left| {\psi \left( Z\right) }\right|  < \left( {1.5}\right) \delta . \)

8.3. Proof that \( {t}_{3} = {t}_{2} \) . At this point we have a product coordinate system on which the metric is almost the Euclidean metric in the \( {C}^{1} \) -sense, and we have the graph flow given by

\[
Y = \frac{\partial \widetilde{\gamma }}{\partial t} = \frac{{\nabla }_{Z}Z}{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}} - \psi \left( Z\right) Z
\]

defined on \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{3}}\right\rbrack \) with image always contained in the given coordinate patch and written as a graph over a fixed interval \( {I}^{\prime } \) in the \( z \) -axis. For every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{3}}\right\rbrack \) the length of \( {\left. {\gamma }_{{t}^{\prime }}\right| }_{{I}^{\prime }} \) in the metric \( h\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) is between \( \left( {0.8}\right) r \) and \( r \) . The function \( f\left( {z, t}\right) \) whose graphs give the flow satisfies \( {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \leq  1/{10} \) . Our next goal is to estimate \( {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \) and show that it is always less than \( 1/{10} \) as long as \( {k}^{2} \leq  2/\left( {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) \) and \( t - {t}^{\prime } \leq  \delta {r}^{2} \) for a sufficiently small \( \delta \) , i.e., for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) ; that is to say, our next goal is to prove that \( {t}_{3} = {t}_{2} \) . In all the arguments that follow \( {C}^{\prime } \) is a constant that depends only on the curvature bound for the ambient Ricci flow, but the value of \( {C}^{\prime } \) is allowed to change from line to line.

The first step in doing this is to consider the angle between \( {\nabla }_{Z}Z \) and \( Z \) .

CLAIM 19.65. Provided that \( \delta  > 0 \) is sufficiently small, the angle (measured in \( h\left( t\right) ) \) between \( Y \) and \( Z = \left( {1,{f}_{z}}\right) \) is greater than \( \pi /4 \) . Also:

(1)

\[
k \leq  \left| Y\right|  < \sqrt{2}k
\]

(2)

\[
\left| \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}Z, Z}\right\rangle  \right|  < \left( {k + {2\delta }}\right) {\left| Z\right| }^{3}.
\]

(3)

\[
\left| {{\nabla }_{Z}Z}\right|  < 2\left( {\left| Y\right|  + \delta }\right)
\]

(4)

\[
\left| {\langle Y, Z\rangle }\right|  \leq  \left| Y\right| \left| {f}_{z}\right| \left( {1 + {3\delta }}\right) .
\]

Proof. Under the hypothesis that \( {\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }} \leq  1/{10} \) , it is easy to see that the Euclidean angle between \( \left( {0,{f}_{zz}}\right) \) and \( \left( {1,{f}_{z}}\right) \) is at most \( \pi /2 - \pi /5 \) . From this, the first statement follows immediately provided that \( \delta \) is sufficiently small. Since \( Y \) is the sum of \( {\nabla }_{S}S \) and a multiple of \( Z \) and since \( {\nabla }_{S}S \) is \( h\left( t\right) \) -orthogonal to \( Z \) , it follows that \( \left| Y\right|  = \left| {{\nabla }_{S}S}\right| {\left( \cos \left( \theta \right) \right) }^{-1} \) , where \( \theta \) is the angle between \( {\nabla }_{S}S \) and \( Y \) . Since \( Y \) is a multiple of \( \left( {0,{f}_{zz}}\right) \) , it follows from the first part of the claim that the \( h\left( t\right) \) -angle between \( Y \) and \( {\nabla }_{S}S \) is less than \( \pi /4 \) . Item (1) of the claim then follows from the fact that by definition \( \left| {{\nabla }_{S}S}\right|  = k. \)

Since

\[
\frac{{\nabla }_{Z}Z}{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}} = Y + \psi \left( Z\right) Z
\]

and \( {\left| Z\right| }^{2} \leq  \left( {1.01}\right) \left( {1 + \delta }\right) \) , the third item is immediate. For item (4), since \( Y \) is \( {h}^{\prime } \) -orthogonal to the \( z \) -axis, we have

\[
\left| {\langle Y, Z{\rangle }_{{h}^{\prime }}}\right|  = \left| {\left\langle  Y,\left( 0,{f}_{z}\right) \right\rangle  }_{{h}^{\prime }}\right|  \leq  {\left| Y\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }}{\left| {f}_{z}\right| }_{{h}^{\prime }}.
\]

From this and the comparison of \( h\left( t\right) \) and \( {h}^{\prime } \) , item (4) is immediate. Lastly, let us consider item (2). We have

\[
\langle Y, Z\rangle  = \frac{\left\langle  {\nabla }_{Z}Z, Z\right\rangle  }{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}} - {\left\langle  \Gamma \left( Z, Z\right) ,{\partial }_{z}\right\rangle  }_{{h}^{\prime }}.
\]

Thus, from item (4) we have

\[
\frac{\left\langle  {\nabla }_{Z}Z, Z\right\rangle  }{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}} \leq  \left| Y\right| \left| {f}_{z}\right| \left( {1 + {3\delta }}\right)  + \left( {1.5}\right) \delta .
\]

Since \( Y < \sqrt{2}k \) and \( \left| {f}_{z}\right|  < 1/{10} \) , item (2) follows.

CLAIM 19.66. The following hold provided that \( \delta  > 0 \) is sufficiently small:

(1) \( \left| {Z\left( {\psi \left( Z\right) }\right) }\right|  < {C}^{\prime }\left( {1 + \delta \left| Y\right| }\right) \) , and

(2) \( \left| {Y\left( {\psi \left( Z\right) }\right) }\right|  < {C}^{\prime }\left( {\left| Y\right|  + \delta \left| {{\nabla }_{Z}Y}\right| }\right) \) .

(Recall that \( {C}^{\prime } \) is a constant depending only on the curvature bound of the ambient Ricci flow.)

Proof. For the first item, we write \( Z\left( {\psi \left( Z\right) }\right) \) as a sum of terms where the differentiation by \( Z \) acts on the various. When the \( Z \) -derivative acts on \( \Gamma \) the resulting term has norm bounded by a constant depending only on the curvature of the ambient Ricci flow. When the \( Z \) -derivative acts on one of the \( Z \) -terms in \( \Gamma \left( {Z, Z}\right) \) the norm of the result is bounded by \( {2\delta }\left| {{\nabla }_{Z}Z}\right| \left| Z\right| \) . Action on each of the other \( Z \) -terms gives a term bounded in norm by the same expression. Lastly, when the \( Z \) -derivative acts on the constant metric \( {h}^{\prime } \) the norm of the result is bounded by \( 2{\delta }^{2} \) . Since \( \left| {{\nabla }_{Z}Z}\right|  \leq  2\left( {\left| Y\right|  + \delta }\right) \) , the first item follows.

We compute \( Y\left( {\psi \left( Z\right) }\right) \) in a similar fashion. When the \( Y \) -derivative acts on the \( \Gamma \) , the norm of the result is bounded by \( {C}^{\prime }\left| Y\right| \) . When the \( Y \) -derivative acts on one of the \( Z \) -terms the norm of the result is bounded by \( {2\delta }\left| {{\nabla }_{Y}Z}\right| \) . Lastly, when the \( Y \) -derivative acts on the constant metric \( {h}^{\prime } \) , the norm of the result is bounded by \( {\delta }^{2}\left| Y\right| \) . Putting all these terms together establishes the second inequality above.

Now we wish to compute \( {\int }_{{I}^{\prime }\times \{ t\} }{\left| Z\right| }^{2}{dz} \) . To do this we first note that using the definition of \( Y \) , and arguing as in the proof of the first equation in of Lemma 19.6 we have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| Z\right| }^{2} =  - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Z, Z}\right)  + 2\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Y}Z, Z}\right\rangle
\]

\[
=  - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Z, Z}\right)  + 2\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}Y, Z}\right\rangle  .
\]

Direct computation shows that

\[
2\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}\left( \frac{{\nabla }_{Z}Z}{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}}\right) , Z}\right\rangle   = Z\left( \frac{Z\left( {\left| Z\right| }^{2}\right) }{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}}\right)  - 2\frac{{\left| {\nabla }_{Z}Z\right| }^{2}}{{\left| Z\right| }^{4}}{\left| Z\right| }^{2}.
\]

Thus from the Claim 19.64, we have

(19.11)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| Z\right| }^{2} = 2\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}Y, Z}\right\rangle   - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Z, Z}\right)
\]

\[
= Z\left( \frac{Z\left( {\left| Z\right| }^{2}\right) }{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}}\right)  - 2\frac{{\left| {\nabla }_{Z}Z\right| }^{2}}{{\left| Z\right| }^{4}}{\left| Z\right| }^{2} - 2\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}\left( {\psi \left( Z\right) Z}\right) , Z}\right\rangle   - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Z, Z}\right)
\]

\[
= Z\left( \frac{Z\left( {\left| Z\right| }^{2}\right) }{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}}\right)  - 2{\left| Y\right| }^{2}{\left| Z\right| }^{2} + V,
\]

where

\[
V =  - 4{\left| Z\right| }^{2}\langle Y,\psi \left( Z\right) Z\rangle  - 2{\psi }^{2}\left( Z\right) {\left| Z\right| }^{4} - 2\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}\left( {\psi \left( Z\right) Z}\right) , Z}\right\rangle   - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Z, Z}\right) .
\]

By item (1) in Claim 19.66 and item (4) in Claim 19.65 we have

(19.12)

\[

{\left( \widetilde{Q} - h\right) }_{t} \leq  \frac{{\widetilde{Q}}_{zz}}{{\left| Z\right| }^{2}} - \frac{{h}_{zz}}{1 - \delta } - {\widetilde{Q}}^{2} + {h}^{2}.
\]

Since both \( h \) and \( {h}_{zz} \) are positive, at any point where \( \widetilde{Q} - h \geq  0 \) and \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{zz} < 0 \) , we have \( {\left( \widetilde{Q} - h\right) }_{t} < 0 \) . At any point where \( {Q}_{zz} \geq  0 \) , using the fact that \( {\left| Z\right| }^{2} \geq  \left( {1 - \delta }\right) \) we have

\[
{\left( \widetilde{Q} - h\right) }_{t} \leq  {\left( 1 - \delta \right) }^{-1}{\left( \widetilde{Q} - h\right) }_{zz} - {\widetilde{Q}}^{2} + {h}^{2}.
\]

Thus, for any fixed \( t \) , at any local maximum for \( \left( {\widetilde{Q} - h}\right) \left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at which \( \left( {\widetilde{Q} - h}\right) \) is \( \geq  0 \) we have \( {\left( \widetilde{Q} - h\right) }_{t} \leq  0 \) . Since \( \widetilde{Q} - h \) equals \( - \infty \) at the end points of \( {I}^{\prime } \) for all times, there is a continuous function \( f\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\max }\limits_{{z \in  {I}^{\prime }}}\left( {\widetilde{Q} - h}\right) \left( {z, t}\right) \) , defined for all \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) approaching \( - \infty \) uniformly as \( t \) approaches \( {t}^{\prime } \) from above. By the previous discussion, at any point where \( f\left( t\right)  \geq  0 \) we have \( {f}^{\prime }\left( t\right)  \leq  0 \) in the sense of forward difference quotients. It now follows that \( f\left( t\right)  \leq  0 \) for all \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) . This means that for all \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) at the \( {h}^{\prime } \) -midpoint \( {x}_{0} \) of \( {I}^{\prime } \) (the point where \( z = l/2 \) ) we have

\[
Q\left( {{x}_{0}, t}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{t - {t}^{\prime }} + \frac{{16} \cdot  4{\left( 1 - \delta \right) }^{-1}}{{l}^{2}} + {C}_{1}^{\prime }.
\]

Since \( l \geq  \left( {0.8}\right) r \) and since \( t - {t}^{\prime } \leq  \delta {r}^{2} \) , we see that provided \( \delta \) is sufficiently small (depending on the bound of the curvature of the ambient flow) we have

\[
Q\left( {{x}_{0}, t}\right)  < \frac{3}{2\left( {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) }
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) . Of course, since \( {\left| Z\right| }^{2} \geq  1 - \delta \) everywhere, this shows that

\[
{k}^{2}\left( {{x}_{0}, t}\right)  \leq  {\left| Y\left( {x}_{0}, t\right) \right| }^{2} = \left( {2 - {\left| Z\left( {x}_{0}, t\right) \right| }^{2}}\right) Q\left( {{x}_{0}, t}\right)  < \frac{2}{\left( t - {t}^{\prime }\right) }
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) . Since \( {x}_{0} \) was an arbitrary point of \( c\left( {\cdot ,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) , this shows that \( k\left( {x, t}\right)  < \sqrt{\frac{2}{t - {t}^{\prime }}} \) for all \( x \in  c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) and all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) . By the definition of \( {t}_{2} \) this implies that \( {t}_{2} = {t}^{\prime } + \delta {r}^{2} \) and completes the proof of Lemma 19.58.

nodes.proof:
Proof. Clearly,

\[
\frac{\partial \varphi \left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t} = {\psi }^{\prime }\left( \frac{s\left( {x, t}\right) }{r}\right)  \cdot  \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial s\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}.
\]

We know that \( \left| {\psi }^{\prime }\right|  \leq  {D}^{\prime } \) so that

\[
\left| \frac{\partial \varphi \left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right|  \leq  \frac{{D}^{\prime }}{r}\left| \frac{\partial s\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right| .
\]

On the other hand,

\[
s\left( {x, t}\right)  = {\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}\left| {X\left( {y, t}\right) }\right| {dy}
\]

so that

\[
\left| \frac{\partial s\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right|  = \left| {{\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}\frac{\partial \left| {X\left( {y, t}\right) }\right| }{\partial t}{dy}}\right| ,
\]

By Lemma 19.6 we have

\[
\frac{\partial \left| {X\left( {y, t}\right) }\right| }{\partial y}{dy} = \left( {-\operatorname{Ric}\left( {S\left( {y, t}\right) , S\left( {y, t}\right) }\right)  - {k}^{2}\left( {y, t}\right) }\right) {ds},
\]

so that there is a constant \( D \) depending only on the bound of the sectional curvatures of the ambient Ricci flow with

\[
\left| \frac{\partial s\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right|  \leq  {\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}\left( {D + {k}^{2}}\right) {ds} \leq  {Dl}\left( {\gamma }_{t}\right)  + {\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}{k}^{2}\left( {y, t}\right) {ds}\left( {y, t}\right) ,
\]

and hence by Claim 19.59

\[
\left| \frac{\partial s\left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right|  \leq  D{D}_{0}r + {\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}{k}^{2}\left( {y, t}\right) {ds}\left( {y, t}\right) .
\]

Using the fact that \( {k}^{2} \leq  2/\left( {t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) \) , we have

\[
{\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}{k}^{2}\left( {y, t}\right) {ds}\left( {y, t}\right)  \leq  \sqrt{\frac{2}{t - {t}^{\prime }}}{\int }_{{x}_{0}}^{x}{kds} \leq  \frac{\sqrt{2}{D}_{0}}{\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}}.
\]

Putting all this together, we see that there is a constant \( {D}_{1} \) such that

\[
\left| \frac{\partial \varphi \left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}\right|  \leq  {D}_{1}\left( {\frac{1}{r\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}} + 1}\right) .
\]

nodes.proof:
Proof. We have

\[
\left| {\frac{d}{dt}{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{\varphi kds}}\right|  \leq  \left| {{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}\frac{\partial \varphi \left( {x, t}\right) }{\partial t}{kds}}\right|  + \left| {{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}\varphi \frac{\partial \left( {kds}\right) }{\partial t}}\right| .
\]

Using Claim 19.60 for the first term and Claim 19.8 and arguing as in the proof of Lemma 19.9 for the second term, we have

\[
\left| {\frac{d}{dt}{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{\varphi kds}}\right|  \leq  {D}_{1}\left( {1 + \frac{1}{r\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}}}\right) {\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{kds} + \left| {{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}\varphi {k}^{\prime \prime }{ds}}\right|  + {\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{C}_{1}^{\prime }{\varphi kds},
\]

where \( {C}_{1}^{\prime } \) depends only on the ambient curvature bound. We bound the first term by

\[
{D}_{1}{D}_{0}\left( {\frac{1}{r\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}} + 1}\right) ,
\]

where \( {D}_{0} \) is the constant depending on \( \Theta \) and the ambient curvature bound from Claim 19.59. Since the ends of \( {\gamma }_{t} \) are at distance at least \( \left( {0.45}\right) r \) from \( {x}_{0} \) all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) , we see that for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) ,

\[
{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}\varphi {k}^{\prime \prime } = {\int }_{c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\varphi {k}^{\prime \prime }.
\]

Integrating by parts we have

\[
{\int }_{c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\varphi {k}^{\prime \prime }{ds} = {\int }_{c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }{\varphi }^{\prime \prime }{kds},
\]

where the prime here refers to the derivative along \( c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) with respect to arc length. Of course \( \left| {\varphi }^{\prime \prime }\right|  \leq  \frac{{D}^{\prime }}{{r}^{2}} \) . Thus, we see that

\[
\left| {{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}\varphi {k}^{\prime \prime }{ds}}\right|  \leq  \frac{{D}^{\prime }}{{r}^{2}}{\int }_{c\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }{kds} \leq  \frac{{D}^{\prime }{D}_{0}}{{r}^{2}}.
\]

Putting all this together, we have

\[
\left| {\frac{d}{dt}{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{\varphi kds}}\right|  \leq  {D}_{2}\left( {1 + \frac{1}{r\sqrt{t - {t}^{\prime }}}}\right)  + \frac{{D}_{2}}{{r}^{2}} + {D}_{3}{\int }_{{\gamma }_{t}}{\varphi kds}
\]

for \( {D}_{2} = {D}_{0}\max \left( {{D}^{\prime },{D}_{1}}\right) \) and \( {D}_{3} = {C}_{1}^{\prime } \) . This gives the required estimate.

From this, the first statement follows immediately provided that \( \delta \) is sufficiently small. Since \( Y \) is the sum of \( {\nabla }_{S}S \) and a multiple of \( Z \) and since \( {\nabla }_{S}S \) is \( h\left( t\right) \) -orthogonal to \( Z \) , it follows that \( \left| Y\right|  = \left| {{\nabla }_{S}S}\right| {\left( \cos \left( \theta \right) \right) }^{-1} \) , where \( \theta \) is the angle between \( {\nabla }_{S}S \) and \( Y \) . nodes.proof: By the previous lemma, if \( \epsilon \) is sufficiently small for every \( n \in \; N \) there is a unique two-plane, \( {P}_{n} \) , at each point on which the sectional curvature is maximal. The sectional curvature on this two-plane is close to \( 1/2 \) and the other two eigenvalues of the curvature operator at \( n \) are close to zero. Furthermore, \( {P}_{n} \) makes small \( g \) -angles with the tangent planes to the \( {S}^{2} \) -factors in the neck structure. Under the condition that the restriction of the metric to \( f\left( {S}^{2}\right) \) is close to the round metric \( {h}_{0} \) and the norm of the second fundamental form is small, we see that for every \( p \in  {S}^{2} \) the two-plane \( {df}\left( {{T}_{p}{S}^{2}}\right) \) makes a small \( g \) -angle with \( {P}_{n} \) and hence with the tangent planes to the family of two-spheres coming from the neck structure. Since \( g \) is close to the product metric, this means that the angle between \( {df}\left( {{T}_{n}{S}^{2}}\right) \) and the tangents to the family of two-spheres coming from the neck structure, measured in the product metric, is also small. Hence, the composition of \( f \) followed by the projection mapping \( N \rightarrow  {S}^{2} \) induced by the neck structure determines a submersion of \( {S}^{2} \) onto itself. Since \( {S}^{2} \) is compact and simply connected, any submersion of \( {S}^{2} \) onto itself is a diffeomorphism. This means that \( f\left( {S}^{2}\right) \) crosses each line \( \{ x\}  \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) transversely and in exactly one point. Clearly then, it is isotopic in \( N \) to any two-sphere of the form \( {S}^{2} \times  \{ s\} \) .

Let us consider a geodesic \( \mu \) in the product Riemannian manifold \( {S}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) with the metric on \( {S}^{2} \) being of constant Gaussian curvature \( 1/2 \) , i.e., radius \( \sqrt{2} \) . Its projections, \( {\mu }_{1} \) and \( {\mu }_{2} \) , to \( {S}^{2} \) and to \( \mathbb{R} \) , respectively, are also geodesics, and \( \left| \mu \right|  = \sqrt{{\left| {\mu }_{1}\right| }^{2} + {\left| {\mu }_{2}\right| }^{2}} \) . For \( \mu \) to be a minimal geodesic, the same is true of each of its projections. In particular, when \( \mu \) is minimal, the length of \( {\mu }_{1} \) is at most \( \sqrt{2}\pi \) . Hence, for any \( {\alpha }^{\prime } > 0 \) , if \( \mu \) is sufficiently long and if the final endpoint has a larger \( s \) -value than the initial point, then the angle between the tangent vectors \( {\mu }^{\prime }\left( s\right) \) and \( \partial /\partial s \) is less than \( {\alpha }^{\prime } \) . This establishes the result for the standard metric on the model for \( \epsilon \) -necks.

The first statement now follows for all \( \epsilon \) sufficiently small and all \( \epsilon \) -necks because minimal geodesics between a pair of points in a manifold vary continuously in the \( {C}^{1} \) -topology as a function of the space of metrics with the \( {C}^{k} \) -topology, since \( k \geq  2 \) . The second statement is obvious since the diameter of any member of the family of two-spheres in the standard metric is \( \sqrt{2}\pi \) .

We parameterize \( \gamma \) as a map from \( \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) . By Corollary A.6, provided that \( \epsilon  > 0 \) is sufficiently small, each component of \( \gamma  \cap  N \) crosses each two-sphere of the neck structure at most once. Suppose that there is some two-sphere \( {S}^{2} \times  \{ x\} \) that is crossed by two different components of \( \gamma \) . Let \( c < d \) be two points of intersection of \( \gamma \) with \( {S}^{2} \times  \{ s\} \) .

There are two cases to consider. Suppose that the two components of \( \gamma  \cap  N \) cross \( {S}^{2} \times  \{ x\} \) in opposite directions. In this case, since each component of \( \gamma  \cap  N \) has length at least \( {\epsilon }^{-1}/8 \) , then applying Corollary A. 5 we can take the two-sphere that they both cross to be \( {S}^{2} \times  \{ s\} \) for some \( s \in  \left( {-\left( {0.9}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1},\left( {0.9}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) . Applying Corollary A. 5 again we see that the distance from this sphere to the complement of \( N \) is at least \( R{\left( x\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1}/{20} \) . Let \( c < d \) be the points of intersection. Remove \( \gamma \left( \left\lbrack  {c, d}\right\rbrack  \right) \) from \( \gamma \) and replace it by a path in \( {S}^{2} \times  \{ s\} \) between \( \gamma \left( c\right) \) and \( \gamma \left( d\right) \) . If \( \epsilon \) is sufficiently small, by Lemma A. 4 we can choose this path to have length at most \( {2\pi } \) , and hence the result will be a shorter path.

The other possibility is that \( \gamma \) crosses \( {S}^{2} \times  \{ s\} \) twice in the same direction. In this case the central two-sphere of \( N \) does not separate \( M \) and \( \gamma \) makes a circuit transverse to the two-sphere. In particular, by Corollary A. 5 the length of \( \gamma \left( \left\lbrack  {c, d}\right\rbrack  \right) \) is bounded below by \( 2\left( {1 - \alpha }\right) R{\left( x\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1} \) where we can take \( \alpha  > 0 \) as close to zero as we want by making \( \epsilon \) smaller. Clearly, then in this case as well, replacing \( \gamma \left( \left\lbrack  {c, d}\right\rbrack  \right) \) with a path of length less than \( {2\pi R}{\left( x\right) }^{-1/2} \) on \( {S}^{2} \times  \{ s\} \) will shorten the length of \( \gamma \) .

nodes.content: COROLLARY A.8. The following holds for all \( \epsilon  > 0 \) sufficiently small and any \( C < \infty \) . We orient the s-direction in \( N \) so that \( Y \) lies off the negative end of \( N \) . Suppose that there are \( {a}^{\prime } < d < {b}^{\prime } \) with \( \gamma \left( {a}^{\prime }\right) \) and \( \gamma \left( {b}^{\prime }\right) \) contained in \( S \) . Then, by Corollary A.5, replacing \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  {a}^{\prime },{b}^{\prime }\right\rbrack  } \) with a path on \( S \) joining \( \gamma \left( {a}^{\prime }\right) \) to \( \gamma \left( {b}^{\prime }\right) \) creates a shorter path with the same endpoints. This shows that at least one of the paths \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  a, d\right\rbrack  } \) or \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  d, b\right\rbrack  } \) , let us say \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  a, d\right\rbrack  } \) , is contained in \( \widehat{Y} \) . The other path \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  d, b\right\rbrack  } \) has an endpoint in \( Y \) and exits from \( \widehat{Y} \) , hence by Corollary A. 6 there is a subinterval \( \left\lbrack  {d,{b}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) such that either \( \gamma \left( {b}^{\prime }\right) \) is contained in the frontier of \( X \) or \( b = {b}^{\prime } \) and furthermore \( \gamma \left( \left\lbrack  {d,{b}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack  \right) \) crosses each two-sphere of the \( \epsilon \) -neck structure on \( N \) at most once. We have constructed a subinterval of the form \( \left\lbrack  {a,{b}^{\prime \prime }}\right\rbrack \) such that \( \gamma \left( \left\lbrack  {a,{b}^{\prime \prime }}\right\rbrack  \right) \) is contained in \( \widehat{Y} \) . This establishes the result in this case. Suppose that \( {b}^{\prime } < b \) . If there is \( c \in  \left\lbrack  {{b}^{\prime }, b}\right\rbrack \) with \( \gamma \left( c\right)  \in  \widehat{Y} \) then the length of \( \gamma \left( \left\lbrack  {{b}^{\prime \prime }, c}\right\rbrack  \right) \) is at least twice the distance from \( S \) to the frontier of the positive end of \( N \) . Thus, we could create a shorter path with the same endpoints by joining \( \gamma \left( {b}^{\prime \prime }\right) \) to \( \gamma \left( c\right) \) by a path of \( S \) . This means that \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  {b}^{\prime }, b\right\rbrack  } \) is disjoint from \( S \) and hence from \( \widehat{Y} \) , proving the result in this case as well.

Proposition A.11. Given \( 0 < \alpha  \leq  {10}^{-2} \) , there is \( {\epsilon }_{5} = {\epsilon }_{5}\left( \alpha \right)  > 0 \) such that the following hold for all \( 0 < \epsilon  \leq  {\epsilon }_{5} \) . Let \( N \) and \( {N}^{\prime } \) be \( \epsilon \) -necks centered at \( x \) and \( {x}^{\prime } \) , respectively, in a Riemannian manifold \( X \) :

(1) If \( N \cap  {N}^{\prime } \neq  \varnothing \) then \( 1 - \alpha  < R\left( x\right) /R\left( {x}^{\prime }\right)  < 1 + \alpha \) . In particular, denoting the scales of \( N \) and \( {N}^{\prime } \) by \( h \) and \( {h}^{\prime } \) we have

\[
1 - \alpha  < \frac{h}{{h}^{\prime }} < 1 + \alpha
\]

(2) Suppose \( y \in  N \cap  {N}^{\prime } \) and \( S \) and \( {S}^{\prime } \) are the two-spheres in the \( \epsilon \) -neck structures on \( N \) and \( {N}^{\prime } \) , respectively, passing through \( y \) . Then the angle between \( T{S}_{y} \) and \( T{S}_{y}^{\prime } \) is less than \( \alpha \) .

(3) Suppose that \( y \in  N \cap  {N}^{\prime } \) . Denote by \( \partial /\partial {s}_{N} \) and \( \partial /\partial {s}_{{N}^{\prime }} \) the tangent vectors in the \( \epsilon \) -neck structures of \( N \) and \( {N}^{\prime } \) , respectively. Then at the point \( y \) , either

\[
\left| {R{\left( x\right) }^{1/2}\left( {\partial /\partial {s}_{N}}\right)  - R{\left( {x}^{\prime }\right) }^{1/2}\partial /\partial {s}_{{N}^{\prime }}}\right|  < \alpha
\]

or

\[
\left| {R{\left( x\right) }^{1/2}\left( {\partial /\partial {s}_{N}}\right)  + R{\left( {x}^{\prime }\right) }^{1/2}\partial /\partial {s}_{{N}^{\prime }}}\right|  < \alpha .
\]

(4) Suppose that one of the two-spheres \( {S}^{\prime } \) of the \( \epsilon \) -neck structure on \( {N}^{\prime } \) is completely contained in \( N \) . Then \( {S}^{\prime } \) is a section of the projection mapping on the first factor

\[
{p}_{1} : {S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)  \rightarrow  {S}^{2}.
\]

In particular, \( {S}^{\prime } \) is isotopic in \( N \) to any one of the two-spheres of the \( \epsilon \) -neck structure on \( N \) by an isotopy that moves all points in the interval directions.

(5) If \( N \cap  {N}^{\prime } \) contains a point \( y \) with \( \left( {-{0.9}}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1} \leq  {s}_{N}\left( y\right)  \leq  \left( {0.9}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1} \) , then there is a point \( {y}^{\prime } \in  N \cap  {N}^{\prime } \) such that

\[
- \left( {0.96}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1} \leq  {s}_{N}\left( {y}^{\prime }\right)  \leq  \left( {0.96}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1},
\]

\[
- \left( {0.96}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1} \leq  {s}_{{N}^{\prime }}\left( {y}^{\prime }\right)  \leq  \left( {0.96}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1}.
\]

The two-sphere \( S\left( {y}^{\prime }\right) \) in the neck structure on \( N \) through \( {y}^{\prime } \) is contained in \( {N}^{\prime } \) and the two-sphere \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {y}^{\prime }\right) \) in the neck structure on \( {N}^{\prime } \) through \( {y}^{\prime } \) is contained in \( N \) . Furthermore, \( S\left( {y}^{\prime }\right) \) and \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {y}^{\prime }\right) \) are isotopic in \( N \cap  {N}^{\prime } \) . Lastly, \( N \cap  {N}^{\prime } \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) under a diffeomorphism mapping \( S\left( y\right) \) to \( {S}^{2} \times  \{ 1/2\} \) , see FIG. 3.

DEFINITION A.12. Let \( \left( {X, g}\right) \) be a Riemannian manifold. By a finite chain of \( \epsilon \) -necks in \( \left( {X, g}\right) \) , we mean a sequence \( {N}_{a},\ldots ,{N}_{b} \) , of \( \epsilon \) -necks in \( \left( {X, g}\right) \) such that:

(1) for all \( i, a \leq  i < b \) , the intersection \( {N}_{i} \cap  {N}_{i + 1} \) contains the positive-most quarter of \( {N}_{i} \) and the negative-most quarter of \( {N}_{i + 1} \) and is contained in the positive-most three-quarters of \( {N}_{i} \) and the negative-most three-quarters of \( {N}_{i + 1} \) , and

(2) for all \( i, a < i \leq  b,{N}_{i} \) is disjoint from the negative end of \( {N}_{a} \) .

By an infinite chain of \( \epsilon \) -necks in \( X \) we mean a collection \( {\left\{  {N}_{i}\right\}  }_{i \in  I} \) for some interval \( I \subset  \mathbb{Z} \) , infinite in at least one direction, so that for each finite subinterval \( J \) of \( I \) the subset of \( {\left\{  {N}_{i}\right\}  }_{i \in  J} \) is a chain of \( \epsilon \) -necks.

Notice that in an \( \epsilon \) -chain \( {N}_{i} \cap  {N}_{j} = \varnothing \) if \( \left| {i - j}\right|  \geq  5 \) .

nodes.proof: Let us first prove the result for finite chains. The proof that \( U \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) is by induction on \( b - a + 1 \) . If \( b = a \) , then the result is clear. Suppose that we know the result for chains of smaller cardinality. Then \( {N}_{a} \cup  \cdots  \cup  {N}_{b - 1} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) . Hence by part (5) of Proposition A. \( {11}, U \) is the union of two manifolds each diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) meeting in an open subset diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) . Furthermore, by the same result in the intersection there is a two-sphere isotopic to each of the two-sphere factors from the two pieces. It now follows easily that the union is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) . Now consider an infinite chain. It is an increasing union of finite chains each diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) and with the two-spheres of one isotopic to the two-spheres of any larger one. It is then immediate that the union is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) .

nodes.proof: Suppose that \( x \) is a point of the frontier of \( U \) . Let \( {x}_{i} \in  U \) be a sequence converging to \( x \) . If the \( {x}_{i} \) were contained in a finite union of the \( {N}_{k} \) , say \( {N}_{0} \cup  \cdots  \cup  {N}_{\ell } \) , then \( x \) would be in the closure of this union and hence by the previous comment would be either in the frontier of the negative end of \( {N}_{0} \) or in the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{\ell } \) . But the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{\ell } \) is contained in \( {N}_{\ell  + 1} \) and hence contains no points of the frontier of \( U \) . Thus, in this case \( x \) is a point of the frontier of the negative end of \( {N}_{0} \) . If \( \left\{  {x}_{i}\right\} \) is not contained in any finite union, then after passing to a subsequence, we can suppose that \( {x}_{i} \in  {N}_{k\left( i\right) } \) where \( k\left( i\right) \) is an increasing sequence tending to infinity. Clearly \( R\left( {x}_{i}\right) \) converges to \( R\left( x\right)  < \infty \) . Hence, there is a uniform lower bound to the scales of the \( {N}_{k\left( i\right) } \) . For all \( i \) sufficiently large, \( {x}_{i} \notin  {N}_{0} \) . Thus, for such \( i \) any path from \( {x}_{i} \) to \( x \) must traverse either \( {N}_{0} \) or \( {N}_{k\left( j\right) } \) for all \( j \geq  i + 5 \) . The length of such a path is at least the minimum of the width of \( {N}_{0} \) and the width of \( {N}_{k\left( j\right) } \) for some \( j \) sufficiently large. But we have just seen that there is a positive lower bound to the scales of the \( {N}_{k\left( j\right) } \) independent of \( j \) , and hence by Corollary A. 5 there is a positive lower bound, independent of \( j \) , to the widths of the \( {N}_{k\left( j\right) } \) . This shows that there is a positive lower bound, independent of \( i \) , to the distance from \( {x}_{i} \) to \( x \) .This is impossible since \( {x}_{i} \) converges to \( x \) .

nodes.content: LEMMA A.18. There exists \( {\epsilon }_{0} > 0 \) such that for all \( 0 < \epsilon  \leq  {\epsilon }_{0} \) the following is true. Suppose that \( \left\{  {{N}_{a},\ldots ,{N}_{b}}\right\} \) is a balanced chain in a Riemannian manifold \( M \) with \( U = { \cup  }_{i = a}^{b}{N}_{i} \) . Suppose that the two-spheres of the neck structure of \( {N}_{a} \) separate \( M \) . nodes.content: Proposition A.19. There exists \( {\epsilon }_{0} > 0 \) such that for all \( 0 < \epsilon  \leq  {\epsilon }_{0} \) the following is true. Let \( X \) be a connected subset of a Riemannian manifold \( M \) with the property that every point \( x \in  X \) is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck \( N\left( x\right) \) in M. Suppose that the central two-spheres of these necks do not separate M. Then there is a subset \( \left\{  {x}_{i}\right\} \) of \( X \) such that the necks \( N\left( {x}_{i}\right) \) (possibly after reversing their s-directions) form a balanced chain of \( \epsilon \) -necks \( \left\{  {N\left( {x}_{i}\right) }\right\} \) whose union \( U \) contains \( X \) . The union \( U \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) . It is an \( \epsilon \) -tube.

nodes.proof:
According to Lemma A. 18 for \( \epsilon  > 0 \) sufficiently small the following holds. Suppose that we have a balanced chain of \( \epsilon \) -necks \( {N}_{a}\ldots ,{N}_{b} \) , with \( {N}_{i} \) centered at \( {x}_{i} \in  X \) , whose union \( U \) does not contain \( X \) . Then one of the following holds:

(1) It is possible to find an \( \epsilon \) -neck \( {N}_{b + 1} \) centered at a point of the intersection of \( X \) with the closure of the positive end of \( {N}_{b} \) so that \( {N}_{a},\ldots ,{N}_{b + 1} \) is a balanced \( \epsilon \) -chain.

(2) It is possible to find an \( \epsilon \) -neck \( {N}_{a - 1} \) centered at a point of the intersection of \( X \) with the closure of the negative end of \( {N}_{a} \) so that \( {N}_{a - 1},{N}_{a},\ldots ,{N}_{b} \) is a balanced \( \epsilon \) -chain.

Now assume that there is no finite balanced chain of \( \epsilon \) -necks \( N\left( {x}_{i}\right) \) containing \( X \) . Then we can repeatedly lengthen a balanced chain of \( \epsilon \) -necks centered at points of \( X \) by adding necks at one end or the other. Suppose that we have a half-infinite balanced chain \( \left\{  {{N}_{0},{N}_{1},\ldots ,}\right\} \) . By Lemma A. 15 the frontier of this union is the frontier of the negative end of \( {N}_{0} \) . Thus, if we can construct a balanced chain which is infinite in both directions, then the union of the necks in this chain is a component of \( M \) and hence contains the connected set \( X \) . If we can construct a balanced chain that is infinite at one end but not the other that cannot be further extended, then the connected set is disjoint from the frontier of the negative end of the first neck in the chain and, as we have see above, the 'infinite' end of the chain has no frontier. Thus, \( X \) is disjoint from the frontier of \( U \) in \( M \) and hence is contained in \( U \) . Thus, in all cases we construct a balanced chain of \( \epsilon \) -necks containing \( X \) . By Lemma A.13 the union of the necks in this chain is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) and hence is an \( \epsilon \) -tube.
