nodes.label: Remark 2.3.3
nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow
nodes.section_title: 2.3. Deformation of geometric quantities as the Riemannian metric is deformed
nodes.content:
Remark 2.3.3. A weakened form of this proposition which suffices for many purposes is

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\nabla Y = Y * \nabla h
\]

where the \( * \) -notation is from Section 2.1. Moreover, if \( \omega  \in  \Gamma \left( {{T}^{ * }\mathcal{M}}\right) \) is a one-form which is independent of \( t \) , then

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\nabla }_{X}\omega }\right) \left( Y\right)  = \frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\nabla }_{X}\left\lbrack  {\omega \left( Y\right) }\right\rbrack   - \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\omega \left( {{\nabla }_{X}Y}\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {X\left\lbrack  {\omega \left( Y\right) }\right\rbrack  }\right)  - \omega \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\nabla }_{X}Y}\right) \tag{2.3.2}
\]

\[
=  - \omega \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\nabla }_{X}Y}\right) ,
\]

and so

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\nabla \omega  = \omega  * \nabla h
\]

By the product rule, we then find the formula

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\nabla A = A * \nabla h,
\]

for any fixed tensor field \( A \) , or more generally, if \( A = A\left( t\right) \) is given a \( t \) - dependency, then we have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\nabla A - \nabla \frac{\partial }{\partial t}A = A * \nabla h. \tag{2.3.3}
\]

This formula may be compared with (2.1.6).

Next we take a first look at how the curvature is changing.

nodes.label: Proposition 2.3.4
nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow
nodes.section_title: 2.3. Deformation of geometric quantities as the Riemannian metric is deformed
nodes.content:
Proposition 2.3.4.

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}R\left( {X, Y}\right) W = \left( {{\nabla }_{Y}\Pi }\right) \left( {X, W}\right)  - \left( {{\nabla }_{X}\Pi }\right) \left( {Y, W}\right)
\]

We want to turn this into a formula for the evolution of the full curvature tensor \( \mathrm{{Rm}} \) in terms only of \( h \mathrel{\text{ := }} \frac{\partial g}{\partial t} \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: Proposition 2.3.4. \[ \frac{\partial }{\partial t}R\left( {X, Y}\right) W = \left( {{\nabla }_{Y}\Pi }\right) \left( {X, W}\right) - \left( {{\nabla }_{X}\Pi }\right) \left( {Y, W}\right) \] We want to turn this into a formula for the evolution of the full curvature tensor \( \mathrm{{Rm}} \) in terms only of \( h \mathrel{\text{ := }} \frac{\partial g}{\partial t} \) .

nodes.proof:
By definition,

\[
R\left( {X, Y}\right) W \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{X}W - {\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{Y}W + {\nabla }_{\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }W,
\]

and so

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}R\left( {X, Y}\right) W = \left\lbrack  {\Pi \left( {Y,{\nabla }_{X}W}\right)  + {\nabla }_{Y}\left( {\Pi \left( {X, W}\right) }\right) }\right\rbrack
\]

\[
- \left\lbrack  {\Pi \left( {X,{\nabla }_{Y}W}\right)  + {\nabla }_{X}\left( {\Pi \left( {Y, W}\right) }\right) }\right\rbrack   + \Pi \left( {\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  , W}\right)
\]

\[
= \left( {{\nabla }_{Y}\Pi }\right) \left( {X, W}\right)  - \left( {{\nabla }_{X}\Pi }\right) \left( {Y, W}\right)
\]

\[
+ \Pi \left( {{\nabla }_{Y}X - {\nabla }_{X}Y + \left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  , W}\right)
\]

\[
= \left( {{\nabla }_{Y}\Pi }\right) \left( {X, W}\right)  - \left( {{\nabla }_{X}\Pi }\right) \left( {Y, W}\right)
\]

since \( \nabla \) is torsion free.

nodes.label: Proposition 2.3.5
nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow
nodes.section_title: 2.3. Deformation of geometric quantities as the Riemannian metric is deformed
nodes.content:
Proposition 2.3.5.

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\operatorname{Rm}\left( {X, Y, W, Z}\right)  = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack  {h\left( {R\left( {X, Y}\right) W, Z}\right)  - h\left( {R\left( {X, Y}\right) Z, W}\right) }\right\rbrack
\]

\[
+ \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack  {{\nabla }_{Y, W}^{2}h\left( {X, Z}\right)  - {\nabla }_{X, W}^{2}h\left( {Y, Z}\right) }\right. \tag{2.3.4}
\]

\[
\left. {+{\nabla }_{X, Z}^{2}h\left( {Y, W}\right)  - {\nabla }_{Y, Z}^{2}h\left( {X, W}\right) }\right\rbrack
\]

Note that the anti-symmetry between \( X \) and \( Y \) , and also between \( W \) and \( Z \) , is automatic in this expression. The tensor Rm also enjoys the symmetry \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {X, Y, W, Z}\right)  = \operatorname{Rm}\left( {W, Z, X, Y}\right) \) (that is, the curvature operator is symmetric) and we see this in the right-hand side of (2.3.4) via the Ricci identity (2.1.2) which in this case tells us that

\[
- {\nabla }_{X, Y}^{2}h\left( {W, Z}\right)  + {\nabla }_{Y, X}^{2}h\left( {W, Z}\right)  =  - h\left( {R\left( {X, Y}\right) W, Z}\right)  - h\left( {R\left( {X, Y}\right) Z, W}\right) .
\]

(2.3.5)

Next we want to compute the evolution of the Ricci and scalar curvatures. Since these arise as traces, we record now the following useful fact.

nodes.proof:
To shorten the calculation, we will check this tensor identity at one point \( p \in  \mathcal{M} \) at which we may assume, without loss of generality, that at a ’time’ \( t \) of your choosing,

\[
\nabla X = \nabla Y = \nabla W = \nabla Z = 0. \tag{2.3.13}
\]

To begin with, since the metric is evolving, we have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\langle R\left( {X, Y}\right) W, Z\rangle  = h\left( {R\left( {X, Y}\right) W, Z}\right)  + \left\langle  {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}R\left( {X, Y}\right) W, Z}\right\rangle
\]

\[
= h\left( {R\left( {X, Y}\right) W, Z}\right)  + \left\langle  {\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}\Pi }\right) \left( {X, W}\right)  - \left( {{\nabla }_{X}\Pi }\right) \left( {Y, W}\right) , Z}\right\rangle
\]

by Proposition 2.3.4. Meanwhile, by Proposition 2.3.1 and (2.3.13) we have

\[
\left\langle  {\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}\Pi }\right) \left( {X, W}\right) , Z}\right\rangle   = Y\langle \Pi \left( {X, W}\right) , Z\rangle
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}Y\left\lbrack  {\left( {{\nabla }_{W}h}\right) \left( {X, Z}\right)  + \left( {{\nabla }_{X}h}\right) \left( {W, Z}\right)  - \left( {{\nabla }_{Z}h}\right) \left( {X, W}\right) }\right\rbrack
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack  {\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{W}h}\right) \left( {X, Z}\right)  + \left( {{\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{X}h}\right) \left( {W, Z}\right)  - \left( {{\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{Z}h}\right) \left( {X, W}\right) }\right\rbrack
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack  {{\nabla }_{Y, W}^{2}h\left( {X, Z}\right)  + {\nabla }_{Y, X}^{2}h\left( {W, Z}\right)  - {\nabla }_{Y, Z}^{2}h\left( {X, W}\right) }\right\rbrack  ,
\]

and hence

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\langle R\left( {X, Y}\right) , W, Z\rangle  = h\left( {R\left( {X, Y}\right) W, Z}\right)  + \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack  {{\nabla }_{Y, W}^{2}h\left( {X, Z}\right)  - {\nabla }_{X, W}^{2}h\left( {Y, Z}\right) }\right.
\]

\[
+ {\nabla }_{Y, X}^{2}h\left( {W, Z}\right)  - {\nabla }_{X, Y}^{2}h\left( {W, Z}\right)
\]

\[
\left. {-{\nabla }_{Y, Z}^{2}h\left( {X, W}\right)  + {\nabla }_{X, Z}^{2}h\left( {Y, W}\right) }\right\rbrack  .
\]

We conclude by using (2.3.5).

Proposition 2.3.6. For any \( t \) -dependent tensor \( \alpha  \in  \Gamma \left( {{ \otimes  }^{2}{T}^{ * }\mathcal{M}}\right) \) , there holds

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {\operatorname{tr}\alpha }\right)  =  - \langle h,\alpha \rangle  + \operatorname{tr}\frac{\partial \alpha }{\partial t}.
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: Proposition 2.3.6. For any \( t \) -dependent tensor \( \alpha \in \Gamma \left( {{ \otimes }^{2}{T}^{ * }\mathcal{M}}\right) \) , there holds \[ \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {\operatorname{tr}\alpha }\right) = - \langle h,\alpha \rangle + \operatorname{tr}\frac{\partial \alpha }{\partial t}. \]

\]

nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow
nodes.section_title: 2.3. Deformation of geometric quantities as the Riemannian metric is deformed
nodes.content:
Proposition 2.3.7.

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\operatorname{Ric} =  - \frac{1}{2}{\Delta }_{L}h - \frac{1}{2}{\mathcal{L}}_{{\left( \delta G\left( h\right) \right) }^{\# }}g, \tag{2.3.6}
\]

where \( {\Delta }_{L} \) is the Lichnerowicz Laplacian

\[

\[

\]

\]

\]

\[
\operatorname{tr}{\nabla }_{X, \cdot  }^{2}h\left( {\cdot , W}\right)  =  - \left( {\nabla {\delta h}}\right) \left( {X, W}\right) .
\]

\[

\]

\[

\[

\]

\[

\]

which together with (2.3.10) is what we wanted to prove.

nodes.content:
Remark 2.3.8. In the definition of the Lichnerowicz Laplacian above, we have viewed the Ricci tensor as a section of \( {T}^{ * }\mathcal{M} \otimes  T\mathcal{M} \) (using the metric). On such occasions, we will tend to write \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( X\right) \) for the vector field defined in terms of the usual \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( {\cdot , \cdot  }\right) \) by \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, Y}\right)  = \langle \operatorname{Ric}\left( X\right) , Y\rangle \) , or equivalently \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( X\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\left( \operatorname{Ric}\left( X, \cdot  \right) \right) }^{\# }. \)

A term \( {\mathcal{L}}_{X}g \) can be viewed as a ’symmetrized gradient’ of \( X \) - see [14, (2.62)] - and for any 1-form \( \omega \) we have

\[
{\mathcal{L}}_{{\omega }^{\# }}g\left( {X, W}\right)  = \nabla \omega \left( {X, W}\right)  + \nabla \omega \left( {W, X}\right) . \tag{2.3.8}
\]

In the special case that \( \omega  = {df} \) for some function \( f : \mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) , we then have

\[
{\mathcal{L}}_{{\left( df\right) }^{\# }}g = {\mathcal{L}}_{\left( \nabla f\right) }g = 2\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \tag{2.3.9}
\]

where \( \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \) is the Hessian - the symmetric tensor \( \nabla {df} \) - as before. Combining with (2.1.8) we can expand the final term of (2.3.6) as

\[
{\mathcal{L}}_{{\left( \delta G\left( h\right) \right) }^{\# }}g = {\mathcal{L}}_{{\left( \delta h\right) }^{\# }}g + \operatorname{Hess}\left( {\operatorname{tr}h}\right) . \tag{2.3.10}
\]

It will be important during the proof \( {}^{3} \) to be able to juggle different formulations of the lower order terms in the definition of \( {\Delta }_{L} \) . First, we have

(2.3.11)

\[
h\left( {X,\operatorname{Ric}\left( W\right) }\right)  = \langle h\left( {X, \cdot  }\right) ,\operatorname{Ric}\left( {W, \cdot  }\right) \rangle  = \operatorname{tr}h\left( {X, \cdot  }\right)  \otimes  \operatorname{Ric}\left( {W, \cdot  }\right)
\]

\[
=  - \operatorname{tr}h\left( {R\left( {W, \cdot  }\right) \cdot , X}\right) ,
\]

which one can easily check with respect to an orthonormal frame \( \left\{  {e}_{i}\right\} \) ; for example

\[
\operatorname{tr}h\left( {X, \cdot  }\right)  \otimes  \operatorname{Ric}\left( {W, \cdot  }\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}h\left( {X,{e}_{i}}\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( {W,{e}_{i}}\right)  = h\left( {X,\operatorname{Ric}\left( {W,{e}_{i}}\right) {e}_{i}}\right)
\]

\[
= h\left( {X,\operatorname{Ric}\left( W\right) }\right) .
\]

Similarly, we have

\[
\operatorname{tr}h\left( {R\left( {X, \cdot  }\right) W, \cdot  }\right)  = \langle \operatorname{Rm}\left( {X,\cdot , W, \cdot  }\right) , h\rangle . \tag{2.3.12}
\]

By Proposition 2.3.6, we have

\[
\frac{\partial R}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Ric}}\right)  =  - \langle h,\operatorname{Ric}\rangle  + \operatorname{tr}\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) .

From Proposition 2.3.7, and (2.3.10) we then see that

\[

\]

Expanding the definition of \( {\Delta }_{L} \) using (2.3.11) and (2.3.12) gives

\[
{\Delta }_{L}\left( {X, W}\right)  = {\Delta h}\left( {X, W}\right)  - \langle h\left( {X, \cdot  }\right) ,\operatorname{Ric}\left( {W, \cdot  }\right) \rangle
\]

\[
- \langle h\left( {W, \cdot  }\right) ,\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, \cdot  }\right) \rangle  + 2\langle \operatorname{Rm}\left( {X,\cdot , W, \cdot  }\right) , h\rangle ,
\]

making it easier to see that

\[
\operatorname{tr}{\Delta }_{L}h = \operatorname{tr}{\Delta h} - \langle h,\operatorname{Ric}\rangle  - \langle h,\operatorname{Ric}\rangle  + 2\langle h,\operatorname{Ric}\rangle  = \Delta \left( {\operatorname{tr}h}\right) . \tag{2.3.16}
\]

Meanwhile, by (2.3.8),

\[
\operatorname{tr}{\mathcal{L}}_{\left( \delta h\right) }\# g =  - 2{\delta }^{2}h \tag{2.3.17}
\]

Combining (2.3.15), (2.3.16) and (2.3.17) gives our conclusion

\[
\frac{\partial R}{\partial t} =  - \langle h,\operatorname{Ric}\rangle  + {\delta }^{2}h - \Delta \left( {\operatorname{tr}h}\right) .
\]

The divergence theorem tells us that for a fixed 1-form \( \alpha \) ,

\[

(Note that \( \delta  = {\left( -1\right) }^{n\left( {p + 1}\right)  + 1} * d * \) on a p-form, and hence \( \left( {\delta \alpha }\right) {dV} = ( \pm   * \; d * \alpha ){dV} =  \pm  d\left( {*\alpha }\right) \) .) This enables us to integrate by parts: if \( f : \mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) , then

\[
\delta \left( {f\alpha }\right)  =  - \langle {df},\alpha \rangle  + f\left( {\delta \alpha }\right) \tag{2.3.18}
\]

so by integrating,

\[
\int \langle {df},\alpha \rangle {dV} = \int f\left( {\delta \alpha }\right) {dV}. \tag{2.3.19}
\]

Applying this formula with \( \alpha \) equal to our time-dependent 1-form \( \omega \) , and differentiating with respect to \( t \) , gives

\[
\int \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {\delta \omega }\right) {fdV} =  - \int h\left( {{df},\omega }\right) {dV} + \int \left\langle  {{df},\frac{\partial \omega }{\partial t}}\right\rangle  {dV}
\]

\[
- \int \left\lbrack  {\left( {\delta \omega }\right) f-\langle {df},\omega \rangle }\right\rbrack  \frac{1}{2}\left( {\operatorname{tr}h}\right) {dV}
\]

where we have used \( \frac{\partial }{\partial t}{g}^{ij} =  - {h}^{ij} \) to obtain the sign in the first term on the right-hand side.

By applying (2.3.18) with \( \alpha  = \omega \) to the final term, and (2.3.19) with \( \alpha  = \frac{\partial \omega }{\partial t} \) to the penultimate term,

\]

\]

\]

In particular, we have the analogue of (2.3.18) in the proof of the last proposition, that for all \( S \in  \Gamma \left( {{\operatorname{Sym}}^{2}{T}^{ * }\mathcal{M}}\right) \)

\[
\left( {\delta S}\right) Z = \delta \left( {S\left( {\cdot , Z}\right) }\right)  + \frac{1}{2}\left\langle  {S,{\mathcal{L}}_{Z}g}\right\rangle  , \tag{2.3.20}
\]

and also, by differentiating, and applying Proposition 2.3.1

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\mathcal{L}}_{Z}g\left( {X, Y}\right)  = h\left( {{\nabla }_{X}Z, Y}\right)  + h\left( {X,{\nabla }_{Y}Z}\right)  + {\nabla }_{Z}h\left( {X, Y}\right) . \tag{2.3.21}
\]

By the definition \( G\left( T\right)  = T - \frac{1}{2}\left( {\operatorname{tr}T}\right) g \) of (2.1.7) and Proposition 2.3.6 we have

\[
\frac{\partial G\left( T\right) }{\partial t} =  - \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial \operatorname{tr}T}{\partial t}g - \frac{1}{2}\left( {\operatorname{tr}T}\right) h = \frac{1}{2}\langle h, T\rangle g - \frac{1}{2}\left( {\operatorname{tr}T}\right) h. \tag{2.3.22}
\]

Having compiled these preliminary formulae, we apply (2.3.20) with \( S = \; G\left( T\right) \) , and differentiate with respect to \( t \) to give

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\delta G}\left( T\right) }\right) Z = \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\delta \left( {G\left( T\right) \left( {\cdot , Z}\right) }\right)  + \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left\langle  {G\left( T\right) ,{\mathcal{L}}_{Z}g}\right\rangle  . \tag{2.3.23}
\]

We deal with the two terms on the right-hand side separately. For the first, by Proposition 2.3.10 and (2.3.22),

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\delta \left( {G\left( T\right) \left( {\cdot , Z}\right) }\right)  = \delta \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {G\left( T\right) \left( {\cdot , Z}\right) }\right)  + \langle h,\nabla \left( {G\left( T\right) \left( {\cdot , Z}\right) }\right) \rangle  - \langle {\delta G}\left( h\right) , G\left( T\right) \left( {\cdot , Z}\right) \rangle
\]

\[

\]

\[
+ \langle h, G\left( T\right) ( \cdot  ,\nabla .Z\rangle  - \langle {\delta G}\left( h\right) , T\left( {\cdot , Z}\right)  - \frac{1}{2}\left( {\operatorname{tr}T}\right) g\left( {\cdot , Z}\right) \rangle
\]

\[
=  - \frac{1}{2}Z\langle h, T\rangle  + \frac{1}{2}\langle h, T\rangle \delta \left( {g\left( {\cdot , Z}\right) }\right)  + h\left( {\nabla \left( \frac{\operatorname{tr}T}{2}\right) , Z}\right)
\]

\[
- \frac{1}{2}\left( {\operatorname{tr}T}\right) \delta \left( {h\left( {\cdot , Z}\right) }\right)  + \langle h,\nabla T\left( {\cdot ,\cdot , Z}\right) \rangle  + \left\langle  {h, - \frac{1}{2}d\left( {\operatorname{tr}T}\right)  \otimes  g\left( {\cdot , Z}\right) }\right\rangle
\]

\[
+ \langle h, G\left( T\right) \left( {\cdot ,\nabla .Z}\right) \rangle  - T\left( {{\left( \delta G\left( h\right) \right) }^{\# }, Z}\right)  + \frac{1}{2}\left( {\operatorname{tr}T}\right) \left( {{\delta G}\left( h\right) }\right) Z.
\]

Using (2.3.20) with \( S = g \) and also with \( S = h \) , and recalling (2.1.8), we then have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\delta \left( {G\left( T\right) \left( {\cdot , Z}\right) }\right)  =  - \frac{1}{2}\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}h, T}\right\rangle   - \frac{1}{2}\left\langle  {h,{\nabla }_{Z}T}\right\rangle   - \frac{1}{4}\langle h, T\rangle \operatorname{tr}{\mathcal{L}}_{Z}g
\]

\[
- \frac{1}{2}\left( {\operatorname{tr}T}\right) \left\lbrack  {\left( {\delta h}\right) Z - \frac{1}{2}\left\langle  {h,{\mathcal{L}}_{Z}g}\right\rangle  }\right\rbrack   + \langle h,\nabla T\left( {\cdot ,\cdot , Z}\right) \rangle
\]

\[
+ \langle h, G\left( T\right) \left( {\cdot ,\nabla .Z}\right) \rangle  - T\left( {{\left( \delta G\left( h\right) \right) }^{\# }, Z}\right)  + \frac{1}{2}\left( {\operatorname{tr}T}\right) \left( {\delta h}\right) Z
\]

\[
+ \frac{1}{4}\left( {\operatorname{tr}T}\right) Z\left( {\operatorname{tr}h}\right)
\]

\[
= \left( {-T\left( {{\left( \delta G\left( h\right) \right) }^{\# }, Z}\right) +\langle h,\nabla T\left( {\cdot ,\cdot , Z}\right) \rangle  - \frac{1}{2}\left\langle  {h,{\nabla }_{Z}T}\right\rangle  }\right)
\]

\[
- \frac{1}{2}\left\langle  {{\nabla }_{Z}h, G\left( T\right) }\right\rangle   - \frac{1}{4}\langle h, T\rangle \operatorname{tr}{\mathcal{L}}_{Z}g + \frac{1}{4}\left( {\operatorname{tr}T}\right) \left\langle  {h,{\mathcal{L}}_{Z}g}\right\rangle
\]

\[
+ \langle h, G\left( T\right) \left( {\cdot ,\nabla .Z}\right) \rangle \text{ . }
\]

For the second term of (2.3.23), we recall (2.3.22) and (2.3.21), and think in the same manner as in the proof of Proposition 2.3.6, to compute

\[
\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left\langle  {G\left( T\right) ,{\mathcal{L}}_{Z}g}\right\rangle   = \frac{1}{2}\left\langle  {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}G\left( T\right) ,{\mathcal{L}}_{Z}g}\right\rangle   + \frac{1}{2}\left\langle  {G\left( T\right) ,\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\mathcal{L}}_{Z}g}\right\rangle
\]

\[
- \langle h, G\left( T\right) \left( {\cdot ,\nabla .Z}\right) \rangle  - \langle G\left( T\right) , h\left( {\cdot ,\nabla .Z}\right) \rangle
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}\left\langle  {\frac{1}{2}\langle h, T\rangle g - \frac{1}{2}\left( {\operatorname{tr}T}\right) h,{\mathcal{L}}_{Z}g}\right\rangle   + \frac{1}{2}\left\langle  {G\left( T\right) ,{2h}\left( {\nabla .Z, \cdot  }\right)  + {\nabla }_{Z}h}\right\rangle
\]

\[
- \langle h, G\left( T\right) \left( {\cdot ,{\nabla }_{ \cdot  }Z}\right) \rangle  - \langle G\left( T\right) , h\left( {\cdot ,{\nabla }_{ \cdot  }Z}\right) \rangle
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{4}\langle h, T\rangle \operatorname{tr}{\mathcal{L}}_{Z}g - \frac{1}{4}\left( {\operatorname{tr}T}\right) \left\langle  {h,{\mathcal{L}}_{Z}g}\right\rangle
\]

\[
+ \frac{1}{2}\left\langle  {G\left( T\right) ,{\nabla }_{Z}h}\right\rangle   - \langle h, G\left( T\right) \left( {\cdot ,\nabla .Z}\right) \rangle .
\]

Combining these two formulae with (2.3.23), we conclude

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\delta G}\left( T\right) }\right) Z =  - T\left( {{\left( \delta G\left( h\right) \right) }^{\# }, Z}\right)  + \langle h,\nabla T\left( {\cdot ,\cdot , Z}\right) \rangle  - \frac{1}{2}\left\langle  {h,{\nabla }_{Z}T}\right\rangle  .
\]

\]

\]

nodes.proof:
This sort of calculation is probably easiest to perform in normal coordinates (or alternatively with respect to an appropriate orthonormal frame) about an arbitrary point \( p \) . The main ingredients are the Bianchi identities. To begin with, we require the second Bianchi identity for the first derivative of Rm,

\[
{\nabla }_{i}{R}_{jkla} + {\nabla }_{j}{R}_{kila} + {\nabla }_{k}{R}_{ijla} = 0.
\]

(Here \( {\nabla }_{i}{R}_{jkla} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \left( {{\nabla }_{\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}}\operatorname{Rm}}\right) \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{j}},\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{k}},\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{l}},\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{a}}}\right) \) .) Taking one further derivative, tracing, and restricting our attention to the point \( p \) , we find that

\[
\Delta {R}_{jkla} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}{R}_{kila} - {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{k}{R}_{jila} = 0. \tag{2.4.1}
\]

(Here \( \Delta {R}_{jkla} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \left( {\Delta \mathrm{{Rm}}}\right) \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{j}},\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{k}},\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{l}},\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{a}}}\right) \) .) Note that when considering expressions at the point \( p \) , where the vectors \( \left\{  \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}\right\} \) are orthonormal, we are able to use only lower indices, and the usual summation convention makes sense.

We focus on the second term of (2.4.1), since the third term differs only by a sign and a permutation of \( k \) and \( j \) . By the Ricci identity (2.1.2) we have

\[
{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}{R}_{kila} - {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{i}{R}_{kila} =  - {R}_{jikc}{R}_{cila} - {R}_{jiic}{R}_{kcla} - {R}_{jilc}{R}_{kica} - {R}_{jiac}{R}_{kilc}.
\]

Now \( {R}_{jiic} =  - {R}_{jc} \) with our sign convention, and we have the first Bianchi identity \( {R}_{\text{ cila }} =  - {R}_{\text{ ilca }} - {R}_{\text{ lcia }} \) , and thus

\[
{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}{R}_{kila} - {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{i}{R}_{kila} = {R}_{jikc}{R}_{ilca} + {R}_{jikc}{R}_{lcia} + {R}_{jc}{R}_{kcla}
\]

\[
- {R}_{jilc}{R}_{kica} - {R}_{jiac}{R}_{kilc}
\]

\[
= {R}_{jc}{R}_{kcla} + {B}_{jkla} - {B}_{jkal} + {B}_{jlka} - {B}_{jakl}.
\]

(2.4.2)

To handle the second term on the left-hand side of (2.4.2), we return to the second Bianchi identity, with permuted indices

\[
{\nabla }_{b}{R}_{laki} + {\nabla }_{l}{R}_{abki} + {\nabla }_{a}{R}_{blki} = 0,
\]

near \( p \) , and trace to give

\[
{g}^{bi}{\nabla }_{b}{R}_{kila} + {\nabla }_{l}{R}_{ak} - {\nabla }_{a}{R}_{lk} = 0.
\]

Applying \( {\nabla }_{j} \) and restricting our attention to \( p \) , we see that

\[
{\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{i}{R}_{kila} = {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{a}{R}_{lk} - {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{l}{R}_{ak},
\]

which may be plugged into (2.4.2) to give

\[
{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}{R}_{kila} = {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{a}{R}_{lk} - {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{l}{R}_{ak} + {R}_{jc}{R}_{kcla}
\]

\[
+ {B}_{jkla} - {B}_{jkal} + {B}_{jlka} - {B}_{jakl}.
\]

Finally, we apply this twice to (2.4.1) (once with \( k \) and \( j \) permuted) to conclude

\[
\Delta {R}_{jkla} =  - {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{a}{R}_{lk} + {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{l}{R}_{ak} + {\nabla }_{k}{\nabla }_{a}{R}_{lj} - {\nabla }_{k}{\nabla }_{l}{R}_{aj}
\]

\[
- {R}_{jc}{R}_{kcla} + {R}_{kc}{R}_{jcla} - 2\left( {{B}_{jkla} - {B}_{jkal} + {B}_{jlka} - {B}_{jakl}}\right) .
\]

nodes.content:
Proposition 2.5.1. Under the Ricci flow, the curvature tensor evolves according to

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\operatorname{Rm}\left( {X, Y, W, Z}\right)  = \left( {\Delta \operatorname{Rm}}\right) \left( {X, Y, W, Z}\right)

\[

\]

\[
+ 2(B\left( {X, Y, W, Z}\right)  - B\left( {X, Y, Z, W}\right)
\]

\[
+ B\left( {X, W, Y, Z}\right)  - B\left( {X, Z, Y, W}\right) ).
\]

Therefore, the curvature tensor Rm evolves under a heat equation.

nodes.content:
Theorem 3.1.1 (Weak maximum principle for scalars). Suppose, for \( t \in \; \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) (where \( 0 < T < \infty \) ) that \( g\left( t\right) \) is a smooth family of metrics, and \( X\left( t\right) \) is a smooth family of vector fields on a closed manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) . Let \( F \) : \( \mathbb{R} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) be smooth. Suppose that \( u \in  {C}^{\infty }\left( {\mathcal{M} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack  ,\mathbb{R}}\right) \) solves

\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} \leq  {\Delta }_{g\left( t\right) }u + \langle X\left( t\right) ,\nabla u\rangle  + F\left( {u, t}\right) . \tag{3.1.1}
\]

Suppose further that \( \phi  : \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) solves

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{ll} \frac{d\phi }{dt} &  = F\left( {\phi \left( t\right) , t}\right) \\  \phi \left( 0\right) &  = \alpha  \in  \mathbb{R}. \end{array}\right. \tag{3.1.2}
\]

If \( u\left( {\cdot ,0}\right)  \leq  \alpha \) , then \( u\left( {\cdot , t}\right)  \leq  \phi \left( t\right) \) for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) .

nodes.proof:
For \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , consider the ODE

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{ll} \frac{d{\phi }_{\varepsilon }}{dt} &  = F\left( {{\phi }_{\varepsilon }\left( t\right) , t}\right)  + \varepsilon \\  {\phi }_{\varepsilon }\left( 0\right) &  = \alpha  + \varepsilon  \in  \mathbb{R}, \end{array}\right. \tag{3.1.3}
\]

for a new function \( {\phi }_{\varepsilon } : \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) . Basic ODE theory tells us that there exists \( {\varepsilon }_{0} > 0 \) such that for \( 0 < \varepsilon  \leq  {\varepsilon }_{0} \) there exists a solution \( {\phi }_{\varepsilon } \) on \( \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . (Here we are using the existence of \( \phi \) asserted in the hypotheses, and the fact that \( T < \infty \) .) Moreover, \( {\phi }_{\varepsilon } \rightarrow  \phi \) uniformly as \( \varepsilon  \downarrow  0 \) . Consequently, we need only prove that \( u\left( {\cdot , t}\right)  < {\phi }_{\varepsilon }\left( t\right) \) for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) and arbitrary \( \varepsilon  \in  \left( {0,{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) \) .

If this were not true, then we could choose \( \varepsilon  \in  \left( {0,{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right) \) and \( {t}_{0} \in  (0, T\rbrack \) where \( u\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right)  < {\phi }_{\varepsilon }\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) fails. Without loss of generality we may assume that \( {t}_{0} \) is the earliest such time, and pick \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) so that \( u\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  = {\phi }_{\varepsilon }\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) . Using the fact that \( u\left( {x, s}\right)  - {\phi }_{\varepsilon }\left( s\right) \) is negative for \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right) \) and zero for \( s = {t}_{0} \) , we must have

\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  - {\phi }_{\varepsilon }^{\prime }\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \geq  0.
\]

Moreover, since \( x \) is a maximum of \( u\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) \) , it follows that \( {\Delta u}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  0 \) and \( \nabla u\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  = 0 \) .

Combining these facts with the inequality (3.1.1) for \( u \) and equation (3.1.3) for \( {\phi }_{\varepsilon } \) , we get the contradiction that

\[
0 \geq  \left\lbrack  {\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} - {\Delta u}-\langle X,\nabla u\rangle  - F\left( {u, \cdot  }\right) }\right\rbrack  \left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {\phi }_{\varepsilon }^{\prime }\left( {t}_{0}\right)  - F\left( {{\phi }_{\varepsilon }\left( {t}_{0}\right) ,{t}_{0}}\right)  = \varepsilon  > 0.
\]

Theorem 3.2.1. Suppose \( g\left( t\right) \) is a Ricci flow on a closed manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) , for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . If \( R \geq  \alpha  \in  \mathbb{R} \) at time \( t = 0 \) , then for all times \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) ,

\[

\]

nodes.content:
Remark 3.2.8. One consequence of Corollary 3.2.7 is the following: If our Ricci flow is defined for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) , then

\[
\bar{V} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  \infty }}\frac{V\left( t\right) }{{\left( 1 + \frac{2\left( {-\alpha }\right) }{n}t\right) }^{\frac{n}{2}}}
\]

exists. A rough principle within the work of Perelman is a local version of an assertion that if \( \bar{V} > 0 \) then the manifold is becoming hyperbolic. (If \( \bar{V} = 0 \) then the manifold is becoming like a graph manifold.) Recall from the discussion in Section 1.2.1 that if \( {g}_{0} \) is exactly hyperbolic then \( g\left( t\right)  = \left( {1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) t}\right) {g}_{0} \) , so \( V\left( t\right)  = {\left( 1 + 2\left( n - 1\right) t\right) }^{\frac{n}{2}}V\left( 0\right) \) . See [32] for more information.

nodes.content: Remark 3.2.9. The scalar curvature is just one of many types of curvature for which positivity is preserved under the Ricci flow on closed manifolds. Other notable preserved curvature conditions include positive curvature operator in any dimension [20], positive isotropic curvature in four dimensions [23], and as we shall see in Chapter 9, in dimension three (or less) positive Ricci curvature. In contrast, negative curvatures are not preserved in general under Ricci flow (with the notable exception of scalar curvature in dimension two).

nodes.content:
Theorem 3.3.1. Suppose that \( M > 0 \) and \( g\left( t\right) \) is a Ricci flow on a closed manifold \( {\mathcal{M}}^{n} \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{M}}\right\rbrack \) . For all \( k \in  \mathbb{N} \) there exists \( C = C\left( {n, k}\right) \) such that if \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right|  \leq  M \) throughout \( \mathcal{M} \times  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{M}}\right\rbrack \) , then for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{M}}\right\rbrack \) ,

\[
\left| {{\nabla }^{k}\mathrm{{Rm}}}\right|  \leq  \frac{CM}{{t}^{\frac{k}{2}}}. \tag{3.3.1}
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: Theorem 3.3.1. Suppose that \( M > 0 \) and \( g\left( t\right) \) is a Ricci flow on a closed manifold \( {\mathcal{M}}^{n} \) for \( t \in \left\lbrack {0,\frac{1}{M}}\right\rbrack \) . For all \( k \in \mathbb{N} \) there exists \( C = C\left( {n, k}\right) \) such that if \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| \leq M \) throughout \( \mathcal{M} \times \left\lbrack {0,\frac{1}{M}}\right\rbrack \) , then for all \( t \...

nodes.proof:
We will just give a proof of the case \( k = 1 \) here. The higher derivative estimates follow along the same lines by induction.

By Remark 2.5.2 we have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{Rm}} = \Delta \mathrm{{Rm}} + \mathrm{{Rm}} * \mathrm{{Rm}}. \tag{3.3.2}
\]

Specialising some of our formulae for commuting derivatives to our situation, we find from (2.1.6) that

\[
\nabla \left( {\Delta \mathrm{{Rm}}}\right)  = \Delta \left( {\nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}}\right)  + \mathrm{{Rm}} * \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}},
\]

and from (2.3.3) that

\[
\nabla \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{Rm}} = \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\nabla \mathrm{{Rm}} + \mathrm{{Rm}} * \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}.
\]

Therefore, taking the covariant derivative of (3.3.2), we have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\nabla \mathrm{{Rm}} = \Delta \left( {\nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}}\right)  + \mathrm{{Rm}} * \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}. \tag{3.3.3}
\]

Computing as in the proof of Proposition 3.2.10, we find that

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {\nabla }^{2}\mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} + C\left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| {\left| \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} \tag{3.3.4}
\]

\[
\leq  \Delta {\left| \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} + C\left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| {\left| \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2}.
\]

Set \( u\left( {x, t}\right)  = t{\left| \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} + \alpha {\left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} \) for some \( \alpha \) to be picked later. Then using (3.3.4) and Proposition 3.2.10, we have that

\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} \leq  {\left| \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} + t\left( {\Delta {\left| \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} + C\left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| {\left| \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2}}\right)
\]

\[
+ \alpha \left( {\Delta {\left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} + C{\left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{3}}\right)
\]

\[
= {\Delta u} + {\left| \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2}\left( {1 + {Ct}\left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right|  - {2\alpha }}\right)  + {C\alpha }{\left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{3}.
\]

By hypothesis, \( \left| \operatorname{Rm}\right|  \leq  M \) and \( t \leq  \frac{1}{M} \) . Thus

\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} \leq  {\Delta u} + {\left| \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2}\left( {1 + C - {2\alpha }}\right)  + {C\alpha }{M}^{3}
\]

for \( C = C\left( n\right) \) . For sufficiently large \( \alpha \) (say \( \left. {\alpha  = \frac{1}{2}\left( {1 + C}\right) }\right) \) we have that

\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} \leq  {\Delta u} + C\left( n\right) {M}^{3}.
\]

Note further that \( u\left( {\cdot ,0}\right)  = \alpha {\left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} \leq  \alpha {M}^{2} \) . Therefore by the weak maximum principle, Theorem 3.1.1 (comparing with \( \phi \left( t\right)  = \alpha {M}^{2} + {Ct}{M}^{3} \) satisfying \( {\phi }^{\prime }\left( t\right)  = C{M}^{3} \) and \( \phi \left( 0\right)  = \alpha {M}^{2} \) ) it follows that

\[
u\left( {\cdot , t}\right)  \leq  \alpha {M}^{2} + {Ct}{M}^{3} \leq  C{M}^{2}.
\]

Hence

\[
t{\left| \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} \leq  u\left( {\cdot , t}\right)  \leq  C{M}^{2},
\]

so

\[
\left| {\nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}}\right|  \leq  \frac{CM}{\sqrt{t}}
\]

for some \( C = C\left( n\right) \) .

Corollary 3.3.2. Suppose that \( M > 0 \) and \( g\left( t\right) \) is a Ricci flow on a closed manifold \( {\mathcal{M}}^{n} \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{M}}\right\rbrack \) . For all \( j, k \in \{ 0\} \cup \mathbb{N} \) , there exists a constant \( C = C\left( {j, k, n}\right) \) such that \( \dot{if}\left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| \leq M \) throughout \( \mathcal{M} \times \left\lbrack {0,\frac{1}{M}}...

nodes.proof:
By rescaling the entire flow, as in Section 1.2.3, we first note that it suffices to prove the corollary at \( t = 1 \) . Since this time lies within the interval \( \left( {0,\frac{1}{M}}\right\rbrack \) , we know that

\[
M \leq  1\text{ . } \tag{3.3.6}
\]

By (2.5.2), we know that

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{Rm}} = \Delta \mathrm{{Rm}} + \mathrm{{Rm}} * \mathrm{{Rm}}
\]

and hence, since \( M \leq  1 \) , we find at \( t = 1 \) that

\[
\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{Rm}}}\right|  \leq  \left| {\Delta \mathrm{{Rm}}}\right|  + \left| {\mathrm{{Rm}} * \mathrm{{Rm}}}\right|  \leq  C\left( {M + {M}^{2}}\right)  \leq  {CM},
\]

by Theorem 3.3.1. Meanwhile, by (3.3.3), we have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\nabla \mathrm{{Rm}} = \Delta \left( {\nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}}\right)  + \mathrm{{Rm}} * \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}},
\]

and may again use the fact that \( M \leq  1 \) to give, at \( t = 1 \) ,

\[
\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}}\right|  \leq  C\left| {{\nabla }^{3}\mathrm{{Rm}}}\right|  + C\left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| \left| {\nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}}\right|  \leq  C\left( {M + {M}^{2}}\right)  \leq  {CM}.
\]

We have dealt with the cases \( \left( {j, k}\right)  = \left( {1,0}\right) \) and \( \left( {1,1}\right) \) . To handle the case \( j = 1 \) and \( k > 1 \) , we can use induction to show that \( \frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\nabla }^{k}\mathrm{{Rm}} \) can be written as a *-composition of terms involving Rm and its covariant derivatives, since by (2.3.3) we know that

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\nabla }^{k}\mathrm{{Rm}} = \nabla \frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\nabla }^{k - 1}\mathrm{{Rm}} + {\nabla }^{k - 1}\mathrm{{Rm}} * \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}.
\]

By taking norms, as for the first two cases, each of these terms is bounded at \( t = 1 \) as required.

We have dealt with the case \( j = 1 \) , using the case \( j = 0 \) handled by Theorem 3.3.1. One can see with hindsight that this is the first inductive step to proving the corollary for all \( j \) . Indeed, by what we have seen above, any expression \( \frac{{\partial }^{l + 1}}{\partial {t}^{l + 1}}{\nabla }^{k}\operatorname{Rm} \) can immediately be written in terms of the \( l \) th \( t \) derivative of terms involving only \( \mathrm{{Rm}} \) and its spacial covariant derivatives.

Theorem 3.3.3 (Shi). Suppose that \( g\left( t\right) \) is a Ricci flow defined on an arbitrary (boundaryless) manifold \( U \) , for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , with no requirement that \( g\left( t\right) \) is complete. Suppose further that \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right|  \leq  M \) on \( U \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , and that \( p \in  U \) and \( r > 0 \) are such that \( \overline{{B}_{g\left( 0\right) }\left( {p, r}\right) } \subset  U \) . Then

\[

nodes.title: 4.1. Linear scalar PDE
nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow

nodes.label: Definition 4.1-extra-1
nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow
nodes.content:
### 4.1 Linear scalar PDE

Consider a second order PDE on \( \Omega  \subset  {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) for a function \( u : \Omega  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) of the form

\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = {a}_{ij}{\partial }_{i}{\partial }_{j}u + {b}_{i}{\partial }_{i}u + {cu} \tag{4.1.1}
\]

where \( {\partial }_{i} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}} \) and \( {a}_{ij},{b}_{i}, c : \Omega  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) are smooth coefficients. Such an equation is called parabolic if \( {a}_{ij} \) is uniformly positive definite - that is, if there exists \( \lambda  > 0 \) such that

\[
{a}_{ij}{\xi }_{i}{\xi }_{j} \geq  \lambda {\left| \xi \right| }^{2} \tag{4.1.2}
\]

for all \( \xi  \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . For example, the heat equation \( \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = {\Delta u} \) is a parabolic PDE.

This notion extends to manifolds. Let \( \mathcal{M} \) be closed and consider the PDE for \( u : \mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) given by

\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = L\left( u\right) \tag{4.1.3}
\]

where \( L : {C}^{\infty }\left( \mathcal{M}\right)  \rightarrow  {C}^{\infty }\left( \mathcal{M}\right) \) can be written with respect to local coordinates \( \left\{  {x}^{i}\right\} \) as

\[
L\left( u\right)  = {a}_{ij}{\partial }_{i}{\partial }_{j}u + {b}_{i}{\partial }_{i}u + {cu}
\]

for \( {a}_{ij},{b}_{i} \) and \( c \) locally defined smooth, real coefficients. Equation (4.1.3) is said to be parabolic if \( {a}_{ij} \) is positive definite for all \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) . Note that this is well defined, independent of the choice of coordinates. (See also Section 4.2.)

nodes.content:
There is a good theory for such equations. For example, given a smooth initial function \( {u}_{0} : \mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) , there exists a smooth solution \( u : \mathcal{M} \times  \lbrack 0,\infty ) \rightarrow \; \mathbb{R} \) to

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{ll} \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = L\left( u\right) & \text{ on }\mathcal{M} \times  \lbrack 0,\infty ) \\  u\left( 0\right)  = {u}_{0} & \text{ on }\mathcal{M}. \end{array}\right.
\]

We also have uniqueness: Suppose that \( \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = L\left( u\right) \) and \( \frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = L\left( v\right) \) on \( \mathcal{M} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . If either \( u\left( 0\right)  = v\left( 0\right) \) or \( u\left( T\right)  = v\left( T\right) \) holds, then \( u\left( t\right)  = v\left( t\right) \) for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) .

nodes.title: 4.2. The principal symbol
nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow

nodes.label: Definition 4.2-extra-1
nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow
nodes.content:
### 4.2 The principal symbol

Define the principal symbol \( \sigma \left( L\right)  : {T}^{ * }\mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) by

\[
\sigma \left( L\right) \left( {x,\xi }\right)  = {a}_{ij}\left( x\right) {\xi }_{i}{\xi }_{j}. \tag{4.2.1}
\]

This is well defined, independent of the choice of coordinates. An alternative definition would be the following: Given \( \left( {x,\xi }\right)  \in  {T}^{ * }\mathcal{M} \) , and \( \phi , f : \mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) smooth with \( {d\phi }\left( x\right)  = \xi \) , define

\[
\sigma \left( L\right) \left( {x,\xi }\right) f\left( x\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{s \rightarrow  \infty }}{s}^{-2}{e}^{-{s\phi }\left( x\right) }L\left( {{e}^{s\phi }f}\right) \left( x\right) . \tag{4.2.2}
\]

To check that this is well defined, and that the two definitions are consistent, we calculate

\[
{\partial }_{i}\left( {{e}^{s\phi }f}\right) \left( x\right)  = s{\partial }_{i}\phi \left( x\right) \left( {{e}^{s\phi }f}\right) \left( x\right)  + {e}^{s\phi }{\partial }_{i}f\left( x\right) ,
\]

and so

\[
{e}^{-{s\phi }}{\partial }_{i}{\partial }_{j}\left( {{e}^{s\phi }f}\right) \left( x\right)  = {s}^{2}{\partial }_{i}\phi \left( x\right) {\partial }_{j}\phi \left( x\right) f\left( x\right)  + s\left( \cdots \right)  + {s}^{0}\left( \cdots \right)
\]

where we have collected up terms according to whether they are quadratic, linear or constant in \( s \) , and care only about the quadratic term. Therefore

\[
{e}^{-{s\phi }\left( x\right) }L\left( {{e}^{s\phi }f}\right) \left( x\right)  = {s}^{2}{a}_{ij}{\partial }_{i}\phi \left( x\right) {\partial }_{j}\phi \left( x\right) f\left( x\right)  + s\left( \cdots \right)  + {s}^{0}\left( \cdots \right)
\]

and so

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{s \rightarrow  \infty }}{s}^{-2}{e}^{-{s\phi }\left( x\right) }L\left( {{e}^{s\phi }f}\right) \left( x\right)  = {a}_{ij}{\partial }_{i}\phi \left( x\right) {\partial }_{j}\phi \left( x\right) f\left( x\right)  = {a}_{ij}{\xi }_{i}{\xi }_{j}f\left( x\right) .
\]

Notice in particular that the second definition is independent of the choice of \( \phi \) and \( f \) (with \( {d\phi }\left( x\right)  = \xi \) ).

nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow

nodes.label: Definition 4.3-extra-1
nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow
nodes.content:
Let \( E \) be a smooth vector bundle over a closed manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) . Whereas above, we looked at functions \( u : \mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) , we now consider sections \( v \in  \Gamma \left( E\right) \) . Locally we may write \( v = {v}^{\alpha }{e}_{\alpha } \) for some local frame \( \left\{  {e}_{\alpha }\right\} \) . Consider the equation

\[
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = L\left( v\right) \tag{4.3.1}
\]

where \( L \) is a linear second order differential operator, by which we mean \( L : \Gamma \left( E\right)  \rightarrow  \Gamma \left( E\right) \) may be given locally, in terms of local coordinates \( \left\{  {x}^{i}\right\} \) on \( \mathcal{M} \) and a local frame \( \left\{  {e}_{\alpha }\right\} \) on \( E \) , as \( {}^{2} \)

\[
L\left( v\right)  = \left\lbrack  {{a}_{\alpha \beta }^{ij}{\partial }_{i}{\partial }_{j}{v}^{\beta } + {b}_{\alpha \beta }^{i}{\partial }_{i}{v}^{\beta } + {c}_{\alpha \beta }{v}^{\beta }}\right\rbrack  {e}_{\alpha }.
\]

We can again define the principal symbol - now \( \sigma \left( L\right)  : {\Pi }^{ * }\left( E\right)  \rightarrow  {\Pi }^{ * }\left( E\right) \) is a vector bundle homomorphism, where \( \Pi  : {T}^{ * }\mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathcal{M} \) denotes the bundle projection. Note that \( {\Pi }^{ * }\left( E\right) \) is a vector bundle over \( {T}^{ * }\mathcal{M} \) whose fibre at \( \left( {x,\xi }\right)  \in  {T}^{ * }\left( \mathcal{M}\right) \) is \( {E}_{x} \) . We define

\[
\sigma \left( L\right) \left( {x,\xi }\right) v = \left( {{a}_{\alpha \beta }^{ij}{\xi }_{i}{\xi }_{j}{v}^{\beta }}\right) {e}_{\alpha }. \tag{4.3.2}
\]

---

\( {}^{2} \) Don’t try to read the usual significance into whether we use lower or upper indices

---

Again, there exists a definition independent of coordinates: Given \( \left( {x,\xi }\right)  \in \; {T}^{ * }\mathcal{M} \) , for all \( v \in  \Gamma \left( E\right) \) and \( \phi  : \mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) with \( {d\phi }\left( x\right)  = \xi \) , define

\[
\sigma \left( L\right) \left( {x,\xi }\right) v = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{s \rightarrow  \infty }}{s}^{-2}{e}^{-{s\phi }\left( x\right) }L\left( {{e}^{s\phi }v}\right) \left( x\right) . \tag{4.3.3}
\]

For example, for a vector bundle with connection \( \nabla \) , if \( \Delta \) denotes the connection Laplacian, then

\[
\Delta \left( {{e}^{s\phi }v}\right)  = {e}^{s\phi }\left( {{s}^{2}{\left| d\phi \right| }^{2}v + \text{ lower order terms in }s}\right) ,
\]

and so \( \sigma \left( \Delta \right) \left( {x,\sigma }\right) v = {\left| \xi \right| }^{2}v \) because \( {d\phi } = \xi \) . Thus \( \sigma \left( \Delta \right) \left( {x,\xi }\right)  = {\left| \xi \right| }^{2} \) id.

nodes.content:
In practice we need to be able to discuss nonlinear PDE of the form

\[
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = P\left( v\right) \tag{4.3.5}
\]

where \( P \) is a quasilinear second order differential operator, by which we mean \( P : \Gamma \left( E\right)  \rightarrow  \Gamma \left( E\right) \) may be given locally, in terms of local coordinates \( \left\{  {x}^{i}\right\} \) on \( \mathcal{M} \) and a local frame \( \left\{  {e}_{\alpha }\right\} \) on \( E \) , as

\[
P\left( v\right)  = \left\lbrack  {{a}_{\alpha \beta }^{ij}\left( {x, v,\nabla v}\right) {\partial }_{i}{\partial }_{j}{v}^{\beta } + {b}^{\alpha }\left( {x, v,\nabla v}\right) }\right\rbrack  {e}_{\alpha }.
\]

Finally, the Ricci flow equation \( \frac{\partial g}{\partial t} =  - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( g\right) \) fits into this category, as we discuss in Section 5.1.

Given an arbitrary fixed section \( w \in  \Gamma \left( E\right) \) (independent of \( t \) ) we call (4.3.5) parabolic (again, strictly and strongly) at \( w \) if the linearisation of (4.3.5) at \( w \)

\[
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = \left\lbrack  {{DP}\left( w\right) }\right\rbrack  v
\]

is parabolic as just defined.

on the bundle \( E = {\operatorname{Sym}}^{2}{T}^{ * }\mathcal{M} \) . The linearisation of (5.1.1) is \( {}^{1} \)

\[
\frac{\partial h}{\partial t} = {Lh} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \left\lbrack  {{DQ}\left( g\right) }\right\rbrack  h = {\Delta }_{L}h + {\mathcal{L}}_{{\left( \delta G\left( h\right) \right) }^{\sharp }}g
\]

by Proposition 2.3.7. We wish to know, for arbitrary initial metric \( g \) , and corresponding \( L \) , whether \( \frac{\partial h}{\partial t} = L\left( h\right) \) is parabolic.

Recall that \( \sigma \left( L\right) \left( {x,\xi }\right) h \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{s \rightarrow  \infty }}{s}^{-2}{e}^{-{s\phi }\left( x\right) }L\left( {{e}^{s\phi }h}\right) \left( x\right) \) for \( \phi \) satisfying \( {d\phi }\left( x\right)  = \xi \) . Since \( {\Delta }_{L} = \Delta  + \) lower order terms,

\[
\sigma \left( {\Delta }_{L}\right) \left( {x,\xi }\right) h = \sigma \left( \Delta \right) \left( {x,\xi }\right) h = {\left| \xi \right| }^{2}h
\]

as calculated earlier. Meanwhile, we saw in (2.1.8) that \( {\delta G}\left( h\right)  = {\delta h} + \; \frac{1}{2}d\left( {\operatorname{tr}h}\right) \) , and so

\[
{\delta G}\left( {{e}^{s\phi }h}\right)  =  - \operatorname{tr}\nabla \left( {{e}^{s\phi }h}\right)  + \frac{1}{2}d\left( {{e}^{s\phi }\operatorname{tr}h}\right)
\]

\[
= {e}^{s\phi }\left\lbrack  {s\left( {-\operatorname{tr}{d\phi } \otimes  h + \frac{1}{2}{d\phi }\operatorname{tr}h}\right)  + {s}^{0}\left( \cdots \right) }\right\rbrack
\]

\[
= {e}^{s\phi }\left\lbrack  {s\left( {-h\left( {{\xi }^{\sharp }, \cdot  }\right)  + \frac{1}{2}\xi \operatorname{tr}h}\right)  + {s}^{0}\left( \cdots \right) }\right\rbrack
\]

---

\( {}^{1} \) Note that the subscript \( L \) for \( \Delta \) denotes the Lichnerowicz Laplacian, and does not refer to the linearisation of \( Q \) .

---

Therefore, since \( {\mathcal{L}}_{{\omega }^{\sharp }}g\left( {X, W}\right)  = \nabla \omega \left( {X, W}\right)  + \nabla \omega \left( {W, X}\right) \) as we saw in (2.3.8), we have

\[
{\mathcal{L}}_{{\left( \delta G\left( {e}^{s\phi }h\right) \right) }^{\sharp }}g = {e}^{s\phi }\left\lbrack  {{s}^{2}\left( {-\xi  \otimes  h\left( {{\xi }^{\sharp }, \cdot  }\right)  - h\left( {{\xi }^{\sharp }, \cdot  }\right)  \otimes  \xi  + \left( {\xi  \otimes  \xi }\right) \operatorname{tr}h}\right) }\right.
\]

\[
\left. {+{s}^{1}\left( \cdots \right)  + {s}^{0}\left( \cdots \right) }\right\rbrack  \text{ . }
\]

By definition of the principal symbol, we then have

\[
\sigma \left( {h \mapsto  {\mathcal{L}}_{{\left( \delta G\left( h\right) \right) }^{\sharp }}g}\right) \left( {x,\xi }\right) h =  - \xi  \otimes  h\left( {{\xi }^{\sharp }, \cdot  }\right)  - h\left( {{\xi }^{\sharp }, \cdot  }\right)  \otimes  \xi  + \left( {\xi  \otimes  \xi }\right) \operatorname{tr}h,
\]

and

\[
\sigma \left( L\right) \left( {x,\xi }\right) h = {\left| \xi \right| }^{2}h - \xi  \otimes  h\left( {{\xi }^{\sharp }, \cdot  }\right)  - h\left( {{\xi }^{\sharp }, \cdot  }\right)  \otimes  \xi  + \left( {\xi  \otimes  \xi }\right) \operatorname{tr}h.
\]

Having computed the principal symbol, we can now check whether \( \frac{\partial h}{\partial t} = \; L\left( h\right) \) is parabolic. This would require \( \langle \sigma \left( L\right) \left( {x,\xi }\right) h, h\rangle  > 0 \) for all \( \left( {x,\xi }\right)  \in \; {T}^{ * }\mathcal{M} \) with \( \xi  \neq  0 \) and all \( h \in  {\operatorname{Sym}}^{2}{T}_{x}^{ * }\mathcal{M} \) . However, setting \( h = \xi  \otimes  \xi \) we see that

\[
\sigma \left( L\right) \left( {x,\xi }\right) h = {\left| \xi \right| }^{2}\xi  \otimes  \xi \left( {1 - 1 - 1 + 1}\right)  = 0,
\]

so \( \frac{\partial h}{\partial t} = L\left( h\right) \) is not parabolic.

\]

nodes.title: 5.3. Curvature blow-up at finite-time singularities
nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow

nodes.label: Theorem 5.3.1
nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow
nodes.content:
Theorem 5.3.1 (Curvature blows up at a singularity). If \( \mathcal{M} \) is closed and \( g\left( t\right) \) is a Ricci flow on a maximal time interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) and \( T < \infty \) , then

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\mathcal{M}}\left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {\cdot , t}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \tag{5.3.1}
\]

as \( t \uparrow  T \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: Theorem 5.3.1 (Curvature blows up at a singularity). If \( \mathcal{M} \) is closed and \( g\left( t\right) \) is a Ricci flow on a maximal time interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) and \( T < \infty \) , then \[ \mathop{\sup }\limits_{\mathcal{M}}\left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {\cdot , t}\right) \rightarrow \infty \tag{5.3.1} \] as \( t \uparrow T \) .

nodes.proof:
We will deal with the contrapositive of this theorem, assuming instead that \( \sup \left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {\cdot , t}\right)  \nrightarrow  \infty \) as \( t \uparrow  T \) , and proving that the Ricci flow can be extended to a larger time interval \( \lbrack 0, T + \varepsilon ) \) .

Note first that by Theorem 3.2.11, if \( \sup \left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {\cdot , t}\right)  \nrightarrow  \infty \) , then there exists \( M > 0 \) such that \( \left| \operatorname{Rm}\right|  \leq  M \) for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) . Indeed, this theorem tells us that if \( \left| \operatorname{Rm}\right|  \leq  M \) at time \( t = T - \varepsilon \) , then

\[
\left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right|  \leq  \frac{M}{1 - {CM}\left\lbrack  {t - \left( {T - \varepsilon }\right) }\right\rbrack  }
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {T - \varepsilon , T}\right\rbrack \) .

We claim that in this case, \( g\left( t\right) \) may be extended from being a smooth solution on \( \lbrack 0, T) \) to a smooth solution on \( \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . We may then take \( g\left( T\right) \) to be an 'initial' metric in our short-time existence theorem (Theorem 5.2.1) in order to extend the flow to a Ricci flow for \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T + \varepsilon ) \) , contradicting the assumption that \( \lbrack 0, T) \) is a maximal time interval. (One should note here that the extended flow is smooth at \( t = T \) - that is, \( \frac{{\partial }^{k}g}{\partial {t}^{k}} \) exists at \( t = T \) for \( k \in  \mathbb{N} \) - which can be seen by differentiating the equation for Ricci flow with respect to \( t \) , away from \( t = T \) , in order to write \( \frac{{\partial }^{k}g}{\partial {t}^{k}} \) in terms of the curvature and its spacial derivatives.)

In order to prove our claim that \( g\left( t\right) \) may be extended to a Ricci flow on \( \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , we first note that by Lemma 5.3.2 and the boundedness of the curvature, the tensor \( g\left( t\right) \) may be extended continuously to the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , and the \( g\left( T\right) \) which has been added will be a metric. (In particular, it will be positive definite.)

All that we need to show now, is that this extension is smooth. We will have achieved this if we can show that within a local coordinate chart, all space-time derivatives of \( {g}_{ij} \) are bounded on \( \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2}T, T}\right) \) , for all indices \( i \) and \( j \) . By our global derivative estimates from Corollary 3.3.2, we have that

\[
\left| {\frac{{\partial }^{l}}{\partial {t}^{l}}{\nabla }^{k}\mathrm{{Rm}}}\right|  \leq  C = C\left( {l, k, T, M, n}\right)
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2}T, T}\right) \) . Working directly with the definition of Ric, and the Ricci flow equation (1.1.1), this may be turned into

\[
\left| {\frac{{\partial }^{l}}{\partial {t}^{l}}{\nabla }^{k}\operatorname{Ric}}\right|  \leq  C\left( {l, k, T, M, n}\right) , \tag{5.3.3}
\]

over the same time interval. Meanwhile, by using the consequence of (2.3.3) that

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\nabla  - \nabla \frac{\partial }{\partial t}}\right) A = A * \nabla \mathrm{{Rm}}
\]

for any \( t \) -dependent tensor field \( A \) , we can check that with respect to local coordinates \( \left\{  {x}^{i}\right\} \) ,

\[
\left| {\frac{{\partial }^{l}}{\partial {t}^{l}}{\nabla }^{k}{\partial }_{i}}\right|  \leq  C
\]

for each index \( i \) , where \( {\partial }_{i} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}} \) , and \( C \) is independent of \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2}T, T}\right) \) . By combining with (5.3.3) we then find that for any indices \( a \) and \( b \) ,

\[
\left| {\frac{{\partial }^{l}}{\partial {t}^{l}}{D}^{\alpha }{R}_{ab}}\right|  \leq  C \tag{5.3.4}
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2}T, T}\right) \) , where \( \alpha  = \left( {{\alpha }_{1},\ldots ,{\alpha }_{p}}\right)  \in  {\left( \{ 0\}  \cup  \mathbb{N}\right) }^{p} \) is any multi-index (that is, \( {D}^{\alpha } \) is a combination of spatial partial derivatives, \( {D}^{\alpha } = \frac{{\partial }^{\left| \alpha \right| }}{\partial {x}^{{\alpha }_{1}}\ldots \partial {x}^{{\alpha }_{p}}} \) , with \( \left. {\left| \alpha \right|  \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\alpha }_{1} + \ldots {\alpha }_{p}}\right) . \)

Now by plugging the equation \( \frac{\partial {g}_{ab}}{\partial t} =  - 2{R}_{ab} \) into the inequality (5.3.4), we obtain the boundedness of

\[
\left| {\frac{{\partial }^{l}}{\partial {t}^{l}}{D}^{\alpha }{g}_{ab}}\right|
\]

for \( l \geq  1 \) , any multi-index \( \alpha \) , and any indices \( a \) and \( b \) , and by integrating with respect to time, we find the same is true also for \( l = 0 \) .

Lemma 5.3.2 (Metric equivalence). If \( g\left( t\right) \) is a Ricci flow for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, s}\right\rbrack \) and \( \left| \operatorname{Ric}\right|  \leq  M \) on \( \mathcal{M} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, s}\right\rbrack \) , then

\[
{e}^{-{2Mt}}g\left( 0\right)  \leq  g\left( t\right)  \leq  {e}^{2Mt}g\left( 0\right) \tag{5.3.2}
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, s}\right\rbrack \) .

nodes.section_title: 6.1. Gradient of total scalar curvature and related functionals
nodes.content:
### 6.1 Gradient of total scalar curvature and re- lated functionals

Given a compact manifold with a Riemannian metric \( g \) , we define the total scalar curvature by

\[
E\left( g\right)  = {\int }_{\mathcal{M}}{RdV}
\]

Let us consider the first variation of \( E \) under an arbitrary change of metric. As before, we write \( h = \frac{\partial g}{\partial t} \) . Using Propositions 2.3.9 and 2.3.12, and keeping in mind that the integral of the divergence of a 1-form must be zero, we compute

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\int {RdV} = \int \frac{\partial R}{\partial t}{dV} + \int R\frac{1}{2}\left( {\operatorname{tr}h}\right) {dV}
\]

\[
= \int \left( {-\langle \operatorname{Ric}, h\rangle  + {\delta }^{2}h - \Delta \left( {\operatorname{tr}h}\right) }\right) {dV} + \int \frac{R}{2}\langle g, h\rangle {dV}
\]

\[
= \int \left\langle  {\frac{R}{2}g - \operatorname{Ric}, h}\right\rangle  {dV}
\]

By definition, the gradient of \( E \) is then given by

\[
\nabla E\left( g\right)  = \frac{R}{2}g - \text{ Ric }.
\]

nodes.content:
### 6.2 The \( \mathcal{F} \) -functional

One of the early joys of the recent work of Perelman [31] is that Ricci flow can in fact be formulated as a gradient flow. To see one such formulation, we consider, for a fixed closed manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) , the following ’Fisher information’ functional \( \mathcal{F} \) on pairs \( \left( {g, f}\right) \) where \( g \) is a Riemannian metric, and \( f \) is a function \( f : \mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) :

\[
\mathcal{F}\left( {g, f}\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \int \left( {R + {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right) {e}^{-f}{dV}.
\]

nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow
nodes.content:
Proposition 6.2.1.

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{F}\left( {g, f}\right)  = \int \langle  - \operatorname{Ric} - \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) , h\rangle {e}^{-f}{dV} + \int \left( {{2\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + R}\right) \left( {\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}h - k}\right) {e}^{-f}{dV}.
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: Proposition 6.2.1. \[ \frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{F}\left( {g, f}\right) = \int \langle - \operatorname{Ric} - \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) , h\rangle {e}^{-f}{dV} + \int \left( {{2\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + R}\right) \left( {\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}h - k}\right) {e}^{-f}{dV}. \]

nodes.proof:
Keeping in mind that \( \frac{\partial }{\partial t}{g}^{ij} =  - {h}^{ij} \) , we may calculate

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} =  - h\left( {\nabla f,\nabla f}\right)  + 2\langle \nabla k,\nabla f\rangle .
\]

Therefore, using Propositions 2.3.9 and 2.3.12, we have

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{F}\left( {g, f}\right)  = \int \left\lbrack  {-h\left( {\nabla f,\nabla f}\right)  + 2\langle \nabla k,\nabla f\rangle -\langle \operatorname{Ric}, h\rangle  + {\delta }^{2}h - \Delta \left( {\operatorname{tr}h}\right) }\right\rbrack  {e}^{-f}{dV}
\]

\[
+ \int \left( {R + {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right) \left\lbrack  {-k + \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}h}\right\rbrack  {e}^{-f}{dV}
\]

Three of these terms may be usefully addressed by integrating by parts. First,

\[
\int 2\langle \nabla k,\nabla f\rangle {e}^{-f}{dV} = \int  - {2k}\left( {{\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right) {e}^{-f}{dV}.
\]

Second, by Remark 2.1.1,

\[
\int \left( {{\delta }^{2}h}\right) {e}^{-f}{dV} = \int \left\langle  {{\delta h}, d\left( {e}^{-f}\right) }\right\rangle  {dV}
\]

\[
= \int \left\langle  {h,\nabla d\left( {e}^{-f}\right) }\right\rangle  {dV}
\]

\[
= \int \left( {h\left( {\nabla f,\nabla f}\right) -\langle \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) , h\rangle }\right) {e}^{-f}{dV}.
\]

Third,

\[
\int  - \Delta \left( {\operatorname{tr}h}\right) {e}^{-f}{dV} = \int  - \left( {\operatorname{tr}h}\right) \Delta \left( {e}^{-f}\right) {dV} = \int \left( {{\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right) \left( {\operatorname{tr}h}\right) {e}^{-f}{dV}.
\]

nodes.label: Theorem 6.4.1

nodes.content:
Theorem 6.4.1. For an arbitrary \( {g}_{0} \) , on a closed manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) , there exist \( T > 0 \) , and an \( n \) -form \( \omega  > 0 \) which is neither arbitrary nor unique, such that there exists a solution on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) to the (upwards) gradient flow for the functional

\[
{\mathcal{F}}^{\omega }\left( g\right)  = \int \left( {R + {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right) \omega
\]

where \( f \) is determined by the constraint \( \omega  = {e}^{-f}{dV} \) , and we compute the gradient with respect to the inner product

\[
\langle g, h{\rangle }_{\omega } = \frac{1}{2}\int \langle g, h\rangle \omega .
\]

We are free to take \( T \) as large as we like, provided that the Ricci flow starting at \( {g}_{0} \) exists for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , although \( \omega \) will depend on the \( T \) chosen.

This gradient flow is just the Ricci flow, modified by a time-dependent diffeomorphism. That is, there exists a smooth family of diffeomorphisms \( {\phi }_{t} : \mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathcal{M} \) such that \( {\phi }_{t}^{ * }\left( {g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is the Ricci flow starting at \( {g}_{0} \) .

nodes.title: 6.5. The classical entropy
nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow

nodes.label: Definition 6.5-extra-1

nodes.content:
### 6.5 The classical entropy

So far in Chapter 6, our exposition has been an expansion of the original comments of Perelman [31]. It is enlightening also to emphasise the function \( u \) from (6.4.7) rather than \( f \) . If we specify \( u\left( T\right) \) as a probability density at time \( T \) , and let it evolve backwards in time under (6.4.8), then \( u\left( t\right) \) represents the probability density of a particle evolving under Brownian motion, backwards in time, on the evolving manifold. A basic building block for constructing interesting functionals for Ricci flow is then the classical, or 'Boltzmann-Shannon' entropy

\[
N =  - {\int }_{\mathcal{M}}u\ln {udV}
\]

as considered in thermodynamics, information theory (Boltzmann, Shannon, Turing etc.) and elsewhere, which gives a measure of the concentration of the probability density. (Note that Brownian diffusion on a fixed manifold represents the gradient flow for this entropy on the space of probability densities endowed with the Wasserstein metric - see the discussion and references in [42].) In this framework, the information functional \( \mathcal{F} \) coincides with the time derivative of \( N \) , up to a sign (see also [30]). By (2.5.7),

\[
- \frac{dN}{dt} = \int \left\lbrack  {\left( {1 + \ln u}\right) \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} - {Ru}\ln u}\right\rbrack  {dV}
\]

\[
=  - \int \left\lbrack  {\left( {1 + \ln u}\right) \left( {{\Delta u} - {Ru}}\right)  + {Ru}\ln u}\right\rbrack  {dV} \tag{6.5.1}
\]

\[
= \int \left( {\frac{{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2}}{u} + {Ru}}\right) {dV}
\]

\[
= \mathcal{F}\text{ . }
\]

It is sometimes convenient to take a renormalised version of the classical entropy

\[
\widetilde{N} = N - \frac{n}{2}\left( {1 + \ln {4\pi }\left( {T - t}\right) }\right) . \tag{6.5.2}
\]

With this adjustment, one can check that \( \widetilde{N} \rightarrow  0 \) as \( t \uparrow  T \) when one takes \( u \) to be a solution of (6.4.8) which is a delta function at \( t = T \) . (In other words, \( u \) is a heat kernel for the conjugate heat equation - the probability density of the backwards Brownian path of a particle whose position is known at time \( t = T \) .) Indeed, this functional applied to the classical fundamental solution of the heat equation on Euclidean space would be zero. One could check that by virtue of the Harnack inequality of Li-Yau [28], the functional \( \widetilde{N} \) applied to a (backwards) heat kernel on a fixed manifold of positive Ricci curvature must be decreasing in \( T - t \) . For Ricci flow, this is true without any curvature hypothesis:

nodes.content: Lemma 6.5.1. If \( g\left( t\right) \) is a Ricci flow on a closed manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) , for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , and \( u : \mathcal{M} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) is a solution to \( {\square }^{ * }u = 0 \) , then the functional \( \widetilde{N} \) defined by (6.5.2) is monotonically increasing in \( t \) .

If \( g\left( t\right) \) is a Ricci flow on a closed manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) , for \( t \in \left\lbrack {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , and \( u : \mathcal{M} \times \left\lbrack {0, T}\right\rbrack \rightarrow \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) is a solution to \( {\square }^{ * }u = 0 \) , then the functional \( \widetilde{N} \) defined by (6.5.2) is monotonically increasing in \( t \) .

nodes.proof:
As observed above, we have

\[
- \frac{d\widetilde{N}}{dt} = \mathcal{F} - \frac{n}{2\left( {T - t}\right) },
\]

so we are reduced to proving that

\[
\mathcal{F} \leq  \frac{n}{2\left( {T - t}\right) } \tag{6.5.3}
\]

The functional \( \mathcal{F} \) evaluated as here on the Ricci flow \( g\left( t\right) \) and the density \( u \) (or its corresponding \( f \mathrel{\text{ := }}  - \ln u \) ) is equal to \( \mathcal{F} \) evaluated on the \( \widehat{g} \) and \( \widehat{f} \) of the previous section. We may then sharpen the monotonicity of \( \mathcal{F} \) , as expressed in (6.4.3) to

\[
\frac{d\mathcal{F}}{dt} = 2\int {\left| \operatorname{Ric} + \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \right| }^{2}{e}^{-f}{dV} \geq  \frac{2}{n}\int {\left| R + \Delta f\right| }^{2}{e}^{-f}{dV}
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{2}{n}{\left( \int \left( R + \Delta f\right) {e}^{-f}dV\right) }^{2} = \frac{2}{n}{\mathcal{F}}^{2} \tag{6.5.4}
\]

where we have estimated the norm of the symmetric tensor Ric \( + \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \) in terms of its trace, appealed to Cauchy-Schwarz, and integrated by parts, as in [31]. If ever (6.5.3) were violated, then the differential inequality (6.5.4) would force \( \mathcal{F}\left( t\right) \) to blow up prior to the time \( T \) until which we are assuming its existence.

nodes.label: Definition 6.6-extra-1
nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow
nodes.content:
### 6.6 The zeroth eigenvalue of \( - {4\Delta } + R \)

It is also useful to rewrite the functional \( \mathcal{F} \) to act on pairs \( \left( {g,\phi }\right) \) where \( \phi  \mathrel{\text{ := }} {e}^{-\frac{f}{2}} \) . In this case, one can easily check that

\[
\mathcal{F} = \int \left( {4{\left| \nabla \phi \right| }^{2} + R{\phi }^{2}}\right) {dV}
\]

and hence that the zeroth eigenvalue of the operator \( - {4\Delta } + R \) is given by

\[
\lambda  = \lambda \left( g\right)  = \inf \left\{  {\mathcal{F}\left( {g,\phi }\right) \mid \int {\phi }^{2}{dV} = 1}\right\}  ,
\]

where we are using the same notation \( \mathcal{F} \) even after the change of variables. By applying the direct method and elliptic regularity theory (see [15, §8.12]) we know that this infimum is attained by some smooth \( {\phi }_{\min } \) (for given smooth \( g \) on a closed manifold) and also that after negating if necessary, we have \( {\phi }_{\min } > 0 \) . (Note that \( \left| {\phi }_{\min }\right| \) will also be a minimiser, and that by the Harnack inequality - see for example [15, Theorem 8.20] - we must then have \( \left| {\phi }_{\text{ min }}\right|  > 0 \) .)

One consequence of this positivity is that the minimiser \( {\phi }_{\min } \) must be unique (up to a sign) or we would be able to take an appropriate linear combination of two distinct minimisers to give a new minimiser which would no longer be nonzero.

Another consequence is that we can write \( {\phi }_{\min } = {e}^{-\frac{{f}_{\min }}{2}} \) for some function \( {f}_{\min } : \mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) , and hence we see that

\[
\lambda  = \min \{ \mathcal{F}\left( {g, f}\right)  \mid  \int {e}^{-f}{dV} = 1\} . \tag{6.6.1}
\]

nodes.label: Definition 7.1.1
nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow
nodes.content:
Definition 7.1.1 (Smooth, pointed "Cheeger-Gromov" convergence of manifolds). A sequence \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{i},{g}_{i},{p}_{i}}\right) \) of smooth, complete, pointed Riemannian manifolds (that is, Riemannian manifolds \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{i},{g}_{i}}\right) \) and points \( {p}_{i} \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{i} \) ) is said to converge (smoothly) to the smooth, complete, pointed manifold \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, g, p}\right) \) as \( i \rightarrow  \infty \) if there exist

(i) a sequence of compact sets \( {\Omega }_{i} \subset  \mathcal{M} \) , exhausting \( \mathcal{M} \) (that is, so that any compact set \( K \subset  \mathcal{M} \) satisfies \( K \subset  {\Omega }_{i} \) for sufficiently large \( i \) ) with \( p \in  \operatorname{int}\left( {\Omega }_{i}\right) \) for each \( i \) ;

(ii) a sequence of smooth maps \( {\phi }_{i} : {\Omega }_{i} \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{i} \) which are diffeomorphic onto their image and satisfy \( {\phi }_{i}\left( p\right)  = {p}_{i} \) for all \( i \) ;

such that,

\[
{\phi }_{i}^{ * }{g}_{i} \rightarrow  g
\]

smoothly as \( i \rightarrow  \infty \) in the sense that for all compact sets \( K \subset  \mathcal{M} \) , the tensor \( {\phi }_{i}^{ * }{g}_{i} - g \) and its covariant derivatives of all orders (with respect to any fixed background connection) each converge uniformly to zero on \( K \) .

nodes.label: Definition 7.2.1

nodes.content:
Definition 7.2.1. Let \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{i},{g}_{i}\left( t\right) }\right) \) be a sequence of smooth families of complete Riemannian manifolds for \( t \in  \left( {a, b}\right) \) where \( - \infty  \leq  a < 0 < b \leq  \infty \) . Let \( {p}_{i} \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{i} \) for each \( i \) . Let \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) be a smooth family of complete Riemannian manifolds for \( t \in  \left( {a, b}\right) \) and let \( p \in  \mathcal{M} \) . We say that

\[
\left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{i},{g}_{i}\left( t\right) ,{p}_{i}}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {\mathcal{M}, g\left( t\right) , p}\right)
\]

as \( i \rightarrow  \infty \) if there exist

(i) a sequence of compact \( {\Omega }_{i} \subset  \mathcal{M} \) exhausting \( \mathcal{M} \) and satisfying \( p \in \) int \( \left( {\Omega }_{i}\right) \) for each \( i \) ;

(ii) a sequence of smooth maps \( {\phi }_{i} : {\Omega }_{i} \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{i} \) , diffeomorphic onto their image, and with \( {\phi }_{i}\left( p\right)  = {p}_{i} \) ;

such that

\[
{\phi }_{i}^{ * }{g}_{i}\left( t\right)  \rightarrow  g\left( t\right)
\]

as \( i \rightarrow  \infty \) in the sense that \( {\phi }_{i}^{ * }{g}_{i}\left( t\right)  - g\left( t\right) \) and its derivatives of every order (with respect to time as well as covariant space derivatives with respect to any fixed background connection) converge uniformly to zero on every compact subset of \( \mathcal{M} \times  \left( {a, b}\right) \) .

nodes.label: Remark 7.3-extra-1
nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow
nodes.content:
### 7.3 Blowing up at singularities I

As we have mentioned before, one application of the compactness of Ricci flows in Theorem 7.2.3 that we have in mind, is to analyse rescalings of Ricci flows near their singularities. Let \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) be a Ricci flow with \( \mathcal{M} \) closed, on the maximal time interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) - as defined at the end of Section 5.2 - with \( T < \infty \) . By Theorem 5.3.1 we know that

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\mathcal{M}}\left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {\cdot , t}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty
\]

as \( t \uparrow  T \) . Let us choose points \( {p}_{i} \in  \mathcal{M} \) and times \( {t}_{i} \uparrow  T \) such that

\[
\left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {{p}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right)  = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  \mathcal{M}, t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{i}}\right\rbrack  }}\left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {x, t}\right) ,
\]

by, for example, picking \( \left( {{p}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right) \) to maximise \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| \) over \( \mathcal{M} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T - \frac{1}{i}}\right\rbrack \) . Notice in particular that \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| \left( {{p}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( i \rightarrow  \infty \) . Define rescaled (and translated) flows \( {g}_{i}\left( t\right) \) by

\[
{g}_{i}\left( t\right)  = \left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {{p}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right) g\left( {{t}_{i} + \frac{t}{\left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {{p}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right) }}\right) .
\]

By the discussion in Section 1.2.3, \( \left( {\mathcal{M},{g}_{i}\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a Ricci flow on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{i}\left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {{p}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right) ,\left( {T - {t}_{i}}\right) \left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {{p}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right) }\right) \) .

Moreover, for each \( i,\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{g}_{i}\left( 0\right) }\right) }\right| \left( {p}_{i}\right)  = 1 \) and for \( t \leq  0 \) ,

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\mathcal{M}}\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{g}_{i}\left( t\right) }\right) }\right|  \leq  1.
\]

Furthermore, by Theorem 3.2.11, for \( t > 0 \) ,

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\mathcal{M}}\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{g}_{i}\left( t\right) }\right) }\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{1 - C\left( n\right) t}.
\]

Therefore, for all \( a < 0 \) and some \( b = b\left( n\right)  > 0,{g}_{i}\left( t\right) \) is defined for \( t \in  \left( {a, b}\right) \) and

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{i}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\mathcal{M} \times  \left( {a, b}\right) }}\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{g}_{i}\left( t\right) }\right) }\right|  < \infty .
\]

By Theorem 7.2.3, we can pass to a subsequence in \( i \) , and get convergence \( \left( {\mathcal{M},{g}_{i}\left( t\right) ,{p}_{i}}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {\mathcal{N},\widehat{g}\left( t\right) ,{p}_{\infty }}\right) \) to a "singularity model" Ricci flow \( \left( {\mathcal{N},\widehat{g}\left( t\right) }\right) \) , provided that we can establish the injectivity radius estimate

\[
\mathop{\inf }\limits_{i}\operatorname{inj}\left( {\mathcal{M},{g}_{i}\left( 0\right) ,{p}_{i}}\right)  > 0. \tag{7.3.1}
\]

\]

nodes.label: Lemma 8.1.7

nodes.content:
Lemma 8.1.7. Let \( g \) denote the flat metric on \( \mathcal{M} = {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . If \( f \) and \( \tau \) are compatible with \( g \) , then

\[
\mathcal{W}\left( {g, f,\tau }\right)  \geq  0 \tag{8.1.4}
\]

with equality if and only if \( f\left( x\right)  \equiv  \frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4\tau } \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: Lemma 8.1.7. Let \( g \) denote the flat metric on \( \mathcal{M} = {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . If \( f \) and \( \tau \) are compatible with \( g \) , then \[ \mathcal{W}\left( {g, f,\tau }\right) \geq 0 \tag{8.1.4} \] with equality if and only if \( f\left( x\right) \equiv \frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4\tau } \) .

nodes.proof:
For now, set \( \tau  = \frac{1}{2} \) and let \( f : {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) be compatible with \( g \) and \( \tau \) , which in this situation means that

\[
{\int }_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}\frac{{e}^{-f}}{{\left( 2\pi \right) }^{\frac{n}{2}}}{dx} = 1.
\]

If we define \( v = {e}^{\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4} - \frac{f}{2}} \) , we have

\[
{v}^{2}{d\mu } = {e}^{\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{2} - f}{\left( 2\pi \right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}{e}^{-\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{2}}{dx} = {\left( 2\pi \right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}{e}^{-f}{dx}
\]

and so \( {\int }_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}{v}^{2}{d\mu } = 1 \) . Therefore, by the log-Sobolev inequality,

\[
\int {v}^{2}\ln \left| v\right| {d\mu } \leq  \int {\left| \nabla v\right| }^{2}{d\mu }
\]

We wish to convert from \( v \) to \( f \) in this inequality. For the left-hand side, we have

\[
\int {v}^{2}\ln \left| v\right| {d\mu } = \int {e}^{\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{2} - f}\left( {\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4} - \frac{f}{2}}\right) {\left( 2\pi \right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}{e}^{-\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{2}}{dx}
\]

\[
= \int \left( {\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4} - \frac{f}{2}}\right) \frac{{e}^{-f}}{{\left( 2\pi \right) }^{\frac{n}{2}}}{dx}.
\]

For the right-hand side, first note that

\[
\nabla v = \left( {\frac{x}{2} - \frac{\nabla f}{2}}\right) {e}^{\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4} - \frac{f}{2}}
\]

which gives us

\[
{\left| \nabla v\right| }^{2} = \left( {\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4} - \frac{x \cdot  \nabla f}{2} + \frac{{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}{4}}\right) {e}^{\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{2} - f},
\]

and thus

\[
{\left| \nabla v\right| }^{2}{d\mu } = \left( {\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4} - \frac{x \cdot  \nabla f}{2} + \frac{{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}{4}}\right) \frac{{e}^{-f}}{{\left( 2\pi \right) }^{\frac{n}{2}}}{dx}.
\]

Before integrating this, we use the fact that \( \nabla .x = n \) to give the integration-by-parts formula

\[
- \int \frac{x \cdot  \nabla f}{2}\frac{{e}^{-f}}{{\left( 2\pi \right) }^{\frac{n}{2}}}{dx} = \frac{1}{2}\int x \cdot  \nabla \left( {e}^{-f}\right) \frac{dx}{{\left( 2\pi \right) }^{\frac{n}{2}}} =  - \frac{n}{2}\int \frac{{e}^{-f}}{{\left( 2\pi \right) }^{\frac{n}{2}}}{dx}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\int {\left| \nabla v\right| }^{2}{d\mu } = \int \left( {\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4} - \frac{n}{2} + \frac{{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}{4}}\right) \frac{{e}^{-f}}{{\left( 2\pi \right) }^{\frac{n}{2}}}{dx},
\]

and the log-Sobolev inequality (8.1) becomes

\[
\int \left( {\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4} - \frac{f}{2}}\right) \frac{{e}^{-f}}{{\left( 2\pi \right) }^{\frac{n}{2}}}{dx} \leq  \int \left( {\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4} - \frac{n}{2} + \frac{{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}{4}}\right) \frac{{e}^{-f}}{{\left( 2\pi \right) }^{\frac{n}{2}}}{dx}
\]

or equivalently

\[
\mathcal{W}\left( {g, f,\frac{1}{2}}\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \int \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2}{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + f - n}\right\rbrack  \frac{{e}^{-f}}{{\left( 2\pi \right) }^{\frac{n}{2}}}{dx} \geq  0,
\]

for this special case where \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, g}\right) \) is Euclidean \( n \) -space, with equality if and only if \( f\left( x\right)  \equiv  \frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{2} \) by Remark 8.1.4. By the scale invariance \( \mathcal{W}\left( {g, f,\tau }\right)  = \; \mathcal{W}\left( {\frac{1}{2\tau }g, f,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \) , the fact that compatibility is preserved under the transformation \( \left( {g, f,\tau }\right)  \mapsto  \left( {\frac{1}{2\tau }g, f,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \) and also the fact that \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, g}\right) \) is preserved under homothetic scaling, we conclude that

\[
\mathcal{W}\left( {g, f,\tau }\right)  \geq  0, \tag{8.1.5}
\]

for any \( f,\tau \) compatible with \( g \) , with equality if and only if \( f\left( x\right)  \equiv  \frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4\tau } \) .
