nodes.content:
Lemma 8.1.8. For any smooth Riemannian metric \( g \) on a closed manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) , and \( \tau  > 0 \) , the infimum of \( \mathcal{W}\left( {g, f,\tau }\right) \) over all compatible \( f \) (as defined in Definition 8.1.1) is attained by a smooth compatible \( f \) .

Defining \( \mu \) as this infimum,

\[
\mu \left( {g,\tau }\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\inf }\limits_{f}\mathcal{W}\left( {g, f,\tau }\right) , \tag{8.1.6}
\]

the function \( \mu \left( {g,\tau }\right) \) is bounded below as \( \tau \) varies within any finite interval \( \left( {0,{\tau }_{0}}\right\rbrack \) .

nodes.proof:
We limit ourselves to proving that the functional \( \mathcal{W} \) is bounded below, for given \( g \) and \( \tau \) , and that a minimising sequence of compatible positive functions \( \phi \) must be bounded in \( {W}^{1,2} \) , and hence that the direct method applies to give a minimiser. (See [15, §8.12].)

By the invariance observed in Proposition 8.1.2, we may scale \( g \) and \( \tau \) simultaneously and assume that \( \tau  = \frac{1}{4\pi } \) , say, which slightly simplifies (8.1.8) and (8.1.9).

It suffices to prove that

\[
\mathcal{W}\left( \phi \right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \int \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{4\pi }\left( {4{\left| \nabla \phi \right| }^{2} + R{\phi }^{2}}\right)  - 2{\phi }^{2}\ln \phi  - n{\phi }^{2}}\right\rbrack  {dV} \tag{8.1.11}
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{1}{2\pi }\int {\left| \nabla \phi \right| }^{2}{dV} - C\left( {g, n}\right) ,
\]

for any positive \( \phi \) satisfying

\[
\int {\phi }^{2}{dV} = 1 \tag{8.1.12}
\]

for some constant \( C\left( {g, n}\right) \) .

To achieve this, we split up the expression (8.1.11) for \( \mathcal{W}\left( \phi \right) \) . First, by (8.1.12) we clearly have

\[
\int \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{4\pi }\left( {R{\phi }^{2}}\right)  - n{\phi }^{2}}\right\rbrack  {dV} \geq   - C\left( {g, n}\right) , \tag{8.1.13}
\]

since our manifold is closed, so \( R \) is bounded.

Meanwhile, we may write

(8.1.14)

\[
\int {\phi }^{2}\ln {\phi dV} = \frac{n - 2}{4}\int {\phi }^{2}\ln {\phi }^{\frac{4}{n - 2}}{dV}
\]

\[
= \frac{n - 2}{4}\int G\left( \sigma \right) {d\mu }
\]

where \( \sigma  : \mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) is defined by \( \sigma  \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\phi }^{\frac{4}{n - 2}} \) , the function \( G : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) defined by \( G\left( y\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \ln y \) is concave, and the measure \( {d\mu } \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\phi }^{2}{dV} \) has unit total mass. We may apply Jensen's inequality

\[
\int G\left( \sigma \right) {d\mu } \leq  G\left( {\int {\sigma d\mu }}\right) ,
\]

(see for example [41, p.11]) to tell us that

\[
\int {\phi }^{2}\ln {\phi dV} \leq  \frac{n - 2}{4}\ln \left\lbrack  {\int {\phi }^{2 + \frac{4}{n - 2}}{dV}}\right\rbrack   = \frac{n}{4}\ln {\left\lbrack  \int {\phi }^{\frac{2n}{n - 2}}dV\right\rbrack  }^{\frac{n - 2}{n}}.
\]

We continue by applying the Sobolev inequality (see [15])

\[
{\left( \int {\phi }^{\frac{2n}{n - 2}}dv\right) }^{\frac{n - 2}{2n}} \leq  C\left( {g, n}\right) {\left\lbrack  \int {\phi }^{2}dV+\int {\left| \nabla \phi \right| }^{2}dV\right\rbrack  }^{\frac{1}{2}},
\]

to give

\[
\int {\phi }^{2}\ln {\phi dV} \leq  C\left( {g, n}\right)  + \frac{n}{4}\ln \left\lbrack  {1+\int {\left| \nabla \phi \right| }^{2}{dV}}\right\rbrack   \leq  \frac{1}{2\pi }\int {\left| \nabla \phi \right| }^{2}{dV} + C\left( {g, n}\right) ,
\]

where the constant \( C\left( {g, n}\right) \) is permitted to change at each step.

Combining with (8.1.13), we conclude that

\[
\mathcal{W}\left( \phi \right)  \geq  \frac{1}{2\pi }\int {\left| \nabla \phi \right| }^{2}{dV} - C\left( {g, n}\right) ,
\]

as required in (8.1.11).

Remark 8.2.2. Under the evolution of the previous proposition, \( u \) satisfies

\[

\]

Indeed, as we discussed in Section 6.5, \( u \) is again evolving as the probability density corresponding to Brownian motion backwards in time. More generally, by Proposition 6.3.1, if \( h \) is a solution of the heat equation \( \square h = 0 \) , then

\[
\int {uhdV}
\]

is constant in time.

Remark 8.2.4. The \( \mathcal{W} \) -functional applied to this backwards Brownian diffusion on a Ricci flow also arises via the (renormalised) classical entropy \( \widetilde{N} \) discussed in Section 6.5. Indeed, if we set \( \tau  = T - t \) , one may calculate (compare with [31] and [30]) that

\[
\mathcal{W}\left( t\right)  =  - \frac{d}{dt}\left( {\tau \widetilde{N}}\right) .
\]

Proposition 8.2.6. Suppose \( g, f \) and \( \tau \) evolve as in Proposition 8.2.1, and \( u \) is defined as in (8.1.1). Then the function \( v \) defined by

\[
v \mathrel{\text{ := }} \left\lbrack  {\tau \left( {{2\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + R}\right)  + f - n}\right\rbrack  u \tag{8.2.3}
\]

satisfies

\[
{\square }^{ * }v =  - {2\tau }{\left| \operatorname{Ric} + \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right)  - \frac{g}{2\tau }\right| }^{2}u.
\]

nodes.proof:
Splitting \( v \) as a product, we find that

\[
{\square }^{ * }v = {\square }^{ * }\left( {\frac{v}{u}u}\right)  = \frac{v}{u}{\square }^{ * }u - u\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} + \Delta }\right) \left( \frac{v}{u}\right)  - 2\langle \nabla \left( \frac{v}{u}\right) ,\nabla u\rangle ,
\]

and since \( {\square }^{ * }u = 0 \) , we have

\[
{u}^{-1}{\square }^{ * }v =  - \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} + \Delta }\right) \left( \frac{v}{u}\right)  - 2{u}^{-1}\langle \nabla \left( \frac{v}{u}\right) ,\nabla u\rangle . \tag{8.2.4}
\]

For the first of the terms on the right-hand side, we compute

\[
- \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} + \Delta }\right) \left( \frac{v}{u}\right)  =  - \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} + \Delta }\right) \left\lbrack  {\tau \left( {{2\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + R}\right)  + f - n}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
= \left( {{2\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + R}\right)
\]

\[
- \tau \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} + \Delta }\right) \left( {{2\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + R}\right)  - \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} + \Delta }\right) f
\]

and using the evolution equation for \( f \) in (8.2.1) on the final term, this reduces to

\[
- \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} + \Delta }\right) \left( \frac{v}{u}\right)  = {2\Delta f} - 2{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + {2R} - \frac{n}{2\tau } - \tau \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} + \Delta }\right) \left( {{2\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + R}\right) .
\]

(8.2.5)

We deal with each part of the final term individually:

By Proposition 2.5.6 and the evolution equation for \( f \) ,

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} + \Delta }\right) {\Delta f} = \Delta \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + 2\langle \operatorname{Ric},\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \rangle  + {\Delta }^{2}f \tag{8.2.6}
\]

\[
= 2\langle \operatorname{Ric},\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \rangle  + \Delta \left( {{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} - R + \frac{n}{2\tau }}\right)
\]

Using also the evolution equation for \( g \) ,

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} + \Delta }\right) {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} = 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {\nabla f,\nabla f}\right)  + 2\left\langle  {\nabla f,\nabla \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}}\right\rangle   + \Delta {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
= 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {\nabla f,\nabla f}\right)  + 2\left\langle  {\nabla f,\nabla \left( {-{\Delta f} + {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} - R}\right) }\right\rangle   + \Delta {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2},
\]

and by Proposition 2.5.4,

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} + \Delta }\right) R = {2\Delta R} + 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\right| }^{2}.
\]

Combining these three expressions gives

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} + \Delta }\right) \left( {{2\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + R}\right)  = 4\langle \operatorname{Ric},\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \rangle  + \Delta {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {\nabla f,\nabla f}\right)
\]

\[
- 2\langle \nabla f,\nabla \left( {-{\Delta f} + {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} - R}\right) \rangle  + 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\right| }^{2}.
\]

(8.2.7)

Also,

\[
\left\langle  {\nabla \frac{v}{u},\nabla u}\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {\tau \nabla \left( {{2\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + R}\right)  + \nabla f, - u\nabla f}\right\rangle
\]

\[
- 2{u}^{-1}\left\langle  {\nabla \frac{v}{u},\nabla u}\right\rangle   = {2\tau }\left\langle  {\nabla \left( {{2\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + R}\right) ,\nabla f}\right\rangle   + 2{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} \tag{8.2.8}
\]

Combining (8.2.4), (8.2.5), (8.2.7) and (8.2.8) we find that

\[
{u}^{-1}{\square }^{ * }v = \frac{1}{\tau }\left( {-\frac{n}{2}}\right)  + \left( {{2\Delta f} + {2R}}\right)
\]

\[
+ \tau \left( {-4\langle \operatorname{Ric},\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \rangle  - 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\right| }^{2}}\right.
\]

\[
\left. {+\left\lbrack  {-\Delta {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {\nabla f,\nabla f}\right)  + 2\langle \nabla f,\nabla {\Delta f}\rangle }\right\rbrack  }\right) \text{ . }
\]

The three terms within square brackets simplify to \( - 2{\left| \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \right| }^{2} \) by the Bochner formula, so

\[
{u}^{-1}{\square }^{ * }v =  - \frac{n}{2\tau } + 2\langle \operatorname{Ric} + \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) , g\rangle  - {2\tau }{\left| \operatorname{Ric} + \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \right| }^{2}
\]

\[
=  - {2\tau }{\left| \operatorname{Ric} + \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right)  - \frac{g}{2\tau }\right| }^{2}
\]

nodes.content:
### 8.3 No local volume collapse where curvature is controlled

Given a complete Riemannian manifold \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, g}\right) \) , a point \( p \in  \mathcal{M} \) and \( s > 0 \) , we use the shorthand

\[
\mathcal{V}\left( {p, s}\right)  = {\mathcal{V}}_{g}\left( {p, s}\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{Vol}\left( {{B}_{g}\left( {p, s}\right) }\right)
\]

for the volume of the geodesic ball \( B\left( {p, s}\right)  = {B}_{g}\left( {p, s}\right) \) centred at \( p \) of radius \( s \) , computed with respect to the metric \( g \) . Our aim is to get a lower bound on the volume ratio

\[
\mathcal{K}\left( {p, r}\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \frac{\mathcal{V}\left( {p, r}\right) }{{r}^{n}}, \tag{8.3.1}
\]

during a Ricci flow which will be turned into a lower bound for the injectivity radius, in terms of the maximum of the curvature |Rm|, in the next section.

nodes.label: Theorem 8.3.1
nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow
nodes.section_title: 8.3. No local volume collapse where curvature is controlled
nodes.content:
Theorem 8.3.1 (No collapsing). Suppose that \( g\left( t\right) \) is a Ricci flow on a closed manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) , for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . Working with respect to the metric \( g\left( T\right) \) , if \( p \in  \mathcal{M} \) , and \( r > 0 \) is sufficiently small so that \( \left| R\right|  \leq  {r}^{-2} \) on \( B\left( {p, r}\right) \) , then

\[
\mathcal{K}\left( {p, r}\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \frac{\mathcal{V}\left( {p, r}\right) }{{r}^{n}} > \xi
\]

for some \( \xi  > 0 \) depending on \( n, g\left( 0\right) \) , and upper bounds for \( r \) and \( T \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: Theorem 8.3.1 (No collapsing). Suppose that \( g\left( t\right) \) is a Ricci flow on a closed manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) , for \( t \in \left\lbrack {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . Working with respect to the metric \( g\left( T\right) \) , if \( p \in \mathcal{M} \) , and \( r > 0 \) is sufficiently small so that \( \left| R\right| \leq {r}^{-2} \) on \( B\left( {p, r}\right) \) , then \[ \mathcal{K}\left( {p, r}\right...

nodes.proof:
Let \( {r}_{0} \) and \( {T}_{0} \) be upper bounds for \( r \) and \( T \) respectively. By Theorem 8.3.4, there exists \( \gamma  = \gamma \left( {n, g\left( 0\right) ,{T}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right)  \in  \mathbb{R} \) such that working with respect to the metric \( g\left( T\right) \) , we have, for all \( s \in  \left( {0,{r}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , that

\[
\gamma  \leq  \frac{\mathcal{V}\left( {p, s}\right) }{\mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{s}{2}}\right) } + \frac{{s}^{2}}{\mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{s}{2}}\right) }{\int }_{B\left( {p, s}\right) }\left| R\right| {dV} + \ln \left\lbrack  {\mathcal{K}\left( {p, s}\right) }\right\rbrack  .
\]

When \( s \in  (0, r\rbrack \) , we have that \( \left| R\right|  \leq  {r}^{-2} \leq  {s}^{-2} \) on \( B\left( {p, s}\right) \) , and therefore

\[
\gamma  \leq  2\frac{\mathcal{V}\left( {p, s}\right) }{\mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{s}{2}}\right) } + \ln \left\lbrack  {\mathcal{K}\left( {p, s}\right) }\right\rbrack  . \tag{8.3.11}
\]

Define \( {\omega }_{n} \) to be the volume of the unit ball in Euclidean \( n \) -space. Since \( g\left( T\right) \) is a smooth metric, we have

\[
\mathcal{K}\left( {p, s}\right)  = \frac{\mathcal{V}\left( {p, s}\right) }{{s}^{n}} \rightarrow  {\omega }_{n} \tag{8.3.12}
\]

as \( s \downarrow  0 \) . We claim that the theorem holds true if we choose

\[
\xi  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \min \left\{  {\frac{{\omega }_{n}}{2},{e}^{\gamma  - {2}^{n + 1}}}\right\}   > 0.
\]

That is, we wish to establish that \( \mathcal{K}\left( {p, r}\right)  > \xi \) .

Claim: If \( s \in  (0, r\rbrack \) and \( \mathcal{K}\left( {p, s}\right)  \leq  \xi \) then \( \mathcal{K}\left( {p,\frac{s}{2}}\right)  \leq  \xi \) .

Indeed if \( \mathcal{K}\left( {p, s}\right)  \leq  \xi \) , then \( \mathcal{K}\left( {p, s}\right)  \leq  {e}^{\gamma  - {2}^{n + 1}} \) , so \( \ln \left\lbrack  {\mathcal{K}\left( {p, s}\right) }\right\rbrack   \leq  \gamma  - {2}^{n + 1} \) , and by (8.3.11),

\[
\gamma  \leq  2\frac{\mathcal{V}\left( {p, s}\right) }{\mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{s}{2}}\right) } + \gamma  - {2}^{n + 1}
\]

Rearranging, we find that

\[
{2}^{n} \leq  \frac{\mathcal{V}\left( {p, s}\right) }{\mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{s}{2}}\right) } = {2}^{n}\frac{\mathcal{K}\left( {p, s}\right) }{\mathcal{K}\left( {p,\frac{s}{2}}\right) },
\]

and hence that \( \mathcal{K}\left( {p,\frac{s}{2}}\right)  \leq  \mathcal{K}\left( {p, s}\right)  \leq  \xi \) , as required for the claim.

Using this claim iteratively, we see that

\[
\mathcal{K}\left( {p, r}\right)  \leq  \xi \; \Rightarrow  \;\mathcal{K}\left( {p,{2}^{-m}r}\right)  \leq  \xi  \leq  \frac{{\omega }_{n}}{2}
\]

for all \( m \geq  1 \) , but this contradicts the limit \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{s \downarrow  0}}\mathcal{K}\left( {p, s}\right)  = {\omega }_{n} \) from (8.3.12).

Theorem 8.3.4. Suppose that \( g\left( t\right) \) is a Ricci flow on a closed manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) , for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , and that \( r > 0 \) and \( p \in  \mathcal{M} \) . First, let us specialise Lemma 8.3.5 to the case \( \lambda  = \frac{1}{36} \) and \( g = g\left( T\right) \) , and estimate

\[
\mu \left( {g\left( T\right) ,\frac{1}{36}{r}^{2}}\right)  \leq  \frac{\mathcal{V}\left( {p, r}\right) }{\mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right) } + \frac{{r}^{2}}{\mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right) }{\int }_{B\left( {p, r}\right) }\left| R\right| {dV} + \ln \left\lbrack  {\mathcal{K}\left( {p, r}\right) }\right\rbrack   - \frac{n}{2}\ln \frac{\pi }{9} - n.
\]

(8.3.8)

By Lemma 8.1.8, there exists a smooth \( {f}_{T} : \mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) compatible with \( g\left( T\right) \) and \( \tau  = \frac{1}{36}{r}^{2} \) such that

\[
\mathcal{W}\left( {g\left( T\right) ,{f}_{T},\frac{1}{36}{r}^{2}}\right)  = \mu \left( {g\left( T\right) ,\frac{1}{36}{r}^{2}}\right) . \tag{8.3.9}
\]

We set \( \tau  = T + \frac{1}{36}{r}^{2} - t \) , and for our given Ricci flow \( g\left( t\right) \) , find the \( f \) : \( \mathcal{M} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) with \( f\left( T\right)  = {f}_{T} \) completing a solution of (8.2.1), as discussed in Remark 8.2.5. By Remark 8.2.2, \( g\left( t\right) , f\left( t\right) \) and \( \tau \) remain compatible for all \( t \) . Using the definition of \( \mu \) , Proposition 8.2.1 and (8.3.9) we then have

\[
\mu \left( {g\left( 0\right) ,\frac{1}{36}{r}^{2} + T}\right)  \leq  \mathcal{W}\left( {g\left( 0\right) , f\left( 0\right) ,\frac{1}{36}{r}^{2} + T}\right)  \leq  \mathcal{W}\left( {g\left( T\right) , f\left( T\right) ,\frac{1}{36}{r}^{2}}\right)
\]

\[
= \mu \left( {g\left( T\right) ,\frac{1}{36}{r}^{2}}\right) ,
\]

(8.3.10)

which coupled with (8.3.8) and the definition of \( \nu \) from (8.1.7) gives

\[
\nu \left( {g\left( 0\right) ,\frac{1}{36}{r}_{0}^{2} + {T}_{0}}\right)  + \frac{n}{2}\ln \frac{\pi }{9} + n \leq  \frac{\mathcal{V}\left( {p, r}\right) }{\mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right) } + \frac{{r}^{2}}{\mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right) }{\int }_{B\left( {p, r}\right) }\left| R\right| {dV} + \ln \left\lbrack  {\mathcal{K}\left( {p, r}\right) }\right\rbrack  ,
\]

\[
\mu \left( {g,\lambda {r}^{2}}\right)  \leq  {36\lambda }\frac{\mathcal{V}\left( {p, r}\right)  - \mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right) }{\mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right) } + \frac{\lambda {r}^{2}}{\mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right) }{\int }_{B\left( {p, r}\right) }\left| R\right| {dV} + \ln \left\lbrack  \frac{\mathcal{V}\left( {p, r}\right) }{{\left( 4\pi \lambda {r}^{2}\right) }^{\frac{n}{2}}}\right\rbrack   - n.

nodes.proof:
If we adopt the change of variables we used in Section 8.1, namely \( \phi  = {e}^{-\frac{f}{2}} \) , and write \( \tau  = \lambda {r}^{2} \) , then we have (abusing notation for \( \mathcal{W} \) as before) that

\[
\mathcal{W}\left( {g,\phi ,\lambda {r}^{2}}\right)  = {\left( 4\pi \lambda {r}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}\int \left\lbrack  {\lambda {r}^{2}\left( {4{\left| \nabla \phi \right| }^{2} + R{\phi }^{2}}\right)  - 2{\phi }^{2}\ln \phi  - n{\phi }^{2}}\right\rbrack  {dV},
\]

(8.3.3)

and the compatibility constraint (8.1.2) becomes

\[
{\left( 4\pi \lambda {r}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}\int {\phi }^{2}{dV} = 1. \tag{8.3.4}
\]

As we remarked before, these expressions have the benefit of making sense when \( \phi \) is merely weakly (rather than strictly) positive, and by approximation,

\[
\mathop{\inf }\limits_{f}\mathcal{W}\left( {g, f,\lambda {r}^{2}}\right)  = \mathop{\inf }\limits_{\phi }\mathcal{W}\left( {g,\phi ,\lambda {r}^{2}}\right) , \tag{8.3.5}
\]

where the infima are taken over \( f : \mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) and \( \phi  : \mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) compatible with \( g \) and \( \tau  = \lambda {r}^{2} \) , and we are abusing notation for \( \mathcal{W} \) as usual.

Let \( \psi  : \lbrack 0,\infty ) \rightarrow  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) be a smooth cut-off function, supported in \( \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) , such that \( \psi \left( y\right)  = 1 \) for \( y \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{2}}\right\rbrack \) and \( \left| {\psi }^{\prime }\right|  \leq  3 \) . We then write

\[
\phi \left( x\right)  = {e}^{-\frac{c}{2}}\psi \left( \frac{d\left( {x, p}\right) }{r}\right) ,
\]

where \( c \in  \mathbb{R} \) is determined by the constraint (8.3.4), and since

\[
\mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right)  \leq  {e}^{c}\int {\phi }^{2}{dV} \leq  \mathcal{V}\left( {p, r}\right) ,
\]

we deduce that

\[
{\left( 4\pi \lambda {r}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}\mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right)  \leq  {e}^{c} \leq  {\left( 4\pi \lambda {r}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}\mathcal{V}\left( {p, r}\right) . \tag{8.3.6}
\]

We now estimate each of the four terms in (8.3.3) separately.

Term 1. For the specific \( \phi \) we have chosen, whose gradient is supported on \( B\left( {p, r}\right)  \smallsetminus  B\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right) \) , and satisfies \( \left| {\nabla \phi }\right|  \leq  {e}^{-\frac{c}{2}}\frac{1}{r}\sup \left| {\psi }^{\prime }\right|  \leq  \frac{3}{r}{e}^{-\frac{c}{2}} \) , we estimate

\[
{\left( 4\pi \lambda {r}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}\int \lambda {r}^{2}4{\left| \nabla \phi \right| }^{2}{dV} \leq  {4\lambda }{r}^{2}{\left( 4\pi \lambda {r}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}\sup {\left| \nabla \phi \right| }^{2}\left( {\mathcal{V}\left( {p, r}\right)  - \mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\leq  {36\lambda }{\left( 4\pi \lambda {r}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}{e}^{-c}\left( {\mathcal{V}\left( {p, r}\right)  - \mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\leq  {36\lambda }\frac{\mathcal{V}\left( {p, r}\right)  - \mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right) }{\mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right) },
\]

the last inequality using the first part of (8.3.6).

Term 2. For the specific \( \phi \) we have chosen, which is supported on \( B\left( {p, r}\right) \) , and satisfies

\[
{\phi }^{2} \leq  {e}^{-c} \leq  \frac{{\left( 4\pi \lambda {r}^{2}\right) }^{\frac{n}{2}}}{\mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right) },
\]

we estimate

\[
{\left( 4\pi \lambda {r}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}\int \lambda {r}^{2}R{\phi }^{2}{dV} \leq  \frac{\lambda {r}^{2}}{\mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right) }{\int }_{B\left( {p, r}\right) }\left| R\right| {dV}.
\]

Term 3. By again using the fact that the support of \( \phi \) lies within \( B\left( {p, r}\right) \) , we rewrite

\[
{\left( 4\pi \lambda {r}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}\int  - 2{\phi }^{2}\ln {\phi dV} = \int G\left( \sigma \right) {d\mu }, \tag{8.3.7}
\]

where \( \sigma  : B\left( {p, r}\right)  \rightarrow  \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) is defined by \( \sigma  \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\phi }^{2} \) , the continuous function \( G : \lbrack 0,\infty ) \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) is defined for \( y > 0 \) by \( G\left( y\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }}  - y\ln y \) , and the measure \( {d\mu } \) is supported on \( B\left( {p, r}\right) \) , where \( {d\mu } \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\left( 4\pi \lambda {r}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}{dV} \) . Because \( G \) is concave, we may apply Jensen's inequality

\[
\oint G\left( \sigma \right) {d\mu } \leq  G\left( {\oint {\sigma d\mu }}\right) ,
\]

as we used in Section 8.1, and since by (8.3.4) we have

\[
\int {\sigma d\mu } = 1
\]

this tells us that

\[
\int G\left( \sigma \right) {d\mu } \leq  \left( {\int {d\mu }}\right) G\left( \frac{1}{\int {d\mu }}\right)  = \ln \left( {\int {d\mu }}\right) .
\]

By (8.3.7) and the definition of \( {d\mu } \) , we conclude that

\[
{\left( 4\pi \lambda {r}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}\int  - 2{\phi }^{2}\ln {\phi dV} \leq  \ln \left\lbrack  \frac{\mathcal{V}\left( {p, r}\right) }{{\left( 4\pi \lambda {r}^{2}\right) }^{\frac{n}{2}}}\right\rbrack  .
\]

Term 4. By the constraint (8.3.4), we have simply

\[
{\left( 4\pi \lambda {r}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}\int  - n{\phi }^{2}{dV} =  - n.
\]

When we combine these calculations with (8.3.3), we find that for the particular \( \phi \) under consideration,

\[
\mathcal{W}\left( {g,\phi ,\lambda {r}^{2}}\right)  \leq  {36\lambda }\frac{\mathcal{V}\left( {p, r}\right)  - \mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right) }{\mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right) } + \frac{\lambda {r}^{2}}{\mathcal{V}\left( {p,\frac{r}{2}}\right) }{\int }_{B\left( {p, r}\right) }\left| R\right| {dV} + \ln \left\lbrack  \frac{\mathcal{V}\left( {p, r}\right) }{{\left( 4\pi \lambda {r}^{2}\right) }^{\frac{n}{2}}}\right\rbrack   - n,
\]

which together with (8.3.5), proves the lemma.

nodes.label: Lemma 8.4.1

nodes.content:
Lemma 8.4.1. There exist \( \bar{r} > 0 \) universal and \( \eta  > 0 \) depending on the dimension \( n \) such that if \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}^{n}, g}\right) \) is a closed Riemannian manifold satisfying \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right|  \leq  1 \) , then there exists \( p \in  \mathcal{M} \) such that

\[
\frac{\mathcal{V}\left( {p, r}\right) }{{r}^{n}} \leq  \frac{\eta }{r}\operatorname{inj}\left( \mathcal{M}\right) \tag{8.4.1}
\]

for all \( r \in  (0,\bar{r}\rbrack \) .

In order to see the sharpness of this lemma, one can consider \( \mathcal{M} \) to be the product of a closed manifold of dimension \( n - 1 \) satisfying \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right|  \leq  1 \) , and a very small \( {S}^{1} \) .

There exist \( \bar{r} > 0 \) universal and \( \eta > 0 \) depending on the dimension \( n \) such that if \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}^{n}, g}\right) \) is a closed Riemannian manifold satisfying \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| \leq 1 \) , then there exists \( p \in \mathcal{M} \) such that \[ \frac{\mathcal{V}\left( {p, r}\right) }{{r}^{n}} \leq \frac{\eta }{r}\operatorname{inj}\left( \mathcal{M}\right)...

nodes.proof:
For the moment, set \( \bar{r} = 1 \) . We will arrive at the constant \( \bar{r} \) whose existence is asserted in the proof by successively reducing it to satisfy a number of constraints.

First we observe that it suffices to prove the theorem under the assumption that \( \operatorname{inj}\left( \mathcal{M}\right) \) is less than \( \pi \) . (We could take any positive upper bound here.) This follows because our curvature hypothesis \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right|  \leq  1 \) implies that all sectional curvatures are no lower than -1 , and hence by Bishop's theorem (see, for example [14, (3.101))]) the volume ratio on the left-hand side of (8.4.1) is bounded above for \( r \leq  1 \) by some n-dependent constant \( C \) (which could be taken to be the volume ratio of the unit ball in hyperbolic space). Whenever \( \inf \left( \mathcal{M}\right)  \geq  \pi \) , the theorem holds with \( \eta  = \frac{C}{\pi } \) .

We now appeal to Klingenberg's lemma (see [4, Theorem 3.4]) which tells us that because all of the sectional curvatures are no more than 1, and \( \operatorname{inj}\left( \mathcal{M}\right)  < \pi \) , there exists a closed geodesic loop \( \gamma \) in \( \mathcal{M} \) with

\[
\operatorname{Length}\left( \gamma \right)  = 2\operatorname{inj}\left( \mathcal{M}\right) \text{ . } \tag{8.4.2}
\]

We are free to pick any \( p \in  \gamma \) .

Let us define \( {N}^{r}\gamma \) to be the subset of the normal bundle of \( \gamma \) within \( \mathcal{M} \) consisting of vectors of length less than \( r \) , and \( {\mathcal{N}}^{r}\gamma \) to be the subset of \( \mathcal{M} \) consisting of all points within a distance \( r \) of \( \gamma \) . There is a natural flat metric \( G \) on the total space of \( {N}^{r}\gamma \) , which can be defined unambiguously at points over a neighbourhood \( U \subset  \gamma \) (small enough to be simply connected) of an arbitrary point \( q \in  \gamma \) as the pullback of the standard product metric on \( \gamma  \times  {N}_{q}^{r}\gamma \) under the map

(8.4.3)

\[
{N}^{r}U \rightarrow  \;\gamma  \times  {N}_{q}^{r}U
\]

\[
v \rightarrow  \;\left( {\pi \left( v\right) ,\Theta \left( v\right) }\right)
\]

where \( \pi  : {N}^{r}\gamma  \rightarrow  \gamma \) is the bundle projection, and \( \Theta \left( v\right) \) is the parallel translate of \( v \) within \( U \) to a vector over \( q \) .

We define a map \( u : {N}^{r}\gamma  \rightarrow  {\mathcal{N}}^{r}\gamma \) by exponentiation. That is, for \( v \in  {N}^{r}\gamma \) ,

\[
u\left( v\right)  = {\exp }_{\pi \left( v\right) }\left( v\right) .
\]

Clearly, \( u \) is a surjection, since if \( y \in  {\mathcal{N}}^{r}\gamma \) and \( q \in  \gamma \) is a point closest to \( y \) , then \( y \) is in the image of an appropriate vector in the fibre over \( q \) . Moreover, by considering the behaviour of Jacobi fields under our constraint \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right|  \leq  1 \) , and in particular by the Rauch comparison theorems (see [4]) after reducing the upper bound \( \bar{r} \) for \( r \) , if necessary (to some positive, universal value) the map \( u \) is an immersion and we have

\[
{u}^{ * }g \leq  {4G},
\]

say. (Note that \( {u}^{ * }g = G \) on \( \gamma \) .) In particular, the volume form of \( {u}^{ * }g \) is bounded by \( {2}^{n} \) times the volume form of \( G \) , and hence

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{g}\left( {{\mathcal{N}}^{r}\gamma }\right)  \leq  {\operatorname{Vol}}_{{u}^{ * }g}\left( {{N}^{r}\gamma }\right)  \leq  {2}^{n}{\operatorname{Vol}}_{G}\left( {{N}^{r}\gamma }\right)  = {2}^{n}\operatorname{Length}\left( \gamma \right) {\omega }_{n - 1}{r}^{n - 1},
\]

where \( {\omega }_{n - 1} \) is the volume of the \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional Euclidean unit ball.

Clearly \( {B}_{g}\left( {p, r}\right)  \subset  {\mathcal{N}}^{r}\gamma \) , and so

\[
\mathcal{V}\left( {p, r}\right)  \leq  \operatorname{Vol}\left( {{\mathcal{N}}^{r}\gamma }\right)  \leq  {2}^{n}{\omega }_{n - 1}\operatorname{Length}\left( \gamma \right) {r}^{n - 1},
\]

and by (8.4.2) we have

\[
\frac{\mathcal{V}\left( {p, r}\right) }{{r}^{n}} \leq  {2}^{n + 1}{\omega }_{n - 1}\frac{\operatorname{inj}\left( \mathcal{M}\right) }{r}.
\]

nodes.content:
Theorem 8.5.1 (Blow-up of singularities). Suppose that \( \mathcal{M} \) is a closed manifold, and \( g\left( t\right) \) is a Ricci flow on a maximal time interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( T < \infty \) . Then there exist sequences \( {p}_{i} \in  \mathcal{M} \) and \( {t}_{i} \uparrow  T \) with

\[
\left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {{p}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right)  = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  \mathcal{M}, t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{i}}\right\rbrack  }}\left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty ,
\]

such that, defining

\[
{g}_{i}\left( t\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {{p}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right) g\left( {{t}_{i} + \frac{t}{\left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {{p}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right) }}\right) ,
\]

there exist \( b = b\left( n\right)  > 0 \) , a complete Ricci flow \( \left( {\mathcal{N},\widehat{g}\left( t\right) }\right) \) for \( t \in  \left( {-\infty , b}\right) \) , and \( {p}_{\infty } \in  \mathcal{N} \) such that

\[
\left( {\mathcal{M},{g}_{i}\left( t\right) ,{p}_{i}}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {\mathcal{N},\widehat{g}\left( t\right) ,{p}_{\infty }}\right)
\]

as \( i \rightarrow  \infty \) . Moreover, \( \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {\widehat{g}\left( 0\right) }\right) }\right| \left( {p}_{\infty }\right)  = 1 \) , and \( \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {\widehat{g}\left( t\right) }\right) }\right|  \leq  1 \) for \( t \leq  0 \) .

nodes.content:
### 9.2 The Einstein Tensor, E

It is often useful to diagonalise the (symmetric) curvature operator \( \mathcal{R} \) : \( \mathop{\bigwedge }\limits^{2}T\mathcal{M} \rightarrow  \mathop{\bigwedge }\limits^{2}T\mathcal{M} \) . In three dimensions, elements of \( \mathop{\bigwedge }\limits^{2} \) are all simple. (That is, we can write each of them as \( e \land  f \) for some vectors \( e \) and \( f \) , as opposed to in higher dimensions where, for example, \( {e}_{1} \land  {e}_{2} + {e}_{3} \land  {e}_{4} \) cannot be written in this way given linearly independent vectors \( {e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{4} \) .) It follows that, at each point \( x \in  \mathcal{M},\mathcal{R} \) can be diagonalised by \( {e}_{2} \land  {e}_{3} \) , \( {e}_{3} \land  {e}_{1},{e}_{1} \land  {e}_{2} \) where \( {e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3} \) form an orthonormal basis for \( {T}_{x}\mathcal{M} \) . All of the curvature information is then given by the eigenvalues of \( \mathcal{R} \) .

In fact, all the curvature information is given by the sectional curvatures \( {\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2},{\lambda }_{3} \) of the three "planes" \( {e}_{2} \land  {e}_{3},{e}_{3} \land  {e}_{1},{e}_{1} \land  {e}_{2} \) respectively, because

\[
{\lambda }_{3} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \text{ sectional curvature of }{e}_{1} \land  {e}_{2} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{Rm}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{1},{e}_{2}}\right)
\]

\[
= \left\langle  {\mathcal{R}\left( {{e}_{1} \land  {e}_{2}}\right) ,{e}_{1} \land  {e}_{2}}\right\rangle
\]

and thus these sectional curvatures are just the eigenvalues of \( \mathcal{R} \) up to some \( {\text{ constant }}^{1} \) .

An efficient way to handle this is in terms of the Einstein tensor, \( E \in \; \Gamma \left( {{\operatorname{Sym}}^{2}{T}^{ * }\mathcal{M}}\right) \) , defined by

\[
E \mathrel{\text{ := }}  - G\left( \operatorname{Ric}\right)  =  - \operatorname{Ric} + \frac{R}{2}g,
\]

which we will normally view as a section \( E \in  \Gamma \left( {{T}^{ * }\mathcal{M} \otimes  T\mathcal{M}}\right) \) using the metric. (That is, \( E\left( X\right)  =  - \operatorname{Ric}\left( X\right)  + \frac{R}{2}X \) , where we are keeping in mind Remark 2.3.8.) Note that Ric is diagonalised by \( \left\{  {e}_{i}\right\} \) , with

\[
\operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{j}}\right)  = \left( \begin{matrix} {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{3} & 0 & 0 \\  0 & {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{3} & 0 \\  0 & 0 & {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \end{matrix}\right)
\]

and \( R = 2\left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{3}}\right) \) . Therefore \( E \) is also diagonalised by \( \left\{  {e}_{i}\right\} \) , and

\[
E\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{j}}\right)  = \left( \begin{matrix} {\lambda }_{1} & 0 & 0 \\  0 & {\lambda }_{2} & 0 \\  0 & 0 & {\lambda }_{3} \end{matrix}\right) .
\]

### 9.3 Evolution of \( E \) under the Ricci flow

In Proposition 2.5.3, we recorded how the Ricci tensor evolves under Ricci flow. We may convert this to the equivalent formula for Ric seen as a section of \( {T}^{ * }\mathcal{M} \otimes  T\mathcal{M} \) by computing

\[
\left\langle  {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\operatorname{Ric}\left( X\right) , W}\right\rangle   = \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\langle \operatorname{Ric}\left( X\right) , W\rangle  + 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {\operatorname{Ric}\left( X\right) , W}\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, W}\right)  + 2\langle \operatorname{Ric}\left( X\right) ,\operatorname{Ric}\left( W\right) \rangle
\]

\[
= \Delta \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, W}\right)  + 2\langle \operatorname{Rm}\left( {X,\cdot , W, \cdot  }\right) ,\operatorname{Ric}\rangle
\]

Moreover \( \frac{\partial R}{\partial t} = {\Delta R} + 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\right| }^{2} \) and thus

\[
\left\langle  {\frac{\partial E}{\partial t}\left( X\right) , W}\right\rangle   =  - \Delta \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, W}\right)  - 2\langle \operatorname{Rm}\left( {X,\cdot , W, \cdot  }\right) ,\operatorname{Ric}\rangle
\]

\[
+ \frac{1}{2}\left( {\Delta R}\right) g\left( {X, W}\right)  + {\left| \operatorname{Ric}\right| }^{2}g\left( {X, W}\right)
\]

\[
= {\Delta E}\left( {X, W}\right)  - 2\langle \operatorname{Rm}\left( {X,\cdot , W, \cdot  }\right) ,\operatorname{Ric}\rangle  + {\left| \operatorname{Ric}\right| }^{2}g\left( {X, W}\right) .
\]

(9.3.1)

Writing this with respect to the basis \( \left\{  {e}_{i}\right\} \) then gives

\[
\frac{\partial E}{\partial t} - {\Delta E} = 2\left( \begin{matrix} {\lambda }_{1}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}{\lambda }_{3} & 0 & 0 \\  0 & {\lambda }_{2}^{2} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{3} & 0 \\  0 & 0 & {\lambda }_{3}^{2} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{2} \end{matrix}\right) . \tag{9.3.2}
\]

There are a number of ways of writing the right-hand side explicitly in terms of \( E \) . For example, it represents the fibre-gradient of the function \( \frac{2}{3}\operatorname{tr}\left( {E}^{3}\right)  + 2\det \left( E\right) \) on \( {T}^{ * }\mathcal{M} \otimes  T\mathcal{M} \) , or can be written in terms of the Lie-algebra square of \( E \) (see [20] for the latter viewpoint) but we are happy to leave it in this form for now.

nodes.label: Theorem 9.6.1

nodes.content:
Theorem 9.6.1. Suppose that \( W \) is a vector bundle over a closed manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) , with bundle projection \( \pi  : W \rightarrow  \mathcal{M} \) , equipped with a fixed fibre metric \( h \) and a smooth family of connections \( A\left( t\right) \) compatible with \( h \) , for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . Suppose that \( g\left( t\right) \) is a smooth family of Riemannian metrics on \( \mathcal{M} \) , for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) .

Suppose that \( \Upsilon  \in  \Gamma \left( {{\pi }^{ * }\left( W\right) }\right) \) , that is, \( \Upsilon \) is a vector field on \( W \) which is parallel to the fibres of \( W \) , and that \( X \subset  W \) is a closed subset which is parallel and convex in the sense of Definition 9.5.5, and preserved under the ODE

\[
\frac{de}{dt} = \Upsilon \left( e\right) \tag{9.6.1}
\]

More precisely, if \( e\left( t\right) \) is a solution to (9.6.1) on some time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,\epsilon }\right\rbrack \) , with \( e\left( 0\right)  \in  X \) then we assume that \( e\left( t\right)  \in  X \) for all \( t \) .

Then the set \( X \) is preserved under the PDE

\[
\frac{\partial E}{\partial t} - {\Delta }_{A}E = \Upsilon \left( E\right) \tag{9.6.2}
\]

for \( E\left( t\right)  \in  \Gamma \left( W\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . In other words, if \( E\left( {x,0}\right)  \in  X \) for all \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) , then \( E\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  X \) for all \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) .

Note that the ODE (9.6.1) preserves each fibre.

Suppose that \( g\left( t\right) \) is a smooth family of Riemannian metrics o...

nodes.proof:
First note that we may assume, without loss of generality, that \( X \) is compact. Indeed, if we had a counterexample to the theorem for \( X \) noncompact, then we could intersect \( X \) with the parallel, convex subset

\[
{T}_{r} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \{ w \in  W : \left| w\right|  < r\} , \tag{9.6.3}
\]

for \( r > 0 \) sufficiently large that the image of the counterexample \( E \) always lay within \( {T}_{r/2} \) , and modify \( \Upsilon \) outside the image of \( E \) appropriately to give a counterexample for \( X \) compact. (Here, and throughout the proof, the quantity \( \left| w\right| \) of a point in \( W \) will always be measured with respect to \( h \) .)

Define \( \psi  : W \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) by \( \psi \left( w\right)  = \operatorname{dist}\left( {w, X}\right) \) , the fibrewise distance function to the convex set \( X \) , using the fibre metric \( h \) . Define \( Y = \{ w \in  W \mid  \psi \left( w\right)  < 2\} \) , and let \( K \) be the (fibrewise) Lipschitz constant for \( \Upsilon \) within \( Y \) . That is, for all \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) , and for all \( v, w \in  {Y}_{x} \) (the part of \( Y \) in the fibre over \( x \) ) we have

\[
\left| {\Upsilon \left( v\right)  - \Upsilon \left( w\right) }\right|  \leq  K\left| {v - w}\right| . \tag{9.6.4}
\]

For a given \( w \in  Y \smallsetminus  X \) , we pick the point \( p \in  \partial X \) in the same fibre as \( w \) which is closest to \( w \) , and define \( x \mathrel{\text{ := }} \pi \left( w\right) \) . It is also convenient to highlight the linear function \( L : {W}_{x} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) defined by \( L\left( v\right)  = d{\psi }_{x}\left( w\right) \left( {v - p}\right) \) , and note that

\[
L \leq  0\text{ on }{X}_{x};\;L \leq  \psi  \leq  \operatorname{dist}\left( {\cdot , p}\right) \text{ near }w\text{ in }{W}_{x}. \tag{9.6.5}
\]

By the ODE hypothesis, we must have

\[
d{\psi }_{x}\left( w\right) \left( {\Upsilon \left( p\right) }\right)  \leq  0. \tag{9.6.6}
\]

If not, we would solve the ODE (9.6.1) with \( e\left( 0\right)  = p \) to find that

\[
{\left. \frac{d}{dt}L\left( e\left( t\right) \right) \right| }_{t = 0} = d{\psi }_{x}\left( w\right) \left( {\Upsilon \left( p\right) }\right)  > 0,
\]

which, by (9.6.5), would make \( \psi \left( {e\left( t\right) }\right)  \geq  L\left( {e\left( t\right) }\right)  > 0 \) for small \( t > 0 \) , a contradiction.

The inequality (9.6.6) then leads to

(9.6.7)

\[
d{\psi }_{\pi \left( w\right) }\left( w\right) \left( {\Upsilon \left( w\right) }\right)  = d{\psi }_{x}\left( w\right) \left( {\Upsilon \left( w\right)  - \Upsilon \left( p\right) }\right)  + d{\psi }_{x}\left( w\right) \left( {\Upsilon \left( p\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \left| {\Upsilon \left( w\right)  - \Upsilon \left( p\right) }\right|  \leq  {K\psi }\left( w\right) ,
\]

for our arbitrary point \( w \in  Y \smallsetminus  X \) .

In order to apply the maximum principle as we stated it in Chapter 3, it will be convenient to work with a slightly smoothed version of \( \psi \) . Since \( \psi \) is \( {C}^{1} \) on \( Y \smallsetminus  X \) (recall (9.6.5)) for any \( \varepsilon  \in  \left( {0,1}\right) \) , we can mollify \( \psi \) (see [15]) by a small amount (depending on \( \varepsilon \) ) on each fibre, using the metric \( h \) , to give a smooth, parallel, convex function \( \Psi  : W \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) for which

\[
\left| {\Psi  - \psi }\right|  < \varepsilon
\]

on \( Y \) , and

\[
d{\Psi }_{\pi \left( w\right) }\left( w\right) \left( {\Upsilon \left( w\right) }\right)  \leq  {2K\Psi }\left( w\right) \tag{9.6.8}
\]

on the set \( \{ w \in  W \mid  \Psi \left( w\right)  \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{\varepsilon }{2},1}\right\rbrack  \}  \subset  Y \) .

Now let us take a solution \( E \) to the PDE as in the theorem. We will constraint the evolution of \( E \) by applying the maximum principle to \( u \mathrel{\text{ := }} \; \Psi  \circ  E : \mathcal{M} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) . By Proposition 9.5.4 and (9.6.8), we have

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - {\Delta }_{\mathcal{M}}}\right) u\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  d{\Psi }_{x}\left( {E\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \left( {\Upsilon \left( {E\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) }\right)  \leq  {2Ku}\left( {x, t}\right) \tag{9.6.9}
\]

whenever \( u\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{\varepsilon }{2},1}\right\rbrack \) . Moreover, if we choose some smooth \( F : \mathbb{R} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) for which \( F\left( v\right)  = 2\widetilde{Kv} \) for \( v \geq  \varepsilon \) , and so that \( d{\Psi }_{\pi \left( w\right) }\left( w\right) \left( {\Upsilon \left( w\right) }\right)  \leq  F\left( {\Psi \left( w\right) }\right) \) for all \( w \in  W \) with \( \Psi \left( w\right)  \leq  1 \) , then

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - {\Delta }_{\mathcal{M}}}\right) u \leq  F\left( u\right) \tag{9.6.10}
\]

for sufficiently small \( t \) so that \( u\left( {\cdot , t}\right)  \leq  1 \) . This is the equation to which we can apply Theorem 3.1.1. Noting that \( u\left( {\cdot ,0}\right)  \leq  \varepsilon \) , we compare \( u \) to the function \( \phi \left( t\right)  = \varepsilon {e}^{2Kt} \) , and find that for \( \varepsilon  < {e}^{-{2KT}} \) , we have \( u\left( {\cdot , t}\right)  \leq  \varepsilon {e}^{2Kt} \leq  \varepsilon {e}^{2KT} < 1 \) , the last of these inequalities being mentioned to emphasise that we need not worry about (9.6.10) failing to hold before time \( T \) . Returning from \( \Psi \) to \( \psi \) , we find that \( \psi  \circ  E \leq  \Psi  \circ  E + \varepsilon  = u + \varepsilon \) , and hence that

\[
\psi  \circ  E \leq  \varepsilon \left( {{e}^{2KT} + 1}\right)
\]

on \( \mathcal{M} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . This last inequality is independent of the mollification, and holds for all sufficiently small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , and hence \( \psi  \circ  E \equiv  0 \) throughout, which is equivalent to having \( E\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  X \) for all \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) as desired.

The only aspect of the ODE hypothesis that we used in the proof is the following property: For all \( p \in  \partial X \) , when we solve the ODE (9.6.1) with \( e\left( 0\right)  = p \) , then

\[
{\left. \frac{d}{dt}L\left( e\left( t\right) \right) \right| }_{t = 0} \leq  0 \tag{9.6.11}
\]

whenever \( L : {W}_{x} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) is a nonconstant linear function such that \( L\left( p\right)  = 0 \) and \( L \leq  0 \) on \( X \) . This property could be shown to be equivalent to the ODE hypothesis, although one should beware of the subtlety that if we only knew that for some \( p \in  \partial X \) , the ODE solution \( e\left( t\right) \) with \( e\left( 0\right)  = p \) satisfied (9.6.11) for all \( L \) as before, then it could still be the case that \( e\left( t\right)  \notin  X \) for all \( t > 0 \) even though \( e\left( 0\right)  = p \in  X \) .

The following consequence of these considerations will be useful:

nodes.content:
Remark 9.7.1. We will apply Theorem 9.6.1 in the case described in Remark 9.5.1. We take the section \( \Upsilon \) so that the PDE (9.6.2) for \( E \) is the PDE (9.4.2) we had for \( \widetilde{E} \) . Note that in this situation, the ODE (9.6.1) preserves the eigenvectors of the symmetric endomorphism \( e \) , and thus can be viewed simply as the coupled ODE

\[
\frac{d{\lambda }_{1}}{dt} = 2\left( {{\lambda }_{1}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}{\lambda }_{3}}\right) ,\;\frac{d{\lambda }_{2}}{dt} = 2\left( {{\lambda }_{2}^{2} + {\lambda }_{3}{\lambda }_{1}}\right) ,\;\frac{d{\lambda }_{3}}{dt} = 2\left( {{\lambda }_{3}^{2} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{2}}\right) \tag{9.7.1}
\]

for the eigenvalues \( {\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2} \) and \( {\lambda }_{3} \) .

By definition of the extension of \( A\left( t\right) \) to \( W \) from \( V \) , and the fact that \( A\left( t\right) \) is compatible with the metric \( h \) , when we parallel translate an element of \( W \) (that is, an endomorphism) the eigenvectors in \( V \) move by parallel translation, and the eigenvalues remain the same.

Consequently, if we define a function \( \Psi \) on \( W \) exclusively in terms of the eigenvalues \( {\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2},{\lambda }_{3} \) , it will automatically be a parallel function, in the sense of Definition 9.5.2.

In order to make \( \Psi \) convex, in the sense of Definition 9.5.3, it suffices to choose a function of \( {\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2},{\lambda }_{3} \) which gives a convex function on the space of symmetric endomorphisms of \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) endowed with the standard metric. This motivates the following lemma.

(i) \( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{3} \) is just the trace of the symmetric endomorphism, which is a linear function.

(ii) Suppose that \( {F}_{1} \) and \( {F}_{2} \) are two symmetric endomorphisms on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) , and that \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . Let \( e \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) be a unit-length eigenvector corresponding to the first eigenvalue of \( s{F}_{1} + \left( {1 - s}\right) {F}_{2} \) . Then

\[
{\lambda }_{1}\left( {s{F}_{1} + \left( {1 - s}\right) {F}_{2}}\right)  = s\left\langle  {{F}_{1}\left( e\right) , e}\right\rangle   + \left( {1 - s}\right) \left\langle  {{F}_{2}\left( e\right) , e}\right\rangle   \geq  s{\lambda }_{1}\left( {F}_{1}\right)  + \left( {1 - s}\right) {\lambda }_{1}\left( {F}_{2}\right)
\]

since \( {\lambda }_{1}\left( {F}_{1}\right)  = \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{\parallel \widetilde{e}\parallel  = 1}}\left\langle  {{F}_{1}\left( \widetilde{e}\right) ,\widetilde{e}}\right\rangle \) .

(a) This follows from (ii) since if \( E \) is a symmetric endomorphism on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) , then \( {\lambda }_{3}\left( E\right)  =  - {\lambda }_{1}\left( {-E}\right) \) .

(b) This follows from (i) and (a) because \( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} = \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{3}}\right)  - {\lambda }_{3} \) .

(c) This follows from (ii) and (a).

For the final claim, since the function \( \beta  : \lbrack 0,\infty ) \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) is concave, for \( {x}_{1},{x}_{2} \in \; {\alpha }^{-1}\left( {\lbrack 0,\infty }\right) ) \subset  \mathcal{X} \) we have

\[
{s\beta }\left( {\alpha \left( {x}_{1}\right) }\right)  + \left( {1 - s}\right) \beta \left( {\alpha \left( {x}_{2}\right) }\right)  \leq  \beta \left\lbrack  {{s\alpha }\left( {x}_{1}\right)  + \left( {1 - s}\right) \alpha \left( {x}_{2}\right) }\right\rbrack   \leq  \beta \left\lbrack  {\alpha \left( {s{x}_{1} + \left( {1 - s}\right) {x}_{2}}\right) }\right\rbrack  ,
\]

where the final inequality uses the monotonicity of \( \beta \) .

We apply Theorem 9.6.1 in the situation described in Remark 9.7.1, with \( X \) the 0-sublevel set of the convex function \( \Psi \left( e\right)  =  - {\lambda }_{1}\left( e\right) \) . (That is, \( X = \{ e \in  W \mid  \Psi \left( e\right)  \leq  0\} \) .) \[

\]

and thus keeping in mind that \( {\lambda }_{2},{\lambda }_{3} \geq  {\lambda }_{1} \geq  0 \) , we see that \( {\lambda }_{1} \geq  0 \) is preserved.

nodes.content:
Theorem 9.7.5. For all \( \varepsilon  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{3}}\right) \) and any Ricci flow \( g\left( t\right) \) on a three-dimensional, closed manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) , the "pinching condition"

\[
\operatorname{Ric} \geq  {\varepsilon Rg} \tag{9.7.2}
\]

is preserved.

Refer back to Remark 5.3.3 for the definition of such inequalities, if necessary.

The significance of the permitted range of values for \( \varepsilon \) is that (9.7.2) then implies \( R \geq  0 \) , and hence that \( \operatorname{Ric} \geq  0 \) , by tracing.

nodes.proof:
The eigenvalues of Ric are (in increasing order)

\[
{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2},\;{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{3},\;{\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{3},
\]

and in particular, \( R = 2\left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{3}}\right) \) . Define \( \delta  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \frac{2\varepsilon }{1 - {2\varepsilon }} \in  \lbrack 0,2) \) . Therefore

\[
\operatorname{Ric} \geq  {\varepsilon Rg} \Leftrightarrow  {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \geq  \varepsilon \left( {2\left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{3}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\Leftrightarrow  {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \geq  \frac{2\varepsilon }{1 - {2\varepsilon }}{\lambda }_{3}
\]

\[
\Leftrightarrow  \delta {\lambda }_{3} - \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)  \leq  0\text{ . }
\]

By Lemma 9.7.2, \( {\lambda }_{3} \) and \( \left( {-{\lambda }_{1} - {\lambda }_{2} - {\lambda }_{3}}\right) \) are convex, and thus \( \left\lbrack  {\delta {\lambda }_{3} - \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right) }\right\rbrack \) is convex.

We apply Theorem 9.6.1 in the situation described in Remark 9.7.1, with \( X \) the 0 -sublevel set of the convex function \( \Psi \left( e\right)  = \left\lbrack  {\delta {\lambda }_{3} - \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right) }\right\rbrack  \left( e\right) \) . The theorem tells us that the condition \( \left\lbrack  {\delta {\lambda }_{3} - \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right) }\right\rbrack   \leq  0 \) is preserved under the Ricci flow (and hence that Ric \( \geq  {\varepsilon Rg} \) is preserved, as desired) provided that the same condition is preserved under the analogous ODE (9.6.1), or equivalently (9.7.1). Therefore, keeping in mind Remark 9.6.2, we must simply prove that

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\left( {\delta {\lambda }_{3} - \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right) }\right)  \equiv  {2\delta }\left( {{\lambda }_{3}^{2} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{2}}\right)  - 2\left( {{\lambda }_{1}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}{\lambda }_{3} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{3}}\right) \tag{9.7.3}
\]

\[
\leq  0,
\]

whenever

\[
\delta {\lambda }_{3} - \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)  = 0. \tag{9.7.4}
\]

In this regard, note that (9.7.4) implies that both \( {\lambda }_{3} \geq  0 \) and \( \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)  \geq  0 \) , since \( \delta  \in  \lbrack 0,2) \) and \( {\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2} \leq  {\lambda }_{3} \) . Neglecting the easy case in which \( {\lambda }_{3} = 0 \) , (9.7.4) then implies that

\[
\delta \left( {{\lambda }_{3}^{2} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{2}}\right)  - \left( {{\lambda }_{1}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}{\lambda }_{3} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{3}}\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{{\lambda }_{3}}\left\lbrack  {\left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right) \left( {{\lambda }_{3}^{2} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{2}}\right)  - {\lambda }_{3}\left( {{\lambda }_{1}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}{\lambda }_{3} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{3}}\right) }\right\rbrack
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{{\lambda }_{3}}\left\lbrack  {{\lambda }_{1}^{2}{\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2}{\lambda }_{1} - {\lambda }_{3}\left( {{\lambda }_{1}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2}}\right) }\right\rbrack
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{1}{{\lambda }_{3}}\left\lbrack  {{\lambda }_{1}^{2}{\lambda }_{3} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2}{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{3}\left( {{\lambda }_{1}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2}}\right) }\right\rbrack
\]

\[
= 0
\]

and hence (9.7.3) is satisfied.

Theorem 9.7.8 (Roundness). For any \( 0 < \beta  < B < \infty \) and \( \gamma  > 0 \) (however small) there exists \( M = M\left( {\beta , B,\gamma }\right)  < \infty \) such that whenever \( g\left( t\right) \) is

a Ricci flow on a closed, three-dimensional manifold, for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , with \( {\beta g}\left( 0\right)  \leq  \operatorname{Ric}\left( {g\left( 0\right) }\right)  \leq  {Bg}\left( 0\right) \) , we have

\[

\]

nodes.proof:
At \( t = 0 \) , we have \( \operatorname{Ric} \geq  {\beta g} > 0 \) . In terms of the eigenvalues \( {\lambda }_{i} \) , this may be phrased

\[
{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \geq  \beta  > 0
\]

We define a first convex parallel function to be

\[
{\Psi }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \beta  - \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)
\]

which will be weakly negative at \( t = 0 \) . We also see readily that the weak negativity of \( {\Psi }_{1} \) is preserved under the ODE (9.7.1).

Returning to \( t = 0 \) , combining the facts \( {\beta g} \leq \) Ric and \( R \leq  {3B} \) tells us that Ric \( \geq  \frac{\beta }{3B}{Rg} \) . After defining \( \varepsilon  = \frac{\beta }{3B} \in  \left( {0,\frac{1}{3}}\right) \) , and \( \delta  = \frac{2\varepsilon }{1 - {2\varepsilon }} \in  \left( {0,2}\right) \) , we know from the proof of Theorem 9.7.5 that this condition is equivalent to

\[
{\Psi }_{2} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \delta {\lambda }_{3} - \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)  \leq  0, \tag{9.7.6}
\]

and is also preserved under the ODE (9.7.1).

Set \( \theta  = \frac{1}{1 + \frac{1}{2}\delta } \in  \left( {\frac{1}{2},1}\right) \) . Note that at \( t = 0,{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1} \leq  {\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1} + \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)  = \; {\lambda }_{3} + {\lambda }_{2} = \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{1}}\right)  \leq  B \) and \( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} = \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{3},{e}_{3}}\right)  \geq  \beta \) . Hence, by choosing \( A > 0 \) sufficiently large (depending on \( \beta \) and \( B \) ) we have

\[
{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1} \leq  A{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta }, \tag{9.7.7}
\]

at \( t = 0 \) .

We claim that (9.7.7) is preserved under our Ricci flow. If this were true, then by Remark 9.7.9 we would have

\[
\left| {\operatorname{Ric} - \frac{1}{3}{Rg}}\right|  \leq  {\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1} \leq  A{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta } \leq  A{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{3}\right) }^{\theta } = \widetilde{A}{R}^{\theta }
\]

for \( \widetilde{A} = \widetilde{A}\left( {\beta , B}\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} A{2}^{-\theta } \) . The theorem would then hold with

\[
M = M\left( {\gamma ,\beta , B}\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{R \geq  0}}\left( {\widetilde{A}{R}^{\theta } - {\gamma R}}\right)  < \infty .
\]

It remains to show that (9.7.7) is preserved under this Ricci flow. By Lemma 9.7.2, \( {\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1} \) is convex, \( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \) is concave and \( {\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta } \) is concave where \( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \geq  0 \) . Therefore,

\[
{\Psi }_{3} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1}}\right)  - A{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta }
\]

is a convex function where \( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \geq  0 \) , and in particular, where \( {\Psi }_{1} \leq  0 \) .

We apply Theorem 9.6.1 in the situation described in Remark 9.7.1, with \( X \) consisting of all points where \( {\Psi }_{1},{\Psi }_{2} \) and \( {\Psi }_{3} \) are all weakly negative. The theorem tells us that the set \( X \) is preserved under the Ricci flow (and in particular that (9.7.7) will continue to hold) provided that \( X \) is preserved under the analogous ODE (9.6.1), or equivalently (9.7.1).

We have already remarked that both the conditions \( {\Psi }_{1} \leq  0 \) and \( {\Psi }_{2} \leq  0 \) are preserved under the ODE (9.7.1). We will conclude by showing that if our eigenvalues solve (9.7.1) and satisfy \( {\Psi }_{1} \leq  0 \) and \( {\Psi }_{2} \leq  0 \) , then whenever \( {\Psi }_{3} \geq  0 \) , the ratio \( \frac{{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1}}{{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta }} \) is decreasing in time.

In this case, our eigenvalues satisfy \( {\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1} > 0 \) and \( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} > 0 \) , and we may calculate that

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\ln \left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1}}\right)  = \frac{2}{{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1}}\left( {{\lambda }_{3}^{2} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{2} - {\lambda }_{1}^{2} - {\lambda }_{2}{\lambda }_{3}}\right)  = 2\left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right)
\]

and that

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\ln \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)  = \frac{2}{{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\left( {{\lambda }_{1}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}{\lambda }_{3} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2} + {\lambda }_{1}{\lambda }_{3}}\right)
\]

\[
= 2\left\lbrack  {{\lambda }_{3} + \frac{{\lambda }_{1}^{2} + {\lambda }_{2}^{2}}{{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}}\right\rbrack   = 2\left\lbrack  {\left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right)  + \frac{2{\lambda }_{2}^{2}}{{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}}\right\rbrack  .
\]

Now \( \delta {\lambda }_{3} \leq  {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \) (since \( {\Psi }_{2} \leq  0 \) ) and \( {\lambda }_{1} \leq  {\lambda }_{2} \) , so

\[
\delta \left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right)  \leq  {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} = \frac{{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{2}}{{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}} \leq  \frac{{\left( 2{\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{2}}{{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}.
\]

Hence

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\ln \left( {{\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}}\right)  \geq  2\left( {1 + \frac{1}{2}\delta }\right) \left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right) .
\]

Thus

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\ln \left\lbrack  \frac{{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1}}{{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta }}\right\rbrack   \leq  2\left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right)  - {2\theta }\left( {1 + \frac{1}{2}\delta }\right) \left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right)
\]

\[
= 2\left( {{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{2} + {\lambda }_{1}}\right) \left( {1 - \theta \left( {1 + \frac{1}{2}\delta }\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= 0
\]

by definition of \( \theta \) . Therefore, \( \frac{{\lambda }_{3} - {\lambda }_{1}}{{\left( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2}\right) }^{\theta }} \) is decreasing as claimed, and (9.7.7) is preserved.

nodes.label: Theorem 10.1.1
nodes.document_title: Peter Topping - Lectures on the Ricci Flow
nodes.content:
Theorem 10.1.1 (Hamilton). If \( \left( {\mathcal{M},{g}_{0}}\right) \) is a closed three-dimensional Riemannian manifold with positive Ricci curvature, then the Ricci flow \( g\left( t\right) \) , with \( g\left( 0\right)  = {g}_{0} \) , on a maximal time interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) becomes round in the following sense. There exist

(i) a metric \( {g}_{\infty } \) on \( \mathcal{M} \) of constant positive sectional curvature,

(ii) a sequence \( {t}_{i} \uparrow  T \) ,

(iii) a point \( {p}_{\infty } \in  \mathcal{M} \) and a sequence \( \left\{  {p}_{i}\right\}   \in  \mathcal{M} \) ,

such that if we define new Ricci flows \( {g}_{i}\left( t\right) \) for \( t \leq  0 \) by

\[
{g}_{i}\left( t\right)  = \left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {{p}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right) g\left( {{t}_{i} + \frac{t}{\left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {{p}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right) }}\right) \tag{10.1.1}
\]

then

\[
\left( {\mathcal{M},{g}_{i}\left( t\right) ,{p}_{i}}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {\mathcal{M},\left( {c - t}\right) {g}_{\infty },{p}_{\infty }}\right)
\]

on the time interval \( ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , for some \( c > 0 \) .

nodes.proof:
First, let us pick \( 0 < \beta  \leq  B < \infty \) such that \( \beta {g}_{0} \leq  \operatorname{Ric}\left( {g}_{0}\right)  \leq  B{g}_{0} \) . This is possible because \( \mathcal{M} \) is compact and \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( {g}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) . Note then that \( R \geq  {3\beta } > 0 \) at \( t = 0 \) , so by Corollary 3.2.4, we have \( T \leq  \frac{1}{2\beta } \) , and in particular, there is a finite-time singularity in the flow.

We are then able to analyse the flow with Theorem 8.5.1, generating a constant \( b > 0 \) , sequences \( \left\{  {p}_{i}\right\}   \subset  \mathcal{M} \) and \( {t}_{i} \uparrow  T \) , rescaled Ricci flows \( {g}_{i}\left( t\right) \) and (for \( t \in  \left( {-\infty , b}\right) \) ) a limit Ricci flow \( \left( {\mathcal{N},\widehat{g}\left( t\right) }\right) \) with a base point \( {p}_{\infty } \in  \mathcal{N} \) .

Applying Theorem 9.7.8 to \( g\left( t\right) \) , we find that for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) and all \( \gamma  > 0 \) ,

\[
\left| {\operatorname{Ric} - \frac{1}{3}{Rg}}\right|  \leq  {\gamma R} + M\left( {\beta , B,\gamma }\right)
\]

with all terms computed with respect to \( g\left( t\right) \) . But \( {g}_{i}\left( t\right) \) is just a rescaling, and translation in time, of \( g\left( t\right) \) , so with respect to \( {g}_{i}\left( 0\right) \) there holds

\[
\left| {\operatorname{Ric} - \frac{1}{3}{Rg}}\right|  \leq  {\gamma R} + \frac{M\left( {\beta , B,\gamma }\right) }{\left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {{p}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right) }
\]

for all \( \gamma  > 0 \) . Taking the limit \( i \rightarrow  \infty \) , we have

\[
\left| {\operatorname{Ric} - \frac{1}{3}{Rg}}\right|  \leq  {\gamma R}
\]

with respect to \( \widehat{g}\left( 0\right) \) . Since \( \gamma  > 0 \) is arbitrary, we must have \( \operatorname{Ric} - \frac{1}{3}{Rg} = 0 \) for \( \widehat{g}\left( 0\right) \) . Thus \( \widehat{g}\left( 0\right) \) is Einstein, and \( R \) must be constant, as we discussed in Section 2.2.

Using the fact that \( \mathcal{M} \) is three dimensional, \( \widehat{g}\left( 0\right) \) then has constant sectional curvature (because the Einstein tensor \( E =  - \operatorname{Ric} + \frac{1}{2}{Rg} = {\lambda g} \) for some \( \lambda  \in \; \mathbb{R}) \) . Moreover, since \( R > 0 \) for \( g\left( t\right) \) , it follows that \( R > 0 \) for \( {g}_{i}\left( t\right) \) and so \( R \geq \) 0 for the limit \( \widehat{g}\left( 0\right) \) , and we deduce that the constant value of the sectional curvatures of \( \widehat{g}\left( 0\right) \) is weakly positive. Recalling that \( \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {\widehat{g}\left( 0\right) }\right) }\right| \left( {p}_{\infty }\right)  = 1 \) , we deduce that in fact, \( \widehat{g}\left( 0\right) \) must have strictly positive, constant sectional curvature.

By Myer's Theorem (which tells us that a positive lower bound for the Ricci curvature of a manifold implies that its diameter is finite - see [27, Theorem 11.8]) \( \mathcal{N} \) must be compact and hence closed. By the definition of convergence of flows, we must then have \( \mathcal{N} = \mathcal{M} \) . By the backwards uniqueness of Ricci flows asserted in Theorem 5.2.2, we must have that \( \widehat{g}\left( t\right)  = \left( {c - t}\right) {g}_{\infty } \) where \( {g}_{\infty } \) is some positive multiple of \( \widehat{g}\left( 0\right) \) . Therefore

\[
\left( {\mathcal{M},{g}_{i}\left( t\right) ,{p}_{i}}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {\mathcal{M},\left( {c - t}\right) {g}_{\infty },{p}_{\infty }}\right) .
\]

## Appendix A Connected sum

In this appendix, we recall the notion of connected sum, as required principally in Section 1.4.

Given any two oriented manifolds \( \mathcal{A} \) and \( \mathcal{B} \) of the same dimension, we first remove a small disc/ball in each.

![019eaffa-82c1-7a9a-a400-be4bdd356265_127_295_1345_1195_426_0.jpg](images/019eaffa-82c1-7a9a-a400-be4bdd356265_127_295_1345_1195_426_0.jpg)

We then paste them together (matching orientations) to get a new manifold which we denote by \( \mathcal{A}\# \mathcal{B} \) .

![019eaffa-82c1-7a9a-a400-be4bdd356265_128_288_31_956_299_0.jpg](images/019eaffa-82c1-7a9a-a400-be4bdd356265_128_288_31_956_299_0.jpg)

For example, \( {T}^{2}\# {T}^{2} \) is shown in figure A.1.

nodes.content: THEOREM 4.1. If the initial metric has its local holonomy group restricted to a subgroup \( G \) of \( {S0}\left( n\right) \) , it remains so under the Ricci Flow.
nodes.content_excerpt: THEOREM 4.1. If the initial metric has its local holonomy group restricted to a subgroup \( G \) of \( {S0}\left( n\right) \) , it remains so under the Ricci Flow.

nodes.proof:
The idea is that the local holonomy is restricted to \( G \) if and only if the image of the curvature operator \( M \) at each point is restricted to the Lie algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) of \( G \) . In this case since \( M \) is self-adjoint, the orthogonal complement \( {\mathcal{G}}^{ \bot  } \) is contained in the kernel of \( M \) . Then the same properties hold for both \( {M}^{2} \) and \( {M}^{\# } \) , and hence are preserved by the Ricci Flow by the maximum principle.

As an example, the local holonomy of a Riemannian manifold of even dimension reduces from \( {S0}\left( {2n}\right) \) to \( U\left( n\right) \) if and only if there is a complex structure with respect to which the metric is Kähler. Also, the local holonomy reduces from \( {S0}\left( n\right) \) to \( {S0}\left( p\right)  \times  {S0}\left( q\right) \) with \( p + q = n \) if and only if the metric is locally a product. (It need not be a product globally, as we see from \( {S}^{2} \times  {S}^{1} \) .)

nodes.content:
THEOREM 7.1. There exist constants \( {C}_{k} \) for \( R \geq  1 \) such that if the curvature is bounded

\[
\left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  M
\]

up to time \( t \) with \( 0 < t \leq  1/M \) then the covariant derivative of the curvature is bounded

\[
\left| {DRm}\right|  \leq  {C}_{1}M/{t}^{1/2}
\]

and the \( {k}^{th} \) covariant derivative of the curvature is bounded

\[
\left| {{D}^{k}{Rm}}\right|  \leq  {C}_{k}M/{T}^{k/2}.
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: THEOREM 7.1. There exist constants \( {C}_{k} \) for \( R \geq 1 \) such that if the curvature is bounded \[ \left| {Rm}\right| \leq M \] up to time \( t \) with \( 0 < t \leq 1/M \) then the covariant derivative of the curvature is bounded \[ \left| {DRm}\right| \leq {C}_{1}M/{t}^{1/2} \] and the \( {k}^{th} \) covariant derivative of the curvature is bounded \[ \left| {{D}^{k}{Rm}}\right| \leq {C}_{k}M/{T}^{k/2}...

nodes.proof:
We denote by \( A * B \) any tensor product of two tensors \( A \) and \( B \) when we do not need the precise expression. We have a formula

\[
{D}_{t}{Rm} = {\Delta Rm} + {Rm} * {Rm}
\]

which gives a formula

\[
{D}_{t}{\left| Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| Rm\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| DRm\right| }^{2} + C{\left| Rm\right| }^{3}
\]

for some constant \( C \) . Taking the covariant space derivative of the first formula yields

\[
{D}_{t}{DRm} = {\Delta DRm} + {Rm} * {DRm}
\]

which leads to a formula

\[
{D}_{t}{\left| DRm\right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| DRm\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {D}^{2}Rm\right| }^{2} + C\left| {Rm}\right| {\left| DRm\right| }^{2}.
\]

Now let \( F \) be the function

\[
F = t{\left| DRm\right| }^{2} + A{\left| Rm\right| }^{2}
\]

where \( A \) is a constant we shall choose in a minute. Then discarding \( {\left| {D}^{2}Rm\right| }^{2} \geq  0 \) we find that

\[
{D}_{t}F \leq  {\Delta F} + \left( {{Ct}\left| {Rm}\right|  - {2A}}\right) {\left| DRm\right| }^{2} + {CA}{\left| Rm\right| }^{3}
\]

for some constant \( C \) . Now we assume \( \left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  M \) and \( {tM} \leq  1 \) ; then if we take \( A \geq  C \) we get

\[
{D}_{t}F \leq  {\Delta F} + C{M}^{3}
\]

for some constant \( C \) . Also

\[
F \leq  C{M}^{2}
\]

at \( t = 0 \) (since \( t{\left| DRm\right| }^{2} = 0 \) !) and hence by the maximum principle

\[
F \leq  C{M}^{2} + {Ct}{M}^{3}.
\]

Now as long as \( {tM} \leq  1 \) this gives \( F \leq  C{M}^{2} \) for some constant \( C \) , and

\[
t{\left| DRm\right| }^{2} \leq  F \leq  C{M}^{2}
\]

yields

\[
\left| {DRm}\right|  \leq  {C}_{1}M/{t}^{1/2}
\]

for some constant \( {C}_{1} \) .

The general case follows in the same way. Differentiating \( k \) times gives a formula

\[
{D}_{t}{D}^{k}{Rm} = \Delta {D}^{k}{Rm} + \sum {D}^{{j}_{1}}{Rm} * {D}^{{j}_{2}}{Rm} * \cdots  * {D}^{{j}_{p}}{Rm}
\]

where the sum extends over \( p \geq  2 \) with

\[
0 \leq  {j}_{1} \leq  {j}_{2} \leq  \cdots  \leq  {j}_{p} \leq  k
\]

with

\[
{j}_{1} + {j}_{2} + \cdots  + {j}_{p} = k + 4 - {2p}.
\]

If we have bounds

\[
\left| {{D}^{k}{Rm}}\right|  \leq  {C}_{k}M/{t}^{k/2}
\]

we get an estimate (using \( {tM} \leq  1 \) )

\[
{D}_{t}{\left| {D}^{k}Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| {D}^{k}Rm\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {D}^{k - 1}Rm\right| }^{2} + C{M}^{3}/{t}^{k}
\]

and another estimate (using \( {tM} \leq  1 \) )

\[
{D}_{t}{\left| {D}^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| {D}^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {D}^{k + 2}Rm\right| }^{2} + {CM}{\left| {D}^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
+ C{M}^{2}\left| {{D}^{k + 1}{Rm}}\right| /{t}^{\left( {k + 1}\right) /2} + C{M}^{3}/{t}^{k + 1}.
\]

Now we can bound

\[
{M}^{2}\left| {{D}^{k + 1}{Rm}}\right| /{t}^{\left( {k + 1}\right) /2} \leq  M{\left| {D}^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} + C{M}^{3}/{t}^{k + 1}
\]

and discard \( {\left| {D}^{k + 2}Rm\right| }^{2} \geq  0 \) to get

\[
{D}_{t}{\left| {D}^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| {D}^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} + {CM}{\left| {D}^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} + C{M}^{3}/{t}^{k + 1}.
\]

Now we let

\[
{F}_{k} = t{\left| {D}^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} + {A}_{k}{\left| {D}^{k}Rm\right| }^{2}
\]

where \( {A}_{k} \) is a constant we shall choose soon. Then

\[
{D}_{t}{F}_{k} \leq  \Delta {F}_{k} + \left( {{CtM} - 2{A}_{k}}\right) {\left| {D}^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} + C{A}_{k}{M}^{3}/{t}^{k}
\]

and if we take \( {tM} \leq  1 \) and \( {A}_{k} \geq  C \) then

\[
{D}_{t}{F}_{k} \leq  \Delta {F}_{k} + {CM}/{t}^{k}
\]

for some constant \( C \) . Also at \( t = 0 \)

\[
{F}_{k} \leq  C{M}^{2}/{t}^{k}
\]

so by the maximum principle for \( t \geq  0 \)

\[
{F}_{k} \leq  C{M}^{2}/{t}^{k} + C{M}^{3}/{t}^{k - 1}.
\]

Now since \( {tM} \leq  1 \) we just get \( {F}_{k} \leq  C{M}^{2}/{t}^{k} \) , and then

\[
t{\left| {D}^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  {F}_{k} \leq  C{M}^{2}/{t}^{k}
\]

gives

\[
\left| {{D}^{k + 1}{Rm}}\right|  \leq  {C}_{R}M/{t}^{\left( {k + 1}\right) /2}
\]

which is the induction step we need. This completes the proof of the Theorem.

nodes.content: THEOREM 8.1. For any smooth initial metric on a compact manifold there exists a maximal time \( T \) on which there is a unique smooth solution to the Ricci flow for \( 0 \leq  t < T \) . Either \( T = \infty \) or else the curvature is unbounded as \( t \rightarrow  T \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: THEOREM 8.1. For any smooth initial metric on a compact manifold there exists a maximal time \( T \) on which there is a unique smooth solution to the Ricci flow for \( 0 \leq t < T \) . Either \( T = \infty \) or else the curvature is unbounded as \( t \rightarrow T \) .

nodes.proof:
, so there is a unique smooth solution on a maximal time interval \( 0 \leq  t < T \) for \( T \leq  \infty \) . Suppose \( T < \infty \) and \( \left| {Rm}\right| \) remains bounded as \( t \rightarrow  T \) . Then so do all the space-time derivatives \( {D}_{t}{D}^{k}{Rm} \) . We claim that the metric \( g \) and all its derivatives, i.e. ordinary derivatives in a local coordinate chart, also remain bounded, and \( g \) remains bounded away from zero below. Then the metric \( {g}_{t} \) at time \( t \) converges to a smooth limit metric \( {g}_{T} \) as \( t \rightarrow  T \) . Once we know this, we can continue the solution past \( T \) , and so \( T \) was not maximal after all.

To see that \( g \) remains bounded above and below, consider the evolution of the length of a vector from

\[
{\left| V\right| }^{2} = g\left( {V, V}\right)
\]

By the equation

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}g\left( {V, V}\right)  =  - {2Rc}\left( {V, V}\right)
\]

and if \( \left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  M \) then

\[
\left| {\operatorname{Rc}\left( {V, V}\right) }\right|  \leq  {CMg}\left( {V, V}\right)
\]

for some constant \( C \) depending on the dimension only. Thus

\[
\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}g\left( {V, V}\right) }\right|  \leq  {CMg}\left( {V, V}\right)
\]

and it follows that

\[
{e}^{-{CMt}}{g}_{0}\left( {V, V}\right)  \leq  {g}_{t}\left( {V, V}\right)  \leq  {e}^{CMt}{g}_{0}\left( {V, V}\right)
\]

and the metrics \( {g}_{t} \) are uniformly bounded above and below for \( 0 \leq  t < T \) . As a result, it does not matter what metric we use to measure the length of a vector or tensor from now on in the argument.

Fix a background connection \( \bar{\Gamma } \) (i.e. the zero connection in a local chart) and let \( \bar{D} \) be the covariant derivative in \( \bar{\Gamma } \) (i.e., an ordinary derivative). Then the difference \( \Gamma  - \bar{\Gamma } \) is a tensor, and in fact

\[
{\left( \Gamma  - \bar{\Gamma }\right) }_{ij}^{\ell } = \frac{1}{2}{g}^{k\ell }\left( {{\bar{D}}_{i}{g}_{jk} + {\bar{D}}_{j}{g}_{ik} - {\bar{D}}_{k}{g}_{ij}}\right) .
\]

We can then compute its evolution

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left( \Gamma  - \bar{\Gamma }\right) }_{ij}^{\ell } = {g}^{k\ell }\left( {{\bar{D}}_{k}{R}_{ij} =  - {\bar{D}}_{i}{R}_{jk} - {\bar{D}}_{j}{R}_{ik}}\right) .
\]

Since there is a formula

\[
\bar{D}{Rc} = {DRc} + \left( {\Gamma  - \bar{\Gamma }}\right)  * {Rc}
\]

we get a formula

\[
\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {\Gamma  - \bar{\Gamma }}\right) }\right|  \leq  C\left| {DRc}\right|  + C\left| {Rc}\right| \left| {\Gamma  - \bar{\Gamma }}\right| .
\]

Bounds on \( \left| {Rc}\right| \) and \( \left| {DRc}\right| \) give

\[
\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {\Gamma  - \bar{\Gamma }}\right) }\right|  \leq  C + C\left| {\Gamma  - \bar{\Gamma }}\right|
\]

from which we get at most exponential growth in \( \Gamma  - \bar{\Gamma } \) . In finite time we bound \( \Gamma  - \bar{\Gamma } \) . Hence from now on in the argument all covariant derivatives are equivalent. Bounds on \( \bar{D}g \) can be recovered from

\[
{\bar{D}}_{i}{g}_{jk} = {g}_{k\ell }{\left( \Gamma  - \bar{\Gamma }\right) }_{ij}^{\ell } + {g}_{j\ell }{\left( \Gamma  - \bar{\Gamma }\right) }_{ik}^{\ell }.
\]

We can now recover the second derivatives \( {\bar{D}}^{2}g \) from a formula for their time evolution

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\bar{D}}^{2}g =  - 2{\bar{D}}^{2}{Rc}
\]

and a formula

\[
{\bar{D}}^{2}{Rc} = {D}^{2}{Rc} + {\bar{D}}^{2}g * {Rc} + \bar{D}g * \bar{D}g * {Rc}
\]

contracting tensors with \( g \) , to see that

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left| {{\bar{D}}^{2}g}\right|  \leq  C + C\left| {{\bar{D}}^{2}g}\right|
\]

and again we get at worst exponential growth, giving bounds on \( {\bar{D}}^{2}g \) . Higher derivatives of \( g \) are the same. This proves the Theorem.
