while there exists some \( {Q}_{j} \) with

\[
R\left( {{Q}_{j},0}\right) d{\left( Q, O,0\right) }^{2} = {A}_{j}\;\text{ and }\;d\left( {Q, O,0}\right)  = {\sigma }_{j}
\]

(or else \( {\sigma }_{j} \) would not be maximal). Now pick \( {P}_{j} \) so that \( d\left( {{P}_{j}, O,0}\right)  \geq  {\sigma }_{j} \) and

\[
R\left( {{P}_{j},0}\right)  \geq  \frac{1}{1 + {\varepsilon }_{j}}\sup \left\{  {R\left( {Q,0}\right)  : d\left( {Q, O,0}\right)  \geq  {\sigma }_{j}}\right\}
\]

which is possible since even on a noncompact set we can come as close to the sup as we wish. Finally pick \( {r}_{j} = {\varepsilon }_{j}{\sigma }_{j} \) .

First we check (a). If \( P \) is in the ball of radius \( {r}_{j} \) around \( {P}_{j} \) at time \( t = 0 \) , either \( d\left( {P, O,0}\right)  \geq  {\sigma }_{j} \) or \( d\left( {P, O,0}\right)  \leq  {\sigma }_{j} \) . In the first case we have from the choice of \( {P}_{j} \)

\[
R\left( {P,0}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\varepsilon }_{j}}\right) R\left( {{P}_{j},0}\right)
\]

which satisfies condition (a) with \( {\delta }_{j} = {\varepsilon }_{j} \) . In the second case, we have from the choice of \( {\sigma }_{j} \)

\[
R\left( {P,0}\right)  \leq  {A}_{j}/d{\left( P, O,0\right) }^{2}
\]

and

\[
d\left( {P, O,0}\right)  \geq  d\left( {{P}_{j}, O,0}\right)  - d\left( {P,{P}_{j},0}\right)  \geq  {\sigma }_{j} - {r}_{j} = \left( {1 - {\varepsilon }_{j}}\right) {\sigma }_{j}
\]

so

\[
R\left( {P,0}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{{\left( 1 - {\varepsilon }_{j}\right) }^{2}} \cdot  \frac{{A}_{j}}{{\sigma }_{j}^{2}}.
\]

On the other hand, from the choice of \( {Q}_{j} \)

\[
R\left( {{Q}_{j},0}\right)  = \frac{{A}_{j}}{{\sigma }_{j}^{2}}
\]

and from the choice of \( {P}_{j} \)

\[
R\left( {{P}_{j},0}\right)  \geq  \frac{1}{1 + {\varepsilon }_{j}}R\left( {{Q}_{j},0}\right)
\]

since \( {Q}_{j} \) is a possible choice of \( Q \) , then

\[
R\left( {{P}_{j},0}\right)  \geq  \frac{1}{1 + {\varepsilon }_{j}} \cdot  \frac{{A}_{j}}{{\sigma }_{j}^{2}}
\]

and

\[
R\left( {P,0}\right)  \leq  \frac{1 + {\varepsilon }_{j}}{{\left( 1 - {\varepsilon }_{j}\right) }^{2}}R\left( {{P}_{j},0}\right)
\]

which satisfies condition (a) with

\[
{\delta }_{j} = \frac{1 + {\varepsilon }_{j}}{{\left( 1 - {\varepsilon }_{j}\right) }^{2}} - 1
\]

and in either case \( {\delta }_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) as \( {\varepsilon }_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) .

Next we check condition (b). We have from our previous estimate

\[
{r}_{j}^{2}R\left( {{P}_{j},0}\right)  \geq  \frac{{\varepsilon }_{j}^{2}}{1 + {\varepsilon }_{j}}{A}_{j} \rightarrow  \infty
\]

by our choice of \( {A}_{j} \) . To check condition (c) note \( {s}_{j} \geq  {\sigma }_{j} \) so that \( {\lambda }_{j} \geq  1/{\varepsilon }_{j} \rightarrow  \infty \) . Finally note that (a), (b) and (c) continue to hold if we pass to a subsequence. Any point \( P \) in \( {B}_{{r}_{j}}\left( {{P}_{j},0}\right) \) has distance from the origin at time 0

\[
d\left( {P,0,0}\right)  \geq  d\left( {{P}_{j},0,0}\right)  - d\left( {P,{P}_{j},0}\right)  \geq  \left( {1 - {\varepsilon }_{j}}\right) {\sigma }_{j}
\]

and since \( {A}_{j} \rightarrow  \infty \) we must have \( {\sigma }_{j} \rightarrow  \infty \) . Thus any fixed compact set does not meet the balls \( B{r}_{j}\left( {{P}_{j},0}\right) \) for large enough \( j \) . If we pass to a subsequence, the balls will all avoid each other. This proves the Lemma.

Then there exists a sequence of dilations around origins \( {P}_{j} \) at time 0 which converges to a limit which splits as a product of \( {R}^{1} \) with a solution of even dimension \( {2n} \) which is ancient and complete with bounded curvature and weakly positive curvature operator.

\[
\left( {\sqrt{M} - \delta }\right) s \leq  f \leq  \left( {\sqrt{M} + \delta }\right) s
\]

which makes \( f \) comparable to \( s \) . Hence on the level set

\[
{S}_{\varphi } = \{ f = \varphi \}
\]

the distance \( s \) is nearly \( \varphi /\sqrt{M} \) for large \( r \) , in particular. Hence on the level set

\[
{S}_{\mu } = \{ f = \mu \}
\]

the distance \( s \) is nearly \( \mu /\sqrt{M} \) , in particular

\[
\mu /\left( {\sqrt{M} + \delta }\right)  \leq  s \leq  \mu /\left( {\sqrt{M} - \delta }\right)
\]

for large \( \mu \) .

Now choose the point \( {P}_{j} \) and radii \( {r}_{j} \) as before and let \( {R}_{j} = R\left( {{P}_{j},0}\right) \) and \( {\mu }_{j} = f\left( {{P}_{j},0}\right) \) . Then the curvature \( R \) at any point \( P \) on any sphere \( {S}_{\mu } \) at time \( = 0 \) with

\[
\left| {\mu  - {\mu }_{j}}\right|  \leq  {r}_{j}/\sqrt{M}
\]

satisfies an estimate

\[
R \leq  \left( {1 + {\varepsilon }_{j}}\right) {R}_{j}
\]

for large \( j \) , where again

\[
{R}_{j}{r}_{j}^{2} \rightarrow  \infty \text{ and }{\varepsilon }_{j} \rightarrow  0.
\]

We can argue as before if we can control the injectivity radii \( {\rho }_{j} \) at \( \left( {{P}_{j},0}\right) \) with an estimate

\[
{\rho }_{j} \geq  c/\sqrt{{R}_{j}}\text{ . }
\]

We get this estimate in odd dimensions as follows.

Each level set \( {S}_{\mu } \) for large \( \mu \) is a smooth submanifold which is strictly convex since \( f \) is convex. The second fundamental form II of \( {S}_{\mu } \) is given by

\[
\operatorname{II}\left( {X, Y}\right)  = {D}^{2}f\left( {X, Y}\right) /\left| {Df}\right|
\]

on vectors \( X \) and \( Y \) where

\[
{Df}\left( X\right)  = {Df}\left( Y\right)  = 0
\]

makes them tangent to \( {S}_{\mu } \) . Since \( \left| {Df}\right|  \rightarrow  \sqrt{M} \) and \( {D}^{2}f = {Rc} \) , we can control the second fundamental form on \( {S}_{\mu } \) by the maximum of \( {Rc} \) on \( {S}_{\mu } \) , hence by \( {R}_{j} \) . Thus

\[
\left| {II}\right|  \leq  C{R}_{j}/\sqrt{M}
\]

on all \( {S}_{\mu } \) with \( \left| {\mu  - {\mu }_{j}}\right|  \leq  {r}_{j}/\sqrt{M} \) . Each \( {S}_{\mu } \) has positive sectional curvature in the induced metric by the Gauss curvature equation, and each \( {S}_{\mu } \) is orientable since the whole soliton is diffeomorphic to \( {R}^{{2n} + 1} \) and the normal bundle is oriented by \( {Df} > 0 \) . If the dimension \( {2n} + 1 \) of the soliton is odd, the dimension \( {2n} \) of \( {S}_{\mu } \) is even. Then by a theorem in [9] the injectivity radius of \( {S}_{\mu } \) in the induced metric can be bounded \( \geq  c/\sqrt{{R}_{j}} \) .

This gives a similar bound on the injectivity radius of the soliton at \( {P}_{j} \) in the following way. Since the curvature is positive it is bounded below, and it suffice to show that a ball around \( {P}_{j} \) in the soliton of radius \( \alpha /\sqrt{{R}_{j}} \) has volume \( \geq  c/\sqrt{{R}_{j}^{{2n} + 1}} \) for some \( \alpha  > 0 \) and \( c > 0 \) independent of \( j \) . We do this by taking a coordinate chart inside the ball and estimating its volume. First go a distance \( \alpha /\sqrt{{R}_{j}} \) from \( {P}_{j} \) in the direction of \( \pm  {Df} \) . This moves us out and back some comparable distance. Then take the exponential map of radius \( \alpha /\sqrt{{R}_{j}} \) out from each point on this curve in the spheres \( {S}_{\mu } \) in their induced metric. Start with a frame on the tangent space at \( {P}_{j} \) and parallelly translate it along the curve in the direction \( {Df} \) to get a frame at each point on this curve, and use it to refer the exponential map on a standard ball in \( {R}^{2n} \) into \( {S}_{\mu } \) for each \( \mu \) . Then this gives a coordinate chart in a neighborhood of \( {P}_{j} \) on the soliton. Since each curvature in the soliton and each second fundamental form on the hypersurfaces \( {S}_{\mu } \) can be controlled by \( {R}_{j} \) , for a suitable small \( \alpha \) the coordinate chart will inject with derivative close to an isometry. This shows the image has volume \( \geq  c/\sqrt{{R}_{j}^{{2n} + 1}} \) . The rest of the proof proceeds just as before, up to taking the first limit. Unfortunately we cannot do the backward limit in time without more injectivity radius control.

If an initial metric \( {g}_{0} \) has the property that every surface which bounds a volume at least \( V \) on each side has area \( A \geq \beta {V}^{2/3} \) , and the initial metric has...

nodes.proof:
defined for \( 0 \leq  t < T \) and \( 0 \leq  V \leq  \mathcal{V}\left( t\right) \) which for \( 0 < V < \mathcal{V}\left( t\right) \) is the infimum of the areas of surfaces of any type which divide the manifold into regions of volumes \( V \) and \( \mathcal{V} - V \) , with \( G = 0 \) if \( V = 0 \) or \( V = \mathcal{V} \) . Then so much is known about the theory of minimal surfaces (see Almgren [1]) that we know \( G \) is continuous in \( V \) and \( t \) , and for any \( t \) in \( 0 \leq  t < T \) and any \( V \) in \( 0 < V < \mathcal{V} \) the infimum is attained on a smooth surface of constant mean curvature \( H \) . Moreover if \( \beta  < {\beta }_{E} \) where \( {\beta }_{E} \) is its Euclidean value

\[
{\beta }_{E} = {\left( {36}\pi \right) }^{1/3}
\]

then for any metric on a compact manifold we can find \( \delta  > 0 \) depending on the metric so that any surface bounding a volume \( V \leq  \delta \) has area \( A \geq  \beta {V}^{2/3} \) . This means we do not need to concern ourselves with very small volumes.

We shall prove a lower bound of the form \( G > F \) for \( 0 < V < \mathcal{V} \) where the function \( F\left( {V, t}\right) \) is chosen of the form

\[
\frac{1}{F} = {e}^{\frac{2}{3}{\rho t}}\left\{  {\frac{Q}{T - t} + \frac{B}{{V}^{2/3}} + \frac{B}{{\left\lbrack  \mathcal{V}\left( t\right)  - V\right\rbrack  }^{2/3}}}\right\}
\]

for some suitably large constants \( Q \) and \( B \) which we are free to choose later. Since \( {e}^{\rho t} \leq  {e}^{\rho T} \) we can find \( \gamma  > 0 \) in terms of \( {e}^{\rho T}, A \) and \( B \) , which will prove the Theorem. If \( B \) is large enough, then by the previous remark we do not have to worry when \( V \) or \( \mathcal{V} - V \) is very small.

If this estimate fails, there will be a first time \( {t}^{ * } \) and a volume \( {V}^{ * } \) with \( 0 < {V}^{ * } < {\left\lbrack  \alpha \left( T - t\right) \right\rbrack  }^{3/2} \) when \( G = F \) , and \( G\left( {{V}^{ * },{t}^{ * }}\right) \) will be attained by the area of a smooth surface \( {\sum }^{ * } \) of constant mean curvature \( H \) . Consider a one-parameter family of smooth surfaces \( \sum \left( r\right) \) for \( r \) near 0 by taking the parallel surface to \( {\sum }^{ * } \) at distance \( r \) , with \( \sum \left( r\right) \) inside the part with volume \( {V}^{ * } \) for \( r < 0 \) and outside for \( r > 0 \) . Note that \( \sum \left( 0\right)  = {\sum }^{ * } \) . Define the smooth functions \( A\left( {r, t}\right) \) and \( V\left( {r, t}\right) \) for \( r \) near 0 and \( t \) near \( {t}^{ * } \) by letting \( A\left( {r, t}\right) \) be the area of \( \sum \left( r\right) \) at time \( t \) , and letting \( V\left( {r, t}\right) \) be the volume enclosed by \( \sum \left( r\right) \) at time \( t \) on the side of the part with volume \( {V}^{ * } \) . Note that \( A\left( {0,{t}^{ * }}\right) \) is the area of \( {\sum }^{ * } \) which is \( G\left( {{V}^{ * },{t}^{ * }}\right) \) , while \( V\left( {0,{t}^{ * }}\right)  = {V}^{ * } \) .

It is clear we have the inequality

\[
A\left( {r,{t}^{ * }}\right)  \geq  G\left( {V\left( {r,{t}^{ * }}\right) ,{t}^{ * }}\right)
\]

since \( G \) is the least area among all surfaces enclosing the given volume at the given time. But \( G \geq  F \) up to time \( {t}^{ * } \) , so

\[
A\left( {r,{t}^{ * }}\right)  \geq  F\left( {V\left( {r,{t}^{ * }}\right) ,{t}^{ * }}\right)
\]

for all \( r \) near 0, and equality is attained at \( r = 0 \) where \( G = F \) at time \( {t}^{ * } \) . Since \( A \) and \( F \) are both smooth, at \( r = 0 \) and \( t = {t}^{ * } \) we get

\[
\frac{\partial A}{\partial r} = \frac{\partial F}{\partial V}\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
\]

and

\[
\frac{{\partial }^{2}A}{\partial {r}^{2}} \geq  \frac{{\partial }^{2}F}{\partial {V}^{2}}{\left( \frac{\partial V}{\partial r}\right) }^{2} + \frac{\partial F}{\partial V}\frac{{\partial }^{2}V}{\partial {r}^{2}}.
\]

In addition, it is also clear that we have the inequality

\[
A\left( {0, t}\right)  \geq  G\left( {V\left( {0, t}\right) , t}\right)
\]

for \( t \leq  {t}^{ * } \) , and since \( G \geq  F \) up to time \( {t}^{ * } \) we get

\[
A\left( {0, t}\right)  \geq  F\left( {V\left( {0, t}\right) , t}\right)
\]

for \( t \leq  {t}^{ * } \) , with equality at \( t = {t}^{ * } \) . Thus at \( r = 0 \) and \( t = {t}^{ * } \) ,

\[
\frac{\partial A}{\partial t} \leq  \frac{\partial F}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial F}{\partial V}\frac{\partial V}{\partial t}
\]

Now at \( r = 0 \) and \( t = {t}^{ * } \) ,

\[
\frac{\partial V}{\partial r} = A = F
\]

and

\[
\frac{{\partial }^{2}V}{\partial {r}^{2}} = \frac{\partial A}{\partial r} = {HA} = {HF}
\]

where \( H \) is the constant mean curvature. Then the equality

\[
\frac{\partial A}{\partial r} = \frac{\partial F}{\partial V}\frac{\partial V}{\partial r}
\]

makes

\[
\frac{\partial F}{\partial V} = H
\]

From this we get

\[
\frac{{\partial }^{2}V}{\partial {r}^{2}} = F\frac{\partial F}{\partial V}
\]

Now our inequality on \( {\partial }^{2}A/\partial {r}^{2} \) becomes

\[
\frac{{\partial }^{2}A}{\partial {r}^{2}} \geq  {F}^{2}\frac{{\partial }^{2}F}{\partial {V}^{2}} + F{\left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial V}\right) }^{2}.
\]

The volume \( V \) shrinks at a rate

\[
\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} =  - \int {Rdv} \leq  {\rho V}
\]

(since the inequality \( R \geq   - \rho \) , which we assume at \( t = 0 \) , is preserved by the Ricci Flow). Since both \( F \) and \( G \) are symmetric in \( V \rightarrow  \mathcal{V}\left( t\right)  - V \) , it is no loss to assume \( {V}^{ * } \leq  \mathcal{V}\left( t\right) /2 \) ; and this makes \( \partial F/\partial V = H \geq  0 \) at \( r = 0 \) and \( t = {t}^{ * } \) . Then our inequality on \( \partial A/\partial t \) becomes

\[
\frac{\partial A}{\partial t} \leq  \frac{\partial F}{\partial t} + {\rho V}\frac{\partial F}{\partial V}
\]

These are the inequalities we need.

The remaining fact we use comes from section 12, where we showed that for a family of parallel surfaces \( \sum \left( r\right) \) we have

\[
\frac{\partial A}{\partial t} = \frac{{\partial }^{2}A}{\partial {r}^{2}} - {4\pi \chi }
\]

where \( \chi \) is the Euler class of \( {\sum }^{ * } \) . We claim that for a suitably large constant \( Q \) in the definition of \( F \) , which makes

\[
F \leq  \left( {T - t}\right) /Q
\]

we can make \( \chi  \leq  0 \) , so that \( {\sum }^{ * } \) is not a sphere or a projective plane. What is required for this? We have

\[
{2\pi \chi } = {\int }_{{\sum }^{ * }}\left\lbrack  {{Rm}\left( P\right)  + K}\right\rbrack  {da}
\]

where \( {Rm}\left( P\right) \) is the ambient curvature of the tangent plane \( P \) to \( {\sum }^{ * } \) , and \( K \) is the determinant of the second fundamental form. We have

\[
\operatorname{Rm}\left( P\right)  \leq  {C\Omega }/\left( {T - t}\right)
\]

for some constant \( C \) . Then

\[
{\int }_{{\sum }^{ * }}\operatorname{Rm}\left( P\right) {da} \leq  {C\Omega }/Q
\]

which is as small as we like for \( Q \) large. Also \( K \leq  {H}^{2}/4 \) and \( H = \partial F/\partial V \) so

\[
{\int }_{{\sum }^{ * }}{Kda} \leq  \frac{1}{4}F{\left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial V}\right) }^{2}.
\]

Now we claim that by making \( B \) large we can make \( F{\left( \partial F/\partial V\right) }^{2} \) as small as we like. Recall

\[
\frac{1}{F} = {e}^{\frac{2}{3}{\rho t}}\left\{  {\frac{Q}{T - t} + \frac{B}{{V}^{2/3}} + \frac{B}{{\left\lbrack  \mathcal{V}\left( t\right)  - V\right\rbrack  }^{2/3}}}\right\}  .
\]

Differentiate implicitly to get

\[
\frac{\partial F}{\partial V} = \frac{2}{3}B{e}^{\frac{2}{3}{\rho t}}{F}^{2}\left\{  {\frac{1}{{V}^{5/3}} - \frac{1}{{\left\lbrack  \mathcal{V}\left( t\right)  - V\right\rbrack  }^{5/3}}}\right\}  .
\]

Since we have assumed \( V \leq  \mathcal{V}\left( t\right) /2 \) ,

\[
0 \leq  \frac{\partial F}{\partial V} \leq  \frac{4}{3}B{e}^{\frac{2}{3}{\rho t}}{F}^{2}/{V}^{5/3}
\]

and

\[
F \leq  {V}^{2/3}/B{e}^{\frac{2}{3}{\rho t}}
\]

This makes

\[
F{\left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial V}\right) }^{2} \leq  {16}/\left( {9{B}^{3}{e}^{2\rho t}}\right)
\]

which is indeed as small as we like when \( B \) is large. Thus \( \chi  < 1 \) , and since it is an integer we must have \( \chi  \leq  0 \) . This makes

\[
\frac{\partial A}{\partial t} \geq  \frac{{\partial }^{2}A}{\partial {r}^{2}}
\]

Now we can combine our inequalities to include that

\[
\frac{\partial F}{\partial t} + {\rho V}\frac{\partial F}{\partial V} \geq  {F}^{2}\frac{{\partial }^{2}F}{\partial {V}^{2}} + F{\left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial V}\right) }^{2}
\]

at \( V = {V}^{ * } \) and \( t = {t}^{ * } \) . However, we claim if \( Q \) and \( B \) are large enough the opposite inequality holds everywhere. This contradiction implies \( G > F \) for all \( t < T \) , which will prove the Theorem.

Then we need

\[
{H}^{3}\left( {\frac{\partial H}{\partial t} + {\rho V}\frac{\partial H}{\partial V}}\right)  + 3{\left( \frac{\partial H}{\partial V}\right) }^{2} \geq  H\frac{{\partial }^{2}H}{\partial {V}^{2}}.
\]

If \( H \) takes the form

\[
H = {e}^{\frac{2}{3}{\rho t}}K
\]

then \( K \) must satisfy

\[
{e}^{\frac{4}{3}{\rho t}}{K}^{3}\left\lbrack  {\frac{\partial K}{\partial t} + \rho \left( {\frac{2}{3}K + V\frac{\partial K}{\partial V}}\right) }\right\rbrack   + 3{\left( \frac{\partial K}{\partial V}\right) }^{2} \geq  K\frac{{\partial }^{2}K}{\partial {V}^{2}}.
\]

Our \( K \) has the form

\[
K = \frac{Q}{T - t} + B\left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{{V}^{2/3}} + \frac{1}{{\left( \mathcal{V} - V\right) }^{2/3}}}\right\rbrack  .
\]

We compute

\[
\frac{\partial K}{\partial t} + \rho \left( {\frac{2}{3}K + V\frac{\partial K}{\partial V}}\right)  = \frac{Q}{{\left( T - t\right) }^{2}} + \frac{2}{3}\frac{\rho Q}{T - t}
\]

\[
+ \frac{2}{3}B \cdot  \frac{1}{{\left( \mathcal{V} - V\right) }^{5/3}}\left( {\rho \mathcal{V} - \frac{\partial \mathcal{V}}{\partial t}}\right) .
\]

Since \( R \geq   - \rho \) makes

\[
\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} \leq  {\rho v}
\]

we have

\[
\frac{\partial K}{\partial t} + \rho \left( {\frac{2}{3}K + V\frac{\partial K}{\partial V}}\right)  \geq  \frac{Q}{{\left( T - t\right) }^{2}}.
\]

Since \( {e}^{\frac{4}{3}{\rho t}} \geq  1 \) it is sufficient to verify

\[
{K}^{3}\frac{Q}{{\left( T - t\right) }^{2}} + 3{\left( \frac{\partial K}{\partial V}\right) }^{2} \geq  K\frac{{\partial }^{2}K}{\partial {V}^{2}}
\]

and now we can forget about \( \rho \) .

We consider two cases. The first is where \( V \leq  \varepsilon \mathcal{V} \) for some small absolute constant \( \varepsilon \) we shall choose shortly. We have

\[
\frac{\partial K}{\partial V} =  - \frac{2}{3}B\left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{{V}^{5/3}} - \frac{1}{{\left( \mathcal{V} - V\right) }^{5/3}}}\right\rbrack
\]

and

\[
\frac{{\partial }^{2}K}{\partial {V}^{2}} = \frac{10}{9}B\left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{{V}^{8/3}} + \frac{1}{{\left( \mathcal{V} - V\right) }^{8/3}}}\right\rbrack  .
\]

Then

\[
3{\left( \frac{\partial K}{\partial V}\right) }^{2} \geq  \frac{12}{9}{B}^{2}{\left\lbrack  1 - {\varepsilon }^{5/3}\right\rbrack  }^{2} \cdot  \frac{1}{{V}^{{10}/3}}
\]

and

\[
\frac{{\partial }^{2}K}{\partial {V}^{2}} \leq  \frac{10}{9}B\left\lbrack  {1 + {\varepsilon }^{8/3}}\right\rbrack   \cdot  \frac{1}{{V}^{8/3}}.
\]

Also

\[
B \cdot  \frac{1}{{V}^{2/3}} \leq  K \leq  \frac{Q}{T - t} + B\left\lbrack  {1 + {\varepsilon }^{2/3}}\right\rbrack   \cdot  \frac{1}{{V}^{2/3}}.
\]

Therefore our inequality will hold if we choose \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) so small that

\[
\frac{12}{9}{\left\lbrack  1 - {\varepsilon }^{5/3}\right\rbrack  }^{2} \geq  \frac{10}{9}\left\lbrack  {1 + {\varepsilon }^{8/3}}\right\rbrack   + \frac{1}{9}
\]

and if in addition we have

\[
{B}^{3}Q \cdot  \frac{1}{{\left( T - t\right) }^{2}{V}^{6/3}} + \frac{1}{9}{B}^{2} \cdot  \frac{1}{{V}^{{10}/3}} \geq  \frac{10}{9}{BQ}\left\lbrack  {1 + {\varepsilon }^{8/3}}\right\rbrack   \cdot  \frac{1}{T - t} \cdot  \frac{1}{{V}^{8/3}}.
\]

Since \( \varepsilon \) is small we can take

\[
\frac{10}{9}\left\lbrack  {1 + {\varepsilon }^{8/3}}\right\rbrack   \leq  2
\]

and then this inequality holds if \( {B}^{3} \geq  {3Q} \) . Thus we have the estimate for \( V \leq  \varepsilon \left( {\mathcal{V} - V}\right) \) by making \( B \) large compared to \( Q \) .

Consider the other case where \( V \geq  \varepsilon \left( {\mathcal{V} - V}\right) \) . This is easier because we can compare everything to \( \mathcal{V} \) and

\[
{\mathcal{V}}^{2/3} \geq  \alpha \left( {T - t}\right)
\]

for some \( \alpha  > 0 \) by our hypothesis. With various constants \( C < \infty \) and \( c > 0 \) independent of \( B, Q \) , and \( \alpha \) (but depending on \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) which is fixed) we have

\[
\frac{{\partial }^{2}K}{\partial {V}^{2}} \leq  {CB} \cdot  \frac{1}{{V}^{8/3}}
\]

and

\[
K \geq  {cB} \cdot  \frac{1}{{\mathcal{V}}^{2/3}}
\]

Our estimate holds if

\[
\frac{{\partial }^{2}K}{\partial {V}^{2}} \leq  {K}^{2}\frac{Q}{{\left( T - t\right) }^{2}}
\]

which holds if \( \mathcal{V} \geq  \alpha {\left( T - t\right) }^{3/2} \) and

\[
{BQ} \geq  C/{\alpha }^{4/3}
\]

for some constant \( C \) as above. This is easily arranged also, and the Theorem is established.

\[

at \( t = 0 \) , and hence for \( t \geq  0 \) by the proof of the previous theorem. Choose the constant \( A \) so that the inequality

\[
\lambda  - \nu  \leq  A{\left( \mu  + \nu \right) }^{1 - \delta }
\]

holds at \( t = 0 \) , which is possible since

\[
\lambda  - \nu  \leq  \lambda  + \mu  \leq  B\text{ and }\mu  + \nu  \geq  \beta
\]

at \( t = 0 \) . We claim this inequality is also preserved by the Ricci Flow. Clearly it defines a convex set of matrices \( M \) with eigenvalues \( \lambda  \geq  \mu  \geq  \nu \) and \( \mu  + \nu  \geq  0 \) . So we only must check that the inequality is preserved by the ODE system. Now

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\left( {\lambda  - \nu }\right)  = {\lambda }^{2} + {\mu \nu } - {\nu }^{2} - {\lambda \mu }
\]

so

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\ln \left( {\lambda  - \nu }\right)  = \lambda  - \mu  + \nu
\]

while

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\left( {\mu  + \nu }\right)  = {\mu }^{2} + {\lambda \nu } + {\nu }^{2} + {\lambda \mu } \geq  \lambda \left( {\mu  + \nu }\right)
\]

so

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\ln \left( {\mu  + \nu }\right)  \geq  \lambda
\]

Then

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\ln \left\lbrack  {\left( {\lambda  - \nu }\right) /{\left( \mu  + \nu \right) }^{1 - \delta }}\right\rbrack   \leq  {\delta \lambda } - \left( {\mu  + \nu }\right)  \leq  0
\]

so the ratio \( \left( {\lambda  - \nu }\right) /{\left( \mu  + \nu \right) }^{1 - \delta } \) decreases. If it is less than \( A \) to start, it remains so.

an explicit estimate using the maximum principle is given in [20]. Suppose the estimate fails for all \( C \) . Pick a sequence \( {C}_{j} \rightarrow  \infty \) , and pick points \( {P}_{j} \) and times \( {\tau }_{j} \) such that

\[
\left| {\operatorname{DRm}\left( {{P}_{j},{\tau }_{j}}\right) }\right|  \geq  \theta \mathop{\max }\limits_{{t \leq  {\tau }_{j}}}\mathop{\max }\limits_{P}{\left| \operatorname{Rm}\left( P, t\right) \right| }^{3/2} + {C}_{j}.
\]

Choose the \( {P}_{j} \) to be the origin, and pull the metric back to a small ball of radius \( {r}_{j} \) proportional to the reciprocal of the square root of the maximum curvature up to time \( \tau \) . Clearly these go to infinity by our derivative bounds. Dilate the metrics so

\[
\mathop{\max }\limits_{{t \leq  {\tau }_{j}}}\mathop{\max }\limits_{P}\left| {{Rm}\left( {P, t}\right) }\right|
\]

becomes 1 and translate so time \( {\tau }_{j} \) becomes time 0 . Then \( {C}_{j} \) dilates to zero, but in the limit metric

\[
\left| {{DRm}\left( {0,0}\right) }\right|  \geq  \theta \text{ . }
\]

However the limit metric has

\[
{Rc} - \frac{1}{3}{Rg} = 0
\]

by the previous theorem. But then it has constant curvature, which is a contradiction. This proves the corollary.

THEOREM 24.4. Suppose we have a solution to the Ricci flow

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{g}_{ij} =  - 2{R}_{ij}
\]

on a compact three-manifold which satisfies the inequalities \( R \geq   - 1 \) and

\[
{M}_{ij} + {f}^{-1}\left( R\right) {g}_{ij} \geq  0
\]

at \( t = 0 \) . Then it will continue to satisfy them for \( t \geq  0 \) .

Note that since \( {f}^{-1}\left( y\right)  \geq   + 1 \) always, any matrix with eigenvalues at least -1 and trace at least -1 satisfies the inequalities. For any metric we can achieve this by dilation. Then the inequalities will continue to hold under the Ricci flow. Then if the curvatures go to infinity, the most negative will be small compared to the most positive.

THEOREM 24.6. Suppose we have a solution to the Ricci Flow on a compact three-manifold on a maximal time interval \( 0 \leq  t < T \) which is Type I, so

\[
\mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  T}}\left( {T - t}\right) \left| M\right|  < \infty
\]

and suppose the manifold never acquires positive sectional curvature everywhere. Then there exists a \( \theta  > 0 \) such that for every \( \tau  < T \) and every \( \delta  > 0 \) we can find a time \( t \) in \( \tau  \leq  t < T \) and a point \( P \) where \( \left( {T - t}\right) \left| M\right|  \geq  \theta \) and a frame at \( P \) in which

\[
\left| {M - {RE}}\right|  \leq  \delta \left| M\right|
\]

where the scalar curvature \( R = \operatorname{tr}M \) is the trace of the curvature operator \( M \) and \( E \) is the curvature operator matrix of a round cylinder \( {S}^{2} \times  {R}^{1} \) given by

\[
E = \left( \begin{array}{lll} 1 & & \\   & 0 & \\   & & 0 \end{array}\right) .
\]

COROLLARY 24.7. The limit of dilations of the solution around these points and times gives an ancient solution with bounded non-negative sectional curvature whose holonomy reduces. Consequently it splits as a product of a surface with \( {R}^{1} \) .

COROLLARY 24.10. We have \( F \rightarrow  0 \) as \( t \rightarrow  T \) .

Proof. Choose any \( \lambda  > 0 \) . When

\[
\left( {T - t}\right) \left| M\right|  \leq  \lambda
\]

since \( \left| {\overset{ \circ  }{ \rightarrow  }M}\right|  \leq  \left| M\right| \) and \( \left| M\right|  \leq  A\left( {R + \rho }\right) \) we have

\[
F \leq  {A}^{2 - \varepsilon }{\lambda }^{\varepsilon }
\]

which is as small as we like if \( \lambda \) is small enough. But when

\[
\left( {T - t}\right) \left| M\right|  \geq  \lambda
\]

we have \( \left| M\right| \) quite large for \( t \) near \( T \) , so

\[
C - c{\left| M\right| }^{2} \leq   - \frac{1}{2}c{\left| M\right| }^{2}
\]

and

\[
{F}^{\prime } \leq   - \frac{1}{2}c{\left| M\right| }^{2}F/\left( {R + \rho }\right) .
\]

On the other hand, now that \( \left| M\right| \) is large

\[
R + \rho  \leq  \sqrt{3}\left| M\right|  + \rho  \leq  2\left| M\right|
\]

so

\[
{F}^{\prime } \leq   - \frac{1}{4}c\left| M\right| F.
\]

Using \( \left| M\right|  \geq  \lambda /\left( {T - t}\right) \) we get

\[
{F}^{\prime } \leq   - \frac{1}{4}{c\lambda F}/\left( {T - t}\right)
\]

for \( t \) near \( T \) . Thus when the maximum \( {F}_{\text{ MAX }} \) of \( F \) exceeds \( {A}^{2 - \varepsilon }{\lambda }^{\varepsilon } \) it must decrease at a rate

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{F}_{\mathrm{{MAX}}} \leq   - p{F}_{\mathrm{{MAX}}}/\left( {T - t}\right)
\]

where \( p = \frac{1}{4}{c\lambda } > 0 \) . This implies

\[
{\left. \frac{d}{dt}\left( T - t\right) \right) }^{-p}{F}_{\mathrm{{MAX}}} \leq  0
\]

so if \( {\left( T - t\right) }^{-p}{F}_{\text{ MAX }} = B \) at some time \( \tau \) close enough to \( T \) for the above estimates to hold then subsequently

\[
{F}_{\mathrm{{MAX}}} \leq  B{\left( T - t\right) }^{p}\;\text{ or }\;{F}_{\mathrm{{MAX}}} \leq  {A}^{2 - \varepsilon }{\lambda }^{\varepsilon }
\]

and so when \( t \) is even closer to \( T \) the second holds. But \( \lambda  > 0 \) is arbitrary, so \( F \rightarrow  0 \) .

nodes.content:
THEOREM 25.1. Suppose we have a sequence of solutions to the Ricci Flow given by metrics \( {G}_{j} \) on manifolds \( {M}_{j} \) with origins \( {O}_{j} \) and frames \( {\mathcal{F}}_{j} \) for times \( \alpha  < t < \omega \) (with \( \alpha  < 0 < \omega \) ) which are all complete, and such that for some \( \rho  > 0 \)

(a) all the sectional curvatures of all the metrics \( {G}_{j} \) are at most \( 1/{\rho }^{2} \)

(b) there is a sequence \( {\delta }_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) such that all the eigenvalues of the curvature operator \( R{m}_{j} \) of the metric \( {G}_{j} \) are at least \( - {\delta }_{j}/{\rho }^{2} \)

(c) there is an \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) such that all the eigenvalues of the curvature operator \( R{m}_{j} \) of \( {G}_{j} \) at the origin \( {O}_{j} \) are at least \( \varepsilon /{\rho }^{2} \)

(d) the diameters \( {d}_{j} \) of the metrics \( {G}_{j} \) go to \( \infty \) .

Then there is a subsequence of the metrics such that all the injectivity radii at the origins are at least this \( \rho  > 0 \) . Hence a subsequence converges to a solution \( {G}_{\infty } \) of the Ricci Flow on \( \alpha  < t < \omega \) .

nodes.proof:
which would want to converge if we could control the injectivity radii. To do this we introduce the notion of a geodesic tube in a manifold \( M \) with origin. Given a frame \( \mathcal{F} = \left( {{F}_{1},{F}_{2},\ldots ,{F}_{n}}\right) \) at the origin \( O \) and a length \( L \) , we begin by constructing the geodesic of length \( L \) out of \( O \) in the direction \( {F}_{1} \) and its opposite. Then we parallelly translate the frame \( \mathcal{F} \) along this geodesic, and take the geodesic out of each point in the direction \( {F}_{2} \) and its opposite of length \( \rho \) . Parallelly translate \( \mathcal{F} \) along these also, and take the geodesic out of each of these points in the direction \( {F}_{3} \) and its opposite of length \( \rho \) , and so on. Notice that only in the first direction do we go a long way \( L \) , while in the other directions we don’t go farther than \( \rho \) . The curvature satisfies \( \left| K\right|  \leq  \rho \) , so this construction gives a local diffeomorphism of

\[
\left( {-L, L}\right)  \times  \left( {-\rho ,\rho }\right)  \times  \cdots  \times  \left( {-\rho ,\rho }\right)  \rightarrow  M.
\]

Consider the pull-back metrics. For the Ricci Flow a bound on the curvature gives a bound on all the derivatives of the curvature. Then by ordinary differential equations we get bounds on the pull-back metric and all its derivatives with respect to the tube coordinates. (Here we omit the details.)

If we consider a fixed reference frame \( {\mathcal{F}}_{j} \) at the origin in each \( {M}_{j} \) and take an element \( A \) of the orthogonal group, then \( A{\mathcal{F}}_{j} \) is a frame at the origin in \( {M}_{j} \) , and we can take the pull-back metric for the geodesic tube on \( A{\mathcal{F}}_{j} \) . For a fixed \( A \) and a fixed \( L \) , we can always find a convergent subsequence of the pull-back metrics. By choosing a countable dense set of \( A \) ’s and a sequence of \( L \) ’s going to infinity, and by a diagonalization argument, we can find a subsequence of metrics so that the pull-back metrics to the tube on the frames \( A{\mathcal{F}}_{j} \) of length \( L \) converge for every \( A \) and every \( L \) . In this case we say the metrics preconverge along geodesic tubes. (Note any convergent sequence would be preconvergent.) The advantage of preconvergence is that we do not need to control the injectivity radius to get it. Form now on we only deal with such a preconvergent sequence.

We can strengthen the notion of preconvergence to compare one tube with another. For any two vectors \( X \) and \( Y \) in \( {R}^{n} \) (which we identify with the tangent spaces at the origins \( {0}_{j} \) in the \( {M}_{j} \) with the frames \( {\mathcal{F}}_{j} \) ) we can consider the sequence of distances

\[
{d}_{j} = {d}_{j}\left( {{\exp }_{j}X,{\exp }_{j}Y}\right)  \leq  \left| X\right|  + \left| Y\right|
\]

in \( {M}_{j} \) ; by picking a subsequence we can assume the \( {d}_{j} \) converge. If we do this by diagonalization for a countable dense set of pairs \( \left( {{X}_{\alpha },{Y}_{\alpha }}\right) \) then in fact \( {d}_{j} \) will converge for every pair \( \left( {X, Y}\right) \) . To see this take any \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) . Choose a sequence of pairs with \( {X}_{\alpha } \rightarrow  X \) and \( {Y}_{\alpha } \rightarrow  Y \) . Since we have preconvergence in geodesic tubes in the directions \( X \) and \( Y \) , the metrics \( {G}_{j} \) converge to a limit \( {G}_{\infty }^{X} \) in the tube on \( X \) , and to a limit \( {G}_{\infty }^{Y} \) in the tube on \( Y \) . We can find a constant \( c > 0 \) depending only on the dimension so that for any \( \zeta  > 0 \) small enough, if \( \left| {\widetilde{X} - X}\right|  \leq  {c\zeta \rho } \) then in the metric \( {G}_{\infty }^{X} \)

\[
{d}_{\infty }^{X}\left( {{\exp }_{\infty }^{X}\widetilde{X},{\exp }_{\infty }^{X}X}\right)  \leq  {\zeta \rho }
\]

and likewise if \( \left| {\widetilde{Y} - Y}\right|  \leq  {c\zeta \rho } \) then in the metric \( {G}_{\infty }^{Y} \)

\[
{d}_{\infty }^{Y}\left( {{\exp }_{\infty }^{Y}\widetilde{Y},{\exp }_{\infty }^{Y}Y}\right)  \leq  {\zeta \rho }
\]

Given \( \zeta  > 0 \) , choose \( \alpha \) so large that

\[
\left| {{X}_{\alpha } - X}\right|  \leq  {c\zeta \rho }\text{ and }\left| {{Y}_{\alpha } - Y}\right|  \leq  {c\zeta \rho }.
\]

Then

\[
{d}_{\infty }^{X}\left( {{\exp }_{\infty }^{X}{X}_{\alpha },{\exp }_{\infty }^{X}X}\right)  \leq  {\zeta \rho }
\]

and

\[
{d}_{\infty }^{Y}\left( {{\exp }_{\infty }^{Y}{Y}_{\alpha },{\exp }_{\infty }^{Y}Y}\right)  \leq  {\zeta \rho }
\]

Now choose \( j \) large enough depending on \( X, Y,\alpha ,\eta \) , and \( \rho \) so that

\[
\left| {{d}_{j}\left( {{\exp }_{j}{X}_{\alpha },{\exp }_{j}X}\right)  - {d}_{\alpha }^{X}\left( {{\exp }_{\infty }^{X}{X}_{\alpha },{\exp }_{\infty }^{X}X}\right) }\right|  \leq  {\zeta \rho }
\]

and

\[
\left| {{d}_{j}\left( {{\exp }_{j}{Y}_{\alpha },{\exp }_{j}Y}\right)  - {d}_{\alpha }^{X}\left( {{\exp }_{\infty }^{Y}{Y}_{\alpha },{\exp }_{\infty }^{Y}Y}\right) }\right|  \leq  {\zeta \rho }.
\]

Finally make \( j \) large enough also depending on \( X, Y,\alpha ,\zeta \) and \( \rho \) so that

\[
{d}_{j}\left( {{\exp }_{j}{X}_{\alpha },{\exp }_{j}{Y}_{\alpha }}\right)  \leq  {\zeta \rho }
\]

since \( {X}_{\alpha } \) and \( {Y}_{\alpha } \) are in the countable set for which the sequence is preconvergent in distances. Then

\[
{d}_{j}\left( {{\exp }_{,}X,{\exp }_{j}Y}\right)  \leq  {5\zeta \rho }.
\]

Since \( \zeta \) is arbitrary, the sequence is preconvergent in distances for all \( X \) and \( Y \) as claimed.

In fact we can do a little better along the lines of [H]. Using the geodesic tube coordinates at \( t = 0 \) , we can also consider the pull-back of the metric at earlier or later times, which we can bound using curvature bounds, since we know the metric evolves by the curvature under Ricci Flow. Then we can actually make the pull-backs of the Ricci Flow converge to a solution of the Ricci Flow in every geodesic tube. We can also keep the solutions preconvergent in the distances \( {d}_{j}\left( {{\exp }_{m}X,{\exp }_{j}Y}\right) \left( t\right) \) for all \( X \) and \( Y \) at every time \( t \) .

Then we can find a sequence of points \( {X}_{j} = {\exp }_{0}\left( {{\ell }_{j}{V}_{j}}\right) \) at distances \( {\ell }_{j} \leq  L \) from the origin in some directions \( {V}_{j} \) with \( \left| {V}_{j}\right|  = 1 \) such that some eigenvalues of the curvature operators at the \( {X}_{j} \) are not bounded away from 0 on the positive side. Since on \( {M}_{j} \) we have there eigenvalues \( \geq   - {\delta }_{j}/{\rho }^{2} \) with \( \delta  \rightarrow  0 \) , they in fact go to zero.

Find a convergent subsequence \( {V}_{j} \rightarrow  V \) and \( {\ell }_{j} \rightarrow  \ell \) and pick a geodesic tube in each \( {M}_{j} \) starting in the direction \( V \) . By preconvergence we get a limit which solves the Ricci Flow in the tube and the limit will have some eigenvalue of the curvature operator equal to zero at the point \( \ell V \) with \( \ell  \leq  L \) . But in the limit all the eigenvalues of the curvature operator are \( \geq  0 \) , so by the strong maximum principle (see[29]; the argument works locally also) there must be a zero eigenvalue of the curvature operator everywhere in the tube at every time, in particular at the origin at \( t = 0 \) . But for the sequence we had the eigenvalues of the curvature operator at \( {O}_{j} \geq  \varepsilon \) , so this holds in the limit also. Since this is a contradiction, the Lemma is established.

nodes.document_title: Richard S. Hamilton - The Formation of Singularities in the Ricci Flow
nodes.section_title: 1. The Formation of Singularities in the Ricci Flow
nodes.content:
THEOREM 26.1. The only solutions to the Ricci Flow on a surface which are complete with bounded curvature on an ancient time interval \( - \infty  < t < T \) and where the curvature \( R \) has

\[
\mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{t \rightarrow   - \infty }}\left( {T - t}\right) \left| R\right|  < \infty
\]

are the round sphere \( {S}^{2} \) and the flat plane \( {R}^{2} \) , and their quotients.
nodes.content_excerpt: THEOREM 26.1. The only solutions to the Ricci Flow on a surface which are complete with bounded curvature on an ancient time interval \( - \infty < t < T \) and where the curvature \( R \) has \[ \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{t \rightarrow - \infty }}\left( {T - t}\right) \left| R\right| < \infty \] are the round sphere \( {S}^{2} \) and the flat plane \( {R}^{2} \) , and their quotients.

nodes.proof:
and the minimum of \( R \) increases, \( R \geq  0 \) . Moreover by the strong maximum principle \( R = 0 \) everywhere and it is flat, or \( R > 0 \) everywhere. If the solution is compact with \( R > 0 \) , either it is the sphere or it is the projective plane \( R{P}^{2} = {S}^{2}/{Z}_{2} \) whose double cover is the sphere. Assume it is the sphere, and we shall see it is round. Then \( R{P}^{2} \) must be round also since its cover is.

We know from [22] that the sphere shrinks to a point at some future time which we can take to be \( T \) , when it becomes round. Its area \( A \) shrinks at a constant rate

\[
\frac{dA}{dt} =  - \int {Rda} =  - {8\pi }
\]

so \( A = {8\pi }\left( {T - t}\right) \) . On an even dimensional oriented manifold the injectivity radius can be bounded by the maximum curvature. Since

\[
R \leq  C/\left( {T - t}\right)
\]

by hypothesis, we must have injectivity radius \( \rho \) with

\[
\rho  \geq  c\sqrt{T - t}
\]

for some \( c \) . Now the diameter \( L \) has

\[
L \leq  {CA}/\rho  \leq  C\sqrt{T - t}
\]

as a bound also. Hence the diameter, the injectivity radius and the maximum curvature all scale proportionally to the time to blow-up.

The scaled entropy

\[
E = \int R\ln \left\lbrack  {R\left( {T - t}\right) }\right\rbrack  {da}
\]

is monotone decreasing in \( t \) . Since

\[
R\left( {T - t}\right)  \leq  C\;\text{ and }\;\int {Rda} = {8\pi }
\]

we have an upper bound

\[
E \leq  {8\pi }\ln C
\]

so

\[
{E}_{-\infty } = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow   - \infty }}{E}_{t}
\]

exists. Pick a sequence of points \( {t}_{j} \rightarrow   - \infty \) and points \( {P}_{j} \) where the curvature is as big as anywhere at time \( {t}_{j} \) . Then it was never larger anywhere at any earlier time, since an ancient solution with \( R > 0 \) has \( R \) pointwise increasing by the Harnack inequality. Make \( {P}_{j} \) the new origin and \( {t}_{j} \) the new time 0 and \( T \) the same blow-up time by translation and dilation. We can then take a limit using the curvature and injectivity radius bounds. The backwards limit is still compact by the diameter bound. Moreover the scaled entropy is now constant at the value \( {E}_{-\infty } \) . But the only way this happens is on a shrinking soliton, and (except for orbifolds) the only one is the round sphere. Then \( E \) has its minimal value at \( t =  - \infty \) , so it was constant all along. hence the sphere was round all along.

nodes.content:
THEOREM 26.5. Suppose we have a solution to the Ricci Flow on a compact three- manifold, and suppose \( R \) becomes unbounded in some finite time \( T \) . Then there exists a sequence of dilations of the solution which converges to \( {S}^{3} \) or \( {S}^{2} \times  {R}^{1} \) or \( {\sum }^{2} \times  {R}^{1} \) (where \( {\sum }^{2} \) is the "cigar" soliton) or to a quotient of one of these solutions by a finite group of isometries acting freely (these quotients are the space forms \( {S}^{3}/\gamma , R{P}^{2} \times  {R}^{1} \) , and \( R{P}^{2} \times  {R}^{1} \) and \( {S}^{2} \times  {S}_{r}^{1}, R{P}^{2} \times  {S}_{r}^{1} \) and \( {\sum }^{2} \times  {S}_{r}^{1} \) for circles \( {S}_{r}^{1} \) of any radius \( r \) ), except possibly for the case of a Type I singularity where the injectivity radius times the square root of the maximum curvature goes to zero.

Proof. When we get an injectivity radius estimate valid for finite time we can always for a singularity model of Type I or II. First consider Type I. If the sectional curvature ever becomes positive everywhere, it becomes round and our limit is \( {S}^{3} \) or \( {S}^{3}/\gamma \) . Otherwise in Type I we get a limit which is an ancient solution with bounded non-negative sectional curvature which splits as a product of a surface with \( {R}^{1} \) . For the surface, if \( \left( {T - t}\right) R \leq  C \) it must be a round sphere or projective plane by Theorem 26.1. Otherwise we can take a backwards limit as \( t \rightarrow   - \infty \) to get a Type II limit, which must be the cigar \( {\sum }^{2} \) . Since a limit of a limit is also a limit, we get \( {\sum }^{2} \times  {R}^{1} \) or \( {\sum }^{2} \times  {S}^{1} \) as a limit of the three-manifold solution.

In order to take this backward limit we need an injectivity radius estimate on the surface in terms of the maximum curvature \( R \) at the current time. Since \( R > 0 \) this is easy. There are three cases. If the surface is compact and oriented, it is \( {S}^{2} \) and the result follows from a theorem for positive sectional curvature in even dimensions of Klingenberg ([9], 5.9). If it is compact but not oriented, it is \( R{P}^{2} \) and the double cover can be handled as before. If it is not compact, it is diffeomorphic to \( {R}^{2} \) and we can use the estimate for complete noncompact manifolds of positive sectional curvature.

If the limit is Type II, it must be a Ricci soliton of weakly positive sectional curvature from our pinching result in Theorem 24.4. If the sectional curvature is not strictly positive, it splits as a product of a surface soliton, which must be \( {\sum }^{2} \) , with a flat factor \( {R}^{2} \) or \( {S}^{1} \) (of any radius). Even if it does not split, we know the asymptotic curvature ratio is infinite

\[
A = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{s \rightarrow  \infty }}R{s}^{2} = \infty
\]

by Theorem 20.2, and by Theorem 22.3 since the dimension \( n = 3 \) is odd, we can do dimension reduction to find a limit of a limit which splits as a product with \( {R}^{1} \) of an ancient solution with bounded positive curvature on a surface. Again a limit of a limit is a limit, and we can classify the surface as a round \( {S}^{2} \) (not \( R{P}^{2} \) because it is oriented) or \( {\sum }^{2} \) . This finishes the proof of the Theorem.

## 2. Notations and conventions

We will use the old-fashioned index notation for tensors, since it is well-adapted to the intense computations we must perform. We denote vectors as \( {v}^{i} \) , covectors as \( {v}_{j} \) , and mixed tensors as \( {T}_{klm}^{ij} \) etc. The summation convention will always hold. The Riemannian metric is \( {g}_{ij} \) , its inverse is \( {g}^{ij} \) , and the induced measure is \( {d\mu } = \mu \left( x\right) {dx} \) where \( \mu \left( x\right)  = \sqrt{\det {g}_{ij}} \) . The Levi-Civita connection is given by the Christöffel symbols

\[
{\Gamma }_{ij}^{h} = \frac{1}{2}{g}^{hk}\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}{g}_{jk} + \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{j}}{g}_{ik} - \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{k}}{g}_{ij}}\right) ,
\]

and the Riemannian curvature tensor is

\[
{R}_{ijk}^{h} = \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}{\Gamma }_{jk}^{h} - \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{j}}{\Gamma }_{ik}^{h} + {\Gamma }_{ip}^{h}{\Gamma }_{jk}^{p} - {\Gamma }_{jp}^{h}{\Gamma }_{ik}^{p}.
\]

We lower the index to the middle position, so that

\[
{R}_{ijkl} = {g}_{hk}{R}_{ijl}^{h}.
\]

Then \( {R}_{ijkl} \) is anti-symmetric in the pairs \( i, j \) and \( k, l \) and symmetric in their interchange, and satisfies a Bianchi identity on the cyclic permutation of any three. For the sphere we have

\[
R\left( {u, v, u, v}\right)  = {R}_{ijkl}{u}^{i}{v}^{j}{u}^{k}{v}^{l} > 0,
\]

which is the opposite of the usual convention, but more symmetric. The Ricci curvature is the contraction

\[
{R}_{ik} = {g}^{jl}{R}_{ijkl},
\]

and on the sphere we have

\[
R\left( {u, u}\right)  = {R}_{ij}{u}^{i}{u}^{j} > 0,
\]

which agrees with the usual convention. The scalar curvature \( R = {g}^{ij}{R}_{ij} \) . We denote the covariant derivative of a vector \( {v}^{j} \) by

\[
{\partial }_{i}{v}^{j} = \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}{v}^{j} + {\Gamma }_{ik}^{j}{v}^{k},
\]

and this definition extends uniquely to tensors so as to preserve the product rule and contractions. For the interchange of two covariant derivatives we have

\[
{\partial }_{i}{\partial }_{j}{v}^{h} - {\partial }_{j}{\partial }_{i}{v}^{h} = {R}_{ijk}^{h}{v}^{k},
\]

\[
{\partial }_{i}{\partial }_{j}{v}_{k} - {\partial }_{j}{\partial }_{i}{v}_{k} = {R}_{ijkl}{g}^{lm}{v}_{m}
\]

and similar formulas for more complicated tensors. To see how to convert from the old coordinate notation to the new coordinate-free notation the reader should consider the formulas

for a vector \( v : v = {v}^{i}\partial /\partial {x}^{i} \) ,

for a covector \( L : L = {L}_{i}d{x}^{i} \) ,

for a pairing: \( L\left( v\right)  = {L}_{i}{v}^{i} \) ,

for a tensor: \( T\left( {\partial /\partial {x}^{j},\partial /\partial {x}^{k}}\right)  = {T}_{jk}^{i}\partial /\partial {x}^{i} \) ,

for a covariant derivative:

\[
{\partial }_{v}T\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{j}},\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{k}}}\right)  = {v}^{h}{\partial }_{h}{T}_{jk}^{i}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}.
\]

For any tensor \( T \) such as \( {T}_{jk}^{i} \) we define its length \( \left| {T}_{jk}^{i}\right| \) by

\[
{\left| {T}_{jk}^{i}\right| }^{2} = {g}_{il}{g}^{jm}{g}^{kn}{T}_{jk}^{i}{T}_{mn}^{l},
\]

and we define its Laplacian \( {\Delta T} \) by

\[
\Delta {T}_{jk}^{i} = {g}^{pq}{\partial }_{p}{\partial }_{q}{T}_{jk}^{i},
\]

the trace of the second iterated covariant derivative. We hope these remarks will aid the reader in following the paper.

nodes.content:
### 3.The evolution equation

We consider the evolution equation on \( {X}^{n} \)

(**)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{g}_{ij} = \frac{2}{n}r{g}_{ij} - 2{R}_{ij},
\]

where \( r = \int {Rd\mu }/\int {d\mu } \) is the average scalar curvature. The factor \( r \) serves to normalize the equation so that the volume is constant. To see this we observe that if \( {d\mu } = \mu \left( x\right) {dx} \) is the measure then \( \mu  = \sqrt{\det {g}_{ij}} \) and

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\log \mu  = \frac{1}{2}{g}^{ij}\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{g}_{ij} = r - R
\]

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\int {d\mu } = \int \left( {r - R}\right) {d\mu } = 0.
\]

Now it is awkward to have the normalizing factor present until we really need it. Therefore we will deal first with the unnormalized evolution equation

(*)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{g}_{ij} =  - 2{R}_{ij},
\]

which is easier to handle. The two equations differ only by a change of scale in space and a change of parametrization in time. To see this we let \( t,{g}_{ij},{R}_{ij}, R \) , \( r \) denote the variables for the unnormalized equation \( \left( *\right) \) and \( \widetilde{t},{\widetilde{g}}_{ij},{\widetilde{R}}_{ij},\widetilde{R},\widetilde{r} \) the corresponding variables for the normalized equation. To make the conversion from \( \left( *\right) \) to \( \left( {* * }\right) \) , we first choose the normalization factor \( \psi  = \psi \left( t\right) \) so that if \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij} = \psi {g}_{ij} \) then \( \int d\widetilde{\mu } = 1 \) , so that the new manifold has measure 1 . Then we choose a new time scale \( \widetilde{t} = \int \psi \left( t\right) {dt} \) . It is easy to see that

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{ij} = {R}_{ij},\;\widetilde{R} = \frac{1}{\psi }R,\;\widetilde{r} = \frac{1}{\psi }r,
\]

and \( \int d\widetilde{\mu } = 1 \) so \( \int {d\mu } = {\psi }^{-n/2} \) . Arguing as before we have \( \left( {\partial /\partial t}\right) \log \mu  =  - R \) and so

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\log \int {d\mu } =  - r,\;\frac{d}{dt}\log \psi  = \frac{2}{n}r.
\]

Then it follows that

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial \widetilde{t}}{\widetilde{g}}_{ij} = \frac{\partial }{\partial t}{g}_{ij} + \left( {\frac{d}{dt}\log \psi }\right) {g}_{ij} = \frac{2}{n}\widetilde{r}{\widetilde{g}}_{ij} - 2{\widetilde{R}}_{ij}.
\]

It is worth noting that for a sphere \( {S}^{n} \) the normalized equation is constant, while the unnormalized equation shrinks to a point in a finite time.

nodes.content:
## 5. Evolution equations with an integrability condition

We shall consider evolution equations

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = E\left( f\right)
\]

where \( E\left( f\right) \) is a nonlinear differential operator of degree 2 in \( f \) . We suppose \( f \) belongs to an open set \( U \) in a vector bundle \( F \) over a compact manifold \( X \) , and \( E\left( f\right) \) takes its values in \( F \) also. Then \( E \) is a smooth map

\[
E : {\mathcal{C}}^{\infty }\left( {X, U}\right)  \subseteq  {\mathcal{C}}^{\infty }\left( {X, F}\right)  \rightarrow  {\mathcal{C}}^{\infty }\left( {X, F}\right)
\]

of an open set in a Fréchet space to itself. In studying the evolution equation it is important to consider its linearization. Letting \( \widetilde{f} \) denote a variation in \( f \) , we get

\[
\frac{\partial \widetilde{f}}{\partial t} = {DE}\left( f\right) \widetilde{f},
\]

where the derivative \( {DE}\left( f\right) \widetilde{f} \) is a linear differential operator in \( \widetilde{f} \) of degree 2 . We say \( E \) is parabolic if its linearization is parabolic around any \( f \) . This can be expressed in terms of the symbol \( {\sigma DE}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right) \) , which is obtained by replacing each derivative \( \partial /\partial {x}^{j} \) by \( {\xi }_{j} \) in the highest order terms. (For simplicity we omit the factor \( i = \sqrt{-1} \) .) If in local coordinates

\[
\partial {f}^{\alpha }/\partial t = {E}^{\alpha }\left( {{x}^{i},{f}^{\beta },{f}_{i}^{\beta },{f}_{ij}^{\beta }}\right) ,
\]

then the symbol of \( {DE}\left( f\right) \) is

\[
{\sigma DE}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right)  = \frac{\partial {E}^{\alpha }}{\partial {f}_{ij}^{\beta }}\left( {{x}^{i},{f}^{\beta },{f}_{i}^{\beta },{f}_{ij}^{\beta }}\right) {\xi }_{i}{\xi }_{j}.
\]

The symbol is an automorphism of the vector bundle \( F \) to itself. Then \( {DE}\left( f\right) \) is parabolic if all the eigenvalues of \( {\sigma DE}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right) \) have strictly positive real parts when \( \xi  \neq  0 \) . In this case it is well known that the evolution equation \( \partial f/\partial t = \; E\left( f\right) \) has a unique smooth solution for the initial value problem \( f = {f}_{0} \) at \( t = 0 \) for at least a short time interval \( 0 \leq  t \leq  \varepsilon \) (where \( \varepsilon \) may depend on \( {f}_{0} \) ).

We shall consider problems where some of the eigenvalues of \( {\sigma DE}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right) \) are zero. This happens when \( E\left( f\right) \) satisfies an integrability condition. Let \( g = \; L\left( f\right) h \) be a differential operator of degree 1 on sections \( f \in  U \subseteq  F \) and \( h \in  F \) with values \( g \) in another vector bundle \( G \) over \( X \) , such that the operator \( Q\left( f\right)  = L\left( f\right) E\left( f\right) \) only has degree at most 1 in \( f \) . We call \( L\left( f\right) \) the integrability condition for \( E\left( f\right) \) . Taking a variation \( \widetilde{f} \) in \( f \) we see that

\[
L\left( f\right) {DE}\left( f\right) \widetilde{f} + {DL}\left( f\right) \{ E\left( f\right) ,\widetilde{f}\}  = {DQ}\left( f\right) \widetilde{f}.
\]

Now the operators \( {DL}\left( f\right) \{ E\left( f\right) ,\widetilde{f}\} \) and \( {DQ}\left( f\right) \widetilde{f} \) only have degree 1 in \( \widetilde{f} \) , and hence the operator \( L\left( f\right) {DE}\left( f\right) \widetilde{f} \) also has degree 1 only. Therefore taking the symbols, \( {\sigma L}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right)  \cdot  {\sigma DE}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right)  = 0 \) . From this we see that

\[
\operatorname{Im}{\sigma DE}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right)  \subseteq  \operatorname{Null}{\sigma L}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right) .
\]

If \( L \) is not trivial then \( {\sigma DE}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right) \) must have a null eigenspace. The most we can hope is that the restriction of \( {\sigma DE}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right) \) to Null \( {\sigma L}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right) \) is positive. We shall prove the following result.

nodes.proof:
We shall use the Nash-Moser inverse function theorem (see [5] for a complete exposition by the author). We shall show that if \( \partial \bar{f}/\partial t - E\left( \bar{f}\right)  = \bar{h} \) is a solution of the evolution equation on \( 0 \leq  t \leq  1 \) , with \( \bar{f} = {\bar{f}}_{0} \) at \( t = 0 \) , then for any \( {f}_{0} \) near \( {\bar{f}}_{0} \) and \( h \) near \( \bar{h} \) there exists a unique solution of the equation \( \partial f/\partial t - E\left( f\right)  = h \) over the interval \( 0 \leq  t \leq  1 \) with \( f = {f}_{0} \) at \( t = 0 \) . To see that this implies the theorem, choose \( \bar{f} \) to be any function whose formal Taylor series at \( t = 0 \) is what it must be to solve \( \partial f/\partial t = E\left( f\right) \) with \( f = {f}_{0} \) at \( t = 0 \) , and let \( \bar{h} = \partial \bar{f}/\partial t - E\left( \bar{f}\right) \) . Then the formal Taylor series of \( \bar{h} \) at \( t = 0 \) is identically zero. By translating \( \bar{h} \) a little, we can find \( h \) arbitrarily close to \( \bar{h} \) and vanishing for a short time \( 0 \leq  t \leq  \varepsilon \) . Then the solution of \( \partial f/\partial t - E\left( f\right)  = h \) with \( f = {f}_{0} \) at \( t = 0 \) solves the equation up to time \( \varepsilon \) .

We can apply the Nash-Moser inverse function theorem to the operator

\[
\delta  : {\mathcal{C}}^{\infty }\left( {X \times  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack  , F}\right)  \rightarrow  {\mathcal{C}}^{\infty }\left( {X \times  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack  , F}\right)  \times  {\mathcal{C}}^{\infty }\left( {X, F}\right) ,
\]

\[
\varepsilon \left( f\right)  = \left( {\partial f/\partial t - E\left( f\right) , f\mid \{ t = 0\} }\right) .
\]

Its derivative is the operator

\[
D\mathcal{E}\left( f\right) \widetilde{f} = \left( {\partial \widetilde{f}/\partial t - {DE}\left( f\right) \widetilde{f},\widetilde{f}\mid \{ t = 0\} }\right) .
\]

We must show that the linearized equation \( \partial \widetilde{f}/\partial t - {DE}\left( f\right) \widetilde{f} = \widetilde{h} \) has a unique solution for the initial value problem \( \widetilde{f} = {\widetilde{f}}_{0} \) at \( t = 0 \) , and verify that the solution \( \widetilde{f} \) is a smooth tame function of \( \widetilde{h} \) and \( {\widetilde{f}}_{0} \) .

We make the substitution \( \widetilde{g} = L\left( f\right) \widetilde{f} \) . Then \( \widetilde{g} \) will satisfy the evolution equation

\[
\frac{\partial \widetilde{g}}{\partial t} = L\left( f\right) \frac{\partial \widetilde{f}}{\partial t} + {DL}\left( f\right) \left\{  {\widetilde{f},\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}}\right\}  .
\]

However \( \partial \widetilde{f}/\partial t = {DE}\left( f\right) \widetilde{f} + \widetilde{h} \) . Moreover differentiating the integrability condition \( L\left( f\right) E\left( f\right)  = Q\left( f\right) \) we get

\[
L\left( f\right) {DE}\left( f\right) \widetilde{f} + {DL}\left( f\right) \{ E\left( f\right) ,\widetilde{f}\}  = {DQ}\left( f\right) \widetilde{f}.
\]

Then we get the equation

\[
\frac{\partial \widetilde{g}}{\partial t} - M\left( f\right) \widetilde{f} = \widetilde{k}
\]

where \( \widetilde{k} = L\left( f\right) \widetilde{h} \) and

\[
M\left( f\right) \widetilde{f} = {DL}\left( f\right) \left\{  {\widetilde{f},\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}}\right\}   - {DL}\left( f\right) \{ E\left( f\right) ,\widetilde{f}\}  + {DQ}\left( f\right) \widetilde{f}
\]

is a linear differential operator in \( \widetilde{f} \) of degree 1 whose coefficients depend smoothly on \( f \) and its derivatives (possibly of degree 3 in space, or 1 in space and 1 in time).

If we choose a measure on \( X \) and inner products on the vector bundles \( F \) and \( G \) , we can form a differential operator \( {L}^{ * }\left( f\right) g = h \) , of degree 1 in \( f \) and \( g \) , which is the adjoint of \( L\left( f\right) \) . Let us write

\[
P\left( f\right)  = {DE}\left( f\right)  + {L}^{ * }\left( f\right) L\left( f\right) .
\]

We claim that the equation \( \partial \widetilde{f}/\partial t = P\left( f\right) \widetilde{f} \) is parabolic. To see this, we must examine the symbol

\[
{\sigma P}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right)  = {\sigma DE}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right)  + \sigma {L}^{ * }\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right)  \cdot  {\sigma L}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right) .
\]

Suppose \( v \) is an eigenvector in \( F \) with eigenvalue \( \lambda \) . Then \( {\sigma P}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right) v = {\lambda v} \) . But \( {\sigma L}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right)  \cdot  {\sigma DE}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right)  = 0 \) , so

\[
{\sigma L}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right)  \cdot  \sigma {L}^{ * }\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right)  \cdot  {\sigma L}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right) v = {\lambda \sigma L}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right) v.
\]

It follows that

\[
{\left| \sigma {L}^{ * }\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right)  \cdot  \sigma L\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right) v\right| }^{2} = \lambda {\left| \sigma L\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right) v\right| }^{2}.
\]

Now if \( \sigma {L}^{ * }\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right)  \cdot  {\sigma L}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right) v = 0 \) then \( {\sigma L}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right) v = 0 \) , and otherwise \( \lambda \) is real and strictly positive. When \( {\sigma L}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right) v = 0 \) then \( {\sigma DE}\left( f\right) \left( \xi \right) v = {\lambda v} \) , and \( \lambda \) has strictly positive real part by our hypothesis (B). Thus \( P\left( f\right) \) is parabolic.

We proceed to solve the system of equations

\[
\frac{\partial \widetilde{f}}{\partial t} - P\left( f\right) \widetilde{f} + {L}^{ * }\left( f\right) \widetilde{g} = \widetilde{h}
\]

\[
\frac{\partial \widetilde{g}}{\partial t} - M\left( f\right) \widetilde{f} = \widetilde{k}
\]

for the unknown functions \( \widetilde{f} \) and \( \widetilde{g} \) for given \( \widetilde{h} \) and \( \widetilde{k} \) and given \( f \) , with initial data \( \widetilde{f} = {\widetilde{f}}_{0} \) and \( \widetilde{g} = {\widetilde{g}}_{0} = L\left( {f}_{0}\right) {\widetilde{f}}_{0} \) at \( t = 0 \) .

It follows from the theorem in the next section that the solution \( \left( {\widetilde{f},\widetilde{g}}\right) \) exists and is unique, and is a smooth tame function of \( \left( {f,\widetilde{h},\widetilde{k},{\widetilde{f}}_{0},{\widetilde{g}}_{0}}\right) \) . Then putting \( \widetilde{l} = \widetilde{g} - L\left( f\right) \widetilde{f} \) we see that \( \widetilde{l} \) satisfies the evolution equation

\[
\frac{\partial \widetilde{l}}{\partial t} = L\left( f\right) {L}^{ * }\left( f\right) \widetilde{l}
\]

and \( \widetilde{l} = 0 \) at \( t = 0 \) . But then the obvious integral inequality

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{\int }_{X}{\left| \widetilde{l}\right| }^{2}{d\mu } + 2{\int }_{X}{\left| {L}^{ * }\left( f\right) \widetilde{l}\right| }^{2}{d\mu } = 0
\]

proves that \( \widetilde{l} = 0 \) . Then it follows that \( \partial \widetilde{f}/\partial t - {DE}\left( f\right) \widetilde{f} = \widetilde{h} \) . This completes the proof of the theorem, except for the result of the following section.

nodes.label: Theorem 6
nodes.document_title: Richard S. Hamilton - Three-Manifolds with Positive Ricci Curvature
nodes.content: 6. Theorem. Suppose the equation \( \partial f/\partial t = {Pf} \) is parabolic. Then for any given \( \left( {{f}_{0},{g}_{0}, h, k}\right) \) there exists a unique smooth solution \( \left( {f, g}\right) \) of the system with \( f = {f}_{0} \) and \( g = {g}_{0} \) at \( t = 0 \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 6. Theorem. Suppose the equation \( \partial f/\partial t = {Pf} \) is parabolic. Then for any given \( \left( {{f}_{0},{g}_{0}, h, k}\right) \) there exists a unique smooth solution \( \left( {f, g}\right) \) of the system with \( f = {f}_{0} \) and \( g = {g}_{0} \) at \( t = 0 \) .

nodes.proof:
We can use the equation to solve formally for the Taylor series of \( f \) and \( g \) at \( t = 0 \) . Choose functions \( \bar{f} \) and \( \bar{g} \) with the given Taylor series, and subtract them off from \( f \) and \( g \) . This reduces us to the case where \( f, g, h, k \) are all known to vanish for \( t \leq  0 \) . We can then use the following regularization device.

We introduce a time lag \( \delta  > 0 \) into the second equation, so that

\[
{\left( \frac{\partial g}{\partial t}\right) }_{t + \delta } = {\left( Mf + Ng + h\right) }_{t}.
\]

The resulting system clearly has a unique smooth solution on \( 0 \leq  t \leq  T \) , for we can alternatively use the first and second equations separately to advance the solution on intervals of length \( \delta  > 0 \) . In the sequel we shall derive a priori estimates for the solutions \( f \) and \( g \) of the evolutionary system. These estimates also clearly hold for the delayed system and are independent of \( \delta  \rightarrow  0 \) . We leave the necessary modification to the reader. Then by passing to a convergent subsequence we get a solution for \( \delta  = 0 \) .

nodes.content:
We turn to the a priori estimates. We introduce the following norms. For a section of \( F \) (or \( G \) ) over \( X \) we let \( {\left| f\right| }_{n} \) measure the \( {L}_{2} \) norm of \( f \) and its derivatives up to degree \( n \) . For a time-dependent section \( f \) over \( X \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) with \( f = \left\{  {{f}_{t} : 0 \leq  t \leq  T}\right\} \) we put

\[
{\left| f\right| }_{n}^{2} = {\int }_{0}^{T}{\left| {f}_{t}\right| }_{n}^{2}{dt}
\]

so that \( {\left| f\right| }_{n} \) measures space derivatives of degree \( \leq  n \) only. Then we put

\[
\parallel f{\parallel }_{n}^{2} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{{2j} \leq  n}}{\begin{Vmatrix}{\left( \partial /\partial t\right) }^{j}f\end{Vmatrix}}_{n - {2j}},
\]

which is a weighted norm counting one time derivative equal to two space derivatives. (We caution the reader that this weighted grading is not tamely equivalent to the usual one.) The differential operators \( P, L, M, N \) are all sections of some appropriate bundles over \( X \) , which could be interpreted in terms of jet bundles. We measure \( P, L, M, N \) in terms of norms \( {\left| \left\lbrack  L\right\rbrack  \right| }_{n} \) where \( {\left\lbrack  L\right\rbrack  }_{n} \) measures the supremum of \( L \) and its space derivatives up to degree \( n \) , and | [ ] | is the corresponding norm counting one time derivative equal to two space derivatives as before. (Note that the gradings \( \parallel {\parallel }_{n} \) and \( \left| \left\lbrack  \right\rbrack  \right| {|}_{n} \) are tamely equivalent. Also from a point of view of tamely equivalent gradings it does not really matter that for odd \( n \) our grading \( \parallel {\parallel }_{n} \) has missed \( \frac{1}{2} \) of a time derivative, compared to the usual one for parabolic equations. This allows us to avoid the nuisance of discussing fractional derivatives.)

nodes.content:
6.3 Lemma. If \( \partial f/\partial t - {Pf} = h \) on \( 0 \leq  t \leq  T \) and \( f = 0 \) at \( t = 0 \) then we can find a constant \( C \) independent of \( \theta \) such that for \( 0 \leq  \theta  \leq  T \)

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {f}_{t}\right| }_{2}^{2}{dt} \leq  C{\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {h}_{t}\right| }_{0}^{2}{dt}
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: 6.3 Lemma. If \( \partial f/\partial t - {Pf} = h \) on \( 0 \leq t \leq T \) and \( f = 0 \) at \( t = 0 \) then we can find a constant \( C \) independent of \( \theta \) such that for \( 0 \leq \theta \leq T \) \[ {\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {f}_{t}\right| }_{2}^{2}{dt} \leq C{\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {h}_{t}\right| }_{0}^{2}{dt} \]

nodes.proof: When \( \theta  = T \) this is a standard result for parabolic equations (see [4]). To see that \( C \) is independent of \( \theta \) for \( 0 \leq  \theta  \leq  T \) we use the following device. We extend \( P \) to be parabolic on the interval \( - T \leq  t \leq  T \) . Note that we may assume all the derivatives of \( f \) vanish at \( t = 0 \) also, for the set of such functions is dense in those with \( {f}_{0} = 0 \) in the norm \( \parallel {\parallel }_{2} \) . Then we may extend \( f \) smoothly to be zero for \( - T \leq  t \leq  0 \) . Now we consider translations by \( T - \theta \) of the original equation. Then \( P \) and \( f \) on \( - T + \theta  \leq  t \leq  \theta \) correspond to their translates on \( 0 \leq  t \leq  T \) . Since the estimate above is coercive for \( P \) , it follows by the usual argument that the same constant \( C \) works for all operators in a neighborhood of \( P \) . Hence we can make one constant \( C \) work for any compact set of parabolic operators \( P \) . But the set of translates is compact, so the lemma follows.

nodes.content:
6.4 Corollary. If \( \partial f/\partial t - {Pf} = h \) on \( 0 \leq  t \leq  T \) and \( f = {f}_{0} \) at \( t = 0 \) then we can find a constant \( C \) independent of \( \theta \) such that for \( 0 \leq  \theta  \leq  T \)

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {f}_{t}\right| }_{2}^{2}{dt} \leq  C{\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {h}_{t}\right| }_{0}^{2}{dt} + C{\left| {f}_{0}\right| }_{1}^{2}.
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: 6.4 Corollary. If \( \partial f/\partial t - {Pf} = h \) on \( 0 \leq t \leq T \) and \( f = {f}_{0} \) at \( t = 0 \) then we can find a constant \( C \) independent of \( \theta \) such that for \( 0 \leq \theta \leq T \) \[ {\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {f}_{t}\right| }_{2}^{2}{dt} \leq C{\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {h}_{t}\right| }_{0}^{2}{dt} + C{\left| {f}_{0}\right| }_{1}^{2}. \]

nodes.proof:
The norm \( {\left| {f}_{0}\right| }_{1} \) is equivalent to the quotient norm \( \inf \left\{  {\parallel f{\parallel }_{2} : f = {f}_{0}}\right. \) at \( t = 0\} \) . It suffices to check this in local coordinates, where we can use the Fourier transform. Given \( {f}_{0}\left( x\right) \) on \( t = 0 \) , we define the extension \( f\left( {x, t}\right) \) by letting

\[
f\left( {\xi ,\tau }\right)  = \psi \left( \frac{\tau }{1 + {\left| \xi \right| }^{2}}\right)  \cdot  \frac{1}{1 + {\left| \xi \right| }^{2}}{\widehat{f}}_{0}\left( \xi \right) ,
\]

where \( \psi \left( \tau \right) \) is a smooth function of compact support with \( \int \psi \left( \tau \right) {d\tau } = 1 \) . Then \( f \) extends \( {f}_{0} \) and if \( \theta  = \tau /\left( {1 + {\left| \xi \right| }^{2}}\right) \)

\[
\parallel f{\parallel }_{2}^{2} = \iint {\left( 1 + {\left| \xi \right| }^{2} + \left| \tau \right| \right) }^{2}{\left| \widehat{f}\left( \xi ,\tau \right) \right| }^{2}{d\xi d\tau }
\]

\[
= \int {\left| \psi \left( \theta \right) \right| }^{2}{\left( 1 + \left| \theta \right| \right) }^{2}{d\theta } \cdot  \int \left( {1 + {\left| \xi \right| }^{2}}\right) {\left| {\widehat{f}}_{0}\left( \xi \right) \right| }^{2}{d\xi }
\]

\[
\leq  C{\left| {f}_{0}\right| }_{1}^{2}
\]

Conversely given on \( t \geq  0 \) with \( f = {f}_{0} \) at \( t = 0 \) , we can first extend \( f \) to \( t \leq  0 \) without increasing \( \parallel f{\parallel }_{2} \) by more than a factor. Then using the Fourier transform, since

\[
{\widehat{f}}_{0}\left( \xi \right)  = \int \widehat{f}\left( {\xi ,\tau }\right) {d\tau }
\]

we have

\[
{\left| {f}_{0}\right| }_{1} = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{\left| g\right| }_{0} \leq  1}}\int {\left( 1 + {\left| \xi \right| }^{2}\right) }^{1/2}{\widehat{f}}_{0}\left( \xi \right) \widehat{g}\left( \xi \right) {d\xi }
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{\left| g\right| }_{0} \leq  1}}\iint {\left( 1 + {\left| \xi \right| }^{2}\right) }^{1/2}\widehat{f}\left( {\xi ,\tau }\right) \widehat{g}\left( \xi \right) {d\xi d\tau }
\]

\[
\leq  \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{\left| g\right| }_{0} \leq  1}}{\left\{  \iint {\left( 1 + {\left| \xi \right| }^{2} + \left| \tau \right| \right) }^{2}{\left| \widehat{f}\left( \xi ,\tau \right) \right| }^{2}d\xi d\tau \right\}  }^{1/2}
\]

\[
\times  {\left\{  \iint \frac{\left( {1 + {\left| \xi \right| }^{2}}\right) {\left| \widehat{g}\left( \xi \right) \right| }^{2}}{{\left( 1 + {\left| \xi \right| }^{2} + \left| \tau \right| \right) }^{2}}d\xi d\tau \right\}  }^{1/2}.
\]

Now the first integral is bounded by \( \parallel f{\parallel }_{2}^{2} \) , and the second is bounded by a constant, since

\[
\int \frac{1 + {\left| \xi \right| }^{2}}{{\left( 1 + {\left| \xi \right| }^{2} + \left| \tau \right| \right) }^{2}}{d\tau } = \int \frac{d\theta }{{\left( 1 + \left| \theta \right| \right) }^{2}} = C < \infty .
\]

Thus \( {\left| {f}_{0}\right| }_{1}^{2} \leq  C\parallel f{\parallel }_{2}^{2} \) , proving our assertion.

We can combine the extension operators in local coordinates to produce a linear extension operator \( {\mathcal{C}}^{\infty }\left( {X, F}\right)  \rightarrow  {\mathcal{C}}^{\infty }\left( {X \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack  , F}\right) \) such that if \( {f}^{ * } \) is the extension of \( {f}_{0} \) then \( {f}^{ * } = {f}_{0} \) at \( t = 0 \) and \( {\begin{Vmatrix}{f}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}_{2} \leq  C{\left| {f}_{0}\right| }_{1} \) . Now given \( f \) satisfying \( \partial f/\partial t - {Pf} = h \) and \( f = {f}_{0} \) at \( t = 0 \) , let \( {f}^{ * } \) be the extension of \( {f}_{0} \) constructed above and let \( \partial {f}^{ * }/\partial t - P{f}^{ * } = {h}^{ * } \) . If \( f = {f}^{ * } + \widetilde{f} \) and \( h = {h}^{ * } + \widetilde{h} \) then \( \partial \widetilde{f}/\partial t - P\widetilde{f} = \widetilde{h} \) , and \( \widetilde{f} = 0 \) at \( t = 0 \) . We can then estimate \( \widetilde{f} \) using the previous lemma, so

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {f}_{t}\right| }_{0}^{2}{dt} \leq  {\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {f}_{t}^{ * }\right| }_{0}^{2}{dt} + {\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {\widetilde{f}}_{t}\right| }_{0}^{2}{dt}
\]

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {f}_{t}^{ * }\right| }_{0}^{2}{dt} \leq  {\int }_{0}^{T}{\left| {f}_{t}^{ * }\right| }_{0}^{2}{dt} \leq  C{\begin{Vmatrix}{f}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}_{2}^{2} \leq  C{\left| {f}_{0}\right| }_{1}^{2},
\]

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {\widetilde{f}}_{t}\right| }_{0}^{2}{dt} \leq  C{\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {\widetilde{h}}_{t}\right| }_{0}^{2}{dt}
\]

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {\widetilde{h}}_{t}\right| }_{0}^{2}{dt} \leq  {\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {h}_{t}\right| }_{0}^{2}{dt} + {\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {h}_{t}^{ * }\right| }_{0}^{2}{dt}
\]

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {h}_{t}^{ * }\right| }_{0}^{2}{dt} \leq  {\int }_{0}^{T}{\left| {h}_{t}^{ * }\right| }_{0}^{2}{dt} \leq  C{\begin{Vmatrix}{h}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}_{0}^{2} \leq  C{\begin{Vmatrix}{f}^{ * }\end{Vmatrix}}_{2}^{2} \leq  C{\left| {f}_{0}\right| }_{1}^{2}.
\]

Combining these estimates the result follows.

6.5 Lemma. If \( \partial g/\partial t = k \) , then for \( 0 \leq  \theta  \leq  T \)

\[
{\left| {g}_{\theta }\right| }_{1}^{2} \leq  C{\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {k}_{t}\right| }_{1}^{2}{dt} + C{\left| {g}_{0}\right| }_{1}^{2}.
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: 6.5 Lemma. If \( \partial g/\partial t = k \) , then for \( 0 \leq \theta \leq T \) \[ {\left| {g}_{\theta }\right| }_{1}^{2} \leq C{\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {k}_{t}\right| }_{1}^{2}{dt} + C{\left| {g}_{0}\right| }_{1}^{2}. \]

nodes.proof:
Since

\[
{g}_{\theta } = {g}_{0} + {\int }_{0}^{\theta }{k}_{t}{dt}
\]

and every norm is convex, we have

\[
{\left| {g}_{\theta }\right| }_{1} \leq  {\left| {g}_{0}\right| }_{1} + {\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {k}_{t}\right| }_{1}{dt}
\]

But we also have

\[
{\left( {\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {k}_{t}\right| }_{1}dt\right) }^{2} \leq  \theta {\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {k}_{t}\right| }_{1}^{2}{dt}
\]

Therefore the above estimate holds with a constant \( C \) independent of \( \theta \) for \( 0 \leq  \theta  \leq  T \) .

Note that if there is a delay \( \delta \) in time, so that \( {\left( \partial g/\partial t\right) }_{t + \delta } = {k}_{t} \) , and if \( g \) and \( k \) vanish for \( t \leq  0 \) , then \( g \) also vanishes for \( t \leq  \delta \) , and we have a better estimate

\[
{\left| {g}_{\theta  + \delta }\right| }_{1}^{2} \leq  C{\int }_{t = 0}^{\theta }{\left| {k}_{t}\right| }_{1}^{2}{dt}
\]

for \( 0 \leq  \theta  \leq  T - \delta \) .

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {f}_{t}\right| }_{2}^{2}{dt} \leq  C{\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {g}_{t}\right| }_{1}^{2}{dt} + C{E}^{2}

\]

\]

nodes.content:
6.7 Corollary. A solution of the system of evolution equations satisfies the a priori estimate

\[
{\left| f\right| }_{2} + {\left| g\right| }_{1} \leq  C\left( {{\left| h\right| }_{0} + {\left| k\right| }_{1} + {\left| {f}_{0}\right| }_{1} + {\left| {g}_{0}\right| }_{1}}\right) .
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: 6.7 Corollary. A solution of the system of evolution equations satisfies the a priori estimate \[ {\left| f\right| }_{2} + {\left| g\right| }_{1} \leq C\left( {{\left| h\right| }_{0} + {\left| k\right| }_{1} + {\left| {f}_{0}\right| }_{1} + {\left| {g}_{0}\right| }_{1}}\right) . \]

nodes.proof:
By the above estimates we have

\[
{\left| {g}_{\theta }\right| }_{1}^{2} \leq  C{\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {g}_{t}\right| }_{1}^{2}{dt} + C{E}^{2}.
\]

Then for any \( \lambda  > 0 \) we have

\[
\lambda {\int }_{\theta  = 0}^{T}{e}^{-{\lambda \theta }}{\left| {g}_{\theta }\right| }_{1}^{2}{d\theta } \leq  C{\int }_{t = 0}^{T}\left\{  {{\int }_{\theta  = t}^{T}\lambda {e}^{\lambda \left( {t - \theta }\right) }{d\theta }}\right\}  {e}^{-{\lambda t}}{\left| {g}_{t}\right| }_{1}^{2}{dt}
\]

\[
+ C\left\{  {{\int }_{\theta  = 0}^{T}\lambda {e}^{-{\lambda \theta }}{d\theta }}\right\}  {E}^{2},
\]

and since the bracketed integrals are \( \leq  1 \) , we have

\[
\left( {\lambda  - C}\right) {\int }_{t = 0}^{T}{e}^{-{\lambda t}}{\left| {g}_{t}\right| }_{1}^{2}{dt} \leq  C{E}^{2}
\]

with a constant \( C \) independent of \( \lambda \) . When \( \lambda  > C \) we get \( {\left| g\right| }_{1}^{2} \leq  C{E}^{2} \) . Then \( {\left| f\right| }_{2}^{2} \leq  C{E}^{2} \) also.

Note that if there is a time delay \( \delta \) , so that

\[
{\left( \partial g/\partial t\right) }_{t + \delta } = {\left( Mf + Ng + h\right) }_{t},
\]

then we get a better estimate

\[
{\left| {g}_{\theta  + \delta }\right| }_{1}^{2} \leq  C{\int }_{0}^{\theta }{\left| {g}_{t}\right| }_{1}^{2}{dt} + C{E}^{2},
\]

and since

\[
{\int }_{\theta  = 0}^{T - \delta }{e}^{-{\lambda \theta }}{\left| {g}_{\theta  + \delta }^{2}\right| }_{1}{d\theta } = {e}^{\lambda \delta }{\int }_{\theta  = 0}^{T}{e}^{-{\lambda \theta }}{\left| {g}_{\theta }\right| }_{1}^{2}{d\theta },
\]

the same argument yields the same estimate with a constant independent of \( \delta \) as \( \delta  \rightarrow  0 \) .

nodes.content:
6.8 Lemma. If \( \delta  > 0 \) is small enough then for all systems \( P, L, M, N \) in the given neighborhood the a priori estimate

\[
{\left| f\right| }_{2} + {\left| g\right| }_{1} \leq  C\left( {{\left| h\right| }_{0} + {\left| k\right| }_{0} + {\left| {f}_{0}\right| }_{1} + {\left| {g}_{0}\right| }_{1}}\right)
\]

holds with a fixed constant \( C \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 6.8 Lemma. If \( \delta > 0 \) is small enough then for all systems \( P, L, M, N \) in the given neighborhood the a priori estimate \[ {\left| f\right| }_{2} + {\left| g\right| }_{1} \leq C\left( {{\left| h\right| }_{0} + {\left| k\right| }_{0} + {\left| {f}_{0}\right| }_{1} + {\left| {g}_{0}\right| }_{1}}\right) \] holds with a fixed constant \( C \) .

nodes.proof:
If \( f \) and \( g \) solve the system of evolution equations for \( P, L, M, N \) , then

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = \bar{P}f + \bar{L}g + \left( {P - \bar{P}}\right) f + \left( {L - \bar{L}}\right) g + h,
\]

\[
\frac{\partial g}{\partial t} = \bar{M}f + \bar{N}g + \left( {M - \bar{M}}\right) f + \left( {N - \bar{N}}\right) g + k.
\]

Applying the estimate for the fixed system \( \bar{P},\bar{L},\bar{M},\bar{N} \) we get

\[
{\left| f\right| }_{2} + {\left| g\right| }_{1} \leq  C\left( {\left| \left( P - \bar{P}\right) f + \left( L - \bar{L}\right) g + h\right| }_{0}\right.
\]

\[
+ {\left| \left( M - \bar{M}\right) f + \left( N - \bar{N}\right) g + k\right| }_{1} + {\left| {f}_{0}\right| }_{1} + {\left| {g}_{0}\right| }_{1},
\]

\[
{\left| f\right| }_{2} + {\left| g\right| }_{1} \leq  {C\delta }\left( {{\left| f\right| }_{2} + {\left| g\right| }_{1}}\right)  + C\left( {{\left| h\right| }_{0} + {\left| k\right| }_{1} + {\left| {f}_{0}\right| }_{1} + {\left| {g}_{0}\right| }_{1}}\right) .
\]

When \( \delta  > 0 \) is sufficiently small, the estimate follows.

We can now estimate higher space derivatives in the usual way by differentiating through the equation. Choose connections in the vector bundles \( F \) and \( G \) and let \( {\partial }_{v}f \) denote the covariant derivative of the section \( f \) in the direction of a vector field \( v \) . There is then a natural way to define the covariant derivative of the linear differential operators so that (for example)

\[
{\partial }_{v}\left( {Lf}\right)  = L\left( {{\partial }_{v}f}\right)  + \left( {{\partial }_{v}L}\right) f.
\]

Note that \( {\partial }_{v}L \) will be a differential operator of the same degree as \( L \) , formed by allowing the derivatives to fall on the coefficients. We will let \( {\sum }_{v} \) denote the sum over a finite number of vector fields which span the tangent space at each point of \( X \) .
