nodes.proof:
Given any point \( y \in  \mathcal{U} \) , let \( \Omega  \subset  \mathcal{U} \) be a connected open set such that \( \bar{\Omega } \) is a compact manifold with smooth boundary and \( \Omega \) contains both \( {x}_{0} \) and \( y \) . Let \( {\varphi }_{1} : \bar{\Omega } \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) be a smooth nonnegative function satisfying

\[
{\varphi }_{1}\left( x\right)  \leq  {\lambda }_{1}\left( u\right) \left( {x,0}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  \bar{\Omega },{\varphi }_{1}\left( {x}_{0}\right)  \geq  \frac{1}{2}{\lambda }_{1}\left( u\right) \left( {{x}_{0},0}\right) \) , and \( {\varphi }_{1} = 0 \) on \( \partial \Omega \) . It is easy to see that such a function \( {\varphi }_{1} \) exists. Given \( A > 0 \) large to be chosen later, there exists a solution \( f : \bar{\Omega } \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) to the following initial-boundary value problem of a linear heat-type equation on \( \bar{\Omega } \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) (this may be proved by adapting §7.1 of [185] to the manifold setting):

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = {\Delta }_{g\left( t\right) }f + X\left( t\right) f - {Af}
\]

\[
{\left. f\right| }_{\partial \Omega  \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack  } = 0\;\text{ and }\;f\left( {x,0}\right)  = {\varphi }_{1}\left( x\right) .
\]

Note that \( u\left( {{x}_{0},0}\right)  > 0 \) implies \( {\varphi }_{1}\left( {x}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) . By the strong maximum principle for scalars (applying Theorem 12.40 to \( - f \) ), we have \( f > 0 \) on \( \Omega  \times  (0, T\rbrack \) . Also, by the weak maximum principle (Theorem 10.2), we have

\[
f\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \mathop{\max }\limits_{\bar{\Omega }}{\varphi }_{1}\left( \cdot \right)  \leq  \mathop{\max }\limits_{\bar{\Omega }}{\lambda }_{1}\left( u\right) \left( {\cdot ,0}\right) \text{ on }\Omega  \times  (0, T\rbrack .
\]

Define the section \( \widetilde{h} \) of \( \mathcal{V} = \operatorname{Hom}\left( {\mathcal{W},\mathcal{W}}\right) \) by

\[
\widetilde{h}\left( W\right)  \Doteq  W
\]

as in (12.41) and define

(12.59)

\[
\widetilde{u}\left( {x, t}\right)  \Doteq  u\left( {x, t}\right)  + \left( {\varepsilon {e}^{At} - f\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \widetilde{h}\left( x\right) ,
\]

where \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) . We claim that for \( \varepsilon \) sufficiently small, \( \widetilde{u} \geq  0 \) on \( \bar{\Omega } \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . The proposition will follow from the claim easily. Taking the limit as \( \varepsilon  \rightarrow  0 \) , we obtain \( u \geq  f\widetilde{h} \) in \( \bar{\Omega } \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) ; in particular, \( u\left( {y, t}\right)  > 0 \) for any \( t > 0 \) since \( y \in  \Omega \) and \( f\left( {y, t}\right)  > 0 \) . Since \( y \in  \mathcal{U} \) is arbitrary, the proposition is proved assuming the claim.

To prove the claim, we compute, using \( \nabla \left( t\right) \widetilde{h} = 0 \) and \( \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\widetilde{h} = 0 \) ,

\[
\frac{\partial \widetilde{u}}{\partial t} \geq  \Delta \widetilde{u} + {\nabla }_{X\left( t\right) }\widetilde{u} + \beta \left( {\widetilde{u}, t}\right)  - \left\lbrack  {\beta \left( {\widetilde{u}, t}\right)  - \beta \left( {u, t}\right) }\right\rbrack   + A\left( {\varepsilon {e}^{At} + f}\right) \widetilde{h}.
\]

Since \( \bar{\Omega } \) is compact, we have \( u \geq  0 \) is uniformly bounded above on \( \bar{\Omega } \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , say by \( {L}_{0}\widetilde{h} \) . Notice that when \( \varepsilon {e}^{AT} \leq  1 \) , we have

\[
- \mathop{\max }\limits_{\bar{\Omega }}{\lambda }_{1}\left( u\right) \left( {\cdot ,0}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{u} \leq  \left( {{L}_{0} + 1}\right) \widetilde{h}
\]

on \( \bar{\Omega } \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . Hence by the locally Lipschitz property of \( \beta \) there exists a constant \( {K}_{0} = K\left( {L}_{0}\right) \) such that \( \left| {\beta \left( {\widetilde{u}, t}\right)  - \beta \left( {u, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {K}_{0}\left| {\varepsilon {e}^{At} - f}\right| \) ; in particular

(12.60)

\[
\beta \left( {\widetilde{u}, t}\right)  - \beta \left( {u, t}\right)  \leq  {K}_{0}\left| {\varepsilon {e}^{At} - f}\right| \widetilde{h}.
\]

Therefore

(12.61)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\widetilde{u} \geq  \Delta \widetilde{u} + {\nabla }_{X\left( t\right) }\widetilde{u} + \beta \left( {\widetilde{u}, t}\right)  + \left( {A - {K}_{0}}\right) \left( {\varepsilon {e}^{At} + f}\right) \widetilde{h}.
\]

Now we first choose \( A \) such that \( A > {K}_{0} \) and then choose \( \varepsilon \) such that \( \varepsilon  \leq  {e}^{-{AT}} \) . We have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\widetilde{u} \geq  \Delta \widetilde{u} + {\nabla }_{X\left( t\right) }\widetilde{u} + \beta \left( {\widetilde{u}, t}\right) .
\]

Since \( u \geq  {\lambda }_{1}\left( u\right) \widetilde{h} \) on \( \Omega  \times  (0, T\rbrack \) , we have \( \widetilde{u} \geq  \varepsilon {e}^{At}\widetilde{h} > 0 \) on \( \left( {\partial \Omega \times \lbrack 0, T}\right) ) \cup \; \left( {\Omega \times \{ 0\} }\right) \) . By adapting Theorem 10.7 to compact manifolds with boundary, it is easy to see that applying the maximum principle for 2-tensors to \( \widetilde{u} \) , while using the above boundary property of \( \widetilde{u} \) , yields

\[
\widetilde{u} \geq  0\;\text{ for all }\varepsilon  \in  \left( {0,{e}^{-{AT}}}\right\rbrack
\]

The claim is proved and so is the proposition.

nodes.proof:
Proof. Given any point \( y \in  \mathcal{U} \) , let \( \Omega  \subset  \mathcal{U} \) be a connected open set such that \( \bar{\Omega } \) is a compact manifold with smooth boundary and \( \Omega \) contains both \( {x}_{0} \) and \( y \) . Let \( {\varphi }_{k} : \bar{\Omega } \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) be a smooth nonnegative function satisfying

\[
k{\varphi }_{k}\left( x\right)  \leq  {\phi }_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  \bar{\Omega }, k{\varphi }_{k}\left( {x}_{0}\right)  \geq  \frac{1}{2}{\phi }_{k}\left( {{x}_{0},0}\right) \) , and \( {\varphi }_{k} = 0 \) on \( \partial \Omega \) . It is easy to see that such a function \( {\varphi }_{k} \) exists. For some constant \( A > 0 \) to be determined later, let \( f : \bar{\Omega } \times  \lbrack 0, T) \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) be the solution to the following initial-boundary value problem on \( \bar{\Omega } \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) (the existence of the solution follows from the same reason given in the proof of Proposition 12.47):

(12.62)

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = {\Delta f} + {Xf} - {Af}
\]

\[
{\left. f\right| }_{\partial \Omega  \times  \lbrack 0, T)} = 0\;\text{ and }\;f\left( {x,0}\right)  = {\varphi }_{k}\left( x\right) .
\]

Note that \( {\phi }_{k}\left( {{x}_{0},0}\right)  > 0 \) implies \( {\varphi }_{k}\left( {x}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) . By the strong maximum principle for scalars (applying Theorem 12.40 to \( - f \) ), we have \( f > 0 \) on \( \Omega  \times  (0, T\rbrack \) . Also, by the weak maximum principle (Theorem 10.2), we have

\[
f\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \mathop{\max }\limits_{\bar{\Omega }}{\varphi }_{k}\left( \cdot \right)  \leq  \frac{1}{k}\mathop{\max }\limits_{\bar{\Omega }}{\phi }_{k}\left( {x,0}\right) \text{ on }\Omega  \times  (0, T\rbrack .
\]

Let \( \widetilde{h} \) be the section of \( \mathcal{V} = \operatorname{Hom}\left( {\mathcal{W},\mathcal{W}}\right) \) as in (12.41). Define

(12.63)

\[
\bar{u}\left( {x, t}\right)  \Doteq  u\left( {x, t}\right)  + \left( {\varepsilon {e}^{At} - f\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \widetilde{h}\left( x\right)
\]

and

\[
{\bar{\phi }}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \Doteq  \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{\left\{  {{e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{k}}\right\}  \text{ orthonormal }}}\left( {\bar{u}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{1}}\right)  + \cdots  + \bar{u}\left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{k}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= {\phi }_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  + k\left( {\varepsilon {e}^{At} - f\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) ,
\]

where \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) . We claim that for \( \varepsilon \) sufficiently small, \( {\bar{\phi }}_{k} > 0 \) on \( \bar{\Omega } \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . The proposition will follow from the claim easily. Taking the limit as \( \varepsilon  \rightarrow  0 \) , we obtain \( {\phi }_{k} \geq  {kf} \) in \( \bar{\Omega } \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) ; in particular, \( {\phi }_{k}\left( {y, t}\right)  > 0 \) for any \( t > 0 \) since \( y \in  \Omega \) and \( f\left( {y, t}\right)  > 0 \) . Since \( y \in  \mathcal{U} \) is arbitrary, the proposition is proved assuming the claim.

We now prove the claim by contradiction. If the claim is false, since by the definition of \( f\left( {x, t}\right) \) we have \( {\bar{\phi }}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  > 0 \) in \( \Omega \) and \( {\left. {\bar{\phi }}_{k}\left( x, t\right) \right| }_{\partial \Omega  \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack  } > 0 \) , there exists \( \left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  \in  \Omega  \times  (0, T\rbrack \) such that \( {\bar{\phi }}_{k}\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  = 0 \) and \( {\bar{\phi }}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  > 0 \) for all \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  \Omega  \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{1}}\right) \) . Let \( \left\{  {{E}_{1}^{0},\ldots ,{E}_{k}^{0}}\right\}   \in  {\mathcal{W}}_{{x}_{1}} \) be orthonormal vectors such that

\[
\bar{u}\left( {{E}_{1}^{0},{E}_{1}^{0}}\right)  + \cdots  + \bar{u}\left( {{E}_{k}^{0},{E}_{k}^{0}}\right)  = 0
\]

at \( \left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right) \) . As in Section 2 of Chapter 10, we extend each \( {E}_{i}^{0} \) in space and time to a local vector field \( {E}_{i} \) by parallel translating \( {E}_{i}^{0} \) along geodesics emanating from \( {x}_{1} \) (with respect to \( \nabla \left( {t}_{1}\right) \) ) and taking \( {E}_{i} \) to be constant in time. Then \( \nabla {E}_{i}\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  = 0,\Delta {E}_{i}\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  = 0 \) , and \( \frac{\partial {E}_{i}}{\partial t}\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  = 0 \) . Define

\[
{\psi }_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \Doteq  \bar{u}\left( {x, t}\right) \left( {{E}_{1},{E}_{1}}\right)  + \cdots  + \bar{u}\left( {x, t}\right) \left( {{E}_{k},{E}_{k}}\right)
\]

in a neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right) \) . We have \( {\psi }_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  {\bar{\phi }}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  0 \) for \( t \leq  {t}_{1} \) and \( {\psi }_{k}\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  = 0 \) . Hence by the second derivative test we have at \( \left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right) \)

\[
\frac{\partial {\psi }_{k}}{\partial t} \leq  0,\;\nabla {\psi }_{k} = 0,\;\text{ and }\;\Delta {\psi }_{k} \geq  0.
\]

Using (12.58),(12.62), and the properties of \( {E}_{i} \) and \( \widetilde{h} \) , we compute at \( \left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right) \)

\[
0 \geq  \frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\psi }_{k} - \Delta {\psi }_{k} - {\nabla }_{X\left( t\right) }{\psi }_{k}
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\left( {\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta  - {\nabla }_{X\left( t\right) }}\right) \bar{u}}\right) \left( {{E}_{i}^{0},{E}_{i}^{0}}\right)
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\beta \left( {\bar{u}, t}\right) \left( {{E}_{i}^{0},{E}_{i}^{0}}\right)  + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\left( {\beta \left( {u, t}\right)  - \beta \left( {\bar{u}, t}\right) }\right) \left( {{E}_{i}^{0},{E}_{i}^{0}}\right)
\]

\[
+ {Ak}\left( {\varepsilon {e}^{At} + f}\right) \text{ . }
\]

Since \( \beta \) satisfies the null-eigenvector assumption, \( \beta \left( {\bar{u}, t}\right) \left( {{E}_{i}^{0},{E}_{i}^{0}}\right)  \geq  0 \) . Hence we have

(12.64)

\[
0 \geq  \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\left( {\beta \left( {u, t}\right)  - \beta \left( {\bar{u}, t}\right) }\right) \left( {{E}_{i}^{0},{E}_{i}^{0}}\right)  + {Ak}\left( {\varepsilon {e}^{At} + f}\right) .
\]

Since \( \bar{\Omega } \) is compact, there exists \( {L}_{1} < \infty \) such that \( \left| u\right|  \leq  {L}_{1} \) and \( \left| f\right|  \leq  {L}_{1} \) on \( \bar{\Omega } \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . When \( \varepsilon {e}^{AT} \leq  1 \) , we have from (12.63) that \( \left| \bar{u}\right|  \leq  {L}_{1} + \operatorname{rank}\mathcal{W} \) . Hence, by the locally Lipschitz assumption on \( \beta \) , there is a constant \( {K}_{1} = \; {K}_{1}\left( {{L}_{1},\operatorname{rank}\mathcal{W}}\right) \) such that

\[
\beta \left( {u, t}\right)  - \beta \left( {\bar{u}, t}\right)  \geq   - {K}_{1}\left| {\varepsilon {e}^{At} - f}\right| \widetilde{h}\left( x\right) .
\]

Applying this to (12.64), we have

\[
0 \geq  \left( {A - {K}_{1}}\right) k\left( {{e}^{At} + f}\right) .
\]

We obtain a contradiction by first choosing \( A > {K}_{1} \) and then choosing \( \varepsilon  \in  \left( {0,{e}^{-{AT}}}\right\rbrack \) . The claim is proved and the proposition follows.

nodes.content:
THEOREM 12.50. Under the assumptions we made before Proposition 12.47, let \( u : \mathcal{U} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathcal{V} = \mathcal{W}{ \otimes  }_{S}\mathcal{W} \) be a \( {C}^{2,1} \) -solution to (12.58), where \( \beta \) satisfies the null-eigenvector assumption (10.15). Suppose \( u \geq  0 \) on \( \mathcal{U} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) .

(i) If \( {t}_{2} > {t}_{1} \) in \( \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , then

(12.65)

\[
\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{x \in  \mathcal{U}}}\operatorname{rank}\left( {u\left( {x,{t}_{2}}\right) }\right)  \geq  \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  \mathcal{U}}}\operatorname{rank}\left( {u\left( {x,{t}_{1}}\right) }\right) .
\]

Hence there exists \( \delta  > 0 \) such that

(12.66)

\[
\operatorname{rank}\left( {u\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \text{ is constant for all }x \in  \mathcal{U}\text{ and }t \in  \left( {0,\delta }\right) \text{ . }
\]

(ii) (Null space depends smoothly on space and time) Let \( \left( {0,\delta }\right) \) be the time interval in part (i). Then for every \( t \in  \left( {0,\delta }\right) \) , null \( \left( {u\left( t\right) }\right)  \subset  \mathcal{W} \) is a smooth subbundle. Moreover, null \( \left( {u\left( t\right) }\right) \) depends smoothly on time.

(iii) (Null space is parallel in space and time) Let \( \left( {0,\delta }\right) \) be the time interval in part (i). Then for \( t \in  \left( {0,\delta }\right) \) , null \( \left( {u\left( t\right) }\right) \) is invariant under parallel translation in space and constant in time. Moreover,

\[
\operatorname{null}\left( {u\left( t\right) }\right)  \subset  \operatorname{null}\left( {\beta \left( {u\left( t\right) , t}\right) }\right) \;\text{ for all }t \in  \left( {0,\delta }\right) .
\]

In particular, we have the time-independent inclusion

\[
\operatorname{null}\left( {u\left( t\right) }\right)  \subset  \bigcap {}_{s \in  \left( {0,\delta }\right) }\operatorname{null}\left( {\beta \left( {u\left( s\right) , s}\right) }\right)
\]

for all \( t \in  \left( {0,\delta }\right) \) .

Proof. (i) Let \( \ell  \doteq  \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  \mathcal{M}}}\operatorname{rank}\left( {u\left( {x,{t}_{1}}\right) }\right) \) . Then there exists \( {x}_{1} \in  \mathcal{U} \) such that \( \operatorname{rank}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right) }\right)  = \ell \) . This implies

\[
{\phi }_{m}\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  > 0,
\]

where \( m \doteq  \operatorname{rank}\left( \mathcal{W}\right)  - \ell  + 1 \) . Since \( {t}_{2} > {t}_{1} \) , by Proposition 12.49 we have \( {\phi }_{m}\left( {x,{t}_{2}}\right)  > 0 \) for all \( x \in  \mathcal{U} \) . Hence

\[
\operatorname{rank}\left( {u\left( {x,{t}_{2}}\right) }\right)  \geq  \operatorname{rank}\left( \mathcal{W}\right)  - m + 1 = \ell
\]

for all \( x \in  \mathcal{U} \) . This proves (12.65).

By (12.65) we have that \( \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{x \in  \mathcal{U}}}\operatorname{rank}\left( {u\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) is a nondecreasing function of \( t \) . Therefore, since it is integer-valued, it is constant on some short time interval \( \left( {0,\delta }\right) \) . However, applying (12.65) again implies

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  \mathcal{U}}}\operatorname{rank}\left( {u\left( {x, t}\right) }\right)  = \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{x \in  \mathcal{U}}}\operatorname{rank}\left( {u\left( {x, t}\right) }\right)
\]

on this time interval and hence \( \operatorname{rank}\left( {u\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) is constant on \( \mathcal{U} \times  \left( {0,\delta }\right) \) .

(ii) Define \( p \Doteq  \dim \left( {\operatorname{null}\left( {u\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) }\right) \) , which is constant on \( \mathcal{U} \times  \left( {0,\delta }\right) \) by part (i). For each \( x \in  \mathcal{U} \) , let \( {G}_{r - p, r}\left( x\right) \) denote the Grassmannian of \( \left( {r - p}\right) \) - dimensional subspaces of \( {\mathcal{W}}_{x} \) , where \( r \Doteq  \operatorname{rank}\left( \mathcal{W}\right) \) . Define

\[
\Phi \left( {x, t}\right)  \Doteq  \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\Pi  \in  {G}_{r - p, r}\left( x\right) }}\left( {\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{W \in  \Pi -\{ 0\} }}\frac{u\left( {W, W}\right) }{{\left| W\right| }^{2}}}\right)  = {\lambda }_{p + 1}\left( {u\left( {x, t}\right) }\right)  \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) ,
\]

where \( {\lambda }_{1} \leq  \cdots  \leq  {\lambda }_{r} \) are the ordered eigenvalues. For each \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  \mathcal{U} \times  \left( {0,\delta }\right) \) , the span \( \Pi \left( {x, t}\right) \) of the eigenspaces corresponding to the nonzero eigenvalues of \( u\left( {x, t}\right) \) is the unique element \( \Pi \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {G}_{r - p, r}\left( x\right) \) such that

\[
\Phi \left( {x, t}\right)  = \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{W \in  \Pi \left( {x, t}\right) -\{ 0\} }}\frac{u\left( {W, W}\right) }{{\left| W\right| }^{2}}.
\]

Since each point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \in  \mathcal{U} \times  \left( {0,\delta }\right) \) is contained in a space-time neighborhood \( \mathcal{N} \) such that \( \Phi \left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  c \) for some constant \( c > 0 \) , we have \( \Pi \left( {x, t}\right) \) depends smoothly on space and time in \( \mathcal{U} \times  \left( {0,\delta }\right)  \cdot  {}^{26} \)

(iii) Let \( W\left( {x, t}\right) \) be a smooth local section of the subbundle null \( \left( {u\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) defined on a space-time neighborhood in \( \mathcal{U} \times  \left( {0,\delta }\right) \) ; that is, \( u\left( {W, Y}\right) \left( {x, t}\right)  \equiv  0 \) for all local tangent vector fields \( Y \) . We have

---

\( {}^{26} \) In general, if \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \in  \mathcal{U} \times  \left( {0,\delta }\right) \) and \( \mu  \in  \mathbb{R} \) is not an eigenvalue of \( u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) , then the subbundles \( \left\{  {W \in  \mathcal{W} : u\left( {W, W}\right)  > \mu {\left| W\right| }^{2}}\right\} \) and \( \left\{  {W \in  \mathcal{W} : u\left( {W, W}\right)  < \mu {\left| W\right| }^{2}}\right\} \) depend smoothly on space and time in a neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) .

(12.67)

\[
0 = \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {u\left( {W, W}\right) }\right)  = \frac{\partial u}{\partial t}\left( {W, W}\right)  + {2u}\left( {\frac{\partial W}{\partial t}, W}\right)
\]

\[
= \left( {{\Delta u} + {\nabla }_{X\left( t\right) }u + \beta \left( {u, t}\right) }\right) \left( {W, W}\right)
\]

\[
= \Delta \left( {u\left( {W, W}\right) }\right)  - {2u}\left( {{\Delta W}, W}\right)  - 2{g}^{ij}u\left( {{\nabla }_{i}W,{\nabla }_{j}W}\right)
\]

\[
- 4{g}^{ij}\left( {{\nabla }_{i}u}\right) \left( {{\nabla }_{j}W, W}\right)  + \left( {{\nabla }_{X\left( t\right) }u}\right) \left( {W, W}\right)  + \beta \left( {u, t}\right) \left( {W, W}\right)
\]

\[
=  - 2{g}^{ij}u\left( {{\nabla }_{i}W,{\nabla }_{j}W}\right)  - 4{g}^{ij}\left( {{\nabla }_{i}u}\right) \left( {{\nabla }_{j}W, W}\right)  + \left( {{\nabla }_{X\left( t\right) }u}\right) \left( {W, W}\right)
\]

\[
+ \beta \left( {u, t}\right) \left( {W, W}\right) .
\]

Now \( {}^{27} \)

\[
0 = \nabla \left( {u\left( W\right) }\right)  = \left( {\nabla u}\right) \left( W\right)  + u\left( {\nabla W}\right) ,
\]

which implies

\[
0 = {g}^{ij}\left( {{\nabla }_{i}u}\right) \left( {{\nabla }_{j}W, W}\right)  + {g}^{ij}u\left( {{\nabla }_{i}W,{\nabla }_{j}W}\right)
\]

and

\[
0 = \left( {{\nabla }_{X\left( t\right) }u}\right) \left( {W, W}\right)  + u\left( {{\nabla }_{X\left( t\right) }W, W}\right)  = \left( {{\nabla }_{X\left( t\right) }u}\right) \left( {W, W}\right) .
\]

Plugging these two equations into (12.67), we obtain

\[
2{g}^{ij}u\left( {{\nabla }_{i}W,{\nabla }_{j}W}\right)  + \beta \left( {u, t}\right) \left( {W, W}\right)  = 0.
\]

Since both terms in the above equation are nonnegative, we conclude that \( \beta \left( {u, t}\right) \left( {W, W}\right)  = 0 \) and \( {g}^{ij}u\left( {{\nabla }_{i}W,{\nabla }_{j}W}\right)  = 0 \) . Therefore

\[
\operatorname{null}\left( {u\left( t\right) }\right)  \subset  \operatorname{null}\left( {\beta \left( {u, t}\right) }\right)
\]

and \( u\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}W,{\nabla }_{Y}W}\right)  = 0 \) for all \( Y \) , that is,

\[
{\nabla }_{Y}W\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  \operatorname{null}\left( {u\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \text{ for all }Y.
\]

Next we prove that null \( \left( {u\left( t\right) }\right) \) is invariant under parallel translation in space using the above infinitesimal invariance. Let \( p \Doteq  \dim \operatorname{null}\left( {u\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Given \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) , let \( {\left\{  {W}_{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{p} \) be a basis of smooth sections of \( \operatorname{null}\left( {u\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) defined in a (spatial) neighborhood of \( {x}_{0} \) in \( \mathcal{U} \) and let \( \gamma  : \lbrack 0,\varepsilon ) \rightarrow  \mathcal{U} \) be a path emanating from \( {x}_{0} \) . Since \( {\nabla }_{\dot{\gamma }}{W}_{i} \in  \operatorname{null}\left( {u\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) along \( \gamma \) , we have

\[
{\nabla }_{\dot{\gamma }}{W}_{i} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{p}{A}_{i}^{j}{W}_{j}
\]

where \( {A}_{i}^{j} \) are functions along \( \gamma \) . Given any vector \( {V}_{0} \in  \operatorname{null}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) , we shall show that the parallel section \( V\left( s\right) \) along \( \gamma \) , with respect to \( g\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) and with \( V\left( 0\right)  = {V}_{0} \) , satisfies

\[
V\left( s\right)  \in  \operatorname{null}\left( {u\left( {\gamma \left( s\right) , t}\right) }\right) ;
\]

---

\( {}^{27} \) We also consider \( u \) as a map \( u : \mathcal{W} \rightarrow  \mathcal{W} \) by using the metric on \( \mathcal{W} \) to identify \( \mathcal{W} \) with \( {\mathcal{W}}^{ * } \) . Note that \( u\left( {\nabla W}\right) \left( Y\right)  \Doteq  u\left( {{\nabla }_{Y}W}\right) \) is a local section of \( \mathcal{W} \) .

---

this will imply the invariance of null \( \left( {u\left( t\right) }\right) \) under parallel translation in space. Let \( {V}_{0} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{p}{f}_{0}^{i}{W}_{i}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Note that the equation

\[
0 = {\nabla }_{\dot{\gamma }}\left( {{f}^{i}{W}_{i}}\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{p}\left( {\frac{d{f}^{i}}{ds}{W}_{i} + {f}^{i}{\nabla }_{\dot{\gamma }}{W}_{i}}\right) ,\;{f}^{i}\left( 0\right)  = {f}_{0}^{i},
\]

is equivalent to the following system of linear ordinary differential equations for \( {f}^{j}\left( s\right) \) :

\[
\frac{d{f}^{j}}{ds} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{p}{f}^{i}{A}_{i}^{j} = 0,\;{f}^{i}\left( 0\right)  = {f}_{0}^{i},
\]

which has a solution. By the uniqueness of parallel translation we have

\[
V\left( s\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{p}{f}^{i}\left( s\right) {W}_{i}\left( {\gamma \left( s\right) , t}\right)  \in  \operatorname{null}\left( {u\left( {\gamma \left( s\right) , t}\right) }\right) .
\]

Finally we prove that null \( \left( {u\left( t\right) }\right) \) is constant in time. Let \( W\left( {x, t}\right) \) be a smooth local section of null \( \left( {u\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) defined in a space-time neighborhood in \( \mathcal{U} \times  \left( {0,\delta }\right) \) . We claim that \( W\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  \operatorname{null}\left( {{\Delta u}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) . Assuming this, since \( W \in  \operatorname{null}\left( {\beta \left( {u, t}\right) }\right) \) and

\[
\left( {{\nabla }_{X\left( t\right) }u}\right) \left( W\right)  = {\nabla }_{X\left( t\right) }\left( {u\left( W\right) }\right)  - u\left( {{\nabla }_{X\left( t\right) }W}\right)  = 0,
\]

we have

\[
0 = \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {u\left( W\right) }\right)  = \left( {{\Delta u} + {\nabla }_{X\left( t\right) }u + \beta \left( {u, t}\right) }\right) \left( W\right)  + u\left( \frac{\partial W}{\partial t}\right)
\]

\[
= u\left( \frac{\partial W}{\partial t}\right) ,
\]

so that \( \frac{\partial W}{\partial t} \in  \operatorname{null}\left( {u\left( t\right) }\right) \) . This implies null \( \left( {u\left( t\right) }\right) \) is constant in time. In particular, given \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \in  \mathcal{U} \times  \left( {0,\delta }\right) \) and \( {V}_{0} \in  \operatorname{null}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) , again we write \( {V}_{0} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{p}{f}_{0}^{i}{W}_{i} \) , where \( {\left\{  {W}_{i}\left( x, t\right) \right\}  }_{i = 1}^{p} \) is a basis of smooth sections of null \( \left( {u\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) defined in a space-time neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Since \( \frac{\partial {W}_{i}}{\partial t} \in \) null \( \left( {u\left( {{x}_{0}, t}\right) }\right) \) for \( t \) near \( {t}_{0} \) , we may write

\[
\frac{\partial {W}_{i}}{\partial t} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{p}{B}_{i}^{j}{W}_{j}
\]

where \( {B}_{i}^{j} \) are functions of \( t \) . We shall show that the constant vector \( {V}_{0} \) is contained in \( \operatorname{null}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0}, t}\right) }\right) \) for \( t \in  \left( {{t}_{0} - \delta ,{t}_{0} + \delta }\right) \) for some \( \delta  > 0 \) . Let

\[
V\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{p}{f}^{i}\left( t\right) {W}_{i}\left( {x, t}\right) ,
\]

where \( {f}^{i}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  = {f}_{0}^{i} \) , and consider the equation

\[
0 = \frac{\partial V}{\partial t} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{p}\left( {\frac{\partial {f}^{j}}{\partial t} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{p}{f}^{i}{B}_{i}^{j}}\right) {W}_{j}.
\]

We may uniquely solve this linear system for \( t \in  \left( {{t}_{0} - \delta ,{t}_{0} + \delta }\right) \) :

\[
\frac{\partial {f}^{j}}{\partial t} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{p}{f}^{i}{B}_{i}^{j} = 0,\;{f}^{i}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  = {f}_{0}^{i}.
\]

Hence we have \( {V}_{0} = V\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{p}{f}^{i}\left( t\right) {W}_{i}\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  \operatorname{null}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0}, t}\right) }\right) \) , so the theorem is proved modulo the claim.

To see the claim \( W\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  \operatorname{null}\left( {{\Delta u}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) , we use the fact that \( \operatorname{null}\left( {u\left( t\right) }\right) \) is invariant under parallel translation, i.e., \( u\left( {{\nabla }_{j}W}\right)  \equiv  0 \) , so that

(12.68)

\[
0 = {g}^{ij}{\nabla }_{i}\left( {u\left( {{\nabla }_{j}W}\right) }\right)  = {g}^{ij}\left( {{\nabla }_{i}u}\right) \left( {{\nabla }_{j}W}\right)  + u\left( {\Delta W}\right) .
\]

Since \( {\nabla }_{Y}W \in  \operatorname{null}\left( u\right) \) for all \( Y \) , by differentiating again, we have \( {\Delta W}\left( {x, t}\right)  \in \) null \( \left( {u\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) , so that from (12.68) we obtain

\[
{g}^{ij}\left( {{\nabla }_{i}u}\right) \left( {{\nabla }_{j}W}\right)  = 0.
\]

Finally we compute

\[
0 = \Delta \left( {u\left( W\right) }\right)  = \left( {\Delta u}\right) \left( W\right)  + u\left( {\Delta W}\right)  + 2{g}^{ij}\left( {{\nabla }_{i}u}\right) \left( {{\nabla }_{j}W}\right)
\]

\[
= \left( {\Delta u}\right) \left( W\right) .
\]

The claim and theorem are now proved.

THEOREM 12.53 (Strong maximum principle for Rm). Let \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}^{n}, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) , \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , be a smooth solution to the Ricci flow with \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {g\left( t\right) }\right)  \geq  0 \) (neither necessarily complete nor necessarily with bounded curvature), where \( \mathcal{M} \) is connected and without boundary.

(i) If \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {{x}_{0},0}\right)  > 0 \) at some point \( {x}_{0} \in  \mathcal{M} \) , then for \( t > 0 \) we have \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right)  > 0 \) for all \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) .

(ii) There exists \( \delta  > 0 \) such that for \( t \in  \left( {0,\delta }\right) \) the set

\[
\text{ image }\left( {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {g\left( t\right) }\right) }\right)  \subset  {\Lambda }^{2}{T}^{ * }\mathcal{M}
\]

is a smooth subbundle which is invariant under parallel translation and constant in time. Moreover, \( \operatorname{image}\left( {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) is a Lie subalgebra of \( {\Lambda }^{2}{T}^{ * }{\mathcal{M}}_{x} \) for all \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) and \( t \in  \left( {0,\delta }\right) \) .

Using Uhlenbeck's trick, we prove the theorem for the pulled-back Riemann curvature tensor \( \mathrm{{Rm}} = {\iota }^{ * }\mathrm{{Rm}} \) , which is a section of \( {\Lambda }^{2}{V}^{ * } \) ; we leave it as an exercise to show that the corresponding statements also hold for Rm, which is a section of \( {\Lambda }^{2}{T}^{ * }\mathcal{M} \) .

(i) Since the null-eigenvector assumption for the curvature operator is verified by (10.39) in the proof of Theorem 10.14, saying that \( \mathrm{{Rm}} \geq  0 \) is preserved, part (i) of Theorem 12.53 follows directly from Proposition 12.47.

(ii) The first statement in part (ii) of Theorem 12.53 follows from Theorem 12.50 directly. To see that image \( \left( {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) is a Lie subalgebra of \( {\Lambda }^{2}{T}^{ * }{\mathcal{M}}_{x} \) for all \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) and \( t \in  \left( {0,\delta }\right) \) , first recall the result that

\[
\operatorname{null}\left( \mathrm{{Rm}}\right)  \subset  \operatorname{null}\left( {{\mathrm{{Rm}}}^{2} + {\mathrm{{Rm}}}^{\# }}\right) ,
\]

which implies \( \operatorname{null}\left( \mathrm{{Rm}}\right)  \subset  \operatorname{null}\left( {\mathrm{{Rm}}}^{\# }\right) \) since \( \mathrm{{Rm}} \geq  0 \) and \( {\mathrm{{Rm}}}^{\# } \geq  0 \) . Let \( p \Doteq  \dim \) null \( \left( \mathrm{{Rm}}\right) \) , which is constant on \( \mathcal{M} \times  \left( {0,\delta }\right) \) . Choose an orthonormal basis \( \left\{  {\varphi }^{\alpha }\right\} \) of \( {\Lambda }^{2}{V}_{x}^{ * } \) such that \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) \) is diagonal:

\[
\operatorname{Rm} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }{\lambda }_{\alpha }{\varphi }^{\alpha } \otimes  {\varphi }^{\alpha }
\]

where \( {\lambda }_{\alpha } = 0 \) for \( \alpha  = 1,\ldots , p \) and \( {\lambda }_{\beta } > 0 \) for \( \beta  > p \) . Since \( \mathrm{{Rm}} \) is diagonal, we have

\[
{\left( {\mathrm{{Rm}}}^{\# }\right) }_{\alpha \beta } = {C}_{\alpha }^{\gamma \delta }{C}_{\beta }^{\gamma \delta }{\mathrm{{Rm}}}_{\gamma \gamma }{\mathrm{{Rm}}}_{\delta \delta }.
\]

Since null \( \left( \mathrm{{Rm}}\right)  \subset \) null \( \left( {\mathrm{{Rm}}}^{\# }\right) \) , we have for \( \alpha  = 1,\ldots , p \) ,

\[
{\left( {\mathrm{{Rm}}}^{\# }\right) }_{\alpha \alpha } = {\left( {C}_{\alpha }^{\gamma \delta }\right) }^{2}{\lambda }_{\gamma }{\lambda }_{\delta } = 0.
\]

Hence \( {C}_{\alpha }^{\gamma \delta } = 0 \) for \( \alpha  \leq  p \) and \( \gamma ,\delta  > p \) . Now image \( \left( \operatorname{Rm}\right)  = \operatorname{span}\left\{  {{\varphi }^{\beta } : \beta  > p}\right\} \) . Thus for \( \gamma ,\delta  > p \) we have \( \left\lbrack  {{\varphi }^{\gamma },{\varphi }^{\delta }}\right\rbrack   = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{\alpha  > p}}{C}_{\alpha }^{\gamma \delta }{\varphi }^{\alpha } \in \) image \( \left( \operatorname{Rm}\right) \) . Therefore image (Rm) is a Lie subalgebra of \( {\Lambda }^{2}{V}_{x}^{ * } \) .

nodes.content: Given a Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}^{n}, g}\right) \) and \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) , let \( {S}_{B}^{2}\left( x\right) \) denote the space of all self-adjoint transformations \( {\Lambda }^{2}\left( {{T}_{x}\mathcal{M}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\Lambda }^{2}\left( {{T}_{x}\mathcal{M}}\right) \) that obey the first Bianchi identity, i.e., the space of algebraic curvature operators. Let \( \Gamma  = \left\{  {\Gamma \left( x\right)  \subseteq  {S}_{B}^{2}\left( x\right)  : x \in  \mathcal{M}}\right\} \) be a collection of subsets that are invariant under parallel transport. We say \( \Gamma \) is a preserved curvature condition for Ricci flow if the fact that \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x,0}\right)  \in  \Gamma \left( x\right) \) for all \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) implies that \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  \Gamma \left( x\right) \) for all \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) and \( t > 0 \) such that a solution of Ricci flow exists. We say \( \Gamma \) is an attractive curvature condition if all complete singularity models \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{\infty }^{n},{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) formed from a finite-time singularity of \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}^{n}, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) have \( {\operatorname{Rm}}_{\infty }\left( {y,0}\right)  \in  \Gamma \left( y\right) \) for all \( y \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{\infty } \) .

EXAMPLE 13.1 (Nonnegative scalar curvature). Because

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}R = {\Delta R} + 2{\left| \operatorname{Rc}\right| }^{2} \geq  {\Delta R}
\]

nonnegative scalar curvature is a preserved cone on any solution \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}^{n}, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) of Ricci flow for which the maximum principle applies. In fact, under the same conditions, one has \( R\left( {\cdot , t}\right)  \geq  {R}_{\min }\left( 0\right) \) . Because a singularity at time \( T < \infty \) implies that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \nearrow  T}}\left( {\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  \mathcal{M}}}\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right| }\right)  = \infty \) , it follows that nonnegative scalar curvature is also an attractive curvature cone.

EXAMPLE 13.2 (Nonnegative curvature operator). Hamilton's tensor maximum principle proves that nonnegative curvature operator is a preserved cone [245] in all dimensions. (Anticipating material below, we note that nonnegative sectional curvature is equivalent to nonnegative curvature operator in dimensions \( n = 2,3 \) but is a weaker notion in dimensions \( n \geq  4 \) .)

Hamilton has also proved that positive isotropic curvature (likewise a weaker condition than positive curvature operator) is preserved in dimension \( n = 4 \) [255]. Recently, Brendle and Schoen [48] and H. Nguyen [376] have independently proved that positive isotropic curvature is preserved in all dimensions.

EXAMPLE 13.3 (Hamilton-Ivey estimate). Hamilton's original paper on Ricci flow [244] proves that nonnegative Ricci curvature is a preserved cone in dimension \( n = 3 \) . Furthermore, pinching estimates for 3-manifolds proved independently by Hamilton [252] and Ivey [286] show that nonnegative curvature operator is an attractive cone in that dimension. In particular, Hamilton's version implies that

\[
R\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  \left| {\lambda }_{1}\right| \left( {\log \left| {\lambda }_{1}\right|  + \log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - 3}\right) ,
\]

where \( {\lambda }_{1} < 0 \) is the smallest eigenvalue of the curvature operator \( \mathrm{{Rm}} \in \; {S}_{B}^{2}\left( x\right) \) . Neckpinch asymptotics indicate it is essentially sharp [11].

nodes.content: EXAMPLE 13.4 ( 2-nonnegative curvature operator). H. Chen has proved that 2-nonnegative curvature operator is a preserved cone in all dimensions [112]. If \( {\lambda }_{1} \leq  \cdots  \leq  {\lambda }_{N} \) are the eigenvalues of \( \operatorname{Rm} \in  {S}_{B}^{2}\left( x\right) \) , where \( N = \dim \left( {\mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right) }\right) \) , then one says that \( \mathrm{{Rm}} \) is 2-nonnegative if \( {\lambda }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \geq  0 \) for all \( x \in  {\mathcal{M}}^{n} \) . Note that 2-nonnegative curvature operator is equivalent to nonnegative Ricci curvature in dimension \( n = 3 \) . In every dimension \( n \geq  2 \) , a manifold admitting a metric with 2-positive curvature operator is diffeomorphic to a space form, i.e. a quotient of \( {\mathcal{S}}^{n} \subset  {\mathbb{R}}^{n + 1} \) by a finite subgroup of \( \mathrm{O}\left( {n + 1}\right) \) acting isometrically, linearly, and freely. See Chapter 11.

To understand the example, it is useful first to recall some basic facts about Riemannian submersions [395]. \( {}^{2} \) Let \( \pi  : \left( {{\mathcal{X}}^{N}, G}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{\mathcal{Y}}^{n}, g}\right) \) be a smooth submersion \( \left( {N > n}\right) \) . For each \( y \in  \mathcal{Y} \) , denote the fiber \( {\pi }^{-1}\left( y\right) \) by \( {\mathcal{Z}}_{y} \) . For each \( x \in  {\mathcal{Z}}_{y} \) , there is an induced linear map \( {\pi }_{ * }\left( x\right)  : {T}_{x}\mathcal{X} \rightarrow  {T}_{y}\mathcal{Y} \) and hence an orthogonal decomposition

\[
{T}_{x}\mathcal{X} = {V}_{x} \oplus  {H}_{x}
\]

where \( {V}_{x} = \ker \left( {{\pi }_{ * }\left( x\right) }\right) \) and \( {H}_{x} = {\left( {V}_{x}\right) }^{ \bot  } \) with respect to \( G\left( x\right) \) . One says \( \pi \) is a Riemannian submersion if

(13.1)

\[
{\pi }_{ * }\left( x\right) \left| {}_{{H}_{x}} : \left( {H}_{x}, G\left( x\right) {|}_{{H}_{x}}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {T}_{y}\mathcal{Y}, g\left( y\right) \right) \right|
\]

is an isometry of inner-product spaces for all \( y \in  \mathcal{Y} \) and all \( x \in  {\mathcal{Z}}_{y} \) .

For each \( x \in  \mathcal{X} \) , let \( {\mathcal{V}}_{x} : {T}_{x}\mathcal{X} \rightarrow  {V}_{x} \) and \( {\mathcal{H}}_{x} : {T}_{x}\mathcal{X} \rightarrow  {H}_{x} \) denote the projections onto the vertical and horizontal subspaces, respectively. If \( \varphi \) is a vector field on \( \mathcal{X} \) , one says \( \varphi \) is vertical if \( \varphi \left( x\right)  \in  {V}_{x} \) for all \( x \in  \mathcal{X} \) ; one says \( \varphi \) is horizontal if \( \varphi \left( x\right)  \in  {H}_{x} \) for all \( x \in  \mathcal{X} \) . (Hereafter, we suppress dependence on \( x \in  \mathcal{X} \) .) O’Neill defines \( \left( {2,1}\right) \) -tensor fields \( A \) and \( T \) on \( \mathcal{X} \) by stipulating that for all vector fields \( \varphi \) and \( \psi \) on \( \mathcal{X} \) ,

\[
{A}_{\varphi }\psi  = \mathcal{H}\left( {{\nabla }_{\mathcal{H}\varphi }\left( {\mathcal{V}\psi }\right) }\right)  + \mathcal{V}\left( {{\nabla }_{\mathcal{H}\varphi }\left( {\mathcal{H}\psi }\right) }\right)
\]

---

\( {}^{2} \) Also see [40,§9].

---

and

\[
{T}_{\varphi }\psi  = \mathcal{H}\left( {{\nabla }_{\mathcal{V}\varphi }\left( {\mathcal{V}\psi }\right) }\right)  + \mathcal{V}\left( {{\nabla }_{\mathcal{V}\varphi }\left( {\mathcal{H}\psi }\right) }\right) .
\]

Their geometric meanings are as follows. The tensor \( A \) vanishes if and only if the horizontal distribution is integrable. (The vertical distribution is of course always integrable.) The tensor \( T \) encodes the second fundamental form of each fiber and hence vanishes if and only if each fiber is totally geodesic. If both \( A \) and \( T \) vanish, then \( \mathcal{X} \) is a Riemannian product, at least locally.

THEOREM 13.9 (Curvatures of a Riemannian submersion). Let \( U \) and \( V \) denote vertical vector fields, and let \( X \) and \( Y \) denote horizontal vector fields. Then

(13.2a)

\[
{K}_{\mathcal{X}}\left( {U, V}\right)  = {K}_{\mathcal{Z}}\left( {U, V}\right)  + \frac{{\left| {T}_{U}V\right| }^{2}-\langle {T}_{U}U,{T}_{V}V\rangle }{{\left| U \land  V\right| }^{2}},
\]

(13.2b)

\[
{K}_{\mathcal{X}}\left( {U, X}\right)  = \frac{{\left| {A}_{X}U\right| }^{2}+\langle {\left( {\nabla }_{X}T\right) }_{U}U, X\rangle  - {\left| {T}_{U}X\right| }^{2}}{{\left| U \land  X\right| }^{2}},
\]

(13.2c)

\[
{K}_{\mathcal{X}}\left( {X, Y}\right)  = {K}_{\mathcal{Y}}\left( {{\pi }_{ * }X,{\pi }_{ * }Y}\right)  - 3\frac{{\left| {A}_{X}Y\right| }^{2}}{{\left| X \land  Y\right| }^{2}}.
\]

Here, \( {\left| X \land  Y\right| }^{2} = {\left| X\right| }^{2}{\left| Y\right| }^{2} - \langle X, Y{\rangle }^{2} \) , and all inner products are computed with respect to \( G \) .

Note that \( {\left| U \land  X\right| }^{2} = {\left| U\right| }^{2}{\left| X\right| }^{2} \) if \( U \) is vertical and \( X \) is horizontal.

THEOREM 13.12. Let \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}^{n}, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) be a solution of Ricci flow that exists for \( 0 \leq  t \leq  \delta \) with uniformly bounded nonnegative sectional curvatures. Let \( \left( {{\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}^{n},\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) }\right) \) denote the lift of the solution to the universal cover \( \widetilde{\mathcal{M}} \) of \( \mathcal{M} \) .

(1) For \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\delta }\right\rbrack  ,\left( {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}},\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) }\right) \) splits isometrically as

\[
{\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}^{n} = {\mathcal{N}}_{1}^{n - k} \times  {\mathcal{N}}_{2}^{k}
\]

where \( {\mathcal{N}}_{1} \) is a compact manifold of nonnegative sectional curvature and \( {\mathcal{N}}_{2}^{k} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{k} \) .

(2) For \( t \in  (0,\delta \rbrack \) , there exists a smooth, strictly convex exhaustion function on \( {\mathcal{N}}_{2} \) with respect to the restriction of \( g\left( t\right) \) to \( {\mathcal{N}}_{2} \) .

(3) The soul of \( {\mathcal{N}}_{2} \) is a point \( \{ p\} \) , and the soul of \( \widetilde{\mathcal{M}} \) is \( {\mathcal{N}}_{1} \times  \{ p\} \) .

We shall merely outline the proof here, referring the reader to [381] for the details.

Step 1. Construct a Busemann function \( {b}_{0} \) on \( \widetilde{\mathcal{M}} \) , noting that with respect to \( \widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) \) , the function \( {b}_{0} \) is weakly convex, uniformly Lipschitz, and exhaustive. By ’exhaustive’, we mean that there exists \( c > 0 \) such that

\[
b\left( x\right)  \geq  c{d}_{\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{0}, x}\right)
\]

for any fixed origin \( {x}_{0} \in  \widetilde{\mathcal{M}} \) and all \( x \in  \widetilde{\mathcal{M}} \) with \( {d}_{\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{0}, x}\right) \) sufficiently large.

Step 2. Let \( \left( {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}},\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) }\right) \) evolve by Ricci flow and let \( b \) denote the solution to the heat equation

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}b = {\Delta b}
\]

(with respect to the evolving metric) satisfying the initial condition \( b\left( {\cdot ,0}\right)  = \; {b}_{0}\left( \cdot \right) \) .

Step 3. Observe that \( b\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) remains weakly convex and exhaustive with respect to \( \widetilde{g}\left( t\right) \) as long as the sectional curvature remains nonnegative. Furthermore, the null space of the covariant Hessian \( \nabla \nabla b \) is a parallel distribution on \( \left( {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}},\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) }\right) \) . (This step uses a tensor maximum principle.)

Step 4. Apply De Rham's decomposition theorem to get an isometric splitting \( \left( {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}},\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) }\right)  = \mathcal{A} \times  \mathcal{B} \) for \( t > 0 \) , where \( \nabla \nabla b = 0 \) on \( \mathcal{A} \) and \( \nabla \nabla b > 0 \) on \( \mathcal{B} \) .

Step 5. Argue that \( \mathcal{A} \) is compact and that the soul of \( \mathcal{B} \) is a point. (This step uses the facts that \( b \) remains exhaustive and is strictly convex on \( \mathcal{B} \) for \( t > 0 \) .)

Step 6. Finally, argue that the isometric splitting \( \left( {\widetilde{\mathcal{M}},\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) }\right)  = \mathcal{A} \times  \mathcal{B} \) persists in the limit as \( t \searrow  0 \) .

The theorem immediately implies the main result of this subsection:

THEOREM 13.15. For each complex dimension \( n \geq  2 \) and all integers \( k \in  \left\lbrack  {1, n - 1}\right\rbrack \) , there exists a 1-parameter family of Kähler metrics on \( {L}_{-k}^{n} \) that are complete, of bounded curvature, and of nonnegative Ricci curvature, but which immediately develop mixed Ricci curvature when evolved by the Kähler-Ricci flow.

---

\( {}^{6} \) Since the complement of the 0-section of \( {L}_{-k}^{n} \) is biholomorphic to \( \left( {{\mathbb{C}}^{n}\smallsetminus \{ 0\} }\right) /{\mathbb{Z}}_{k} \) , one may construct \( {L}_{-k}^{n} \) by gluing a \( {\mathbb{{CP}}}^{n - 1} \) onto \( \left( {{\mathbb{C}}^{n}\smallsetminus \{ 0\} }\right) /{\mathbb{Z}}_{k} \) at the origin. In particular, \( {L}_{-1}^{n} \) is the tautological line bundle, i.e., \( {\mathbb{C}}^{n} \) blown up at the origin.

nodes.content:
However, it is conjectured by Feldman, Ilmanen, and one of the authors that nonnegative Ricci curvature is not an attractive cone for Kähler-Ricci flow. Here is why. For \( n \geq  2 \) , the noncompact line bundles \( \mathbb{C} \hookrightarrow  {L}_{-k}^{n} \rightarrow  {\mathbb{{CP}}}^{n - 1} \) admit soliton solutions discovered in [191] and described in Section 7 of Chapter 2 of Part I of this volume. These solitons are conjectured to occur as blow-ups of singularities of perturbed metrics on the total space of projective line bundles \( {\mathbb{{CP}}}^{1} \hookrightarrow  {F}_{k}^{n} \rightarrow  {\mathbb{{CP}}}^{n - 1}\left( {0 < k < n}\right) \) . (These compact bundles, also described in Chapter 2 of Part I of this volume, were introduced by Calabi [66] and form the underlying spaces for the Koiso solitons [315].) One reason for our conjecture is as follows.

At \( t = 0 \) , let \( {\sum }_{0} \) be a \( {\mathbb{{CP}}}^{1} \) in the 0 -section of \( {F}_{k}^{m} \) ; let \( {\sum }_{\infty } \) be a \( {\mathbb{{CP}}}^{1} \) in the \( \infty \) -section; and let \( T \) denote a fiber. Then \( {H}_{2}\left( {{F}_{k}^{n};\mathbb{Z}}\right)  \cong  \mathbb{Z} \oplus  \mathbb{Z} \) is generated by \( \left\lbrack  {\sum }_{0}\right\rbrack \) and \( \left\lbrack  T\right\rbrack \) , and one has \( \left\lbrack  {\sum }_{\infty }\right\rbrack   = \left\lbrack  {\sum }_{0}\right\rbrack   + k\left\lbrack  T\right\rbrack \) . Under unnormalized Kähler-Ricci flow \( \frac{\partial }{\partial t}g =  - \mathrm{{Rc}} \) , the area \( \left| \sum \right| \left( t\right) \) of any complex curve \( \sum \) evolves by

\[
\left| \sum \right| \left( t\right)  = \left| \sum \right| \left( 0\right)  - {2\pi }\left\langle  {{c}_{1},\left\lbrack  \sum \right\rbrack  }\right\rangle  t.
\]

Noting that \( \left\langle  {{c}_{1},\left\lbrack  {\sum }_{0}\right\rbrack  }\right\rangle   = n - k \) and \( \left\langle  {{c}_{1},\left\lbrack  T\right\rbrack  }\right\rangle   = 2 \) , we conjecture that for initial data with \( \left| {\sum }_{0}\right| /\left| T\right|  < \left( {n - k}\right) /2 \) , the Kähler-Ricci flow forms a local singularity as \( \left| {\sum }_{0}\right| \left( t\right)  \searrow  0 \) . Its singularity model should be the \( \mathrm{U}\left( n\right) \) -invariant soliton on the bundle \( \mathbb{C} \hookrightarrow  {L}_{-k}^{n} \rightarrow  {\mathbb{{CP}}}^{n - 1} \) . This solution does not have nonnegative Ricci curvature. (See Example 2.2 of [191] for more details.)

EXERCISE 13.18 (Criterion for real analyticity). Let \( \left( {{\mathcal{N}}^{n}, h}\right) \) be a complete flat Riemannian manifold. Show that a sufficient condition for a \( {C}^{\infty } \) function \( f : \mathcal{N} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) to be real analytic is that for every \( a \in  \mathcal{N} \) there exists \( r > 0 \) and \( C < \infty \) such that

(13.16)

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{m = 0}}^{\infty }\frac{{r}^{m}}{m!}{\left| {\nabla }^{m}f\right| }^{2}\left( x\right)  \leq  C
\]

for all \( x \in  B\left( {a, r}\right) \) , where \( {\nabla }^{m}f \) denotes the \( m \) -th covariant derivative of \( f \) . Note that (13.16) implies

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\frac{\left| {{\nabla }^{m}f}\right| \left( x\right) }{m!}{\left( \frac{r}{2}\right) }^{m} = 0.
\]

HINT: Since the problem is local, we may assume that \( \left( {{\mathcal{N}}^{n}, h}\right) \) is Euclidean space. Recall the formula for the remainder and estimate this remainder.

Proposition 13.19 (Real analyticity of solutions to the heat equation). Let \( \left( {{\mathcal{N}}^{n}, h}\right) \) be a closed flat Riemannian manifold. If \( f : \mathcal{N} \times  \lbrack 0, T) \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) is a smooth solution to the heat equation \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = {\Delta }_{h}f \) , then for all \( x \in  \mathcal{N} \) and \( t \geq  0 \) we have

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{\infty }\frac{{\left( 2t\right) }^{k}}{k!}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}f\right| }^{2}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \mathop{\max }\limits_{\mathcal{N}}{\left| f\left( \cdot ,0\right) \right| }^{2}.
\]

Hence, by Exercise 13.18, we have that for every \( t > 0 \) , the function \( f\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) : \( \mathcal{N} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) is real analytic.

If \( f : \mathcal{N} \times \lbrack 0, T) \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) is a smooth solution to the heat equation \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = {\Delta }_{h}f \) , then for all \( x \in \mathcal{N} \) and \( t \geq 0 \) we have \[ \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k =...

nodes.proof:
Recall that, from (14.13) and the maximum principle, we have

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{1}\frac{{\left( 2t\right) }^{k}}{k!}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}f\right| }^{2} = {2t}{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + {f}^{2} \leq  \mathop{\max }\limits_{\mathcal{N}}{\left| f\left( \cdot ,0\right) \right| }^{2}.
\]

The idea is to extend this formula to higher derivatives. Since we are on a flat manifold, the Riemann curvature tensor is zero, so we may commute covariant derivatives for free. We have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {{\nabla }^{k}f}\right)  = {\nabla }^{k}\left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\right)  = {\nabla }^{k}\left( {\Delta f}\right)  = \Delta \left( {{\nabla }^{k}f}\right) .
\]

Hence

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}f\right| }^{2} = 2\left\langle  {{\nabla }^{k}f,\Delta \left( {{\nabla }^{k}f}\right) }\right\rangle   = \Delta {\left| {\nabla }^{k}f\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}f\right| }^{2}.
\]

The nonpositive terms \( - 2{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}f\right| }^{2} \) on the RHS enable us to introduce powers of \( t \) and to sum. In particular, for any \( \ell  \in  \mathbb{N} \) we have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{\ell }\frac{{\left( 2t\right) }^{k}}{k!}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}f\right| }^{2}}\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{\ell }\frac{{\left( 2t\right) }^{k}}{k!}\left( {\Delta {\left| {\nabla }^{k}f\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}f\right| }^{2}}\right)
\]

\[
+ \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{\ell }2\frac{{\left( 2t\right) }^{k - 1}}{\left( {k - 1}\right) !}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}f\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
= \Delta \left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{\ell }\frac{{\left( 2t\right) }^{k}}{k!}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}f\right| }^{2}}\right)  - 2\frac{{\left( 2t\right) }^{\ell }}{\ell !}{\left| {\nabla }^{\ell  + 1}f\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
\leq  \Delta \left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{\ell }\frac{{\left( 2t\right) }^{k}}{k!}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}f\right| }^{2}}\right) .
\]

Since the initial-value of this subsolution of the heat equation is less than or equal to \( \mathop{\max }\limits_{\mathcal{N}}{\left| f\left( \cdot ,0\right) \right| }^{2} \) , we conclude that for any \( \ell  \in  \mathbb{N} \) ,

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 0}}^{\ell }\frac{{\left( 2t\right) }^{k}}{k!}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}f\right| }^{2}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \mathop{\max }\limits_{\mathcal{N}}{\left| f\left( \cdot ,0\right) \right| }^{2}
\]

for all \( x \) and \( t \) . The proposition follows.

2.2. Real analyticity of solutions to the Ricci flow. Given a manifold \( {\mathcal{M}}^{n} \) , a real analytic structure on \( \mathcal{M} \) is an atlas (i.e., collection of charts covering \( \mathcal{M} \) )

\[
{\left\{  \left( {U}_{\alpha },{\left\{  {x}_{\alpha }^{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{n}\right) \right\}  }_{\alpha  \in  \Lambda },
\]

where \( \Lambda \) is some index set, such that the overlap maps (transition functions) are real analytic. \( {}^{10} \) Coordinate systems compatible with this atlas are called real analytic coordinates. By definition, the collection of all real analytic coordinates is called the completion of the atlas and forms a complete atlas; from now on we shall assume the atlas is complete. The manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) together with such an atlas is called a real analytic manifold.

We say that a Riemannian metric \( g \) , on a real analytic manifold \( \mathcal{M} \) , is a real analytic metric if, with respect to a subatlas of real analytic coordinates, the components \( {g}_{ij} \) of the metric are real analytic functions. \( {}^{11} \) This is equivalent to \( {g}_{ij} \) being real analytic functions for all charts in the complete atlas of all real analytic coordinates. Note that on a real analytic Riemannian manifold \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, g}\right) \) any exponential coordinate system is real analytic; \( {}^{12} \) hence the \( {g}_{ij} \) are real analytic functions with respect to normal coordinates. By the above remarks, conversely, we have the following.

\]

Here our notation is such that if \( C \in  \mathbb{N} \) and \( A \) and \( B \) are tensors, then \( {CA} * B \) denotes a tensor consisting of \( C \) terms of the form contraction \( \left( {A \otimes  B}\right) {.}^{14} \)

nodes.proof:
We compute (with respect to an orthonormal frame at a point)

\[
\left( {{\nabla }_{i}\Delta  - \Delta {\nabla }_{i}}\right) A = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{n}\left( {{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{j} - {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{i}}\right) A
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{n}\left( {{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j} - {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{i}}\right) {\nabla }_{j}A
\]

\[
+ \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{n}{\nabla }_{j}\left( {{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j} - {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{i}}\right) A
\]

\[
= n\left( {\ell  + 1}\right) {\operatorname{Rm}}_{i} * \nabla A + \ell \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{n}{\nabla }_{j}\left( {{\operatorname{Rm}}_{ij} * A}\right)
\]

\[
= n\left( {2\ell  + 1}\right) {\operatorname{Rm}}_{i} * \nabla A + \ell \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{n}{\nabla }_{j}{\operatorname{Rm}}_{ij} * A,
\]

which yields the lemma. Here only some of the subscripts are written explicitly.

nodes.content:
LEMMA 13.24 (Commutator of \( {\nabla }^{k} \) and \( \Delta \) acting on tensors). If \( T \) is a (covariant) p-tensor with \( p \geq  1 \) , then

\[
{\nabla }^{k}{\Delta T} - \Delta {\nabla }^{k}T \lessapprox  n\left( {p + 1}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) !}{2!k!}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k}T
\]

(13.19)

\[
+ n\left( {{2p} + 1}\right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) !}{\left( {i + 2}\right) !\left( {k - i}\right) !}{\nabla }^{i}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k - i}T.
\]

In particular,

(13.20)

\[
{\nabla }^{k}{\Delta T} - \Delta {\nabla }^{k}T \lessapprox  {2n}\left( {p + 1}\right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{k}\frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) !}{\left( {i + 2}\right) !\left( {k - i}\right) !}{\nabla }^{i}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k - i}T.
\]

---

\( {}^{13} \) Later we shall take this tensor to be a covaiant derivative of Rm.

\( {}^{14} \) Similarly for sums of such terms.

\( {}^{15} \) The second Bianchi identity is \( {\nabla }_{m}{R}_{{ijk}\ell } + {\nabla }_{i}{R}_{{jmk}\ell } + {\nabla }_{j}{R}_{{mik}\ell } = 0 \) .

---

Here, when we write that a tensor \( S \) satisfies \( S \lesssim  {CA} * B \) , where \( C \in  \mathbb{N} \) and \( A \) and \( B \) are tensors, we mean that \( S \) is equal to the sum of at most \( C \) terms of the form contraction \( \left( {A \otimes  B}\right) .{}^{16} \)

nodes.proof:
We prove (13.19) by induction on \( k \) . Note that by (13.18) the lemma holds for \( k = 1 \) . Assume that (13.19) holds for some \( k \in  \mathbb{N} \) . We shall prove the same formula with \( k \) replaced by \( k + 1 \) .

Taking the covariant derivative of (13.19) and using (13.18), we compute \( {}^{18} \)

(13.21)

\[
{\nabla }^{k + 1}{\Delta T} - \Delta {\nabla }^{k + 1}T
\]

\[
= \nabla \left( {{\nabla }^{k}{\Delta T} - \Delta {\nabla }^{k}T}\right)  + \left( {\nabla \Delta  - \Delta \nabla }\right) {\nabla }^{k}T
\]

(13.22)

\[
\lessapprox  n\left( {p + 1}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) !}{2!k!}\nabla \operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k}T + n\left( {p + 1}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) !}{2!k!}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k + 1}T
\]

\[
+ n\left( {{2p} + 1}\right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) !}{\left( {i + 2}\right) !\left( {k - i}\right) !}{\nabla }^{i + 1}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k - i}T
\]

\[
+ n\left( {{2p} + 1}\right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) !}{\left( {i + 2}\right) !\left( {k - i}\right) !}{\nabla }^{i}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k + 1 - i}T
\]

\[
+ n\left( {2\left( {k + p}\right)  + 1}\right) \operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k + 1}T + n\left( {k + p}\right) \nabla \operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k}T.
\]

Using

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) !}{\left( {i + 2}\right) !\left( {k - i}\right) !}{\nabla }^{i + 1}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k - i}T
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 2}}^{{k + 1}}\frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) !}{\left( {i + 1}\right) !\left( {k + 1 - i}\right) !}{\nabla }^{i}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k + 1 - i}T
\]

and combining terms, we have the following equalities concerning the coefficients on the RHS of (13.22).

---

\( {}^{16} \) Again, similarly for sums of such terms.

\( {}^{17} \) This is unlike the usual case where we cannot differentiate an inequality.

\( {}^{18} \) When we write \( {CA} * B \lessapprox  {C}^{\prime }{A}^{\prime } * {B}^{\prime } \) , we actually mean that a sum of at most \( C \) terms of the form \( A * B \) is equal to a sum of at most \( {C}^{\prime } \) terms of the form \( {A}^{\prime } * {B}^{\prime } \) .

---

(1) For the \( \operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k + 1}T \) -terms in (13.22) we have the coefficient

\[
n\left( {p + 1}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) !}{2!k!} + n\left( {2\left( {k + p}\right)  + 1}\right)
\]

\[
= n\left( {\left( {p + 1}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) \left( {k + 1}\right) }{2} + {2k} + {2p} + 1}\right) .
\]

Since \( p \geq  1 \) , the above number is clearly less than or equal to \( n\left( {p + 1}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 3}\right) !}{2!\left( {k + 1}\right) !} \) , which is the coefficient of the Rm \( * {\nabla }^{k + 1}T \) -term on the RHS of formula (13.19) for \( {\nabla }^{k + 1}{\Delta T} - \Delta {\nabla }^{k + 1}T \) .

(2) For the \( \nabla \operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k}T \) -terms in (13.22) we have the coefficient

\[
n\left( {p + 1}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) !}{2!k!} + n\left( {{2p} + 1}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) !}{3!\left( {k - 1}\right) !} + n\left( {k + p}\right)
\]

\[
= n\left( {\left( {p + 1}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) \left( {k + 1}\right) }{2} + \left( {{2p} + 1}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) \left( {k + 1}\right) k}{6} + k + p}\right) .
\]

Since \( p \geq  1 \) , the above number is less than or equal to \( n\left( {{2p} + 1}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 3}\right) !}{3!k!} \) , which is the coefficient of the \( \nabla \operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k}T \) -term on the RHS of (13.19) for \( {\nabla }^{k + 1}{\Delta T} - \Delta {\nabla }^{k + 1}T \) .

(3) For the \( {\nabla }^{i}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k + 1 - i}T \) -terms \( \left( {2 \leq  i \leq  k}\right) \) we have the coefficient

\[
n\left( {{2p} + 1}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) !}{\left( {i + 1}\right) !\left( {k + 1 - i}\right) !} + n\left( {{2p} + 1}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) !}{\left( {i + 2}\right) !\left( {k - i}\right) !}
\]

\[
= n\left( {{2p} + 1}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 3}\right) !}{\left( {i + 2}\right) !\left( {k + 1 - i}\right) !}.
\]

The above number is clearly equal to the coefficient of the \( {\nabla }^{i}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k + 1 - i}T \) - term in (13.19) for \( {\nabla }^{k + 1}{\Delta T} - \Delta {\nabla }^{k + 1}T \) .

(4) For the \( {\nabla }^{k + 1}\operatorname{Rm} * T \) -term in (13.22) we have the coefficient \( n\left( {{2p} + 1}\right) \) , which is equal to the coefficient of the \( {\nabla }^{k + 1}\operatorname{Rm} * T \) -term in (13.19) for \( {\nabla }^{k + 1}{\Delta T} - \Delta {\nabla }^{k + 1}T \)

Now we have proved that (13.19) holds for \( {\nabla }^{k + 1}{\Delta T} - \Delta {\nabla }^{k + 1}T \) ; by induction the lemma is proved.

nodes.proof:
Similarly to the proof of Lemma 13.24, we prove this by induction. By (13.23), we have (13.24) is true for \( k = 1 \) . Now assume that (13.24) is true for some \( k \in  \mathbb{N} \) . We compute

\[
{\nabla }^{k + 1}\frac{\partial }{\partial t}T - \frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\nabla }^{k + 1}T
\]

\[
= \nabla \left( {{\nabla }^{k}\frac{\partial }{\partial t}T - \frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\nabla }^{k}T}\right)  + \left( {\nabla \frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\nabla }\right) {\nabla }^{k}T
\]

\[
\lessapprox  {3n}\left( {p + 1}\right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\frac{\left( {k + 1}\right) !}{\left( {i + 1}\right) !\left( {k - i}\right) !}\left( {{\nabla }^{i + 1}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k - i}T + {\nabla }^{i}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k + 1 - i}T}\right)
\]

\[
+ {3n}\left( {k + p}\right) \nabla \operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k}T
\]

\[
\lesssim  {3n}\left( {p + 1}\right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 2}}^{k}\left( {\frac{\left( {k + 1}\right) !}{\left( {i + 1}\right) !\left( {k - i}\right) !} + \frac{\left( {k + 1}\right) !}{i!\left( {k + 1 - i}\right) !}}\right) {\nabla }^{i}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k + 1 - i}T
\]

\[
+ \left( {{3n}\left( {p + 1}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 1}\right) !}{2!\left( {k - 1}\right) !} + {3n}\left( {k + p}\right) }\right) \nabla \operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k}T
\]

\[
+ {3n}\left( {p + 1}\right) {\nabla }^{k + 1}\operatorname{Rm} * T
\]

\[
\lessapprox  {3n}\left( {p + 1}\right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 2}}^{k}\frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) !}{\left( {i + 1}\right) !\left( {k + 1 - i}\right) !}{\nabla }^{i}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k + 1 - i}T
\]

\[
+ \left( {{3n}\left( {p + 1}\right) \frac{k\left( {k + 1}\right) }{2} + {3n}\left( {k + p}\right) }\right) \nabla \operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k}T
\]

\[
+ {3n}\left( {p + 1}\right) {\nabla }^{k + 1}\operatorname{Rm} * T.
\]

So to obtain the lemma, it suffices to have

\[
{3n}\left( {p + 1}\right) \frac{k\left( {k + 1}\right) }{2} + {3n}\left( {k + p}\right)  \leq  {3n}\left( {p + 1}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) \left( {k + 1}\right) }{2},
\]

that is,

\[
{3n}\left( {k + p}\right)  \leq  {3n}\left( {p + 1}\right) \left( {k + 1}\right) ,
\]

which is true.

\[
{\nabla }^{k}\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta }\right) T - \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta }\right) {\nabla }^{k}T
\]

(13.25)

\[
\lessapprox  {3n}\left( {p + 1}\right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{k}\left( {i + k + 4}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 1}\right) !}{\left( {i + 2}\right) !\left( {k - i}\right) !}{\nabla }^{i}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k - i}T.
\]

nodes.proof:
We compute

\[
{\nabla }^{k}\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta }\right) T - \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta }\right) {\nabla }^{k}T
\]

\[
\lessapprox  {3n}\left( {p + 1}\right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\frac{\left( {k + 1}\right) !}{\left( {i + 1}\right) !\left( {k - i}\right) !}{\nabla }^{i}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k - i}T
\]

\[
+ {3n}\left( {p + 1}\right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{k}\frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) !}{\left( {i + 2}\right) !\left( {k - i}\right) !}{\nabla }^{i}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k - i}T
\]

\[
\lessapprox  {3n}\left( {p + 1}\right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\left( {i + k + 4}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 1}\right) !}{\left( {i + 2}\right) !\left( {k - i}\right) !}{\nabla }^{i}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k - i}T
\]

\[
+ {3n}\left( {p + 1}\right) \frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) \left( {k + 1}\right) }{2}\operatorname{Rm} * {\nabla }^{k}T,
\]

and the lemma follows from comparing the last line to the \( i = 0 \) case of the RHS of (13.25).

LEMMA 13.28. There exists a constant \( {C}_{n} \in  \mathbb{N} \) depending only on \( n \) such that

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}\mathrm{\;{Rm}}\right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| {\nabla }^{k}\mathrm{\;{Rm}}\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}\mathrm{\;{Rm}}\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
+ {C}_{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{k}\frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) !}{\left( {i + 2}\right) !\left( {k - i}\right) !}\left| {{\nabla }^{i}\mathrm{{Rm}}}\right| \left| {{\nabla }^{k - i}\mathrm{{Rm}}}\right| \left| {{\nabla }^{k}\mathrm{{Rm}}}\right| .
\]

nodes.proof:
We compute using (13.26) that \( {}^{19} \)

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta }\right) {\left| {\nabla }^{k}\mathrm{\;{Rm}}\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
= 2\left\langle  {\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta }\right) {\nabla }^{k}\mathrm{\;{Rm}},{\nabla }^{k}\mathrm{\;{Rm}}}\right\rangle   - 2{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}\mathrm{\;{Rm}}\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
+ 2\left( {k + 4}\right) \mathrm{{Rc}} * {\left( {\nabla }^{k}\mathrm{\;{Rm}}\right) }^{*2}
\]

\[
\leq  2\left( {{34n} + 5}\right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{k}\frac{\left( {k + 2}\right) !}{\left( {i + 2}\right) !\left( {k - i}\right) !}\left| {{\nabla }^{i}\mathrm{\;{Rm}}}\right| \left| {{\nabla }^{k - i}\mathrm{\;{Rm}}}\right| \left| {{\nabla }^{k}\mathrm{\;{Rm}}}\right|
\]

\[
- 2{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}\mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} + {2n}\left( {k + 4}\right) \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| {\left| {\nabla }^{k}\mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2}
\]

and the lemma follows easily.

EXERCISE 13.30 (Computing using Uhlenbeck's trick). Carry out the computations for \( \left\lbrack  {{\nabla }^{k},\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta }\right) }\right\rbrack  \mathrm{{Rm}} \) and \( \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta }\right) {\left| {\nabla }^{k}\mathrm{{Rm}}\right| }^{2} \) using Uhlen-beck's trick. In this case we have

\[

\]

and (F.27), i.e.,

\[

nodes.label: Remark 14.1-extra-1
nodes.document_title: Bennett Chow et al. - The Ricci Flow Techniques and Applications Part II Analytic Aspects
nodes.content:
1.1. The distinction between fine and coarse estimates. It is useful to distinguish between what we may call fine estimates with what we may call coarse estimates. Since we apply these terminologies in a casual way, we describe our distinction between them in terms of examples. Examples of fine estimates in the theory of Ricci flow are curvature pinching estimates, Harnack-type estimates, entropy formulas, and monotonicity formulas. We may decree that an aspect of the fineness of an estimate is its sensitivity to perturbation. \( {}^{1} \) Although the matrix and trace Harnack estimates for the Ricci flow are known assuming nonnegative curvature operator in dimensions 2 and above, so far no substantial improvements (i.e., perturbations) seem to be known for dimensions 3 and above (in dimension 2 there is a trace Harnack estimate for arbitrary solutions on closed surfaces). On the other hand, one may think of the Hamilton-Ivey curvature estimate as a perturbation of the 'nonnegative sectional curvature is preserved' estimate in dimension 3. In this sense Harnack-type estimates appear finer than curvature pinching estimates although an analogy exists between them via the space-time approach. \( {}^{2} \) A further comment is that curvature pinching estimates in dimension 3 may be thought of as (large) perturbations of the 'nonnegative sectional (or Ricci) curvature is preserved' estimate.

Another aspect of the fineness of an estimate is how sharp it is; in general, finer estimates are sharper. A classical sharp example in Riemannian geometry is the Bishop-Gromov volume comparison theorem. In the Ricci flow, the matrix Harnack estimate is sharp (i.e., equality is attained in certain directions) on expanding gradient Ricci solitons. Moreover, for the corresponding Harnack estimate for ancient solutions we have that equality is attained on steady gradient Ricci solitons. Strikingly, Perelman has proved sharp monotonicity formulas for complete solutions of the Ricci flow on both closed and noncompact manifolds (without curvature sign restrictions). These estimates are sharp, as are monotonicity formulas in geometric flows in general.

On the other hand, in deriving coarse estimates, the ability to successfully apply the maximum principle to the evolution equations of the relevant quantities does not depend in a sensitive way on the constants in these quantities. For this reason we consider the global and local derivative of curvature estimates to be coarse estimates. Perhaps for the same reason derivative estimates hold for a number of different geometric evolution equations besides the Ricci flow including the heat equation on Riemannian manifolds and the mean curvature flow.

---

\( {}^{1} \) That is, the finer the estimate, the more difficult it is to perturb.

\( {}^{2} \) However, the reader may argue that a Harnack estimate in dimension \( n \) corresponds to a curvature estimate in dimension \( n + 1 \) since time adds a dimension, so that the apparent increase in fineness really corresponds to an increase in dimension.

---

The fineness or coarseness of an estimate may not be related to its relative importance to the study of a geometric flow; however, it may be related to its geometric significance. We venture to say that, in general, finer estimates are positively correlated to more geometrically significant estimates. An example of what we mean by this is that in many monotonicity formulas, the equality case, i.e., the case where the geometric invariant is constant under the flow, is characterized as occurring if and only if the solution is self-similar.

LEMMA 14.3 (Gradient and Laplacian estimate for cutoff function). Let \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}^{n}, g\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , be a solution to the Ricci flow. Assume \( \mathcal{U} \subset  \mathcal{M} \) is an open set and \( {\bar{B}}_{g\left( 0\right) }\left( {p, r}\right)  \subset  \mathcal{U} \) is compact. Assume

\[
\left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right|  \leq  K\;\text{ in }{B}_{g\left( 0\right) }\left( {p, r}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {0,\tau }\right\rbrack  ,
\]

where \( \tau  \leq  \alpha /K \) , and let \( \Theta \left( {x, t}\right)  \Doteq  t{K}^{2}{\left| \nabla \operatorname{Rc}\left( x, t\right) \right| }^{2} \) . There exist constants \( C\left( {\alpha , n}\right) \) and \( C\left( {\alpha ,\sqrt{K}r, n}\right) \) and there exists a cutoff function \( \eta  : \mathcal{U} \rightarrow  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) with support in \( {B}_{g\left( 0\right) }\left( {p, r}\right) \) and with \( \eta  = 1 \) in \( {B}_{g\left( 0\right) }\left( {p, r/2}\right) \) such that in \( B\left( {p, r}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {0,\tau }\right\rbrack \) we have

(14.1)

\[
{\left| \nabla \eta \left( x\right) \right| }_{g\left( t\right) }^{2} \leq  \frac{C\left( {\alpha , n}\right) }{{r}^{2}}\eta \left( x\right) ,
\]

(14.2)

\[
- {\Delta }_{g\left( t\right) }\eta \left( x\right)  \leq  \frac{C\left( {\alpha ,\sqrt{K}r, n}\right) }{{r}^{2}} + \frac{C\left( {\alpha , n}\right) }{{K}^{3/2}r}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{s \in  \left\lbrack  {0, t}\right\rbrack  }}{\left( \eta \Theta \right) }^{1/2}\left( {x, s}\right) .
\]

Let \( \lambda  : \lbrack 0,\infty ) \rightarrow  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) be a smooth nonincreasing function which satisfies \( \lambda \left( u\right)  = 1 \) for \( u \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1/2}\right\rbrack  ,\lambda \left( u\right)  = 0 \) for \( u \geq  7/8,0 \leq   - {\lambda }^{\prime }\left( u\right)  \leq  3 \) , and \( \left| {{\lambda }^{\prime \prime }\left( u\right) }\right|  \leq  {100} \) . Define the function \( \kappa \left( u\right)  \Doteq  {\lambda }^{2}\left( \frac{u}{r}\right) \) . Then \( \kappa \left( u\right)  = 1 \) for \( u \in  \left\lbrack  {0, r/2}\right\rbrack  ,\kappa \left( u\right)  = 0 \) for \( u \geq  {7r}/8 \) ,

(14.3)

\[
0 \leq   - {\kappa }^{\prime }\left( u\right)  \leq  6\sqrt{\kappa \left( u\right) }/r
\]

and

(14.4)

\[
\left| {{\kappa }^{\prime \prime }\left( u\right) }\right|  \leq  {250}/{r}^{2}.
\]

Let \( \eta  : \mathcal{U} \rightarrow  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) be the radial function \( \eta \left( x\right)  = \kappa \left( {{d}_{g\left( 0\right) }\left( {x, p}\right) }\right) \) , which is Lipschitz continuous. We have

\[
{\left| \nabla \eta \right| }_{g\left( 0\right) }^{2} \leq  \frac{36\eta }{{r}^{2}}
\]

a.e. on \( \mathcal{U} \) , and \( \eta \) has compact support in \( {B}_{g\left( 0\right) }\left( {p, r}\right) \) . Since \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right|  \leq  K \) in \( B\left( {p, r}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {0,\tau }\right\rbrack \) and \( \tau  \leq  \alpha /K \) , we have by Lemma 14.1,

\[
g\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  {e}^{-C\left( n\right) \alpha }g\left( {x,0}\right) .
\]

Hence

\[
{\left| \nabla \eta \left( x\right) \right| }_{g\left( t\right) }^{2} \leq  {e}^{C\left( n\right) \alpha }{\left| \nabla \eta \left( x\right) \right| }_{g\left( 0\right) }^{2} \leq  \frac{{36}{e}^{C\left( n\right) \alpha }}{{r}^{2}}\eta \left( x\right) .
\]

Part 2: Inequality (14.2). Let \( s\left( x\right)  = {d}_{g\left( 0\right) }\left( {x, p}\right) \) and for convenience of notation, let \( {g}^{t} \) also denote \( g\left( t\right) \) and \( {\nabla }^{t} \Doteq  \nabla \left( t\right) \) denote the covariant derivative with respect to \( g\left( t\right) {.}^{3} \) Since \( \left| \operatorname{Rm}\right|  \leq  K \) , we have sect \( \geq   - K \) , and by the Hessian comparison theorem (see for example [173] or [218])

\[
{\nabla }_{i}^{0}{\nabla }_{j}s \leq  \sqrt{K}\coth \left( {\sqrt{K}s}\right) {g}_{ij}^{0} \leq  \sqrt{K}r\coth \left( {\sqrt{K}r}\right) \frac{1}{s}{g}_{ij}^{0}
\]

for \( 0 < s \leq  r \) . So we have

\[
{\nabla }_{i}^{0}{\nabla }_{j}s \leq  \frac{C\left( {\sqrt{K}r}\right) }{s}{g}_{ij}^{0}
\]

---

\( {}^{3} \) Note that when acting on a function \( f \) , we have \( {\nabla }^{t}f = {df} \) , so often we just denote this by \( \nabla f \) .

---

for \( 0 < s \leq  r \) .

Hence, by (14.3) and (14.4) we have

\[
\left( {{\nabla }_{i}^{0}{\nabla }_{j}\eta }\right) \left( x\right)  = {\kappa }^{\prime }\left( s\right) {\nabla }_{i}^{0}{\nabla }_{j}s + {\kappa }^{\prime \prime }\left( s\right) {\nabla }_{i}s{\nabla }_{j}s
\]

\[
\geq  \left( {-6\sqrt{\kappa \left( s\right) }\frac{1}{r}\frac{C\left( {\sqrt{K}r}\right) }{r/2} - \frac{C}{{r}^{2}}}\right) {g}_{ij}^{0}
\]

(14.5)

\[
\geq   - \frac{C\left( {\sqrt{K}r}\right) }{{r}^{2}}{g}_{ij}^{0}
\]

since \( 0 \leq  s \leq  r \) and \( {\kappa }^{\prime }\left( s\right)  = 0 \) for \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0, r/2}\right\rbrack \) .

Now that we have a lower bound for \( {\nabla }_{i}^{0}{\nabla }_{j}\eta \) , the next step is to obtain a lower bound for \( {\nabla }_{i}^{t}{\nabla }_{j}\eta \) . We compute

\[
{\Delta }_{g\left( t\right) }\eta  = {g}^{ij}{\nabla }_{i}^{t}{\nabla }_{j}\eta  = {g}^{ij}{\nabla }_{i}^{0}{\nabla }_{j}\eta  - {g}^{ij}\left( {{\nabla }_{i}^{0} - {\nabla }_{i}^{t}}\right) {\nabla }_{j}\eta
\]

(14.6)

\[
= {g}^{ij}{\nabla }_{i}^{0}{\nabla }_{j}\eta  + {g}^{ij}\left( {{\left( {\Gamma }^{0}\right) }_{ij}^{k} - {\left( {\Gamma }^{t}\right) }_{ij}^{k}}\right) {\nabla }_{k}\eta ,
\]

where \( {\left( {\Gamma }^{t}\right) }_{ij}^{k} \Doteq  {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) . To clarify notation, in the following we call the time at which we compute \( {t}_{0} \) instead of \( t \) . Given \( x \in  {B}_{g\left( 0\right) }\left( {p, r}\right) \) and choosing coordinates such that \( {g}_{ij}\left( x\right)  = {\delta }_{ij} \) , we have

\[
\left| {{\left( {\Gamma }^{{t}_{0}}\right) }_{ij}^{k}\left( x\right)  - {\left( {\Gamma }^{0}\right) }_{ij}^{k}\left( x\right) }\right|  \leq  {\int }_{0}^{{t}_{0}}\left| {\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}}\right) \left( {x, t}\right) }\right| {dt} \leq  3{\int }_{0}^{{t}_{0}}\left| {{\nabla }_{k}{R}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right| {dt}
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{3}{K}{\int }_{0}^{{t}_{0}}{\Theta }^{1/2}\left( {x, t}\right) \frac{dt}{{t}^{1/2}}
\]

Hence

\[
\left| {{g}^{ij}\left( {{\left( {\Gamma }^{0}\right) }_{ij}^{k} - {\left( {\Gamma }^{{t}_{0}}\right) }_{ij}^{k}}\right) {\nabla }_{k}\eta }\right| \left( x\right)  \leq  \left| {{\left( {\Gamma }^{0}\right) }_{ij}^{k} - {\left( {\Gamma }^{{t}_{0}}\right) }_{ij}^{k}}\right| \left( x\right) \frac{C\left( {\alpha , n}\right) }{r}\eta {\left( x\right) }^{1/2}.
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{C\left( {\alpha , n}\right) }{Kr}{\int }_{0}^{{t}_{0}}\eta {\left( x\right) }^{1/2}{\Theta }^{1/2}\left( {x, t}\right) \frac{dt}{{t}^{1/2}}
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{C\left( {\alpha , n}\right) }{Kr}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }}{\left( \eta \Theta \right) }^{1/2}\left( {x, t}\right) {\int }_{0}^{{t}_{0}}\frac{dt}{{t}^{1/2}}
\]

(14.7)

\[
\leq  \frac{C\left( {\alpha , n}\right) }{{K}^{3/2}r}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }}{\left( \eta \Theta \right) }^{1/2}\left( {x, t}\right) ,
\]

where we used \( {\int }_{0}^{{t}_{0}}\frac{dt}{{t}^{1/2}} = 2{t}_{0}^{1/2} \leq  2\sqrt{\alpha }/\sqrt{K} \) (since \( {t}_{0} \leq  \alpha /K \) ).

Combining (14.6),(14.5), and (14.7), we obtain for any \( x \in  {B}_{g\left( 0\right) }\left( {p, r}\right) \) and \( {t}_{0} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\tau }\right\rbrack \) ,

\[
{\Delta }_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\eta \left( x\right)  \geq   - \frac{C\left( {\sqrt{K}r}\right) }{{r}^{2}}{g}^{ij}\left( {t}_{0}\right) {g}_{ij}^{0} - \frac{C\left( {\alpha , n}\right) }{{K}^{3/2}r}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }}{\left( \eta \Theta \right) }^{1/2}\left( {x, t}\right)
\]

\[
\geq   - \frac{C\left( {\sqrt{K}r}\right) }{{r}^{2}}n{e}^{-C\left( n\right) \alpha } - \frac{C\left( {\alpha , n}\right) }{{K}^{3/2}r}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }}{\left( \eta \Theta \right) }^{1/2}\left( {x, t}\right) ,
\]

where we also used \( g\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {e}^{-C\left( n\right) \alpha }g\left( {x,0}\right) \) from Lemma 14.1.

THEOREM 14.5 (Global derivative estimates). For any \( \alpha  > 0 \) and any \( m, n \in  \mathbb{N} \) , there exists a constant \( C = C\left( {m, n,\max \{ \alpha ,1\} }\right)  < \infty \) depending only on \( m, n \) , and \( \max \{ \alpha ,1\} \) such that if \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}^{n}, g\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , is a solution of the Ricci flow for which the maximum principle applies to all the quantities that we consider (this is true in particular if \( \mathcal{M} \) is closed) and if

\[

\]
