Then the normalized Ricci flow evolv...

nodes.proof:
Let \( {\mathrm{R}}_{p} \) denote the curvature operator of \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) at a point \( p \in  M \) . For all \( p \in  M \) we have

\[
{\mathrm{R}}_{p} \in  \left\{  {\mathrm{R} \mid  \text{ scal } \leq  {h}_{0}}\right\}   \cap  C\left( \varepsilon \right)
\]

for a sufficiently small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) and a sufficiently large \( {h}_{0} \) , since the family of cones is continuous and \( M \) is compact. For this pair \( \varepsilon ,{h}_{0} \) we consider an invariant set \( F \) as in Theorem 4.1.

By the maximum principle the Ricci flow evolves \( g \) to metrics \( {g}_{t} \) whose curvature operators at each point are contained in \( F \) . We also know that the solution of the Ricci flow exists as long as the curvature does not tend to infinity. Furthermore it follows from the maximum principle that the Ricci flow exists only on a finite time interval \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Subsequently we only consider times \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0}/2,{t}_{0}}\right) \) such that twice of the maximum of the scalar curvature at time \( t \) bounds the scalar curvature at all previous times. We will establish among other things that the scalar curvature is nearly constant for such a time \( t \) close to \( {t}_{0} \) . Since the minimum of the scalar curvature increases, it follows a postiori that the additional assumption holds for all \( t \) close to \( {t}_{0} \) . By Shi [Sh] it follows from the maximum principle applied to the evolution equation for the \( i \) -th derivative of the curvature operator that

\[
\max {\begin{Vmatrix}{\nabla }^{i}{\mathrm{R}}_{t}\end{Vmatrix}}^{2} \leq  {C}_{i}\max {\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathrm{R}}_{t}\end{Vmatrix}}^{i + 2}
\]

where we used the fact that by our choice of \( t \) the maximum of the norm of the curvature operator at time \( t \) controls the norm of the curvature operator at all previous times.

We now rescale each metric \( {g}_{t} \) to a metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{t} \) such that the maximal sectional curvature is equal to 1 . From the above estimates we get a priori bounds for all derivatives of the curvature tensor of the metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{t} \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0}/2,{t}_{0}}\right) \) .

Next, we pick a point \( {p}_{t} \in  \left( {M,{\widetilde{g}}_{t}}\right) \) such that the sectional curvature attains its maximum in the ball \( {B}_{\pi }\left( {p}_{t}\right) \) of radius \( \pi \) around \( {p}_{t} \) . We pull the metric via the exponential map back to the ball of radius \( \pi \) in \( {T}_{{p}_{t}}M \) . By choosing a linear isometry \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \rightarrow  {T}_{{p}_{t}}M \) we identify this ball with the ball \( {B}_{\pi }\left( 0\right)  \subset  {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) and denote by \( {\bar{g}}_{t} \) the induced metric on \( {B}_{\pi }\left( 0\right) \) . From the above estimates on the derivatives of the curvature tensor it is clear that for any sequence \( \left( {t}_{k}\right) \) in \( \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right) \) converging to \( {t}_{0} \) there is a subsequence of \( \left( {\bar{g}}_{{t}_{k}}\right) \) converging in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) topology to a limit metric.

Now, let \( {\lambda }_{j} \) denote the scaling factors of these metrics \( {\bar{g}}_{{t}_{j}} \) which by assumption tend to infinity. At each point of \( M \) the curvature operator of the limit metric is contained in the set

\[
\bigcap \frac{1}{{\lambda }_{j}^{2}}F = {\mathbb{R}}^{ + }I
\]

Thus the limit metric on \( {B}_{\pi }\left( 0\right) \) has pointwise constant sectional curvature. Since \( n \geq  3 \) , it has constant curvature one by Schur’s theorem.

Since the sequence was arbitrary, the minimal sectional curvature converges on a ball of radius \( \pi \) around \( {p}_{t} \) in \( \left( {M,{\widetilde{g}}_{t}}\right) \) to 1 as well as \( t \) tends to \( {t}_{0} \) . Notice that this argument works for all \( {p}_{t} \in  {B}_{\pi }\left( {q}_{t}\right) \) , where \( {q}_{t} \) denotes a point where the sectional curvature attains its maximum 1. Therefore the minimal sectional curvature converges on the ball of radius \( {2\pi } \) around \( {q}_{t} \) to 1 as well. By the theorem of Bonnet Myers \( \operatorname{diam}\left( {M,{\widetilde{g}}_{t}}\right)  \leq  {3\pi }/2 \) for large \( t < {t}_{0} \) and consequently, also the minimum of the sectional curvature of \( \left( {M,{\widetilde{g}}_{t}}\right) \) tends to 1 for \( t \rightarrow  {t}_{0} \) .

In the case of manifolds one is done since by Klingenberg's injectivity radius estimate [CE] collapse can not occur. Alternatively, one can use the fact that \( \left( {M,{g}_{t}}\right) \) satisfies the assumption of Huisken’s theorem [Hu] for suitable large \( t \) . In the case of orbifolds one has to use additionally Proposition 5.2 from below.

Let us remark that collapse in the above situation can also be ruled out by applying Perelman's local injectivity radius estimate for the Ricci flow [Pe].

nodes.label: Proposition 5.2
nodes.document_title: Christoph Boehm and Burkhard Wilking - Manifolds with Positive Curvature Operators Are Space Forms
nodes.content: Proposition 5.2. Let \( \left( {X, g}\right) \) be a compact orbifold with sectional curvature \( K \) . If \( n \geq  3 \) and \( g \) is strictly quarter pinched, that is \( 1/4 < K \leq  1 \) , then \( X \) is the quotient of a Riemannian manifold by a finite isometric group action.
nodes.content_excerpt: Proposition 5.2. Let \( \left( {X, g}\right) \) be a compact orbifold with sectional curvature \( K \) . If \( n \geq 3 \) and \( g \) is strictly quarter pinched, that is \( 1/4 < K \leq 1 \) , then \( X \) is the quotient of a Riemannian manifold by a finite isometric group action.

nodes.proof:
By replacing \( X \) by a cover if necessary we may assume that \( X \) is not a nontrivial quotient of an orbifold by a finite group action. We then have to show that \( X \) is a manifold. Recall that the frame bundle \( {FX} \) of the orbifold \( X \) , endowed with the connection metric of \( g \) , is a Riemannian manifold. We consider an \( \mathrm{{SO}}\left( n\right) \) orbit \( \mathrm{{SO}}\left( n\right) v \) in \( {FX} \) . Clearly the normal exponential map of the orbit \( \mathrm{{SO}}\left( n\right) v \) has a focal radius \( \geq  \pi \) . Similarly to Klingenberg’s injectivity radius estimate we show below that the normal exponential map of the orbit \( \mathrm{{SO}}\left( n\right) v \) has injectivity radius \( \geq  \pi \) . Since the orbit was arbitrary, this rules out exceptional orbits and hence \( X \) is then a manifold.

From the assumption that \( X \) is not a nontrivial quotient it follows that the natural map \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {\mathrm{{SO}}\left( n\right) }\right)  \rightarrow  {\pi }_{1}\left( {FX}\right) \) is surjective. This implies that the space \( {\Omega }_{\mathrm{{SO}}\left( n\right) v}{FX} \) of all curves starting and ending in \( \mathrm{{SO}}\left( n\right) v \) is connected. The critical levels of the energy functional in \( {\Omega }_{\mathrm{{SO}}\left( n\right) v}{FX} \) are in one-to-one correspondence to the geodesic loops in the orbifold.

Suppose on the contrary that the injectivity radius of the normal exponential map of \( \mathrm{{SO}}\left( n\right) v \) is equal to \( r < \pi \) . It is then easy to see that there is a horizontal geodesic \( c \) of length \( {2r} \) in \( {\Omega }_{\mathrm{{SO}}\left( n\right) v}{FX} \) . Analogously to Klingen-berg’s long homotopy lemma one can show that every path \( {c}_{s} \) in \( {\Omega }_{\mathrm{{SO}}\left( n\right) v}{FX} \) that connects \( c = {c}_{0} \) with a constant curve \( {c}_{1} \) satisfies \( L\left( {c}_{s}\right)  \geq  {2\pi } \) for some \( s \) . In other words the space of paths of energy \( < 2{\pi }^{2} \) is not connected.

On the other hand it is straightforward to check that the critical points of the energy function with energy \( \geq  2{\pi }^{2} \) have indices at least \( n - 1 \geq  2 \) . But then by a standard degenerate Morse theory argument the loop space \( {\Omega }_{\mathrm{{SO}}\left( n\right) v}{FX} \) itself is not connected - a contradiction.

nodes.content: 1. The main difference between dimension two and the higher dimensional case is that in dimension two Schur's theorem fails. Notice also that in dimension two Proposition 5.2 does not remain valid either. In fact given any positive \( \delta  < 1 \) , there exists a \( \delta \) pinched two-dimensional orbifold \( X \) which is not the quotient of a manifold: Consider two discs of constant curvature 1 with totally geodesic boundary. Divide out the cyclic group of order \( \left( {p + 1}\right) \) from the first disc and the cyclic group of order \( p \) from the second. After scaling the first disc by the factor \( \frac{p + 1}{p} \) the two orbifolds can be glued along their common boundary. By smoothing this example for some large \( p \) one obtains the claimed result.

nodes.content:
4. We turn now to the Kähler analogue of Theorem 1: On a compact Kähler manifold the Kähler-Ricci flow converges to the symmetric metric of the complex projective space \( {\mathbb{{CP}}}^{n} \) if the initial Kähler metric has positive bisectional curvature. This result follows from Chen's and Tian's work [CT] on Ricci flow on Kähler-Einstein manifolds and the solution to the Frankel conjecture by Mori [Mo] and Siu and Yau [SY].

We would like to mention that the above result cannot be proved just carrying over the methods of this paper to the Kähler case. Notice first that an analogue of Theorem 2 holds for Kähler curvature operators. However, unlike the curvature operator of the round sphere in the real case the curvature operator of the symmetric metric on \( {\mathbb{{CP}}}^{n} \) it not a local attractor for the ordinary differential equation (1) restricted to the space of Kähler curvature operators. To be more precise there exists a maximal solution \( \mathrm{R}\left( s\right) , s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{s}_{0}}\right) \) , of (1) such that the initial Kähler curvature operator \( \mathrm{R}\left( 0\right) \) can be chosen arbitrarily close to the curvature operator of the symmetric metric on \( {\mathbb{{CP}}}^{n} \) but the rescaled limit \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{s \rightarrow  {s}_{0}}}\frac{\mathrm{R}\left( s\right) }{\parallel \mathrm{R}\left( s\right) \parallel } \) is the curvature operator of a symmetric metric on \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  {\mathbb{C}}^{n - 1} \) .

Proposition 1.1. The curvature tensor satisfies

\[
R\left( {X, Y, Z, W}\right)  =  - R\left( {Y, X, Z, W}\right)  = R\left( {Z, W, X, Y}\right)
\]

and

\[
R\left( {X, Y, Z, W}\right)  + R\left( {Y, Z, X, W}\right)  + R\left( {Z, X, Y, W}\right)  = 0
\]

for all vector fields \( X, Y, Z, W \) .

Since \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) is complete, we can find a vector \( v \in  {T}_{\gamma \left( 0\right) }M \) such that \( {\exp }_{\gamma \left( 0\right) }\left( v\right)  = q \) and \( \left| v\right|  = d\left( {\gamma \left( 0\right) , q}\right) \) . If \( v = 0 \) , the assertion is trivial. Hence, it suffices to consider the case \( v \neq  0 \) . We can find a smooth map \( \alpha  : \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack   \times  ( - \varepsilon ,0\rbrack  \rightarrow  M \) such that \( \alpha \left( {0, s}\right)  = \gamma \left( s\right) \) for all \( s \in  ( - \varepsilon ,0\rbrack ,\alpha \left( {1, s}\right)  = q \) for all \( s \in  ( - \varepsilon ,0\rbrack \) , and \( \alpha \left( {t,0}\right)  = {\exp }_{\gamma \left( 0\right) }\left( {tv}\right) \) for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . Then

\[
L\left( {\alpha \left( {\cdot , s}\right) }\right)  \geq  d\left( {\gamma \left( s\right) , q}\right)  \geq  d\left( {\gamma \left( 0\right) , q}\right)  + {\mu s}
\]

for all \( s \in  ( - \varepsilon ,0\rbrack \) , and the inequality is sharp for \( s = 0 \) . Using the formula for the first variation of arc length (cf. [26]), we obtain

\[

\]

From this, the assertion follows.

nodes.content: Proposition 1.14. Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a compact Riemannian manifold of dimension \( n \) with sectional curvature \( K \geq  1 \) . Suppose that \( p \) and \( q \) are two points in \( M \) such that \( d\left( {p, q}\right)  = \operatorname{diam}\left( {M, g}\right)  > \frac{\pi }{2} \) . Moreover, suppose that \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) is a geodesic satisfying \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = \gamma \left( 1\right)  = p \) . Then \( \gamma \) has Morse index at least \( n - 1 \) .

nodes.proof:
By assumption, we have \( d\left( {\gamma \left( s\right) , q}\right)  \leq  d\left( {\gamma \left( 0\right) , q}\right) \) for all \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . By Lemma 1.13, there exists a vector \( v \in  {T}_{p}M \) such that \( {\exp }_{p}\left( v\right)  = q \) , \( \left| v\right|  = d\left( {p, q}\right) \) , and \( \left\langle  {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) , v}\right\rangle   \geq  0 \) .

We claim that \( L\left( \gamma \right)  > \pi \) . To prove this, we argue by contradiction. If \( L\left( \gamma \right)  \leq  \pi \) , then the hinge version of Toponogov’s theorem (see e.g. [26], Theorem 2.2B) implies that

\[
\cos \left( {d\left( {\gamma \left( 1\right) , q}\right) }\right)  \geq  \cos \left( {L\left( \gamma \right) }\right) \cos \left( {d\left( {\gamma \left( 0\right) , q}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
+ \sin \left( {L\left( \gamma \right) }\right) \sin \left( {d\left( {\gamma \left( 0\right) , q}\right) }\right) \cos \left( {\sphericalangle \left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) , v}\right) }\right) .
\]

By assumption, we have \( L\left( \gamma \right)  \in  (0,\pi \rbrack \) and \( d\left( {\gamma \left( 0\right) , q}\right)  \in  \left( {\frac{\pi }{2},\pi }\right\rbrack \) . Moreover, the inequality \( \left\langle  {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) , v}\right\rangle   \geq  0 \) implies \( \cos \left( {-\chi \left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( 0\right) , v}\right) }\right)  \geq  0 \) . Putting these facts together, we obtain

\[
\cos \left( {d\left( {\gamma \left( 1\right) , q}\right) }\right)  \geq  \cos \left( {L\left( \gamma \right) }\right) \cos \left( {d\left( {\gamma \left( 0\right) , q}\right) }\right)  > \cos \left( {d\left( {\gamma \left( 0\right) , q}\right) }\right) .
\]

This contradicts the fact that \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = \gamma \left( 1\right) \) . Consequently, we have \( L\left( \gamma \right)  > \pi \) .

Let \( \mathcal{H} \) be the space of all vector fields of the form \( V\left( s\right)  = \sin \left( {\pi s}\right) X\left( s\right) \) , where \( X \) is a parallel vector field along \( \gamma \) satisfying \( \left\langle  {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) , X\left( s\right) }\right\rangle   = 0 \) for all \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . Then

\[
I\left( {V, V}\right)  = {\int }_{0}^{1}\left( {{\left| {D}_{\frac{d}{ds}}V\left( s\right) \right| }^{2} - R\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) , V\left( s\right) ,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) , V\left( s\right) }\right) }\right) {ds}
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {{\pi }^{2} - L{\left( \gamma \right) }^{2}}\right) {\int }_{0}^{1}{\left| V\left( s\right) \right| }^{2}{ds}
\]

for all \( V \in  \mathcal{H} \) . Since \( L\left( \gamma \right)  > \pi \) , the restriction of \( I \) to \( \mathcal{H} \) is negative definite. This implies \( \operatorname{ind}\left( \gamma \right)  \geq  \dim \mathcal{H} = n - 1 \) .

nodes.content: Theorem 1.15 (K. Grove, K. Shiohama [42]). Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a compact Riemannian manifold of dimension \( n \geq  4 \) with sectional curvature \( K \geq  1 \) and diameter \( \operatorname{diam}\left( {M, g}\right)  > \frac{\pi }{2} \) . nodes.proof:
We claim that \( M \) is \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -connected. Suppose this false. Then there exists an integer \( k \in  \{ 1,\ldots , n - 1\} \) such that \( {\pi }_{k}\left( M\right)  \neq  0 \) . Let us fix two points \( p, q \in  M \) such that \( d\left( {p, q}\right)  = \operatorname{diam}\left( {M, g}\right)  > \frac{\pi }{2} \) . Since \( {\pi }_{k}\left( M\right)  \neq  0 \) , there exists a geodesic \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) such that \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = \gamma \left( 1\right)  = p \) and ind \( \left( \gamma \right)  < k \) . On the other hand, we have \( \operatorname{ind}\left( \gamma \right)  \geq  n - 1 \) by Proposition 1.14. This is a contradiction.

Therefore, \( M \) is \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -connected. This implies that \( M \) is a homotopy sphere. Hence, it follows from results of Freedman and Smale that \( M \) is homeomorphic to \( {S}^{n} \) (cf. [36], Theorem 1.6, and [81], Theorem A).

nodes.content:
#### 1.4.The Sphere Theorem of Micallef and Moore

In this section, we describe a generalization of Theorem 1.10 due to Micallef and Moore. Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a Riemannian manifold of dimension \( n \geq  4 \) , and let \( f \) be a smooth map from \( {S}^{2} \) into \( M \) . In the following, we identify \( {S}^{2} \) with \( {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \cup  \{ \infty \} \) via stereographic projection. Moreover, we denote by \( \left( {x, y}\right) \) the standard Cartesian coordinates on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \) . The energy of \( f \) is defined by

\[
\mathcal{E}\left( f\right)  = \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{S}^{2}}\left( {{\left| \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right| }^{2} + {\left| \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right| }^{2}}\right) {dxdy}.
\]

A map \( f : {S}^{2} \rightarrow  M \) is called harmonic if \( {D}_{\frac{\partial }{\partial x}}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + {D}_{\frac{\partial }{\partial y}}\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 0 \) .

Throughout this section, we assume that \( f : {S}^{2} \rightarrow  M \) is a nonconstant harmonic map. This implies that \( f \) is a critical point of the functional \( \mathcal{E} \) . Moreover, the second variation of \( \mathcal{E} \) is given by

\[
I\left( {W, W}\right)  = {\int }_{{S}^{2}}\left\lbrack  {{\left| {D}_{\frac{\partial }{\partial x}}W\right| }^{2} + {\left| {D}_{\frac{\partial }{\partial y}}W\right| }^{2}}\right\rbrack  {dxdy}
\]

\[
- {\int }_{{S}^{2}}\left\lbrack  {R\left( {\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}, W,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}, W}\right)  + R\left( {\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}, W,\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}, W}\right) }\right\rbrack  {dxdy}
\]

for all vector fields \( W \in  \Gamma \left( {{f}^{ * }\left( {TM}\right) }\right) \) . Here, \( R \) denotes the Riemann curvature tensor of \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) .

For each point \( p \in  M \) , we denote by \( {T}_{p}^{\mathbb{C}}M = {T}_{p}M{ \otimes  }_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{C} \) the com-plexified tangent space to \( M \) at \( p \) . We may extend the inner product \( g : {T}_{p}M \times  {T}_{p}M \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) to a complex bilinear form \( g : {T}_{p}^{\mathbb{C}}M \times  {T}_{p}^{\mathbb{C}}M \rightarrow  \mathbb{C} \) . Similarly, the Riemann curvature tensor extends to a complex multilinear form \( R : {T}_{p}^{\mathbb{C}}M \times  {T}_{p}^{\mathbb{C}}M \times  {T}_{p}^{\mathbb{C}}M \times  {T}_{p}^{\mathbb{C}}M \rightarrow  \mathbb{C}. \)

\]

\]

Moreover, for each section \( W \in  \Gamma \left( {{f}^{ * }\left( {{T}^{\mathbb{C}}M}\right) }\right) \) we define

\[
{D}_{\frac{\partial }{\partial z}}W = \frac{1}{2}\left( {{D}_{\frac{\partial }{\partial x}}W - i{D}_{\frac{\partial }{\partial y}}W}\right)

nodes.content: Proposition 1.18. There exists a holomorphic subbundle \( E \subset  {f}^{ * }\left( {{T}^{\mathbb{C}}M}\right) \) such that \( {\operatorname{rank}}_{\mathbb{C}}E \geq  n - 2,{c}_{1}\left( E\right)  = 0 \) , and \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} \notin  \Gamma \left( E\right) \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: Proposition 1.18. There exists a holomorphic subbundle \( E \subset {f}^{ * }\left( {{T}^{\mathbb{C}}M}\right) \) such that \( {\operatorname{rank}}_{\mathbb{C}}E \geq n - 2,{c}_{1}\left( E\right) = 0 \) , and \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} \notin \Gamma \left( E\right) \) .

nodes.proof:
By a theorem of Grothendieck [40], there exist holomorphic line bundles \( {L}_{1},\ldots ,{L}_{n} \subset  {f}^{ * }\left( {{T}^{\mathbb{C}}M}\right) \) such that \( {f}^{ * }\left( {{T}^{\mathbb{C}}M}\right)  = {L}_{1} \oplus  {L}_{2} \oplus  \cdots  \oplus  {L}_{n} \) . We assume that the line bundles \( {L}_{1},\ldots ,{L}_{n} \) are chosen so that

\[
{c}_{1}\left( {L}_{1}\right)  \geq  {c}_{1}\left( {L}_{2}\right)  \geq  \ldots  \geq  {c}_{1}\left( {L}_{n}\right) .
\]

The line bundles \( {L}_{1},\ldots ,{L}_{n} \) are not unique. However, the sequence of Chern classes \( {c}_{1}\left( {L}_{1}\right) ,\ldots ,{c}_{1}\left( {L}_{n}\right) \) is uniquely determined (i.e. it is independent of the particular choice of \( {L}_{1},\ldots ,{L}_{n} \) ).

Recall that \( {f}^{ * }\left( {{T}^{\mathbb{C}}M}\right) \) is the complexification of a real vector bundle. Hence, the bundle \( {f}^{ * }\left( {{T}^{\mathbb{C}}M}\right) \) is isomorphic to its dual bundle, which, in turn, is isomorphic to \( {L}_{n}^{ * } \oplus  {L}_{n - 1}^{ * } \oplus  \cdots  \oplus  {L}_{1}^{ * } \) . Since the sequence of Chern classes is unique, we conclude that

\[
{c}_{1}\left( {L}_{k}\right)  = {c}_{1}\left( {L}_{n - k + 1}^{ * }\right)  =  - {c}_{1}\left( {L}_{n - k + 1}\right)
\]

for \( k = 1,\ldots , n \) .

We now write \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} = {W}_{1} + \cdots  + {W}_{n} \) , where \( {W}_{j} \in  \Gamma \left( {L}_{j}\right) \) for \( j = 1,\ldots , n \) . Since \( f \) is nonconstant, we can find an integer \( k \in  \{ 1,\ldots , n\} \) such that \( {W}_{k} \) does not vanish identically. We then define \( E = {\bigoplus }_{j \in  J}{L}_{j} \) , where \( J = \; \{ 1,\ldots , n\}  \smallsetminus  \{ k, n - k + 1\} \) . It is straightforward to verify that \( E \) has all the required properties.

nodes.content: Theorem 1.19 (M. Micallef, J.D. Moore [60]). Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a Riemannian manifold of dimension \( n \geq  4 \) . Let us assume that \( R\left( {\zeta ,\eta ,\bar{\zeta },\bar{\eta }}\right)  > 0 \) for all points \( p \in  M \) and all linearly independent vectors \( \zeta ,\eta  \in  {T}_{p}^{\mathbb{C}}M \) satisfying \( g\left( {\zeta ,\zeta }\right)  = g\left( {\zeta ,\eta }\right)  = g\left( {\eta ,\eta }\right)  = 0 \) . Finally, let \( f : {S}^{2} \rightarrow  M \) be a nonconstant harmonic map. Then \( f \) has Morse index at least \( \left\lbrack  \frac{n - 2}{2}\right\rbrack \) .

nodes.proof:
Let \( E \subset  {f}^{ * }\left( {{T}^{\mathbb{C}}M}\right) \) be the holomorphic subbundle constructed in Proposition 1.18, and let \( \mathcal{H} \) be the space of holomorphic sections of \( E \) . Given two sections \( {W}_{1},{W}_{2} \in  \mathcal{H} \) , the inner product \( g\left( {{W}_{1},{W}_{2}}\right) \) is a holomorphic function on \( {S}^{2} \) . Consequently, the function \( g\left( {{W}_{1},{W}_{2}}\right) \) is constant. This gives a complex bilinear form

\[
\mathcal{H} \times  \mathcal{H} \rightarrow  \mathbb{C},\;\left( {{W}_{1},{W}_{2}}\right)  \mapsto  g\left( {{W}_{1},{W}_{2}}\right) .
\]

By the Riemann-Roch theorem, we have \( {\dim }_{\mathbb{C}}\mathcal{H} \geq  n - 2 \) . Hence, there exists a subspace \( {\mathcal{H}}_{0} \subset  \mathcal{H} \) such that \( \mathop{\dim }\limits_{\mathbb{C}}{\mathcal{H}}_{0} \geq  \left\lbrack  \frac{n - 2}{2}\right\rbrack \) and \( g\left( {W, W}\right)  = 0 \) for all \( W \in  {\mathcal{H}}_{0} \) .

We now consider an arbitrary section \( W \in  {\mathcal{H}}_{0} \) . Since \( W \) is holomorphic, it follows from Proposition 1.17 that \( g\left( {\frac{\partial f}{\partial z},\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}}\right)  = g\left( {\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}, W}\right)  = 0 \) at each point on \( {S}^{2} \) . Moreover, we have \( g\left( {W, W}\right)  = 0 \) at each point on \( {S}^{2} \) . Using the curvature assumption, we obtain

\[
R\left( {\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}, W,\frac{\partial f}{\partial \bar{z}},\bar{W}}\right)  \geq  0,
\]

with equality if and only if \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} \) and \( W \) are linearly dependent. Since \( W \) is holomorphic, we conclude that

\[
I\left( {W,\bar{W}}\right)  =  - 4{\int }_{{S}^{2}}R\left( {\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}, W,\frac{\partial f}{\partial \bar{z}},\bar{W}}\right) {dxdy} \leq  0
\]

by Proposition 1.16. We next analyze the case of equality. If \( I\left( {W,\bar{W}}\right)  = 0 \) , then \( W = \psi \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} \) for some meromorphic function \( \psi  : {S}^{2} \rightarrow  \mathbb{C} \) . Since \( W \in \; \Gamma \left( E\right) \) and \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} \notin  \Gamma \left( E\right) \) , the function \( \psi \) vanishes identically. Thus, we conclude that \( I\left( {W,\bar{W}}\right)  < 0 \) for every nonvanishing section \( W \in  {\mathcal{H}}_{0} \) .

We now complete the proof of Theorem 1.19. Suppose that \( f \) has Morse index \( m < \left\lbrack  \frac{n - 2}{2}\right\rbrack \) . Then \( \mathop{\dim }\limits_{\mathbb{C}}{\mathcal{H}}_{0} \geq  \left\lbrack  \frac{n - 2}{2}\right\rbrack   > m \) . Consequently, there exists a nonvanishing section \( W \in  {\mathcal{H}}_{0} \) which is orthogonal to the first \( m \) eigenfunctions of the second variation operator. Since \( W \in  {\mathcal{H}}_{0} \) , we have \( I\left( {W,\bar{W}}\right)  < 0 \) . On the other hand, we have \( I\left( {W,\bar{W}}\right)  \geq  0 \) since \( W \) is orthogonal to the first \( m \) eigenfunctions of the second variation operator. This is a contradiction.

Then \( M \) is homeomorphic to \( {S}^{n} \) .

nodes.proof:
We claim that \( M \) is \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -connected. Suppose this is false. Then there exists an integer \( k \in  \{ 2,\ldots , n - 1\} \) such that \( {\pi }_{k}\left( M\right)  \neq  0 \) and \( {\pi }_{j}\left( M\right)  = \) 0 for \( j = 1,\ldots , k - 1 \) . Using the Hurewicz theorem (cf. [16], Chapter VII, Corollary 10.8), we obtain \( {H}_{k}\left( {M,\mathbb{Z}}\right)  \neq  0 \) and \( {H}_{j}\left( {M,\mathbb{Z}}\right)  = 0 \) for \( j = \; 1,\ldots , k - 1 \) . Hence, the universal coefficient theorem for cohomology implies that \( {H}^{j}\left( {M,\mathbb{Z}}\right)  = 0 \) for \( j = 1,\ldots , k - 1 \) (see [16], Chapter V, Corollary 7.3). Using Poincaré duality (see e.g. [16], Chapter VI, Corollary 8.4), we conclude that \( {H}_{n - j}\left( {M,\mathbb{Z}}\right)  = 0 \) for \( j = 1,\ldots , k - 1 \) . Since \( {H}_{k}\left( {M,\mathbb{Z}}\right)  \neq  0 \) , it follows that \( k \leq  \left\lbrack  \frac{n}{2}\right\rbrack \) .

We now apply an existence theorem for harmonic two-spheres. Since \( k \geq  2 \) and \( {\pi }_{k}\left( M\right)  \neq  0 \) , there exists a nonconstant harmonic map \( f : {S}^{2} \rightarrow  M \) with Morse index less than \( k - 1 \) (see [75], Chapter VII, Theorem 2). On the other hand, it follows from Theorem 1.19 that \( f \) has Morse index at least \( \left\lbrack  \frac{n - 2}{2}\right\rbrack \) . Putting these facts together, we conclude that \( k > \left\lbrack  \frac{n}{2}\right\rbrack \) . This is a contradiction.

Therefore, \( M \) is \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -connected. Consequently, \( M \) is a homotopy sphere. It now follows from work of Freedman [36] and Smale [81] that \( M \) is homeomorphic to \( {S}^{n} \) .

Definition 2.1. Let \( M \) be a manifold, and let \( g\left( t\right) , t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , be a one-parameter family of Riemannian metrics on \( M \) . We say that \( g\left( t\right) \) is a solution to the Ricci flow if

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}g\left( t\right)  =  - 2{\operatorname{Ric}}_{g\left( t\right) }.
\]

2.1.1. Einstein manifolds. Let \( \left( {M,{g}_{0}}\right) \) be a Riemannian manifold. We say that \( {g}_{0} \) is an Einstein metric if \( {\operatorname{Ric}}_{{g}_{0}} = \rho {g}_{0} \) for some constant \( \rho \) . In that case, the metrics

\[
g\left( t\right)  = \left( {1 - {2\rho t}}\right) {g}_{0}
\]

form a solution to the Ricci flow.

nodes.content:
2.1.2. Ricci solitons. Let \( \left( {M,{g}_{0}}\right) \) be a Riemannian manifold. We say that \( \left( {M,{g}_{0}}\right) \) is a Ricci soliton if there exists a constant \( \rho \) and a vector field \( \xi \) such that

\[
{\operatorname{Ric}}_{{g}_{0}} + \frac{1}{2}{\mathcal{L}}_{\xi }{g}_{0} = \rho {g}_{0},
\]

where \( {\mathcal{L}}_{\xi }{g}_{0} \) denotes the Lie derivative of \( {g}_{0} \) along the vector field \( \xi \) . Depending on the sign of \( \rho \) , a Ricci soliton is called shrinking \( \left( {\rho  > 0}\right) \) , steady \( \left( {\rho  = 0}\right) \) , or expanding \( \left( {\rho  < 0}\right) \) . If the vector field \( \xi \) is the gradient of a function, we say that \( \left( {M,{g}_{0}}\right) \) is a gradient Ricci soliton.

Suppose that \( \left( {M,{g}_{0}}\right) \) is a Ricci soliton. For each point \( p \in  M \) , we denote by \( {\varphi }_{t}\left( p\right) \) the unique solution of the ordinary differential equation (ODE)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\varphi }_{t}\left( p\right)  = {\left. \frac{1}{1 - {2\rho t}}\xi \right| }_{{\varphi }_{t}\left( p\right) }
\]

with initial condition \( {\varphi }_{0}\left( p\right)  = p \) . This defines a one-parameter family of diffeomorphisms \( {\varphi }_{t} : M \rightarrow  M \) . Then the metrics

\[
g\left( t\right)  = \left( {1 - {2\rho t}}\right) {\varphi }_{t}^{ * }\left( {g}_{0}\right)
\]

form a solution to the Ricci flow.

nodes.content:
2.1.3. The cigar soliton. The simplest example of a Ricci soliton is the cigar soliton on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \) . For each \( t \in  \left( {-\infty ,\infty }\right) \) , we define a metric \( g\left( t\right) \) on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \) by

\[
{g}_{ij}\left( t\right)  = \frac{4}{{e}^{t} + {\left| x\right| }^{2}}{\delta }_{ij}
\]

for \( x \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \) . The scalar curvature of \( g\left( t\right) \) is given by

\[
{\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( t\right) } = \frac{{e}^{t}}{{e}^{t} + {\left| x\right| }^{2}}.
\]

This implies

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}g\left( t\right)  =  - {\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( t\right) }g\left( t\right)  =  - 2{\operatorname{Ric}}_{g\left( t\right) }.
\]

Consequently, the metrics \( g\left( t\right) , t \in  \left( {-\infty ,\infty }\right) \) , form a solution to the Ricci flow. Moreover, we have \( g\left( t\right)  = {\varphi }_{t}^{ * }\left( {g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) , where \( {\varphi }_{t} : {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \rightarrow  {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \) is defined by \( {\varphi }_{t}\left( x\right)  = {e}^{-\frac{t}{2}}x \) . Thus, \( g\left( 0\right) \) is a steady Ricci soliton.

nodes.content:
2.1.4. The Rosenau solution. There is an interesting closed-form solution to the Ricci flow on \( {S}^{2} \) . For each \( t \in  \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) , we define a metric \( g\left( t\right) \) on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \) by

\[
{g}_{ij}\left( t\right)  = \frac{8\sinh \left( {-t}\right) }{1 + 2\cosh \left( {-t}\right) {\left| x\right| }^{2} + {\left| x\right| }^{4}}{\delta }_{ij}
\]

for \( x \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \) . Note that \( g\left( t\right) \) extends to a smooth metric on \( {S}^{2} \) . The scalar curvature of \( g\left( t\right) \) is given by

\[
{\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( t\right) } = \frac{\cosh \left( {-t}\right) }{\sinh \left( {-t}\right) } - \frac{2\sinh \left( {-t}\right) {\left| x\right| }^{2}}{1 + 2\cosh \left( {-t}\right) {\left| x\right| }^{2} + {\left| x\right| }^{4}}.
\]

This implies

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}g\left( t\right)  =  - {\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( t\right) }g\left( t\right)  =  - 2{\operatorname{Ric}}_{g\left( t\right) }.
\]

Consequently, the metrics \( g\left( t\right) , t \in  \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) , form a solution to the Ricci flow.

Definition 2.2. Let \( f \) be a smooth map from a Riemannian manifold \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) into a Riemannian manifold \( \left( {N, h}\right) \) . The harmonic map Laplacian of \( f \) is defined by

\[
{\Delta }_{g, h}f = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{{e}_{k}}{df}}\right) \left( {e}_{k}\right) ,
\]

where \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n}}\right\} \) is a local orthonormal frame on \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) . Here, the differential \( {df} \) is viewed as a section of the vector bundle \( T{M}^{ * } \otimes  {f}^{ * }\left( {TN}\right) \) , and \( D \) denotes the induced connection on that bundle. Note that \( {\Delta }_{g, h}f \) is a section of the vector bundle \( {f}^{ * }\left( {TN}\right) \) .

Clearly, the harmonic map Laplacian is invariant under the action of the diffeomorphism group of \( M \) .

\]

Definition 2.4. Let \( M \) be a compact manifold, and let \( h \) be a fixed background metric on \( M \) . Moreover, suppose that \( \widetilde{g}\left( t\right) , t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , is a one-parameter family of Riemannian metrics on \( M \) . We say that \( \widetilde{g}\left( t\right) \) is a solution of the Ricci-DeTurck flow if

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\widetilde{g}\left( t\right)  =  - 2{\operatorname{Ric}}_{\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) } - {\mathcal{L}}_{{\xi }_{t}}\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) ,
\]

where \( {\xi }_{t} = {\Delta }_{\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) , h} \) id.

nodes.content: Proposition 2.5. Let \( M \) be a compact manifold, and let \( h \) be a fixed background metric on \( M \) . Given any initial metric \( {g}_{0} \) , there exist a real number \( T > 0 \) and a smooth one-parameter family of metrics \( \widetilde{g}\left( t\right) , t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , such that \( \widetilde{g}\left( t\right) \) is a solution of the Ricci-DeTurck flow and \( \widetilde{g}\left( 0\right)  = {g}_{0} \) . Moreover, the solution \( \widetilde{g}\left( t\right) \) is unique.

nodes.proof:
In local coordinates, the Ricci tensor of \( \widetilde{g} \) is given by

\[
{\operatorname{Ric}}_{\widetilde{g}} =  - \frac{1}{2}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i, j, k, l = 1}}^{n}{\widetilde{g}}^{ik}\left( {{\partial }_{i}{\partial }_{k}{\widetilde{g}}_{jl} - {\partial }_{i}{\partial }_{l}{\widetilde{g}}_{jk} - {\partial }_{j}{\partial }_{k}{\widetilde{g}}_{il} + {\partial }_{j}{\partial }_{l}{\widetilde{g}}_{ik}}\right) d{x}^{j} \otimes  d{x}^{l}
\]

+ lower order terms.

Moreover, the vector field \( \xi  = {\Delta }_{\widetilde{g}, h} \) id can be written in the form

\[
\xi  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i, k, l = 1}}^{n}{\widetilde{g}}^{ik}\left( {{\left( {\Gamma }^{h}\right) }_{ik}^{l} - {\left( {\Gamma }^{\widetilde{g}}\right) }_{ik}^{l}}\right) {\partial }_{l},
\]

where \( {\Gamma }^{\widetilde{g}} \) and \( {\Gamma }^{h} \) denote the Christoffel symbols associated with the metrics \( \widetilde{g} \) and \( h \) , respectively. This implies

\[
\xi  =  - \frac{1}{2}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i, j, k, l = 1}}^{n}{\widetilde{g}}^{ik}{\widetilde{g}}^{jl}\left( {{\partial }_{i}{\widetilde{g}}_{jk} + {\partial }_{k}{\widetilde{g}}_{ij} - {\partial }_{j}{\widetilde{g}}_{ik}}\right) {\partial }_{l}
\]

\[
\text{ + lower order terms. }
\]

From this, we deduce that

\[
{\mathcal{L}}_{\xi }\widetilde{g} =  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i, j, k, l = 1}}^{n}{\widetilde{g}}^{ik}\left( {{\partial }_{i}{\partial }_{l}{\widetilde{g}}_{jk} + {\partial }_{j}{\partial }_{k}{\widetilde{g}}_{il} - {\partial }_{j}{\partial }_{l}{\widetilde{g}}_{ik}}\right) d{x}^{j} \otimes  d{x}^{l}
\]

\[
\text{ + lower order terms. }
\]

Putting these facts together, we obtain

\[
- 2{\operatorname{Ric}}_{\widetilde{g}} - {\mathcal{L}}_{\xi }\widetilde{g} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i, j, k, l = 1}}^{n}{\widetilde{g}}^{ik}{\partial }_{i}{\partial }_{k}{\widetilde{g}}_{jl}d{x}^{j} \otimes  d{x}^{l}
\]

\[
\text{ + lower order terms. }
\]

This shows that the Ricci-DeTurck flow is strictly parabolic. Hence, the assertion follows from standard existence and uniqueness theorems for parabolic systems.

Proposition 2.7. Fix a compact manifold \( M \) and a background metric \( h \) on \( M \) . Assume that \( g\left( t\right) , t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , is a solution to the Ricci flow on M. Moreover, we assume that \( {\varphi }_{t}, t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , is a one-parameter family of diffeomorphisms on \( M \) evolving under the harmonic map heat flow

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\varphi }_{t} = {\Delta }_{g\left( t\right) , h}{\varphi }_{t}.
\]

For each \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , we define a metric \( \widetilde{g}\left( t\right) \) by \( {\varphi }_{t}^{ * }\left( {\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) }\right)  = g\left( t\right) \) . Then

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\widetilde{g}\left( t\right)  =  - 2{\operatorname{Ric}}_{\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) } - {\mathcal{L}}_{{\xi }_{t}}\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) ,
\]

where \( {\xi }_{t} = {\Delta }_{\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) , h} \) id. Furthermore, we have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\varphi }_{t}\left( p\right)  = {\left. {\xi }_{t}\right| }_{{\varphi }_{t}\left( p\right) }
\]

for all points \( p \in  M \) and all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) .

Using Lemma 2.3, we obtain

\[
{\left. \frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\varphi }_{t}\left( p\right)  = \left( {\Delta }_{g\left( t\right) , h}{\varphi }_{t}\right) \right| }_{p} = {\left. \left( {\Delta }_{{\varphi }_{t}^{ * }\left( {\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) }\right) , h}{\varphi }_{t}\right) \right| }_{p} = {\left. \left( {\Delta }_{\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) , h}\mathrm{\;{id}}\right) \right| }_{{\varphi }_{t}\left( p\right) } = {\left. {\xi }_{t}\right| }_{{\varphi }_{t}\left( p\right) }
\]

for all points \( p \in  M \) and all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) . Since \( {\varphi }_{t}^{ * }\left( {\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) }\right)  = g\left( t\right) \) , it follows that

\[
{\varphi }_{t}^{ * }\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\widetilde{g}\left( t\right)  + {\mathcal{L}}_{{\xi }_{t}}\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) }\right)  = \frac{\partial }{\partial t}g\left( t\right) .
\]

By assumption, the metrics \( g\left( t\right) \) form a solution to the Ricci flow. Thus, we conclude that

\[
{\varphi }_{t}^{ * }\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\widetilde{g}\left( t\right)  + 2{\operatorname{Ric}}_{\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) } + {\mathcal{L}}_{{\xi }_{t}}\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) }\right)  = \frac{\partial }{\partial t}g\left( t\right)  + 2{\operatorname{Ric}}_{g\left( t\right) } = 0.
\]

This implies

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\widetilde{g}\left( t\right)  =  - 2{\operatorname{Ric}}_{\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) } - {\mathcal{L}}_{{\xi }_{t}}\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) ,
\]

as claimed.

nodes.content: Theorem 2.8 (R. Hamilton [44]). Let \( M \) be a compact manifold and let \( {g}_{0} \) be a smooth metric on \( M \) . Then there exist a real number \( T > 0 \) and a smooth one-parameter family of metrics \( g\left( t\right) , t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , such that \( g\left( t\right) \) is a solution of the Ricci flow and \( g\left( 0\right)  = {g}_{0} \) . Moreover, the solution \( g\left( t\right) \) is unique.
nodes.content_excerpt: Theorem 2.8 (R. Hamilton [44]). Let \( M \) be a compact manifold and let \( {g}_{0} \) be a smooth metric on \( M \) . Then there exist a real number \( T > 0 \) and a smooth one-parameter family of metrics \( g\left( t\right) , t \in \lbrack 0, T) \) , such that \( g\left( t\right) \) is a solution of the Ricci flow and \( g\left( 0\right) = {g}_{0} \) . Moreover, the solution \( g\left( t\right) \) is unique.

nodes.proof:
We first prove the existence statement. By Proposition 2.5, there exists a solution \( \widetilde{g}\left( t\right) \) of the Ricci-DeTurck flow which is defined on some time interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) and satisfies \( \widetilde{g}\left( 0\right)  = {g}_{0} \) . Consequently, we have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\widetilde{g}\left( t\right)  =  - 2{\operatorname{Ric}}_{\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) } - {\mathcal{L}}_{{\xi }_{t}}\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) ,
\]

where \( {\xi }_{t} = {\Delta }_{\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) , h} \) id. For each point \( p \in  M \) , we denote by \( {\varphi }_{t}\left( p\right) \) the solution of the ODE

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\varphi }_{t}\left( p\right)  = {\left. {\xi }_{t}\right| }_{{\varphi }_{t}\left( p\right) }
\]

with initial condition \( {\varphi }_{0}\left( p\right)  = p \) . By Proposition 2.6, the metrics \( g\left( t\right)  = \; {\varphi }_{t}^{ * }\left( {\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , form a solution of the Ricci flow with \( g\left( 0\right)  = {g}_{0} \) .

We now describe the proof of the uniqueness statement. Suppose that \( {g}^{1}\left( t\right) \) and \( {g}^{2}\left( t\right) \) are two solutions to the Ricci flow which are defined on some time interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) and satisfy \( {g}^{1}\left( 0\right)  = {g}^{2}\left( 0\right) \) . We claim that \( {g}^{1}\left( t\right)  = {g}^{2}\left( t\right) \) for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) . In order to prove this, we argue by contradiction. Suppose that that \( {g}^{1}\left( t\right)  \neq  {g}^{2}\left( t\right) \) for some \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) . We define a real number \( \tau  \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) by

\[
\tau  = \inf \left\{  {t \in  \lbrack 0, T) : {g}^{1}\left( t\right)  \neq  {g}^{2}\left( t\right) }\right\}  .
\]

Clearly, \( {g}^{1}\left( \tau \right)  = {g}^{2}\left( \tau \right) \) . Let \( {\varphi }_{t}^{1} \) be the solution of the harmonic map heat flow

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\varphi }_{t}^{1} = {\Delta }_{{g}^{1}\left( t\right) , h}{\varphi }_{t}^{1}
\]

with initial condition \( {\varphi }_{\tau }^{1} = \) id. Similarly, we denote by \( {\varphi }_{t}^{2} \) the solution of the harmonic map heat flow

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\varphi }_{t}^{2} = {\Delta }_{{g}^{2}\left( t\right) , h}{\varphi }_{t}^{2}
\]

with initial condition \( {\varphi }_{\tau }^{2} = \) id. It follows from standard parabolic theory that \( {\varphi }_{t}^{1} \) and \( {\varphi }_{t}^{2} \) are defined on some time interval \( \lbrack \tau ,\tau  + \varepsilon ) \) , where \( \varepsilon \) is a positive real number. Moreover, if we choose \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) small enough, then \( {\varphi }_{t}^{1} : M \rightarrow  M \) and \( {\varphi }_{t}^{2} : M \rightarrow  M \) are diffeomorphisms for all \( t \in  \lbrack \tau ,\tau  + \varepsilon ) \) .

For each \( t \in  \lbrack \tau ,\tau  + \varepsilon ) \) , we define two Riemannian metrics \( {\widetilde{g}}^{1}\left( t\right) \) and \( {\widetilde{g}}^{2}\left( t\right) \) on \( M \) by \( {\left( {\varphi }_{t}^{1}\right) }^{ * }\left( {{\widetilde{g}}^{1}\left( t\right) }\right)  = {g}^{1}\left( t\right) \) and \( {\left( {\varphi }_{t}^{2}\right) }^{ * }\left( {{\widetilde{g}}^{2}\left( t\right) }\right)  = {g}^{2}\left( t\right) \) . It follows from Proposition 2.7 that \( {\widetilde{g}}^{1}\left( t\right) \) and \( {\widetilde{g}}^{2}\left( t\right) \) are solutions of the Ricci-DeTurck flow. Since \( {\widetilde{g}}^{1}\left( \tau \right)  = {\widetilde{g}}^{2}\left( \tau \right) \) , the uniqueness statement in Proposition 2.5 implies that \( {\widetilde{g}}^{1}\left( t\right)  = {\widetilde{g}}^{2}\left( t\right) \) for all \( t \in  \lbrack \tau ,\tau  + \varepsilon ) \) . For each \( t \in  \lbrack \tau ,\tau  + \varepsilon ) \) , we define a vector field \( {\xi }_{t} \) on \( M \) by

\[
{\xi }_{t} = {\Delta }_{{\widetilde{g}}^{1}\left( t\right) , h}\mathrm{{id}} = {\Delta }_{{\widetilde{g}}^{2}\left( t\right) , h}\mathrm{{id}}.
\]

By Proposition 2.7, we have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\varphi }_{t}^{1}\left( p\right)  = {\left. {\xi }_{t}\right| }_{{\varphi }_{t}^{1}\left( p\right) }
\]

and

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\varphi }_{t}^{2}\left( p\right)  = {\left. {\xi }_{t}\right| }_{{\varphi }_{t}^{2}\left( p\right) }
\]

for all points \( p \in  M \) and all \( t \in  \lbrack \tau ,\tau  + \varepsilon ) \) . Since \( {\varphi }_{\tau }^{1} = {\varphi }_{\tau }^{2} = \) id, it follows that \( {\varphi }_{t}^{1} = {\varphi }_{t}^{2} \) for all \( t \in  \lbrack \tau ,\tau  + \varepsilon ) \) . Putting these facts together, we conclude that

\[
{g}^{1}\left( t\right)  = {\left( {\varphi }_{t}^{1}\right) }^{ * }\left( {{\widetilde{g}}^{1}\left( t\right) }\right)  = {\left( {\varphi }_{t}^{2}\right) }^{ * }\left( {{\widetilde{g}}^{2}\left( t\right) }\right)  = {g}^{2}\left( t\right)
\]

for all \( t \in  \lbrack \tau ,\tau  + \varepsilon ) \) . This contradicts the definition of \( \tau \) .

Proposition 2.9. Let \( X, Y, Z \) be fixed vector fields on \( M \) . Then

\[
g\left( {A\left( {X, Y}\right) , Z}\right)  =  - \left( {{D}_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Z}\right)  - \left( {{D}_{Y}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {X, Z}\right)  + \left( {{D}_{Z}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {X, Y}\right) .
\]

nodes.proof:
By definition of the Levi-Civita connection, we have

\[
{2g}\left( {{D}_{X}Y, Z}\right)  = X\left( {g\left( {Y, Z}\right) }\right)  + Y\left( {g\left( {X, Z}\right) }\right)  - Z\left( {g\left( {X, Y}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
+ g\left( {\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  , Z}\right)  - g\left( {\left\lbrack  {X, Z}\right\rbrack  , Y}\right)  - g\left( {\left\lbrack  {Y, Z}\right\rbrack  , X}\right)
\]

(cf. Section 1.1). We now differentiate this identity with respect to \( t \) . This yields

\[
g\left( {A\left( {X, Y}\right) , Z}\right)  = \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {g\left( {{D}_{X}Y, Z}\right) }\right)  + 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {{D}_{X}Y, Z}\right)
\]

\[
=  - X\left( {\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Z}\right) }\right)  - Y\left( {\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, Z}\right) }\right)  + Z\left( {\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, Y}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
- \operatorname{Ric}\left( {\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  , Z}\right)  + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {\left\lbrack  {X, Z}\right\rbrack  , Y}\right)  + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {\left\lbrack  {Y, Z}\right\rbrack  , X}\right)
\]

\[
+ 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {{D}_{X}Y, Z}\right) \text{ . }
\]

Since \( A \) is a tensor, we conclude that

\[
g\left( {A\left( {X, Y}\right) , Z}\right)  =  - \left( {{D}_{X}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Z}\right)  - \left( {{D}_{Y}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {X, Z}\right)  + \left( {{D}_{Z}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {X, Y}\right) ,
\]

as claimed.

nodes.proof:
We have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {{D}_{X}{D}_{Y}Z - {D}_{Y}{D}_{X}Z - {D}_{\left\lbrack  X, Y\right\rbrack  }Z}\right)
\]

\[
= {D}_{X}\left( {A\left( {Y, Z}\right) }\right)  - {D}_{Y}\left( {A\left( {X, Z}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
+ A\left( {X,{D}_{Y}Z}\right)  - A\left( {Y,{D}_{X}Z}\right)  - A\left( {\left\lbrack  {X, Y}\right\rbrack  , Z}\right)
\]

\[
= \left( {{D}_{X}A}\right) \left( {Y, Z}\right)  - \left( {{D}_{Y}A}\right) \left( {X, Z}\right) .
\]

This implies

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}R\left( {X, Y, Z, W}\right)  =  - g\left( {\left( {{D}_{X}A}\right) \left( {Y, Z}\right) , W}\right)  + g\left( {\left( {{D}_{Y}A}\right) \left( {X, Z}\right) , W}\right)
\]

\[
- 2\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}R\left( {X, Y, Z,{e}_{k}}\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{k}, W}\right) .
\]

Using Proposition 2.9, we obtain

\[
g\left( {\left( {{D}_{X}A}\right) \left( {Y, Z}\right) , W}\right)
\]

\[
=  - \left( {{D}_{X, Y}^{2}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Z, W}\right)  - \left( {{D}_{X, Z}^{2}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, W}\right)  + \left( {{D}_{X, W}^{2}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Z}\right) .
\]

Interchanging the roles of \( X \) and \( Y \) yields

\[
g\left( {\left( {{D}_{Y}A}\right) \left( {X, Z}\right) , W}\right)
\]

\[
=  - \left( {{D}_{Y, X}^{2}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Z, W}\right)  - \left( {{D}_{Y, Z}^{2}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {X, W}\right)  + \left( {{D}_{Y, W}^{2}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {X, Z}\right) .
\]

Moreover, we have

\[
\left( {{D}_{X, Y}^{2}\mathrm{{Ric}}}\right) \left( {Z, W}\right)  - \left( {{D}_{Y, X}^{2}\mathrm{{Ric}}}\right) \left( {Z, W}\right)
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}R\left( {X, Y, Z,{e}_{k}}\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{k}, W}\right)  + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}R\left( {X, Y, W,{e}_{k}}\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Z,{e}_{k}}\right) .
\]

Putting these facts together, we obtain

\[

\]

\[

\]

\[
- \left( {{D}_{Y, X}^{2}\mathrm{{Ric}}}\right) \left( {Z, W}\right)  - \left( {{D}_{Y, Z}^{2}\mathrm{{Ric}}}\right) \left( {X, W}\right)  + \left( {{D}_{Y, W}^{2}\mathrm{{Ric}}}\right) \left( {X, Z}\right)
\]

\[
- 2\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}R\left( {X, Y, Z,{e}_{k}}\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{k}, W}\right)
\]

\[
= \left( {{D}_{X, Z}^{2}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, W}\right)  - \left( {{D}_{X, W}^{2}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {Y, Z}\right)
\]

\[
- \left( {{D}_{Y, Z}^{2}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {X, W}\right)  + \left( {{D}_{Y, W}^{2}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {X, Z}\right)
\]

\[
+ \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}R\left( {X, Y, W,{e}_{k}}\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Z,{e}_{k}}\right)  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}R\left( {X, Y, Z,{e}_{k}}\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{k}, W}\right) ,
\]

as claimed.

nodes.proof:
Note that

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{X,{e}_{k}}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, Y, Z, W}\right)  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{{e}_{k}, X}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, Y, Z, W}\right)
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k, l = 1}}^{n}R\left( {X,{e}_{k},{e}_{k},{e}_{l}}\right) R\left( {{e}_{l}, Y, Z, W}\right)  + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k, l = 1}}^{n}R\left( {X,{e}_{k}, Y,{e}_{l}}\right) R\left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{l}, Z, W}\right)
\]

\[
+ \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k, l = 1}}^{n}R\left( {X,{e}_{k}, Z,{e}_{l}}\right) R\left( {{e}_{k}, Y,{e}_{l}, W}\right)  + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k, l = 1}}^{n}R\left( {X,{e}_{k}, W,{e}_{l}}\right) R\left( {{e}_{k}, Y, Z,{e}_{l}}\right) .
\]

Interchanging the roles of \( X \) and \( Y \) yields

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{Y,{e}_{k}}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, X, Z, W}\right)  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{{e}_{k}, Y}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, X, Z, W}\right)
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k, l = 1}}^{n}R\left( {Y,{e}_{k},{e}_{k},{e}_{l}}\right) R\left( {{e}_{l}, X, Z, W}\right)  + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k, l = 1}}^{n}R\left( {Y,{e}_{k}, X,{e}_{l}}\right) R\left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{l}, Z, W}\right)
\]

\[
+ \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k, l = 1}}^{n}R\left( {Y,{e}_{k}, Z,{e}_{l}}\right) R\left( {{e}_{k}, X,{e}_{l}, W}\right)  + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k, l = 1}}^{n}R\left( {Y,{e}_{k}, W,{e}_{l}}\right) R\left( {{e}_{k}, X, Z,{e}_{l}}\right) .
\]

We now subtract the second identity from the first. This implies

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{X,{e}_{k}}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, Y, Z, W}\right)  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{Y,{e}_{k}}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, X, Z, W}\right)
\]

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{{e}_{k}, X}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, Y, Z, W}\right)  + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{{e}_{k}, Y}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, X, Z, W}\right)
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k, l = 1}}^{n}\left\lbrack  {R\left( {X,{e}_{k}, Y,{e}_{l}}\right)  - R\left( {Y,{e}_{k}, X,{e}_{l}}\right) }\right\rbrack  R\left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{l}, Z, W}\right)
\]

\[
+ 2\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k, l = 1}}^{n}R\left( {X,{e}_{k}, Z,{e}_{l}}\right) R\left( {Y,{e}_{k}, W,{e}_{l}}\right)  - 2\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k, l = 1}}^{n}R\left( {X,{e}_{k}, W,{e}_{l}}\right) R\left( {Y,{e}_{k}, Z,{e}_{l}}\right)
\]

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{l = 1}}^{n}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X,{e}_{l}}\right) R\left( {{e}_{l}, Y, Z, W}\right)  + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{l = 1}}^{n}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y,{e}_{l}}\right) R\left( {{e}_{l}, X, Z, W}\right) .
\]

It follows from the first Bianchi identity that

\[
R\left( {X,{e}_{k}, Y,{e}_{l}}\right)  - R\left( {Y,{e}_{k}, X,{e}_{l}}\right)  = R\left( {X, Y,{e}_{k},{e}_{l}}\right) .
\]

Hence, we obtain

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{X,{e}_{k}}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, Y, Z, W}\right)  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{Y,{e}_{k}}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, X, Z, W}\right)
\]

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{{e}_{k}, X}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, Y, Z, W}\right)  + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{{e}_{k}, Y}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, X, Z, W}\right)
\]

\[
= Q\left( R\right) \left( {X, Y, Z, W}\right)
\]

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{l = 1}}^{n}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X,{e}_{l}}\right) R\left( {{e}_{l}, Y, Z, W}\right)  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{l = 1}}^{n}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y,{e}_{l}}\right) R\left( {X,{e}_{l}, Z, W}\right) .
\]

Using the second Bianchi identity, we obtain

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{X,{e}_{k}}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, Y, Z, W}\right)
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{X, Z}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, Y,{e}_{k}, W}\right)  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{X, W}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, Y,{e}_{k}, Z}\right)
\]

\[
= \left( {{D}_{X, Z}^{2}\mathrm{{Ric}}}\right) \left( {Y, W}\right)  - \left( {{D}_{X, W}^{2}\mathrm{{Ric}}}\right) \left( {Y, Z}\right) .
\]

Interchanging the roles of \( X \) and \( Y \) yields

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{Y,{e}_{k}}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, X, Z, W}\right)
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{Y, Z}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, X,{e}_{k}, W}\right)  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{Y, W}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, X,{e}_{k}, Z}\right)
\]

\[
= \left( {{D}_{Y, Z}^{2}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {X, W}\right)  - \left( {{D}_{Y, W}^{2}\operatorname{Ric}}\right) \left( {X, Z}\right) .
\]

Moreover, the second Bianchi identity implies that

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{{e}_{k}, X}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, Y, Z, W}\right)  - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{n}\left( {{D}_{{e}_{k}, Y}^{2}R}\right) \left( {{e}_{k}, X, Z, W}\right)
\]

\[

### 3.1. Estimates for the derivatives of the curvature tensor

In this section, we establish estimates for the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor. These estimates were proved by W.X. Shi [78] (see also [49], Section 7). Throughout this section, we assume that \( M \) is a compact manifold and \( g\left( t\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\tau }\right\rbrack \) , is a solution to the Ricci flow on \( M \) . To fix notation, we denote by \( {D}^{m}R \) the \( m \) th iterated covariant derivative of the Riemann curvature tensor. Given two tensors \( A, B \) , we shall write \( A * B \) for any bilinear expression in \( A \) and \( B \) .

nodes.label: Lemma 3.1
nodes.document_title: Simon Brendle - Ricci Flow and the Sphere Theorem
nodes.section_title: 3.1. Estimates for the derivatives of the curvature tensor
nodes.content:
Lemma 3.1. Let \( M \) be a smooth manifold, and let \( g\left( t\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\tau }\right\rbrack \) , be a solution to the Ricci flow on \( M \) . Then

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{D}^{m}R = \Delta {D}^{m}R + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{l = 0}}^{m}{D}^{l}R * {D}^{m - l}R
\]

for \( m = 0,1,2,\ldots \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: Lemma 3.1. Let \( M \) be a smooth manifold, and let \( g\left( t\right) , t \in \left\lbrack {0,\tau }\right\rbrack \) , be a solution to the Ricci flow on \( M \) . Then \[ \frac{\partial }{\partial t}{D}^{m}R = \Delta {D}^{m}R + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{l = 0}}^{m}{D}^{l}R * {D}^{m - l}R \] for \( m = 0,1,2,\ldots \) .

nodes.proof:
The proof is by induction on \( m \) . By Corollary 2.12, the assertion holds for \( m = 0 \) . We next assume that \( m \geq  1 \) and

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{D}^{m - 1}R = \Delta {D}^{m - 1}R + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{l = 0}}^{{m - 1}}{D}^{l}R * {D}^{m - l - 1}R.
\]

This implies

\[
D\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{D}^{m - 1}R = {D\Delta }{D}^{m - 1}R + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{l = 0}}^{m}{D}^{l}R * {D}^{m - l}R.
\]

Using Proposition 2.9, we obtain

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{D}^{m}R = D\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{D}^{m - 1}R + {DR} * {D}^{m - 1}R.
\]

Moreover, we have

\[
\Delta {D}^{m}R = {D\Delta }{D}^{m - 1}R + R * {D}^{m}R + {DR} * {D}^{m - 1}R.
\]

Putting these facts together, we conclude that

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{D}^{m}R = \Delta {D}^{m}R + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{l = 0}}^{m}{D}^{l}R * {D}^{m - l}R.

\[

\[

Moreover, we have

\[
\Delta {D}^{m}H = {D\Delta }{D}^{m - 1}H + R * {D}^{m}H + {DR} * {D}^{m - 1}H.

Putting these facts together, we conclude that

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{D}^{m}H = \Delta {D}^{m}H + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{l = 0}}^{m}{D}^{l}R * {D}^{m - l}H.
\]

This completes the proof.

Theorem 3.7 (R. Hamilton [44]). Let \( M \) be a compact manifold, and let \( g\left( t\right) , t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , be a maximal solution to the Ricci flow on \( M \) . Moreover, suppose that \( T < \infty \) . Then

\]

nodes.content_excerpt: Lemma 4.2. Let \( t \) be an arbitrary real number. Then \[ \frac{at}{2\pi } \in \mathbb{Z} \Leftrightarrow {\varphi }_{t} = \mathrm{{id}} \Leftrightarrow \frac{bt}{2\pi } \in \mathbb{Z}. \]

nodes.proof:
Suppose that \( \frac{at}{2\pi } \) is an integer. Using (15), we obtain \( {\left( d{\varphi }_{t}\right) }_{p}\left( v\right)  = v \) for all \( v \in  {T}_{p}{S}^{2} \) . Since \( {\varphi }_{t} \) is an isometry, it follows that

\[
{\varphi }_{t}\left( {{\exp }_{p}\left( v\right) }\right)  = {\exp }_{{\varphi }_{t}\left( p\right) }\left( {{\left( d{\varphi }_{t}\right) }_{p}\left( v\right) }\right)  = {\exp }_{p}\left( v\right)
\]

for all vectors \( v \in  {T}_{p}{S}^{2} \) . Consequently, \( {\varphi }_{t} = \mathrm{{id}} \) .

Conversely, if \( {\varphi }_{t} = \mathrm{{id}} \) , then \( {\left( d{\varphi }_{t}\right) }_{p}\left( v\right)  = v \) for all vectors \( v \in  {T}_{p}{S}^{2} \) . Hence, it follows from (15) that \( \frac{at}{2\pi } \) is an integer.

To summarize, we have proved that \( \frac{at}{2\pi } \in  \mathbb{Z} \Leftrightarrow  {\varphi }_{t} = \mathrm{{id}} \) . An analogous argument shows that \( \frac{bt}{2\pi } \in  \mathbb{Z} \Leftrightarrow  {\varphi }_{t} = \mathrm{{id}} \) .

nodes.label: Proposition 4.3
nodes.document_title: Simon Brendle - Ricci Flow and the Sphere Theorem
nodes.content: Proposition 4.3. Assume that \( \left( {{S}^{2}, g}\right) \) is a gradient Ricci soliton. Then \( g \) has constant scalar curvature.
nodes.content_excerpt: Proposition 4.3. Assume that \( \left( {{S}^{2}, g}\right) \) is a gradient Ricci soliton. Then \( g \) has constant scalar curvature.

nodes.proof:
We closely follow the arguments in [29]. There exists a unit-speed geodesic \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,\sigma }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left( {{S}^{2}, g}\right) \) such that \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p,\gamma \left( \sigma \right)  = q \) , and \( \sigma  = d\left( {p, q}\right) \) . By Lemma 4.1, the map \( {\varphi }_{t} : \left( {{S}^{2}, g}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{S}^{2}, g}\right) \) is an isometry. Hence, for each \( t \in  \mathbb{R} \) , the curve \( s \mapsto  {\varphi }_{t}\left( {\gamma \left( s\right) }\right) \) is a unit-speed geodesic.

We define a vector field \( V \) along \( \gamma \) by

\[
V\left( s\right)  = {\left. \frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\varphi }_{t}\left( \gamma \left( s\right) \right) \right| }_{t = 0} = {\left. J\xi \right| }_{\gamma \left( s\right) }
\]

for all \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\sigma }\right\rbrack \) . Clearly, \( V \) is a Jacobi field along \( \gamma \) with \( V\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) and \( V\left( \sigma \right)  = 0 \) . This implies \( \left\langle  {V\left( s\right) ,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) }\right\rangle   = 0 \) for all \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\sigma }\right\rbrack \) . Hence, there exists a smooth function \( u : \left\lbrack  {0,\sigma }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) such that \( V\left( s\right)  = u\left( s\right) J{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) \) for all \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\sigma }\right\rbrack \) . Moreover, \( u\left( 0\right)  = u\left( \sigma \right)  = 0 \) .

Since \( V \) is a Jacobi field, we have

(17)

\[
{u}^{\prime \prime }\left( s\right)  + \frac{1}{2}u\left( s\right) {\operatorname{scal}}_{g}\left( {\gamma \left( s\right) }\right)  = 0
\]

for all \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\sigma }\right\rbrack \) . We next observe that

\[
\left\langle  {{\left. \xi \right| }_{\gamma \left( s\right) },{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) }\right\rangle   = \left\langle  {V\left( s\right) , J{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) }\right\rangle   = u\left( s\right)
\]

for all \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\sigma }\right\rbrack \) . Differentiating this identity with respect to \( s \) yields

\[
{\left( {D}^{2}f\right) }_{\gamma \left( s\right) }\left( {{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) ,{\gamma }^{\prime }\left( s\right) }\right)  = {u}^{\prime }\left( s\right)
\]

for all \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\sigma }\right\rbrack \) . Using the identity (14), we obtain

(18)

\[
\rho  - \frac{1}{2}{\operatorname{scal}}_{g}\left( {\gamma \left( s\right) }\right)  = {u}^{\prime }\left( s\right)
\]

for all \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\sigma }\right\rbrack \) . Substituting (18) into (17), we conclude that

(19)

\[
{u}^{\prime \prime }\left( s\right)  + {\rho u}\left( s\right)  = u\left( s\right) {u}^{\prime }\left( s\right)
\]

for all \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\sigma }\right\rbrack \) .

The identity (18) implies that

\[
a = \rho  - \frac{1}{2}{\operatorname{scal}}_{g}\left( p\right)  = {u}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)
\]

and

\[
b = \rho  - \frac{1}{2}{\operatorname{scal}}_{g}\left( q\right)  = {u}^{\prime }\left( \sigma \right) .
\]

Moreover, it follows from Lemma 4.2 that \( {a}^{2} = {b}^{2} \) . Thus, we conclude that \( {u}^{\prime }{\left( 0\right) }^{2} = {u}^{\prime }{\left( \sigma \right) }^{2} \) . Using (19), we obtain

\[
0 = \frac{1}{2}\left( {{u}^{\prime }{\left( \sigma \right) }^{2} - {u}^{\prime }{\left( 0\right) }^{2}}\right)  + \frac{1}{2}\rho \left( {u{\left( \sigma \right) }^{2} - u{\left( 0\right) }^{2}}\right)  = {\int }_{0}^{\sigma }u\left( s\right) {u}^{\prime }{\left( s\right) }^{2}{ds}.
\]

Consequently, there exists a real number \( {s}_{0} \in  \left( {0,\sigma }\right) \) such that \( u\left( {s}_{0}\right)  = 0 \) . Since \( \gamma \) is free of conjugate points, it follows that \( u\left( s\right)  = 0 \) for all \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\sigma }\right\rbrack \) . In particular, we have \( a = {u}^{\prime }\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) and \( b = {u}^{\prime }\left( \sigma \right)  = 0 \) . Using Lemma 4.2, we obtain \( {\varphi }_{t} = \mathrm{{id}} \) for all \( t \in  \mathbb{R} \) . Therefore, the vector field \( {J\xi } \) vanishes identically. Consequently, \( f \) is constant and \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{g} = {2\rho } \) .

nodes.label: Lemma 4.4

nodes.content: Lemma 4.4. We have \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {{S}^{2}, g\left( t\right) }\right)  = {8\pi }\left( {1 - t}\right) \) for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) . In particular, \( T \leq  1 \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: Lemma 4.4. We have \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {{S}^{2}, g\left( t\right) }\right) = {8\pi }\left( {1 - t}\right) \) for all \( t \in \lbrack 0, T) \) . In particular, \( T \leq 1 \) .

nodes.proof:
Using the Gauss-Bonnet theorem, we obtain

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{vol}\left( {{S}^{2}, g\left( t\right) }\right)  =  - {\int }_{{S}^{2}}\operatorname{scal}d\operatorname{vol} =  - {8\pi }.
\]

From this, the assertion follows.

nodes.content: Lemma 4.5. We have \( \mathcal{E}\left( t\right)  \geq  0 \) for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) .

We have the pointwise estimate

\[

Using the Gauss-Bonnet theorem and Lemma 4.4, we obtain

\[

\]

\[
\geq  {\int }_{{S}^{2}}\left( {\operatorname{scal} - \frac{1}{1 - t}}\right) d\operatorname{vol} = 0,
\]

as claimed.

nodes.label: Lemma 4.6
nodes.document_title: Simon Brendle - Ricci Flow and the Sphere Theorem
nodes.content:
Lemma 4.6. For each \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , we have

\[
{\int }_{{S}^{2}}\frac{1}{\operatorname{scal}}{\left| d\operatorname{scal}\right| }^{2}d\operatorname{vol} \geq  {\int }_{{S}^{2}}{\left( \Delta f\right) }^{2}d\operatorname{vol} + 2{\int }_{{S}^{2}}{\left| M\right| }^{2}d\operatorname{vol}.
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: Lemma 4.6. For each \( t \in \lbrack 0, T) \) , we have \[ {\int }_{{S}^{2}}\frac{1}{\operatorname{scal}}{\left| d\operatorname{scal}\right| }^{2}d\operatorname{vol} \geq {\int }_{{S}^{2}}{\left( \Delta f\right) }^{2}d\operatorname{vol} + 2{\int }_{{S}^{2}}{\left| M\right| }^{2}d\operatorname{vol}. \]

nodes.proof:
We use an argument due to B. Chow. Since the sum scal \( + {\Delta f} \) is constant, we have

\[
{\int }_{{S}^{2}}\frac{1}{\text{ scal }}{\left| d\text{ scal }\right| }^{2}d\text{ vol } - 2{\int }_{{S}^{2}}{\left( \Delta f\right) }^{2}d\text{ vol } + {\int }_{{S}^{2}}\text{ scal }{\left| df\right| }^{2}d\text{ vol }
\]

\[
= {\int }_{{S}^{2}}\frac{1}{\text{ scal }}{\left| d\text{ scal }\right| }^{2}d\text{ vol } - 2{\int }_{{S}^{2}}\langle d\text{ scal },{df}\rangle d\text{ vol } + {\int }_{{S}^{2}}\text{ scal }{\left| df\right| }^{2}d\text{ vol }
\]

\[
= {\int }_{{S}^{2}}\frac{1}{\text{ scal }}{\left| d\text{ scal } - \operatorname{scal}df\right| }^{2}d\text{ vol } \geq  0.
\]

Moreover, it follows from the Bochner formula that

\[
2{\int }_{{S}^{2}}{\left( \Delta f\right) }^{2}d\operatorname{vol} - {\int }_{{S}^{2}}\operatorname{scal}{\left| df\right| }^{2}d\operatorname{vol} = 2{\int }_{{S}^{2}}{\left| {D}^{2}f\right| }^{2}d\operatorname{vol}.
\]

Putting these facts together, we obtain

\[
{\int }_{{S}^{2}}\frac{1}{\operatorname{scal}}{\left| d\operatorname{scal}\right| }^{2}d\operatorname{vol} \geq  2{\int }_{{S}^{2}}{\left| {D}^{2}f\right| }^{2}d\operatorname{vol}.
\]

Since \( {\left| {D}^{2}f\right| }^{2} = \frac{1}{2}{\left( \Delta f\right) }^{2} + {\left| M\right| }^{2} \) , the assertion follows.

nodes.content: Proposition 4.7. We have \( \frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{E}\left( t\right)  \leq   - 2\mathcal{M}\left( t\right) \) for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) . In particular, the function \( t \mapsto  \mathcal{E}\left( t\right) \) is monotone decreasing.
nodes.content_excerpt: Proposition 4.7. We have \( \frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{E}\left( t\right) \leq - 2\mathcal{M}\left( t\right) \) for all \( t \in \lbrack 0, T) \) . In particular, the function \( t \mapsto \mathcal{E}\left( t\right) \) is monotone decreasing.

nodes.proof:
By Corollary 2.16, the scalar curvature of \( g\left( t\right) \) satisfies the evolution equation

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\operatorname{scal} = \Delta \operatorname{scal} + {\operatorname{scal}}^{2}.
\]

This implies

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{E}\left( t\right)  =  - {\int }_{{S}^{2}}\frac{1}{\text{ scal }}{\left| d\text{ scal }\right| }^{2}d\text{ vol } + {\int }_{{S}^{2}}{\operatorname{scal}}^{2}d\text{ vol } - \frac{8\pi }{1 - t}
\]

\[
=  - {\int }_{{S}^{2}}\frac{1}{\text{ scal }}{\left| d\text{ scal }\right| }^{2}d\text{ vol } + {\int }_{{S}^{2}}{\left( \Delta f\right) }^{2}d\text{ vol }.
\]

Hence, the assertion follows from Lemma 4.6.

nodes.label: Proposition 4.8
nodes.document_title: Simon Brendle - Ricci Flow and the Sphere Theorem
nodes.content:
Proposition 4.8. We have \( T = 1 \) and

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \lbrack 0,1)}}\left\lbrack  {\left( {1 - t}\right) \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{S}^{2}}{\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( t\right) }}\right\rbrack   < \infty .
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: Proposition 4.8. We have \( T = 1 \) and \[ \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in \lbrack 0,1)}}\left\lbrack {\left( {1 - t}\right) \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{S}^{2}}{\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( t\right) }}\right\rbrack < \infty . \]

nodes.proof:
The assertion follows from Theorem 3.7 if we can show that

(24)

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \lbrack 0, T)}}\left\lbrack  {\left( {1 - t}\right) \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{S}^{2}}{\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( t\right) }}\right\rbrack   < \infty .
\]

To prove (24), we argue by contradiction. Suppose that (24) is false. We define a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) by

\[
{t}_{k} = \inf \left\{  {t \in  \lbrack 0, T) : \left( {1 - t}\right) \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{S}^{2}}{\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( t\right) } \geq  {2k}}\right\}  .
\]

In the following, we will choose \( k \) sufficiently large so that \( {t}_{k} > 0 \) . For each \( k \) , we choose a point \( {p}_{k} \in  {S}^{2} \) where the scalar curvature of \( g\left( {t}_{k}\right) \) attains its maximum. This implies

\[
{\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\left( {p}_{k}\right)  = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{S}^{2}}{\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( {t}_{k}\right) } = \frac{2k}{1 - {t}_{k}}.
\]

By Corollary 3.3, there exists a uniform constant \( N \geq  1 \) such that

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{S}^{2}}{\left| d{\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right| }^{2} \leq  N{\left( \frac{k}{1 - {t}_{k}}\right) }^{3}
\]

for all \( k \) . Hence, if we define

\[
{\Omega }_{k} = \left\{  {x \in  {S}^{2} : {d}_{g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\left( {{p}_{k}, x}\right)  \leq  \sqrt{\frac{1 - {t}_{k}}{Nk}}}\right\}  ,
\]

then

\[
\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{x \in  {\Omega }_{k}}}{\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\left( x\right)  \geq  {\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\left( {p}_{k}\right)  - \frac{k}{1 - {t}_{k}} = \frac{k}{1 - {t}_{k}}
\]

for all \( k \) . This implies

\[
{\int }_{{\Omega }_{k}}{\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\log \left( {\left( {1 - {t}_{k}}\right) {\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }}\right) d{\operatorname{vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }
\]

(25)

\[
\geq  \frac{k\log k}{1 - {t}_{k}}\operatorname{vol}\left( {{\Omega }_{k}, g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) .
\]

Using the pointwise estimate

\[
\left( {1 - {t}_{k}}\right) {\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\log \left( {\left( {1 - t}\right) {\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }}\right)  \geq   - 1,
\]

we obtain

\[
{\int }_{{S}^{2} \smallsetminus  {\Omega }_{k}}{\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\log \left( {\left( {1 - {t}_{k}}\right) {\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }}\right) d{\operatorname{vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }
\]

(26)

\[
\geq   - \frac{1}{1 - {t}_{k}}\operatorname{vol}\left( {{S}^{2} \smallsetminus  {\Omega }_{k}, g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right)  \geq   - {8\pi }.
\]

Adding (25) and (26) yields

\[
\mathcal{E}\left( {t}_{k}\right)  = {\int }_{{S}^{2}}{\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\log \left( {\left( {1 - {t}_{k}}\right) {\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }}\right) d{\operatorname{vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }
\]

(27)

\[
\geq  \frac{k\log k}{1 - {t}_{k}}\operatorname{vol}\left( {{\Omega }_{k}, g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right)  - {8\pi }.
\]

By a theorem of Klingenberg (see [26], Theorem 5.9), the injectivity radius of \( \left( {{S}^{2}, g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) is bounded from below by

\[
\operatorname{inj}\left( {{S}^{2}, g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right)  \geq  \pi \sqrt{\frac{1 - {t}_{k}}{k}}.
\]

Therefore, the radius of the ball \( {\Omega }_{k} \) is smaller than the injectivity radius of \( \left( {{S}^{2}, g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) . This implies

\[
\mathop{\liminf }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}\frac{k}{1 - {t}_{k}}\operatorname{vol}\left( {{\Omega }_{k}, g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right)  > 0.
\]

Hence, it follows from (27) that \( \mathcal{E}\left( {t}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) . This contradicts Proposition 4.7.

By Proposition 4.8, we have

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \lbrack 0,1)}}\left\lbrack  {\left( {1 - t}\right) \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{S}^{2}}{\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( t\right) }}\right\rbrack   < \infty .
\]

Using Corollary 3.3, we obtain

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \lbrack 0,1)}}\left\lbrack  {{\left( 1 - t\right) }^{m + 2}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{S}^{2}}{\left| {D}^{m}{\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( t\right) }\right| }^{2}}\right\rbrack   < \infty
\]

for \( m = 1,2,\ldots \) . From this, the first statement follows. The second statement is a consequence of Proposition 4.8 and Klingenberg's injectivity radius estimate (cf. [26], Theorem 5.9).

Hence, it remains to prove the third statement. To that end, we argue by contradiction. Suppose that there exists a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \in  \lbrack 0,1) \) such that

\[
\operatorname{diam}\left( {{S}^{2},\widetilde{g}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right)  \geq  k
\]

for all \( k \) . For each \( k \) , we can find a unit-speed geodesic \( {\gamma }_{k} : \left\lbrack  {0, k}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow \; \left( {{S}^{2},\widetilde{g}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) such that \( {d}_{\widetilde{g}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\left( {{\gamma }_{k}\left( 0\right) ,{\gamma }_{k}\left( k\right) }\right)  = k \) . We next define

\[
{\Omega }_{i, k} = \left\{  {x \in  {S}^{2} : {d}_{\widetilde{g}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\left( {{\gamma }_{k}\left( i\right) , x}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{4}}\right\}
\]

for \( i = 0,1,\ldots , k \) . Since the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{S}^{2},\widetilde{g}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) is uniformly bounded from above and the injectivity radius of \( \left( {{S}^{2},\widetilde{g}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) is uniformly bounded from below, we conclude that

\[
\mathop{\min }\limits_{{i = 0,1,\ldots , k}}\operatorname{vol}\left( {{\Omega }_{i, k},\widetilde{g}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right)  \geq  \varepsilon
\]

where \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) is independent of \( k \) . Since the sets \( {\Omega }_{i, k}, i = 0,1,\ldots , k \) , are disjoint, it follows that

\[
\operatorname{vol}\left( {{S}^{2},\widetilde{g}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right)  \geq  \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{k}\operatorname{vol}\left( {{\Omega }_{i, k},\widetilde{g}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right)  \geq  \varepsilon \left( {k + 1}\right)
\]

for all \( k \) . On the other hand, we have \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {{S}^{2},\widetilde{g}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right)  = {8\pi } \) by Lemma 4.4. This is a contradiction.

nodes.document_title: Simon Brendle - Ricci Flow and the Sphere Theorem
nodes.content:
Proposition 4.10. We have

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{S}^{2}}\left| {\left( {1 - t}\right) {\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( t\right) } - 1}\right|  \rightarrow  0
\]

as \( t \rightarrow  1 \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: Proposition 4.10. We have \[ \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{S}^{2}}\left| {\left( {1 - t}\right) {\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( t\right) } - 1}\right| \rightarrow 0 \] as \( t \rightarrow 1 \) .

nodes.proof:
We argue by contradiction. If the assertion is false, we can find a real number \( \varepsilon  \in  \left( {0,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \) and a sequence of times \( {\tau }_{k} \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2},1}\right) \) such that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{\tau }_{k} = 1 \) and

(28)

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{S}^{2}}\left| {\left( {1 - {\tau }_{k}}\right) {\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) } - 1}\right|  > {2\varepsilon }
\]

for all \( k \) .

For each \( k \) , we can find a real number \( {t}_{k} \in  \left\lbrack  {2{\tau }_{k} - 1,{\tau }_{k}}\right\rbrack \) such that \( \mathcal{M}\left( {t}_{k}\right)  = \; \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {2{\tau }_{k} - 1,{\tau }_{k}}\right\rbrack  }}\mathcal{M}\left( t\right) \) . This implies

\[
\left( {1 - {t}_{k}}\right) \mathcal{M}\left( {t}_{k}\right)  \leq  2\left( {1 - {\tau }_{k}}\right) \mathcal{M}\left( {t}_{k}\right)  \leq  2{\int }_{2{\tau }_{k} - 1}^{{\tau }_{k}}\mathcal{M}\left( t\right) {dt}
\]

for all \( k \) . Moreover, it follows from Lemma 4.5 and Proposition 4.7 that \( {\int }_{0}^{1}\mathcal{M}\left( t\right) {dt} < \infty \) . Putting these facts together, we conclude that

(29)

\[
\left( {1 - {t}_{k}}\right) \mathcal{M}\left( {t}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow  0
\]

as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) . After passing to a subsequence if necessary, the rescaled metrics \( \widetilde{g}\left( {t}_{k}\right)  = \frac{1}{1 - {t}_{k}}g\left( {t}_{k}\right) \) converge in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a smooth limit metric \( \bar{g} \) on \( {S}^{2} \) (see [2], Theorem 2.2, or [49], Theorem 16.1). It follows from (29) that \( \left( {{S}^{2},\bar{g}}\right) \) is a gradient Ricci soliton. Moreover, we have \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {{S}^{2},\bar{g}}\right)  = \; {8\pi } \) . Consequently, the limit metric \( \bar{g} \) has constant scalar curvature 1 by Proposition 4.3.

Hence, if \( k \) is sufficiently large, then we have

\[
\frac{1 - {2\varepsilon }}{\left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) \left( {1 - {t}_{k}}\right) } \leq  {\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( {t}_{k}\right) } \leq  \frac{1 + {2\varepsilon }}{\left( {1 + \varepsilon }\right) \left( {1 - {t}_{k}}\right) }
\]

at each point on \( {S}^{2} \) . Using the maximum principle, we obtain

\[
\frac{1 - {2\varepsilon }}{\left( {1 - {2\varepsilon }}\right) \left( {1 - {\tau }_{k}}\right)  + \varepsilon \left( {1 - {t}_{k}}\right) } \leq  {\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) } \leq  \frac{1 + {2\varepsilon }}{\left( {1 + {2\varepsilon }}\right) \left( {1 - {\tau }_{k}}\right)  - \varepsilon \left( {1 - {t}_{k}}\right) }
\]

for all points on \( {S}^{2} \) . Since \( 1 - {t}_{k} \leq  2\left( {1 - {\tau }_{k}}\right) \) , we conclude that

\[
\frac{1 - {2\varepsilon }}{1 - {\tau }_{k}} \leq  {\operatorname{scal}}_{g\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) } \leq  \frac{1 + {2\varepsilon }}{1 - {\tau }_{k}}
\]

at each point on \( {S}^{2} \) . This contradicts (28).

Lemma 4.11. The tensor \( M \) satisfies the evolution equation

\[
{D}_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}M = {\Delta M} + \frac{1}{1 - t}M - \operatorname{scal}M.
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: Lemma 4.11. The tensor \( M \) satisfies the evolution equation \[ {D}_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}M = {\Delta M} + \frac{1}{1 - t}M - \operatorname{scal}M. \]

nodes.proof:
For abbreviation, let \( \bar{M} = {D}^{2}f \) denote the Hessian of \( f \) . Moreover, let us fix two vector fields \( X, Y \) on \( {S}^{2} \) . Using Proposition 2.9, we obtain

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\bar{M}\left( {X, Y}\right)  = {D}_{X, Y}^{2}\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}f}\right)  - A\left( {X, Y}\right) \left( f\right)
\]

\[
= {D}_{X, Y}^{2}\left( {\Delta f}\right)  + \frac{1}{1 - t}{D}_{X, Y}^{2}f
\]

\[
+ \frac{1}{2}X\left( \text{ scal }\right) Y\left( f\right)  + \frac{1}{2}Y\left( \text{ scal }\right) X\left( f\right)  - \frac{1}{2}\langle d\text{ scal, }{df}\rangle g\left( {X, Y}\right) .
\]

On the other hand, a straightforward calculation shows that

\[
\left( {\Delta \bar{M}}\right) \left( {X, Y}\right)  = {D}_{X, Y}^{2}\left( {\Delta f}\right)  + 2\operatorname{scal}M\left( {X, Y}\right)
\]

\[
+ \frac{1}{2}X\left( \mathrm{{scal}}\right) Y\left( f\right)  + \frac{1}{2}Y\left( \mathrm{{scal}}\right) X\left( f\right)  - \frac{1}{2}\langle d\mathrm{{scal}},{df}\rangle g\left( {X, Y}\right) .
\]

Putting these facts together, we obtain

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\bar{M}\left( {X, Y}\right)  = \left( {\Delta \bar{M}}\right) \left( {X, Y}\right)  + \frac{1}{1 - t}\bar{M}\left( {X, Y}\right)  - 2\operatorname{scal}M\left( {X, Y}\right) ,
\]

hence,

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}M\left( {X, Y}\right)  = \left( {\Delta M}\right) \left( {X, Y}\right)  + \frac{1}{1 - t}M\left( {X, Y}\right)  - 2\operatorname{scal}M\left( {X, Y}\right) .
\]

From this, the assertion follows.

nodes.content:
Lemma 4.12. Fix a real number \( \alpha  \in  \left( {0,1}\right) \) . There exists a positive constant C such that

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{S}^{2}}{\left| M\right| }^{2} \leq  C{\left( 1 - t\right) }^{{2\alpha } - 2}
\]

for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0,1) \) .
