nodes.proof:
We argue by contradiction. Suppose that the assertion is false. Then we can find a sequence of Ricci flows with surgery \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) and a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) in space-time with the following properties:

(i) The flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{j}}\right) \) and has surgery parameters \( \varepsilon ,{\widehat{r}}_{j},{h}_{j},{\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) , where \( {\widehat{r}}_{j} \leq  \frac{1}{j} \) and \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \leq  \min \left\{  {\widetilde{\widetilde{\delta }}\left( {\widehat{r}}_{j}\right) ,\frac{1}{j}}\right\} \) . Here, \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( \cdot \right) \) is the function introduced in Proposition 10.9.

(ii) \( {Q}_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 2{\widehat{r}}_{j}\right) }^{-2} \) .

(iii) The point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) does not satisfy the conclusion of Theorem 10.10.

Condition (iii) means that at least one of the following statements is true:

- There does not exist a neighborhood \( B \) of \( {x}_{j} \) with the property that \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{\left( 2{C}_{1}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},2{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) and \( {\left( 2{C}_{2}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \leq  \operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{j}}\right)  \leq  2{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) for all \( x \in  B \) , and such that \( B \) is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck (in the sense of [35]) with center at \( {x}_{j} \) or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap.

- \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  > {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) .

- \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  > {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) .

We will proceed in several steps:

Step 1: By Definition 10.1, we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq \; {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) for each point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  4{Q}_{j} \) . Moreover, by Proposition 10.9, the flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales less than \( \varepsilon \) for some uniform constant \( \kappa \) that may depend on the initial data, but it is independent of \( j \) .

Step 2: Suppose that \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) is a point in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \; + {Q}_{j} \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . The pointwise curvature derivative estimate implies that scal \( \leq \; 8{r}_{0}^{-2} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{{r}_{0}}{100\eta }, - \frac{{r}_{0}^{2}}{100\eta }}\right) \) . Using Proposition 10.4, we conclude that \( \left| {{D}^{m}R}\right|  \leq  C\left( {n, m,\eta }\right) {r}_{0}^{-m - 2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Moreover, Proposition 10.9 implies \( {\operatorname{vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}_{0}^{n} \) for some uniform constant \( \kappa \) that is independent of \( j \) .

Step 3: We next prove a long-range curvature estimate. Given any \( \rho  > 0 \) , we put

\[
\mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{j}}\right) .
\]

The pointwise curvature derivative estimate implies that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  \leq  {16} \) for \( 0 < \; \rho  < \frac{1}{100\eta }. \)

We claim that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \) for all \( \rho  > 0 \) . Suppose this is false. Let

\[
{\rho }^{ * } = \sup \{ \rho  \geq  0 : \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \}  < \infty .
\]

By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , we have an upper bound for the curvature in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . Using the results in Step 2, we obtain bounds for all the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . Moreover, the noncollapsing estimate in Step 2 gives a lower bound for the volume. We rescale around \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) and pass to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) . In the limit, we obtain an incomplete manifold \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) that is weakly PIC2 (cf. [31, Th. 5.6]).

By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , there exists a sequence of points \( {y}_{j} \) such that

\[
{\rho }_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {Q}_{j}^{\frac{1}{2}}{d}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{y}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }^{ * }\;\text{ and }\;{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty .
\]

Let \( {\gamma }_{j} : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) be a unit-speed geodesic such that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( 0\right)  = {x}_{j} \) and \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  = {y}_{j} \) , and let \( {\gamma }_{\infty } : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }^{ * }}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) denote the limit of \( {\gamma }_{j} \) . Using the estimate \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) we obtain for \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) ,

\[
{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( s\right) }\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {s{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 2\eta \left( {\rho }^{ * } - s\right) \right) }^{-2} \geq  {100}.
\]

Let us consider a real number \( \bar{s} \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) such that \( {64}{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s} \) . We claim that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) lies at the center of a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ). Indeed, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption implies that the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap. Furthermore, the Canonical Neighborhood is contained in a geodesic ball around \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) of radius \( 8{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , and the scalar curvature is at most \( 8{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) at each point in the Canonical Neighborhood. Since \( \mathbb{M}\left( \bar{s}\right)  < \infty \) , we obtain \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  = \infty \) ; consequently, \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {16}{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {y}_{j} \) . We next observe that \( {32}{C}_{1}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}{\left( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  {64}{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s} \) . This implies \( {16}{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {x}_{j} \) . If the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap, then the geodesic \( {\gamma }_{j} \) must enter and exit this \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap, but this is impossible since \( {\gamma }_{j} \) minimizes length. To summarize, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck. In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) . \)

Passing to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) , we conclude that \( \left| {D{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) . Integrating this estimate along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) gives \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) }\right)  \geq \; {\left( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \left( {\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-2} \) . Moreover, since \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies at the center of a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck for \( j \) sufficiently large, the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) must lie on a strong \( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) .

As in \( \left\lbrack  {{33},§{12.1}}\right\rbrack \) , there is a sequence of rescalings that converges to a piece of a nonflat metric cone in the limit. Let us fix a point on this metric cone. In view of the preceding discussion, this point must lie on a strong \( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \) -neck. This gives a locally defined solution to the Ricci flow that is weakly PIC2 and that, at the final time, is a piece of nonflat metric cone. This contradicts Proposition 6.5.

Step 4: We now dilate the manifold \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) around the point \( {x}_{j} \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) . By Step 3, we have uniform bounds for the curvature at bounded distance. Using the results in Step 2, we obtain bounds for all the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor at bounded distance. Using these estimates together with the noncollapsing estimate in Step 2, we conclude that the rescaled manifolds converge in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a complete limit manifold \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) . Since \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) has \( \left( {f,\theta }\right) \) -pinched curvature, the curvature tensor of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is weakly PIC2 and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC. Using the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption, we conclude that every point in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with scalar curvature greater than 4 has a neighborhood that is either a strong \( {8\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {8\varepsilon } \) -cap.

We claim that \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature. Indeed, if there is a sequence of points in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with curvature going to infinity, then \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) contains a sequence of necks with radii converging to 0 , contradicting Proposition 6.9. This shows that \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature.

Step 5: We now extend the limit \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time. By Step 4, the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is bounded from above by a constant \( \Lambda  > 4 \) . We claim that, given any \( A > 1 \) , the parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right)
\]

is free of surgeries if \( j \) is sufficiently large. To prove this, fix \( A > 1 \) and suppose that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) contains points modified by surgery. Let \( {s}_{j} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }}\right\rbrack \) be the largest number such that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries. The pointwise curvature derivative estimate gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\left. P\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\right) \right) }\operatorname{scal} \leq  {2\Lambda }{Q}_{j}
\]

if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Since the scalar curvature is greater than \( \frac{1}{2}{h}_{j}^{-2} \) at each point modified by surgery, we deduce that \( \frac{1}{2}{h}_{j}^{-2} \leq  {2\Lambda }{Q}_{j} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. In particular, \( {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1} \leq  \frac{1}{10\eta }{h}_{j}^{2} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Since \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) ,

Proposition 10.5 implies that the parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right)
\]

is, after dilating by the factor \( {h}_{j} \) , arbitrarily close to a piece of the standard solution when \( j \) is sufficiently large. Using Corollary 9.3, we conclude that \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap when \( j \) is sufficiently large. If \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on an \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, then this neck is actually a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, since we are assuming that each \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) -neck on which we perform surgery has a large backward parabolic neighborhood that is free of surgeries (cf. Definition 10.1). Moreover, Corollary 9.3 implies that \( \left| {D\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . Therefore, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10, and this contradicts statement (iii). Thus, given any \( A > 1 \) , the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries if \( j \) is sufficiently large.

Let \( {\tau }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }}  - \frac{1}{200\eta \Lambda } \) . In view of the preceding discussion, we may extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  {2\Lambda } \) .

We now repeat this process. Suppose that we can extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack \) , and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{m} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } < \infty \) . Let \( {\tau }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{200\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} \) . We claim that we can extend the solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) backward to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and \( {\Lambda }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m} \) .

Indeed, if this is not possible, then there exists a number \( A > 1 \) with the property that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) contains points modified by surgery for \( j \) sufficiently large. Let \( {s}_{j} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}}}\right\rbrack \) be the largest number such that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries. The pointwise curvature derivative estimate gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\left. P\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}\right) \right) }\operatorname{scal} \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m}{Q}_{j}
\]

if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Let us choose \( {\alpha }_{m} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{n - 1}{2}}\right) \) so that \( \frac{{\alpha }_{m}}{{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) } \geq \; 8{\Lambda }_{m}\left( {\frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) \) . If \( \left( {{s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1} \geq  {\alpha }_{m}{h}_{j}^{2} \) for \( j \) sufficiently large, then Proposition 10.5 together with the lower bound for the scalar curvature on the standard solution (cf. Theorem 9.1) gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal} \geq  \frac{1}{2{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) }{h}_{j}^{-2}
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{{\alpha }_{m}}{2{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) }{\left( {s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}\right) }^{-1}{Q}_{j}
\]

\[
\geq  4{\Lambda }_{m}{Q}_{j}
\]

for \( j \) sufficiently large, which is impossible. Consequently, \( \left( {{s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1} \leq  {\alpha }_{m}{h}_{j}^{2} \) for \( j \) sufficiently large. Since \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) , Proposition 10.5 implies that the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is, after dilating by the factor \( {h}_{j} \) , arbitrarily close to a piece of the standard solution when \( j \) is sufficiently large. Using Corollary 9.3, we conclude that \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap when \( j \) is sufficiently large. If \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on an \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, then this neck is actually a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, since we are assuming that each \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) -neck on which we perform surgery has a large backward parabolic neighborhood that is free of surgeries (cf. Definition 10.1). Moreover, Corollary 9.3 implies that \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . Therefore, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10, and this contradicts statement (iii). Thus, we may extend the flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) backward to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack \) , where \( {\tau }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{200\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} \) , and we have \( {\Lambda }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m}. \)

Let \( {\tau }^{ * } = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\tau }_{m} \leq   - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda } \) . Using a standard diagonal sequence argument, we obtain a complete, smooth limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined on the interval \( \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) and that has bounded curvature for each \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Step 6: We next show that \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) . Indeed, if \( {\tau }^{ * } >  - \infty \) , it follows that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {\tau }_{m + 1}}\right)  = 0 \) , hence \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) . Arguing as in Step 6 in the proof of Theorem 7.2, we can show that the limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) has bounded curvature. This contradicts the fact that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) . Thus, \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) . Hence, if we dilate the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) around the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) , then (after passing to a subsequence) the rescaled flows converge to an ancient solution that is complete, has bounded curvature, is weakly PIC2, and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC. By Proposition 10.9, the limiting ancient solution is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed for some \( \kappa  > 0 \) that depends only on the initial data. By Corollary 6.22, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck with center at \( {x}_{j} \) ; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap; or a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) ; or a quotient neck. Recall that we have discarded all connected components that are diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) (see Definition 10.1). Hence, the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) cannot be a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) . If the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a quotient neck, then Theorem A. 1 in [6] implies that the underlying manifold contains a nontrivial incompressible \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional space form, contrary to our assumption. Consequently, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck with center at \( {x}_{j} \) or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap. Finally, Corollary 6.20 implies that \( \left| {D\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\mathrm{{scal}}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . In summary, we have shown that the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10. This contradicts statement (iii). This completes the proof of Theorem 10.10.

nodes.content: Proposition 11.1 (cf. G. Perelman [35, Lemma 4.3]). Given \( \varepsilon ,\widehat{r},\widehat{\delta } \) , we can find a small number \( h \in  \left( {0,\widehat{\delta }\widehat{r}}\right) \) with the following property: Suppose that we have a Ricci flow with surgery with parameters \( \varepsilon ,\widehat{r},\widehat{\delta }, h \) that is defined on the time interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) and goes singular at time \( T \) . Let \( x \) be a point that lies in an \( {4\varepsilon } \) -horn in \( \left( {\Omega , g\left( T\right) }\right) \) and has curvature \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {x, T}\right)  = {h}^{-2} \) . Then the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {x, T,{\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}h, - {\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}^{2}}\right) \) is free of surgeries. Moreover, \( P\left( {x, T,{\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}h, - {\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}^{2}}\right) \) is a \( \widehat{\delta } \) -neck.

nodes.proof:
Suppose that the assertion is false. Then there exists a sequence of positive numbers \( {h}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) , a sequence of Ricci flows with surgery \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) and a sequence of points \( {x}_{j} \) with the following properties:

(i) The flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) has surgery parameters \( \varepsilon ,\widehat{r},{h}_{j},\widehat{\delta } \) . It is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{j}}\right) \) and goes singular as \( t \rightarrow  {T}_{j} \) .

(ii) The point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) lies on an \( {4\varepsilon } \) -horn and \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right)  = {h}_{j}^{-2} \) .

(iii) The parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j},{\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}_{j}, - {\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}_{j}^{2}}\right) \) contains points modified by surgery, or it is not a \( \widehat{\delta } \) -neck.

By Definition 10.1, we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) whenever scal \( \geq  {\widehat{r}}^{-2} \) . Since \( {h}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) , it follows that \( \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{h}_{j}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{T}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 1 + 2\eta A\right) }^{-2}{h}_{j}^{-2} \) . In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( A \) ), then

\[
\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{h}_{j}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{T}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {10}{\left( \widehat{\delta }\widehat{r}\right) }^{-2}.
\]

We claim that for each \( A > 1 \) there exists a constant \( Q\left( A\right) \) (depending on \( A \) , but not on \( j \) ) such that \( \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{h}_{j}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{T}_{j}}\right)  \leq  Q\left( A\right) {h}_{j}^{-2} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. The proof of this statement is analogous to Claim 2 in Theorem 12.1 in [33]. Indeed, if no such constant \( Q\left( A\right) \) exists, then we can find a sequence of points \( \left( {{y}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) (lying on the same horn as \( \left. \left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \right) \) such that the blow-up limit around \( \left( {{y}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) is a piece of nonflat metric cone. Since the flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) satisfies the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption with accuracy \( {4\varepsilon } \) , the point \( \left( {{y}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) either lies on a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck or on a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap. The second case can easily be ruled out, so \( \left( {{y}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) must lie on a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck. In particular, there exists a small parabolic neighborhood of \( \left( {{y}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) that is free of surgeries. In view of Proposition 10.3, the blow-up limit around \( \left( {{y}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) is weakly PIC2. Hence, Proposition 6.5 implies that the limit cannot be a piece of a nonflat metric cone. This proves the claim.

In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( A \) ), then the distance of the point \( {x}_{j} \) from either end of the horn is at least \( A{h}_{j} \) .

We now continue with the proof of Proposition 11.1. Let us fix a number \( A > 1 \) . Since the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -horn, no point in \( {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{h}_{j}}\right) \) can lie on a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap. Hence, the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption implies that every point in \( {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{h}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck. Using Shi’s estimate, we obtain bounds for all the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor in \( {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\frac{1}{2}A{h}_{j}}\right) \) . Note that these bounds may depend on \( A \) , but are independent of \( j \) . We now pass to the limit, sending \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) first and \( A \rightarrow  \infty \) second. In the limit, we obtain a complete manifold with two ends that, by Proposition 10.3, is uniformly PIC and weakly PIC2. By the Cheeger-Gromoll splitting theorem, the limit is isometric to a product \( X \times  \mathbb{R} \) ; moreover, the cross-section \( X \) is compact and is nearly isometric to \( {S}^{n - 1} \) . Since every point in \( {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{h}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck, we conclude that, for each \( A > 1 \) , the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}, A{h}_{j}, - \frac{3{h}_{j}^{2}}{4}}\right) \) is free of surgeries if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( A \) ). After rescaling and passing to the limit, we obtain a solution to the Ricci flow that is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-\frac{1}{2},0}\right\rbrack \) and that splits off a line. Now, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( A) \) , then no point in \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}, A{h}_{j}, - \frac{{h}_{j}^{2}}{2}}\right) \) can lie on a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( A \) ), then every point in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}, A{h}_{j}, - \frac{{h}_{j}^{2}}{2}}\right) \) lies on a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck. This allows us to extend the limit solution backward in time to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {-1,0}\right\rbrack \) . Repeating this argument, we can extend the limit solution backwards in time, so that it is defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-1,0}\right\rbrack  ,\left\lbrack  {-\frac{3}{2},0}\right\rbrack  ,\left\lbrack  {-2,0}\right\rbrack \) , etc. To summarize, we produce a limit solution that is ancient, uniformly PIC, weakly PIC2, and splits as a product of a line with a manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n - 1} \) . By Theorem 6.4, the limiting solution is a family of standard cylinders. Therefore, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j},{\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}_{j}, - {\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}_{j}^{2}}\right) \) is free of surgeries, and \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j},{\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}_{j}, - {\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}_{j}^{2}}\right) \) is a \( \widehat{\delta } \) -neck. This contradicts (iii).

nodes.proof:
We evolve the initial metric \( {g}_{0} \) by smooth Ricci flow until the flow becomes singular for the first time. It follows from Theorem 10.10 and a standard continuity argument that the flow satisfies the Canonical Neighborhood Property with accuracy \( {2\varepsilon } \) on all scales less than \( 2\widehat{r} \) , up until the first singular time. At the first singular time, we perform finitely many surgeries on \( \widehat{\delta } \) -necks that have curvature level \( {h}^{-2} \) . The existence of such necks is ensured by Proposition 11.1. After performing surgery, we restart the flow and continue until the second singular time. Using Theorem 10.10 and a standard continuity argument, we conclude that the flow with surgery satisfies the Canonical Neighborhood Property with accuracy \( {2\varepsilon } \) on all scales less than \( 2\widehat{r} \) , up until the second singular time. Consequently, Proposition 11.1 ensures that, at the second singular time, we can again find \( \widehat{\delta } \) -necks on which to perform surgery. After performing surgery, we continue the flow until the third singular time. Again, Theorem 10.10 guarantees that the flow with surgery satisfies the Canonical Neighborhood Property with accuracy \( {2\varepsilon } \) on all scales less than \( 2\widehat{r} \) , up until the third singular time. We can now perform surgery again and repeat the process.

Since each surgery reduces the volume by at least \( c\left( n\right) {h}^{n} \) , we have an upper bound for the number of surgeries. By Proposition 10.2, the flow with surgery must become extinct by time \( \frac{n}{2\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{x \in  M}}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,0}\right) } \) at the latest. This completes the proof of Theorem 11.2.

LEMMA A.1. Let \( 0 \leq  \zeta  \leq  1 \) and \( 0 < \rho  \leq  1 \) . Assume that \( H \) is a symmetric bilinear form with the property that the largest eigenvalue of \( H \) is bounded from above by \( \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}\left( H\right) \) , and the sum of the two smallest eigenvalues of \( H \) is bounded from below by \( \frac{2\left( {1 - \zeta }\right) }{n}\operatorname{tr}\left( H\right) \) . Then

\[
\frac{n - 2}{n}\operatorname{tr}\left( H\right) \left( {{H}_{11} + {H}_{22}}\right)  - \rho \left( {{\left( {\overset{ \circ  }{H}}^{2}\right) }_{11} + {\left( {\overset{ \circ  }{H}}^{2}\right) }_{22}}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{2}{{n}^{2}}\left( {\left( {n - 2}\right) \left( {1 - \zeta }\right)  - 2{\zeta }^{2}\rho \frac{{n}^{2} - {2n} + 2}{{\left( n - 2\right) }^{2}}}\right) \operatorname{tr}{\left( H\right) }^{2}
\]

for every pair of orthonormal vectors \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2}}\right\} \) , where \( \overset{ \circ  }{H} \) denotes the tracefree part of \( H \) .

nodes.proof:
By scaling, we may assume that \( \operatorname{tr}\left( H\right)  = n \) . Moreover, we may assume that \( H \) is diagonal with diagonal entries \( {\lambda }_{1} \leq  \cdots  \leq  {\lambda }_{n} \) . By assumption, each eigenvalue is bounded from above by \( \frac{n}{2} \) , and the sum of any two distinct eigenvalues of \( H \) is bounded from below by \( 2\left( {1 - \zeta }\right) \) . It suffices to prove that

\[
\left( {n - 2}\right) \left( {{\lambda }_{i} + {\lambda }_{j}}\right)  - \rho \left( {{\left( {\lambda }_{i} - 1\right) }^{2} + {\left( {\lambda }_{j} - 1\right) }^{2}}\right)  \geq  2\left( {n - 2}\right) \left( {1 - \zeta }\right)  - 4{\zeta }^{2}\rho \frac{{n}^{2} - {2n} + 2}{{\left( n - 2\right) }^{2}}
\]

or, equivalently,

\[
{\lambda }_{i}\left( {\frac{n - 2}{\rho } + 2 - {\lambda }_{i}}\right)  + {\lambda }_{j}\left( {\frac{n - 2}{\rho } + 2 - {\lambda }_{j}}\right)  \geq  2\left( {1 - \zeta }\right) \left( {\frac{n - 2}{\rho } + 1 + \zeta }\right)  - \frac{2{n}^{2}{\zeta }^{2}}{{\left( n - 2\right) }^{2}}
\]

for \( i < j \) . Note that \( \frac{n - 2}{\rho } + 2 \geq  n \) . Moreover, \( {\lambda }_{n} \leq  \frac{n}{2} \) by assumption. We distinguish two cases:

Case 1: Suppose first that \( {\lambda }_{i} \geq  1 - \zeta \) . Since \( i < j \) , we have \( 1 - \zeta  \leq  {\lambda }_{i} \leq \; {\lambda }_{j} \leq  \frac{n}{2} \) . Since the function \( \lambda  \mapsto  \lambda \left( {\frac{n - 2}{\rho } + 2 - \lambda }\right) \) is monotone increasing on the interval \( \left( {-\infty ,\frac{n}{2}}\right\rbrack \) , we obtain

\[
{\lambda }_{i}\left( {\frac{n - 2}{\rho } + 2 - {\lambda }_{i}}\right)  + {\lambda }_{j}\left( {\frac{n - 2}{\rho } + 2 - {\lambda }_{j}}\right)  \geq  2\left( {1 - \zeta }\right) \left( {\frac{n - 2}{\rho } + 1 + \zeta }\right) ,
\]

which implies the claim.

Case 2: Suppose finally that \( {\lambda }_{i} \leq  1 - \zeta \) . Since the sum of any two distinct eigenvalues is at least \( 2\left( {1 - \zeta }\right) \) , we obtain \( 2\left( {1 - \zeta }\right)  - {\lambda }_{i} \leq  {\lambda }_{j} \leq  \frac{n}{2} \) . Since the function \( \lambda  \mapsto  \lambda \left( {\frac{n - 2}{\rho } + 2 - \lambda }\right) \) is monotone increasing on the interval \( \left( {-\infty ,\frac{n}{2}}\right\rbrack \) , we obtain

\[
{\lambda }_{i}\left( {\frac{n - 2}{\rho } + 2 - {\lambda }_{i}}\right)  + {\lambda }_{j}\left( {\frac{n - 2}{\rho } + 2 - {\lambda }_{j}}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  {\lambda }_{i}\left( {\frac{n - 2}{\rho } + 2 - {\lambda }_{i}}\right)  + \left( {2\left( {1 - \zeta }\right)  - {\lambda }_{i}}\right) \left( {\frac{n - 2}{\rho } + {2\zeta } + {\lambda }_{i}}\right)
\]

\[
= 2\left( {1 - \zeta }\right) \left( {\frac{n - 2}{\rho } + 1 + \zeta }\right)  - 2{\left( 1 - \zeta  - {\lambda }_{i}\right) }^{2}.
\]

Since the sum of any two distinct eigenvalues is at least \( 2\left( {1 - \zeta }\right) \) , it follows that \( {\lambda }_{i} \geq  1 - \frac{2\left( {n - 1}\right) \zeta }{n - 2} \) . Consequently, \( 0 \leq  1 - \zeta  - {\lambda }_{i} \leq  \frac{n\zeta }{n - 2} \) . Thus, we conclude that

\[
{\lambda }_{i}\left( {\frac{n - 2}{\rho } + 2 - {\lambda }_{i}}\right)  + {\lambda }_{j}\left( {\frac{n - 2}{\rho } + 2 - {\lambda }_{j}}\right)  \geq  2\left( {1 - \zeta }\right) \left( {\frac{n - 2}{\rho } + 1 + \zeta }\right)  - \frac{2{n}^{2}{\zeta }^{2}}{{\left( n - 2\right) }^{2}},
\]

as claimed.

\]

Let \( S\left( t\right)  = R\left( t\right)  - \frac{1}{2}\kappa \left( t\right) \) id \( \oslash \) id. As in [4], we compute

\[
Q\left( {S\left( t\right) }\right)  + {2\kappa }\left( t\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( S\right)  \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} + \left( {n - 1}\right) \kappa {\left( t\right) }^{2}\mathrm{{id}} \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} = Q\left( {R\left( t\right) }\right) .
\]

This gives

\[
\frac{d}{dt}S\left( t\right)  = Q\left( {S\left( t\right) }\right)  + {2\kappa }\left( t\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( {S\left( t\right) }\right)  \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} - \frac{1}{2}\left( {\frac{d}{dt}\kappa \left( t\right)  - 2\left( {n - 1}\right) \kappa {\left( t\right) }^{2}}\right) \mathrm{{id}} \oslash  \mathrm{{id}}.
\]

If \( S \in \) PIC, then Proposition 7.5 in [5] implies \( Q\left( S\right)  \in  {T}_{S} \) PIC. Moreover, if \( S \in \) PIC, then the sum of the four smallest eigenvalues of \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( S\right) \) is nonnegative by Lemma A.4, and consequently \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( S\right)  \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC. Therefore, the condition \( S\left( t\right)  \in \) PIC is preserved.

nodes.proof:
Since \( S \in \) PIC, we have

\[
{S}_{1313} + {S}_{1414} + {S}_{2323} + {S}_{2424} - 2{S}_{1234} \geq  0
\]

for every orthonormal four-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) . We now replace \( {e}_{4} \) by \( \lambda {e}_{4} \pm \; \sqrt{1 - {\lambda }^{2}}{e}_{p} \) for some fixed \( p \in  \{ 5,\ldots , n\} \) , and we take the arithmetic mean of the resulting inequalities. This gives

\[
{S}_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}{S}_{1414} + {S}_{2323} + {\lambda }^{2}{S}_{2424} - {2\lambda }{S}_{1234} + \left( {1 - {\lambda }^{2}}\right) \left( {{S}_{1p1p} + {S}_{2p2p}}\right)  \geq  0
\]

for all \( p \in  \{ 5,\ldots , n\} \) . In the next step, we take the mean value over all \( p \in  \{ 5,\ldots , n\} \) . Using the inequality

\[
\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p = 5}}^{n}\left( {{S}_{1p1p} + {S}_{2p2p}}\right)  \leq  \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p = 3}}^{n}\left( {{S}_{1p1p} + {S}_{2p2p}}\right)  = \operatorname{Ric}{\left( S\right) }_{11} + \operatorname{Ric}{\left( S\right) }_{22} - 2{S}_{1212},
\]

we obtain

\[
{S}_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}{S}_{1414} + {S}_{2323} + {\lambda }^{2}{S}_{2424} - {2\lambda }{S}_{1234}
\]

\[
+ \frac{1 - {\lambda }^{2}}{n - 4}\left( {\operatorname{Ric}{\left( S\right) }_{11} + \operatorname{Ric}{\left( S\right) }_{22} - 2{S}_{1212}}\right)  \geq  0.
\]

This proves the assertion.

\[
{T}_{ijkl} = {S}_{ijkl},\;{T}_{ijk0} = 0,\;{T}_{i0k0} = {H}_{ik}
\]

for \( i, j, k, l \in  \{ 1,\ldots , n\} \) . If

\[
{S}_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}{S}_{1414} + {S}_{2323} + {\lambda }^{2}{S}_{2424} - {2\lambda }{S}_{1234} + \left( {1 - {\lambda }^{2}}\right) \left( {{H}_{11} + {H}_{22}}\right)  \geq  0
\]

for every orthonormal four-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) and every \( \lambda  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) , then \( T \in \) PIC.

Let \( \widetilde{\zeta },\widetilde{\eta } \in  {\mathbb{C}}^{n + 1} \) be two linearly independent vectors satisfying \( g\left( {\widetilde{\zeta },\widetilde{\zeta }}\right)  = g\left( {\widetilde{\zeta },\widetilde{\eta }}\right)  = g\left( {\widetilde{\eta },\widetilde{\eta }}\right)  = 0 \) . We claim that \( T\left( {\widetilde{\zeta },\widetilde{\eta },\overline{\widetilde{\zeta }},\overline{\widetilde{\eta }}}\right)  \geq  0 \) . We can find a nonzero vector \( \widetilde{z} \in  \operatorname{span}\{ \widetilde{\zeta },\widetilde{\eta }\} \) such that \( \widetilde{z} = \left( {z,0}\right) \) for some \( z \in  {\mathbb{C}}^{n} \) . Moreover, we can find a nonzero vector \( \widetilde{w} \in  \operatorname{span}\{ \widetilde{\zeta },\widetilde{\eta }\} \) such that \( g\left( {\widetilde{z},\overline{\widetilde{w}}}\right)  = 0 \) . We normalize \( \widetilde{z} \) and \( \widetilde{w} \) such that \( g\left( {\widetilde{z},\overline{\widetilde{z}}}\right)  = g\left( {\widetilde{w},\overline{\widetilde{w}}}\right)  = 2 \) . We can further arrange that \( \widetilde{w} = \left( {w,{ia}}\right) \) , where \( w \in  {\mathbb{C}}^{n} \) and \( a \in  \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) . The identities \( g\left( {\widetilde{\zeta },\widetilde{\zeta }}\right)  = g\left( {\widetilde{\zeta },\widetilde{\eta }}\right)  = g\left( {\widetilde{\eta },\widetilde{\eta }}\right)  = 0 \) imply \( g\left( {\widetilde{z},\widetilde{z}}\right)  = g\left( {\widetilde{z},\widetilde{w}}\right)  = g\left( {\widetilde{w},\widetilde{w}}\right)  = 0. \)

Consequently, we may write \( z = {e}_{1} + i{e}_{2}, w = {e}_{3} + {i\lambda }{e}_{4} \) , and \( a = \sqrt{1 - {\lambda }^{2}} \) for some orthonormal four-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\}   \subset  {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) and some \( \lambda  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . This implies

\[
T\left( {\widetilde{z},\widetilde{w},\overline{\widetilde{z}},\overline{\widetilde{w}}}\right)  = {S}_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}{S}_{1414} + {S}_{2323}
\]

\[
+ {\lambda }^{2}{S}_{2424} - {2\lambda }{S}_{1234} + \left( {1 - {\lambda }^{2}}\right) \left( {{H}_{11} + {H}_{22}}\right)  \geq  0.
\]

Since \( \operatorname{span}\{ \widetilde{\zeta },\widetilde{\eta }\}  = \operatorname{span}\{ \widetilde{z},\widetilde{w}\} \) , it follows that \( T\left( {\widetilde{\zeta },\widetilde{\eta },\bar{\widetilde{\zeta }},\bar{\widetilde{\eta }}}\right)  \geq  0 \) , as claimed.

Proposition A.8. Let \( S \) be an algebraic curvature tensor, and let \( H \) be a symmetric bilinear form on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) such that

\[
Z \mathrel{\text{ := }} {S}_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}{S}_{1414} + {S}_{2323} + {\lambda }^{2}{S}_{2424} - {2\lambda }{S}_{1234} + \left( {1 - {\lambda }^{2}}\right) \left( {{H}_{11} + {H}_{22}}\right)  \geq  0
\]

for every orthonormal four-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) and every \( \lambda  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . Moreover, suppose that \( Z = 0 \) for one particular orthonormal four-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) and one particular \( \lambda  \in  \lbrack 0,1) \) . Then

\[
Q{\left( S\right) }_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}Q{\left( S\right) }_{1414} + Q{\left( S\right) }_{2323} + {\lambda }^{2}Q{\left( S\right) }_{2424} - {2\lambda Q}{\left( S\right) }_{1234}
\]

\[
+ {\left( H \odot  H\right) }_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}{\left( H \odot  H\right) }_{1414}
\]

\[
+ {\left( H \odot  H\right) }_{2323} + {\lambda }^{2}{\left( H \odot  H\right) }_{2424}
\]

\[
- {2\lambda }{\left( H \oslash  H\right) }_{1234}
\]

\[
+ 2\left( {1 - {\lambda }^{2}}\right) \left( {{\left( S * H\right) }_{11} + {\left( S * H\right) }_{22}}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  \left( {1 + {\lambda }^{2}}\right) {\left( {H}_{11} + {H}_{22}\right) }^{2}
\]

for this particular four-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) and this particular \( \lambda  \in  \lbrack 0,1) \) . Here, \( S * H \) is defined by \( {\left( S * H\right) }_{ik} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 1}}^{n}{S}_{ipkq}{H}_{pq} \) .

nodes.proof:
We define a curvature tensor \( T \) on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n + 1} \) by

\[
{T}_{ijkl} = {S}_{ijkl},\;{T}_{ijk0} = 0,\;{T}_{i0k0} = {H}_{ik}
\]

for \( i, j, k, l \in  \{ 1,\ldots , n\} \) . By Lemma A.7, we know that \( T \in \) PIC. Suppose that \( Z = 0 \) for one particular orthonormal four-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\}   \subset  {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) and one particular \( \lambda  \in  \lbrack 0,1) \) . Then \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},\lambda {e}_{4} + \sqrt{1 - {\lambda }^{2}}{e}_{0}}\right\} \) is an orthonormal four-frame in \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n + 1} \) that has zero isotropic curvature for \( T \) . Using Proposition 7.4 in [5], we obtain

\[
0 \leq  \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 0}}^{n}\left( {{T}_{1p1q} + {T}_{2p2q}}\right)
\]

\[
\cdot  \left( {{T}_{3p3q} + {\lambda }^{2}{T}_{4p4q} + \lambda \sqrt{1 - {\lambda }^{2}}{T}_{4p0q} + \lambda \sqrt{1 - {\lambda }^{2}}{T}_{0p4q} + \left( {1 - {\lambda }^{2}}\right) {T}_{0p0q}}\right)
\]

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 0}}^{n}{T}_{12pq}\left( {\lambda {T}_{34pq} + \sqrt{1 - {\lambda }^{2}}{T}_{30pq}}\right)
\]

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 0}}^{n}\left( {{T}_{1p3q} + \lambda {T}_{2p4q} + \sqrt{1 - {\lambda }^{2}}{T}_{2p0q}}\right) \left( {{T}_{3p1q} + \lambda {T}_{4p2q} + \sqrt{1 - {\lambda }^{2}}{T}_{0p2q}}\right)
\]

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 0}}^{n}\left( {\lambda {T}_{1p4q} + \sqrt{1 - {\lambda }^{2}}{T}_{1p0q} - {T}_{2p3q}}\right) \left( {\lambda {T}_{4p1q} + \sqrt{1 - {\lambda }^{2}}{T}_{0p1q} - {T}_{3p2q}}\right)
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 0}}^{n}\left( {{T}_{1p1q} + {T}_{2p2q}}\right) \left( {{T}_{3p3q} + {\lambda }^{2}{T}_{4p4q} + \left( {1 - {\lambda }^{2}}\right) {T}_{0p0q}}\right)
\]

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 0}}^{n}{T}_{12pq}\lambda {T}_{34pq}
\]

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 0}}^{n}\left( {{T}_{1p3q} + \lambda {T}_{2p4q}}\right) \left( {{T}_{3p1q} + \lambda {T}_{4p2q}}\right)
\]

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 0}}^{n}\left( {\lambda {T}_{1p4q} - {T}_{2p3q}}\right) \left( {\lambda {T}_{4p1q} - {T}_{3p2q}}\right) .
\]

This implies

\[
0 \leq  \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 1}}^{n}\left( {{T}_{1p1q} + {T}_{2p2q}}\right) \left( {{T}_{3p3q} + {\lambda }^{2}{T}_{4p4q} + \left( {1 - {\lambda }^{2}}\right) {T}_{0p0q}}\right)
\]

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 1}}^{n}{T}_{12pq}\lambda {T}_{34pq}
\]

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 1}}^{n}\left( {{T}_{1p3q} + \lambda {T}_{2p4q}}\right) \left( {{T}_{3p1q} + \lambda {T}_{4p2q}}\right)
\]

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 1}}^{n}\left( {\lambda {T}_{1p4q} - {T}_{2p3q}}\right) \left( {\lambda {T}_{4p1q} - {T}_{3p2q}}\right)
\]

\[
+ \left( {{H}_{11} + {H}_{22}}\right) \left( {{H}_{33} + {\lambda }^{2}{H}_{44}}\right)
\]

\[
- {\left( {H}_{13} + \lambda {H}_{24}\right) }^{2} - {\left( \lambda {H}_{14} - {H}_{23}\right) }^{2}
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 1}}^{n}\left( {{S}_{1p1q} + {S}_{2p2q}}\right) \left( {{S}_{3p3q} + {\lambda }^{2}{S}_{4p4q} + \left( {1 - {\lambda }^{2}}\right) {H}_{pq}}\right)
\]

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 1}}^{n}{S}_{12pq}\lambda {S}_{34pq}
\]

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 1}}^{n}\left( {{S}_{1p3q} + \lambda {S}_{2p4q}}\right) \left( {{S}_{3p1q} + \lambda {S}_{4p2q}}\right)
\]

\[
- \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 1}}^{n}\left( {\lambda {S}_{1p4q} - {S}_{2p3q}}\right) \left( {\lambda {S}_{4p1q} - {S}_{3p2q}}\right)
\]

\[
+ \left( {{H}_{11} + {H}_{22}}\right) \left( {{H}_{33} + {\lambda }^{2}{H}_{44}}\right)
\]

\[
- {\left( {H}_{13} + \lambda {H}_{24}\right) }^{2} - {\left( \lambda {H}_{14} - {H}_{23}\right) }^{2}
\]

Since \( \lambda  \in  \lbrack 0,1) \) , we have \( Z = \frac{\partial Z}{\partial \lambda } = 0 \) . This gives \( \lambda {S}_{1414} + \lambda {S}_{2424} - {S}_{1234} = \; \lambda \left( {{H}_{11} + {H}_{22}}\right) \) and \( {S}_{1313} + {S}_{2323} - \lambda {S}_{1234} =  - \left( {{H}_{11} + {H}_{22}}\right) \) . Consequently,

\[
\left( {1 + {\lambda }^{2}}\right) {\left( {H}_{11} + {H}_{22}\right) }^{2} = {\left\lbrack  \left( \lambda {S}_{1414} + {S}_{1423}\right)  + \left( \lambda {S}_{2424} - {S}_{1324}\right) \right\rbrack  }^{2}
\]

\[
+ {\left\lbrack  \left( {S}_{1313} - \lambda {S}_{1324}\right)  + \left( {S}_{2323} + \lambda {S}_{1423}\right) \right\rbrack  }^{2}
\]

\[
\leq  2{\left( \lambda {S}_{1414} + {S}_{1423}\right) }^{2} + 2{\left( \lambda {S}_{2424} - {S}_{1324}\right) }^{2}
\]

\[
+ 2{\left( {S}_{1313} - \lambda {S}_{1324}\right) }^{2} + 2{\left( {S}_{2323} + \lambda {S}_{1423}\right) }^{2}
\]

\[
\leq  \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 1}}^{n}{\left( {S}_{13pq} - \lambda {S}_{24pq}\right) }^{2} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 1}}^{n}{\left( \lambda {S}_{14pq} + {S}_{23pq}\right) }^{2}.
\]

Putting these facts together, we conclude that

\[
Q{\left( S\right) }_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}Q{\left( S\right) }_{1414} + Q{\left( S\right) }_{2323} + {\lambda }^{2}Q{\left( S\right) }_{2424} - {2\lambda Q}{\left( S\right) }_{1234}
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 1}}^{n}{\left( {S}_{13pq} - \lambda {S}_{24pq}\right) }^{2} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 1}}^{n}{\left( \lambda {S}_{14pq} + {S}_{23pq}\right) }^{2}
\]

\[
+ 2\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 1}}^{n}\left( {{S}_{1p1q} + {S}_{2p2q}}\right) \left( {{S}_{3p3q} + {\lambda }^{2}{S}_{4p4q}}\right)
\]

\[
- 2\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 1}}^{n}{S}_{12pq}\lambda {S}_{34pq}
\]

\[
- 2\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 1}}^{n}\left( {{S}_{1p3q} + \lambda {S}_{2p4q}}\right) \left( {{S}_{3p1q} + \lambda {S}_{4p2q}}\right)
\]

\[
- 2\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 1}}^{n}\left( {\lambda {S}_{1p4q} - {S}_{2p3q}}\right) \left( {\lambda {S}_{4p1q} - {S}_{3p2q}}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  \left( {1 + {\lambda }^{2}}\right) {\left( {H}_{11} + {H}_{22}\right) }^{2} - 2\left( {1 - {\lambda }^{2}}\right) \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p, q = 1}}^{n}\left( {{S}_{1p1q} + {S}_{2p2q}}\right) {H}_{pq}
\]

\[
- 2\left( {{H}_{11} + {H}_{22}}\right) \left( {{H}_{33} + {\lambda }^{2}{H}_{44}}\right)
\]

\[
+ 2{\left( {H}_{13} + \lambda {H}_{24}\right) }^{2} + 2{\left( \lambda {H}_{14} - {H}_{23}\right) }^{2}.
\]

This completes the proof.

nodes.proof:
Consider a complex two-form \( \varphi \) with the property that \( \varphi  = \; \left( {{e}_{1} + i{e}_{2}}\right)  \land  \left( {{e}_{3} + i{e}_{4}}\right) \) for some orthonormal four-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) and \( U\left( {\varphi ,\bar{\varphi }}\right)  = 0 \) . Since \( U \in  \operatorname{PIC}, U\left( {{e}^{-{t\sigma }}\varphi {e}^{t\sigma },\overline{{e}^{-{t\sigma }}\varphi {e}^{t\sigma }}}\right)  \geq  0 \) for all \( \sigma  \in  \mathfrak{{so}}\left( {n,\mathbb{C}}\right) \) and all \( t \in  \mathbb{R} \) . This implies \( {\left. \frac{{d}^{2}}{d{t}^{2}}U\left( {e}^{-{t\sigma }}\varphi {e}^{t\sigma },\overline{{e}^{-{t\sigma }}\varphi {e}^{t\sigma }}\right) \right| }_{t = 0} \geq  0 \) for all \( \sigma  \in \; \mathfrak{{so}}\left( {n,\mathbb{C}}\right) \) ; consequently,

\[
U\left( {\left\lbrack  {\left\lbrack  {\varphi ,\sigma }\right\rbrack  ,\sigma }\right\rbrack  ,\bar{\varphi }}\right)  + U\left( {\varphi ,\overline{\left\lbrack  \left\lbrack  \varphi ,\sigma \right\rbrack  ,\sigma \right\rbrack  }}\right)  + {2U}\left( {\left\lbrack  {\varphi ,\sigma }\right\rbrack  ,\overline{\left\lbrack  \varphi ,\sigma \right\rbrack  }}\right)  \geq  0
\]

for all \( \sigma  \in  \mathfrak{{so}}\left( {n,\mathbb{C}}\right) \) (cf. [36]). If we replace \( \sigma \) by \( {i\sigma } \) and add the resulting inequalities, we obtain \( U\left( {\left\lbrack  {\varphi ,\sigma }\right\rbrack  ,\overline{\left\lbrack  \varphi ,\sigma \right\rbrack  }}\right)  \geq  0 \) for all \( \sigma  \in  \mathfrak{{so}}\left( {n,\mathbb{C}}\right) \) . Since \( S - U \geq  0 \) , it follows that \( S\left( {\left\lbrack  {\varphi ,\sigma }\right\rbrack  ,\overline{\left\lbrack  \varphi ,\sigma \right\rbrack  }}\right)  \geq  0 \) for all \( \sigma  \in  \mathfrak{{so}}\left( {n,\mathbb{C}}\right) \) . Let us define a linear transformation \( L : \mathfrak{{so}}\left( {n,\mathbb{C}}\right)  \rightarrow  \mathfrak{{so}}\left( {n,\mathbb{C}}\right) \) by \( {L\sigma } = \left\lbrack  {\varphi ,\sigma }\right\rbrack \) . The adjoint \( {L}^{ * } : \mathfrak{{so}}\left( {n,\mathbb{C}}\right)  \rightarrow  \mathfrak{{so}}\left( {n,\mathbb{C}}\right) \) is given by \( {L}^{ * }\sigma  =  - \left\lbrack  {\bar{\varphi },\sigma }\right\rbrack \) . Let \( P : \mathfrak{{so}}\left( {n,\mathbb{C}}\right)  \rightarrow  \mathfrak{{so}}\left( {n,\mathbb{C}}\right) \) be a linear transformation with the property that \( \sigma  = {LP\sigma } \) whenever \( \sigma \) lies in the image of \( L \) . Clearly, \( L = {LPL} \) , and consequently \( {L}^{ * } = {L}^{ * }{P}^{ * }{L}^{ * } \) . Since \( {L}^{ * }{SL} \geq  0 \) and \( {LS}{L}^{ * } \geq  0 \) , we obtain

\[
\operatorname{tr}\left( {{SLS}{L}^{ * }}\right)  = \operatorname{tr}\left( {\left( {{L}^{ * }{SL}}\right) P\left( {{LS}{L}^{ * }}\right) {P}^{ * }}\right)  \geq  0.
\]

From this, we deduce that \( {S}^{\# }\left( {\varphi ,\bar{\varphi }}\right)  \geq  0 \) . Since this inequality holds for every two-form \( \varphi  = \left( {{e}_{1} + i{e}_{2}}\right)  \land  \left( {{e}_{3} + i{e}_{4}}\right) \) satisfying \( U\left( {\varphi ,\bar{\varphi }}\right)  = 0 \) , we conclude that \( {S}^{\# } \in  {T}_{U} \) PIC.

nodes.content:
3.1. The definition of Ricci flow, and some basic properties. Let \( M \) be a compact 3-manifold and let \( \{ g\left( t\right) {\} }_{t \in  \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack  } \) be a smoothly varying family of Riemannian metrics on \( M \) . Then \( g\left( \cdot \right) \) satisfies the Ricci flow equation if

(3.1)

\[
\frac{\partial g}{\partial t}\left( t\right)  =  - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {g\left( t\right) }\right)
\]

holds for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack \) . Hamilton showed in [35] that for any Riemannian metric \( {g}_{0} \) on \( M \) , there is a \( T \in  (0,\infty \rbrack \) with the property that there is a (unique) solution \( g\left( \cdot \right) \) to the Ricci flow equation defined on the time interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( g\left( 0\right)  = {g}_{0} \) , so that if \( T < \infty \) then the curvature of \( g\left( t\right) \) becomes unbounded as \( t \rightarrow  T \) . We refer to this maximal solution as the Ricci flow with initial condition \( {g}_{0} \) . If \( T < \infty \) then we call \( T \) the blow-up time. A basic example is the shrinking round 3-sphere, with \( {g}_{0} = {r}_{0}^{2}{g}_{{S}^{3}} \) and \( g\left( t\right)  = \left( {{r}_{0}^{2} - {4t}}\right) {g}_{{S}^{3}} \) , in which case \( T = \frac{{r}_{0}^{2}}{4} \) .

Let \( \left( {p,{t}_{0}}\right) \) be a fixed spacetime point. Define backward time by \( \tau  = {t}_{0} - t \) . Given a curve \( \gamma \left( \tau \right) \) in \( M \) defined for \( 0 \leq  \tau  \leq  \bar{\tau } \) (i.e. going backward in real time) with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p \) , its \( \mathcal{L} \) -length is

(4.1)

\[
\mathcal{L}\left( \gamma \right)  = {\int }_{0}^{\bar{\tau }}\sqrt{\tau }\left( {{\left| \dot{\gamma }\left( \tau \right) \right| }^{2} + R\left( {\gamma \left( \tau \right) ,{t}_{0} - \tau }\right) }\right) {d\tau }.
\]

One can compute the first and second variations of \( \mathcal{L} \) , in analogy to what is done in Riemannian geometry.

Let \( L\left( {q,\bar{\tau }}\right) \) be the infimum of \( \mathcal{L}\left( \gamma \right) \) over curves \( \gamma \) with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = p \) and \( \gamma \left( \bar{\tau }\right)  = q \) . Put \( l\left( {q,\bar{\tau }}\right)  = \; \frac{L\left( {q,\bar{\tau }}\right) }{2\sqrt{\bar{\tau }}} \) . The reduced volume is defined by \( \widetilde{V}\left( \bar{\tau }\right)  = {\int }_{M}{\bar{\tau }}^{-\frac{n}{2}}{e}^{-l\left( {q,\bar{\tau }}\right) }\operatorname{dvol}\left( q\right) \) . The remarkable fact is that if \( g\left( \cdot \right) \) is a Ricci flow solution then \( \widetilde{V} \) is nonincreasing in \( \bar{\tau } \) , i.e. nondecreasing in real time \( t \) . Furthermore, it is constant if and only if \( g\left( \cdot \right) \) is a gradient shrinking soliton that terminates at time \( {t}_{0} \) . The proof of monotonicity uses a subtle cancellation between the \( \bar{\tau } \) - derivative of \( l\left( {\gamma \left( \bar{\tau }\right) ,\bar{\tau }}\right) \) along an \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic and the Jacobian of the so-called \( \mathcal{L} \) -exponential map.

(5.2)

\[
\mathcal{F}\left( {g, f}\right)  = {\int }_{M}\left( {R + {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right) {e}^{-f}{dV}.
\]

Given \( {v}_{ij} \in  {T}_{g}\mathcal{M} \) and \( h \in  {T}_{f}{C}^{\infty }\left( M\right) \) , the evaluation of the differential \( d\mathcal{F} \) on \( \left( {{v}_{ij}, h}\right) \) is written as \( \delta \mathcal{F}\left( {{v}_{ij}, h}\right) \) . Put \( v = {g}^{ij}{v}_{ij} \) .

nodes.label: Proposition 5.3
nodes.document_title: Bruce Kleiner and John Lott - Notes on Perelman's Papers
nodes.section_title: 5. I.1.1. THE F-FUNCTIONAL AND ITS MONOTONICITY
nodes.content:
Proposition 5.3. (cf. I.1.1) We have

(5.4)

\[
\text{ 5.4) }\delta \mathcal{F}\left( {{v}_{ij}, h}\right)  = {\int }_{M}{e}^{-f}\left\lbrack  {-{v}_{ij}\left( {{R}_{ij} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f}\right)  + \left( {\frac{v}{2} - h}\right) \left( {{2\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + R}\right) }\right\rbrack  {dV}\text{ . }
\]

nodes.proof:
From a standard formula,

(5.5)

\[
{\delta R} =  - \bigtriangleup v + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}{v}_{ij} - {R}_{ij}{v}_{ij}.
\]

As

(5.6)

\[
{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} = {g}^{ij}{\nabla }_{i}f{\nabla }_{j}f
\]

we have

(5.7)

\[
\delta {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} =  - {v}^{ij}{\nabla }_{i}f{\nabla }_{j}f + 2\langle \nabla f,\nabla h\rangle .
\]

As \( {dV} = \sqrt{\det \left( g\right) }d{x}_{1}\ldots d{x}_{n} \) , we have \( \delta \left( {dV}\right)  = \frac{v}{2}{dV} \) , so

(5.8)

\[
\delta \left( {{e}^{-f}{dV}}\right)  = \left( {\frac{v}{2} - h}\right) {e}^{-f}{dV}.
\]

Putting this together gives

(5.9)

\[
\delta \mathcal{F} = {\int }_{M}{e}^{-f}\left\lbrack  {-{\Delta v} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}{v}_{ij} - {R}_{ij}{v}_{ij} - {v}_{ij}{\nabla }_{i}f{\nabla }_{j}f + }\right.
\]

\[
2\langle \nabla f,\nabla h\rangle  + \left( {R + {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right) \left( {\frac{v}{2} - h}\right) \rbrack {dV}
\]

The goal now is to rewrite the right-hand side of (5.9) so that \( {v}_{ij} \) and \( h \) appear algebraically, i.e. without derivatives. As

(5.10)

\[
\Delta {e}^{-f} = \left( {{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} - {\Delta f}}\right) {e}^{-f},
\]

we have

(5.11)

\[
{\int }_{M}{e}^{-f}\left\lbrack  {-\bigtriangleup v}\right\rbrack  {dV} =  - {\int }_{M}\left( {\bigtriangleup {e}^{-f}}\right) {vdV} = {\int }_{M}{e}^{-f}\left( {\bigtriangleup f - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right) {vdV}.
\]

Next,

(5.12)

\[
{\int }_{M}{e}^{-f}{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}{v}_{ij}{dV} = {\int }_{M}\left( {{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}{e}^{-f}}\right) {v}_{ij}{dV} =  - {\int }_{M}{\nabla }_{i}\left( {{e}^{-f}{\nabla }_{j}f}\right) {v}_{ij}{dV}
\]

\[
= {\int }_{M}{e}^{-f}\left( {{\nabla }_{i}f{\nabla }_{j}f - {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f}\right) {v}_{ij}{dV}
\]

Finally,

(5.13)

\[
2{\int }_{M}{e}^{-f}\langle \nabla f,\nabla h\rangle {dV} =  - 2{\int }_{M}\left\langle  {\nabla {e}^{-f},\nabla h}\right\rangle  {dV} = 2{\int }_{M}\left( {\bigtriangleup {e}^{-f}}\right) {hdV}
\]

\[
= 2{\int }_{M}{e}^{-f}\left( {{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} - \bigtriangleup f}\right) {hdV}.
\]

Then

(5.14)

\[
\delta \mathcal{F} = {\int }_{M}{e}^{-f}\left\lbrack  {\left( {\frac{v}{2} - h}\right) \left( {{2\Delta f} - 2{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right)  - {v}_{ij}\left( {{R}_{ij} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f}\right) }\right.
\]

\[
\left. {+\left( {\frac{v}{2} - h}\right) \left( {R + {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right) }\right\rbrack  {dV}
\]

\[
= {\int }_{M}{e}^{-f}\left\lbrack  {-{v}_{ij}\left( {{R}_{ij} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f}\right)  + \left( {\frac{v}{2} - h}\right) \left( {2\bigtriangleup f - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + R}\right) }\right\rbrack  {dV}.
\]

This proves the proposition.

nodes.content:
## 6. BASIC EXAMPLE FOR I.1

In this section we compute \( \mathcal{F} \) in a Euclidean example.

Consider \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) with the standard metric, constant in time. Fix \( {t}_{0} > 0 \) . Put \( \tau  = {t}_{0} - t \) and

(6.1)

\[
f\left( {t, x}\right)  = \frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4\tau } + \frac{n}{2}\ln \left( {4\pi \tau }\right) ,
\]

so

(6.2)

\[
{e}^{-f} = {\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{-n/2}{e}^{-\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4\tau }}.
\]

This is the standard heat kernel when considered for \( \tau \) going from 0 to \( {t}_{0} \) , i.e. for \( t \) going from \( {t}_{0} \) to 0 . One can check that \( \left( {g, f}\right) \) solves (5.21). As

(6.3)

\[
{\int }_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}{e}^{-\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4\tau }}{dV} = {\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{n/2}
\]

\( f \) is properly normalized. Then \( \nabla f = \frac{\mathbf{x}}{2\tau } \) and \( {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} = \frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4{\tau }^{2}} \) . Differentiating (6.3) with respect to \( \tau \) gives

(6.4)

\[
{\int }_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4{\tau }^{2}}{e}^{-\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4\tau }}{dV} = {\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{n/2}\frac{n}{2\tau },
\]

so

(6.5)

\[
{\int }_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}{e}^{-f}{dV} = \frac{n}{2\tau }.
\]

Then \( \mathcal{F}\left( t\right)  = \frac{n}{2\tau } = \frac{n}{2\left( {{t}_{0} - t}\right) } \) . In particular, this is nondecreasing as a function of \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{0}}\right) \) .

nodes.content_excerpt: Proposition 7.1. Given a metric \( g \) , there is a unique minimizer \( \bar{f} \) of \( \mathcal{F}\left( {g, f}\right) \) under the constraint \( {\int }_{M}{e}^{-f}{dV} = 1 \) .

nodes.proof:
Write

(7.2)

\[
\mathcal{F} = {\int }_{M}\left( {R{e}^{-f} + 4{\left| \nabla {e}^{-f/2}\right| }^{2}}\right) {dV}.
\]

Putting \( \Phi  = {e}^{-f/2} \) ,

(7.3)

\[
\mathcal{F} = {\int }_{M}\left( {4{\left| \nabla \Phi \right| }^{2} + R{\Phi }^{2}}\right) {dV} = {\int }_{M}\Phi \left( {-4\bigtriangleup \Phi  + {R\Phi }}\right) {dV}.
\]

The constraint equation becomes \( {\int }_{M}{\Phi }^{2}{dV} = 1 \) . Then \( \lambda \) is the smallest eigenvalue of \( - 4\bigtriangleup  + \; R \) and \( {e}^{-\bar{f}/2} \) is a corresponding normalized eigenvector. As the operator is a Schrödinger operator, there is a unique normalized positive eigenvector [55, Chapter XIII.12].

nodes.content: Proposition 7.5. (cf. I.2.2) If \( g\left( \cdot \right) \) is a Ricci flow solution then \( \lambda \left( {g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is nondecreasing in \( t \) .

nodes.proof:
Consider a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{1},{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) , and the minimizer \( \bar{f}\left( {t}_{2}\right) \) . In particular, \( \lambda \left( {t}_{2}\right)  = \; \mathcal{F}\left( {g\left( {t}_{2}\right) ,\bar{f}\left( {t}_{2}\right) }\right) \) . Put \( u\left( {t}_{2}\right)  = {e}^{-\bar{f}\left( {t}_{2}\right) } \) . Solve the backward heat equation

(7.6)

\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} =  - {\Delta u} + {Ru}
\]

backward on \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{1},{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) .

We claim that \( u\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  > 0 \) for all \( {x}^{\prime } \in  M \) and \( {t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{1},{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) . To see this, we take \( {t}^{\prime } \in \; \left\lbrack  {{t}_{1},{t}_{2}}\right) \) , and let \( h \) be the solution to the forward heat equation \( \frac{\partial h}{\partial t} = \bigtriangleup h \) on \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime }}}h\left( t\right)  = {\delta }_{{x}^{\prime }} \) . We have

(7.7)

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{\int }_{M}u\left( t\right) h\left( t\right) {dV} = {\int }_{M}\left\lbrack  {\left( {{\partial }_{t}u + \bigtriangleup u - {Ru}}\right) v + u\left( {{\partial }_{t}h - \bigtriangleup h}\right) }\right\rbrack  {dV} = 0.
\]

One knows that \( h\left( t\right)  > 0 \) for all \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) . Then(7.8)

\[
\text{ (7.8) }u\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  = {\int }_{M}u\left( {x,{t}^{\prime }}\right) {\delta }_{{x}^{\prime }}\left( x\right) {dV}\left( x\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime }}}{\int }_{M}u\left( t\right) h\left( t\right) {dV} = {\int }_{M}u\left( {t}_{2}\right) h\left( {t}_{2}\right) {dV} > 0\text{ . }
\]

For \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{1},{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) , define \( f\left( t\right) \) by \( u\left( t\right)  = {e}^{-f\left( t\right) } \) . By (5.22), \( \mathcal{F}\left( {g\left( {t}_{1}\right) , f\left( {t}_{1}\right) }\right)  \leq  \mathcal{F}\left( {g\left( {t}_{2}\right) , f\left( {t}_{2}\right) }\right) \) . By the definition of \( \lambda ,\lambda \left( {t}_{1}\right)  = \mathcal{F}\left( {g\left( {t}_{1}\right) ,\bar{f}\left( {t}_{1}\right) }\right)  \leq  \mathcal{F}\left( {g\left( {t}_{1}\right) , f\left( {t}_{1}\right) }\right) \) . (We are using the fact that \( {\int }_{M}{e}^{-f\left( {t}_{1}\right) }{dV}\left( {t}_{1}\right)  = {\int }_{M}{e}^{-f\left( {t}_{2}\right) }{dV}\left( {t}_{2}\right)  = 1 \) .) Thus \( \lambda \left( {t}_{1}\right)  \leq  \lambda \left( {t}_{2}\right) \) .

nodes.content_excerpt: Lemma 7.11. (cf. Proposition I.1.2) (7.12) \[ \frac{d\lambda }{dt} \geq \frac{2}{n}{\lambda }^{2}\left( t\right) \]

nodes.proof:
Given a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{1},{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) , with the notation of the proof of Proposition 7.5 we have

(7.13)

\[
\lambda \left( {t}_{1}\right)  \leq  \mathcal{F}\left( {g\left( {t}_{1}\right) , f\left( {t}_{1}\right) }\right)  = \mathcal{F}\left( {g\left( {t}_{2}\right) , f\left( {t}_{2}\right) }\right)  - 2{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}{\int }_{M}{\left| {R}_{ij} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f\right| }^{2}{e}^{-f}{dVdt}
\]

\[
= \lambda \left( {t}_{2}\right)  - 2{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}{\int }_{M}{\left| {R}_{ij} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f\right| }^{2}{e}^{-f}{dVdt}.
\]

Then

(7.14)

\[
{\left. \frac{d\lambda }{dt}\right| }_{t = {t}_{2}} = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{{t}_{1} \rightarrow  {t}_{2}^{ - }}}\frac{\lambda \left( {t}_{2}\right)  - \lambda \left( {t}_{1}\right) }{{t}_{2} - {t}_{1}} \geq  2{\int }_{M}{\left| {R}_{ij} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f\right| }^{2}{e}^{-f}{dV},
\]

where the right-hand side is evaluated at time \( {t}_{2} \) .

Hence for all \( t \) ,

(7.15)

\[
\frac{d\lambda }{dt} \geq  2{\int }_{M}{\left| {R}_{ij} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}\bar{f}\right| }^{2}{e}^{-\bar{f}}{dV}
\]

and so

(7.16)

\[

###### 8.I.2.3.THE RESCALED \( \lambda \) -INVARIANT

In this section we show the monotonicity of a scale-invariant version of \( \lambda \) . This will be used in Section 93. We then show that an expanding breather on a compact manifold is a gradient expanding soliton.

Put \( \bar{\lambda }\left( g\right)  = \lambda \left( g\right) V{\left( g\right) }^{\frac{2}{n}} \) . As \( \bar{\lambda } \) is scale-invariant, it is constant in \( t \) along a steady, shrinking or expanding soliton solution.

A smooth Ricci flow solution \( g\left( \cdot \right) \) on a time interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) is said to be locally collapsing at \( T \) if there is a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow  T \) and a sequence of metric balls \( {B}_{k} = B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) \) at times \( {t}_{k} \) such that \( {r}_{k}^{2}/{t}_{k} \) is bounded, \( \mid  \operatorname{Rm} \mid  \left( {g\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right)  \leq  {r}_{k}^{-2} \) in \( {B}_{k} \) and \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{r}_{k}^{-n}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B}_{k}\right)  = 0. \)

nodes.content: Theorem 13.3. (cf. Theorem I.4.1) If \( M \) is closed and \( T < \infty \) then \( g\left( \cdot \right) \) is not locally collapsing at \( T \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: Theorem 13.3. (cf. Theorem I.4.1) If \( M \) is closed and \( T < \infty \) then \( g\left( \cdot \right) \) is not locally collapsing at \( T \) .

nodes.proof:
We first sketch the idea of the proof. In Section 11 we showed that in the case of flat \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) , taking \( {e}^{-f}\left( x\right)  = {e}^{-\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4\tau }} \) , we get \( \mathcal{W}\left( {g, f,\tau }\right)  = 0 \) . So putting \( \tau  = {r}_{k}^{2} \) and \( {e}^{-{f}_{k}}\left( x\right)  = {e}^{-\frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4{r}_{k}^{2}}} \) , we have \( \mathcal{W}\left( {g,{f}_{k},{r}_{k}^{2}}\right)  = 0 \) . In the collapsing case, the idea is to use a test function \( {f}_{k} \) so that

(13.4)

\[
{e}^{-{f}_{k}}\left( x\right)  \sim  {e}^{-{c}_{k}}{e}^{-\frac{{\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{k}}{\left( x,{p}_{k}\right) }^{2}}{4{r}_{k}^{2}}},
\]

where \( {c}_{k} \) is determined by the normalization condition

(13.5)

\[
{\int }_{M}{\left( 4\pi {r}_{k}^{2}\right) }^{-n/2}{e}^{-{f}_{k}}{dV} = 1.
\]

The main difference between computing (13.5) in \( M \) and in \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) comes from the difference in volumes, which means that \( {e}^{-{c}_{k}} \sim  \frac{1}{{r}_{k}^{-n}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B}_{k}\right) } \) . In particular, as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) , we have \( {c}_{k} \rightarrow   - \infty \) .

Now that \( {f}_{k} \) is normalized correctly, the main difference between computing \( \mathcal{W}\left( {g\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{f}_{k},{r}_{k}^{2}}\right) \) in \( M \) , and the analogous computation for the Gaussian in \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) , comes from the \( f \) term in the integrand of \( \mathcal{W} \) . Since \( {f}_{k} \sim  {c}_{k} \) , this will drive \( \mathcal{W}\left( {g\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{f}_{k},{r}_{k}^{2}}\right) \) to \( - \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) , so \( \mu \left( {g\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{r}_{k}^{2}}\right)  \rightarrow   - \infty \) ; by the monotonicity of \( \mu \left( {g\left( t\right) ,{t}_{0} - t}\right) \) it follows that \( \mu \left( {g\left( 0\right) ,{t}_{k} + {r}_{k}^{2}}\right)  \rightarrow \; - \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) . This contradicts the fact that \( \mu \left( {g\left( 0\right) ,\tau }\right) \) is a continuous function of \( \tau \) .

To write this out precisely, let us put \( \Phi  = {e}^{-f/2} \) , so that

(13.6)

\[
\mathcal{W}\left( {g, f,\tau }\right)  = {\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{-n/2}{\int }_{M}\left\lbrack  {{4\tau }{\left| \nabla \Phi \right| }^{2} + \left( {{\tau R} - 2\ln \Phi  - n}\right) {\Phi }^{2}}\right\rbrack  {dV}.
\]

For the argument, it is enough to obtain small values of \( \mathcal{W} \) for positive \( \Phi \) . Since \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{s \rightarrow  0}}\left( {-2\ln s}\right) {s}^{2} = \) 0, by an approximation it is enough to obtain small values of \( \mathcal{W} \) for nonnegative \( \Phi \) , where the integrand is declared to be \( {4\tau }{\left| \nabla \Phi \right| }^{2} \) at points where \( \Phi \) vanishes. Take

(13.7)

\[
{\Phi }_{k}\left( x\right)  = {e}^{-{c}_{k}/2}\phi \left( {{\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {x,{p}_{k}}\right) /{r}_{k}}\right) ,
\]

where \( \phi  : \lbrack 0,\infty ) \rightarrow  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) is a monotonically nonincreasing function such that \( \phi \left( s\right)  = 1 \) if \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1/2}\right\rbrack  ,\phi \left( s\right)  = 0 \) if \( s \geq  1 \) and \( \left| {{\phi }^{\prime }\left( s\right) }\right|  \leq  {10} \) for \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {1/2,1}\right\rbrack \) . The function \( {\Phi }_{k} \) is \( a \) priori only Lipschitz, but by smoothing it slightly we can use \( {\Phi }_{k} \) in the variational formula to bound \( \mathcal{W} \) from above.

The constant \( {c}_{k} \) is determined by

(13.8)

\[
{e}^{{c}_{k}} = {\int }_{M}{\left( 4\pi {r}_{k}^{2}\right) }^{-n/2}{\phi }^{2}\left( {{\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {x,{p}_{k}}\right) /{r}_{k}}\right) {dV} \leq  {\left( 4\pi {r}_{k}^{2}\right) }^{-n/2}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B}_{k}\right) .
\]

Thus \( {c}_{k} \rightarrow   - \infty \) . Next,

(13.9)

\[
\text{ ) }\mathcal{W}\left( {g\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{f}_{k},{r}_{k}^{2}}\right)  = {\left( 4\pi {r}_{k}^{2}\right) }^{-n/2}{\int }_{M}\left\lbrack  {4{r}_{k}^{2}{\left| \nabla {\Phi }_{k}\right| }^{2} + \left( {{r}_{k}^{2}R - 2\ln {\Phi }_{k} - n}\right) {\Phi }_{k}^{2}}\right\rbrack  {dV}\text{ . }
\]

Let \( {A}_{k}\left( s\right) \) be the mass of the distance sphere \( S\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}s}\right) \) around \( {p}_{k} \) . Put

(13.10)

\[
{\bar{R}}_{k}\left( s\right)  = {r}_{k}^{2}{A}_{k}{\left( s\right) }^{-1}{\int }_{S\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}s}\right) }{Rd}\text{ area }.
\]

We can compute the integral in (13.9) radially to get (13.11)

\[
\mathcal{W}\left( {g\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{f}_{k},{r}_{k}^{2}}\right)  = \frac{{\int }_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack  {4{\left( {\phi }^{\prime }\left( s\right) \right) }^{2} + \left( {{\bar{R}}_{k}\left( s\right)  + {c}_{k} - 2\ln \phi \left( s\right)  - n}\right) {\phi }^{2}\left( s\right) }\right\rbrack  {A}_{k}\left( s\right) {ds}}{{\int }_{0}^{1}{\phi }^{2}\left( s\right) {A}_{k}\left( s\right) {ds}}.
\]

The expression \( 4{\left( {\phi }^{\prime }\left( s\right) \right) }^{2} - 2\ln \phi \left( s\right) {\phi }^{2}\left( s\right) \) vanishes if \( s \notin  \left\lbrack  {1/2,1}\right\rbrack \) , and is bounded above by \( {400} + {e}^{-1} \) if \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {1/2,1}\right\rbrack \) . Then the lower bound on the Ricci curvature and the Bishop-Gromov inequality give

(13.12)

\[
\frac{{\int }_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack  {4{\left( {\phi }^{\prime }\left( s\right) \right) }^{2} - 2\ln \phi \left( s\right) {\phi }^{2}\left( s\right) }\right\rbrack  {A}_{k}\left( s\right) {ds}}{{\int }_{0}^{1}{\phi }^{2}\left( s\right) {A}_{k}\left( s\right) {ds}} \leq  {401}\frac{\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) }\right)  - \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}/2}\right) }\right) }{\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}/2}\right) }\right) }
\]

\[
\leq  {401}\left( {\frac{{\int }_{0}^{1}{\sinh }^{n - 1}\left( s\right) {ds}}{{\int }_{0}^{1/2}{\sinh }^{n - 1}\left( s\right) {ds}} - 1}\right) .
\]

Next, from the upper bound on scalar curvature, \( {\bar{R}}_{k}\left( s\right)  \leq  n\left( {n - 1}\right) \) for \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . Putting this together gives \( \mathcal{W}\left( {g\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{f}_{k},{r}_{k}^{2}}\right)  \leq \) const. \( + {c}_{k} \) and so \( \mathcal{W}\left( {g\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{f}_{k},{r}_{k}^{2}}\right)  \rightarrow   - \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow  \infty \) .

Thus \( \mu \left( {g\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{r}_{k}^{2}}\right)  \rightarrow   - \infty \) . For any \( {t}_{0} > t,\mu \left( {g\left( t\right) ,{t}_{0} - t}\right) \) is nondecreasing in \( t \) . Hence \( \mu \left( {g\left( 0\right) ,{t}_{k} + {r}_{k}^{2}}\right)  \leq  \mu \left( {g\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{r}_{k}^{2}}\right) \) , so \( \mu \left( {g\left( 0\right) ,{t}_{k} + {r}_{k}^{2}}\right)  \rightarrow   - \infty \) . Since \( T \) is finite, \( {t}_{k} \) and \( {r}_{k}^{2} \) are uniformly bounded, and \( {t}_{k} \) uniformly positive, which contradicts the fact that \( \mu \left( {g\left( 0\right) ,\tau }\right) \) is a continuous function of \( \tau \) .

nodes.content:
Remark 13.13. In the preceding argument we only used the upper bound on scalar curvature and the lower bound on Ricci curvature, i.e. in the definition of local collapsing one could have assumed that \( R\left( {{g}_{ij}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right)  \leq  n\left( {n - 1}\right) {r}_{k}^{-2} \) in \( {B}_{k} \) and \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{g}_{ij}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right)  \geq   - \left( {n - 1}\right) {r}_{k}^{-2} \) in \( {B}_{k} \) . In fact, one can also remove the lower bound on Ricci curvature (observation of Perelman, communicated by Gang Tian). The necessary ingredients of the preceding argument were that

1. \( {r}_{k}^{-n}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) }\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) ,

2. \( {r}_{k}^{2}R \) is uniformly bounded above on \( B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) \) and

3. \( \frac{\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) }\right) }{\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}/2}\right) }\right) } \) is uniformly bounded above.

Suppose only that \( {r}_{k}^{-n}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) }\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) and for all \( k,{r}_{k}^{2}R \leq  n\left( {n - 1}\right) \) on \( B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) \) . If \( \frac{\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) }\right) }{\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}/2}\right) }\right) } < {3}^{n} \) for all \( k \) then we are done. If not, suppose that for a given \( k,\frac{\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) }\right) }{\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}/2}\right) }\right) } \geq \; {3}^{n} \) . Putting \( {r}_{k}^{\prime } = {r}_{k}/2 \) , we have that \( {\left( {r}_{k}^{\prime }\right) }^{-n}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}^{\prime }}\right) }\right)  \leq  {r}_{k}^{-n}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) }\right) \) and \( {\left( {r}_{k}^{\prime }\right) }^{2}R \leq  n\left( {n - 1}\right) \) on \( B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}^{\prime }}\right) \) . We replace \( {r}_{k} \) by \( {r}_{k}^{\prime } \) . If now \( \frac{\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) }\right) }{\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}/2}\right) }\right) } < {3}^{n} \) then we stop. If not then we repeat the process and replace \( {r}_{k} \) by \( {r}_{k}/2 \) . Eventually we will achieve that \( \frac{\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) }\right) }{\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{r}_{k}/2}\right) }\right) } < {3}^{n} \) . Then we can apply the preceding argument to this new sequence of pairs \( {\left\{  \left( {p}_{k},{r}_{k}\right) \right\}  }_{k = 1}^{\infty } \) .

nodes.content: Definition 13.14. (cf. Definition I.4.2) We say that a metric \( g \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on the scale \( \rho \) if every metric ball \( B \) of radius \( r < \rho \) , which satisfies \( \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( x\right) }\right|  \leq  {r}^{-2} \) for every \( x \in  B \) , has volume at least \( \kappa {r}^{n} \) .
