nodes.content: Corollary 40.1. (cf. Corollary I.11.3) The only oriented two-dimensional \( \kappa \) -solution is the shrinking round 2-sphere.
nodes.content_excerpt: Corollary 40.1. (cf. Corollary I.11.3) The only oriented two-dimensional \( \kappa \) -solution is the shrinking round 2-sphere.

nodes.proof:
First, the only nonflat oriented nonnegatively curved gradient shrinking 2-D soliton is the round \( {S}^{2} \) . The reference [30] given in I.11.3 for this fact does not actually cover it, as the reference only deals with compact solitons. A proof using Proposition 39.1 to rule out the noncompact case appears in [68].

Given this, the limit solution in Proposition 39.1 is a shrinking round 2-sphere. Thus the rescalings \( {\bar{\tau }}_{i}^{-1}g\left( {{t}_{0} - {\bar{\tau }}_{i}}\right) \) converge to a round 2-sphere as \( i \rightarrow  \infty \) . However, by [30] the Ricci flow makes an almost-round 2-sphere become more round. Thus any given time slice of the original \( \kappa \) -solution must be a round 2-sphere.

nodes.content: Definition 41.1. If \( M \) is a complete connected Riemannian manifold then its asymptotic scalar curvature ratio is \( \mathcal{R} = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{x \rightarrow  \infty }}R\left( x\right) d{\left( x, p\right) }^{2} \) . It is independent of the choice of basepoint \( p \) .

nodes.content: Theorem 41.2. Let \( \left( {M, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be a noncompact \( \kappa \) -solution. Then the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( \mathcal{R} \) is infinite for each time slice.
nodes.content_excerpt: Theorem 41.2. Let \( \left( {M, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be a noncompact \( \kappa \) -solution. Then the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( \mathcal{R} \) is infinite for each time slice.

nodes.proof:
Suppose that \( M \) is \( n \) -dimensional, with \( n \geq  2 \) . Pick \( p \in  M \) and consider a time- \( {t}_{0} \) slice \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . We deal with the cases \( \mathcal{R} \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) and \( \mathcal{R} = 0 \) separately and show that they lead to contradictions.

Case 1: \( 0 < \mathcal{R} < \infty \) . We choose a sequence \( {x}_{k} \in  M \) such that \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k}, p}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k}, p}\right)  \rightarrow  \mathcal{R} \) . Consider the rescaled pointed solution \( \left( {M,{x}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) }\right) \) with \( {g}_{k}\left( t\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {{t}_{0} + \frac{t}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) \) and \( t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) . We have \( {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right)  = 1 \) , and for all \( b > 0 \) , for sufficiently large \( k \) , we have \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {R}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  \frac{2\mathcal{R}}{{d}_{k}^{2}\left( {x, p}\right) } \) for all \( x \) such that \( {d}_{k}\left( {x, p}\right)  > b \) . Fix numbers \( b, B > 0 \) so that \( b < \sqrt{\mathcal{R}} < B \) . The \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing assumption gives a uniform positive lower bound on the injectivity radius of \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) \) at \( {x}_{k} \) , and so by Appendix E we may extract a pointed limit solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) , defined on a time interval \( ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) from the sequence \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) where \( {M}_{k} = \left\{  {x \in  M \mid  b < {d}_{k}\left( {x, p}\right)  < B}\right\} \) . Note that \( {g}_{\infty } \) has nonnegative curvature operator and the time slice \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is locally isometric to an annular portion of a nonflat metric cone, since \( \left( {{M}_{k}, p,{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) Gromov-Hausdorff converges to the Tits cone \( {C}_{T}\left( {M, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . (We use the word "locally" because the annulus in \( {C}_{T}\left( {M, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) need not be geodesically convex in \( {C}_{T}\left( {M, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) , so we are only saying that the distance functions in small balls match up.) When \( n = 2 \) this contradicts the fact that \( {R}_{\infty }\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1 \) . When \( n \geq  3 \) , we will derive a contradiction from Hamilton’s curvature evolution equation

(41.3)

\[
{\mathrm{{Rm}}}_{t} = \Delta \mathrm{{Rm}} + Q\left( \mathrm{{Rm}}\right) .
\]

Let \( {d}_{v} : {C}_{T}\left( {M, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) be the distance function from the vertex and let \( \rho  : {M}_{\infty } \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) be the pullback of \( {d}_{v} \) under the inclusion of the annulus \( {M}_{\infty } \) in \( {C}_{T}\left( {M, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) .

nodes.content: Lemma 41.4. The metric cone structure on \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is smooth, i.e. \( \rho \) is a smooth function.
nodes.content_excerpt: Lemma 41.4. The metric cone structure on \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is smooth, i.e. \( \rho \) is a smooth function.

nodes.proof:
Consider a unit speed geodesic segment \( \gamma \) in the Tits cone \( {C}_{T}\left( {M, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) , such that \( \gamma \) is disjoint from the vertex \( v \in  {C}_{T}\left( {M, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . Note that since \( {C}_{T}\left( {M, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) is a Euclidean cone over the Tits boundary \( {\partial }_{T}\left( {M, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) , the geodesic \( \gamma \) lies in the cone over a geodesic segment \( \widehat{\gamma } \subset  {\partial }_{T}\left( {M, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . Thus \( \gamma \) lies in a 2-dimensional locally convex flat subspace of \( {C}_{T}\left( {M, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . Also, as in a flat 2-dimensional cone, the second derivative of the composite function \( {d}_{v}^{2} \circ  \gamma \) is identically 2 .

Since \( \rho \) is obtained from \( {d}_{v} \) by composition with a locally isometric embedding \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right)  \rightarrow \; {C}_{T}\left( {M, g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) , the composition of \( {\rho }^{2} \) with any unit speed geodesic segment in \( {M}_{\infty } \) also has second derivative identically equal to 2.

Since \( {\rho }^{2} \) is Lipschitz, Rademacher’s theorem implies that \( {\rho }^{2} \) is differentiable almost everywhere. Let \( y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) be a point of differentiability of \( {\rho }^{2} \) . If the injectivity radius of \( {g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) \) at \( y \) is \( > a \) , then the function \( {h}_{y} \) given by the composition

\[
{T}_{y}{M}_{\infty } \supset  B\left( {0, a}\right) \overset{{\exp }_{y}}{ \rightarrow  }{M}_{\infty }\overset{{\rho }^{2}}{ \rightarrow  }\mathbb{R}
\]

has the property that its second radial derivative is identically 2 , and it is differentiable at the origin \( 0 \in  {T}_{y}{M}_{\infty } \) . Therefore \( {h}_{y} \) is a second order polynomial with Hessian identically 2, and is smooth. As the injectivity radius is a continuous function, this implies that \( {\rho }^{2} \) is smooth everywhere in \( {M}_{\infty } \) .

Since \( {\rho }^{2} \) is strictly positive on \( {M}_{\infty } \) , it follows that \( \rho  = \sqrt{{\rho }^{2}} \) is smooth as well.

As \( \mathcal{R} = \infty \) , there are sequences \( {x}_{k} \in  M \) and \( {s}_{k} > 0 \) such that \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k}, p}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty ,\frac{{s}_{k}}{{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k}, p}\right) } \rightarrow  0, R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {s}_{k}^{2} \rightarrow  \infty \) , and \( R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {2R}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) for all \( x \in  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{s}_{k}}\right) \) [33, Lemma 22.2]. Consider the rescaled pointed solution \( \left( {M,{x}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) }\right) \) with \( {g}_{k}\left( t\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {{t}_{0} + \frac{t}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) \) and \( t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) . As \( {R}_{t} \geq  0 \) , we have \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  2 \) whenever \( t \leq  0 \) and \( {d}_{k}\left( {x,{x}_{k}}\right)  \leq  R{\left( {x}_{k},{t}_{0}\right) }^{1/2}{s}_{k} \) , where \( {d}_{k} \) is the distance function for \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) \) and \( {R}_{k}\left( {\cdot , \cdot  }\right) \) is the scalar curvature of \( {g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) . The \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing assumption gives a uniform positive lower bound on the injectivity radius of \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) \) at \( {x}_{k} \) , so by Appendix E we may extract a complete pointed limit solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , of a subsequence of the sequence of pointed Ricci flows. By relative volume comparison, \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) has positive asymptotic volume ratio. By Appendix G, the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is isometric to an Alexandrov space which splits off a line, which means that it is a Riemannian product \( \mathbb{R} \times  N \) . This implies a product structure for earlier times; see Appendix A. Now when \( n = 2 \) , we have a contradiction, since \( R\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1 \) but \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is a product surface, and must therefore be flat. When \( n > 2 \) we obtain a \( \kappa \) -solution on an \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -manifold with positive asymptotic volume ratio at time zero, and by induction this is impossible.

nodes.title: 42. IN A κ-SOLUTION, THE CURVATURE AND THE NORMALIZED VOLUME CONTROL EACH OTHER
nodes.document_title: Bruce Kleiner and John Lott - Notes on Perelman's Papers

nodes.label: Corollary 42.1
nodes.document_title: Bruce Kleiner and John Lott - Notes on Perelman's Papers
nodes.section_title: 42. IN A κ-SOLUTION, THE CURVATURE AND THE NORMALIZED VOLUME CONTROL EACH OTHER
nodes.content:
Corollary 42.1. 1. If \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) is a ball in a time slice of a \( \kappa \) -solution, then the normalized volume \( {r}_{0}^{-n}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is controlled (i.e. bounded away from zero) \( \Leftrightarrow \) the normalized scalar curvature \( {r}_{0}^{2}R\left( {x}_{0}\right) \) is controlled (i.e. bounded above).

2. If \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) is a ball in a time slice of a \( \kappa \) -solution, then the normalized volume \( {r}_{0}^{-n}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is almost maximal \( \Leftrightarrow \) the normalized scalar curvature \( {r}_{0}^{2}R\left( {x}_{0}\right) \) is almost zero.

3. (Precompactness) If \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) is a sequence of pointed \( \kappa \) -solutions (without the assumption that \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = 1 \) ) and for some \( r > 0 \) , the \( r \) -balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k}, r}\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) have controlled normalized volume, then a subsequence converges to an ancient solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right) ,{g}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) which has nonnegative curvature operator, and is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed (though a priori the curvature may be unbounded on a given time slice).

4. There is a constant \( \eta  = \eta \left( {n,\kappa }\right) \) such that for every \( n \) -dimensional \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {M, g\left( \right) }\right) \) , and all \( x \in  M \) , we have \( \left| {\nabla R}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \eta {R}^{\frac{3}{2}}\left( {x, t}\right) \) and \( \left| {R}_{t}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \eta {R}^{2}\left( {x, t}\right) \) . More generally, there are scale invariant bounds on all derivatives of the curvature tensor, that only depend on \( n \) and \( \kappa \) . That is, for each \( \rho , k, l < \infty \) there is a constant \( C = C\left( {n,\rho , k, l,\kappa }\right)  < \infty \) such that \( \left| {\frac{{\partial }^{k}}{\partial {t}^{k}}{\nabla }^{l}\operatorname{Rm}}\right| \left( {y, t}\right)  \leq  {CR}{\left( x, t\right) }^{\left( k + \frac{l}{2} + 1\right) } \) for any \( y \in  {B}_{t}\left( {x,{\rho R}{\left( x, t\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) .

5. There is a function \( \alpha  : \lbrack 0,\infty ) \rightarrow  \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) depending only on \( \kappa \) such that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{s \rightarrow  \infty }}\alpha \left( s\right)  = \; \infty \) , and for every \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {M, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) and \( x, y \in  M \) , we have \( R\left( y\right) {d}^{2}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  \alpha \left( {R\left( x\right) {d}^{2}\left( {x, y}\right) }\right) \) .

Assertion \( 1, \Rightarrow \) . Suppose we have a sequence of \( \kappa \) -solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) , and sequences \( {t}_{k} \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack ,{x}_{k} \in  {M}_{k},{r}_{k} > 0 \) , such that at time \( {t}_{k} \) , the normalized volume of \( B\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) \) is \( \geq  c > 0 \) , and \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) {r}_{k}^{2} \rightarrow  \infty \) . By Appendix H, for each \( k \) , we can find \( {y}_{k} \in  B\left( {{x}_{k},5{r}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{r}}_{k} \leq  {r}_{k} \) , such that \( R\left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) {\bar{r}}_{k}^{2} \geq  R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) {r}_{k}^{2} \) , and \( R\left( {z,{t}_{k}}\right)  \leq  {2R}\left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) for all \( z \in  B\left( {{y}_{k},{\bar{r}}_{k}}\right) \) . Note that by relative volume comparison, whenever \( {\widetilde{r}}_{k} \leq  {\bar{r}}_{k} \) we have

(42.2)

\[
\frac{\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{y}_{k},{\widetilde{r}}_{k}}\right) }\right) }{{\widetilde{r}}_{k}^{n}} \geq  \frac{\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{y}_{k},{\bar{r}}_{k}}\right) }\right) }{{\bar{r}}_{k}^{n}} \geq  \frac{\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{y}_{k},{10}{r}_{k}}\right) }\right) }{{\left( {10}{r}_{k}\right) }^{n}} \geq  \frac{\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) }\right) }{{\left( {10}{r}_{k}\right) }^{n}} \geq  \frac{c}{{10}^{n}}.
\]

Rescaling the sequence of pointed solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) by \( R\left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , we get a sequence satisfying the hypotheses of Appendix E (we use here the fact that \( {R}_{t} \geq  0 \) for an ancient solution), so it accumulates on a limit flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{y}_{\infty },0}\right) ,{g}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) which is a \( \kappa \) -solution. By (42.2), the asymptotic volume ratio of \( \left( {M,{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is \( \geq  \frac{c}{{10}^{n}} > 0 \) . This contradicts Proposition 41.13.

Assertion 3. By relative volume comparison, it follows that every \( r \) -ball in \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) has normalized volume bounded below by a ( \( k \) -independent) function of its distance to \( {x}_{k} \) . By 1, this implies that the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) is bounded by a \( k \) -independent function of the distance to \( {x}_{k} \) , and hence we can apply Appendix E to extract a smoothly converging subsequence.

Assertion \( 1, \Leftarrow \) . Suppose we have a sequence \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) of \( \kappa \) -solutions, and sequences \( {x}_{k} \in  {M}_{k},{r}_{k} > 0 \) , such that \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) {r}_{k}^{2} < c \) for all \( k \) , but \( {r}_{k}^{-n}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) }\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) . For large \( k \) , we can choose \( {\bar{r}}_{k} \in  \left( {0,{r}_{k}}\right) \) such that \( {\bar{r}}_{k}^{-n}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{k},{\bar{r}}_{k}}\right) }\right)  = \frac{1}{2}{c}_{n} \) where \( {c}_{n} \) is the volume of the unit Euclidean \( n \) -ball. By relative volume comparison, \( \frac{{\bar{r}}_{k}}{{r}_{k}} \rightarrow  0 \) . Applying 3, we see that the pointed sequence \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) , rescaled by the factor \( {\bar{r}}_{k}^{-2} \) , accumulates on a pointed ancient solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right) ,{g}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) , such that the ball \( B\left( {{x}_{\infty },1}\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) has normalized volume \( \frac{1}{2}{c}_{n} \) at \( t = 0 \) .

Suppose the ball \( B\left( {{x}_{\infty },1}\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) were flat. Then by the Harnack inequality (F.14) (applied to the approximators) we would have \( {R}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  = 0 \) for all \( x \in  {M}_{\infty }, t \leq \) 0, i.e. \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) would be a time-independent flat manifold. It cannot be \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) since \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{\infty },1}\right) }\right)  = \frac{1}{2}{c}_{n} \) . But flat manifolds other than Euclidean space have zero asymptotic volume ratio (as follows from the Bieberbach theorem that if \( N = {\mathbb{R}}^{n}/\Gamma \) is a flat manifold and \( \Gamma \) is nontrivial then there is a \( \Gamma \) -invariant affine subspace \( A \subset  {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) of dimension at least 1 on which \( \Gamma \) acts cocompactly). This contradicts the assumption that the sequence \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed. Thus \( B\left( {{x}_{\infty },1}\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is not flat, which means, by the Harnack inequality, that the scalar curvature of \( {g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) \) is strictly positive everywhere. Therefore, with respect to \( {g}_{k} \) , we have

(42.3)

\[

\]

which is a contradiction.

Assertion 2, \( \Rightarrow \) . Apply 1, the precompactness criterion, and the fact that a nonnegatively-curved manifold whose balls have normalized volume \( {c}_{n} \) must be flat.

Assertion 2, \( \Leftarrow \) . Apply 1, the precompactness criterion, and the Harnack inequality (F.14) (to the approximators).

Assertion 4. This follows by rescaling \( g \) so that \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  = 1 \) , and applying 1 and 3 .

Assertion 5. The quantity \( R\left( z\right) {d}^{2}\left( {u, v}\right) \) is scale invariant. This contradicts 1 and 3 .

nodes.proof:
If the lemma were not true then there would be a sequence \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) of 2-dimensional \( \kappa \) -solutions, and sequences \( {x}_{k},{y}_{k} \in  {M}_{k},{t}_{k} \in  \mathbb{R} \) such that \( {r}_{k}^{-2}\operatorname{vol}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) }\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) , where \( {r}_{k} = d\left( {{x}_{k},{y}_{k}}\right) \) . Let \( {z}_{k} \) be the midpoint of a shortest segment from \( {x}_{k} \) to \( {y}_{k} \) in the \( {t}_{k} \) -time slice \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) . For large \( k \) , choose \( {\bar{r}}_{k} \in  \left( {0,{r}_{k}/2}\right) \) such that

(43.3)

\[
{\bar{r}}_{k}^{-2}\operatorname{vol}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{z}_{k},{\bar{r}}_{k}}\right) }\right)  = \frac{\pi }{2},
\]

i.e. half the area of the unit disk in \( {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \) . As

(43.4)

\[
\frac{\pi }{2} = {\bar{r}}_{k}^{-2}\operatorname{vol}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{z}_{k},{\bar{r}}_{k}}\right) }\right)  \leq  {\bar{r}}_{k}^{-2}\operatorname{vol}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) }\right)  = {\left( {\bar{r}}_{k}/{r}_{k}\right) }^{-2}{r}_{k}^{-2}\operatorname{vol}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) }\right)
\]

it follows that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}\frac{{\bar{r}}_{k}}{{r}_{k}} = 0 \) . Then by part 3 of Corollary 42.1, the sequence of pointed Ricci flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{z}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) , when rescaled by \( {\bar{r}}_{k}^{-2} \) , accumulates on a complete Ricci flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{z}_{\infty },0}\right) ,{g}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) . The segments from \( {z}_{k} \) to \( {x}_{k} \) and \( {y}_{k} \) accumulate on a line in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) , and hence \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) splits off a line. By (43.3), \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) cannot be isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \) , and hence must be a cylinder. Considering the approximating Ricci flows, we get a contradiction to the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing assumption.

Given \( \epsilon  > 0 \) , suppose that the corollary is not true. Then there is a sequence of such Ricci flow solutions with \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{k},{A}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }\right)  > \epsilon {\left( {A}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) }^{n} \) at time zero, where \( {A}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) . By Bishop-Gromov, \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{k},{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }\right)  > \epsilon {Q}_{k}^{-\frac{n}{2}} \) at time zero, so we can parabolically rescale by \( {Q}_{k} \) and take a convergent subsequence. The limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) will be a nonflat complete ancient solution with nonnegative curvature operator, bounded curvature and \( \mathcal{V}\left( 0\right)  > 0 \) . By Proposition 41.13, it cannot be \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed for any \( \kappa \) . Thus for each \( \kappa  > 0 \) , there are a point \( \left( {{x}_{\kappa },{t}_{\kappa }}\right)  \in  {M}_{\infty } \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) and a radius \( {r}_{\kappa } \) so that \( \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{x}_{\kappa },{t}_{\kappa }}\right) }\right|  \leq  {r}_{\kappa }^{-2} \) on the time- \( {t}_{\kappa } \) ball \( B\left( {{x}_{\kappa },{r}_{\kappa }}\right) \) , but \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{\kappa },{r}_{\kappa }}\right) }\right)  < \kappa {r}_{\kappa }^{n} \) . From the Bishop-Gromov inequality, \( \mathcal{V}\left( {t}_{\kappa }\right)  < \kappa \) for the limit solution.

We claim that \( \mathcal{V}\left( t\right) \) is nonincreasing in \( t \) . To see this, we have \( \frac{\operatorname{dvol}\left( U\right) }{dt} = {\int }_{U}{RdV} \geq  0 \) for any domain \( U \subset  {M}_{\infty } \) . Also, as \( R \leq  2 \) on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , Corollary 27.16 gives that distances on \( {M}_{\infty } \) decrease at most linearly in \( t \) , which implies the claim.

Thus \( \mathcal{V}\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) for the limit solution, which is a contradiction.

For part (a), we can assume that \( {r}_{0} = 1 \) . Given \( B, C > 0 \) , suppose that \( g\left( \cdot \right) \) is a Ricci flow solution for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) that satisfies the hypotheses of the corollary, with \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  > C + B{\left( t - {t}_{0}\right) }^{-1} \) for some \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) satisfying \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{4} \) . Following the notation of the proof of Theorem 30.1, except changing the \( A \) of Theorem 30.1 to \( \widehat{A} \) , put \( \widehat{A} = \lambda {C}^{\frac{1}{2}} \) and \( \alpha  = \min \left( {{\lambda }^{2}{C}^{\frac{1}{2}}, B}\right) \) , where we will take \( \lambda \) to be a sufficiently small number that only depends on \( n \) . Put

(45.5)

\[

\]

Clearly \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {M}_{\alpha } \) .

We first go through the analog of the proof of Lemma 31.1. We claim that there is some \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  \in  {M}_{\alpha } \) , with \( \bar{t} \in  \left( {{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{3} \) , such that \( R\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \leq  {2Q} = {2R}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) whenever \( \left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \in  {M}_{\alpha },{t}^{\prime } \in  \left( {{t}_{0},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}^{\prime },{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  + \widehat{A}{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . Put \( \left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  = \; \left( {x, t}\right) \) . Inductively, if we cannot take \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) for \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) then there is some \( \left( {{x}_{k + 1},{t}_{k + 1}}\right)  \in  {M}_{\alpha } \) with \( {t}_{k + 1} \in  \left( {{t}_{0},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack  , R\left( {{x}_{k + 1},{t}_{k + 1}}\right)  > {2R}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{k + 1}}\left( {{x}_{k + 1},{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  + \; \widehat{A}R{\left( {x}_{k},{t}_{k}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . As the process must terminate, we end up with \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) satisfying

(45.6)

\[
{\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{1 - \sqrt{1/2}}\widehat{A}R{\left( x, t\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  \frac{1}{3}
\]

if \( \lambda \) is sufficiently small.

Next, we go through the analog of the proof of Lemma 32.1. As in the proof of Lemma 32.1, \( R\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \leq  {2R}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) whenever \( \bar{t} - \frac{1}{2}\alpha {Q}^{-1} \leq  {t}^{\prime } \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}^{\prime },{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  + \widehat{A}{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . We claim that the time- \( \bar{t} \) ball \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  + \frac{1}{10}\widehat{A}{Q}^{-1/2}}\right) \) is contained in the time- \( {t}^{\prime } \) ball \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  + \widehat{A}{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) . To see this, we apply Lemma 27.8 with \( {r}_{0} = \frac{1}{2}{Q}^{-1/2} \) to give

(45.7)

\[
{\operatorname{dist}}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},\bar{x}}\right)  - {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {{x}_{0},\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  \operatorname{const}.\left( n\right) \alpha {Q}^{-1/2} \leq  \lambda \operatorname{const}.\left( n\right) \widehat{A}{Q}^{-1/2}.
\]

If \( \lambda \) is sufficiently small then the claim follows. The argument also shows that it is consistent to use the curvature bound when applying Lemma 27.8.

Hence \( R\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \leq  {2R}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) whenever \( \bar{t} - \frac{1}{2}\alpha {Q}^{-1} \leq  {t}^{\prime } \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {{x}^{\prime },{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  + \; \frac{1}{10}\widehat{A}{Q}^{-1/2} \) . It follows that \( R\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \leq  {2R}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) whenever \( \bar{t} - \frac{1}{2}\alpha {Q}^{-1} \leq  {t}^{\prime } \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {{x}^{\prime },\bar{x}}\right)  \leq \; \frac{1}{10}\widehat{A}{Q}^{-1/2} \) . This shows that there is an \( {A}^{\prime } = {A}^{\prime }\left( {B, C}\right) \) , which goes to infinity as \( B, C \rightarrow  \infty \) , so that \( R\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \leq  {2R}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) whenever \( \bar{t} - {A}^{\prime }{Q}^{-1} \leq  {t}^{\prime } \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {{x}^{\prime },\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  {A}^{\prime }{Q}^{-1/2} \) .

Now suppose that Corollary 45.1(a) is not true. Fixing \( w > 0 \) , for any sequences \( {\left\{  {B}_{k}\right\}  }_{k = 1}^{\infty } \) and \( {\left\{  {C}_{k}\right\}  }_{k = 1}^{\infty } \) going to infinity and for each \( k \) , there is a Ricci flow solution \( {g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) which satisfies the hypotheses of the corollary but for which \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \geq  {C}_{k} + {B}_{k}{\left( {t}_{k} - {t}_{0, k}\right) }^{-1} \) for some point \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) satisfying \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0, k}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{4} \) . We can assume that \( {\lambda }^{2}{C}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}} \geq  {B}_{k} \) . From the preceding discussion, there is a sequence \( {A}_{k}^{\prime } \rightarrow  \infty \) and points \( \left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{\bar{t}}_{k}}\right) \) with \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{\bar{t}}_{k}}\left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{x}_{0, k}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{3} \) so that \( R\left( {{x}_{k}^{\prime },{t}_{k}^{\prime }}\right)  \leq  {2R}\left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{\bar{t}}_{k}}\right) \) whenever \( {\bar{t}}_{k} - {A}_{k}^{\prime }{Q}_{k}^{-1} \leq  {t}_{k}^{\prime } \leq  {\bar{t}}_{k} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{\bar{t}}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k}^{\prime },{\bar{x}}_{k}}\right)  \leq  {A}_{k}^{\prime }{Q}_{k}^{-1/2} \) , where

(45.8)

\[
{Q}_{k} = R\left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{\bar{t}}_{k}}\right)  \geq  {B}_{k}{\left( {\bar{t}}_{k} - {t}_{0, k}\right) }^{-1} \geq  {B}_{k}.
\]

By Corollary 44.1, for any \( \epsilon  > 0 \) there is some \( A = A\left( \epsilon \right)  < \infty \) so that for large \( k \) ,

(45.9)

\[
\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{\bar{x}}_{k}, A/\sqrt{{Q}_{k}}}\right) }\right)  \leq  \epsilon {\left( A/\sqrt{{Q}_{k}}\right) }^{n}
\]

at time zero. By the Bishop-Gromov inequality, \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},1}\right) }\right)  \leq  \epsilon \) for large \( k \) , since \( {Q}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) . If we took \( \epsilon \) sufficiently small from the beginning then we would get a contradiction to the fact that

(45.10)

\[
\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},1}\right) }\right)  \geq  \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{0, k},\frac{2}{3}}\right) }\right)  \geq  {\left( \frac{2}{3}\right) }^{n}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{0, k},1}\right) }\right)  \geq  {\left( \frac{2}{3}\right) }^{n}w.
\]

For part (b), the idea is to choose the parameter \( {\tau }_{0} \) sufficiently small so that we will still have the estimate \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  {5}^{-n}w{r}_{0}^{n} \) for the time- \( t \) ball \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) when \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{\tau }_{0}{r}_{0}^{2},0}\right\rbrack \) , and so we can apply part (a) with \( w \) replaced by \( \frac{w}{5} \) . The value of \( {\tau }_{0} \) will emerge from the proof. More precisely, putting \( {r}_{0} = 1 \) and with a given \( {\tau }_{0} \) , let \( \tau \) be the largest number in \( \left\lbrack  {0,{\tau }_{0}}\right\rbrack \) so that the time- \( t \) ball \( B\left( {{x}_{0},1}\right) \) satisfies \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{0},1}\right) }\right)  \geq  {5}^{-n}w \) whenever \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-\tau ,0}\right\rbrack \) . If \( \tau  < {\tau }_{0} \) then at time \( - \tau \) , we have \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{0},1}\right) }\right)  = {5}^{-n}w \) . The conclusion of part (a) holds in the sense that

(45.11)

\[
R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C\left( {{5}^{-n}w}\right)  + B\left( {{5}^{-n}w}\right) {\left( t + \tau \right) }^{-1}
\]

whenever \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-\tau ,0}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{4} \) . Lemma 27.8, along with (45.11), implies that the time- \( \left( {-\tau }\right) \) ball \( B\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{4}}\right) \) contains the time-0 ball \( B\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{4} - {10}\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {\tau \sqrt{C} + 2\sqrt{B\tau }}\right) }\right) \) . From the nonnegative curvature, the time- \( \left( {-\tau }\right) \) volume of the first ball is at least as large as the time-0 volume of the second ball. Then

(45.12)

\[
{5}^{-n}w = \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{0},1}\right) }\right)  \geq  \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{4}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\geq  \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{4} - {10}\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {\tau \sqrt{C} + 2\sqrt{B\tau }}\right) }\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\geq  {\left( \frac{1}{4} - {10}\left( n - 1\right) \left( \tau \sqrt{C} + 2\sqrt{B\tau }\right) \right) }^{n}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{0},1}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\geq  {\left( \frac{1}{4} - {10}\left( n - 1\right) \left( \tau \sqrt{C} + 2\sqrt{B\tau }\right) \right) }^{n}w,
\]

where the balls on the top line of (45.12) are at time- \( \left( {-\tau }\right) \) , and the other balls are at time-0 . Thus \( \frac{1}{4} - {10}\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {\tau \sqrt{C} + 2\sqrt{B\tau }}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{5} \) . This contradicts our assumption that \( \tau  < {\tau }_{0} \) provided that \( \frac{1}{4} - {10}\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {{\tau }_{0}\sqrt{C} + 2\sqrt{B{\tau }_{0}}}\right)  = \frac{1}{5} \) .

(cf. end of Section I.11.6) For every \( w > 0 \) , there are \( B = B\left( w\right)  < \infty \) , \( C = C\left( w\right)  < \infty \) and \( {\tau }_{0} = {\tau }_{0}\left( w\right)  > 0 \) with the following property. Suppose that for each \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{\tau }_{0}{r}_{0}^{2},0}\right\rbrack \) , the curvature operator in the time-t ball \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) is bounded below by \( - {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . If we assume a time-zero volume bound \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {{B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  w{r}_{0}^{n} \) then

nodes.label: Theorem 46.1
nodes.document_title: Bruce Kleiner and John Lott - Notes on Perelman's Papers
nodes.section_title: 46. I.11.7. COMPACTNESS OF THE SPACE OF THREE-DIMENSIONAL κ-SOLUTIONS
nodes.content: Theorem 46.1. (cf. Theorem I.11.7) Given \( \kappa  > 0 \) , the set of oriented three-dimensional \( \kappa \) -solutions is compact modulo scaling. That is, from any sequence of such solutions and points \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) , after appropriate dilations we can extract a smoothly converging subsequence that satisfies the same conditions.
nodes.content_excerpt: Theorem 46.1. (cf. Theorem I.11.7) Given \( \kappa > 0 \) , the set of oriented three-dimensional \( \kappa \) -solutions is compact modulo scaling. That is, from any sequence of such solutions and points \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) , after appropriate dilations we can extract a smoothly converging subsequence that satisfies the same conditions.

nodes.proof:
If \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) ,{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) is a sequence of such \( \kappa \) -solutions with \( R\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right)  = 1 \) then parts 1 and 3 of Corollary 42.1 imply there is a subsequence that converges to an ancient solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right) ,{g}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) which has nonnegative curvature operator and is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed. The remaining issue is to show that it has bounded curvature. Note that \( {R}_{t} \geq  0 \) since \( {g}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) \) is a limit of a sequence of Ricci flows satisfying \( {R}_{t} \geq  0 \) . Hence it is enough to show that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty }, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) has bounded scalar curvature.

If not, there is a sequence of points \( {y}_{i} \) going to infinity in \( {M}_{\infty } \) such that \( R\left( {{y}_{i},0}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( R\left( {y,0}\right)  \leq  {2R}\left( {{y}_{i},0}\right) \) for \( y \in  B\left( {{y}_{i},{A}_{i}R{\left( {y}_{i},0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) , where \( {A}_{i} \rightarrow  \infty \) ; compare [33, Lemma 22.2]. Using the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing, a subsequence of the rescalings \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{y}_{i}, R\left( {{y}_{i},0}\right) {g}_{\infty }}\right) \) will converge to a limit manifold \( {N}_{\infty } \) . As in the proof of Proposition 41.13 from Appendix G, \( {N}_{\infty } \) will split off a line. By Corollary 40.1 or Section 43, \( {N}_{\infty } \) must be the standard solution on \( \mathbb{R} \times  {S}^{2} \) . Thus \( \left( {{M}_{\infty }, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) contains a sequence \( {D}_{i} \) of neck regions, with their cross-sectional radii tending to zero as \( i \rightarrow  \infty \) .

Note that \( {M}_{\infty } \) has to be 1-ended. Otherwise, it would contain a line, and would therefore have to split off a line isometrically [18, Theorem 8.17]. But then \( {M}_{\infty } \) , the product of a line and a surface, could not have neck regions with cross-sections tending to zero.

From the theory of nonnegatively curved manifolds [18, Chapter 8.5], there is an exhaustion \( {M}_{\infty } = \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{t > 0}}{C}_{t} \) by nonempty totally convex compact sets \( {C}_{t} \) so that \( \left( {{t}_{1} \leq  {t}_{2}}\right)  \Rightarrow  \left( {{C}_{{t}_{1}} \subset  }\right. \; \left. {C}_{{t}_{2}}\right) \) , and

(46.2)

\[
{C}_{{t}_{1}} = \left\{  {q \in  {C}_{{t}_{2}} : \operatorname{dist}\left( {q,\partial {C}_{{t}_{2}}}\right)  \geq  {t}_{2} - {t}_{1}}\right\}  .
\]

Now consider a neck region \( D \) which is close to a cylinder. Note by triangle comparison - or simply because the distance function in \( D \) is close to that of a product metric - any minimizing geodesic segment \( \gamma  \subset  D \) of length large compared to cross-sectional radius of \( D \) must be nearly orthogonal to the cross-section. It follows from this and (46.2) that if \( t > 0 \) and \( \partial {C}_{t} \) contains a point \( p \in  D \) such that \( d\left( {p,\partial D}\right) \) is large compared to the cross-section of \( D \) , then \( \partial {C}_{t} \cap  D \) is an approximate 2-sphere cross-section of \( D \) . Fix such a neck region \( {D}_{0} \) and let \( {C}_{{t}_{0}} \) be the corresponding convex set. As \( {M}_{\infty } \) has one end, \( \partial {C}_{{t}_{0}} \) has only one connected component, namely the approximate 2-sphere cross-section.

For all \( t > {t}_{0} \) , there is a distance-nonincreasing retraction \( r : {C}_{t} \rightarrow  {C}_{{t}_{0}} \) which maps \( {C}_{t} - {C}_{{t}_{0}} \) onto \( \partial {C}_{{t}_{0}}\left\lbrack  {60}\right\rbrack \) . Let \( D \) be a neck region with a very small cross-section and let \( {C}_{t} \) be a convex set so that \( \partial {C}_{t} \) intersects \( D \) in an approximate 2-sphere cross-section. Then \( \partial {C}_{t} \) consists entirely of this approximate cross-section. The restriction of \( r \) to \( \partial {C}_{t} \) is distance-nonincreasing, but will map the 2-sphere \( \partial {C}_{t} \) onto the 2-sphere \( \partial {C}_{{t}_{0}} \) . This is a contradiction.

nodes.content: Remark 46.4. One may wonder where we have used the fact that we have a Ricci flow solution, i.e. whether the curvature is bounded for any \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed Riemannian 3- manifold with nonnegative sectional curvature. Following the above argument, we could again split off a line in a rescaling around high-curvature points. However, we would not necessarily know that the ensuing nonnegatively-curved surface is compact. (A priori, it could be a smoothed-out cone, for example.) In the case of a Ricci flow, the compactness comes from Corollary 40.1 or Section 43.

Definition 47.1. Fix \( \epsilon  > 0 \) . Let \( \left( {M, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be an oriented three-dimensional \( \kappa \) -solution. We say that a point \( {x}_{0} \in  M \) is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck if the solution \( g\left( \cdot \right) \) in the set \( \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  :  - {\left( \epsilon Q\right) }^{-1} < t \leq  0,{\operatorname{dist}}_{0}{\left( x,{x}_{0}\right) }^{2} < {\left( \epsilon Q\right) }^{-1}}\right\} \) , where \( Q = R\left( {{x}_{0},0}\right) \) , is, after scaling with the factor \( Q,\epsilon \) -close in some fixed smooth topology to the corresponding subset of the evolving round cylinder (having scalar curvature one at time zero). (See Definition 58.1 below for a more precise statement.)

We let \( {M}_{\epsilon } \) denote the points in \( M \) that are not centers of \( \epsilon \) -necks.

nodes.proof:
We prove here the claims of Corollary 47.2, except for the diameter bound. In the next section we give another argument which also proves the diameter bound.

We claim first that \( {M}_{\epsilon } \) is compact. Suppose not. Then there is a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \in  {M}_{\epsilon } \) going to infinity. Fix a basepoint \( {x}_{0} \in  M \) . Then \( R\left( {x}_{0}\right) {\operatorname{dist}}_{0}^{2}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) . By part 5 of Corollary 42.1, \( R\left( {x}_{k}\right) {\operatorname{dist}}_{0}^{2}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) . Rescaling around \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) to make its scalar curvature one, we can use Theorem 46.1 to extract a convergent subsequence \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) . As in the proof of Proposition 41.13, we can say that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) splits off a line. Hence for large \( k,{x}_{k} \) is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck, which is a contradiction.

Next we claim that for any \( \epsilon \) , there exists \( C = C\left( {\epsilon ,\kappa }\right)  > 0 \) such that if \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) is a \( \kappa \) -solution then for any point \( x \in  {M}_{\epsilon } \) , there is a point \( {x}_{0} \in  \partial {M}_{\epsilon } \) such that \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{0}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  C{Q}^{-1/2} \) and \( {C}^{-1}Q \leq  R\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  {CQ} \) , where \( Q = R\left( {{x}_{0},0}\right) \) .

If not then there is a sequence \( {\left\{  {M}_{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) of \( \kappa \) -solutions along with points \( {x}_{i} \in  {M}_{i,\epsilon } \) such that for each \( {y}_{i} \in  \partial {M}_{i,\epsilon } \) , we have

1. \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{0}^{2}\left( {{x}_{i},{y}_{i}}\right) R\left( {{y}_{i},0}\right)  \geq  i \) or

2. \( R\left( {{y}_{i},0}\right)  \geq  {iR}\left( {{x}_{i},0}\right) \) or

3. \( R\left( {{x}_{i},0}\right)  \geq  {iR}\left( {{y}_{i},0}\right) \) .

Rescale the metric on \( {M}_{i} \) so that \( R\left( {{x}_{i},0}\right)  = 1 \) . From Theorem 46.1, a subsequence of the pointed spaces \( \left( {{M}_{i},{x}_{i}}\right) \) will converge smoothly to a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) . Also, \( {x}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty ,\epsilon } \) .

Taking a subsequence, we can assume that 1 . occurs for each \( i \) , or 2 . occurs for each \( i \) , or 3. occurs for each \( i \) . If \( {M}_{\infty } \neq  {M}_{\infty ,\epsilon } \) , choose \( {y}_{\infty } \in  \partial {M}_{\infty ,\epsilon } \) . Then \( {y}_{\infty } \) is the limit of a subsequence of points \( {y}_{i} \in  \partial {M}_{i,\epsilon } \) .

If 1. occurs for each \( i \) then \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{0}^{2}\left( {{x}_{\infty },{y}_{\infty }}\right) R\left( {{y}_{\infty },0}\right)  = \infty \) , which is impossible. If 2. occurs for each \( i \) then \( R\left( {{y}_{\infty },0}\right)  = \infty \) , which is impossible. If 3 . occurs for each \( i \) then \( R\left( {{y}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 0 \) . It follows from (F.14) that \( {M}_{\infty } \) is flat, which is impossible, as \( R\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1 \) .

Hence \( {M}_{\infty } = {M}_{\infty ,\epsilon } \) , i.e. no point in the noncompact ancient solution \( {M}_{\infty } \) is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck. This contradicts the previous conclusion that \( {M}_{\infty ,\epsilon } \) is compact.

Corollary 48.1. For all \( \kappa  > 0 \) , there exists an \( {\epsilon }_{0} > 0 \) such that for all \( 0 < \epsilon  < {\epsilon }_{0} \) there exists an \( \alpha  = \alpha \left( {\epsilon ,\kappa }\right) \) with the property that for any \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {M, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) , and at any time \( t \) , precisely one of the following holds \( \left( {M}_{\epsilon }\right. \) denotes the set of points which are not centers of \( \epsilon \) -necks at time \( t \) ):

A. \( \left( {M, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) is round cylindrical flow, and so every point at every time is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck for all \( \epsilon  > 0 \) .

B. \( M \) is noncompact, \( {M}_{\epsilon } \neq  \varnothing \) , and for all \( x, y \in  {M}_{\epsilon } \) , we have \( R\left( x\right) {d}^{2}\left( {x, y}\right)  < \alpha \) .

C. \( M \) is compact, and there is a pair of points \( x, y \in  {M}_{\epsilon } \) such that \( R\left( x\right) {d}^{2}\left( {x, y}\right)  > \alpha \) ,

(48.2)

\[
{M}_{\epsilon } \subset  B\left( {x,{\alpha R}{\left( x\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \cup  B\left( {y,{\alpha R}{\left( y\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,
\]

and there is a minimizing geodesic \( \overline{xy} \) such that every \( z \in  M - {M}_{\epsilon } \) satisfies \( R\left( z\right) {d}^{2}\left( {z,\overline{xy}}\right)  < \; \alpha \) .

D. \( M \) is compact and there exists a point \( x \in  {M}_{\epsilon } \) such that \( R\left( x\right) {d}^{2}\left( {x, z}\right)  < \alpha \) for all \( z \in  M \) .

nodes.proof:
Let \( \left( {M, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be a \( \kappa \) -solution, and \( \epsilon  > 0 \) .

Case 1: Every \( x \in  \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck. In this case, if \( \epsilon  > 0 \) is sufficiently small, \( M \) fibers over a 1-manifold with fiber \( {S}^{2} \) . If the 1-manifold is homeomorphic to \( \mathbb{R} \) , then \( M \) has two ends, which implies that the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) is an evolving round cylinder. If the base of the fibration were a circle, then the universal cover \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) }\right) \) would split off a line, which would imply that the universal covering flow would be a round cylindrical flow; but this would violate the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed assumption at very negative times. Thus A holds in this case.

Case 2: There exist \( x, y \in  {M}_{\epsilon } \) such that \( R\left( x\right) {d}^{2}\left( {x, y}\right)  > \alpha \) . By Lemma 48.3 and Corollary 42.1 part 5, for all \( z \in  M - \left( {B\left( {x,{\alpha R}{\left( x\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \cup  B\left( {y,{\alpha R}{\left( y\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }\right) \) , we have \( R\left( z\right) {d}^{2}\left( {z,\overline{xy}}\right)  < \alpha \) and \( z \notin  {M}_{\epsilon } \) . This implies (again by Corollary 42.1 part 5) that there exists a \( \gamma  = \gamma \left( {\epsilon ,\kappa }\right) \) such that for every \( z \in  M \) there is a \( {z}^{\prime } \in  \overline{xy} \) for which \( R\left( {z}^{\prime }\right) {d}^{2}\left( {{z}^{\prime }, z}\right)  < \gamma \) , which means that \( M \) must be compact, and \( \mathrm{C} \) holds.

Case 3: \( {M}_{\epsilon } \neq  \varnothing \) , and for all \( x, y \in  {M}_{\epsilon } \) , we have \( R\left( x\right) {d}^{2}\left( {x, y}\right)  < \alpha \) . If \( M \) is noncompact then we are in case B and are done, so assume that \( M \) is compact. Pick \( x \in  {M}_{\epsilon } \) , and suppose \( z \in  M \) maximizes \( R\left( x\right) {d}^{2}\left( {\cdot , x}\right) \) . If \( R\left( x\right) {d}^{2}\left( {z, x}\right)  \geq  \alpha \) , then \( z \) is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck, and we may look at the cross-section \( \sum \) of the neck region. If \( \sum \) separates \( M \) , then when \( \epsilon  > 0 \) is sufficiently small, we get a contradiction to the assumption that \( z \) maximizes \( R\left( x\right) {d}^{2}\left( {x, \cdot  }\right) \) . Hence \( \sum \) cannot separate \( M \) , and there is a loop passing through \( x \) which intersects \( \sum \) transversely at one point. It follows that the universal covering flow \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) is cylindrical flow, a contradiction. Hence \( R\left( x\right) {d}^{2}\left( {x, z}\right)  < \alpha \) for all \( z \in  M \) , so \( \mathrm{D} \) holds.

Pick \( \epsilon  > 0,\kappa  > 0 \) , and suppose no such \( \alpha \) exists. Then there is a sequence \( {\alpha }_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) , a sequence of \( \kappa \) -solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) , and sequences \( {x}_{k},{y}_{k},{z}_{k} \in  {M}_{k},{t}_{k} \in  \mathbb{R} \) violating the

\( {\alpha }_{k} \) -version of the statement for all \( k \) . In particular, \( {x}_{k},{y}_{k} \in  {\left( {M}_{k}\right) }_{\epsilon } \) and

\[
\text{ (48.4) }R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{k}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{y}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty , R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{k}}^{2}\left( {{z}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \text{ , and }R\left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{k}}^{2}\left( {{z}_{k},{y}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \text{ . }
\]

Let \( {z}_{k}^{\prime } \in  \overline{{x}_{k}{y}_{k}} \) be a point in \( \overline{{x}_{k}{y}_{k}} \) nearest \( {z}_{k} \) in \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) .

We first show that \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{k}}^{2}\left( {{z}_{k}^{\prime },{x}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) . If not, we may pass to a subsequence on which \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{k}}^{2}\left( {{z}_{k}^{\prime },{x}_{k}}\right) \) remains bounded. Applying Theorem 46.1, we may pass to a subsequence and rescale by \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , to make the sequence \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) converge to a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right) ,{g}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) , the segments \( \overline{{x}_{k}{y}_{k}} \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) converge to a ray \( \overline{{x}_{\infty }\xi } \subset \; \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) , and the segments \( \overline{{z}_{k}^{\prime }{z}_{k}} \) converge to a ray \( \overline{{z}_{\infty }^{\prime }\eta } \) . Recall that the comparison angle \( {Z}_{{z}_{\infty }^{\prime }}\left( {u, v}\right) \) tends to the Tits angle \( {\partial }_{T}\left( {\xi ,\eta }\right) \) as \( u \in  \overline{{z}_{\infty }^{\prime }\xi }, v \in  \overline{{z}_{\infty }^{\prime }\eta } \) tend to infinity. Since \( d\left( {{z}_{k},{z}_{k}^{\prime }}\right)  = d\left( {{z}_{k},\overline{{x}_{k}{y}_{k}}}\right) \) we must have \( {\partial }_{T}\left( {\xi ,\eta }\right)  \geq  \frac{\pi }{2} \) . Now consider a sequence \( {u}_{k} \in  \overline{{z}_{\infty }^{\prime }\xi } \) tending to infinity. By Theorem 46.1, part 5 of Corollary 42.1, and the remarks about Alexandrov spaces in Appendix G, if we rescale \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{u}_{k},0}\right) ,{g}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) by \( R\left( {{u}_{k},0}\right) \) , we get round cylindrical flow as a limit. When \( k \) is sufficiently large, we may find an almost product region \( D \subset  \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) containing \( {u}_{k} \) which is disjoint from \( \overline{{z}_{\infty }^{\prime }\eta } \) , and whose cross-section \( \sum  \times  \{ 0\}  \subset  \sum  \times  \left( {-1,1}\right)  \simeq  D \) intersects the ray \( \overline{{z}_{\infty }^{\prime }\xi } \) transversely at a single point. This implies that \( \sum  \times  \{ 0\} \) separates the two ends of \( \overline{{z}_{\infty }^{\prime }\xi } \cup  \overline{{z}_{\infty }^{\prime }\eta } \) from each other; hence \( {M}_{\infty } \) is two-ended, and \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) is round cylindrical flow. This contradicts the assumption that \( {x}_{k} \) is not the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck. Hence \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{k}}^{2}\left( {{z}_{k}^{\prime },{x}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) , and similar reasoning shows that \( R\left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{k}}^{2}\left( {{z}_{k}^{\prime },{y}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) .

By part 5 of Corollary 42.1, we therefore have \( R\left( {{z}_{k}^{\prime },{t}_{k}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{k}}^{2}\left( {{z}_{k}^{\prime },{x}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( R\left( {{z}_{k}^{\prime },{t}_{k}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{k}}^{2}\left( {{z}_{k}^{\prime },{y}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow \; \infty \) . Rescaling the sequence \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{z}_{k}^{\prime },{t}_{k}}\right) ,{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) by \( R\left( {{z}_{k}^{\prime },{t}_{k}}\right) \) , we get convergence to round cylindrical flow (since any limit flow contains a line), and \( \overline{{z}_{k}^{\prime }{z}_{k}} \) subconverges to a segment orthogonal to the \( \mathbb{R} \) -factor, which implies that \( R\left( {{z}_{k}^{\prime },{t}_{k}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{k}}^{2}\left( {{z}_{k},{z}_{k}^{\prime }}\right) \) is bounded and \( {z}_{k} \) is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck for large \( k \) . This contradicts our assumption that the \( {\alpha }_{k} \) -version of the lemma is violated for each \( k \) .

is sufficiently large, we can apply the preceding proposition to the triple \( {z}^{\prime },{y}_{1},{y}_{2} \) , to conclude that \( {z}^{\prime } \) is the center of an \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) -neck. Since the shortest segment from \( z \) to \( {z}^{\prime } \) is orthogonal to \( \eta \) , when \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) is small enough the segment \( \overline{z{z}^{\prime }} \) will lie close to an \( {S}^{2} \) cross-section in the approximating round cylinder, which gives \( R\left( {z}^{\prime }\right) {d}^{2}\left( {z,{z}^{\prime }}\right)  \lesssim  2{\pi }^{2} \) .

nodes.label: Proposition 50.1
nodes.document_title: Bruce Kleiner and John Lott - Notes on Perelman's Papers
nodes.section_title: 50. I.11.9. GETTING A UNIFORM VALUE OF κ
nodes.content: Proposition 50.1. There is a \( {\kappa }_{0} > 0 \) so that if \( \left( {M, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) is an oriented three-dimensional \( \kappa \) -solution, for some \( \kappa  > 0 \) , then it is a \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution or it is a quotient of the round shrinking \( {S}^{3} \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: Proposition 50.1. There is a \( {\kappa }_{0} > 0 \) so that if \( \left( {M, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) is an oriented three-dimensional \( \kappa \) -solution, for some \( \kappa > 0 \) , then it is a \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution or it is a quotient of the round shrinking \( {S}^{3} \) .

nodes.proof:
Let \( \left( {M, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be a \( \kappa \) -solution. Suppose that for some \( {\kappa }^{\prime } > 0 \) , the solution is \( {\kappa }^{\prime } \) - collapsed at some scale. After rescaling, we can assume that there is a point \( \left( {{x}_{0},0}\right) \) so that \( \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  1 \) for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) satisfying \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{0}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < 1 \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-1,0}\right\rbrack \) , with \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {{B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{0},1}\right) }\right)  < \; {\kappa }^{\prime } \) . Let \( \widetilde{V}\left( t\right) \) denote the reduced volume as a function of \( t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , as defined using curves from \( \left( {{x}_{0},0}\right) \) . It is nondecreasing in \( t \) . As in the proof of Theorem 26.2, there is an estimate \( \widetilde{V}\left( {-{\kappa }^{\prime }}\right)  \leq  3{\left( {\kappa }^{\prime }\right) }^{3/2} \) . Take a sequence of times \( {t}_{i} \rightarrow   - \infty \) . For each \( {t}_{i} \) , choose \( {q}_{i} \in  M \) so that \( l\left( {{q}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right)  \leq  \frac{3}{2} \) . From the proof of Proposition 39.1, for all \( \epsilon  > 0 \) there is a \( \delta  > 0 \) such that \( l\left( {q, t}\right) \) does not exceed \( {\delta }^{-1} \) whenever \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{i},{t}_{i}/2}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{i}}^{2}\left( {q,{q}_{i}}\right)  \leq  {\epsilon }^{-1}{t}_{i} \) . Given the monotonicity of \( \widetilde{V} \) and the upper bound on \( l\left( {q, t}\right) \) , we obtain an upper bound on the volume of the time- \( {t}_{i} \) ball \( B\left( {{q}_{i},\sqrt{{t}_{i}/\epsilon }}\right) \) of the form const. \( {t}_{i}^{3/2}{e}^{{\delta }^{-1}}{\left( {\kappa }^{\prime }\right) }^{3/2} \) .

On the other hand, from Proposition 39.1, a subsequence of the rescalings of the ancient solution around \( \left( {{q}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right) \) converges to a nonflat gradient shrinking soliton. If the gradient shrinking soliton is compact then it must be a quotient of the round shrinking \( {S}^{3} \) [35]. Otherwise, Corollary 51.22 says that if the gradient shrinking soliton is noncompact then it must be an evolving cylinder or its \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) -quotient. Fixing \( \epsilon \) , this gives a lower bound on \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{i}}\left( {{q}_{i},\sqrt{{t}_{i}/\epsilon }}\right) }\right) \) in terms of the noncollapsing constants of the evolving cylinder and its \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) -quotient. Hence there is a universal constant \( {\kappa }_{0} \) so that if \( {\kappa }^{\prime } < {\kappa }_{0} \) then we obtain a contradiction to the assumption of \( {\kappa }^{\prime } \) -collapsing.

nodes.label: Lemma 51.1
nodes.document_title: Bruce Kleiner and John Lott - Notes on Perelman's Papers
nodes.section_title: 51. II.1.2. THREE-DIMENSIONAL NONCOMPACT κ-NONCOLLAPSED GRADIENT SHRINKERS ARE STANDARD
nodes.content: Lemma 51.1. (cf. Lemma of II.1.2) There is no complete oriented 3-dimensional noncom-pact \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed gradient shrinking soliton with bounded positive sectional curvature.
nodes.content_excerpt: Lemma 51.1. (cf. Lemma of II.1.2) There is no complete oriented 3-dimensional noncom-pact \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed gradient shrinking soliton with bounded positive sectional curvature.

nodes.proof:
The idea of the proof is to show that the soliton has the qualitative features of a shrinking cylinder, and then to get a contradiction to the assumption of positive sectional curvature.

Applying \( {\nabla }_{i} \) to the gradient shrinker equation

(51.2)

\[
{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f + {R}_{ij} + \frac{1}{2t}{g}_{ij} = 0
\]

gives

(51.3)

\[
\Delta {\nabla }_{j}f + {\nabla }_{i}{R}_{ij} = 0.
\]

As \( {\nabla }_{i}{R}_{ij} = \frac{1}{2}{\nabla }_{j}R \) and \( \bigtriangleup {\nabla }_{j}f = {\nabla }_{j}\bigtriangleup f + {R}_{jk}{\nabla }_{k}f = {\nabla }_{j}\left( {-R - \frac{n}{2t}}\right)  + {R}_{jk}{\nabla }_{k}f \) , we obtain

(51.4)

\[
{\nabla }_{i}R = 2{R}_{ij}{\nabla }_{j}f
\]

Fix a basepoint \( {x}_{0} \in  M \) and consider a normalized minimal geodesic \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{s}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) in the time -1 slice with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = {x}_{0} \) . Put \( X\left( s\right)  = \frac{d\gamma }{ds} \) . As in the proof of Lemma 27.8, \( {\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) {ds} \leq \) const. for some constant independent of \( \bar{s} \) . If \( {\left\{  {Y}_{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{3} \) are orthonormal parallel vector fields along \( \gamma \) then

(51.5)

\[
{\left( {\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( X,{Y}_{1}\right) \right| ds\right) }^{2} \leq  \bar{s}{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( X,{Y}_{1}\right) \right| }^{2}{ds} \leq  \bar{s}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( X,{Y}_{i}\right) \right| }^{2}{ds}.
\]

Thinking of Ric as a self-adjoint linear operator on \( {TM},\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{3}{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( X,{Y}_{i}\right) \right| }^{2} = \left\langle  {X,{\operatorname{Ric}}^{2}X}\right\rangle \) . In terms of a pointwise orthonormal frame \( \left\{  {e}_{i}\right\} \) of eigenvectors of Ric, with eigenvalues \( {\lambda }_{i} \) , write \( X = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{3}{X}_{i}{e}_{i} \) . Then

(51.6)

\[
\left\langle  {X,{\operatorname{Ric}}^{2}X}\right\rangle   = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{3}{\lambda }_{i}^{2}{X}_{i}^{2} \leq  \left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{3}{\lambda }_{i}}\right) \left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{3}{\lambda }_{i}{X}_{i}^{2}}\right)  = R \cdot  \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) .
\]

Hence

(51.7)

\[
{\left( {\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( X,{Y}_{1}\right) \right| ds\right) }^{2} \leq  \left( {\mathop{\sup }\limits_{M}R}\right) \bar{s}{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) {ds} \leq  \text{ const. }\bar{s}.
\]

Multiplying (51.2) by \( {X}^{i}{X}^{j} \) and summing gives \( \frac{{d}^{2}f\left( {\gamma \left( s\right) }\right) }{d{s}^{2}} + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  - \frac{1}{2} = 0 \) . Then

(51.8)

\[
{\left. \frac{{df}\left( {\gamma \left( s\right) }\right) }{ds}\right| }_{s = \bar{s}} = {\left. \frac{{df}\left( {\gamma \left( s\right) }\right) }{ds}\right| }_{s = 0} + \frac{1}{2}\bar{s} - {\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) {ds} \geq  \frac{1}{2}\bar{s} - \text{ const. }
\]

This implies that there is a compact subset of \( M \) outside of which \( f \) has no critical points.

If \( Y \) is a unit vector field perpendicular to \( X \) then multiplying (51.2) by \( {X}^{i}{Y}^{j} \) and summing gives \( \frac{d}{ds}\left( {Y \cdot  f}\right) \left( {\gamma \left( s\right) }\right)  + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, Y}\right)  = 0 \) . Then

(51.9)

\[
\left( {Y \cdot  f}\right) \left( {\gamma \left( \bar{s}\right) }\right)  = \left( {Y \cdot  f}\right) \left( {\gamma \left( 0\right) }\right)  - {\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, Y}\right) {ds}
\]

and

(51.10)

\[
\left| {\left( {Y \cdot  f}\right) \left( {\gamma \left( \bar{s}\right) }\right) }\right|  \leq  \text{ const. }\left( {\sqrt{\bar{s}} + 1}\right) .
\]

For large \( \bar{s},\left| {\left( {Y \cdot  f}\right) \left( {\gamma \left( \bar{s}\right) }\right) }\right| \) is small compared to \( \left( {X \cdot  f}\right) \left( {\gamma \left( \bar{s}\right) }\right) \) . This means that as one approaches infinity, the gradient of \( f \) becomes more and more parallel to the gradient of the distance function from \( {x}_{0} \) , where by the latter we mean the vectors \( X \) that are tangent to minimal geodesics.

The gradient flow of \( f \) is given by the equation

(51.11)

\[
\frac{dx}{du} = \left( {\nabla f}\right) \left( x\right) .
\]

Then along a flowline, equation (51.4) implies that

(51.12)

\[
\frac{{dR}\left( x\right) }{du} = \left\langle  {\nabla R,\frac{dx}{du}}\right\rangle   = 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {\nabla f,\nabla f}\right) .
\]

In particular, outside of a compact set, \( R \) is strictly increasing along the flowlines. Put \( \bar{R} = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{x \rightarrow  \infty }}R \) . Take points \( {x}_{\alpha } \) tending toward infinity, with \( R\left( {x}_{\alpha }\right)  \rightarrow  \bar{R} \) . Putting \( {r}_{\alpha } = \sqrt{{\operatorname{dist}}_{-1}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{\alpha }}\right) } \) , we have \( \frac{{r}_{\alpha }}{{\operatorname{dist}}_{-1}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{\alpha }}\right) } \rightarrow  0 \) and \( R\left( {x}_{\alpha }\right) {r}_{\alpha }^{2} \rightarrow  \infty \) . Then the argument of the proof of Proposition 41.13 shows that any convergent subsequence of the rescalings around \( \left( {{x}_{\alpha }, - 1}\right) \) splits off a line. Hence the limit is a shrinking round cylinder with scalar curvature \( \bar{R} \) at time -1 . Because our original solution exists up to time zero, we must have \( \bar{R} \leq  1 \) . Now equation (C.13) says that the Ricci flow is given by \( g\left( {-t}\right)  =  - t{\phi }_{t}^{ * }g\left( {-1}\right) \) , where \( {\phi }_{t} \) is the flow generated by \( \nabla f \) . It follows that \( \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{x \in  M}}R\left( {x, t}\right)  = C{t}^{-1} \) for some \( C > 0 \) . That is, the curvature blows up uniformly as \( t \rightarrow  0 \) . Comparing this with the singularity time of the shrinking round cylinder implies that \( \bar{R} = 1 \) . Performing a similar argument with any sequence of \( {x}_{\alpha } \) ’s tending toward infinity, with the property that \( R\left( {x}_{\alpha }\right) \) has a limit, shows that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{x \rightarrow  \infty }}R\left( x\right)  = 1 \) .

Let \( N \) denote a (connected component of a) level surface of \( f \) . At a point of \( N \) , choose an orthonormal frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3}}\right\} \) with \( {e}_{3} = X \) normal to \( N \) . From the Gauss-Codazzi equation,

(51.13)

\[
{R}^{N} = 2{K}^{N}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{2}}\right)  = 2\left( {{K}^{M}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{2}}\right)  + \det \left( S\right) }\right) ,
\]

where \( S \) is the shape operator. As \( R = 2\left( {{K}^{M}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{2}}\right)  + {K}^{M}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{3}}\right)  + {K}^{M}\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{3}}\right) }\right) \) and \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  = {K}^{M}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{3}}\right)  + {K}^{M}\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{3}}\right) \) , we obtain

(51.14)

\[
{R}^{N} = R - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  + 2\det \left( S\right) .
\]

The shape operator is given by \( S = \frac{{\left. Hessf\right| }_{TN}}{\left| \nabla f\right| } \) . From (51.2), Hess \( f = \frac{1}{2} \) - Ric. We can diagonalize \( {\left. \operatorname{Ric}\right| }_{TN} \) to write \( \operatorname{Ric} = \left( \begin{matrix} {r}_{1} & 0 & {c}_{1} \\  0 & {r}_{2} & {c}_{2} \\  {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {r}_{3} \end{matrix}\right) \) , where \( {r}_{3} = \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) \) . Then

(51.15)

\[
\det \left( {\left. \operatorname{Hess}f\right| }_{TN}\right)  = \left( {\frac{1}{2} - {r}_{1}}\right) \left( {\frac{1}{2} - {r}_{2}}\right)  = \frac{1}{4}\left( {{\left( 1 - {r}_{1} - {r}_{2}\right) }^{2} - {\left( {r}_{1} - {r}_{2}\right) }^{2}}\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{1}{4}{\left( 1 - {r}_{1} - {r}_{2}\right) }^{2} = \frac{1}{4}{\left( 1 - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( X, X\right) \right) }^{2}.
\]

This shows that the scalar curvature of \( N \) is bounded above by

(51.16)

\[
R - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  + \frac{{\left( 1 - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( X, X\right) \right) }^{2}}{2{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}.
\]

If \( \left| {\nabla f}\right| \) is large then \( 1 - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  < 2{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} \) . As \( 1 - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) \) is positive when the distance from \( x \) to \( {x}_{0} \) is large enough,

(51.17)

\[
{\left( 1 - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( X, X\right) \right) }^{2} < 2\left( {1 - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) }\right) {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
\leq  2\left( {1 - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) }\right) {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + 2{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)
\]

and so

(51.18)

\[
\frac{{\left( 1 - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( X, X\right) \right) }^{2}}{2{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}} < 1 - R + 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) .
\]

Hence

(51.19)

\[
R - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  + \frac{{\left( 1 - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( X, X\right) \right) }^{2}}{2{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}} < 1.
\]

This shows that \( {R}^{N} < 1 \) if \( N \) is sufficiently far from \( {x}_{0} \) .

If \( Y \) is a unit vector that is tangential to \( N \) then from (51.2),

(51.20)

\[
{\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{Y}f = \frac{1}{2} - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right)
\]

If \( \{ Y, Z, W\} \) is an orthonormal basis then

(51.21)

\[
\text{ (51.21) }\operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right)  = {K}^{M}\left( {Y, Z}\right)  + {K}^{M}\left( {Y, W}\right)  \leq  {K}^{M}\left( {Y, Z}\right)  + {K}^{M}\left( {Y, W}\right)  + {K}^{M}\left( {Z, W}\right)  = \frac{1}{2}R\text{ . }
\]

Hence \( {\nabla }_{Y}{\nabla }_{Y}f \geq  \frac{1}{2}\left( {1 - R}\right) \) , which is positive if \( N \) is sufficiently far from \( {x}_{0} \) . Thus \( N \) is convex and so the area of the level set increases as the level increases. On the other hand, we can take points \( {x}_{\alpha } \) on the level sets going to infinity, apply the previous splitting argument and use the fact that grad \( f \) becomes almost parallel to grad \( d\left( {\cdot ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) . Within one of the approximate cylinders coming from the splitting argument, there is a projection \( \pi \) to its base \( {S}^{2} \) . As a tangent plane of \( N \) is almost perpendicular to \( \operatorname{Ker}\left( {d\pi }\right) \) , the restriction of \( \pi \) to \( N \) is an almost-isometry from \( N \) to \( {S}^{2} \) . By the monotonicity of \( \operatorname{area}\left( N\right) \) , we conclude that \( \operatorname{area}\left( N\right)  \leq  {8\pi } \) if \( N \) is sufficiently far from \( {x}_{0} \) . However as \( N \) is a topologically a 2-sphere, the Gauss-Bonnet theorem says that \( {\int }_{N}{R}^{N}{dA} = {8\pi } \) . This contradicts the facts that \( {R}^{N} < 1 \) and \( \operatorname{area}\left( N\right)  \leq  {8\pi } \) .

A Ricci flow solution is said to have \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature if for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) , we have

(52.2)

\[
\operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq   - \Phi \left( {R\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) .

nodes.label: Remark 52.3
nodes.document_title: Bruce Kleiner and John Lott - Notes on Perelman's Papers
nodes.content:
Remark 52.3. Note that \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature implies that the scalar curvature is uniformly bounded below by \( - {6\Phi }\left( 0\right) \) . The formulation of the pinching condition in [51, Section 12] is that there is a decreasing function \( \phi \) , tending to zero at infinity, so that \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq   - \phi \left( {R\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) R\left( {x, t}\right) \) for each \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) . This formulation has a problem when \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  < 0 \) , if one takes \( \phi \) to be defined on all of \( \mathbb{R} \) . The condition in Definition 52.1 is what comes out of the three-dimensional Hamilton-Ivey pinching result (applied to the rescaled metric \( \widetilde{g}\left( t\right)  = \frac{g\left( t\right) }{t} \) ) if we assume normalized initial conditions; see Appendix B.

We note that since the sectional curvatures have to add up to \( R \) , the lower bound (52.2) implies a double-sided bound on the sectional curvatures. Namely,

(52.4)

\[
- \Phi \left( R\right)  \leq  \operatorname{Rm} \leq  \frac{R}{2} + \left( {\frac{n\left( {n - 1}\right) }{2} - 1}\right) \Phi \left( R\right) .
\]

The main use of the pinching condition is to show that blowup limits have nonnegative sectional curvature.
