nodes.proof:
We give a proof which differs in some points from the proof in [51] but which has the same ingredients. We first outline the argument.

Suppose that the theorem is false. Then for some \( \epsilon ,\kappa ,\sigma  > 0 \) , we have a sequence of such \( \Phi \) -nonnegatively curved 3-dimensional Ricci flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) defined on intervals \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) , and sequences \( {r}_{k} \rightarrow  0,{\widehat{x}}_{k} \in  {M}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k} \geq  1 \) such that \( {M}_{k} \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales \( < \sigma \) and \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{k}^{-2} \) , but the \( {Q}_{k} \) -rescaled solution in \( {B}_{{\left( \epsilon {Q}_{k}\right) }^{-1/2}}\left( {\widehat{x}}_{k}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{\widehat{t}}_{k} - {\left( \epsilon {Q}_{k}\right) }^{-1},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) is not \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of any \( \kappa \) -solution.

We note that if the statement were false for \( \epsilon \) then it would also be false for any smaller \( \epsilon \) . Because of this, somewhat paradoxically, we will begin the argument with a given \( \epsilon \) but will allow ourselves to make \( \epsilon \) small enough later so that the argument works. To be clear, we will eventually get a contradiction using a fixed (small) value of \( \epsilon \) , but as the proof goes along we will impose some upper bounds on this value in order for the proof to work. (If we tried to list all of the constraints at the beginning of the argument then they would look unmotivated.)

The goal is to get a contradiction based on the "bad" points \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) . In a sense, the method of proof of Theorem 52.7 is an induction on the curvature scale. For example, if we were to make the additional assumption in the theorem that \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) for all \( x \in  M \) and \( t \leq  {t}_{0} \) then the theorem would be very easy to prove. We would just take a convergent subsequence of the rescaled solutions, based at \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) , to get a \( \kappa \) -solution; this would give a contradiction. This simple argument can be considered to be the first step in a proof by induction on curvature scale. In the proof of Theorem 52.7 one effectively proves the result at a given curvature scale inductively by assuming that the result is true at higher curvature scales.

The actual proof consists of four steps. Step 1 consists of replacing the sequence \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) by another sequence of "bad" points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) which have the property that points near \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) with distinctly higher scalar curvature are "good" points. It then suffices to get a contradiction based on the existence of the sequence \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

In steps 2-4 one uses the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) to build up a \( \kappa \) -solution, whose existence then contradicts the "badness" of the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . More precisely, let \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be the result of rescaling \( {g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) by \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . We will show that the sequence of pointed flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) accumulates on a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) , thereby obtaining a contradiction.

In step 2 one takes a pointed limit of the manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) in order to construct what will become the final time slice of the \( \kappa \) -solution, \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . In order to take this limit, it is necessary to show that the manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) have uniformly bounded curvature on distance balls of a fixed radius. If this were not true then for some radius, a subsequence of the manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) would have curvatures that asymptotically blowup on the ball of that radius. One shows that geometrically, the curvature blowup is due to the asymptotic formation of a cone-like point at the blowup radius. Doing a further rescaling at this cone-like point, one obtains a Ricci flow solution that ends on a part of a nonflat metric cone. This gives a contradiction as in the case \( 0 < \mathcal{R} < \infty \) of Theorem 41.2.

Thus one can construct the pointed limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . The goal now is to show that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) is the final time slice of a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) . In step 3 one shows that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) extends backward to a Ricci flow solution on some time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - \Delta ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , and that the time slices have bounded nonnegative curvature. In step 4 one shows that the Ricci flow solution can be extended all the way to time \( \left( {-\infty ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , thereby constructing a \( \kappa \) -solution

Step 1: Adjusting the choice of basepoints.

We first modify the points \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) slightly in time to points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) so that in the given Ricci flow solution, there are no other "bad" points with much larger scalar curvature in a earlier time interval whose length is large compared to \( R{\left( {x}_{k},{t}_{k}\right) }^{-1} \) . (The phrase "nearly the smallest curvature \( Q \) " in [51, Proof of Theorem 12.1] should read "nearly the largest curvature \( Q \) ". This is clear from the sentence in parentheses that follows.) The proof of the next lemma is by pointpicking, as in Appendix H.

Lemma 52.9. We can find \( {H}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty ,{x}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) , and \( {t}_{k} \geq  \frac{1}{2} \) such that \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) , and for all \( k \) the conclusion of Theorem 52.7 fails at \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , but holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right)  \in \; {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - {H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for which \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  \geq  {2R}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

Proof. Choose \( {H}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) such that \( {H}_{k}{\left( R\left( {\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}\right) \right) }^{-1} \leq  \frac{1}{10} \) for all \( k \) . For each \( k \) , initially set \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) . Put \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) and look for a point in \( {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - {H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) at which Theorem 52.7 fails, and the scalar curvature is at least \( {2R}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . If such a point exists, replace \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) by this point; otherwise do nothing. Repeat this until the second alternative occurs. This process must terminate with a new choice of \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) satisfying the lemma.

Hereafter we use this modified sequence \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . Let \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be the result of rescaling \( {g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) by \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . We use \( {\bar{R}}_{k} \) to denote its scalar curvature; in particular, \( {\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = 1 \) . Note that the rescaled time interval of Lemma 52.9 has duration \( {H}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) ; this is what we want in order to try to extract an ancient solution.

Step 2: For every \( \rho  < \infty \) , the scalar curvature \( {\bar{R}}_{k} \) is uniformly bounded on the \( \rho \) -balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) (the argument for this is essentially equivalent to [51, Pf. of Claim 2 of Theorem I.12.1]). Before proceeding, we need some bounds which come from our choice of basepoints, and the derivative bounds inherited (by approximation) from \( \kappa \) -solutions.

Lemma 52.10. There is a constant \( C = C\left( \kappa \right) \) so that for any \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in a Ricci flow solution, if \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  > 0 \) and the solution in \( {B}_{t}\left( {x,{\left( \epsilon R\left( x, t\right) \right) }^{-1/2}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {t - {\left( \epsilon R\left( x, t\right) \right) }^{-1}, t}\right\rbrack \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to a corresponding subset of a \( \kappa \) -solution then \( \left| {\nabla {R}^{-1/2}}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C \) and \( \left| {{\partial }_{t}{R}^{-1}}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C \) .

Proof. This follows from the compactness in Theorem 46.1.

Note that the same value of \( C \) in Lemma 52.10 also works for smaller \( \epsilon \) .

Lemma 52.11. (cf. Claim 1 of I.12.1) For each \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{k} - \frac{1}{2}{H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  {t}_{k} \) , we have \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4{\bar{Q}}_{k} \) whenever \( \bar{t} - c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1/2} \) , where \( {\bar{Q}}_{k} = {Q}_{k} + \left| {{R}_{k}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) }\right| \) and \( c = c\left( \kappa \right)  > 0 \) is a small constant.

Proof. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  2{Q}_{k} \) then there is nothing to show. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  > 2{Q}_{k} \) , consider a spacetime curve \( \gamma \) that goes linearly from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) , and then goes from \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) to \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) along a minimizing geodesic. If there is a point on \( \gamma \) with curvature \( 2{Q}_{k} \) , let \( p \) be the nearest such point to \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) . If not, put \( p = \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) . From the conclusion of Lemma 52.9, we can apply Lemma 52.10 along \( \gamma \) from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( p \) . The claim follows from integrating the ensuing derivative bounds along \( \gamma \) .

Lemma 52.12. In terms of the rescaled solution \( {\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) , for each \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{k} - \frac{1}{2}{H}_{k} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  {t}_{k} \) , we have \( {\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4{\widetilde{Q}}_{k} \) whenever \( \bar{t} - c{\widetilde{Q}}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  c{\widetilde{Q}}_{k}^{-1/2} \) , where \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{k} = 1 + \left| {{\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) }\right| . \)

Proof. This is just the rescaled version of Lemma 52.11.

For all \( \rho  \geq  0 \) , put

(52.13)

\[
D\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {{\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {x,{t}_{k}}\right)  \mid  k \geq  1, x \in  B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) }\right\}  ,
\]

and let \( {\rho }_{0} \) be the supremum of the \( \rho \) ’s for which \( D\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \) . Note that \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) , in view of Lemma 52.12 (taking \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  = \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) ). Suppose that \( {\rho }_{0} < \infty \) . After passing to a subsequence if necessary, we can find a sequence \( {y}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) with \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},{y}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} \) and \( \bar{R}\left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) . Let \( {\eta }_{k} \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) be a minimizing geodesic segment from \( {x}_{k} \) to \( {y}_{k} \) . Let \( {z}_{k} \in  {\eta }_{k} \) be the point on \( {\eta }_{k} \) closest to \( {y}_{k} \) at which \( \bar{R}\left( {{z}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = 2 \) , and let \( {\gamma }_{k} \) be the subsegment of \( {\eta }_{k} \) running from \( {y}_{k} \) to \( {z}_{k} \) . By Lemma 52.12 the length of \( {\gamma }_{k} \) is bounded away from zero independent of \( k \) . Due to the \( \Phi \) -pinching (see (52.4)), for all \( \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) , we have a uniform bound on \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| \) on the balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) . The injectivity radius is also controlled in \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right) \) , in view of the curvature bounds and the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing. Therefore after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the pointed sequence \( \left( {B\left( {{x}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the pointed Gromov-Hausdorff topology (i.e. for all \( \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) we have the usual Gromov-Hausdorff convergence) to a pointed \( {C}^{1} \) -Riemannian manifold \( \left( {Z,{\bar{g}}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , the segments \( {\eta }_{k} \) converge to a segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\eta }_{\infty } \subset  Z \) emanating from \( {x}_{\infty } \) , and \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converges to \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {\eta }_{\infty } \) . Let \( \bar{Z} \) denote the completion of \( \left( {Z,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) , and \( {y}_{\infty } \in  \bar{Z} \) the limit point of \( {\eta }_{\infty } \) . Note that by Lemma 52.9 and part 4 of Corollary 42.1, the Riemannian structure near \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) may be chosen to be many times differentiable. (Alternatively, this follows from Lemma 52.12 and the Shi estimates of Appendix D.) In particular the scalar curvature \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty } \) is defined, differentiable, and satisfies the bound in Lemma 52.10 near \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) .

Lemma 52.14. 1. There is a function \( c : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) depending only on \( \kappa \) , with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}c\left( t\right)  = \; \infty \) , such that if \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) then \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) d{\left( {y}_{\infty }, w\right) }^{2} > c\left( \epsilon \right) \) .

2. There is a function \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \cup  \{ \infty \} \) depending only on \( \kappa \) , with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}{\epsilon }^{\prime }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) , such that if \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) and \( d\left( {{y}_{\infty }, w}\right) \) is sufficiently small then the pointed manifold \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( 2{\epsilon }^{\prime }\left( \epsilon \right) \) -close to a round cylinder in the \( {C}^{2} \) topology.

Proof. It follows from Lemma 52.9 that for all \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) , the pointed Riemannian manifold \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to (a time slice of) a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution. From the definition of pointed closeness, there is an embedded region around \( w \) , large on the scale defined by \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) \) , which is close to the corresponding subset of a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution. This gives a lower bound on the distance \( {\rho }_{0} - d\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) to the point of curvature blowup, thereby proving part 1 of the lemma.

We know that \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {N,\star , h\left( t\right) }\right) \) in the pointed \( {C}^{2} \) -topology. By Lemma 52.10, we know \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) \) tends to \( \infty \) as \( d\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} \) , for \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . In particular, \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {d}^{2}\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) . From part 1 above, we can choose \( \epsilon \) small enough in order to make \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {d}^{2}\left( {w,{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) large enough to apply Proposition 49.1. Hence the pointed manifold \( \left( {N,\star , R\left( \star \right) h\left( t\right) }\right) \) is \( {\epsilon }^{\prime \prime }\left( \epsilon \right) \) -close to a round cylinder, where \( {\epsilon }^{\prime \prime } : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) is a function with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}{\epsilon }^{\prime \prime }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) . The lemma follows.

Note that the function \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) in Lemma 52.14 is independent of the particular manifold \( Z \) that arises in our proof.

From part 2 of Lemma 52.14, if \( \epsilon \) is small and \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) is sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) then \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {C}^{2} \) -close to a round cylinder. The cross-section of the cylinder has diameter approximately \( \pi {\left( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) /2\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . If we form the union of the balls \( B\left( {w,{2\pi }{\left( {R}_{\infty }\left( w\right) /2\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) , as \( w \) ranges over such points in \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) , then we obtain a connected Riemannian manifold \( W \) . By adding in the point \( {y}_{\infty } \) , we get a metric space \( \bar{W} \) which is locally complete, and geodesic near \( {y}_{\infty } \) . As the original manifolds \( {M}_{k} \) had \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature, it follows from Lemma 52.5 that \( W \) is nonnegatively curved. Furthermore, \( {y}_{\infty } \) cannot be an interior point of any geodesic segment in \( \bar{W} \) , since such a geodesic would have to pass through a cylindrical region near \( {y}_{\infty } \) twice. The usual proof of the Toponogov triangle comparison inequality now applies near \( {y}_{\infty } \) since minimizers remain in the smooth nonnegatively curved part of \( \bar{W} \) . Then \( \bar{W} \) has nonnegative curvature in the Alexandrov sense.

This implies that blowups of \( \left( {\bar{W},{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) converge to the tangent cone \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) . As \( \bar{W} \) is three-dimensional, so is \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) [12, Corollary 7.11]. It will be \( {C}^{2} \) -smooth away from the vertex and nowhere flat, by part 2 of Lemma 52.14. Pick \( z \in  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) such that \( d\left( {z,{y}_{\infty }}\right)  = 1 \) . Then for any \( \delta  < \frac{1}{2} \) , the ball \( B\left( {z,\delta }\right)  \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) is the Gromov-Hausdorff limit of a sequence of rescaled balls \( B\left( {{\widehat{z}}_{k},{\widehat{r}}_{k}}\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) where \( {\widehat{r}}_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) , whose center points \( \left( {{\widehat{z}}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) satisfy the conclusions of Theorem 52.7. Applying Lemma 52.12 and Appendix B, if \( \delta  = \delta \left( \kappa \right) \) is taken small enough then we get the curvature bounds needed to extract a limiting Ricci flow solution whose time zero slice is isometric to \( B\left( {z,\delta }\right) \) . Now we can apply the reasoning from the \( 0 < \mathcal{R} < \infty \) case of Theorem 41.2 to get a contradiction. This completes step 2.

Step 3: The sequence of pointed flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) ,\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right) \) accumulates on a pointed Ricci flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) ,\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) which is defined on a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) with \( {t}^{\prime } < {t}_{0} \) . By step 2, we know that the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) at \( y \in  {M}_{k} \) is bounded by a function of the distance from \( y \) to \( {x}_{k} \) . Lemma 52.12 extends this curvature control to a backward parabolic neighborhood centered at \( y \) whose radius depends only on \( d\left( {y,{x}_{k}}\right) \) . Thus we can conclude, using \( \Phi \) -pinching (52.4) and Shi’s estimates (Appendix D), that all derivatives of the curvature \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) are controlled as a function of the distance from \( {x}_{k} \) , which means that the sequence of pointed manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) accumulates to a smooth manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) .

From Lemma 52.5, \( {M}_{\infty } \) has nonnegative sectional curvature. We claim that \( {M}_{\infty } \) has bounded curvature. If not then there is a sequence of points \( {q}_{k} \in  {M}_{\infty } \) so that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}\bar{R}\left( {q}_{k}\right)  = \; \infty \) and \( \bar{R}\left( q\right)  \leq  2\bar{R}\left( {q}_{k}\right) \) for \( q \in  B\left( {{y}_{k},{A}_{k}\bar{R}{\left( {q}_{k}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) , where \( {A}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) ; compare [33, Lemma 22.2]. Lemma 52.9 implies that for large \( k \) , a rescaled neighborhood of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{q}_{k}}\right) \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of a time slice of a \( \kappa \) -solution. As in the proof of Theorem 46.1, we obtain a sequence of neck-like regions in \( {M}_{\infty } \) with smaller and smaller cross-sections, which contradicts the existence of the Sharafutdinov retraction.

By Lemma 52.12 again, we now get curvature control on \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) for a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \Delta ,{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for some \( \Delta  > 0 \) , and hence we can extract a subsequence which converges to a pointed Ricci flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - \Delta ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , which has nonnegative curvature and bounded curvature on compact time intervals.

Step 4: Getting an ancient solution. Let \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) be the maximal time interval on which we can extract a limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) with bounded curvature on compact time intervals. Suppose that \( {t}^{\prime } >  - \infty \) . By Lemma 52.12 the maximum of the scalar curvature on the time slice \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) must tend to infinity as \( t \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) . From the trace Harnack inequality, \( {R}_{t} + \frac{R}{t - {t}^{\prime }} \geq  0 \) , and so

(52.15)

\[
{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  Q\frac{{t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }}{t - {t}^{\prime }},
\]

where \( Q \) is the maximum of the scalar curvature on \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . Combining this with Corollary 27.16, we get

(52.16)

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  \text{ const. }\sqrt{Q\frac{{t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }}{t - {t}^{\prime }}}.
\]

Since the right hand side is integrable on \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , and using the fact that distances are nonincreasing in time (since \( \mathrm{{Rm}} \geq  0 \) ), it follows that there is a constant \( C \) such that

(52.17)

\[
\left| {{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  - {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, y}\right) }\right|  < C
\]

for all \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty }, t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) .

If \( {M}_{\infty } \) is compact then by (52.17) the diameter of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is bounded independent of \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . Since the minimum of the scalar curvature is increasing in time, it is also bounded independent of \( t \) . Now the argument in Step 2 shows that the curvature is bounded everywhere independent of \( t \) . (We can apply the argument of Step 2 to the time- \( t \) slice because the main ingredient was Lemma 52.9, which holds for rescaled time \( t \) .)

We may therefore assume \( {M}_{\infty } \) is noncompact. To be consistent with the notation of I.12.1, we now relabel the basepoint \( \left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) \) as \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Since nonnegatively curved manifolds are asymptotically conical (see Appendix G), there is a constant \( D \) such that if \( y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) , and \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right)  > D \) , then there is a point \( x \in  {M}_{\infty } \) such that

(52.18)

\[
{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, y}\right)  = {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right) \;\text{ and }\;{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  \frac{3}{2}{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right) ;
\]

by (52.17) the same conditions hold at all times \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , up to error \( C \) . If for some such \( y \) , and some \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) the scalar curvature were large, then \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {y, t}\right) ,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( {y, t}\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) would be \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {N, h\left( \cdot \right) ,\left( {z,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) . When \( \epsilon \) is small we could use Proposition 49.1 to see that \( y \) lies in a neck region \( U \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) of diameter \( \approx  R{\left( y, t\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \ll  1 \) .

We claim that \( U \) separates \( {x}_{0} \) from \( x \) in the sense that \( {x}_{0} \) and \( x \) belong to disjoint components of \( {M}_{\infty } - U \) , where \( {x}_{0}, y \) , and \( x \) satisfy (52.18). To see this, we recall that if \( {M}_{\infty } \) has more than one end then it splits isometrically, in which case the claim is clear. If \( {M}_{\infty } \) has one end then we consider an exhaustion of \( {M}_{\infty } \) by totally convex compact sets \( {C}_{t} \) as in Section 46. One of the sets \( {C}_{t} \) will have boundary consisting of an approximate 2-sphere cross-section in the neck region \( U \) , giving the separation.

(For another argument, suppose that \( U \) does not separate \( {x}_{0} \) from \( x \) . Since \( {\widetilde{Z}}_{y}\left( {{x}_{0}, x}\right)  > \frac{\pi }{2} \) (from Proposition 49.1), the segments \( \overline{y{x}_{0}} \) and \( \overline{yx} \) must exit \( U \) by different ends. If \( {x}_{0} \) and \( x \) can be joined by a curve avoiding \( U \) then there is a nonzero element of \( {\mathrm{H}}^{1}\left( {{M}_{\infty },\mathbb{Z}}\right) \) . The corresponding infinite cyclic cover of \( {M}_{\infty } \) will then isometrically split off a line and its quotient \( {M}_{\infty } \) will be compact, which is a contradiction. We thank one of the referees for this argument.)

Obviously, at time \( {t}_{0} \) the set \( U \) still separates \( {x}_{0} \) from \( x \) . Since \( {\bar{g}}_{\infty } \) has nonnegative curvature, we have \( {\operatorname{diam}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( U\right)  \leq  {\operatorname{diam}}_{t}\left( U\right)  \ll  1 \) . Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) has bounded geometry, there cannot be topologically separating subsets of arbitrarily small diameter. Thus there must be a uniform upper bound on \( R\left( {y, t}\right) \) and the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is uniformly bounded (in space and time) outside a set of uniformly bounded diameter. Repeating the reasoning from Step 2, we get uniform bounds everywhere. This contradicts our assumption that the curvature blows up as \( t \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) .

It remains to show that the ancient solution is a \( \kappa \) -solution. The only remaining point is to show that it is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed at all scales. This follows from the fact that the original Ricci flow solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) were \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales less than the fixed number \( \sigma \) .

nodes.content:
Remark 52.8. Our statement of Theorem 52.7 differs slightly from that in [51, Theorem 12.1]. First, we allow \( M \) to be noncompact, provided that there is bounded sectional curvature on compact time intervals. This generalization will be useful for later work. More importantly, the statement in [51, Theorem 12.1] has noncollapsing at scales less than \( {r}_{0} \) , whereas we require noncollapsing at scales less than \( \sigma \) . See Remark 52.19 for further comment.

In the phrase " \( {t}_{0} \geq  1 \) " there is an implied scale which comes from the \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegativity assumption, and similarly for the statement "scales less than \( \sigma \) ".

It follows from Lemma 52.9 that for all \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) , the pointed Riemannian manifold \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to (a time slice of) a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution. From the definition of pointed closeness, there is an embedded region around \( w \) , large on the scale defined by \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) \) , which is close to the corresponding subset of a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution. This gives a lower bound on the distance \( {\rho }_{0} - d\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) to the point of curvature blowup, thereby proving part 1 of the lemma.

We know that \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {N,\star , h\left( t\right) }\right) \) in the pointed \( {C}^{2} \) -topology. By Lemma 52.10, we know \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) \) tends to \( \infty \) as \( d\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} \) , for \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . In particular, \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {d}^{2}\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) . From part 1 above, we can choose \( \epsilon \) small enough in order to make \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {d}^{2}\left( {w,{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) large enough to apply Proposition 49.1. Hence the pointed manifold \( \left( {N,\star , R\left( \star \right) h\left( t\right) }\right) \) is \( {\epsilon }^{\prime \prime }\left( \epsilon \right) \) -close to a round cylinder, where \( {\epsilon }^{\prime \prime } : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) is a function with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}{\epsilon }^{\prime \prime }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) . The lemma follows.

nodes.content: Remark 52.19. As mentioned in Remark 52.8, the statement of [51, Theorem 12.1] instead assumes noncollapsing at all scales less than \( {r}_{0} \) . Bing Wang pointed out that with this assumption, after constructing the ancient solution in Step 4 of the proof, one only gets that it is \( \kappa \) -collapsed at all scales less than one. Hence it may not be a \( \kappa \) -solution. The literal statement of [51, Theorem 12.1] is not used in the rest of [51, 52], but rather its method of proof. Because of this, the change of hypotheses does not seem to lead to any problems. The method of proof of Theorem 52.7 is used in two different ways. The first way is to construct the Ricci flow with surgery on a fixed finite time interval, as in Section 77. In this case the noncollapsing at a given scale \( \sigma \) comes from Theorem 26.2, and its extension when surgeries are allowed. The second way is to analyze the large-time behavior of the Ricci flow, as in the next few sections.

nodes.content: Theorem 53.1. For any \( A < \infty \) , there exist \( K = K\left( A\right)  < \infty \) and \( \rho  = \rho \left( A\right)  > 0 \) with the following property. Suppose in dimension three we have a Ricci flow solution with \( \Phi \) - almost nonnegative curvature. Given \( {x}_{0} \in  M \) and \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) , suppose that \( {r}_{0}^{2}\Phi \left( {r}_{0}^{-2}\right)  < \rho \) , the solution is defined for \( 0 \leq  t \leq  {r}_{0}^{2} \) and it has \( \left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{3{r}_{0}^{2}} \) for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) satisfying \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{0}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < {r}_{0} \) . Suppose in addition that the volume of the metric ball \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) at time zero is at least \( {A}^{-1}{r}_{0}^{3} \) . Then \( R\left( {x,{r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  \leq  K{r}_{0}^{-2} \) whenever \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < A{r}_{0} \) .

nodes.proof:
To prove the lemma, suppose that there is a sequence of such pointed solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{0, k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) , along with points \( {\widehat{x}}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) , so that \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{x}_{0, k}}\right)  < A{r}_{0} \) and \( {r}_{0}^{2}R\left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  \rightarrow \; \infty \) , but \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{r}_{0}^{2}}\right) \) does not satisfy conclusion (b) of the lemma. As in the proof of Theorem 52.7, we will allow ourselves to make \( \epsilon \) smaller during the course of the proof.

We first show that there is a sequence \( {D}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) and modified points \( \left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{\bar{t}}_{k}}\right) \) with \( \frac{3}{4}{r}_{0}^{2} \leq \; {\bar{t}}_{k} \leq  {r}_{0}^{2},{\operatorname{dist}}_{{\bar{t}}_{k}}\left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{x}_{0, k}}\right)  < \left( {A + 1}\right) {r}_{0} \) and \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{\bar{t}}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) , so that any point \( \left( {{x}_{k}^{\prime },{t}_{k}^{\prime }}\right) \) with \( R\left( {{x}_{k}^{\prime },{t}_{k}^{\prime }}\right)  > 2{Q}_{k},{\bar{t}}_{k} - {D}_{k}^{2}{Q}_{k}^{-1} \leq  {t}_{k}^{\prime } \leq  {\bar{t}}_{k} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{k}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{k}^{\prime },{x}_{0, k}}\right)  < {\operatorname{dist}}_{{\bar{t}}_{k}}\left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{x}_{0, k}}\right)  + {D}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1/2} \) satisfies conclusion (b) of the lemma, but \( \left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{\bar{t}}_{k}}\right) \) does not satisfy conclusion (b) of the lemma. (Of course, in saying " \( \left( {{x}_{k}^{\prime },{t}_{k}^{\prime }}\right) \) satisfies conclusion (b)" or " \( \left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{\bar{t}}_{k}}\right) \) does not satisfy conclusion (b)", we mean that the \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in conclusion (b) is replaced by \( \left( {{x}_{k}^{\prime },{t}_{k}^{\prime }}\right) \) or \( \left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{\bar{t}}_{k}}\right) \) , respectively.)

The construction of \( \left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{\bar{t}}_{k}}\right) \) is by a pointpicking argument. Put \( {D}_{k} = \frac{{r}_{0}R{\left( {\widehat{x}}_{k},{r}_{0}^{2}\right) }^{1/2}}{10} \) . Start with \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{r}_{0}^{2}}\right) \) and look if there is a point \( \left( {{x}_{k}^{\prime },{t}_{k}^{\prime }}\right) \) with \( R\left( {{x}_{k}^{\prime },{t}_{k}^{\prime }}\right)  > {2R}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , \( {\bar{t}}_{k} - {D}_{k}^{2}R{\left( {x}_{k},{t}_{k}\right) }^{-1} \leq  {t}_{k}^{\prime } \leq  {\bar{t}}_{k} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{k}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{k}^{\prime },{x}_{0, k}}\right)  < {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0, k}}\right)  + {D}_{k}R{\left( {x}_{k},{t}_{k}\right) }^{-1/2} \) , but which does not have a neighborhood that is \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of a \( \kappa \) - solution. If there is such a point, we replace \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) by \( \left( {{x}_{k}^{\prime },{t}_{k}^{\prime }}\right) \) and repeat the process. The process must terminate after a finite number of steps to give a point \( \left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{\bar{t}}_{k}}\right) \) with the desired property.

(Note that the condition \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{k}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{k}^{\prime },{x}_{0, k}}\right)  < {\operatorname{dist}}_{{\bar{t}}_{k}}\left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{x}_{0, k}}\right)  + {D}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1/2} \) involves the metric at time \( {t}_{k}^{\prime } \) . In order to construct an ancient solution, one of the issues will be to replace this by a condition that only involves the metric at time \( {\bar{t}}_{k} \) , i.e. that involves a parabolic neighborhood around \( \left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{\bar{t}}_{k}}\right) \) .)

Let \( {\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) denote the rescaling of the solution \( {g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) by \( {Q}_{k} \) . We normalize the time interval of the rescaled solution by fixing a number \( {t}_{\infty } \) and saying that for all \( k \) , the time- \( {\bar{t}}_{k} \) slice of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}}\right) \) corresponds to the time- \( {t}_{\infty } \) slice of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}}\right) \) . Then the scalar curvature \( {\bar{R}}_{k} \) of \( {\bar{g}}_{k} \) satisfies \( {\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{t}_{\infty }}\right)  = 1 \) .

By the argument of Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 52.7, a subsequence of the pointed spaces \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{x}}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{\infty }\right) }\right) \) will smoothly converge to a nonnegatively-curved pointed space \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{x}}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) . By the pointpicking, if \( m \in  {M}_{\infty } \) has \( \bar{R}\left( m\right)  \geq  3 \) then a parabolic neighborhood of \( m \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding region in a \( \kappa \) -solution. It follows, as in Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 52.7, that the sectional curvature of \( {M}_{\infty } \) will be bounded above by some \( C < \infty \) . Using Lemma 52.12, the metric on \( {M}_{\infty } \) is the time- \( {t}_{\infty } \) slice of a nonnegatively-curved Ricci flow solution defined on some time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty } - c,{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) , with \( c > 0 \) , and one has convergence of a subsequence \( {\bar{g}}_{k}\left( t\right)  \rightarrow  {\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty } - c,{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) . As \( {\bar{R}}_{t} \geq  0 \) , the scalar curvature on this time interval will be uniformly bounded above by \( {6C} \) and so from the \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature (see (52.4)), the sectional curvature will be uniformly bounded above on the time interval. Hence we can apply Lemma 27.8 to get a uniform additive bound on the length distortion between times \( {t}_{\infty } - c \) and \( {t}_{\infty } \) (see Step 4 of the proof of Theorem 52.7). More precisely, in applying Lemma 27.8, we use the curvature bound coming from the hypotheses of the theorem near \( {x}_{0} \) , and the just-derived upper curvature bound near \( {\bar{x}}_{k} \) .

It follows that for a given \( {A}^{\prime } > 0 \) , for large \( k \) , if \( {t}_{k}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{\bar{t}}_{k} - c{Q}_{k}^{-1}/2,{\bar{t}}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{\bar{t}}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k}^{\prime },{\bar{x}}_{k}}\right)  < \; {A}^{\prime }{Q}_{k}^{-1/2} \) then \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{k}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{k}^{\prime },{x}_{0, k}}\right)  < {\operatorname{dist}}_{{\bar{t}}_{k}}\left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{x}_{0, k}}\right)  + {D}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1/2} \) . In particular, if a point \( \left( {{x}_{k}^{\prime },{t}_{k}^{\prime }}\right) \) lies in the parabolic neighborhood given by \( {t}_{k}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{\bar{t}}_{k} - c{Q}_{k}^{-1}/2,{\bar{t}}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{\bar{t}}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k}^{\prime },{\bar{x}}_{k}}\right)  < {A}^{\prime }{Q}_{k}^{-1/2} \) , and has \( R\left( {{x}_{k}^{\prime },{t}_{k}^{\prime }}\right)  > 2{Q}_{k} \) , then it has a neighborhood that is \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of a \( \kappa \) -solution.

As in Step 4 of the proof of Theorem 52.7, we now extend \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty },{\bar{x}}_{\infty }}\right) \) backward to an ancient solution \( {\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) \) , defined for \( t \in  \left( {-\infty ,{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) . To do so, we use the fact that if the solution is defined backward to a time- \( t \) slice then the length distortion bound, along with the pointpicking, implies that a point \( m \) in a time- \( t \) slice with \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( m\right)  > 3 \) has a neighborhood that is \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of a \( \kappa \) -solution. The ancient solution is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed at all scales since the original solution was \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed at some scale, by Theorem 28.2. Then we obtain smooth convergence of parabolic regions of the points \( \left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{\bar{t}}_{k}}\right) \) to the \( \kappa \) -solution, which is a contradiction to the choice of the \( \left( {{\bar{x}}_{k},{\bar{t}}_{k}}\right) \) ’s.

nodes.content: Lemma 54.1. Given \( {w}^{\prime } > 0 \) and \( n \in  {\mathbb{Z}}^{ + } \) , there is a number \( c = c\left( {{w}^{\prime }, n}\right)  > 0 \) with the following property. Let \( B \) be a radius-r ball with compact closure in an \( n \) -dimensional Riemannian manifold. Suppose that the sectional curvatures of \( B \) are bounded below by \( - {r}^{-2} \) . Suppose that \( \operatorname{vol}\left( B\right)  \geq  {w}^{\prime }{r}^{n} \) . Then there is a subball \( {B}^{\prime } \subset  B \) of radius \( {r}^{\prime } \geq  {cr} \) so that \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {B}^{\prime }\right)  \geq  \frac{1}{2}{\omega }_{n}{\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{n} \) , where \( {\omega }_{n} \) is the volume of the unit ball in \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) .

Then there is a sequence of Riemannian manifolds \( {\left\{  {M}_{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) with balls \( B\left( {{x}_{i},1}\right)  \subset  {M}_{i} \) having compact closure so that \( {\left. \operatorname{Rm}\right| }_{B\left( {{x}_{i},1}\right) } \geq   - 1 \) and \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{i},1}\right) }\right)  \geq  {w}^{\prime } \) , but with the property that all balls \( B\left( {{x}_{i}^{\prime },{r}^{\prime }}\right)  \subset  B\left( {{x}_{i},1}\right) \) with \( {r}^{\prime } \geq  {i}^{-1} \) satisfy \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{i}^{\prime },{r}^{\prime }}\right) }\right)  < \frac{1}{2}{\omega }_{n}{\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{n} \) . After taking a subsequence, we can assume that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{i \rightarrow  \infty }}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{i},1}\right) ,{x}_{i}}\right)  = \left( {X,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) in the pointed Gromov-Hausdorff topology. From [12, Theorem 10.8], the Riemannian volume forms \( {\operatorname{dvol}}_{{M}_{i}} \) converge weakly to the three-dimensional Hausdorff measure \( \mu \) of \( X \) . From [12, Corollary 6.7 and Section 9], for any \( \epsilon  > 0 \) , there are small balls \( B\left( {{x}_{\infty }^{\prime },{r}^{\prime }}\right)  \subset  X \) with compact closure in \( X \) such that \( \mu \left( {B\left( {{x}_{\infty }^{\prime },{r}^{\prime }}\right) }\right)  \geq  \left( {1 - \epsilon }\right) {\omega }_{n}{\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{n} \) . This gives a contradiction.

Theorem I.12.3) For any \( w > 0 \) there exist \( \tau  = \tau \left( w\right)  > 0, K = \; K\left( w\right)  < \infty \) and \( \rho  = \rho \left( w\right)  > 0 \) with the following property. Suppose that \( g\left( \cdot \right) \) is a Ricci flow on a closed three-manifold \( M \) , defined for \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , with \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature. Let \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) be a spacetime point and let \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) be a radius with \( {t}_{0} \geq  {4\tau }{r}_{0}^{2} \) and \( {r}_{0}^{2}\Phi \left( {r}_{0}^{-2}\right)  < \rho \) . Suppose that \( {\operatorname{vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  w{r}_{0}^{3} \) and the time- \( {t}_{0} \) sectional curvatures on \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) are bounded below by \( - {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . Then \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  K{r}_{0}^{-2} \) whenever \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - \tau {r}_{0}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq \; \frac{1}{4}{r}_{0} \) .

nodes.proof:
Let \( {\tau }_{0}\left( w\right) , B\left( w\right) \) and \( C\left( w\right) \) be the constants of Corollary 45.13. Put \( \tau \left( w\right)  = \frac{1}{2}{\tau }_{0}\left( w\right) \) and \( K\left( w\right)  = C\left( w\right)  + 2\frac{B\left( w\right) }{{\tau }_{0}\left( w\right) } \) . The function \( \rho \left( w\right) \) will be specified in the course of the proof.

Suppose that the theorem is not true. Take a counterexample with a point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) and a radius \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) such that the time- \( {t}_{0} \) ball \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) satisfies the assumptions of the theorem, but the conclusion of the theorem fails. We claim there is a counterexample coming from a point \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{0},{\widehat{t}}_{0}}\right) \) and a radius \( {\widehat{r}}_{0} > 0 \) , with the additional property that for any \( \left( {{x}_{0}^{\prime },{t}_{0}^{\prime }}\right) \) and \( {r}_{0}^{\prime } \) having \( {t}_{0}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{\widehat{t}}_{0} - {2\tau }{\widehat{r}}_{0}^{2},{\widehat{t}}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) and \( {r}_{0}^{\prime } \leq  \frac{1}{2}{\widehat{r}}_{0} \) , if \( {\operatorname{vol}}_{{t}_{0}^{\prime }}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{0}^{\prime },{r}_{0}^{\prime }}\right) }\right)  \geq  w{\left( {r}_{0}^{\prime }\right) }^{3} \) and the time- \( {t}_{0}^{\prime } \) sectional curvatures on \( B\left( {{x}_{0}^{\prime },{r}_{0}^{\prime }}\right) \) are bounded below by \( - {\left( {r}_{0}^{\prime }\right) }^{-2} \) then \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  K{\left( {r}_{0}^{\prime }\right) }^{-2} \) whenever \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0}^{\prime } - \tau {\left( {r}_{0}^{\prime }\right) }^{2},{t}_{0}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}^{\prime }}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{r}_{0}^{\prime } \) . This follows from a pointpicking argument - suppose that it is not true for the original \( {x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0} \) . Then there are \( \left( {{x}_{0}^{\prime },{t}_{0}^{\prime }}\right) \) and \( {r}_{0}^{\prime } \) with \( {t}_{0}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {2\tau }{r}_{0}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) and \( {r}_{0}^{\prime } \leq  \frac{1}{2}{r}_{0} \) , for which the assumptions of the theorem hold but the conclusion does not. If the triple \( \left( {{x}_{0}^{\prime },{t}_{0}^{\prime },{r}_{0}^{\prime }}\right) \) satisfies the claim then we stop, and otherwise we iterate the procedure. The iteration must terminate, which provides the desired triple \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{0},{\widehat{t}}_{0},{\widehat{r}}_{0}}\right) \) . Note that \( {\widehat{t}}_{0} > {t}_{0} - {4\tau }{r}_{0}^{2} \geq  0 \) .

We relabel \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{0},{\widehat{t}}_{0},{\widehat{r}}_{0}}\right) \) as \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) . For simplicity, let us assume that the time- \( {t}_{0} \) sectional curvatures on \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) are strictly greater than \( - {r}_{0}^{-2} \) ; the general case will follow from continuity. Let \( {\tau }^{\prime } > 0 \) be the largest number such that \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq   - {r}_{0}^{-2} \) whenever \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {\tau }^{\prime }{r}_{0}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {r}_{0} \) . If \( {\tau }^{\prime } \geq  {2\tau } = {\tau }_{0}\left( w\right) \) then Corollary 45.13 implies that \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C{r}_{0}^{-2} + B{\left( t - {t}_{0} + 2\tau {r}_{0}^{2}\right) }^{-1} \) whenever \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {2\tau }{r}_{0}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{r}_{0} \) . In particular, \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  K \) whenever \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - \tau {r}_{0}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{r}_{0} \) , which contradicts our assumption that the conclusion of the theorem fails.

Now suppose that \( {\tau }^{\prime } < {2\tau } \) . Put \( {t}^{\prime } = {t}_{0} - {\tau }^{\prime }{r}_{0}^{2} \) . From estimates on the length and volume distortion under the Ricci flow, we know that there are numbers \( \alpha  = \alpha \left( w\right)  > 0 \) and \( {w}^{\prime } = \; {w}^{\prime }\left( w\right)  > 0 \) so that the time- \( {t}^{\prime } \) ball \( B\left( {{x}_{0},\alpha {r}_{0}}\right) \) has volume at least \( {w}^{\prime }{\left( \alpha {r}_{0}\right) }^{3} \) . From Lemma 54.1, there is a subball \( B\left( {{x}^{\prime },{r}^{\prime }}\right)  \subset  B\left( {{x}_{0},\alpha {r}_{0}}\right) \) with \( {r}^{\prime } \geq  {c\alpha }{r}_{0} \) and \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}^{\prime },{r}^{\prime }}\right) }\right)  \geq  \frac{1}{2}{\omega }_{3}{\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{3} \) . From the preceding pointpicking argument, we have the estimate \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  K{\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{-2} \) whenever \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \tau {\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{2},{t}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{t}\left( {x,{x}^{\prime }}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{r}^{\prime } \) . From the \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature, we have

a bound \( \left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq \) const. \( K{\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{-2} + \) const. \( \Phi \left( {K{\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{-2}}\right) \) at such a point (see (52.4)). If \( \rho \left( w\right) \) is taken sufficiently small then we can ensure that \( {r}_{0} \) is small enough, and hence \( {r}^{\prime } \) is small enough, to make \( K{\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{-2} + \Phi \left( {K{\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{-2}}\right)  \leq  {2K}{\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{-2} \) . Then we can apply Theorem 53.1 to a time interval ending at time \( {t}^{\prime } \) , after a redefinition of its constants, to obtain a bound of the form \( R\left( {x,{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \leq  {K}^{\prime }{\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{-2} \) whenever \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{t}\left( {x,{x}^{\prime }}\right)  \leq  {10}{r}_{0} \) , where \( {K}^{\prime } \) is related to the constant \( K \) of Theorem 53.1. (We also obtain a similar estimate at times slightly less than \( {t}^{\prime } \) .) Thus at such a point, \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x,{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \geq   - \Phi \left( {{K}^{\prime }{\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{-2}}\right) \) . If we choose \( \rho \left( w\right) \) to be sufficiently small to force \( {r}^{\prime } \) to be sufficiently small to force \( - \Phi \left( {{K}^{\prime }{\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{-2}}\right)  >  - {r}_{0}^{-2} \) then we have \( \mathrm{{Rm}} >  - {r}_{0}^{-2} \) on \( \overline{{B}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) } \subset  {B}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}^{\prime },{10}{r}_{0}}\right) \) , which contradicts the assumed maximality of \( {\tau }^{\prime } \) .

We note that in the application of Theorem 53.1 at the end of the proof, we must take into account the extra hypothesis, in the notation of Theorem 53.1, that \( {r}_{0}^{2}\Phi \left( {r}_{0}^{-2}\right)  < \rho \) (see Remark 53.2). This will be satisfied if the \( {r}_{0} \) in Theorem 53.1 is small enough, which is ensured by taking the \( \rho \) of Theorem 54.2 small enough.

Fix \( w > 0 \) . The number \( \rho \) will be specified in the course of the proof. Suppose that the corollary is not true, i.e. there is a Ricci flow solution as in the statement of the corollary along with a metric ball \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) at a time \( {t}_{0} \geq  1 \) so that \( \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{x \in  B\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }}\operatorname{Rm}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  =  - {r}_{0}^{-2} \) and \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  > w{r}_{0}^{n} \) . The idea is to use Theorem 54.2, along with the \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature, to get a double-sided sectional curvature bound on a smaller ball at an earlier time. Then one goes forward in time using Theorem 53.1, along with the \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature, to get a lower sectional curvature bound on the original ball, thereby obtaining a contradiction.

If in addition \( {r}_{0} \) is sufficiently small then it follows that \( \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq \) const. \( \Phi \left( {K{r}_{0}^{-2}}\right)  \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) .

nodes.section_title: 57. OVERVIEW OF Ricci Flow with Surgery on Three-Manifolds [52]
nodes.content: A Ricci flow with surgery consists of a sequence of smooth 3-dimensional Ricci flows on adjacent time intervals with the property that for any two adjacent intervals, there is a a compact 3-dimensional submanifold-with-boundary that is common to the final slice of the first time interval and the initial slice of the second time interval.

Definition 58.1. We say that a Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{1},{g}_{1}}\right) \) has distance \( \leq  \epsilon \) in the \( {C}^{N} \) - topology to another Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{2},{g}_{2}}\right) \) if there is a diffeomorphism \( \phi  : {M}_{2} \rightarrow  {M}_{1} \) so that \( \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{\left| I\right|  \leq  N}}\frac{1}{\left| I\right| !}{\begin{Vmatrix}{\nabla }^{I}\left( {\phi }^{ * }{g}_{1} - {g}_{2}\right) \end{Vmatrix}}_{\infty } \leq  \epsilon \) . An open set \( U \) in a Riemannian 3-manifold \( M \) is an \( \epsilon \) -neck if modulo rescaling, it has distance less than \( \epsilon \) , in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  {1/\epsilon }\right\rbrack   + 1} \) -topology, to the product of the round 2-sphere of scalar curvature 1 (and therefore Gaussian curvature \( \left. \frac{1}{2}\right) \) with an interval \( I \) of length greater than \( 2{\epsilon }^{-1} \) . If a point \( x \in  M \) and a neighborhood \( U \) of \( x \) are specified then we will understand that "distance" refers to the pointed topology, where the basepoint in \( {S}^{2} \times  I \) projects to the center of \( I \) .

We make a similar definition of \( \epsilon \) -closeness in the spacetime case, where \( {\nabla }^{I} \) now includes time derivatives. A subset of the form \( U \times  \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack   \subset  M \times  \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack \) , where \( U \subset  M \) is open, sitting in the spacetime of a Ricci flow is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck if after parabolic rescaling and time shifting, it has distance less than \( \epsilon \) to the product Ricci flow defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-1,0}\right\rbrack \) which, at its final time, is isometric to the product of a round 2-sphere of scalar curvature 1 with an interval of length greater than \( 2{\epsilon }^{-1} \) . (Evidently, the time- 0 slice of the product has 3-dimensional scalar curvature equal to 1.)

nodes.content:
Definition 58.2. A metric on \( {S}^{2} \times  \mathbb{I} \) such that each point is contained in some \( \epsilon \) -neck is called an \( \epsilon \) -tube, or an \( \epsilon \) -horn, or a double \( \epsilon \) -horn, if the scalar curvature stays bounded on both ends, stays bounded on one end and tends to infinity on the other, or tends to infinity on both ends, respectively.

A metric on \( {B}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} - \overline{{B}^{3}} \) , such that each point outside some compact subset is contained in an \( \epsilon \) -neck, is called an \( \epsilon \) -cap or a capped \( \epsilon \) -horn, if the scalar curvature stays bounded or tends to infinity on the end, respectively.

An example of an \( \epsilon \) -tube is \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) with the product metric. For a relevant example of an \( \epsilon \) -horn, consider the metric

(58.3)

\[
g = d{r}^{2} + \frac{1}{8\ln \frac{1}{r}}{r}^{2}d{\theta }^{2}
\]

on \( \left( {0, R}\right)  \times  {S}^{2} \) , where \( d{\theta }^{2} \) is the metric on \( {S}^{2} \) with \( R = 1 \) . From [6], the metric \( g \) models a rotationally symmetric neckpinch. Rescaling around \( {r}_{0} \) , we put \( s = \sqrt{8\ln \frac{1}{{r}_{0}}}\left( {\frac{r}{{r}_{0}} - 1}\right) \) and find

(58.4)

\[
\frac{8\ln \frac{1}{{r}_{0}}}{{r}_{0}^{2}}g = d{s}^{2} + \left( {1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{8\ln \frac{1}{{r}_{0}}}}\left( {2 + \frac{1}{\ln \frac{1}{{r}_{0}}}}\right) s + O\left( {s}^{2}\right) }\right) d{\theta }^{2}.
\]

For small \( {r}_{0} \) , if we take \( \epsilon  \sim  {\left( \ln \frac{1}{{r}_{0}}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{4}} \) then the region with \( s \in  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) will be \( \epsilon \) - biLipschitz close to the standard cylinder. Note that as \( {r}_{0} \rightarrow  0 \) , the constant \( \epsilon \) improves; this is related to Lemma 71.1.

An \( \epsilon \) -cap is the result of capping off an \( \epsilon \) -tube by a 3-ball or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} - \overline{{B}^{3}} \) with an arbitrary metric. A capped \( \epsilon \) -horn is the result of capping off an \( \epsilon \) -horn by a 3-ball or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} - \overline{{B}^{3}} \) with an arbitrary metric.

nodes.content: Remark 58.5. Throughout the rest of these notes, \( \epsilon \) denotes a small positive constant that is meant to be universal. The precise value of \( \epsilon \) is unspecified. If the statement of a lemma or theorem invokes \( \epsilon \) then the statement is meant to be true uniformly with respect to the other variables, provided \( \epsilon \) is sufficiently small. When going through the proofs one is allowed to make \( \epsilon \) small enough so that the arguments work, but one is only allowed to make a finite number of such reductions.

nodes.content: Lemma 58.6. Let \( U \) be an \( \epsilon \) -neck in an \( \epsilon \) -tube (or horn) and let \( S \) be a cross-sectional sphere in \( U \) . Then \( S \) separates the two ends of the tube (or horn).
nodes.content_excerpt: Lemma 58.6. Let \( U \) be an \( \epsilon \) -neck in an \( \epsilon \) -tube (or horn) and let \( S \) be a cross-sectional sphere in \( U \) . Then \( S \) separates the two ends of the tube (or horn).

nodes.proof:
Let \( W \) denote the tube (or horn). As any point \( m \in  W \) lies in some \( \epsilon \) -neck, there is a unique lowest eigenvalue of the Ricci operator \( \operatorname{Ric} \in  \operatorname{End}\left( {{T}_{m}W}\right) \) at \( m \) . Let \( {\xi }_{m} \subset  {T}_{m}W \) be the corresponding eigenspace. As \( m \) varies, the \( {\xi }_{m} \) ’s form a smooth line field \( \xi \) on \( W \) , to which \( S \) is transverse.

Suppose that \( S \) does not separate the two ends of \( W \) . Then \( S \) represents a trivial element of \( {\mathrm{H}}_{2}\left( {{S}^{2} \times  I}\right)  \cong  {\pi }_{2}\left( {{S}^{2} \times  I}\right) \) and there is an embedded 3-disk \( D \subset  W \) for which \( \partial D = S \) . This contradicts the fact that the line field \( \xi \) is transverse to \( S \) and extends over \( D \) .

nodes.content: Lemma 59.1. If \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a time slice of a noncompact \( \kappa \) -solution and \( {M}_{\epsilon } \neq  \varnothing \) then there is a compact submanifold-with-boundary \( X \subset  M \) so that \( {M}_{\epsilon } \subset  X, X \) is diffeomorphic to \( \overline{{B}^{3}} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} - {B}^{3} \) , and \( M - \operatorname{int}\left( X\right) \) is diffeomorphic to \( \lbrack 0,\infty ) \times  {S}^{2} \) .

nodes.proof:
If \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) does not have positive sectional curvature and \( {M}_{\epsilon } \neq  \varnothing \) then \( M \) must be isometric to \( \mathbb{R}{ \times  }_{{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}}{S}^{2} \) , in which case the lemma is easily seen to be true with \( X \) diffeomorphic to \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} - {B}^{3} \) . Suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) has positive sectional curvature. Choose \( x \in  {M}_{\epsilon } \) . Let \( \gamma  : \lbrack 0,\infty ) \rightarrow  M \) be a ray with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = x \) . As \( {M}_{\epsilon } \) is compact, there is some \( a > 0 \) so that if \( t > a \) then \( \gamma \left( t\right)  \notin  {M}_{\epsilon } \) . We can cover \( \left( {a,\infty }\right) \) by open intervals \( {V}_{j} \) so that \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{{V}_{i}} \) is a geodesic segment in an \( \epsilon \) -neck of rescaled length approximately \( 2{\epsilon }^{-1} \) . Then we can find a cover of \( \left( {a,\infty }\right) \) by linearly ordered open intervals \( {U}_{i} \) , refining the previous cover, so that 1. The rescaled length of \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{{U}_{i}} \) is approximately \( \frac{1}{10}{\epsilon }^{-1} \) .

2. Choosing some \( {x}_{i} \in  {U}_{i} \cap  {U}_{i + 1} \) , the rescaled length (with rescaling at \( {x}_{i} \) ) of \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{{U}_{i} \cap  {U}_{i + 1}} \) is approximately \( \frac{1}{40}{\epsilon }^{-1} \) and \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{{U}_{i} \cap  {U}_{i + 1}} \) lies in an \( \epsilon \) -neck \( {W}_{i} \) centered at \( {x}_{i} \) .

Let \( {\phi }_{i} \) be projection on the first factor in the assumed diffeomorphism \( {W}_{i} \cong  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)  \times \; {S}^{2} \) . If \( \epsilon \) is sufficiently small then the composition \( {\left. {\phi }_{i} \circ  \gamma \right| }_{{U}_{i}} : {U}_{i} \rightarrow  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) is a diffeomorphism onto its image. Put \( {N}_{i} = {\phi }_{i}^{-1}\left( {\operatorname{Im}\left( {\left. {\phi }_{i} \circ  \gamma \right| }_{{U}_{i}}\right) }\right)  \subset  {W}_{i} \) and \( {p}_{i} = {\left( {\left. {\phi }_{i} \circ  \gamma \right| }_{{U}_{i}}\right) }^{-1} \circ  {\phi }_{i} \) : \( {N}_{i} \rightarrow  {U}_{i} \subset  \left( {a,\infty }\right) \) . Then \( {p}_{i} \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to being a Riemannian submersion and on overlaps \( {N}_{i} \cap  {N}_{i + 1} \) , the maps \( {p}_{i} \) and \( {p}_{i + 1} \) are \( {C}^{K} \) -close. Choosing an appropriate partition of unity \( \left\{  {b}_{i}\right\} \) subordinate to the \( {U}_{i} \) ’s, if \( \epsilon \) is small then the function \( f = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{i}{b}_{i}{p}_{i} \) is a submersion from \( \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{i}{N}_{i} \) to \( \left( {a,\infty }\right) \) . The fiber is seen to be \( {S}^{2} \) . Given \( t \in  \left( {a,\infty }\right) \) , put \( X = M - {f}^{-1}\left( {t,\infty }\right) \) . Then \( M - \operatorname{int}\left( X\right)  = {f}^{-1}\left( {\lbrack t,\infty }\right) ) \) is diffeomorphic to \( \lbrack 0,\infty ) \times  {S}^{2} \) .

Recall from Section 46 that we have an exhaustion of \( M \) by certain convex compact subsets. As \( M \) is one-ended, the subsets have connected boundary. As in Section 46, if the boundary of such a subset intersects an \( \epsilon \) -neck then the intersection will be a nearly cross-sectional 2-sphere in the \( \epsilon \) -neck. Hence with an appropriate choice of \( t \) , the set \( X \) will be isotopic to one of our convex subsets and so diffeomorphic to a closed 3-ball.

Then the universal cover \( \widetilde{M} \) is \( \mathbb{R} \times  {S}^{2} \) . As it has nonnegative sectional curvature and two ends, Toponogov's theorem implies that \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) }\right) \) splits off an \( \mathbb{R} \) -factor. Using the strong maximum principle, the Ricci flow on \( \widetilde{M} \) splits off an \( \mathbb{R} \) -factor; see Theorem A.7. Using Corollary 40.1, it follows that \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( t\right) }\right) \) is the evolving round cylinder \( \mathbb{R} \times  {S}^{2} \) . From the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing, the quotient \( M \) cannot be \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \)

nodes.content: Lemma 59.3. If a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {M, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) is compact and has a noncompact asymptotic soliton then \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: Lemma 59.3. If a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {M, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) is compact and has a noncompact asymptotic soliton then \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

nodes.proof:
We use Corollary 48.1 in Section 48. First, we claim that the time slices of the type-D \( \kappa \) -solutions of Corollary 48.1 have a universal upper bound on \( \mathop{\max }\limits_{M}R \cdot  \operatorname{diam}{\left( M\right) }^{2} \) . To see this, we can rescale at the point \( x \in  {M}_{\epsilon } \) by \( R\left( x\right) \) , after which the diameter is bounded above by \( 2\sqrt{\alpha } \) . We then use Theorem 46.1 to get an upper bound on the rescaled scalar curvature, which proves the claim. Given an upper bound on \( \mathop{\max }\limits_{M}R \cdot  \operatorname{diam}{\left( M\right) }^{2} \) , the asymptotic soliton cannot be noncompact.

Thus we are in case \( \mathrm{C} \) of Corollary 48.1. Take a sequence \( {t}_{i} \rightarrow   - \infty \) and choose points \( {x}_{i},{y}_{i} \in  {M}_{\epsilon }\left( {t}_{i}\right) \) as in Corollary 48.1.C. Rescale by \( R\left( {{x}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right) \) and take a subsequence that converges to a pointed Ricci flow solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty }}\right) }\right) \) . The limit \( {M}_{\infty } \) cannot be compact, as otherwise we would have a uniform upper bound on \( R \cdot  {\operatorname{diam}}^{2} \) for \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{i}\right) }\right) \) , which would contradict the existence of the noncompact asymptotic soliton. Thus \( {M}_{\infty } \) is a noncompact \( \kappa \) -solution. We can find compact sets \( {X}_{i} \subset  M \) containing \( B\left( {{x}_{i},{\alpha R}{\left( {x}_{i},{t}_{i}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) so that \( \left\{  {X}_{i}\right\} \) converges to a set \( {X}_{\infty } \subset  {M}_{\infty } \) as in Lemma 59.1. Taking a further subsequence, we find similar compact sets \( {Y}_{i} \subset  M \) containing \( B\left( {{y}_{i},{\alpha R}{\left( {y}_{i},{t}_{i}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) so that \( \left\{  {Y}_{i}\right\} \) converges to a set \( {Y}_{\infty } \subset  {M}_{\infty } \) as in Lemma 59.1. In particular, for large \( i,{X}_{i} \) and \( {Y}_{i} \) are each diffeomorphic to either \( \overline{{B}^{3}} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} - {B}^{3} \) . Considering a minimizing geodesic segment \( \overline{{x}_{i}{y}_{i}} \) as in the statement of Corollary 48.1.C, we can use an argument as in the proof of Lemma 59.1 to construct a submersion from \( M - \left( {{X}_{i} \cup  {Y}_{i}}\right) \) to an interval, with fiber \( {S}^{2} \) . Hence \( M \) is diffeomorphic to the result of gluing \( {X}_{i} \) and \( {Y}_{i} \) along a 2-sphere. As \( M \) has finite fundamental group, no more than one of \( {X}_{i} \) and \( {Y}_{i} \) can be diffeomorphic to \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} - {B}^{3} \) . Thus \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

nodes.content:
Lemma 59.7. For every sufficiently small \( \epsilon  > 0 \) one can find \( {C}_{1} = {C}_{1}\left( \epsilon \right) \) and \( {C}_{2} = {C}_{2}\left( \epsilon \right) \) such that for each point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in every \( \kappa \) -solution there is a radius \( r \in  \left\lbrack  {R{\left( x, t\right) }^{-1/2},{C}_{1}R{\left( x, t\right) }^{-1/2}}\right\rbrack \) and a neighborhood \( B,\overline{B\left( {x, t, r}\right) } \subset  B \subset  B\left( {x, t,{2r}}\right) \) , which falls into one of the four categories:

(a) \( B \) is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck (more precisely, \( B \) is the slice of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck at its maximal time, and an appropriate parabolic neighborhood of B satisfies the condition to be a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck), or

(b) \( B \) is an \( \epsilon \) -cap, or

(c) \( B \) is a closed manifold, diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) , or

(d) \( B \) is a closed manifold of constant positive sectional curvature.

Furthermore:

- The scalar curvature in \( B \) at time \( t \) is between \( {C}_{2}^{-1}R\left( {x, t}\right) \) and \( {C}_{2}R\left( {x, t}\right) \) .

- The volume of \( B \) in cases (a),(b) and (c) is greater than \( {C}_{2}^{-1}R{\left( x, t\right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}} \) .

- In case (b), there is an \( \epsilon \) -neck \( U \subset  B \) with compact complement in \( B \) (i.e. the end of \( B \) is entirely contained in the \( \epsilon \) -neck) such that the distance from \( x \) to \( U \) is at least \( {10000R}{\left( x, t\right) }^{-1/2} \) .

- In case (c) the sectional curvature in \( B \) at time \( t \) is greater than \( {C}_{2}^{-1}R\left( {x, t}\right) \) .

nodes.proof:
We may assume that we are talking about a \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution, as if \( M \) is a metric quotient of a round sphere then it falls into category (d) for any \( r > \pi {\left( R\left( {x}_{i},{t}_{i}\right) /6\right) }^{-1/2} \) (since then \( M = \overline{B\left( {{x}_{i},{t}_{i}, r}\right) } = B\left( {{x}_{i},{t}_{i},{2r}}\right) ). \)

Fix a small \( \epsilon \) and suppose that the claim is not true. Then there is a sequence of \( {\kappa }_{{0}^{ - }} \) solutions \( {M}_{i} \) that together provide a counterexample. That is, there is a sequence \( {C}_{i} \rightarrow  \infty \) and a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right)  \in  {M}_{i} \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) so that for any \( r \in  \left\lbrack  {R{\left( {x}_{i},{t}_{i}\right) }^{-1/2},{C}_{i}R{\left( {x}_{i},{t}_{i}\right) }^{-1/2}}\right\rbrack \) one cannot find a \( B \) between \( \overline{B\left( {{x}_{i},{t}_{i}, r}\right) } \) and \( B\left( {{x}_{i},{t}_{i},{2r}}\right) \) falling into one of the four categories and satisfying the subsidiary conditions with parameter \( {C}_{2} = {C}_{i} \) . Rescale the metric by \( R\left( {{x}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right) \) and take a convergent subsequence of \( \left( {{M}_{i},\left( {{x}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right) }\right) \) to obtain a limit \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty }}\right) }\right) \) . Then for any \( r > 1 \) , one cannot find a \( {B}_{\infty } \) between \( \overline{B\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty }, r}\right) } \) and \( B\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty },{2r}}\right) \) falling into one of the four categories and satisfying the subsidiary conditions for any parameter \( {C}_{2} \) .

If \( {M}_{\infty } \) is compact then for any \( r \) greater than the diameter of the time- \( {t}_{\infty } \) slice of \( {M}_{\infty } \) , \( \overline{B\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty }, r}\right) } = {M}_{\infty } = B\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty },{2r}}\right) \) falls into category (c) or (d). For the subsidiary conditions, \( {M}_{\infty } \) clearly has a lower volume bound, a positive lower scalar curvature bound and an upper scalar curvature bound. As a compact \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution has positive sectional curvature, \( {M}_{\infty } \) also has a lower sectional curvature bound. This is a contradiction.

If \( {M}_{\infty } \) is noncompact then Lemma 59.1 (or more precisely its proof) and Lemma 59.2 imply that for some \( r > 1 \) , there will be a \( B \) between \( \overline{B\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty }, r}\right) } \) and \( B\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty },{2r}}\right) \) falling into category (a) or (b). In case (b), by choosing the parameter \( r \) sufficiently large, the existence of the \( \epsilon \) -neck \( U \) with the desired properties follows from the proof of Lemma 59.1. For the other subsidiary conditions, \( B \) clearly has a lower volume bound, a positive lower scalar curvature bound and an upper scalar curvature bound. This contradiction completes the proof of the lemma.

A Ricci flow \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) defined on a time interval \( \lbrack 0, a) \) is a standard solution if it has initial condition \( {g}_{0} \) , the curvature \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| \) is bounded on compact time intervals \( \left\lbrack  {0,{a}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack   \subset  \lbrack 0, a) \) , and it cannot be extended to a Ricci flow with the same properties on a strictly longer time interval.

nodes.label: Lemma 60.3
nodes.document_title: Bruce Kleiner and John Lott - Notes on Perelman's Papers
nodes.content:
Lemma 60.3. Let \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be a standard solution. Then

(1) The curvature operator of \( g \) is nonnegative.

(2) All derivatives of curvature are bounded for small time, independent of the standard solution.

(3) The scalar curvature satisfies \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  {a}^{ - }}}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {\mathbb{R}}^{3}}}R\left( {x, t}\right)  = \infty \) .

(4) \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed at scales below 1 on any time interval contained in \( \left\lbrack  {0,2}\right\rbrack \) , where \( \kappa \) depends only on the choice of the initial condition \( {g}_{0} \) .

(5) \( \left( {{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 52.7, in the sense that for any \( {\Delta t} > 0 \) , there is an \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) so that for any point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{0} \geq  {\Delta t} \) and \( Q = R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , the solution in \( \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  : {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < {\left( \epsilon Q\right) }^{-1},{t}_{0} - {\left( \epsilon Q\right) }^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{0}}\right\} \) is, after scaling by the factor \( Q,\epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of a \( \kappa \) -solution.

Moreover, any Ricci flow which satisfies all of the conditions of Definition 60.2 except maximality of the time interval can be extended to a standard solution. In particular, using short-time existence [62, Theorem 1.1], there is at least one standard solution.

nodes.document_title: Bruce Kleiner and John Lott - Notes on Perelman's Papers
nodes.content: Lemma 61.1. (cf. Claim 2 of II.2) Let \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{S}}\right) \) be the maximal time interval such that the curvature of all standard solutions is uniformly bounded for every compact subinterval \( \left\lbrack  {0, a}\right\rbrack   \subset  \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{S}}\right) \) . Then on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{S}}\right) \) , the family of standard solution converges uniformly at (spatial) infinity to the standard Ricci flow on the round infinite cylinder \( {S}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) of scalar curvature one. In particular, \( {T}_{S} \) is at most 1 .

nodes.proof:
Let \( {\left\{  {\mathcal{M}}_{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) be a sequence of standard solutions, and let \( {\left\{  {x}_{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) be a sequence tending to infinity in the time-zero slice \( M \) .

By (2) of Lemma 60.3, the gradient estimates in Appendix D, and Appendix E, every subsequence of \( {\left\{  {\mathcal{M}}_{i},\left( {x}_{i},0\right) \right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) has a subsequence which converges in the pointed smooth topology on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{S}}\right) \) . Therefore, it suffices to show that if \( {\left\{  {\mathcal{M}}_{i},\left( {x}_{i},0\right) \right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) converges to some pointed Ricci flow \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right) }\right) \) then \( {\mathcal{M}}_{\infty } \) is round cylindrical flow.

Since \( {g}_{i}\left( 0\right)  = {g}_{0} \) for all \( i \) , the sequence of pointed time-zero slices \( {\left\{  \left( M,{x}_{i},{g}_{i}\left( 0\right) \right) \right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) converges in the pointed smooth topology to the round cylinder, i.e. \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is a round cylinder of scalar curvature 1. Each time slice \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is biLipschitz equivalent to \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) . In particular, it has two ends. As it also has nonnegative sectional curvature, Toponogov’s theorem implies that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) splits off an \( \mathbb{R} \) -factor. Using the strong maximum principle, the Ricci flow \( {\mathcal{M}}_{\infty } \) splits off an \( \mathbb{R} \) -factor; see Theorem A.7. Then using the uniqueness of the Ricci flow on the round \( {S}^{2} \) , it follows that \( {\mathcal{M}}_{\infty } \) is a standard shrinking cylinder, which proves the lemma.

In particular, \( {T}_{S} \leq  1 \) .
