nodes.label: Lemma 62.1
nodes.document_title: Bruce Kleiner and John Lott - Notes on Perelman's Papers
nodes.content: Lemma 62.1. (cf. Claim 4 of II.2) Let \( {T}_{S} \) be as in Lemma 61.1. Then \( {T}_{S} = 1 \) . In particular, every standard solution survives until time 1.
nodes.content_excerpt: Lemma 62.1. (cf. Claim 4 of II.2) Let \( {T}_{S} \) be as in Lemma 61.1. Then \( {T}_{S} = 1 \) . In particular, every standard solution survives until time 1.

nodes.proof:
First, there is an \( \alpha  > 0 \) so that \( {T}_{S} > \alpha \) [62, Theorem 1.1]. In what follows we will apply Theorem 52.7. The hypothesis of Theorem 52.7 says that the flow should exist on a time interval of duration at least one, but by rescaling we can apply Theorem 52.7 just as well with the alternative hypothesis that the flow exists on a time interval of duration at least \( \alpha \) .

Suppose that \( {T}_{S} < 1 \) . Then there is a sequence of standard solutions \( {\left\{  {\mathcal{M}}_{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) , times \( {t}_{i} \rightarrow  {T}_{S} \) and points \( \left( {{x}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right)  \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{i} \) so that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{i \rightarrow  \infty }}R\left( {{x}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right)  = \infty \) .

We first argue that no subsequence of the points \( {x}_{i} \) can go to infinity (with respect to the time-zero slice). Suppose, after relabeling the subsequence, that \( {\left\{  {x}_{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) goes to infinity. From Lemma 61.1, for any fixed \( {t}^{\prime } < {T}_{S} \) the pointed solutions \( \left( {M,\left( {{x}_{i},0}\right) ,{g}_{i}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) , defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) , approach that of the shrinking cylinder on the same time interval. Lemma 60.3 and the characterization of high-curvature regions from Theorem 52.7 implies a uniform bound on high-curvature regions of the time derivative of \( R \) , of the form (59.5). Then taking \( {t}^{\prime } \) sufficiently close to \( {T}_{S} \) , we get a contradiction. We conclude that outside of a compact region the curvature stays uniformly bounded as \( t \rightarrow  {T}_{S} \) ; compare with the proof of Lemma 52.11. (Alternatively, one could apply Theorem 30.1 to compact approximants, as is done in II.2.)

Thus we may assume that the sequence \( {\left\{  {x}_{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) stays in a compact region of the time-zero slice. By Theorem 52.7, there is a sequence \( {\epsilon }_{i} \rightarrow  0 \) so that after rescaling the pointed solution \( \left( {\mathcal{M},\left( {{x}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right) }\right) \) by \( R\left( {{x}_{i},{t}_{i}}\right) \) , the result is \( {\epsilon }_{i} \) -close to the corresponding subset of an ancient solution. By Proposition 41.13, the ancient solutions have vanishing asymptotic volume ratio. Hence for every \( \beta  > 0 \) , there is some \( L < \infty \) so that in the original unscaled solution, for large \( i \) we have \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{i},{t}_{i},{LR}{\left( {x}_{i},{t}_{i}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }\right)  \leq  \beta {\left( LR{\left( {x}_{i},{t}_{i}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) }^{3} \) . Applying the Bishop-Gromov inequality to the time- \( {t}_{i} \) slices, we conclude that for any \( D > 0 \) , \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{i \rightarrow  \infty }}{D}^{-3}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{i},{t}_{i}, D}\right) }\right)  = 0 \) . However, this contradicts the previously-shown fact that the solution extends smoothly to time \( {T}_{S} < 1 \) outside of a compact set.

Thus \( {T}_{S} = 1 \) .

nodes.content: Lemma 62.2. The infimal scalar curvature on the time-t slice tends to infinity as \( t \rightarrow  {1}^{ - } \) uniformly for all standard solutions.

nodes.proof:
Suppose the lemma failed and let \( {\left\{  \left( {\mathcal{M}}_{i},\left( {x}_{i},{t}_{i}\right) \right) \right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) be a sequence of pointed standard solutions, with \( {\left\{  R\left( {x}_{i},{t}_{i}\right) \right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) uniformly bounded and \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{i \rightarrow  \infty }}{t}_{i} = 1 \) .

Suppose first that after passing to a subsequence, the points \( {x}_{i} \) go to infinity in the time-zero slice. From Lemma 61.1, for any \( {t}^{\prime } \in  \lbrack 0,1) \) we have \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{i \rightarrow  \infty }}{R}^{-1}\left( {{x}_{i},{t}^{\prime }}\right)  = 1 - {t}^{\prime } \) . Combining this with the derivative estimate \( \left| \frac{\partial {R}^{-1}}{\partial t}\right|  \leq  \eta \) at high curvature regions gives a contradiction; compare with the proof of Lemma 52.11. Thus the points \( {x}_{i} \) stay in a compact region. We can now use the bounded-curvature-at-bounded-distance argument in Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 52.7 to extract a convergent subsequence of \( {\left\{  \left( {\mathcal{M}}_{i},\left( {x}_{i},0\right) \right) \right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) with a limit Ricci flow solution \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right) }\right) \) that exists on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . (In this case, the nonnegative curvature of the blowup region \( W \) comes from the fact that a standard solution has nonnegative curvature.) As in Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 52.7, \( {\mathcal{M}}_{\infty } \) will have bounded curvature for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . Note that \( {\mathcal{M}}_{\infty } \) is a standard solution. This contradicts Lemma 61.1.

nodes.content:
Lemma 63.1. (cf. Claim 5 of II.2) Given \( \epsilon  > 0 \) sufficiently small, there are constants \( \eta  = \eta \left( \epsilon \right) ,{C}_{1} = {C}_{1}\left( \epsilon \right) \) and \( {C}_{2} = {C}_{2}\left( \epsilon \right) \) so that every standard solution \( \mathcal{M} \) satisfies the conclusions of Lemmas 59.4 and 59.7, except that the \( \epsilon \) -neck neighborhood need not be strong. (Here the constants do not depend on the standard solution.) More precisely, any point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is covered by one of the following cases :

1. The time \( t \) lies in \( \left( {\frac{3}{4},1}\right) \) and \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) has an \( \epsilon \) -cap neighborhood or a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck neighborhood as in Lemma 59.7.

2. \( x \in  B\left( {p,0,{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{3}{4}}\right\rbrack \) and \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) has an \( \epsilon \) -cap neighborhood as in Lemma 59.7.

3. \( x \notin  B\left( {p,0,{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{3}{4}}\right\rbrack \) and there is an \( \epsilon \) -neck \( B\left( {x, t,{\epsilon }^{-1}r}\right) \) such that the solution in \( P\left( {x, t,{\epsilon }^{-1}r, - t}\right) \) is, after scaling with the factor \( {r}^{-2} \) , \( \epsilon \) -close to the appropriate piece of the evolving round infinite cylinder.

Moreover, we have an estimate \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \geq \) const. \( {\left( 1 - t\right) }^{-1} \) , where the constant does not depend on the standard solution.

(Here the co...

nodes.proof:
We first show that the conclusion of Lemma 59.7 is satisfied.

In view of Lemma 62.2, there is a \( \delta  > 0 \) so that if \( t \in  \left( {1 - \delta ,1}\right) \) then we can apply Theorem 52.7 and Lemma 59.7 to a point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to see that the conclusions of Lemma 59.7 are satisfied in this case. If \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1 - \delta }\right\rbrack \) and \( x \) is sufficiently far from \( p \) (i.e. dist \( {\mathrm{t}}_{0}\left( {x, p}\right)  \geq  D \) for an appropriate \( D \) ) then Lemma 61.1 implies that \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) has a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck neighborhood or there is an \( \epsilon \) -neck \( B\left( {x, t,{\epsilon }^{-1}r}\right) \) such that the solution in \( P\left( {x, t,{\epsilon }^{-1}r, - t}\right) \) is, after scaling with the factor \( {r}^{-2},\epsilon \) -close to the appropriate piece of the evolving round infinite cylinder.

(To elaborate a bit on the last possibility, the issue here is that there is no backward extension of the solution to \( t < 0 \) . Because of this, if \( t > 0 \) is close to 0 then the backward neighborhood \( P\left( {x, t,{\epsilon }^{-1}r, - t}\right) \) will not exist for rescaled time one, as required to have a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck neighborhood. Since \( \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{x \in  M}}R\left( {x,0}\right)  = 1 \) , we know from (B.2) that \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq \; \frac{1}{1 - \frac{2}{3}t} \) . Then if \( t > \frac{3}{5} \) , the time from the initial slice to \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) , after rescaled by the scalar curvature, is bounded below by \( t\frac{1}{1 - \frac{2}{3}t} > 1 \) . In particular, if \( t \geq  \frac{3}{4} \) then \( {r}^{2}t \) is at least one and we are ensured that the backward neighborhood \( P\left( {x, t,{\epsilon }^{-1}r, - t}\right) \) does contain a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck neighborhood.)

If \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1 - \delta }\right\rbrack \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{0}\left( {x, p}\right)  < D \) then, provided that \( D \) and \( \epsilon \) are chosen appropriately, we can say that \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) has an \( \epsilon \) -cap neighborhood.

We now show that the conclusion of Lemma 59.4 is satisfied. If \( t \in  \lbrack 1 - \delta ,1) \) then the conclusion follows from Theorem 52.7 and Lemma 59.4. If \( {\delta }^{\prime } > 0 \) is sufficiently small and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{\delta }^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) then the conclusion follows from Appendix D. If \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2}{\delta }^{\prime },1 - \frac{1}{2}\delta }\right\rbrack \) then we have an upper scalar curvature bound from Lemma 62.1. From Hamilton-Ivey pinching (see Appendix B), this implies a double-sided sectional curvature bound. The conclusion of Lemma 59.4, when \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2}{\delta }^{\prime },1 - \frac{1}{2}\delta }\right\rbrack \) , now follows from the Shi estimates of Appendix D.

The last statement of the lemma follows from the estimate \( \left| \frac{\partial {R}^{-1}}{\partial t}\right|  \leq \) const., which holds for \( t \) near 1 (see Lemmas 59.4,60.3(5) and 62.2) and then can be extended to all \( t \in  \lbrack 0,1) \) (see Lemma 61). From Lemma 62.2, \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  1}}{R}^{-1}\left( {x, t}\right)  = 0 \) for every \( x \) . Thus

\( {R}^{-1}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq \) const. \( \left( {1 - t}\right) \) for any \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) . Equivalently,

(63.2)

\[
R\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  \text{ const. }{\left( 1 - t\right) }^{-1}.
\]

nodes.section_title: 65. CLAIM 1 OF II.2. ROTATIONAL SYMMETRY OF STANDARD SOLUTIONS
nodes.content: Lemma 65.1. (cf. Claim 1 of II.2) Any Ricci flow solution in the space \( \mathcal{S}T \) is rotationally symmetric for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0,1) \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: Lemma 65.1. (cf. Claim 1 of II.2) Any Ricci flow solution in the space \( \mathcal{S}T \) is rotationally symmetric for all \( t \in \lbrack 0,1) \) .

nodes.proof:
We first describe an evolution equation for vector fields which turns out to send Killing vector fields to Killing vector fields. Suppose that a vector field \( u = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{m}{u}^{m}{\partial }_{m} \) evolves by

(65.2)

\[
{u}_{t}^{m} = {u}^{m};{}^{k} + {R}^{m}{}_{i}{u}^{i}.
\]

Then

(65.3)

\[
{\partial }_{t}\left( {{u}_{j, i}^{m}}\right)  = {u}_{t, i}^{m} + \left( {{\partial }_{t}{\Gamma }_{ki}^{m}}\right) {u}^{k}
\]

\[
= {\left( {u}^{m}{}_{;k}^{k} + {R}^{m}{}_{k}{u}^{k}\right) }_{;i} + \left( {{\partial }_{t}{\Gamma }_{ki}^{m}}\right) {u}^{k}
\]

\[
= {u}^{m}{}_{;{ik}}^{k} + {R}^{m}{}_{k;i}{u}^{k} + {R}^{m}{}_{k}{u}^{k}{}_{;i} + \left( {{\partial }_{t}{\Gamma }_{ki}^{m}}\right) {u}^{k}
\]

\[
= {u}_{\;;{ik}}^{m} - {R}_{\;{lki}}^{m}{u}_{\;;k}^{l\;k} - {R}_{\;{lki}}^{k}{u}_{\;;}^{m\;l} + {R}_{\;k;i}^{m}{u}^{k} + {R}_{\;k}^{m}{u}_{\;;i}^{k} + \left( {{\partial }_{t}{\Gamma }_{\;{ki}}^{m}}\right) {u}^{k}
\]

\[
= {u}_{i;{ki}}^{m}{}^{k} - {R}^{m}{}_{lki}{u}^{l}{}_{i}{}^{k} - {R}_{li}{u}^{m}{}_{;}{}^{l} + {R}^{m}{}_{k;i}{u}^{k} + {R}^{m}{}_{k}{u}^{k}{}_{;i} + \left( {{\partial }_{t}{\Gamma }_{ki}^{m}}\right) {u}^{k}
\]

\[
= {u}^{m}{}_{;{ik}}{}^{k} - \left( {{R}^{m}{}_{lki}{u}^{l}}\right) {}_{;}{}^{k} - {R}^{m}{}_{lki}{u}^{l}{}_{;}{}^{k} - {R}_{ki}{u}^{m}{}_{;}{}^{k} + {R}^{m}{}_{k;i}{u}^{k} + {R}^{m}{}_{k}{u}^{k}{}_{;i} + \left( {{\partial }_{t}{\Gamma }^{m}{}_{ki}}\right) {u}^{k}
\]

\[
= {u}^{m}{}_{;{ik}}{}^{k} - {R}^{m}{}_{{lki};}{}^{k}{u}^{l} - 2{R}^{m}{}_{lki}{u}^{l}{}_{;}{}^{k} - {R}_{ik}{u}^{m}{}_{;}{}^{k} + {R}^{m}{}_{k;i}{u}^{k} + {R}^{m}{}_{k}{u}^{k}{}_{;i} + \left( {{\partial }_{t}{\Gamma }^{m}{}_{ki}}\right) {u}^{k}.
\]

Contracting the second Bianchi identity gives

(65.4)

\[
{R}_{{mlki};}{}^{k} = {R}_{{il};m} - {R}_{{im};l}.
\]

Also,

(65.5)

\[
{\partial }_{t}{\Gamma }_{ki}^{m} = {\partial }_{t}\left( {{g}^{ml}{\Gamma }_{lki}}\right)  = 2{R}^{ml}{\Gamma }_{lki} - {g}^{ml}\left( {{R}_{{lk}, i} + {R}_{{li}, k} - {R}_{{ik}, l}}\right)
\]

\[
=  - {R}^{m}{}_{k;i} - {R}^{m}{}_{i;k} + {R}_{{ik};}{}^{m}.
\]

Substituting (65.4) and (65.5) in (65.3) gives

(65.6)

\[
{\partial }_{t}\left( {u}_{;i}^{m}\right)  = {u}_{;{ik}}^{m}{}^{k} - 2{R}^{m}{}_{lki}{u}^{l}{}_{;}{}^{k} - {R}_{ik}{u}^{m}{}_{;}{}^{k} + {R}^{m}{}_{k}{u}^{k}{}_{;i}.
\]

Then

(65.7)

\[
{\partial }_{t}\left( {u}_{j;i}\right)  = {\partial }_{t}\left( {{g}_{jm}{u}_{\;;i}^{m}}\right)  =  - 2{R}_{jm}{u}_{\;;i}^{m} + {g}_{jm}{\partial }_{t}\left( {u}_{\;;i}^{m}\right)
\]

\[
= {u}_{j;{ik}}{}^{k} - 2{R}_{jlki}{u}^{l}{}_{;}{}^{k} - {R}_{ik}{u}_{j}{}_{;}{}^{k} - {R}_{jk}{u}^{k}{}_{;i}
\]

\[
= {u}_{j;{ik}}{}^{k} + 2{R}_{ikjl}{u}^{l}{}_{;}{}^{k} - {R}_{ik}{u}_{j}{}_{;}{}^{k} - {R}_{kj}{u}^{k}{}_{;i}.
\]

Equivalently, writing \( {v}_{ij} = {u}_{j;i} \) gives

\[
{\partial }_{t}{v}_{ij} = {v}_{{ij};k}{}^{k} + 2{R}_{i}{}_{j}^{k}{}^{l}{v}_{kl} - {R}_{i}{}^{k}{v}_{kj} - {R}^{k}{}_{j}{v}_{ik}.
\]

Then putting \( {L}_{ij} = {v}_{ij} + {v}_{ji} \) gives

\[
{\partial }_{t}{L}_{ij} = {L}_{{ij};k}{}^{k} + 2{R}_{i}{}_{j}^{k}{}^{l}{L}_{kl} - {R}_{i}{}^{k}{L}_{kj} - {R}^{k}{}_{j}{L}_{ik}.
\]

For any \( \lambda  \in  \mathbb{R} \) , we have

(65.8)

\[
\text{ (65.8) }{\partial }_{t}\left( {{e}^{2\lambda t}{L}_{ij}{L}^{ij}}\right)  = {2\lambda }\left( {{e}^{2\lambda t}{L}_{ij}{L}^{ij}}\right)  + {\left( {e}^{2\lambda t}{L}_{ij}{L}^{ij}\right) }_{;k}{}^{k} - 2{e}^{2\lambda t}{L}_{{ij};k}{L}^{{ij};k} + Q\left( {\mathrm{{Rm}},{e}^{\lambda t}L}\right) \text{ , }
\]

where \( Q\left( {\mathrm{{Rm}}, L}\right) \) is an algebraic expression that is linear in the curvature tensor \( \mathrm{{Rm}} \) and quadratic in \( L \) . Putting \( {M}_{ij} = {e}^{\lambda t}{L}_{ij} \) gives

(65.9)

\[
{\partial }_{t}\left( {{M}_{ij}{M}^{ij}}\right)  = {2\lambda }{M}_{ij}{M}^{ij} + {\left( {M}_{ij}{M}^{ij}\right) }_{;k}{}^{k} - 2{M}_{{ij};k}{M}^{{ij};k} + Q\left( {\mathrm{{Rm}}, M}\right) .
\]

Suppose that we have a Ricci flow solution \( g\left( t\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , with \( g\left( 0\right)  = {g}_{0} \) . Let \( u\left( 0\right) \) be a rotational Killing vector field for \( {g}_{0} \) . Let \( {u}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) \) be its restriction to (any) \( {S}^{2} \) , which we will think of as the 2-sphere at spatial infinity. Solve (65.2) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) with \( u\left( t\right) \) bounded at spatial infinity for each \( t \) ; due to the asymptotics coming from Lemma 61.1 (which is independent of the rotational symmetry question), there is no problem in doing so. Arguing as in the proof of Lemma 61.1, one can show that for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , at spatial infinity \( u\left( t\right) \) converges to \( {u}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) \) . Construct \( {M}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) from \( u\left( t\right) \) . As \( u\left( 0\right) \) is a Killing vector field, \( {M}_{ij}\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) . For any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) , at spatial infinity the tensor \( {M}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) converges smoothly to zero. Suppose that \( \lambda \) is sufficiently negative, relative to the \( {L}^{\infty } \) -norm of the sectional curvature on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . We can apply the maximum principle to (65.9) to conclude that \( {M}_{ij}\left( t\right)  = 0 \) for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . Thus \( u\left( t\right) \) is a Killing vector field for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) .

To finish the argument, as Ben Chow pointed out, any Killing vector field \( u \) satisfies

(65.10)

\[
{u}^{m};{}^{k} + {R}^{m}{}_{i}{u}^{i} = 0.
\]

To see this, we use the Killing field equation to write

(65.11)

\[
0 = {u}_{m;k}{}^{k} + {u}_{k;m}{}^{k} = {u}_{m;k}{}^{k} + {u}_{k;m}{}^{k} - {u}_{k;m} = {u}_{m;k} + {u}^{k}{}_{;{mk}} - {u}^{k}{}_{;{km}}
\]

\[
= {u}_{m;k} - {R}^{k}{}_{imk}{u}^{i} = {u}_{m;k} + {R}_{mi}{u}^{i}.
\]

Then from (65.2), \( {u}_{t}^{m} = 0 \) and the Killing vector fields are not changing at all. This implies that \( g\left( t\right) \) is rotationally symmetric for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) .

nodes.content:
## 66. CLAIM 3 OF II.2. UNIQUENESS OF THE STANDARD SOLUTION

In this section, which is not needed for the sequel, we outline an argument for the uniqueness of the standard solution. We do this for the convenience of the reader. Papers on the uniqueness issue are [21, 41]. Our argument is somewhat different than that of [52, Proof of Claim 3 of Section 2], which seems to have some unjustified statements.

In general, suppose that we have two Ricci flow solutions \( \mathcal{M} \equiv  \left( {M, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) and \( \widehat{\mathcal{M}} \equiv \; \left( {M,\widehat{g}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) with bounded curvature on each compact time interval and the same initial condition. We want to show that they coincide. As the set of times for which \( g\left( t\right)  = \widehat{g}\left( t\right) \) is closed, it suffices to show that it is relatively open. Thus it is enough to show that \( g \) and \( \widehat{g} \) agree on \( \lbrack 0, T) \) for some small \( T \) .

We will carry out the Deturck trick in this noncompact setting, using a time-dependent background metric as in [5, Section 2]. The idea is to define a 1-parameter family of metrics \( \{ h\left( t\right) {\} }_{t \in  \lbrack 0, T)} \) by \( h\left( t\right)  = {\phi }^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }g\left( t\right) \) , where \( \{ \phi \left( t\right) {\} }_{t \in  \lbrack 0, T)} \) is a 1-parameter family of diffeomorphisms of \( M \) whose generator is the negative of the time-dependent vector field

(66.1)

\[
{W}^{i}\left( t\right)  = {h}^{jk}\left( {\Gamma {\left( h\right) }_{jk}^{i} - \Gamma {\left( \widehat{g}\right) }_{jk}^{i}}\right) ,
\]

with \( {\phi }_{0} = \) Id. More geometrically, as in [33, Section 6], we consider the solution of the harmonic heat flow equation \( \frac{\partial F}{\partial t} = \bigtriangleup F \) for maps \( F : M \rightarrow  M \) between the manifolds \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) and \( \left( {M,\widehat{g}\left( t\right) }\right) \) , with \( F\left( 0\right)  = \mathrm{{Id}} \) .

We now specialize to the case when \( \left( {M, g\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) and \( \left( {M,\widehat{g}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) come from standard solutions. The technical issue, which we do not address here, is to show that a solution to the harmonic heat flow will exist for some time interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) with uniformly bounded derivatives; see [21]. One is allowed to use the asymptotics of Section 61 here and from Section 65, one can also assume that all of the metrics are rotationally invariant. In the rest of this section we assume the existence of such a solution \( F \) . By further reducing the time interval if necessary, we may assume that \( F\left( t\right) \) is a diffeomorphism of \( M \) for each \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) . Then \( h\left( t\right)  = {F}^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }g\left( t\right) \) . Clearly \( h\left( 0\right)  = g\left( 0\right)  = \widehat{g}\left( 0\right) \) .

By Section 61, \( g \) and \( \widehat{g} \) have the same spatial asymptotics, namely that of the shrinking cylinder. We claim that this is also true for \( h \) . That is, we claim that \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, h\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) converges smoothly to the shrinking cylinder solution on \( \lbrack 0, T) \) . It suffices to show that \( F \) converges smoothly to the identity on \( \lbrack 0, T) \) . Suppose not. Let \( {\left\{  {x}_{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) be a sequence of points in the time-zero slice so that no subsequence of the pointed spacetime maps \( \left( {F,\left( {{x}_{i},0}\right) }\right) \) converges to the identity. Using the derivative bounds, we can extract a subsequence that converges to some \( \widetilde{F} : \lbrack 0, T) \times  \mathbb{R} \times  {S}^{2} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \times  {S}^{2} \) in the pointed smooth topology. However, \( \widetilde{F} \) will satisfy the harmonic heat flow equation from the shrinking cylinder \( \mathbb{R} \times  {S}^{2} \) to itself, with \( \widetilde{F}\left( 0\right) \) being the identity, and will have bounded derivatives. The uniqueness of \( \widetilde{F} \) follows by standard methods. Hence \( \widetilde{F}\left( t\right) \) is the identity for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , which is a contradiction.

By construction, the family of metrics \( \{ h\left( t\right) {\} }_{t \in  \lbrack 0, T)} \) satisfies the equation

(66.2)

\[
\frac{d{h}_{ij}}{dt} =  - 2{R}_{ij}\left( h\right)  + \nabla {\left( h\right) }_{i}{W}_{j} + \nabla {\left( h\right) }_{j}{W}_{i}.
\]

In local coordinates, the right-hand side of (66.2) is a polynomial in \( {h}_{ij},{h}^{ij},{h}_{{ij}, k} \) and \( {h}_{{ij},{kl}} \) . The leading term in (66.2) is

(66.3)

\[
\frac{d{h}_{ij}}{dt} = {h}^{kl}{\partial }_{k}{\partial }_{l}{h}_{ij} + \ldots
\]

A particular solution of (66.2) is \( h\left( t\right)  = \widehat{g}\left( t\right) \) , since if we had \( g = \widehat{g} \) then we would have \( W = 0 \) and \( {\phi }_{t} = \mathrm{{Id}} \) .

Put \( w\left( t\right)  = h\left( t\right)  - \widehat{g}\left( t\right) \) . We claim that \( w \) satisfies an equation of the form

(66.4)

\[
\frac{dw}{dt} =  - \nabla {\left( \widehat{g}\right) }^{ * }\nabla \left( \widehat{g}\right) w + {Pw} + {Qw},
\]

where \( P \) is a first-order operator and \( Q \) is a zeroth-order operator. To obtain the leading derivative terms in (66.4), using (66.3) we write

(66.5)

\[
\frac{d{w}_{ij}}{dt} = {h}^{kl}{\partial }_{k}{\partial }_{l}{h}_{ij} - {\widehat{g}}^{kl}{\partial }_{k}{\partial }_{l}{\widehat{g}}_{ij} + \ldots
\]

\[
= {\widehat{g}}^{kl}{\partial }_{k}{\partial }_{l}{w}_{ij} + \left( {{h}^{kl} - {\widehat{g}}^{kl}}\right) {\partial }_{k}{\partial }_{l}{h}_{ij} + \ldots
\]

\[
= {\widehat{g}}^{kl}{\partial }_{k}{\partial }_{l}{w}_{ij} - {\widehat{g}}^{ka}{w}_{ab}{h}^{bl}{\partial }_{k}{\partial }_{l}{h}_{ij} + \ldots
\]

\[
= {\widehat{g}}^{kl}{\partial }_{k}{\partial }_{l}{w}_{ij} - {\widehat{g}}^{ka}{h}^{bl}{\partial }_{k}{\partial }_{l}{h}_{ij}{w}_{ab} + \ldots
\]

A similar procedure can be carried out for the lower order terms, leading to (66.4). By construction the operators \( P \) and \( Q \) have smooth coefficients which, when expressed in terms of orthonormal frames, will be bounded on \( M \) . In fact, as \( h \) and \( \widehat{g} \) have the same spatial asymptotics, it follows from [5, Proposition 4] that the operator on the right-hand side of (66.4) converges at spatial infinity to the Lichnerowicz Laplacian \( {\bigtriangleup }_{L}\left( \widehat{g}\right) \) .

By assumption, \( w\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) . We now claim that \( w\left( t\right)  = 0 \) for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) . Let \( K \subset  M \) be a codimension-zero compact submanifold-with-boundary. For any \( \lambda  \in  \mathbb{R} \) , we have

(66.6)

\[
{e}^{2\lambda t}\frac{d}{dt}\left( {\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-{2\lambda t}}{\int }_{K}{\left| w\left( t\right) \right| }^{2}{\operatorname{dvol}}_{\widehat{g}\left( t\right) }}\right)  =
\]

\[
{\int }_{K}\left\lbrack  {\left( {-\lambda  - \frac{R}{2}}\right) {\left| w\right| }^{2} + \left\langle  {w,\frac{dw}{dt}}\right\rangle  }\right\rbrack  {\operatorname{dvol}}_{\widehat{g}\left( t\right) } =
\]

\[
{\int }_{K}\left\lbrack  {\left( {-\lambda  - \frac{R}{2}}\right) {\left| w\right| }^{2} - {\left| \nabla \left( \widehat{g}\right) w\right| }^{2} + {w}_{ab}{P}^{abcdi}\nabla {\left( \widehat{g}\right) }_{i}{w}_{cd} + \langle w,{Qw}\rangle }\right\rbrack  {\operatorname{dvol}}_{\widehat{g}\left( t\right) } \pm
\]

\[
{\int }_{\partial K}\left\langle  {w,{\nabla }_{n}w}\right\rangle  {\operatorname{dvol}}_{\partial \widehat{g}\left( t\right) } =
\]

\[
{\int }_{K}\left\lbrack  {\left( {-\lambda  - \frac{R}{2}}\right) {\left| w\right| }^{2} - {\left| \nabla {\left( \widehat{g}\right) }_{i}{w}^{cd} - \frac{1}{2}{P}^{abcdi}{w}_{ab}\right| }^{2} + \frac{1}{4}{\left| {P}^{abcdi}{w}_{ab}\right| }^{2} + \langle w,{Qw}\rangle }\right\rbrack  {\operatorname{dvol}}_{\widehat{g}\left( t\right) } \pm
\]

\[
{\int }_{\partial K}\left\langle  {w,{\nabla }_{n}w}\right\rangle  {\operatorname{dvol}}_{\partial \widehat{g}\left( t\right) }.
\]

Choose

(66.7)

\[
\lambda  > \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{v \neq  0}}\frac{\frac{1}{4}{\left| {P}^{abcdi}{v}_{ab}\right| }^{2}+\langle v,{Qv}\rangle }{\langle v, v\rangle }.
\]

On any subinterval \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack   \subset  \lbrack 0, T) \) , since \( w \) converges to zero at infinity and \( \left( {M,\widehat{g}\left( t\right) }\right) \) is standard at infinity, by choosing \( K \) appropriately we can make \( {\int }_{\partial K}\left\langle  {w,{\nabla }_{n}w}\right\rangle  {\operatorname{dvol}}_{\partial \widehat{g}\left( t\right) } \) small. It follows that there is an exhaustion \( {\left\{  {K}_{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) of \( M \) so that

(66.8)

\[
{e}^{2\lambda t}\frac{d}{dt}\left( {\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-{2\lambda t}}{\int }_{{K}_{i}}{\left| w\left( t\right) \right| }^{2}{\operatorname{dvol}}_{\widehat{g}\left( t\right) }}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{i}
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{T}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) . Then

(66.9)

\[
{\int }_{{K}_{i}}{\left| w\left( t\right) \right| }^{2}{\operatorname{dvol}}_{\widehat{g}\left( t\right) } \leq  \frac{{e}^{2\lambda t} - 1}{\lambda i}
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{T}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) . Taking \( i \rightarrow  \infty \) gives \( w\left( t\right)  = 0 \) .

Thus \( h = \widehat{g} \) . From (66.1), \( W = 0 \) and so \( h = g \) . This shows that if \( \mathcal{M},\widehat{\mathcal{M}} \in  \mathcal{S}T \) then \( \mathcal{M} = \widehat{\mathcal{M}} \)

Definition 67.1. Define a subset \( \Omega \) of \( M \) by

(67.2)

\[
\Omega  = \left\{  {x \in  M : \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \lbrack 0, T)}}\left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  < \infty }\right\}
\]

Suppose that \( x \in  M - \Omega \) , so there is a sequence of times \( \left\{  {t}_{i}\right\} \) in \( \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{i \rightarrow  \infty }}{t}_{i} = T \) and \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{i \rightarrow  \infty }}\left| \operatorname{Rm}\right| \left( {x,{t}_{i}}\right)  = \infty \) . As \( \mathop{\min }\limits_{M}R\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) in nondecreasing in \( t \) , the largest sectional curvature at \( \left( {x,{t}_{i}}\right) \) goes to infinity as \( i \rightarrow  \infty \) . Then by the \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative sectional curvature result of Appendix B, \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{i \rightarrow  \infty }}R\left( {x,{t}_{i}}\right)  = \infty \) . From the time-derivative estimate of (59.5), \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  {T}^{ - }}}R\left( {x, t}\right)  = \infty \) . Thus \( x \in  M - \Omega \) if and only if \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  {T}^{ - }}}R\left( {x, t}\right)  = \infty \) .

nodes.proof: Given \( x \in  \Omega \) , using the time-derivative estimate in (59.6) gives a bound of the form \( \left| {R\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  C \) for \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) . Then using the spatial-derivative estimate in (59.6) gives a number \( \widehat{r} > 0 \) so that so that \( \left| {R\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {2C} \) on \( B\left( {x, t,\widehat{r}}\right) \) , for each \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) . The \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative sectional curvature implies a bound of the form \( \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {C}^{\prime } \) on \( B\left( {x, t,\widehat{r}}\right) \) , for each \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) . nodes.content: Lemma 67.5. If \( \Omega  = \varnothing \) then \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{3},\mathbb{R}{P}^{3},{S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

nodes.proof:
The time-derivative estimate in (59.6) implies that for \( t \) slightly less than \( T \) , we have \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  {r}^{-2} \) for all \( x \in  M \) . Thus at that time, every \( x \in  M \) has a neighborhood that is in an \( \epsilon \) -neck or an \( \epsilon \) -cap, as described in Lemma 59.7. (Recall that we have already excluded the positively-curved case of the lemma.)

As in the proof of Lemma 59.1, by splicing together the projection maps associated with neck regions, one obtains an open subset \( U \subset  M \) and a 2-sphere fibration \( U \rightarrow  N \) where the fibers are nearly totally geodesic, and the complement of \( U \) is contained in a union of \( \epsilon \) -caps. It follows that \( U \) is connected. If there are any \( \epsilon \) -caps then there must be exactly two of them \( {U}_{1},{U}_{2} \) , and they may be chosen to intersect \( U \) in connected open sets \( {V}_{i} = {U}_{i} \cap  U \) which are isotopic to product regions in both \( U \) and in the \( {U}_{i} \) ’s. The caps being diffeomorphic to \( \overline{{B}^{3}} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} - {B}^{3} \) , it follows that \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{3},\mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) if \( U \neq  M \) ; otherwise \( M \) is diffeomorphic to an \( {S}^{2} \) bundle over a circle, and the orientability assumption implies that this bundle is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) .

nodes.content:
An open subset \( R \) of a Riemannian manifold is a good cylinder if:

- It is \( \epsilon \) -close, modulo rescaling, to a segment of a round cylinder of scalar curvature 1.

- The diameter of \( R \) is approximately 100 times its cross-section.

- Every point in \( R \) , lies in an \( \epsilon \) -neck in the ambient Riemannian manifold.

From Lemma 59.7, every \( \epsilon \) -cap neighborhood \( {B}_{x} \) contains a good cylinder lying in the \( \epsilon \) -neck at the end of \( {B}_{x} \) .

nodes.proof:
Put \( {p}_{1} = x \) . Let \( R \) be a good cylinder in the \( \epsilon \) -neck at the end of \( {B}_{{p}_{1}} \) . Now glue on successive good cylinders to \( R \) , as in the proof of the preceding lemma, going away from \( {p}_{1} \) .

Case 1 : Suppose this gluing process can be continued indefinitely. Then taking the union of \( {B}_{{p}_{1}} \) with the good cylinders, we obtain an open subset \( W \) of \( C \) which is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} - \overline{{B}^{3}} \) . We claim that \( W \) is a closed subset of \( \Omega \) . If not then there is a sequence \( {\left\{  {x}_{k}\right\}  }_{k = 1}^{\infty } \subset  W \) converging to some \( {x}_{\infty } \in  \Omega  - W \) . This implies that \( {\left\{  \bar{R}\left( {x}_{k}\right) \right\}  }_{k = 1}^{\infty } \) remains bounded. In view of the overlap condition between successive good cylinders, a subsequence of \( {\left\{  {x}_{k}\right\}  }_{k = 1}^{\infty } \) lies in an infinite number of mutually disjoint good cylinders, whose volumes have a positive lower bound (because of the upper scalar curvature bound at the points \( {x}_{k} \) ). This contradicts Lemma 67.6.

Thus \( W \) is open and closed in \( \Omega \) . Hence \( W = C \) and we are done.

Case 2 : Now suppose that the gluing process cannot be continued beyond some good cylinder \( {R}_{1} \) . Then there must be a point \( {p}_{2} \in  {R}_{1} \) such that \( {B}_{{p}_{2}} \) is an \( \epsilon \) -cap. Also, note that the union \( {W}_{1} \) of \( {B}_{{p}_{1}} \) with the good cylinders is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} - \overline{{B}^{3}} \) , and that \( {R}_{1} \) has compact complement in \( {W}_{1} \) . Let \( \sum  \subset  {R}_{1} \) be a cross-sectional 2-sphere passing through \( {p}_{2} \) .

We first claim that if \( V \) is the compact side of \( \sum \) in \( {W}_{1} \) , then \( V \) coincides with the compact side \( {V}^{\prime } \) of \( \sum \) in \( {B}_{{p}_{2}} \) . To see this, note that \( V \) and \( {V}^{\prime } \) are both connected open sets disjoint from \( \sum \) , with topological frontiers \( \partial V = \partial {V}^{\prime } = \sum \) . Then \( V - {V}^{\prime } = V \cap  \left( {C - \left( {{V}^{\prime } \cup  \sum }\right) }\right) \) and we obtain two open decompositions

(67.12)

\[
V = \left( {V \cap  {V}^{\prime }}\right)  \sqcup  \left( {V - {V}^{\prime }}\right) ,\;{V}^{\prime } = \left( {V \cap  {V}^{\prime }}\right)  \sqcup  \left( {{V}^{\prime } - V}\right) .
\]

If \( V \cap  {V}^{\prime } = \varnothing \) , then \( \bar{V} \cup  \overline{{V}^{\prime }} \) is a union of two compact manifolds with the same boundary \( \sum \) , and disjoint interiors. Hence it is an open and closed subset of the connected component \( C \) , which contradicts Lemma 67.4. Thus \( V \cap  {V}^{\prime } \) is nonempty. By (67.12) and the connectedness of \( V \) and \( {V}^{\prime } \) , we get \( V \subset  {V}^{\prime } \) and \( {V}^{\prime } \subset  V \) , so \( V = {V}^{\prime } \) as claimed.

Next, we claim that if \( {R}_{2} \subset  {B}_{{p}_{2}} \) is a good cylinder with compact complement in \( {B}_{{p}_{2}} \) , then \( {R}_{2} \) is disjoint from \( {W}_{1} \) . To see this, note that \( {R}_{2} \) is disjoint from \( \sum \) because \( {p}_{2} \in  \sum \) and the diameter of \( \sum \) is close to \( \pi {\left( \overline{R}\left( {p}_{2}\right) /6\right) }^{-1/2} \) , whereas by Lemma 59.7 there is an \( \epsilon \) -neck \( U \subset  {B}_{{p}_{2}} \) with compact complement in \( {B}_{{p}_{2}} \) , at distance at least \( {9000}\bar{R}{\left( {p}_{2}\right) }^{-1/2} \) from \( {p}_{2} \) . Thus \( {R}_{2} \) must lie in the noncompact side of \( \sum \) in \( {B}_{{p}_{2}} \) , and hence is disjoint from \( V \) . As the good cylinder \( {R}_{1} \ni  {p}_{2} \) lies within \( B\left( {{p}_{2},{1000}\bar{R}{\left( {p}_{2}\right) }^{-1/2}}\right)  \subset  \Omega \) , it follows that \( {R}_{2} \) is also disjoint from \( {R}_{1} \) , so \( {R}_{2} \) is disjoint from \( {W}_{1} = V \cup  {R}_{1} \subset  {B}_{{p}_{2}} \) .

We continue adding good cylinders to \( {R}_{2} \) as long as we can. If we come to another cap point \( {p}_{3} \) then we jump to its cap \( {B}_{{p}_{3}} \) and continue the process. When so doing, we encounter successive cap points \( {p}_{1},{p}_{2},\ldots \) with associated caps \( {B}_{{p}_{1}} \subset  {B}_{{p}_{2}} \subset  \ldots \) and disjoint good cylinders \( {R}_{1},{R}_{2},\ldots \) . Since the ratio \( \frac{\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{B}_{{p}_{k}}}\bar{R}}{\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{B}_{{p}_{k}}}\bar{R}} \) has an a priori bound by Lemma 59.7, in view of the disjoint good cylinders in \( {B}_{{p}_{k}} \) we get \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {B}_{{p}_{k}}\right)  \geq \) const. \( k\bar{R}{\left( {p}_{1}\right) }^{-3/2} \) . Then

Lemma 67.6 gives an upper bound on \( k \) . Hence we encounter a finite number of cap points. Arguing as in Case 1, we conclude that \( C \) is a capped \( \epsilon \) -horn.

For later use, we now summarize the relevant notation that we introduce. More precise definitions will be given below. We will avoid using new notation as much as possible.

- \( \mathcal{M} \) is a Ricci flow with surgery.

- \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t} \) is the time- \( t \) slice of \( \mathcal{M} \) .

- \( {\mathcal{M}}_{\text{ reg }} \) is the set of regular points of \( \mathcal{M} \) .

- If \( T \) is a singular time then \( {M}_{T}^{ - } \) is the limit of time slices \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t} \) as \( t \rightarrow  {T}^{ - } \) (called \( \Omega \) in II.4.1) and \( {M}_{T}^{ + } \) is the outgoing time slice (for example, the result of performing surgery on \( \Omega ) \) . If \( T \) is a nonsingular time then \( {\mathcal{M}}_{T}^{ - } = {\mathcal{M}}_{T}^{ + } = {\mathcal{M}}_{T} \) .

nodes.content:
Definition 68.1. A Ricci flow with surgery is given by

- A collection of Ricci flows \( {\left\{  \left( {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {t}_{k}^{ - },{t}_{k}^{ + }\right) ,{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \right) \right\}  }_{1 \leq  k \leq  N} \) , where \( N \leq  \infty ,{M}_{k} \) is a compact (possibly empty) manifold, \( {t}_{k}^{ + } = {t}_{k + 1}^{ - } \) for all \( 1 \leq  k < N \) , and the flow \( {g}_{k} \) goes singular at \( {t}_{k}^{ + } \) for each \( k < N \) . We allow \( {t}_{N}^{ + } \) to be \( \infty \) .

- A collection of limits \( {\left\{  \left( {\Omega }_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\right) \right\}  }_{1 \leq  k \leq  N} \) , in the sense of Section 67, at the respective final times \( {t}_{k}^{ + } \) that are singular if \( k < N \) . (Recall that \( {\Omega }_{k} \) is an open subset of \( {M}_{k} \) .)

- A collection of isometric embeddings \( {\left\{  {\psi }_{k} : {X}_{k}^{ + } \rightarrow  {X}_{k + 1}^{ - }\right\}  }_{1 \leq  k < N} \) where \( {X}_{k}^{ + } \subset  {\Omega }_{k} \) and \( {X}_{k + 1}^{ - } \subset  {M}_{k + 1},1 \leq  k < N \) , are compact 3-dimensional submanifolds with boundary. The \( {X}_{k}^{ \pm  } \) ’s are the subsets which survive the transition from one flow to the next, and the \( {\psi }_{k} \) ’s give the identifications between them.

We will say that \( t \) is a singular time if \( t = {t}_{k}^{ + } = {t}_{k + 1}^{ - } \) for some \( 1 \leq  k < N \) , or \( t = {t}_{N}^{ + } \) and the metric goes singular at time \( {t}_{N}^{ + } \) .

nodes.content:
It will be convenient to associate a (non-manifold) spacetime \( \mathcal{M} \) to the Ricci flow with surgery. This is constructed by taking the disjoint union of the smooth manifolds-with-boundary

(68.2)

\[
\left( {{M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k}^{ - },{t}_{k}^{ + }}\right) }\right)  \cup  \left( {{\Omega }_{k} \times  \left\{  {t}_{k}^{ + }\right\}  }\right)  \subset  {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k}^{ - },{t}_{k}^{ + }}\right\rbrack
\]

for \( 1 \leq  k \leq  N \) and making identifications using the \( {\psi }_{k} \) ’s as gluing maps. We denote the quotient space by \( \mathcal{M} \) and the quotient map by \( \pi \) . We will sometimes also use \( \mathcal{M} \) to refer to the whole Ricci flow with surgery structure, rather than just the associated spacetime. The time-t slice \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t} \) of \( \mathcal{M} \) is the image of the time- \( t \) slices of the constituent Ricci flows under the quotient map.

If \( t = {t}_{k}^{ + } \) is a singular time then we put \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ - } = \pi \left( {{\Omega }_{k} \times  \left\{  {t}_{k}^{ + }\right\}  }\right) \) ; if in addition \( t \neq  {t}_{N}^{ + } \) then we put \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } = \pi \left( {{M}_{k + 1} \times  \left\{  {t}_{k + 1}^{ - }\right\}  }\right) \) . If \( t \) is not a singular time then we put \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } = {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ - } = {\mathcal{M}}_{t} \) . We refer to \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) and \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ - } \) as the forward and backward time slices, respectively.

Let us summarize the structure of \( \mathcal{M} \) near a singular time \( t = {t}_{k}^{ + } = {t}_{k + 1}^{ - } \) . The backward time slice \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ - } \) is a copy of \( {\Omega }_{k} \) . The forward time slice \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) is a copy of \( {M}_{k + 1} \) . The time slice \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t} \) is the result of gluing \( {\Omega }_{k} \) and \( {M}_{k + 1} \) using \( {\psi }_{k} \) . Thus it is the disjoint union of \( {\Omega }_{k} - {X}_{k}^{ + } \) , \( {M}_{k + 1} - {X}_{k + 1}^{ - } \) and \( {X}_{k}^{ + } \cong  {X}_{k + 1}^{ - } \) . If \( s > 0 \) is small then in going from \( {M}_{t - s} \) to \( {M}_{t + s} \) , the topological change is that we remove \( {M}_{k} - {X}_{k}^{ + } \) from \( {M}_{k} \) and add \( {M}_{k + 1} - {X}_{k + 1}^{ - } \) .

We let \( {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( t,{t}^{\prime }\right) } = { \cup  }_{\bar{t} \in  \left( {t,{t}^{\prime }}\right) }{\mathcal{M}}_{\bar{t}} \) denote the time slab between \( t \) and \( {t}^{\prime } \) , i.e. the union of the time slices between \( t \) and \( {t}^{\prime } \) . The closed time slab \( {\mathcal{M}}_{\left\lbrack  t,{t}^{\prime }\right\rbrack  } \) is defined to be the closure of \( {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( t,{t}^{\prime }\right) } \) in \( \mathcal{M} \) , so \( {\mathcal{M}}_{\left\lbrack  t,{t}^{\prime }\right\rbrack  } = {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \cup  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( t,{t}^{\prime }\right) } \cup  {\mathcal{M}}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{ - } \) . We (ab)use the notation \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to denote a point \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) lying in the time \( t \) slice \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t} \) , even though \( \mathcal{M} \) may no longer be a product.

The spacetime \( \mathcal{M} \) has three types of points:

1. The 4-manifold points, which include all points at nonsingular times in \( \left( {{t}_{1}^{ - },{t}_{N}^{ + }}\right) \) and all points in \( \pi \left( {\operatorname{Interior}\left( {X}_{k}^{ + }\right)  \times  \left\{  {t}_{k}^{ + }\right\}  }\right) \) (or \( \pi \left( {\operatorname{Interior}\left( {X}_{k}^{ - }\right)  \times  \left\{  {t}_{k}^{ - }\right\}  }\right) \) ) for \( 1 \leq  k < N \) ,

2. The boundary points of \( \mathcal{M} \) , which are the images in \( \mathcal{M} \) of \( {M}_{1} \times  \left\{  {t}_{1}^{ - }\right\}  ,{\Omega }_{N} \times  \left\{  {t}_{N}^{ + }\right\} \) , \( \left( {{\Omega }_{k} - {X}_{k}^{ + }}\right)  \times  \left\{  {t}_{k}^{ + }\right\} \) for \( 1 \leq  k < N \) , and \( \left( {{M}_{k} - {X}_{k}^{ - }}\right)  \times  \left\{  {t}_{k}^{ - }\right\} \) for \( 1 < k \leq  N \) , and 3. The "splitting" points, which are the images in \( \mathcal{M} \) of \( \partial {X}_{k}^{ + } \times  \left\{  {t}_{k}^{ + }\right\} \) for \( 1 \leq  k < N \) .

Here the classification of points is according to the smooth structure, not the topology. In fact, \( \mathcal{M} \) is a topological manifold-with-boundary. We say that \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is regular if it is either a 4-manifold point, or it lies in the initial time slice \( {\mathcal{M}}_{{t}_{1}^{ - }} \) or final time slice \( {\mathcal{M}}_{{t}_{N}^{ + }} \) . Let \( {\mathcal{M}}_{\text{ reg }} \) denote the set of regular points. It has a natural smooth structure since the gluing maps \( {\psi }_{k} \) , being isometries between smooth Riemannian manifolds, are smooth maps.

Note that the Ricci flows on the \( {M}_{k} \) ’s define a Riemannian metric \( g \) on the "horizontal" subbundle of the tangent bundle of \( {\mathcal{M}}_{\text{ reg }} \) . It follows from the definition of the Ricci flow that \( g \) is actually smooth on \( {\mathcal{M}}_{\text{ reg }} \) .

Definition 69.1. (Canonical neighborhoods, cf. Definition in II.4.1) Let \( \epsilon  > 0 \) be small enough so that Lemmas 59.7 and 63.1 hold. Let \( {C}_{1} \) be the maximum of \( {30}{\epsilon }^{-1} \) and the \( {C}_{1}\left( \epsilon \right) \) ’s of Lemmas 59.7 and 63.1. Let \( {C}_{2} \) be the maximum of the \( {C}_{2}\left( \epsilon \right) \) ’s of Lemmas 59.7 and 63.1. Let \( r : \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) be a positive nonincreasing function. A Ricci flow with surgery \( \mathcal{M} \) defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack \) satisfies the \( r \) -canonical neighborhood assumption if every \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ \pm  } \) with scalar curvature \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  r{\left( t\right) }^{-2} \) has a canonical neighborhood in the corresponding (forward/backward) time slice, as in Lemma 59.7. More precisely, there is an \( \widehat{r} \in  \left( {R{\left( x, t\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}},{C}_{1}R{\left( x, t\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) and an open set \( U \subset  {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ \pm  } \) with \( \overline{{B}^{ \pm  }\left( {x, t,\widehat{r}}\right) } \subset  U \subset  {B}^{ \pm  }\left( {x, t,2\widehat{r}}\right) \) that falls into one of the following categories :

(a) \( U \times  \left\lbrack  {t - {\Delta t}, t}\right\rbrack   \subset  \mathcal{M} \) is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck for some \( {\Delta t} > 0 \) . (Note that after parabolic rescaling the scalar curvature at \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) becomes 1, so the scale factor must be \( \approx  R\left( {x, t}\right) \) , which implies that \( {\Delta t} \approx  R{\left( x, t\right) }^{-1} \) .)

(b) \( U \) is an \( \epsilon \) -cap which, after rescaling, is \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding piece of a \( {\kappa }_{0} \) - solution or a time slice of a standard solution (cf. Section 60).

(c) \( U \) is a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{3} \) or \( R{P}^{3} \) .

(d) \( U \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to a closed manifold of constant positive sectional curvature.

Moreover, the scalar curvature in \( U \) lies between \( {C}_{2}^{-1}R\left( {x, t}\right) \) and \( {C}_{2}R\left( {x, t}\right) \) . In cases (a), (b), and (c), the volume of \( U \) is greater than \( {C}_{2}^{-1}R{\left( x, t\right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}} \) . In case (c), the infimal sectional curvature of \( U \) is greater than \( {C}_{2}^{-1}R\left( {x, t}\right) \) .

Finally, we require that

(69.2)

\[
\left| {\nabla R\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  < {\eta R}{\left( x, t\right) }^{\frac{3}{2}},\;\left| {\frac{\partial R}{\partial t}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  < {\eta R}{\left( x, t\right) }^{2},
\]

where \( \eta \) is the constant from (59.5). Here the time dervative \( \frac{\partial R}{\partial t}\left( {x, t}\right) \) should be interpreted as a one-sided derivative when the point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is added or removed during surgery at time \( t \) .

nodes.content: Definition 69.6. A Ricci flow with surgery satisfies the a priori assumptions if it satisfies the \( \Phi \) -pinching and \( r \) -canonical neighborhood assumptions on the time interval of the flow. Note that the a priori assumptions depend on \( \epsilon \) , the function \( r\left( t\right) \) of Definition 69.1 and the function \( \Phi \) of Definition 69.5.

nodes.content:
Lemma 71.1. (cf. Lemma II.4.3)

Given the pinching function \( \Phi \) , a number \( \widehat{T} \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) , a positive nonincreasing function \( r : \left\lbrack  {0,\widehat{T}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) and a number \( \delta  \in  \left( {0,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \) , there is a nonincreasing function \( h : \left\lbrack  {0,\widehat{T}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) with \( 0 < h\left( T\right)  < {\delta }^{2}r\left( T\right) \) so that the following property is satisfied. Let \( \mathcal{M} \) be a Ricci flow with surgery defined on \( \lbrack 0, T) \) , with \( T < \widehat{T} \) , which satisfies the a priori assumptions (Definition 69.6) and which goes singular at time \( T \) . Let \( \left( {\Omega ,\bar{g}}\right) \) denote the time- \( T \) limit, in the sense of Section 67. Put \( \rho  = {\delta r}\left( T\right) \) and

(71.2)

\[
{\Omega }_{\rho } = \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  \Omega  \mid  \bar{R}\left( {x, T}\right)  \leq  {\rho }^{-2}}\right\}  .
\]

Suppose that \( \left( {x, T}\right) \) lies in an \( \epsilon \) -horn \( \mathcal{H} \subset  \Omega \) whose boundary is contained in \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) . Suppose also that \( \bar{R}\left( {x, T}\right)  \geq  {h}^{-2}\left( T\right) \) . Then the parabolic region \( P\left( {x, T,{\delta }^{-1}\bar{R}{\left( x, T\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \bar{R}{\left( x, T\right) }^{-1}}\right) \) is contained in a strong \( \delta \) -neck. (As usual, \( \epsilon \) is a fixed constant that is small enough so that the result holds uniformly with respect to the other variables.)

nodes.proof:
Fix \( \delta  \in  \left( {0,1}\right) \) . Suppose that the claim is not true. Then there is a sequence of Ricci flows with surgery \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\alpha } \) and points \( \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right)  \in  {\mathcal{M}}^{\alpha } \) with \( {T}^{\alpha } < \widehat{T} \) such that

1. \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\alpha } \) satisfies the \( \Phi \) -pinching and \( r \) -canonical neighborhood assumptions,

2. \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\alpha } \) goes singular at time \( {T}^{\alpha } \) ,

3. \( \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right) \) belongs to an \( \epsilon \) -horn \( {\mathcal{H}}^{\alpha } \subset  {\Omega }^{\alpha } \) whose boundary is contained in \( {\Omega }_{\rho }^{\alpha } \) , and

4. \( \bar{R}\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) , but

5. For each \( \alpha , P\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha },{\delta }^{-1}\bar{R}{\left( {x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \bar{R}{\left( {x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-1}}\right) \) is not contained in a strong \( \delta \) -neck.

Recall that when \( \epsilon \) is small enough, any cross-sectional 2-sphere sitting in an \( \epsilon \) -neck \( V \subset  {\mathcal{H}}^{\alpha } \) separates the ends of \( {\mathcal{H}}^{\alpha } \) ; see Section 58. We may find a properly embedded minimizing geodesic \( {\gamma }^{\alpha } \subset  {\mathcal{H}}^{\alpha } \) which joins the two ends of \( {\mathcal{H}}^{\alpha } \) . As \( {\gamma }^{\alpha } \) must intersect a cross-sectional 2-sphere containing \( \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right) \) , it must pass within distance \( \leq  {10}\bar{R}{\left( {x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) of \( \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right) \) , when \( \epsilon \) is small. Let \( {y}^{\alpha } \) be the endpoint of \( {\gamma }^{\alpha } \) contained in \( {\Omega }_{\rho }^{\alpha } \) and let \( {\widehat{y}}^{\alpha } \) be the first point, moving along \( {\gamma }^{\alpha } \) from the noncompact end of \( {\mathcal{H}}^{\alpha } \) toward \( {y}^{\alpha } \) , where \( \bar{R}\left( {{\widehat{y}}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right)  = {\rho }^{-2} \) . As the gradient bound \( \left| {\nabla {\bar{R}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{2}\eta \) is valid along \( {\gamma }^{\alpha } \) starting from \( {\widehat{y}}^{\alpha } \) and going out the noncompact end (since such points on \( {\gamma }^{\alpha } \) have scalar curvature greater than \( \left. {r{\left( {T}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2}}\right) \) , we have \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{T}^{\alpha }}\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{y}^{\alpha }}\right)  \geq  {\operatorname{dist}}_{{T}^{\alpha }}\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{\widehat{y}}^{\alpha }}\right)  \geq  \frac{2}{\eta }\left( {\rho  - \bar{R}{\left( {x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) . Let \( {L}^{\alpha } \) denote the time- \( {T}^{\alpha } \) distance from \( {x}^{\alpha } \) to the other end of \( {\mathcal{H}}^{\alpha } \) . Since \( \bar{R} \) goes to infinity as one exits the end, Lemma 70.2 implies that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha  \rightarrow  \infty }}\bar{R}{\left( {x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}{L}^{\alpha } = \infty \) . From the existence of \( {\gamma }^{\alpha } \) , whose length in either direction from \( {x}^{\alpha } \) is large compared to \( \bar{R}{\left( {x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , it is clear that for large \( \alpha \) , the canonical neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right) \) must be of type (a) or (b) in the terminology of Definition 69.1. By Lemmas 67.9 and 70.2, we also know that for any fixed \( \sigma  < \infty \) , for large \( \alpha \) the ball \( B\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha },\sigma \bar{R}{\left( {x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) has compact closure in the time- \( {T}^{\alpha } \) slice of \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\alpha } \) .

By Lemma 70.2, after rescaling the metric on the time- \( {T}^{\alpha } \) slice by \( \bar{R}\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right) \) we have uniform curvature bounds on distance balls. We also have a uniform lower bound on the injectivity radius at \( \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right) \) of the rescaled solution, in view of its canonical neighborhood. Hence after passing to a subsequence, we may take a pointed smooth complete limit \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{x}^{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) of the time- \( {T}^{\alpha } \) slices, where the derivative bounds needed to take a smooth limit come from the canonical neighborhood assumption. By the \( \Phi \) -pinching assumption, \( {M}^{\infty } \) will have nonnegative curvature.

After passing to a subsequence, we can also assume that the \( {\gamma }^{\alpha } \) ’s converge to a minimizing geodesic \( \gamma \) in \( {M}^{\infty } \) that passes within distance 10 from \( {x}^{\infty } \) . The rescaled length of \( {\gamma }^{\alpha } \) from \( {x}^{\alpha } \) to \( {y}^{\alpha } \) is bounded below by \( \frac{2}{\eta }\left( {\bar{R}{\left( {x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}\rho  - 1}\right) \) , which tends to infinity as \( \alpha  \rightarrow  \infty \) . We have shown that the rescaled length of \( {\gamma }^{\alpha } \) from \( {x}^{\alpha } \) to the other end of \( {\mathcal{H}}^{\alpha } \) also tends to infinity as \( \alpha  \rightarrow  \infty \) . It follows that \( \gamma \) is bi-infinite. Thus by Toponogov’s theorem, \( {M}^{\infty } \) splits off an \( \mathbb{R} \) -factor. Then for large \( \alpha \) , the canonical neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right) \) must be an \( \epsilon \) -neck, and \( {M}^{\infty } = \mathbb{R} \times  {S}^{2} \) for some positively curved metric on \( {S}^{2} \) . In particular, \( {M}^{\infty } \) has scalar curvature uniformly bounded above.

Any point \( \widehat{x} \in  {M}^{\infty } \) is a limit of points \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right)  \in  {\mathcal{M}}^{\alpha } \) . As \( {R}_{\infty }\left( \widehat{x}\right)  > 0 \) and \( R\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right)  \rightarrow \; \infty \) , it follows that \( R\left( {{\widehat{x}}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) . Then for large \( \alpha ,\left( {{\widehat{x}}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right) \) is in a canonical neighborhood which, in view of the \( \mathbb{R} \) -factor in \( {M}^{\infty } \) , must be a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. From the upper bound on the scalar curvature of \( {M}^{\infty } \) , along with the time interval involved in the definition of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck, it follows that we can parabolically rescale the pointed flows \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}^{\alpha },{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right) \) by \( R\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right) \) , shift time and extract a smooth pointed limiting Ricci flow \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}^{\infty },{x}^{\infty },0}\right) \) which is defined on a time interval \( (\xi ,0\rbrack \) , for some \( \xi  < 0 \) .

In view of the strong \( \epsilon \) -necks around the points \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right) \) , if we take \( \xi \) close to zero then we are ensured that the Ricci flow \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}^{\infty },{x}^{\infty },0}\right) \) has positive scalar curvature \( {R}_{\infty } \) . Given \( \left( {\widehat{x}, t}\right)  \in  {\mathcal{M}}^{\infty } \) , as \( {R}_{\infty }\left( {\widehat{x}, t}\right)  > 0 \) and \( R\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) , the \( \Phi \) -pinching implies that the time- \( t \) slice \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{\infty } \) has nonnegative curvature at \( \widehat{x} \) . Thus \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\infty } \) has nonnegative curvature. The time- 0 slice \( {\mathcal{M}}_{0}^{\infty } \) splits off an \( \mathbb{R} \) -factor, which means that the same will be true of all time slices; cf. the proof of Lemma 61.1. Hence \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\infty } \) is a product Ricci flow.

Let \( \xi \) be the minimal negative number so that after parabolically rescaling the pointed flows \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}^{\alpha },{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right) \) by \( R\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right) \) , we can extract a limit Ricci flow \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}^{\infty },\left( {{x}^{\infty },0}\right) ,{g}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) which is the product of \( \mathbb{R} \) with a positively curved Ricci flow on \( {S}^{2} \) , and is defined on the time interval \( (\xi ,0\rbrack \) . We claim that \( \xi  =  - \infty \) . Suppose not, i.e. \( \xi  >  - \infty \) . Given \( \left( {\widehat{x}, t}\right)  \in  {\mathcal{M}}^{\infty } \) , as \( {R}_{\infty }\left( {\widehat{x}, t}\right)  > 0 \) and \( R\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) , it follows that \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is a limit of points \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  \in  {\mathcal{M}}^{\alpha } \) that lie in canonical neighborhoods. In view of the \( \mathbb{R} \) -factor in \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\infty } \) , for large \( \alpha \) these canonical neighborhoods must be strong \( \epsilon \) -necks. This implies in particular that \( \left( {{R}_{\infty }^{-2}\frac{\partial {R}_{\infty }}{\partial t}}\right) \left( {\widehat{x}, t}\right)  > 0 \) , so \( \frac{\partial {R}_{\infty }}{\partial t}\left( {\widehat{x}, t}\right)  > 0 \) . Then there is a uniform upper bound \( Q \) for the scalar curvature on \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\infty } \) . Extending backward from a time- \( \left( {\xi  + \frac{1}{100Q}}\right) \) slice, we can construct a limit Ricci flow that exists on some time interval \( \left( {{\xi }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) with \( {\xi }^{\prime } < \xi \) . As before, using the strong \( \epsilon \) -neck condition and the \( \Phi \) -pinching, if \( {\xi }^{\prime } \) is sufficiently close to \( \xi \) then we are ensured that the Ricci flow on \( \left( {{\xi }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) is the product of \( \mathbb{R} \) with a positively curved Ricci flow on \( {S}^{2} \) . This is a contradiction.

Thus we obtain an ancient solution \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\infty } \) with the property that each point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) lies in a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. Removing the \( \mathbb{R} \) -factor gives an ancient solution on \( {S}^{2} \) . In view of the fact that each time slice is \( \epsilon \) -close to the round \( {S}^{2} \) , up to rescaling, it follows that the ancient solution on \( {S}^{2} \) must be the standard shrinking solution (see Sections 40 and 43). Then \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\infty } \) is the standard shrinking solution on \( \mathbb{R} \times  {S}^{2} \) . Hence for an infinite number of \( \alpha , P\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha },{\delta }^{-1}R{\left( {x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - R{\left( {x}^{\alpha },{T}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-1}}\right) \) is in fact in a strong \( \delta \) -neck, which is a contradiction.

nodes.content: Remark 71.3. If a given \( h \) makes Lemma 71.1 work for a given function \( r \) then one can check that logically, \( h \) also works for any \( {r}^{\prime } \) with \( {r}^{\prime } \geq  r \) . Because of this, we may assume that \( h \) only depends on \( \min r = r\left( T\right) \) and is monotonically nondecreasing as a function of \( r\left( T\right) \) . Similarly, if a given \( h \) makes Lemma 71.1 work for a given value of \( \delta \) then \( h \) also works for any \( {\delta }^{\prime } \) with \( {\delta }^{\prime } \geq  \delta \) . Thus we may assume that \( h \) is monotonically nondecreasing as a function of \( \delta \) .

nodes.content:
Lemma 72.1. Let \( {g}_{cyl} \) denote the round cylindrical metric of scalar curvature 1 on \( \mathbb{R} \times  {S}^{2} \) . Let \( z \) denote the coordinate in the \( \mathbb{R} \) -direction. Given \( A > 0 \) , suppose that \( f : ( - A,0\rbrack  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) is a smooth function such that

- \( {f}^{\left( k\right) }\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) for all \( k \geq  0 \) .

- On \( \left( {-A,0}\right) \) ,

(72.2)

\[
f\left( z\right)  < 0,\;{f}^{\prime }\left( z\right)  > 0,\;{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( z\right)  < 0.
\]

- \( \parallel f{\parallel }_{{C}^{2}} < \epsilon \) .

- For every \( z \in  \left( {-A,0}\right) \) ,

(72.3)

\[
\max \left( {\left| {f\left( z\right) }\right| ,\left| {{f}^{\prime }\left( z\right) }\right| }\right)  \leq  \epsilon \left| {{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( z\right) }\right| .
\]

Then if \( {h}_{0} \) is a smooth metric on \( \left( {-A,0}\right\rbrack   \times  {S}^{2} \) with \( {\begin{Vmatrix}{h}_{0} - {g}_{cyl}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{2}} < \epsilon \) and we set \( {h}_{1} = \; {e}^{{2f}\left( z\right) }{h}_{0} \) , it follows that for all \( p \in  \left( {-A,0}\right)  \times  {S}^{2} \) we have \( {R}_{{h}_{1}}\left( p\right)  > {R}_{{h}_{0}}\left( p\right)  - {f}^{\prime \prime }\left( {z\left( p\right) }\right) \) . Also, if \( {\lambda }_{1}\left( p\right) \) denotes the lowest eigenvalue of the curvature operator at \( p \) then \( {\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{1}}\left( p\right)  > \; {\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{0}}\left( p\right)  - {f}^{\prime \prime }\left( {z\left( p\right) }\right) . \)

nodes.proof:
We will use the variational characterization of \( {\lambda }_{1}\left( p\right) \) :

(72.4)

\[
{\lambda }_{1}\left( p\right)  = \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{\omega  \neq  0}}\frac{{\omega }_{ij}{R}_{kl}^{ij}{\omega }^{kl}}{{\omega }_{ij}{\omega }^{ij}}
\]

where \( \omega  \in  {\Lambda }^{2}\left( {{T}_{p}M}\right) \) . We will also use the following formulas about curvature quantities for conformally related metrics in dimension 3 :

(72.5)

\[
{R}_{{h}_{1}} = {e}^{-{2f}}\left( {{R}_{{h}_{0}} - 4\bigtriangleup f - 2{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right)
\]

and

(72.6)

\[
{R}^{ij}{}_{kl}\left( {h}_{1}\right)  = {e}^{-{2f}}\left( {{R}^{ij}{}_{kl}\left( {h}_{0}\right)  - {\widetilde{f}}^{i}{}_{k}{\delta }^{j}{}_{l} + {\widetilde{f}}^{i}{}_{l}{\delta }^{j}{}_{k} + {\widetilde{f}}^{j}{}_{k}{\delta }^{i}{}_{l} - {\widetilde{f}}^{l}{}_{l}{\delta }^{i}{}_{k} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}\left( {{\delta }^{i}{}_{k}{\delta }^{j}{}_{l} - {\delta }^{i}{}_{l}{\delta }^{j}{}_{k}}\right) }\right) ,
\]

where \( {\widetilde{f}}_{ij} = {f}_{;{ij}} - {f}_{;i}{f}_{;j} \) . That is, \( \widetilde{f} = \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right)  - {df} \otimes  {df} \) . The right-hand sides of these expressions are computed using the metric \( {h}_{0} \) .

To motivate the proof, let us first consider the linearization of these expressions around \( {h}_{0} \) . Keeping only the linear terms in \( f \) gives to leading order,

(72.7)

\[
{R}_{{h}_{1}} \sim  {R}_{{h}_{0}} - {2f}{R}_{{h}_{0}} - 4\bigtriangleup f
\]

and

(72.8)

\[
{R}^{ij}{}_{kl}\left( {h}_{1}\right)  \sim  {R}^{ij}{}_{kl}\left( {h}_{0}\right)  - {2f}{R}^{ij}{}_{kl}\left( {h}_{0}\right)  - {f}_{;}^{i}{}_{k}{\delta }^{j}{}_{l} + {f}_{;}^{i}{}_{l}{\delta }^{j}{}_{k} + {f}_{;}^{j}{}_{k}{\delta }^{i}{}_{l} - {f}_{;}^{j}{}_{l}{\delta }^{i}{}_{k}.
\]

From the assumptions, \( {R}_{{h}_{0}} \sim  1 \) and \( f < 0 \) on \( \left( {-A,0}\right)  \times  {S}^{2} \) . As \( {h}_{0} \) is close to \( {g}_{cul} \) , we have \( \bigtriangleup f \sim  {f}^{\prime \prime }\left( z\right) \) , so \( - {2f}{R}_{{h}_{0}} - 4\bigtriangleup f \geq   - {f}^{\prime \prime }\left( z\right) \) . Similarly, in the case of \( {g}_{cyl} \) a minimizer \( \omega \) in (72.4) is of the form \( \omega  = X \land  {\partial }_{z} \) , where \( X \) is a unit vector in the \( {S}^{2} \) -direction. As \( {h}_{0} \) is close to \( {g}_{cyl} \) , a minimizing \( \omega \) for \( {h}_{0} \) will be close to something of the form \( X \land  {\partial }_{z} \) . Then

(72.9)

\[
{\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{1}} \sim  {\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{0}} - {2f}{\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{0}} - 2{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( z\right)  \geq  {\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{0}} + {2f}\left( z\right) \left| {\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{0}}\right|  - 2{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( z\right) .
\]

As \( {h}_{0} \) is close to \( {g}_{cyl},{\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{0}} \) is close to \( {\lambda }_{1}^{{g}_{cyl}} = 0 \) . Then we can use (72.3) to say that \( {2f}\left( z\right) \left| {\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{0}}\right|  - \; 2{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( z\right)  \geq   - {f}^{\prime \prime }\left( z\right) . \)

The remaining issue is to show that the increase in \( R \) and \( {\lambda }_{1} \) coming from the linear approximation is still approximately valid in the nonlinear case, provided that \( \epsilon \) is sufficiently small. For this, we have to show that the increase from the linear approximation dominates the error terms that we have neglected.

To deal with the scalar curvature first, from (72.5) we have

(72.10)

\[
{R}_{{h}_{1}} = {e}^{-{2f}}\left( {{R}_{{h}_{0}} - 4{\bigtriangleup }_{{g}_{cyl}}f}\right)  + 4{e}^{-{2f}}\left( {{\bigtriangleup }_{{g}_{cyl}}f - \bigtriangleup f}\right)  - 2{e}^{-{2f}}{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
\geq  {R}_{{h}_{0}} - 4{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( z\right)  + 4{e}^{-{2f}}\left( {{\bigtriangleup }_{{g}_{cyl}}f - \bigtriangleup f}\right)  - 2{e}^{-{2f}}{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}.
\]

Next, there is an estimate of the form

(72.11)

\[
\left| {{\bigtriangleup }_{{g}_{cyl}}f - \bigtriangleup f}\right|  \leq  \text{ const. }{\begin{Vmatrix}{h}_{0} - {g}_{cyl}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{2}}\left( {\left| {f\left( z\right) }\right|  + \left| {{f}^{\prime }\left( z\right) }\right|  + \left| {{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( z\right) }\right| }\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \text{ const. }\epsilon \left( {\left| {f\left( z\right) }\right|  + \left| {{f}^{\prime }\left( z\right) }\right|  + \left| {{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( z\right) }\right| }\right) .
\]

As \( {e}^{-{2f}} \leq  {e}^{2\epsilon } \) , if \( \epsilon \) is small then

(72.12)

\[
\left| {{e}^{-{2f}}\left( {{\bigtriangleup }_{{g}_{cyl}}f - \bigtriangleup f}\right) }\right|  \leq  \text{ const. }\epsilon \left( {\left| {f\left( z\right) }\right|  + \left| {{f}^{\prime }\left( z\right) }\right|  + \left| {{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( z\right) }\right| }\right)
\]

Similarly,

(72.13)

\[
{e}^{-{2f}}{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} \leq  \text{ const. }{\left| {f}^{\prime }\left( z\right) \right| }^{2} \leq  \text{ const. }\epsilon \left| {{f}^{\prime }\left( z\right) }\right| .
\]

When combined with (72.3), if \( \epsilon \) is taken sufficiently small then

(72.14)

\[
- 4{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( z\right)  + 4{e}^{-{2f}}\left( {{\bigtriangleup }_{{g}_{cyl}}f - \bigtriangleup f}\right)  - 2{e}^{-{2f}}{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} \geq   - {f}^{\prime \prime }\left( z\right) .
\]

This shows the desired estimate for \( {R}_{{h}_{1}}\left( p\right) \) .

To estimate \( {\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{1}} \) we use (72.4) and (72.6) to write

(72.15)

\[
{\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{1}}\left( p\right)  = {e}^{-{2f}\left( z\right) }\left( {\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{\omega  \neq  0}}\frac{{\omega }_{ij}{R}_{\;{kl}}^{ij}\left( {h}_{0}\right) {\omega }^{kl} - 4{\omega }_{ij}{\widetilde{f}}_{k}^{i}{\omega }^{kj}}{{\omega }_{ij}{\omega }^{ij}} - 2{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}\left( z\right) }\right) .
\]

Comparing with

(72.16)

\[
{\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{0}}\left( p\right)  = \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{\omega  \neq  0}}\frac{{\omega }_{ij}{R}_{ikl}^{ij}\left( {h}_{0}\right) {\omega }^{kl}}{{\omega }_{ij}{\omega }^{ij}}
\]

gives

(72.17)

\[
{\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{0}}\left( p\right)  \leq  {e}^{{2f}\left( z\right) }{\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{1}}\left( p\right)  + \frac{4{\omega }_{ij}{\widetilde{f}}_{k}{\omega }^{kj}}{{\omega }_{ij}{\omega }^{ij}} + 2{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}\left( z\right) ,
\]

where \( \omega \) is a minimizer in (72.15), or

(72.18)

\[
{\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{1}}\left( p\right)  \geq  {e}^{-{2f}\left( z\right) }{\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{0}}\left( p\right)  - 4{e}^{-{2f}\left( z\right) }\frac{{\omega }_{ij}{\widetilde{f}}_{k}{\omega }^{kj}}{{\omega }_{ij}{\omega }^{ij}} - 2{e}^{-{2f}\left( z\right) }{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}\left( z\right) .
\]

Using the variational formula (72.4), one can show that \( \left| {{\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{0}}\left( p\right) }\right|  \leq \) const. \( \epsilon \) . From eigenvalue perturbation theory [55, Chapter 12], \( \omega \) will be of the form \( X \land  {\partial }_{z} + O\left( \epsilon \right) \) for some unit vector \( X \) tangential to \( {S}^{2} \) . Then we get an estimate

(72.19)

\[
{\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{1}}\left( p\right)  \geq  {\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{0}}\left( p\right)  - 2{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( z\right)  - \text{ const. }\epsilon \left( {\left| {f\left( z\right) }\right|  + \left| {{f}^{\prime }\left( z\right) }\right|  + \left| {{f}^{\prime \prime }\left( z\right) }\right| }\right) .
\]

From (72.3), if \( \epsilon \) is taken sufficiently small then \( {\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{1}}\left( p\right)  - {\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{0}}\left( p\right)  \geq   - {f}^{\prime \prime }\left( z\right) \) .

Lemma 72.20. Given \( A > 0 \) , we can choose \( B > A \) and \( F \in  {C}^{\infty }\left( {-B,\infty }\right) \) so that

1. \( F \equiv  0 \) on \( \lbrack 0,\infty ) \times  {S}^{2} \) .

2. The restriction of \( F \) to \( ( - A,0\rbrack  \times  {S}^{2} \) satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma 72.1.

3. The metric \( {e}^{{2F}\left( z\right) }{g}_{cyl} \) on \( \left( {-B,\infty }\right)  \times  {S}^{2} \) has nonnegative sectional curvature and extends smoothly to a metric on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) by adding a ball of constant positive curvature at \( \{  - B\}  \times  {S}^{2} \) .

nodes.proof:
For a metric of the form \( {e}^{{2F}\left( z\right) }{g}_{cyl} \) , one computes that the sectional curvatures are \( - {e}^{-{2F}}{F}^{\prime \prime } \) and \( {e}^{-{2F}}\left( {\frac{1}{2} - {\left( {F}^{\prime }\right) }^{2}}\right) \) . In particular, the conditions for positive sectional curvature are \( {F}^{\prime \prime } < 0 \) and \( \left| {F}^{\prime }\right|  < \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \) .

The 3-sphere of constant sectional curvature \( {k}^{2} \) , with two points removed, has a metric given by

(72.21)

\[
{F}_{k}\left( z\right)  = \log \left( \frac{\sqrt{2}}{k}\right)  + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}z - \log \left( {1 + {e}^{\sqrt{2}z}}\right) .
\]

(Shifting \( z \) gives other metrics of constant curvature \( {k}^{2} \) . We have normalized so that the \( z = 0 \) slice is the slice of maximal area.) Note that the derivative

(72.22)

\[
D\left( z\right)  = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \sqrt{2}\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{2}z}}{1 + {e}^{\sqrt{2}z}}
\]

is independent of \( k \) .

Given \( A > 0 \) , we take \( F \) to be 0 on \( \lbrack 0,\infty ) \) and of the form \( {c}_{1}{e}^{{c}_{2}/z} \) on \( ( - A,0\rbrack \) . We can take the constant \( {c}_{1} > 0 \) sufficiently small and the constant \( {c}_{2} < \infty \) sufficiently large so that the hypotheses of Lemma 72.1 are satisfied. It remains to smoothly cap off \( (\lbrack  - A,\infty ) \times \; {S}^{2},{e}^{{2F}\left( z\right) }{g}_{cyl}) \) with something of positive sectional curvature.

With our given choice of \( {\left. F\right| }_{( - A,0\rbrack } \) , we have \( {F}^{\prime }\left( {-A}\right)  \in  \left( {0,\epsilon }\right) \) . As \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{z \rightarrow   - \infty }}D\left( z\right)  = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \) , we can choose \( B > A \) so that \( D\left( {-B}\right)  > {F}^{\prime }\left( {-A}\right) \) . As \( {F}^{\prime \prime }\left( {-A}\right)  < 0 \) and \( {D}^{\prime }\left( {-B}\right)  < 0 \) , we can extend \( {F}^{\prime } \) to a smooth function \( \widetilde{D} : \left( {-B,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {0,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}\right) \) which has \( {\widetilde{D}}^{\prime } < 0 \) and which coincides with \( D \) on a small interval \( \left( {-B, - B + \delta }\right) \) . Putting

(72.23)

\[
F\left( z\right)  = F\left( 0\right)  + {\int }_{0}^{z}\widetilde{D}\left( w\right) {dw}
\]

we obtain \( F \in  {C}^{\infty }\left( {B,\infty }\right) \) which coincides with \( {F}_{k} \) on \( \left( {-B, - B + \delta }\right) \) , for some \( k > 0 \) . Then we can glue on a round metric ball of constant curvature \( {k}^{2} \) to \( \{  - B\}  \times  {S}^{2} \) , in order to obtain the desired metric.

nodes.content:
Lemma 72.24. There exists \( {\delta }^{\prime } = {\delta }^{\prime }\left( \delta \right) \) with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\delta  \rightarrow  0}}{\delta }^{\prime }\left( \delta \right)  = 0 \) and a constant \( {\delta }_{0} > 0 \) such that the following holds. Suppose that \( \delta  < {\delta }_{0}, x \in  \{ 0\}  \times  {S}^{2} \) and \( {h}_{0} \) is a Riemannian metric on \( \left( {-A,\frac{1}{\delta }}\right)  \times  {S}^{2} \) with \( R\left( x\right)  > 0 \) such that:

- \( {h}_{0} \) satisfies the time-t Hamilton-Ivey pinching condition of Definition B.5.

- \( R\left( x\right) {h}_{0} \) is \( \delta \) -close to \( {g}_{cyl} \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  \frac{1}{\delta }\right\rbrack   + 1} \) -topology.

Then there is a smooth metric \( h \) on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} = {D}^{3} \cup  \left( {\left( {-B,\frac{1}{\delta }}\right)  \times  {S}^{2}}\right) \) such that

- \( h \) satisfies the time-t pinching condition.

- The restriction of \( h \) to \( \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{\delta }}\right)  \times  {S}^{2} \) is \( {h}_{0} \) .

- The restriction of \( R\left( x\right) h \) to \( \left( {-B, - A}\right)  \times  {S}^{2} \) is \( {g}_{0} \) , the initial metric of a standard solution.

- The restriction of \( R\left( x\right) h \) to \( {D}^{3} \) has constant curvature \( {k}^{2} \) .

- \( R\left( x\right) h \) is \( {\delta }^{\prime } \) -close to \( {e}^{2F}{g}_{cyl} \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  \frac{1}{{\delta }^{\prime }}\right\rbrack   + 1} \) -topology on \( \left( {-B,\frac{1}{\delta }}\right)  \times  {S}^{2} \) .

nodes.proof:
Put

(72.25)

\[
{U}_{1} = \left( {-B, - \frac{A}{2}}\right)  \times  {S}^{2},\;{U}_{2} = \left( {-A,\frac{1}{\delta }}\right)  \times  {S}^{2}
\]

and let \( \left\{  {{\alpha }_{1},{\alpha }_{2}}\right\} \) be a \( {C}^{\infty } \) partition of unity subordinate to the open cover \( \left\{  {{U}_{1},{U}_{2}}\right\} \) of \( \left( {-B,\frac{1}{\delta }}\right)  \times  {S}^{2} \) . We set

(72.26)

\[
h = {\alpha }_{1}R{\left( x\right) }^{-1}{g}_{0} + {\alpha }_{2}{e}^{2F}{h}_{0}
\]

on \( \left( {-B,\frac{1}{\delta }}\right)  \times  {S}^{2} \) and cap it off with a 3-ball of constant curvature \( k \) , as in Lemma 72.20.

Given \( {\delta }^{\prime } \) , we claim that if \( \delta \) is sufficiently small then the conclusion of the lemma holds. The only part of the lemma that is not obvious is the pinching condition. Note that on \( \left( {-\frac{A}{2},\frac{1}{\delta }}\right)  \times  {S}^{2} \) the metric \( h \) agrees with \( {e}^{2F}{h}_{0} \) and hence, when \( \delta \) is sufficiently small, the pinching condition will hold on \( \left( {-\frac{A}{2},\frac{1}{\delta }}\right)  \times  {S}^{2} \) by Lemmas 72.1 and B.6. On the other hand, when \( \delta \) is sufficiently small, the restrictions of the metrics \( {g}_{0} = {e}^{2F}{g}_{cyl} \) and \( R\left( x\right) {e}^{2F}{h}_{0} \) to \( \left( {-A, - \frac{A}{2}}\right)  \times  {S}^{2} \) will be very close and will have strictly positive curvature. (The positive curvature for \( {e}^{2F}{h}_{0} \) also follows from Lemma 72.1; if \( \delta \) is small enough then \( {\lambda }_{1}^{{h}_{0}} \) will be close to zero, while \( - {f}^{\prime \prime }\left( z\right) \) is strictly positive for \( z \in  \left( {-A, - \frac{A}{2}}\right) \) .) Thus \( h \) will have positive curvature on \( \left( {-B, - \frac{A}{2}}\right)  \times  {S}^{2} \) and the pinching condition will hold there.

We have now fixed the initial condition \( {g}_{0} \) for a standard solution, along with the procedure to meld \( {g}_{0} \) to an approximate cylinder.

nodes.content:
Definition 73.1. (Ricci flow with cutoff) Suppose that \( a \geq  0 \) and let \( \mathcal{M} \) be a Ricci flow with surgery defined on \( \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack \) that satisfies the a priori assumptions of Definition 69.6. Let \( \delta  : \left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left( {0,{\delta }_{0}}\right) \) be a nonincreasing function, where \( {\delta }_{0} \) is the parameter of Lemma 72.24. Then \( \mathcal{M} \) is a Ricci flow with \( \left( {r,\delta }\right) \) -cutoff if at each singular time \( t \) , the forward time slice \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) is obtained from the backward time slice \( \Omega  = {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ - } \) by applying the following procedure:

A. Discard each component of \( \Omega \) that does not intersect

(73.2)

\[
{\Omega }_{\rho } = \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  \Omega  \mid  R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {\rho }^{-2}}\right\}  ,
\]

where \( \rho  = \delta \left( t\right) r\left( t\right) \) .

B. In each \( \epsilon \) -horn \( {\mathcal{H}}_{ij} \) of each of the remaining components \( {\Omega }_{i} \) , find a point \( \left( {{x}_{ij}, t}\right) \) such that \( R\left( {{x}_{ij}, t}\right)  = {h}^{-2} \) , where \( h = h\left( t\right) \) is as in Lemma 71.1.

C. Find a strong \( \delta \) -neck \( {U}_{ij} \times  \left\lbrack  {t - {h}^{2}, t}\right\rbrack \) containing \( P\left( {{x}_{ij}, t,{\delta }^{-1}R{\left( {x}_{ij}, t\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - R{\left( {x}_{ij}, t\right) }^{-1}}\right) \) ; this is guaranteed to exist by Lemma 71.1.

D. For each \( {ij} \) , let \( {S}_{ij} \subset  {U}_{ij} \) be a cross-sectional 2-sphere containing \( \left( {{x}_{ij}, t}\right) \) . Cut \( \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{i}{\Omega }_{i} \) along the \( {S}_{ij} \) ’s and throw away the tips of the horns \( {\mathcal{H}}_{ij} \) , to obtain a compact manifold-with-boundary \( X \) having a spherical boundary component for each \( {ij} \) .

E. Glue caps onto \( X \) , using Lemma 72.24, to obtain the closed manifold \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) .

For concreteness, we take the parameter \( A \) of Lemma 72.24 to be 10 . The neighborhood of a boundary component of \( X \) is parametrized as \( \left\lbrack  {-A,{\delta }^{-1}}\right)  \times  {S}^{2} \) , with \( {S}_{ij} = \{  - A\}  \times  {S}^{2} \) . The metric on \( \left\lbrack  {0,{\delta }^{-1}}\right)  \times  {S}^{2} \) is unaltered by the surgery procedure. The corresponding region in the new manifold \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) , minus a metric ball of constant curvature, is parametrized by \( \left( {-B,{\delta }^{-1}}\right)  \times  {S}^{2} \) . Put \( {S}_{ij}^{\prime } = \{ 0\}  \times  {S}^{2} \subset  {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ - } \) . We will consider the part added by surgery on \( {\mathcal{H}}_{ij} \) to be the 3-disk in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) bounded by \( {S}_{ij}^{\prime } \) . In terms of Definition 68.1, if \( t = {t}_{k}^{ + } \) then the subset \( {X}_{k}^{ + } \) of \( {\Omega }_{k} = {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ - } \) has boundary \( \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{ij}}{S}_{ij}^{\prime } \) . The added part \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } - {X}_{k + 1}^{ - } \) is a union of 3-balls.
