nodes.proof:
The proof of part (a) is analogous to the proof of Theorem 28.2. The proof of part (b) is analogous to the proof of Lemma 53.3. The proof of part (c) is analogous to the proof of Theorem 53.1. We will be brief on the parts of the proof of Proposition 84.1 that are along the same lines as was done before, and will concentrate on the differences.

For part (a), we first remark that the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing that we want does not follow from the noncollapsing estimate used in the proof of Proposition 77.2, which would give a time-dependent \( \kappa \) . So suppose that \( \left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \in  B\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}, A{r}_{0}}\right) ,\rho  < {r}_{0} \) , the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {x,{t}_{0},\rho , - {\rho }^{2}}\right) \) is unscathed and \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right|  \leq  {\rho }^{-2} \) there. We want to get a lower bound on \( {\rho }^{-3}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {x,{t}_{0},\rho }\right) }\right) \) . We first reduce the case \( \rho  < \frac{r\left( {t}_{0}\right) }{100} \) to the case \( \rho  \geq  \frac{r\left( {t}_{0}\right) }{100} \) .

Suppose that \( \rho  < \frac{r\left( {t}_{0}\right) }{100} \) and let \( s \) be the largest number so that the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {x,{t}_{0}, s, - {s}^{2}}\right) \) is unscathed and \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right|  \leq  {s}^{-2} \) there. Clearly \( s \geq  \rho \) . If \( s < \frac{r\left( {t}_{0}\right) }{100} \) then we obtain a lower bound on \( {\rho }^{-3}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {x,{t}_{0},\rho }\right) }\right) \) as in Sublemma 79.23; a canonical neighborhood of type (d) with small volume cannot occur, in view of condition 3 of Proposition 84.1.

If \( s \geq  \frac{r\left( {t}_{0}\right) }{100} \) and \( \frac{r\left( {t}_{0}\right) }{100} < {r}_{0} \) then once we have proved part (a) of the proposition at scale \( \frac{r\left( {t}_{0}\right) }{100} \) , the Bishop-Gromov inequality will give a lower bound on \( {\rho }^{-3}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {x,{t}_{0},\rho }\right) }\right) \) and prove part (a) of the proposition at scale \( \rho \) .

Suppose that \( s \geq  \frac{r\left( {t}_{0}\right) }{100} \geq  {r}_{0} \) . Let \( D \) be the largest radius so that \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right|  \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) on \( B\left( {x,{t}_{0}, D}\right) \) . Clearly \( D \geq  s \geq  \rho \) . If \( D \geq  \left( {A + 1}\right) {r}_{0} \) then assumption 3 . of the proposition implies that \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {x,{t}_{0},\left( {A + 1}\right) {r}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {A}^{-1}{r}_{0}^{-3}}\right. \) . Since \( \rho  < {r}_{0} \) , the Bishop-Gromov inequality implies a lower bound on \( {\rho }^{-3}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {x,{t}_{0},\rho }\right) }\right) \) .

Finally, if \( D < \left( {A + 1}\right) {r}_{0} \) then there is some \( {x}_{1} \) with \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{1}}\right)  = D \) so that \( \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right|  = \; {r}_{0}^{-2} \geq  {10000}{\left( r\left( {t}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-2} \) . Slightly moving \( {x}_{1} \) inward toward \( x \) , there is a point \( {x}_{2} \in  B\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{0}, D - }\right. \; \left. {{cr}\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) with \( \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{x}_{2},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right|  \geq  {5000}{\left( r\left( {t}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-2} \) , for a universal constant \( c \) ; cf. case (b) of the proof of Sublemma 79.23. If \( \bar{r} \) is small then Hamilton-Ivey pinching implies that \( \left( {{x}_{2},{t}_{0}}\right) \) is in a canonical neighborhood, which gives an estimate

(85.2)

\[
\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {x,{t}_{0}, D}\right) }\right)  \geq  \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{2},{t}_{0},\operatorname{cr}\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) }\right)  \geq  \text{ const. }{\left( r\left( {t}_{0}\right) \right) }^{3} \geq  {10}^{6}\text{ const. }{r}_{0}^{3}.
\]

Since \( \rho  \leq  D \) , the Bishop-Gromov inequality now implies a lower bound on \( {\rho }^{-3}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {x,{t}_{0},\rho }\right) }\right) \) , depending on \( A \) .

This shows that it suffices to consider scales \( \rho \) that are at least \( r\left( {t}_{0}\right) /{100} \) . To continue, we recall the idea of the proof of Theorem 28.2. With the notation of Theorem 28.2, after rescaling so that \( {r}_{0} = {t}_{0} = 1 \) , we had a point \( x \in  B\left( {{x}_{0},1, A}\right) \) around which we wanted to prove noncollapsing. Defining \( l \) using curves starting at \( \left( {x,1}\right) \) , we wanted to find a point \( \left( {y,1/2}\right)  \in  B\left( {{x}_{0},1/2,1/2}\right) \) so that \( l\left( {y,1/2}\right) \) was bounded above by a universal constant. Given such a point, we concatenated a minimizing \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic (from \( \left( {x,1}\right) \) to \( \left( {y,1/2}\right) \) ) with curves emanating backward in time from \( \left( {y,1/2}\right) \) . Then the bounded geometry near \( \left( {y,1/2}\right) \) allowed us to estimate from below the reduced volume at a time slightly less than \( 1/2 \) .

We knew that there was some point \( y \in  M \) so that \( l\left( {y,1/2}\right)  \leq  \frac{3}{2} \) , but the issue in Theorem 28.2 was to find a point \( \left( {y,1/2}\right)  \in  B\left( {{x}_{0},1/2,1/2}\right) \) with \( l\left( {y,1/2}\right) \) bounded above by a universal constant. The idea was to take the proof that some point \( y \in  M \) has \( l\left( {y,1/2}\right)  \leq  \frac{3}{2} \) and localize it near \( {x}_{0} \) . The proof of Theorem 28.2 used the function \( h\left( {y, t}\right)  = \; \phi \left( {d\left( {y, t}\right)  - A\left( {{2t} - 1}\right) }\right) \left( {\bar{L}\left( {y,1 - t}\right)  + 7}\right) \) . Here \( \phi \) was a certain nondecreasing function that is one on \( \left( {-\infty ,1/{20}}\right) \) and infinite on \( \lbrack 1/{10},\infty ) \) , and \( \bar{L}\left( {q,\tau }\right)  = 2\sqrt{\tau }L\left( {q,\tau }\right) \) . Clearly min \( h\left( {\cdot ,1}\right)  \leq  7 \) and \( \min h\left( {\cdot ,1/2}\right) \) is achieved in \( B\left( {{x}_{0},1/2,1/{10}}\right) \) . The equation \( \square h \geq   - \left( {6 + C\left( A\right) }\right) h \) implied that \( \frac{d}{dt}\min h \geq   - \left( {6 + C\left( A\right) }\right) \min h \) , and \( \operatorname{so}\left( {\min h}\right) \left( t\right)  \leq  7{e}^{\left( {6 + C\left( A\right) }\right) \left( {1 - t}\right) } \) .

In the present case, if one knew that the possible contribution of a barely admissible curve to \( h\left( {y, t}\right) \) was greater than \( 7{e}^{\left( {6 + C\left( A\right) }\right) \left( {1 - t}\right) } + \epsilon \) then one could still apply the maximum principle to find a point \( \left( {y,1/2}\right) \) with \( h\left( {y,1/2}\right)  \leq  7{e}^{\left( {6 + C\left( A\right) }\right) /2} \) . For this, it suffices to know that the possible contribution of a barely admissible curve to \( \bar{L}\left( {q,\tau }\right) \) can be bounded below by a sufficiently large number. However, Lemma 79.3 only says that we can make the contribution of a barely admissible curve to \( L \) large (using the lower scalar curvature bound to pass from \( {\mathcal{L}}_{ + } \) to \( \mathcal{L} \) ). Because of the factor \( 2\sqrt{\tau } \) in the definition of \( \bar{L}\left( {q,\tau }\right) \) , we cannot necessarily say that its contribution to \( \bar{L}\left( {q,\tau }\right) \) is large. To salvage the argument, the idea is to redefine \( h \) and redo the proof of Theorem 28.2 in order to get an extra factor of \( \sqrt{\tau } \) in \( \min h \) .

(The use of Lemma 79.3 is similar to what was done in the proof of Proposition 77.2. However, there is a difference in scales. In Proposition 77.2 one was working at a microscopic scale in order to construct the Ricci flow with surgery. The function \( \bar{\delta }\left( t\right) \) in Proposition 77.2 was relevant to this scale. In the present case we are working at the macroscopic scale \( {r}_{0} \sim  \sqrt{{t}_{0}} \) in order to analyze the long-time behavior of the Ricci flow with surgery. The function \( {\delta }_{A}\left( t\right) \) of Proposition 84.1 is relevant to this scale. Thus we will end up further reducing the surgery function \( \bar{\delta }\left( t\right) \) of Proposition 77.2 in order to be able to apply Proposition 84.1.)

By assumption, \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right|  \leq  1 \) at \( t = 0 \) . From Lemma 79.11, \( R \geq   - \frac{3}{2}\frac{1}{t + 1/4} \) . Then for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}/2,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  , \)

(85.3)

\[
R{r}_{0}^{2} \geq   - \frac{3}{2}\frac{{r}_{0}^{2}}{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}/2} \geq   - \frac{3}{2}\frac{{r}_{0}^{2}}{2{r}_{0}^{2} - {r}_{0}^{2}/2} =  - 1.
\]

After rescaling so that \( {r}_{0} = 1 \) , the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) is shifted to \( \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . Then for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2},1}\right\rbrack \) , we certainly have \( R \geq   - 3 \) .

From this, if \( 0 < \tau  \leq  \frac{1}{2} \) then \( \bar{L}\left( {y,\tau }\right)  \geq   - 6\sqrt{\tau }{\int }_{0}^{\tau }\sqrt{v}{dv} =  - 4{\tau }^{2} \) , so \( \widehat{L}\left( {y,\tau }\right)  \equiv \; \bar{L}\left( {y,\tau }\right)  + 2\sqrt{\tau } > 0. \)

Putting

(85.4)

\[
h\left( {y,\tau }\right)  = \phi \left( {{d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0}, y}\right)  - A\left( {{2t} - 1}\right) }\right) \widehat{L}\left( {y,\tau }\right)
\]

and using the fact that \( \frac{d}{dt}\sqrt{\tau } =  - \frac{d}{d\tau }\sqrt{\tau } =  - \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\tau }} \) , the computations of the proof of Theorem 28.2 give

(85.5)

\[
\square h \geq   - \left( {\bar{L} + 2\sqrt{\tau }}\right) C\left( A\right) \phi  - {6\phi } - \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}\phi
\]

\[
=  - C\left( A\right) h - \left( {6 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}}\right) \phi .
\]

Then if \( {h}_{0}\left( \tau \right)  = \min h\left( {\cdot ,\tau }\right) \) , we have

(85.6)

\[
\frac{d}{d\tau }\left( {\log \left( \frac{{h}_{0}\left( \tau \right) }{\sqrt{\tau }}\right) }\right)  = {h}_{0}^{-1}\frac{d{h}_{0}}{d\tau } - \frac{1}{2\tau } \leq  C\left( A\right)  + \left( {6 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}}\right) \frac{\phi }{{h}_{0}} - \frac{1}{2\tau }
\]

\[
= C\left( A\right)  + \left( {6 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}}\right) \frac{1}{\bar{L} + 2\sqrt{\tau }} - \frac{1}{2\tau }
\]

\[
= C\left( A\right)  + \frac{6\sqrt{\tau } + 1}{\sqrt{\tau L} + {2\tau }} - \frac{1}{2\tau }.
\]

As \( \bar{L} \geq   - 4{\tau }^{2} \) ,

(85.7)

\[
\frac{d}{d\tau }\left( {\log \left( \frac{{h}_{0}\left( \tau \right) }{\sqrt{\tau }}\right) }\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)  + \frac{6\sqrt{\tau } + 1}{{2\tau } - 4{\tau }^{2}\sqrt{\tau }} - \frac{1}{2\tau } \leq  C\left( A\right)  + \frac{50}{\sqrt{\tau }}.
\]

As \( \tau  \rightarrow  0 \) , the Euclidean space computation gives \( \bar{L}\left( {q,\tau }\right)  \sim  {\left| q\right| }^{2} \) , so \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\tau  \rightarrow  0}}\frac{{h}_{0}\left( \tau \right) }{\sqrt{\tau }} = 2 \) . Then

(85.8)

\[
{h}_{0}\left( \tau \right)  \leq  2\sqrt{\tau }\exp \left( {C\left( A\right) \tau  + {100}\sqrt{\tau }}\right) .
\]

This estimate has the desired extra factor of \( \sqrt{\tau } \) .

It now suffices to show that for a barely admissible curve \( \gamma \) that hits a surgery region at time \( 1 - \tau \) ,

(85.9)

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\tau }\sqrt{v}\left( {R\left( {\gamma \left( {1 - v}\right) , v}\right)  + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\left( v\right) \right| }^{2}}\right) {dv} \geq  \exp \left( {C\left( A\right) \tau  + {100}\sqrt{\tau }}\right)  + \epsilon ,
\]

where \( 0 < \tau  \leq  \frac{1}{2} \) . Choosing \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) small enough, this follows from Lemma 79.3 along with the lower scalar curvature bound. Then we can apply the maximum principle and follow the proof of Theorem 28.2. In our case the bounded geometry near \( \left( {y,1/2}\right)  \in  B\left( {{x}_{0},1/2,1/2}\right) \) comes from assumptions 2 and 3 of the Proposition. The function \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A} \) is now determined. After reintroducing the scale \( {r}_{0} \) , this proves part (a) of the proposition.

The proof of part (b) is similar to the proofs of Lemma 53.3 and Proposition 77.2. Suppose that for some \( A > 0 \) the claim is not true. Then there is a sequence of Ricci flows \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\alpha } \) which together provide a counterexample. In particular, some point \( \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  \in  B\left( {{x}_{0}^{\alpha },{t}_{0}^{\alpha }, A{r}_{0}^{\alpha }}\right) \) has \( R\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  \geq  {K}_{1}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \) but does not have a canonical neighborhood, where \( {K}_{1}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( \alpha  \rightarrow \; \infty \) . Because of the canonical neighborhood assumption, we must have \( {K}_{1}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \leq  r{\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \) . Then \( 2{K}_{1}^{\alpha } \leq  {K}_{1}^{\alpha }{t}_{0}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \leq  {t}_{0}^{\alpha }r{\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \) . Since \( {K}_{1}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  \infty \) and the function \( t \rightarrow  \operatorname{tr}{\left( t\right) }^{-2} \) is bounded on any finite \( t \) -interval, it follows that \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  \infty \) . Applying point selection to each \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\alpha } \) and removing the superscripts, there are points \( \bar{x} \in  B\left( {{x}_{0},\bar{t},{2A}{r}_{0}}\right) \) with \( \bar{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}/2,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) such that \( \bar{Q} \equiv  R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  \geq  {K}_{1}{r}_{0}^{-2} \) and \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) does not have a canonical neighborhood, but each point \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  \bar{P} \) with \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  4\bar{Q} \) does have a canonical neighborhood, where \( \bar{P} = \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  : {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0}, x}\right)  \leq  {d}_{\bar{t}}\left( {{x}_{0},\bar{x}}\right)  + {K}_{1}^{1/2}{\bar{Q}}^{-1/2}, t \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} - \frac{1}{4}{K}_{1}{\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) . From (a), we have noncollapsing in \( \bar{P} \) . Rescaling by \( {\bar{Q}}^{-1} \) , we have bounded curvature at bounded distances from \( \bar{x} \) ; see Lemma 70.2. Then we can extract a pointed limit \( {X}_{\infty } \) , which we think of as a time zero slice, that will have nonnegative sectional curvature. (The required pinching for the last statement comes from the assumption that \( 2{r}_{0}^{2} < {t}_{0} \) , along with the fact that \( {K}_{1}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  \infty \) .) The fact that points \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  \bar{P} \) with \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  4\bar{Q} \) have a canonical neighborhood implies that regions of large scalar curvature in \( {X}_{\infty } \) have canonical neighborhoods, from which one can deduce as in Section 46 that the sectional curvatures of \( {X}_{\infty } \) are globally bounded above by some \( {Q}_{0} > 0 \) . Then for each \( \bar{A} \) , Lemmas 27.8 and 70.1 imply that for large \( \alpha \) , the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t},\bar{A}{\bar{Q}}^{-1/2}, - \epsilon {\eta }^{-1}{Q}_{0}^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) is contained in \( \bar{P} \) . (Here \( \epsilon \) is a small parameter, which we absorb in the global parameter \( \epsilon \) .) In applying Lemma 27.8 we use the curvature bound near \( {x}_{0} \) coming from the hypothesis of the proposition along with the curvature bound near \( \bar{x} \) just derived; cf. the proof of Lemma 53.3. In addition, we claim that \( P\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t},\bar{A}{\bar{Q}}^{-1/2}, - \epsilon {\eta }^{-1}{Q}_{0}^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) is unscathed. This is proved as in Section 80. Recall that the idea is to show that a surgery in \( P\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t},\bar{A}{\bar{Q}}^{-1/2}, - \epsilon {\eta }^{-1}{Q}_{0}^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) implies that \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) lies in a canonical neighborhood, which contradicts our assumption. In the argument we use the fact that \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  \infty \) implies \( \delta \left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) in order to rule out surgeries; this is the replacement for the condition \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) that was used in Section 80.

We extend \( {X}_{\infty } \) to the maximal backward-time limit and obtain an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, which contradicts the assumption that the points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) did not have canonical neighborhoods. This proves part (b) of the proposition.

To prove part (c), we can rescale \( {t}_{0} \) to 1 and then apply Lemma 70.2; see the end of the proof of Theorem 53.1. The \( \Phi \) -pinching that we use comes from the Hamilton-Ivey estimate of (B.4). We recall that in the proof of Theorem 53.1 we need to get nonnegative curvature in the region \( W \) near the blowup point; this comes from the fact that \( {\bar{r}}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) in the contradiction argument, along with the Hamilton-Ivey pinching.

This proves the proposition.

##### 87.II.7.1. NONCOLLAPSED POINTED LIMITS ARE HYPERBOLIC

In this section we start the analysis of the long-time decomposition into hyperbolic and graph manifold pieces. In the section, \( \mathcal{M} \) will denote a Ricci flow with \( \left( {r,\delta }\right) \) -cutoff whose initial time slice \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{0}, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is compact and has normalized metric.

Lemma 87.4. On any time interval which is free of singular times, and on which \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \leq \) 0 for all \( t \) (which we are assuming), we have

From (B.1), \( \frac{d{R}_{\min }}{dt} \geq  \frac{2}{3}{R}_{\min }^{2} \) . Then

(87.6)

\[
\frac{d\widehat{R}}{dt} = \frac{d{R}_{\min }}{dt}{V}^{\frac{2}{3}} + \frac{2}{3}{R}_{\min }{V}^{-\frac{1}{3}}\frac{dV}{dt} \geq  \frac{2}{3}{R}_{\min }^{2}{V}^{\frac{2}{3}} - \frac{2}{3}{R}_{\min }{V}^{-\frac{1}{3}}{\int }_{M}{RdV},
\]

from which the lemma follows.

nodes.proof:
Suppose that \( \bar{V} > 0 \) . Using Lemma 79.11,(87.9)

\[
\bar{R}{\bar{V}}^{-2/3} = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  \infty }}{R}_{\min }\left( t\right) V{\left( t\right) }^{\frac{2}{3}}{\left( V\left( t\right) {\left( t + \frac{1}{4}\right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\right) }^{-\frac{2}{3}} = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  \infty }}\left( {t + \frac{1}{4}}\right) {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \geq   - \frac{3}{2}.
\]

In particular, there is a limit as \( t \rightarrow  \infty \) of \( \left( {t + \frac{1}{4}}\right) {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) \) . Suppose that

(87.10)

\[
\bar{R}{\bar{V}}^{-2/3} = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  \infty }}\left( {t + \frac{1}{4}}\right) {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  = c >  - \frac{3}{2}.
\]

Combining this with (87.2) gives that for any \( \mu  > 0, V\left( t\right)  \leq \) const. \( {t}^{\mu  - c} \) whenever \( t \) is sufficiently large. Then \( V\left( t\right) {t}^{-3/2} \leq \) const. \( {t}^{-\left( {c + 3/2 - \mu }\right) } \) . Taking \( \mu  = \frac{1}{2}\left( {c + \frac{3}{2}}\right) \) , we contradict the assumption that \( \bar{V} > 0 \) .

nodes.proof:
Suppose first that the flow is surgery-free. Because of the assumed existence of the limit \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{\infty },\left( {\bar{x},1}\right) ,{g}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) , the original solution \( \mathcal{M} \) has \( \bar{V} > 0 \) . We claim that the scalar curvature on \( P\left( {\bar{x},1, r, - {r}^{2}}\right) \) is spatially constant. If not then there are numbers \( c < 0 \) and \( {s}_{0},\mu  > 0 \) so that

(87.12)

\[
{\int }_{B\left( {\bar{x}, s, r}\right) }\left( {{R}_{\min }^{\prime }\left( s\right)  - R\left( {x, s}\right) }\right) {dV} \leq  c
\]

whenever \( s \in  \left( {{s}_{0} - \mu ,{s}_{0} + \mu }\right)  \subset  \left\lbrack  {1 - {r}^{2},1}\right\rbrack \) , where \( {R}_{\min }^{\prime }\left( s\right) \) is the minimum of \( R \) over \( B\left( {\bar{x}, s, r}\right) \) . Then for large \( \alpha \) ,

(87.13)

\[
{\int }_{B\left( {{x}^{\alpha }, s{t}^{\alpha }, r\sqrt{{t}^{\alpha }}}\right) }\left( {{R}_{\min }^{\prime }\left( {s{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  - R\left( {x, s{t}^{\alpha }}\right) }\right) {dV} < \frac{c}{2}\sqrt{{t}^{\alpha }},
\]

where \( {R}_{\min }^{\prime }\left( {s{t}^{\alpha }}\right) \) is now the minimum of \( R \) over \( B\left( {{x}^{\alpha }, s{t}^{\alpha }, r\sqrt{{t}^{\alpha }}}\right) \) . Thus

(87.14)

\[
{\int }_{B\left( {{x}^{\alpha }, s{t}^{\alpha }, r\sqrt{{t}^{\alpha }}}\right) }\left( {{R}_{\min }\left( {s{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  - R\left( {x, s{t}^{\alpha }}\right) }\right) {dV} < \frac{c}{2}\sqrt{{t}^{\alpha }}.
\]

After passing to a subsequence, we can assume that \( \frac{{t}^{\alpha  + 1}}{{t}^{\alpha }} > \frac{{s}_{0} + \mu }{{s}_{0} - \mu } \) for all \( \alpha \) . From (87.5), (87.15)

\[
\bar{R} - \widehat{R}\left( 0\right)  \geq  \frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\widehat{R}\left( t\right) V{\left( t\right) }^{-1}{\int }_{M}\left( {{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  - R\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) {dV}\left( x\right) {dt}
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{2}{3}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }{t}^{\alpha }{\int }_{{s}_{0} - \mu }^{{s}_{0} + \mu }\widehat{R}\left( {s{t}^{\alpha }}\right) V{\left( s{t}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-1}{\int }_{M}\left( {{R}_{\min }\left( {s{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  - R\left( {x, s{t}^{\alpha }}\right) }\right) {dV}\left( x\right) {ds}
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{2}{3}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{\alpha }{t}^{\alpha }{\int }_{{s}_{0} - \mu }^{{s}_{0} + \mu }\widehat{R}\left( {s{t}^{\alpha }}\right) V{\left( s{t}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-1}{\int }_{B\left( {{x}^{\alpha }, s{t}^{\alpha }, r\sqrt{{t}^{\alpha }}}\right) }\left( {{R}_{\min }\left( {s{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  - R\left( {x, s{t}^{\alpha }}\right) }\right) {dV}\left( x\right) {ds}.
\]

Using the definitions of \( \bar{V} \) and \( \bar{R} =  - \frac{3}{2}{\bar{V}}^{\frac{2}{3}} \) , along with (87.14), it follows that the right-hand side of (87.15) is infinite. This contradicts the fact that \( \bar{R} < \infty \) .

Thus \( R \) is spatially constant on \( P\left( {\bar{x},1, r, - {r}^{2}}\right) \) . As \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \sim   - \frac{3}{2t} \) on \( M \) , we know that the scalar curvature \( R \) at \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {\bar{x},1, r, - {r}^{2}}\right) \) , which only depends on \( t \) , satisfies \( R\left( t\right)  \geq   - \frac{3}{2t} \) . It does not immediately follow that the scalar curvature on \( P\left( {\bar{x},1, r, - {r}^{2}}\right) \) equals \( - \frac{3}{2t} \) , as \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) \) is the minimum of the scalar curvature on all of \( M \) . However, if the scalar curvature is not identically \( - \frac{3}{2t} \) on \( P\left( {\bar{x},1, r, - {r}^{2}}\right) \) then again we can find \( c < 0 \) and \( {s}_{0},\mu  > 0 \) so that for large \( \alpha ,\left( {87.14}\right) \) holds for \( s \in  \left( {{s}_{0} - \mu ,{s}_{0} + \mu }\right)  \subset  \left\lbrack  {1 - {r}^{2},1}\right\rbrack \) . Again we get a contradiction using (87.5). Thus \( R\left( t\right)  =  - \frac{3}{2t} \) on \( P\left( {\bar{x},1, r, - {r}^{2}}\right) \) . Then from (B.1), each time-slice of \( P\left( {\bar{x},1, r, - {r}^{2}}\right) \) has an Einstein metric. Thus the sectional curvature on \( P\left( {\bar{x},1, r, - {r}^{2}}\right) \) is \( - \frac{1}{4t} \) .

The argument goes through if one allows surgeries. The main ingredient was the monotonicity formulas, which still hold if there are surgeries. Note that for large \( \alpha \) there are no surgeries in \( P\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }, r\sqrt{{t}^{\alpha }}, - {r}^{2}{t}^{\alpha }}\right) \) by assumption.

Lemma 88.1. (cf. Lemma II.7.2)

(a) Given \( w, r,\xi  > 0 \) one can find \( T = T\left( {w, r,\xi }\right)  < \infty \) such that if the ball \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}, r\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right)  \subset \; {\mathcal{M}}_{{t}_{0}}^{ + } \) at some time \( {t}_{0} \geq  T \) has volume at least \( w{r}^{3}{t}_{0}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and sectional curvatures at least \( - {r}^{-2}{t}_{0}^{-1} \) then the curvature at \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) satisfies

(88.2)

\[
{\left| 2t{R}_{ij}\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0}\right)  + {g}_{ij}\right| }^{2} = \left( {{2t}{R}_{ij}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  + {g}_{ij}}\right) \left( {{2t}{R}^{ij}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  + {g}^{ij}}\right)  < {\xi }^{2}.
\]

(b) Given in addition \( A < \infty \) and allowing \( T \) to depend on \( A \) , we can ensure (88.2) for all points in \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) \) .

(c) The same is true for \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}, A{r}^{2}{t}_{0}}\right) \) .

Note that the time \( T \) will depend on the initial metric.

nodes.proof:
To prove (a), suppose that there is a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{0}^{\alpha },{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\right) \) with \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  \infty \) that provide a counterexample. We wish to apply Corollary 81.3 with the parameter \( {r}_{0} \) of the corollary equal to \( r\sqrt{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }} \) . Putting

(88.3)

\[
\widehat{w} = \left( {\mathop{\min }\limits_{{x \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack  }}\frac{{\int }_{0}^{x}{\sinh }^{2}\left( s\right) {ds}}{{x}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\sinh }^{2}\left( s\right) {ds}}}\right) w,
\]

if \( r > \bar{r}\left( \widehat{w}\right) \) , where \( \bar{r} \) is from Corollary 81.3, then the hypotheses of the lemma will still be satisfied upon replacing \( w \) by \( \widehat{w} \) and \( r \) by \( \bar{r}\left( \widehat{w}\right) \) . Thus after redefining \( w \) , if necessary, we may assume that \( r \leq  \bar{r}\left( w\right) \) . As the function \( {h}_{\max }\left( t\right) \) is nonincreasing, if \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \) is sufficiently large then \( {\theta }^{-1}\left( w\right) {h}_{\max }\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right)  \leq  r\sqrt{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }} \) . Using Corollary 81.3 with a redefinition of \( w \) , we can take a convergent pointed subsequence as \( \alpha  \rightarrow  \infty \) of the \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \) -rescalings, whose limit is defined in an abstract parabolic neighborhood. From Proposition 87.11 the limit will be hyperbolic, which is a contradiction.

For part (b), Corollary 81.3 gives a bound \( R \leq  K{r}_{0}^{-2} \) in the unscathed parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}/4, - \tau {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) \) , where \( {r}_{0} = \min \left( {r,\bar{r}\left( {w}^{\prime }\right) }\right) \sqrt{{t}_{0}} \) . We apply Proposition 84.1 to the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}^{\prime }, - {\left( {r}_{0}^{\prime }\right) }^{2}}\right) \) where \( K{r}_{0}^{-2} = {\left( {r}_{0}^{\prime }\right) }^{-2} \) . By Proposition 84.1(b), each point \( y \in  B\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) \) with scalar curvature at least \( Q = {K}^{\prime }\left( A\right) {r}_{0}^{-2} \) has a canonical neighborhood. Suppose that there is such a point. From part (a) we have \( R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  < 0 \) , so along a geodesic from \( {x}_{0} \) to \( y \) there will be some point \( {x}_{0}^{\prime } \in  B\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) \) with scalar curvature \( Q \) . It also has a canonical neighborhood, necessarily of type (a) or (b). We can apply part (a) to a ball around \( {x}_{0}^{\prime } \) with a radius on the order of \( {\left( {K}^{\prime }\left( A\right) \right) }^{-1/2}{r}_{0} \) , and with a value of \( w \) coming from the canonical neighborhood condition, to get a contradiction for large \( {t}_{0} \) . (Note that \( {\left( {K}^{\prime }\left( A\right) \right) }^{-1/2}{r}_{0} \) is proportionate to \( \sqrt{{t}_{0}} \) .) Thus \( R \leq  {K}^{\prime }\left( A\right) {r}_{0}^{-2} \) on \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) \) . If \( T \) is large enough then the \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature implies that \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right|  \leq  {K}^{\prime }\left( A\right) {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . Then the noncollapsing in Proposition 84.1(a) gives a lower local volume bound. Hence we can apply part (a) of the lemma to appropriate-sized balls in \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{A}{2}r\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) \) . As \( A \) is arbitrary, this proves (b) of the lemma.

For part (c), without loss of generality we can take \( \xi \) small. Suppose that the claim is not true. Then there is a point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) that satisfies the hypotheses of the lemma but for which there is a point \( \left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  \in  P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}, A{r}^{2}{t}_{0}}\right) \) with \( \left| {2{t}_{1}{R}_{ij}\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  + {g}_{ij}}\right|  \geq  \xi \) . Without loss of generality, we can take \( \left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right) \) to be a first such point in \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}, A{r}^{2}{t}_{0}}\right) \) . By part (b), \( {t}_{1} > {t}_{0} \) . Then \( \left| {{2t}{R}_{ij} + {g}_{ij}}\right|  \leq  \xi \) on \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}},{t}_{1} - {t}_{0}}\right) \) . If \( \xi \) is small then this region has negative sectional curvature and there are no surgeries in the region. Using the length distortion estimates of Section 27, we can find \( {r}^{\prime } = {r}^{\prime }\left( {r, A}\right)  > 0 \) so that the sectional curvature is bounded below by \( - {\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{-2}{t}_{1}^{-1} \) on \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{1},{r}^{\prime }\sqrt{{t}_{1}}}\right) \) . Also, by the evolution of volume under Ricci flow, there will be a \( {w}^{\prime } = {w}^{\prime }\left( {r, w,\xi , A}\right) \) so that the volume of \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{1},{r}^{\prime }\sqrt{{t}_{1}}}\right) \) is bounded below by \( {w}^{\prime }{\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{3}{\left( {t}_{1}\right) }^{\frac{3}{2}} \) . Thus for large \( {t}_{0} \) we can apply (b) to \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{1},{A}^{\prime }{r}^{\prime }\sqrt{{t}_{1}}}\right) \) with an appropriate choice of \( {A}^{\prime } \) to obtain a contradiction.

Definition 89.1. For \( x \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) , let \( \rho \left( {x, t}\right) \) be the unique number \( \rho  \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) such that \( \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{{B}^{ + }\left( {x, t,\rho }\right) }}\operatorname{Rm} =  - {\rho }^{-2} \) , if such a \( \rho \) exists, and put \( \rho \left( {x, t}\right)  = \infty \) otherwise.

The function \( \rho \left( {x, t}\right) \) is well-defined because \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) is a compact smooth Riemannian manifold, so for fixed \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) the quantity \( \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{{B}^{ + }\left( {x, t,\rho }\right) }}\operatorname{Rm} \) is a continuous nonincreasing function of \( \rho \) which is negative for sufficiently large \( \rho \) if and only if \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) lies in a connected component with negative sectional curvature somewhere; on the other hand the function \( - {\rho }^{-2} \) is continuous and strictly increasing. We note that when it is finite, the quantity \( \rho \left( {x, t}\right) \) may be larger than the diameter of the component of \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t} \) containing \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) .

As an example, if \( \mathcal{M} \) is the flow on a manifold \( M \) with spatially constant negative curvature then for large \( t,\rho \left( {x, t}\right)  \sim  2\sqrt{t} \) uniformly on \( M \) . The "thin" part of \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t} \) , in the sense of hyperbolic geometry, can then be characterized as the points \( x \) so that \( \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {x, t,\rho \left( {x, t}\right) }\right)  < }\right. \; w{\rho }^{3}\left( {x, t}\right) \) , for an appropriate constant \( w \) .

(89.3)

\[

\]

nodes.proof:
If the lemma is not true then there is a sequence \( \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) \) with \( {t}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  \infty ,\rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) {\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-1/2} \rightarrow \) 0 and vol \( \left( {B\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha },\rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) }\right) }\right)  \geq  w{\rho }^{3}\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) \) . The first step is to apply Corollary 81.3, but we need to know that for large \( \alpha \) we have \( \rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  \geq  {\theta }^{-1}\left( w\right) {h}_{\max }\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) \) , where \( \theta \left( w\right) \) and \( {h}_{\max } \) are from Corollary 81.3. Suppose that this is not the case. Then after passing to a subsequence we have \( \rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  < {\theta }^{-1}\left( w\right) {h}_{\max }\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right)  \leq  r\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) \) for all \( \alpha \) , where we used Remark 86.9 in the last inequality. There are points \( {x}^{\alpha ,\prime } \in  \overline{B\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha },\rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) }\right) } \) with a sectional curvature equal to \( - {\rho }^{-2}\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) \) . Applying the Hamilton-Ivey pinching estimate of (B.4) with \( {X}^{\alpha } = {\rho }^{-2}\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) \) , and using the fact that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha  \rightarrow  \infty }}{t}^{\alpha }{X}^{\alpha } = \infty \) , gives

(89.4)

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha  \rightarrow  \infty }}R\left( {{x}^{\alpha ,\prime },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) {\rho }^{2}\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  = \infty .
\]

We claim that the curvatures at the centers of the balls satisfy

(89.5)

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha  \rightarrow  \infty }}R\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) {\rho }^{2}\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  = \infty .
\]

Suppose not. Then there is some number \( C \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) so that after passing to a subsequence, \( R\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) {\rho }^{2}\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  \leq  C \) for all \( \alpha \) . By continuity and (89.4), after passing to another subsequence we can assume that there is a point \( {x}^{\alpha \prime \prime } \) on a time- \( {t}^{\alpha } \) geodesic segment between \( {x}^{\alpha } \) and \( {x}^{\alpha \prime } \) so that \( R\left( {{x}^{\alpha \prime \prime },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) {\rho }^{2}\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  = {2C} \) , for all \( \alpha \) . We now apply Lemma 70.2 around \( \left( {{x}^{\alpha \prime \prime },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) \) to get a contradiction to (89.4). (More precisely, we apply a version of Lemma 70.2 that applies along geodesics, as in Claim 2 of II.4.2.) In applying Lemma 70.2, we use the fact that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha  \rightarrow  \infty }}{t}^{\alpha }{\rho }^{-2}\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  = \infty \) in order to say that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha  \rightarrow  \infty }}\frac{\Phi \left( {{2C}{\rho }^{-2}\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) }\right) }{{2C}{\rho }^{-2}\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) } = 0 \) , with the notation of Lemma 70.2.

Making a similar argument centered at other points in \( B\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha },\rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) }\right) \) , we deduce that

(89.6)

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha  \rightarrow  \infty }}\left( {\left. \inf R\right| }_{B\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha },\rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) }\right) }\right) {\rho }^{2}\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  = \infty .
\]

In particular, since \( \rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  \leq  r\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) \) , if \( \alpha \) is large then each point \( {y}^{\alpha } \in  B\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha },\rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) }\right) \) is the center of a canonical neighborhood. As \( \alpha  \rightarrow  \infty \) , the intrinsic scales \( R{\left( {y}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-1/2} \) become arbitrarily small compared to \( \rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) \) . However, by Lemma 83.1 there is a subball \( {B}^{\alpha ,\prime } \) of \( B\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha },\rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) }\right) \) with radius \( {\theta }_{0}\left( w\right) \rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) \) so that every subball of \( {B}^{\alpha ,\prime } \) has almost Euclidean volume. This contradicts the existence of a small canonical neighborhood around each point of \( B\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha },\rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) }\right) \) .

We now know that for large \( \alpha ,\rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  \geq  {\theta }^{-1}\left( w\right) {h}_{\max }\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) \) . Thus we can apply Corollary 81.3 to get an unscathed solution on the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha },\rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) /4, - \tau {\rho }^{2}\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) }\right) \) with \( R < {K}_{0}\rho {\left( {x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \) there. Applying Proposition 84.1(c), along with the fact that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha  \rightarrow  \infty }}{t}^{\alpha }{\rho }^{-2}\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  = \infty \) , gives an estimate \( R \leq  {K}_{2}\rho {\left( {x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \) on \( B\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha },\rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) }\right) \) . But then for large \( \alpha \) , the Hamilton-Ivey pinching gives \( \operatorname{Rm} >  - \frac{1}{2}\rho {\left( {x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \) on \( B\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha },\rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) }\right) \) , which is a contradiction.

Proposition 90.1. There exist a number \( {T}_{0} < \infty \) , a nonincreasing function \( \alpha  : \left\lbrack  {{T}_{0},\infty }\right)  \rightarrow \; \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  \infty }}\alpha \left( t\right)  = 0 \) , a (possibly empty) collection \( \left\{  {\left( {{H}_{1},{x}_{1}}\right) ,\ldots ,\left( {{H}_{k},{x}_{k}}\right) }\right\} \) of complete connected pointed finite-volume hyperbolic 3-manifolds and a family of smooth maps

nodes.proof:
If for some \( w > 0 \) we have \( {\Lambda }_{w} = \varnothing \) then \( {M}^{ + }\left( {w, t}\right)  = \varnothing \) for large \( t \) . Thus if \( {\Lambda }_{w} = \varnothing \) for all \( w > 0 \) , we can take the empty collection of pointed hyperbolic manifolds and then 1 and 2 will be satisfied vacuously, and \( \alpha \left( t\right) \) may be chosen so that 3 holds. So we assume that \( {\Lambda }_{w} \neq  \varnothing \) for some \( w > 0 \) .

Since every complete finite-volume hyperbolic 3-manifold has a point with injectivity radius \( \geq  {\mu }_{0} \) , there is a \( {w}_{0} > 0 \) such that the collections \( {\left\{  {\Lambda }_{w}\right\}  }_{w \leq  {w}_{0}} \) contain the same sets of underlying hyperbolic manifolds (although the basepoints have more freedom when \( w \) is small). We let \( {H}_{1} \) be a hyperbolic manifold from this collection with the fewest cusps and we choose a basepoint \( {x}_{1} \in  {H}_{1} \) so that \( \left( {{H}_{1},{x}_{1}}\right)  \in  {\Lambda }_{{w}_{0}} \) . Put \( {w}_{1} = \frac{{w}_{0}}{2} \) . Note that \( {x}_{1} \) lies in the \( {w}_{1} \) -thick part of \( {H}_{1} \) . In what follows we will use the fact that if \( f \) is a \( \epsilon \) -approximation from \( {H}_{1} \) , for sufficiently small \( \epsilon \) , then \( f\left( {x}_{1}\right) \) will lie in the \( {.9}{w}_{0} \) -thick part of the image.

The idea of the first step of the proof is to define a family \( \left\{  {{f}_{0}\left( t\right) }\right\} \) of \( \delta \) -approximations \( \left( {{H}_{1},{x}_{1}}\right)  \rightarrow  {Z}_{t} \) , for all \( t \) sufficiently large, by taking a \( \delta \) -approximation \( \left( {{H}_{1},{x}_{1}}\right)  \rightarrow  {Z}_{t} \) , pushing it along static curves, and arguing using Lemma 90.11 that one can make small adjustments from time to time to keep it a \( \delta \) -approximation. The family \( \left\{  {{f}_{0}\left( t\right) }\right\} \) will not vary continuously with time, but it will have controlled "jumps".

More precisely, pick \( {T}_{0} < \infty \) and let \( {\xi }_{1},\ldots ,{\xi }_{4} > 0 \) be parameters to be specified later. We assume that \( {T}_{0} \) is large enough so that \( {2\beta }\left( {T}_{0}\right)  < {\xi }_{1} \) , where \( \beta \) is from Lemma 90.14. By the definition of \( {\Lambda }_{{w}_{1}} \) , we may pick \( {T}_{0} \) so that there is a point \( \left( {{\bar{x}}_{0},{T}_{0}}\right)  \in  {M}^{ + }\left( {{w}_{1},{T}_{0}}\right)  \subset  {\mathcal{M}}_{{T}_{0}}^{ + } \) and a \( {\xi }_{1} \) -approximation \( {f}_{0}\left( {T}_{0}\right)  : \left( {{H}_{1},{x}_{1}}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{Z}_{{T}_{0}},{\bar{x}}_{0}}\right) \) .

To do the induction step, for a given \( j \geq  0 \) suppose that at time \( {2}^{j}{T}_{0} \) there is a point \( \left( {{\bar{x}}_{j},{2}^{j}{T}_{0}}\right)  \in  {M}^{ + }\left( {{w}_{1},{2}^{j}{T}_{0}}\right)  \subset  {\mathcal{M}}_{{2}^{j}{T}_{0}}^{ + } \) and a \( {\xi }_{1} \) -approximation \( {f}_{0}\left( {{2}^{j}{T}_{0}}\right)  : \left( {{H}_{1},{x}_{1}}\right)  \rightarrow \; \left( {{Z}_{{2}^{j}{T}_{0}},{\bar{x}}_{j}}\right) \) . As mentioned above, if \( {\xi }_{1} \) is small then in fact \( {\bar{x}}_{j} \in  {M}^{ + }\left( {{.9}{w}_{0},{2}^{j}{T}_{0}}\right) \) .

By part 2 of Lemma 90.14, provided that \( {T}_{0} \) is sufficiently large we may define, for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{2}^{j}{T}_{0},{2}^{j + 1}{T}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , a \( 2{\xi }_{1} \) -approximation \( {f}_{0}\left( t\right)  : \left( {{H}_{1},{x}_{1}}\right)  \rightarrow  {Z}_{t} \) by moving \( {f}_{0}\left( {{2}^{j}{T}_{0}}\right) \) along static curves. Provided that \( {\xi }_{1} \) is sufficiently small we will have \( {f}_{0}\left( {{2}^{j + 1}{T}_{0}}\right) \left( {x}_{1}\right)  \in  {M}^{ + }\left( {{w}_{1},{2}^{j + 1}{T}_{0}}\right) \) and then part 1 of Lemma 90.14 says there is some \( \left( {{H}^{\prime },{x}^{\prime }}\right)  \in  {\Lambda }_{{w}_{1}} \) with a \( \beta \left( {{2}^{j + 1}{T}_{0}}\right) \) - approximation \( \phi  : \left( {{H}^{\prime },{x}^{\prime }}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{Z}_{{2}^{j + 1}{T}_{0}},{f}_{0}\left( {{2}^{j + 1}{T}_{0}}\right) \left( {x}_{1}\right) }\right) \) . Provided that \( \beta \left( {{2}^{j + 1}{T}_{0}}\right) \) and \( {\xi }_{1} \) are sufficiently small, the partially defined map \( {\phi }^{-1} \circ  {f}_{0}\left( {{2}^{j + 1}{T}_{0}}\right) \) will define a \( {\xi }_{2} \) -approximation from \( \left( {{H}_{1},{x}_{1}}\right) \) to \( \left( {{H}^{\prime },{x}^{\prime }}\right) \) . Hence provided that \( {\xi }_{2} \) is sufficiently small, by Lemma 90.11 the map will be \( {\xi }_{3} \) -close to an isometry \( \psi  : \left( {{H}_{1},{x}_{1}}\right)  \rightarrow  {H}^{\prime } \) . (In applying Lemma 90.11 we use the fact that \( {H}_{1} \) is also a manifold with the fewest number of cusps in \( {\Lambda }_{{w}_{1}} \) .) Put \( {\phi }_{1} = \phi  \circ  \psi \) . Provided that \( {\xi }_{3} \) is sufficiently small, \( {f}_{0}\left( {{2}^{j + 1}{T}_{0}}\right) \) and \( {\phi }_{1} \) will be \( {\xi }_{4} \) -close as maps from \( \left( {{H}_{1},{x}_{1}}\right) \) to \( {Z}_{{2}^{j + 1}{T}_{0}} \) . Since \( {\phi }_{1} \) is a \( \beta \left( {{2}^{j + 1}{T}_{0}}\right) \) -approximation precomposed with an isometry which shifts basepoints a distance at most \( {\xi }_{3} \) , it will be a \( {2\beta }\left( {{2}^{j + 1}{T}_{0}}\right) \) -approximation provided that \( {\xi }_{3} < 1 \) and \( \beta \left( {{2}^{j + 1}{T}_{0}}\right)  < \frac{1}{2} \) . We now redefine \( {f}_{0}\left( {{2}^{j + 1}{T}_{0}}\right) \) to be \( {\phi }_{1} \) and let \( {\bar{x}}_{j + 1} \) be the image of \( {x}_{1} \) under \( {\phi }_{1} \) . This completes the induction step.

In this way we define a family of partially defined maps \( {\left\{  {f}_{0}\left( t\right)  : \left( {H}_{1},{x}_{1}\right)  \rightarrow  {Z}_{t}\right\}  }_{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{T}_{0},\infty }\right) } \) . From the construction, \( {f}_{0}\left( {{2}^{j}{T}_{0}}\right) \) is a \( {2\beta }\left( {{2}^{j}{T}_{0}}\right) \) -approximation for all \( j \geq  0 \) . Lemma 90.14 then implies that there is a function \( {\alpha }_{1} : \left\lbrack  {{T}_{0},\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) decreasing to zero at infinity such that for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{T}_{0},\infty }\right) ,{f}_{0}\left( t\right) \) is an \( {\alpha }_{1}\left( t\right) \) -approximation, and for every \( \bar{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {t,{2t}}\right\rbrack \) we may slide \( {f}_{0}\left( t\right) \) along static curves to define an \( {\alpha }_{1}\left( t\right) \) -approximation \( h\left( \bar{t}\right)  : \left( {{H}_{1},{x}_{1}}\right)  \rightarrow  {Z}_{t} \) which is \( {\alpha }_{1}\left( t\right) \) -close to \( {f}_{0}\left( \bar{t}\right) \) .

One may now employ a standard smoothing argument to convert the family \( {\left\{  {f}_{0}\left( t\right) \right\}  }_{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{T}_{0},\infty }\right) } \) into a family \( {\left\{  {f}_{1}\left( t\right) \right\}  }_{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{T}_{0},\infty }\right) } \) which satisfies the first two conditions of the proposition. If condition 3 fails to hold then we redefine the \( {\Lambda }_{w} \) ’s by considering limits of only those \( {\left\{  \left( {\mathcal{M}}_{{t}_{i}}^{ + },\left( {x}_{i},{t}_{i}\right) ,{t}_{i}^{-1}g\left( {t}_{i}\right) \right) \right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) with \( {t}_{i} \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( {x}_{i} \in  {M}^{ + }\left( {w,{t}_{i}}\right)  \subset  {\mathcal{M}}_{{t}_{i}}^{ + } \) not in the image of \( {f}_{1}\left( {t}_{i}\right) \) . Repeating the construction we obtain a pointed hyperbolic manifold \( \left( {{H}_{2},{x}_{2}}\right) \) and a family \( \left\{  {{f}_{2}\left( t\right) }\right\} \) defined for large \( t \) satisfying conditions 1 and 2, where \( \operatorname{im}\left( {{f}_{2}\left( t\right) }\right) \) is disjoint from \( \operatorname{im}\left( {{f}_{1}\left( t\right) }\right) \) for large \( t \) . Iteration of this procedure must stop after \( k \) steps for some finite number \( k \) , in view of the fact that \( \bar{V} < \infty \) and the fact that there is a positive lower bound on the volumes of complete hyperbolic 3-manifolds. We get the desired family \( \{ f\left( t\right) \} \) by taking the union of the maps \( {f}_{1}\left( t\right) ,\ldots ,{f}_{k}\left( t\right) \) .

nodes.content: Remark 90.5. The analogous statement in [52, Section 7.3] is in terms of a fixed \( w \) . That is, for a given \( w \) one considers pointed limits of \( {\left\{  \left( {\mathcal{M}}_{{t}_{j}}^{ + },\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}\right) ,{t}_{j}^{-1}g\left( {t}_{j}\right) \right) \right\}  }_{j = 1}^{\infty } \) with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}{t}_{j} = \infty \) and the basepoint satisfying \( {x}_{j} \in  {M}^{ + }\left( {w,{t}_{j}}\right)  \subset  {\mathcal{M}}_{{t}_{j}}^{ + } \) for all \( j \) . Considering the possible limit spaces in a certain order, as described below, one extracts complete pointed finite-volume hyperbolic manifolds \( {\left\{  \left( {H}_{i},{x}_{i}\right) \right\}  }_{i = 1}^{k} \) with \( {x}_{i} \) in the \( w \) -thick part of \( {H}_{i} \) . There is a number \( {w}_{0} > 0 \) so that as long as \( w \leq  {w}_{0} \) , the hyperbolic manifolds \( {H}_{i} \) are independent of \( w \) . For any \( {w}^{\prime } > 0 \) , as time goes on the \( {w}^{\prime } \) -thick part of \( \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}{H}_{i} \) better approximates \( {M}^{ + }\left( {{w}^{\prime }, t}\right) \) . Hence the formulation of Proposition 90.1 is equivalent to that of [52, Section 7.3].

nodes.content:
Definition 90.6. If \( \left( {X, x}\right) \) and \( \left( {Y, y}\right) \) are pointed smooth Riemannian manifolds and \( \epsilon  > 0 \) then \( \left( {X, x}\right) \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to \( \left( {Y, y}\right) \) if there is a pointed map \( f : \left( {X, x}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {Y, y}\right) \) such that

(90.7)

\[
{\left. f\right| }_{\overline{B\left( {x,{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) }} : \overline{B\left( {x,{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) } \rightarrow  Y
\]

is a diffeomorphism onto its image and

(90.8)

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{f}^{ * }{g}_{Y} - {g}_{X}\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{{\epsilon }^{-1}}} < \epsilon
\]

where the norm is taken on \( \overline{B\left( {x,{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) } \) . Note that nothing is required of \( f \) on the complement of \( \overline{B\left( {x,{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) } \) . Such a map \( f \) is called an \( \epsilon \) -approximation.

We will sometimes refer to a partially defined map \( f : \left( {X, x}\right)  \supset  \left( {W, x}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {Y, y}\right) \) as an \( \epsilon \) -approximation provided that \( W \) contains \( \overline{B\left( {x,{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) } \) and the conditions above are satisfied. By convention we will permit \( X \) and \( Y \) to be disconnnected, in which case \( \epsilon \) -closeness only says something about the components containing the basepoints. We say that two maps \( {f}_{1},{f}_{2} : \left( {X, x}\right)  \rightarrow  Y \) (not necessarily basepoint-preserving) are \( \epsilon \) -close if

(90.9)

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{p \in  \overline{B\left( {x,{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) }}}{d}_{Y}\left( {{f}_{1}\left( p\right) ,{f}_{2}\left( p\right) }\right)  < \epsilon .
\]

nodes.content: Lemma 90.11. Let \( \left( {X, x}\right) \) be a pointed complete connected finite-volume hyperbolic 3- manifold. Then for each \( \zeta  > 0 \) there exists \( \xi  > 0 \) such that if \( {X}^{\prime } \) is a complete finite-volume hyperbolic manifold with at least as many cusps as \( X \) , and \( f : \left( {X, x}\right)  \rightarrow  {X}^{\prime } \) is a \( \xi \) -approximation, then there is an isometry \( \widehat{f} : \left( {X, x}\right)  \rightarrow  {X}^{\prime } \) which is \( \zeta \) -close to \( f \) .

nodes.proof:
The main step is to show that for the fixed \( \left( {X, x}\right) \) , if \( \xi \) is sufficiently small then for any \( \xi \) -approximation \( f : \left( {X, x}\right)  \rightarrow  {X}^{\prime } \) satisfying the hypotheses of the lemma, the manifolds \( X \) and \( {X}^{\prime } \) are diffeomorphic. The proof of this will use the Margulis thick-thin decomposition. The rest of the assertion then follows readily from Mostow-Prasad rigidity [47, 54].

Pick \( {\mu }_{1} \in  \left( {0,{\mu }_{0}}\right) \) so that \( X - {X}_{{\mu }_{1}} \) consists only of cusps \( {U}_{1},\ldots ,{U}_{k} \) . The thick part \( {X}_{{\mu }_{1}} \) is compact and connected. Given \( \xi  > 0 \) , let \( f : \left( {B\left( {x,{\xi }^{-1}}\right) , x}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{X}^{\prime },{x}^{\prime }}\right) \) be a \( \xi \) -approximation as in (90.8). The intuitive idea is that because of the compactness of \( {X}_{{\mu }_{1}} \) , if \( \xi \) is sufficiently small then \( {\left. f\right| }_{{X}_{{\mu }_{1}}} \) is close to being an isometry from \( {X}_{{\mu }_{1}} \) to its image. Then \( f\left( {X}_{{\mu }_{1}}\right) \) is close to a connected component of the thick part \( {X}_{{\mu }_{1}}^{\prime } \) of \( {X}^{\prime } \) . As \( f\left( {X}_{{\mu }_{1}}\right) \) and \( {X}_{{\mu }_{1}}^{\prime } \) are connected, this means that \( f\left( {X}_{{\mu }_{1}}\right) \) is close to \( {X}_{{\mu }_{1}}^{\prime } \) . We will show that in fact \( {X}_{{\mu }_{1}} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {X}_{{\mu }_{1}}^{\prime } \) . The boundary components of \( {X}_{{\mu }_{1}} \) correspond to the cusps of \( X \) and the boundary components of \( {X}_{{\mu }_{1}}^{\prime } \) correspond to the connected components of \( {X}^{\prime } - {X}_{{\mu }_{1}}^{\prime } \) . As \( {X}^{\prime } \) has at least as many cusps as \( X \) by assumption, it follows that the connected components of \( {X}^{\prime } - {X}_{{\mu }_{1}}^{\prime } \) are all cusps. Hence \( X \) and \( {X}^{\prime } \) are diffeomorphic.

In order to show that \( {X}_{{\mu }_{1}} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {X}_{{\mu }_{1}}^{\prime } \) , we will take a larger region \( W \supset  {X}_{{\mu }_{1}} \) that is diffeomorphic to \( {X}_{{\mu }_{1}} \) and show that \( f\left( W\right) \) can be isotoped to \( {X}_{{\mu }_{1}}^{\prime } \) by sliding it inward along the radial direction. More precisely, in each cusp \( {U}_{i} \) put \( {V}_{i} = {\rho }_{i}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {-{3L}, - L}\right\rbrack  \right) \) , where \( L \gg  1 \) is large enough that every cuspidal torus \( {\rho }_{i}^{-1}\left( s\right) \) with \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {-{3L}, - L}\right\rbrack \) has diameter much less than one. Let \( W \subset  X \) be the complement of the open horoballs at height \( - {2L} \) , i.e.

(90.12)

\[
W = X - \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}{\rho }_{i}^{-1}\left( {-\infty , - {2L}}\right) .
\]

When \( \xi \) is sufficiently small, \( f \) will preserve injectivity radius to within a factor close to 1 for points \( p \in  B\left( {x,{\xi }^{-1}}\right) \) with \( d\left( {p,\partial B\left( {x,{\xi }^{-1}}\right) }\right)  > 2\operatorname{InjRad}\left( {X, p}\right) \) . Therefore when \( \xi \) is small, \( f \) will map each \( {V}_{i} \) into \( {X}^{\prime } - {X}_{{\mu }_{1}}^{\prime } \) , and hence into one of the connected components \( {U}_{{k}_{i}}^{\prime } \) of \( {X}^{\prime } - {X}_{{\mu }_{1}}^{\prime } \) . Let \( {Z}_{i}^{\prime } \) be the image of \( {Z}_{i} = {\rho }_{i}^{-1}\left( {-{2L}}\right) \) under \( f \) . Note that \( d\left( {\operatorname{core}\left( {U}_{{k}_{i}}^{\prime }\right) ,{Z}_{i}^{\prime }}\right)  \gtrsim  L \) (if \( \operatorname{core}\left( {U}_{{k}_{i}}^{\prime }\right)  \neq  \varnothing \) ), for otherwise \( {f}^{-1}\left( {\operatorname{core}\left( {U}_{{k}_{i}}^{\prime }\right) }\right) \) would be a closed curve with small diameter and curvature lying in \( {U}_{i} \) , which contradicts the fact that the horospheres have principal curvatures \( - \frac{1}{2} \) (because of our normalization that the sectional curvatures are \( - \frac{1}{4} \) ). Thus for each point \( {z}^{\prime } \in  {Z}_{i}^{\prime } \) there is a minimizing radial geodesic segment \( {\gamma }^{\prime } \) passing through \( {z}^{\prime } \) with \( d\left( {{z}^{\prime },\partial {\gamma }^{\prime }}\right)  \gtrsim  L \) . The preimage of \( {\gamma }^{\prime } \) under \( f \) is a curve \( \gamma  \subset  X \) with small curvature and length \( \gtrsim  L \) passing through \( {Z}_{i} \) . This forces the direction of \( \gamma \) to be nearly radial and so transverse to \( {Z}_{i} \) . Hence \( {Z}_{i}^{\prime } \) is transverse to the radial direction in \( {U}_{{k}_{i}}^{\prime } \) . Combining this with the fact that \( {Z}_{i}^{\prime } \) is embedded implies that \( {Z}_{i}^{\prime } \) is isotopic in \( \overline{{U}_{{k}_{i}}^{\prime }} \) to \( \partial {U}_{{k}_{i}}^{\prime } \) . It follows that \( f\left( W\right) \) is isotopic to \( {X}_{{\mu }_{1}}^{\prime } \) . Then by the preceding argument involving counting the number of cusps, \( X \) and \( {X}^{\prime } \) are diffeomorphic. We apply Mostow-Prasad rigidity \( \left\lbrack  {{47},{54}}\right\rbrack \) to deduce that \( X \) is isometric to \( {X}^{\prime } \) .

We now claim that for any \( \zeta  > 0 \) , if \( \xi \) is sufficiently small then the map \( f \) is \( \zeta \) -close to an isometry from \( X \) to \( {X}^{\prime } \) . Suppose not. Then there are a number \( \zeta  > 0 \) and a sequence of \( \frac{1}{i} \) -approximations \( {f}_{i} : \left( {X, x}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{X}_{i}^{\prime },{x}_{i}^{\prime }}\right) \) so that none of the \( {f}_{i} \) ’s are \( \zeta \) -close to any isometry from \( \left( {X, x}\right) \) to \( \left( {{X}_{i}^{\prime },{x}_{i}^{\prime }}\right) \) . Taking a convergent subsequence of the maps \( {f}_{i} \) gives a limit isometry \( {f}_{\infty } : \left( {X, x}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{X}_{\infty }^{\prime },{x}_{\infty }^{\prime }}\right) \) . From what has already been proven, for large \( i \) we know that \( {X}_{i}^{\prime } \) is isometric to \( X \) , and so isometric to \( {X}_{\infty }^{\prime } \) . This is a contradiction.

Lemma 90.14. Given \( w > 0 \) , there is a decreasing function \( \beta  : \lbrack 0,\infty ) \rightarrow  (0,\infty \rbrack \) with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{s \rightarrow  \infty }}\beta \left( s\right)  = 0 \) such that if \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {M}^{ + }\left( {w, t}\right)  \subset  {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) , and \( {Z}_{t} \) denotes the forward time slice \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) rescaled by \( {t}^{-1} \) , then

2. \( B\left( {x, t,\beta {\left( t\right) }^{-1}\sqrt{t}}\right)  \subset  {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) is unscathed on the interval \( \left\lbrack  {t,{2t}}\right\rbrack \) and if \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {t,{2t}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathcal{M} \) is a static curve starting at \( \left( {x, t}\right) ,\bar{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {t,{2t}}\right\rbrack \) , then the map

\]

defined by following static curves induces a map

\]

satisfying

(90.17)

\[

\]

Proposition 91.2. The homomorphism

The homomorphism (91.3) \[ {\pi }_{1}\left( {f\left( t\right) }\right) : {\pi }_{1}\left( {Z, \star }\right) \rightarrow {\pi }_{1}\left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + }, f\left( t\right) \left( \star \right) }\right) \] is a monomorphism for all \( t \geq {T}_{a} \) .

nodes.proof:
Pick \( D < {2\pi } \) . Let \( a < {a}_{0} \) and \( {T}_{a}^{\prime } \) be as in Lemma 91.12.

By Lemma 91.12, \( A \) is bounded on compact subsets of \( \left\lbrack  {{T}_{a}^{\prime },\infty }\right) \) . By Lemma 91.10, for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{T}_{a}^{\prime },\infty }\right) \) we can find a compact set \( {K}_{t} \subset  {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) so that for all \( {t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{T}_{a}^{\prime },\infty }\right) \) sufficiently close to \( t \) , the compressing disk \( {N}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) lies in \( {K}_{t} \) . If \( \left( {{K}_{t}, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) and \( \left( {{K}_{t}, g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) }\right) \) are \( {e}^{\sigma } \) -biLipschitz equivalent then \( A\left( t\right)  \leq  {e}^{2\sigma }\operatorname{area}\left( {N}_{{t}^{\prime }}\right)  = {e}^{2\sigma }A\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) and \( A\left( {t}^{\prime }\right)  \leq  {e}^{2\sigma }\operatorname{area}\left( {N}_{t}\right)  = {e}^{2\sigma }A\left( t\right) \) . It follows that \( A \) is continuous on \( \left\lbrack  {{T}_{a}^{\prime },\infty }\right) \) .

For \( t \geq  {T}_{a}^{\prime } \) , put

(91.24)

\[
F\left( t\right)  = {\left( t + \frac{1}{4}\right) }^{-\frac{3}{4}}A\left( t\right)  + 4\left( {{2\pi } - D}\right) {\left( t + \frac{1}{4}\right) }^{\frac{1}{4}}.
\]

We claim that \( F\left( t\right)  \leq  F\left( {T}_{a}^{\prime }\right) \) for all \( t \geq  {T}_{a}^{\prime } \) . Suppose not. Put \( {t}_{0} = \inf \left\{  {t \geq  {T}_{a}^{\prime } : F\left( t\right)  > }\right. \; \left. {F\left( {T}_{a}^{\prime }\right) }\right\} \) . By continuity, \( F\left( {t}_{0}\right)  = F\left( {T}_{a}^{\prime }\right) \) . Consider the function \( \bar{A} \) of Lemma 91.12. Put

(91.25)

\[
\bar{F}\left( t\right)  = {\left( t + \frac{1}{4}\right) }^{-\frac{3}{4}}\bar{A}\left( t\right)  + 4\left( {{2\pi } - D}\right) {\left( t + \frac{1}{4}\right) }^{\frac{1}{4}}.
\]

Then \( \bar{F}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  = F\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) and in a small interval around \( {t}_{0} \) , we have \( \bar{F} \geq  F \) . However,(91.13) implies that \( {\bar{F}}^{\prime }\left( {t}_{0}\right)  < 0 \) . There is some \( \sigma  > 0 \) so that for \( t \in  \left( {{t}_{0},{t}_{0} + \sigma }\right) \) , we have

(91.26)

\[
F\left( t\right)  \leq  \bar{F}\left( t\right)  \leq  \bar{F}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  + \frac{1}{2}{\bar{F}}^{\prime }\left( {t}_{0}\right) \left( {t - {t}_{0}}\right)  < \bar{F}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  = F\left( {t}_{0}\right)  = F\left( {T}_{a}^{\prime }\right) ,
\]

which contradicts the definition of \( {t}_{0} \) .

Thus if \( t \geq  {T}_{a}^{\prime } \) then \( F\left( t\right)  \leq  F\left( {T}_{a}^{\prime }\right) \) . This implies that \( A\left( t\right) \) is negative for large \( t \) , which contradicts the fact that an area is nonnegative.

We have shown that the homomorphism (91.3) is injective if \( t \) is sufficiently large. In view of Lemma 91.4, the same statement holds for all \( t \geq  {T}_{a} \) .

nodes.proof:
The argument for the second one is similar.

The kernel obviously remains constant on any time interval which is free of singular times. Suppose that \( {t}_{0} \geq  {T}_{a} \) is a singular time. Then the intersection \( {\mathcal{M}}_{{t}_{0}}^{ + } \cap  {\mathcal{M}}_{{t}_{0}}^{ - } \) includes into \( {\mathcal{M}}_{{t}_{0}}^{ + } \) and, by using static curves, into \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t} \) for \( t \neq  {t}_{0} \) close to \( {t}_{0} \) . By Van Kampen’s theorem, these inclusions induce monomorphisms of the fundamental groups. Therefore for \( t \) close to \( {t}_{0} \) , the kernel of (91.5) is the same as the kernel of

(91.6)

\[
{\pi }_{1}\left( {f\left( t\right) }\right)  : {\pi }_{1}\left( {Z, \star  }\right)  \rightarrow  {\pi }_{1}\left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{{t}_{0}}^{ + } \cap  {\mathcal{M}}_{{t}_{0}}^{ - }}\right) ,
\]

which is independent of \( t \) for times \( t \) close to \( {t}_{0} \) .

We now assume that the kernel of

(91.7)

\[
{\pi }_{1}\left( {f\left( t\right) }\right)  : {\pi }_{1}\left( {Z, \star  }\right)  \rightarrow  {\pi }_{1}\left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + }, f\left( t\right) \left( \star \right) }\right)
\]

is nontrivial for some, and hence every, \( t \geq  {T}_{a} \) . By Van Kampen’s theorem and the fact that the cuspidal torus \( Z \subset  Y \) is incompressible in \( Y \) , it follows that the kernel \( K \) of

(91.8)

\[
{\pi }_{1}\left( {f\left( t\right) }\right)  : {\pi }_{1}\left( {Z, \star  }\right)  \rightarrow  {\pi }_{1}\left( {{\widehat{W}}_{t}, f\left( t\right) \left( \star \right) }\right)
\]

in nontrivial for all \( t \geq  {T}_{a} \) . By Poincaré duality, \( \operatorname{Im}\left( {{\mathrm{H}}^{1}\left( {{\widehat{W}}_{t};\mathbb{R}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\mathrm{H}}^{1}\left( {\partial {\widehat{W}}_{t};\mathbb{R}}\right) }\right) \) is a Lagrangian subspace of \( {\mathrm{H}}^{1}\left( {\partial {\widehat{W}}_{t};\mathbb{R}}\right) \) . In particular, \( \operatorname{Im}\left( {{\mathrm{H}}^{1}\left( {{\widehat{W}}_{t};\mathbb{R}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\mathrm{H}}^{1}\left( {Z;\mathbb{R}}\right) }\right) \) has rank one. Dually, \( \operatorname{Ker}\left( {{\mathrm{H}}_{1}\left( {Z;\mathbb{R}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\mathrm{H}}_{1}\left( {{\widehat{W}}_{t};\mathbb{R}}\right) }\right) \) has rank one and so \( K \) , a subgroup of a rank-two free abelian group, has rank one. We note that for all large \( t,{\widehat{Z}}_{t} \) is a convex boundary component of \( {\widehat{W}}_{t} \) . The main theorem of [43] implies that for every such \( t \) , there is is a least-area compressing disk

(91.9)

\[
\left( {{N}_{t}^{2},\partial {N}_{t}^{2}}\right)  \subset  \left( {{\widehat{W}}_{t},{\widehat{Z}}_{t}}\right) .
\]

We recall that a compressing disk is an embedded disk whose boundary curve is essential in \( {\widehat{Z}}_{t} \) . We note that by definition, \( {\widehat{W}}_{t} \) is a compact manifold even when \( t \) is a singular time. The embedded curve \( f{\left( t\right) }^{-1}\left( {\partial {N}_{t}}\right)  \subset  Z \) represents a primitive element of \( {\pi }_{1}\left( Z\right) \) which, since \( K \) has rank one, must therefore generate \( K \) . It follows that modulo taking inverses, the homotopy class of \( f{\left( t\right) }^{-1}\left( {\partial {N}_{t}}\right)  \subset  Z \) is independent of \( t \) .

We define a function \( A : \left\lbrack  {{T}_{a},\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) by letting \( A\left( t\right) \) be the infimum of the areas of such embedded compressing disks. We now show that the least-area compressing disks avoid the surgery regions.

nodes.proof: If the lemma were not true then there would be a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) and for each \( k \) an area-minimizing compressing disk \( \left( {{N}_{{t}_{k}},\partial {N}_{{t}_{k}}}\right)  \subset  \left( {{\widehat{W}}_{{t}_{k}},{\widehat{Z}}_{{t}_{k}}}\right) \) , along with a point \( {x}_{k} \in  {N}_{{t}_{k}} \) that is in the center of a \( {10\delta }\left( {t}_{k}\right) \) -neck. Note that the scalar curvature near \( \partial {N}_{{t}_{k}} \) is comparable to \( - \frac{3}{2{t}_{k}} \) . We now rescale by \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , and consider the map of pointed manifolds \( {f}_{k} : \left( {{N}_{{t}_{k}},\partial {N}_{{t}_{k}},{x}_{k}}\right)  \hookrightarrow  \left( {{\widehat{W}}_{{t}_{k}},{\widehat{Z}}_{{t}_{k}},{x}_{k}}\right) \) where the domain is equipped with the pullback Riemannian metric. By [57] and standard elliptic regularity, for all \( \rho  < \infty \) and every integer \( j \) , the \( {j}^{th} \) covariant derivative of the second fundamental form of \( {f}_{k} \) is uniformly bounded on the ball \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  {N}_{{t}_{k}} \) , for sufficiently large \( k \) . Therefore the pointed Riemannian manifolds \( \left( {{N}_{{t}_{k}},\partial {N}_{{t}_{k}},{x}_{k}}\right) \) subconverge in the smooth topology to a pointed, complete, connected, smooth manifold \( \left( {{N}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) . Using the same bounds on the derivatives of the second fundamental form, we may extract a limit mapping \( {\phi }_{\infty } : {N}_{\infty } \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \times  {S}^{2} \) which is a 2-sided isometric stable minimal immersion. By [58, Theorem 2], \( {\phi }_{\infty } \) is a totally geodesic immersion whose normal vector field in \( M \) has vanishing Ricci curvature. It follows that \( {\phi }_{\infty } \) is a cover of a fiber \( \{ \mathrm{{pt}}\}  \times  {S}^{2} \) . This contradicts the fact that \( {N}_{\infty } \) is noncompact.

nodes.proof:
This is proved in [34, Sections 11 and 12]. We just state the main idea. For the purposes of this proof, we give \( {\widehat{W}}_{t} \) the metric \( {t}^{-1}g\left( t\right) \) . First, \( \partial {N}_{t} \) is the intersection of \( {N}_{t} \) with \( {\widehat{Z}}_{t} \) . Because \( {N}_{t} \) is minimal with respect to free boundary conditions (i.e. the only constraint is that \( \partial {N}_{t} \) is in the right homotopy class in \( {\widehat{Z}}_{t} \) ), it follows that \( {N}_{t} \) meets \( {\widehat{Z}}_{t} \) orthogonally. Then \( {\kappa }_{\partial {N}_{t}} = \Pi \left( {v, v}\right) \) , where \( \Pi \) is the second fundamental form of \( {\widehat{Z}}_{t} \) in \( {\widehat{W}}_{t} \) and \( v \) is the unit tangent vector of \( \partial {N}_{t} \) . Given \( a > 0 \) , let \( Z \) be the horospherical torus in \( {V}_{j} \) of diameter \( a \) . By Proposition 90.1, for large \( t \) the map \( f\left( t\right) \) is close to being an isometry of pairs \( \left( {Y, Z}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{\widehat{Y}}_{t},{\widehat{Z}}_{t}}\right) \) . As \( Z \) has principal curvatures \( \frac{1}{2} \) , we may assume that \( \Pi \left( {v, v}\right) \) is close to \( \frac{1}{2} \) . This reduces the problem to showing that with an appropriate choice of \( {a}_{0} \) , if \( a \in  \left( {0,{a}_{0}}\right) \) then for large values of \( t \) the length of \( \partial {N}_{t} \) is guaranteed to be small. The intuition is that since \( {\widehat{W}}_{t} \) is close to being the standard cusp \( {V}_{j} \) , a large piece of the minimal disk \( {N}_{t} \) should be like a minimal surface \( {N}_{\infty } \) in \( {V}_{j} \) that intersects \( Z \) in the given homotopy class. Such a minimal surface in \( {V}_{j} \) essentially consists of a geodesic curve in \( Z \) going all the way down the cusp. The length of the intersection of \( {N}_{\infty } \) with the horospherical torus of diameter \( a \) is proportionate to \( a \) . Hence if \( {a}_{0} \) is small enough, one would expect that if \( a < {a}_{0} \) and if \( t \) is large then the length of \( \partial {N}_{t} \) is small. In particular, the length of \( \partial {N}_{t} \) is uniformly bounded with respect to \( a \) . A detailed proof appears in [34, Section 12].

Rescaling from the metric \( {t}^{-1}g\left( t\right) \) to the original metric \( g\left( t\right) ,{\int }_{\partial {N}_{t}}{\kappa }_{\partial {N}_{t}}{ds} \) is unchanged and length \( \left( {\partial {N}_{t}}\right) \) is multiplied by \( \sqrt{t} \) .

Lemma 91.12. For every \( D > 0 \) there is a number \( {a}_{0} > 0 \) with the following property. Given \( a \in  \left( {0,{a}_{0}}\right) \) , suppose that we take \( Z \) to be the torus cross-section in \( {V}_{j} \) of diameter a. Then there is a number \( {T}_{a}^{\prime } < \infty \) so that as long as \( {t}_{0} \geq  {T}_{a}^{\prime } \) , there is a smooth function \( \bar{A} \) defined on a neighborhood of \( {t}_{0} \) such that \( \bar{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  = A\left( {t}_{0}\right) ,\bar{A} \geq  A \) everywhere, and

(91.13)

\[
{\bar{A}}^{\prime }\left( {t}_{0}\right)  < \frac{3}{4}\left( \frac{1}{{t}_{0} + \frac{1}{4}}\right) A\left( {t}_{0}\right)  - {2\pi } + D.
\]

nodes.proof:
Take \( {a}_{0} \) as in Lemma 91.11.

For \( {t}_{0} > {T}_{a} \) , we begin with the minimizing compressing disk \( {N}_{{t}_{0}} \subset  {\mathcal{M}}_{{t}_{0}}^{ + } \) . If \( {t}_{0} \) is a surgery time and \( {N}_{{t}_{0}} \) intersected the surgery region \( {\mathcal{M}}_{{t}_{0}}^{ + } - \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{{t}_{0}}^{ + } \cap  {\mathcal{M}}_{{t}_{0}}^{ - }}\right) \) then \( {N}_{{t}_{0}} \) would have to pass through a \( {10\delta }\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) -neck, which is impossible by Lemma 91.10. Thus \( {N}_{{t}_{0}} \) avoids any parts added by surgery.

For \( t \) close to \( {t}_{0} \) we define an embedded compressing disk \( {S}_{t} \subset  {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) as follows. We take \( {N}_{{t}_{0}} \) and extend it slightly to a smooth surface \( {N}_{{t}_{0}}^{\prime } \subset  {\mathcal{M}}_{{t}_{0}}^{ + } \) which contains \( {N}_{{t}_{0}} \) in its interior. The surface \( {N}_{{t}_{0}}^{\prime } \) will be unscathed on some open time interval containing \( {t}_{0} \) . If we let \( {S}_{t}^{\prime } \subset  {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) be the surface obtained by moving \( {N}_{{t}_{0}}^{\prime } \) along static curves then for some \( b > 0 \) , the surface \( {S}_{t}^{\prime } \) will intersect \( \partial {\widehat{W}}_{t} \) transversely for all \( t \in  \left( {{t}_{0} - b,{t}_{0} + b}\right) \) . Putting

(91.14)

\[
{S}_{t} = {S}_{t}^{\prime } \cap  {\widehat{W}}_{t}
\]

defines a compressing disk for \( {\widehat{Z}}_{t} \subset  {\widehat{W}}_{t} \) .

Define \( \bar{A} : \left( {{t}_{0} - b,{t}_{0} + b}\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) by

(91.15)

\[
\bar{A}\left( t\right)  = \operatorname{area}\left( {S}_{t}\right) .
\]

Clearly \( \bar{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  = A\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) and \( \bar{A} \geq  A \) .

For the rest of the calculation, we will view \( {S}_{t} \) as a surface sitting in a fixed manifold \( M \) (a fattening of \( {\widehat{W}}_{t} \) ) with a varying metric \( g\left( \cdot \right) \) , and put \( S = {S}_{{t}_{0}} = {N}_{{t}_{0}} \) .

By the first variation formula for area,

(91.16)

\[
{\bar{A}}^{\prime }\left( {t}_{0}\right)  = {\int }_{\partial S}\left\langle  {X,{\nu }_{\partial S}}\right\rangle  {ds} + {\left. {\int }_{S}\frac{d}{dt}\right| }_{t = {t}_{0}}{\mathrm{{dvol}}}_{S},
\]

where \( X \) denotes the variation vector field for \( {\widehat{Z}}_{t} \) , viewed as a surface moving in \( M \) , and \( {\nu }_{\partial S} \) is the outward normal vector along \( \partial S \) . By Proposition 90.1, there is an estimate \( \left| X\right|  \leq  \alpha \left( {t}_{0}\right) {t}_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , where \( \alpha \left( {t}_{0}\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) as \( {t}_{0} \rightarrow  \infty \) . Therefore

(91.17)

\[
\left| {{\int }_{\partial {S}_{{t}_{0}}}\left\langle  {X,{\nu }_{\partial {S}_{{t}_{0}}}}\right\rangle  {ds}}\right|  \leq  \alpha \left( {t}_{0}\right) {t}_{0}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\operatorname{length}\left( {\partial {N}_{{t}_{0}}}\right) .
\]

By Lemma 91.11, the right-hand side of (91.17) is bounded above by \( \frac{D}{2} \) if \( {t}_{0} \) is large.

We turn to the second term in (91.16). Pick \( p \in  S \) and let \( {e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3} \) be an orthonormal basis for \( {T}_{p}M \) with \( {e}_{1} \) and \( {e}_{2} \) tangent to \( S \) . Then

(91.18)

\[
{\left. \frac{1}{{\operatorname{dvol}}_{S}}\frac{d}{dt}\right| }_{t = {t}_{0}}{\operatorname{dvol}}_{S} = \frac{1}{2}{\left. \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{2}\frac{dg}{dt}\right| }_{t = {t}_{0}}\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{i}}\right)  =  - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{1}}\right)  - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{2}}\right) .
\]

Now

(91.19)

\[
\left. {-\operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{1}}\right)  - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{2}}\right) }\right)  =  - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{3},{e}_{3}}\right)  =  - R + K\left( {{e}_{3},{e}_{1}}\right)  + K\left( {{e}_{3},{e}_{2}}\right)
\]

\[
=  - \frac{R}{2} - K\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{2}}\right)  =  - \frac{R}{2} - {K}_{S} + {\mathrm{{GK}}}_{S},
\]

where \( {K}_{S} \) denotes the Gauss curvature of \( S \) and \( {\mathrm{{GK}}}_{S} \) denotes the product of the principal curvatures. Applying the Gauss-Bonnet formula

(91.20)

\[
{\int }_{\partial S}{\kappa }_{\partial S}{ds} = {2\pi } - {\int }_{S}{K}_{S}{\operatorname{vol}}_{S},
\]

the fact that \( {\mathrm{{GK}}}_{S} \leq  0 \) (since \( S \) is time- \( {t}_{0} \) minimal) and the inequality

(91.21)

\[
{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \geq   - \frac{3}{2}\left( \frac{1}{t + \frac{1}{4}}\right)
\]

from Lemma 79.11, we obtain

(91.22)

\[
{\int }_{S}{\left. \frac{d}{dt}\right| }_{t = {t}_{0}}{\operatorname{dvol}}_{S} \leq  {\int }_{S}\frac{3}{4}\left( \frac{1}{{t}_{0} + \frac{1}{4}}\right) {\operatorname{dvol}}_{S} + {\int }_{\partial S}{\kappa }_{\partial S}{ds} - {2\pi }.
\]

By Lemma 91.11, if \( a \in  \left( {0,{a}_{0}}\right) ,\operatorname{diam}\left( Z\right)  = a \) and \( {t}_{0} \) is sufficiently large then \( {\int }_{\partial S}{\kappa }_{\partial S}{ds} \leq  \frac{D}{2} \) . Using (91.16),(91.17) and (91.22), if \( {t}_{0} \) is large then

(91.23)

\[
{\bar{A}}^{\prime }\left( {t}_{0}\right)  < \frac{3}{4}\left( \frac{1}{{t}_{0} + \frac{1}{4}}\right) A\left( {t}_{0}\right)  - {2\pi } + D.
\]

This proves the lemma.

Theorem 92.1. (cf. Theorem II.7.4) Suppose that \( \left( {{M}^{\alpha },{g}^{\alpha }}\right) \) is a sequence of compact oriented Riemannian 3-manifolds, closed or with convex boundary, and \( {w}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) . Assume that

(1) for each point \( x \in  {M}^{\alpha } \) there exists a radius \( \rho  = {\rho }^{\alpha }\left( x\right) \) not exceeding the diameter of \( {M}^{\alpha } \) such that the ball \( B\left( {x,\rho }\right) \) in the metric \( {g}^{\alpha } \) has volume at most \( {w}^{\alpha }{\rho }^{3} \) and sectional curvatures at least \( - {\rho }^{-2} \) .

(2) each component of the boundary of \( {M}^{\alpha } \) has diameter at most \( {w}^{\alpha } \) , and has a (topologically trivial) collar of length one, where the sectional curvatures are between \( - \frac{1}{4} - \epsilon \) and \( - \frac{1}{4} - \epsilon \) .

Then for large \( \alpha ,{M}^{\alpha } \) is diffeomorphic to a graph manifold.

Theorem 92.3. (cf. Theorem II.7.4) Suppose that \( \left( {{M}^{\alpha },{g}^{\alpha }}\right) \) is a sequence of compact oriented Riemannian 3-manifolds, closed or with convex boundary, and \( {w}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) . Assume that

(1) for each point \( x \in  {M}^{\alpha } \) there exists a radius \( \rho  = {\rho }^{\alpha }\left( x\right) \) such that the ball \( B\left( {x,\rho }\right) \) in the metric \( {g}^{\alpha } \) has volume at most \( {w}^{\alpha }{\rho }^{3} \) and sectional curvatures at least \( - {\rho }^{-2} \) .

(2) each component of the boundary of \( {M}^{\alpha } \) has diameter at most \( {w}^{\alpha } \) , and has a (topologically trivial) collar of length one, where the sectional curvatures are between \( - \frac{1}{4} - \epsilon \) and \( - \frac{1}{4} - \epsilon \) . (3) for every \( {w}^{\prime } > 0 \) and \( m \in  \left\{  {0,1,\ldots ,\left\lbrack  {\epsilon }^{-1}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , there exist \( \bar{r} = \bar{r}\left( {w}^{\prime }\right)  > 0 \) and \( {K}_{m} = {K}_{m}\left( {w}^{\prime }\right)  < \; \infty \) such that for sufficiently large \( \alpha \) , if \( r \in  (0,\bar{r}\rbrack \) and a ball \( B\left( {x, r}\right) \) in the metric \( {g}^{\alpha } \) has volume at least \( {w}^{\prime }{r}^{3} \) and sectional curvatures at least \( - {r}^{-2} \) then \( \left| {{\nabla }^{m}\operatorname{Rm}}\right| \left( x\right)  \leq  {K}_{m}{r}^{-m - 2} \) .

Then for large \( \alpha ,{M}^{\alpha } \) is diffeomorphic to a graph manifold.
