Remark 92.7. We give some simple examples where the collapsing theorems apply. Let \( \left( {\sum ,{g}_{hyp}}\right) \) be a closed surface with the hyperbolic metric. Let \( {S}^{1}\left( \mu \right) \) be a circle of length \( \mu \) and consider the Ricci flow on \( {S}^{1} \times  \sum \) with the initial metric \( {S}^{1}\left( \mu \right)  \times  \left( {\sum ,{c}_{0}{g}_{hyp}}\right) \) . The Ricci flow solution at time \( t \) is \( {S}^{1}\left( \mu \right)  \times  \left( {\sum ,\left( {{c}_{0} + {2t}}\right) {g}_{hyp}}\right) \) . In the rest of this example we consider the rescaled metric \( {t}^{-1}g\left( t\right) \) . Its diameter goes like \( O\left( {t}^{0}\right) \) and its sectional curvatures go like \( O\left( {t}^{0}\right) \) . If we take \( \rho \) to be a small constant then for large \( t, B\left( {x, t,\rho }\right) \) is approximately a circle bundle over a ball in a hyperbolic surface of constant sectional curvature \( - \frac{1}{2} \) , with circle lengths that go like \( {t}^{-1/2} \) . The sectional curvature on \( B\left( {x, t,\rho }\right) \) is bounded below by \( - {\rho }^{-2} \) , and \( {\rho }^{-3}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {x, t,\rho }\right) }\right)  \sim  {t}^{-1/2} \) . Theorems 92.1 and 92.3 both apply.

Next, consider a compact 3-dimensional nilmanifold that evolves under the Ricci flow. Let \( {\theta }_{1},{\theta }_{2},{\theta }_{3} \) be affine-parallel 1-forms on \( M \) which lift to Maurer-Cartan forms on the Heisenberg group, with \( d{\theta }_{1} = d{\theta }_{2} = 0 \) and \( d{\theta }_{3} = {\theta }_{1} \land  {\theta }_{2} \) . Consider the metric

(92.8)

\[
g\left( t\right)  = {\alpha }^{2}\left( t\right) {\theta }_{1}^{2} + {\beta }^{2}\left( t\right) {\theta }_{2}^{2} + {\gamma }^{2}\left( t\right) {\theta }_{3}^{2}.
\]

Its sectional curvatures are \( {R}_{1212} =  - \frac{3}{4}\frac{{\gamma }^{2}}{{\alpha }^{2}{\beta }^{2}} \) and \( {R}_{1313} = {R}_{2323} = \frac{1}{4}\frac{{\gamma }^{2}}{{\alpha }^{2}{\beta }^{2}} \) . The Ricci tensor is

(92.9)

\[
\operatorname{Ric} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{{\gamma }^{2}}{{\alpha }^{2}{\beta }^{2}}\left( {-{\alpha }^{2}{\theta }_{1}^{2} - {\beta }^{2}{\theta }_{2}^{2} + {\gamma }^{2}{\theta }_{3}^{2}}\right) .
\]

The general solution to the Ricci flow equation is of the form(92.10)

\[
{\alpha }^{2}\left( t\right)  = {A}_{0}{\left( t + {t}_{0}\right) }^{1/3}
\]

\[
{\beta }^{2}\left( t\right)  = {B}_{0}{\left( t + {t}_{0}\right) }^{1/3},
\]

\[
{\gamma }^{2}\left( t\right)  = \frac{{A}_{0}{B}_{0}}{3}{\left( t + {t}_{0}\right) }^{-1/3}.
\]

In the rest of this example we consider the rescaled metric \( {t}^{-1}g\left( t\right) \) . Its diameter goes like \( {t}^{-1/3} \) , its volume goes like \( {t}^{-4/3} \) and its sectional curvatures go like \( {t}^{0} \) . If we take \( \rho \left( x\right)  = \operatorname{diam} \) then \( {\rho }^{-3}\operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {x,\rho }\right) }\right)  \sim  {t}^{-1/3} \) , so both Theorem 92.1 and Theorem 92.3 apply. We could also take \( \rho \left( x\right) \) to be a small constant \( c > 0 \) , in which case Theorem 92.3 applies.

In general, among the eight maximal homogeneous geometries, the rescaled solution for a compact 3-manifold with geometry \( {H}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or \( {\mathrm{{SL}}}_{2}\left( \mathbb{R}\right) \) will collapse to a hyperbolic surface of constant sectional curvature \( - \frac{1}{2} \) . The rescaled solution for a Sol geometry will collapse to a circle. The rescaled solution for an \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) or Nil geometry will collapse to a point.

We remark that although these homogeneous solutions are collapsing in the sense of Theorem 92.1, there is no contradiction with the no local collapsing result of Theorem 26.2, which only rules out local collapsing on a finite time interval.

Returning to our Ricci flow with surgery, recall the statement of Proposition 90.1. If the collection \( \left\{  {{H}_{1},\ldots ,{H}_{k}}\right\} \) of Proposition 90.1 is nonempty then for large \( t \) , let \( {\widehat{H}}_{i}\left( t\right) \) be the result of removing from \( {H}_{i} \) the horoballs whose boundaries are at distance approximately \( \frac{1}{2}\alpha \left( t\right) \) from the basepoint \( {x}_{i} \) . (If there are no such horoballs then \( {\widehat{H}}_{i}\left( t\right)  = {H}_{i} \) .) Put

(92.11)

\[
{M}_{\text{ thin }}\left( t\right)  = {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } - f\left( t\right) \left( {{\widehat{H}}_{1}\left( t\right)  \cup  \ldots {\widehat{H}}_{k}\left( t\right) }\right) .
\]

nodes.content: Proposition 92.12. For large \( t,{M}_{\text{ thin }}\left( t\right) \) is a graph manifold.
nodes.content_excerpt: Proposition 92.12. For large \( t,{M}_{\text{ thin }}\left( t\right) \) is a graph manifold.

nodes.proof:
We continue with the proof of Proposition 92.12. By construction there is a sequence \( {w}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) so that conditions (1) and (2) of Theorem 92.3 hold with \( {\rho }^{\alpha }\left( {x}^{\alpha }\right)  = {\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) \) .

Hence for large \( \alpha ,{M}^{\alpha } \) is diffeomorphic to a graph manifold. This is a contradiction to the choice of the \( {M}^{\alpha } \) ’s and proves the theorem.

We now give a proof that instead uses Theorem 92.1. Let \( {d}^{\alpha } \) denote the diameter of \( {M}^{\alpha } \) . If we take \( {\rho }^{\alpha }\left( {x}^{\alpha }\right)  = {\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\rho \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) \) then we can apply Theorem 92.1 as long as that the diameter statement in condition (1) of Theorem 92.1 is satisfied. If it is not satisfied then there is some point \( {x}^{\alpha } \in  {M}^{\alpha } \) with \( {\rho }^{\alpha }\left( {x}^{\alpha }\right)  > {d}^{\alpha } \) . The sectional curvatures of \( {M}^{\alpha } \) are bounded below by \( - \frac{1}{{\rho }^{\alpha }{\left( {x}^{\alpha }\right) }^{2}} \) , and so are bounded below by \( - \frac{1}{{\left( {d}^{\alpha }\right) }^{2}} \) . If there is a subsequence with \( \frac{{\rho }^{\alpha }\left( {x}^{\alpha }\right) }{{d}^{\alpha }} \leq  C < \infty \) then

(92.14)

\[
\operatorname{vol}\left( {M}^{\alpha }\right)  = \operatorname{vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{\rho }^{\alpha }\left( {x}^{\alpha }\right) }\right) }\right)  \leq  {w}^{\alpha }{\rho }^{\alpha }{\left( {x}^{\alpha }\right) }^{3} \leq  {w}^{\alpha }{C}^{3}{\left( {d}^{\alpha }\right) }^{3}
\]

and we can apply Theorem 92.1 with \( {\rho }^{\alpha } = {d}^{\alpha } \) , after redefining \( {w}^{\alpha } \) . Thus we may assume that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha  \rightarrow  \infty }}\frac{{\rho }^{\alpha }\left( {x}^{\alpha }\right) }{{d}^{\alpha }} = \infty \) . If there is a subsequence with \( \frac{\operatorname{vol}\left( {M}^{\alpha }\right) }{{\left( {d}^{\alpha }\right) }^{3}} \rightarrow  0 \) then we can apply Theorem 92.1 with \( {\rho }^{\alpha } = {d}^{\alpha } \) . Thus we may assume that \( \frac{\operatorname{vol}\left( {M}^{\alpha }\right) }{{\left( {d}^{\alpha }\right) }^{3}} \) is bounded away from zero. After rescaling the metric to make the diameter one, we are in a noncollapsing situation with the lower sectional curvature bound going to zero. By the argument in the proof of Lemma 92.13 (which used Corollary 81.3) there are uniform \( {L}^{\infty } \) -bounds on \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {M}^{\alpha }\right) \) and its covariant derivatives. After passing to a subsequence, there is a limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) in the smooth topology which is diffeomorphic to \( {M}^{\alpha } \) for large \( \alpha \) , and carries a metric of nonnegative sectional curvature. As any boundary component of \( {M}_{\infty } \) would have to have a neighborhood of negative sectional curvature (see the definition of \( {M}_{\text{ thin }} \) and condition (2) of Theorem 92.1), \( {M}_{\infty } \) is closed. However, by construction \( {M}^{\alpha } \) has no connected components which are closed and admit metrics of nonnegative sectional curvature. This contradiction shows that the diameter statement in condition (1) of Theorem 92.1 is satisfied. The other conditions of Theorem 92.1 are satisfied as before.

Thus for large \( t,{\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) has a decomposition into a piece \( f\left( t\right) \left( {{\widehat{H}}_{1}\left( t\right)  \cup  \ldots {\widehat{H}}_{k}\left( t\right) }\right) \) , whose interior admits a complete finite-volume hyperbolic metric, and the complement, which is a graph manifold.

In addition, by Section 91 the cuspidal tori are incompressible in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) . By Lemma 73.4, the initial (connected) manifold \( {\mathcal{M}}_{0} \) is diffeomorphic to a connected sum of the connected components of \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t} \) , along with some possible additional connected sums with a finite number of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s and quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) . This proves the geometrization conjecture of Appendix I.

nodes.content_excerpt: Lemma 92.13. Condition (3) in Theorem 92.3 holds for the \( {M}^{\alpha } \) ’s.

nodes.proof:
With \( {w}^{\prime } \) being a parameter as in Condition (3) in Theorem 92.3, let \( \bar{r} = \bar{r}\left( {w}^{\prime }\right) \) be the parameter of Corollary 81.3. It is enough to show that for large \( \alpha \) , if \( r \in  \left( {0,\bar{r}\sqrt{{t}^{\alpha }}}\right\rbrack \) , \( {x}^{\alpha } \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{{t}^{\alpha }}^{ + } \) , and \( B\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }, r}\right) \) has volume at least \( {w}^{\prime }{r}^{3} \) and sectional curvatures bounded below by \( - {r}^{-2} \) , then \( \left| {{\nabla }^{m}\operatorname{Rm}}\right| \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  \leq  {K}_{m}{r}^{-m - 2} \) for an appropriate choice of constants \( {K}_{m} \) .

To prove this by contradiction, we assume that after passing to a subsequence if necessary, there are \( {r}^{\alpha } \in  \left( {0,\bar{r}\sqrt{{t}^{\alpha }}}\right\rbrack \) and \( {x}^{\alpha } \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{{t}^{\alpha }}^{ + } \) such that \( B\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha },{r}^{\alpha }}\right) \) has volume at least \( {w}^{\prime }{\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{3} \) and sectional curvature at least \( - {\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \) , but \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha  \rightarrow  \infty }}{\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{m + 2}\left| {{\nabla }^{m}\operatorname{Rm}}\right| \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  = \infty \) for some \( m \leq  \left\lbrack  {\epsilon }^{-1}\right\rbrack \) .

In the notation of Corollary 81.3, if \( {r}^{\alpha } \geq  {\theta }^{-1}\left( {w}^{\prime }\right) {h}_{\max }\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) \) for infinitely many \( \alpha \) then for these \( \alpha \) , Corollary 81.3 gives a curvature bound on an unscathed parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha },{r}^{\alpha }/4, - \tau {\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{2}}\right) \) and hence, by Appendix D, derivative bounds at \( \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) \) . This is a contradiction. Therefore we may assume that \( {r}^{\alpha } < {\theta }^{-1}\left( {w}^{\prime }\right) {h}_{\max }\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right)  \leq  r\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) \) for all \( \alpha \) , where we used Remark 86.9 for the last inequality.

Suppose first that \( R\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  \leq  {\left( r\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) \right) }^{-2} \) . By Lemma 70.1, there is an estimate \( R \leq \; {16}{\left( r\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) \right) }^{-2} \) on the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha },\frac{1}{4}{\eta }^{-1}r\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) , - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}{\left( r\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) \right) }^{2}}\right) \) . A surgery in this neighborhood could only occur where \( R \geq  {h}_{\max }{\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \) . For large \( \alpha ,{h}_{\max }{\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} >  > \; r{\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \) by Remark 86.9. Hence this neighborhood is unscathed. Appendix D now gives bounds of the form \( \left| {{\nabla }^{m}\operatorname{Rm}}\right| \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  \leq \) const. \( {\left( r\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) \right) }^{-m - 2} \leq \) const. \( {\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-m - 2} \) , which is a contradiction..

Suppose now that \( R\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  > {\left( r\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) \right) }^{-2} \) . Then \( \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) \) is in the center of a canonical neighborhood and there are universal estimates \( \left| {{\nabla }^{m}\operatorname{Rm}}\right| \left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  \leq \) const. \( \left( m\right) R{\left( {x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }\right) }^{\frac{m + 2}{2}} \) for all \( m \leq  \left\lbrack  {\epsilon }^{-1}\right\rbrack \) . Hence in this case, it suffices to show that \( R\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) \) is bounded above by a constant times \( {\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \) , i.e. it suffices to get a contradiction just to the assumption that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha  \rightarrow  \infty }}{\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{2}R\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  = \infty . \)

So suppose that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha  \rightarrow  \infty }}{\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{2}R\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  = \infty \) . We claim that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha  \rightarrow  \infty }}{\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{2}\inf {\left. R\right| }_{B\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha },{r}^{\alpha }}\right) } = \; \infty \) . Suppose not. Then there is some \( C \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) so that after passing to a subsequence, there are points \( {x}^{\alpha \prime } \in  B\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha },{r}^{\alpha }}\right) \) with \( {\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{2}R\left( {{x}^{\alpha \prime },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  < C \) . Considering points along the time- \( {t}^{\alpha } \) geodesic segment from \( {x}^{\alpha \prime } \) to \( {x}^{\alpha } \) , for large \( \alpha \) we can find points \( {x}^{\alpha \prime \prime } \in  B\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha },{r}^{\alpha }}\right) \) with \( {\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{2}R\left( {{x}^{\alpha \prime \prime },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  = {2C} \) . Applying Lemma 70.2 at \( \left( {{x}^{\alpha \prime \prime },{t}^{\alpha }}\right) \) , or more precisely a version that applies along geodesics as in Claim 2 of II.4.2, we obtain a contradiction to the assumption that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha  \rightarrow  \infty }}{\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{2}R\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha }}\right)  = \infty \) . In applying Lemma 70.2 we use that \( {r}^{\alpha } < r\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right) \) and \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha  \rightarrow  \infty }}r\left( {t}^{\alpha }\right)  = 0 \) , giving \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha  \rightarrow  \infty }}{\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2}{t}^{\alpha } = \infty \) , in order to say that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\alpha  \rightarrow  \infty }}\frac{\Phi \left( {{2C}{\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2}}\right) }{{2C}{\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2}} = 0 \) .

Hence for large \( \alpha \) , every point \( x \in  B\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha },{r}^{\alpha }}\right) \) is in the center of a canonical neighborhood of size comparable to \( R{\left( x,{t}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , which is small compared to \( {r}^{\alpha } \) . On the other hand, from Lemma 83.1, there is a ball \( {B}^{\prime } \) of radius \( {\theta }_{0}\left( {w}^{\prime }\right) {r}^{\alpha } \) in \( B\left( {{x}^{\alpha },{t}^{\alpha },{r}^{\alpha }}\right) \) so that every subball of \( {B}^{\prime } \) has almost-Euclidean volume. This is a contradiction.

This proves the lemma.

nodes.content:
93.1. The approach using the \( \sigma \) -invariant. We first give some well-known results about the sigma-invariant. We recall that the sigma-invariant of a closed connected manifold \( M \) of dimension \( n \geq  3 \) is given by

(93.4)

\[
\sigma \left( M\right)  = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{\mathcal{C}}\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{g \in  \mathcal{C}}}\frac{{\int }_{M}R\left( g\right) \operatorname{dvol}\left( g\right) }{\operatorname{vol}{\left( M, g\right) }^{\frac{n - 2}{n}}},
\]

where \( \mathcal{C} \) runs over the conformal classes of Riemannian metrics on \( M \) . From the solution to the Yamabe problem, the infimum in (93.4) is realized by a metric of constant scalar curvature in the given conformal class. It follows that if \( \sigma \left( M\right)  > 0 \) then \( M \) admits a metric with positive scalar curvature. Conversely, suppose that \( M \) admits a metric \( {g}_{0} \) with positive scalar curvature. Let \( \mathcal{C} \) be the conformal class containing \( {g}_{0} \) . Then

(93.5)

\[
\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{g \in  \mathcal{C}}}\frac{{\int }_{M}R\left( g\right) \operatorname{dvol}\left( g\right) }{\operatorname{vol}{\left( M, g\right) }^{\frac{n - 2}{n}}} = \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{u > 0}}\frac{{\int }_{M}\left( {\frac{4\left( {n - 1}\right) }{n - 2}{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2} + R\left( {g}_{0}\right) {u}^{2}}\right) {\operatorname{dvol}}_{M}\left( {g}_{0}\right) }{{\left( {\int }_{M}{u}^{\frac{2n}{n - 2}}{\operatorname{dvol}}_{M}\left( {g}_{0}\right) \right) }^{\frac{n - 2}{n}}}
\]

is positive, in view of the Sobolev embedding theorem, and so \( \sigma \left( M\right)  > 0 \) .

We claim that if \( \sigma \left( M\right)  \leq  0 \) then

(93.6)

\[
\sigma \left( M\right)  = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{g}{R}_{\min }\left( g\right) V{\left( g\right) }^{\frac{2}{n}}.
\]

To see this, as the infimum in (93.4) is realized by a metric of constant scalar curvature in the given conformal class, it follows that \( \sigma \left( M\right)  \leq  \mathop{\sup }\limits_{g}{R}_{\min }\left( g\right) V{\left( g\right) }^{\frac{2}{n}} \) . Now given a Riemannian metric \( g \) , the infimum in (93.4) within the corresponding conformal class \( \mathcal{C} \) equals \( \widetilde{R}V{\left( \widetilde{g}\right) }^{\frac{2}{n}} \) for a metric \( \widetilde{g} = {u}^{\frac{4}{n - 2}}g \) with constant scalar curvature \( \widetilde{R} \) . Then

(93.7)

\[
\widetilde{R}V{\left( \widetilde{g}\right) }^{\frac{2}{n}} = \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{u > 0}}\frac{{\int }_{M}\left( {\frac{4\left( {n - 1}\right) }{n - 2}{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2} + R{u}^{2}}\right) {\operatorname{dvol}}_{M}}{{\left( {\int }_{M}{u}^{\frac{2n}{n - 2}}{\operatorname{dvol}}_{M}\right) }^{\frac{n - 2}{n}}}.
\]

As

(93.8)

\[
\frac{{\int }_{M}\left( {\frac{4\left( {n - 1}\right) }{n - 2}{\left| \nabla u\right| }^{2} + R{u}^{2}}\right) {\operatorname{dvol}}_{M}}{{\left( {\int }_{M}{u}^{\frac{2n}{n - 2}}{\operatorname{dvol}}_{M}\right) }^{\frac{n - 2}{n}}} \geq  {R}_{\min }\left( g\right) \frac{{\int }_{M}{u}^{2}{\operatorname{dvol}}_{M}}{{\left( {\int }_{M}{u}^{\frac{2n}{n - 2}}{\operatorname{dvol}}_{M}\right) }^{\frac{n - 2}{n}}}
\]

and \( {R}_{\min }\left( g\right)  \leq  0 \) , Holder’s inequality implies that \( \widetilde{R}V{\left( \widetilde{g}\right) }^{\frac{2}{n}} \geq  {R}_{\min }\left( g\right) V{\left( g\right) }^{\frac{2}{n}} \) . It follows that \( \sigma \left( M\right)  \geq  \mathop{\sup }\limits_{g}{R}_{\min }\left( g\right) V{\left( g\right) }^{\frac{2}{n}} \) .

nodes.content:
Proposition 93.9. Let \( M \) be a closed connected oriented 3-manifold.

(a) If \( \sigma \left( M\right)  > 0 \) then \( M \) is diffeomorphic to a connected sum of a finite number of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s and metric quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) . Conversely, each such manifold has \( \sigma \left( M\right)  > 0 \) .

(b) \( M \) is a graph manifold if and only if \( \sigma \left( M\right)  \geq  0 \) .

(c) If \( \sigma \left( M\right)  < 0 \) then \( {\left( -\frac{2}{3}\sigma \left( M\right) \right) }^{\frac{3}{2}} \) is the minimum of the numbers \( V \) with the following property : M can be decomposed as a connected sum of a finite collection of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s, metric quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) and some other components, the union of which is denoted by \( {M}^{\prime } \) , and there exists a (possibly disconnected) complete finite-volume manifold \( N \) with constant sectional curvature \( - \frac{1}{4} \) and volume \( V \) which can be embedded in \( {M}^{\prime } \) so that the complement \( {M}^{\prime } - N \) (if nonempty) is a graph manifold.

Moreover, if \( \operatorname{vol}\left( N\right)  = {\left( -\frac{2}{3}\sigma \left( M\right) \right) }^{\frac{3}{2}} \) then the cusps of \( N \) (if any) are incompressible in \( {M}^{\prime } \) .

nodes.proof:
If \( \sigma \left( M\right)  > 0 \) then \( M \) has a metric \( g \) of positive scalar curvature. From Lemmas 81.1 and \( {81.2}, M \) is a connected sum of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s and metric quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) . Conversely, if \( M \) is a connected sum of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s and metric quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) then \( M \) admits a metric \( g \) of positive scalar curvature and so \( \sigma \left( M\right)  > 0 \) .

Now suppose that \( \sigma \left( M\right)  \leq  0 \) . If \( M \) is a graph manifold then \( M \) volume-collapses with bounded curvature, so (93.6) implies that \( \sigma \left( M\right)  = 0 \) .

Suppose that \( M \) is not a graph manifold. Suppose that we have a given decomposition of \( M \) as a connected sum of a finite collection of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s, metric quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) and some other components, the union of which is denoted by \( {M}^{\prime } \) , and there exists a (possibly disconnected) finite-volume complete manifold \( N \) with constant sectional curvature \( - \frac{1}{4} \) which can be embedded in \( {M}^{\prime } \) so that the complement (if nonempty) is a graph manifold. Let \( {V}_{hyp} \) denote the hyperbolic volume of \( N \) . We do not assume that the cusps of \( N \) are incompressible in \( {M}^{\prime } \) . For any \( \epsilon  > 0 \) , we claim that there is a metric \( {g}_{\epsilon } \) on \( M \) with \( R \geq   - 6 \cdot  \frac{1}{4} - \epsilon \) and volume \( V\left( {g}_{\epsilon }\right)  \leq  {V}_{\text{ hyp }} + \epsilon \) . This comes from collapsing the graph manifold pieces, along with the fact that the connected sum operation can be performed while decreasing the scalar curvature arbitrarily little and increasing the volume arbitrarily little. Then \( {R}_{\min }\left( {g}_{\epsilon }\right) V{\left( {g}_{\epsilon }\right) }^{\frac{2}{3}} \geq   - \frac{3}{2}{V}_{hyp}^{2/3} - \) const. \( \epsilon \) . Thus \( \sigma \left( M\right)  \geq   - \frac{3}{2}{V}_{hyp}^{2/3} \) .

Let \( \widehat{V} \) denote the minimum of \( {V}_{hyp} \) over all such decompositions of \( M \) . (As the set of volumes of complete finite-volume 3-manifolds with constant curvature \( - \frac{1}{4} \) is well-ordered, there is a minimum.) Then \( \sigma \left( M\right)  \geq   - \frac{3}{2}{\widehat{V}}^{2/3} \) .

Next, take an arbitrary metric \( {g}_{0} \) on \( M \) and consider the Ricci flow \( g\left( t\right) \) with initial metric \( {g}_{0} \) . From Sections 90 and 92, there is a nonempty manifold \( N \) with a complete finite-volume metric of constant curvature \( - \frac{1}{4} \) so that for large \( t \) , there is a decomposition \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } = \; {M}_{1}\left( t\right)  \cup  {M}_{2}\left( t\right) \) of the time- \( t \) manifold, where \( {M}_{1}\left( t\right) \) is a graph manifold and \( \left( {{M}_{2}\left( t\right) ,{\left. \frac{1}{t}g\left( t\right) \right| }_{{M}_{2}\left( t\right) }}\right) \) is close to a large piece of \( N \) . In terms of condition (c) of Proposition 93.9, we will think of \( {M}^{\prime } \) as being \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) . Because of the presence of \( N \) , we know that \( t{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \leq   - \frac{3}{2} + \epsilon \left( t\right) \) and \( V\left( t\right)  \geq  {t}^{2/3}{V}_{hyp}\left( N\right)  - \epsilon \left( t\right) \) for a function \( \epsilon \left( t\right) \) with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  \infty }}\epsilon \left( t\right)  = 0 \) . The monotonicity of \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) {V}^{2/3}\left( t\right) \) , even through surgeries, implies that

(93.10)

\[
{R}_{\min }\left( {g}_{0}\right) {V}^{2/3}\left( {g}_{0}\right)  \leq   - \frac{3}{2}{V}_{\text{ hyp }}{\left( N\right) }^{2/3} \leq   - \frac{3}{2}{\widehat{V}}^{2/3}.
\]

Thus \( \sigma \left( M\right)  \leq   - \frac{3}{2}{\widehat{V}}^{2/3} \) .

This shows that \( \sigma \left( M\right)  =  - \frac{3}{2}{\widehat{V}}^{2/3} \) . Now take a decomposition of \( M \) as in condition (c) of Proposition 93.9, with \( {V}_{hyp}\left( N\right)  = \widehat{V} \) . We claim that the cuspidal 2-tori of \( N \) are incompressible in \( {M}^{\prime } \) . If not then there would be a metric \( g \) on \( M \) with \( R\left( g\right)  \geq   - \frac{3}{2} \) and \( \operatorname{vol}\left( g\right)  < {V}_{hyp}\left( N\right) \) [3, Pf. of Theorem 2.9]. This would contradict the fact that \( \sigma \left( M\right)  =  - \frac{3}{2}{V}_{hyp}{\left( N\right) }^{2/3}. \)

nodes.content:
Proposition 93.11. (cf. II.8.2) Let \( M \) be a closed connected oriented 3-manifold.

(a) If \( M \) admits a metric \( g \) with \( \lambda \left( g\right)  > 0 \) then it is diffeomorphic to a connected sum of a finite number of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s and metric quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) . Conversely, each such manifold admits a metric \( g \) with \( \lambda \left( g\right)  > 0 \) .

(b) Suppose that \( M \) does not admit any metric \( g \) with \( \lambda \left( g\right)  > 0 \) . Let \( \bar{\lambda } \) denote the supremum of \( \lambda \left( g\right) V{\left( g\right) }^{\frac{2}{3}} \) over all metrics \( g \) on \( M \) . Then \( M \) is a graph manifold if and only if \( \bar{\lambda } = 0 \) . (c) Suppose that \( M \) does not admit any metric \( g \) with \( \lambda \left( g\right)  > 0 \) , and \( \bar{\lambda } < 0 \) . Then \( {\left( -\frac{2}{3}\bar{\lambda }\right) }^{\frac{3}{2}} \) is the minimum of the numbers \( V \) with the following property : \( M \) can be decomposed as a connected sum of a finite collection of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s, metric quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) and some other components, the union of which is denoted by \( {M}^{\prime } \) , and there exists a (possibly disconnected) complete manifold \( N \) with constant sectional curvature \( - \frac{1}{4} \) and volume \( V \) which can be embedded in \( {M}^{\prime } \) so that the complement \( {M}^{\prime } - N \) (if nonempty) is a graph manifold.

Moreover, if \( \operatorname{vol}\left( N\right)  = {\left( -\frac{2}{3}\bar{\lambda }\right) }^{\frac{3}{2}} \) then the cusps of \( N \) (if any) are incompressible in \( {M}^{\prime } \) .

Conversely, each such manifold admits a metric \( g \) with \( \lambda \left( g\right) > 0 \) . (b) Supp...

nodes.proof:
We first give the argument for Proposition 93.11 under the pretense that all Ricci flows are smooth, except for possible extinction of components. (Of course this is not the case, but it will allow us to present the main idea of the proof.)

If \( \lambda \left( g\right)  > 0 \) for some metric \( g \) then from (93.2), the Ricci flow starting from \( g \) will become extinct within time \( \frac{3}{{2\lambda }\left( g\right) } \) . Hence Lemma 81.2 applies. Conversely, if \( M \) is a connected sum of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s and metric quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) then \( M \) admits a metric \( g \) of positive scalar curvature. From (93.3), \( \lambda \left( g\right)  > 0 \) .

Now suppose that \( M \) does not admit any metric \( g \) with \( \lambda \left( g\right)  > 0 \) . If \( M \) is a graph manifold then \( M \) volume-collapses with bounded curvature, so (93.3) implies that \( \bar{\lambda } = 0 \) .

Suppose that \( M \) is not a graph manifold. Suppose that we have a given decomposition of \( M \) as a connected sum of a finite collection of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s, metric quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) and some other components, the union of which is denoted by \( {M}^{\prime } \) , and there exists a (possibly disconnected) complete manifold \( N \) with constant sectional curvature \( - \frac{1}{4} \) which can be embedded in \( {M}^{\prime } \) so that the complement (if nonempty) is a graph manifold. Let \( {V}_{hyp} \) denote the hyperbolic volume of \( N \) . We do not assume that the cusps of \( N \) are incompressible in \( {M}^{\prime } \) . For any \( \epsilon  > 0 \) , we claim that there is a metric \( {g}_{\epsilon } \) on \( M \) with \( R \geq   - 6 \cdot  \frac{1}{4} - \epsilon \) and volume \( V\left( {g}_{\epsilon }\right)  \leq  {V}_{hyp} + \epsilon \) . This comes from collapsing the graph manifold pieces, along with the fact that the connected sum operation can be performed while decreasing the scalar curvature arbitrarily little and increasing the volume arbitrarily little. Then (93.3) implies that \( \lambda \left( {g}_{\epsilon }\right) V{\left( {g}_{\epsilon }\right) }^{\frac{2}{3}} \geq   - \frac{3}{2}{V}_{hyp}^{2/3} \) - const. \( \epsilon \) . Thus \( \bar{\lambda } \geq   - \frac{3}{2}{V}_{hyp}^{2/3} \) .

Let \( \widehat{V} \) denote the minimum of \( {V}_{hyp} \) over all such decompositions of \( M \) . (As the set of volumes of complete finite-volume 3-manifolds with constant curvature \( - \frac{1}{4} \) is well-ordered, there is a minimum.) Then \( \bar{\lambda } \geq   - \frac{3}{2}{\widehat{V}}^{2/3} \) .

Next, take an arbitrary metric \( {g}_{0} \) on \( M \) and consider the Ricci flow \( g\left( t\right) \) with initial metric \( {g}_{0} \) . From Sections 90 and 92, there is a nonempty manifold \( N \) with a finite-volume complete metric of constant curvature \( - \frac{1}{4} \) so that for large \( t \) , there is a decomposition of the time- \( t \) manifold \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } = {M}_{1}\left( t\right)  \cup  {M}_{2}\left( t\right) \) where \( {M}_{1}\left( t\right) \) is a graph manifold and \( \left( {{M}_{2}\left( t\right) ,{\left. \frac{1}{t}g\left( t\right) \right| }_{{M}_{2}\left( t\right) }}\right) \) is close to a large piece of \( N \) . As \( N \) has finite volume, a constant function on \( N \) is square-integrable and so inf spec \( \left( {-{\bigtriangleup }_{N}}\right)  = 0 \) . Equivalently,

(93.12)

\[
\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{f \in  {C}_{c}^{\infty }\left( N\right) , f \neq  0}}\frac{{\int }_{N}{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}{\mathrm{{dvol}}}_{N}}{{\int }_{N}{f}^{2}{\mathrm{{dvol}}}_{N}} = 0.
\]

Taking an appropriate test function \( \Phi \) on \( M \) with compact support in \( {M}_{2}\left( t\right) \) gives \( {t\lambda }\left( t\right)  \leq \; - \frac{3}{2} + {\epsilon }_{1}\left( t\right) \) , with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  \infty }}{\epsilon }_{1}\left( t\right)  = 0 \) . In terms of condition (c) of Proposition 93.11, we will think of \( {M}^{\prime } \) as being \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) . From the presence of \( N \) , we know that \( V\left( t\right)  \geq  {t}^{2/3}{V}_{\text{ hyp }}\left( N\right)  - {\epsilon }_{2}\left( t\right) \) , with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  \infty }}{\epsilon }_{2}\left( t\right)  = 0 \) . As we are assuming that the Ricci flow is nonsingular, the monotonicity of \( \lambda \left( t\right) {V}^{2/3}\left( t\right) \) implies that

(93.13)

\[
\lambda \left( {g}_{0}\right) {V}^{2/3}\left( {g}_{0}\right)  \leq   - \frac{3}{2}{V}_{\text{ hyp }}{\left( N\right) }^{2/3} \leq   - \frac{3}{2}{\widehat{V}}^{2/3}.
\]

Thus \( \bar{\lambda } \leq   - \frac{3}{2}{\widehat{V}}^{2/3} \) .

This shows that \( \bar{\lambda } =  - \frac{3}{2}{\widehat{V}}^{2/3} \) . Now take a decomposition of \( M \) as in condition (c) of Proposition 93.11, with \( {V}_{hyp}\left( N\right)  = \widehat{V} \) . We claim that the cuspidal 2-tori of \( N \) are incompressible in \( {M}^{\prime } \) . If not then there would be a metric \( g \) on \( M \) with \( R\left( g\right)  \geq   - \frac{3}{2} \) and vol \( \left( g\right)  < {V}_{hyp}\left( N\right) \) [3, Pf. of Theorem 2.9]. Using (93.3), one would obtain a contradiction to the fact that \( \bar{\lambda } =  - \frac{3}{2}{V}_{hyp}{\left( N\right) }^{2/3} \) .

To handle the behaviour of \( \lambda \left( t\right) {V}^{\frac{2}{3}}\left( t\right) \) under Ricci flows with surgery, we first state a couple of general facts about Schrödinger operators.

nodes.content:
Lemma 93.14. Given a closed Riemannian manifold \( M \) , let \( X \) be a codimension-0 submanifold-with-boundary of \( M \) . Given \( R \in  {C}^{\infty }\left( M\right) \) , let \( {\lambda }_{M} \) be the lowest eigenvalue of \( - 4\bigtriangleup  + R \) on \( M \) , with corresponding eigenfunction \( \psi \) . Let \( {\lambda }_{X} \) be the lowest eigenvalue of the corresponding operator on \( X \) , with Dirichlet boundary conditions, and similarly for \( {\lambda }_{M - \operatorname{int}\left( X\right) } \) . Then for all \( \eta  \in  {C}_{c}^{\infty }\left( {\operatorname{int}\left( X\right) }\right) \) , we have

(93.15)

\[
{\lambda }_{M} \leq  \min \left( {{\lambda }_{X},{\lambda }_{M - \operatorname{int}\left( X\right) }}\right)
\]

and

(93.16)

\[
{\lambda }_{X} \leq  {\lambda }_{M} + 4\frac{{\int }_{M}{\left| \nabla \eta \right| }^{2}{\psi }^{2}{dV}}{{\int }_{M}{\eta }^{2}{\psi }^{2}{dV}}.
\]

Equation (93.15) follows from Dirichlet-Neumann bracketing [55, Chapter XIII.15]. To prove (93.16), \( {\eta \psi } \) is supported in \( \operatorname{int}\left( X\right) \) and so

(93.17)

\[
{\lambda }_{X} \leq  \frac{{\int }_{M}\left( {4{\left| \nabla \left( \eta \psi \right) \right| }^{2} + R{\eta }^{2}{\psi }^{2}}\right) {dV}}{{\int }_{M}{\eta }^{2}{\psi }^{2}{dV}}
\]

\[
= \frac{{\int }_{M}\left( {4{\left| \nabla \eta \right| }^{2}{\psi }^{2} + 8\langle \nabla \eta ,\nabla \psi \rangle {\eta \psi } + 4{\eta }^{2}{\left| \nabla \psi \right| }^{2} + R{\eta }^{2}{\psi }^{2}}\right) {dV}}{{\int }_{M}{\eta }^{2}{\psi }^{2}{dV}}.
\]

As \( - {4\Delta \psi } + {R\psi } = {\lambda }_{M}\psi \) , we have

(93.18)

\[
{\lambda }_{M}{\int }_{M}{\eta }^{2}{\psi }^{2}{dV} =  - 4{\int }_{M}{\eta }^{2}\psi \bigtriangleup {\psi dV} + {\int }_{M}R{\eta }^{2}{\psi }^{2}{dV}
\]

\[
= 4{\int }_{M}\left\langle  {\nabla \left( {{\eta }^{2}\psi }\right) ,\nabla \psi }\right\rangle  {dV} + {\int }_{M}R{\eta }^{2}{\psi }^{2}{dV}
\]

\[
= 4{\int }_{M}{\eta }^{2}{\left| \nabla \psi \right| }^{2}{dV} + 8{\int }_{M}\langle \nabla \eta ,\nabla \psi \rangle {\eta \psi dv} + {\int }_{M}R{\eta }^{2}{\psi }^{2}{dV}
\]

Equation (93.16) follows.

Lemma 93.19. With the notation of Lemma 93.14, given a nonnegative function \( \phi  \in \; {C}^{\infty }\left( M\right) \) , suppose that \( f \in  {C}^{\infty }\left( M\right) \) satisfies

(93.20)

\[
4{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} \leq  R - {\lambda }_{M} - c
\]

on \( \operatorname{supp}\left( \phi \right) \) , for some \( c > 0 \) . Then

(93.21)

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{e}^{f}\phi \psi \end{Vmatrix}}_{2} \leq  4{c}^{-1}\left( {{\begin{Vmatrix}{e}^{f}\bigtriangleup \phi \end{Vmatrix}}_{\infty } + {\begin{Vmatrix}{e}^{f}\nabla \phi \end{Vmatrix}}_{\infty }{\left( {\lambda }_{M} - \min R\right) }^{1/2}}\right) \parallel \psi {\parallel }_{2}.
\]

nodes.proof:
Put \( H =  - {4\Delta } + R \) . By assumption,

(93.22)

\[
\phi \left( {R - 4{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} - {\lambda }_{M}}\right) \phi  \geq  c{\phi }^{2}
\]

and so there is an inequality of operators on \( {L}^{2}\left( M\right) \) :

(93.23)

\[
\phi \left( {H - 4{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} - {\lambda }_{M}}\right) \phi  = {4\phi }{d}^{ * }{d\phi } + \phi \left( {R - 4{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} - {\lambda }_{M}}\right) \phi  \geq  c{\phi }^{2}.
\]

In particular,

(93.24)

\[
{\int }_{M}{e}^{f}{\psi \phi }\left( {H - 4{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} - {\lambda }_{M}}\right) \phi {e}^{f}{\psi dV} \geq  c{\int }_{M}{\phi }^{2}{e}^{2f}{\psi }^{2}{dV}.
\]

For \( \rho  \in  {C}^{\infty }\left( M\right) \) ,

(93.25)

\[
{e}^{f}H\left( {{e}^{-f}\rho }\right)  = {H\rho } + 4\nabla  \cdot  \left( {\left( {\nabla f}\right) \rho }\right)  + 4\langle \nabla f,\nabla \rho \rangle  - 4{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}\rho
\]

and so

(93.26)

\[
{\int }_{M}\rho {e}^{f}H\left( {{e}^{-f}\rho }\right) {dV} = {\int }_{M}\rho \left( {H - 4{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right) {\rho dV}.
\]

Taking \( \rho  = {e}^{f}{\phi \psi } \) gives

(93.27)

\[
{\int }_{M}{e}^{2f}{\phi \psi H}\left( {\phi \psi }\right) {dV} = {\int }_{M}{e}^{f}{\phi \psi }\left( {H - 4{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right) {e}^{f}{\phi \psi dV}.
\]

From (93.24) and (93.27),

(93.28)

\[
c{\begin{Vmatrix}{e}^{f}\phi \psi \end{Vmatrix}}_{2}^{2} \leq  {\int }_{M}{e}^{2f}{\phi \psi }\left( {H - {\lambda }_{M}}\right) \left( {\phi \psi }\right) {dV} = {\int }_{M}{e}^{2f}{\phi \psi }\left\lbrack  {H,\phi }\right\rbrack  {\psi dV} = {\left\langle  {e}^{f}\phi \psi ,{e}^{f}\left\lbrack  H,\phi \right\rbrack  \psi \right\rangle  }_{2}.
\]

Thus

(93.29)

\[
c{\begin{Vmatrix}{e}^{f}\phi \psi \end{Vmatrix}}_{2} \leq  {\begin{Vmatrix}{e}^{f}\left\lbrack  H,\phi \right\rbrack  \psi \end{Vmatrix}}_{2}.
\]

Now

(93.30)

\[
{e}^{f}\left\lbrack  {H,\phi }\right\rbrack  \psi  =  - 4{e}^{f}\left( {\bigtriangleup \phi }\right) \psi  - 8{e}^{f}\langle \nabla \phi ,\nabla \psi \rangle .
\]

Then

(93.31)

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{e}^{f}\left\lbrack  H,\phi \right\rbrack  \psi \end{Vmatrix}}_{2} \leq  4{\begin{Vmatrix}{e}^{f}\bigtriangleup \phi \end{Vmatrix}}_{\infty }\parallel \psi {\parallel }_{2} + 8{\begin{Vmatrix}{e}^{f}\nabla \phi \end{Vmatrix}}_{\infty }\parallel \nabla \psi {\parallel }_{2}.
\]

Finally,

(93.32)

\[
4\parallel \nabla \psi {\parallel }_{2}^{2} = {\int }_{M}\left( {{\lambda }_{M} - R}\right) {\psi }^{2}{dV}
\]

and so

(93.33)

\[
2\parallel \nabla \psi {\parallel }_{2} \leq  {\left( {\lambda }_{M} - \min R\right) }^{1/2}\parallel \psi {\parallel }_{2}.
\]

This proves the lemma.

Theorem A.1. Let \( M \) be a closed manifold. Let \( \{ g\left( t\right) {\} }_{t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack  } \) be a smooth one-parameter family of Riemannian metrics on \( M \) and let \( \{ X\left( t\right) {\} }_{t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack  } \) be a smooth one-parameter family of vector fields on \( M \) . Let \( F : \mathbb{R} \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) be a Lipschitz function. Suppose that \( u = u\left( {x, t}\right) \) is \( {C}^{2} \) -regular in \( x,{C}^{1} \) -regular in \( t \) and

(A.2)

\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} \leq  {\bigtriangleup }_{g\left( t\right) }u + X\left( t\right) u + F\left( {u, t}\right) .
\]

Let \( \phi  : \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) be the solution of \( \frac{d\phi }{dt} = F\left( {\phi \left( t\right) , t}\right) \) with \( \phi \left( 0\right)  = \alpha \) . If \( u\left( {\cdot ,0}\right)  \leq  \alpha \) then \( u\left( {\cdot , t}\right)  \leq  \phi \left( t\right) \) for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack  . \)

Let \( \{ g\left( t\right) {\} }_{t \in  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack  } \) be a smooth one-parameter family of Riemannian metrics on \( M \) with nonnegative curvature operator that satisfy the Ricci flow equation. Then for each \( t \in  (0, T\rbrack \) , the image \( \operatorname{Im}\left( {\operatorname{Rm}}_{g\left( t\right) }\right) \) of the curvature operator is a smooth subbundle of \( {\Lambda }^{2}\left( {{T}^{ * }M}\right) \) which is invariant under spatial parallel translation. There is a sequence of times \( 0 = {t}_{0} < {t}_{1} < \ldots  < {t}_{k} = T \) such that for each \( 1 \leq  i \leq  k \) , \( \operatorname{Im}\left( {\operatorname{Rm}}_{g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a Lie subalgebra of \( {\Lambda }^{2}\left( {{T}_{m}^{ * }M}\right)  \cong  o\left( n\right) \) that is independent of \( t \) for \( t \in  \left( {{t}_{i - 1},{t}_{i}}\right\rbrack \) . Furthermore, \( \operatorname{Im}\left( {\operatorname{Rm}}_{g\left( {t}_{i}\right) }\right)  \subset  \operatorname{Im}\left( {\operatorname{Rm}}_{g\left( {t}_{i + 1}\right) }\right) \) .

nodes.title: C. RICCI SOLITONS
nodes.document_title: Bruce Kleiner and John Lott - Notes on Perelman's Papers

nodes.label: Remark C-extra-1
nodes.document_title: Bruce Kleiner and John Lott - Notes on Perelman's Papers
nodes.content:
## APPENDIX C. RICCI SOLITONS

Let \( \{ V\left( t\right) \} \) be a time-dependent family of vector fields on a manifold \( M \) . The solution to the equation

(C.1)

\[
\frac{dg}{dt} = {\mathcal{L}}_{V\left( t\right) }g
\]

is

(C.2)

\[
g\left( t\right)  = {\phi }^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }g\left( {t}_{0}\right)
\]

where \( \{ \phi \left( t\right) \} \) is the 1-parameter group of diffeomorphisms generated by \( - V \) , normalized by \( \phi \left( {t}_{0}\right)  = \) Id. (If \( M \) is noncompact then we assume that \( V \) can be integrated. The reason for the funny signs is that if a 1-parameter family of diffeomorphisms \( \eta \left( t\right) \) is generated by vector fields \( W\left( t\right) \) then \( {\left. {\mathcal{L}}_{W\left( t\right) } = {\eta }^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }\frac{{d\eta }{\left( t + \epsilon \right) }^{ * }}{d\epsilon }\right| }_{\epsilon  = 0} =  - {\left. \frac{d{\eta }^{-1}{\left( t + \epsilon \right) }^{ * }}{d\epsilon }\right| }_{\epsilon  = 0}\eta {\left( t\right) }^{ * } \) .)

The equation for a steady soliton is

(C.3)

\[
2\operatorname{Ric} + {\mathcal{L}}_{V}g = 0,
\]

where \( V \) is a time-independent vector field. The corresponding Ricci flow is given by

(C.4)

\[
g\left( t\right)  = {\phi }^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }g\left( {t}_{0}\right) ,
\]

where \( \{ \phi \left( t\right) \} \) is the 1-parameter group of diffeomorphisms generated by \( - V \) . (Of course, in this case \( \left\{  {{\phi }^{-1}\left( t\right) }\right\} \) is the 1-parameter group of diffeomorphisms generated by \( V \) .)

A gradient steady soliton satisfies the equations

(C.5)

\[
\frac{\partial {g}_{ij}}{\partial t} =  - 2{R}_{ij} = 2{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f
\]

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}
\]

It follows from (C.5) that

(C.6)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {{g}^{ij}{\partial }_{j}f}\right)  = 2{R}^{ij}{\nabla }_{j}f + {g}^{ij}{\nabla }_{j}{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} =  - 2\left( {{\nabla }^{i}{\nabla }^{j}f}\right) {\nabla }_{j}f + {\nabla }^{i}{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} = 0,
\]

showing that \( V = \nabla f \) is indeed constant in \( t \) . The solution to (C.5) is

(C.7)

\[
g\left( t\right)  = {\phi }^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }g\left( {t}_{0}\right) ,
\]

\[
f\left( t\right)  = {\phi }^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }f\left( {t}_{0}\right) .
\]

Conversely, given a metric \( \widehat{g} \) and a function \( \widehat{f} \) satisfying

(C.8)

\[
{\widehat{R}}_{ij} + {\widehat{\nabla }}_{i}{\widehat{\nabla }}_{j}\widehat{f} = 0
\]

put \( V = \widehat{\nabla }\widehat{f} \) . If we define \( g\left( t\right) \) and \( f\left( t\right) \) by

(C.9)

\[
g\left( t\right)  = {\phi }^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }\widehat{g}
\]

\[
f\left( t\right)  = {\phi }^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }\widehat{f}
\]

then they satisfy (C.5).

A solution to (C.5) satisfies

(C.10)

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} - \bigtriangleup f - R
\]

or

(C.11)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{e}^{-f} =  - \bigtriangleup {e}^{-f} + R{e}^{-f}.
\]

This perhaps motivates Perelman's use of the backward heat equation (5.23).

A shrinking soliton lives on a time interval \( \left( {-\infty , T}\right) \) . For convenience, we take \( T = 0 \) . Then the equation is

(C.12)

\[
2\operatorname{Ric} + {\mathcal{L}}_{V}g + \frac{g}{t} = 0.
\]

The vector field \( V = V\left( t\right) \) satisfies \( V\left( t\right)  =  - \frac{1}{t}V\left( {-1}\right) \) . The corresponding Ricci flow is given by

(C.13)

\[
g\left( t\right)  =  - t{\phi }^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }g\left( {-1}\right) ,
\]

where \( \{ \phi \left( t\right) \} \) is the 1-parameter group of diffeomorphisms generated by \( - V \) , normalized by \( \phi \left( {-1}\right)  = \) Id.

A gradient shrinking soliton satisfies the equations

(C.14)

\[
\frac{\partial {g}_{ij}}{\partial t} =  - 2{R}_{ij} = 2{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f + \frac{{g}_{ij}}{t}
\]

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}
\]

It follows from (C.14) that \( V = \nabla f \) satisfies \( V\left( t\right)  =  - \frac{1}{t}V\left( {-1}\right) \) . The solution to (C.14) is

(C.15)

\[
g\left( t\right)  =  - t{\phi }^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }g\left( {-1}\right)
\]

\[
f\left( t\right)  = {\phi }^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }f\left( {-1}\right) .
\]

Conversely, given a metric \( \widehat{g} \) and a function \( \widehat{f} \) satisfying

(C.16)

\[
{\widehat{R}}_{ij} + {\widehat{\nabla }}_{i}{\widehat{\nabla }}_{j}\widehat{f} - \frac{1}{2}\widehat{g} = 0,
\]

put \( V\left( t\right)  =  - \frac{1}{t}\widehat{\nabla }\widehat{f} \) . If we define \( g\left( t\right) \) and \( f\left( t\right) \) by

(C.17)

\[
g\left( t\right)  =  - t{\phi }^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }\widehat{g}
\]

\[
f\left( t\right)  = {\phi }^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }\widehat{f}
\]

then they satisfy (C.14).

An expanding soliton lives on a time interval \( \left( {T,\infty }\right) \) . For convenience, we take \( T = 0 \) . Then the equation is

(C.18)

\[
2\operatorname{Ric} + {\mathcal{L}}_{V}g + \frac{g}{t} = 0.
\]

The vector field \( V = V\left( t\right) \) satisfies \( V\left( t\right)  = \frac{1}{t}V\left( 1\right) \) . The corresponding Ricci flow is given by

(C.19)

\[
g\left( t\right)  = t{\phi }^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }g\left( 1\right) ,
\]

where \( \{ \phi \left( t\right) \} \) is the 1-parameter group of diffeomorphisms generated by \( - V \) , normalized by \( \phi \left( 1\right)  = \) Id.

A gradient expanding soliton satisfies the equations

(C.20)

\[
\frac{\partial {g}_{ij}}{\partial t} =  - 2{R}_{ij} = 2{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f + \frac{{g}_{ij}}{t}
\]

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}
\]

It follows from (C.20) that \( V = \nabla f \) satisfies \( V\left( t\right)  = \frac{1}{t}V\left( 1\right) \) . The solution to (C.20) is

(C.21)

\[
g\left( t\right)  = t{\phi }^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }g\left( 1\right)
\]

\[
f\left( t\right)  = {\phi }^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }f\left( 1\right)
\]

Conversely, given a metric \( \widehat{g} \) and a function \( \widehat{f} \) satisfying

(C.22)

\[
{\widehat{R}}_{ij} + {\widehat{\nabla }}_{i}{\widehat{\nabla }}_{j}\widehat{f} + \frac{1}{2}\widehat{g} = 0,
\]

put \( V\left( t\right)  = \frac{1}{t}\widehat{\nabla }\widehat{f} \) . If we define \( g\left( t\right) \) and \( f\left( t\right) \) by

(C.23)

\[
g\left( t\right)  = t{\phi }^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }\widehat{g}
\]

\[
f\left( t\right)  = {\phi }^{-1}{\left( t\right) }^{ * }\widehat{f}
\]

then they satisfy (C.20).

Obvious examples of solitons are given by Einstein metrics, with \( V = 0 \) . Any steady or expanding soliton on a closed manifold comes from an Einstein metric. Other examples of solitons (see [22, Chapter 2]) are :

1. (Gradient steady soliton) The cigar soliton on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \) and the Bryant soliton on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) .

2. (Gradient shrinking soliton) Flat \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) with \( f =  - \frac{{\left| x\right| }^{2}}{4t} \) .

3. (Gradient shrinking soliton) The shrinking cylinder \( \mathbb{R} \times  {S}^{n - 1} \) with \( f =  - \frac{{x}^{2}}{4t} \) , where \( x \) is the coordinate on \( \mathbb{R} \) .

4. (Gradient shrinking soliton) The Koiso soliton on \( \mathbb{C}{P}^{2}\# \overline{\mathbb{C}{P}^{2}} \) .

nodes.content:
Theorem E.1. Given \( {r}_{0} \in  (0,\infty \rbrack \) , let \( {\left\{  {g}_{i}\left( t\right) \right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) be a sequence of Ricci flow solutions on connected pointed manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{i},{m}_{i}}\right) \) , defined for \( t \in  \left( {A, B}\right) \) with \( - \infty  \leq  A < 0 < B \leq  \infty \) . We assume that for all \( i,{M}_{i} \) equals the time-zero ball \( {B}_{0}\left( {{m}_{i},{r}_{0}}\right) \) and for all \( r \in  \left( {0,{r}_{0}}\right) \) , \( \overline{{B}_{0}\left( {{m}_{i}, r}\right) } \) is compact. Suppose that the following two conditions are satisfied :

1. For each \( r \in  \left( {0,{r}_{0}}\right) \) and each compact interval \( I \subset  \left( {A, B}\right) \) , there is an \( {N}_{r, I} < \infty \) so that for all \( t \in  I \) and all \( i,\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{B}_{0}\left( {{m}_{i}, r}\right)  \times  I}}\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {g}_{i}\right) }\right|  \leq  {N}_{r, I} \) , and

2. The time-0 injectivity radii \( {\left\{  \operatorname{inj}\left( {g}_{i}\left( 0\right) \right) \left( {m}_{i}\right) \right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) are uniformly bounded below by a positive number.

Then after passing to a subsequence, the solutions converge smoothly to a Ricci flow solution \( {g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) \) on a connected pointed manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{m}_{\infty }}\right) \) , defined for \( t \in  \left( {A, B}\right) \) , for which \( {M}_{\infty } = {B}_{0}\left( {{m}_{\infty },{r}_{0}}\right) \) and \( \overline{{B}_{0}\left( {{m}_{\infty }, r}\right) } \) is compact for all \( r \in  \left( {0,{r}_{0}}\right) \) . That is, for any compact interval \( I \subset  \left( {A, B}\right) \) and any \( r < {r}_{0} \) , there are pointed time-independent diffeomorphisms \( {\phi }_{r, i} : {B}_{0}\left( {{m}_{\infty }, r}\right)  \rightarrow  {B}_{0}\left( {{m}_{i}, r}\right) \) so that \( {\left\{  {\left( {\phi }_{r, i} \times  \mathrm{{Id}}\right) }^{ * }{g}_{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) converges smoothly to \( {g}_{\infty } \) on \( {B}_{0}\left( {{m}_{\infty }, r}\right)  \times  I \) .

Corollary E.2. Let \( {\left\{  {g}_{i}\left( t\right) \right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) be a sequence of Ricci flow solutions on connected pointed manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{i},{m}_{i}}\right) \) , defined for \( t \in  (A,0\rbrack \) with \( - \infty  \leq  A < 0 \) . Suppose that each time-zero slice \( \left( {{M}_{i},{m}_{i},{g}_{i}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is complete. Suppose that the following three conditions are satisfied :

1. For each \( r \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) and each compact interval \( I \subset  (A,0\rbrack \) , there is an \( {N}_{r, I} < \infty \) so that for all \( i \) , \( \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{B}_{0}\left( {{m}_{i}, r}\right)  \times  I}}\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {g}_{i}\right) }\right|  \leq  {N}_{r, I} \) ,

2. For each compact interval \( I \subset  (A,0\rbrack \) , there is some \( {N}_{I}^{\prime } \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) with the following property : for each \( r \in  \left( {0,\infty }\right) \) , there is some \( {J}_{r, I} \in  {\mathbb{Z}}^{ + } \) so that whenever \( i \geq  {J}_{r, I} \) , we have \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( {g}_{i}\right)  \geq   - {N}_{I}^{\prime }{g}_{i} \) on \( {B}_{0}\left( {{m}_{i}, r}\right)  \times  I \) , and

3. The time-0 injectivity radii \( {\left\{  \operatorname{inj}\left( {g}_{i}\left( 0\right) \right) \left( {m}_{i}\right) \right\}  }_{i = 1}^{\infty } \) are uniformly bounded below by a positive number.

Then after passing to a subsequence, the solutions converge smoothly to a Ricci flow solution \( {g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) \) on a connected pointed manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{m}_{\infty }}\right) \) , defined for \( t \in  (A,0\rbrack \) , with complete time slices.

nodes.proof:
Let \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{m}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be constructed as in Theorem E.1. Then on each compact time interval \( I \subset  (A,0\rbrack \) , we have \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( {g}_{\infty }\right)  \geq   - {N}_{I}^{\prime }{g}_{\infty } \) . By (27.5), if \( t \in  I \) then for any \( {m}_{0},{m}_{1} \in  {M}_{\infty } \) , we have

(E.3)

\[
{\operatorname{dist}}_{t}\left( {{m}_{0},{m}_{1}}\right)  \geq  {e}^{-{N}_{I}^{\prime }t}{\operatorname{dist}}_{0}\left( {{m}_{0},{m}_{1}}\right) .
\]

Suppose that \( {\left\{  {m}_{j}\right\}  }_{j = 1}^{\infty } \) is a Cauchy sequence in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) . From (E.3), it is also a Cauchy sequence in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) , and so has a subsequence, which we relabel as \( {\left\{  {m}_{j}\right\}  }_{j = 1}^{\infty } \) , that converges to some \( {m}^{\prime } \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) . nodes.content:
We first recall the statement of the matrix Harnack inequality. Put

(F.1)

\[
{P}_{abc} = {\nabla }_{a}{R}_{bc} - {\nabla }_{b}{R}_{ac}
\]

\[
{M}_{ab} = \bigtriangleup {R}_{ab} - \frac{1}{2}{\nabla }_{a}{\nabla }_{b}R + 2{R}_{acbd}{R}_{cd} - {R}_{ac}{R}_{bc} + \frac{{R}_{ab}}{2t}.
\]

Given a 2-form \( U \) and a 1-form \( W \) , put

(F.2)

\[
Z\left( {U, W}\right)  = {M}_{ab}{W}_{a}{W}_{b} + 2{P}_{abc}{U}_{ab}{W}_{c} + {R}_{abcd}{U}_{ab}{U}_{cd}.
\]

nodes.content: Suppose that we have a Ricci flow for \( t > 0 \) on a complete manifold with bounded curvature on each compact time interval and nonnegative curvature operator. \]

nodes.content:
In the rest of this section we assume that the solution is defined for all \( t \in  \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) . Changing the origin point of time, we have

(F.10)

\[
{R}_{t} + \frac{1}{t - {t}_{0}}R + 2\langle \nabla R, X\rangle  + 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  \geq  0
\]

whenever \( {t}_{0} \leq  t \) . Taking \( {t}_{0} \rightarrow   - \infty \) gives

(F.11)

\[
{R}_{t} + 2\langle \nabla R, X\rangle  + 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  \geq  0
\]

In particular, taking \( X = 0 \) shows that the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in \( t \) for any ancient solution with nonnegative curvature operator, assuming again that the metric is complete on each time slice with bounded curvature on each compact time interval. More generally,

(F.12)

\[
0 \leq  {R}_{t} + 2\langle \nabla R, X\rangle  + 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  \leq  {R}_{t} + 2\langle \nabla R, X\rangle  + {2R}\langle X, X\rangle .
\]

If \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {{t}_{1},{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) is a curve parametrized by \( s \) then taking \( X = \frac{1}{2}\frac{d\gamma }{ds} \) gives

(F.13)

\[
\frac{{dR}\left( {\gamma \left( s\right) , s}\right) }{ds} = {R}_{t}\left( {\gamma \left( s\right) , s}\right)  + \left\langle  {\frac{d\gamma }{ds},\nabla R}\right\rangle   \geq   - \frac{1}{2}R\left\langle  {\frac{d\gamma }{ds},\frac{d\gamma }{ds}}\right\rangle  .
\]

Integrating \( \frac{d\ln R\left( {\gamma \left( s\right) , s}\right) }{ds} \) with respect to \( s \) and using the fact that \( g\left( t\right) \) is nonincreasing in \( t \) gives

(F.14)

\[
R\left( {{x}_{2},{t}_{2}}\right)  \geq  \exp \left( {-\frac{{d}_{{t}_{1}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{1},{x}_{2}}\right) }{2\left( {{t}_{2} - {t}_{1}}\right) }}\right) R\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right) .
\]

whenever \( {t}_{1} < {t}_{2} \) and \( {x}_{1},{x}_{2} \in  M \) . (If \( n = 2 \) then one can replace \( \frac{{d}_{{t}_{1}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{1},{x}_{2}}\right) }{2\left( {{t}_{2} - {t}_{1}}\right) } \) by \( \frac{{d}_{{t}_{1}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{1},{x}_{2}}\right) }{4\left( {{t}_{2} - {t}_{1}}\right) } \) .) In particular, if \( R\left( {{x}_{2},{t}_{2}}\right)  = 0 \) for some \( \left( {{x}_{2},{t}_{2}}\right) \) then \( g\left( t\right) \) must be flat for all \( t \) .

nodes.label: Conjecture I-extra-1
nodes.document_title: Bruce Kleiner and John Lott - Notes on Perelman's Papers
nodes.section_title: I. STATEMENT OF THE GEOMETRIZATION CONJECTURE
nodes.content:
Let \( M \) be a connected orientable closed \( ( = \) compact boundaryless) 3-manifold. One formulation of the geometrization conjecture says that \( M \) is the connected sum of closed 3-manifolds \( {\left\{  {M}_{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{n} \) , each of which admits a codimension-0 compact submanifold-with-boundary \( {G}_{i} \) so that

- \( {G}_{i} \) is a graph manifold

- \( {M}_{i} - {G}_{i} \) is hyperbolic, i.e. admits a complete Riemannian metric with constant negative sectional curvature and finite volume

- Each component \( T \) of \( \partial {G}_{i} \) is an incompressible torus in \( {M}_{i} \) , i.e. with respect to a basepoint \( t \in  T \) , the induced map \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {T, t}\right)  \rightarrow  {\pi }_{1}\left( {{M}_{i}, t}\right) \) is injective.

We allow \( {G}_{i} = \varnothing \) or \( {G}_{i} = {M}_{i} \) .

nodes.document_title: Bruce Kleiner and John Lott - Notes on Perelman's Papers
nodes.section_title: I. STATEMENT OF THE GEOMETRIZATION CONJECTURE
nodes.content: The definition is as follows. One takes a collection \( {\left\{  {P}_{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{N} \) of pairs of pants (i.e. closed 2-disks with two balls removed) and a collection of closed 2-disks \( {\left\{  {D}_{j}^{2}\right\}  }_{j = 1}^{{N}^{\prime }} \) . The 3-manifolds \( {\left\{  {S}^{1} \times  {P}_{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{N} \cup  {\left\{  {S}^{1} \times  {D}_{j}^{2}\right\}  }_{j = 1}^{{N}^{\prime }} \) have toral boundary components. One takes an even number of these tori, matches them in pairs by homeomorphisms, and glues \( {\left\{  {S}^{1} \times  {P}_{i}\right\}  }_{i = 1}^{N} \cup  {\left\{  {S}^{1} \times  {D}_{j}^{2}\right\}  }_{j = 1}^{{N}^{\prime }} \) by these homeomorphisms. The resulting 3-manifold \( G \) is a graph manifold, and all graph manifolds arise in this way. We will assume that the gluing homeomorphisms are such that \( G \) is orientable. Clearly the boundary of \( G \) , if nonempty, is a disjoint union of tori. It is also clear that the result of gluing two graph manifolds along some collection of boundary tori is a graph manifold. The connected sum of two 3-manifolds is a graph manifold if and only if each factor is a graph manifold [42, Proposition 2.4.3].

nodes.content: 1.2. Proposition. Suppose that the gradient flow for \( {\mathcal{F}}^{m} \) exists for \( t \in \; \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . Then at \( t = 0 \) we have \( {\mathcal{F}}^{m} \leq  \frac{n}{2T}{\int }_{M}{dm} \) .
nodes.content_excerpt: 1.2. Proposition. Suppose that the gradient flow for \( {\mathcal{F}}^{m} \) exists for \( t \in \; \left\lbrack {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . Then at \( t = 0 \) we have \( {\mathcal{F}}^{m} \leq \frac{n}{2T}{\int }_{M}{dm} \) .

nodes.proof:
We may assume \( {\int }_{M}{dm} = 1 \) . The evolution equations for the gradient flow of \( {\mathcal{F}}^{m} \) are

\[
{\left( {g}_{ij}\right) }_{t} =  - 2\left( {{R}_{ij} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f}\right) ,\;{f}_{t} =  - R - \bigtriangleup f, \tag{1.1}
\]

and \( {\mathcal{F}}^{m} \) satisfies

\[
{\mathcal{F}}_{t}^{m} = 2\int {\left| {R}_{ij} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f\right| }^{2}{dm} \tag{1.2}
\]

Modifying by an appropriate diffeomorphism, we get evolution equations

\[
{\left( {g}_{ij}\right) }_{t} =  - 2{R}_{ij},{f}_{t} =  - \bigtriangleup f + {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} - R, \tag{1.3}
\]

and retain (1.2) in the form

\[
{\mathcal{F}}_{t} = 2\int {\left| {R}_{ij} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f\right| }^{2}{e}^{-f}{dV} \tag{1.4}
\]

Now we compute

\[
{\mathcal{F}}_{t} \geq  \frac{2}{n}\int {\left( R + \bigtriangleup f\right) }^{2}{e}^{-f}{dV} \geq  \frac{2}{n}{\left( \int \left( R + \bigtriangleup f\right) {e}^{-f}dV\right) }^{2} = \frac{2}{n}{\mathcal{F}}^{2},
\]

and the proposition follows.

nodes.content: 2.2. Define \( \lambda \left( {g}_{ij}\right)  = \inf \mathcal{F}\left( {{g}_{ij}, f}\right) \) , where infimum is taken over all smooth \( f \) , satisfying \( {\int }_{M}{e}^{-f}{dV} = 1 \) . Clearly, \( \lambda \left( {g}_{ij}\right) \) is just the lowest eigenvalue of the operator \( - 4\bigtriangleup  + R \) . Then formula (1.4) implies that \( \lambda \left( {{g}_{ij}\left( t\right) }\right) \) is nondecreasing in \( t \) , and moreover, if \( \lambda \left( {t}_{1}\right)  = \lambda \left( {t}_{2}\right) \) , then for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{1},{t}_{2}}\right\rbrack \) we have \( {R}_{ij} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f = \) 0 for \( f \) which minimizes \( \mathcal{F} \) . Thus a steady breather is necessarily a steady soliton.

3.1. In order to handle the shrinking case when \( \lambda  > 0 \) , we need to replace our functional \( \mathcal{F} \) by its generalization, which contains explicit insertions of the scale parameter, to be denoted by \( \tau \) . Thus consider the functional

\[
\mathcal{W}\left( {{g}_{ij}, f,\tau }\right)  = {\int }_{M}\left\lbrack  {\tau \left( {{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + R}\right)  + f - n}\right\rbrack  {\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}{e}^{-f}{dV}, \tag{3.1}
\]

restricted to \( f \) satisfying

\[
{\int }_{M}{\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}{e}^{-f}{dV} = 1, \tag{3.2}
\]

\( \tau  > 0 \) . Clearly \( \mathcal{W} \) is invariant under simultaneous scaling of \( \tau \) and \( {g}_{ij} \) . The evolution equations, generalizing (1.3) are

\[
{\left( {g}_{ij}\right) }_{t} =  - 2{R}_{ij},{f}_{t} =  - \bigtriangleup f + {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} - R + \frac{n}{2\tau },{\tau }_{t} =  - 1 \tag{3.3}
\]

The evolution equation for \( f \) can also be written as follows: \( {\square }^{ * }u = 0 \) , where \( u = {\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}{e}^{-f} \) , and \( {\square }^{ * } =  - \partial /\partial t - \bigtriangleup  + R \) is the conjugate heat operator. Now a routine computation gives

\[
d\mathcal{W}/{dt} = {\int }_{M}{2\tau }{\left| {R}_{ij} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f - \frac{1}{2\tau }{g}_{ij}\right| }^{2}{\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}{e}^{-f}{dV}. \tag{3.4}
\]

Therefore, if we let \( \mu \left( {{g}_{ij},\tau }\right)  = \inf \mathcal{W}\left( {{g}_{ij}, f,\tau }\right) \) over smooth \( f \) satisfying (3.2), and \( \nu \left( {g}_{ij}\right)  = \inf \mu \left( {{g}_{ij},\tau }\right) \) over all positive \( \tau \) , then \( \nu \left( {{g}_{ij}\left( t\right) }\right) \) is nondecreasing along the Ricci flow. It is not hard to show that in the definition of \( \mu \) there always exists a smooth minimizer \( f \) (on a closed \( M \) ). nodes.proof:
(sketch) Assume that \( \bar{\tau } > 0 \) is so small that Ricci flow starting from \( {g}_{ij} \) exists on \( \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{\tau }}\right\rbrack \) . Let \( u = {\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}{e}^{-f} \) be the solution of the conjugate heat equation, starting from a \( \delta \) -function at \( t = \bar{\tau },\tau \left( t\right)  = \; \bar{\tau } - t \) . Then \( \mathcal{W}\left( {{g}_{ij}\left( t\right) , f\left( t\right) ,\tau \left( t\right) }\right) \) tends to zero as \( t \) tends to \( \bar{\tau } \) , and therefore \( \mu \left( {{g}_{ij},\bar{\tau }}\right)  \leq  \mathcal{W}\left( {{g}_{ij}\left( 0\right) , f\left( 0\right) ,\tau \left( 0\right) }\right)  < 0 \) by (3.4).

Now let \( \tau  \rightarrow  0 \) and assume that \( {f}^{\tau } \) are the minimizers, such that

\[
\mathcal{W}\left( {\frac{1}{2}{\tau }^{-1}{g}_{ij},{f}^{\tau },\frac{1}{2}}\right)  = \mathcal{W}\left( {{g}_{ij},{f}^{\tau },\tau }\right)  = \mu \left( {{g}_{ij},\tau }\right)  \leq  c < 0.
\]

The metrics \( \frac{1}{2}{\tau }^{-1}{g}_{ij} \) "converge" to the euclidean metric, and if we could extract a converging subsequence from \( {f}^{\tau } \) , we would get a function \( f \) on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) , such that \( {\int }_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}{\left( 2\pi \right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}{e}^{-f}{dx} = 1 \) and

\[
{\int }_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}\left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2}{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + f - n}\right\rbrack  {\left( 2\pi \right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}{e}^{-f}{dx} < 0
\]

The latter inequality contradicts the Gaussian logarithmic Sobolev inequality, due to L.Gross. (To pass to its standard form, take \( f = {\left| x\right| }^{2}/2 - 2\log \phi \) and integrate by parts) This argument is not hard to make rigorous; the details are left to the reader.

nodes.title: 5. A statistical analogy
nodes.document_title: Grisha Perelman - The Entropy Formula for the Ricci Flow and Its Geometric Applications

nodes.label: Remark 5.1
nodes.document_title: Grisha Perelman - The Entropy Formula for the Ricci Flow and Its Geometric Applications
nodes.content:
5.1 Recall that the partition function for the canonical ensemble at temperature \( {\beta }^{-1} \) is given by \( Z = \int \exp \left( {-{\beta E}}\right) {d\omega }\left( E\right) \) , where \( \omega \left( E\right) \) is a "density of states" measure, which does not depend on \( \beta \) . Then one computes the average energy \( \langle E\rangle  =  - \frac{\partial }{\partial \beta }\log Z \) , the entropy \( S = \beta \langle E\rangle  + \log Z \) , and the fluctuation \( \sigma  =  < {\left( E - \langle E > \right) }^{2} >  = \frac{{\partial }^{2}}{{\left( \partial \beta \right) }^{2}}\log Z \) .

Now fix a closed manifold \( M \) with a probability measure \( m \) , and suppose that our system is described by a metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( \tau \right) \) , which depends on the temperature \( \tau \) according to equation \( {\left( {g}_{ij}\right) }_{\tau } = 2\left( {{R}_{ij} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f}\right) \) , where \( {dm} = {udV}, u = \; {\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}{e}^{-f} \) , and the partition function is given by \( \log Z = \int \left( {-f + \frac{n}{2}}\right) {dm} \) . (We do not discuss here what assumptions on \( {g}_{ij} \) guarantee that the corresponding "density of states" measure can be found) Then we compute

\[
< E >  =  - {\tau }^{2}{\int }_{M}\left( {R + {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} - \frac{n}{2\tau }}\right) {dm},
\]

\[
S =  - {\int }_{M}\left( {\tau \left( {R + {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right)  + f - n}\right) {dm},
\]

\[
\sigma  = 2{\tau }^{4}{\int }_{M}{\left| {R}_{ij} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f - \frac{1}{2\tau }{g}_{ij}\right| }^{2}{dm}
\]

Alternatively, we could prescribe the evolution equations by replacing the \( t \) -derivatives by minus \( \tau \) -derivatives in (3.3 ), and get the same formulas for \( Z, < E > , S,\sigma \) , with \( {dm} \) replaced by \( {udV} \) .

Clearly, \( \sigma \) is nonnegative; it vanishes only on a gradient shrinking soliton. \( < E > \) is nonnegative as well, whenever the flow exists for all sufficiently small \( \tau  > 0 \) (by proposition 1.2). Furthermore, if (a) \( u \) tends to a \( \delta \) -function as \( \tau  \rightarrow  0 \) , or (b) \( u \) is a limit of a sequence of functions \( {u}_{i} \) , such that each \( {u}_{i} \) tends to a \( \delta \) -function as \( \tau  \rightarrow  {\tau }_{i} > 0 \) , and \( {\tau }_{i} \rightarrow  0 \) , then \( S \) is also nonnegative. In case (a) all the quantities \( < E > , S,\sigma \) tend to zero as \( \tau  \rightarrow  0 \) , while in case (b), which may be interesting if \( {g}_{ij}\left( \tau \right) \) goes singular at \( \tau  = 0 \) , the entropy \( S \) may tend to a positive limit.

If the flow is defined for all sufficiently large \( \tau \) (that is, we have an ancient solution to the Ricci flow, in Hamilton's terminology), we may be interested in the behavior of the entropy \( S \) as \( \tau  \rightarrow  \infty \) . A natural question is whether we have a gradient shrinking soliton whenever \( S \) stays bounded.

nodes.content:
6.1 Consider the manifold \( \widetilde{M} = M \times  {\mathbb{S}}^{N} \times  {\mathbb{R}}^{ + } \) with the following metric:

\[
{\widetilde{g}}_{ij} = {g}_{ij},{\widetilde{g}}_{\alpha \beta } = \tau {g}_{\alpha \beta },{\widetilde{g}}_{00} = \frac{N}{2\tau } + R,{\widetilde{g}}_{i\alpha } = {\widetilde{g}}_{i0} = {\widetilde{g}}_{\alpha 0} = 0,
\]

where \( i, j \) denote coordinate indices on the \( M \) factor, \( \alpha ,\beta \) denote those on the \( {\mathbb{S}}^{N} \) factor, and the coordinate \( \tau \) on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{ + } \) has index \( 0;{g}_{ij} \) evolves with \( \tau \) by the backward Ricci flow \( {\left( {g}_{ij}\right) }_{\tau } = 2{R}_{ij},{g}_{\alpha \beta } \) is the metric on \( {\mathbb{S}}^{N} \) of constant curvature \( \frac{1}{2N} \) . It turns out that the components of the curvature tensor of this metric coincide (modulo \( {N}^{-1} \) ) with the components of the matrix Harnack expression (and its traces), discovered by Hamilton [H 3]. One can also compute that all the components of the Ricci tensor are equal to zero (mod \( {N}^{-1} \) ). The heat equation and the conjugate heat equation on \( M \) can be interpreted via Laplace equation on \( \widetilde{M} \) for functions and volume forms respectively: \( u \) satisfies the heat equation on \( M \) iff \( \widetilde{u} \) (the extension of \( u \) to \( \widetilde{M} \) constant along the \( {\mathbb{S}}^{N} \) fibres) satisfies \( \widetilde{\bigtriangleup }\widetilde{u} = 0{\;\operatorname{mod}\;{N}^{-1}} \) ; similarly, \( u \) satisfies the conjugate heat equation on \( M \) iff \( {\widetilde{u}}^{ * } = {\tau }^{-\frac{N - 1}{2}}\widetilde{u} \) satisfies \( \widetilde{\bigtriangleup }{\widetilde{u}}^{ * } = \) 0 mod \( {N}^{-1} \) on \( \widetilde{M} \) .

To achieve this, first apply to \( \widetilde{g} \) a (small) diffeomorphism, mapping each point \( \left( {{x}^{i},{y}^{\alpha },\tau }\right) \) into \( \left( {{x}^{i},{y}^{\alpha },\tau \left( {1 - \frac{2f}{N}}\right) }\right) \) ; we would get a metric \( {\widetilde{g}}^{m} \) , with components \( \left( {{\;\operatorname{mod}\;{N}^{-1}}\text{ ) }}\right) \)

\[
{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{m} = {\widetilde{g}}_{ij},{\widetilde{g}}_{\alpha \beta }^{m} = \left( {1 - \frac{2f}{N}}\right) {\widetilde{g}}_{\alpha \beta },{\widetilde{g}}_{00}^{m} = {\widetilde{g}}_{00} - 2{f}_{\tau } - \frac{f}{\tau },{\widetilde{g}}_{i0}^{m} =  - {\nabla }_{i}f,{\widetilde{g}}_{i\alpha }^{m} = {\widetilde{g}}_{\alpha 0}^{m} = 0;
\]

then apply a horizontal (that is, along the \( M \) factor) diffeomorphism to get \( {g}^{m} \) satisfying \( {\left( {g}_{ij}^{m}\right) }_{\tau } = 2\left( {{R}_{ij} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f}\right) \) ; the other components of \( {g}^{m} \) become \( \left( {\;\operatorname{mod}\;{N}^{-1}}\right) \)

\[
{g}_{\alpha \beta }^{m} = \left( {1 - \frac{2f}{N}}\right) {\widetilde{g}}_{\alpha \beta },{g}_{00}^{m} = {\widetilde{g}}_{00}^{m} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} = \frac{1}{\tau }\left( {\frac{N}{2} - \left\lbrack  {\tau \left( {2\bigtriangleup f - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + R}\right)  + f - n}\right\rbrack  }\right) ,
\]

\[
{g}_{i0}^{m} = {g}_{\alpha 0}^{m} = {g}_{i\alpha }^{m} = 0
\]

Note that the hypersurface \( \tau  = \) const in the metric \( {g}^{m} \) has the volume form \( {\tau }^{N/2}{e}^{-f} \) times the canonical form on \( M \) and \( {\mathbb{S}}^{N} \) , and the scalar curvature of this hypersurface is \( \frac{1}{\tau }\left( {\frac{N}{2} + \tau \left( {2\bigtriangleup f - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + R}\right)  + f}\right) {\;\operatorname{mod}\;{N}^{-1}} \) . Thus the entropy \( S \) multiplied by the inverse temperature \( \beta \) is essentially minus the total scalar curvature of this hypersurface.

Our formula for the reduced volume resembles the expression in Huisken monotonicity formula for the mean curvature flow [Hu]; however, in our case the monotonicity is in the opposite direction.

nodes.content: 9.6 Remark. Ricci flow can be characterized among all other evolution equations by the infinitesimal behavior of the fundamental solutions of the conjugate heat equation. Namely, suppose we have a riemannian metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) evolving with time according to an equation \( {\left( {g}_{ij}\right) }_{t} = {A}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) . Then we have the heat operator \( \square  = \frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \bigtriangleup \) and its conjugate \( {\square }^{ * } =  - \frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \bigtriangleup  - \frac{1}{2}A \) , so that \( \frac{d}{dt}\int {uv} = \int \left( {\left( {\square u}\right) v - u\left( {{\square }^{ * }v}\right) }\right) \) . (Here \( A = {g}^{ij}{A}_{ij} \) ) Consider the fundamental solution \( u = {\left( -4\pi t\right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}{e}^{-f} \) for \( {\square }^{ * } \) , starting as \( \delta \) -function at some point \( \left( {p,0}\right) \) . Then for general \( {A}_{ij} \) the function \( \left( {\square \bar{f} + \frac{\bar{f}}{t}}\right) \left( {q, t}\right) \) , where \( \bar{f} = f - \int {fu} \) , is of the order \( O\left( 1\right) \) for \( \left( {q, t}\right) \) near \( \left( {p,0}\right) \) . The Ricci flow \( {A}_{ij} =  - 2{R}_{ij} \) is characterized by the condition \( \left( {\square \bar{f} + \frac{\bar{f}}{t}}\right) \left( {q, t}\right)  = o\left( 1\right) \) ; in fact, it is \( O\left( {{\left| pq\right| }^{2} + \left| t\right| }\right) \) in this case.

nodes.label: Theorem 10.1

nodes.content:
10.1. Theorem. For every \( \alpha  > 0 \) there exist \( \delta  > 0,\epsilon  > 0 \) with the following property. Suppose we have a smooth solution to the Ricci flow \( {\left( {g}_{ij}\right) }_{t} = \; - 2{R}_{ij},0 \leq  t \leq  {\left( \epsilon {r}_{0}\right) }^{2} \) , and assume that at \( t = 0 \) we have \( R\left( x\right)  \geq   - {r}_{0}^{-2} \) and \( {Vol}{\left( \partial \Omega \right) }^{n} \geq  \left( {1 - \delta }\right) {c}_{n}{Vol}{\left( \Omega \right) }^{n - 1} \) for any \( x,\Omega  \subset  B\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) , where \( {c}_{n} \) is the euclidean isoperimetric constant. Then we have an estimate \( \left| {Rm}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq \; \alpha {t}^{-1} + {\left( \epsilon {r}_{0}\right) }^{-2} \) whenever \( 0 < t \leq  {\left( \epsilon {r}_{0}\right) }^{2}, d\left( {x, t}\right)  = {\operatorname{dist}}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < \epsilon {r}_{0} \) .

Thus, under the Ricci flow, the almost singular regions (where curvature is large) can not instantly significantly influence the almost euclidean regions. Or, using the interpretation via renormalization group flow, if a region looks trivial (almost euclidean) on higher energy scale, then it can not suddenly become highly nontrivial on a slightly lower energy scale.
