nodes.proof:
It is an argument by contradiction. The idea is to pick a point \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) not far from \( \left( {{x}_{0},0}\right) \) and consider the solution \( u \) to the conjugate heat equation, starting as \( \delta \) -function at \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , and the corresponding nonpositive function \( v \) as in 9.3. If the curvatures at \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) are not small compared to \( {\bar{t}}^{-1} \) and are larger than at nearby points, then one can show that \( \int v \) at time \( t \) is bounded away from zero for (small) time intervals \( \bar{t} - t \) of the order of \( {\left| Rm\right| }^{-1}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) . By monotonicity we conclude that \( \int v \) is bounded away from zero at \( t = 0 \) . In fact, using (9.1) and an appropriate cut-off function, we can show that at \( t = 0 \) already the integral of \( v \) over \( B\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) \) is bounded away from zero, whereas the integral of \( u \) over this ball is close to 1, where \( r \) can be made as small as we like compared to \( {r}_{0} \) . Now using the control over the scalar curvature and isoperimetric constant in \( B\left( {{x}_{0}{r}_{0}}\right) \) , we can obtain a contradiction to the logarithmic Sobolev inequality.

Now let us go into details. By scaling assume that \( {r}_{0} = 1 \) . We may also assume that \( \alpha \) is small, say \( \alpha  < \frac{1}{100n} \) . From now on we fix \( \alpha \) and denote by \( {M}_{\alpha } \) the set of pairs \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) , such that \( \left| {Rm}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  \alpha {t}^{-1} \) .

Claim 1.For any \( A > 0 \) , if \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) solves the Ricci flow equation on \( 0 \leq \; t \leq  {\epsilon }^{2},{A\epsilon } < \frac{1}{100n} \) , and \( \left| {Rm}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  > \alpha {t}^{-1} + {\epsilon }^{-2} \) for some \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) , satisfying \( 0 \leq \; t \leq  {\epsilon }^{2}, d\left( {x, t}\right)  < \epsilon \) , then one can find \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  \in  {M}_{\alpha } \) , with \( 0 < \bar{t} \leq  {\epsilon }^{2}, d\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  < \; \left( {{2A} + 1}\right) \epsilon \) , such that

\[
\left| {Rm}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4\left| {Rm}\right| \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) , \tag{10.1}
\]

whenever

\[
\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {M}_{\alpha },0 < t \leq  \bar{t}, d\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  d\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  + A{\left| Rm\right| }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \tag{10.2}
\]

Proof of Claim 1. We construct \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) as a limit of a (finite) sequence \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , defined in the following way. Let \( \left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right) \) be an arbitrary point, satisfying \( 0 < {t}_{1} \leq  {\epsilon }^{2}, d\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  < \epsilon ,\left| {Rm}\right| \left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  \geq  \alpha {t}^{-1} + {\epsilon }^{-2} \) . Now if \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) is already constructed, and if it can not be taken for \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , because there is some \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) satisfying (10.2), but not (10.1), then take any such \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) for \( \left( {{x}_{k + 1},{t}_{k + 1}}\right) \) . Clearly, the sequence, constructed in such a way, satisfies \( \left| {Rm}\right| \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \geq  {4}^{k - 1}\left| {Rm}\right| \left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  \geq  {4}^{k - 1}{\epsilon }^{-2} \) , and therefore, \( d\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \leq  ({2A} + \) 1) \( \epsilon \) . Since the solution is smooth, the sequence is finite, and its last element fits.

Claim 2. For \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , constructed above,(10.1) holds whenever

\[
\bar{t} - \frac{1}{2}\alpha {Q}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t},{\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{10}A{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, \tag{10.3}
\]

where \( Q = \left| {Rm}\right| \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) .

Proof of Claim 2. We only need to show that if \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) satisfies (10.3), then it must satisfy (10.1) or (10.2). Since \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  \in  {M}_{\alpha } \) , we have \( Q \geq  \alpha {\bar{t}}^{-1} \) , so \( \bar{t} - \frac{1}{2}\alpha {Q}^{-1} \geq  \frac{1}{2}\bar{t} \) . Hence, if \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) does not satisfy (10.1), it definitely belongs to \( {M}_{\alpha } \) . Now by the triangle inequality, \( d\left( {x,\bar{t}}\right)  \leq  d\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  + \frac{1}{10}A{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . On the other hand, using lemma 8.3(b) we see that, as \( t \) decreases from \( \bar{t} \) to \( \bar{t} - \frac{1}{2}\alpha {Q}^{-1} \) , the point \( x \) can not escape from the ball of radius \( d\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  + A{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) centered at \( {x}_{0} \) .

Continuing the proof of the theorem, and arguing by contradiction, take sequences \( \epsilon  \rightarrow  0,\delta  \rightarrow  0 \) and solutions \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) , violating the statement; by reducing \( \epsilon \) , we’ll assume that

\[
\left| {Rm}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \alpha {t}^{-1} + 2{\epsilon }^{-2}\text{ whenever }0 \leq  t \leq  {\epsilon }^{2}\text{ and }d\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \epsilon \tag{10.4}
\]

Take \( A = \frac{1}{100n\epsilon } \rightarrow  \infty \) , construct \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , and consider solutions \( u = ({4\pi }(\bar{t} - \) t)) \( {)}^{-\frac{n}{2}}{e}^{-f} \) of the conjugate heat equation, starting from \( \delta \) -functions at \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , and corresponding nonpositive functions \( v \) .

Claim 3. \( {As\epsilon },\delta  \rightarrow  0 \) , one can find times \( \widetilde{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} - \frac{1}{2}\alpha {Q}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) , such that the integral \( {\int }_{B}v \) stays bounded away from zero, where \( B \) is the ball at time \( \widetilde{t} \) of radius \( \sqrt{\bar{t} - \widetilde{t}} \) centered at \( \bar{x} \) .

Proof of Claim 3(sketch). The statement is invariant under scaling, so we can try to take a limit of scalings of \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) at points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with factors \( Q \) . If the injectivity radii of the scaled metrics at \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) are bounded away from zero, then a smooth limit exists, it is complete and has \( \left| {Rm}\right| \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  = 1 \) and \( \left| {Rm}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4 \) when \( \bar{t} - \frac{1}{2}\alpha  \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) . It is not hard to show that the fundamental solutions \( u \) of the conjugate heat equation converge to such a solution on the limit manifold. But on the limit manifold, \( {\int }_{B}v \) can not be zero for \( \widetilde{t} = \bar{t} - \frac{1}{2}\alpha \) , since the evolution equation (9.1) would imply in this case that the limit is a gradient shrinking soliton, and this is incompatible with \( \left| {Rm}\right| \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  = 1 \) .

If the injectivity radii of the scaled metrics tend to zero, then we can change the scaling factor, to make the scaled metrics converge to a flat manifold with finite injectivity radius; in this case it is not hard to choose \( \widetilde{t} \) in such a way that \( {\int }_{B}v \rightarrow   - \infty \) .

The positive lower bound for \( - {\int }_{B}v \) will be denoted by \( \beta \) .

Our next goal is to construct an appropriate cut-off function. We choose it in the form \( h\left( {y, t}\right)  = \phi \left( \frac{\widetilde{d}\left( {y, t}\right) }{10A\epsilon }\right) \) , where \( \widetilde{d}\left( {y, t}\right)  = d\left( {y, t}\right)  + {200n}\sqrt{t} \) , and \( \phi \) is a smooth function of one variable, equal one on \( ( - \infty ,1\rbrack \) and decreasing to zero on \( \left\lbrack  {1,2}\right\rbrack \) . Clearly, \( h \) vanishes at \( t = 0 \) outside \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{20A\epsilon }}\right) \) ; on the other hand, it is equal to one near \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) .

Now \( \square h = \frac{1}{10A\epsilon }\left( {{d}_{t} - \bigtriangleup d + \frac{100n}{\sqrt{t}}}\right) {\phi }^{\prime } - \frac{1}{{\left( {10}A\epsilon \right) }^{2}}{\phi }^{\prime \prime } \) . Note that \( {d}_{t} - \bigtriangleup t + \frac{100n}{\sqrt{t}} \geq  0 \) on the set where \( {\phi }^{\prime } \neq  0 \) - this follows from the lemma 8.3(a) and our assumption (10.4). We may also choose \( \phi \) so that \( {\phi }^{\prime \prime } \geq   - {10\phi },{\left( {\phi }^{\prime }\right) }^{2} \leq  {10\phi } \) . Now we can compute \( {\left( {\int }_{M}hu\right) }_{t} = {\int }_{M}\left( {\square h}\right) u \leq  \frac{1}{{\left( A\epsilon \right) }^{2}} \) , so \( {\int }_{M}{hu}{ \mid  }_{t = 0} \geq  {\int }_{M}{hu}{ \mid  }_{t = \bar{t}} \; - \frac{\bar{t}}{{\left( A\epsilon \right) }^{2}} \geq  1 - {A}^{-2} \) . Also, by (9.1), \( {\left( {\int }_{M} - hv\right) }_{t} \leq  {\int }_{M} - \left( {\square h}\right) v \leq  \frac{1}{{\left( A\epsilon \right) }^{2}}{\int }_{M} - {hv}, \) so by Claim 3, \( - {\int }_{M}{hv}{ \mid  }_{t = 0} \geq  \beta \exp \left( {-\frac{\bar{t}}{{\left( A\epsilon \right) }^{2}}}\right)  \geq  \beta \left( {1 - {A}^{-2}}\right) \) .

From now on we’ll work at \( t = 0 \) only. Let \( \widetilde{u} = {hu} \) and correspondingly \( \widetilde{f} = f - \log h \) . Then

\[
\beta \left( {1 - {A}^{-2}}\right)  \leq   - {\int }_{M}{hv} = {\int }_{M}\left\lbrack  {\left( {-2\bigtriangleup f + {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} - R}\right) \bar{t} - f + n}\right\rbrack  {hu}
\]

\[
= {\int }_{M}\left\lbrack  {-\bar{t}{\left| \nabla \widetilde{f}\right| }^{2} - \widetilde{f} + n}\right\rbrack  \widetilde{u} + {\int }_{M}\left\lbrack  {\bar{t}\left( {{\left| \nabla h\right| }^{2}/h - {Rh}}\right)  - h\log h}\right\rbrack  u
\]

\[
\leq  {\int }_{M}\left\lbrack  {-\bar{t}{\left| \nabla \widetilde{f}\right| }^{2} - \widetilde{f} - n}\right\rbrack  \widetilde{u} + {A}^{-2} + {100}{\epsilon }^{2}
\]

( Note that \( {\int }_{M} - {uh}\log h \) does not exceed the integral of \( u \) over \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{20A\epsilon }}\right)  \smallsetminus  \widetilde{B}\left( {{x}_{0},{10A\epsilon }}\right) \) , and \( {\int }_{B\left( {{x}_{0},{10A\epsilon }}\right) }u \geq  {\int }_{M}\bar{h}u \geq  1 - {A}^{-2} \) , where \( \left. {\bar{h} = \phi \left( \frac{\widetilde{d}}{5A\epsilon }\right) }\right) \)

Now scaling the metric by the factor \( \frac{1}{2}{\bar{t}}^{-1} \) and sending \( \epsilon ,\delta \) to zero, we get a sequence of metric balls with radii going to infinity, and a sequence of compactly supported nonnegative functions \( u = {\left( 2\pi \right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}{e}^{-f} \) with \( \int u \rightarrow  1 \) and \( \int \left\lbrack  {-\frac{1}{2}{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} - f + n}\right\rbrack  u \) bounded away from zero by a positive constant. We also have isoperimetric inequalities with the constants tending to the euclidean one. This set up is in conflict with the Gaussian logarithmic Sobolev inequality, as can be seen by using spherical symmetrization.

nodes.proof:
The statement is invariant under scaling, so we can try to take a limit of scalings of \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) at points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with factors \( Q \) . If the injectivity radii of the scaled metrics at \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) are bounded away from zero, then a smooth limit exists, it is complete and has \( \left| {Rm}\right| \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  = 1 \) and \( \left| {Rm}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4 \) when \( \bar{t} - \frac{1}{2}\alpha  \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) . It is not hard to show that the fundamental solutions \( u \) of the conjugate heat equation converge to such a solution on the limit manifold. But on the limit manifold, \( {\int }_{B}v \) can not be zero for \( \widetilde{t} = \bar{t} - \frac{1}{2}\alpha \) , since the evolution equation (9.1) would imply in this case that the limit is a gradient shrinking soliton, and this is incompatible with \( \left| {Rm}\right| \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  = 1 \) .

If the injectivity radii of the scaled metrics tend to zero, then we can change the scaling factor, to make the scaled metrics converge to a flat manifold with finite injectivity radius; in this case it is not hard to choose \( \widetilde{t} \) in such a way that \( {\int }_{B}v \rightarrow   - \infty \) .

nodes.content:
11.1. In this section we consider smooth solutions to the Ricci flow \( {\left( {g}_{ij}\right) }_{t} = \; - 2{R}_{ij}, - \infty  < t \leq  0 \) , such that for each \( t \) the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) is a complete non-flat metric of bounded curvature and nonnegative curvature operator. Hamilton discovered a remarkable differential Harnack inequality for such solutions; we need only its trace version

\[
{R}_{t} + 2 < X,\nabla R >  + 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  \geq  0 \tag{11.1}
\]

and its corollary, \( {R}_{t} \geq  0 \) . In particular, the scalar curvature at some time \( {t}_{0} \leq  0 \) controls the curvatures for all \( t \leq  {t}_{0} \) .

We impose one more requirement on the solutions; namely, we fix some \( \kappa  > 0 \) and require that \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) be \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on all scales (the definitions 4.2 and 8.1 are essentially equivalent in this case). It is not hard to show that this requirement is equivalent to a uniform bound on the entropy \( S \) , defined as in 5.1 using an arbitrary fundamental solution to the conjugate heat equation.

Now, since \( \widetilde{V}\left( \tau \right) \) is nonincreasing and bounded away from zero (because the scaled metrics are not collapsed near \( q\left( \tau \right) ) \) the limit function \( \bar{V}\left( \tau \right) \) must be a positive constant; this constant is strictly less than \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\tau  \rightarrow  0}}\widetilde{V}\left( \tau \right)  = {\left( 4\pi \right) }^{\frac{n}{2}} \) , since \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) is not flat. Therefore, on the one hand,(7.14) must become an equality, hence \( \bar{l} \) is smooth, and on the other hand, by the description of the equality case in (7.12), \( {\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( \tau \right) \) must be a gradient shrinking soliton with \( {\bar{R}}_{ij} + {\bar{\nabla }}_{i}{\bar{\nabla }}_{j}\bar{l} - \frac{1}{2\tau }{\bar{g}}_{ij} = 0 \) . If this soliton is flat, then \( \bar{l} \) is uniquely determined by the equality in (7.14), and it turns out that the value of \( \bar{V} \) is exactly \( {\left( 4\pi \right) }^{\frac{n}{2}} \) , which was ruled out.

nodes.proof: Hamilton [H 10] proved that round sphere is the only non-flat oriented nonnegatively curved gradient shrinking soliton in dimension two. Thus, the scalings of our ancient solution must converge to a round sphere. However, Hamilton [H 10] has also shown that an almost round sphere is getting more round under Ricci flow, therefore our ancient solution must be round.

nodes.proof:
Induction on dimension. In dimension two the statement is vacuous, as we have just shown. Now let \( n \geq  3 \) , suppose that \( \mathcal{V} > 0 \) for some \( t = {t}_{0} \) , and consider the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( \mathcal{R} = \; \lim \sup R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) {d}^{2}\left( x\right) \) as \( d\left( x\right)  \rightarrow  \infty .(d\left( x\right) \) denotes the distance, at time \( {t}_{0} \) , from \( x \) to some fixed point \( {x}_{0} \) ) If \( \mathcal{R} = \infty \) , then we can find a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) and radii \( {r}_{k} > 0 \) , such that \( {r}_{k}/d\left( {x}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow  0, R\left( {x}_{k}\right) {r}_{k}^{2} \rightarrow  \infty \) , and \( R\left( x\right)  \leq  {2R}\left( {x}_{k}\right) \) whenever \( x \in  B\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) \) . Taking blow-up limit of \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) at \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) with factors \( R\left( {x}_{k}\right) \) , we get a smooth non-flat ancient solution, satisfying the assumptions of 11.1, which splits off a line (this follows from a standard argument based on the Aleksandrov-Toponogov concavity). Thus, we can do dimension reduction in this case (cf. [H 4,§22]).

If \( 0 < \mathcal{R} < \infty \) , then a similar argument gives a blow-up limit in a ball of finite radius; this limit has the structure of a non-flat metric cone. This is ruled out by Hamilton's strong maximum principle for nonnegative curvature operator.

Finally, if \( \mathcal{R} = 0 \) , then (in dimensions three and up) it is easy to see that the metric is flat.

By scaling assume \( {r}_{0} = 1 \) . (a) Arguing by contradiction, consider a sequence of \( B, C \rightarrow  \infty \) , of solutions \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) and points \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) , such that \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{4} \) and \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  > C + B{\left( t - {t}_{0}\right) }^{-1} \) . Then, arguing as in the proof of claims 1,2 in 10.1, we can find a point \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , satisfying \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  < \; \frac{1}{3}, Q = R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  > C + B{\left( \bar{t} - {t}_{0}\right) }^{-1} \) , and such that \( R\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \leq  {2Q} \) whenever \( \bar{t} - A{Q}^{-1} \leq  {t}^{\prime } \leq  \bar{t},{\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {{x}^{\prime },\bar{x}}\right)  < A{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , where \( A \) tends to infinity with \( B, C \) . Applying the previous corollary at \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) and using the relative volume comparison, we get a contradiction with the assumption involving \( w \) .

(b) Let \( B\left( w\right) , C\left( w\right) \) be good for (a). We claim that \( B = B\left( {{5}^{-n}w}\right) , C = \; C\left( {{5}^{-n}w}\right) \) are good for (b), for an appropriate \( {\tau }_{0}\left( w\right)  > 0 \) . Indeed, let \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) be a solution with nonnegative curvature operator, such that \( \operatorname{Vol}B\left( {{x}_{0},1}\right)  \geq  w \) at \( t = 0 \) , and let \( \left\lbrack  {-\tau ,0}\right\rbrack \) be the maximal time interval, where the assumption of (a) still holds, with \( {5}^{-n}w \) in place of \( w \) and with \( - \tau \) in place of \( {t}_{0} \) . Then at time \( t =  - \tau \) we must have \( \operatorname{Vol}B\left( {{x}_{0},1}\right)  \leq  {5}^{-n}w \) . On the other hand, from lemma 8.3 (b) we see that the ball \( B\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{4}}\right) \) at time \( t =  - \tau \) contains the ball \( B\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{4} - {10}\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {\tau \sqrt{C} + 2\sqrt{B\tau }}\right) }\right) \) at time \( t = 0 \) , and the volume of the former is at least as large as the volume of the latter. Thus, it is enough to choose \( {\tau }_{0} = {\tau }_{0}\left( w\right) \) in such a way that the radius of the latter ball is \( > \frac{1}{5} \) .

Clearly, the proof also works if instead of assuming that curvature operator is nonnegative, we assumed that it is bounded below by \( - {r}_{0}^{-2} \) in the (time-dependent) metric ball of radius \( {r}_{0} \) , centered at \( {x}_{0} \) .

11.7. From now on we restrict our attention to oriented manifolds of dimension three. Under the assumptions in 11.1, the solutions on closed manifolds must be quotients of the round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) or \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) - this is proved in the same way as in two dimensions, since the gradient shrinking solitons are known from the work of Hamilton [H 1,10]. The noncompact solutions are described below.

Theorem. The set of non-compact ancient solutions , satisfying the assumptions of 11.1, is compact modulo scaling. That is, from any sequence of such solutions and points \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) with \( R\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right)  = 1 \) , we can extract a smoothly converging subsequence, and the limit satisfies the same conditions.

To ensure a converging subsequence it is enough to show that whenever \( R\left( {{y}_{k},0}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) , the distances at \( t = 0 \) between \( {x}_{k} \) and \( {y}_{k} \) go to infinity as well. Assume the contrary. Define a sequence \( {z}_{k} \) by the requirement that \( {z}_{k} \) be the closest point to \( {x}_{k} \) (at \( t = 0 \) ), satisfying \( R\left( {{z}_{k},0}\right) {\operatorname{dist}}_{0}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{z}_{k}}\right)  = 1 \) . We claim that \( R\left( {z,0}\right) /R\left( {{z}_{k},0}\right) \) is uniformly bounded for \( z \in  B\left( {{z}_{k},{2R}{\left( {z}_{k},0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) . Indeed, otherwise we could show, using 11.5 and relative volume comparison in nonnegative curvature, that the balls \( B\left( {{z}_{k}, R{\left( {z}_{k},0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) are collapsing on the scale of their radii. Therefore, using the local derivative estimate, due to W.-X.Shi (see [H 4,§13]), we get a bound on \( {R}_{t}\left( {{z}_{k}, t}\right) \) of the order of \( {R}^{2}\left( {{z}_{k},0}\right) \) . Then we can compare \( 1 = R\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right)  \geq  {cR}\left( {{z}_{k}, - c{R}^{-1}\left( {{z}_{k},0}\right) }\right)  \geq  {cR}\left( {{z}_{k},0}\right) \) for some small \( c > 0 \) , where the first inequality comes from the Harnack inequality, obtained by integrating (11.1). Thus, \( R\left( {{z}_{k},0}\right) \) are bounded. But now the existence of the sequence \( {y}_{k} \) at bounded distance from \( {x}_{k} \) implies, via 11.5 and relative volume comparison, that balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k}, c}\right) \) are collapsing - a contradiction.

It remains to show that the limit has bounded curvature at \( t = 0 \) . If this was not the case, then we could find a sequence \( {y}_{i} \) going to infinity, such that \( R\left( {{y}_{i},0}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( R\left( {y,0}\right)  \leq  {2R}\left( {{y}_{i},0}\right) \) for \( y \in  B\left( {{y}_{i},{A}_{i}R{\left( {y}_{i},0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{A}_{i} \rightarrow \; \infty \) . Then the limit of scalings at \( \left( {{y}_{i},0}\right) \) with factors \( R\left( {{y}_{i},0}\right) \) satisfies the assumptions in 11.1 and splits off a line. Thus by 11.3 it must be a round infinite cylinder. It follows that for large \( i \) each \( {y}_{i} \) is contained in a round cylindrical "neck" of radius \( {\left( \frac{1}{2}R\left( {y}_{i},0\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \rightarrow  0 \) ,- something that can not happen in an open manifold of nonnegative curvature.

11.9 Remark. It can be shown that there exists \( {\kappa }_{0} > 0 \) , such that if an ancient solution on a noncompact three-manifold satisfies the assumptions in 11.1 with some \( \kappa  > 0 \) , then it would satisfy these assumptions with \( \kappa  = {\kappa }_{0} \) . This follows from the arguments in 7.3, 11.2, and the statement (which is not hard to prove) that there are no noncompact three-dimensional gradient shrinking solitons, satisfying 11.1, other than the round cylinder and its \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{{2}^{ - }} \) quotients.

Furthermore, I believe that there is only one (up to scaling) noncom-pact three-dimensional \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed ancient solution with bounded positive curvature - the rotationally symmetric gradient steady soliton, studied by R.Bryant. In this direction, I have a plausible, but not quite rigorous argument, showing that any such ancient solution can be made eternal, that is, can be extended for \( t \in  \left( {-\infty , + \infty }\right) \) ; also I can prove uniqueness in the class of gradient steady solitons.

nodes.content: 12.1 Let \( \phi \) be a decreasing function of one variable, tending to zero at infinity. A solution to the Ricci flow is said to have \( \phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature if it satisfies \( {Rm}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq   - \phi \left( {R\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) R\left( {x, t}\right) \) for each \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) .

nodes.proof:
An argument by contradiction. Take a sequence of \( {r}_{0} \) converging to zero, and consider the solutions \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) , such that the conclusion does not hold for some \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) ; moreover, by tampering with the condition \( {t}_{0} \geq  1 \) a little bit, choose among all such \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) , in the solution under consideration, the one with nearly the smallest curvature \( Q \) . (More precisely, we can choose \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) in such a way that the conclusion of the theorem holds for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) , satisfying \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  > {2Q},{t}_{0} - H{Q}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{0} \) , where \( H \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( {r}_{0} \rightarrow  0 \) ) Our goal is to show that the sequence of blow-ups of such solutions at such points with factors \( Q \) would converge, along some subsequence of \( {r}_{0} \rightarrow  0 \) , to an ancient solution, satisfying 11.1.

Claim 1. For each \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{0} - H{Q}^{-1} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  {t}_{0} \) we have \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4\bar{Q} \) whenever \( \bar{t} - c{\bar{Q}}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  c{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , where \( \bar{Q} = Q + R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) and \( c = c\left( \kappa \right)  > 0 \) is a small constant.

Proof of Claim 1. Use the fact (following from the choice of \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) and the description of the ancient solutions) that for each \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  > \; {2Q} \) and \( {t}_{0} - H{Q}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{0} \) we have the estimates \( \left| {{R}_{t}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  C{R}^{2}\left( {x, t}\right) \) , \( \left| {\nabla R}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C{R}^{\frac{3}{2}}\left( {x, t}\right) . \)

Claim 2. There exists \( c = c\left( \kappa \right)  > 0 \) and for any \( A > 0 \) there exist \( D = D\left( A\right)  < \infty ,{\rho }_{0} = {\rho }_{0}\left( A\right)  > 0 \) , with the following property. Suppose that \( {r}_{0} < {\rho }_{0} \) , and let \( \gamma \) be a shortest geodesic with endpoints \( \bar{x}, x \) in \( {g}_{ij}\left( \bar{t}\right) \) , for some \( \bar{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - H{Q}^{-1},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , such that \( R\left( {y,\bar{t}}\right)  > {2Q} \) for each \( y \in  \gamma \) . Let \( z \in  \gamma \) satisfy \( {cR}\left( {z,\bar{t}}\right)  > R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  = \bar{Q} \) . Then \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x}, z}\right)  \geq  A{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) whenever \( R\left( {x,\bar{t}}\right)  \geq  D\bar{Q} \) .

Proof of Claim 2. Note that from the choice of \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) and the description of the ancient solutions it follows that an appropriate parabolic (backward in time) neighborhood of a point \( y \in  \gamma \) at \( t = \bar{t} \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to the evolving round cylinder, provided \( {c}^{-1}\bar{Q} \leq  R\left( {y,\bar{t}}\right)  \leq  {cR}\left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) for an appropriate \( c = c\left( \kappa \right) \) . Now assume that the conclusion of the claim does not hold, take \( {r}_{0} \) to zero, \( R\left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) - to infinity, and consider the scalings around \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with factors \( \bar{Q} \) . We can imagine two possibilities for the behavior of the curvature along \( \gamma \) in the scaled metric: either it stays bounded at bounded distances from \( \bar{x} \) , or not. In the first case we can take a limit (for a subsequence) of the scaled metrics along \( \gamma \) and get a nonnegatively curved almost cylindrical metric, with \( \gamma \) going to infinity. Clearly, in this case the curvature at any point of the limit does not exceed \( {c}^{-1} \) ; therefore, the point \( z \) must have escaped to infinity, and the conclusion of the claim stands.

In the second case, we can also take a limit along \( \gamma \) ; it is a smooth non-negatively curved manifold near \( \bar{x} \) and has cylindrical shape where curvature is large; the radius of the cylinder goes to zero as we approach the (first) singular point, which is located at finite distance from \( \bar{x} \) ; the region beyond the first singular point will be ignored. Thus, at \( t = \bar{t} \) we have a metric, which is a smooth metric of nonnegative curvature away from a single singular point \( o \) . Since the metric is cylindrical at points close to \( o \) , and the radius of the cylinder is at most \( \epsilon \) times the distance from \( o \) , the curvature at \( o \) is nonnegative in Aleksandrov sense. Thus, the metric near \( o \) must be cone-like. In other words, the scalings of our metric at points \( {x}_{i} \rightarrow  o \) with factors \( R\left( {{x}_{i},\bar{t}}\right) \) converge to a piece of nonnegatively curved non-flat metric cone. Moreover, using claim 1, we see that we actually have the convergence of the solutions to the Ricci flow on some time interval, and not just metrics at \( t = \bar{t} \) . Therefore, we get a contradiction with the strong maximum principle of Hamilton [H 2].

Now continue the proof of theorem, and recall that we are considering scalings at \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) with factor \( Q \) . It follows from claim 2 that at \( t = {t}_{0} \) the curvature of the scaled metric is bounded at bounded distances from \( {x}_{0} \) . This allows us to extract a smooth limit at \( t = {t}_{0} \) (of course, we use the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing assumption here). The limit has bounded nonnegative curvature (if the curvatures were unbounded, we would have a sequence of cylindrical necks with radii going to zero in a complete manifold of nonnegative curvature). Therefore, by claim 1, we have a limit not only at \( t = {t}_{0} \) , but also in some interval of times smaller than \( {t}_{0} \) .

We want to show that the limit actually exists for all \( t < {t}_{0} \) . Assume that this is not the case, and let \( {t}^{\prime } \) be the smallest value of time, such that the blowup limit can be taken on \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . From the differential Harnack inequality of Hamilton [H 3] we have an estimate \( {R}_{t}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq   - R\left( {x, t}\right) {\left( t - {t}^{\prime }\right) }^{-1} \) , therefore, if \( \widetilde{Q} \) denotes the maximum of scalar curvature at \( t = {t}_{0} \) , then \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{Q}\frac{{t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }}{t - {t}^{\prime }} \) . Hence by lemma 8.3(b) \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, y}\right)  + C \) for all \( t \) , where \( C = \; {10n}\left( {{t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }}\right) \sqrt{\widetilde{Q}} \) .

The next step is needed only if our limit is noncompact. In this case there exists \( D > 0 \) , such that for any \( y \) satisfying \( d = {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, y}\right)  > D \) , one can find \( x \) satisfying \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, y}\right)  = d,{\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  > \frac{3}{2}d \) . We claim that the scalar curvature \( R\left( {y, t}\right) \) is uniformly bounded for all such \( y \) and all \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . Indeed, if \( R\left( {y, t}\right) \) is large, then the neighborhood of \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) is like in an ancient solution; therefore,(long) shortest geodesics \( \gamma \) and \( {\gamma }_{0} \) , connecting at time \( t \) the point \( y \) to \( x \) and \( {x}_{0} \) respectively, make the angle close to 0 or \( \pi \) at \( y \) ; the former case is ruled out by the assumptions on distances, if \( D > {10C} \) ; in the latter case, \( x \) and \( {x}_{0} \) are separated at time \( t \) by a small neighborhood of \( y \) , with diameter of order \( R{\left( y, t\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , hence the same must be true at time \( {t}_{0} \) , which is impossible if \( R\left( {y, t}\right) \) is too large.

Thus we have a uniform bound on curvature outside a certain compact set, which has uniformly bounded diameter for all \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . Then claim 2 gives a uniform bound on curvature everywhere. Hence, by claim 1, we can extend our blow-up limit past \( {t}^{\prime } \) - a contradiction.

nodes.proof:
In the first step of the proof we check the following

Claim. There exists \( K = K\left( A\right)  < \infty \) , such that a point \( \left( {x,1}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of the previous theorem 12.1 (for some fixed small \( \epsilon  > 0 \) ), whenever \( R\left( {x,1}\right)  > K \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{1}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < A \) .

The proof of this statement essentially repeats the proof of the previous theorem (the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing assumption is ensured by theorem 8.2). The only difference is in the beginning. So let us argue by contradiction, and suppose we have a sequence of solutions and points \( x \) with \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{1}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < A \) and \( R\left( {x,1}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) , which do not satisfy the conclusion of 12.1. Then an argument, similar to the one proving claims 1,2 in 10.1, delivers points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( \frac{1}{2} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  1,{\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  < {2A} \) , with \( Q = R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) , and such that \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of 12.1 whenever \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  > {2Q},\bar{t} - D{Q}^{-1} \leq  t \leq \; \bar{t},{\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x}, x}\right)  < D{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , where \( D \rightarrow  \infty \) . (There is a little subtlety here in the application of lemma 8.3(b); nevertheless, it works, since we need to apply it only when the endpoint other than \( {x}_{0} \) either satisfies the conclusion of 12.1, or has scalar curvature at most \( {2Q} \) ) After such \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) are found, the proof of 12.1 applies.

Now, having checked the claim, we can prove the theorem by applying the claim 2 of the previous theorem to the appropriate segment of the shortest geodesic, connecting \( x \) and \( {x}_{0} \) .

nodes.proof:
If we knew that sectional curvatures are \( \geq   - {r}_{0}^{-2} \) for all \( t \) , then we could just apply corollary 11.6(b) (with the remark after its proof) and take \( \tau \left( w\right)  = {\tau }_{0}\left( w\right) /2, K\left( w\right)  = C\left( w\right)  + {2B}\left( w\right) /{\tau }_{0}\left( w\right) \) . Now fix these values of \( \tau , K \) , consider a \( \phi \) -almost nonnegatively curved solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) , a point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) and a radius \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) , such that the assumptions of the theorem do hold whereas the conclusion does not. We may assume that any other point \( \left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) and radius \( {r}^{\prime } > 0 \) with that property has either \( {t}^{\prime } > {t}_{0} \) or \( {t}^{\prime } < {t}_{0} - {2\tau }{r}_{0}^{2} \) , or \( 2{r}^{\prime } > {r}_{0} \) . Our goal is to show that \( \phi \left( {r}_{0}^{-2}\right) \) is bounded away from zero.

Let \( {\tau }^{\prime } > 0 \) be the largest time interval such that \( {Rm}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq   - {r}_{0}^{-2} \) whenever \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {\tau }^{\prime }{r}_{0}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  ,{\operatorname{dist}}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {r}_{0} \) . If \( {\tau }^{\prime } \geq  {2\tau } \) , we are done by corollary 11.6(b). Otherwise, by elementary Aleksandrov space theory, we can find at time \( {t}^{\prime } = {t}_{0} - {\tau }^{\prime }{r}_{0}^{2} \) a ball \( B\left( {{x}^{\prime },{r}^{\prime }}\right)  \subset  B\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) with \( \operatorname{Vol}B\left( {{x}^{\prime },{r}^{\prime }}\right)  \geq  \frac{1}{2}{\omega }_{n}{\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{n} \) , and with radius \( {r}^{\prime } \geq  c{r}_{0} \) for some small constant \( c = c\left( w\right)  > 0 \) . By the choice of \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) and \( {r}_{0} \) , the conclusion of our theorem holds for \( \left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right) ,{r}^{\prime } \) . Thus we have an estimate \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  K{\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{-2} \) whenever \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \tau {\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{2},{t}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack  ,{\operatorname{dist}}_{t}\left( {x,{x}^{\prime }}\right)  \leq \; \frac{1}{4}{r}^{\prime } \) . Now we can apply the previous theorem (or rather its scaled version) and get an estimate on \( R\left( {x, t}\right) \) whenever \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{1}{2}\tau {\left( {r}^{\prime }\right) }^{2},{t}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack  ,{\operatorname{dist}}_{t}\left( {{x}^{\prime }, x}\right)  \leq  {10}{r}_{0} \) . Therefore, if \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) is small enough, we have \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq   - {r}_{0}^{-2} \) for those \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) , which is a contradiction to the choice of \( {\tau }^{\prime } \) .

nodes.content: Given any compact three-manifold \( M \) with an arbitrary Riemannian metric, one evolves the metric by the Ricci flow. Then, as Hamilton showed in [58], the solution \( g\left( t\right) \) to the Ricci flow exists for a short time and is unique (also see Theorem 1.2.1). In fact, Hamilton [58] showed that the solution \( g\left( t\right) \) will exist on a maximal time interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) , where either \( T = \infty \) , or \( 0 < T < \infty \) and the curvature becomes unbounded as \( t \) tends to \( T \) . We call such a solution \( g\left( t\right) \) a maximal solution of the Ricci flow. If \( T < \infty \) and the curvature becomes unbounded as \( t \) tends to \( T \) , we say the maximal solution develops singularities as \( t \) tends to \( T \) and \( T \) is the singular time.

nodes.content:
1.1. The Ricci Flow. Let \( M \) be an \( n \) -dimensional complete Riemannian manifold with the Riemannian metric \( {g}_{ij} \) . The Levi-Civita connection is given by the Christoffel symbols

\[
{\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} = \frac{1}{2}{g}^{kl}\left( {\frac{\partial {g}_{jl}}{\partial {x}^{i}} + \frac{\partial {g}_{il}}{\partial {x}^{j}} - \frac{\partial {g}_{ij}}{\partial {x}^{l}}}\right)
\]

where \( {g}^{ij} \) is the inverse of \( {g}_{ij} \) . The summation convention of summing over repeated indices is used here and throughout the book. The Riemannian curvature tensor is given by

\[
{R}_{ijl}^{k} = \frac{\partial {\Gamma }_{jl}^{k}}{\partial {x}^{i}} - \frac{\partial {\Gamma }_{il}^{k}}{\partial {x}^{j}} + {\Gamma }_{ip}^{k}{\Gamma }_{jl}^{p} - {\Gamma }_{jp}^{k}{\Gamma }_{il}^{p}.
\]

We lower the index to the third position, so that

\[
{R}_{ijkl} = {g}_{kp}{R}_{ijl}^{p}.
\]

The curvature tensor \( {R}_{ijkl} \) is anti-symmetric in the pairs \( i, j \) and \( k, l \) and symmetric in their interchange:

\[
{R}_{ijkl} =  - {R}_{jikl} =  - {R}_{ijlk} = {R}_{klij}.
\]

Also the first Bianchi identity holds

(1.1.1)

\[
{R}_{ijkl} + {R}_{jkil} + {R}_{kijl} = 0.
\]

The Ricci tensor is the contraction

\[
{R}_{ik} = {g}^{jl}{R}_{ijkl},
\]

and the scalar curvature is

\[
R = {g}^{ij}{R}_{ij}
\]

We denote the covariant derivative of a vector field \( v = {v}^{j}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{j}} \) by

\[
{\nabla }_{i}{v}^{j} = \frac{\partial {v}^{j}}{\partial {x}^{i}} + {\Gamma }_{ik}^{j}{v}^{k}
\]

and of a 1-form by

\[
{\nabla }_{i}{v}_{j} = \frac{\partial {v}_{j}}{\partial {x}^{i}} - {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}{v}_{k}.
\]

These definitions extend uniquely to tensors so as to preserve the product rule and contractions. For the exchange of two covariant derivatives, we have

(1.1.2)

\[
{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}{v}^{l} - {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{i}{v}^{l} = {R}_{ijk}^{l}{v}^{k},
\]

(1.1.3)

\[
{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}{v}_{k} - {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{i}{v}_{k} = {R}_{ijkl}{g}^{lm}{v}_{m},
\]

and similar formulas for more complicated tensors. The second Bianchi identity is given by

(1.1.4)

\[
{\nabla }_{m}{R}_{ijkl} + {\nabla }_{i}{R}_{jmkl} + {\nabla }_{j}{R}_{mikl} = 0.
\]

For any tensor \( T = {T}_{jk}^{i} \) we define its length by

\[
{\left| {T}_{jk}^{i}\right| }^{2} = {g}_{il}{g}^{jm}{g}^{kp}{T}_{jk}^{i}{T}_{mp}^{l},
\]

and we define its Laplacian by

\[
\Delta {T}_{jk}^{i} = {g}^{pq}{\nabla }_{p}{\nabla }_{q}{T}_{jk}^{i},
\]

the trace of the second iterated covariant derivatives. Similar definitions hold for more general tensors.

The Ricci flow of Hamilton [58] is the evolution equation

(1.1.5)

\[
\frac{\partial {g}_{ij}}{\partial t} =  - 2{R}_{ij}
\]

for a family of Riemannian metrics \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) on \( M \) . It is a nonlinear system of second order partial differential equations on metrics.

nodes.document_title: Huai-Dong Cao and Xi-Ping Zhu - A Complete Proof of the Poincare and Geometrization Conjectures
nodes.content:
(1) Einstein metrics

A Riemannian metric \( {g}_{ij} \) is called Einstein if

\[
{R}_{ij} = \lambda {g}_{ij}
\]

for some constant \( \lambda \) . A smooth manifold \( M \) with an Einstein metric is called an Einstein manifold.

If the initial metric is Ricci flat, so that \( {R}_{ij} = 0 \) , then clearly the metric does not change under (1.1.5). Hence any Ricci flat metric is a stationary solution of the Ricci flow. This happens, for example, on a flat torus or on any \( {K3} \) -surface with a Calabi-Yau metric.

If the initial metric is Einstein with positive scalar curvature, then the metric will shrink under the Ricci flow by a time-dependent factor. Indeed, since the initial metric is Einstein, we have

\[
{R}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right)  = \lambda {g}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right) ,\;\forall x \in  M
\]

and some \( \lambda  > 0 \) . Let

\[
{g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right)  = {\rho }^{2}\left( t\right) {g}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right) .
\]

From the definition of the Ricci tensor, one sees that

\[
{R}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right)  = {R}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right)  = \lambda {g}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right) .
\]

Thus the equation (1.1.5) corresponds to

\[
\frac{\partial \left( {{\rho }^{2}\left( t\right) {g}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right) }\right) }{\partial t} =  - {2\lambda }{g}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right) .
\]

This gives the ODE

(1.1.6)

\[
\frac{d\rho }{dt} =  - \frac{\lambda }{\rho }
\]

whose solution is given by

\[
{\rho }^{2}\left( t\right)  = 1 - {2\lambda t}
\]

Thus the evolving metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) \) shrinks homothetically to a point as \( t \rightarrow  T = 1/{2\lambda } \) . Note that as \( t \rightarrow  T \) , the scalar curvature becomes infinite like \( 1/\left( {T - t}\right) \) .

By contrast, if the initial metric is an Einstein metric of negative scalar curvature, the metric will expand homothetically for all times. Indeed if

\[
{R}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right)  =  - \lambda {g}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right)
\]

with \( \lambda  > 0 \) and

\[
{g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right)  = {\rho }^{2}\left( t\right) {g}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right) .
\]

Then \( \rho \left( t\right) \) satisfies the ODE

(1.1.7)

\[
\frac{d\rho }{dt} = \frac{\lambda }{\rho }
\]

with the solution

\[
{\rho }^{2}\left( t\right)  = 1 + {2\lambda t}
\]

Hence the evolving metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right)  = {\rho }^{2}\left( t\right) {g}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right) \) exists and expands homothetically for all times, and the curvature will fall back to zero like \( - 1/t \) . Note that now the evolving metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) \) only goes back in time to \( - 1/{2\lambda } \) , when the metric explodes out of a single point in a "big bang".

nodes.content:
## (2) Ricci Solitons

We will call a solution to an evolution equation which moves under a one-parameter subgroup of the symmetry group of the equation a steady soliton. The symmetry group of the Ricci flow contains the full diffeomorphism group. Thus a solution to the Ricci flow (1.1.5) which moves by a one-parameter group of diffeomor-phisms \( {\varphi }_{t} \) is called a steady Ricci soliton.

If \( {\varphi }_{t} \) is a one-parameter group of diffeomorphisms generated by a vector field \( V \) on \( M \) , then the Ricci soliton is given by

(1.1.8)

\[
{g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right)  = {\varphi }_{t}^{ * }{g}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right)
\]

which implies that the Ricci term -2Ric on the RHS of (1.1.5) is equal to the Lie derivative \( {\mathcal{L}}_{V}g \) of the evolving metric \( g \) . In particular, the initial metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right) \) satisfies the following steady Ricci soliton equation

(1.1.9)

\[
2{R}_{ij} + {g}_{ik}{\nabla }_{j}{V}^{k} + {g}_{jk}{\nabla }_{i}{V}^{k} = 0.
\]

If the vector field \( V \) is the gradient of a function \( f \) then the soliton is called a steady gradient Ricci soliton. Thus

(1.1.10)

\[
{R}_{ij} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f = 0,\;\text{ or }\;\operatorname{Ric} + {\nabla }^{2}f = 0,
\]

is the steady gradient Ricci soliton equation.

Conversely, it is clear that a metric \( {g}_{ij} \) satisfying (1.1.10) generates a steady gradient Ricci soliton \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) given by (1.1.8). For this reason we also often call such a metric \( {g}_{ij} \) a steady gradient Ricci soliton and do not necessarily distinguish it with the solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) it generates.

More generally, we can consider a solution to the Ricci flow (1.1.5) which moves by diffeomorphisms and also shrinks or expands by a (time-dependent) factor at the same time. Such a solution is called a homothetically shrinking or homothetically expanding Ricci soliton. The equation for a homothetic Ricci soliton is

(1.1.11)

\[
2{R}_{ij} + {g}_{ik}{\nabla }_{j}{V}^{k} + {g}_{jk}{\nabla }_{i}{V}^{k} - {2\lambda }{g}_{ij} = 0,
\]

or for a homothetic gradient Ricci soliton,

(1.1.12)

\[
{R}_{ij} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f - \lambda {g}_{ij} = 0,
\]

where \( \lambda \) is the homothetic constant. For \( \lambda  > 0 \) the soliton is shrinking, for \( \lambda  < 0 \) it is expanding. The case \( \lambda  = 0 \) is a steady Ricci soliton, the case \( V = 0 \) (or \( f \) being a constant function) is an Einstein metric. Thus Ricci solitons can be considered as natural extensions of Einstein metrics. In fact, the following result states that there are no nontrivial gradient steady or expanding Ricci solitons on any compact manifold.

We remark that if the underlying manifold \( M \) is a complex manifold and the initial metric is Kähler, then it is well known (see, e.g., [62, 11]) that the solution metric to the Ricci flow (1.1.5) remains Kähler. For this reason, the Ricci flow on a Kähler manifold is called the Kähler-Ricci flow. A (steady, or shrinking, or expanding) Ricci soliton to the Kähler-Ricci flow is called a (steady, or shrinking, or expanding repectively) Kähler-Ricci soliton.

nodes.content: PROPOSITION 1.1.1. On a compact n-dimensional manifold \( M \) , a gradient steady or expanding Ricci soliton is necessarily an Einstein metric.
nodes.content_excerpt: PROPOSITION 1.1.1. On a compact n-dimensional manifold \( M \) , a gradient steady or expanding Ricci soliton is necessarily an Einstein metric.

nodes.proof:
We shall only prove the steady case and leave the expanding case as an exercise. Our argument here follows that of Hamilton [63].

Let \( {g}_{ij} \) be a complete steady gradient Ricci soliton on a manifold \( M \) so that

\[
{R}_{ij} + {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f = 0.
\]

Taking the trace, we get

(1.1.13)

\[
R + {\Delta f} = 0.
\]

Also, taking the covariant derivatives of the Ricci soliton equation, we have

\[
{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{k}f - {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{k}f = {\nabla }_{j}{R}_{ik} - {\nabla }_{i}{R}_{jk}.
\]

On the other hand, by using the commutating formula (1.1.3), we otain

\[
{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{k}f - {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{k}f = {R}_{ijkl}{\nabla }_{l}f.
\]

Thus

\[
{\nabla }_{i}{R}_{jk} - {\nabla }_{j}{R}_{ik} + {R}_{ijkl}{\nabla }_{l}f = 0.
\]

Taking the trace on \( j \) and \( k \) , and using the contracted second Bianchi identity

(1.1.14)

\[
{\nabla }_{j}{R}_{ij} = \frac{1}{2}{\nabla }_{i}R
\]

we get

\[
{\nabla }_{i}R - 2{R}_{ij}{\nabla }_{j}f = 0.
\]

Then

\[
{\nabla }_{i}\left( {{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} + R}\right)  = 2{\nabla }_{j}f\left( {{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f + {R}_{ij}}\right)  = 0.
\]

Therefore

(1.1.15)

\[
R + {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} = C
\]

for some constant \( C \) .

Taking the difference of (1.1.13) and (1.1.15), we get

(1.1.16)

\[
{\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2} =  - C
\]

We claim \( C = 0 \) when \( M \) is compact. Indeed, this follows either from

(1.1.17)

\[
0 =  - {\int }_{M}\Delta \left( {e}^{-f}\right) {dV} = {\int }_{M}\left( {{\Delta f} - {\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}\right) {e}^{-f}{dV},
\]

or from considering (1.1.16) at both the maximum point and minimum point of \( f \) . Then, by integrating (1.1.16) we obtain

\[
{\int }_{M}{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}{dV} = 0.
\]

Therefore \( f \) is a constant and \( {g}_{ij} \) is Ricci flat. \( \square \)

nodes.label: Remark 1.1.2
nodes.document_title: Huai-Dong Cao and Xi-Ping Zhu - A Complete Proof of the Poincare and Geometrization Conjectures
nodes.content:
REMARK 1.1.2. By contrast, there do exist nontrivial compact gradient shrinking Ricci solitons (see Koiso [80], Cao [13] and Wang-Zhu [127] ). Also, there exist complete noncompact steady gradient Ricci solitons that are not Ricci flat. In two dimensions Hamilton [60] wrote down the first such example on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{2} \) , called the cigar soliton, where the metric is given by

(1.1.18)

\[
d{s}^{2} = \frac{d{x}^{2} + d{y}^{2}}{1 + {x}^{2} + {y}^{2}},
\]

and the vector field is radial, given by \( V =  - \partial /\partial r =  - \left( {x\partial /\partial x + y\partial /\partial y}\right) \) . This metric has positive curvature and is asymptotic to a cylinder of finite circumference \( {2\pi } \) at \( \infty \) . Higher dimensional examples were found by Robert Bryant [10] on \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) in the Riemannian case, and by the first author [13] on \( {\mathbb{C}}^{n} \) in the Kähler case. These examples are complete, rotationally symmetric, of positive curvature and found by solving certain nonlinear ODE (system). Noncompact expanding solitons were also constructed by the first author [13]. More recently, Feldman, Ilmanen and Knopf [46] constructed new examples of noncompact shrinking and expanding Kähler-Ricci solitons.

nodes.content: LEMMA 1.2.1. The modified evolution equation (1.2.5) is a strictly parabolic system.
nodes.content_excerpt: LEMMA 1.2.1. The modified evolution equation (1.2.5) is a strictly parabolic system.

nodes.proof:
The RHS of the equation (1.2.5) is given by

\[
- 2{R}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right)  + {\nabla }_{i}{V}_{j} + {\nabla }_{j}{V}_{i}
\]

\[
= \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}\left\{  {{g}^{kl}\frac{\partial {g}_{kl}}{\partial {x}^{j}}}\right\}   - \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{k}}\left\{  {{g}^{kl}\left( {\frac{\partial {g}_{jl}}{\partial {x}^{i}} + \frac{\partial {g}_{il}}{\partial {x}^{j}} - \frac{\partial {g}_{ij}}{\partial {x}^{l}}}\right) }\right\}
\]

\[
+ {g}_{jk}{g}^{pq}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}\left\{  {\frac{1}{2}{g}^{kl}\left( {\frac{\partial {g}_{pl}}{\partial {x}^{q}} + \frac{\partial {g}_{ql}}{\partial {x}^{p}} - \frac{\partial {g}_{pq}}{\partial {x}^{l}}}\right) }\right\}
\]

\[
+ {g}_{ik}{g}^{pq}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{j}}\left\{  {\frac{1}{2}{g}^{kl}\left( {\frac{\partial {g}_{pl}}{\partial {x}^{q}} + \frac{\partial {g}_{ql}}{\partial {x}^{p}} - \frac{\partial {g}_{pq}}{\partial {x}^{l}}}\right) }\right\}
\]

\[
\text{ + (lower order terms) }
\]

\[
= {g}^{kl}\left\{  {\frac{{\partial }^{2}{g}_{kl}}{\partial {x}^{i}\partial {x}^{j}} - \frac{{\partial }^{2}{g}_{jl}}{\partial {x}^{i}\partial {x}^{k}} - \frac{{\partial }^{2}{g}_{il}}{\partial {x}^{j}\partial {x}^{k}} + \frac{{\partial }^{2}{g}_{ij}}{\partial {x}^{k}\partial {x}^{l}}}\right\}
\]

\[
+ \frac{1}{2}{g}^{pq}\left\{  {\frac{{\partial }^{2}{g}_{pj}}{\partial {x}^{i}\partial {x}^{q}} + \frac{{\partial }^{2}{g}_{qj}}{\partial {x}^{i}\partial {x}^{p}} - \frac{{\partial }^{2}{g}_{pq}}{\partial {x}^{i}\partial {x}^{j}}}\right\}
\]

\[
+ \frac{1}{2}{g}^{pq}\left\{  {\frac{{\partial }^{2}{g}_{pi}}{\partial {x}^{j}\partial {x}^{q}} + \frac{{\partial }^{2}{g}_{qi}}{\partial {x}^{j}\partial {x}^{p}} - \frac{{\partial }^{2}{g}_{pq}}{\partial {x}^{i}\partial {x}^{j}}}\right\}
\]

\[
\text{ + (lower order terms) }
\]

\[
= {g}^{kl}\frac{{\partial }^{2}{g}_{ij}}{\partial {x}^{k}\partial {x}^{l}} + \text{ (lower order terms). }
\]

Thus its symbol is \( \left( {{g}^{kl}{\zeta }_{k}{\zeta }_{l}}\right) {\widetilde{g}}_{ij} \) . Hence the equation in (1.2.5) is strictly parabolic. I

Now since the equation (1.2.5) is strictly parabolic and the manifold \( M \) is compact, it follows from the standard theory of parabolic equations (see for example [81]) that (1.2.5) has a solution for a short time. From the solution of (1.2.5) we can obtain a solution of the Ricci flow from (1.2.4) and (1.2.2). This shows existence. Now we argue the uniqueness of the solution. Since

\[
{\Gamma }_{jl}^{k} = \frac{\partial {y}^{\alpha }}{\partial {x}^{j}}\frac{\partial {y}^{\beta }}{\partial {x}^{l}}\frac{\partial {x}^{k}}{\partial {y}^{\gamma }}{\widehat{\Gamma }}_{\alpha \beta }^{\gamma } + \frac{\partial {x}^{k}}{\partial {y}^{\alpha }}\frac{{\partial }^{2}{y}^{\alpha }}{\partial {x}^{j}\partial {x}^{l}},
\]

the initial value problem (1.2.4) can be written as

(1.2.6)

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} \frac{\partial {y}^{\alpha }}{\partial t} = {g}^{jl}\left( {\frac{{\partial }^{2}{y}^{\alpha }}{\partial {x}^{j}\partial {x}^{l}} - {\overset{o}{\Gamma }}_{jl}^{k}\frac{\partial {y}^{\alpha }}{\partial {x}^{k}} + {\overset{o}{\Gamma }}_{\gamma \beta }^{\alpha }\frac{\partial {y}^{\beta }}{\partial {x}^{j}}\frac{\partial {y}^{\gamma }}{\partial {x}^{l}}}\right) , \\  {y}^{\alpha }\left( {x,0}\right)  = {x}^{\alpha }. \end{array}\right.
\]

This is clearly a strictly parabolic system. For any two solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\left( 1\right) }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) and \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\left( 2\right) }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) of the Ricci flow (1.1.5) with the same initial data, we can solve the initial value problem (1.2.6) (or equivalently,(1.2.4)) to get two families \( {\varphi }_{t}^{\left( 1\right) } \) and \( {\varphi }_{t}^{\left( 2\right) } \) of dif-feomorphisms of \( M \) . Thus we get two solutions, \( {g}_{ij}^{\left( 1\right) }\left( {\cdot , t}\right)  = {\left( {\varphi }_{t}^{\left( 1\right) }\right) }^{ * }{\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\left( 1\right) }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) and \( {g}_{ij}^{\left( 2\right) }\left( {\cdot , t}\right)  = {\left( {\varphi }_{t}^{\left( 2\right) }\right) }^{ * }{\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\left( 2\right) }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) , to the modified evolution equation (1.2.5) with the same initial metric. The uniqueness result for the strictly parabolic equation (1.2.5) implies that \( {g}_{ij}^{\left( 1\right) } = {g}_{ij}^{\left( 2\right) } \) . Then by equation (1.2.4) and the standard uniqueness result of ODE systems, the corresponding solutions \( {\varphi }_{t}^{\left( 1\right) } \) and \( {\varphi }_{t}^{\left( 2\right) } \) of (1.2.4) (or equivalently (1.2.6)) must agree. Consequently the metrics \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\left( 1\right) } \) and \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\left( 2\right) } \) must agree also. Thus we have proved the following result.

Proposition 1.3.1 (Hamilton [58]). Under the Ricci flow (1.1.5), the curvature tensor satisfies the evolution equation

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{R}_{ijkl} = \Delta {R}_{ijkl} + 2\left( {{B}_{ijkl} - {B}_{ijlk} - {B}_{iljk} + {B}_{ikjl}}\right)
\]

\[
- {g}^{pq}\left( {{R}_{pjkl}{R}_{qi} + {R}_{ipkl}{R}_{qj} + {R}_{ijpl}{R}_{qk} + {R}_{ijkp}{R}_{ql}}\right)
\]

where \( {B}_{ijkl} = {g}^{pr}{g}^{qs}{R}_{piqj}{R}_{rksl} \) and \( \Delta \) is the Laplacian with respect to the evolving metric.

nodes.proof:
Choose \( \left\{  {{x}^{1},\ldots ,{x}^{m}}\right\} \) to be a normal coordinate system at a fixed point. At this point, we compute

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\Gamma }_{jl}^{h} = \frac{1}{2}{g}^{hm}\left\{  {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{j}}\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{g}_{lm}}\right)  + \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{l}}\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{g}_{jm}}\right)  - \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{m}}\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{g}_{jl}}\right) }\right\}
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}{g}^{hm}\left( {{\nabla }_{j}\left( {-2{R}_{lm}}\right)  + {\nabla }_{l}\left( {-2{R}_{jm}}\right)  - {\nabla }_{m}\left( {-2{R}_{jl}}\right) }\right) ,
\]

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{R}_{ijl}^{h} = \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\Gamma }_{jl}^{h}}\right)  - \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{j}}\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\Gamma }_{il}^{h}}\right) ,
\]

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{R}_{ijkl} = {g}_{hk}\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{R}_{ijl}^{h} + \frac{\partial {g}_{hk}}{\partial t}{R}_{ijl}^{h}.
\]

Combining these identities we get

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{R}_{ijkl} = {g}_{hk}\left\lbrack  \left( {\frac{1}{2}{\nabla }_{i}\left\lbrack  {{g}^{hm}\left( {{\nabla }_{j}\left( {-2{R}_{lm}}\right)  + {\nabla }_{l}\left( {-2{R}_{jm}}\right)  - {\nabla }_{m}\left( {-2{R}_{jl}}\right) }\right) }\right\rbrack  }\right) \right.
\]

\[
\left. {-\left( {\frac{1}{2}{\nabla }_{j}\left\lbrack  {{g}^{hm}\left( {{\nabla }_{i}\left( {-2{R}_{lm}}\right)  + {\nabla }_{l}\left( {-2{R}_{im}}\right)  - {\nabla }_{m}\left( {-2{R}_{il}}\right) }\right) }\right\rbrack  }\right) }\right\rbrack
\]

\[
- 2{R}_{hk}{R}_{ijl}^{h}
\]

\[
= {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{k}{R}_{jl} - {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{l}{R}_{jk} - {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{k}{R}_{il} + {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{l}{R}_{ik}
\]

\[
- {R}_{ijlp}{g}^{pq}{R}_{qk} - {R}_{ijkp}{g}^{pq}{R}_{ql} - 2{R}_{ijpl}{g}^{pq}{R}_{qk}
\]

\[
= {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{k}{R}_{jl} - {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{l}{R}_{jk} - {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{k}{R}_{il} + {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{l}{R}_{ik}
\]

\[
- {g}^{pq}\left( {{R}_{ijkp}{R}_{ql} + {R}_{ijpl}{R}_{qk}}\right) .
\]

Here we have used the exchanging formula (1.1.3).

Now it remains to check the following identity, which is analogous to the Simon's identity in extrinsic geometry,

(1.3.1)

\[
\Delta {R}_{ijkl} + 2\left( {{B}_{ijkl} - {B}_{ijlk} - {B}_{iljk} + {B}_{ikjl}}\right)
\]

\[
= {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{k}{R}_{jl} - {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{l}{R}_{jk} - {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{k}{R}_{il} + {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{l}{R}_{ik}
\]

\[
+ {g}^{pq}\left( {{R}_{pjkl}{R}_{qi} + {R}_{ipkl}{R}_{qj}}\right) .
\]

Indeed, from the second Bianchi identity (1.1.4), we have

\[
\Delta {R}_{ijkl} = {g}^{pq}{\nabla }_{p}{\nabla }_{q}{R}_{ijkl}
\]

\[
= {g}^{pq}{\nabla }_{p}{\nabla }_{i}{R}_{qjkl} - {g}^{pq}{\nabla }_{p}{\nabla }_{j}{R}_{qikl}.
\]

Let us examine the first term on the RHS. By using the exchanging formula (1.1.3) and the first Bianchi identity (1.1.1), we have

\[
{g}^{pq}{\nabla }_{p}{\nabla }_{i}{R}_{qjkl} - {g}^{pq}{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{p}{R}_{qjkl}
\]

\[
= {g}^{pq}{g}^{mn}\left( {{R}_{piqm}{R}_{njkl} + {R}_{pijm}{R}_{qnkl} + {R}_{pikm}{R}_{qjnl} + {R}_{pilm}{R}_{qjkn}}\right)
\]

\[
= {R}_{im}{g}^{mn}{R}_{njkl} + {g}^{pq}{g}^{mn}{R}_{pimj}\left( {{R}_{qkln} + {R}_{qlnk}}\right)
\]

\[
+ {g}^{pq}{g}^{mn}{R}_{pikm}{R}_{qjnl} + {g}^{pq}{g}^{mn}{R}_{pilm}{R}_{qjkn}
\]

\[
= {R}_{im}{g}^{mn}{R}_{njkl} - {B}_{ijkl} + {B}_{ijlk} - {B}_{ikjl} + {B}_{iljk},
\]

while using the contracted second Bianchi identity

(1.3.2)

\[
{g}^{pq}{\nabla }_{p}{R}_{qjkl} = {\nabla }_{k}{R}_{jl} - {\nabla }_{l}{R}_{jk},
\]

we have

\[
{g}^{pq}{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{p}{R}_{qjkl} = {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{k}{R}_{jl} - {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{l}{R}_{jk}.
\]

Thus

\[
{g}^{pq}{\nabla }_{p}{\nabla }_{i}{R}_{qjkl}
\]

\[
= {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{k}{R}_{jl} - {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{l}{R}_{jk} - \left( {{B}_{ijkl} - {B}_{ijlk} - {B}_{iljk} + {B}_{ikjl}}\right)  + {g}^{pq}{R}_{pjkl}{R}_{qi}.
\]

Therefore we obtain

\[
\Delta {R}_{ijkl}
\]

\[
= {g}^{pq}{\nabla }_{p}{\nabla }_{i}{R}_{qjkl} - {g}^{pq}{\nabla }_{p}{\nabla }_{j}{R}_{qikl}
\]

\[
= {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{k}{R}_{jl} - {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{l}{R}_{jk} - \left( {{B}_{ijkl} - {B}_{ijlk} - {B}_{iljk} + {B}_{ikjl}}\right)  + {g}^{pq}{R}_{pjkl}{R}_{qi}
\]

\[
- {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{k}{R}_{il} + {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{l}{R}_{ik} + \left( {{B}_{jikl} - {B}_{jilk} - {B}_{jlik} + {B}_{jkil}}\right)  - {g}^{pq}{R}_{pikl}{R}_{qj}
\]

\[
= {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{k}{R}_{jl} - {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{l}{R}_{jk} - {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{k}{R}_{il} + {\nabla }_{j}{\nabla }_{l}{R}_{ik}
\]

\[
+ {g}^{pq}\left( {{R}_{pjkl}{R}_{qi} + {R}_{ipkl}{R}_{qj}}\right)  - 2\left( {{B}_{ijkl} - {B}_{ijlk} - {B}_{iljk} + {B}_{ikjl}}\right)
\]

as desired, where in the last step we used the symmetries

(1.3.3)

\[
{B}_{ijkl} = {B}_{klij} = {B}_{jilk}.
\]

\[

\]

\[

\]

\[
- 2{g}^{pq}{R}_{pk}{R}_{qi}
\]

We claim that \( {g}^{jl}\left( {{B}_{ijkl} - 2{B}_{ijlk}}\right)  = 0 \) . Indeed by using the first Bianchi identity, we have

\[
{g}^{jl}{B}_{ijkl} = {g}^{jl}{g}^{pr}{g}^{qs}{R}_{piqj}{R}_{rksl}
\]

\[
= {g}^{jl}{g}^{pr}{g}^{qs}{R}_{pqij}{R}_{rskl}
\]

\[
= {g}^{jl}{g}^{pr}{g}^{qs}\left( {{R}_{piqj} - {R}_{pjqi}}\right) \left( {{R}_{rksl} - {R}_{rlsk}}\right)
\]

\[
= 2{g}^{jl}\left( {{B}_{ijkl} - {B}_{ijlk}}\right)
\]

as desired.

Thus we obtain

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{R}_{ik} = \Delta {R}_{ik} + 2{g}^{pr}{g}^{qs}{R}_{piqk}{R}_{rs} - 2{g}^{pq}{R}_{pi}{R}_{qk}.
\]

nodes.content:
THEOREM 1.4.1 (Shi [114]). There exist constants \( {C}_{m}, m = 1,2,\ldots \) , such that if the curvature of a complete solution to Ricci flow is bounded by

\[
\left| {R}_{ijkl}\right|  \leq  M
\]

up to time \( t \) with \( 0 < t \leq  \frac{1}{M} \) , then the covariant derivative of the curvature is bounded by

\[
\left| {\nabla {R}_{ijkl}}\right|  \leq  {C}_{1}M/\sqrt{t}
\]

and the \( {m}^{th} \) covariant derivative of the curvature is bounded by

\[
\left| {{\nabla }^{m}{R}_{ijkl}}\right|  \leq  {C}_{m}M/{t}^{\frac{m}{2}}.
\]

Here the norms are taken with respect to the evolving metric.

nodes.proof:
We shall only give the proof for the compact case. The noncompact case can be deduced from the next local derivative estimate theorem. Let us denote the curvature tensor by \( {Rm} \) and denote by \( A * B \) any tensor product of two tensors \( A \) and \( B \) when we do not need the precise expression. We have from Proposition 1.3.1 that

(1.4.1)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{Rm} = {\Delta Rm} + {Rm} * {Rm}.
\]

Since

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\Gamma }_{jk}^{i} = \frac{1}{2}{g}^{il}\left\{  {{\nabla }_{j}\frac{\partial {g}_{kl}}{\partial t} + {\nabla }_{k}\frac{\partial {g}_{jl}}{\partial t} - {\nabla }_{l}\frac{\partial {g}_{jk}}{\partial t}}\right\}
\]

\[
= \nabla {Rm},
\]

it follows that

(1.4.2)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {\nabla {Rm}}\right)  = \Delta \left( {\nabla {Rm}}\right)  + {Rm} * \left( {\nabla {Rm}}\right) .
\]

Thus

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| Rm\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2} + C{\left| Rm\right| }^{3}
\]

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {\nabla }^{2}Rm\right| }^{2} + C\left| {Rm}\right|  \cdot  {\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2},
\]

for some constant \( C \) depending only on the dimension \( n \) .

Let \( A > 0 \) be a constant (to be determined) and set

\[
F = t{\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2} + A{\left| Rm\right| }^{2}.
\]

We compute

\[
\frac{\partial F}{\partial t} = {\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2} + t\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2} + A\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| Rm\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
\leq  \Delta \left( {t{\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2} + A{\left| Rm\right| }^{2}}\right)  + {\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2}\left( {1 + {tC}\left| {Rm}\right|  - {2A}}\right)  + {CA}{\left| Rm\right| }^{3}.
\]

Taking \( A \geq  C + 1 \) , we get

\[
\frac{\partial F}{\partial t} \leq  {\Delta F} + \bar{C}{M}^{3}
\]

for some constant \( \bar{C} \) depending only on the dimension \( n \) . We then obtain

\[
F \leq  F\left( 0\right)  + \bar{C}{M}^{3}t \leq  \left( {A + \bar{C}}\right) {M}^{2},
\]

and then

\[
{\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  \left( {A + \bar{C}}\right) {M}^{2}/t
\]

The general case follows in the same way. If we have bounds

\[
\left| {{\nabla }^{k}{Rm}}\right|  \leq  {C}_{k}M/{t}^{\frac{k}{2}},
\]

we know from (1.4.1) and (1.4.2) that

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| {\nabla }^{k}Rm\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} + \frac{C{M}^{3}}{{t}^{k}},
\]

and

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 2}Rm\right| }^{2} + {CM}{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} + \frac{C{M}^{3}}{{t}^{k + 1}}.
\]

Let \( {A}_{k} > 0 \) be a constant (to be determined) and set

\[
{F}_{k} = {t}^{k + 2}{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} + {A}_{k}{t}^{k + 1}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}Rm\right| }^{2}.
\]

Then

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{F}_{k} = \left( {k + 2}\right) {t}^{k + 1}{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} + {t}^{k + 2}\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
+ {A}_{k}\left( {k + 1}\right) {t}^{k}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}Rm\right| }^{2} + {A}_{k}{t}^{k + 1}\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}Rm\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {k + 2}\right) {t}^{k + 1}{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
+ {t}^{k + 2}\left\lbrack  {\Delta {\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 2}Rm\right| }^{2} + {CM}{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} + \frac{C{M}^{3}}{{t}^{k + 1}}}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
+ {A}_{k}\left( {k + 1}\right) {t}^{k}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}Rm\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
+ {A}_{k}{t}^{k + 1}\left\lbrack  {\Delta {\left| {\nabla }^{k}Rm\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} + \frac{C{M}^{3}}{{t}^{k}}}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
\leq  \Delta {F}_{k} + {C}_{k + 1}{M}^{2}
\]

for some positive constant \( {C}_{k + 1} \) , by choosing \( {A}_{k} \) large enough. This implies that

\[
\left| {{\nabla }^{k + 1}{Rm}}\right|  \leq  \frac{{C}_{k + 1}M}{{t}^{\frac{k + 1}{2}}}.
\]

The above derivative estimate is a somewhat standard Bernstein estimate in PDEs. By using a cutoff argument, we will derive the following local version, which is called Shi's derivative estimate. The following proof is adapted from Hamilton [63].

nodes.content:
THEOREM 1.4.2 (Shi [114]). There exist positive constants \( \theta ,{C}_{k}, k = 1,2,\ldots \) , depending only on the dimension with the following property. Suppose that the curvature of a solution to the Ricci flow is bounded

\[
\left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  M,\;\text{ on }U \times  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{\theta }{M}}\right\rbrack
\]

where \( U \) is an open set of the manifold. Assume that the closed ball \( {B}_{0}\left( {p, r}\right) \) , centered at \( p \) of radius \( r \) with respect to the metric at \( t = 0 \) , is contained in \( U \) and the time \( t \leq  \theta /M \) . Then we can estimate the covariant derivatives of the curvature at \( \left( {p, t}\right) \) by

\[
{\left| \nabla Rm\left( p, t\right) \right| }^{2} \leq  {C}_{1}{M}^{2}\left( {\frac{1}{{r}^{2}} + \frac{1}{t} + M}\right) ,
\]

and the \( {k}^{\text{ th }} \) covariant derivative of the curvature at \( \left( {p, t}\right) \) by

\[
{\left| {\nabla }^{k}Rm\left( p, t\right) \right| }^{2} \leq  {C}_{k}{M}^{2}\left( {\frac{1}{{r}^{2k}} + \frac{1}{{t}^{k}} + {M}^{k}}\right) .
\]
