nodes.proof:
From the evolution equation of the Ricci flow, we know that the metrics \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) are equivalent to each other on \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{r}_{0}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) . Thus, without loss of generality, we may assume that the curvature of the solution is uniformly bounded for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{r}_{0}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) and all points in \( {B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) . Fix a point \( \left( {x,{r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  \in  M \times  \left\{  {r}_{0}^{2}\right\} \) . By scaling we may assume \( {r}_{0} = 1 \) . We may also assume \( {d}_{1}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  = A \) . Let \( p = x \) , \( \bar{\tau } = 1 - t \) , and consider Perelman’s reduced volume

\[
\widetilde{V}\left( \bar{\tau }\right)  = {\int }_{M}{\left( 4\pi \bar{\tau }\right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,\bar{\tau }}\right) }\right) d{V}_{1 - \bar{\tau }}\left( q\right) ,
\]

where

\[
l\left( {q,\bar{\tau }}\right)  = \inf \left\{  {\left. {\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\bar{\tau }}}{\int }_{0}^{\bar{\tau }}\sqrt{\tau }\left( {R + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}}\right) {d\tau }}\right| \;\gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{\tau }}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M}\right.
\]

\[
\text{ with }\left. {\gamma \left( 0\right)  = p,\gamma \left( \bar{\tau }\right)  = q}\right\}
\]

is the Li-Yau-Perelman distance. We argue by contradiction. Suppose for some \( 0 < \; r < 1 \) we have

\[
\left| {Rm}\right| \left( {y, t}\right)  \leq  {r}^{-2}
\]

whenever \( y \in  {B}_{1}\left( {x, r}\right) \) and \( 1 - {r}^{2} \leq  t \leq  1 \) , but \( \epsilon  = {r}^{-1}{\operatorname{Vol}}_{1}{\left( {B}_{1}\left( x, r\right) \right) }^{\frac{1}{n}} \) is very small. Then arguing as in the proof of the no local collapsing theorem I (Theorem 3.3.2), we see that Perelman's reduced volume

\[
\widetilde{V}\left( {\epsilon {r}^{2}}\right)  \leq  2{\epsilon }^{\frac{n}{2}}.
\]

On the other hand, from the monotonicity of Perelman's reduced volume we have

\[
{\left( 4\pi \right) }^{-\frac{n}{2}}{\int }_{M}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,1}\right) }\right) d{V}_{0}\left( q\right)  = \widetilde{V}\left( 1\right)  \leq  \widetilde{V}\left( {\epsilon {r}^{2}}\right) .
\]

Thus once we bound the function \( l\left( {q,1}\right) \) over \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{0},1}\right) \) from above, we will get the desired contradiction and will prove the theorem.

For any \( q \in  {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{0},1}\right) \) , exactly as in the proof of the no local collapsing theorem I, we choose a path \( \gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = x,\gamma \left( 1\right)  = q,\gamma \left( \frac{1}{2}\right)  = y \in  {B}_{\frac{1}{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{10}}\right) \) and \( \gamma \left( \tau \right)  \in  {B}_{1 - \tau }\left( {{x}_{0},1}\right) \) for \( \tau  \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2},1}\right\rbrack \) such that

\[
\mathcal{L}\left( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  0,\frac{1}{2}\right\rbrack  }\right)  = 2\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}l\left( {y,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \;\left( { = L\left( {y,\frac{1}{2}}\right) }\right) .
\]

Now \( \mathcal{L}\left( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  \frac{1}{2},1\right\rbrack  }\right)  = {\int }_{\frac{1}{2}}^{1}\sqrt{\tau }\left( {R\left( {\gamma \left( \tau \right) ,1 - \tau }\right)  + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\left( \tau \right) \right| }_{{g}_{ij}\left( {1 - \tau }\right) }^{2}}\right) {d\tau } \) is bounded from above by a uniform constant since all geometric quantities in \( {g}_{ij} \) are uniformly bounded on \( \left\{  {\left( {y, t}\right)  \mid  t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1/2}\right\rbrack  , y \in  {B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},1}\right) }\right\} \) (where \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1/2}\right\rbrack \) is equivalent to \( \tau  \in  \left\lbrack  {1/2,1}\right\rbrack \) ). Thus all we need is to estimate the minimum of \( l\left( {\cdot ,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \) , or equivalently \( \bar{L}\left( {\cdot ,\frac{1}{2}}\right)  = \; 4\frac{1}{2}l\left( {\cdot ,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \) , in the ball \( {B}_{\frac{1}{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{10}}\right) \) .

Recall that \( \bar{L} \) satisfies the differential inequality

(3.4.1)

\[
\frac{\partial \bar{L}}{\partial \tau } + \Delta \bar{L} \leq  {2n}.
\]

We will use this in a maximum principle argument. Let us define

\[
h\left( {y, t}\right)  = \phi \left( {d\left( {y, t}\right)  - A\left( {{2t} - 1}\right) }\right)  \cdot  \left( {\bar{L}\left( {y,1 - t}\right)  + {2n} + 1}\right)
\]

where \( d\left( {y, t}\right)  = {d}_{t}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right) \) , and \( \phi \) is a function of one variable, equal to 1 on \( \left( {-\infty ,\frac{1}{20}}\right) \) , and rapidly increasing to infinity on \( \left( {\frac{1}{20},\frac{1}{10}}\right) \) in such a way that:

(3.4.2)

\[
2\frac{{\left( {\phi }^{\prime }\right) }^{2}}{\phi } - {\phi }^{\prime \prime } \geq  \left( {{2A} + {100n}}\right) {\phi }^{\prime } - C\left( A\right) \phi
\]

for some constant \( C\left( A\right)  <  + \infty \) . The existence of such a function \( \phi \) can be justified as follows: put \( v = \frac{{\phi }^{\prime }}{\phi } \) , then the condition (3.4.2) for \( \phi \) can be written as

\[
3{v}^{2} - {v}^{\prime } \geq  \left( {{2A} + {100n}}\right) v - C\left( A\right)
\]

which can be solved for \( v \) .

Since the scalar curvature \( R \) evolves by

\[
\frac{\partial R}{\partial t} = {\Delta R} + 2{\left| Rc\right| }^{2} \geq  {\Delta R} + \frac{2}{n}{R}^{2},
\]

we can apply the maximum principle as in Chapter 2 to deduce

\[
R\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq   - \frac{n}{2t}\text{ for }t \in  (0,1\rbrack \text{ and }x \in  M.
\]

Thus for \( \bar{\tau } = 1 - t \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{2}}\right\rbrack \) ,

\[
\bar{L}\left( {\cdot ,\bar{\tau }}\right)  = 2\sqrt{\bar{\tau }}{\int }_{0}^{\bar{\tau }}\sqrt{\tau }\left( {R + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}}\right) {d\tau }
\]

\[
\geq  2\sqrt{\bar{\tau }}{\int }_{0}^{\bar{\tau }}\sqrt{\tau }\left( {-\frac{n}{2\left( {1 - \tau }\right) }}\right) {d\tau }
\]

\[
\geq  2\sqrt{\bar{\tau }}{\int }_{0}^{\bar{\tau }}\sqrt{\tau }\left( {-n}\right) {d\tau }
\]

\[
>  - {2n}\text{ . }
\]

That is

(3.4.3)

\[
\bar{L}\left( {\cdot ,1 - t}\right)  + {2n} + 1 \geq  1,\;\text{ for }t \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2},1}\right\rbrack  .
\]

Clearly \( \mathop{\min }\limits_{{y \in  M}}h\left( {y,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \) is achieved by some \( y \in  {B}_{\frac{1}{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{10}}\right) \) and

(3.4.4)

\[
\mathop{\min }\limits_{{y \in  M}}h\left( {y,1}\right)  \leq  h\left( {x,1}\right)  = {2n} + 1.
\]

We compute

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta }\right) h = \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta }\right) \phi  \cdot  \left( {\bar{L}\left( {y,1 - t}\right)  + {2n} + 1}\right)
\]

\[
+ \phi  \cdot  \left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta }\right) \bar{L}\left( {y,1 - t}\right)  - 2\langle \nabla \phi ,\nabla \bar{L}\left( {y,1 - t}\right) \rangle
\]

\[
= \left( {{\phi }^{\prime }\left\lbrack  {\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta }\right) d - {2A}}\right\rbrack   - {\phi }^{\prime \prime }{\left| \nabla d\right| }^{2}}\right)  \cdot  \left( {\bar{L} + {2n} + 1}\right)
\]

\[
+ \phi  \cdot  \left( {-\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau } - \Delta }\right) \bar{L} - 2\langle \nabla \phi ,\nabla \bar{L}\rangle
\]

\[
\geq  \left( {{\phi }^{\prime }\left\lbrack  {\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta }\right) d - {2A}}\right\rbrack   - {\phi }^{\prime \prime }}\right)  \cdot  \left( {\bar{L} + {2n} + 1}\right)
\]

\[
- {2n\phi } - 2\langle \nabla \phi ,\nabla \bar{L}\rangle
\]

by using (3.4.1). At a minimizing point of \( h \) we have

\[
\frac{\nabla \phi }{\phi } =  - \frac{\nabla \bar{L}}{\left( \bar{L} + 2n + 1\right) }.
\]

Hence

\[
- 2\langle \nabla \phi ,\nabla \bar{L}\rangle  = 2\frac{{\left| \nabla \phi \right| }^{2}}{\phi }\left( {\bar{L} + {2n} + 1}\right)  = 2\frac{{\left( {\phi }^{\prime }\right) }^{2}}{\phi }\left( {\bar{L} + {2n} + 1}\right) .
\]

Then at the minimizing point of \( h \) , we compute

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta }\right) h \geq  \left( {{\phi }^{\prime }\left\lbrack  {\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta }\right) d - {2A}}\right\rbrack   - {\phi }^{\prime \prime }}\right)  \cdot  \left( {\bar{L} + {2n} + 1}\right)
\]

\[
- {2n\phi } + 2\frac{{\left( {\phi }^{\prime }\right) }^{2}}{\phi }\left( {\bar{L} + {2n} + 1}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  \left( {{\phi }^{\prime }\left\lbrack  {\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta }\right) d - {2A}}\right\rbrack   - {\phi }^{\prime \prime }}\right)  \cdot  \left( {\bar{L} + {2n} + 1}\right)
\]

\[
- {2nh} + 2\frac{{\left( {\phi }^{\prime }\right) }^{2}}{\phi }\left( {\bar{L} + {2n} + 1}\right)
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2},1}\right\rbrack \) and

\[
{\Delta h} \geq  0\text{ . }
\]

Let us denote by \( {h}_{\min }\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\min }\limits_{{y \in  M}}h\left( {y, t}\right) \) . By applying Lemma 3.4.1(i) to the set where \( {\phi }^{\prime } \neq  0 \) , we further obtain

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{h}_{\min } \geq  \left( {\bar{L} + {2n} + 1}\right)  \cdot  \left\lbrack  {{\phi }^{\prime }\left( {-{100n} - {2A}}\right)  - {\phi }^{\prime \prime } + 2\frac{{\left( {\phi }^{\prime }\right) }^{2}}{\phi }}\right\rbrack   - {2n}{h}_{\min }
\]

\[
\geq   - \left( {{2n} + C\left( A\right) }\right) {h}_{\min },\;\text{ for }t \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2},1}\right\rbrack  .
\]

This implies that \( {h}_{\min }\left( t\right) \) cannot decrease too fast. By combining (3.4.3) and (3.4.4) we get the required estimate for the minimum \( \bar{L}\left( {\cdot ,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \) in the ball \( {B}_{\frac{1}{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{10}}\right) \) .

Therefore we have completed the proof of the theorem.

Let \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k},{p}_{k}}\right) \) be a sequence of marked complete Riemannian manifolds, with metrics \( {g}_{k} \) and marked points \( {p}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) . Let \( B\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{k}}\right)  \subset  {M}_{k} \) denote the geodesic ball centered at \( {p}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) and of radius \( {s}_{k}\left( {0 < {s}_{k} \leq   + \infty }\right) \) . We say a sequence of marked geodesic balls \( \left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{k}}\right) ,{g}_{k},{p}_{k}}\right) \) with \( {s}_{k} \rightarrow  {s}_{\infty }\left( { \leq   + \infty }\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (maybe noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{p}_{\infty }}\right) \) , which is an open geodesic ball centered at \( {p}_{\infty } \in  {B}_{\infty } \) and of radius \( {s}_{\infty } \) with respect to the metric \( {g}_{\infty } \) , if we can find a sequence of exhausting open sets \( {U}_{k} \) in \( {B}_{\infty } \) containing \( {p}_{\infty } \) and a sequence of diffeomorphisms \( {f}_{k} \) of the sets \( {U}_{k} \) in \( {B}_{\infty } \) to open sets \( {V}_{k} \) in \( B\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{k}}\right)  \subset  {M}_{k} \) mapping \( {p}_{\infty } \) to \( {p}_{k} \) such that the pull-back metrics \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k} = {\left( {f}_{k}\right) }^{ * }{g}_{k} \) converge in \( {C}^{\infty } \) topology to \( {g}_{\infty } \) on every compact subset of \( {B}_{\infty } \) .

nodes.content:
THEOREM 4.1.2 (Hamilton [62]). Let \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k},{p}_{k}}\right) \) be a sequence of marked complete Riemannian manifolds of dimension \( n \) . Consider a sequence of geodesic balls \( B\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{k}}\right)  \subset  {M}_{k} \) of radius \( {s}_{k}\left( {0 < {s}_{k} \leq  \infty }\right) \) , with \( {s}_{k} \rightarrow  {s}_{\infty }\left( { \leq  \infty }\right) \) , around the base point \( {p}_{k} \) of \( {M}_{k} \) in the metric \( {g}_{k} \) . Suppose

(a) for every radius \( r < {s}_{\infty } \) and every integer \( l \geq  0 \) there exists a constant \( {B}_{l, r} \) , independent of \( k \) , and positive integer \( k\left( {r, l}\right)  <  + \infty \) such that as \( k \geq \; k\left( {r, l}\right) \) , the curvature tensors \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {g}_{k}\right) \) of the metrics \( {g}_{k} \) and their \( {l}^{\text{ th }} \) -covariant derivatives satisfy the bounds

\[
\left| {{\nabla }^{l}\operatorname{Rm}\left( {g}_{k}\right) }\right|  \leq  {B}_{l, r}
\]

on the balls \( B\left( {{p}_{k}, r}\right) \) of radius \( r \) around \( {p}_{k} \) in the metrics \( {g}_{k} \) ; and

(b) there exists a constant \( \delta  > 0 \) independent of \( k \) such that the injectivity radii inj \( \left( {{M}_{k},{p}_{k}}\right) \) of \( {M}_{k} \) at \( {p}_{k} \) in the metric \( {g}_{k} \) satisfy the bound

\[
\operatorname{inj}\left( {{M}_{k},{p}_{k}}\right)  \geq  \delta
\]

Then there exists a subsequence of the marked geodesic balls \( \left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{k}}\right) ,{g}_{k},{p}_{k}}\right) \) which converges to a marked geodesic ball \( \left( {B\left( {{p}_{\infty },{s}_{\infty }}\right) ,{g}_{\infty },{p}_{\infty }}\right) \) in \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology. Moreover the limit is complete if \( {s}_{\infty } =  + \infty \) .

nodes.proof:
In [62] and Theorem 16.1 of [63], Hamilton proved this convergence theorem for the case \( {s}_{\infty } =  + \infty \) . In the following we only need to modify Hamilton’s argument to prove the remaining case of \( {s}_{\infty } <  + \infty \) . Suppose we are given a sequence of geodesic balls \( \left( {B\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{k}}\right) ,{g}_{k},{p}_{k}}\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k},{p}_{k}}\right) \) , with \( {s}_{k} \rightarrow  {s}_{\infty }\left( { <  + \infty }\right) \) , satisfying the assumptions of Theorem 4.1.2. We will split the proof into three steps.

Step 1: Picking the subsequence.

By the local injectivity radius estimate (4.2.2) in Corollary 4.2.3 of the next section, we can find a positive decreasing \( {C}^{1} \) function \( \rho \left( r\right) ,0 \leq  r < {s}_{\infty } \) , independent of \( k \) such that

(4.1.1)

\[
\rho \left( r\right)  < \frac{1}{100}\left( {{s}_{\infty } - r}\right) ,
\]

(4.1.2)

\[
0 \geq  {\rho }^{\prime }\left( r\right)  \geq   - \frac{1}{1000},
\]

and a sequence of positive constants \( {\varepsilon }_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) so that the injectivity radius at any point \( x \in  B\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{k}}\right) \) with \( {r}_{k} = {d}_{k}\left( {x,{p}_{k}}\right)  < {s}_{\infty } - {\varepsilon }_{k} \) is bounded from below by

(4.1.3)

\[
\operatorname{inj}\left( {{M}_{k}, x}\right)  \geq  {500\rho }\left( {{r}_{k}\left( x\right) }\right) ,
\]

where \( {r}_{k}\left( x\right)  = {d}_{k}\left( {x,{p}_{k}}\right) \) is the distance from \( x \) to \( {p}_{k} \) in the metric \( {g}_{k} \) of \( {M}_{k} \) . We define

\[
\widetilde{\rho }\left( r\right)  = \rho \left( {r + {20\rho }\left( r\right) }\right) ,\;\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}\left( r\right)  = \widetilde{\rho }\left( {r + {20}\widetilde{\rho }\left( r\right) }\right) .
\]

By (4.1.2) we know that both \( \widetilde{\rho }\left( r\right) \) and \( \widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}\left( r\right) \) are nonincreasing positive functions on \( \left\lbrack  {0,{s}_{\infty }}\right) \) .

In each \( B\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{\infty }}\right) \) we choose inductively a sequence of points \( {x}_{k}^{\alpha } \) for \( \alpha  = 0,1,2,\ldots \) in the following way. First we let \( {x}_{k}^{0} = {p}_{k} \) . Once \( {x}_{k}^{\alpha } \) are chosen for \( \alpha  = 0,1,2,\ldots ,\sigma \) , we pick \( {x}_{k}^{\sigma  + 1} \) closest to \( {p}_{k} \) so that \( {r}_{k}^{\sigma  + 1} = {r}_{k}\left( {x}_{k}^{\sigma  + 1}\right) \) is as small as possible, subject to the requirement that the open ball \( B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\sigma  + 1},{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\sigma  + 1}}\right) \) around \( {x}_{k}^{\sigma  + 1} \) of radius \( {\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\sigma  + 1} \) is disjoint from the balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha }}\right) \) for \( \alpha  = 0,1,2,\ldots ,\sigma \) , where \( {\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha } = \widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}\left( {r}_{k}^{\alpha }\right) \) and \( {r}_{k}^{\alpha } = {r}_{k}\left( {x}_{k}^{\alpha }\right) \) . In particular, the open balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha }}\right) ,\alpha  = 0,1,2,\ldots \) , are all disjoint. We claim the balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },2{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha }}\right) \) cover \( B\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{\infty } - {\varepsilon }_{k}}\right) \) and moreover for any \( r,0 < r < {s}_{\infty } - {\varepsilon }_{k} \) , we can find \( \lambda \left( r\right) \) independent of \( k \) such that for \( k \) large enough, the geodesic balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },2{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha }}\right) \) for \( \alpha  \leq  \lambda \left( r\right) \) cover the ball \( B\left( {{p}_{k}, r}\right) \) .

To see this, let \( x \in  B\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{\infty } - {\varepsilon }_{k}}\right) \) and let \( r\left( x\right) \) be the distance from \( x \) to \( {p}_{k} \) and let \( \widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }} = \widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}\left( {r\left( x\right) }\right) \) . Consider those \( \alpha \) with \( {r}_{k}^{\alpha } \leq  r\left( x\right)  < {s}_{\infty } - {\varepsilon }_{k} \) . Then

\[
\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }} \leq  {\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha }
\]

Now the given point \( x \) must lie in one of the balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },2{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha }}\right) \) . If not, we could choose the next point in the sequence of \( {x}_{k}^{\beta } \) to be \( x \) instead, for since \( {\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha } + \widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }} \leq  2{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha } \) the ball \( B\left( {x,\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}\right) \) would miss \( B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha }}\right) \) with \( {r}_{k}^{\alpha } \leq  r\left( x\right) \) . But this is a contradiction. Moreover for any \( r,0 < r < {s}_{\infty } - {\varepsilon }_{k} \) , using the curvature bound and the injectivity radius bound, each ball \( B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha }}\right) \) with \( {r}_{k}^{\alpha } \leq  r \) has volume at least \( \epsilon \left( r\right) {\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{n} \) where \( \epsilon \left( r\right)  > 0 \) is some constant depending on \( r \) but independent of \( k \) . Now these balls are all disjoint and contained in the ball \( B\left( {{p}_{k},\left( {r + {s}_{\infty }}\right) /2}\right) \) . On the other hand, for large enough \( k \) , we can estimate the volume of this ball from above, again using the curvature bound, by a positive function of \( r \) that is independent of \( k \) . Thus there is a \( {k}^{\prime }\left( r\right)  > 0 \) such that for each \( k \geq  {k}^{\prime }\left( r\right) \) , there holds

(4.1.4)

\[
\# \left\{  {\alpha  \mid  {r}_{k}^{\alpha } \leq  r}\right\}   \leq  \lambda \left( r\right)
\]

for some positive constant \( \lambda \left( r\right) \) depending only on \( r \) , and the geodesic balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },2{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha }}\right) \) for \( \alpha  \leq  \lambda \left( r\right) \) cover the ball \( B\left( {{p}_{k}, r}\right) \) .

By the way, since

\[
{r}_{k}^{\alpha } \leq  {r}_{k}^{\alpha  - 1} + {\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha  - 1} + {\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha }
\]

\[
\leq  {r}_{k}^{\alpha  - 1} + 2{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha  - 1},
\]

and by (4.1.1)

\[
{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha  - 1} \leq  \frac{1}{100}\left( {{s}_{\infty } - {r}_{k}^{\alpha  - 1}}\right) ,
\]

we get by induction

\[
{r}_{k}^{\alpha } \leq  \frac{49}{50}{r}_{k}^{\alpha  - 1} + \frac{1}{50}{s}_{\infty }
\]

\[
\leq  {\left( \frac{49}{50}\right) }^{\alpha }{r}_{k}^{0} + \frac{1}{50}\left( {1 + \frac{49}{50} + \cdots  + {\left( \frac{49}{50}\right) }^{\alpha  - 1}}\right) {s}_{\infty }
\]

\[
= \left( {1 - {\left( \frac{49}{50}\right) }^{\alpha }}\right) {s}_{\infty }.
\]

So for each \( \alpha \) , with \( \alpha  \leq  \lambda \left( r\right) \left( {r < {s}_{\infty }}\right) \) , there holds

(4.1.5)

\[
{r}_{k}^{\alpha } \leq  \left( {1 - {\left( \frac{49}{50}\right) }^{\lambda \left( r\right) }}\right) {s}_{\infty }
\]

for all \( k \) . And by passing to a subsequence (using a diagonalization argument) we may assume that \( {r}_{k}^{\alpha } \) converges to some \( {r}^{\alpha } \) for each \( \alpha \) . Then \( {\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha } \) (respectively \( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{k}^{\alpha },{\rho }_{k}^{\alpha } \) ) converges to \( {\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\alpha } = \widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) \) (respectively \( {\widetilde{\rho }}^{\alpha } = \widetilde{\rho }\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) ,{\rho }^{\alpha } = \rho \left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) \) ).

Hence for all \( \alpha \) we can find \( k\left( \alpha \right) \) such that

\[
\frac{1}{2}{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\alpha } \leq  {\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha } \leq  2{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\alpha }
\]

\[
\frac{1}{2}{\widetilde{\rho }}^{\alpha } \leq  {\widetilde{\rho }}_{k}^{\alpha } \leq  2{\widetilde{\rho }}^{\alpha }\;\text{ and }\;\frac{1}{2}{\rho }^{\alpha } \leq  {\rho }_{k}^{\alpha } \leq  2{\rho }^{\alpha }
\]

whenever \( k \geq  k\left( \alpha \right) \) . Thus for all \( \alpha ,{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\alpha } \) are comparable when \( k \) is large enough so we can work with balls of a uniform size, and the same is true for \( {\widetilde{\rho }}_{k}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\widetilde{\rho }}^{\alpha } \) , and \( {\rho }_{k}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\rho }^{\alpha } \) . Let \( {\widehat{B}}_{k}^{\alpha } = B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },4{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\alpha }}\right) \) , then \( {\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha } \leq  2{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\alpha } \) and \( B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },2{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha }}\right)  \subset  B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },4{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\alpha }}\right)  = {\widehat{B}}_{k}^{\alpha } \) . So for every \( r \) if we let \( k\left( r\right)  = \max \{ k\left( \alpha \right)  \mid  \alpha  \leq  \lambda \left( r\right) \} \) then when \( k \geq  k\left( r\right) \) , the balls \( {\widehat{B}}_{k}^{\alpha } \) for \( \alpha  \leq  \lambda \left( r\right) \) cover the ball \( B\left( {{p}_{k}, r}\right) \) as well. Suppose that \( {\widehat{B}}_{k}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\widehat{B}}_{k}^{\beta } \) meet for \( k \geq  k\left( \alpha \right) \) and \( k \geq  k\left( \beta \right) \) , and suppose \( {r}_{k}^{\beta } \leq  {r}_{k}^{\alpha } \) . Then, by the triangle inequality, we must have

\[
{r}_{k}^{\alpha } \leq  {r}_{k}^{\beta } + 4{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\alpha } + 4{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\beta } \leq  {r}_{k}^{\beta } + 8{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\beta } < {r}_{k}^{\beta } + {16}{\widetilde{\rho }}_{k}^{\beta }.
\]

This then implies

\[
{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\beta } = \widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}\left( {r}_{k}^{\beta }\right)  = \widetilde{\rho }\left( {{r}_{k}^{\beta } + {20}\widetilde{\rho }\left( {r}_{k}^{\beta }\right) }\right)  < \widetilde{\rho }\left( {r}_{k}^{\alpha }\right)  = {\widetilde{\rho }}_{k}^{\alpha }
\]

and hence

\[
{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\beta } \leq  4{\widetilde{\rho }}^{\alpha }.
\]

Therefore \( {\widehat{B}}_{k}^{\beta } \subset  B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },{36}{\widetilde{\rho }}^{\alpha }}\right) \) whenever \( {\widehat{B}}_{k}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\widehat{B}}_{k}^{\beta } \) meet and \( k \geq  \max \{ k\left( \alpha \right) , k\left( \beta \right) \} \) .

Next we define the balls \( {B}_{k}^{\alpha } = B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },5{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\alpha }}\right) \) and \( {\widetilde{B}}_{k}^{\alpha } = B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\alpha }/2}\right) \) . Note that \( {\widetilde{B}}_{k}^{\alpha } \) are disjoint since \( {\widetilde{B}}_{k}^{\alpha } \subset  B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha }}\right) \) . Since \( {\widehat{B}}_{k}^{\alpha } \subset  {B}_{k}^{\alpha } \) , the balls \( {B}_{k}^{\alpha } \) cover \( B\left( {{p}_{k}, r}\right) \) for \( \alpha  \leq  \lambda \left( r\right) \) as before. If \( {B}_{k}^{\alpha } \) and \( {B}_{k}^{\beta } \) meet for \( k \geq  k\left( \alpha \right) \) and \( k \geq  k\left( \beta \right) \) and \( {r}_{k}^{\beta } \leq  {r}_{k}^{\alpha } \) , then by the triangle inequality we get

\[
{r}_{k}^{\alpha } \leq  {r}_{k}^{\beta } + {10}{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\beta } < {r}_{k}^{\beta } + {20}{\widetilde{\rho }}_{k}^{\beta },
\]

and hence

\[
{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\beta } \leq  4{\widetilde{\rho }}^{\alpha }
\]

again. Similarly,

\[
{\widetilde{\rho }}_{k}^{\beta } = \widetilde{\rho }\left( {r}_{k}^{\beta }\right)  = \rho \left( {{r}_{k}^{\beta } + {20\rho }\left( {r}_{k}^{\beta }\right) }\right)  < \rho \left( {r}_{k}^{\alpha }\right)  = {\rho }_{k}^{\alpha }.
\]

This makes

\[
{\widetilde{\rho }}^{\beta } \leq  4{\rho }^{\alpha }.
\]

Now any point in \( {B}_{k}^{\beta } \) has distance at most

\[
5{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\alpha } + 5{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\beta } + 5{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\beta } \leq  {45}{\widetilde{\rho }}^{\alpha }
\]

from \( {x}_{k}^{\alpha } \) , so \( {B}_{k}^{\beta } \subset  B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },{45}{\widetilde{\rho }}^{\alpha }}\right) \) . Likewise, whenever \( {B}_{k}^{\alpha } \) and \( {B}_{k}^{\beta } \) meet for \( k \geq  k\left( \alpha \right) \) and \( k \geq  k\left( \beta \right) \) , any point in the larger ball \( B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\beta },{45}{\widetilde{\rho }}^{\beta }}\right) \) has distance at most

\[
5{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\alpha } + 5{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\beta } + {45}{\widetilde{\rho }}^{\beta } \leq  {205}{\rho }^{\alpha }
\]

from \( {x}_{k}^{\alpha } \) and hence \( B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\beta },{45}{\widetilde{\rho }}^{\beta }}\right)  \subset  B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },{205}{\rho }^{\alpha }}\right) \) . Now we define \( {\bar{B}}_{k}^{\alpha } = B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },{45}{\widetilde{\rho }}^{\alpha }}\right) \) and \( {\overline{\bar{B}}}_{k}^{\alpha } = B\left( {{x}_{k}^{\alpha },{205}{\rho }^{\alpha }}\right) \) . Then the above discussion says that whenever \( {B}_{k}^{\alpha } \) and \( {B}_{k}^{\beta } \) meet for \( k \geq  k\left( \alpha \right) \) and \( k \geq  k\left( \beta \right) \) , we have

(4.1.6)

\[
{B}_{k}^{\beta } \subset  {\bar{B}}_{k}^{\alpha }\;\text{ and }\;{\bar{B}}_{k}^{\beta } \subset  {\overline{\bar{B}}}_{k}^{\alpha }.
\]

Note that \( {\overline{\bar{B}}}_{k}^{\alpha } \) is still a nice embedded ball since, by (4.1.3), \( {205}{\rho }^{\alpha } \leq  {410}{\rho }_{k}^{\alpha } < \; \operatorname{inj}\left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k}^{\alpha }}\right) \) .

We claim there exist positive numbers \( N\left( r\right) \) and \( {k}^{\prime \prime }\left( r\right) \) such that for any given \( \alpha \) with \( {r}^{\alpha } < r \) , as \( k \geq  {k}^{\prime \prime }\left( r\right) \) , there holds

(4.1.7)

\[
\# \left\{  {\beta  \mid  {B}_{k}^{\alpha } \cap  {B}_{k}^{\beta } \neq  \phi }\right\}   \leq  N\left( r\right) .
\]

Indeed, if \( {B}_{k}^{\alpha } \) meets \( {B}_{k}^{\beta } \) then there is a positive \( {k}^{\prime \prime }\left( \alpha \right) \) such that as \( k \geq  {k}^{\prime \prime }\left( \alpha \right) \) ,

\[
{r}_{k}^{\beta } \leq  {r}_{k}^{\alpha } + {10}{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}_{k}^{\alpha }
\]

\[
\leq  r + {20\rho }\left( r\right)
\]

\[
\leq  r + \frac{1}{5}\left( {{s}_{\infty } - r}\right) ,
\]

where we used (4.1.2) in the third inequality. Set

\[
{k}^{\prime \prime }\left( r\right)  = \max \left\{  {{k}^{\prime \prime }\left( \alpha \right) ,{k}^{\prime }\left( r\right)  \mid  \alpha  \leq  \lambda \left( r\right) }\right\}
\]

and

\[
N\left( r\right)  = \lambda \left( {r + \frac{1}{5}\left( {{s}_{\infty } - r}\right) }\right) .
\]

Then by combining with (4.1.4), these give the desired estimate (4.1.7)

Next we observe that by passing to another subsequence we can guarantee that for any pair \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) we can find a number \( k\left( {\alpha ,\beta }\right) \) such that if \( k \geq  k\left( {\alpha ,\beta }\right) \) then either \( {B}_{k}^{\alpha } \) always meets \( {B}_{k}^{\beta } \) or it never does.

Hence by setting

\[
\bar{k}\left( r\right)  = \max \left\{  {k\left( {\alpha ,\beta }\right) , k\left( \alpha \right) , k\left( \beta \right) ,{k}^{\prime \prime }\left( r\right)  \mid  \alpha  \leq  \lambda \left( r\right) \text{ and }}\right.
\]

\[
\left. {\beta  \leq  \lambda \left( {r + \frac{1}{5}\left( {{s}_{\infty } - r}\right) }\right) }\right\}  ,
\]

we have shown the following results: for every \( r < {s}_{\infty } \) , if \( k \geq  \bar{k}\left( r\right) \) , we have

(i) the ball \( B\left( {{p}_{k}, r}\right) \) in \( {M}_{k} \) is covered by the balls \( {B}_{k}^{\alpha } \) for \( \alpha  \leq  \lambda \left( r\right) \) ,

(ii) whenever \( {B}_{k}^{\alpha } \) and \( {B}_{k}^{\beta } \) meet for \( \alpha  \leq  \lambda \left( r\right) \) , we have

\[
{B}_{k}^{\beta } \subset  {\bar{B}}_{k}^{\alpha }\;\text{ and }\;{\bar{B}}_{k}^{\beta } \subset  {\overline{\bar{B}}}_{k}^{\alpha },
\]

(iii) for each \( \alpha  \leq  \lambda \left( r\right) \) , there no more than \( N\left( r\right) \) balls ever meet \( {B}_{k}^{\alpha } \) , and

(iv) for any \( \alpha  \leq  \lambda \left( r\right) \) and any \( \beta \) , either \( {B}_{k}^{\alpha } \) meets \( {B}_{k}^{\beta } \) for all \( k \geq  \bar{k}\left( r\right) \) or none for all \( k \geq  \bar{k}\left( r\right) \) .

Now we let \( {\widehat{E}}^{\alpha },{E}^{\alpha },{\bar{E}}^{\alpha } \) , and \( {\overline{\bar{E}}}^{\alpha } \) be the balls of radii \( 4{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\alpha },5{\widetilde{\widetilde{\rho }}}^{\alpha },{45}{\widetilde{\rho }}^{\alpha } \) , and \( {205}{\rho }^{\alpha } \) around the origin in Euclidean space \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . At each point \( {x}_{k}^{\alpha } \in  B\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{k}}\right) \) we define coordinate charts \( {H}_{k}^{\alpha } : {E}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  {B}_{k}^{\alpha } \) as the composition of a linear isometry of \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) to the tangent space \( {T}_{{x}_{k}^{\alpha }}{M}_{k} \) with the exponential map \( {\exp }_{{x}_{k}^{\alpha }} \) at \( {x}_{k}^{\alpha } \) . We also get maps \( {\bar{H}}_{k}^{\alpha } : {\bar{E}}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  {\bar{B}}_{k}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\overline{\bar{H}}}_{k}^{\alpha } : {\overline{\bar{E}}}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  {\overline{\bar{B}}}_{k}^{\alpha } \) in the same way. Note that (4.1.3) implies that these maps are all well defined. We denote by \( {g}_{k}^{\alpha } \) (and \( {\bar{g}}_{k}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\overline{\bar{g}}}_{k}^{\alpha } \) ) the pull-backs of the metric \( {g}_{k} \) by \( {H}_{k}^{\alpha } \) (and \( {\bar{H}}_{k}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\overline{\bar{H}}}_{k}^{\alpha } \) ). We also consider the coordinate transition functions \( {J}_{k}^{\alpha \beta } : {E}^{\beta } \rightarrow  {\bar{E}}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\bar{J}}_{k}^{\alpha \beta } : {\bar{E}}^{\beta } \rightarrow  {\overline{\bar{E}}}^{\alpha } \) defined by

\[
{J}_{k}^{\alpha \beta } = {\left( {\bar{H}}_{k}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-1}{H}_{k}^{\beta }\;\text{ and }\;{\bar{J}}_{k}^{\alpha \beta } = {\left( {\bar{\bar{H}}}_{k}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-1}{\bar{H}}_{k}^{\beta }.
\]

Clearly \( {\bar{J}}_{k}^{\alpha \beta }{J}_{k}^{\beta \alpha } = I \) . Moreover \( {J}_{k}^{\alpha \beta } \) is an isometry from \( {g}_{k}^{\beta } \) to \( {\bar{g}}_{k}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\bar{J}}_{k}^{\alpha \beta } \) from \( {\bar{g}}_{k}^{\beta } \) to \( {\overline{\bar{g}}}_{k}^{\alpha } \) .

Now for each fixed \( \alpha \) , the metrics \( {g}_{k}^{\alpha } \) are in geodesic coordinates and have their curvatures and their covariant derivatives uniformly bounded.

nodes.proof:
It suffices to show the following general result:

There exists a constant \( c > 0 \) depending only on the dimension, and constants \( {C}_{q} \) depending only on the dimension and \( q \) and bounds \( {B}_{j} \) on the curvature and its derivatives for \( j \leq  q \) where \( \left| {{D}^{j}{Rm}}\right|  \leq  {B}_{j} \) , so that for any metric \( {g}_{k\ell } \) in geodesic coordinates in the ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) , we have

\[
\frac{1}{2}{I}_{k\ell } \leq  {g}_{k\ell } \leq  2{I}_{k\ell }
\]

and

\[
\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{{j}_{1}}}\cdots \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{{j}_{q}}}{g}_{k\ell }}\right|  \leq  {C}_{q}
\]

where \( {I}_{k\ell } \) is the Euclidean metric.

Suppose we are given a metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( x\right) d{x}^{i}d{x}^{j} \) in geodesic coordinates in the ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) as in Claim 1. Then by definition every line through the origin is a geodesic (parametrized proportional to arc length) and \( {g}_{ij} = {I}_{ij} \) at the origin. Also, the Gauss Lemma says that the metric \( {g}_{ij} \) is in geodesic coordinates if and only if \( {g}_{ij}{x}^{i} = {I}_{ij}{x}^{i} \) . Note in particular that in geodesic coordinates

\[
{\left| x\right| }^{2} = {g}_{ij}{x}^{i}{x}^{j} = {I}_{ij}{x}^{i}{x}^{j}
\]

is unambiguously defined. Also, in geodesic coordinates we have \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) , and all the first derivatives for \( {g}_{jk} \) vanish at the origin.

Introduce the symmetric tensor

\[
{A}_{ij} = \frac{1}{2}{x}^{k}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{k}}{g}_{ij}.
\]

Since we have \( {g}_{jk}{x}^{k} = {I}_{jk}{x}^{k} \) , we get

\[
{x}^{k}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}{g}_{jk} = {I}_{ij} - {g}_{ij} = {x}^{k}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{j}}{g}_{ik}
\]

and hence from the formula for \( {\Gamma }_{jk}^{i} \)

\[
{x}^{j}{\Gamma }_{jk}^{i} = {g}^{i\ell }{A}_{k\ell }
\]

Hence \( {A}_{k\ell }{x}^{k} = 0 \) . Let \( {D}_{i} \) be the covariant derivative with respect to the metric \( {g}_{ij} \) . Then

\[
{D}_{i}{x}^{k} = {I}_{i}^{k} + {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}{x}^{j} = {I}_{i}^{k} + {g}^{k\ell }{A}_{i\ell }.
\]

Introduce the potential function

\[
P = {\left| x\right| }^{2}/2 = \frac{1}{2}{g}_{ij}{x}^{i}{x}^{j}.
\]

We can use the formulas above to compute

\[
{D}_{i}P = {g}_{ij}{x}^{j}.
\]

Also we get

\[
{D}_{i}{D}_{j}P = {g}_{ij} + {A}_{ij}.
\]

The defining equation for \( P \) gives

\[
{g}^{ij}{D}_{i}P{D}_{j}P = {2P}.
\]

If we take the covariant derivative of this equation we get

\[
{g}^{k\ell }{D}_{j}{D}_{k}P{D}_{\ell }P = {D}_{j}P
\]

which is equivalent to \( {A}_{jk}{x}^{k} = 0 \) . But if we take the covariant derivative again we get

\[
{g}^{k\ell }{D}_{i}{D}_{j}{D}_{k}P{D}_{\ell }P + {g}^{k\ell }{D}_{j}{D}_{k}P{D}_{i}{D}_{\ell }P = {D}_{i}{D}_{j}P.
\]

Now switching derivatives

\[
{D}_{i}{D}_{j}{D}_{k}P = {D}_{i}{D}_{k}{D}_{j}P = {D}_{k}{D}_{i}{D}_{j}P + {R}_{{ikj}\ell }{g}^{\ell m}{D}_{m}P
\]

and if we use this and \( {D}_{i}{D}_{j}P = {g}_{ij} + {A}_{ij} \) and \( {g}^{k\ell }{D}_{\ell }P = {x}^{k} \) we find that

\[
{x}^{k}{D}_{k}{A}_{ij} + {A}_{ij} + {g}^{k\ell }{A}_{ik}{A}_{j\ell } + {R}_{{ikj}\ell }{x}^{k}{x}^{\ell } = 0.
\]

From our assumed curvature bounds we can take \( \left| {R}_{{ijk}\ell }\right|  \leq  {B}_{0} \) . Then we get the following estimate:

\[
\left| {{x}^{k}{D}_{k}{A}_{ij} + {A}_{ij}}\right|  \leq  C{\left| {A}_{ij}\right| }^{2} + C{B}_{0}{r}^{2}
\]

on the ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \) for some constant \( C \) depending only on the dimension.

We now show how to use the maximum principle on such equations. First of all, by a maximum principle argument, it is easy to show that if \( f \) is a function on a ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \) and \( \lambda  > 0 \) is a constant, then

\[
\lambda \sup \left| f\right|  \leq  \sup \left| {{x}^{k}\frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}^{k}} + {\lambda f}}\right| .
\]

For any tensor \( T = \left\{  {T}_{i\cdots j}\right\} \) and any constant \( \lambda  > 0 \) , setting \( f = {\left| T\right| }^{2} \) in the above inequality, we have

(4.1.8)

\[
\lambda \sup \left| T\right|  \leq  \sup \left| {{x}^{k}{D}_{k}T + {\lambda T}}\right| .
\]

Applying this to the tensor \( {A}_{ij} \) we get

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left| x\right|  \leq  r}}\left| {A}_{ij}\right|  \leq  C\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left| x\right|  \leq  r}}{\left| {A}_{ij}\right| }^{2} + C{B}_{0}{r}^{2}
\]

for some constant depending only on the dimension.

It is fairly elementary to see that there exist constants \( c > 0 \) and \( {C}_{0} < \infty \) such that if the metric \( {g}_{ij} \) is in geodesic coordinates with \( \left| {R}_{{ijk}\ell }\right|  \leq  {B}_{0} \) in the ball of radius \( r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) then

\[
\left| {A}_{ij}\right|  \leq  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{r}^{2}.
\]

Indeed, since the derivatives of \( {g}_{ij} \) vanish at the origin, so does \( {A}_{ij} \) . Hence the estimate holds near the origin. But the inequality

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left| x\right|  \leq  r}}\left| {A}_{ij}\right|  \leq  C\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left| x\right|  \leq  r}}{\left| {A}_{ij}\right| }^{2} + C{B}_{0}{r}^{2}
\]

says that \( \left| {A}_{ij}\right| \) avoids an interval when \( c \) is chosen small. In fact the inequality

\[
X \leq  C{X}^{2} + D
\]

is equivalent to

\[
\left| {{2CX} - 1}\right|  \geq  \sqrt{1 - {4CD}}
\]

which makes \( X \) avoid an interval if \( {4CD} < 1 \) . (Hence in our case we need to choose \( c \) with \( 4{C}^{2}{c}^{2} < 1 \) .) Then if \( X \) is on the side containing 0 we get

\[
X \leq  \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - {4CD}}}{2C} \leq  {2D}.
\]

This gives \( \left| {A}_{ij}\right|  \leq  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{r}^{2} \) with \( {C}_{0} = {2C} \) .

We can also derive bounds on all the covariant derivatives of \( P \) in terms of bounds on the covariant derivatives of the curvature. To simplify the notation, we let

\[
{D}^{q}P = \left\{  {{D}_{{j}_{1}}{D}_{{j}_{2}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}P}\right\}
\]

denote the \( {q}^{\text{ th }} \) covariant derivative, and in estimating \( {D}^{q}P \) we will lump all the lower order terms into a general slush term \( {\Phi }^{q} \) which will be a polynomial in \( {D}^{1}P,{D}^{2}P,\ldots ,{D}^{q - 1}P \) and \( {Rm},{D}^{1}{Rm},\ldots ,{D}^{q - 2}{Rm} \) . We already have estimates on a ball of radius \( r \)

\[
P \leq  {r}^{2}/2
\]

\[
\left| {{D}^{1}P}\right|  \leq  r
\]

\[
\left| {A}_{ij}\right|  \leq  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{r}^{2}
\]

and since \( {D}_{i}{D}_{j}P = {g}_{ij} + {A}_{ij} \) and \( r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) if we choose \( c \) small we can make

\[
\left| {A}_{ij}\right|  \leq  1/2
\]

and we get

\[
\left| {{D}^{2}P}\right|  \leq  {C}_{2}
\]

for some constant \( {C}_{2} \) depending only on the dimension.

Start with the equation \( {g}^{ij}{D}_{i}P{D}_{j}P = {2P} \) and apply repeated covariant derivatives. Observe that we get an equation which starts out

\[
{g}^{ij}{D}_{i}P{D}^{q}{D}_{j}P + \cdots  = 0
\]

where the omitted terms only contain derivatives \( {D}^{q}P \) and lower. If we switch two derivatives in a term \( {D}^{q + 1}P \) or lower, we get a term which is a product of a covariant derivative of \( {Rm} \) of order at most \( q - 2 \) (since the two closest to \( P \) commute) and a covariant derivative of \( P \) of order at most \( q - 1 \) ; such a term can be lumped in with the slush term \( {\Phi }^{q} \) . Therefore up to terms in \( {\Phi }^{q} \) we can regard the derivatives as commuting. Then paying attention to the derivatives in \( {D}^{1}P \) we get an equation

\( {g}^{ij}{D}_{i}P{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}}P + {g}^{ij}{D}_{i}{D}_{{k}_{1}}P{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{2}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}}P \; + {g}^{ij}{D}_{i}{D}_{{k}_{2}}P{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{1}}{D}_{{k}_{3}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}}P + \cdots  + {g}^{ij}{D}_{i}{D}_{{k}_{q}}P{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q - 1}}P \; = {D}_{{k}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}}P + {\Phi }^{q}. \)

Recalling that \( {D}_{i}{D}_{j}P = {g}_{ij} + {A}_{ij} \) we can rewrite this as

\[
{\Phi }^{q} = {g}^{ij}{D}_{i}P{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}} + \left( {q - 1}\right) {D}_{{k}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}}P
\]

\[
+ {g}^{ij}{A}_{i{k}_{1}}{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{2}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}}P + \cdots  + {g}^{ij}{A}_{i{k}_{q}}{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q - 1}}P.
\]

Estimating the product of tensors in the usual way gives

\[
\left| {{x}^{i}{D}_{i}{D}^{q}P + \left( {q - 1}\right) {D}^{q}P}\right|  \leq  q\left| A\right| \left| {{D}^{q}P}\right|  + \left| {\Phi }^{q}\right| .
\]

Applying the inequality \( \lambda \sup \left| T\right|  \leq  \sup \left| {{x}^{k}{D}_{k}T + {\lambda T}}\right| \) with \( T = {D}^{q}P \) gives

\[
\left( {q - 1}\right) \sup \left| {{D}^{q}P}\right|  \leq  \sup \left( {q\left| A\right| \left| {{D}^{q}P}\right|  + \left| {\Phi }^{q}\right| }\right) .
\]

Now we can make \( \left| A\right|  \leq  1/2 \) by making \( r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) with \( c \) small; it is important here that \( c \) is independent of \( q \) ! Then we get

\[
\left( {q - 2}\right) \sup \left| {{D}^{q}P}\right|  \leq  2\sup \left| {\Phi }^{q}\right|
\]

which is a good estimate for \( q \geq  3 \) . The term \( {\Phi }^{q} \) is estimated inductively from the terms \( {D}^{q - 1}P \) and \( {D}^{q - 2}{Rm} \) and lower. This proves that there exist constants \( {C}_{q} \) for \( q \geq  3 \) depending only on \( q \) and the dimension and on \( \left| {{D}^{j}{Rm}}\right| \) for \( j \leq  q - 2 \) such that

\[
\left| {{D}^{q}P}\right|  \leq  {C}_{q}
\]

on the ball \( r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) .

Now we turn our attention to estimating the Euclidean metric \( {I}_{jk} \) and its covariant derivatives with respect to \( {g}_{jk} \) . We will need the following elementary fact: suppose that \( f \) is a function on a ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \) with \( f\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) and

\[
\left| {{x}^{i}\frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}^{i}}}\right|  \leq  C{\left| x\right| }^{2}
\]

for some constant \( C \) . Then

(4.1.9)

\[
\left| f\right|  \leq  C{\left| x\right| }^{2}
\]

for the same constant \( C \) . As a consequence, if \( T = \left\{  {T}_{j\cdots k}\right\} \) is a tensor which vanishes at the origin and if

\[
\left| {{x}^{i}{D}_{i}T}\right|  \leq  C{\left| x\right| }^{2}
\]

on a ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \) then \( \left| T\right|  \leq  C{\left| x\right| }^{2} \) with the same constant \( C \) . (Simply apply the inequality (4.1.9) to the function \( f = \left| T\right| \) . In case this is not smooth, we can use \( f = \sqrt{{\left| T\right| }^{2} + {\epsilon }^{2}} - \epsilon \) and then let \( \epsilon  \rightarrow  0 \) .)

Our application will be to the tensor \( {I}_{jk} \) which gives the Euclidean metric as a tensor in geodesic coordinates. We have

\[
{D}_{i}{I}_{jk} =  - {\Gamma }_{ij}^{p}{I}_{pk} - {\Gamma }_{ik}^{p}{I}_{pj}
\]

and since

\[
{x}^{i}{\Gamma }_{ij}^{p} = {g}^{pq}{A}_{jq}
\]

we get the equation

\[
{x}^{i}{D}_{i}{I}_{jk} =  - {g}^{pq}{A}_{jp}{I}_{kq} - {g}^{pq}{A}_{kp}{I}_{jq}.
\]

We already have \( \left| {A}_{jk}\right|  \leq  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{\left| x\right| }^{2} \) for \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) . The tensor \( {I}_{jk} \) doesn’t vanish at the origin, but the tensor

\[
{h}_{jk} = {I}_{jk} - {g}_{jk}
\]

does. We can then use

\[
{x}^{i}{D}_{i}{h}_{jk} =  - {g}^{pq}{A}_{jp}{h}_{kq} - {g}^{pq}{A}_{kq}{h}_{jq} - 2{A}_{jk}.
\]

Suppose \( M\left( s\right)  = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left| x\right|  \leq  s}}\left| {h}_{jk}\right| \) . Then

\[
\left| {{x}^{i}{D}_{i}{h}_{jk}}\right|  \leq  2\left\lbrack  {1 + M\left( s\right) }\right\rbrack  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{\left| x\right| }^{2}
\]

and we get

\[
\left| {h}_{jk}\right|  \leq  2\left\lbrack  {1 + M\left( s\right) }\right\rbrack  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{\left| x\right| }^{2}
\]

on \( \left| x\right|  \leq  s \) . This makes

\[
M\left( s\right)  \leq  2\left\lbrack  {1 + M\left( s\right) }\right\rbrack  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{s}^{2}.
\]

Then for \( s \leq  r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) with \( c \) small compared to \( {C}_{0} \) we get \( 2{C}_{0}{B}_{0}{s}^{2} \leq  1/2 \) and \( M\left( s\right)  \leq  4{C}_{0}{B}_{0}{s}^{2} \) . Thus

\[
\left| {{I}_{jk} - {g}_{jk}}\right|  = \left| {h}_{jk}\right|  \leq  4{C}_{0}{B}_{0}{\left| x\right| }^{2}
\]

for \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) , and hence for \( c \) small enough

\[
\frac{1}{2}{g}_{jk} \leq  {I}_{jk} \leq  2{g}_{jk}
\]

Thus the metrics are comparable. Note that this estimate only needs \( r \) small compared to \( {B}_{0} \) and does not need any bounds on the derivatives of the curvature.

Now to obtain bounds on the covariant derivative of the Eucliden metric \( {I}_{k\ell } \) with respect to the Riemannian metric \( {g}_{k\ell } \) we want to start with the equation

\[
{x}^{i}{D}_{i}{I}_{k\ell } + {g}^{mn}{A}_{km}{I}_{\ell n} + {g}^{mn}{A}_{\ell m}{I}_{kn} = 0
\]

and apply \( q \) covariant derivatives \( {D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}} \) . Each time we do this we must interchange \( {D}_{j} \) and \( {x}^{i}{D}_{i} \) , and since this produces a term which helps we should look at it closely. If we write \( {R}_{ji} = \left\lbrack  {{D}_{j},{D}_{i}}\right\rbrack \) for the commutator, this operator on tensors involves the curvature but no derivatives. Since

\[
{D}_{j}{x}^{i} = {I}_{j}^{i} + {g}^{im}{A}_{jm}
\]

we can compute

\[
\left\lbrack  {{D}_{j},{x}^{i}{D}_{i}}\right\rbrack   = {D}_{j} + {g}^{im}{A}_{jm}{D}_{i} + {x}^{i}{R}_{ji}
\]

and the term \( {D}_{j} \) in the commutator helps, while \( {A}_{jm} \) can be kept small and \( {R}_{ji} \) is zero order. It follows that we get an equation of the form

\[
0 = {x}^{i}{D}_{i}{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{k\ell } + q{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{k\ell }
\]

\[
+ \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{h = 1}}^{q}{g}^{im}{A}_{{j}_{h}m}{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{h - 1}}{D}_{i}{D}_{{j}_{h + 1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{k\ell }
\]

\[
+ {g}^{mn}{A}_{km}{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{\ell n} + {g}^{mn}{A}_{\ell m}{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{kn} + {\Psi }^{q},
\]

where the slush term \( {\Psi }^{q} \) is a polynomial in derivatives of \( {I}_{k\ell } \) of degree no more than \( q - 1 \) and derivatives of \( P \) of degree no more than \( q + 2 \) (remember \( {x}^{i} = {g}^{ij}{D}_{j}P \) and \( {A}_{ij} = {D}_{i}{D}_{j}P - {g}_{ij} \) ) and derivatives of the curvature \( {Rm} \) of degree no more than \( q - 1 \) . We now estimate

\[
{D}^{q}{I}_{k\ell } = \left\{  {{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{k\ell }}\right\}
\]

by induction on \( q \) using (4.1.8) with \( \lambda  = q \) . Noticing a total of \( q + 2 \) terms contracting \( {A}_{ij} \) with a derivative of \( {I}_{k\ell } \) of degree \( q \) , we get the estimate

\[
q\sup \left| {{D}^{q}{I}_{k\ell }}\right|  \leq  \left( {q + 2}\right) \sup \left| A\right| \sup \left| {{D}^{q}{I}_{k\ell }}\right|  + \sup \left| {\Psi }^{q}\right| .
\]

and everything works. This proves that there exists a constant \( c > 0 \) depending only on the dimension, and constants \( {C}_{q} \) depending only on the dimension and \( q \) and bounds \( {B}_{j} \) on the curvature and its derivatives for \( j \leq  q \) where \( \left| {{D}^{j}{Rm}}\right|  \leq  {B}_{j} \) , so that for any metric \( {g}_{k\ell } \) in geodesic coordinates in the ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) the Euclidean metric \( {I}_{k\ell } \) satisfies

\[
\frac{1}{2}{g}_{k\ell } \leq  {I}_{k\ell } \leq  2{g}_{k\ell }
\]

and the covariant derivatives of \( {I}_{k\ell } \) with respect to \( {g}_{k\ell } \) satisfy

\[
\left| {{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{k\ell }}\right|  \leq  {C}_{q}.
\]

The difference between a covariant derivative and an ordinary derivative is given by the connection

\[
- {\Gamma }_{ij}^{p}{I}_{pk} - {\Gamma }_{ik}^{p}{I}_{pj}
\]

to get

\[
{\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} = \frac{1}{2}{I}^{k\ell }\left( {{D}_{\ell }{I}_{ij} - {D}_{i}{I}_{j\ell } - {D}_{j}{I}_{i\ell }}\right) .
\]

This gives us bounds on \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} \) . We then obtain bounds on the first derivatives of \( {g}_{ij} \) from

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}{g}_{jk} = {g}_{k\ell }{\Gamma }_{ij}^{\ell } + {g}_{j\ell }{\Gamma }_{ik}^{\ell }.
\]

Always proceeding inductively on the order of the derivative, we now get bounds on covariant derivatives of \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} \) from the covariant derivatives of \( {I}_{pk} \) and bounds of the ordinary derivatives of \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} \) by relating the to the covariant derivatives using the \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} \) , and bounds on the ordinary derivatives of the \( {g}_{jk} \) from bounds on the ordinary derivatives of the \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{\ell } \) . Consequently, we have estimates

\[
\frac{1}{2}{I}_{k\ell } \leq  {g}_{k\ell } \leq  2{I}_{k\ell }
\]

and

\[
\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{{j}_{1}}}\cdots \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{{j}_{q}}}{g}_{k\ell }}\right|  \leq  {\widetilde{C}}_{q}
\]

for similar constants \( {\widetilde{C}}_{q} \) .

Therefore we have finished the proof of Claim 1.

nodes.proof:
We need to show how to estimate the derivatives of an isometry. We will prove that if \( y = F\left( x\right) \) is an isometry from a ball in Euclidean space with a metric \( {g}_{ij}d{x}^{i}d{x}^{j} \) to a ball in Euclidean space with a metric \( {h}_{kl}d{y}^{k}d{y}^{l} \) . Then we can bound all of the derivatives of \( y \) with respect to \( x \) in terms of bounds on \( {g}_{ij} \) and its derivatives with respect to \( x \) and bound on \( {h}_{kl} \) and its derivatives with respect to \( y \) . This would imply Claim 2.

Since \( y = F\left( x\right) \) is an isometry we have the equation

\[
{h}_{pq}\frac{\partial {y}^{p}}{\partial {x}^{j}}\frac{\partial {y}^{q}}{\partial {x}^{k}} = {g}_{jk}.
\]

Using bounds \( {g}_{jk} \leq  C{I}_{jk} \) and \( {h}_{pq} \geq  c{I}_{pq} \) comparing to the Euclidean metric, we easily get estimates

\[
\left| \frac{\partial {y}^{p}}{\partial {x}^{j}}\right|  \leq  C
\]

Now if we differentiate the equation with respect to \( {x}^{i} \) we get

\[
{h}_{pq}\frac{{\partial }^{2}{y}^{p}}{\partial {x}^{i}\partial {x}^{j}}\frac{\partial {y}^{q}}{\partial {x}^{k}} + {h}_{pq}\frac{\partial {y}^{p}}{\partial {x}^{j}}\frac{{\partial }^{2}{y}^{q}}{\partial {x}^{i}\partial {x}^{k}} = \frac{\partial {g}_{jk}}{\partial {x}^{i}} - \frac{\partial {h}_{pq}}{\partial {y}^{r}}\frac{\partial {y}^{r}}{\partial {x}^{i}}\frac{\partial {y}^{p}}{\partial {x}^{j}}\frac{\partial {y}^{q}}{\partial {x}^{k}}.
\]

Now let

\[
{T}_{ijk} = {h}_{pq}\frac{\partial {y}^{p}}{\partial {x}^{i}}\frac{{\partial }^{2}{y}^{q}}{\partial {x}^{j}\partial {x}^{k}}
\]

and let

\[
{U}_{ijk} = \frac{\partial {g}_{jk}}{\partial {x}^{i}} - \frac{\partial {h}_{pq}}{\partial {y}^{r}}\frac{\partial {y}^{r}}{\partial {x}^{i}}\frac{\partial {y}^{p}}{\partial {x}^{j}}\frac{\partial {y}^{q}}{\partial {x}^{k}}.
\]

Then the above equation says

\[
{T}_{kij} + {T}_{jik} = {U}_{ijk}.
\]

Using the obvious symmetries \( {T}_{ijk} = {T}_{ikj} \) and \( {U}_{ijk} = {U}_{ikj} \) we can solve this in the usual way to obtain

\[
{T}_{ijk} = \frac{1}{2}\left( {{U}_{jik} + {U}_{kij} - {U}_{ijk}}\right) .
\]

We can recover the second derivatives of \( y \) with respect to \( x \) from the formula

\[
\frac{{\partial }^{2}{y}^{p}}{\partial {x}^{i}\partial {x}^{j}} = {g}^{k\ell }{T}_{kij}\frac{\partial {y}^{p}}{\partial {x}^{\ell }}.
\]

Combining these gives an explicit formula giving \( {\partial }^{2}{y}^{p}/\partial {x}^{i}\partial {x}^{j} \) as a function of \( {g}^{ij},{h}_{pq},\partial {g}_{jk}/\partial {x}^{i},\partial {h}_{pq}/\partial {y}^{r} \) , and \( \partial {y}^{p}/\partial {y}^{i} \) . This gives bounds

\[
\left| \frac{{\partial }^{2}{y}^{p}}{\partial {y}^{i}\partial {y}^{j}}\right|  \leq  C
\]

and bounds on all higher derivatives follow by differentiating the formula and using induction. This completes the proof of Claim 2 and hence the proof of Theorem 4.1.2. 0

Let \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) be a Riemannian manifold, \( K \) a compact subset of \( M \) , and \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( t\right) \) a collection of solutions to Ricci flow defined on neighborhoods of \( K \times  \left\lbrack  {\alpha ,\beta }\right\rbrack \) with \( \left\lbrack  {\alpha ,\beta }\right\rbrack \) containing 0 . Suppose that for each \( l \geq  0 \) ,

nodes.proof:
First by using the equation

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\widetilde{g}}_{k} =  - 2{\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k}
\]

and the assumption (c) we immediately get

(4.1.10)

\[
{\widetilde{{C}_{0}}}^{-1}g \leq  {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( t\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{C}}_{0}g,\text{ on }K \times  \left\lbrack  {\alpha ,\beta }\right\rbrack
\]

for some positive constant \( {\widetilde{C}}_{0} \) independent of \( k \) .

Next we want to bound \( \nabla {\widetilde{g}}_{k} \) . The difference of the connection \( {\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{k} \) of \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k} \) and the connection \( \Gamma \) of \( g \) is a tensor. Taking \( \Gamma \) to be fixed in time, we get

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {{\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{k} - \Gamma }\right)  = \frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {\frac{1}{2}{\left( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\right) }^{\gamma \delta }\left\lbrack  {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{\alpha }}{\left( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\right) }_{\delta \beta } + \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{\beta }}{\left( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\right) }_{\delta \alpha } - \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{\delta }}{\left( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\right) }_{\alpha \beta }}\right\rbrack  }\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}{\left( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\right) }^{\gamma \delta }\left\lbrack  {{\left( {\widetilde{\nabla }}_{k}\right) }_{\alpha }\left( {-2{\left( {\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k}\right) }_{\beta \delta }}\right)  + {\left( {\widetilde{\nabla }}_{k}\right) }_{\beta }\left( {-2{\left( {\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k}\right) }_{\alpha \delta }}\right) }\right.
\]

\[
\left. {-{\left( {\widetilde{\nabla }}_{k}\right) }_{\delta }\left( {-2{\left( {\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k}\right) }_{\alpha \beta }}\right) }\right\rbrack
\]

and then by the assumption (c) and (4.1.10),

\[
\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {{\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{k} - \Gamma }\right) }\right|  \leq  C,\;\text{ for all }k.
\]

Note also that at a normal coordinate of the metric \( g \) at a fixed point and at the time \( t = 0, \)

(4.1.11)

\[
{\left( {\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{k}\right) }_{\alpha \beta }^{\gamma } - {\Gamma }_{\alpha \beta }^{\gamma } = \frac{1}{2}{\left( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\right) }^{\gamma \delta }\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{\alpha }}{\left( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\right) }_{\delta \beta } + \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{\beta }}{\left( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\right) }_{\delta \alpha } - \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{\delta }}{\left( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\right) }_{\alpha \beta }}\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}{\left( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\right) }^{\gamma \delta }\left( {{\nabla }_{\alpha }{\left( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\right) }_{\delta \beta } + {\nabla }_{\beta }{\left( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\right) }_{\delta \alpha } - {\nabla }_{\delta }{\left( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\right) }_{\alpha \beta }}\right) ,
\]

thus by the assumption (b) and (4.1.10),

\[
\left| {{\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{k}\left( 0\right)  - \Gamma }\right|  \leq  C,\text{ for all }k.
\]

Integrating over time we deduce that

(4.1.12)

\[
\left| {{\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{k} - \Gamma }\right|  \leq  C,\text{ on }K \times  \left\lbrack  {\alpha ,\beta }\right\rbrack  ,\text{ for all }k.
\]

By using the assumption (c) and (4.1.10) again, we have

\[
\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {\nabla {\widetilde{g}}_{k}}\right) }\right|  = \left| {-2\nabla {\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k}}\right|
\]

\[
= \left| {-2{\widetilde{\nabla }}_{k}{\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k} + \left( {{\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{k} - \Gamma }\right)  * {\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k}}\right|
\]

\[
\leq  C\text{ , for all }k\text{ . }
\]

Hence by combining with the assumption (b) we get bounds

(4.1.13)

\[
\left| {\nabla {\widetilde{g}}_{k}}\right|  \leq  {\widetilde{C}}_{1},\text{ on }K \times  \left\lbrack  {\alpha ,\beta }\right\rbrack
\]

for some positive constant \( {\widetilde{C}}_{1} \) independent of \( k \) .

Further we want to bound \( {\nabla }^{2}{\widetilde{g}}_{k} \) . Again regarding \( \nabla \) as fixed in time, we see

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {{\nabla }^{2}{\widetilde{g}}_{k}}\right)  =  - 2{\nabla }^{2}\left( {\widetilde{R}i{c}_{k}}\right) .
\]

Write

\[
{\nabla }^{2}{\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k} = \left( {\nabla  - {\widetilde{\nabla }}_{k}}\right) \left( {\nabla {\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k}}\right)  + {\widetilde{\nabla }}_{k}\left( {\nabla  - {\widetilde{\nabla }}_{k}}\right) {\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k} + {\widetilde{\nabla }}_{k}^{2}{\mathop{\operatorname{Ric}}\limits^{ \circ  }}_{k}
\]

\[
= \left( {\Gamma  - {\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{k}}\right)  * \nabla {\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k} + {\widetilde{\nabla }}_{k}\left( {\left( {\Gamma  - {\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{k}}\right)  * {\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k}}\right)  + {\widetilde{\nabla }}_{k}^{2}{\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k}
\]

\[
= \left( {\Gamma  - {\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{k}}\right)  * \left\lbrack  {\left( {\nabla  - {\widetilde{\nabla }}_{k}}\right) {\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k} + {\widetilde{\nabla }}_{k}{\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k}}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
+ {\widetilde{\nabla }}_{k}\left( {{\widetilde{g}}_{k}^{-1} * \nabla {\widetilde{g}}_{k} * {\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k}}\right)  + {\widetilde{\nabla }}_{k}^{2}{\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k}
\]

\[
= \left( {\Gamma  - {\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{k}}\right)  * \left\lbrack  {\left( {\Gamma  - {\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{k}}\right)  * {\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k} + {\widetilde{\nabla }}_{k}{\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k}}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
+ {\widetilde{\nabla }}_{k}\left( {{\widetilde{g}}_{k}^{-1} * \nabla {\widetilde{g}}_{k} * {\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k}}\right)  + {\widetilde{\nabla }}_{k}^{2}{\widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}}_{k}
\]

where we have used (4.1.11). Then by the assumption (c), (4.1.10), (4.1.12) and (4.1.13) we have

\[
\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\nabla }^{2}{\widetilde{g}}_{k}}\right|  \leq  C + C \cdot  \left| {{\widetilde{\nabla }}_{k}\nabla {\widetilde{g}}_{k}}\right|
\]

\[
= C + C \cdot  \left| {{\nabla }^{2}{\widetilde{g}}_{k} + \left( {{\widetilde{\Gamma }}_{k} - \Gamma }\right)  * \nabla {\widetilde{g}}_{k}}\right|
\]

\[
\leq  C + C\left| {{\nabla }^{2}{\widetilde{g}}_{k}}\right| .
\]

Hence by combining with the assumption (b) we get

\[
\left| {{\nabla }^{2}{\widetilde{g}}_{k}}\right|  \leq  {\widetilde{C}}_{2},\text{ on }K \times  \left\lbrack  {\alpha ,\beta }\right\rbrack  ,
\]

for some positive constant \( {\widetilde{C}}_{2} \) independent of \( k \) .

The bounds on the higher derivatives can be derived by the same argument. Therefore we have completed the proof of the lemma. \( \square \)

THEOREM 4.1.5 (Hamilton’s compactness theorem). Let \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( t\right) ,{p}_{k}}\right) , t \in \; (A,\Omega \rbrack \) with \( A < 0 \leq  \Omega \) , be a sequence of evolving marked complete Riemannian manifolds. Consider a sequence of geodesic balls \( {B}_{0}\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{k}}\right)  \subset  {M}_{k} \) of radii \( {s}_{k}(0 < \; {s}_{k} \leq   + \infty ) \) , with \( {s}_{k} \rightarrow  {s}_{\infty }\left( { \leq   + \infty }\right) \) , around the base points \( {p}_{k} \) in the metrics \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) \) . Suppose each \( {g}_{k}\left( t\right) \) is a solution to the Ricci flow on \( {B}_{0}\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{k}}\right)  \times  (A,\Omega \rbrack \) . Suppose also

(i) for every radius \( r < {s}_{\infty } \) there exist positive constants \( C\left( r\right) \) and \( k\left( r\right) \) independent of \( k \) such that the curvature tensors \( \operatorname{Rm}\left( {g}_{k}\right) \) of the evolving metrics \( {g}_{k}\left( t\right) \) satisfy the bound

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {g}_{k}\right) }\right|  \leq  C\left( r\right)
\]

on \( {B}_{0}\left( {{p}_{k}, r}\right)  \times  (A,\Omega \rbrack \) for all \( k \geq  k\left( r\right) \) , and

(ii) there exists a constant \( \delta  > 0 \) such that the injectivity radii of \( {M}_{k} \) at \( {p}_{k} \) in the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) \) satisfy the bound

\[
\operatorname{inj}\left( {{M}_{k},{p}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right)  \geq  \delta  > 0,
\]

for all \( k = 1,2,\ldots \)

Then there exists a subsequence of evolving marked \( \left( {{B}_{0}\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{k}}\right) ,{g}_{k}\left( t\right) ,{p}_{k}}\right) \) over \( t \in \; (A,\Omega \rbrack \) which converge in \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a solution \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,{p}_{\infty }}\right) \) over \( t \in  (A,\Omega \rbrack \) to the Ricci flow, where, at the time \( t = 0,{B}_{\infty } \) is a geodesic open ball centered at \( {p}_{\infty } \in  {B}_{\infty } \) with the radius \( {s}_{\infty } \) . Moreover the limiting solution is complete if \( {s}_{\infty } =  + \infty \) .

THEOREM 4.2.1 (The Gromoll-Meyer injectivity radius estimate). Let \( M \) be a complete, noncompact Riemannian manifold with positive sectional curvature. Then the injectivity radius of \( M \) satisfies the following estimate

\[
\operatorname{inj}\left( M\right)  \geq  \frac{\pi }{\sqrt{{K}_{\max }}}.
\]
nodes.content_excerpt: THEOREM 4.2.1 (The Gromoll-Meyer injectivity radius estimate). Let \( M \) be a complete, noncompact Riemannian manifold with positive sectional curvature. Then the injectivity radius of \( M \) satisfies the following estimate \[ \operatorname{inj}\left( M\right) \geq \frac{\pi }{\sqrt{{K}_{\max }}}. \]

nodes.proof:
Let \( O \) be an arbitrary fixed point in \( M \) . We need to show that the injectivity radius at \( O \) is not less than \( \pi /\sqrt{{K}_{\max }} \) . We argue by contradiction. Suppose not, then by Klingenberg’s lemma there exists a closed geodesic loop \( \gamma \) on \( M \) starting and ending at \( O \) (may be not smooth at \( O \) ).

Since \( M \) has positive sectional curvature, we know from the work of Gromoll-Meyer [52] (see also Proposition 8.5 in Cheeger & Ebin [22]) that there exists a compact totally convex subset \( C \) of \( M \) containing the geodesic loop \( \gamma \) . Among all geodesic loops starting and ending at the same point and lying entirely in the compact totally convex set \( C \) there will be a shortest one. Call it \( {\gamma }_{0} \) , and suppose \( {\gamma }_{0} \) starts and ends at a point we call \( {p}_{0} \) .

First we claim that \( {\gamma }_{0} \) must be also smooth at the point \( {p}_{0} \) . Indeed by the curvature bound and implicit function theorem, there will be a geodesic loop \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) close to \( {\gamma }_{0} \) starting and ending at any point \( \widetilde{p} \) close to \( {p}_{0} \) . Let \( \widetilde{p} \) be along \( {\gamma }_{0} \) . Then by total convexity of the set \( C,\widetilde{\gamma } \) also lies entirely in \( C \) . If \( {\gamma }_{0} \) makes an angle different from \( \pi \) at \( {p}_{0} \) , the first variation formula will imply that \( \widetilde{\gamma } \) is shorter than \( {\gamma }_{0} \) . This contradicts with the choice of the geodesic loop \( {\gamma }_{0} \) being the shortest.

Now let \( L : \lbrack 0, + \infty ) \rightarrow  M \) be a ray emanating from \( {p}_{0} \) . Choose \( r > 0 \) large enough and set \( q = L\left( r\right) \) . Consider the distance between \( q \) and the geodesic loop \( {\gamma }_{0} \) . It is clear that the distance can be realized by a geodesic \( \beta \) connecting the point \( q \) to a point \( p \) on \( {\gamma }_{0} \) .

Let \( X \) be the unit tangent vector of the geodesic loop \( {\gamma }_{0} \) at \( p \) . Clearly \( X \) is orthogonal to the tangent vector of \( \beta \) at \( p \) . We then translate the vector \( X \) along the geodesic \( \beta \) to get a parallel vector field \( X\left( t\right) ,0 \leq  t \leq  r \) . By using this vector field we can form a variation fixing one endpoint \( q \) and the other on \( {\gamma }_{0} \) such that the variational vector field is \( \left( {1 - \frac{t}{r}}\right) X\left( t\right) \) . The second variation of the arclength of this family of curves is given by

\[
I\left( {\left( {1 - \frac{t}{r}}\right) X\left( t\right) ,\left( {1 - \frac{t}{r}}\right) X\left( t\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= {\int }_{0}^{r}\left\lbrack  {\left| {\nabla }_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}\left( \left( 1 - \frac{t}{r}\right) X\left( t\right) \right) \right| }^{2}\right.
\]

\[
\left. {-R\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t},\left( {1 - \frac{t}{r}}\right) X\left( t\right) ,\frac{\partial }{\partial t},\left( {1 - \frac{t}{r}}\right) X\left( t\right) }\right) }\right\rbrack  {dt}
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{r} - {\int }_{0}^{r}{\left( 1 - \frac{t}{r}\right) }^{2}R\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}, X\left( t\right) ,\frac{\partial }{\partial t}, X\left( t\right) }\right) {dt}
\]

\[
< 0
\]

when \( r \) is sufficiently large, since the sectional curvature of \( M \) is strictly positive everywhere. This contradicts with the fact that \( \beta \) is the shortest geodesic connecting the point \( q \) to the shortest geodesic loop \( {\gamma }_{0} \) . Thus we have proved the injectivity radius estimate. \( \square \)

It is well known (cf. Lemma 5.6 in Cheeger and Ebin [22]) that

\[
\operatorname{inj}\left( {M,{x}_{0}}\right)  = \min \left\{  {\text{ conjugate radius of }{x}_{0},\frac{1}{2}{l}_{M}\left( {x}_{0}\right) }\right\}
\]

where \( {l}_{M}\left( {x}_{0}\right) \) denotes the length of the shortest (nontrivial) closed geodesic starting and ending at \( {x}_{0} \) . Since by assumption \( r \leq  \pi /\left( {4\sqrt{\Lambda }}\right) \) if \( \Lambda  > 0 \) , the conjugate radius of \( {x}_{0} \) is at least \( {4r} \) . Thus it suffices to show

(4.2.1)

\[
{l}_{M}\left( {x}_{0}\right)  \geq  {2r} \cdot  \frac{\operatorname{Vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) }\right) }{\operatorname{Vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) }\right)  + {V}_{\lambda }^{n}\left( {2r}\right) }.
\]

Now we follow the argument presented in [1]. The idea for proving this inequality, as indicated in [1], is to compare the geometry of the ball \( B\left( {{x}_{0},{4r}}\right)  \subseteq  B\left( {{x}_{0},4{r}_{0}}\right)  \subset \; M \) with the geometry of its lifting \( {\widetilde{B}}_{4r} \subset  {T}_{{x}_{0}}\left( M\right) \) , via the exponential map \( {\exp }_{{x}_{0}} \) , equipped with the pull-back metric \( \widetilde{g} = {\exp }_{{x}_{0}}^{ * }g \) . Thus \( {\exp }_{{x}_{0}} : {\widetilde{B}}_{4r} \rightarrow  B\left( {{x}_{0},{4r}}\right) \) is a length-preserving local diffeomorphism.

Let \( {\widetilde{x}}_{0},{\widetilde{x}}_{1},\ldots ,{\widetilde{x}}_{N} \) be the preimages of \( {x}_{0} \) in \( {\widetilde{B}}_{r} \subset  {\widetilde{B}}_{4r} \) with \( {\widetilde{x}}_{0} = 0 \) . Clearly they one-to-one correspond to the geodesic loops \( {\gamma }_{0},{\gamma }_{1},\ldots ,{\gamma }_{N} \) at \( {x}_{0} \) of length less than \( r \) , where \( {\gamma }_{0} \) is the trivial loop. Now for each point \( {\widetilde{x}}_{i} \) there exists exactly one isometric immersion \( {\varphi }_{i} : {\widetilde{B}}_{r} \rightarrow  {\widetilde{B}}_{4r} \) mapping 0 to \( {\widetilde{x}}_{i} \) and such that \( {\exp }_{{x}_{0}}{\varphi }_{i} = {\exp }_{{x}_{0}} \) .

Without loss of generality, we may assume \( {\gamma }_{1} \) is the shortest nontrivial geodesic loop at \( {x}_{0} \) . By analyzing short homotopies, one finds that \( {\varphi }_{i}\left( \widetilde{x}\right)  \neq  {\varphi }_{j}\left( \widetilde{x}\right) \) for all \( \widetilde{x} \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{r} \) and \( 0 \leq  i < j \leq  N \) . This fact has two consequences:

(a) \( N \geq  {2m} \) , where \( m = \left\lbrack  {r/{l}_{M}\left( {x}_{0}\right) }\right\rbrack \) . To see this, we first observe that the points \( {\varphi }_{1}^{k}\left( 0\right) , - m \leq  k \leq  m \) , are preimages of \( {x}_{0} \) in \( {\widetilde{B}}_{r} \) because \( {\varphi }_{1} \) is an isometric immersion satisfying \( {\exp }_{{x}_{0}}{\varphi }_{1} = {\exp }_{{x}_{0}} \) . Moreover we claim they are distinct. For otherwise \( {\varphi }_{1} \) would act as a permutation on the set \( \left\{  {{\varphi }_{1}^{k}\left( 0\right)  \mid   - m \leq  k \leq  m}\right\} \) . Since the induced metric \( \widetilde{g} \) at each point in \( {\widetilde{B}}_{r} \) has the injectivity radius at least \( {2r} \) , it follows from the Whitehead theorem (see for example [22]) that \( {\widetilde{B}}_{r} \) is geodesically convex. Then there would exist the unique center of mass \( \widetilde{y} \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{r} \) . But then \( \widetilde{y} = {\varphi }_{0}\left( \widetilde{y}\right)  = {\varphi }_{1}\left( \widetilde{y}\right) \) , a contradiction.

(b) Each point in \( B\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) \) has at least \( N + 1 \) preimages in \( \Omega  = { \cup  }_{i = 0}^{N}B\left( {{\widetilde{x}}_{i}, r}\right)  \subset  {\widetilde{B}}_{2r} \) . Hence by the Bishop volume comparison,

\[
\left( {N + 1}\right) \operatorname{Vol}\left( {B\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) }\right)  \leq  {\operatorname{Vol}}_{\widetilde{g}}\left( \Omega \right)  \leq  {\operatorname{Vol}}_{\widetilde{g}}\left( {\widetilde{B}}_{2r}\right)  \leq  {V}_{\lambda }^{n}\left( {2r}\right) .
\]

Now the inequality (4.2.1) follows by combining the fact \( N \geq  2\left\lbrack  {r/{l}_{M}\left( {x}_{0}\right) }\right\rbrack \) with the above volume estimate. D

Corollary 4.2.3. Suppose \( B\left( {{p}_{0},{s}_{0}}\right) \left( {0 < {s}_{0} \leq  \infty }\right) \) is a geodesic ball in an n-dimensional complete Riemannian manifold \( M \) having the property that for any \( 0 < s < {s}_{0} \) the sectional curvature \( K \) on \( B\left( {{p}_{0}, s}\right) \) satisfies the bound

\[
\left| K\right|  \leq  \Lambda \left( s\right)
\]

for some positive increasing function \( \Lambda \) defined on \( \left\lbrack  {0,{s}_{0}}\right) \) . Then for any point \( p \in  B\left( {{p}_{0},{s}_{0}}\right) \) with \( d\left( {{p}_{0}, p}\right)  = s \) and any positive number \( r \leq \; \min \left\{  {\pi /4\sqrt{\Lambda \left( {s + 2{r}_{0}}\right) },{r}_{0}}\right\} \) with \( {r}_{0} = \left( {{s}_{0} - s}\right) /4 \) , the injectivity radius of \( M \) at \( p \) is bounded below by

\[
\text{ inj }\left( {M, p}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  r\frac{{V}_{-\Lambda \left( {s + 2{r}_{0}}\right) }^{n}\left( r\right)  \cdot  \operatorname{Vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right) }{{V}_{-\Lambda \left( {s + 2{r}_{0}}\right) }^{n}\left( r\right) \operatorname{Vol}\left( {B\left( {{p}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  + {V}_{-\Lambda \left( {s + 2{r}_{0}}\right) }^{n}\left( {2r}\right) {V}_{-\Lambda \left( {s + 2{r}_{0}}\right) }^{n}\left( {s + 2{r}_{0}}\right) }.
\]

In particular, we have

(4.2.2)

\[
\operatorname{inj}\left( {M, p}\right)  \geq  {\rho }_{n,\delta ,\Lambda }\left( s\right)
\]

where \( \delta  > 0 \) is a lower bound of the injectivity radius \( \operatorname{inj}\left( {M,{p}_{0}}\right) \) at the origin \( {p}_{0} \) and \( {\rho }_{n,\delta ,\Lambda } : \left\lbrack  {0,{s}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\mathbb{R}}^{ + } \) is a positive decreasing function that depends only on the dimension \( n \) , the lower bound \( \delta \) of the injectivity radius \( \operatorname{inj}\left( {M,{p}_{0}}\right) \) , and the function \( \Lambda \) .

THEOREM 4.2.4 (Little Loop Lemma). Let \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) ,0 \leq  t < T <  + \infty \) , be a solution of the Ricci flow on a compact manifold \( M \) . Then there exists a constant \( \rho  > 0 \) having the following property: if at a point \( {x}_{0} \in  M \) and a time \( {t}_{0} \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) ,

\[
\left| {Rm}\right| \left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {r}^{-2}\;\text{ on }{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right)
\]

for some \( r \leq  \sqrt{T} \) , then the injectivity radius of \( M \) with respect to the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) at \( {x}_{0} \) is bounded from below by

\[
\operatorname{inj}\left( {M,{x}_{0},{g}_{ij}\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right)  \geq  {\rho r}\text{ . }
\]

\]

nodes.content:
DEFINITION 4.3.2. We say that the solution satisfies injectivity radius condition if for any sequence of (almost) maximum points \( \left\{  \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \right\} \) , there exists a constant \( {c}_{2} > 0 \) independent of \( k \) such that

\[
\operatorname{inj}\left( {M,{x}_{k},{g}_{ij}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right)  \geq  \frac{{c}_{2}}{\sqrt{{K}_{\max }\left( {t}_{k}\right) }}\text{ for all }k.
\]

Clearly, by the Little Loop Lemma, a maximal solution on a compact manifold with the maximal time \( T <  + \infty \) always satisfies the injectivity radius condition. Also by the Gromoll-Meyer injectivity radius estimate, a solution on a complete noncom-pact manifold with positive sectional curvature also satisfies the injectivity radius condition.

\]

nodes.label: Definition 4.3.3
nodes.document_title: Huai-Dong Cao and Xi-Ping Zhu - A Complete Proof of the Poincare and Geometrization Conjectures
nodes.content:
DEFINITION 4.3.3. A solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) \) to the Ricci flow on the manifold \( M \) , where either \( M \) is compact or at each time \( t \) the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) is complete and has bounded curvature, is called a singularity model if it is not flat and of one of the following three types:

Type I: The solution exists for \( t \in  \left( {-\infty ,\Omega }\right) \) for some constant \( \Omega \) with \( 0 < \Omega  <  + \infty \) and

\[
\left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  \Omega /\left( {\Omega  - t}\right)
\]

everywhere with equality somewhere at \( t = 0 \) ;

Type II: The solution exists for \( t \in  \left( {-\infty , + \infty }\right) \) and

\[
\left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  1
\]

everywhere with equality somewhere at \( t = 0 \) ;

Type III: The solution exists for \( t \in  \left( {-A, + \infty }\right) \) for some constant \( A \) with \( 0 < A < \; + \infty \) and

\[
\left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  A/\left( {A + t}\right)
\]

everywhere with equality somewhere at \( t = 0 \) .

nodes.content: THEOREM 4.3.4. For any maximal solution to the Ricci flow which satisfies the injectivity radius condition and is of Type I, II(a), (b), or III(a), there exists a sequence of dilations of the solution along (almost) maximum points which converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a singularity model of the corresponding type.
