nodes.proof:
The proof is by induction on the dimension. When the dimension is two, the lemma is valid by Theorem 6.2.2. For dimension \( \geq  3 \) , we argue by contradiction.

Suppose the lemma is valid for dimensions \( \leq  n - 1 \) and suppose \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) for some \( n \) -dimensional nonflat ancient solution with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature at some time \( {t}_{0} \leq  0 \) . Fixing a point \( {x}_{0} \in  M \) , we consider the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio

\[
A = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty }}R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right) .
\]

We divide the proof into three cases.

Case 1: \( A =  + \infty \) .

By Lemma 6.1.3, there exist sequences of points \( {x}_{k} \in  M \) divergent to infinity, of radii \( {r}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) , and of positive constants \( {\delta }_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) such that

(i) \( R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{k}}\right) R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) for all \( x \) in the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) \) of radius \( {r}_{k} \) around \( {x}_{k} \) ,

(ii) \( {r}_{k}^{2}R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) ,

(iii) \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right) /{r}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) .

By scaling the solution around the points \( {x}_{k} \) with factor \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) , and shifting the time \( {t}_{0} \) to the new time zero, we get a sequence of rescaled solutions

\[
{g}_{k}\left( s\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right)
\]

to the Ricci flow. Since the ancient solution has nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature, there holds the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.5). Thus the rescaled solutions satisfy

\[
{R}_{k}\left( {x, s}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{k}}\right)
\]

for all \( s \leq  0 \) and \( x \in  {B}_{{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) \) . Since \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , it follows from the standard volume comparison and Theorem 4.2.2 that the injectivity radii of the rescaled solutions \( {g}_{k} \) at the points \( {x}_{k} \) and the new time zero is uniformly bounded below by a positive number. Then by Hamilton's compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) will converge to a solution \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) , O}\right) \) to the Ricci flow with

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {y, s}\right)  \leq  1\text{ , for all }s \leq  0\text{ and }y \in  \widetilde{M}\text{ , }
\]

and

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {O,0}\right)  = 1\text{ . }
\]

Since the metric is shrinking, by (ii) and (iii), we get

\[
R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) }^{2}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{k}}\right)  \geq  R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }^{2}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{k}}\right)
\]

which tends to \( + \infty \) , as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) , for all \( s \leq  0 \) . Thus by Proposition 6.1.2, for each \( s \leq  0,\left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) }\right) \) splits off a line. We now consider the lifting of the solution \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) }\right) , s \leq  0 \) , to its universal cover and denote it by \( \left( {\widetilde{\widetilde{M}},\widetilde{\widetilde{g}}\left( s\right) }\right) , s \leq  0 \) . Clearly we still have

\[
{\nu }_{\widetilde{M}}\left( 0\right)  > 0\text{ and }{\nu }_{\widetilde{\widetilde{M}}}\left( 0\right)  > 0\text{ . }
\]

By applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle and the de Rham decomposition theorem, the universal cover \( \widetilde{\widetilde{M}} \) splits isometrically as \( X \times  \mathbb{R} \) for some \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) - dimensional nonflat (complete) ancient solution \( X \) with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature. These imply that \( {\nu }_{X}\left( 0\right)  > 0 \) , which contradicts the induction hypothesis.

Case 2: \( 0 < A <  + \infty \) .

Take a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) divergent to infinity such that

\[
R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow  A,\text{ as }k \rightarrow   + \infty .
\]

Consider the rescaled solutions \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) }\right) \) (around the fixed point \( {x}_{0} \) ), where

\[
{g}_{k}\left( s\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) , s \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack .
\]

Then there is a constant \( C > 0 \) such that

(6.3.1)

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} {R}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  C/{d}_{k}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right) , \\  {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right)  = 1, \\  {d}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0},0}\right)  \rightarrow  \sqrt{A} > 0, \end{array}\right.
\]

where \( {d}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,{x}_{0},0}\right) \) is the distance function from the point \( {x}_{0} \) in the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) \) .

Since \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , it is a basic result in Alexandrov space theory (see for example Theorem 7.6 of [20]) that a subsequence of \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) converges in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to an \( n \) -dimensional metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) with vertex \( {x}_{0} \) .

By (6.3.1), the standard volume comparison and Theorem 4.2.2, we know that the injectivity radius of \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) at \( {x}_{k} \) is uniformly bounded from below by a positive number \( {\rho }_{0} \) . After taking a subsequence, we may assume \( {x}_{k} \) converges to a point \( {x}_{\infty } \) in \( M \smallsetminus  \left\{  {x}_{0}\right\} \) . Then by Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), we can take a subsequence such that the metrics \( {g}_{k}\left( s\right) \) on the metric balls \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \left( { \subset  M}\right. \) with respect to the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) ) \) converge in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a solution of the Ricci flow on a ball \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{\infty },\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) . Clearly the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) limit has nonnegative curvature operator and it is a piece of the metric cone at the time \( s = 0 \) . By (6.3.1), we have

(6.3.2)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1
\]

Let \( x \) be any point in the limiting ball \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{\infty },\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) and \( {e}_{1} \) be any radial direction at \( x \) . Clearly \( \widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{1}}\right)  = 0 \) . Recall that the evolution equation of the Ricci tensor in frame coordinates is

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\widetilde{R}}_{ab} = \widetilde{\bigtriangleup }{\widetilde{R}}_{ab} + 2{\widetilde{R}}_{acbd}{\widetilde{R}}_{cd}.
\]

Since the curvature operator is nonnegative, by applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle (Theorem 2.2.1) to the above equation, we deduce that the null space of Ric is invariant under parallel translation. In particular, all radial directions split off locally and isometrically. While by (6.3.2), the piece of the metric cone is nonflat. This gives a contradiction.

Case 3: \( A = 0 \) .

The gap theorem as was initiated by Mok-Siu-Yau [93] and established by Greene-Wu [49, 50], Eschenberg-Shrader-Strake [45], and Drees [44] shows that a complete noncompact \( n \) -dimensional (except \( n = 4 \) or 8) Riemannian manifold with nonnegative sectional curvature and the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( A = 0 \) must be flat. So the present case is ruled out except in dimension \( n = 4 \) or 8 . Since in our situation the asymptotic volume ratio is positive and the manifold is the solution of the Ricci flow, we can give an alternative proof for all dimensions as follows.

We claim the sectional curvature of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is positive everywhere. Indeed, by Theorem 2.2.2, the image of the curvature operator is just the restricted holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) of the manifold. If the sectional curvature vanishes for some two-plane, then the holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) cannot be \( {so}\left( n\right) \) . We observe the manifold is not Einstein since it is noncompact, nonflat and has nonnegative curvature operator. If \( \mathcal{G} \) is irreducible, then by Berger’s Theorem [7], \( \mathcal{G} = u\left( \frac{n}{2}\right) \) . Thus the manifold is Kähler with bounded and nonnegative bisectional curvature and with curvature decay faster than quadratic. Then by the gap theorem obtained by Chen and the second author in [31], this Kähler manifold must be flat. This contradicts the assumption. Hence the holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) is reducible and the universal cover of \( M \) splits isometrically as \( {\widetilde{M}}_{1} \times  {\widetilde{M}}_{2} \) nontrivially. Clearly the universal cover of \( M \) has positive asymptotic volume ratio. So \( {\widetilde{M}}_{1} \) and \( {\widetilde{M}}_{2} \) still have positive asymptotic volume ratio and at least one of them is nonflat. By the induction hypothesis, this is also impossible. Thus our claim is proved.

Now we know that the sectional curvature of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is positive everywhere. Choose a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) divergent to infinity such that

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  = \sup \left\{  {R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \mid  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right) }\right\}  , \\  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  k, \\  R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  = {\varepsilon }_{k} \rightarrow  0. \end{array}\right.
\]

Consider the rescaled metric

\[
{g}_{k}\left( 0\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right)
\]

as before. Then

(6.3.3)

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} {R}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  {\varepsilon }_{k}/{d}_{k}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right) ,\;\text{ for }{d}_{k}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right)  \geq  \sqrt{{\varepsilon }_{k}}, \\  {d}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0},0}\right)  = \sqrt{{\varepsilon }_{k}} \rightarrow  0. \end{array}\right.
\]

As in Case 2, the rescaled marked solutions \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) will converge in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to a metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) . And by the virtue of Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), up to a subsequence, the convergence is in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology in \( \widetilde{M} \smallsetminus  \left\{  {x}_{0}\right\} \) . We next claim the metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) .

Indeed, let us write the metric cone \( \widetilde{M} \) as a warped product \( {\mathbb{R}}_{ + }{ \times  }_{r}{X}^{n - 1} \) for some \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional manifold \( {X}^{n - 1} \) . By (6.3.3), the metric cone must be flat and \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is isometric to a quotient of the round sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{n - 1} \) by fixed point free isometries in the standard metric. To show \( \widetilde{M} \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) , we only need to verify that \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is simply connected.

Let \( \varphi \) be the Busemann function of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) with respect to the point \( {x}_{0} \) . Since \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) has nonnegative sectional curvature, it is easy to see that for any small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there is a \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) such that

\[
\left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \varphi \left( x\right)  \leq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  M \smallsetminus  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) . The strict positivity of the sectional curvature of the manifold \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) implies that the square of the Busemann function is strictly convex (and exhausting). Thus every level set \( {\varphi }^{-1}\left( a\right) \) , with \( a > \inf \{ \varphi \left( x\right)  \mid  x \in  M\} \) , of the Busemann function \( \varphi \) is diffeomorphic to the \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{n - 1} \) . In particular, \( {\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {a,\frac{3}{2}a}\right\rbrack  \right) \) is simply connected for \( a > \inf \{ \varphi \left( x\right)  \mid  x \in  M\} \) since \( n \geq  3 \) .

Consider an annulus portion \( \left\lbrack  {1,2}\right\rbrack   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) of the metric cone \( \widetilde{M} = {\mathbb{R}}_{ + }{ \times  }_{r}{X}^{n - 1} \) . It is the limit of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) , where

\[
{M}_{k} = \left\{  {x \in  M\left| {\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }} \leq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{2}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right. }\right\}  .
\]

It is clear that

\[
{\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }},\frac{2\left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) }{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right\rbrack  \right)  \subset  {M}_{k} \subset  {\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {\frac{1 - \varepsilon }{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }},\frac{2}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right\rbrack  \right)
\]

for \( k \) large enough. Thus any closed loop in \( \left\{  \frac{3}{2}\right\}   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) can be shrunk to a point by a homotopy in \( \left\lbrack  {1,2}\right\rbrack   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) . This shows that \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is simply connected. Hence we have proven that the metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Consequently,

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow   + \infty }}\frac{{\operatorname{Vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right)  \smallsetminus  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{\sigma r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right) }\right) }{{\left( \frac{r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) }^{n}} = {\alpha }_{n}\left( {1 - {\sigma }^{n}}\right)
\]

for any \( r > 0 \) and \( 0 < \sigma  < 1 \) , where \( {\alpha }_{n} \) is the volume of the unit ball in the Euclidean space \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Finally, by combining with the monotonicity of the Bishop-Gromov volume comparison, we conclude that the manifold \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is flat and isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . This contradicts the assumption.

Therefore, we have proved the lemma. Ⓡ

Finally we would like to include an alternative simpler argument, inspired by Ni [98], for the above Case 2 and Case 3 to avoid the use of the gap theorem, holonomy groups, and asymptotic cone structure.

Alternative Proof for Case 2 and Case 3. Let us consider the situation of \( 0 \leq \; A <  + \infty \) in the above proof. Observe that \( {\nu }_{M}\left( t\right) \) is nonincreasing in time \( t \) by using Lemma 3.4.1(ii) and the fact that the metric is shrinking in \( t \) . Suppose \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , then the solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed for \( t \leq  {t}_{0} \) for some uniform \( \kappa  > 0 \) . By combining with Theorem 6.2.1, there exist a sequence of points \( {q}_{k} \) and a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow   - \infty \) such that the scalings of \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) around \( {q}_{k} \) with factor \( {\left| {t}_{k}\right| }^{-1} \) and with the times \( {t}_{k} \) shifting to the new time zero converge to a nonflat gradient shrinking soliton \( \bar{M} \) in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology. This gradient soliton also has maximal volume growth (i.e. \( {\nu }_{\bar{M}}\left( t\right)  > 0 \) ) and satisfies the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.5). If the curvature of the shrinking soliton \( \bar{M} \) at the time -1 is bounded, then we see from the proof of Theorem 6.2.2 that by using the equations (6.2.24)-(6.2.26), the scalar curvature has a positive lower bound everywhere on \( \bar{M} \) at the time -1 . In particular, this implies the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( A = \infty \) for the soliton at the time -1 , which reduces to Case 1 and arrives at a contradiction by the dimension reduction argument. On the other hand, if the scalar curvature is unbounded, then by Lemma 6.1.4, the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.5) and Lemma 6.1.2, we can do the same dimension reduction as in Case 1 to arrive at a contradiction also. 0

The following lemma is a local and space-time version of Lemma 6.1.4 on picking local (almost) maximum curvature points. We formulate it from Perelman's arguments in the section 10 of [103].

LEMMA 6.3.2. For any positive constants \( B, C \) with \( B > 4 \) and \( C > {1000} \) , there exists \( 1 \leq  A < \min \left\{  {\frac{1}{4}B,\frac{1}{1000}C}\right\} \) which tends to infinity as \( B \) and \( C \) tend to infinity and satisfies the following property. Suppose we have a (not necessarily complete) solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) to the Ricci flow, defined on \( M \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) , so that at each time \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) the metric ball \( {B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},1}\right) \) is compactly contained in \( M \) . Suppose there exists a point \( \left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \in  M \times  \left( {-{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) such that

\[
{d}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  < \frac{1}{3}\text{ with }Q = \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) }\right|  > C + B{\left( \bar{t} + {t}_{0}\right) }^{-1},

and

\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {4Q}
\]

for all \( \left( {-{t}_{0} < }\right) \bar{t} - A{Q}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {d}_{t}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{10}{A}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) .

We first claim that there exists a point \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( - {t}_{0} < \bar{t} \leq  0 \) and \( {d}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  < \frac{1}{3} \) such that

\[
Q = \left| {{Rm}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) }\right|  > C + B{\left( \bar{t} + {t}_{0}\right) }^{-1},
\]

and

(6.3.4)

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {4Q}
\]

wherever \( \bar{t} - A{Q}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t},\;{d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {d}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  + {\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) .

We will construct such \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) as a limit of a finite sequence of points. Take an arbitrary \( \left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right) \) such that

\[
{d}_{{t}_{1}}\left( {{x}_{1},{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{4},\; - {t}_{0} < {t}_{1} \leq  0\text{ and }\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right) }\right|  > C + B{\left( {t}_{1} + {t}_{0}\right) }^{-1}.
\]

Such a point clearly exists by our assumption. Assume we have already constructed \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . If we cannot take the point \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) to be the desired point \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , then there exists a point \( \left( {{x}_{k + 1},{t}_{k + 1}}\right) \) such that

\[
{t}_{k} - A{\left| Rm\left( {x}_{k},{t}_{k}\right) \right| }^{-1} \leq  {t}_{k + 1} \leq  {t}_{k},
\]

and

\[
{d}_{{t}_{k + 1}}\left( {{x}_{k + 1},{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {d}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  + {\left( A{\left| \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x}_{k},{t}_{k}\right) \right| }^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}},
\]

but

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k + 1},{t}_{k + 1}}\right) }\right|  > 4\left| {{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right| .
\]

It then follows that

\[
{d}_{{t}_{k + 1}}\left( {{x}_{k + 1},{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {d}_{{t}_{1}}\left( {{x}_{1},{x}_{0}}\right)  + {A}^{\frac{1}{2}}\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}{\left| \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x}_{i},{t}_{i}\right) \right| }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{1}{4} + {A}^{\frac{1}{2}}\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}{2}^{-\left( {i - 1}\right) }{\left| \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x}_{1},{t}_{1}\right) \right| }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{1}{4} + 2{\left( A{C}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}
\]

\[
< \frac{1}{3}
\]

\[
{t}_{k + 1} - \left( {-{t}_{0}}\right)  = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\left( {{t}_{i + 1} - {t}_{i}}\right)  + \left( {{t}_{1} - \left( {-{t}_{0}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\geq   - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}A{\left| Rm\left( {x}_{i},{t}_{i}\right) \right| }^{-1} + \left( {{t}_{1} - \left( {-{t}_{0}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\geq   - A\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}{4}^{-\left( {i - 1}\right) }{\left| \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x}_{1},{t}_{1}\right) \right| }^{-1} + \left( {{t}_{1} - \left( {-{t}_{0}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\geq   - \frac{2A}{B}\left( {{t}_{1} + {t}_{0}}\right)  + \left( {{t}_{1} + {t}_{0}}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{1}{2}\left( {{t}_{1} + {t}_{0}}\right)
\]

and

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k + 1},{t}_{k + 1}}\right) }\right|  > {4}^{k}\left| {{Rm}\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right) }\right|
\]

\[
\geq  {4}^{k}C \rightarrow   + \infty \text{ as }k \rightarrow   + \infty \text{ . }
\]

Since the solution is smooth, the sequence \( \left\{  \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \right\} \) is finite and its last element fits. Thus we have proved assertion (6.3.4).

From the above construction we also see that the chosen point \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) satisfies

\[
{d}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  < \frac{1}{3}
\]

and

\[
Q = \left| {{Rm}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) }\right|  > C + B{\left( \bar{t} + {t}_{0}\right) }^{-1}.
\]

Clearly, up to some adjustment of the constant \( A \) , we only need to show that

(6.3.4)

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {4Q}
\]

wherever \( \bar{t} - \frac{1}{200n}{A}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {d}_{t}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{10}{A}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) .

For any point \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( {d}_{\bar{t}}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{10}{A}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , we have

\[
{d}_{\bar{t}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {d}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  + {d}_{\bar{t}}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)
\]

\[
\leq  {d}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  + {\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}
\]

and then by (6.3.4)

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) }\right|  \leq  {4Q}.
\]

Thus by continuity, there is a minimal \( {\bar{t}}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} - \frac{1}{200n}{A}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) such that

(6.3.5)

\[
\sup \left\{  {\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \mid  {\bar{t}}^{\prime } \leq  t \leq  \bar{t},\;{d}_{t}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{10}{A}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\}   \leq  {5Q}.
\]

For any point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( {\bar{t}}^{\prime } \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {d}_{t}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{10}{\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) , we divide the discussion into two cases.

Case (1): \( {d}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{3}{10}{\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) .

From assertion (6.3.4) we see that

\( {\left( {6.3}{.5}\right) }^{\prime } \)

\[
\sup \left\{  {\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \mid  {\bar{t}}^{\prime } \leq  t \leq  \bar{t},\;{d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}}\right\}   \leq  {4Q}.
\]

Since \( {d}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{3}{10}{\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) , we have

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {d}_{t}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  + {d}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{1}{10}{\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} + \frac{3}{10}{\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}
\]

\[
\leq  {\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}
\]

which implies the estimate \( \left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {4Q} \) from \( {\left( {6.3}{.5}\right) }^{\prime } \) .

Case (2): \( {d}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  > \frac{3}{10}{\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) .

From the curvature bounds in (6.3.5) and \( {\left( {6.3}{.5}\right) }^{\prime } \) , we can apply Lemma 3.4.1 (ii) with \( {r}_{0} = \frac{1}{10}{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) to get

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\left( {{d}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq   - {40}\left( {n - 1}\right) {Q}^{\frac{1}{2}}
\]

and then

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {d}_{\widehat{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  + {40n}\left( {Q}^{\frac{1}{2}}\right) \left( {\frac{1}{200n}{A}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}^{-1}}\right)
\]

\[
\leq  {d}_{\widehat{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  + \frac{1}{5}{\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}
\]

where \( \widehat{t} \in  (t,\bar{t}\rbrack \) satisfies the property that \( {d}_{s}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  \frac{3}{10}{\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) whenever \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {t,\widehat{t}}\right\rbrack \) . So we have either

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {d}_{t}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  + {d}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{1}{10}{\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} + \frac{3}{10}{\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} + \frac{1}{5}{\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}
\]

\[
\leq  {\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}
\]

or

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {d}_{t}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  + {d}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{1}{10}{\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} + {d}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  + \frac{1}{5}{\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}
\]

\[
\leq  {d}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  + {\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}.
\]

It then follows from (6.3.4) that \( \left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {4Q} \) .

Hence we have proved

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {4Q}
\]

for any point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( {\bar{t}}^{\prime } \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {d}_{t}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{10}{\left( A{Q}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) . By combining with the choice of \( {\bar{t}}^{\prime } \) in (6.3.5), we must have \( {\bar{t}}^{\prime } = \bar{t} - \frac{1}{200n}{A}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}^{-1} \) . This proves assertion (6.3.4)

Therefore we have completed the proof of the lemma. I

We now use the volume lower bound assumption to establish the crucial curvature upper bound estimate of Perelman [103] for the Ricci flow. For the Ricci flow on Kähler manifolds, a global version of this estimate (i.e., curvature decaying linear in time and quadratic in space) was independently obtained in [29] and [32]. Note that the volume estimate conclusion in the following Theorem 6.3.3 (ii) was not stated in Corollary 11.6 (b) of Perelman [103]. The estimate will be used later in the proof of Theorem 7.2.2 and Theorem 7.5.2.

nodes.content:
THEOREM 6.3.3 (Perelman [103]). For every \( w > 0 \) there exist \( B = B\left( w\right)  < \; + \infty ,\;C = C\left( w\right)  <  + \infty ,\;{\tau }_{0} = {\tau }_{0}\left( w\right)  > 0 \) , and \( \xi  = \xi \left( w\right)  > 0 \) (depending also on the dimension) with the following properties. Suppose we have a (not necessarily complete) solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) to the Ricci flow, defined on \( M \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{0}{r}_{0}^{2},0}\right\rbrack \) , so that at each time \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{0}{r}_{0}^{2},0}\right\rbrack \) the metric ball \( {B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) is compactly contained in \( M \) .

(i) If at each time \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{0}{r}_{0}^{2},0}\right\rbrack \) ,

\[
{Rm}\left( {., t}\right)  \geq   - {r}_{0}^{-2}\text{ on }{B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right)
\]

\[
\text{ and }{\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( {{B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  w{r}_{0}^{n}\text{ , }
\]

then we have the estimate

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  C{r}_{0}^{-2} + B{\left( t + {t}_{0}{r}_{0}^{2}\right) }^{-1}
\]

whenever \( - {t}_{0}{r}_{0}^{2} < t \leq  0 \) and \( {d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{r}_{0} \) .

(ii) If for some \( 0 < \bar{\tau } \leq  {t}_{0} \) ,

\[
{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq   - {r}_{0}^{-2}\text{ for }t \in  \left\lbrack  {-\bar{\tau }{r}_{0}^{2},0}\right\rbrack  , x \in  {B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) ,
\]

\[
\text{ and }{\operatorname{Vol}}_{0}\left( {{B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  w{r}_{0}^{n}\text{ , }
\]

then we have the estimates

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( {{B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  \xi {r}_{0}^{n}\text{ for all }\max \left\{  {-\bar{\tau }{r}_{0}^{2}, - {\tau }_{0}{r}_{0}^{2}}\right\}   \leq  t \leq  0\text{ , }
\]

and

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  C{r}_{0}^{-2} + B{\left( t - \max \left\{  -\bar{\tau }{r}_{0}^{2}, - {\tau }_{0}{r}_{0}^{2}\right\}  \right) }^{-1}
\]

whenever \( \max \left\{  {-\bar{\tau }{r}_{0}^{2}, - {\tau }_{0}{r}_{0}^{2}}\right\}   < t \leq  0 \) and \( {d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{r}_{0} \) .

nodes.proof:
By scaling we may assume \( {r}_{0} = 1 \) .

(i) By the standard (relative) volume comparison, we know that there exists some \( {w}^{\prime } > 0 \) , with \( {w}^{\prime } \leq  w \) , depending only on \( w \) , such that for each point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( - {t}_{0} \leq  t \leq  0 \) and \( {d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{3} \) , and for each \( r \leq  \frac{1}{3} \) , there holds

(6.3.6)

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( {{B}_{t}\left( {x, r}\right) }\right)  \geq  {w}^{\prime }{r}^{n}.
\]

We argue by contradiction. Suppose there are sequences \( B, C \rightarrow   + \infty \) , of solutions \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) and points \( \left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right) \) such that

\[
{d}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}^{\prime },{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{4},\; - {t}_{0} < {t}^{\prime } \leq  0\text{ and }\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right|  > C + B{\left( {t}^{\prime } + {t}_{0}\right) }^{-1}.
\]

Then by Lemma 6.3.2, we can find a sequence of points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) such that

\[
{d}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  < \frac{1}{3}
\]

\[
Q = \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) }\right|  > C + B{\left( \bar{t} + {t}_{0}\right) }^{-1},
\]

and

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {4Q}
\]

wherever \( \left( {-{t}_{0} < }\right) \bar{t} - A{Q}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t},\;{d}_{t}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{10}{A}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , where \( A \) tends to infinity with \( B, C \) . Thus we may take a blow-up limit along the points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with factors \( Q \) and get a non-flat ancient solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{ij}^{\left( \infty \right) }\left( t\right) }\right) \) with nonnegative curvature operator and with the asymptotic volume ratio \( {\nu }_{{M}_{\infty }}\left( t\right)  \geq  {w}^{\prime } > 0 \) for each \( t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) (by (6.3.6)). This contradicts Lemma 6.3.1.

(ii) Let \( B\left( w\right) , C\left( w\right) \) be good for the first part of the theorem. By the volume assumption at \( t = 0 \) and the standard (relative) volume comparison, we still have the estimate

(6.3.6)

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{0}\left( {{B}_{0}\left( {x, r}\right) }\right)  \geq  {w}^{\prime }{r}^{n}
\]

for each \( x \in  M \) with \( {d}_{0}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{3} \) and \( r \leq  \frac{1}{3} \) . We will show that \( \xi  = {5}^{-n}{w}^{\prime } \) , \( B = B\left( {{5}^{-n}{w}^{\prime }}\right) \) and \( C = C\left( {{5}^{-n}{w}^{\prime }}\right) \) are good for the second part of the theorem.

By continuity and the volume assumption at \( t = 0 \) , there is a maximal subinterval \( \left\lbrack  {-\tau ,0}\right\rbrack \) of the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-\bar{\tau },0}\right\rbrack \) such that

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( {{B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},1}\right) }\right)  \geq  w \geq  {5}^{-n}{w}^{\prime }\;\text{ for all }t \in  \left\lbrack  {-\tau ,0}\right\rbrack  .
\]

This says that the assumptions of (i) hold with \( {5}^{-n}{w}^{\prime } \) in place of \( w \) and with \( \tau \) in place of \( {t}_{0} \) . Thus the conclusion of the part (i) gives us the estimate

(6.3.7)

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  C + B{\left( t + \tau \right) }^{-1}
\]

whenever \( t \in  ( - \tau ,0\rbrack \) and \( {d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{4} \) .

We need to show that one can choose a positive \( {\tau }_{0} \) depending only on \( w \) and the dimension such that the maximal \( \tau  \geq  \min \left\{  {\bar{\tau },{\tau }_{0}}\right\} \) .

For \( t \in  ( - \tau ,0\rbrack \) and \( \frac{1}{8} \leq  {d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{4} \) , we use (6.3.7) and Lemma 3.4.1(ii) to get

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq   - {10}\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {\sqrt{C} + \left( {\sqrt{B}/\sqrt{t + \tau }}\right) }\right)
\]

which further gives

\[
{d}_{0}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {d}_{-\tau }\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  - {10}\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {\tau \sqrt{C} + 2\sqrt{B\tau }}\right) .
\]

This means

(6.3.8)

\[
{B}_{\left( -\tau \right) }\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{4}}\right)  \supset  {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{4} - {10}\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {\tau \sqrt{C} + 2\sqrt{B\tau }}\right) }\right) .
\]

Note that the scalar curvature \( R \geq   - C\left( n\right) \) for some constant \( C\left( n\right) \) depending only on the dimension since \( {Rm} \geq   - 1 \) . We have

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( {{B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{4} - {10}\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {\tau \sqrt{C} + 2\sqrt{B\tau }}\right) }\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= {\int }_{{B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{4} - {10}\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {\tau \sqrt{C} + 2\sqrt{B\tau }}\right) }\right) }\left( {-R}\right) d{V}_{t}
\]

\[
\leq  C\left( n\right) {\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( {{B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{4} - {10}\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {\tau \sqrt{C} + 2\sqrt{B\tau }}\right) }\right) }\right)
\]

and then

(6.3.9)

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( {{B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{4} - {10}\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {\tau \sqrt{C} + 2\sqrt{B\tau }}\right) }\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\leq  {e}^{C\left( n\right) \tau }{\operatorname{Vol}}_{\left( -\tau \right) }\left( {{B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{4} - {10}\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {\tau \sqrt{C} + 2\sqrt{B\tau }}\right) }\right) }\right) .
\]

Thus by (6.3.6) \( {}^{\prime },\left( {6.3.8}\right) \) and (6.3.9),

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{\left( -\tau \right) }\left( {B}_{\left( -\tau \right) }\right) \left( {{x}_{0},1}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  {\operatorname{Vol}}_{\left( -\tau \right) }\left( {B}_{\left( -\tau \right) }\right) \left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{4}}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  {\operatorname{Vol}}_{\left( -\tau \right) }\left( {{B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{4} - {10}\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {\tau \sqrt{C} + 2\sqrt{B\tau }}\right) }\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\geq  {e}^{-C\left( n\right) \tau }{\operatorname{Vol}}_{0}\left( {{B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{4} - {10}\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {\tau \sqrt{C} + 2\sqrt{B\tau }}\right) }\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\geq  {e}^{-C\left( n\right) \tau }{w}^{\prime }{\left( \frac{1}{4} - {10}\left( n - 1\right) \left( \tau \sqrt{C} + 2\sqrt{B\tau }\right) \right) }^{n}.
\]

So it suffices to choose \( {\tau }_{0} = {\tau }_{0}\left( w\right) \) small enough so that

\[
{e}^{-C\left( n\right) {\tau }_{0}}{\left( \frac{1}{4} - {10}\left( n - 1\right) \left( {\tau }_{0}\sqrt{C} + 2\sqrt{B{\tau }_{0}}\right) \right) }^{n} \geq  {\left( \frac{1}{5}\right) }^{n}.
\]

Therefore we have proved the theorem.

nodes.content_excerpt: LEMMA 6.4.1 (Classification of three-dimensional shrinking solitons). Let \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( t\right) }\right) \) be a nonflat gradient shrinking soliton on a three-manifold. Suppose \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( t\right) }\right) \) has bounded and nonnegative sectional curvature and is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on all scales for some \( \kappa > 0 \) . Then \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( t\right) }\right) \...

nodes.proof:
We first consider the case that the sectional curvature of the nonflat gradient shrinking soliton is not strictly positive. Let us pull back the soliton to its universal cover. Then the pull-back metric is again a nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. By Hamilton's strong maximum principle (Theorem 2.2.1), we know that the pull-back solution splits as the metric product of a two-dimensional nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution and \( \mathbb{R} \) . Since the two-dimensional nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is simply connected, it follows from Theorem 6.2.2 that it must be the round sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) . Thus, the gradient shrinking soliton must be \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R}/\Gamma \) , a metric quotient of the round cylinder.

For each \( \sigma  \in  \Gamma \) and \( \left( {x, s}\right)  \in  {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , we write \( \sigma \left( {x, s}\right)  = \left( {{\sigma }_{1}\left( {x, s}\right) ,{\sigma }_{2}\left( {x, s}\right) }\right)  \in \; {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Since \( \sigma \) sends lines to lines, and sends cross spheres to cross spheres, we have \( {\sigma }_{2}\left( {x, s}\right)  = {\sigma }_{2}\left( {y, s}\right) \) , for all \( x, y \in  {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) . This says that \( {\sigma }_{2} \) reduces to a function of \( s \) alone on \( \mathbb{R} \) . Moreover, for any \( \left( {x, s}\right) ,\left( {{x}^{\prime },{s}^{\prime }}\right)  \in  {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , since \( \sigma \) preserves the distances between cross spheres \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \{ s\} \) and \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \left\{  {s}^{\prime }\right\} \) , we have \( \left| {{\sigma }_{2}\left( {x, s}\right)  - {\sigma }_{2}\left( {{x}^{\prime },{s}^{\prime }}\right) }\right|  = \left| {s - {s}^{\prime }}\right| \) . So the projection \( {\Gamma }_{2} \) of \( \Gamma \) to the second factor \( \mathbb{R} \) is an isometry subgroup of \( \mathbb{R} \) . If the metric quotient \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R}/\Gamma \) were compact, it would not be \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on sufficiently large scales as \( t \rightarrow   - \infty \) . Thus the metric quotient \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R}/\Gamma \) is noncompact. It follows that \( {\Gamma }_{2} = \{ 1\} \) or \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) . In particular, there is a \( \Gamma \) -invariant cross sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) in the round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Denote it by \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \{ 0\} \) . Then \( \Gamma \) acts on the round two-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \{ 0\} \) isometrically without fixed points. This implies \( \Gamma \) is either \( \{ 1\} \) or \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) . Hence we conclude that the gradient shrinking soliton is either the round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , or \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , or the twisted product \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) where \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) flips both \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) and \( \mathbb{R} \) .

We next consider the case that the gradient shrinking soliton is compact and has strictly positive sectional curvature everywhere. By the proof of Theorem 5.2.1 (see also Remark 5.2.8) we see that the compact gradient shrinking soliton is getting round and tends to a space form (with positive constant curvature) as the time approaches the maximal time \( t = 0 \) . Since the shape of a gradient shrinking Ricci soliton does not change up to reparametrizations and homothetical scalings, the gradient shrinking soliton has to be the round three-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) or a metric quotient of \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) .

Finally we want to exclude the case that the gradient shrinking soliton is non-compact and has strictly positive sectional curvature everywhere.

Suppose there is a (complete three-dimensional) noncompact \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed gradient shrinking soliton \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) , - \infty  < t < 0 \) , with bounded and positive sectional curvature at each \( t \in  \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) and satisfying the equation (6.4.1). Then as in (6.2.25), we have

(6.4.2)

\[
{\nabla }_{i}R = 2{R}_{ij}{\nabla }_{j}f
\]

Fix some \( t < 0 \) , say \( t =  - 1 \) , and consider a long shortest geodesic \( \gamma \left( s\right) ,0 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s} \) . Let \( {x}_{0} = \gamma \left( 0\right) \) and \( X\left( s\right)  = \dot{\gamma }\left( s\right) \) . Let \( U\left( 0\right) \) be any unit vector orthogonal to \( \dot{\gamma }\left( 0\right) \) and translate \( U\left( 0\right) \) along \( \gamma \left( s\right) \) to get a parallel vector field \( U\left( s\right) ,0 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s} \) , on \( \gamma \) . Set

\[
\widetilde{U}\left( s\right)  = \left\{  \begin{array}{lll} {sU}\left( s\right) , & \text{ for } & 0 \leq  s \leq  1, \\  U\left( s\right) , & \text{ for } & 1 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s} - 1 \\  \left( {\bar{s} - s}\right) U\left( s\right) , & \text{ for } & \bar{s} - 1 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s}. \end{array}\right.
\]

It follows from the second variation formula of arclength that

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\left( {{\left| \dot{\widetilde{U}}\left( s\right) \right| }^{2} - R\left( {X,\widetilde{U}, X,\widetilde{U}}\right) }\right) {ds} \geq  0.
\]

Since the curvature of the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {-1}\right) \) is bounded, we clearly have

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}R\left( {X, U, X, U}\right) {ds} \leq  \text{ const. }
\]

and then

(6.4.3)

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) {ds} \leq  \text{ const.. }
\]

Moreover, since the curvature of the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {-1}\right) \) is positive, it follows from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality that for any unit vector field \( Y \) along \( \gamma \) and orthogonal to \( X\left( { = \dot{\gamma }\left( s\right) }\right) \) , we have

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( X, Y\right) \right| }^{2}{ds} \leq  {\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right) {ds}
\]

\[
\leq  \text{ const. } \cdot  {\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) {ds}
\]

\[
\leq  \text{ const. }
\]

and then

(6.4.4)

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\left| {\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, Y}\right) }\right| {ds} \leq  \text{ const. } \cdot  \left( {\sqrt{\bar{s}} + 1}\right) .
\]

From (6.4.1) we know

\[
{\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{X}f + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  - \frac{1}{2} = 0
\]

and by integrating this equation we get

\[
X\left( {f\left( {\gamma \left( \bar{s}\right) }\right) }\right)  - X\left( {f\left( {\gamma \left( 0\right) }\right) }\right)  + {\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) {ds} - \frac{1}{2}\bar{s} = 0.
\]

Thus by (6.4.3) we deduce

(6.4.5)

\[
\frac{\bar{s}}{2} - \text{ const. } \leq  \langle X,\nabla f\left( {\gamma \left( \bar{s}\right) }\right) \rangle  \leq  \frac{\bar{s}}{2} + \text{ const. }
\]

Similarly by integrating (6.4.1) and using (6.4.4) we can deduce

(6.4.6)

\[
\left| {\langle Y,\nabla f\left( {\gamma \left( \bar{s}\right) }\right) \rangle }\right|  \leq  \text{ const. } \cdot  \left( {\sqrt{\bar{s}} + 1}\right) .
\]

These two inequalities tell us that at large distances from the fixed point \( {x}_{0} \) the function \( f \) has no critical point, and its gradient makes a small angle with the gradient of the distance function from \( {x}_{0} \) .

Now from (6.4.2) we see that at large distances from \( {x}_{0}, R \) is strictly increasing along the gradient curves of \( f \) , in particular

\[
\bar{R} = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{{d}_{\left( -1\right) }\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty }}R\left( {x, - 1}\right)  > 0.
\]

Let us choose a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{k}, - 1}\right) \) where \( R\left( {{x}_{k}, - 1}\right)  \rightarrow  \bar{R} \) . By the noncol-lapsing assumption we can take a limit along this sequence of points of the gradient soliton and get an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution defined on \( - \infty  < t < 0 \) . By Proposition 6.1.2, we deduce that the limiting ancient \( \kappa \) -solution splits off a line. Since the soliton has positive sectional curvature, we know from Gromoll-Meyer [52] that it is orientable. Then it follows from Theorem 6.2.2 that the limiting solution is the shrinking round infinite cylinder with scalar curvature \( \bar{R} \) at time \( t =  - 1 \) . Since the limiting solution exists on \( \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) , we conclude that \( \bar{R} \leq  1 \) . Hence

\[
R\left( {x, - 1}\right)  < 1
\]

when the distance from \( x \) to the fixed \( {x}_{0} \) is large enough on the gradient shrinking soliton.

Let us consider the level surface \( \{ f = a\} \) of \( f \) . The second fundamental form of the level surface is given by

\[
{h}_{ij} = \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{i}\left( \frac{\nabla f}{\left| \nabla f\right| }\right) ,{e}_{j}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
= {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f/\left| {\nabla f}\right| ,\;i, j = 1,2,
\]

where \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2}}\right\} \) is an orthonormal basis of the level surface. By (6.4.1), we have

\[
{\nabla }_{{e}_{i}}{\nabla }_{{e}_{i}}f = \frac{1}{2} - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{i}}\right)  \geq  \frac{1}{2} - \frac{R}{2} > 0,\;i = 1,2,
\]

since for a three-manifold the positivity of sectional curvature is equivalent to \( R \geq \) 2Ric. It then follows from the first variation formula that

(6.4.7)

\[
\frac{d}{da}\operatorname{Area}\{ f = a\}  = {\int }_{\{ f = a\} }\operatorname{div}\left( \frac{\nabla f}{\left| \nabla f\right| }\right)
\]

\[
\geq  {\int }_{\{ f = a\} }\frac{1}{\left| \nabla f\right| }\left( {1 - R}\right)
\]

\[
> {\int }_{\{ f = a\} }\frac{1}{\left| \nabla f\right| }\left( {1 - \bar{R}}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  0
\]

for \( a \) large enough. We conclude that Area \( \{ f = a\} \) strictly increases as \( a \) increases. From (6.4.5) we see that for \( s \) large enough

\[
\left| {\frac{df}{ds} - \frac{s}{2}}\right|  \leq  \text{ const., }
\]

and then

\[
\left| {f - \frac{{s}^{2}}{4}}\right|  \leq  \text{ const. } \cdot  \left( {s + 1}\right) .
\]

Thus we get from (6.4.7)

\[
\frac{d}{da}\operatorname{Area}\{ f = a\}  > \frac{1 - \bar{R}}{2\sqrt{a}}\operatorname{Area}\{ f = a\}
\]

for \( a \) large enough. This implies that

\[
\log \operatorname{Area}\{ f = a\}  > \left( {1 - \bar{R}}\right) \sqrt{a} - \text{ const. }
\]

for \( a \) large enough. But it is clear from (6.4.7) that Area \( \{ f = a\} \) is uniformly bounded from above by the area of the round sphere of scalar curvature \( \bar{R} \) for all large \( a \) . Thus we deduce that \( \bar{R} = 1 \) . So

(6.4.8)

\[
\text{ Area }\{ f = a\}  < {8\pi }
\]

for a large enough.

Denote by \( X \) the unit normal vector to the level surface \( \{ f = a\} \) . By using the Gauss equation and (6.4.1), the intrinsic curvature of the level surface \( \{ f = a\} \) can be computed as

(6.4.9) intrinsic curvature

\[
= {R}_{1212} + \det \left( {h}_{ij}\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}\left( {R - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) }\right)  + \frac{\det \left( {\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) }\right) }{{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{1}{2}\left( {R - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) }\right)  + \frac{1}{4{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}{\left( \operatorname{tr}\left( \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \right) \right) }^{2}
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}\left( {R - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) }\right)  + \frac{1}{4{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}{\left( 1 - \left( R - \operatorname{Ric}\left( X, X\right) \right) \right) }^{2}
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack  {1 - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  - \left( {1 - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) }\right)  + \frac{{\left( 1 - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( X, X\right) \right) }^{2}}{2{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
< \frac{1}{2}
\]

for sufficiently large \( a \) , since \( \left( {1 - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) }\right)  > 0 \) and \( \left| {\nabla f}\right| \) is large when \( a \) is large. Thus the combination of (6.4.8) and (6.4.9) gives a contradiction to the Gauss-Bonnet formula.

Therefore we have proved the lemma.
nodes.proof_excerpt: We first consider the case that the sectional curvature of the nonflat gradient shrinking soliton is not strictly positive. Let us pull back the soliton to its universal cover. Then the pull-back metric is again a nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. nodes.label: Proposition 6.4.2
nodes.document_title: Huai-Dong Cao and Xi-Ping Zhu - A Complete Proof of the Poincare and Geometrization Conjectures
nodes.content: PROPOSITION 6.4.2 (Universal noncollapsing). There exists a positive constant \( {\kappa }_{0} \) with the following property. Suppose we have a nonflat three-dimensional ancient \( \kappa \) -solution for some \( \kappa  > 0 \) . Then either the solution is \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -noncollapsed on all scales, or it is a metric quotient of the round three-sphere.
nodes.content_excerpt: PROPOSITION 6.4.2 (Universal noncollapsing). There exists a positive constant \( {\kappa }_{0} \) with the following property. Suppose we have a nonflat three-dimensional ancient \( \kappa \) -solution for some \( \kappa > 0 \) . Then either the solution is \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -noncollapsed on all scales, or it is a metric quotient of the round three-sphere.

nodes.proof:
Let \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) , x \in  M \) and \( t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , be a nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution for some \( \kappa  > 0 \) . For an arbitrary point \( \left( {p,{t}_{0}}\right)  \in  M \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , we define as in Chapter 3 that

\[
\tau  = {t}_{0} - t,\;\text{ for }t < {t}_{0},
\]

\[
l\left( {q,\tau }\right)  = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\tau }}\inf \left\{  {{\int }_{0}^{\tau }\sqrt{s}\left( {R\left( {\gamma \left( s\right) ,{t}_{0} - s}\right)  + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\left( s\right) \right| }_{{g}_{ij}\left( {{t}_{0} - s}\right) }^{2}}\right) {ds} \mid  }\right.
\]

\[
\gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,\tau }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M\text{ with }\left. {\gamma \left( 0\right)  = p,\gamma \left( \tau \right)  = q}\right\}  ,
\]

\[
\text{ and }\widetilde{V}\left( \tau \right)  = {\int }_{M}{\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,\tau }\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - \tau }\left( q\right) \text{ . }
\]

Recall from (6.2.1) that for each \( \tau  > 0 \) we can find \( q = q\left( \tau \right) \) such that \( l\left( {q,\tau }\right)  \leq  \frac{3}{2} \) . In view of Lemma 6.4.1, we may assume that the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is not a gradient shrinking Ricci soliton. Thus by (the proof of) Theorem 6.2.1, the scalings of \( {g}_{ij}\left( {{t}_{0} - \tau }\right) \) at \( q\left( \tau \right) \) with factor \( {\tau }^{-1} \) converge along a subsequence of \( \tau  \rightarrow   + \infty \) to a nonflat gradient shrinking soliton with nonnegative curvature operator which is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on all scales. We now show that the limit has bounded curvature.

Denote the limiting nonflat gradient shrinking soliton by \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) with \( - \infty  < \; t \leq  0 \) . Note that there holds the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Theorem 2.5.4) on any ancient \( \kappa \) -solution and in particular, the scalar curvature of the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is pointwise nondecreasing in time. This implies that the scalar curvature of the limiting soliton \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) is still pointwise nondecreasing in time. Thus we only need to show that the limiting soliton has bounded curvature at \( t = 0 \) .

We argue by contradiction. By lifting to its orientable cover, we may assume that \( \bar{M} \) is orientable. Suppose the curvature of the limiting soliton is unbounded at \( t = 0 \) . Of course in this case the limiting soliton \( \bar{M} \) is noncompact. Then by applying Lemma 6.1.4, we can choose a sequence of points \( {x}_{j}, j = 1,2,\ldots \) , divergent to infinity such that the scalar curvature \( \bar{R} \) of the limit satisfies

\[
\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)  \geq  j\text{ and }\bar{R}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  4\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{j}, j/\sqrt{\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }}\right) \) and \( j = 1,2,\ldots \) Since the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time, we have

(6.4.10)

\[
\bar{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) ,
\]

for all \( x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{j}, j/\sqrt{\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }}\right) \) , all \( t \leq  0 \) and \( j = 1,2,\ldots \) By combining with Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5) and the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing, we know that a subsequence of the rescaled solutions

\[
\left( {\bar{M},\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) {\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t/\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }\right) ,{x}_{j}}\right) ,\;j = 1,2,\ldots ,
\]

converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a nonflat smooth solution of the Ricci flow. Then Proposition 6.1.2 implies that the new limit at the new time \( \{ t = 0\} \) must split off a line. By pulling back the new limit to its universal cover and applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle, we deduce that the pull-back of the new limit on the universal cover splits off a line for all time \( t \leq  0 \) . Thus by combining with Theorem 6.2.2 and the argument in the proof of Lemma 6.4.1, we further deduce that the new limit is either the round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or the round \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Since \( \bar{M} \) is orientable, the new limit must be \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Since \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right) }\right) \) has nonnegative curvature operator and the points \( \left\{  {x}_{j}\right\} \) going to infinity and \( \bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) , this gives a contradiction to Proposition 6.1.1. So we have proved that the limiting gradient shrinking soliton has bounded curvature at each time.

Hence by Lemma 6.4.1, the limiting gradient shrinking soliton is either the round three-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) or its metric quotients, or the infinite cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or one of its \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) quotients. If the asymptotic gradient shrinking soliton is the round three-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) or its metric quotients, it follows from Lemma 5.2.4 and Proposition 5.2.5 that the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution must be round. Thus in the following we may assume the asymptotic gradient shrinking soliton is the infinite cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or a \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) quotient of \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) .

We now come back to consider the original ancient \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) . By rescaling, we can assume that \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  1 \) for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) satisfying \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, p}\right)  \leq  2 \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - 1,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . We will argue as in the proof of Theorem 3.3.2 (Perelman’s no local collapsing theorem I) to obtain a positive lower bound for \( {\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {p,1}\right) }\right) \) .

Denote by \( \xi  = {\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}{\left( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( p,1\right) \right) }^{\frac{1}{3}} \) . For any \( v \in  {T}_{p}M \) we can find an \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic \( \gamma \left( \tau \right) \) , starting at \( p \) , with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\tau  \rightarrow  {0}^{ + }}}\sqrt{\tau }\dot{\gamma }\left( \tau \right)  = v \) . It follows from the \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic equation (3.2.1) that

\[
\frac{d}{d\tau }\left( {\sqrt{\tau }\dot{\gamma }}\right)  - \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\tau }\nabla R + 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {\sqrt{\tau }\dot{\gamma }, \cdot  }\right)  = 0.
\]

By integrating as before we see that for \( \tau  \leq  \xi \) with the property \( \gamma \left( \sigma \right)  \in  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {p,1}\right) \) as long as \( \sigma  < \tau \) , there holds

\[
\left| {\sqrt{\tau }\dot{\gamma }\left( \tau \right)  - v}\right|  \leq  {C\xi }\left( {\left| v\right|  + 1}\right)
\]

where \( C \) is some positive constant depending only on the dimension. Without loss of generality, we may assume \( {C\xi } \leq  \frac{1}{4} \) and \( \xi  \leq  \frac{1}{100} \) . Then for \( v \in  {T}_{p}M \) with \( \left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) and for \( \tau  \leq  \xi \) with the property \( \gamma \left( \sigma \right)  \in  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {p,1}\right) \) as long as \( \sigma  < \tau \) , we have

\[
{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {p,\gamma \left( \tau \right) }\right)  \leq  {\int }_{0}^{\tau }\left| {\dot{\gamma }\left( \sigma \right) }\right| {d\sigma }
\]

\[
< \frac{1}{2}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}{\int }_{0}^{\tau }\frac{d\sigma }{\sqrt{\sigma }}
\]

\[
= 1\text{ . }
\]

This shows

(6.4.11)

\[
\mathcal{L}\exp \left\{  {\left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\}  \left( \xi \right)  \subset  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {p,1}\right) .
\]

We decompose Perelman’s reduced volume \( \widetilde{V}\left( \xi \right) \) as

(6.4.12)

\[
\widetilde{V}\left( \xi \right)  = {\int }_{\mathcal{L}\exp \left\{  {\left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\}  \left( \xi \right) }
\]

\[
+ {\int }_{M \smallsetminus  \mathcal{L}\exp \left\{  {\left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\}  \left( \xi \right) }{\left( 4\pi \xi \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,\xi }\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - \xi }\left( q\right) .
\]

By using (6.4.11) and the metric evolution equation of the Ricci flow, the first term on the RHS of (6.4.12) can be estimated by

\[
{\int }_{\mathcal{L}\exp \left\{  {\left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\}  \left( \xi \right) }{\left( 4\pi \xi \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,\xi }\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - \xi }\left( q\right)
\]

\[
\leq  {\int }_{{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {p,1}\right) }{\left( 4\pi \xi \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}{e}^{3\xi }d{V}_{{t}_{0}}\left( q\right)
\]

\[
= {\left( 4\pi \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}{e}^{3\xi }{\xi }^{\frac{3}{2}}
\]

\[
< {\xi }^{\frac{3}{2}}\text{ , }
\]

while by using Theorem 3.2.7 (Perelman's Jacobian comparison theorem), the second term on the RHS of (6.4.12) can be estimated by

(6.4.13)

\[
{\int }_{M \smallsetminus  \mathcal{L}\exp \left\{  {\left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\}  \left( \xi \right) }{\left( 4\pi \xi \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,\xi }\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - \xi }\left( q\right)
\]

\[
\leq  {\int }_{\left\{  \left| v\right|  > \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right\}  }{\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}{\left. \exp \left( -l\left( \tau \right) \right) \mathcal{J}\left( \tau \right) \right| }_{\tau  = 0}{dv}
\]

\[
= {\left( 4\pi \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}{\int }_{\left\{  \left| v\right|  > \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right\}  }\exp \left( {-{\left| v\right| }^{2}}\right) {dv}
\]

\[
< {\xi }^{\frac{3}{2}}
\]

since \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\tau  \rightarrow  {0}^{ + }}}{\tau }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\mathcal{J}\left( \tau \right)  = 1 \) and \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\tau  \rightarrow  {0}^{ + }}}l\left( \tau \right)  = {\left| v\right| }^{2} \) by (3.2.18) and (3.2.19) respectively. Thus we obtain

(6.4.14)

\[
\widetilde{V}\left( \xi \right)  < 2{\xi }^{\frac{3}{2}}.
\]

On the other hand, we recall that there exist a sequence \( {\tau }_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) and a sequence of points \( q\left( {\tau }_{k}\right)  \in  M \) with \( l\left( {q\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) ,{\tau }_{k}}\right)  \leq  \frac{3}{2} \) so that the scalings of the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution at \( q\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) \) with factor \( {\tau }_{k}^{-1} \) converge to either round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or one of its \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) quotients. For sufficiently large \( k \) , we construct a path \( \gamma  : \;\left\lbrack  {0,2{\tau }_{k}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) , connecting \( p \) to any given point \( q \in  M \) , as follows: the first half path \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  0,{\tau }_{k}\right\rbrack  } \) connects \( p \) to \( q\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) \) such that

\[
l\left( {q\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) ,{\tau }_{k}}\right)  = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{{\tau }_{k}}}{\int }_{0}^{{\tau }_{k}}\sqrt{\tau }\left( {R + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\left( \tau \right) \right| }^{2}}\right) {d\tau } \leq  2,
\]

and the second half path \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  {\tau }_{k},2{\tau }_{k}\right\rbrack  } \) is a shortest geodesic connecting \( q\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) \) to \( q \) with respect to the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {{t}_{0} - {\tau }_{k}}\right) \) . Note that the rescaled metric \( {\tau }_{k}^{-1}{g}_{ij}\left( {{t}_{0} - \tau }\right) \) over the domain \( {B}_{{t}_{0} - {\tau }_{k}}\left( {q\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) ,\sqrt{{\tau }_{k}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - 2{\tau }_{k},{t}_{0} - {\tau }_{k}}\right\rbrack \) is sufficiently close to the round

\( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or its \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) quotients. Then there is a universal positive constant \( \beta \) such that

\[
l\left( {q,2{\tau }_{k}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2{\tau }_{k}}}\left( {{\int }_{0}^{{\tau }_{k}} + {\int }_{{\tau }_{k}}^{2{\tau }_{k}}}\right) \sqrt{\tau }\left( {R + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\left( \tau \right) \right| }^{2}}\right) {d\tau }
\]

\[
\leq  \sqrt{2} + \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2{\tau }_{k}}}{\int }_{{\tau }_{k}}^{2{\tau }_{k}}\sqrt{\tau }\left( {R + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\left( \tau \right) \right| }^{2}}\right) {d\tau }
\]

\[
\leq  \beta
\]

for all \( q \in  {B}_{{t}_{0} - {\tau }_{k}}\left( {q\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) ,\sqrt{{\tau }_{k}}}\right) \) . Thus

\[
\widetilde{V}\left( {2{\tau }_{k}}\right)  = {\int }_{M}{\left( 4\pi \left( 2{\tau }_{k}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,2{\tau }_{k}}\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - 2{\tau }_{k}}\left( q\right)
\]

\[
\geq  {e}^{-\beta }{\int }_{{B}_{{t}_{0} - {\tau }_{k}}\left( {q\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) ,\sqrt{{\tau }_{k}}}\right) }{\left( 4\pi \left( 2{\tau }_{k}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}d{V}_{{t}_{0} - 2{\tau }_{k}}\left( q\right)
\]

\[
\geq  \widetilde{\beta }
\]

for some universal positive constant \( \widetilde{\beta } \) . Here we have used the curvature estimate (6.2.6). By combining with the monotonicity of Perelman's reduced volume (Theorem 3.2.8) and (6.4.14), we deduce that

\[
\widetilde{\beta } \leq  \widetilde{V}\left( {2{\tau }_{k}}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{V}\left( \xi \right)  < 2{\xi }^{\frac{3}{2}}.
\]

This proves

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {p,1}\right) }\right)  \geq  {\kappa }_{0} > 0
\]

for some universal positive constant \( {\kappa }_{0} \) . So we have proved that the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is also an ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution. \( \square \)

THEOREM 6.4.3 (Elliptic type estimate). There exist a positive constant \( \eta \) and a positive increasing function \( \omega  : \;\lbrack 0, + \infty ) \rightarrow  \left( {0, + \infty }\right) \) with the following properties. Suppose we have a three-dimensional ancient \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( t\right) }\right) , - \infty  < t \leq  0 \) , for some \( \kappa  > 0 \) . Then

(i) for every \( x, y \in  M \) and \( t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , there holds

\[
R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  R\left( {y, t}\right)  \cdot  \omega \left( {R\left( {y, t}\right) {d}_{t}^{2}\left( {x, y}\right) }\right) ;
\]

(ii) for all \( x \in  M \) and \( t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , there hold

\[
\left| {\nabla R}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \eta {R}^{\frac{3}{2}}\left( {x, t}\right) \text{ and }\left| \frac{\partial R}{\partial t}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \eta {R}^{2}\left( {x, t}\right) .
\]

nodes.proof:
(i) Consider a three-dimensional nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) \) on \( M \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) . In view of Proposition 6.4.2, we may assume that the ancient solution is universal \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -noncollapsed. Obviously we only need to establish the estimate at \( t = 0 \) . Let \( y \) be an arbitrarily fixed point in \( M \) . By rescaling, we can assume \( R\left( {y,0}\right)  = 1 \) .

Let us first consider the case that \( \sup \left\{  {R\left( {x,0}\right) {d}_{0}^{2}\left( {x, y}\right)  \mid  x \in  M}\right\}   > 1 \) . Define \( z \) to be the closest point to \( y \) (at time \( t = 0 \) ) satisfying \( R\left( {z,0}\right) {d}_{0}^{2}\left( {z, y}\right)  = 1 \) . We want to bound \( R\left( {x,0}\right) /R\left( {z,0}\right) \) from above for \( x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {z,{2R}{\left( z,0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) .

Connect \( y \) and \( z \) by a shortest geodesic and choose a point \( \widetilde{z} \) lying on the geodesic satisfying \( {d}_{0}\left( {\widetilde{z}, z}\right)  = \frac{1}{4}R{\left( z,0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . Denote by \( B \) the ball centered at \( \widetilde{z} \) and with radius \( \frac{1}{4}R{\left( z,0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) (with respect to the metric at \( t = 0 \) ). Clearly the ball \( B \) lies in \( {B}_{0}\left( {y, R{\left( z,0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) and lies outside \( {B}_{0}\left( {y,\frac{1}{2}R{\left( z,0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) . Thus for \( x \in  B \) , we have

\[
R\left( {x,0}\right) {d}_{0}^{2}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  1\;\text{ and }\;{d}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  \frac{1}{2}R{\left( z,0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}
\]

and hence

\[
R\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{{\left( \frac{1}{2}R{\left( z,0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) }^{2}}\text{ for all }x \in  B.
\]

Then by the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality and the \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -noncollapsing, we have

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{0}\left( B\right)  \geq  {\kappa }_{0}{\left( \frac{1}{4}R{\left( z,0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) }^{3},
\]

and then

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{0}\left( {{B}_{0}\left( {z,{8R}{\left( z,0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }\right)  \geq  \frac{{\kappa }_{0}}{{2}^{15}}{\left( 8R{\left( z,0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) }^{3}.
\]

So by Theorem 6.3.3(ii), there exist positive constants \( B\left( {\kappa }_{0}\right) , C\left( {\kappa }_{0}\right) \) , and \( {\tau }_{0}\left( {\kappa }_{0}\right) \) such that

(6.4.15)

\[
R\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  \left( {C\left( {\kappa }_{0}\right)  + \frac{B\left( {\kappa }_{0}\right) }{{\tau }_{0}\left( {\kappa }_{0}\right) }}\right) R\left( {z,0}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {z,{2R}{\left( z,0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) .

We now consider the remaining case. If \( R\left( {x,0}\right) {d}_{0}^{2}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  1 \) everywhere, we choose a point \( z \) satisfying \( \sup \{ R\left( {x,0}\right)  \mid  x \in  M\}  \leq  {2R}\left( {z,0}\right) \) . Obviously we also have the estimate (6.4.15) in this case.

We next want to bound \( R\left( {z,0}\right) \) for the chosen \( z \in  M \) . By (6.4.15) and the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality, we have

\[
R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \left( {C\left( {\kappa }_{0}\right)  + \frac{B\left( {\kappa }_{0}\right) }{{\tau }_{0}\left( {\kappa }_{0}\right) }}\right) R\left( {z,0}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {z,{2R}{\left( z,0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) and all \( t \leq  0 \) . It then follows from the local derivative estimates of Shi that

\[
\frac{\partial R}{\partial t}\left( {z, t}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{C}\left( {\kappa }_{0}\right) R{\left( z,0\right) }^{2},\;\text{ for all } - {R}^{-1}\left( {z,0}\right)  \leq  t \leq  0
\]

which implies

(6.4.16)

\[
R\left( {z, - c{R}^{-1}\left( {z,0}\right) }\right)  \geq  {cR}\left( {z,0}\right)
\]

for some small positive constant \( c \) depending only on \( {\kappa }_{0} \) . On the other hand, by using the Harnack estimate in Corollary 2.5.7, we have

(6.4.17)

\[
1 = R\left( {y,0}\right)  \geq  \widetilde{c}R\left( {z, - c{R}^{-1}\left( {z,0}\right) }\right)
\]

for some small positive constant \( \widetilde{c} \) depending only on \( {\kappa }_{0} \) , since \( {d}_{0}\left( {y, z}\right)  \leq  R{\left( z,0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) and the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) is equivalent on

\[
{B}_{0}\left( {z,{2R}{\left( z,0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-c{R}^{-1}\left( {z,0}\right) ,0}\right\rbrack
\]

with \( c > 0 \) small enough. Thus we get from (6.4.16) and (6.4.17) that

(6.4.18)

\[
R\left( {z,0}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{A}
\]

for some positive constant \( \widetilde{A} \) depending only on \( {\kappa }_{0} \) .

Since \( {B}_{0}\left( {z,{2R}{\left( z,0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \supset  {B}_{0}\left( {y, R{\left( z,0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) and \( R{\left( z,0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \geq  {\left( \widetilde{A}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , the combination of (6.4.15) and (6.4.18) gives

(6.4.19)

\[
R\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  \left( {C\left( {\kappa }_{0}\right)  + \frac{B\left( {\kappa }_{0}\right) }{{\tau }_{0}\left( {\kappa }_{0}\right) }}\right) \widetilde{A}
\]

whenever \( x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {y,{\left( \widetilde{A}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) . Then by the \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -noncollapsing there exists a positive constant \( {r}_{0} \) depending only on \( {\kappa }_{0} \) such that

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{0}\left( {{B}_{0}\left( {y,{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  {\kappa }_{0}{r}_{0}^{3}\text{ . }
\]

For any fixed \( {R}_{0} \geq  {r}_{0} \) , we then have

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{0}\left( {{B}_{0}\left( {y,{R}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  {\kappa }_{0}{r}_{0}^{3} = {\kappa }_{0}{\left( \frac{{r}_{0}}{{R}_{0}}\right) }^{3} \cdot  {R}_{0}^{3}.
\]

By applying Theorem 6.3.3 (ii) again and noting that the constant \( {\kappa }_{0} \) is universal, there exists a positive constant \( \omega \left( {R}_{0}\right) \) depending only on \( {R}_{0} \) such that

\[
R\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  \omega \left( {R}_{0}^{2}\right) \;\text{ for all }x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {y,\frac{1}{4}{R}_{0}}\right) .
\]

This gives the desired estimate.

(ii) This follows immediately from conclusion (i), the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality and the local derivative estimate of Shi. 0

nodes.proof:
Consider any sequence of three-dimensional ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solutions and marking points \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) with \( R\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right)  = 1 \) . By Theorem 6.4.3(i), the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality and Hamilton's compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), we can extract a \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) converging subsequence such that the limit \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) , with \( - \infty  < t \leq  0 \) , is an ancient solution to the Ricci flow with nonnegative curvature operator and \( {\kappa }_{{0}^{ - }} \) noncollapsed on all scales. Since any ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution satisfies the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality, it implies that the scalar curvature \( \bar{R}\left( {x, t}\right) \) of the limit \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) is pointwise nondecreasing in time. Thus it remains to show that the limit solution has bounded curvature at \( t = 0 \) .

Obviously we may assume the limiting manifold \( \bar{M} \) is noncompact. By pulling back the limiting solution to its orientable cover, we can assume that the limiting manifold \( \bar{M} \) is orientable. We now argue by contradiction. Suppose the scalar curvature \( \bar{R} \) of the limit at \( t = 0 \) is unbounded.

By applying Lemma 6.1.4, we can choose a sequence of points \( {x}_{j} \in  \bar{M}, j = \; 1,2,\ldots \) , divergent to infinity such that the scalar curvature \( \bar{R} \) of the limit satisfies

\[
\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)  \geq  j\text{ and }\bar{R}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  4\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)
\]

for all \( j = 1,2,\ldots \) , and \( x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{j}, j/\sqrt{\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }}\right) \) . Then from the fact that the limiting scalar curvature \( \bar{R}\left( {x, t}\right) \) is pointwise nondecreasing in time, we have

(6.4.20)

\[
\bar{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)
\]

for all \( j = 1,2,\ldots , x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{j}, j/\sqrt{\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }}\right) \) and \( t \leq  0 \) . By combining with Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5) and the \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -noncollapsing, we know that a subsequence of the rescaled solutions

\[
\left( {\bar{M},\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) {\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t/\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }\right) ,{x}_{j}}\right) ,\;j = 1,2,\ldots ,
\]

converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a nonflat smooth solution of the Ricci flow. Then Proposition 6.1.2 implies that the new limit at the new time \( \{ t = 0\} \) must split off a line. By pulling back the new limit to its universal cover and applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle, we deduce that the pull-back of the new limit on the universal cover splits off a line for all time \( t \leq  0 \) . Thus by combining with Theorem 6.2.2 and the argument in the proof of Lemma 6.4.1, we further deduce that the new limit is either the round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or the round \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Since \( \bar{M} \) is orientable, the new limit must be \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Moreover, since \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right) }\right) \) has nonnegative curvature operator and the points \( \left\{  {x}_{j}\right\} \) are going to infinity and \( \bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) , this gives a contradiction to Proposition 6.1.1. So we have proved that the limit \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) has uniformly bounded curvature. \( \square \)

COROLLARY 6.4.5. For any \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) there exists \( C = C\left( \varepsilon \right)  > 0 \) , such that if \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) is a nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution on a noncompact three-manifold \( M \) for some \( \kappa  > 0 \) , and \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) denotes the set of points in \( M \) which are not centers of evolving \( \varepsilon \) -necks at \( t = 0 \) , then at \( t = 0 \) , either the whole manifold \( M \) is the round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or its \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) metric quotients, or \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) satisfies the following

(i) \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) is compact,

(ii) diam \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \leq  C{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) and \( {C}^{-1}Q \leq  R\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  {CQ} \) , whenever \( x \in  {M}_{\varepsilon } \) , where \( Q = R\left( {{x}_{0},0}\right) \) for some \( {x}_{0} \in  \partial {M}_{\varepsilon } \) .
