nodes.proof:
We first consider the easy case that the curvature operator of the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution has a nontrivial null vector somewhere at some time. Let us pull back the solution to its universal cover. By applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle and Theorem 6.2.2, we see that the universal cover is the evolving round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Thus in this case, by the argument in the proof of Lemma 6.4.1, we conclude that the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is either isometric to the round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or one of its \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) metric quotients (i.e., \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , or the twisted product \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) where \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) flips both \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) , or \( \mathbb{R} \) ).

We then assume that the curvature operator of the nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is positive everywhere. Firstly we want to show \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) is compact. We argue by contradiction. Suppose there exists a sequence of points \( {z}_{k}, k = 1,2,\ldots \) , going to infinity (with respect to the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( 0\right) \) ) such that each \( {z}_{k} \) is not the center of any evolving \( \varepsilon \) -neck. For an arbitrarily fixed point \( {z}_{0} \in  M \) , it follows from Theorem 6.4.3(i) that

\[
0 < R\left( {{z}_{0},0}\right)  \leq  R\left( {{z}_{k},0}\right)  \cdot  \omega \left( {R\left( {{z}_{k},0}\right) {d}_{0}^{2}\left( {{z}_{k},{z}_{0}}\right) }\right)
\]

which implies that

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}R\left( {{z}_{k},0}\right) {d}_{0}^{2}\left( {{z}_{k},{z}_{0}}\right)  =  + \infty .
\]

Since the sectional curvature of the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is positive everywhere, the underlying manifold is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) , and in particular, orientable. Then as before, by Proposition 6.1.2, Theorem 6.2.2 and Corollary 6.4.4, we conclude that \( {z}_{k} \) is the center of an evolving \( \varepsilon \) -neck for \( k \) sufficiently large. This is a contradiction, so we have proved that \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) is compact.

Again, we notice that \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) since the curvature operator is positive. According to the resolution of the Schoenflies conjecture in three-dimensions, every approximately round two-sphere cross-section through the center of an evolving \( \varepsilon \) -neck divides \( M \) into two parts such that one of them is diffeomorphic to the three-ball \( {\mathbb{B}}^{3} \) . Let \( \varphi \) be the Busemann function on \( M \) , it is a standard fact that \( \varphi \) is convex and proper. Since \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) is compact, \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) is contained in a compact set \( K = {\varphi }^{-1}\left( {( - \infty , A\rbrack }\right) \) for some large \( A \) . We note that each point \( x \in  M \smallsetminus  {M}_{\varepsilon } \) is the center of an \( \varepsilon \) -neck. It is clear that there is an \( \varepsilon \) -neck \( N \) lying entirely outside \( K \) . Consider a point \( x \) on one of the boundary components of the \( \varepsilon \) -neck \( N \) . Since \( x \in  M \smallsetminus  {M}_{\varepsilon } \) , there is an \( \varepsilon \) -neck adjacent to the initial \( \varepsilon \) -neck, producing a longer neck. We then take a point on the boundary of the second \( \varepsilon \) -neck and continue. This procedure can either terminate when we get into \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) or go on infinitely to produce a semi-infinite (topological) cylinder. The same procedure can be repeated for the other boundary component of the initial \( \varepsilon \) -neck. This procedure will give a maximal extended neck \( \widetilde{N} \) . If \( \widetilde{N} \) never touches \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) , the manifold will be diffeomorphic to the standard infinite cylinder, which is a contradiction. If both ends of \( \widetilde{N} \) touch \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) , then there is a geodesic connecting two points of \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) and passing through \( N \) . This is impossible since the function \( \varphi \) is convex. So we conclude that one end of \( \widetilde{N} \) will touch \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) and the other end will tend to infinity to produce a semi-infinite (topological) cylinder. Thus we can find an approximately round two-sphere cross-section which encloses the whole set \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) and touches some point \( {x}_{0} \in  \partial {M}_{\varepsilon } \) . We next want to show that \( R{\left( {x}_{0},0\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \cdot  \operatorname{diam}\left( {M}_{\varepsilon }\right) \) is bounded from above by some positive constant \( C = C\left( \varepsilon \right) \) depending only on \( \varepsilon \) .

Suppose not; then there exists a sequence of nonflat noncompact three-dimensional ancient \( \kappa \) -solutions with positive curvature operator such that for the above chosen points \( {x}_{0} \in  \partial {M}_{\varepsilon } \) there would hold

(6.4.21)

\[
R{\left( {x}_{0},0\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \cdot  \operatorname{diam}\left( {M}_{\varepsilon }\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty .
\]

By Proposition 6.4.2, we know that the ancient solutions are \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -noncollapsed on all scales for some universal positive constant \( {\kappa }_{0} \) . Let us dilate the ancient solutions around the points \( {x}_{0} \) with the factors \( R\left( {{x}_{0},0}\right) \) . By Corollary 6.4.4, we can extract a convergent subsequence. From the choice of the points \( {x}_{0} \) and (6.4.21), the limit has at least two ends. Then by Toponogov's splitting theorem the limit is isometric to \( X \times  \mathbb{R} \) for some nonflat two-dimensional ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution \( X \) . Since \( M \) is orientable, we conclude from Theorem 6.2.2 that limit must be the evolving round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . This contradicts the fact that each chosen point \( {x}_{0} \) is not the center of any evolving \( \varepsilon \) -neck. Therefore we have proved

\[
\operatorname{diam}\left( {M}_{\varepsilon }\right)  \leq  C{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}}
\]

for some positive constant \( C = C\left( \varepsilon \right) \) depending only on \( \varepsilon \) , where \( Q = R\left( {{x}_{0},0}\right) \) .

Finally by combining this diameter estimate with Theorem 6.4.3(i), we immediately deduce

\[
{\widetilde{C}}^{-1}Q \leq  R\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{C}Q,\text{ whenever }x \in  {M}_{\varepsilon },
\]

for some positive constant \( \widetilde{C} \) depending only on \( \varepsilon \) . \( \square \)

THEOREM 6.4.6 (Canonical neighborhood theorem). For any \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) one can find positive constants \( {C}_{1} = {C}_{1}\left( \varepsilon \right) \) and \( {C}_{2} = {C}_{2}\left( \varepsilon \right) \) with the following property. Suppose we have a three-dimensional nonflat (compact or noncompact) ancient \( \kappa \) - solution \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) . Then either the ancient solution is the round \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , or every point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) has an open neighborhood \( B \) , with \( {B}_{t}\left( {x, r}\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{t}\left( {x,{2r}}\right) \) for some \( 0 < r < {C}_{1}R{\left( x, t\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , which falls into one of the following three categories:

(a) \( B \) is an evolving \( \varepsilon \) -neck (in the sense that it is the slice at the time \( t \) of the parabolic region \( \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  B,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {t - {\varepsilon }^{-2}R{\left( x, t\right) }^{-1}, t}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) which is, after scaling with factor \( R\left( {x, t}\right) \) and shifting the time \( t \) to zero, \( \varepsilon \) -close (in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  {\varepsilon }^{-1}\right\rbrack  } \) topology) to the subset \( \left( {{\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{I}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{\varepsilon }^{-2},0}\right\rbrack \) of the evolving standard round cylinder with scalar curvature 1 and length \( 2{\varepsilon }^{-1} \) to \( \mathbb{I} \) at the time zero), or

(b) \( B \) is an evolving \( \varepsilon \) -cap (in the sense that it is the time slice at the time \( t \) of an evolving metric on \( {\mathbb{B}}^{3} \) or \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{3} \smallsetminus  {\mathbb{B}}^{3} \) such that the region outside some suitable compact subset of \( {\mathbb{B}}^{3} \) or \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{3} \smallsetminus  {\mathbb{B}}^{3} \) is an evolving \( \varepsilon \) -neck), or

(c) \( B \) is a compact manifold (without boundary) with positive sectional curvature (thus it is diffeomorphic to the round three-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) or a metric quotient of \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3}) \)

furthermore, the scalar curvature of the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution on \( B \) at time \( t \) is between \( {C}_{2}^{-1}R\left( {x, t}\right) \) and \( {C}_{2}R\left( {x, t}\right) \) , and the volume of \( B \) in case (a) and case (b) satisfies

\[
{\left( {C}_{2}R\left( x, t\right) \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}} \leq  {\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( B\right)  \leq  \varepsilon {r}^{3}.
\]

nodes.proof:
As before, we first consider the easy case that the curvature operator has a nontrivial null vector somewhere at some time. By pulling back the solution to its universal cover and applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle and Theorem 6.2.2, we deduce that the universal cover is the evolving round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Then exactly as before, by the argument in the proof of Lemma 6.4.1, we conclude that the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is isometric to the round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R},{\mathbb{{RP}}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , or the twisted product \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2}\widetilde{ \times  }\mathbb{R} \) where \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) flips both \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) and \( \mathbb{R} \) . Clearly each point of the round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or the twisted product \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2}\widetilde{ \times  }\mathbb{R} \) has a neighborhood falling into the category (a) or (b) (over \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{3} \smallsetminus  \overline{{\mathbb{B}}^{3}} \) ).

We now assume that the curvature operator of the nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is positive everywhere. Then the manifold is orientable by the Cheeger-Gromoll theorem [23] for the noncompact case or the Synge theorem [22] for the compact case.

Without loss of generality, we may assume \( \varepsilon \) is suitably small, say \( 0 < \varepsilon  < \frac{1}{100} \) . If the nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is noncompact, the conclusions follow immediately from the combination of Corollary 6.4.5 and Theorem 6.4.3(i). Thus we may assume the nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is compact. By Proposition 6.4.2, either the compact ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is isometric to a metric quotient of the round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) , or it is \( {\kappa }_{{0}^{ - }} \) noncollapsed on all scales for the universal positive constant \( {\kappa }_{0} \) . Clearly each point of a metric quotient of the round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) has a neighborhood falling into category (c). Thus we may further assume the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is also \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -noncollapsing.

We argue by contradiction. Suppose that for some \( \varepsilon  \in  \left( {0,\frac{1}{100}}\right) \) , there exist a sequence of compact orientable ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}}\right) \) with positive curvature operator, a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) with \( {x}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) and sequences of positive constants \( {C}_{1k} \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( {C}_{2k} = \omega \left( {4{C}_{1k}^{2}}\right) \) , with the function \( \omega \) given in Theorem 6.4.3, such that for every radius \( r,0 < r < {C}_{1k}R{\left( {x}_{k},0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , any open neighborhood \( B \) , with \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k}, r}\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},{2r}}\right) \) , does not fall into one of the three categories (a),(b) and (c), where in the case (a) and case (b), we require the neighborhood \( B \) to satisfy the volume estimate

\[
{\left( {C}_{2k}R\left( {x}_{k},0\right) \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}} \leq  {\operatorname{Vol}}_{0}\left( B\right)  \leq  \varepsilon {r}^{3}.
\]

By Theorem 6.4.3(i) and the choice of the constants \( {C}_{2k} \) we see that the diameter of each \( {M}_{k} \) at \( t = 0 \) is at least \( {C}_{1k}R{\left( {x}_{k},0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) ; otherwise we can choose suitable \( r \in  \left( {0,{C}_{1k}R{\left( {x}_{k},0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) and \( B = {M}_{k} \) , which falls into the category (c) with the scalar curvature between \( {C}_{2k}^{-1}R\left( {x,0}\right) \) and \( {C}_{2k}R\left( {x,0}\right) \) on \( B \) . Now by scaling the ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solutions along the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) with factors \( R\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) , it follows from Corollary 6.4.4 that a sequence of the ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solutions converge in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a noncompact orientable ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution.

If the curvature operator of the noncompact limit has a nontrivial null vector somewhere at some time, it follows exactly as before by using the argument in the proof of Lemma 6.4.1 that the orientable limit is isometric to the round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , or the twisted product \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) where \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) flips both \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) and \( \mathbb{R} \) . Then for \( k \) large enough, a suitable neighborhood \( B \) (for suitable \( r \) ) of the point \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) would fall into the category (a) or (b) (over \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{3} \smallsetminus  {\mathbb{B}}^{3} \) ) with the desired volume estimate. This is a contradiction.

If the noncompact limit has positive sectional curvature everywhere, then by using Corollary 6.4.5 and Theorem 6.4.3(i) for the noncompact limit we see that for \( k \) large enough, a suitable neighborhood \( B \) (for suitable \( r \) ) of the point \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) would fall into category (a) or (b) (over \( {\mathbb{B}}^{3} \) ) with the desired volume estimate. This is also a contradiction.

Finally, the statement on the curvature estimate in the neighborhood \( B \) follows directly from Theorem 6.4.3(i). 0

nodes.content: THEOREM 7.1.1 (Singularity structure theorem). Given \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) and \( {T}_{0} > 1 \) , one can find \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) with the following property. If \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) , x \in  M \) and \( t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( 1 < T \leq  {T}_{0} \) , is a solution to the Ricci flow on a compact orientable three-manifold \( M \) with normalized initial metric, then for any point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{0} \geq  1 \) and \( Q = \; R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , the solution in \( \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < {\varepsilon }^{-2}{Q}^{-1},\;{t}_{0} - {\varepsilon }^{-2}{Q}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{0}}\right\} \) is, after scaling by the factor \( Q,\varepsilon \) -close (in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  {\varepsilon }^{-1}\right\rbrack  } \) -topology) to the corresponding subset of some orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution (for some \( \kappa  > 0 \) ).

nodes.proof:
Since the initial metric is normalized, it follows from the no local collapsing theorem I or I' (and their proofs) that there is a positive constant \( \kappa \) , depending only on \( {T}_{0} \) , such that the solution in Theorem 7.1.1 is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on all scales less than \( \sqrt{{T}_{0}} \) . Let \( C\left( \varepsilon \right) \) be a positive constant larger than or equal to \( {\varepsilon }^{-2} \) . It suffices to prove that there exists \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) such that for any point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{0} \geq  1 \) and \( Q = \; R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , the solution in the parabolic region \( \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  M\times \lbrack 0, T) \mid  {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < }\right. \; \left. {C\left( \varepsilon \right) {Q}^{-1},{t}_{0} - C\left( \varepsilon \right) {Q}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{0}}\right\} \) is, after scaling by the factor \( Q,\varepsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of some orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. The constant \( C\left( \varepsilon \right) \) will be determined later.

We argue by contradiction. Suppose for some \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there exist a sequence of solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) to the Ricci flow on compact orientable three-manifolds with normalized initial metrics, defined on the time intervals \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{k}}\right) \) with \( 1 < {T}_{k} \leq  {T}_{0} \) , a sequence of positive numbers \( {r}_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) , and a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) and times \( {t}_{k} \geq  1 \) with \( {Q}_{k} = {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{k}^{-2} \) such that each solution \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) in the parabolic region \( \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{k}}\right)  \mid  {d}_{{t}_{k}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{k}}\right)  < C\left( \varepsilon \right) {Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k} - C\left( \varepsilon \right) {Q}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{k}}\right\} \) is not, after scaling by the factor \( {Q}_{k},\varepsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of any orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, where \( {R}_{k} \) denotes the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}}\right) \) .

For each solution \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) , we may adjust the point \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{k} \geq  \frac{1}{2} \) and with \( {Q}_{k} = {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) to be as large as possible so that the conclusion of the theorem fails at \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , but holds for any \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - {H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) satisfying \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  2{Q}_{k} \) , where \( {H}_{k} = \frac{1}{4}{r}_{k}^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Indeed, suppose not, by setting \( \left( {{x}_{{k}_{1}},{t}_{{k}_{1}}}\right)  = \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , we can choose a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{{k}_{l}},{t}_{{k}_{l}}}\right)  \in  {M}_{k} \times \; \left\lbrack  {{t}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }} - {H}_{k}{R}_{k}{\left( {x}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }},{t}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }}\right) }^{-1},{t}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }}}\right\rbrack \) such that \( {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{l}},{t}_{{k}_{l}}}\right)  \geq  2{R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }},{t}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }}}\right) \) and the conclusion of the theorem fails at \( \left( {{x}_{{k}_{l}},{t}_{{k}_{l}}}\right) \) for each \( l = 2,3,\ldots \) . Since the solution is smooth, but

\[
{R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{l}},{t}_{{k}_{l}}}\right)  \geq  2{R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }},{t}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }}}\right)  \geq  \cdots  \geq  {2}^{l - 1}{R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,
\]

and

\[
{t}_{{k}_{l}} \geq  {t}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }} - {H}_{k}{R}_{k}{\left( {x}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }},{t}_{{k}_{\left( l - 1\right) }}\right) }^{-1}
\]

\[
\geq  {t}_{k} - {H}_{k}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{{l - 1}}\frac{1}{{2}^{i - 1}}{R}_{k}{\left( {x}_{k},{t}_{k}\right) }^{-1}
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{1}{2}
\]

this process must terminate after a finite number of steps and the last element fits.

Let \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) be the rescaled solutions obtained by rescaling \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) around \( {x}_{k} \) with the factors \( {Q}_{k} = {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) and shifting the time \( {t}_{k} \) to the new time zero. Denote by \( {\widetilde{R}}_{k} \) the rescaled scalar curvature. We will show that a subsequence of the orientable rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, which is a contradiction. In the following we divide the argument into four steps.

Step 1. First of all, we need a local bound on curvatures.

Lemma 7.1.2. For each \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{k} - \frac{1}{2}{H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  {t}_{k} \) , we have \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4{\bar{Q}}_{k} \) whenever \( \bar{t} - c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {d}_{\bar{t}}^{2}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1} \) , where \( {\bar{Q}}_{k} = {Q}_{k} + {R}_{k}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) and \( c > 0 \) is a small universal constant.

Proof. Consider any point \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {B}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{\left( c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} - c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) with \( c > 0 \) to be determined. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  2{Q}_{k} \) , there is nothing to show. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  > 2{Q}_{k} \) , consider a space-time curve \( \gamma \) from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) that goes straight from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) and goes from \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) to \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) along a minimizing geodesic (with respect to the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,\bar{t}}\right) \) ). If there is a point on \( \gamma \) with the scalar curvature \( 2{Q}_{k} \) , let \( {y}_{0} \) be the nearest such point to \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) . If not, put \( {y}_{0} = \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) . On the segment of \( \gamma \) from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( {y}_{0} \) , the scalar curvature is at least \( 2{Q}_{k} \) . According to the choice of the point \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , the solution along the segment is \( \varepsilon \) -close to that of some ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. It follows from Theorem 6.4.3 (ii) that

\[
\left| {\nabla \left( {R}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) }\right|  \leq  {2\eta }\text{ and }\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {R}_{k}^{-1}\right) }\right|  \leq  {2\eta }
\]

on the segment. (Here, without loss of generality, we may assume \( \varepsilon \) is suitably small). Then by choosing \( c > 0 \) (depending only on \( \eta \) ) small enough we get the desired curvature bound by integrating the above derivative estimates along the segment. This proves the lemma.

Step 2. Next we want to show that for each \( A <  + \infty \) , there exist a positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) (independent of \( k \) ) such that the curvatures of the rescaled solutions

\( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at the new time \( t = 0 \) (corresponding to the original times \( {t}_{k} \) ) satisfy the estimate

\[
\left| \widetilde{R{m}_{k}}\right| \left( {y,0}\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)
\]

whenever \( {d}_{{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) }\left( {y,{x}_{k}}\right)  \leq  A \) and \( k \geq  1 \) .

For each \( \rho  \geq  0 \) , set

\[
M\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {{\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \mid  k \geq  1, x \in  {M}_{k}\text{ with }{d}_{0}\left( {x,{x}_{k}}\right)  \leq  \rho }\right\}
\]

and

\[
{\rho }_{0} = \sup \{ \rho  \geq  0 \mid  M\left( \rho \right)  <  + \infty \} .
\]

By the pinching estimate (7.1.1), it suffices to show \( {\rho }_{0} =  + \infty \) .

Note that \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) by applying Lemma 7.1.2 with \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  = \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . We now argue by contradiction to show \( {\rho }_{0} =  + \infty \) . Suppose not, we may find (after passing to a subsequence if necessary) a sequence of points \( {y}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) with \( {d}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},{y}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) and \( {\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {{y}_{k},0}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Let \( {\gamma }_{k}\left( { \subset  {M}_{k}}\right) \) be a minimizing geodesic segment from \( {x}_{k} \) to \( {y}_{k} \) . Let \( {z}_{k} \in  {\gamma }_{k} \) be the point on \( {\gamma }_{k} \) closest to \( {y}_{k} \) with \( {\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {{z}_{k},0}\right)  = 2 \) , and let \( {\beta }_{k} \) be the subsegment of \( {\gamma }_{k} \) running from \( {z}_{k} \) to \( {y}_{k} \) . By Lemma 7.1.2 the length of \( {\beta }_{k} \) is bounded away from zero independent of \( k \) . By the pinching estimate (7.1.1), for each \( \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) , we have a uniform bound on the curvatures on the open balls \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}}\right) \) . The injectivity radii of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k} \) at the points \( {x}_{k} \) and the time \( t = 0 \) are also uniformly bounded from below by the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property. Therefore by Lemma 7.1.2 and Hamilton's compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the marked sequence \( \left( {{B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , the segments \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( {x}_{\infty } \) , and \( {\beta }_{k} \) converges to a subsegment \( {\beta }_{\infty } \) of \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . Let \( {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) denote the completion of \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) , and \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) the limit point of \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) .

Denote by \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty } \) the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) . Since the rescaled scalar curvatures \( {\widetilde{R}}_{k} \) along \( {\beta }_{k} \) are at least 2, it follows from the choice of the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) that for any \( {q}_{0} \in  {\beta }_{\infty } \) , the manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) in \( \left\{  {q \in  {B}_{\infty } \mid  {\operatorname{dist}}_{{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }}^{2}\left( {q,{q}_{0}}\right)  < C\left( \varepsilon \right) {\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-1}}\right\} \) is \( {2\varepsilon } \) -close to the corresponding subset of (a time slice of) some orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. Then by Theorem 6.4.6, we know that the orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution at each point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) has a radius \( r,0 < r < {C}_{1}\left( {2\varepsilon }\right) R{\left( x, t\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , such that its canonical neighborhood \( B \) , with \( {B}_{t}\left( {x, r}\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{t}\left( {x,{2r}}\right) \) , is either an evolving \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, or an evolving \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap, or a compact manifold (without boundary) diffeomorphic to a metric quotient of the round three-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) , and moreover the scalar curvature is between \( {\left( {C}_{2}\left( 2\varepsilon \right) \right) }^{-1}R\left( {x, t}\right) \) and \( {C}_{2}\left( {2\varepsilon }\right) R\left( {x, t}\right) \) , where \( {C}_{1}\left( {2\varepsilon }\right) \) and \( {C}_{2}\left( {2\varepsilon }\right) \) are the positive constants in Theorem 6.4.6.

We now choose \( C\left( \varepsilon \right)  = \max \left\{  {2{C}_{1}^{2}\left( {2\varepsilon }\right) ,{\varepsilon }^{-2}}\right\} \) . By the local curvature estimate in Lemma 7.1.2, we see that the scalar curvature \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty } \) becomes unbounded when approaching \( {y}_{\infty } \) along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . This implies that the canonical neighborhood around \( {q}_{0} \) cannot be a compact manifold (without boundary) diffeomorphic to a metric quotient of the round three-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) . Note that \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) is shortest since it is the limit of a sequence of shortest geodesics. Without loss of generality, we may assume \( \varepsilon \) is suitably small (say, \( \varepsilon  \leq  \frac{1}{100} \) ). These imply that as \( {q}_{0} \) gets sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) , the canonical neighborhood around \( {q}_{0} \) cannot be an evolving \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap. Thus we conclude that each \( {q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) is the center of an evolving \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck.

Let

\[
U = \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{{q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty }}}B\left( {{q}_{0},{4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \;\left( { \subset  \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }}\right) }\right) ,
\]

where \( B\left( {{q}_{0},{4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) is the ball centered at \( {q}_{0} \in  {B}_{\infty } \) with the radius \( {4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . Clearly \( U \) has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching estimate (7.1.1). Since the metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{\infty } \) is cylindrical at any point \( {q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) which is sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) , we see that the metric space \( \bar{U} = U \cup  \left\{  {y}_{\infty }\right\} \) by adding in the point \( {y}_{\infty } \) , is locally complete and intrinsic near \( {y}_{\infty } \) . Furthermore \( {y}_{\infty } \) cannot be an interior point of any geodesic segment in \( \bar{U} \) . This implies the curvature of \( \bar{U} \) at \( {y}_{\infty } \) is nonnegative in the Alexandrov sense. It is a basic result in Alexandrov space theory (see for example Theorem 10.9.3 and Corollary 10.9.5 of [9]) that there exists a three-dimensional tangent cone \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{U} \) at \( {y}_{\infty } \) which is a metric cone. It is clear that its aperture is \( \leq  {10\varepsilon } \) , thus the tangent cone is nonflat.

Pick a point \( p \in  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{U} \) such that the distance from the vertex \( {y}_{\infty } \) to \( p \) is one and it is nonflat around \( p \) . Then the ball \( B\left( {p,\frac{1}{2}}\right)  \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{U} \) is the Gromov-Hausdorff limit of the scalings of a sequence of balls \( {B}_{0}\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{k}}\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) }\right) \) by some factors \( {a}_{k} \) , where \( {s}_{k} \rightarrow  {0}^{ + } \) . Since the tangent cone is three-dimensional and nonflat around \( p \) , the factors \( {a}_{k} \) must be comparable with \( {\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right) \) . By using the local curvature estimate in Lemma 7.1.2, we actually have the convergence in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology for the solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) on the balls \( {B}_{0}\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{k}}\right) \) and over some time interval \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-\delta ,0}\right\rbrack \) for some sufficiently small \( \delta  > 0 \) . The limiting ball \( B\left( {p,\frac{1}{2}}\right)  \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{U} \) is a piece of the nonnegative curved and nonflat metric cone whose radial directions are all Ricci flat. On the other hand, by applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle to the evolution equation of the Ricci curvature tensor as in the proof of Lemma 6.3.1, the limiting ball \( B\left( {p,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \) would split off all radial directions isometrically (and locally). Since the limit is nonflat around \( p \) , this is impossible. Therefore we have proved that the curvatures of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at the new times \( t = 0 \) (corresponding to the original times \( {t}_{k} \) ) stay uniformly bounded at bounded distances from \( {x}_{k} \) for all \( k \) .

We have proved that for each \( A <  + \infty \) , the curvature of the marked manifold \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) at each point \( y \in  {M}_{k} \) with distance from \( {x}_{k} \) at most \( A \) is bounded by \( C\left( A\right) \) . Lemma 7.1.2 extends this curvature control to a backward parabolic neighborhood centered at \( y \) whose radius depends only on the distance from \( y \) to \( {x}_{k} \) . Thus by Shi's local derivative estimates (Theorem 1.4.2) we can control all derivatives of the curvature in such backward parabolic neighborhoods. Then by using the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing and Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), we can take a \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) subsequent limit to obtain \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , which is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on all scales and is defined on a space-time open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing the time slice \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \{ 0\} \) . Clearly it follows from the pinching estimate (7.1.1) that the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) has nonnegative curvature operator (and hence nonnegative sectional curvature).

Step 3. We further claim that the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) at the time slice \( \{ t = 0\} \) has bounded curvature.

We know that the sectional curvature of the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) is nonnegative everywhere. Argue by contradiction. Suppose the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) is not bounded, then by Lemma 6.1.4, there exists a sequence of points \( {q}_{j} \in  {M}_{\infty } \) diverging to infinity such that their scalar curvatures \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{j},0}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) as \( j \rightarrow   + \infty \)

and

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  4{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{j},0}\right)
\]

for \( x \in  B\left( {{q}_{j}, j/\sqrt{{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{j},0}\right) }}\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) }\right) \) . By combining with Lemma 7.1.2 and the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing, a subsequence of the rescaled and marked manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{j},0}\right) {\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{q}_{j}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a smooth nonflat limit \( Y \) . By Proposition 6.1.2, the new limit \( Y \) is isometric to a metric product \( N \times  \mathbb{R} \) for some two-dimensional manifold \( N \) . On the other hand, in view of the choice of the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , the original limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) at the point \( {q}_{j} \) has a canonical neighborhood which is either a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap, or a compact manifold (without boundary) diffeomorphic to a metric quotient of the round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) . It follows that for \( j \) large enough, \( {q}_{j} \) is the center of a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck of radius \( {\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{j},0\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . Without loss of generality, we may further assume that \( {2\varepsilon } < {\varepsilon }_{0} \) , where \( {\varepsilon }_{0} \) is the positive constant given in Proposition 6.1.1. Since \( {\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{j},0\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \rightarrow  0 \) as \( j \rightarrow   + \infty \) , this contradicts Proposition 6.1.1. So the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) }\right) \) is bounded.

Step 4. Finally we want to extend the limit backwards in time to \( - \infty \) .

By Lemma 7.1.2 again, we now know that the limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) is defined on a backward time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-a,0}\right\rbrack \) for some \( a > 0 \) .

Denote by

\( {t}^{\prime } = \inf \{ \widetilde{t} \mid \) we can take a smooth limit on \( (\widetilde{t},0\rbrack \) (with bounded curvature at each time slice) from a subsequence of the convergent rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k} \) \}.

We first claim that there is a subsequence of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k} \) which converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a smooth limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) on the maximal time interval \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Indeed, let \( {t}_{k}^{\prime } \) be a sequence of negative numbers such that \( {t}_{k}^{\prime } \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) and there exist smooth limits \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }^{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) defined on \( \left( {{t}_{k}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . For each \( k \) , the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature and has bounded curvature at each time slice. Moreover by Lemma 7.1.2, the limit has bounded curvature on each subinterval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \subset  \left( {{t}_{k}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . Denote by \( \widetilde{Q} \) the scalar curvature upper bound of the limit at time zero (where \( \widetilde{Q} \) is the same for all \( k \) ). Then we can apply the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.7) to get

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }^{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{Q}\left( \frac{-{t}_{k}^{\prime }}{t - {t}_{k}^{\prime }}\right) ,
\]

where \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }^{k}\left( {x, t}\right) \) are the scalar curvatures of the limits \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }^{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) . Hence by the definition of convergence and the above curvature estimates, we can find a subsequence of the above convergent rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k} \) which converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a smooth limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) on the maximal time interval \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) .

We next claim that \( {t}^{\prime } =  - \infty \) .

Suppose not, then by Lemma 7.1.2, the curvature of the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) becomes unbounded as \( t \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } >  - \infty \) . By applying the maximum principle to the evolution equation of the scalar curvature, we see that the infimum of the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time. Note that \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1 \) . Thus there exists some point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty } \) such that

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{10}}\right)  < \frac{3}{2}
\]

where \( c > 0 \) is the universal constant in Lemma 7.1.2. By using Lemma 7.1.2 again we see that the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) in a small neighborhood of the point \( \left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{10}}\right) \) extends backwards to the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{10},{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{10}}\right\rbrack \) . We remark that the distances at time \( t \) and time 0 are roughly equivalent in the following sense

(7.1.3)

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  {d}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  {d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  - \text{ const. }
\]

for any \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . Indeed from the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.7) we have the estimate

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{Q}\left( \frac{-{t}^{\prime }}{t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) ,\;\text{ on }{M}_{\infty } \times  \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack  .
\]

By applying Lemma 3.4.1 (ii), we have

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {d}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  + {30}\left( {-{t}^{\prime }}\right) \sqrt{\widetilde{Q}}
\]

for any \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . On the other hand, since the curvature of the limit metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) is nonnegative, we have

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  {d}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)
\]

for any \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . Thus we obtain the estimate (7.1.3).

Let us still denote by \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) the subsequence which converges on the maximal time interval \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . Consider the rescaled sequence \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) with the marked points \( {x}_{k} \) replaced by the associated sequence of points \( {y}_{k} \rightarrow  {y}_{\infty } \) and the (original unshifted) times \( {t}_{k} \) replaced by any \( {s}_{k} \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} + \left( {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{20}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k} + \left( {{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{20}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) . It follows from Lemma 7.1.2 that for \( k \) large enough, the rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) at \( {y}_{k} \) satisfy

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {{y}_{k}, t}\right)  \leq  {10}
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{10},{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{10}}\right\rbrack \) . By applying the same arguments as in the above Step 2, we conclude that for any \( A > 0 \) , there is a positive constant \( C\left( A\right)  <  + \infty \) such that

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( {d}_{t}\left( {x,{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  A \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{20},{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{20}}\right\rbrack \) . The estimate (7.1.3) implies that there is a positive constant \( {A}_{0} \) such that for arbitrarily given small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \in  \left( {0,\frac{c}{100}}\right) \) , for \( k \) large enough, there hold

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{k},{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  {A}_{0}
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . By combining with Lemma 7.1.2, we then conclude that for any \( A > 0 \) , there is a positive constant \( \widetilde{C}\left( A\right) \) such that for \( k \) large enough, the rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) satisfy

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{C}\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{100}{\left( C\left( A\right) \right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) .

Now, by taking convergent subsequences from the (original) rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) , we see that the limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) is defined on a spacetime open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . By repeating the argument of Step 3 and using Lemma 7.1.2, we further conclude the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) has uniformly bounded curvature on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . This is a contradiction.

Therefore we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) converges to an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, which gives the desired contradiction. This completes the proof of the theorem. 0

nodes.proof:
Consider any point \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {B}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{\left( c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} - c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) with \( c > 0 \) to be determined. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  2{Q}_{k} \) , there is nothing to show. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  > 2{Q}_{k} \) , consider a space-time curve \( \gamma \) from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) that goes straight from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) and goes from \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) to \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) along a minimizing geodesic (with respect to the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,\bar{t}}\right) \) ). If there is a point on \( \gamma \) with the scalar curvature \( 2{Q}_{k} \) , let \( {y}_{0} \) be the nearest such point to \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) . If not, put \( {y}_{0} = \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) . On the segment of \( \gamma \) from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( {y}_{0} \) , the scalar curvature is at least \( 2{Q}_{k} \) . According to the choice of the point \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , the solution along the segment is \( \varepsilon \) -close to that of some ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. It follows from Theorem 6.4.3 (ii) that

\[
\left| {\nabla \left( {R}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) }\right|  \leq  {2\eta }\text{ and }\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {R}_{k}^{-1}\right) }\right|  \leq  {2\eta }
\]

on the segment. (Here, without loss of generality, we may assume \( \varepsilon \) is suitably small). Then by choosing \( c > 0 \) (depending only on \( \eta \) ) small enough we get the desired curvature bound by integrating the above derivative estimates along the segment. This proves the lemma.

nodes.label: Theorem 7.2.1
nodes.document_title: Huai-Dong Cao and Xi-Ping Zhu - A Complete Proof of the Poincare and Geometrization Conjectures
nodes.content:
THEOREM 7.2.1 (Perelman [103]). For any \( A <  + \infty \) , there exist \( K = K\left( A\right)  < \; + \infty \) and \( \alpha  = \alpha \left( A\right)  > 0 \) with the following property. Suppose we have a solution to the Ricci flow on a three-dimensional, compact and orientable manifold \( M \) with normalized initial metric. Suppose that for some \( {x}_{0} \in  M \) and some \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) with \( {r}_{0} < \alpha \) , the solution is defined for \( 0 \leq  t \leq  {r}_{0}^{2} \) and satisfies

\[
\left| {Rm}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2},\;\text{ for }0 \leq  t \leq  {r}_{0}^{2},{d}_{0}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {r}_{0},
\]

and

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{0}\left( {{B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  {A}^{-1}{r}_{0}^{3}\text{ . }
\]

Then \( R\left( {x,{r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  \leq  K{r}_{0}^{-2} \) whenever \( {d}_{{r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < A{r}_{0} \) .

nodes.proof:
Given any large \( A > 0 \) and letting \( \alpha  > 0 \) be chosen later, by Perelman’s no local collapsing theorem II (Theorem 3.4.2), there exists a positive constant \( \kappa  = \kappa \left( A\right) \) (independent of \( \alpha \) ) such that any complete solution satisfying the assumptions of the theorem is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales \( \leq  {r}_{0} \) over the region \( \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right) \left| {\;\frac{1}{5}{r}_{0}^{2} \leq  t \leq  }\right. }\right. \; \left. {{r}_{0}^{2},{d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {5A}{r}_{0}}\right\} \) . Set

\[
\varepsilon  = \min \left\{  {\frac{1}{4}{\varepsilon }_{0},\frac{1}{100}}\right\}  ,
\]

where \( {\varepsilon }_{0} \) is the positive constant in Proposition 6.1.1. We first prove the following assertion.

CLAIM. For the above fixed \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , one can find \( K = K\left( {A,\varepsilon }\right)  <  + \infty \) such that if we have a three-dimensional complete orientable solution with normalized initial metric and satisfying

\[
\left| {Rm}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2}\text{ for }0 \leq  t \leq  {r}_{0}^{2},{d}_{0}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {r}_{0},
\]

and

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{0}\left( {{B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  {A}^{-1}{r}_{0}^{3}
\]

for some \( {x}_{0} \in  M \) and some \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) , then for any point \( x \in  M \) with \( {d}_{{r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < {3A}{r}_{0} \) , either

\[
R\left( {x,{r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  < K{r}_{0}^{-2}
\]

or the subset \( \left\{  {\left( {y, t}\right)  \mid  {d}_{{r}_{0}^{2}}^{2}\left( {y, x}\right)  \leq  {\varepsilon }^{-2}R{\left( x,{r}_{0}^{2}\right) }^{-1},{r}_{0}^{2} - {\varepsilon }^{-2}R{\left( x,{r}_{0}^{2}\right) }^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {r}_{0}^{2}}\right\} \) around the point \( \left( {x,{r}_{0}^{2}}\right) \) is \( \varepsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) - solution.

Notice that in this assertion we don’t impose the restriction of \( {r}_{0} < \alpha \) , so we can consider for the moment \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) to be arbitrary in proving the above claim. Note that the assumption on the normalization of the initial metric is just to ensure the pinching estimate. By scaling, we may assume \( {r}_{0} = 1 \) . The proof of the claim is essentially adapted from that of Theorem 7.1.1. But we will meet the difficulties of adjusting points and verifying a local curvature estimate.

Suppose that the claim is not true. Then there exist a sequence of solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) to the Ricci flow satisfying the assumptions of the claim with the origins \( {x}_{{0}_{k}} \) , and a sequence of positive numbers \( {K}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) , times \( {t}_{k} = 1 \) and points \( {x}_{k} \in \; {M}_{k} \) with \( {d}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  < {3A} \) such that \( {Q}_{k} = {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \geq  {K}_{k} \) and the solution in \( \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  {t}_{k} - C\left( \varepsilon \right) {Q}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{k},{d}_{{t}_{k}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{k}}\right)  \leq  C\left( \varepsilon \right) {Q}_{k}^{-1}}\right\} \) is not, after scaling by the factor \( {Q}_{k},\varepsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of any orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, where \( {R}_{k} \) denotes the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) and \( C\left( \varepsilon \right) \left( { \geq  {\varepsilon }^{-2}}\right) \) is the constant defined in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1. As before we need to first adjust the point \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{k} \geq  \frac{1}{2} \) and \( {d}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  < {4A} \) so that \( {Q}_{k} = {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \geq  {K}_{k} \) and the conclusion of the claim fails at \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , but holds for any \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) satisfying \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq \; 2{Q}_{k},{t}_{k} - {H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{k} \) and \( {d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  < {d}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  + {H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , where \( {H}_{k} = \; \frac{1}{4}{K}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) , as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) .

Indeed, by starting with \( \left( {{x}_{{k}_{1}},{t}_{{k}_{1}}}\right)  = \left( {{x}_{k},1}\right) \) we can choose \( \left( {{x}_{{k}_{2}},{t}_{{k}_{2}}}\right)  \in  {M}_{k} \times \; (0,1\rbrack \) with \( {t}_{{k}_{1}} - {H}_{k}{R}_{k}{\left( {x}_{{k}_{1}},{t}_{{k}_{1}}\right) }^{-1} \leq  {t}_{{k}_{2}} \leq  {t}_{{k}_{1}} \) , and \( {d}_{{t}_{{k}_{2}}}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{2}},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  < {d}_{{t}_{{k}_{1}}}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{1}},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  + \; {H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}{R}_{k}{\left( {x}_{{k}_{1}},{t}_{{k}_{1}}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) such that \( {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{2}},{t}_{{k}_{2}}}\right)  \geq  2{R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{1}},{t}_{{k}_{1}}}\right) \) and the conclusion of the claim fails at \( \left( {{x}_{{k}_{2}},{t}_{{k}_{2}}}\right) \) ; otherwise we have the desired point. Repeating this process, we can choose points \( \left( {{x}_{{k}_{i}},{t}_{{k}_{i}}}\right) , i = 2,\ldots , j \) , such that

\[
{R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{i}},{t}_{{k}_{i}}}\right)  \geq  2{R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{i - 1}},{t}_{{k}_{i - 1}}}\right)
\]

\[
{t}_{{k}_{i - 1}} - {H}_{k}{R}_{k}{\left( {x}_{{k}_{i - 1}},{t}_{{k}_{i - 1}}\right) }^{-1} \leq  {t}_{{k}_{i}} \leq  {t}_{{k}_{i - 1}},
\]

\[
{d}_{{t}_{{k}_{i}}}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{i}},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  < {d}_{{t}_{{k}_{i - 1}}}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{i - 1}},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  + {H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}{R}_{k}{\left( {x}_{{k}_{i - 1}},{t}_{{k}_{i - 1}}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}},
\]

and the conclusion of the claim fails at the points \( \left( {{x}_{{k}_{i}},{t}_{{k}_{i}}}\right) , i = 2,\ldots , j \) . These inequalities imply

\[
{R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{j}},{t}_{{k}_{j}}}\right)  \geq  {2}^{j - 1}{R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{1}},{t}_{{k}_{1}}}\right)  \geq  {2}^{j - 1}{K}_{k}
\]

\[
1 \geq  {t}_{{k}_{j}} \geq  {t}_{{k}_{1}} - {H}_{k}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{{j - 2}}\frac{1}{{2}^{i}}{R}_{k}{\left( {x}_{{k}_{1}},{t}_{{k}_{1}}\right) }^{-1} \geq  \frac{1}{2},
\]

and

\[
{d}_{{t}_{{k}_{j}}}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{j}},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  < {d}_{{t}_{{k}_{1}}}\left( {{x}_{{k}_{1}},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  + {H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 0}}^{{j - 2}}\frac{1}{{\left( \sqrt{2}\right) }^{i}}{R}_{k}{\left( {x}_{{k}_{1}},{t}_{{k}_{1}}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} < {4A}.
\]

Since the solutions are smooth, this process must terminate after a finite number of steps to give the desired point, still denoted by \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

For each adjusted \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , let \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) be the maximal subinterval of \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon }^{-2}{Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) so that the conclusion of the claim with \( K = 2{Q}_{k} \) holds on

\[
P\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k},\frac{1}{10}{H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}},{t}^{\prime } - {t}_{k}}\right)
\]

\[
= \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  x \in  {B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{k},\frac{1}{10}{H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack  }\right\}
\]

for all sufficiently large \( k \) . We now want to show \( {t}^{\prime } = {t}_{k} - \frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon }^{-2}{Q}_{k}^{-1} \) .

Consider the scalar curvature \( {R}_{k} \) at the point \( {x}_{k} \) over the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) . If there is a time \( \widetilde{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) satisfying \( {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},\widetilde{t}}\right)  \geq  2{Q}_{k} \) , we let \( \widetilde{t} \) be the first of such time from \( {t}_{k} \) . Then the solution \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) around the point \( {x}_{k} \) over the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\widetilde{t} - \frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon }^{-2}{Q}_{k}^{-1},\widetilde{t}}\right\rbrack \) is \( \varepsilon \) -close to some orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. Note from the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality that the scalar curvature of any ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is pointwise nondecreasing in time. Consequently, we have the following curvature estimate

\[
{R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k}, t}\right)  \leq  2\left( {1 + \varepsilon }\right) {Q}_{k}
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\widetilde{t} - \frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon }^{-2}{Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) (or \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) if there is no such time \( \widetilde{t} \) ). By combining with the elliptic type estimate for ancient \( \kappa \) -solutions (Theorem 6.4.3) and the Hamilton-Ivey pinching estimate, we further have

(7.2.1)

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {5\omega }\left( 1\right) {Q}_{k}
\]

for all \( x \in  {B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{k},{\left( 3{Q}_{k}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\widetilde{t} - \frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon }^{-2}{Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) (or \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) ) and all sufficiently large \( k \) , where \( \omega \) is the positive function in Theorem 6.4.3.

For any point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( \widetilde{t} - \frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon }^{-2}{Q}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{k} \) (or \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) ) and \( {d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{k}}\right)  \leq \; \frac{1}{10}{H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , we divide the discussion into two cases.

Case (1): \( {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  \leq  \frac{3}{10}{H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) .

(7.2.2)

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  \leq  {d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{k}}\right)  + {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{1}{10}{H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}} + \frac{3}{10}{H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}}
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{1}{2}{H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}}.
\]

Case (2): \( {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  > \frac{3}{10}{H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) .

From the curvature bound (7.2.1) and the assumption, we apply Lemma 3.4.1(ii) with \( {r}_{0} = {Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) to get

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\left( {{d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right) }\right)  \geq   - {20}\left( {\omega \left( 1\right)  + 1}\right) {Q}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}},
\]

and then for \( k \) large enough,

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  \leq  {d}_{\widehat{t}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  + {20}\left( {\omega \left( 1\right)  + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{-2}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}}
\]

\[
\leq  {d}_{\widehat{t}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  + \frac{1}{10}{H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}},
\]

where \( \widehat{t} \in  \left( {t,{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) satisfies the property that \( {d}_{s}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  \geq  \frac{3}{10}{H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) whenever \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {t,\widehat{t}}\right\rbrack \) . So we have

(7.2.3)

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  \leq  {d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{k}}\right)  + {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{1}{10}{H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}} + {d}_{\widehat{t}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  + \frac{1}{10}{H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}}
\]

\[
\leq  {d}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  + \frac{1}{2}{H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}},
\]

for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Then the combination of (7.2.2),(7.2.3) and the choice of the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) implies \( {t}^{\prime } = {t}_{k} - \frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon }^{-2}{Q}_{k}^{-1} \) for all sufficiently large \( k \) . (Here we also used the maximality of the subinterval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) in the case that there is no time in \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) with \( {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k}, \cdot  }\right)  \geq  2{Q}_{k} \) .)

Now we rescale the solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) into \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) around the points \( {x}_{k} \) by the factors \( {Q}_{k} = {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) and shift the times \( {t}_{k} \) to the new times zero. Then the same arguments from Step 1 to Step 3 in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1 prove that a subsequence of the rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a limiting (complete) solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) , which is defined on a backward time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-a,0}\right\rbrack \) for some \( a > 0 \) . (The only modification is in Lemma 7.1.2 of Step 1 by further requiring \( {t}_{k} - \frac{1}{4}{\varepsilon }^{-2}{Q}_{k}^{-1} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  {t}_{k} \) ).

We next study how to adapt the argument of Step 4 in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1. As before, we have a maximal time interval \( \left( {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) for which we can take a smooth limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) from a subsequence of the rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) . We want to show \( {t}_{\infty } =  - \infty \) .

Suppose not; then \( {t}_{\infty } >  - \infty \) . Let \( c > 0 \) be a positive constant much smaller than \( \frac{1}{10}{\varepsilon }^{-2} \) . Note that the infimum of the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time. Then we can find some point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and some time \( t = {t}_{\infty } + \theta \) with \( 0 < \theta  < \frac{c}{3} \) such that \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty } + \theta }\right)  \leq  \frac{3}{2} \) .

Consider the (unrescaled) scalar curvature \( {R}_{k} \) of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) at the point \( {x}_{k} \) over the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) . Since the scalar curvature \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty } \) of the limit on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{3},0}\right\rbrack \) is uniformly bounded by some positive constant \( C \) , we have the curvature estimate

\[
{R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k}, t}\right)  \leq  {2C}{Q}_{k}
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) and all sufficiently large \( k \) . Then by repeating the same arguments as in deriving (7.2.1), (7.2.2) and (7.2.3), we deduce that the conclusion of the claim with \( K = 2{Q}_{k} \) holds on the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k},\frac{1}{10}{H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1}}\right) \) for all sufficiently large \( k \) .

Let \( \left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{k} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{k}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1}}\right) \) be a sequence of associated points and times in the (unrescaled) solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) so that after rescaling, the sequence converges to the \( \left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty } + \theta }\right) \) in the limit. Clearly \( \frac{\theta }{2} \leq  {\theta }_{k} \leq  {2\theta } \) for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Then, by considering the scalar curvature \( {\bar{R}}_{k} \) at the point \( {y}_{k} \) over the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{k}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) , the above argument (as in deriving the similar estimates (7.2.1)-(7.2.3)) implies that the conclusion of the claim with \( K = 2{Q}_{k} \) holds on the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{k},\frac{1}{10}{H}_{k}^{\frac{1}{2}}{Q}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1}}\right) \) for all sufficiently large \( k \) . In particular, we have the curvature estimate

\[
{R}_{k}\left( {{y}_{k}, t}\right)  \leq  4\left( {1 + \varepsilon }\right) {Q}_{k}
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{k}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) for all sufficiently large \( k \) .

We now consider the rescaled sequence \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) with the marked points replaced by \( {y}_{k} \) and the times replaced by \( {s}_{k} \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{4}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{c}{4}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) . By applying the same arguments from Step 1 to Step 3 in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1 and the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality as in Step 4 of Theorem 7.1.1, we conclude that there is some small constant \( {a}^{\prime } > 0 \) such that the original limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) is actually well defined on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty } - {a}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) with uniformly bounded curvature. This is a contradiction. Therefore we have checked the claim.

To finish the proof, we next argue by contradiction. Suppose there exist sequences of positive numbers \( {K}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty ,{\alpha }_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) , as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) , and a sequence of solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) to the Ricci flow satisfying the assumptions of the theorem with origins \( {x}_{{0}_{k}} \) and with radii \( {r}_{{0}_{k}} \) satisfying \( {r}_{{0}_{k}} < {\alpha }_{k} \) such that for some points \( {x}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) with \( {d}_{{r}_{{0}_{k}}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  < A{r}_{{0}_{k}} \) we have

(7.2.4)

\[
R\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{{0}_{k}}^{2}}\right)  > {K}_{k}{r}_{{0}_{k}}^{-2}
\]

for all \( k \) . Let \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widehat{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right) \) be the rescaled solutions of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) around the origins \( {x}_{{0}_{k}} \) by the factors \( {r}_{{0}_{k}}^{-2} \) and shifting the times \( {r}_{{0}_{k}}^{2} \) to the new times zero. The above claim tells us that for \( k \) large, any point \( \left( {y,0}\right)  \in  \left( {{M}_{k},{\widehat{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right) \) with \( {d}_{{\widehat{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) }\left( {y,{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right)  < {3A} \) and with the rescaled scalar curvature \( {\widehat{R}}_{k}\left( {y,0}\right)  > {K}_{k} \) has a canonical neighborhood which is either a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap, or a compact manifold (without boundary) diffeomorphic to a metric quotient of the round three-sphere. Note that the pinching estimate (7.1.1) and the condition \( {\alpha }_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) imply any subsequential limit of the rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widehat{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{{0}_{k}}}\right) \) must have nonnegative sectional curvature. Thus the same argument as in Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 7.1.1 shows that for all sufficiently large \( k \) , the curvatures of the rescaled solutions at the time zero stay uniformly bounded at those points whose distances from the origins \( {x}_{{0}_{k}} \) do not exceed \( {2A} \) . This contradicts (7.2.4) for \( k \) large enough.

Therefore we have completed the proof of the theorem. [
